asplos-2025-001.method: Voyager examines each incoming graph's structure—how many connections each node has (degree distribution), how densely packed the nodes are (density), and how sparse the connections are—to decide which transformations to apply on the fly. Rather than using one fixed optimization strategy for all graphs, it measures the graph's properties and generates a custom execution plan that reorders and combines operations (a process called algebraic transformation) specifically matched to that graph's shape. This means a graph with many high-degree nodes gets optimized differently than a sparse one, because the performance bottlenecks are fundamentally different.
asplos-2025-001.key_novelty: Voyager chooses how to transform and reorder operations for each graph at runtime based on the graph's actual topology, instead of using a single fixed transformation strategy for all graphs.

asplos-2025-000.method: The paper surveys machine learning's progress across systems research—spanning task scheduling, compiler design, storage, networking, and more—and compares how quickly each area has adopted ML approaches to known inflection points (turning points where machine learning became dominant) in other fields. It searches for signs of maturity: whether ML solutions are deployed in production systems rather than just research settings, whether researchers have standardized benchmarks for consistent testing, and whether machine learning has replaced the hand-written heuristics (decision rules) that engineers traditionally created.
asplos-2025-000.key_novelty: The paper asks whether machine learning has reached an inflection point in systems research (a turning point where it becomes the dominant approach) by comparing the field's progress to how deep learning transformed computer vision after the AlexNet breakthrough in 2012.

asplos-2025-002.method: The method uses statistics—specifically hypothesis testing (a mathematical way to make decisions with measurable confidence)—to decide when to stop classifying. Rather than using an arbitrary cutoff, it checks the similarity scores between the input and each class category (represented as high-dimensional vectors), computes statistical confidence bounds around those scores, and stops inference as soon as it's mathematically confident which category is correct. This provides a provable guarantee on how much accuracy might be lost while reducing unnecessary computation.
asplos-2025-002.key_novelty: This is the first application of formal statistics with provable confidence bounds to determine when to stop inference early in hyperdimensional computing.

asplos-2025-012.method: Phoenix assigns criticality tags—labels marking which services are essential versus optional—to each container. When capacity runs low, it uses diagonal scaling to automatically shut down non-critical containers, freeing resources for critical services. A Kubernetes controller (the software that manages containerized applications) orchestrates this by optimizing both the application's criticality requirements and the operator's infrastructure goals. Phoenix can recover from failures across a cluster of 100,000 nodes in 10 seconds.
asplos-2025-012.key_novelty: Diagonal scaling uses application-defined criticality tags to selectively shut down non-critical containers during failures, keeping critical services available.

asplos-2025-007.method: The system redesigns how a key-value storage device (KV-SSD) manages its index. Instead of storing each full key directly in the index—which becomes huge if keys are large—AnyKey stores only a small, fixed-size reference to each key, such as a hash or compact descriptor, while keeping the full key data elsewhere. This keeps the index lean no matter how big the keys grow, preventing the performance collapse that normally happens when key sizes balloon.
asplos-2025-007.key_novelty: Instead of storing full keys in the index, store only small fixed-size references—this keeps the index size constant regardless of how large the actual keys are.

asplos-2025-011.method: Velosiraptor takes a formal hardware model (a precise specification of the memory hardware's configuration options and how they work) and automatically generates the OS driver code needed to configure it. The system builds this code using a component library of pre-built translation operations and either a constraint solver (automated logic that figures out which settings work together) or template-based code generation (filling in patterns with hardware-specific details). The resulting code is guaranteed correct because it's assembled from verified components, eliminating the manual mistakes that happen when programmers adapt code for each new hardware design.
asplos-2025-011.key_novelty: Automatically generating correct OS memory-translation drivers from a formal hardware specification instead of writing them by hand for each hardware design.

asplos-2025-013.method: PartIR incrementally transforms a neural network's internal representation (the standard format compilers use to represent programs) as you apply each parallelization strategy—whether splitting data, splitting the model itself, or splitting optimizer state. Each strategy is specified declaratively (you describe what should happen, not how), and they're composable (you can combine multiple strategies together). Because these transformations follow general rules that work on any hardware or runtime system, each step can be verified independently as correct.
asplos-2025-013.key_novelty: PartIR decouples sharding strategies (ways to split neural network training across multiple processors) from the implementation code by incrementally rewriting the program's internal representation, enabling predictable and verifiable composition of arbitrary strategies.

asplos-2025-015.method: Necro-reaper combines software and hardware. A compiler uses profiling data (measurements from running real code) to analyze how long each chunk of memory stays allocated, then inserts special CPU instructions at allocation sites. A customized memory allocator uses these instructions to signal the hardware when memory is deallocated. The hardware then skips unnecessary memory traffic for dead regions without needing its own logic to track which data is still in use.
asplos-2025-015.key_novelty: Special CPU instructions allow the compiler and memory allocator to signal dead heap memory to the hardware, which then skips unnecessary writebacks and fetches without needing its own tracking.

asplos-2025-014.method: CXLfork implements a remote fork interface (a way to copy a running process to a different computer in a cluster) using CXL-attached shared memory—specialized memory physically connected to multiple machines that can all access it directly. Instead of copying the process's pages and metadata over the network, it stores everything in this globally-shared CXL memory, so if multiple processes need the same data, it only exists once instead of being duplicated. The system smartly splits storage between fast local DRAM and the slower shared CXL memory: pages that are frequently used stay in local DRAM for speed, while pages that are rarely used or shared across processes live in CXL memory. CXL-porter builds on this to efficiently scale serverless functions (small on-demand tasks) by spawning multiple copies of a function across cluster nodes without the network copying overhead.
asplos-2025-014.key_novelty: Using CXL-attached globally-shared memory for cluster-wide deduplication of process state, so remote process cloning runs nearly as fast as local cloning.

asplos-2025-010.method: OS2G moves the object storage reader onto a DPU (a specialized data-processing chip) instead of the host CPU, allowing the DPU to fetch data and send it directly to GPU memory via GPU-Direct or RDMA (technologies that let devices transfer data without going through the main CPU). On the DPU side, a processing pipeline decompresses and reformats the incoming data into the tensor structures deep learning models need. By eliminating the host CPU from the data path, the system removes the bottleneck that was limiting how fast the GPU could ingest training data.
asplos-2025-010.key_novelty: OS2G provides an end-to-end direct path from the DPU (a specialized processor) to the GPU for object storage data, eliminating the host CPU and the redundant copies that slow deep learning training in large clusters.

asplos-2025-004.method: Mint looks at request traces—the detailed logs of what happens as requests move through a system—and finds the common structure shared by similar requests. It then creates a template from those common parts and stores each request as only its differences from that template, rather than storing complete traces. This dramatically reduces storage while preserving all per-request details needed to understand what each request did.
asplos-2025-004.key_novelty: Mint collects all requests but stores only their differences from a shared template, replacing the traditional keep-or-discard trace sampling with full coverage at drastically lower storage cost.

asplos-2025-009.method: Cascade groups events that don't depend on each other spatially into larger batches for parallel processing. As training progresses, it identifies nodes whose memory has stabilized—stopped changing significantly—and treats these as safe to process in any order, removing the strict sequence requirement (breaking temporal dependencies). An adaptive mechanism reduces redundant memory updates, achieving 2.3x average speedup (up to 5.1x) without accuracy loss.
asplos-2025-009.key_novelty: Using memory-state similarity to identify stabilized nodes (ones whose memory stopped changing significantly) enables breaking temporal dependencies and training with much larger batches without accuracy loss.

asplos-2025-005.method: EXIST reduces tracing overhead by redesigning how the system collects trace data. It adds minimal measurement points that avoid expensive operations like context-switching (switching between different execution contexts) or waiting for locks. It collects and stores the trace data asynchronously (in the background, not during the app's main execution) so tracing doesn't slow down the actual work. Finally, it compresses trace data intelligently—combining or removing redundant information while preserving the cause-and-effect chain of events.
asplos-2025-005.key_novelty: EXIST redesigns the tracing pipeline end-to-end—from measurement to storage—to cut overhead to roughly one-tenth of a percent (about 10-50x lower than existing systems) while preserving the cause-and-effect relationships between events.

asplos-2025-008.method: PipeLLM encrypts data while the GPU computes, rather than waiting for one to finish before starting the other—similar to how modern CPUs run multiple instructions at the same time. The challenge is that the encryption system doesn't know what data to encrypt until the GPU actually requests it. PipeLLM solves this by predicting what will need encrypting next, based on patterns in how AI models typically serve requests—like token generation and KV-cache access (a buffer storing prior tokens)—and encrypting it before the GPU asks. When a prediction is wrong, a lightweight mechanism recovers without any errors.
asplos-2025-008.key_novelty: PipeLLM uses speculative prediction of what needs encrypting—based on LLM serving patterns—to overlap encryption with GPU computation, nearly eliminating encryption latency.

asplos-2025-006.method: TempGraph breaks a temporal graph (a network of events happening in time order) into separate chains, then runs them in parallel on a GPU using the Generate-Activate-Compute model. Generate creates shortcut references (pointers between chains), Activate identifies which steps across all chains are ready to execute right now, and Compute runs all those steps simultaneously with thousands of GPU threads. The shortcuts let chains proceed without waiting for each other, enabling the full computation to finish quickly while using all of the GPU's parallel capacity.
asplos-2025-006.key_novelty: The Generate-Activate-Compute model with inter-chain shortcut references breaks the sequential constraint of temporal dependencies, allowing GPU threads to process time-dependent chains concurrently.

asplos-2025-019.method: The paper examines existing Java performance benchmarks and testing methods to find where they diverge from how real Java applications perform. It identifies three key problems: warm-up time (when Java's runtime translates and optimizes code at startup), just-in-time compilation artifacts (unexpected performance variations from the translation process itself), and measurement mistakes common in managed languages with automatic garbage collection. It then proposes better testing guidelines and practices that accurately reflect real-world Java performance.
asplos-2025-019.key_novelty: Java's runtime features (just-in-time compilation and garbage collection) create measurement artifacts that invalidate standard performance testing practices.

asplos-2025-020.method: Einsum Tree IR represents a sequence of tensor contractions (step-by-step combinations of multi-dimensional arrays) as a tree structure, then chooses how to arrange the data for all contractions together, rather than deciding separately for each one. This global approach reduces how much data needs to move between the CPU's main memory and its fast cache. The optimized contraction sequences execute on standard CPUs (Arm and x86) using existing high-performance tensor libraries.
asplos-2025-020.key_novelty: Einsum Tree IR optimizes how tensor data is arranged across an entire sequence of contractions at once to minimize data movement, rather than optimizing each contraction's data arrangement separately.

asplos-2025-021.method: The method uses treewidth—a measure of how tree-like a program's control-flow graph is—rather than the graph's size to determine algorithm speed. It breaks the control-flow graph (the map of code branches and loops) into tree-shaped pieces through grammatical decomposition (like parsing a sentence). Register allocation (assigning the CPU's limited fast memory slots to variables) is solved using dynamic programming on these pieces. Since real program control-flow graphs naturally have small treewidth, this enables exact or near-exact solutions to be computed fast enough for practical use.
asplos-2025-021.key_novelty: The key insight is that program control-flow graphs have tree-like structure (small treewidth), enabling much faster register allocation through tree decomposition.

asplos-2025-022.method: MoE models only activate (use) a subset of experts (specialized sub-networks) per token, so most expert parameters never get updated in a given training step. MoC-System exploits this sparsity by saving (checkpointing) only the experts that were actually activated and updated, completely skipping the dormant ones—drastically reducing checkpoint file sizes. To manage I/O overhead, the system overlaps checkpoint writes with forward and backward computation, and spreads checkpoint data across nodes by expert grouping (expert-parallel sharding) to minimize per-node storage.
asplos-2025-022.key_novelty: Instead of saving all expert parameters, the system only saves the ones actually used in each training step, which dramatically shrinks checkpoint files and reduces I/O overhead while keeping the system able to recover from failures.

asplos-2025-023.method: SmoothE reformulates e-graph extraction from discrete yes/no choices to a continuous problem with smooth weights, then applies gradient descent to find good answers faster than exact methods. This approach works with any cost function that has gradients—including learned neural models—whereas existing methods only support linear costs. The method ensures the smooth solution maps to a valid extraction from the original e-graph.
asplos-2025-023.key_novelty: Reformulating e-graph extraction as a smooth, continuous optimization that gradient descent can solve with arbitrary learned cost functions instead of just linear ones.

asplos-2025-017.method: The paper introduces four lossless compression algorithms built specifically for floating-point numbers (the standard way computers represent decimals, with an exponent that sets the scale and a mantissa holding the significant digits). The algorithms work identically on both CPUs and GPUs, producing the same compressed format so data can move between them without re-encoding. The compression works by identifying and removing redundancy in the patterns of exponent and mantissa bits. Both implementations are tuned for CPU vector units and GPU streaming multiprocessors—parallel processing systems that handle many data items simultaneously—to maximize compression and decompression speed.
asplos-2025-017.key_novelty: The core innovation is four lossless floating-point compression algorithms that work identically on both CPUs and GPUs, producing the same compressed data on either platform while achieving over 500 GB/s throughput on an RTX 4090 GPU without sacrificing compression quality.

asplos-2025-029.method: HALO is a compiler that automatically places bootstrapping (noise-clearing operations) inside loops for encrypted programs. Encrypted programs accumulate noise from repeated multiplications, and this gets worse in loops where the same operation repeats many times; bootstrapping resets the noise but is expensive, so HALO figures out the minimum number of times it's needed. The compiler analyzes the loop to determine where noise levels get dangerous, then automatically inserts bootstrapping at loop boundaries or inside the loop body only where strictly necessary.
asplos-2025-029.key_novelty: First compiler to automatically place bootstrapping (noise-clearing operations) inside loops for encrypted programs, enabling iterative encrypted computations without programmer intervention.

asplos-2025-026.method: OctoCache accelerates OctoMap entirely in software on standard CPUs. It restructures octree traversal to organize the tree's data so nearby parts stay close in memory, improving cache efficiency. It reorders ray-casting updates (calculations that scan through 3D space) to group accesses to the same memory together, maximizing cache reuse. It parallelizes these independent updates across multiple cores to run them simultaneously.
asplos-2025-026.key_novelty: It reorders voxel updates to optimize cache performance and parallelizes their scheduling, transforming OctoMap's irregular memory-access pattern into a cache-efficient concurrent workload without modifying the octree structure.

asplos-2025-031.method: AnA inserts three components between planning and perception: a query interface where the planner requests specific perception tasks based on driving context, a query executor that selects which tasks to run, and a monitor that catches execution problems. Rather than analyzing every scene uniformly, the system switches between a fast, broad scan and a detailed analysis of safety-critical elements, mirroring how human drivers focus attention where it matters most.
asplos-2025-031.key_novelty: The system empowers the driving planner to selectively activate perception tasks based on driving context, reducing unnecessary computation by 44% while cutting collisions in half on adversarial benchmarks.

asplos-2025-028.method: Concerto is a compiler that automatically schedules communication in distributed deep learning without being tied to any specific framework or way of splitting work across machines. It uses a general algorithm to solve the scheduling problem—like organizing a project with limited computational resources and time—automatically breaking up the large synchronous communication operations (moments when all machines pause to exchange data) into smaller pieces that can run alongside the actual GPU computations. The result is a schedule that works with any training setup, requiring no manual tuning.
asplos-2025-028.key_novelty: Concerto automatically breaks up synchronous communication operations to enable computation overlap using a general scheduling algorithm that adapts to any training configuration without requiring manual tuning.

asplos-2025-027.method: HyperHammer exploits Rowhammer—a technique that flips bits in RAM by repeatedly accessing nearby memory cells—to bypass protections built into KVM (a virtualization system that isolates guest VMs from the hypervisor). The attack likely uses either hammering techniques that KVM didn't block, or exploits how a guest's virtual memory addresses map to physical hardware memory, especially through huge pages (large memory blocks). By inducing bit flips in the hypervisor's protected memory regions, the attack corrupts the hypervisor's code or data structures, allowing the guest VM to escape isolation and gain hypervisor-level control.
asplos-2025-027.key_novelty: HyperHammer is the first Rowhammer attack (a technique that flips bits in RAM by repeatedly accessing nearby memory cells) to escape KVM guest isolation and directly compromise the hypervisor, overcoming defenses that had previously blocked such attacks.

asplos-2025-024.method: MoE-Lightning pipelines expert weights between CPU and GPU memory: while the GPU computes with current weights, the system simultaneously prefetches the next weights from CPU, reducing GPU idle time. It stores these weights in fixed-size pages and uses a Hierarchical Roofline Model (a performance model that predicts throughput based on batch size, GPU memory, CPU memory, and I/O bandwidth) to automatically select optimal settings. The system scales to multi-GPU configurations for larger models like Mixtral 8x22B and DBRX on 2-4 T4 GPUs.
asplos-2025-024.key_novelty: CGOPipe pipelines expert weights between CPU and GPU, guided by a Hierarchical Roofline Model that predicts throughput, enabling efficient large-model inference on memory-limited GPUs.

asplos-2025-016.method: xUI extends Intel's UIPI with four hardware capabilities: (1) tracked interrupts that confirm when notifications arrive, (2) hardware safepoints—points where the processor safely pauses thread execution—enabling thread management without kernel help, (3) a user-space timer for deadline-driven scheduling without kernel overhead, and (4) interrupt forwarding (based on Intel's DSA) routing notifications directly to accelerators. Together, these solve key limitations: delivery confirmation, kernel-free preemption, deadline-driven scheduling, and accelerator communication. The design is evaluated through gem5, a full-system computer simulator, measuring latency for three distinct use cases.
asplos-2025-016.key_novelty: The core innovation is extending Intel's user-interrupt model with hardware safepoints that enable thread pausing without the kernel, combined with interrupt forwarding that routes notifications directly to accelerators.

asplos-2025-037.method: H-Houdini speeds up finding invariants—properties that always stay true in a hardware design—by breaking the problem into smaller pieces. Instead of searching for invariants across the entire design at once (which becomes impossible as designs get larger), it breaks the hardware into sub-modules, learns invariants for each piece separately, and reuses those invariants when checking the whole system. This hierarchical approach avoids having to explore every possible state combination, which would grow exponentially with design size.
asplos-2025-037.key_novelty: H-Houdini enables formal verification of large hardware designs that previously couldn't be verified due to computational complexity.

asplos-2025-030.method: The authors identify two new timing-based information leaks in AMD systems: cache flush timing (how fast the CPU cache clears) and memory block contention (delays when VMs compete for memory). They develop Reload+Reload attacks—methods that repeatedly load data and measure response times—to expose memory access patterns from other VMs, replacing the disabled Flush+Reload technique. The cache-timing variant creates a covert channel (hidden communication path) for Spectre attacks (a CPU exploit that reads secrets), while the memory-contention variant extracts AES-128 encryption keys by measuring memory response delays even though the VMs are isolated by SEV-SNP.
asplos-2025-030.key_novelty: Two new timing-based side channels in AMD systems—cache flush timing (measuring how long the CPU cache takes to clear) and memory block contention (timing when VMs compete for memory access)—enable Reload+Reload attacks that break through SEV-SNP isolation and outperform Prime+Probe by being more reliable under system noise and leaking information faster.

asplos-2025-038.method: Earth+ runs compression software directly on the satellite. Ground stations on Earth upload recent images from other satellites in the same constellation to each satellite, using the uplink signal. The satellite then compares each newly captured image to the most recent matching reference image and sends only the changed pixels (delta encoding—transmitting just the differences rather than the whole image). This works well because it keeps the reference images fresh and stored on-board, so most new images are very similar to the references, creating sparse differences to transmit.
asplos-2025-038.key_novelty: Earth+ exploits similarity between images from the same constellation by having ground stations upload reference images from other satellites to each on-board satellite, achieving 3.3x reduction in downlink data compared to previous methods without quality loss.

asplos-2025-039.method: The key insight is that on each incoming symbol, only a small subset of the state machines actually need to process it—most are idle. Hopps tracks which state machines are active at any moment using a compact bitmap (a compressed list of which machines are 'turned on') and skips over the inactive ones entirely. It also arranges the memory using tiled SRAM storage, so that state-transition rules for active machines are fetched in batches rather than one at a time, which cuts down the amount of data pulled from slower off-chip memory in proportion to how many machines are actually active.
asplos-2025-039.key_novelty: Hopps is the first automata processing accelerator to completely eliminate wasted processing on inactive state machines by using a bitmap to track which machines are active on each input symbol.

asplos-2025-034.method: COGENT compiles code to RISC-V with metadata tags (small labels attached to code for tracking and security). The toolchain lets you create tags of any width—from 1 to 32 bits per instruction—and attach them at different scales (per instruction, per basic block or chunk of code, or per function), while automatically checking the tags stay intact in the final binary. It also marks jump and function-call points, so downstream security tools can enforce control-flow integrity (verifying the code only jumps to allowed places). You can add new tagging policies without modifying the core compiler.
asplos-2025-034.key_novelty: One flexible toolchain for RISC-V that handles metadata tags of any width (1 to 32 bits) at any scale (instruction, basic block, or function) with automatic integrity checking, eliminating the need for custom compilers for each tagging policy.

asplos-2025-025.method: Modern applications have instruction footprints so large they cause frequent misses in two memory structures: the instruction TLB (which maps instruction addresses) and the instruction cache (which stores frequently used code). Because instruction misses cause the processor to wait idle before continuing, unlike data misses, this approach treats instructions as a higher priority. It coordinates the TLB and cache so that when one evicts an instruction address, the other is informed and does the same, preventing both from wastefully evicting and reloading the same code. The eviction decisions are guided by how often and how recently each instruction is accessed.
asplos-2025-025.key_novelty: The innovation is coordinating the instruction TLB and cache based on how often and how recently instructions are accessed, so they don't independently evict and reload the same code.

asplos-2025-036.method: BlockDepend is an ML compiler tool that analyzes how computations depend on each other at the block level—a middle ground between tracking individual data elements and whole operations. It groups computation into blocks, identifies which blocks need data from which others, and simplifies the dependency graph. This reveals opportunities to fuse operations that produce and consume each other's data, to reuse data in shared GPU memory, and to run independent work in parallel. The compiler uses these insights to reduce data movement and schedule parallel work across different GPU compute units.
asplos-2025-036.key_novelty: BlockDepend simplifies how ML compilers track which operations depend on which others by analyzing blocks of computation instead of individual elements or operations, which reveals hidden opportunities for parallel work and data reuse, achieving up to 2.88x speedup over production compilers.

asplos-2025-035.method: Quetzal combines a simple hardware power-measurement circuit with scheduling software. The scheduler decides which job to run by calculating the total time needed—including how long for the battery to recharge—not just the job's execution time. Before running a job, software uses queueing theory (mathematical models for how fast items pile up in queues) to predict whether incoming data will arrive faster than the job can process it; if overflow is about to happen, the system intentionally makes the job simpler or shorter to speed up processing and prevent data loss.
asplos-2025-035.key_novelty: The system prevents data loss on devices powered by ambient energy by combining three coordinated techniques—predicting buffer overflow using queue models, choosing jobs based on available power, and automatically simplifying jobs when overflow threatens—all made possible by a simple hardware power meter.

asplos-2025-032.method: The solution uses three techniques. First, ray virtualization: after the ray-generation shaders send rays to hardware, they stop and free GPU processor cores (CUDA cores), allowing those cores to generate more rays while hardware traces earlier batches—this multiplies concurrent rays and enables cache reuse within treelet subtrees. Second, a dynamic queue switches between traversal modes (within-treelet vs. across-treelet) at runtime depending on efficiency. Third, warp repacking reorganizes work groups in the ray-tracing hardware unit to optimize parallel execution.
asplos-2025-032.key_novelty: Ray virtualization frees GPU processor cores by stopping ray-generation shaders after dispatch, multiplying concurrent rays and enabling cache reuse within treelets, paired with a dynamic queue switching traversal strategies at runtime—achieving 95% average speedup.

asplos-2025-046.method: StreamGrid solves a memory bottleneck in point cloud processors: point clouds have irregular, unpredictable data access patterns that break conventional streaming buffers—systems that efficiently prefetch data by assuming regular access patterns like those in images. The solution uses two techniques: compulsory splitting, which divides the point cloud into fixed-size grid cells to make data access predictable and keep it all in on-chip memory; and deterministic termination, which precomputes when each processor finishes so the system avoids stalling while waiting for memory. Together, these enable point cloud processors to use the same efficient streaming approach that already works for images. An automated optimizer then minimizes the on-chip memory (SRAM) needed to maintain accuracy.
asplos-2025-046.key_novelty: By partitioning point clouds into fixed-size regions and precomputing when processing finishes, StreamGrid enables point cloud processors to use conventional streaming buffers—systems designed for regular, predictable data access.

asplos-2025-043.method: These circuits are 'latency-insensitive'—they work no matter how fast or slow data arrives—which means standard circuit verification fails. ElasticMiter creates a 'miter' circuit (a testing harness that runs both the original and simplified circuits with the same inputs and checks for output mismatches) that verifies each simplification works under all possible arrival timings. Before applying any simplification rule, the system proves it with this miter, guaranteeing the result still works. The approach handles HLS-specific features like elastic buffering (delay-absorbing queues), fork/join nodes (where data splits and recombines), and control tokens.
asplos-2025-043.key_novelty: This is the first formally verified system for transforming HLS dataflow circuits by building a miter that accounts for latency-insensitive timing to prove each simplification is correct.

asplos-2025-049.method: The Past-Future scheduler predicts how long each request's output will be by examining the actual lengths from the last ~1,000 completed requests, then continuously updates this prediction as each request generates more text. It then calculates memory usage at every future point when requests finish, and finds the maximum memory needed across all those future moments. A new request is only accepted if adding it keeps the peak future memory below the hardware's capacity. LightLLM implements this with less than 1% scheduling overhead by running the calculations in parallel on the GPU.
asplos-2025-049.key_novelty: Output lengths from AI models are stable enough within short time periods that the scheduler can predict peak future memory needs precisely by sampling from historical request data, without requiring model-specific tuning.

asplos-2025-040.method: In 3D rendering models that compute gradients for learning, many GPU threads simultaneously try to add their values to the same shared locations, creating contention (competition for the same resource). These requests pile up at the atomic units in the GPU's L2 cache (the hardware coordinating simultaneous updates), creating stalls that slow training. ARC intercepts these requests at the warp level—a group of 32 threads that communicate quickly with each other—before they reach that bottleneck. Threads updating the same memory location first combine their updates into one using fast warp communication, then send that single combined update instead of many separate ones, with automatic detection to apply this combining only when contention is detected.
asplos-2025-040.key_novelty: ARC combines atomic operations at the warp level before they reach the GPU's bottleneck, with automatic detection to enable this combining only when many operations are trying to happen simultaneously.

asplos-2025-045.method: Klotski processes multiple requests in parallel instead of one at a time. When different requests' computations need the same expert module (a specialized part of the trillion-parameter model), Klotski groups those token computations together, making the total work on that module long enough to keep the GPU busy while loading it from disk into fast memory—eliminating idle processor gaps. The system predicts which expert modules upcoming requests will use and pre-loads them, while also deciding which computations to run next, balancing the load across the memory bus and GPU processors so both operate at full capacity.
asplos-2025-045.key_novelty: Klotski groups token computations from multiple concurrent requests that target the same expert module, making the computation work long enough to fully hide the time spent loading that module.

asplos-2025-050.method: Snowplow trains a machine learning model to make smarter choices about how to mutate (modify) test programs. Instead of guessing randomly or following hand-written rules, the model learns from analyzing the actual kernel source code—specifically how instructions are ordered (control flow graphs) and how data moves between them (data flow). During testing, it predicts which mutations—like adding system calls, changing argument values, or restructuring the test—would most likely guide execution into untested kernel code regions. The model improves by learning from real coverage feedback showing which code actually ran.
asplos-2025-050.key_novelty: Snowplow replaces hand-written mutation rules with a machine learning model that learns from kernel code which test changes will reach untested code.

asplos-2025-047.method: AMuLeT automatically tests whether proposed defenses against Spectre attacks work during hardware design, before building physical chips. It generates small test programs (litmus tests) that deliberately trigger speculative execution—when a CPU predicts ahead and runs instructions it might need—and varies both the timing windows when this speculation happens and the different ways an attacker could observe the side effects. The tool runs these tests on a software simulator of the hardware to find which Spectre attack variants each defense fails to block, giving designers rapid feedback to improve their solutions.
asplos-2025-047.key_novelty: The key idea is automatically creating and running security tests during hardware design to catch whether speculative-execution attack defenses work, so engineers can quickly iterate without manual security analysis.

asplos-2025-048.method: TNIC places a tamper-proof security layer (a formally verified silicon root-of-trust) on the network card (SmartNIC hardware) instead of in the CPU. It uses hardware-accelerated cryptographic primitives running in network processing logic: transferable authentication (signed messages proving who sent them) and non-equivocation (monotonic counters preventing a sender from denying they sent something). Because security stays at the network card level, it works with any CPU. It provides APIs and patterns for Byzantine-fault-tolerant systems (where some components can fail or lie but the system still works), demonstrated by four working distributed systems.
asplos-2025-048.key_novelty: Instead of relying on the CPU's security features (called a TEE), TNIC builds a tamper-proof security layer (formally verified silicon root-of-trust) directly on the network card (SmartNIC hardware) to provide network-level trust guarantees (transferable authentication and non-equivocation) that work with any CPU.

asplos-2025-054.method: PAPI combines two types of processors: PIM units (processors built directly into memory chips to reduce how much data moves around) and traditional compute accelerators (like GPUs), plus a runtime system that watches what the LLM is doing and automatically sends each piece of work to whichever processor is best suited for it at that moment. The PIM units are designed specifically to handle different kinds of memory-heavy operations—like multiplying matrices by single vectors, computing attention (where the model weighs which past tokens matter most), and applying gates (switches that control information flow)—because these operations behave differently. A scheduler watches as parameters change during execution (like batch size or sequence length) and steers work to either the PIM or compute units based on what would be fastest right now.
asplos-2025-054.key_novelty: The system automatically reassigns work between memory-embedded and traditional processors based on real-time workload changes, using specialized memory-embedded processor designs that efficiently handle different types of memory-intensive operations.

asplos-2025-042.method: Orion is an automated compiler that translates deep neural networks from PyTorch into programs that compute directly on encrypted data (fully homomorphic encryption). The core problem is that encrypted computation requires packing numbers into encrypted slots, and different packing arrangements cause combinatorial explosion—Orion's single-shot multiplexed packing strategy efficiently handles arbitrary convolutions without generating all those possibilities. It also automatically decides where to insert bootstrap operations (which refresh the noise budget in encrypted computation) by tracking noise accumulation across layers and placing bootstraps where they cost the least. This approach enables end-to-end compilation of large networks including ResNet-20, ResNet-50, and YOLO-v1 (139 million parameters) without manual FHE engineering.
asplos-2025-042.key_novelty: Orion combines a single-shot multiplexed packing strategy for arbitrary convolutions with automated bootstrap placement that minimizes noise-refresh costs, enabling fully automatic compilation of large convolutional neural networks to fully homomorphic encryption (computation on encrypted data).

asplos-2025-041.method: Hardware Sentinel connects software failures—like crashes and error logs—to underlying CPU defects by analyzing patterns in application behavior. It builds statistical models (mathematical patterns showing how failures relate to specific CPUs) that enable engineers to identify which machines have hardware-caused errors. This approach was validated using 6 years of real production data spanning 13 workloads across 27 data center regions, combining fleet-wide monitoring with both in-production hardware tests (Ripple) and dedicated offline tests (Fleetscanner).
asplos-2025-041.key_novelty: It detects faulty CPUs by observing application failures rather than running specialized hardware tests, finding problems that traditional testing methods miss.

asplos-2025-055.method: The researchers used Isabelle/HOL, an interactive theorem prover (a tool for mathematically proving software correctness), to create a complete chain of formal proofs for seL4. They proved the C source code was correct, then proved the compiled binary faithfully executed it, then proved the binary enforces security properties like confidentiality (data privacy) and integrity (preventing unauthorized changes), and finally gave a mathematically sound guarantee of worst-case execution time (the maximum time any operation takes) across 4 processor instruction sets. The work also included early-stage exploration of extending this methodology to general-purpose operating systems.
asplos-2025-055.key_novelty: seL4 achieved the first complete, mathematically verified proof chain from human-written source code through compiled machine instructions all the way to proven security guarantees and maximum execution time limits, across 4 different processor architectures.

asplos-2025-056.method: ShadowLoad crafts memory access patterns that train the CPU's prefetcher (a hardware unit predicting which memory locations will be needed next) to a desired state by manipulating its internal prediction structures: stride tables and stream buffers. When a victim process runs, it inherits this attacker-controlled prefetcher state, causing speculative memory fetches that alter the victim's cache contents and execution timing. The attack works across process, user/kernel, and secure-enclave boundaries because CPUs don't clear or isolate prefetcher state during privilege transitions.
asplos-2025-056.key_novelty: The core novelty is actively injecting attacker-controlled state into a victim's prefetcher to influence execution, as opposed to passively observing prefetcher side-channel leaks.

asplos-2025-063.method: GraphPipe represents a neural network as a network of interconnected operations (a DAG, or directed acyclic graph) rather than a simple sequence. It identifies which operations can run in parallel and assigns them to separate processing devices (like GPUs). A scheduling algorithm then decides when to feed batches of data through these parallel stages, timing everything so devices stay busy without idle gaps.
asplos-2025-063.key_novelty: Instead of forcing neural network computations into a sequential pipeline, it exploits the branching structure of the computation graph to run parallel sections on different devices simultaneously.

asplos-2025-057.method: Rather than using separate software layers that each independently manage small data chunks (a decoupled approach), the paper combines them into one integrated system working with larger chunks. These larger chunks align with the natural erase boundaries the hardware uses when erasing memory, which significantly reduces index updates—the frequent catalog rewrites needed to track data locations. Wear leveling (the mechanism for distributing writes evenly to prevent memory wear) is restructured to operate at these same larger granularities, eliminating the scanning overhead from managing tiny chunks. The simplified system reduces both the interdependencies between software components and the total I/O operations required.
asplos-2025-057.key_novelty: The core innovation is consolidating separate block-management layers into one unified system aligned with hardware erase boundaries, which jointly eliminates index-update overhead and wear-leveling scan overhead.

asplos-2025-058.method: Wave moves system management programs (the code handling task scheduling, memory management, and program-to-program messaging) from the main server CPU to a SmartNIC—a network card with built-in ARM processors. These programs need to respond in microseconds (millionths of a second), so Wave provides a new communication channel between server and SmartNIC that's fast enough to support time-critical decisions. The framework runs existing Linux programs mostly unchanged and without requiring kernel modifications, making the approach practical.
asplos-2025-058.key_novelty: Wave's core innovation is a microsecond-speed communication link that enables system management tasks—task scheduling, memory allocation, and program-to-program messaging—to run on the SmartNIC's ARM processors without extensive code rewrites.

asplos-2025-064.method: The system keeps computed intermediate results (KV-cache—saved calculations from neural network attention) from prior conversation turns, eliminating wasteful recalculation when a new message arrives. Instead of processing requests in strict arrival order (FCFS), a smarter scheduler reorders or interrupts long requests to prevent them from blocking shorter ones and wasting GPU capacity. Memory allocation dynamically balances how much of these old results to keep in storage versus when to discard and recompute them.
asplos-2025-064.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining KV-cache retention across conversation turns (reusing prior computed attention results) with a head-of-line blocking-aware scheduler (one that deprioritizes long requests so short ones don't wait) specifically designed for multi-turn dialogue serving.

asplos-2025-052.method: The tool proves that checking whether a particular memory state could result from a crash is equivalent to checking whether the execution is valid under additional ordering constraints. It searches all possible partial pre-crash executions and post-crash memory states, using an SMT solver (an automated logic-solving tool) to verify each combination by symbolically encoding the program. The DPLL(T) framework speeds up the search by eliminating impossible branches, and the approach is implemented in the tool PMVerify.
asplos-2025-052.key_novelty: The key idea—reducing crash-consistency verification to an SMT reachability problem under the NVM memory model—enables the first fully automated robustness verification without user-written test inputs.

asplos-2025-075.method: Relax builds a single unified representation (called a compiler IR, or intermediate representation) that describes three normally separate aspects of ML programs: high-level computational graphs, low-level loop-based tensor operations (called TIR), and calls to external libraries—all in one language. Instead of treating shape sizes (how big tensors are) as information that gets lost between these levels, Relax marks them as first-class values that flow through the entire program, enabling the compiler to optimize based on shape information at every stage. The compiler then uses this unified view to fuse multiple operations into single kernels (combining operations for speed), specialize operators for their actual inputs, and finally generate deployment code for GPUs, mobile phones (Android/iOS), embedded microcontrollers, and web-based targets (WebAssembly and WebGPU).
asplos-2025-075.key_novelty: Relax unifies three separate aspects of ML programs (computational graphs, low-level tensor loop operations, and external library calls) with first-class symbolic shapes that flow throughout the program, enabling shape-aware optimizations that work across all these different levels.

asplos-2025-069.method: Virtuoso uses a lightweight simulator that learns from real operating system behavior. It records the decisions an OS makes about managing virtual memory—allocating memory pages, freeing unused ones, and managing the TLB (a hardware cache that stores address translations). The simulator learns to copy these patterns, then replays them with accurate timing measurements when testing new hardware or OS designs. This runs much faster than simulating the entire operating system.
asplos-2025-069.key_novelty: A simulator learns from real OS behavior to quickly reproduce virtual memory decisions in new hardware and software designs, avoiding the need for full operating system simulation.

asplos-2025-059.method: Exo 2 lets programmers add new code-optimization strategies (scheduling operations) outside the compiler by combining small building blocks—actions that modify code, inspections that examine code structure, and references that point to locations. It introduces Cursors, a unifying abstraction that lets code references work the same way across all these building blocks, keeping user-written transformations safe and separated from the compiler's core. Programmers then build reusable scheduling libraries that apply the same transformation across many related kernels (compute-intensive code patterns), instead of requiring compiler changes each time.
asplos-2025-059.key_novelty: Cursors enable programmers to safely externalize and compose reusable scheduling libraries, letting the language grow without modifying the compiler's core.

asplos-2025-067.method: Homomorphic encryption lets you compute on encrypted data without decrypting it, but it's slow because multiplication and rotation operations cost a lot of computation, and the encrypted data takes up lots of memory and uses lots of bandwidth. CIPHERMATCH tackles this three ways: it packs encrypted data more efficiently to use less memory, redesigns the string matching algorithm to use cheaper addition operations instead of expensive multiplication and rotation, and moves computation close to flash storage to avoid repeatedly transferring encrypted data between storage and main memory.
asplos-2025-067.key_novelty: The core idea is combining algorithm redesign to eliminate expensive multiplication with in-flash processing (computing near flash storage to avoid moving data between storage and main memory).

asplos-2025-065.method: The paper restructures the NTT algorithm so data stays within each GPU's memory as long as possible, delaying transfers between GPUs until they're necessary. The butterfly computation stages (the ordered steps that transform numbers) are planned based on which GPUs are physically connected, with expensive data-reorganization steps grouped together and run simultaneously with computation to reduce their cost. The approach also selects the most efficient physical connection path between GPUs—either NVLink for direct high-speed connections or PCIe—to maximize the rate at which data moves.
asplos-2025-065.key_novelty: Map where NTT computation stages execute based on GPU physical connections, so butterfly permutations require less data transfer between GPUs.

asplos-2025-062.method: Cinnamon breaks the work of fully homomorphic encryption (FHE—computation on encrypted data) into parts that run in parallel across multiple small chips (chiplets) instead of one large chip. A compiler identifies where this parallelism exists and assigns specific operations to different chips—polynomial transformations (NTT), number decompositions (RNS), and key-switching. Hardware and algorithm designs reduce resource needs per chip and data transfer between chips, enabling economical scaling with more chips.
asplos-2025-062.key_novelty: The key innovation is using multiple small chips (chiplets) with a co-designed compiler and algorithms to distribute encrypted polynomial calculations, enabling practical encrypted AI inference on large models like BERT for the first time.

asplos-2025-066.method: BQSim represents quantum gates using decision diagrams (compressed representations that identify repeated patterns), making it easy to spot identical operations across a batch of inputs. It converts this representation into a format that GPUs can process in parallel, then uses a task graph (which maps out how computations depend on each other) to group related operations into single GPU kernel launches instead of many small ones, reducing overhead. By also eliminating redundant calculations shared across the batch and overlapping data transfers with computation, it minimizes total work and keeps the GPU continuously busy.
asplos-2025-066.key_novelty: It combines decision diagrams (which identify shared patterns across inputs) with GPU task-graph execution (which batches operations) to create the first GPU-accelerated batch quantum circuit simulator.

asplos-2025-051.method: CENT uses a hierarchical processing-in-memory (PIM) and near-memory (PNM) architecture deployed across 32 GDDR6-PIM memory devices connected via CXL 3.0. Each PIM device contains 16 multiply-accumulate units (32 billion operations per second in BF16), handling over 99% of the arithmetic, plus PNM units with 32 accumulators, reduction trees, special hardware for exponential functions, and 8 CPU cores for operations like Softmax (attention probability calculation), RMSNorm (normalization), square roots, and RoPE (rotary embeddings). A custom instruction set with commands like MAC_ABK (for matrix operations) and BCAST_CXL (for broadcasting) orchestrates computation and data movement across the CXL network. Pipeline parallelism assigns each transformer layer to one device with multiple prompts flowing through in sequence, while tensor parallelism splits a transformer layer across all devices synchronized via CXL broadcast and gather, with a hybrid mode for balancing throughput and responsiveness.
asplos-2025-051.key_novelty: CENT replaces GPUs with a hierarchical PIM-PNM system connected via CXL 3.0 with a novel broadcast primitive, leveraging GDDR6-PIM's 512 trillion bytes per second internal bandwidth to achieve 2.3x higher LLM inference throughput than 4x A100 GPUs at 2.9x lower energy and 5.2x better TCO.

asplos-2025-071.method: ZRAID uses ZRWA—a small random-write buffer built into ZNS SSDs (solid-state drives with sequential write zones)—to temporarily hold partial parity (information needed to rebuild a failed drive). Instead of writing partial parity to reserved zones, which causes throughput slowdowns and extra wear, ZRAID accumulates multiple partial writes in ZRWA until they combine into complete data blocks (called stripes) ready for sequential writing to the drive. This eliminates both the throughput bottleneck and the accelerated wear that come from logging fragments. ZRAID coordinates this buffering across multiple drives to maintain data consistency.
asplos-2025-071.key_novelty: ZRAID uses ZNS SSDs' built-in random-write buffers (ZRWA) for temporary parity storage instead of reserved zones, eliminating the throughput bottlenecks and extra wear from partial parity logging.

asplos-2025-073.method: Aqua pages LLM request state using the high-bandwidth cables that connect GPUs (NVLink/NVSwitch fabric), storing data on remote GPU memory instead of the system's slow main memory or disk. When the system needs to pause a request to handle a higher-priority one, it moves that request's key-value cache—the data structure tracking what the model computed so far—across these fast GPU cables to another GPU's memory. When the paused request resumes, retrieving this data from a nearby GPU is much faster than reading from slow storage, so the system can efficiently time-slice many requests on a single GPU without performance loss.
asplos-2025-073.key_novelty: Using the fast cables that connect GPUs (NVLink/NVSwitch) to page LLM key-value caches instead of slow storage, enabling quick pause-resume of requests without throughput loss.

asplos-2025-080.method: ByteFS is a file system built for CXL memory-semantic SSDs—drives that offer both byte-level access (like regular computer memory) and block-level access (like traditional storage) via the CXL protocol. It routes each file operation to whichever interface handles it faster: sending metadata and small random-access requests through the byte-level interface (which has lower latency), and large sequential data transfers through the block interface (which has higher throughput). The file system also redesigns operating system abstractions for space allocation, caching, and I/O operations to leverage both interfaces and account for the SSD's persistent, byte-addressable storage semantics.
asplos-2025-080.key_novelty: A file system that intelligently routes operations between byte-level and block-level interfaces of CXL-attached SSDs based on access characteristics, with OS structures designed for NAND flash's persistent byte-addressable nature.

asplos-2025-076.method: NeuSight breaks down the task of predicting how long a deep-learning kernel (a single GPU operation) will take into smaller pieces called "tiles" that match the GPU's streaming multiprocessors—the parallel processing units it actually uses to execute work. A machine-learning model predicts the execution time for each tile, and these predictions are added together to estimate the total time. The predictions stay realistic by constraining them with fundamental performance limits (the roofline model, which describes the maximum speed possible given the hardware design) and by incorporating actual GPU specifications plus optimization tricks from libraries like cuDNN and cuBLAS. This approach works on new, unseen GPU models by learning their core hardware properties rather than encoding specific GPU identities, so it can predict performance without running code on the target hardware.
asplos-2025-076.key_novelty: The core idea is decomposing deep-learning kernel predictions into tiles matching the GPU's execution units and constraining them with performance laws, which enables those predictions to generalize to new GPU models without requiring code execution.

asplos-2025-083.method: FEDORA moves ORAM (a structure that hides which parts of a database are accessed) from fast memory to SSDs and optimizes how it accesses storage to reduce unnecessary writes that degrade hardware over time. It introduces epsilon-FDP (Federated Differential Privacy), a framework that trades off perfect privacy for performance by setting a controlled numerical budget on how much privacy loss is acceptable, which cuts the total number of access operations needed. The system supports modern federated learning modes where users participate asynchronously and selectively, making it compatible with production systems.
asplos-2025-083.key_novelty: Epsilon-FDP is a formal privacy framework that balances ORAM's access-hiding against practical performance using a controlled privacy budget, enabling federated recommendation training on SSDs.

asplos-2025-077.method: Plaid observes that dataflow programs repeatedly use three-node communication patterns (fan-in, fan-out, unicast) and designs processor units (PCUs) where three arithmetic units (ALUs) share a single lightweight local router to handle these patterns, while a separate global router connects PCUs together. A compiler based on the Morpher toolchain, using simulated-annealing-based modulo scheduling (testing different arrangements and keeping the best), automatically identifies these patterns and maps them onto the PCU array. Implemented in 22nm FDSOI silicon at 100MHz, a 2x2 array of PCUs delivers 16 functional units—as much compute as a traditional 4x4 spatio-temporal architecture, but using far fewer routers.
asplos-2025-077.key_novelty: Plaid groups three arithmetic units (ALUs) into processor units (PCUs) that share one lightweight local router—matching communication hardware to the repeating three-node dataflow patterns programs execute—replacing overprovisioned individual crossbars.

asplos-2025-078.method: Harmonia introduces a standard interface (called a shell interface specification) that all FPGA types must follow, letting user accelerators be written once and work across different FPGA types without code changes. The framework defines platform-specific logic (the shell) according to this standard for each FPGA type on the hardware side. A software layer on top handles the differences between FPGA types automatically, so applications don't need custom code for each one.
asplos-2025-078.key_novelty: A standardized interface specification and software abstraction layer that separate user accelerator code from FPGA-specific logic, allowing accelerators to be written once and deployed across different FPGA types.

asplos-2025-086.method: MDPeek exploits the Memory Disambiguation Unit (the CPU component that predicts whether memory operations will conflict, enabling parallel execution). By crafting memory access patterns dependent on secret values, the attacker makes the MDU predict differently for each secret, leaving observable timing traces. A spy process running on the same CPU measures these timing differences, leaking the secret despite defenses that balance both branches to take equal time.
asplos-2025-086.key_novelty: MDPeek discovers that the Memory Disambiguation Unit (which predicts memory conflicts in the CPU) leaks secret-dependent timing variations, breaking SGX protections that balance branch execution time.

asplos-2025-085.method: ASDR performs neural rendering calculations directly in specialized memory chips (computing-in-memory arrays) rather than sending data back and forth to a processor, eliminating expensive transfers. It uses adaptive sampling to reduce computation by adjusting how many sample points to process per ray based on scene complexity, and data reuse to further cut computation by exploiting similarities in nearby rays and consecutive frames so the memory chip can reuse earlier calculations. Together, these techniques reduce both the number of operations and the energy required per operation.
asplos-2025-085.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining adaptive ray sampling and data reuse techniques—specifically designed to work together on in-memory computation arrays—to simultaneously reduce the irregular memory access and total computation in neural rendering.

asplos-2025-084.method: CIDRE is an algorithm that decides when to keep containers running versus start new ones, by tracking detailed information about each container—whether it's currently handling tasks and when it will free up—combined with signals about how many tasks are arriving at once. When a new task arrives, it predicts whether waiting for a busy container to finish (a 'warm start' that reuses the existing container) is faster than starting a completely new container from scratch (a 'cold start'). For deciding which containers to shut down, it combines how recently each was used with predictions of whether it will be needed soon, which prevents the mistake of deleting containers that new tasks will immediately require. The algorithm was tested on two production serverless workload traces.
asplos-2025-084.key_novelty: CIDRE is the first serverless keep-alive policy to explicitly track concurrency state (how many tasks each container is handling) and use it to make both warm-vs-cold-start decisions and balanced shutdown choices simultaneously.

asplos-2025-081.method: MetaSapiens makes real-time neural rendering possible on phones by combining two techniques. First, it removes Gaussian primitives (small 3D shapes that build the image) that don't meaningfully matter, deciding which to keep based on visual importance and computational cost on the specific phone hardware. Second, it renders the center of your view in full detail and the edges in lower resolution or with fewer primitives, exploiting the fact that human peripheral vision can't perceive fine details, with both optimized together on mobile hardware.
asplos-2025-081.key_novelty: The key innovation is combining efficient removal of 3D primitives with rendering that shows the center of vision in full detail and edges in lower quality, both working together on mobile devices.

asplos-2025-082.method: COMET makes practical 4-bit quantization (storing weights and intermediate calculations as 4-bit integers instead of higher precision) by identifying extreme activation values and keeping those at 8-bit precision instead—most values compress to 4-bit without losing accuracy. The GPU kernel efficiently handles this mixed 4-bit/8-bit data by placing elements close together in memory to speed up dequantization (converting back to regular precision for computation), overlapping data loading with calculation to reduce idle time, and balancing work across streaming multiprocessors (the GPU's parallel processing units). This enables large models like LLaMA-3-70B to run efficiently on a single A100-80G GPU with 4-bit key-value caches.
asplos-2025-082.key_novelty: COMET achieves practical 4-bit weight and activation (W4A4) quantization by keeping extreme activation values at 8-bit while compressing others to 4-bit, combined with a GPU kernel that co-locates mixed 4-bit/8-bit data and balances work across processors to fully utilize INT4 tensor cores.

asplos-2025-087.method: Melody is a testing framework that systematically measures CXL memory performance by running 265 different workloads across 4 real CXL devices, 5 different CPU platforms, and 7 different injected latency levels. The key insight is SPA (Sub-operation Performance Analysis), which breaks down the time for each memory access into individual steps to identify exactly where CXL's extra latency comes from. Melody also measures tail latencies (the slowest outlier accesses) and tests how well CPU hardware prefetchers (circuits that try to predict and fetch future data before it's explicitly requested) work under CXL's slower speeds.
asplos-2025-087.key_novelty: SPA breaks down CXL memory latency into sub-operations to pinpoint bottlenecks, and Melody systematically characterizes performance across multiple CXL devices, CPU platforms, and latency levels including tail latencies (the slowest outlier accesses).

asplos-2025-091.method: BatchZK generates multiple zero-knowledge proofs simultaneously on a GPU by running them through different computational stages in parallel—while one proof handles polynomial commitment, another handles multi-scalar multiplication, and a third handles the number-theoretic transform (a fast algorithm for multiplying polynomials). This pipeline keeps the GPU constantly busy and amortizes (spreads) the expensive overhead of data transfer and computation launches across many proofs instead of paying those costs once per proof. The system works with standard blockchain proof schemes like Groth16 and PLONK-family.
asplos-2025-091.key_novelty: BatchZK is the first system to use full pipeline parallelism for zero-knowledge proof generation on GPU, allowing multiple proofs to move through different computational stages simultaneously instead of completing one proof entirely before starting the next.

asplos-2025-090.method: The approach represents neural network data—both inputs and the intermediate outputs from each layer (called activations)—as matrices and explores how rearranging their rows and columns exposes different reuse opportunities. This simple reframing unlocks far more reuse patterns than previous methods could access because they were limited to fixed pattern definitions. To navigate this expanded space efficiently, they build two prediction models: one estimates the accuracy cost of using a reuse pattern (approximate computation—calculating less precisely to save time), and another predicts how fast the pattern will execute on the microcontroller. Together, these models enable automatic search to find the reuse pattern that best trades off accuracy against speed for a given neural network and hardware.
asplos-2025-090.key_novelty: Reframing computation reuse as a matrix row/column reordering problem reveals a much larger set of reuse patterns, which dual models can then search to balance accuracy and latency.

asplos-2025-079.method: MVQ combines two complementary techniques. At the algorithm level, it removes unimportant weights using N:M structured pruning (eliminating weights in a regular, predictable pattern), then applies masked k-means clustering—which groups only important weights and ignores pruned zeros so they don't distort the cluster centers—converts to 8-bit symmetric quantization of the codebook, and refines accuracy by updating only unpruned weights during finetuning. At the hardware level, a specialized accelerator using Enhanced Weight Stationary dataflow reconstructs sparse weights dynamically from the codebook and N:M mask using a Codebook Register File and LZC-based mask decoder, and employs a systolic array (grid of processing elements) with Q=N/M × d active elements per subvector instead of the full d, reducing multiplier and register file count by 55%. The design was synthesized at 40nm using 0.99V low-threshold transistors with Synopsys Design Compiler.
asplos-2025-079.key_novelty: Masked k-means clustering that only includes important, unpruned weights when assigning to clusters and updating their centers, preventing pruned zeros from distorting the averages so the codebook stays close to the weights that matter for accuracy.

asplos-2025-088.method: The approach uses a min-cut algorithm—a graph technique for finding the minimum number of 'cuts' needed to divide a network into parts—to determine where bootstrapping (the expensive recovery step for encrypted data) needs to be placed in a computation. It divides the computation into regions, each kept within multiplicative level limits (the maximum number of times encrypted values can be multiplied together). At compile time, the min-cut method mathematically proves it has found the smallest possible number of bootstrapping operations, while assigning scales (sizes) to the encrypted values within each region to prevent overflow.
asplos-2025-088.key_novelty: The core innovation is to formulate where to place bootstrap operations as a min-cut optimization problem on the computation graph, which mathematically guarantees finding the minimal set needed at compile time.

asplos-2025-093.method: The system continuously measures response speed (latency and throughput) for each container in a microservice to detect performance imbalances—which occur because containers on the same shared hardware experience resource contention from other processes. Rather than trying to make all containers perform identically (which requires over-provisioning), it exploits these differences by sending more requests to fast containers and fewer to slow ones. This directs computational work to where it executes fastest, allowing the cluster to handle more total work with the same hardware without adding servers. The system integrates with existing load balancers and cluster schedulers to implement this intelligent request routing.
asplos-2025-093.key_novelty: Instead of trying to make all containers perform equally, the system uses their performance differences to route requests more effectively.

asplos-2025-096.method: BitSpec has the compiler (which translates source code to machine instructions) and hardware work together. The compiler guesses how many bits each variable needs (fewer than its declared size) and writes instructions using those smaller sizes. The hardware watches the actual values flowing through these variables; if a value needs more bits than predicted and overflows (doesn't fit), the hardware detects this mismatch and signals software to re-run that calculation using the original, safe bitwidth. By doing the right-sized computation most of the time but falling back when needed, BitSpec saves energy without ever producing wrong results.
asplos-2025-096.key_novelty: BitSpec lets compilers automatically narrow how many bits each variable uses by guessing what values will actually appear, with hardware detecting when those guesses are wrong—all without programmers having to annotate code or run test cases to guide the optimization.

asplos-2025-089.method: Lambda-trim works in three automated stages. First, a static analyzer traces through the code to identify which modules (pre-written code packages) the function actually needs—the dependency graph. Second, it profiles the code using serverless billing costs (measuring both memory usage and execution time—the two things you pay for in serverless computing) to assess each module's time and money impact. Third, it removes unnecessary code and unused modules while keeping the functionality intact; the cleaned-up function then runs directly on serverless platforms with no further changes needed.
asplos-2025-089.key_novelty: The innovation is profiling code with awareness of both memory and execution time—serverless's two billing dimensions—to prioritize what gets removed during initialization, the loading phase.

asplos-2025-094.method: Dilu introduces Introspective Elasticity, a system that adjusts GPU resources in two ways: within each running task (changing compute and memory allocation) and across multiple instances (adding or removing copies). To do this, it profiles how sensitive each deep-learning function is to compute and memory constraints, then uses a scheduler to pack compatible tasks together to fill up wasted GPU space on the hardware. At runtime, a controller continuously watches whether tasks are meeting their performance targets and adjusts both the per-task GPU allocation and the number of instances to reduce GPU waste while keeping all tasks meeting their performance goals.
asplos-2025-094.key_novelty: Introspective Elasticity enables real-time, two-dimensional GPU resource adjustment for serverless deep-learning functions without restarting, eliminating the static allocation that causes GPU fragmentation.

asplos-2025-099.method: The organizers created a benchmark suite—a set of test problems using real neural network operations—and asked participants to develop algorithms that decide how to split each operation across multiple accelerators (specialized computers for AI) to minimize total execution time. Over several months, competitors submitted their solutions and were evaluated on this benchmark. The paper then examined the problem structure, how the benchmark was designed, the key challenges participants faced (like the combinatorial explosion of possible ways to split operations), and how well different solutions performed.
asplos-2025-099.key_novelty: A structured community competition and benchmark suite that revealed how far current techniques are from solving the problem of splitting neural network operations optimally across multiple accelerators.

asplos-2025-097.method: Helix converts the challenge of splitting an LLM across different GPUs into a flow optimization problem, represented as a graph where each GPU is a node and edges are labeled with their capacity (compute throughput and network bandwidth). A mathematical optimization solver (Mixed Integer Linear Programming, which searches for the best solution among all possibilities) then solves two problems together: deciding which model layers go on which GPU and how to route token requests through the cluster, finding the best placement and scheduling as a single system rather than optimizing them one at a time.
asplos-2025-097.key_novelty: Unlike approaches that solve model placement and request scheduling independently, Helix solves them jointly as a single max-flow optimization problem, exposing trade-offs between the two decisions that separate approaches would miss.

asplos-2025-092.method: Fusion reorganizes how analytics data files (like Parquet files) are split across storage nodes in erasure-coded environments (systems that spread data redundantly for fault tolerance). Instead of reassembling the full file over the network before filtering, Fusion arranges the data so each storage node can evaluate which rows match the query conditions locally. The nodes coordinate their partial results, minimizing data movement across the network.
asplos-2025-092.key_novelty: Designing how data is stored and how queries run together for erasure-coded systems (data spread redundantly across nodes) so filtering can happen locally without full data reassembly.

asplos-2025-095.method: PhasePrint deliberately creates timing glitches by stressing the FPGA — using ring oscillators (self-oscillating circuits whose speed reveals timing characteristics) or changing voltage and clock frequency. Each physical FPGA responds uniquely to this stress because of manufacturing variations in propagation delays (the time signals take to travel through the chip). The system collects these fault patterns to generate a unique fingerprint for each FPGA, enabling identification without needing privileged hardware access.
asplos-2025-095.key_novelty: The breakthrough is using deliberately-induced timing faults to create unique fingerprints for each individual FPGA, bypassing cloud vendor restrictions on hardware identification.

asplos-2025-102.method: TFHE consists of three core operations—bootstrapping, key-switching, and FFT operations—that the paper restructures so data accessed together is stored in the same processing-in-memory vault or bank. An offline scheduler analyzes which data operands are used together and how frequently, then determines the optimal operation order to minimize remote data accesses (fetches across memory banks) while maintaining sufficient parallelism. The approach was tested on a modified existing processing-in-memory device with minimal hardware changes and validated on an FPGA-based processing-in-memory system emulator.
asplos-2025-102.key_novelty: The core idea is applying affinity-aware offline scheduling to TFHE so that operations sharing data run on the same processing-in-memory unit, minimizing remote data accesses.

asplos-2025-101.method: NACHO embeds detection of Write After Read hazards (when modified data is read before being permanently saved) directly into the data cache (fast temporary memory between processor and permanent storage). When the cache detects this hazard, it handles it immediately without a separate tracking system. This lets the system save its state less often by catching hazards early, and keeps modified data in the cache longer before writing to permanent storage, reducing both runtime slowdown and storage wear.
asplos-2025-101.key_novelty: Putting Write After Read (data modified but not yet saved) hazard detection inside the data cache, instead of using a separate tracking system.
