asplos-2025-107.method: Skia creates lightweight 'shadow branch' records (containing just the instruction address and target hint) when branches are about to be evicted from the BTB (the small buffer that normally stores branch predictions). Later, when the FDIP prefetching engine—which tries to fetch instructions before they're needed—encounters a branch that's been evicted, it checks the shadow records instead of stalling. This lets FDIP continue prefetching along the correct path without wasting cache space on wrong-path instructions.
asplos-2025-107.key_novelty: Skia preserves evicted branch information as lightweight 'shadow branch' records, letting the prefetching engine continue correct predictions without needing to restore full branch buffer entries.

asplos-2025-100.method: Vela runs virtual machines (using KVM) where GPUs on different machines send data directly to each other (GPU Direct) without involving the host CPU. It uses SRIOV to give each virtual machine direct network access, and RoCE (a protocol that runs on standard Ethernet) for communication—avoiding specialized interconnects like InfiniBand. The team tested this on NVIDIA A100 GPUs in IBM Cloud with roughly 1500 machines, using model parallelism to train a 50-billion-parameter decoder-based language model. Insights from 2.5 years of production operation guided the design recommendations.
asplos-2025-100.key_novelty: Vela shows that virtualized AI training with direct GPU communication and commodity Ethernet hardware achieves about 80% of bare-metal performance at 1500-GPU scale without specialized interconnects.

asplos-2025-106.method: Pave creates a locked processing box (PaveBox) on a remote server using Intel SGX—a hardware feature that runs code in a private, tamper-proof zone. A monitor inside watches all data entering and leaving, applying information flow control rules (policies that block dangerous data movements while allowing safe ones). Allowed flows work normally to keep programs functional; blocked flows prevent user data from being exposed. The system's security is mathematically proven, and users can verify its trustworthiness through remote attestation.
asplos-2025-106.key_novelty: A remote data-processing service that runs programs in a hardware-protected box (Intel SGX) with a monitor enforcing information flow control (rules that prevent data leaks), mathematically proven secure and verifiable through remote attestation.

asplos-2025-104.method: The approach has two parts: a type system that statically identifies which values depend on secrets and could leak through speculative execution channels (like the CPU cache or port contention) during any known Spectre variant including Spectre-RSB; and a compiler that rewrites low-level code to block these leaks by inserting fences (instructions that force the CPU to wait), reordering instructions, or masking values. Both the type system and compiler transformation are mathematically verified using Coq (a proof assistant) and implemented in Jasmin, a framework for high-assurance cryptographic code.
asplos-2025-104.key_novelty: A Coq-verified combination of an analysis system (identifying which values depend on secrets) and code rewriter (preventing leaks during Spectre attacks) that protects all known Spectre variants (including Spectre-RSB) with below 5-7% overhead for complex cryptographic operations.

asplos-2025-103.method: Segue encodes each Wasm sandbox's memory bounds into x86-64 segment registers (the FS/GS base registers), which the CPU checks automatically on every memory access—eliminating the runtime's need to insert explicit boundary-checking code into Wasm programs. This removes 44.7% of Wasm overhead on SPEC CPU 2006 benchmarks and cuts Firefox's font-rendering sandbox cost by 75%. ColorGuard uses memory protection keys (a CPU-level memory tagging feature), assigning each Wasm instance a unique tag so they can safely coexist in the same address space; this enables up to 15 times more concurrent instances without separate memory partitions.
asplos-2025-103.key_novelty: Offloading WebAssembly sandbox enforcement from software instrumentation to hardware—using x86-64 segment registers for bounds and memory protection keys for instance isolation.

asplos-2025-111.method: PICACHU adds a flexible, programmable processor (called a Coarse-Grained Reconfigurable Array, or CGRA) designed to speed up the nonlinear operations in language models—like softmax, layer norm, and GELU—which don't work well with standard accelerators. The CGRA has small compute units arranged in a grid that can be rewired and adjusted for different data types for each operation. It connects to existing accelerators (like GPUs), handling only the nonlinear operations while they do the matrix math. Before running the model, a compiler tool assigns compute units, configures their connections, and sets precision for each operation.
asplos-2025-111.key_novelty: PICACHU is a plug-in reconfigurable processor that adapts its internal wiring and precision for each nonlinear operation (softmax, layer norm, GELU) in language models—operations that fixed accelerators cannot handle efficiently.

asplos-2025-098.method: FlexProf uses two types of memory scheduling slots (called turns), each sized and structured for its dominant operation: read-optimized turns and write-optimized turns. It determines which type each application needs through coarse-grain profiling (measuring patterns) that observes read/write ratios without revealing sensitive timing information. When a read-optimized turn finishes reading, it can opportunistically handle writes if the read slots are idle, and vice versa, keeping the memory bus busier. This flexible approach preserves the fixed-turn structure that blocks timing attacks—where one program measures memory speed to deduce secrets—between co-scheduled VMs.
asplos-2025-098.key_novelty: Splitting memory scheduling into read-optimized and write-optimized types—chosen by secure, coarse profiling (measuring safely without leaking timing information)—recovers speed wasted by overly cautious worst-case scheduling.

asplos-2025-108.method: Before the program runs, the approach analyzes the code to identify behaviors that are definitely safe—these are called static invariants (unchanging properties proven to be secure). It removes these safe behaviors from what the ML-based predictor needs to check, shrinking the 'attack surface' (the set of actions that could be security risks). Now the ML predictor only makes predictions on genuinely ambiguous situations, so when it flags something as suspicious, it's much more likely to be an actual attack rather than a false alarm, making it safe to enforce security policies like control flow integrity (blocking unexpected code jumps) and debloating (removing unused code).
asplos-2025-108.key_novelty: The core idea is using static analysis to identify definitely-safe program behaviors and exclude them from the ML predictor's evaluation, so the predictor operates only on genuinely risky situations where its predictions reliably distinguish attacks from false alarms.

asplos-2025-116.method: Coach introduces CoachVM, which splits each resource into a reserved portion (guaranteed allocation) and a shareable portion (drawn from a common pool on demand). For memory, it uses a technique called zNUMA that deprioritizes cold pages so they can be temporarily displaced without disrupting the VM. A machine learning model (random forest regressor) predicts how much of each resource each VM will actually need at different times of day, based on the VM's configuration, time of week, usage history, and customer-specific patterns. The cluster scheduler uses these predictions to pack together VMs with complementary usage patterns—like a daytime-heavy workload with a nighttime-heavy one—and a local monitor prevents resource conflicts by reassigning resources between VMs or migrating a VM to another server when contention occurs.
asplos-2025-116.key_novelty: Coach enables oversubscription of all cloud resources by predicting how each VM's resource needs change throughout the day and colocating VMs with non-overlapping demand peaks, using a split-memory technique (zNUMA) that transparently oversubscribes memory without guest OS modifications.

asplos-2025-113.method: MOAT defends against Rowhammer attacks (where rapid repeated accesses to one memory row corrupt nearby rows) by counting how many times each row is accessed. It uses two thresholds to respond: an Eligibility Threshold (ETH) that triggers preventive measures during periodic memory refreshes, and an ALERT Threshold (ATH) that triggers a back-off slowdown when breached. Unlike Panopticon's 8-entry queue per memory bank (which lost counter information and was exploitable via a Jailbreak attack causing 9 times the configured activations), MOAT tracks only the single highest-access row in a Current Tracked Address register, plus one row being actively mitigated, using just 7 bytes of fast storage per bank total. When memory refreshes occur, it safely preserves counter values by copying boundary-row data to backup registers, and testing shows it can securely handle 99 activation attempts with ATH set to 64.
asplos-2025-113.key_novelty: MOAT replaces Panopticon's multi-entry queue with a single Current Tracked Address (CTA) register tracking the highest-access row, enabling a provably secure dual-threshold defense (preventive Eligibility Threshold and reactive ALERT Threshold) with only 7 bytes of storage per bank.

asplos-2025-112.method: The paper profiles multiple RAG execution pipelines to characterize how retrieval time (finding documents) and generation time (creating answers) interact. It demonstrates that exact nearest-neighbor search—which finds the truly closest documents rather than using faster approximations—actually outperforms approximate retrieval end-to-end because it returns a smaller, higher-precision set of documents, reducing the inference burden on the language model's generation stage. The paper proposes hardware and system optimizations to accelerate exact nearest-neighbor search.
asplos-2025-112.key_novelty: Exact nearest-neighbor retrieval—finding the truly closest document matches rather than approximations—reduces RAG's end-to-end latency compared to approximate retrieval because it feeds the generation model fewer, higher-quality documents, motivating hardware acceleration of exact search.

asplos-2025-105.method: FSMoE divides each mixture-of-experts layer into six customizable pieces (Gate, Order, I-Order, Dispatch, Combine, Expert) with a two-phase profiler measuring matrix operations (GEMM) and network communications. It overlaps three streams simultaneously—each node sending data to all others (AlltoAll), coordinating data within each node (ESP-AllGather/ReduceScatter), and expert computation—by identifying the bottleneck and selecting the optimal batch-size per scenario through optimization (SLSQP), while also splitting synchronization (Gradient-AllReduce) into chunks that fit idle computation gaps, refined by greedy search then evolutionary optimization.
asplos-2025-105.key_novelty: FSMoE is the first mixture-of-experts system to overlap both between-node communication (AlltoAll) and within-node communication (ESP-AllGather/ReduceScatter) with expert computation by adapting batch-sizes per scenario, while also partitioning gradient synchronization (Gradient-AllReduce) work into idle pipeline gaps.

asplos-2025-109.method: vAttention uses operating system memory management primitives—specifically demand paging (where memory is only loaded when actually accessed) and virtual address reservation—to give key-value caches continuous virtual memory addresses while allocating actual physical memory on demand. Unlike PagedAttention, which manually manages fragmented memory locations, vAttention reserves large contiguous virtual address ranges upfront and lets the operating system provide the underlying physical memory as needed. This approach preserves the contiguous virtual memory layout that standard GPU (CUDA) attention kernels expect, so they can run unchanged. It also prevents physical memory fragmentation that would otherwise degrade performance.
asplos-2025-109.key_novelty: vAttention achieves dynamic key-value cache allocation with contiguous virtual addresses by using operating system demand paging, eliminating custom non-contiguous memory management.

asplos-2025-110.method: Pruner uses a two-stage 'Draft-then-Verify' process to find better tensor program schedules (how computations are arranged on hardware) faster. In the first 'Draft' stage, a fast Symbol-based Analyzer (a tool using mathematical rules) rapidly filters thousands of schedule candidates down to the most promising ones. In the 'Verify' stage, only these finalists are checked by the expensive learned cost model—an AI system trained to predict program performance. An extended version called MoA-Pruner adds online adaptation using momentum-based updates (iterative adjustments building on previous changes) to gradually adjust the learned model to new hardware during tuning, eliminating the need for complete retraining.
asplos-2025-110.key_novelty: Draft-then-Verify uses a fast symbolic analysis filter to eliminate unpromising candidates, so the expensive learned cost model only needs to evaluate the most promising options, drastically reducing the number of expensive evaluations.

asplos-2025-115.method: ClosureX is a compiler tool that identifies which parts of your program's state (memory, file handles, global variables) change during each test case and determines the minimal set that must be reset between tests. The tool automatically inserts code into the fuzzing loop to save a snapshot of this state before each test and restore it afterward. This approach lets you run many tests in one process (persistent fuzzing) while preventing one test's leftover state from affecting the next, without needing to restart the entire process.
asplos-2025-115.key_novelty: A compiler that automatically identifies the minimal program state requiring reset between fuzzing iterations, enabling correct persistent fuzzing without process recreation overhead.

asplos-2025-114.method: TaOPT analyzes an app to identify UI subspaces—parts of the app that can be tested independently from each other. It then coordinates testing across multiple devices by assigning each device to explore different subspaces, without modifying the testing tools. As testing progresses, TaOPT dynamically updates which subspaces each device should test next based on what's already been covered, preventing redundant exploration across devices.
asplos-2025-114.key_novelty: The core idea is automatically identifying independent testable parts of an app, then assigning different testing devices to explore different parts without modifying the testing tool.

asplos-2025-120.method: Chassis takes a mathematical expression and generates multiple implementations for a specific target—like a GPU, a vector ISA (the instructions for processing multiple numbers at once), or optimized library functions—each offering different trade-offs between accuracy and speed. It measures how accurate and how fast each implementation will be on that hardware. Then it picks and generates the code for whichever implementation works best for that target by optimizing both accuracy and speed together, based on what the hardware can actually do.
asplos-2025-120.key_novelty: A compiler that improves both numerical accuracy and speed at the same time, designed for specific hardware and instruction sets, doing what traditional compiler backends and numerical compilers used to do separately.

asplos-2025-121.method: GOLF uses Go's garbage collector—the system that automatically frees unused memory—to detect when goroutines (lightweight concurrent tasks) get stuck indefinitely waiting on channels (message pipes). It treats a goroutine as 'alive' only if its channel connections can be traced back to the main program entry points. During garbage collection, any goroutine blocked on a channel with no active senders is flagged as deadlocked; GOLF automatically cancels these goroutines to reclaim memory and let the program continue. This detection happens as part of the garbage collector's normal cycle, adding negligible overhead.
asplos-2025-121.key_novelty: By treating garbage collection's reachability tracking as a goroutine liveness check, GOLF can automatically spot and fix goroutines stuck waiting on channels with no active senders.

asplos-2025-119.method: SylQ-SV tests hardware designs written in SystemVerilog by exploring multiple execution paths (called symbolic execution) to find bugs. During this exploration, it encounters mathematical questions that an SMT solver must answer; instead of solving each one from scratch, it remembers answers (caches them) and reuses them when encountering equivalent questions in different paths, saving computation. The tool fully supports SystemVerilog's features including SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), enabling verification of complete real-world hardware designs.
asplos-2025-119.key_novelty: The core idea is that hardware testing through multiple paths generates the same mathematical questions repeatedly, so caching solver answers avoids redundant work while maintaining full verification coverage.

asplos-2025-127.method: TAPAS is a scheduler that manages AI language model computations on shared cloud computers, tracking how much heat and power each model uses during different inference phases (prefill—processing the prompt—and decode—generating tokens one at a time) at millisecond scale. Instead of running models at full strength, it adjusts three knobs: how to split computation across processors (model parallelism), the size of the model, and the precision of calculations (quantization). These adjustments let it balance four competing goals: speed, temperature, power consumption, and output quality. The scheduler handles multiple customers on the same hardware, using different control strategies depending on whether it can fully monitor and control each workload.
asplos-2025-127.key_novelty: What's new is that TAPAS tracks how heat and power change at millisecond scale during inference (prefill vs. decode phases) and adjusts model size, quantization, and parallelism to simultaneously optimize temperature, power, speed, and quality in shared cloud servers.

asplos-2025-129.method: EDM moves the entire remote memory access protocol into the Ethernet PHY layer (the physical signaling layer), completely bypassing the MAC layer (which normally processes packets) to avoid the delays that layer introduces. At each network switch, EDM implements a centralized scheduler inspired by the Parallel Iterative Matching algorithm that dynamically creates reserved bandwidth channels—called virtual circuits—between compute nodes and memory nodes. These reserved channels eliminate queuing delays and the overhead of Layer 2 packet processing by the switch. An FPGA testbed demonstrates approximately 300 nanoseconds of latency for accessing remote memory when the network is unloaded.
asplos-2025-129.key_novelty: Move the entire remote memory access protocol stack into the Ethernet PHY layer (bypassing the MAC layer) and implement a Parallel Iterative Matching-based scheduler at switches to create dedicated bandwidth channels (virtual circuits) that eliminate queuing.

asplos-2025-125.method: HybridTier tracks two different signals simultaneously to decide which pages should stay in fast DRAM: long-term frequency (which pages are accessed often overall) and short-term momentum (which pages are being used right now). To reduce memory overhead, it uses probabilistic tracking—sampling access patterns and inferring behavior rather than recording every access—which is slightly less precise but uses far less memory. It minimizes cache overhead by organizing tracking metadata in compact structures that keep related data close together, reducing cache misses during lookups. Migration decisions combine both signals together, achieving better accuracy than either signal alone.
asplos-2025-125.key_novelty: HybridTier combines long-term access frequency and short-term momentum—two complementary signals that capture both steady usage patterns and immediate workload shifts—using probabilistic tracking to accurately decide which pages stay in fast memory while minimizing memory and cache overhead.

asplos-2025-124.method: When code modifies instructions already in the L1 instruction cache, the x86 processor pauses and clears its pipeline—discarding all unfinished work to stay correct—adding 235–425 observable clock cycles. Researchers identified which instructions cause this pause (clflush, clflushopt, store, lock+inc, prefetch, clwb), then built attacks called Prime+iProbe and Flush+iReload that exploit the delay: they fill the cache with dummy instructions and measure the delay spike when victim code evicts them, leaking which instructions the victim ran. In practice, they recovered 70% of a 2048-bit RSA key from 10 measurements, extracted encryption keys from OpenSSL servers in a single measurement (65–90% recovery), and built a Spectre-v1 variant that achieves up to 4,105 bytes/second throughput.
asplos-2025-124.key_novelty: This paper shows how to exploit the x86 processor's self-modifying code detection mechanism as a side channel on the L1 instruction cache, producing 100–350 times larger timing signals than previous attacks and enabling information theft between unprivileged sibling threads.

asplos-2025-117.method: DarwinGame runs multiple copies of an application with different configurations on the same virtual machine simultaneously, so they all face the same interference—this lets you directly compare them rather than guessing their performance from separate runs with different interference levels. It searches 10,000 configurations through four tournament stages: (1) a Swiss-style regional phase where the search space divides into 10,000 regions and configurations compete in parallel with early stopping when a winner emerges (judged by how much work gets done), (2) a double-elimination phase where both winners and losers advance to re-compete (judged on speed and consistency), (3) a barrage-style playoff where top survivors compete head-to-head without early stopping, and (4) a final match. This finds configurations that are both fast and reliable under cloud interference.
asplos-2025-117.key_novelty: The core innovation is running multiple application copies with different configurations on the same virtual machine so they experience identical interference, enabling direct comparison, then using a tournament structure (Swiss regional, double-elimination global, barrage playoff, finals) to find configurations that are both fast and reliable under unpredictable cloud interference.

asplos-2025-128.method: PCcheck saves neural network models to durable storage while training continues, by overlapping the storage I/O with GPU computation so neither blocks the other. It uses copy-on-write snapshots (capturing only what changes in model state) and pipelined multi-stage I/O (sending data to storage in stages). The system tracks consistency across concurrent training steps to guarantee each checkpoint is valid and recoverable.
asplos-2025-128.key_novelty: PCcheck overlaps checkpoint storage with training compute using copy-on-write snapshots and pipelined I/O, enabling frequent durable checkpoints without slowing training.

asplos-2025-123.method: RESCQ is a real-time scheduler for quantum computers using continuous-angle error correction—a technique where quantum states are constantly rotated in small angles to fix errors as they happen. RESCQ predicts how reliably each quantum state can be created using expected production rates, and uses those predictions to dynamically allocate resources to the most urgent tasks. When state creation actually fails (which is unpredictable), RESCQ quickly reassigns resources from less urgent to more urgent operations to keep total runtime short. To prevent excessive overhead from constant rescheduling, RESCQ also adjusts how often it recalculates its schedule based on system stability.
asplos-2025-123.key_novelty: RESCQ's key innovation is dynamically redistributing quantum resources on-demand in continuous-angle error correction systems, adaptively adjusting rescheduling frequency to balance speed against scheduling overhead.

asplos-2025-131.method: FleetIO assigns each tenant a separate learning agent (using reinforcement learning, where agents improve through trial and error) that learns three coordination tasks: when to process I/O requests, how much storage each tenant gets, and which requests to accept. All agents watch the same system state and coordinate to simultaneously achieve per-tenant performance isolation (preventing noisy neighbors from slowing you down) and efficient overall storage utilization. Since the agents learn automatically rather than relying on hand-tuned policies, the system adapts to changing workloads and jointly optimizes tail latency (the slowest requests) and storage efficiency.
asplos-2025-131.key_novelty: FleetIO replaces hand-tuned storage policies with one learning agent per tenant (software that automatically improves through trial-and-error) that balances giving each tenant isolated, predictable performance with overall storage efficiency, by coordinating through shared system observations.

asplos-2025-118.method: PowerMove is a compiler for neutral atom quantum computers that decides four things together: which quantum gates (operations) to execute in what order, where each atom should be positioned, how to move atoms between zones (regions of the machine), and when to cross zone boundaries. Because these atoms can move physically, existing compilers waste moves by scheduling gates first and then moving atoms as needed afterward. PowerMove treats atom movement as a core optimization target from the start, jointly exploring movement strategies with gate orderings to minimize both moves and zone crossings. The approach works for both current quantum computers (NISQ, near-term intermediate-scale) and future error-corrected ones (FTQC, which use quantum error correction codes to encode logical qubits), achieving up to 216.9x faster compilation.
asplos-2025-118.key_novelty: Jointly optimizing atom movement with gate scheduling and qubit positioning for both current quantum computers (NISQ) and future error-corrected ones (FTQC) in zoned architectures, achieving orders-of-magnitude improvements in quantum-operation accuracy.

asplos-2025-135.method: Ayo breaks application pipelines into smaller pieces than existing systems do, letting it coordinate decisions across different components instead of optimizing each separately. It creates a complete map of how all parts depend on each other (called a DAG or dependency graph), then jointly optimizes when the language model runs and when the other computation happens, making the entire pipeline faster.
asplos-2025-135.key_novelty: Ayo schedules the entire pipeline by optimizing language model and non-LLM parts together, rather than treating each as a separate piece to optimize independently.

asplos-2025-136.method: Tela predicts how I/O load patterns (the read/write traffic over time) will vary for each storage warehouse, rather than just looking at current conditions. It then places cloud virtual disks (CVD—chunks of data storage that live on physical hardware) onto warehouses in a way that spreads the workload both now and into the future, avoiding placements that would later overload a warehouse.
asplos-2025-136.key_novelty: The key idea is using predictions of how load will change over time when deciding where to place virtual disks, so storage warehouses stay balanced over time rather than just at one moment.

asplos-2025-138.method: In disaggregated memory systems (where CPU and memory servers are separated by network), following a chain of pointers normally requires the CPU to send many individual requests to memory—and each request must wait for the previous answer before asking the next question, creating network delays. pulse eliminates this by placing processing elements directly on the memory servers; these local engines can follow the pointer chains in place, fetching each next address immediately without network round-trips. The framework supports different types of linked structures (linked lists, trees, graphs) and can distribute work across multiple memory servers so multiple traversals run in parallel, improving speed, power efficiency, and throughput.
asplos-2025-138.key_novelty: Rather than having the CPU repeatedly request the next pointer over the network, pulse runs the traversal directly on the memory servers, eliminating network delays for each step.

asplos-2025-132.method: GPUlog implements Datalog on data center GPUs by using a data structure called Hash-Indexed Sorted Array (HISA). HISA packs data into arrays that GPUs can efficiently parallelize while supporting fast range-based lookups. The system implements database operations like joins, unions, and set differences using HISA, and optimizes recursive queries by only recomputing new results at each iteration, using less memory than earlier GPU approaches.
asplos-2025-132.key_novelty: HISA (Hash-Indexed Sorted Array) combines array storage optimized for GPU parallelism with fast range-based lookups that allow recursive Datalog queries to recompute only new results at each step.

asplos-2025-134.method: The authors built a formal model of the CXL.cache protocol using Isabelle (a tool for proving systems mathematically correct), encoding 20 system components like caches and message buffers, plus 68 transition rules covering all legal message flows. They tested the model against real protocol scenarios (called litmus tests) and verified that removing safety restrictions like Snoop-pushes-GO would break cache coherence. To prove the model guarantees only one device can write shared data at a time (the Single-Writer-Multiple-Reader property), they created a mathematical invariant with 796 parts that stays true through all 68 rules, automatically generating and checking 53,332 proof steps using a custom tool called super_sketch.
asplos-2025-134.key_novelty: The first formally verified proof that the CXL.cache protocol correctly implements the Single-Writer-Multiple-Reader property (only one device can write at a time), built with a 796-part mathematical invariant and 53,332 verification steps, which led directly to five accepted fixes in the CXL standard.

asplos-2025-143.method: Existing mobile tracing tools use per-core or per-thread distributed buffers that prioritize speed but lose events when buffers overflow. BTrace replaces this with a centralized or coordinated buffering approach—all events flow through a single collection point rather than independent buffers on each core—which preserves event completeness and ordering. This design maintains acceptable performance overhead while ensuring trace reliability, essential for diagnosing smartphone stability issues.
asplos-2025-143.key_novelty: BTrace trades processing throughput for trace completeness by using centralized or coordinated buffering instead of per-core/per-thread distributed buffers, preventing the event loss endemic to existing mobile tracing.

asplos-2025-130.method: M5 puts access counters directly in the CXL hardware controller, where they track which 4KB pages and which 64-byte chunks within those pages get accessed most often. Unlike CPU-based approaches that guess at hot pages by counting page faults (which often misidentifies warm pages as hot), the CXL controller sees every actual access. When it finds that only certain chunks within a page get used frequently, it can move just those chunks to faster memory instead of moving the entire page—avoiding unnecessary movement.
asplos-2025-130.key_novelty: Embed access counters in the CXL hardware controller—rather than having the CPU guess via page faults—so it can precisely track which 64-byte chunks get used frequently and selectively move only the hot chunks instead of entire pages.

asplos-2025-142.method: UniZK builds a systolic array—a grid of specialized processors that work together on repetitive computations—and enhances it with extra direct connections between nearby processors and a new vector processing mode. This makes the single array flexible enough to execute all three types of zero-knowledge proof computations: number-theoretic transforms (NTT, a fast polynomial transform), cryptographic hash functions, and general polynomial operations. Intelligent mapping strategies route each computation across the shared hardware optimally, keeping all processors utilized instead of having separate dedicated units for each computation type.
asplos-2025-142.key_novelty: The innovation is a systolic array with added local connections and vector processing that works as a unified, efficient hardware substrate for all zero-knowledge proof computations by mapping kernels flexibly, instead of having separate hardware for each computation type.

asplos-2025-147.method: D-VSync breaks the tight link between rendering and the display refresh cycle (VSync—the regular signal that tells the screen when it needs new images). Instead of forcing all rendering to finish within one VSync interval, the system lets rendering jobs run as long as needed and stores completed frames in a buffer. A predictive scheduling layer then matches each finished frame with the next available display refresh window, eliminating the forced frame drops that occur when rendering takes longer than one VSync period.
asplos-2025-147.key_novelty: The core idea is to decouple rendering from the display refresh cycle using predictive frame scheduling, so rendering can finish asynchronously and get matched to the display's refresh windows rather than being dropped when it overshoots.

asplos-2025-126.method: HetEC combines two complementary error-correction codes into a single quantum computer. Surface codes arrange qubits in a 2D grid and detect errors using physical geometry; they handle operations requiring magic state distillation (which enables the full set of quantum operations). qLDPC codes scale more efficiently for error correction. The architecture transfers error-corrected logical qubits between code regions and executes quantum gates remotely across boundaries through gate teleportation, enabling any quantum computation with fewer qubits than either code alone.
asplos-2025-126.key_novelty: HetEC enables universal quantum computation by using surface codes for operations requiring magic state distillation and qLDPC codes for efficient error correction, combining their complementary strengths in a single architecture.

asplos-2025-137.method: Contract Shadow Logic adds a verification layer (called shadow logic) to a processor's hardware design (RTL). This layer encodes contracts—rules defining what information the processor can leak when it speculatively executes ahead (runs instructions before confirming they're needed). The shadow logic tracks information flow through speculative execution, and automated verification tools (model checking or equivalence checking) verify that no possible execution violates the contracts. The result is a formal proof that the hardware is secure against speculative execution side-channel attacks.
asplos-2025-137.key_novelty: By embedding verification logic (shadow logic) that tracks information leakage directly in processor hardware code (RTL), you can mathematically prove the design is secure against speculative execution attacks.

asplos-2025-140.method: CTXNL combines software and hardware to speed up transactions on CXL servers. It lets developers specify for each piece of data whether it needs automatic synchronization across servers—a requirement called cache coherence. Most transaction data doesn't need constant synchronization during normal execution, so skipping this overhead saves time. The system only forces synchronization when transactions commit or conflicts are detected, ensuring correctness.
asplos-2025-140.key_novelty: CTXNL's innovation is giving developers selective, per-data-item control over CXL cache coherence, so transactions only pay the synchronization cost when data actually needs coordination.

asplos-2025-141.method: Neuralink tackles an on-device inference bottleneck: sparse neural network inference (activating only necessary neurons) requires loading scattered neurons from flash storage, creating random memory access patterns, but smartphones face severe IOPS constraints on random flash operations. The system uses a two-stage approach: offline, it analyzes co-activation patterns (which neurons activate together) and reorganizes flash storage to place frequently co-activated neurons contiguously; online, it applies caching and sequential read strategies tuned to both the new layout and the target phone's hardware. By converting random access into sequential reads—which mobile flash handles orders of magnitude more efficiently—it substantially reduces the I/O operations required for sparse LLM inference.
asplos-2025-141.key_novelty: Offline co-activation analysis (finding which neurons activate together) reorders flash storage to place frequently co-activated neurons next to each other, converting random I/O patterns into sequential reads that mobile flash handles orders of magnitude more efficiently.

asplos-2025-145.method: Spindle breaks model execution into 'waves'—groups of different computational tasks—and uses two strategies to run them efficiently. First, it sends each wave to devices based on how much computation it needs, accounting for the fact that different data types (images, text, etc.) have different computational costs. Second, it schedules waves based on which waves need output from other waves, allowing new waves to start before old ones finish, so devices never sit idle waiting. This overlapping execution fills the gaps that normally occur when some devices finish their work before others.
asplos-2025-145.key_novelty: The innovation is 'wavefront scheduling'—jointly optimizing how to assign different types of tasks to devices and when they should run based on data dependencies, all in one unified system instead of separately.

asplos-2025-133.method: CoServe takes advantage of a key property of Collaboration-of-Experts systems: they pre-determine which experts each request needs before execution, making expert requirements predictable—unlike Mixture-of-Experts systems where routing is decided at runtime. It uses three strategies to leverage this predictability: grouping requests that use the same expert to keep it loaded in GPU memory longer, removing experts that won't be needed for upcoming requests when GPU memory fills up (starting with the largest ones to free space quickly, then removing rarely-used ones), and using hardware benchmarks beforehand to find the optimal GPU memory allocation and CPU-GPU computation split.
asplos-2025-133.key_novelty: CoServe's core idea is exploiting the fact that Collaboration-of-Experts systems determine expert requirements before execution, enabling intelligent request scheduling and expert eviction strategies that Mixture-of-Experts systems cannot achieve since their routing is only determined at runtime.

asplos-2025-146.method: Most voltage/frequency scaling happens at the program level because the switching overhead exceeds individual operation duration. But operations have different needs: memory-bound operations (waiting for data) and compute-bound operations (needing raw speed) benefit from different settings. The paper uses an analytical model to predict each operation's type, plus a hardware mechanism to reduce switching overhead, enabling per-operation voltage/frequency scaling: memory-bound operations run slower (saving energy during waits) and compute-bound operations run at full speed.
asplos-2025-146.key_novelty: An analytical model predicts the energy-speed trade-off for each AI operation (how much slower it gets if you run at lower voltage/frequency), enabling per-operation voltage/frequency scaling without hardware profiling.

asplos-2025-150.method: Frugal addresses communication bottlenecks by: (1) spreading embedding tables (lookup tables the model needs during training) across GPUs in a pattern that minimizes lookups between GPUs, (2) compressing or bundling embedding gradients (the training signals sent back across the network) to reduce bandwidth demand, and (3) scheduling work so computation and data transfer overlap, hiding the delay from network waits. Since commodity GPUs lack direct GPU-to-GPU connections, the system routes all communication through the CPU's host memory instead.
asplos-2025-150.key_novelty: The system co-designs embedding table partitioning, gradient communication optimization, and compute-communication overlap to fit commodity GPUs' specific communication limitations.

asplos-2025-144.method: FlexSP improves sequence parallelism—splitting long sequences across multiple devices—by adjusting how many devices each sequence is split across based on its actual length. The system dynamically determines this for each batch: short sequences are split across fewer devices, long sequences across more. This keeps the workload balanced so no device sits idle. The system also optimizes how devices communicate with each other and how attention works to match this flexible strategy.
asplos-2025-144.key_novelty: The core innovation is adjusting how many devices split each sequence based on that sequence's length, rather than using the same split for all sequences.

asplos-2025-156.method: The system stacks four independent layers: automatic hardware configuration and monitoring, fair GPU allocation across users, a user interface for job submission with access controls, and automated incident detection and logging. By automating routine maintenance tasks and scheduling jobs intelligently based on their computational needs, the design keeps the cluster running efficiently with minimal staff. This approach was built specifically for campus environments rather than adapting industrial cluster management systems.
asplos-2025-156.key_novelty: A four-layer cluster management system designed specifically for campus environments—with limited staff and mixed hardware—rather than adapted from industrial systems.

asplos-2025-151.method: Stramash creates a single operating system kernel that runs on heterogeneous CPUs—ones using different instruction sets like x86 and RISC-V—by treating cache-coherent shared memory (memory that all CPUs can access and modify while staying synchronized) as its primary foundation. Unlike traditional multi-kernel operating systems that coordinate separate kernels through message-passing, Stramash puts its core data structures directly in shared memory and adds new mechanisms for synchronization, memory management, and task scheduling that work transparently regardless of which instruction set a CPU uses. The team built this by adapting Linux (Stramash-Linux) and validated it with a multi-ISA simulator (Stramash-QEMU) that achieves less than 4% average simulation error.
asplos-2025-151.key_novelty: The fused-kernel OS unifies CPUs with different instruction sets by running a single operating system kernel built directly on cache-coherent shared memory, rather than coordinating separate kernels per ISA.

asplos-2025-155.method: The algorithm guoq alternates between two steps: fast pattern-matching rewrites that simplify local regions of the circuit and identify which parts would benefit from deeper optimization, and targeted exhaustive synthesis that finds the best possible equivalent circuit for those identified regions. Since these targeted subcircuits are small enough to search exhaustively, this division breaks down the otherwise exponential problem into manageable pieces. This fast-slow interleaving works because rewriting guides synthesis to high-value targets, while synthesis achieves improvements that local pattern-matching alone could never reach.
asplos-2025-155.key_novelty: The guoq algorithm unifies fast rewriting and slow synthesis: rewriting identifies which subcircuits deserve expensive global optimization by simplifying locally, then synthesis exhaustively optimizes those identified regions, achieving stronger results than either technique alone because each guides the other.

asplos-2025-161.method: Diffuse creates a common language—called an intermediate representation or IR—that describes computation tasks from different libraries in the same format, enabling cross-library analysis. At runtime, when task graphs become available, a JIT compiler (just-in-time compiler running during execution) identifies compatible tasks and combines them into single merged tasks, then further fuses the GPU kernels (the programs that run on graphics processors) within those merged tasks. This approach works with computations from cuPyNumeric and Legate Sparse without requiring any changes to application code.
asplos-2025-161.key_novelty: Diffuse uses a shared representation of distributed computations to automatically combine tasks and GPU kernels across different libraries at runtime, allowing high-level Python programs to match or exceed MPI performance.

asplos-2025-153.method: CRUSH prevents deadlock by giving each shared functional unit a limited pool of 'credits' (vouchers that allow operations to use it). When an operation needs the unit, it grabs a credit first; when the operation finishes, the credit goes back to the pool. If no credits are available, backpressure signals propagate through the handshake network (the connections between circuit components) to pause upstream operations, preventing the hardware unit from being overloaded and stuck (deadlock). The system is implemented as a compiler transformation that automatically adds this credit tracking when synthesizing the hardware circuit.
asplos-2025-153.key_novelty: A credit-based control system that lets hardware units be safely shared among multiple operations without deadlock, regardless of when those operations actually execute.

asplos-2025-160.method: Apophenia watches the stream of parallel tasks an application creates and automatically finds repeating patterns in them. When it spots a repeating pattern, it saves the task-dependency analysis for that pattern, so the system doesn't have to recompute it each time. The system integrates with existing parallel runtime systems by intercepting the task-creation API, and unlike previous approaches, needs no manual annotations from programmers.
asplos-2025-160.key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically detecting repeating patterns in the task stream (using sequence-analysis techniques like finding repeated sequences in text) to achieve near-manual-trace performance without any programmer annotations.

asplos-2025-157.method: Mosaic uses iTex (instruction-level texture) tessellation, a compiler technique that partitions a tensor computation into sub-pieces, each optimized for a different arithmetic unit type: scalar for single values, vector for multiple values in parallel, and tensor for matrix operations. The compiler analyzes the operation and hardware capabilities to determine the optimal partitioning. It then generates code that executes all these pieces simultaneously within a single kernel, overlapping their execution to exploit all available instruction-level parallelism.
asplos-2025-157.key_novelty: iTex tessellation splits tensor operations into sub-pieces optimized for different arithmetic unit types (scalar, vector, tensor) to execute in parallel within a kernel, exploiting instruction-level parallelism.

asplos-2025-148.method: The system pairs a CPU with an FPGA (a programmable logic chip) to run the blossom algorithm. The FPGA assigns a separate processor to each data point and connection in the problem graph, enabling massive parallelism. Processors maintain only local state and talk only to neighboring processors; conflicts are resolved entirely in hardware without CPU involvement, reducing CPU interactions from O(p*|V|+1) to O(p^2*|V|+1). The system processes measurement data incrementally as it arrives, achieving constant decoding speed regardless of data volume.
asplos-2025-148.key_novelty: The first exact quantum error correction decoder to achieve sub-microsecond latency using the blossom algorithm on programmable hardware (an FPGA), where dedicated processors for each data point and edge resolve conflicts entirely in hardware.

asplos-2025-163.method: KernelGPT feeds kernel source code and documentation to a large language model, asking it to write specifications for system calls (the interfaces that let programs request operations from the kernel) in the format Syzkaller—a fuzzing tool—expects. When fuzzing runs and finds problems, the tool sends those results back to the LLM to fix incomplete or incorrect specifications, refining them through repeated iterations. This approach automatically covers system calls previously left out of fuzzing and ensures the generated specifications correctly describe how system calls actually behave.
asplos-2025-163.key_novelty: Using a language model to automatically write and repair system-call specifications through iterative feedback from fuzzing, covering system calls previously left out of existing specifications.

asplos-2025-154.method: Fat-Tree QRAM replaces single router nodes with multiple router copies in a tree structure: the root contains log(N) copies while the leaves contain one (matching the traditional design). This allows different queries to flow through different routers simultaneously instead of all queueing at a single control point. Each query progresses through alternating steps: addressing steps that load the target memory address using CSWAP gates (quantum operations that conditionally swap values between qubits, taking 4 circuit layers), and routing steps using local SWAP gates within each router node (taking 1 circuit layer per step). Two alternating SWAP types—SWAP-I and SWAP-II—cycle each query through progressively larger QRAM sub-components while keeping all data movement local within individual nodes.
asplos-2025-154.key_novelty: Fat-Tree QRAM achieves parallel quantum memory access by duplicating the bottleneck control node throughout the tree (log(N) copies at the root instead of one), enabling O(log(N)) queries to pipeline simultaneously while using O(N) qubits and maintaining constant access speed independent of memory size.

asplos-2025-149.method: The framework predicts how fast network functions (programs that process network traffic) will run when multiple are co-located on a SmartNIC (a specialized network processor card), by measuring how they interfere when competing for shared resources: CPU cores, memory bandwidth, data transfer engines, and packet queues. It accounts for how incoming traffic patterns affect queuing delays, using machine learning to predict each function's latency (how long operations take) and throughput (how much data it processes), given its resource allocation and traffic conditions.
asplos-2025-149.key_novelty: It predicts network function performance on SmartNICs by jointly modeling how co-located functions compete for multiple resources (CPU, memory, data transfer engines, queues), with competition patterns that depend on incoming traffic.

asplos-2025-166.method: Instead of repeating expensive setup work on every cold start, Medusa pre-computes and saves that work as materialized snapshots on disk. Specifically, it saves two things: the KV cache initialization state (memory pre-allocated and configured for inference) and CUDA graphs (pre-compiled GPU execution instructions for each batch size). When a cold start occurs, the system loads these saved snapshots directly into the GPU, skipping the expensive initialization and compilation steps that normally repeat every time. This pre-computation happens offline or on the first warm start, with minimal overhead to restore the saved state.
asplos-2025-166.key_novelty: Medusa's core idea is materializing the KV cache initialization state and CUDA graphs—storing pre-built copies on disk—so cold starts can reload them directly into the GPU instead of rebuilding them each time.

asplos-2025-158.method: The system first identifies where the mobile NPU (a specialized hardware chip for AI) becomes the bottleneck in LLM inference, then redesigns the inference pipeline to exploit how the NPU actually works. It merges multiple operations into single steps (operator fusion) and breaks computation into chunks that fit the NPU's memory layout. The approach specifically speeds up the prefill stage (where the model processes your initial prompt) by bundling token processing so the cost of invoking the NPU is shared across more work, and restructuring the attention computation (where the model decides which input parts matter) to fit the NPU's built-in hardware units.
asplos-2025-158.key_novelty: The innovation is restructuring how language models focus on input (their attention mechanism) specifically for mobile AI chips, and combining operations to reduce the number of times the chip must be called.

asplos-2025-164.method: QECC-Synth automatically arranges quantum error correction circuits on quantum computers with limited qubit connections. It works by inserting extra helper qubits (called ancillas) that relay information between distant qubits, then uses mathematical optimization (MaxSAT—a technique for finding the best solution among many possibilities) to determine the best placement and routing for these helpers. The system systematically explores all the different ways to set up these helpers and selects the combination that works best for a given error-correction pattern and hardware architecture. This approach works for different types of quantum hardware and different error-correction codes (like surface code or color code) without requiring manual customization.
asplos-2025-164.key_novelty: The core idea is treating quantum circuit arrangement on limited-connection hardware as a mathematical optimization problem (MaxSAT) solved over all possible helper-qubit placements, enabling automated solutions that work across hardware types and error-correction patterns.

asplos-2025-162.method: Cross-Level Debugging compares two debugging views of the same program: source-level debugging (showing the code you wrote) and instruction-level debugging (showing what the CPU actually executes). It checks that three things must be true between them: the program must visit the same code locations in both views, must visit them in the same order, and variables must have the same values at each location. A tool called Devil automates this by generating test programs, running them through both debug views, and flagging any violations as bugs in the debugger toolchain.
asplos-2025-162.key_novelty: It detects debugger bugs by comparing source-level and instruction-level debugging views of the same executable, which catches errors other methods miss in unoptimized binaries.

asplos-2025-170.method: PUSHtap stores OLTP and OLAP data in a single unified format by exploiting how different processors naturally access data: it arranges rows for the CPU's row-by-row scanning (called interleaved access, or ADE), and the exact same data is automatically available to PIM processors as columns (called localized access, or IDE). To pack data efficiently without wasting space, it groups columns of similar widths together using a bin-packing algorithm, then spreads the columns across PIM devices in a rotating pattern every 1024 rows so all devices stay equally busy. For transactional updates, it uses a two-region approach: a main data region and a delta region for recent changes, with visibility snapshots stored as compact bitmaps written in parallel to all devices; cleanup is done by PIM units when needed. A modified memory controller coordinates all this by scheduling fine-grained access from both the CPU and PIM processors, limiting CPU idle time to 300 microseconds during the load phase of analytical queries.
asplos-2025-170.key_novelty: A single data format works for both OLTP and OLAP because CPU and PIM processors access data along perpendicular directions—CPUs scan rows (interleaved access/ADE) while PIM scans columns (localized access/IDE)—eliminating format duplication and rebuilding.

asplos-2025-168.method: The system analyzes the server binary to identify larger functional code regions called Bundles (10s–100s of kilobytes) that tend to execute together. Hardware then uses a record-and-replay prefetcher that watches which Bundles are executed and replays that pattern, prefetching entire Bundles when their entry points are detected rather than individual cache lines. Bundle metadata lives mostly in main memory with under 2KB stored on-chip to save space. This approach tolerates control flow variability because prefetching entire functional regions works even when execution takes unexpected paths that would defeat line-by-line prediction.
asplos-2025-168.key_novelty: The core idea is defining large functional code Bundles (10s–100s kilobytes) and prefetching them as complete units rather than individual cache lines, so that execution stays on track even when control flow diverges from predictions.

asplos-2025-159.method: DejaVuzz combines two complementary techniques: Dynamic Swappable Memory (DSM) swaps physical memory pages at runtime to precisely control the processor's microarchitectural state—its TLBs (address-translation caches), caches, and branch predictors—which enables triggering transient execution bugs. Differential Information Flow Tracking (DIFT) instruments the processor simulator to detect whether secret data leaks through these bugs by monitoring if information flows from a secret source to an observable side channel like cache timing. The fuzzer generates test programs using DSM to reset the microarchitectural state between tests, then uses DIFT differential analysis to identify which tests actually cause information leakage, achieving both comprehensive coverage and precise detection.
asplos-2025-159.key_novelty: Combining dynamic swappable memory to control processor state with information flow tracking to detect secret data leaks enables both reliable triggering and detection of transient execution bugs.

asplos-2025-174.method: DeepContext uses an interceptor—a monitoring layer that watches operations without modifying them—placed between the deep learning framework and C/C++ libraries to record each operation and match it with GPU performance data and the Python code that triggered it. Without changing the framework code itself, this approach traces high-level operations directly to the GPU instructions that executed them. An automated analyzer then examines these linked traces to identify which layers are causing slowdowns and recommend optimizations.
asplos-2025-174.key_novelty: A framework-agnostic interceptor that automatically links Python operations down through the framework and libraries to GPU execution, exposing exactly where performance bottlenecks occur in the entire software stack.

asplos-2025-167.method: The approach treats the DPU chip and host server as redundant peers using a hybrid synchronization protocol. This protocol keeps each VM's complete state mirrored on both components with minimal overhead (kilobytes per VM), smartly prioritizing frequently-changing VM data (hot state) over rarely-changing data (cold state) to reduce bandwidth. When one component fails, the VMs immediately resume on the other side instead of waiting for the failed component to recover.
asplos-2025-167.key_novelty: The system maintains complete VM state on both the DPU and host, treating them as redundant peers, so virtual machines can instantly escape to whichever component is still working.

asplos-2025-172.method: CMSwitch tells the compiler about a hardware capability it previously ignored: CIM accelerators can switch between compute mode (performing calculations) and memory mode (storing or accessing data). The compiler uses optimization techniques—dynamic programming (trying different solutions systematically) and mixed-integer programming (math for finding the best outcome when some variables must be whole numbers)—to determine where to split the network and how much hardware resources to allocate to compute versus memory modes. The result is packaged in a form that works across different CIM hardware targets.
asplos-2025-172.key_novelty: It's the first compiler to jointly optimize compute and memory mode resource allocation using dynamic programming and mixed-integer programming, adapting resources dynamically to each neural network layer's requirements.

asplos-2025-171.method: Tally shares a GPU among multiple programs by intercepting the work they send to it. Instead of running all of one program's work then all of another's, Tally dynamically schedules individual thread blocks (small units of parallel computation, much smaller than a full kernel) from high-priority inference and lower-priority training tasks, controlling how much the programs interfere with each other. All of this works without requiring any changes to the programs or frameworks themselves.
asplos-2025-171.key_novelty: Thread-block-level scheduling isolates concurrent programs' performance on a shared GPU without modifying the applications or frameworks.

asplos-2025-178.method: Gigaflow breaks down packet processing into stages and caches the filtering results from each stage, rather than only caching the final result. When the SmartNIC processes new packets, it can reuse these cached intermediate results for stages that match, avoiding redundant searches through the flow rule tables. By knowing which intermediate results are safe to reuse, Gigaflow improves cache performance and maintains high throughput even when flow rule tables are very large.
asplos-2025-178.key_novelty: Gigaflow caches intermediate filtering results from each pipeline stage instead of just the final lookup, allowing SmartNICs to reuse results across packets and handle very large flow tables efficiently.

asplos-2025-169.method: Pirate sends only one eye's video at a time (alternating left and right), since the two views in VR are almost identical. Each transmission includes lightweight geometric information—disparity maps showing object distance and optical flow showing pixel motion—that let the device recreate the missing eye's view without large AI models, at bitrates as low as 0.1 bits per pixel. By alternating transmission, the system can also reuse frames recreated earlier, further saving bandwidth.
asplos-2025-169.key_novelty: Reconstructing VR's missing eye view step-by-step using only distance and motion information (disparity and optical flow)—not large AI models—to enable 90 FPS streaming at 0.1 bits per pixel on edge devices.

cgo-2025-003.method: PreFix watches your program as it runs and uses context information to identify which data objects get accessed most frequently (hot objects) with high accuracy. It then reserves specific memory regions ahead of time and places these frequently-used objects there, allowing it to group them together even if they were originally allocated separately. The system also recycles this reserved memory—when one object is no longer needed, it reuses that space for a new object, saving memory when object lifetimes don't overlap.
cgo-2025-003.key_novelty: PreFix's core idea is using runtime context information to identify hot objects with near-perfect precision, enabling it to reorder and group frequently-accessed data together in memory.

asplos-2025-177.method: Syno works by defining small, composable building blocks that operate on tensor dimensions (the multi-dimensional arrays used in neural networks) and enforcing rules that keep model training stable—like ensuring dimensions match between operations and follow the associative property (where the order doesn't affect the result). To avoid searching redundant designs, the system uses expression canonicalization to identify and prune equivalent forms. It then uses stochastic tree search (a Monte Carlo-style method of randomly exploring design branches) to navigate the enormous design space while respecting input/output dimension constraints, and compiles and evaluates the resulting operators on real hardware.
asplos-2025-177.key_novelty: Syno is an end-to-end system that automatically discovers neural operators by assembling small, reusable components operating on tensor dimensions (multi-dimensional arrays) and using stochastic tree search (random exploration of design possibilities) to find operators that outperform both hand-designed ones and those from automated neural architecture search.

asplos-2025-175.method: The paper breaks down Ascend's hardware into individual components—compute units, memory subsystems, and data pipelines—and calculates a performance ceiling for each one to identify which component is slowing things down. This analysis is combined with a structured optimization process based on real case studies, which identifies common bottlenecks like memory bandwidth saturation (when memory can't move data fast enough) and pipeline bubbles (when data waits idle in transit), then applies targeted fixes for each.
asplos-2025-175.key_novelty: A component-based roofline model—analyzing each hardware component's performance ceiling separately—to identify bottlenecks and optimize operators (individual operations) on domain-specific architectures like Ascend that require manual memory management.

cgo-2025-002.method: ASDF converts basis-oriented quantum programs (where you pick a coordinate system first) into quantum circuits using MLIR, a compiler toolkit. It automatically generates inverse and conditional versions of functions. The result is OpenQASM 3 or QIR code that runs on quantum simulators or hardware, with gate counts comparable to compilers built specifically for circuits.
cgo-2025-002.key_novelty: The key idea is designing the compiler's intermediate representation around basis-oriented concepts—letting the compiler understand and preserve basis choices during compilation—rather than starting from generic quantum circuits.

asplos-2025-176.method: The attacker uses an unprivileged mechanism to control exactly when the operating system pauses their program and runs the victim program (called preemption). By timing these pauses precisely, the attacker can measure the victim's CPU behavior—specifically patterns in cache access and memory use. This synchronized, finely-timed measurement greatly amplifies side-channel attacks (techniques that steal secrets by observing CPU timing and resource patterns) without requiring special privileges or custom hardware.
asplos-2025-176.key_novelty: A mechanism allowing unprivileged users to control precisely when the operating system pauses programs, which amplifies attacks that steal secrets through observing CPU behavior patterns.

cgo-2025-000.method: FastFlip identifies code vulnerable to silent hardware errors by combining actual error injection (running code with deliberately introduced faults) with mathematical error-propagation analysis. When code changes, it only re-analyzes the modified sections using compositional (modular, reusable) analysis instead of starting from scratch. This efficiency guides compilers to add error-detection code only to the vulnerable instructions.
cgo-2025-000.key_novelty: FastFlip is the first to enable compositional (modular, reusable) and incremental error injection analysis, reanalyzing only changed program sections instead of running fresh analyses each time.

cgo-2025-001.method: Cage uses two Arm hardware features for memory safety. Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) tags memory locations so the processor can catch both out-of-bounds access and use-after-free bugs (when freed memory is accidentally reused) in heap and stack allocations. Pointer Authentication (PAC) digitally signs pointers to prevent them from being forged or reused across WebAssembly instances. An LLVM compiler automatically adds function wrappers and safety metadata to the original code, enabling these hardware protections.
cgo-2025-001.key_novelty: This is the first work to use Arm Memory Tagging Extension and Pointer Authentication together to provide memory safety for WebAssembly while improving the performance of its isolation mechanism.

cgo-2025-008.method: Tensorize automatically converts code to use tensor DSLs (specialized languages for efficient numerical operations) by creating a symbolic trace—a mathematical record of what the program does. It then finds equivalent patterns (sketches) from the target DSL and uses an algebraic solver (a tool that simplifies mathematical expressions) to transform these into the most efficient tensor form. Since the solver works by proven mathematical rules, the result is guaranteed to produce identical outputs to the original program.
cgo-2025-008.key_novelty: Using an algebraic solver on symbolic program traces enables fast, provably-correct automatic translation to tensor DSLs.

asplos-2025-173.method: Random testing of concurrent programs (where multiple threads execute simultaneously) typically misses bugs because it samples interleavings (the order in which operations from different threads execute) non-uniformly — some orderings get tested far more often than others. SURW (Selectively Uniform Random Walk) is an online testing algorithm that fixes this: it picks a subset of the program's events (points where threads interact or synchronize) and generates all possible orderings with equal probability. The algorithm works as a black-box technique requiring only minimal information about the program, achieving uniform sampling across broad classes of programs and arbitrary event subsets.
asplos-2025-173.key_novelty: The method provably achieves uniform sampling of interleavings (the order in which threads' operations execute) without requiring program-specific knowledge, giving each possible sequence equal probability and enabling systematic discovery of bugs hidden in rare orderings.

cgo-2025-006.method: The tool automatically scans your code to identify places where you can replace header includes with forward declarations—instead of loading entire header files at compile time, forward declarations just tell the compiler what it needs to know. It uses LLVM, the compiler infrastructure, along with a specialized tool called Yalla to perform these transformations. For situations where normal forward declarations don't work—specifically class methods and functions that take lambda functions as parameters—the tool instead generates wrapper functions, simpler interfaces that achieve the same goal. The system uses profitability analysis to determine which transformations will meaningfully improve compilation speed, preventing unnecessary changes.
cgo-2025-006.key_novelty: It automatically transforms header includes into forward declarations, handling even the previously impossible cases—methods and lambda-parameter functions—with wrapper functions.

cgo-2025-005.method: Honey Potion translates Elixir code into eBPF binaries (kernel programs). The compiler treats the eBPF verifier's requirement that programs must terminate in bounded time not as a restriction, but as an optimization opportunity: it applies constant propagation (computing values at compile time), type specialization (tailoring code for specific types), and partial evaluation (simplifying by pre-computing what can be determined ahead of time). The compiler includes compile-time proofs to ensure the optimized code preserves the original program's behavior and satisfies the verifier's safety checks.
cgo-2025-005.key_novelty: Honey Potion is the first compiler to translate a functional programming language (Elixir) to eBPF, exploiting the verifier's termination requirement as an optimization opportunity.

cgo-2025-013.method: Proteus compiles GPU kernels just-in-time (recompiling the code right before it runs rather than beforehand), using LLVM IR—an intermediate code format that works across programming languages. Users mark specific points in the code where it can be specialized for the actual input data and GPU launch settings. By using LLVM's portable infrastructure instead of language-specific tools, Proteus works across different GPU vendors without needing separate compilers.
cgo-2025-013.key_novelty: Proteus is the first to use JIT compilation (compiling code right before it runs) on GPU kernels with language-agnostic code that works across all GPU vendors, delivering faster compilation than existing language-specific approaches.

cgo-2025-012.method: Instead of forcing researchers to choose between working inside a production compiler (messy but useful) or building their own from scratch (clean but too much work), this approach creates multiple specialized compilers that work together. They share the same text format for describing code structure (called IR, or intermediate representation) and use a declarative system called IRDL to define how each compiler's extensions work, so each one can focus on what it does best—prototyping, teaching, or production use—while still sharing code with others. The paper demonstrates this with xDSL, a specialized compiler that works alongside MLIR (an existing production framework) and can exchange code with it because they use the same textual IR.
cgo-2025-012.key_novelty: This is the first system that lets multiple specialized compilers—each optimized for different purposes like prototyping, teaching, or production—work together by sharing code in the same text format and using declarative rules to define their extensions.

cgo-2025-007.method: The approach profiles the application to record the exact order in which methods are called and objects are accessed. It then reorders code and objects in the startup snapshot based on this access sequence, placing frequently-accessed items close together in memory to minimize page faults (slow memory loads). The system uses three different strategies to arrange heap objects. Since object identities can change between profiling and compilation into the native binary, it includes logic to match profiled objects to their built versions.
cgo-2025-007.key_novelty: This is the first approach to use profiling data to reorder heap objects in AOT-compiled native code, reducing startup page faults.

cgo-2025-016.method: It works by analyzing examples of your keys to automatically discover patterns in them—like fixed-length sections or repeating bytes—using regular expressions (a system for describing text patterns). One algorithm identifies which patterns matter in your keys, while another generates a custom hash function optimized for those patterns. This is faster than general-purpose hash functions because it takes advantage of the predictable structure in real-world keys.
cgo-2025-016.key_novelty: It automatically generates custom hash functions by learning patterns from your actual keys, rather than hand-tuning templates for each data format.

cgo-2025-010.method: Creates a mathematical model of how PyPM's pattern matching language works. Specifies the behavior two ways: declaratively (rules for which patterns should match which code), and algorithmically (step-by-step procedures for testing matches). Uses Coq—a tool that mechanically verifies mathematical proofs—to prove both specifications are equivalent.
cgo-2025-010.key_novelty: First formal verification of an ML compiler pattern matching language, using mechanized proof in Coq.

cgo-2025-019.method: The paper builds an LLVM-based framework (a compiler tool that instruments code) to systematically test two memory-safety approaches: Low-Fat Pointers and SoftBound. The framework automates the common tasks that these approaches share—figuring out where to add safety checks and removing redundant ones—so researchers can compare them fairly. It then measures what fraction of memory accesses don't actually need checking (are provably safe) and breaks down where the performance cost comes from.
cgo-2025-019.key_novelty: The paper's key idea is an LLVM framework that automates the shared tasks between different memory-safety approaches, making it possible to compare them fairly and identify exactly where practical adoption breaks down.

cgo-2025-014.method: Modern processors have separate execution pipelines for vector operations (processing multiple data items together) and scalar operations (processing one at a time). Current compilers typically vectorize entire loops, forcing all operations through the vector pipeline and leaving the scalar pipeline underused. Scalar Interpolation runs some loop iterations on the scalar pipeline and others on the vector pipeline, avoiding the data movement overhead of forcing scalar operations into vector registers. The technique uses either a cost model or runtime testing to determine the optimal ratio of scalar to vectorized iterations.
cgo-2025-014.key_novelty: The first technique to balance scalar and vector pipeline utilization by inserting scalar-only iterations into vectorized loops.

cgo-2025-009.method: MTE4JNI labels Java heap objects using ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (a hardware feature that marks memory regions with small tags). When native code tries to access these objects through a pointer (a memory reference), the processor verifies the pointer's tag matches the object's tag, blocking the access if they don't match. This real-time verification prevents unauthorized access with minimal performance cost.
cgo-2025-009.key_novelty: This is the first method using ARM's Memory Tagging Extension to protect Java heap from unauthorized access via JNI (the interface that lets native code access Java).

cgo-2025-011.method: The approach extends the use of post-increment instructions—memory operations that fetch or store data and then automatically update the address to the next location—from basic blocks (small sections of straightforward sequential code) to loops at different nesting levels and patterns that connect multiple loops. Rather than always using post-increment whenever possible, it uses profitability analysis to check whether it actually helps (smaller code, better speed) compared to other compiler optimizations before applying it. The implementation is done in LLVM, a widely-used compiler framework, and works across multiple processor architectures.
cgo-2025-011.key_novelty: This is the first compiler to systematically use post-increment instructions (memory operations that automatically advance to the next data location after reading or writing) across all nested loops and patterns that span multiple loops.

cgo-2025-033.method: The approach tests pairs of compiler optimization passes on benchmark programs and uses clustering (a technique to group similar patterns) to identify which pairs work best when applied in sequence. These successful combinations are collected into a small representative set called a coreset. A machine learning model is then trained on these coresets to predict which combinations will work for new programs without testing each possibility individually. Various search strategies are applied to quickly converge to good solutions.
