cgo-2025-033.key_novelty: Identifying synergistic optimization-pass pairs (combinations that work well together) and collecting them into small representative sets (coresets) makes the search space manageable and enables machine learning to predict good strategies for new programs.

cgo-2025-025.method: ANT-ACE takes neural network models in standard ONNX format (a common way to describe machine learning models) and automatically generates C/C++ code that performs inference—makes predictions—on encrypted data using a custom 44,000-line cryptography library. The compiler uses a multi-level intermediate representation (a format that sits between the original model and the final executable code) that can adapt to different model types and different encryption schemes. The current implementation uses the RNS-CKKS encryption scheme to run these encrypted computations on CPUs.
cgo-2025-025.key_novelty: The core innovation is a multi-level intermediate representation that abstracts different encryption schemes and input formats, enabling automatic conversion of standard neural network models into efficient encrypted code.

cgo-2025-027.method: Teapot rewrites compiled binaries without source code to run two parallel execution paths: one normal, one simulating speculative execution (the CPU's process of guessing what code to run ahead of time). This technique, Speculation Shadows, tracks whether timing differences in speculative paths could leak secrets. Runtime integrity checks flag exploitable patterns, and automated testing (fuzzing) confirms which vulnerabilities actually work.
cgo-2025-027.key_novelty: Speculation Shadows: a technique that instruments compiled binaries to run normal and speculative execution paths in parallel, enabling detection of exploitable Spectre gadgets.

cgo-2025-004.method: Janitizer combines static analysis with runtime checks to protect compiled binaries. It uses static analysis to examine the code (without running it) and identify where security needs to be added, then places runtime checks (safeguards) at those locations. This hybrid approach provides the performance of static analysis with the correctness of runtime checking. It protects against memory corruption (through memory sanitization) and control flow attacks (through control flow integrity).
cgo-2025-004.key_novelty: Janitizer achieves both comprehensive security and practical performance by combining static analysis with runtime checks in binary rewriting.

cgo-2025-026.method: Calibro reduces binary size by extracting duplicate code into single locations, using a two-stage process. During compilation, it identifies code regions that likely repeat. During linking (when all code is assembled into the final binary), it uses a parallel suffix tree—a fast data structure for detecting repeated patterns—to find actual duplicates and extract them. To avoid slowing the app, it only extracts code from infrequently-called functions.
cgo-2025-026.key_novelty: It finds and removes duplicate code using compilation-stage hints to guide a fast link-time search, optimizing only infrequently-called functions to preserve performance.

cgo-2025-022.method: SkipFlow improves points-to analysis—a technique for determining what values variables can hold—by analyzing code in two stages: a quick pass treating each function separately, then refinement using information about which functions call which. Throughout, it tracks both primitive values (numbers, booleans) and objects, using predicate edges (edges representing which branches code takes) to capture control flow, gaining precision without the cost of flow-sensitivity (tracking every possible execution path).
cgo-2025-022.key_novelty: Predicate edges (edges representing control-flow branches) combined with primitive value tracking improve points-to analysis precision without needing flow-sensitivity (tracking every possible execution path).

cgo-2025-020.method: The PIM-LLM framework optimizes matrix multiplication (the core LLM operation) on Processing-In-Memory hardware by dividing problems into smaller tiles (PGEMMlib) and using an analytical model (Tile-Selector) to automatically pick optimal tile sizes. Integrated into TVM (a compiler for hardware-specific code), it employs several techniques: pre-compilation data reorganization, combining PIM resources for efficiency, coordinating CPU-PIM work, and fusing attention steps (Q, K, V generation) to reduce host-PIM data transfer overhead.
cgo-2025-020.key_novelty: The approach combines a matrix-multiplication tiling method optimized for PIM hardware (PGEMMlib) with an analytical model that automatically selects tile sizes (Tile-Selector), minimizing data transfers between host and PIM.

cgo-2025-018.method: The method rearranges quantum gates and assigns them to zones to reduce atom movement. It uses three strategies: fountain-shaped chains of controlled-Z gates to group related gates, a ZZ-interaction protocol that separates single- and two-qubit gate execution (preventing interleaved operations that force zone jumps), and preemptive gate scheduling (determining the full schedule before execution begins). By jointly optimizing gate order and zone placement, atoms spend less time traveling between zones.
cgo-2025-018.key_novelty: Fountain-shaped chains of controlled-Z gates combined with a ZZ-interaction protocol (which separates single- and two-qubit gate execution) reduce zone transitions.

cgo-2025-028.method: The compiler transforms code step-by-step through multiple layers, each one matched to what the hardware can actually do. Rather than assigning all variables to storage slots at once (and moving extras to slower memory when registers fill up—a technique called spilling), it gradually assigns storage as it transforms the code. This lets it directly use the processor's specialized features—like hardware loops and streaming registers (fast memory paths for continuous data flow)—that general-purpose compilers typically miss.
cgo-2025-028.key_novelty: Instead of converting code through a single generic form that loses hardware details, this uses multiple intermediate representations designed to preserve and directly use specialized hardware features like loops and streaming registers.

cgo-2025-024.method: Stack filtering removes false pointer relations in Rust by using the language's explicit lifetime information for stack objects—temporary variables that stop existing after a certain point in the program. It works in two phases: first, it determines which stack objects are currently alive via function reachability analysis and a call graph (showing which functions can reach which others); second, it removes pointer relations mentioning dead stack objects during analysis. This filtering happens within context-sensitive pointer analysis (tracking what variables point to while following specific execution paths) and is built into the Ruypē framework.
cgo-2025-024.key_novelty: The core idea is using Rust's explicit stack object lifetimes to eliminate false pointer relations without needing full flow-sensitivity—analyzing how data changes at every step of the program.

cgo-2025-032.method: Vectron takes Python code that implements dynamic programming algorithms (like sequence alignment problems that build up solutions by filling arrays) and automatically converts it to faster C++ code. The C++ version uses SIMD (a CPU feature that applies the same operation to many data values in parallel) and GPU acceleration to speed up computation. It processes multiple problem instances together simultaneously rather than one at a time, letting the parallel hardware handle them efficiently without requiring you to modify your original algorithm.
cgo-2025-032.key_novelty: It automatically converts Python code for dynamic programming into SIMD and GPU-accelerated C++, eliminating the need for manual algorithm redesign.

cgo-2025-031.method: GraalNN uses Graph Neural Networks—a machine learning approach that works on connected graphs—to automatically learn patterns from control-flow graphs (diagrams showing which lines of code execute next) rather than relying on hand-designed patterns. It makes predictions in two stages: first, a basic prediction of how many times each piece of code runs without knowing what calls it, then a refinement using the call graph (the map of which functions call which others) to account for different calling contexts.
cgo-2025-031.key_novelty: Rather than using manually-designed patterns, GraalNN automatically learns from code-flow diagrams using machine learning, then refines this by considering which functions call each other.

cgo-2025-030.method: IntelliGen optimizes deep neural network code by making instruction-level choices about memory access patterns on NVIDIA, AMD, and Cambricon hardware. It relies on a key insight: memory optimizations are "monotonic," meaning if two optimizations each improve performance independently, combining them still improves performance without conflicts. This property lets it efficiently explore thousands of parameter combinations instead of billions.
cgo-2025-030.key_novelty: Instruction-level auto-tuning is made practical through monotonic memory optimization: a principle where each improvement adds on top of others without creating conflicts, which lets the system explore efficiently instead of checking exponentially many possibilities.

cgo-2025-023.method: CUrator takes LLM models (BERT, GPT, Llama) and converts them into a form that can be optimized using TVM, a compiler framework. It systematically tests configuration options for CUTLASS (NVIDIA's optimized matrix multiplication library) to find the best settings for each operation. To improve performance, it applies Split-K optimization (a technique for breaking matrix operations into smaller parallel pieces that efficiently combine their results, with special support for batch operations). Finally, it selects the faster option between cuBLAS and CUTLASS for each operation.
cgo-2025-023.key_novelty: CUrator systematically tunes CUTLASS within TVM (a compiler framework) and selects the faster library between CUTLASS and cuBLAS for each operation, with extended Split-K support for both batch and regular multiplications.

cgo-2025-043.method: DialEgg connects Egglog (an equality saturation engine—a tool that systematically generates and tests all mathematically equivalent forms of code to find the fastest version) to MLIR, a compiler optimization framework used across many programming languages. Rather than writing separate optimization rules for each MLIR variant (dialect), DialEgg automatically translates code back and forth between MLIR and Egglog formats. It comes with pre-built definitions for common MLIR operations, types, and attributes, so developers can benefit from equality saturation immediately.
cgo-2025-043.key_novelty: DialEgg applies equality saturation (systematically finding all mathematically equivalent forms of code and choosing the fastest) to MLIR without needing separate implementations for each compiler dialect.

cgo-2025-036.method: The system uses MLIR, a compilation framework that represents code at multiple abstraction levels, to translate regex patterns into efficient hardware instructions. They created two specialized mini-languages within MLIR: one for describing regex patterns in a hardware-independent way, and another for the domain-specific architecture (DSA) instruction set. By maintaining both representations, the compiler can optimize intelligently—translating high-level pattern logic into parallel hardware operations. The DSA hardware itself was redesigned to exploit the parallelization patterns that become apparent when you structure the problem this way.
cgo-2025-036.key_novelty: Using MLIR's multi-level compilation framework to optimize regex matching by connecting high-level patterns and specialized hardware.

cgo-2025-044.method: Parallaft detects hardware faults using software versions of techniques from fault-tolerant hardware systems. It creates memory snapshots using copy-on-write (saving only changed data), tracks memory modifications, and synchronizes performance counters to spot when computations produce different results. The error checking runs on the little cores (smaller, lower-power processors in chips like Apple M2) rather than on special fault-detection hardware.
cgo-2025-044.key_novelty: Using software on the little cores (smaller processors already built into chips like Apple M2) to detect hardware faults, instead of relying on special fault-tolerance hardware.

dac-2025-000.method: CREST-CiM stores each binary weight using two magnetic tunnel junctions—tiny devices that switch between magnetic states to encode data—connected together per memory cell, one storing +1 and one storing −1. Cross-coupling them (linking their magnetic states) dramatically increases the difference between the electrical current when reading the +1 state versus the −1 state, achieving an 8100-fold ratio. This much larger difference makes the reading circuit much more reliable, allowing it to correctly identify weights despite manufacturing variations and other hardware imperfections.
dac-2025-000.key_novelty: Linking two magnetic storage devices per weight creates an 8100-fold difference in readable current with only 7.9% additional chip area.

cgo-2025-042.method: The method expresses the convolution problem as polynomial multiplication: the filter and input patches are represented as polynomial coefficients, and multiplying those polynomials yields the convolution outputs as the result's coefficients. Using fast polynomial multiplication algorithms computes this in a single pass without duplicating data—avoiding both the data redundancy of im2col and the multi-pass overhead of traditional FFT convolution.
cgo-2025-042.key_novelty: The key insight is expressing convolution as polynomial multiplication, which achieves efficiency gains unavailable through either standard im2col or FFT approaches alone.

dac-2025-001.method: Flip-FET flips the lower transistor in a vertically-stacked transistor pair (CFET—complementary field-effect transistor), creating connection points (pins) directly accessible from both the top and bottom metal wiring layers without requiring tap-cells (helper cells needed for routing). To implement this, the optimization process synthesizes multiple Flip-FET cell variants with different pin layouts, optimizes their placement to minimize tap-cells, and rebalances wiring between the top and bottom layers.
dac-2025-001.key_novelty: Flip-FET eliminates tap-cell overhead by reversing transistor orientation to create connection points directly accessible from both wiring layers, enabling full use of the new backside routing layer.

cgo-2025-038.method: LFQS automatically synthesizes efficient quantum simulator code in C and CUDA from an intermediate language specification (a formal notation between human-readable code and machine instructions). It recognizes that quantum gate matrices—the mathematical representations of quantum operations—naturally contain many zeros and structured patterns that general dense matrix libraries can't exploit. Rather than treating all values equally, it generates code that only computes where needed, skipping the zeros. The result is simulators significantly faster than those using standard dense tensor frameworks.
cgo-2025-038.key_novelty: Automatically generating quantum simulator code by exploiting sparsity in quantum gate matrices, producing simulators faster than both hand-written implementations and dense tensor libraries.

dac-2025-002.method: ReVeil plants a hidden backdoor into a neural network by poisoning the training data before training even begins—without needing to access the model or have extra reference data. The poison creates a dormant trigger in the trained model that appears weak (low attack success rate), making it undetectable before deployment. After deployment, machine unlearning (a technique that selectively removes learned behaviors from a trained model) reactivates and strengthens the hidden trigger to make the attack reliable.
dac-2025-002.key_novelty: A hidden backdoor attack that requires no model access and no auxiliary data, achieved by poisoning the training data during data collection.

cgo-2025-035.method: GoFree uses escape analysis—a compiler technique that runs in O(n^2) time to identify short-lived objects that can be safely freed—to insert explicit freeing instructions instead of relying on garbage collection. These freeing operations use thread-safe mechanisms and operate transparently within Go's memory model without changing the garbage collector. The result is fewer garbage collection pauses and lower peak memory usage.
cgo-2025-035.key_novelty: GoFree's core novelty is using O(n^2) escape analysis to automatically insert compiler-based freeing for identified short-lived objects, thereby reducing garbage collection overhead while preserving thread-safety and requiring no modifications to the garbage collector.

cgo-2025-046.method: Qiwu eliminates wasted space in encrypted computations by combining multiple encrypted chunks (ciphertexts) that contain gaps (bubbles) into tightly-packed encrypted chunks without gaps. These gaps appear inevitably from reduction operations on encrypted data. The system uses a domain-specific language to specify which gaps are expected, data-flow analysis to track where they occur, and cost-benefit calculation to decide which chunks are worth combining.
cgo-2025-046.key_novelty: Qiwu merges encrypted chunks to eliminate gaps from encrypted reduction operations, complementing plaintext-level SIMD parallelism.

dac-2025-007.method: DARIS is a scheduler that decides what work runs on a GPU when. It combines two techniques: NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets multiple tasks share different parts of the same GPU at the same time (space-sharing), while CUDA streams run tasks at different times in sequence (time-sharing). The system synchronizes these tasks so work can move between GPU sections instantly without waiting. By analyzing how tasks can run concurrently, it packs more work onto the GPU than conventional approaches allow.
dac-2025-007.key_novelty: The core insight is combining GPU space-sharing (via MPS) and time-sharing (via CUDA streams) with zero-delay work migration, which lets you run more real-time neural network tasks on one GPU than standard scheduling methods.

dac-2025-003.method: Instead of relying on a single authority to verify if an IoT device is trustworthy, this protocol spreads verification across many independent computers in a blockchain network—each checks the device and votes on whether it's legitimate. All the votes and verification results are recorded permanently on the blockchain, creating a complete and unchangeable history that auditors can review. This distributed approach removes the single weak point that attackers could exploit.
dac-2025-003.key_novelty: Many independent computers verify and vote on a blockchain instead of a single trusted authority, eliminating the single point of failure in device attestation for IoT.

dac-2025-005.method: Qubit routing places quantum bits (qubits) on a quantum computer's physical layout to satisfy interaction constraints, typically by inserting SWAP operations that move qubits to compatible positions. DDRoute solves this routing problem using a depth-driven heuristic: when choosing where to place each SWAP, it selects the position that reduces circuit depth—the total number of sequential operations—the most. This contrasts with existing methods that try to balance multiple competing objectives like minimizing SWAPs while also reducing depth.
dac-2025-005.key_novelty: The core idea is optimizing qubit routing by prioritizing circuit depth—the number of sequential operations—over other objectives, achieving up to 70% depth reduction compared to existing methods.

dac-2025-006.method: The system uses an encoder-decoder diffusion transformer—an AI model with attention mechanisms that generates solutions by iteratively refining random noise. During training, it learns the relationship between circuit performance targets (like desired power and speed) and the device sizes needed to achieve them. Given new performance targets, the model generates IC sizing solutions directly, without expensive optimization loops. This produces accurate results in seconds and generalizes to designs not seen during training.
dac-2025-006.key_novelty: Encoder-decoder diffusion transformers (AI models that iteratively refine solutions from random noise) enable analog IC sizing by learning relationships between circuit performance targets and device sizes.

cgo-2025-047.method: VEGA organizes the functions (pieces of code) that compilers use into groups and creates customizable templates for each group. Using a pre-trained transformer (a type of machine learning model), it learns which parts of the templates are the same for all hardware and which parts differ depending on the hardware. VEGA then automatically generates compiler code for new hardware targets by filling in the templates with the hardware description, eliminating the need for manual engineering.
cgo-2025-047.key_novelty: Using a pre-trained transformer (a machine learning model) to automatically generate compiler code from target descriptions, eliminating manual engineering work.

dac-2025-009.method: Pipirima predicts where non-zero values will appear in sparse matrices using simple counters inspired by CPU branch predictors. When streaming through a compressed matrix (CSR, a compact way to store sparse matrices), these predictions let the accelerator prepare its processing units in advance, preventing load imbalance where some units sit idle while others are overloaded. The system is tested on sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) and sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (SpMM).
dac-2025-009.key_novelty: Pipirima uses simple counters to predict where non-zero values appear in sparse matrices, which helps accelerators distribute work evenly across their processors.

cgo-2025-040.method: The algorithm uses A* search—a technique that systematically tries different solutions while using heuristics to steer toward the best answers. To stay efficient, it employs two types of shortcuts: some guarantee it never skips the optimal solution, while others speed things up by pruning unpromising branches (even if they might contain an answer). For arrays of length 3, it exhaustively tries all correct sorting kernels; for larger arrays, it intelligently samples the best candidates. This approach runs about 100 times faster than prior work (AlphaDev) without requiring specialized hardware like TPU clusters.
cgo-2025-040.key_novelty: The core idea is using A* search with specialized heuristics and pruning to find optimal sorting kernels on standard hardware, thereby establishing the theoretical minimum size these kernels must have.

dac-2025-011.method: The system reads brain signals using the BrainFlow library and trains deep learning models to interpret them for prosthetic control. It searches through different combinations of settings—such as network size, learning algorithms, data window sizes, and whether to combine multiple models—using evolutionary search (testing random variations and keeping what works best) to find configurations that maintain accuracy while running on resource-limited hardware. To make these models small enough for the prosthetic device, it removes unnecessary connections from the networks (pruning) and converts numbers to lower precision (quantization). Users can switch between different control modes with voice commands.
dac-2025-011.key_novelty: It searches for and compresses deep learning models that balance accuracy and speed for real-time prosthetic control on resource-limited hardware.

dac-2025-004.method: The researchers tested how predictable responses were from different PLPUF chips by varying how long they let circuits run before recording outputs (activation duration). They discovered that certain activation durations create mathematical relationships between chips' responses — if you know one chip's output, you can calculate another's with 96% accuracy. This reveals that activation duration is a critical security parameter: wrong choices destroy the unpredictability that protects these chips.
dac-2025-004.key_novelty: The security of PLPUFs critically depends on activation duration selection, with unsuitable choices enabling 96% accurate response prediction.

dac-2025-010.method: Binary numbers are converted to unary representation—expressing a value N as N ones in a sequence—traditionally using comparison circuits (comparators) that check if one number is larger than another. These circuits consume significant power and chip space, especially as input size increases. This design eliminates comparators entirely and instead uses alternative conversion logic to accomplish the same transformation. It provides three implementations: a serial approach that processes one value at a time (simpler, slower), and two parallel approaches (faster) that either compute the exact result or approximate it to reduce costs further.
dac-2025-010.key_novelty: A binary-to-unary conversion method that eliminates expensive comparison circuits (comparators) required by traditional approaches, removing their power and area overhead.

dac-2025-008.method: EdgeMM pairs a multi-core CPU with two specialized hardware types: systolic arrays (processing units designed for rapid parallel calculations) handle the compute-intensive encoding stage, while compute-in-memory chips (processors built directly into memory to minimize data movement) handle the memory-bound decoding stage. Dynamic activation-aware weight pruning (removing less important learned parameters based on which parts of the network are actually active) further improves efficiency. The system is built using 22-nanometer manufacturing technology.
dac-2025-008.key_novelty: A heterogeneous CPU that pairs specialized hardware types—systolic arrays for encoding and compute-in-memory chips for decoding—rather than identical processors.

dac-2025-012.method: This paper examines the security risks that come from breaking computer systems into separate, independent pieces (CPU, memory, storage, networking) connected by networks. The authors look at three real-world contexts: enterprise networks where data travels between separate routers (network fabric), systems that manage radio signals through software (O-RAN), and hardware designed to run trusted code safely (trusted execution environments). They identify the new attack points that appear when pieces are separate—such as data getting exposed during network transfer, losing track of where data came from (provenance), systems not being properly isolated from each other, and problems with how different parts communicate through APIs.
dac-2025-012.key_novelty: This paper examines the security threats and opportunities that come from breaking computer systems into separate networked pieces, focusing on radio systems controlled by software (O-RAN).

dac-2025-015.method: They create FreeSet, a dataset of 220k Verilog files automatically checked to ensure fair-use licensing compliance. A Llama model is then trained on FreeSet through continual pre-training (teaching an existing model new code while keeping its prior knowledge) to create FreeV. They then test FreeV's output against a benchmark that measures copyright violation risk in the generated Verilog code.
dac-2025-015.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically checking copyright licenses in training data so that models trained on legally-approved code can generate new Verilog without risk of copyright infringement.

dac-2025-019.method: The method uses integer linear programming (a mathematical optimization technique that systematically tests combinations to find the best solution) to decide where to place circuit elements in a chip while accounting for secondary power routing—backup power paths that activate when the main power supply can't handle peak demand. It specifically adjusts placement of cross-domain cells (circuit elements that require power from multiple independent power sources simultaneously), reducing competition between power lines and signal lines for routing space. The solution is validated against commercial chip design tools.
dac-2025-019.key_novelty: This is the first detailed placement method that explicitly optimizes secondary power network routing in multi-domain chip designs.

dac-2025-020.method: The method takes a statistical timing graph—a diagram showing all possible execution times for a chip's computations—and runs it on a GPU (graphics processor) using a specialized scheduling algorithm. To work around GPU memory constraints, which are much tighter than traditional computers, the algorithm schedules the computation strategically so data chunks fit in GPU memory. The approach was validated on an 18.2 GB statistical timing graph, demonstrating it handles large designs that would otherwise exceed GPU capacity.
dac-2025-020.key_novelty: The first statistical timing analysis method that runs on GPUs by using a specialized scheduling algorithm to work around GPU memory constraints.

dac-2025-016.method: The technique breaks down CAN bus messages—the signals vehicles use to control functions like acceleration and steering—by systematically testing which individual bits trigger which car actions. It does this through bit-level signal extraction (isolating the specific control bits that matter) combined with exhaustive mapping (systematically checking every bit pattern combination against observed vehicle behavior). The researchers validated the approach on a Tesla Model 3 and Leapmotor C10/C11 vehicles, and demonstrated it runs efficiently enough on a Raspberry Pi.
dac-2025-016.key_novelty: It shows how to precisely identify which individual bits in vehicle control messages trigger which actions, using minimal computing power—efficient enough to run on inexpensive hardware like a Raspberry Pi.

dac-2025-014.method: The DLU model calculates how much space wires need inside routing tiles by analyzing their exact shapes and positions, instead of using a fixed guess. It adds tip-to-tip penalty extensions—extra costs when wires come close together—to accurately predict how tightly wires can pack. Routing algorithms then use these real congestion measurements to choose better paths for wires. The model also handles incremental updates, such as when connection points move.
dac-2025-014.key_novelty: Instead of guessing routing space with fixed estimates, this model measures congestion dynamically based on actual wire shapes and positions.

dac-2025-021.method: Photonic accelerators speed up AI computations by using light, but they need digital-to-analog converters (DACs)—devices that convert digital signals into the analog electrical voltages needed to control light intensity. The problem is that DACs consume so much power they waste most of the energy savings. P-DAC reduces this wasted power by jointly optimizing the DAC itself and how it drives the optical modulators (Mach-Zehnder modulators, which control light intensity).
dac-2025-021.key_novelty: This work focuses on DAC power consumption as a critical bottleneck in photonic accelerators for transformer inference.

dac-2025-013.method: The framework runs compiled code directly (rather than simulating each step, which is slow) with a fast but approximate model of how long operations take on 1024 RISC-V cores working together. It connects to wireless channel models to test 5G signal detection functions in realistic conditions. Single-threaded, it simulates each symbol in 9.5 seconds to 3 minutes—about 1000 times faster than traditional RTL simulation—and can split the work across 128 threads for an additional 73–121× speedup.
dac-2025-013.key_novelty: A simulator that runs compiled code directly (via binary translation) with a fast but approximate timing model, enabling rapid end-to-end exploration of many-core SDR (software-defined radio) baseband processor designs.

dac-2025-027.method: The framework combines four complementary models. First, a wire-area model predicts how much routing space power and signal connections will consume, accounting for congestion. Second, a pad-to-pad clearance model enforces minimum distances between connection points to prevent interference. Third, a two-sided density model prevents component bodies from overlapping with each other and prevents pads (connection points) from overlapping. Fourth, a quadratic programming-based legalizer (a mathematical optimizer) adjusts component positions to resolve any remaining clearance violations and overlaps.
dac-2025-027.key_novelty: This is the first PCB placement framework that directly enforces clearance between pads and handles components of different sizes and shapes simultaneously.

dac-2025-024.method: The system uses contrastive learning—comparing hotspot and non-hotspot examples to teach the model their differences—on both sequence and image representations of chip layouts. A technique called Layout2Seq converts the actual shapes of polygons into numerical vectors. Rather than using the standard position markers that Transformers typically employ, it uses absolute position embeddings that better capture the geometry and topology (spatial arrangement and shapes) of the polygons.
dac-2025-024.key_novelty: The first contrastive learning framework that explicitly encodes the geometric and topological properties of polygons for hotspot detection.

dac-2025-018.method: The system uses multiple specialized AI agents, each focused on a specific quantum optimization: error correction (fixing quantum computational errors) or circuit synthesis (designing efficient quantum circuits). A semantic analyzer—a component that understands code meaning—runs multiple passes to refine the results, applying Chain-of-Thought reasoning (where the AI thinks step-by-step) alongside an error correction decoder to catch and fix quantum mistakes. Testing measures each agent's contribution.
dac-2025-018.key_novelty: Multiple AI agents, each specializing in a different quantum code optimization like error correction or circuit design, work together in one framework.

dac-2025-025.method: The system uses pulse widths (signal durations) as the data format and implements a two-layer ReLU network using RRAM (resistive random-access memory), all operating in the time domain to avoid expensive analog-to-digital-to-analog conversions. The Dynamic Loss-Responsive Subset Enhancement (DLRSE) algorithm optimizes which elements contribute to each calculation, improving the network's ability to approximate any nonlinear function. A pulse-driven programmable current source generates the computation signals, while a low-latency timing comparator determines the output pulse width.
dac-2025-025.key_novelty: First time-domain universal nonlinear operator (representing signals as pulse widths) that eliminates the energy cost of converting between analog and digital domains.

dac-2025-023.method: Instead of computing attention (relevance between all token pairs) for every position, the method only computes it fully for nearby tokens and uses approximate top-K search (AKAttention) to select important distant ones, reducing computation significantly. The key-value cache needed during decoding is stored in a tree-structured processing-in-memory architecture (TreePIM), where computation happens inside memory units rather than moving data to the processor, improving both memory capacity and access speed.
dac-2025-023.key_novelty: The core innovation is using distance to select which token pairs to compute attention for, combined with a hierarchical processing-in-memory architecture for storing the key-value cache, while maintaining accuracy on ultra-long sequences over 1 million tokens.

dac-2025-017.method: Multiple AI models running at the same time on a chip's shared cache compete for space, degrading performance. This approach uses three techniques: hardware support for dedicating cache regions to each model (controlled by the NPU, the processor managing the models), mapping that adapts based on available capacity, and dynamic reallocation that adjusts which model gets which region in real time as their demands change.
dac-2025-017.key_novelty: The core idea is a joint hardware-and-software design using NPU-controlled exclusive cache regions with dynamic allocation to prevent multiple AI models from competing for shared cache.

dac-2025-026.method: YAP creates a mathematical model that predicts yield (the number of working chips produced) when using copper-copper bonding (a metal-joining technique for connecting chiplets) in wafer-to-wafer and die-to-wafer configurations. The model accounts for five sources of failure: misalignment during bonding, particle contamination, copper layer thickness variations, wafer surface roughness, and variations in copper density. Instead of running thousands of simulations like traditional Monte Carlo approaches, YAP uses direct mathematical equations to calculate yield 10,000 times faster.
dac-2025-026.key_novelty: YAP is the first yield model for copper-copper hybrid bonding that accounts for all failure sources, making it fast enough to test many design variations.

dac-2025-035.method: The algorithm extracts the circuit's timing paths iteratively rather than building the complete circuit graph. It uses timing propagation—tracking how clock delays spread through connections—to dynamically identify only the edges (connections) it needs, skipping unnecessary ones. This targeted approach lets it calculate clock skew adjustments (synchronizing clock signals across the chip) while handling multiple clock latency constraints, then applies slack optimization (maximizing timing margin) to achieve target latencies.
dac-2025-035.key_novelty: First iterative clock skew scheduling algorithm that dynamically identifies only the necessary circuit edges using timing propagation instead of building the full graph, reducing extracted edges by 90.05%.

dac-2025-029.method: AttenPIM moves computations into memory banks (processing-in-memory) with dual-mode execution specialized for attention's two distinct operations: multiplying queries by keys to compute scores, and multiplying scores by values to produce results. Each memory bank has configurable processing units that work on key-value data arranged specifically for in-memory execution. The system maintains high throughput by processing multiple tokens and attention heads in parallel, dynamically allocates resources based on sequence-length-dependent matrix sizes, and fuses operations to reduce data movement.
dac-2025-029.key_novelty: The key innovation is a dual-mode processing-in-memory architecture that recognizes attention has two distinct matrix-vector operations (score and value combination) with sequence-length-dependent matrix dimensions.

dac-2025-032.method: The framework removes unnecessary parts from spiking neural networks to reduce energy use by combining three techniques. It uses multi-stage masking to precisely control when individual neurons fire, temporal attention batch normalization (TABN) that adjusts information flow over time with learnable time scaling (letting the network learn how fast to process time), and a dynamic sparse strategy that decides which parts to remove based on real-time synaptic operations (the actual computations between connected neurons).
dac-2025-032.key_novelty: The framework jointly adjusts both spike patterns over time (spatiotemporal spike sparsity) and connection strengths (weight sparsity) dynamically to minimize synaptic operations during inference.

dac-2025-028.method: E-morphic generates multiple circuit structures using equality saturation (systematic exploration of logically-equivalent circuit forms) after the initial technology-independent optimization phase, when standard methods would settle on just one structure. It stores all equivalent forms in an e-graph data structure, prunes unlikely candidates to reduce search complexity, and uses simulated annealing (guided random search) to identify promising structures before converting them back to circuits. This enables parallel exploration of different structures before the final hardware-specific optimization stage.
dac-2025-028.key_novelty: E-morphic is the first to apply equality saturation—exploration of logically-equivalent circuit variations—in the resynthesis stage after initial optimization, solving the problem that standard synthesis methods get locked into a single structure.

dac-2025-031.method: A neural network called a transformer learns how chip components relate to and connect with each other (nodes and edges in a floorplan graph). It then generates improved component arrangements in parallel while simultaneously checking for and correcting thermal warpage—the material distortion that occurs when different materials in densely packed advanced packaging heat unevenly. The method jointly minimizes component displacement and warpage by directly incorporating thermal-mechanical coupling constraints (understanding how materials actually bend under heat) into the optimization.
dac-2025-031.key_novelty: This is the first method to use a transformer neural network to automatically design chip layouts while jointly minimizing component displacement and thermal warpage—the material distortion from uneven heating in advanced IC packaging.

dac-2025-033.method: The algorithm uses ADMM (alternating direction method of multipliers—a technique that breaks complex optimization into simpler parts solved back-and-forth) to repeatedly optimize global cell placement, then recalculate routing based on the new placement. It applies bilevel optimization (where one solution step directly accounts for its effects on the next step) and Wasserstein distance (a mathematical measure of how spread-out distributions are). During this process, a mathematical model determines the optimal amount to expand each cell during placement, while the overall approach directly minimizes wiring congestion in the final routed design.
dac-2025-033.key_novelty: It unifies placement and routing into a single optimization problem using ADMM for the first time, with mathematical theory (bilevel optimization and Wasserstein distance) to directly minimize wiring congestion instead of solving them separately.

dac-2025-037.method: Anchor combines software and hardware design to maximize data that stays in place. Software uses the Mastav algorithm, a graph-partitioning technique that divides vertices and edges to keep as much data as possible within the same memory banks that process it. Hardware uses a custom dataflow design that ensures any data needing to move between banks is fetched exactly once instead of repeatedly. An optimized communication system further reduces unnecessary transfers by analyzing the critical path—the sequence of dependent operations that determines overall speed.
dac-2025-037.key_novelty: The first processing-in-memory architecture for graph neural networks that maximizes stationary data through locality-preserving graph partitioning (Mastav, which groups related data) and single-pass access to data that must move.

dac-2025-036.method: Rimast places compute directly on memory chips—3D-stacked processing-in-memory hardware—so data doesn't have to travel long distances. The software is designed to work with this hardware: it organizes data flow in hierarchical levels to reduce transfers, spreads data evenly across memory to avoid bottlenecks (skew-free mapping), and dynamically decides which retrieval operations run on which parts of the system (adaptive offloading). This approach handles the irregular, hard-to-predict access patterns that come with retrieval-augmented language models.
dac-2025-036.key_novelty: Rimast is the first processing-in-memory system (putting compute directly on memory chips) specifically optimized for retrieval-augmented language models, using hierarchical data flow and balanced data distribution to achieve 273× speedup over CPUs.

dac-2025-038.method: The system progressively simplifies the graph by merging similar nodes (coarsening) while a neural network learns patterns about the graph structure at each level. Once reduced to its smallest form, the system rebuilds the graph back to original size, and the neural network uses its learned patterns to guide which nodes should move between partitions, improving the quality of the final split. This learning-based approach produces better results than traditional methods that rely on fixed rules.
dac-2025-038.key_novelty: It's the first multilevel graph partitioner to use a neural network that adapts partitioning decisions based on learned graph patterns instead of predetermined heuristics.

dac-2025-030.method: SAGA groups vertices that have the same starting point during graph construction, reducing memory waste by storing similar data only once. It splits vertices into two types: 'key' vertices (primary references) and 'non-key' variants that store only small differences from their key vertex. Since these differences fall in a narrow range, they need fewer bits to represent, enabling mixed-precision quantization (using variable numbers of bits for different data). A specialized two-level hardware scheduler with a bit-serial mixed-precision unit executes this efficiently.
dac-2025-030.key_novelty: SAGA reduces memory bottlenecks in dynamic nearest-neighbor graph construction by grouping similar vertices to enable mixed-precision quantization (storing different data with different numbers of bits).

dac-2025-022.method: Testing a chip requires test patterns—binary sequences applied to each input to verify functionality. Traditional SAT-based methods force every input to be set to 0 or 1, causing test bloat that becomes unmanageable for large circuits. This approach uses a specialized SAT solver (PA-MiniSat) that can leave inputs unspecified when they don't influence whether the test passes. The solver includes two efficiency techniques: full-literal watching (fast tracking of logical constraints that remain unsatisfied) and circuit-adapted branching heuristics (decision rules optimized for the circuit's structure), integrated in a hybrid ATPG framework combining structural test algorithms with partial-assignment solving.
dac-2025-022.key_novelty: The first SAT solver to support partial assignments in test generation, reducing specified bits in test cubes by allowing inputs to remain unspecified when they don't affect test success.

dac-2025-042.method: GSIM speeds up software simulation of hardware logic by reducing wasted computation at three levels of detail: groups of operations together (supernode-level), individual logic gates (node-level), and bit-by-bit calculations (bit-level). By using efficient data structures and smart scheduling to optimize all three levels simultaneously instead of just one, it makes complex processor simulations run much faster.
dac-2025-042.key_novelty: GSIM is the first hardware simulator that optimizes at all three abstraction levels (supernode, node, and bit) simultaneously, reaching a 19.94× speedup on realistic processor simulations.

dac-2025-034.method: A neural network predicts how heat will spread through the chip based on its shape, materials, and power consumption. Instead of iteratively refining the mesh (repeatedly tweaking the computational grid to get better results), the network's predictions directly optimize an initial rough mesh. The network identifies thermal hotspots where detail is needed and automatically reduces mesh detail in cooler regions, cutting computation while maintaining accuracy.
dac-2025-034.key_novelty: A neural network generates thermally accurate meshes directly from heat predictions, eliminating iterative refinement and achieving 45× speedup while staying within 0.8% of COMSOL accuracy.

dac-2025-041.method: The April framework improves results from floating-point approximations (techniques like Mitchell's logarithm that use cheaper integer operations instead of expensive floating-point multiplication) by combining two strategies: down-sampling-based compensation, which detects errors by creating lower-resolution versions of the data, and a bias mechanism that adapts to different data patterns. It provides configurable templates for systolic arrays—the grid-structured processing units used in neural network accelerators—that integrate these approximated operations into hardware. The framework automatically generates the actual accelerator design, adjusting the trade-off between accuracy and the amount of silicon required.
dac-2025-041.key_novelty: April is the first framework to combine down-sampling-based error detection with distribution-aware bias adjustment, making floating-point approximation practical in neural network accelerators using configurable systolic arrays.

dac-2025-040.method: PatLabor computes all the best possible ways to connect circuit pins (routing trees) when balancing two opposing goals: minimizing wire length versus minimizing signal delay. For nets up to 9 pins, it explores the entire trade-off space and returns every solution that can't be improved on one goal without hurting the other (called Pareto-optimal). The algorithm avoids parameter tuning by directly mapping all best solutions, with proven guarantees on computation time and solution quality.
dac-2025-040.key_novelty: PatLabor is the first to directly compute all Pareto-optimal solutions (every best delay-wirelength trade-off) for circuit routing, instead of using parameter tuning.

dac-2025-039.method: A CAM (memory that retrieves data by searching its content rather than using an address) traditionally wastes FPGA resources by using LUTs (basic logic building blocks) and BRAM (dedicated memory blocks). This design repurposes DSP blocks—circuits originally built for signal processing—which have built-in storage and comparison logic. These blocks perform many parallel searches across stored values simultaneously and can process multiple search queries without slowing down, speeding up both search and update operations. You can configure the memory width, capacity, and degree of parallelism to match your application.
dac-2025-039.key_novelty: This design uses DSP blocks (circuits built for signal processing) as the primary resource instead of traditional FPGA memory blocks, which reduces search and update time and enables multiple simultaneous queries.

dac-2025-044.method: The approach builds mathematical models that predict how much signal power successfully travels through a microring resonator (MRR) when manufacturing creates tiny variations in its physical dimensions. It then simultaneously adjusts two things: the radius (size) of each MRR and the light wavelength assigned to each signal path, choosing values that maximize signal power despite these manufacturing imperfections. This works because the MRR's size and the wavelengths are coupled — changing the radius changes which wavelengths transmit most strongly, so tuning them together exploits this interdependence to achieve better results than tuning separately.
dac-2025-044.key_novelty: First to jointly tune microring resonator (MRR) sizes and signal wavelengths together while mathematically predicting how manufacturing variations affect performance in wavelength-routed optical networks-on-chip.

dac-2025-046.method: The algorithm reformulates community detection—finding groups of densely connected nodes in a network—as an optimization problem where each node is either in a group or not (a binary choice written as a QUBO, or Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization). It then applies Quantum Hamiltonian Descent, a quantum-inspired optimization technique that finds good solutions by simulating how quantum systems settle into low-energy states. To scale to large networks, the approach uses a multi-level strategy: solving simplified versions of the problem first, then using those results to iteratively refine community assignments across progressively larger sections of the full network.
dac-2025-046.key_novelty: By pairing a quantum-inspired solver (Quantum Hamiltonian Descent) with a QUBO reformulation of the community-detection problem, the approach can find communities in large networks where classical optimization becomes impractical.

dac-2025-050.method: Chameleon-SAT is a specialized computer chip (an ASIC) that solves Boolean satisfiability problems—puzzles where you find true/false values satisfying a set of logical rules. It uses mixed-signal in-memory computing (calculations done directly in memory using both digital and analog signals) to run three different solving strategies: local search (making small changes to find solutions), DPLL (systematic exploration with backtracking), and CDCL (learning from conflicts to avoid repeating failed attempts). By reconfiguring to use the best strategy for each problem's type and size, it efficiently handles the full range from small high-complexity cases to large high-complexity problems.
dac-2025-050.key_novelty: Chameleon-SAT is the first ASIC that can adaptively switch between three satisfiability-solving strategies (local search, DPLL, and CDCL) using mixed-signal in-memory computing.

dac-2025-043.method: Alchemy learns the best cache decisions for each host by running a reinforcement learning agent while the system operates. To learn, it tries different choices—deciding what data to evict from cache and which requests to bypass the cache for—and rewards choices that improve each host's performance metrics. By tracking which host made each request, it discovers strategies tailored to each host instead of using one fixed cache policy for everyone.
dac-2025-043.key_novelty: For CXL disaggregated memory, the system uses reinforcement learning aware of each host's access patterns to jointly optimize cache eviction and bypassing decisions.

dac-2025-051.method: ZXNet converts quantum circuits into simplified diagram representations using ZX calculus, a mathematical notation that expresses quantum operations as connected shapes. Machine learning models called graph neural networks then learn patterns in these diagrams to determine if two circuits are equivalent. This approach dramatically reduces the computational work needed to verify whether different circuit implementations perform the same function.
dac-2025-051.key_novelty: ZXNet combines mathematical representations of quantum circuits (ZX calculus) with machine learning models that learn patterns in connected data (graph neural networks) to verify circuit equivalence.

dac-2025-045.method: CirSTAG uses graph neural networks (AI systems that understand connections between circuit components) to measure circuit stability without running many simulations. It calculates a stability score—the local Lipschitz constant, which measures how much the circuit responds to small input changes—for each component and connection, considering both the network structure and how changing component values affects behavior. When nearby components on the input map to distant components on the output (mapping distortion), this reveals poor stability and identifies the most critical circuit elements.
dac-2025-045.key_novelty: For the first time, it applies spectral manifold analysis using graph neural networks to circuit stability, enabling scalable robustness assessment through local Lipschitz constants instead of running countless simulations.

dac-2025-054.method: Flip-flops store data in two sequential parts: master and slave latches. Using slower transistors reduces power but makes both input timing (setup time) and output speed (clock-to-Q delay) worse together. This design uses faster transistors in the slave latch (to meet timing requirements on critical paths) and slower, power-saving transistors in the master latch (where input timing is less strict). This decoupled control enables power reduction throughout the design while satisfying all timing constraints.
dac-2025-054.key_novelty: First flip-flop design using different transistor speeds in master and slave latches to independently control setup time and output speed for power optimization on critical timing paths.

dac-2025-052.method: ArbiterQ customizes a quantum neural network (machine-learning model on quantum hardware) for each quantum processor by building two profiles: model vector (the mathematical parameters the network learns) and behavioral vector (measurements of how that specific processor performs). During training, it shares gradient updates (improvements to the model) between processors with similar behavioral profiles, allowing them to work in parallel while accounting for hardware differences. It also optimizes inference—running the trained model—by scheduling tasks (shot-oriented inference scheduling) to balance workload and improve accuracy.
dac-2025-052.key_novelty: The core innovation is personalizing quantum neural networks to each processor's behavioral profile (measurements of its actual hardware performance), then sharing training improvements between processors with similar profiles to enable distributed training across heterogeneous quantum hardware.

dac-2025-056.method: The researchers evaluated over 35,000 multiply-accumulate (MAC) circuits—the basic arithmetic components in neural networks—using six different number formats (INT, FP, posit, LNS, MX, VSQ) and various design parameters like operation size and accumulation width. Each design was tested for three qualities: chip area, power efficiency (measured in calculations per watt), and arithmetic accuracy (using signal-to-quantization noise ratio). The analysis then identified the Pareto frontier—the optimal designs where you can't improve one metric without worsening another.
dac-2025-056.key_novelty: The work comprehensively evaluates three relatively new number formats (LNS, MX, VSQ) for multiply-accumulate circuits used in LLM inference, showing which designs best balance performance, power consumption, and accuracy.

dac-2025-048.method: The technique bundles multiple electrical connections (nets) into a single routing pass (sweep) instead of routing them separately, which reduces GPU memory usage and the cost of repeatedly launching GPU operations. When a path gets blocked, the algorithm selectively recalculates only the problematic segment (edge-level rip-up-and-reroute) rather than starting over, preserving successful routes and speeding up the solution.
dac-2025-048.key_novelty: This technique is the first to route multiple electrical connections (nets) simultaneously within a single computational pass (sweep) rather than using multiple passes, reducing GPU memory consumption and computational overhead.

dac-2025-055.method: Develops the COPIFT methodology and RISC-V ISA extensions (instruction set additions) to enable low-cost dual-issue execution—processing two instructions per cycle—for mixed integer and floating-point workloads. The approach couples the integer and floating-point functional units (execution hardware) together, which reduces the extra chip area and complexity needed for dual-issue while maintaining timing performance. By issuing different instruction types in parallel each cycle, it achieves instruction-level parallelism (multiple computations at once) without the full hardware cost of a traditional dual-issue system.
dac-2025-055.key_novelty: ISA extensions that enable lean dual-issue execution by coupling integer and floating-point functional units for mixed workloads.

dac-2025-047.method: EPOC uses ZX-Calculus, a mathematical form that reveals equivalent ways to arrange a quantum circuit, to explore more parallelizable circuit organizations. The framework breaks pulse generation into smaller, more controllable units (finer granularity) and partitions the circuit into independent segments that can process in parallel. Synthesis techniques then optimize these segments into efficient pulse instructions, reducing both the computational cost of pulse generation and circuit execution time.
dac-2025-047.key_novelty: EPOC is the first to combine ZX-Calculus circuit representation, circuit partitioning, and synthesis techniques to generate quantum pulses with reduced computational overhead and increased parallelism.

dac-2025-059.method: The system uses reinforcement learning (machine learning that learns through trial-and-error) to automatically create a Self-Test Library—a customized set of test patterns for each hardware design. These patterns run during idle periods when the system isn't performing its normal job, allowing the hardware to test itself for defects without disrupting operations. The learning algorithm discovers which test patterns work best, maximizing the range of hardware faults detected while keeping the system available.
dac-2025-059.key_novelty: Reinforcement learning automatically generates design-specific test patterns (a Self-Test Library) that find hardware defects during idle time without interrupting normal system operation.

dac-2025-058.method: IntraFuzz finds bugs in SGX applications (programs running in Intel's hardware-protected memory called enclaves) using coverage-guided fuzzing—a method that repeatedly sends random test data to the program while tracking which code paths execute, then uses that feedback to generate new tests targeting unexplored code. The system runs directly on actual Intel hardware, not in simulation, integrating with the SGX runtime to monitor enclave code during testing. By observing real hardware execution rather than simulated behavior, IntraFuzz can uncover vulnerabilities that appear only under actual hardware-protected conditions.
dac-2025-058.key_novelty: IntraFuzz is the first to perform coverage-guided fuzzing (testing by tracking code execution and generating inputs to reach more code paths) inside actual Intel SGX hardware enclaves rather than simulation.

dac-2025-062.method: FastPath combines two different security verification approaches: simulation, which can quickly test the hardware design on many cases but might miss edge-case attacks, and formal verification, which mathematically guarantees finding all security flaws but takes much longer. Rather than choosing one, FastPath analyzes the hardware design's structure to automatically decide for each part whether simulation or formal methods will be more efficient. This structural automation splits the verification work—using fast simulation for simpler parts and thorough formal checking for critical security-sensitive parts—making verification practical for real hardware designs.
dac-2025-062.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically splitting hardware security verification between simulation and formal methods based on the design's structure.

dac-2025-053.method: The method combines two components: a sequence-based generator that creates candidate power-grid layouts step-by-step (like how text models build text word-by-word), and a Transformer neural network that accurately estimates voltage drop for each design. The neural network learns patterns that help identify the most promising designs along the Pareto frontier—the set of designs where improving one goal (like power efficiency) requires sacrificing another (like performance). This combination lets the system efficiently explore the design space and find high-quality power-grid layouts.
dac-2025-053.key_novelty: It combines sequence-based power-grid structure generation with a Transformer neural network that estimates voltage drop to optimize industrial power-grid designs.

dac-2025-057.method: The framework starts by applying application-specific rules to reduce the design space (the set of possible design choices) before the main search. This pre-refinement step is much faster than exploring the entire original space and shrinks what the main search must evaluate. The main search then uses a cost-performance formula (customized per application) to find the best design by weighing tradeoffs between efficiency and accuracy.
dac-2025-057.key_novelty: This work combines a pre-refinement step that shrinks the design space for each application with a cost-performance-based algorithm to find the best design option.

dac-2025-060.method: ChipAlign merges two trained AI models—one designed to follow instructions, one trained on chip-design knowledge—by blending their internal weights without any retraining. It uses geodesic interpolation (finding the mathematically optimal path through the high-dimensional space where weights live) to fuse these models smoothly. The result is a single model that has both strong instruction-following ability and chip-design expertise.
dac-2025-060.key_novelty: Geodesic interpolation through weight space lets you merge two models without retraining, simultaneously achieving instruction alignment and chip-design expertise.

dac-2025-063.method: A central neural network (the "critic") monitors the overall system and evaluates performance under temperature constraints. Separate neural networks on each processor core (the "actors") independently choose DVFS actions—that is, how to adjust each core's speed and power consumption. All these networks learn together through actor-critic reinforcement learning, where the critic scores the actors' decisions and the actors improve based on that feedback. This centralized training resolves two problems: cores no longer make conflicting DVFS decisions, and each core gets better visibility into the full system state.
dac-2025-063.key_novelty: Using centralized training with decentralized actors for multicore DVFS control, so individual cores coordinate their speed-and-power decisions instead of conflicting.

dac-2025-066.method: DuQTTA reduces model size by decomposing the network into tensor-train structures (sets of smaller connected matrices) and then quantizing these pieces in two stages to further reduce precision. During training, it separately adjusts the magnitude (size) and direction of weight changes, allowing efficient fine-tuning without storing all model parameters. This achieves up to 65x compression on LLaMA2-7B while outperforming LoRA, enabling deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
dac-2025-066.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining dual-stage quantization with decoupled magnitude-direction updates applied to tensor-train structures to achieve extreme model compression without full parameter fine-tuning.

dac-2025-065.method: The method trains a deep learning model using two types of data from a PUF (a unique hardware identifier built into FPGAs): the test inputs sent to it and the electrical power it consumes while responding. By learning from both information types simultaneously, rather than separately, the model discovers patterns that more effectively break the PUF's security. This combination approach demonstrates its effectiveness on arbiter-style PUFs, a common design, showing that fusing both data sources produces much stronger attacks than using either alone.
dac-2025-065.key_novelty: The innovation is combining test-input data and power-consumption measurements in a single deep learning model to attack PUFs, rather than analyzing them separately.

dac-2025-068.method: During quantum neural network training, this approach continuously detects errors—both everyday noise and catastrophic failures that halt computation—and adjusts the training strategy in real-time based on what it finds. Because quantum errors aren't stable (they change over time and vary between individual quantum bits), a fixed training approach fails, but adapting to the actual errors as they occur lets the network keep learning effectively.
dac-2025-068.key_novelty: Training quantum neural networks by continuously adapting to errors as they occur, since quantum noise changes over time and differs across individual quantum bits.

dac-2025-061.method: CLADO learns how reducing a layer's precision (using fewer bits to represent numbers) doesn't just affect that layer—it also affects other layers. It builds mathematical equations to predict these cross-layer interactions from a small sample of data, then uses Integer Quadratic Programming (a method for optimizing combinations of choices) to assign each layer an optimal number of bits. By accounting for how layers actually depend on each other, rather than treating each as an independent problem, it finds better tradeoffs between accuracy and efficiency.
dac-2025-061.key_novelty: Rather than treating each layer's quantization error (accuracy loss from reduced precision) as independent, this method optimizes for cross-layer dependencies—how one layer's precision choice affects other layers' accuracy.

dac-2025-067.method: 3D-CIMlet stacks heterogeneous memory chiplets (using RRAM—resistive memory—and eDRAM—embedded dynamic RAM) in 3D architectures to accelerate AI language model processing on edge devices. The framework uses thermal simulations to predict where overheating will occur, then intelligently places each chiplet to minimize heat and energy waste. By matching different memory types to different processing tasks and considering thermal patterns during placement, it enables edge devices to both run trained AI models (inference) and continuously update those models with new data (continual learning).
dac-2025-067.key_novelty: The innovation is using thermal modeling to optimize how different memory technologies (RRAM and eDRAM) are arranged in 3D chip stacks for efficient edge AI inference and continual learning.

dac-2025-049.method: Drift-aware Binary Code (DBC) is a binary encoding scheme that makes neural networks resistant to phase change memory's conductance drift—the gradual degradation of memory cell performance over time. It maps smaller decimal values to the most stable levels in the memory cells, so when drift occurs, stored values naturally decrease rather than increase. This works because neural networks tolerate weight reductions much better than weight increases, so storing the most important network weights at the most stable levels keeps accuracy consistent over years of use. The approach requires no additional hardware and works seamlessly with existing error correction codes.
dac-2025-049.key_novelty: Binary encoding for phase change memory that maps values to minimize conductance drift errors by ensuring that memory degradation shifts stored values toward smaller magnitudes rather than larger ones.

dac-2025-064.method: GNNVault splits a graph neural network into two parts: a public backbone and a private rectifier component. Both run inside Intel SGX, a secure enclave on the processor that keeps code and data hidden from attack. By keeping only the small private part inside SGX, the system protects both the model parameters and the graph topology without needing to fit the entire model in the secure space.
dac-2025-064.key_novelty: The key novelty is designing the model with a partition built in from the start—a small private GNN rectifier—so protected inference runs on edge devices while keeping the secure enclave's memory footprint manageable.

dac-2025-074.method: The system arranges functional units (called cells) on a chip to minimize the total wire distance needed to connect them—a measure called HPWL, or Half-Perimeter Wire Length. It uses two optimization approaches: a classical method called Simulated Annealing that explores arrangements through random adjustments, and a quantum-based solver from D-Wave that frames the problem as a Constrained Quadratic Model. Both solvers are integrated with OpenROAD, an industry-standard tool for chip physical design and routing. The approach was tested on real chip designs using ASAP7 7nm technology rules.
dac-2025-074.key_novelty: Combining quantum and hybrid optimization (using D-Wave's Constrained Quadratic Model solver) with OpenROAD, the industry-standard chip design tool, to arrange the functional units on chips.

dac-2025-069.method: Binary Vector Symbolic Architecture does AI inference with minimal memory, but normally sacrifices accuracy to stay efficient. UniVSA fixes this by redesigning both the algorithm and the hardware at the same time. It uses lightweight modules—small, efficient components—and a specialized design flow that optimizes both together. The result is better accuracy while maintaining a small memory footprint and efficient execution on ultra-lightweight devices.
dac-2025-069.key_novelty: The key idea is designing the algorithm and hardware together as one integrated system instead of separate pieces, which lets binary Vector Symbolic Architecture achieve better accuracy while staying efficient on tiny devices.

dac-2025-071.method: VISTA is a GPU scheduler that watches for data-sharing patterns between warps (groups of 32 threads) and CTAs (larger thread blocks) during execution, even when those warps or blocks aren't next to each other in the GPU's execution order. Once it spots these patterns, VISTA reschedules the work so that computations that access the same data run closer together in time. This keeps the data they need in the GPU's fast cache memory longer, cutting down on expensive memory traffic that would otherwise slow down memory-intensive programs.
dac-2025-071.key_novelty: VISTA detects at runtime when non-adjacent warps and CTAs share data, then schedules them together to reduce memory accesses.

dac-2025-077.method: UniCoS uses a training-free accuracy proxy—a method that predicts how well a network will perform in seconds without actually training it—to quickly evaluate candidate CNN and ViT architectures. It combines this with a clustering-based algorithm that explores heterogeneous hardware dataflows (different patterns for how computations can be organized in accelerators). Together, these enable rapid joint searching: finding the best combination of network architecture and accelerator design at the same time.
dac-2025-077.key_novelty: A training-free accuracy proxy that predicts network performance in seconds (without full training) combined with clustering-based exploration of hardware dataflows enables rapid co-search of both CNN and ViT architectures with their accelerators.

dac-2025-075.method: Bayesian optimization learns from each processor design test to predict which untested configurations look promising—avoiding wasteful random exploration. This work improves three stages of that process: initial sampling (strategically selecting starting configurations), surrogate model construction (building a fast approximate model of expensive simulation), and acquisition function design (deciding which designs to test next). By improving all three stages, the method navigates the massive design space efficiently and identifies Pareto-optimal Arm Neoverse V1 configurations that balance power, performance, and physical area.
dac-2025-075.key_novelty: By systematically improving all three stages of Bayesian optimization together, this method identifies Pareto-optimal processor designs more efficiently than standard Bayesian optimization approaches.

dac-2025-072.method: SQ-DM reduces neural network numbers to 4 bits (instead of standard 32-bit) for both stored weights and intermediate calculations. It exploits sparsity (values that are zero and can be skipped) that varies across data channels and generation timesteps. The team built a custom accelerator with three key features: heterogeneous mixed-precision dense-sparse architecture (hardware that handles both dense and sparse calculations with different bit precisions), channel-last data layout (organizing memory so channel data comes last, for cache efficiency), and timestep-aware sparsity detection (identifying which values can be skipped at each step).
dac-2025-072.key_novelty: Extreme 4-bit quantization combined with dynamic detection of sparsity patterns that vary by data channel and generation timestep, supported by specialized hardware for dense-sparse computation.

dac-2025-070.method: The researchers built a hardware accelerator — a specialized circuit that runs Kalman Filters, which predict motion from brain signals. The hardware is configurable, meaning you can adjust how fast it responds (latency) versus how accurate its predictions are (accuracy). This flexibility lets engineers explore different settings to find the right balance for their specific brain-computer interface. The accelerator plugs into a processor system and can dynamically adjust its settings while processing neural data.
dac-2025-070.key_novelty: A Kalman Filter hardware accelerator for brain-computer interfaces with precise, adjustable speed-versus-accuracy settings.

dac-2025-073.method: NetTAG represents circuits as diagrams of interconnected logic gates, where each gate is annotated with text describing its logical function and physical properties. The system combines two neural network approaches: a language model that interprets the gate descriptions to understand what each gate does, and a graph neural network (a technique for learning from connected structures) that learns how gates interact through their connections. It learns these patterns automatically from unlabeled data and is then aligned with both the high-level circuit specifications (RTL) and the physical chip layout.
dac-2025-073.key_novelty: The innovation is combining a language model's understanding of gate semantics with graph-network learning of circuit structure in a single text-attributed graph representation that supports both functional and physical design tasks.

dac-2025-080.method: CND-IDS continuously learns which patterns matter in network traffic, updating its understanding as new data arrives. To detect anomalies, it uses PCA (a technique that identifies the main patterns in normal data and flags anything significantly different from them). Because it spots deviations from normal behavior rather than matching known attacks, it doesn't need labeled examples of attacks to learn from.
dac-2025-080.key_novelty: It combines continuous learning (updating as new traffic arrives) with unsupervised anomaly detection (flagging traffic that deviates from normal patterns) to catch unknown attacks without requiring labeled attack examples.

dac-2025-079.method: They extract vertex features—metrics describing each circuit region's local structure and compatibility with different optimization methods—by analyzing subgraph neighborhoods and testing how various optimization approaches perform. They use these features to partition the circuit into clusters, applying each cluster's optimal optimization method. To avoid expensive testing, they use self-supervised learning to predict these vertex features for any circuit region, enabling rapid hybrid optimization without simulation.
dac-2025-079.key_novelty: A self-supervised learning model predicts vertex features describing optimization-method compatibility, enabling rapid circuit partitioning and hybrid optimization without expensive simulation.

dac-2025-078.method: PairGraph recognizes that when you run multiple queries on a graph simultaneously, they often explore the same regions of the graph structure. It detects these overlapping search spaces (the parts of the graph that multiple queries traverse) and reuses the data across queries instead of fetching it separately each time.
