By sharing this common graph data, it reduces how much information needs to travel to and from off-chip memory, which is the primary bottleneck in these workloads.
dac-2025-078.key_novelty: A processing model aware of search spaces (the paths concurrent queries explore) that reuses their overlapping data to reduce off-chip bandwidth.

dac-2025-081.method: EVA builds novel circuits by using an AI model called a decoder-only transformer that predicts where electronic components should connect, one connection at a time, starting from scratch. First, the model learns general patterns by studying thousands of existing circuit designs (pretraining). Then it's optimized using PPO and DPO—techniques that reward high-performing designs—to generate circuits tailored for specific performance goals.
dac-2025-081.key_novelty: Discovers entirely new circuit designs from scratch by sequentially predicting how to connect electronic components, using a decoder-only transformer optimized with PPO and DPO.

dac-2025-082.method: Augmented Lagrangian optimization—a mathematical technique that directly enforces power constraints—is built into the training process, so the network learns to stay within a power budget while maintaining accuracy all in one run. Traditionally, finding good power-accuracy tradeoffs requires 150+ separate training attempts; this method does it once. The approach was tested on 13 benchmarks using different activation functions (p-tanh and p-Clipped_ReLU).
dac-2025-082.key_novelty: Augmented Lagrangian optimization directly enforces power constraints during training to compute all optimal power-accuracy tradeoffs in a single run, versus the 150+ runs needed by traditional penalty-based methods.

dac-2025-076.method: ReSMiPS combines optimized matrix reordering with 64-bit floating-point calculation in analog ReRAM arrays—memory using variable electrical resistance instead of 0s and 1s. The hybrid approach merges these analog calculations with digital orchestration, avoiding the memory-bandwidth bottleneck by keeping data inside the memory where computation happens rather than shuttling it to and from a separate processor.
dac-2025-076.key_novelty: ReSMiPS performs 64-bit floating-point sparse matrix solving directly in analog ReRAM arrays—memory chips using resistance for calculations—rather than separate CPUs or GPUs, achieving BiCGSTAB-level precision (< 10^-15 error) with 100× better speed and energy efficiency.

dac-2025-085.method: VersaSlot divides each FPGA into variable-sized slots—some large, some small—so different-length tasks can run at the same time instead of queuing while the FPGA reconfigures (reprograms itself). It uses smart allocation to match each task to the right-size slot and live migration (moving a running task between FPGAs) to spread workload across a cluster. On Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGAs, this eliminates the performance bottleneck where reconfiguration delays become the limiting factor, the primary source of slowdown in shared FPGA environments.
dac-2025-085.key_novelty: The core idea is the Big.Little slot architecture—mixing different-sized slots on each FPGA with live migration across the cluster—to prevent the task queuing caused by reconfiguration bottlenecks.

dac-2025-088.method: PracMHBench is a testing platform for federated learning algorithms where each device uses a different model architecture. It tests these algorithms under realistic constraints—memory, power, and computing limits from actual phones or IoT sensors—across multiple datasets and resource scenarios. It classifies different techniques for handling heterogeneity (device capability differences) and measures their performance.
dac-2025-088.key_novelty: It's the first testing system to evaluate heterogeneous federated learning (where devices use different model architectures) against realistic edge device constraints.

dac-2025-093.method: Device-Aware Test (DAT) adds a second layer to traditional manufacturing testing, which only checks if circuits are wired correctly. DAT uses models of actual transistor physics—how semiconductors behave, especially at tiny technology sizes—to design tests that expose defects these physical models predict. By grounding tests in real device behavior rather than just logical structure, DAT catches defects that traditional structural testing misses.
dac-2025-093.key_novelty: Device-Aware Test shifts from testing based purely on circuit logic to testing based on actual transistor device physics.

dac-2025-083.method: ParGNN measures how much computation each GPU receives (profiling), then breaks the graph into extra pieces and redistributes them to make the work more even (graph over-partitioning and adaptive load balancing). It arranges the work in a pipeline where each GPU processes multiple graph pieces in sequence, timed so that while one GPU is computing, another is simultaneously receiving or sending data (computation-communication overlap). This keeps data flowing and GPUs busy at the same time, eliminating the idle waiting that happens when data arrives late.
dac-2025-083.key_novelty: Profile the workload to dynamically rebalance graphs across GPUs, and use pipelining to overlap data transfer with computation.

dac-2025-090.method: The method uses a two-part approach: it first runs a numerical solver called AMG-PCG (which finds approximate solutions without fully solving the system) to create initial rough estimates of where power is lost in the chip's power grid, then uses graph-based machine learning to refine them. It represents the power grid nodes as a point cloud—a set of interconnected points—and feeds this into a graph transformer, a type of neural network that learns how nodes relate to each other based on their connections. The key innovation is a technique called Neighbor Distance Attention (NDA) that weights nearby nodes based on physical distance, allowing the model to capture both local fine-grained details and large-scale patterns in how power distributes across the grid.
dac-2025-090.key_novelty: The core innovation is using graph-based learning to make precise per-node power-loss predictions, rather than CNN methods that only produce rough grid-level maps, while grounding these predictions in accurate numerical solutions.

dac-2025-084.method: MemSeer predicts memory chip failures in data-center clusters using both x86 and ARM processors (two different chip architectures), by recognizing that each fails in different ways. It monitors warning signs at multiple time scales (from hours to weeks ahead) and feeds predictions to automated systems that can replace failing chips before outages occur. This improves prediction accuracy by 17.3% and catches 27% more failures.
dac-2025-084.key_novelty: Predicting memory failures works better by recognizing that different processor types like x86 and ARM fail in distinct ways and monitoring multiple time scales.

dac-2025-086.method: The decoder uses a polygon to enclose the locations where errors were detected (called flipped syndromes), guaranteeing coverage of all possible error chains. Within this geometric boundary, it tunes the Ising model's parameters—the coupling strengths (how variables interact) and field coefficients (external biases)—through constraint-based optimization to find settings that preserve error-detection accuracy while keeping calculations manageable.
dac-2025-086.key_novelty: A geometric constraint (a polygon) around error locations reduces the Ising model variables by 97.8x, enabling O(n) worst-case runtime that beats union-find and achieving a 10.71-11.0% error threshold superior to MWPM.

dac-2025-089.method: LightRIM protects the Linux kernel (the core of the operating system) by hashing its components in two stages to create a fingerprint for detecting tampering. Instead of checking constantly and wasting CPU power, it only measures when something security-relevant changes. To stay within strict CPU budgets, it randomizes when checks happen, making it harder for attackers to time their modifications between checks and actual use (called TOCTOU vulnerabilities).
dac-2025-089.key_novelty: LightRIM checks kernel integrity only when security-relevant changes occur, using randomized timing to maximize attack detection while staying within CPU limits and preventing attackers from timing modifications between checks and use.

dac-2025-087.method: KLiNQ shrinks neural networks by 99% using knowledge distillation—teaching a small network to mimic a large one—while keeping 91% accuracy in identifying quantum states. Each qubit runs its own compact neural network on a Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGA (reprogrammable hardware), achieving independent 32-nanosecond readouts. This enables fast, simultaneous measurements across all qubits, supporting mid-circuit measurements critical for quantum error correction.
dac-2025-087.key_novelty: Knowledge distillation compresses neural networks by 99% to enable efficient independent qubit readouts in 32 nanoseconds on Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGAs, maintaining 91% accuracy for quantum error correction.

dac-2025-092.method: DM-Tune uses a simpler approach to compress models: instead of using different precision levels for different parts (which requires costly switching between formats), it converts everything to a single low-precision format. To maintain image quality despite the lower precision, it adds a tuning step that learns to compensate for what was lost, using a mathematical function based on Gaussian distributions (smooth probability curves) and linear adjustments. The system identifies which layers lose quality most easily, measures the quantization errors throughout the model, and runs this compensation efficiently on GPUs with custom code.
dac-2025-092.key_novelty: A unified low-precision format with Gaussian-guided noise tuning produces better image quality and alignment than mixed-precision quantization while simplifying execution.

dac-2025-091.method: GEM creates a virtual Very Long Instruction Word architecture (VLIW — a compact way to represent operations, inspired by FPGA emulator design) that runs on NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA. It maps circuit logic into this VLIW form using a CAD process (computer-aided design) based on FPGA place-and-route — the step that assigns circuit logic to physical locations and routes their connections. This solves two problems that prevented earlier GPU simulators from working: irregular memory access patterns (when threads access memory unpredictably) and thread divergence (when different threads take different execution paths), both of which severely reduce GPU efficiency.
dac-2025-091.key_novelty: GEM uses a virtual VLIW architecture to let GPUs (which run the same instruction across many threads simultaneously) simulate circuits with heterogeneous parts (different sections needing different processing).

dac-2025-096.method: FLAG addresses latency by moving heavy work offline. It precomputes the neural network's intermediate results (embeddings) and compresses them using vector quantization (storing full vectors as indices into a small lookup table, reducing memory and computation). At serving time, an FPGA accelerator loads these compressed embeddings and quickly combines neighbor information without expensive recalculations. This eliminates the bottleneck that happens when computation is done live for each query.
dac-2025-096.key_novelty: Precomputing compressed embeddings offline via vector quantization enables an FPGA to efficiently serve graph neural network predictions without hitting the exponential neighbor-growth bottleneck.

dac-2025-095.method: Instead of building a unique circuit for each data sample, EnQode groups similar samples and creates a single circuit template—an ansatz—that represents each group's average state. This ansatz is designed to be shallow (short) and tailored to the specific quantum hardware, minimizing the number of quantum gates. Since all samples in a group share the same circuit, noise from quantum hardware imperfections stays consistent rather than varying unpredictably per sample. This consistency, combined with reduced gates, ensures reliable learning on noisy quantum computers.
dac-2025-095.key_novelty: Amplitude embedding that clusters samples symbolically, then standardizes circuit depth while minimizing gates to ensure consistent noise levels on NISQ devices.

dac-2025-094.method: BBAL improves Block Floating Point quantization—a technique that compresses numbers by fitting them all to one shared scale—by making the scale selection smarter. Instead of simply using the maximum value's scale (which causes small numbers to lose precision), the bidirectional approach selects the scale by considering both extremes, resulting in better overall accuracy. The system uses a processing element array (a bank of specialized circuits) optimized for this bidirectional quantization, along with an efficient circuit for the nonlinear math operations that language models need. This enables accurate low-bit inference (very few bits per number) on edge accelerators—small, power-efficient devices.
dac-2025-094.key_novelty: Selecting the Block Floating Point scale bidirectionally (considering both extremes rather than just the maximum) reduces quantization errors caused by outliers, enabling practical hardware acceleration for language models.

dac-2025-099.method: The approach designs the algorithm and hardware together. First, they developed a revised MX format (called RMX) that uses a "group direction strategy"—dividing data into groups and optimizing each group's scaling to reduce precision loss during compression. Second, they built specialized hardware (RMFA) with an architecture and encoding scheme designed to work efficiently with RMX on low-bit operations.
dac-2025-099.key_novelty: A revised MX format with group direction strategy, paired with custom hardware accelerator, makes 4-bit and 6-bit quantization practical to deploy.

dac-2025-102.method: The system creates neural networks on surface acoustic wave hardware (chip-integrated systems using sound waves to process information) by shaping diffractive patterns—physical structures that control how waves bounce and interfere. The training approach combines finite element analysis (detailed physics simulations) with gradient descent (automatic machine learning optimization). This hybrid method lets them discover useful wave-scattering patterns by balancing physical accuracy with training efficiency.
dac-2025-102.key_novelty: This demonstrates the first diffractive neural network on surface acoustic wave hardware, enabled by a training method that combines physics simulation with machine learning optimization.

dac-2025-097.method: SCONE protects hardware designs by combining two techniques. First, it uses an SMT solver (a tool that finds solutions to logical constraints) to automatically identify which input patterns must be blocked to secure the circuit. Then it uses a circuit encoding scheme (a way to scramble the circuit logic) that hides these patterns, making them invisible to attackers who try to reverse-engineer the design by analyzing the circuit structure. This dual approach handles large, complex circuits while allowing flexibility in how the secret key is generated and structured.
dac-2025-097.key_novelty: Combining an SMT solver with a circuit encoding scheme achieves 350 times better scalability while resisting five types of attacks on circuit inputs and circuit structure.

dac-2025-100.method: The researchers discovered that mathematical matrices for converting between DCT2 and DST7 transforms have most values concentrated along the diagonals. Using an optimization technique (least-squares fitting), they remove unnecessary values to create sparse matrices—mostly zeros with a few key values. This sparse structure enables a single hardware unit using only shift and add operations to handle all block sizes (4, 8, 16, and 32 points) and support all three VVC transform types.
dac-2025-100.key_novelty: Transform conversion matrices for DCT2-to-DST7 conversion concentrate important values along diagonals, enabling high-precision approximate conversion using sparse combinations (mostly zeros) instead of full matrices.

dac-2025-118.method: PASK loads GPU code ahead of time (while the GPU is computing earlier operations) rather than waiting until it's needed, eliminating delays from last-minute code loading. The system organizes GPU code by type in a cache, allowing it to reuse the same code across multiple layers of a neural network instead of reloading new code for each layer. By overlapping code loading with GPU computation, PASK keeps both the CPU and GPU busy, improving overall efficiency.
dac-2025-118.key_novelty: The core idea is to proactively load GPU code while the GPU is already computing, reusing applicable code across layers to avoid redundant loading work.

dac-2025-103.method: SpMMTC looks at where the non-zeros are in your input matrices before compilation and generates optimized instruction sequences specifically designed for that sparsity pattern—this is faster than generic code because the custom version can skip zeros and efficiently use the CPU's parallel capabilities (SIMD, which executes multiple operations simultaneously). The compiler automatically adapts to what the hardware can actually do, checking the CPU's parallel width (SIMD width) and memory cache structure, so it generates fast code without requiring manual programming. It employs two key optimization techniques: vectorization guidance ensures the CPU's parallel hardware is used effectively, and pattern-aware loop unrolling (expanding loops to expose more parallelism) maximizes the opportunities for parallel execution.
dac-2025-103.key_novelty: A compiler that inspects each input matrix's non-zero pattern and automatically creates optimized code specialized for that pattern, without manual per-matrix tuning.

dac-2025-120.method: The algorithm uses three stages. First, it scans for violations within each row, considering both timing (speed) and power consumption. Second, it creates an initial arrangement using a directed acyclic graph (a dependency diagram showing how cells relate to each other) and selects which version of each cell to use—choosing between power-efficient and faster variants. Third, it removes violations between rows using dynamic programming (an optimization technique that builds solutions step-by-step), while ensuring manufacturing minimum implant area requirements are satisfied.
dac-2025-120.key_novelty: It's the first systematic approach to FinFlex cell legalization that combines power-driven cell version selection with minimum implant area constraint handling, using both directed acyclic graphs (dependency diagrams) and dynamic programming (an optimization technique).

dac-2025-101.method: The paper describes how to automate design of multi-chip systems in four stages: first, deciding which parts of a design go on which chiplet and optimizing their interactions; second, verifying the designs with fast machine-learning models early in design and detailed physics simulations (analyzing heat and mechanical stress) before release; third, physically placing chiplets on a substrate, routing connections between them, and managing power distribution; fourth, providing reusable chiplet designs, standard file formats, and shared specifications. Together, these methods address the complete flow of multi-chip system design.
dac-2025-101.key_novelty: The paper identifies what comprehensive automated-design capabilities are needed for multi-chip systems, spanning from how designs partition across chips to their physical arrangement.

dac-2025-116.method: ANGraph starts with intermediate data from system-level simulations—fast but approximate predictions of hardware behavior—and converts them into graph structures where each node represents a circuit component and edges show how components connect. It trains a Graph Neural Network (a machine-learning model that learns patterns in connected data) using over one million detailed gate-level circuit simulations, which are highly accurate but computationally expensive. The GNN learns to predict latency—how long hardware takes to complete operations—by recognizing recurring patterns in the circuit graphs. A separate ResNet model predicts power consumption, and both models generalize across different hardware sizes, manufacturing process nodes, and varying input workloads without requiring retraining.
dac-2025-116.key_novelty: Using a Graph Neural Network to predict how fast neuromorphic hardware runs, bridging the gap between fast-but-rough system-level simulations and slow-but-precise gate-level simulations while remaining accurate across different hardware designs.

dac-2025-098.method: The architecture stacks memory (DRAM) directly on top of the compute chip using 3D hybrid bonding, drastically shortening how far data must travel. Instead of scattered control units across the chip, a single centralized controller manages everything, saving significant chip area. This controller reconfigures between two types of matrix operations—vector-matrix multiplication (GEMV) and matrix-matrix multiplication (GEMM)—depending on the phase of LLM inference. Dual-IO pathways (two separate data routes) prevent data traffic jams.
dac-2025-098.key_novelty: A centralized controller with dual-IO on 3D hybrid-bonded DRAM-to-logic avoids the chip-area cost of distributed controllers while enabling efficient, reconfigurable LLM inference.

dac-2025-119.method: The approach uses vector quantization (representing data using values from a learned lookup table) to convert expensive dynamic matrix operations in attention into static, predetermined operations. This eliminates runtime memory writes because the values and operations are precomputed, avoiding the slow compute-write-compute cycles of traditional approaches. The method combines residual quantization (iterative quantization of remainders to improve accuracy) and product quantization (splitting vectors into parts and quantizing each independently) to maintain precision. Ferroelectric transistors (non-volatile memory retaining data without power) in compute-in-memory crossbars execute these lookups and static matrix multiplications without write-back cycles.
dac-2025-119.key_novelty: Using a vector quantization scheme combining residual and product quantization converts the dynamic attention operations in transformers into static operations that ferroelectric compute-in-memory hardware can execute without memory writes.

dac-2025-104.method: Hydra routes tokens to experts based on which experts are most likely to be used (their popularity distribution), reducing cross-chip communication overhead. In hardware, it uses Content Addressable Memory (CAM—memory that locates data by content rather than by address) to eliminate expensive data rearrangement after matrix multiplication. The system also adds a softmax engine (the component that decides which experts to use) that avoids exponential and division calculations for experts unlikely to be selected.
dac-2025-104.key_novelty: Hydra exploits non-uniform gating—the fact that Mixture-of-Expert models don't use all experts equally—through software routing to popular experts and hardware that skips unnecessary softmax calculations and data rearrangement.

dac-2025-111.method: The approach uses two matching modes on the same 3D NAND chip (MCAM—content-addressable memory, which compares data directly without fetching it first). First, it runs a cheap exact-search mode to filter out vectors that definitely aren't similar. Then, for only the remaining candidates, it runs an approximate-search mode that finds close matches—avoiding expensive comparisons on vectors already ruled out. They optimize this with three techniques: range encoding for multi-level cells to improve filtering, search voltage adjustments that reduce power without losing accuracy, and special training for reliability.
dac-2025-111.key_novelty: A dual-mode NAND chip that uses cheap exact-search filtering to eliminate non-matching vectors before expensive approximate-search, cutting energy waste by orders of magnitude.

dac-2025-122.method: DRAFT solves the problem of expensive gradient calculations during fine-tuning on edge devices by splitting backpropagation (the process of calculating weight updates) into two separate pathways via Feedback Decoupling Approximation (FDA): a trainable adapter and a sparse ternary Bypass Network (a network using mostly-zero weights to efficiently approximate gradients). Custom hardware—a reconfigurable DRAFT accelerator—runs these pathways by exploiting sparsity (the many zeros) and data parallelism (splitting work across processors) through sparse gather networks and dynamic workflows.
dac-2025-122.key_novelty: The key innovation is algorithm-hardware co-design (designing a special algorithm and custom hardware together) where Feedback Decoupling Approximation splits backpropagation (gradient calculation) into two lightweight pathways rather than computing through the entire pre-trained model, reducing computational cost while preserving training accuracy.

dac-2025-121.method: The method defines how to represent and organize task chains in autonomous systems (vehicles, drones) where tasks must run at specific times and pass data between each other. It applies topology optimization—a technique that reorganizes task connections to minimize end-to-end latency (the total time from the first task starting to all dependent tasks completing)—achieving 4.8x faster results than the simpler Floyd algorithm. The approach has O(n²) complexity (computation grows quadratically with task count) and adapts to systems where tasks change dynamically.
dac-2025-121.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of how to construct optimal task graphs (rather than just schedule them) for autonomous systems with time-triggered tasks, using topology optimization.

dac-2025-126.method: The approach uses conformal prediction—a technique that generates ranges of possible future energy harvest with mathematical guarantees they'll contain the actual value a set percentage of the time. Instead of making a single energy-management guess, it tests multiple decisions against many possible energy scenarios sampled from these ranges (Monte Carlo sampling), then combines the results using a lightweight machine-learning model to determine a near-optimal energy strategy.
dac-2025-126.key_novelty: The core idea is using conformal prediction to quantify energy-harvest uncertainty and enable energy-management decisions based on ranges of probable values rather than single guesses, with mathematical guarantees the ranges cover real outcomes.

dac-2025-127.method: Instead of doing arithmetic in a processor, PIMPAL pre-computes and stores the results of calculations as lookup tables inside DRAM memory, then looks up these values in parallel across multiple sections of DRAM banks. This avoids the energy cost of moving data back and forth between memory and a processor. The system uses smart data placement to minimize DRAM row activations (the expensive operation of reading different parts of memory), and combines results from multiple small lookup tables to support multiple precision levels.
dac-2025-127.key_novelty: PIMPAL uses lookup tables stored in DRAM memory instead of traditional arithmetic operations to accelerate matrix-vector multiplication with low chip area overhead while supporting multiple precision levels on edge devices.

dac-2025-125.method: The approach uses a neural network called SAU-FNO (Self-Attention UNet Fourier Neural Operator) that learns to predict how heat flows through 3D chips. It combines three complementary techniques: self-attention (which lets the network track how temperature changes in one part of the chip affect distant regions), U-Net architecture (which processes thermal features at multiple scales simultaneously), and Fourier Neural Operators (which efficiently model both fine-grained temperature details and broader heat patterns). To train this network efficiently, the method uses transfer learning: it starts with low-fidelity simulations (fast but less precise) and fine-tunes on high-fidelity data (slow but accurate), which reduces the need for expensive high-fidelity training data.
dac-2025-125.key_novelty: The hybrid architecture combines self-attention (which captures thermal interactions across the chip), U-Net (which preserves fine temperature details), and Fourier Neural Operators (which model heat patterns) to capture both high-frequency temperature information and long-range thermal dependencies, trained efficiently via transfer learning using low-fidelity simulation data.

dac-2025-129.method: The system uses large language models (AI trained on massive amounts of text) to learn from just a few examples by building knowledge graphs that map out task-specific requirements and attributes. It provides two different vision transformers (neural networks for image recognition): one specialized and compressed for particular tasks, achieving 15% higher accuracy on those specific tasks, and another heavily compressed version (quantized—reducing precision to shrink size) that works across multiple different tasks with reasonable performance. A custom hardware acceleration circuit enables these models to run directly on edge devices (resource-constrained hardware like phones or sensors) for real-time processing without sending data to the cloud.
dac-2025-129.key_novelty: The core innovation is using large language models to automatically generate task-specific knowledge graphs that enable object detection from just a few examples, paired with two different vision transformers (one optimized for accuracy on specific tasks, another compressed for flexibility across tasks) and a custom hardware circuit for real-time edge processing.

dac-2025-124.method: Instead of one mapping entry per logical page (data as seen by the user), the system groups multiple compressed logical pages that fit into one physical page (actual storage location) into a single entry, eliminating redundant records. As compression patterns change, entries dynamically migrate to physical pages with different capacities—promoted to consolidate more aggressively when compression is strong, demoted to spread out when compression weakens. The garbage collection algorithm accounts for this grouping, minimizing data copying during cleanup of invalid entries.
dac-2025-124.key_novelty: An N-to-1 mapping design (consolidating multiple compressed logical pages into single entries instead of separate ones) that dynamically adjusts to changing compression patterns, reducing memory overhead.

dac-2025-128.method: The researchers tested whether attackers can steal neural network weights using correlation power analysis—a technique that extracts secrets by observing electrical consumption during computation. They tested against three energy-saving techniques: overclocking (running faster than designed), voltage reduction, and circuit-level bitwise approximation. They measured Signal-to-Noise Ratio (how much noise obscures the signal) and Measurement-to-Disclosure (how many observations attackers need), then analyzed the security-power-speed tradeoff using a combined metric (Security-Power-Delay).
dac-2025-128.key_novelty: Energy-saving approximation techniques in neural networks increase resistance to power-analysis attacks, requiring attackers to collect 4 to over 20 times more measurements to extract model weights.

dac-2025-130.method: The system puts two types of processing cores directly into memory chips—one built for speed, one built for low power—each with both nonvolatile memory (MRAM, which retains data without power) and fast memory (SRAM). An algorithm watches what computation each piece of data needs and automatically moves data to the core type that will handle it most efficiently, shifting workload between cores as demands change. By keeping simple tasks on low-power cores and complex ones on fast cores, the system avoids wasting energy on unnecessary high-performance processing.
dac-2025-130.key_novelty: The key innovation is using two different types of processing cores and automatically choosing which one processes each piece of data, adapting in real-time to minimize energy use.

dac-2025-131.method: TinyMP combines two techniques to train models on tiny devices. Gradient Condensing simplifies the gradient data (the directional information for updating model weights), reducing memory use while keeping model accuracy. Alternant Partial Update alternately selects essential model parameters (the weights that matter most) to update at each step, rather than updating everything, which reduces computation without needing external search processes.
dac-2025-131.key_novelty: By condensing gradient data and updating only essential model parameters, on-device fine-tuning becomes practical on tiny embedded devices with less than 1 MB SRAM and 2 MB Flash.

dac-2025-132.method: FireGuard is a microarchitecture enabling instruction-level security analysis on real out-of-order superscalar processors—modern chips that run multiple instructions simultaneously. It combines hardware design, system-on-chip integration, new processor instructions, and a programming model that lets developers instrument security checks without slowing the processor's critical path (longest chain of dependent operations) or causing contention (waits for shared resources). The design was validated on Apple M1-Pro, Huawei Kirin-960, and Intel i7-12700F.
dac-2025-132.key_novelty: FireGuard is the first programmable system for analyzing individual instructions' security on real out-of-order superscalar processors with minimal silicon overhead.

dac-2025-123.method: The Seg-Cos framework divides vectors into segments and encodes them as ranges on a circle based on angles and magnitudes (direction and length). This encoding works directly on TCAM hardware (EX-TCAM and Best-TCAM), which can search all ranges in parallel. Locality-aware Compute Mapping minimizes memory row activations, and LUT Aggregation combines multiple small look-up table results to handle different precision levels.
dac-2025-123.key_novelty: This framework is the first to directly approximate cosine similarity (an angular metric for measuring vector alignment) within TCAM hardware, compatible with both EX-TCAM and Best-TCAM.

dac-2025-136.method: The method builds a clock distribution network by organizing it hierarchically (in levels), placing signal amplifiers and tiny silicon holes (Through-Silicon-Vias, or nTSVs) across both the front and back of the chip. After establishing the routing, it refines the layout on both sides to reduce timing mismatches (skew) between different paths. Throughout this process, it uses a single unified optimization framework to balance four competing goals: signal arrival time (latency), timing uniformity, total wire length, and the count of amplifiers and vias needed.
dac-2025-136.key_novelty: Unlike single-side techniques adapted for double-sided use, this method simultaneously optimizes four competing goals—signal arrival time (latency), timing uniformity, wire length, and resource count—when building double-sided clock trees with Through-Silicon-Vias.

dac-2025-133.method: RustBrain uses a large language model (LLM—a machine learning system trained on vast text) to find and fix undefined behaviors in Rust 'unsafe' code. It employs two complementary thinking modes inspired by cognitive science: a 'fast thinking' phase that quickly identifies code patterns and proposes fixes, and a 'slow thinking' phase that carefully breaks down those proposals, verifies whether they work, and generalizes them (adapts them to similar patterns). A feedback loop connects verification and generalization results back to generation, so each cycle improves the system's future proposals.
dac-2025-133.key_novelty: It applies dual-process thinking (a cognitive science framework where the mind uses both quick intuition and careful deliberation) through a large language model to identify and fix undefined behaviors in Rust code.

dac-2025-135.method: MEEK detects hardware errors using two types of processors working in parallel: a fast main processor executes instructions speculatively (running ahead while assuming everything is safe), while slower, power-efficient backup processors re-run the same code to verify correctness. Software and minimal operating-system changes compare the results between main and backup paths and report any mismatches within microseconds. The approach avoids major rewiring of existing processors by dividing the error-detection work across three layers: the instruction set (the software-hardware interface), the processor's internal design, and the operating system.
dac-2025-135.key_novelty: MEEK is the first complete implementation of heterogeneous parallel error detection (using different processor types to catch hardware faults) in an open-source chip, detecting faults in microseconds while requiring minimal changes to existing processor design through hardware-software partitioning.

dac-2025-134.method: Instead of storing control rules for every single frame, METAS keeps just one persistent rule per flow and generates specific frame-level rules on-demand. This approach trades memory for computation: less upfront storage but slightly more work when each frame arrives. An FPGA implementation demonstrates the payoff: memory usage drops from 14.34 megabits to 288 kilobits for 1,024 flows (a 98% reduction), using only 1.56% of FPGA logic resources while maintaining microsecond-level latency and nanosecond-level jitter guarantees.
dac-2025-134.key_novelty: Store a single rule per traffic flow and generate per-frame rules on-demand instead of storing them all, slashing memory by 98% while maintaining strict timing guarantees.

dac-2025-139.method: The method uses active learning (strategically selecting the most informative queries to understand the detector's behavior) to probe a security detector while maintaining stealth through adaptive query budgeting (limiting the total number of queries to avoid triggering alarms). It builds a time series model (a mathematical pattern of how sensor readings normally evolve) from the extracted information, then generates attack sequences from this model that remain hidden within normal-looking sensor behavior.
dac-2025-139.key_novelty: This is the first active learning method for stealthy sensor attacks that maintains stealth both during the learning phase (limiting detector queries) and in the final attack (bypassing the detector).

dac-2025-140.method: GraphFI avoids testing billions of possible fault scenarios by finding patterns in how graphs execute on GPUs. It selects representative moments in execution when similar vertices are computing (iteration-driven), groups vertices by how similarly they fail when faults occur (topology-driven), and uses fault monotonicity—the principle that worse faults always produce worse outcomes—to predict which failures would be severe without testing all possibilities. Combining these three strategies cuts the test scenarios needed by up to 100x.
dac-2025-140.key_novelty: GraphFI is the first fault-injection framework to use graph-specific execution patterns—iteration phases, vertex grouping, and fault monotonicity—to reduce testing trials by 2.1–15.2x while improving reliability assessment.

dac-2025-141.method: AARC represents the workflow as a graph (showing how tasks depend on each other) and identifies the critical path—the longest sequence of tasks that determines overall execution time. Rather than testing every possible combination of CPU and memory amounts, it uses priority-based scheduling to focus on configuration choices with the biggest impact. This targeted approach maintains performance guarantees (service-level objectives) while dramatically reducing the search time for optimal configurations.
dac-2025-141.key_novelty: AARC is the first to automatically optimize separate CPU and memory in serverless workflows (systems where code runs without managing servers) by analyzing which tasks form bottlenecks and prioritizing configuration choices that matter most, achieving 85-89% faster search.

dac-2025-137.method: NDFT reduces data-movement bottlenecks by using near-data processing—executing calculations on processing units built into the memory system instead of shipping data to distant accelerators. It splits the quantum chemistry calculation into stages and assigns each to whichever processor (CPU or on-chip unit) is most efficient for that task. The hardware and software are then co-designed: the chip's architecture and the algorithms are redesigned together, rather than separately, to further squeeze out data movement and reduce delays.
dac-2025-137.key_novelty: This is the first near-data processing system for quantum chemistry calculations, dividing computational work between the CPU and on-chip processing units to minimize long-distance data movement, and achieving 5.2× speedup over pure CPU and 2.5× over GPU.

dac-2025-147.method: This approach uses reinforcement learning (AI that learns through trial and error) to intelligently choose which sections of the chip to repair and how large each section should be, instead of treating all areas equally. It positions sections based on where design rule violations (places where routing breaks manufacturing rules) occur, focusing effort on high-congestion areas. The AI learns which window placements eliminate the most violations most efficiently, achieving routing without any violations while maintaining competitive wire length and via count.
dac-2025-147.key_novelty: This is the first use of reinforcement learning to automatically adjust repair-section size and position based on where design rule violations occur, eliminating all violations while improving wire length and via count.

dac-2025-143.method: BLAST extracts delay measurements from data and clock paths in sequential cells (memory-holding logic elements) and feeds these into a machine learning model called multi-gate mixture-of-experts (MMoE). The model learns to predict setup and hold constraints—the timing windows that specify when data must be stable relative to clock transitions—by understanding how these constraints depend on each other through multi-task learning. To make training more efficient, BLAST uses active learning to identify and focus on the most informative examples.
dac-2025-143.key_novelty: BLAST predicts circuit timing constraints (setup and hold) directly from signal delays using multi-task mixture-of-experts learning, eliminating traditional bisection analysis and achieving 76.9% runtime reduction.

dac-2025-146.method: The researchers tested classical neural networks and hybrid quantum-classical networks (simulated on regular computers) across problems of increasing complexity, ranging from 10 to 110 features. They measured how two key metrics scaled: the computational work required (floating-point operations, or FLOPs—the math calculations computers perform) and the number of adjustable parameters. By comparing how these metrics grew with problem complexity, they could see which architecture remained more efficient as problems became harder.
dac-2025-146.key_novelty: Hybrid quantum-classical networks scale more efficiently than classical networks with increasing problem complexity, requiring only 53.1% more floating-point operations compared to 88.1% for classical networks and 81.4% more parameters compared to 88.5%, demonstrating genuine computational advantage even when simulated on conventional computers.

dac-2025-144.method: GS-TG groups small rectangular image tiles together during sorting—the phase that arranges which pixels to compute—to reduce redundant work, then uses binary flags during rendering (converting the scene to pixels) to identify which tiles actually need processing. This hybrid approach combines the efficiency of handling large regions together during sorting with the efficiency of computing only necessary regions during rendering, without requiring model retraining.
dac-2025-144.key_novelty: GS-TG is the first to address the sorting-rendering trade-off in 3D Gaussian Splatting through tile grouping and binary-flag identification, achieving 1.54x speedup without retraining.

dac-2025-138.method: The method combines meta-learning (training a system to learn how to adapt quickly to new problems) with a multi-gate mixture-of-experts model (multiple specialized sub-networks with several decision gates routing inputs to the right expert) and asynchronous multi-task learning (where different components are trained independently rather than all at once). The CNN's feature detection (identifying hotspot indicators) and classification (deciding if it's a hotspot) components are updated separately, which allows them to specialize independently. A topology-based sampling strategy (selecting training examples based on circuit structure) guides the adaptation process, enabling the system to generalize to new designs using only one training layout clip.
dac-2025-138.key_novelty: This is the first meta-learning (learning how to quickly adapt to new problems) approach for lithographic hotspot detection, enabling rapid generalization to new circuit layouts from just one training sample through asynchronously trained multi-gate mixture-of-experts (multiple specialized sub-networks updated independently) that decouple feature detection and classification.

dac-2025-149.method: FedEDA enables teams to train a shared machine learning model for circuit design without revealing their proprietary designs—instead, they share only trained model weights (numerical patterns the model learned from data). The algorithm uses Rent's Rule, which describes how circuit connections scale with size, to capture the hierarchical structure of circuit data; this lets the system fairly combine everyone's trained weights even when participants have different amounts of training data.
dac-2025-149.key_novelty: FedEDA is the first federated learning algorithm for EDA that uses Rent's Rule to encode circuit hierarchy, enabling collaborative training of models for routability, RC parasitic, and wirelength prediction without sharing proprietary circuit designs.

dac-2025-145.method: The system stores and processes data using light instead of electricity, combining a photonic memory cell (pSRAM) with a matrix-multiplication processor built from integrated photonic components on a single chip. After the processor multiplies numbers using light signals, a specialized light-to-digital converter (called an eoADC, using 1-hot encoding where one signal is active at a time) quickly translates the results back into electrical data. This approach eliminates the slow step where data normally travels between memory and the processor, since everything stays in the photonic domain.
dac-2025-145.key_novelty: The system integrates photonic memory with a photonic matrix-multiplication processor and a light-to-digital converter using 1-hot encoding (one signal active at a time), performing calculations entirely in the optical domain.

dac-2025-150.method: Traditional checkpoint designs for energy-harvesting systems (devices that run on intermittently available power from solar, vibration, or similar sources) assume simplified hardware behavior that doesn't match reality. The paper builds a more accurate model—a step-by-step description of what actually happens when power fails mid-operation—that accounts for the true energy budget and physical limits of small-scale systems. Using this realistic model, the authors derive better rules for when to save state in both pre-planned and adaptive ways, avoiding both the wasted energy of saving too often and the crashes that happen when designs assume more power is available than actually is.
dac-2025-150.key_novelty: When you model how intermittent hardware truly behaves under low-power constraints, you discover that traditional checkpoint strategies waste far more energy than necessary.

dac-2025-148.method: The solution adds two new ways to specify memory addresses in processor-memory instructions: indexed addressing (combining a base address with a register value) and base-offset addressing (combining a base address with a constant offset). These methods reduce the size and complexity of each instruction because they avoid repeating full addresses. By making instructions more efficient, the system reduces the amount of data transferred between the processor and memory, and decreases the code overhead for memory operations.
dac-2025-148.key_novelty: This is the first system to support register-based addressing modes in Direct Memory Access-based in-DRAM processing-in-memory, achieving 1.94x speedup with minimal chip area and power overhead.

dac-2025-142.method: PiSPICE uses adjoint sensitivity analysis (a mathematical technique for finding which components affect results) on pre-layout circuits (before physical layout) to identify critical parasitic elements (unwanted electrical components that appear in densely packed circuits). Only these critical parasitics are kept in the post-layout simulation; model order reduction (a technique that simplifies their representation) minimizes their computational impact while non-critical parasitics are removed entirely. This reduces simulation scale from billions or trillions of nodes to just the essential ones.
dac-2025-142.key_novelty: PiSPICE is the first to use adjoint sensitivity analysis (a technique that finds which components affect results) on pre-layout circuits to identify essential parasitic elements (unwanted circuit components), avoiding expensive analysis of billion-node post-layout circuits and achieving 17.27x speedup.

dac-2025-154.method: The approach uses a statistical model to learn how well different simulation quality levels predict actual chip yield, so it can tell when a fast, rough simulation is reliable enough. It then continuously adjusts the simulation quality for each design based on what it learns about that design's promise — running more precise simulations on promising candidates and rougher ones on less likely designs. This smart allocation of simulation detail converges using fewer than 1,000 total simulations, over 10 times fewer than traditional methods.
dac-2025-154.key_novelty: The key insight is using variable simulation quality (continuous precision levels rather than fixed predefined counts) that adapts to each design's predicted quality, so better designs get more expensive detailed simulations and weaker ones get cheaper rough ones.

dac-2025-156.method: A BiLSTM neural network (an AI that reads sequences in both directions to find patterns) learns to predict the best circuit layout for power amplifiers built with HEMT transistors (fast-switching semiconductor devices). The network's settings—like how many processing layers it has—are tuned using multi-objective Pareto optimization, which balances competing goals like power and efficiency. Tested on gallium-nitride HEMT designs, the method produced amplifiers with 40 dBm output power, 50%+ power-added efficiency (the percentage of input power converted to useful amplified signal), and over 10 dB of gain.
dac-2025-156.key_novelty: The key idea is using a BiLSTM neural network to automatically select power-amplifier designs from data rather than having engineers manually explore different circuit layouts.

dac-2025-151.method: DiTTO uses diffusion models—machine learning techniques that gradually refine random noise into realistic patterns—to generate synthetic storage traces. The approach captures temporal dynamics (how storage activity changes over time) and inter-device dependencies (how storage devices interact), while allowing users to specify desired configurations. The framework maintains high fidelity to real storage patterns, achieving only 8% configuration errors.
dac-2025-151.key_novelty: Using diffusion models to generate storage traces that users can configure while accurately capturing how multiple storage devices behave over time.

dac-2025-152.method: GLOVA uses a machine learning strategy that learns to prioritize worst-case scenarios (risk-sensitive reinforcement learning) and employs multiple AI judges working together (ensemble-based critic) to determine optimal circuit component sizes. To account for real-world variations from manufacturing and environmental factors, it measures both average performance and how much performance fluctuates (mu-sigma evaluation), and runs simulations in a smart order—checking the most critical cases first (simulation reordering). The system validates designs using both extreme corner cases and randomized testing methods (Monte Carlo) to ensure industrial-grade reliability.
dac-2025-152.key_novelty: The core innovation combines a learning strategy that prioritizes worst-case performance (risk-sensitive reinforcement learning) with multiple AI judges (ensemble critics) to design circuits that work reliably despite manufacturing and environmental variations.

dac-2025-160.method: When chip designers move cells, the resulting voltage drop becomes unpredictable. This approach trains a machine learning model (XGBoost) on examples of cell movements and their voltage effects, using the electrical context around each cell to predict outcomes. Instead of running expensive simulations (SPICE) that take over an hour each, the model predicts voltage impact in minutes, letting designers test multiple placement options in the same design session.
dac-2025-160.key_novelty: An XGBoost machine learning model predicts voltage drop immediately after moving cells in chip design, replacing hour-long simulation runs and enabling designers to test multiple placement options in parallel.

dac-2025-153.method: 333-eDRAM stacks three types of transistors in a single chip, each chosen for what it does best: IGZO transistors have nearly zero power drain when idle, so stored data lasts longer; Carbon Nanotube transistors push high current quickly, enabling fast data access; and Silicon transistors efficiently handle support circuits. The design jointly optimizes energy use, chip area, and access speed—metrics known together as EADP (energy-area-delay product)—at 7-nanometer scale. The researchers verified performance through cycle-accurate simulation and physics-based models calibrated to lab measurements.
dac-2025-153.key_novelty: Stacking three different transistor materials—IGZO, Carbon Nanotube, and Silicon—in a single 3D chip allows one memory design to achieve high density, long retention time, high endurance, fast speed, low power use, and minimal standby power drain all simultaneously, breaking the fundamental tradeoffs of traditional single-material DRAM.

dac-2025-157.method: This design uses NAND gates in a 1T1R RRAM crossbar (a grid of resistive memory cells, each paired with a transistor) to build multiplexers—circuits that pick one of four inputs—in 3 steps instead of 10. The same approach works for adders, subtractors, and comparators built directly in memory, cutting execution time by 75%. While it uses more memristors (resistive memory elements), the speed gain makes it practical for in-memory computing where calculations happen right where the data sits.
dac-2025-157.key_novelty: Using NAND-gate logic to build 4:1 multiplexers in RRAM crossbars reduces the execution steps from 10 to 3, enabling fast logic operations directly in memory.

dac-2025-158.method: Quartz is a tool that finds where quantum-unsafe encryption currently exists in systems and how that vulnerability spreads through interconnected supply chains. It works by building dependency graphs (detailed maps showing which systems rely on which encryption methods) to trace connections between components. The system generates a Cryptography Bill of Materials (an inventory of all cryptographic components in use), providing visibility into where quantum vulnerabilities exist.
dac-2025-158.key_novelty: A system that uses dependency maps to identify and track quantum-unsafe encryption across interconnected systems and supply chains.

dac-2025-155.method: GPS finds efficient loop mappings for CGRAs in two stages. First, it uses Integer Linear Programming—a mathematical method that systematically searches for optimal solutions within constraints—to identify promising regions and set initial boundaries. Second, it applies a Graph Neural Network, a machine learning approach that learns patterns from graph-structured data, to explore within those boundaries and prune away poor mappings while refining the best ones. This two-stage combination significantly reduces the search space, enabling the compiler to find good mappings faster while maintaining or improving their quality.
dac-2025-155.key_novelty: GPS combines a first stage of Integer Linear Programming with a second stage of Graph Neural Network refinement to reduce the CGRA loop mapping search space, achieving faster compilation while maintaining or improving solution quality.

dac-2025-159.method: GraphAccel is specialized hardware built into SSDs that speeds up vector similarity searches—finding similar numerical representations (like embeddings for text or images) by navigating a graph (network of connected nodes). It works two ways: first, it physically groups related nodes together on disk so queries require fewer storage page reads; second, it predicts which data paths you'll explore next and fetches them in advance, while the SSD's idle processing channels simultaneously work on multiple search paths. Results are compared against existing approaches like DiskANN and DiskANN++.
dac-2025-159.key_novelty: GraphAccel puts specialized hardware inside SSDs for faster vector similarity searches by keeping related graph nodes close together and fetching likely future data before it's requested.

dac-2025-161.method: BEVSA is a specialized chip that speeds up a computer vision task where multiple camera feeds are converted into a bird's-eye view and processed to identify objects. It uses two innovations: hierarchical BEV pooling, which converts and combines camera views more efficiently by breaking the problem into blocks suited for multi-camera systems, achieving a 43.2x speedup over edge devices; and zero-skipping convolution, which accelerates image processing (convolution) by skipping unnecessary calculations on sparse data—both at the channel level and across image tiles—improving throughput 1.61x. Built at 28 nanometer scale, it targets edge devices where real-time performance is critical.
dac-2025-161.key_novelty: A specialized chip that makes multi-camera semantic segmentation real-time by efficiently converting multiple camera views into a bird's-eye perspective and adaptively handling sparse data during processing.

dac-2025-167.method: The approach uses static analysis to examine code structure and determine which speculative execution paths require rollback capability—the circuits that undo work when the hardware's guess was wrong. It then applies linear programming, a mathematical optimization technique, to eliminate unnecessary control logic, keeping only the circuitry needed for actual rollback in complex control flow.
dac-2025-167.key_novelty: First work combining static analysis with linear programming to systematically reduce the hardware area overhead from rollback control logic in speculative synthesis.

dac-2025-171.method: GauRast accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting by modifying the rasterizer—the part of a GPU that normally converts triangles into pixels—to work with Gaussian splats instead. It can do this because the math behind 3DGS (which renders scenes using overlapping Gaussian blobs) turns out to be similar to how triangle rendering works. The enhancement tweaks the rasterizer's datapath (the circuits that process data) to handle Gaussian primitives and their blending operations, which means existing GPUs can render 3DGS in real time without needing expensive custom accelerator hardware.
dac-2025-171.key_novelty: GauRast accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting by enhancing existing GPU rasterizer hardware instead of building dedicated accelerators.

dac-2025-164.method: The approach uses machine-learning models that predict circuit behavior, combined with data-driven techniques that simulate design conditions without running the slow SPICE simulator. Pre-trained models quickly adapt to new manufacturing processes through fine-tuning. The data-driven techniques recreate design environments—accounting for instance binning, process variations, and layout-dependent effects—without actually running SPICE. This delivers fast feedback for rapid technology exploration.
dac-2025-164.key_novelty: Machine-learning models that efficiently adapt to new manufacturing processes, combined with data-driven simulation that replaces SPICE, accelerate design-technology iteration.

dac-2025-170.method: Compresses the state information needed for adjoint calculations using specialized algorithms that recognize patterns in how circuit simulation data changes across different circuit parts and over time. The compression is lossy—it throws away some information—but error-bounded, so it only discards information in carefully controlled ways that won't break the final gradient calculation. This cuts memory requirements while keeping numerical accuracy.
dac-2025-170.key_novelty: First adjoint method using lossy compression with error bounds to reduce memory without sacrificing numerical accuracy.

dac-2025-168.method: PipeLink solves the coordination problem by splitting hardware synthesis into two stages: compilation (converting the program into individual operations) and linking (assembling these operations into final circuits). This separation allows multiple function calls to shared hardware modules to overlap and execute simultaneously (fully pipelined) without waiting for each other, running in asynchronous dataflow circuits where operations trigger as soon as their input data arrives. The system applies asynchronous design principles consistently across both the computational functions and the memory subsystem, creating one unified framework instead of separate solutions.
dac-2025-168.key_novelty: PipeLink is the first high-level synthesis system to achieve fully-pipelined access to shared resources by decomposing synthesis into compilation and linking stages in asynchronous dataflow architecture.

dac-2025-163.method: CVMAX combines software and specialized hardware to accelerate complex-number operations in neural networks. It represents complex numbers using polar form—as a magnitude (size) and phase (angle)—instead of the standard rectangular form (real part plus imaginary part), and applies quantization (using fewer bits per number) through hardware-efficient bit-shifting operations. A dedicated hardware accelerator optimizes for this polar representation, making multiplication faster since multiplying in polar form simply requires multiplying magnitudes and adding phases, rather than the more complex rectangular multiplication.
dac-2025-163.key_novelty: The core innovation is using polar form to represent complex numbers, which enables efficient quantization and specialized hardware for low-overhead multiplication.

dac-2025-169.method: StreamCSD measures how much data compresses within the SSD using built-in compression engines. It continuously groups data into separate streams based on compression similarity using streaming K-means—an algorithm that updates groupings as new data arrives. Because the SSD performs this work on its own, the host computer doesn't require any modifications.
dac-2025-169.key_novelty: StreamCSD is the first system to manage SSD data streams autonomously on the drive itself, using compression measurements to decide how to group data together.

dac-2025-174.method: STREAM groups incoming data into buckets that exploit patterns in how data changes over time and space. Rather than recalculating each time, it reuses information from previous bucket states to speed up the median calculation. The algorithm includes a tunable-grained bucket mechanism—you can adjust the bucket size to control the trade-off between accuracy and speed, with finer buckets giving more precise results but taking longer. This allows applications to choose the speed-versus-accuracy balance that fits their needs.
dac-2025-174.key_novelty: STREAM is the first approximate median algorithm that takes advantage of patterns in how streaming data changes over time and space, while letting you adjust the bucket size to balance accuracy and speed.

dac-2025-162.method: iG-kway divides circuit graphs into k groups on a GPU while updating incrementally—when a circuit is modified, it updates only affected vertices' group assignments rather than recomputing everything from scratch. It uses a data structure that tracks which vertices changed and a GPU program that improves the partition in only those affected regions. This avoids wasted computation on unchanged parts while maintaining quality—essential for CAD where circuits are iteratively tweaked.
dac-2025-162.key_novelty: The first GPU-based incremental k-way partitioner that efficiently updates only affected vertices during circuit design, avoiding full re-partitioning.

dac-2025-177.method: Espresso builds an FPGA processor that works with event cameras—sensors that capture only pixels where the image changes, producing sparse (mostly empty) event streams. Rather than converting this sparse data into dense pixel grids like traditional processors do, it organizes events by their space and time location, then processes them with specialized hardware patterns that keep the data sparse throughout.
dac-2025-177.key_novelty: The key innovation is using spatiotemporal ordering—organizing events by when and where they occur—to process event camera streams on an FPGA without converting them to dense representations.

dac-2025-178.method: MARIO runs multiple optimization algorithms in parallel and dynamically shifts computing resources between them to achieve results better than any single algorithm could (called superadditivity—the combination is worth more than the parts separately). It predicts which algorithm works best for different circuits using a statistical model (multitask Gaussian process regression), then allocates computing power like a portfolio manager allocates capital, favoring algorithms making progress. The algorithms share evaluation data and work asynchronously, so slower algorithms don't block faster ones.
dac-2025-178.key_novelty: It combines multiple optimization algorithms and dynamically redirects computing power to the best-performing ones, achieving results stronger than any single algorithm could deliver.

dac-2025-165.method: BiNeuroRAM puts ReRAM—memory chips that can store and process data simultaneously—to work accelerating spiking neural networks (which process information through sparse electrical pulses), with three key innovations: first, it supports spike-tracing bipolar-integrate-and-fire neurons (which track both positive and negative signals) for higher accuracy. Second, it uses a specialized low-power voltage sense amplifier to read data more efficiently, cutting ReRAM read power by 14.7 to 58.2 times. Third, it uses an asynchronous architecture that responds to events on-demand rather than running on a clock, exploiting how spiking neural networks naturally produce sparse bursts of activity.
dac-2025-165.key_novelty: It's the first ReRAM accelerator supporting spike-tracing bipolar-integrate-and-fire neurons while reducing sensing power 14.7 to 58.2 times using a specialized low-power voltage sense amplifier.

dac-2025-175.method: When multiple resource-constrained devices train a shared model together (federated learning), they normally send all their updates back to a central server, but limited bandwidth makes this impractical. This method solves it by having each device check how different its local model is from the global shared model using a similarity score—and only transmit updates when that score indicates meaningful divergence, sending compressed updates instead. As training progresses and models converge toward the final solution, this transmission strategy automatically adapts to send less frequently.
dac-2025-175.key_novelty: The core idea is using a similarity score between the local and global models to adaptively decide when to transmit gradient updates, instead of using a fixed transmission policy.

dac-2025-166.method: The method protects complex cells—like adders and multiplexers—by boxing them (treating them as indivisible units) before optimization and keeping them boxed throughout. Rather than black-boxing these cells (keeping them completely opaque), transparent-boxing lets the optimizer see and use information about their internal logic. This allows the algorithm to reoptimize the wiring between cells while preserving each cell's internal structure.
dac-2025-166.key_novelty: The core innovation is transparent-boxing: preserving complex cells as intact units while allowing the optimizer to see and use their internal logic to better optimize how different circuit blocks interact.

dac-2025-181.method: The approach uses physics-inspired forces to reposition flip-flops (memory elements) to reduce timing problems. It combines clustering (grouping single-bit flip-flops into multi-bit units) and legalization (fixing placement violations), making them work together to minimize damage from moving things around. A scoring system that balances multiple competing goals—timing performance, power consumption, chip area, and efficient bin usage—determines which flip-flops to group.
dac-2025-181.key_novelty: It's the first MBFF placement method that explicitly accounts for pre-placed cells (circuit elements locked in fixed positions) during clustering and legalization while simultaneously optimizing timing, power, chip area, and bin utilization.

dac-2025-186.method: It computes routing paths between computing nodes by analyzing how data flows from one node to another. Rather than deciding where to place each node individually, it identifies locations where multiple nodes can share routing resources. It then uses the actual data connections between nodes as constraints, placing multiple nodes in their final positions all at once instead of one-by-one.
dac-2025-186.key_novelty: It places multiple computing nodes together in a single step, using shared routing paths and data dependencies to guide placement rather than deciding each node's location separately.

dac-2025-180.method: Circuits are represented as heterogeneous hypergraphs (network models with different types of connections). The method uses directed graph neural networks to quickly find approximate circuit matches while reformulating the problem as a directed acyclic graph to reduce missed matches. These approximate results then serve as starting points for an optimization solver (MINLP—mixed-integer nonlinear programming), which finds exact matches faster because it starts with a candidate solution rather than from scratch.
dac-2025-180.key_novelty: Hypergraph-based circuit representation with directed graph neural networks that reformulate the matching problem as directed acyclic graphs while embedding circular structures to reduce missed matches.

dac-2025-172.method: The system combines ferroelectric FET transistors (devices that create unique fingerprints from natural manufacturing variations) with compute-in-memory architecture (storing and computing model data in the same hardware). It generates encryption keys from these fingerprints and stores both the fingerprints and model weights together using multi-level cells (multiple bits per transistor), eliminating extra storage for encrypted data. By integrating fingerprint-based key generation directly with the computation process, the system creates and verifies encryption keys during normal operation. It also includes enhancement techniques and a new mapping scheme to make fingerprints more stable and reliable across varying conditions.
dac-2025-172.key_novelty: This is the first system to combine physical fingerprint-based security (extracted from ferroelectric transistors) with compute-in-memory in a single unified design, providing complete protection for edge AI without needing extra storage for encrypted weights.

dac-2025-183.method: The approach lets the computer manage read refreshing at fine-grained block level rather than waiting for entire zones to degrade. It remaps metadata to track individual blocks separately and reconstructs complete zones from these remapped blocks. By prioritizing remapped data for reads until the next refresh cycle, it avoids the performance damage of refreshing all valid data in a zone at once.
dac-2025-183.key_novelty: Instead of refreshing entire zones at once, the approach uses block-level metadata remapping to manage read refreshing in smaller chunks and efficiently reconstruct zones.

dac-2025-179.method: FT-MUX analyzes how to design multiplexers that keep working when control channels break. It models this using coding theory—the mathematical framework that makes error-correcting codes work—specifically as a binary constant weight code to find efficient designs that minimize wasted resources. This reveals design rules that ensure the multiplexer functions with up to n defective control channels. The result is that fault-tolerant designs can actually route fluids through more channels than standard multiplexers, even with equal or fewer control channels.
dac-2025-179.key_novelty: FT-MUX is the first framework that uses coding theory to formally design microfluidic multiplexers that tolerate broken control channels.

dac-2025-185.method: The approach tracks cell inflation over time using momentum-based ratios to prevent over-inflation in local congestion areas. It models global congestion through Poisson's equation (a physics equation describing how quantities spread through space), making this model differentiable for gradient-based optimization to guide net placement. Virtual cells guide each two-pin net placement, while cell density around power and ground rails adjusts based on congestion patterns.
dac-2025-185.key_novelty: It uses Poisson's equation to create a differentiable model of global congestion, enabling gradient-based optimization for net placement with virtual cell guidance.

dac-2025-173.method: ATLAS trains a deep learning model to predict per-cycle power (power at each clock cycle) at the layout stage using only the gate-level netlist, without requiring physical layout. It uses self-supervised learning (extracting training patterns by predicting missing information within the data) in a two-stage approach: pre-training across many circuits to learn general power patterns, then fine-tuning to specific designs. To work from incomplete information, it makes three separate power predictions for the clock network, registers (memory storage), and combinational logic (computation gates), using per-cycle power measurements from commercial simulation tools as training targets.
dac-2025-173.key_novelty: ATLAS is the first model to predict per-cycle power across different chip designs with near-layout accuracy from gate-level netlists without physical layout, using circuit-specific deep learning.

dac-2025-184.method: Partitions points using locality-sensitive hashing (E2LSH, which groups similar points together to narrow the search space). A precomparator module then quickly screens out obviously distant candidates before expensive distance calculations begin. The distance computation is optimized to minimize wasted work while maintaining accuracy.
dac-2025-184.key_novelty: Combining locality-sensitive hashing partitioning with precomparator filtering to significantly reduce expensive distance calculations while maintaining accuracy.

dac-2025-187.method: The approach first profiles ML models running on multi-accelerator edge devices to find which computational stages are slowest—the bottleneck. It then automatically allocates unequal amounts of computing resources across accelerators, giving more power to slow stages and less to fast ones. To make this efficient, it uses the unified memory system in edge SoCs, which is a shared pool of memory that all processors (CPU, GPU, NPU, TPU) can access, so data can move between model stages without being copied.
dac-2025-187.key_novelty: The core idea is allocating unequal computing resources to match performance bottlenecks, while using the device's shared unified memory to keep accelerators from wasting time copying data between model stages.

dac-2025-193.method: The system uses a large language model (LLM) to improve Bayesian optimization—a statistical approach that explores many possible processor designs while balancing competing performance metrics. It starts with a smart initialization phase: the language model reads LLVM compiler code and expert knowledge to generate a good starting set of candidate designs, rather than guessing randomly. From there, the language model helps improve the surrogate model (a simplified predictor of how well each design will perform) even when only a small amount of real test data is available.
dac-2025-193.key_novelty: A large language model improves Bayesian optimization for processor design exploration by providing expert knowledge during initialization and making performance predictions more accurate with limited data.

dac-2025-176.method: KVO-LLM accelerates batched LLM inference by coupling algorithm and hardware optimization. The algorithm reduces KV cache size through quantization that prioritizes tokens important to attention (salient tokens), followed by pruning of KV channels and tokens based on attention patterns. The hardware uses a multi-core accelerator with operator fusion (combining operations to reduce memory transfers) and cross-batch interleaving (mixing requests to maximize processor and DRAM bandwidth utilization). This works because smaller data volumes mean less memory pressure and more opportunities to keep processors busy.
dac-2025-176.key_novelty: The core novelty is co-designing the algorithm (quantization and attention-guided pruning of KV cache) and hardware architecture (operator fusion and cross-batch interleaving) as a single integrated system.

dac-2025-190.method: Creates a graph neural network—an AI model that learns patterns from interconnected structures like atomic arrangements—scaled up to billions of parameters and trained on terabyte-scale datasets. Applies training techniques from large language models that enable efficient management of computation and memory at this scale. Tests three scaling dimensions: network architecture design, dataset size, and training methods to find what works best for billion-parameter models.
dac-2025-190.key_novelty: This is the first study to scale graph neural networks to billions of parameters and terabyte-scale datasets for modeling materials at the atomic level, using training techniques adapted from large language models.

dac-2025-182.method: The approach uses logic inferencing—analyzing how signals logically depend on each other—to identify redundant multiplexers, which are circuit structures that select inputs based on control signals. It eliminates these unnecessary multiplexers entirely.
