For the remaining multiplexers, it restructures them by leveraging the discovered signal dependencies, reducing the total number of logic gates in the design.
dac-2025-182.key_novelty: The core innovation is analyzing signal dependencies to both identify and restructure redundant multiplexers, rather than only tracking control values.

dac-2025-191.method: The algorithm automatically finds the mapping between two circuit designs—showing which states in one design correspond to states in the other—by checking whether they produce identical outputs over time (sequential equivalence checking). To make this mapping concise and understandable, it groups states that behave the same way (relational mapping abstraction). This automation eliminates the tedious manual mapping work that would normally require deep expertise in formal methods and hardware design.
dac-2025-191.key_novelty: Automatically discovering the refinement relation (state correspondence) between two circuit designs by grouping equivalent states—a technique called relational mapping abstraction—to create readable, automatically-generated mappings.

dac-2025-194.method: The work represents circuits through transistor electrical properties—the fundamental ways transistors behave—rather than transistor sizes, which differ across technologies. It then maps these technology-independent electrical properties to actual transistor sizes for a specific chip technology. To predict circuit performance without expensive simulations, it uses a radial basis functions-based Kolmogorov-Arnold network (RBF-KAN, a type of neural network for approximating complex nonlinear relationships), trained on a limited number of simulations.
dac-2025-194.key_novelty: Representing circuits by transistor electrical properties (which remain consistent across chip technologies) instead of transistor sizes enables technology-agnostic surrogate modeling using an RBF-KAN neural network.

dac-2025-196.method: Efficient-GMS analyzes dataflow (how data flows through computation) to identify shared patterns in gather-matmul-scatter operations across different neural network types like RGCN, SpConv, and MoE. It creates four optimized dataflow variants by fusing (combining) operations either vertically or horizontally—different structural ways to merge computation steps. A performance model predicts execution speed for each configuration, and a lightweight heuristic selects the best dataflow variant based on input characteristics and hardware, avoiding expensive search across all possibilities.
dac-2025-196.key_novelty: Shared dataflow patterns in gather-matmul-scatter operations enable the same optimizations to work across different neural networks (RGCN, SpConv, MoE) without per-model tuning.

dac-2025-188.method: The system stacks a processor chip directly on a memory chip via hybrid bonding (a technique that bonds them tightly together) and embeds SRAM-based processing-in-memory units in the processor, allowing computation to happen close to data. It uses bit-level non-zero gathering to exploit sparsity—the prevalence of zeros in graph data—skipping unnecessary work. It then assigns graph subproblems across processor-memory pairs for load balancing and distributes the global pooling step (neural network aggregation) across these pairs rather than centralizing it, minimizing data movement between blocks.
dac-2025-188.key_novelty: The core idea is using 3D hybrid bonding (a technique that physically stacks processor and memory chips tightly together) with embedded SRAM-based processing-in-memory units, exploiting graph sparsity through bit-level gathering, and distributing pooling across the stack to minimize data movement for subgraph neural networks.

dac-2025-192.method: The system reorganizes data into blocks distributed across memory channels (separate storage pathways), which packs information more densely and removes limits on the context length an LLM can handle. It redesigns how attention computation—the operation where an LLM determines which input parts matter most—works across these distributed channels while staying compatible with Processing-in-Memory hardware (processors located beside memory rather than far away).
dac-2025-192.key_novelty: A block memory layout distributed across channels consolidates fragmented data in Processing-in-Memory systems, enabling long-context LLM inference.

dac-2025-197.method: Instead of sending raw high-resolution images to a computer, this approach embeds a compression algorithm directly in the image sensor. The algorithm uses a 1-bit encoder (compressing each pixel value down to 1 bit, essentially binary information) that learns which visual features matter for your specific task. The encoder and the downstream deep learning task are jointly optimized together during training, so the sensor learns what details to keep and what to discard for that particular job. This shrinks the data right at the source, eliminating the energy cost of transmitting unnecessary image data.
dac-2025-197.key_novelty: A 1-bit encoder embedded in the image sensor and jointly optimized with the downstream vision task achieves 10× data compression while maintaining task accuracy.

dac-2025-200.method: ZK-Hammer uses a hardware vulnerability called Rowhammer (repeatedly accessing memory to flip bits in nearby locations) to corrupt the variables used in the mathematical calculations of zk-SNARK proofs—a type of cryptographic proof scheme designed to hide secrets. It targets the exponentiation step in the proof's mathematical representation (called a Quadratic Arithmetic Program). By analyzing these deliberately corrupted proofs using bilinear pairings (a cryptographic technique that works with pairs of values in a special mathematical structure), the attack recovers the secret parameters that should have remained hidden.
dac-2025-200.key_novelty: ZK-SNARK cryptographic proofs, which were thought to be secure, can be broken by Rowhammer attacks (hardware faults that flip bits in memory during calculations), allowing recovery of the secret parameters.

dac-2025-195.method: Sphinx speeds up lookups by replacing sequential tree navigation—where you ask about one branch at a time and wait for each answer—with parallel hash reads. It uses an Inner Node Hash Table to check multiple branches at once, cutting down network round trips. A Succinct Filter Cache on the computing side further reduces network traffic by keeping track of which remote data locations are likely to contain your target, staying small and coherent.
dac-2025-195.key_novelty: An Inner Node Hash Table replaces sequential tree traversal (checking one branch at a time) with parallel hash lookups, eliminating network bottlenecks.

dac-2025-204.method: SSpMV combines expert-designed matrix measurements with a machine learning model called MM-Adapter that analyzes multiple characteristics of a sparse matrix (its sparsity patterns, density, and structure) to predict the fastest-running algorithm. Rather than using the same algorithm for every matrix, it learns which matrix features correspond to which algorithms, then selects the best algorithm and settings for each specific matrix.
dac-2025-204.key_novelty: It uses machine learning that examines multiple types of information about matrices—expert measurements and patterns learned from data—to automatically pick the best algorithm instead of using one fixed algorithm for all cases.

dac-2025-198.method: AutoClock automatically manages clocks in FPGA designs by choosing which clock resources to use, assigning modules to separate clock domains (so different parts run at different speeds), and hierarchically gating clocks (turning them on and off in layers) to save power. It uses heuristics (practical rules of thumb) and constraint satisfaction (checking that all requirements are met) to find the best clock domain assignments and gating strategy, while preventing metastability issues (glitches from signals crossing between different clock speeds) and time-division multiplexing problems (when one clock signal is reused in complex ways).
dac-2025-198.key_novelty: Automatic optimization of clock domain assignments and hierarchical clock gating to prevent metastability glitches (from signals crossing between clock speeds) and time-division multiplexing problems (from reusing clocks in complex ways).

dac-2025-201.method: AutoRE tests many different physical layouts of a microfluidic chip—adjusting component sizes and positions—while keeping the connections between parts the same. It uses Bayesian optimization (a search method that learns from each test to find good solutions efficiently) to explore these variations and identify the layout that works most reliably when manufactured.
dac-2025-201.key_novelty: It's the first automatic tool to make microfluidic biochips more reliable by exploring different physical layouts using Bayesian optimization (a search method that learns as it tests).

dac-2025-205.method: SRAM cells storing zeros experience asymmetric aging—they fail differently depending on whether you read them as zeros or ones. The method exploits this by testing each operation at a tailored voltage: writes at normal voltage, reads of zeros at aggressive voltage, and reads of ones at less-aggressive voltage. This replaces the uniform over-testing of standard approaches with targeted stress only where needed. Statistical sampling and simulation then quickly identify which chips actually fail.
dac-2025-205.key_novelty: Using different test voltages for each SRAM operation based on how it actually ages, rather than uniform aggressive conditions, reduces false rejections by 3-5× while still catching real failures.

dac-2025-189.method: The approach breaks the attention computation into chunks that process sequentially rather than all at once, keeping computation on fast on-chip SRAM memory instead of constantly moving data to slower external storage. To support this, it uses SRAM-based computing-in-memory (computing directly in fast memory) paired with RRAM (nonvolatile resistive memory) for persistent storage. The hardware includes processing blocks that reconfigure themselves to switch between different computational modes—bit-precision or element-size—to efficiently handle the varying layer sizes that pyramid Vision Transformers create. Coordinated scheduling of the work across the hardware balances the load and reduces the amount of intermediate data that must be stored between steps.
dac-2025-189.key_novelty: The core contribution is decoupled chunk attention—processing attention sequentially rather than all at once—executed on reconfigurable hybrid hardware that mixes fast computation with nonvolatile storage, adapting to different pyramid layer sizes.

dac-2025-202.method: The approach performs stochastic computing (calculations using random bit-streams to approximate results) entirely inside ReRAM, a memory type that stores data by changing electrical resistance. Rather than generating random bit-streams in a separate circuit and moving them back and forth to the processor—which wastes power—this system generates random patterns directly in the ReRAM using its natural electrical variation. The same ReRAM cells then do the stochastic calculations and convert results back to ordinary binary numbers. This works because ReRAM naturally tolerates electrical errors, aligning with stochastic computing's design, which remains accurate even with noisy, imperfect data.
dac-2025-202.key_novelty: Stochastic computing can run entirely within ReRAM memory using the memory's natural electrical variation for randomness, eliminating costly data movement between memory and processor.

dac-2025-208.method: SNAPPIX compresses pixel data directly at the camera using coded exposure (where different pixels capture light for different durations), which automatically removes redundancy based on efficient coding theory—a mathematical framework that minimizes data waste. The system learns which pixels to sample without needing to know the specific vision task ahead of time. The downstream AI models are redesigned to handle the uneven pixel brightness that results from this variable exposure. Lightweight hardware additions to the sensor enable this compression without significant power overhead.
dac-2025-208.key_novelty: SNAPPIX's key innovation is to use efficient-coding-inspired coded exposure—where pixels capture light for different durations—at the camera sensor for task-agnostic compression, with AI models and hardware specifically co-designed to support this approach.

dac-2025-206.method: Re4PUF generates a unique hardware fingerprint using 3 transistors and 2 resistor elements (ReRAM), combined with digital voltage dividers that stabilize readings. When read noise and temperature fluctuations degrade the fingerprint's reliability, instead of permanently rewriting the ReRAM chip, the system adjusts the voltages powering its inverter circuits (the basic logic gates) to compensate. These voltage tweaks can be applied repeatedly at low cost. The adjustable voltages also strengthen security by reducing the predictability that neural-network attacks and side-channel attacks (like power-consumption monitoring) depend on.
dac-2025-206.key_novelty: Instead of rewriting a ReRAM chip to fix an unreliable fingerprint, Re4PUF adjusts the inverter voltages in a 3-transistor, 2-resistor circuit—a simple, cheap reconfiguration that also blocks neural-network and side-channel attacks.

dac-2025-203.method: The approach leverages metal routing on both the backside and frontside of the chip to pack transistors more efficiently. Euler path analysis, a graph-based optimization method, determines the minimum spacing between transistor gates (contacted poly pitch); dynamic programming then calculates the number of routing channels required on the frontside. A mathematical constraint solver finalizes exact transistor placement and routing.
dac-2025-203.key_novelty: This is the first cell-synthesis approach to combine backside metal routing with efficient transistor folding (arranging transistors in space-saving patterns), using Euler path analysis and dynamic programming.

dac-2025-199.method: Harrow designs optical logic circuits starting with a binary decision diagram (a tree-like representation of logic operations) and then optimizes optical combiners—devices that merge light signals. It improves how efficiently these combiners preserve signal strength using harmonic mean optimization (a mathematical method that finds the best balance between multiple objectives). It also removes redundant combiners using integer partition (a technique for systematically grouping components to identify and eliminate duplicates). Finally, it arranges these optimizations in a sequence that produces the best overall circuit performance.
dac-2025-199.key_novelty: Harrow combines harmonic mean optimization of DC combiners (devices that merge light signals) with integer partition-based redundancy elimination to improve signal efficiency in optical logic circuits.

dac-2025-212.method: A compiler automatically identifies branches in secret-dependent code where different execution paths would take different amounts of time, then balances them using three instruction-level techniques: shadowing (duplicating operations), cogging (interleaving operations), and spiraling (rearranging operations). By making all paths take equal time, the technique prevents attackers from using timing measurements to deduce secrets. It works on code compiled for Intel SGX and AMD SEV, which are trusted execution environments—hardware-protected regions where sensitive computations run isolated.
dac-2025-212.key_novelty: It hardens branches at the instruction level to mask timing differences that source-level defenses miss, targeting Intel SGX and AMD SEV.

dac-2025-209.method: Point-CIM accelerates point cloud processing with a reconfigurable compute-in-memory unit (a special chip that performs calculations where data is stored and can be configured for different tasks). It uses three techniques to reduce unnecessary work: skipping multiplications by zero, reorganizing 3D point data in a spatial order (Voxel-Morton-sorted Partitioning) with minimum reference points per feature channel for better compression, and storing numbers in fewer bits (Bit-level Truncation Quantization) without needing extra hardware. An optimized data arrangement loads everything to the compute array in one sequence, avoiding repeated transfers between buffer and array.
dac-2025-209.key_novelty: Point-CIM's core idea is a reconfigurable compute-in-memory architecture that accelerates point cloud neural networks by exploiting bit-level sparsity (using fewer bits per number) through feature decomposition and compression-aware optimization.

dac-2025-216.method: Uses graphics processors (GPUs) to speed up track assignment by breaking the work into small, independent tasks that run in parallel. It separates routing resource computation from track assignment, allowing them to execute asynchronously (without waiting for each other in sequence). By considering both global network paths and local connections simultaneously, it produces better estimates of whether the routing will fit.
dac-2025-216.key_novelty: Separates routing resource computation from track assignment into independent tasks that the GPU can execute asynchronously, enabling efficient scheduling.

dac-2025-211.method: The system places approximate nearest neighbor search operations at different levels of the memory hierarchy based on their data-access patterns. Vector loading and distance computation—which read large amounts of data—run directly at the memory bank level (the hardware storage where data is kept), while sorting runs at the memory controller level (the hardware that manages data access) with selective filtering to block unnecessary data transfers. Since computation happens where data already is, there's no need for costly back-and-forth movement to the CPU or GPU. The architecture requires only minimal modifications to existing DRAM.
dac-2025-211.key_novelty: Approximate nearest neighbor search operations are distributed across the memory hierarchy—placing computation at the bank and controller levels where data naturally resides—using a unified execution model to eliminate redundant data transfers and reuse existing hardware.

dac-2025-207.method: Guarder jointly designs hardware and software to protect neural network models in RRAM (resistive memory). The hardware uses 3T2R cells (3 transistors and 2 resistors each) to reliably perform the multiply-accumulate operations neural networks need, and encodes the encryption key into the memory by tuning inverter voltages to set specific resistance levels. The software applies contrastive training (teaching the model to distinguish strongly between authorized and unauthorized cases) to make the model operate accurately only on authorized chips and poorly on unauthorized ones.
dac-2025-207.key_novelty: Guarder's core idea is encoding encryption keys in 3T2R RRAM cells via tuned inverter voltages, combined with contrastive training to make models work accurately only on authorized hardware.

dac-2025-210.method: A simulator models performance and cost across different hardware combinations (CPUs, GPUs, and specialized accelerators). Design space exploration tests many different ways to allocate hardware resources to prefill versus decoding stages, finding Pareto-optimal solutions where you can't improve one stage's performance without hurting the other's. This ensures the hardware chosen matches what each phase actually needs.
dac-2025-210.key_novelty: Instead of one hardware configuration for all LLM serving, this work separately optimizes hardware allocation for the prefill and decoding phases.

dac-2025-218.method: The approach treats a circuit as a graph (network of connected logic components and wires) and uses a graph transformer network—an AI model trained to learn structural relationships—to predict how electrical signals propagate through it. It learns these predictions from accurate but expensive SPICE simulations, capturing waveforms (signal shapes over time) and timing delays. The model achieves ~3% error compared to SPICE while running 3510× faster.
dac-2025-218.key_novelty: A graph transformer network learns to predict electrical signal propagation directly, replacing lookup-table timing methods with a structural model that maintains simulation accuracy at advanced chip nodes.

dac-2025-214.method: The system combines quick-rough estimates with slow-accurate simulations using a Gaussian process, which is a statistical model that predicts outcomes and estimates its own uncertainty. It learns which rough estimates are reliable by comparing them to accurate results, then runs expensive accurate simulations only when it needs confirmation of uncertain designs. This avoids both the cost of always running slow simulations and the inaccuracy of relying only on rough estimates.
dac-2025-214.key_novelty: The core idea is a statistical model that explicitly treats rough and accurate estimates as different-quality information, then identifies the best designs by checking which options beat others rather than assigning exact scores.

dac-2025-219.method: ALLMod reduces the hardware area required for LUT-based modular reduction by splitting the computation into two balanced workloads, inspired by iterative reduction. A template fairly distributes the work between them. The system explores different timing options for combining results from both workloads to find the optimal approach. By trading computation across the two workloads this way, ALLMod shrinks the total number of lookup tables needed while maintaining throughput.
dac-2025-219.key_novelty: Hybrid workload decomposition—splitting the computation into two balanced parts—reduces the hardware area required without sacrificing computation speed.

dac-2025-213.method: Older approaches to protecting memory use either backup copies or send data back and forth for error checking, creating heavy traffic on the CXL connection. This method uses Locally Recoverable Codes (LRC)—a type of error-correction code where you fix corrupted data using only nearby data blocks—running on the controller chip inside the CXL expander. By doing error correction where the data lives (on the expander), the main computer avoids sending redundant requests across the CXL fabric. This balances reliability against bandwidth cost, providing robust error protection without the overhead of traditional approaches.
dac-2025-213.key_novelty: The method offloads error correction to the CXL expander controller using Locally Recoverable Codes—a technique where error-fixing uses only nearby data blocks—eliminating redundant memory requests across the CXL fabric.

dac-2025-215.method: The system uses multiple AI agents trained with reinforcement learning—learning which settings produce good results by trying configurations and receiving reward signals—to adjust Image Signal Processor (ISP) parameters in real-time, without needing a proxy model as an intermediary. A master agent coordinates the others to ensure consistent adjustments across consecutive video frames. Two hardware optimizations, Strip Convolution Kernel and Stride-Aware Dual-Buffer Memory, reduce the neural network computation required for image processing, enabling real-time operation on FPGA or ASIC hardware.
dac-2025-215.key_novelty: Instead of using offline tuning or a proxy model, this system uses multiple AI agents trained with reinforcement learning to adjust Image Signal Processor (ISP) settings in real-time as the car drives, responding instantly to lighting and weather changes.

dac-2025-220.method: The accelerator solves the data-movement bottleneck in matrix operations (BLAS) by performing calculations directly inside non-volatile memory (persistent storage) where the data lives, rather than shuttling data to the CPU or GPU. It contains a unified floating-point arithmetic unit that adapts to handle different precision levels, since BLAS operations vary widely in their numerical requirements. The internal data pathways (dataflows) reconfigure to match the operation type: for operations limited by memory speed, it executes calculations in-memory; for computation-limited operations, it exploits the high parallelism from having many arithmetic units close to the data.
dac-2025-220.key_novelty: It's the first accelerator to perform matrix operations directly inside memory chips, with a flexible arithmetic unit and reconfigurable data pathways that handle simple operations through complex ones.

dac-2025-225.method: The method uses a diffusion-based generative model (an AI trained to reverse the process of corrupting data) to create circuit designs represented as directed acyclic graphs—connection diagrams with no loops. Constraint refinement then validates that the generated circuits follow valid digital logic rules. Finally, Monte Carlo tree search (a strategic exploration technique) removes redundant components to optimize each circuit.
dac-2025-225.key_novelty: The core idea is using a diffusion-based generative model to automatically generate circuit designs represented as directed acyclic graphs, with constraint-guided refinement to ensure the generated circuits follow valid digital logic.

dac-2025-221.method: ClusterKV compresses the KV cache by grouping tokens that mean similar things (semantic clustering) and deciding which clusters to keep—rather than permanently erasing tokens or simply grouping by position in the text. When processing long contexts, it selectively recalls only the most relevant semantic clusters, shrinking the cache to a 1K–2K token budget even for 32K-token inputs. The system uses efficient algorithms for clustering tokens, selecting which ones matter, indexing them, and caching the results.
dac-2025-221.key_novelty: Compressing the KV cache by grouping tokens by meaning (semantic clustering) and selectively recalling clusters, rather than permanently deleting tokens or using position-based grouping.

dac-2025-224.method: The system converts RTL code (the textual descriptions engineers write for circuits) into graph representations showing how components connect and data flows between them. A deep neural network then examines these graphs and learns to classify each node as either a security asset or regular component based on the structural patterns it observes in training data. The network's learned ability to recognize these patterns lets it automatically identify security assets without human intervention.
dac-2025-224.key_novelty: A deep neural network learns to automatically identify security assets by recognizing structural patterns in graph representations of RTL code (how engineers describe circuits in text), eliminating manual identification.

dac-2025-217.method: McPAL breaks down sparse weight matrices (collections of numbers where most are zero, allowing skipped computations) into irregular sparse vectors, then routes active computations through an in-memory butterfly network (an efficient traffic-distribution circuit) connected to processing-in-memory arrays (chips that do calculations where the data is stored). It scales vertically by stacking memory chips in 3D-HBM to minimize data travel distance, and horizontally via a 2.5D IO chiplet that handles inter-chip connections, avoiding the power and yield constraints of a single massive die.
dac-2025-217.key_novelty: Using an in-memory butterfly network (an efficient routing circuit) to route arbitrary sparse computations across multiple chiplets connected via stacked memory, avoiding monolithic die scaling limits.

dac-2025-226.method: The system moves similarity search computation to UPMEM units—processors built into or adjacent to memory chips—instead of doing it on the CPU. This avoids the data-movement bottleneck: since the search runs where the data already lives, far less data has to travel between memory and the processor. The system divvies up search tasks across multiple UPMEM processors based on their architecture and capabilities, keeping all of them busy to maximize total computing power.
dac-2025-226.key_novelty: Optimizing vector similarity search for UPMEM's in-memory processor architecture—rather than trying to run it on the CPU—eliminates the data-movement bottleneck.

dac-2025-222.method: DroidFuzz finds security bugs in proprietary device drivers by testing them at the boundary between hardware drivers and the operating system. It first explores which driver interfaces exist on the device, then generates test inputs that are valid on both sides of this boundary. Rather than using random data, it watches how the code behaves during testing and uses that feedback to probe deeper into driver logic.
dac-2025-222.key_novelty: The key idea is testing vendor-specific drivers and the operating system together at their boundary by generating test inputs that work on both sides, guided by how the code actually executes.

dac-2025-228.method: The server uses multiple different model branches (variations of the neural network) and combines their predictions together. When an attacker tries to reverse-engineer the original input from the mathematical calculation signals (called gradients), they see a scrambled mix from all the branches instead of a clear pattern. This obfuscation makes the attack much harder while keeping accuracy nearly the same, with under 5% overhead.
dac-2025-228.key_novelty: Multiple model branches working together hide the input's fingerprint in the gradients that attackers need to reconstruct it.

dac-2025-229.method: The method runs many different test patterns simultaneously across a GPU's thousands of cores to check whether two hardware designs always produce identical outputs. Each core runs a different test pattern in parallel, which is much faster than checking patterns one at a time on a CPU. When parallel simulation cannot definitively prove the designs are equivalent, it switches to a SAT-based solver (ABC) to complete the verification. On certain large designs, this GPU-based approach achieves 88x faster results than traditional CPU-based SAT solving.
dac-2025-229.key_novelty: Using parallel GPU simulation instead of SAT-based methods to check if two hardware designs produce equivalent outputs.

dac-2025-223.method: The approach organizes convolutional neural network computations into data streams that flow through multiple processor cores sequentially, which reduces expensive communication within and between cores. It strategically assigns the neural network's weights (the learned parameters) across the crossbar arrays (the hardware grids where calculations happen) to maximize their utilization. By minimizing handoffs between cores, the system reduces latency.
dac-2025-223.key_novelty: The core innovation combines stream-based scheduling with strategic weight placement to maximize crossbar utilization for convolutional neural network deployment on multi-core CIM (computing-in-memory) systems.

dac-2025-234.method: The compiler restructures nested loops using CGRA-specific transformations to expose parallelism and enable dataflow (direct data flow between operations without memory). It optimizes task pipelining across loops (overlapping iterations and stages so multiple loop passes execute in parallel). A scheduling algorithm coordinates the timing across the entire computation, creating efficient mappings that keep CGRA hardware heavily utilized with minimal user input.
dac-2025-234.key_novelty: The compiler jointly optimizes loop restructuring and task pipelining (overlapping iterations), rather than handling them separately, to efficiently map computation onto CGRA hardware.

dac-2025-230.method: The framework uses bit-slicing (storing each number as separate groups of individual bits) to handle outliers and normal values with different precision levels. Outliers—the rare, high-magnitude values—keep 8-bit precision, while regular values compress into 4-bit integers. By arranging these bits in an interleaved pattern, the system finds empty spaces (sparsity) in the high-precision sections, enabling the processor to optimize how data flows without expensive packing and unpacking. This avoids the serialization bottleneck that made previous outlier-aware compression methods impractical.
dac-2025-230.key_novelty: The core idea is using bit-slicing to separate outliers and normal values into different precision levels, eliminating the serialization work that slowed previous methods.

dac-2025-231.method: The researchers use Gem5, a computer system simulator, to test how well PCIe (the standard connection between a computer's main processor and accelerator cards) works with different memory configurations—DDR4, DDR5, GDDR6, and HBM2. They simulate a transformer accelerator that performs matrix multiplication as a realistic test case, measuring how performance varies across different memory setups. Their results show that the best configurations achieve 80% of the performance you'd get if the memory lived directly on the accelerator chip itself.
dac-2025-231.key_novelty: The core innovation is a system-level simulation framework for exploring how standard interconnects like PCIe perform with different accelerator designs.

dac-2025-236.method: The toolchain scans quantum circuits for unused qubits and fuses active gates together while skipping the empty ones—this 'sparsity-aware gate fusion' reduces the amount of computation needed. It then generates optimized code for the target platform: vectorized LLVM code for CPUs (processing multiple values in parallel) or PTX code for Nvidia GPUs. The system automatically selects the best fusion approach and platform for each circuit.
dac-2025-236.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining sparsity-aware gate fusion (skipping unused qubits) with platform-specific compilation (LLVM vectorization for CPUs, PTX generation for Nvidia GPUs).

dac-2025-232.method: The system caches successfully-created entangled pairs (connected quantum bits that affect each other) so they're ready immediately when needed. While quantum operations (individual computational steps) run, it continuously generates new pairs asynchronously in the background—meaning generation happens in parallel without pausing other work. A scheduler then adapts which operations execute next based on which pairs are currently available, eliminating idle waiting time.
dac-2025-232.key_novelty: The key idea is to adaptively schedule quantum operations as pairs become available while generating new pairs asynchronously in the background, preventing idle time from unpredictable entanglement latency.

dac-2025-239.method: Quorum is a quantum autoencoder that detects anomalies without training. It works by compressing normal data patterns into a compact quantum state, then reconstructing them—if anomalies fail to reconstruct well, they score higher as anomalies. This avoids the usual quantum learning problem of computing gradients, instead letting quantum properties handle the compression naturally.
dac-2025-239.key_novelty: Quorum detects anomalies by using quantum autoencoders (quantum circuits that compress and reconstruct data) without any training.

dac-2025-238.method: The accelerator combines different processor types on a Xilinx Versal ACAP chip—FPGA logic, CPUs, and specialized AI Engine cores designed for matrix math. The SVD algorithm is reorganized to align with what the AI Engines do best, and an automated tool explores different ways to split work across these components, picking the layout with the fastest speed and lowest power consumption.
dac-2025-238.key_novelty: The core idea is jointly optimizing the SVD algorithm and hardware layout to exploit Versal ACAP's AI Engine processors.

dac-2025-233.method: The solution runs the Poseidon hash algorithm on an FPGA (a chip that can be rewired to solve different problems), with hardware and software designed together to move data smoothly through the pipeline. Instead of building many separate multipliers for modular math (which wastes chip space), the design reuses one multiplier repeatedly, accomplishing the same work in less area. Intermediate results are stored in hierarchical caches on the chip (like layers of faster memory), so frequent lookups stay fast. The system schedules work to keep every stage of the pipeline busy, letting it build large Merkle trees efficiently with flexible parameters.
dac-2025-233.key_novelty: The key innovation is to accelerate Merkle tree construction by reusing the modular multiplier within each Poseidon hash and caching intermediate results on the chip.

dac-2025-241.method: This approach uses measurement-based uncomputation (MBU)—a technique where quantum measurement results eliminate the need for certain quantum gates—applied to single-qubit registers performing modular arithmetic. Rather than building all gates upfront, MBU probabilistically uses measurement outcomes to skip expensive Toffoli gates (the most resource-intensive operations in quantum circuits). The method is formalized specifically for modular arithmetic and tested across different modular adder architectures to verify it reduces both Toffoli gate counts and circuit depth.
dac-2025-241.key_novelty: The core contribution is formalizing measurement-based uncomputation for single-qubit modular arithmetic circuits, showing how quantum measurement outcomes can reduce Toffoli gate counts and circuit depth in resource-constrained quantum systems.

dac-2025-235.method: The approach uses a graphics processor (GPU) to speed up static timing analysis—the process of checking whether signals in a chip design propagate fast enough to meet timing targets. It starts from delay predictions of a commercial reference tool (one-time initialization), then fine-tunes itself on the GPU to match that tool's delay model. Because the engine's math is differentiable (you can compute how small changes propagate through the calculations), it can calculate gradients—directions for tweaking gate sizes and placements to improve timing—making incremental design updates 25 times faster than traditional methods.
dac-2025-235.key_novelty: A GPU-accelerated timing analyzer that is calibrated to match commercial tools (achieving 0.999 correlation) and differentiable, enabling gradient-based optimization across chip designs.

dac-2025-227.method: The system makes multimodal retrieval faster using three steps. It starts with in-memory hashing (where the hardware computes hashes right where data lives, avoiding expensive data movement), which quickly ranks candidates. Then content-addressable memory—specialized hardware that searches many items in parallel—filters the list further. Finally, it reranks survivors using cosine similarity to fix accuracy lost during the approximate hashing step.
dac-2025-227.key_novelty: The core idea is combining in-memory hashing (exploiting hardware's native ability to compute without data movement) and content-addressable memory (for parallel search) to eliminate both memory-bandwidth and search-speed bottlenecks.

dac-2025-237.method: The system builds a specialized processor on an FPGA that addresses three performance bottlenecks in Mamba models. First, it combines (fuses) multiplication and addition operations into single steps, using backward shifting to embed multiplication into subsequent operations and reduce intermediate data storage. Second, it skips computation on sparse data—mostly-empty tensors—by reorganizing data into groups and using a specialized fetcher that only retrieves non-zero values. Third, it uses a reconfigurable systolic array—a flexible grid of connected processing elements—to perform linear calculations while improving data reuse by keeping values in faster local memory.
dac-2025-237.key_novelty: A specialized FPGA processor combining operator fusion (merging operations), sparse skipping (computing only non-zero values), and a reconfigurable processing grid to speed up state-space models like Mamba by reducing data movement bottlenecks.

dac-2025-243.method: Tropical dynamically schedules the prompt-processing phase (prefill) and token-generation phase (decode) on shared workers, shifting work between them based on measured queue lengths and latencies. Instead of either permanently separating these phases onto different machines—which creates long queues—or always running them together—which causes slowdowns from interference—it adapts in real time. This balancing act lets the system simultaneously meet latency targets for both time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-token (TPOT).
dac-2025-243.key_novelty: Tropical combines the benefits of disaggregated LLM serving (low interference) and non-disaggregated serving (short queues) through dynamic scheduling, simultaneously achieving both time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-token (TPOT) latency targets.

dac-2025-240.method: The approach creates a kernel—a mathematical comparison tool—that respects how hardware designs are structured: as nested hierarchies of components rather than flat lists of parameters. It weights this comparison by analyzing synthesis reports to determine which components matter most. A clustering algorithm then uses this weighted comparison to group designs with similar architectural patterns, enabling rapid exploration of many design options in parallel on Gemmini-based RISC-V processors.
dac-2025-240.key_novelty: This is the first application of structure-aware comparison tools to hardware design space exploration, enabling direct comparison of designs based on their hierarchical organization.

dac-2025-244.method: The approach combines the Forward-Forward training method (which trains layers one at a time instead of using backpropagation) with INT8 quantization (using 8-bit integers instead of full-precision numbers), reducing memory and computation needs on edge devices. Training layers sequentially keeps gradients—the values that adjust network weights—stable when using low-bit numbers, because each layer processes independently. A look-ahead mechanism at each layer helps recover accuracy that would otherwise be lost from using fewer bits. The method is tested on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, a compact edge device with limited resources.
dac-2025-244.key_novelty: This is the first method that applies INT8 quantization to training neural networks, using the Forward-Forward algorithm's layer-by-layer approach to keep gradients stable and a look-ahead refinement to recover accuracy.

dac-2025-250.method: Easz moves the computationally expensive encoding work to a server instead of placing it on resource-limited IoT devices. The server uses a patch-erase algorithm (strategically removing image regions based on a learned sampler) to compress the image data. The IoT device then runs a small transformer-based neural network (a type of AI model) to reconstruct the erased pixels and recover the full image. The approach works at any compression level without switching between different models.
dac-2025-250.key_novelty: The first neural image compression system that does all the heavy encoding on a server and leaves only a lightweight reconstruction task on the edge device.

dac-2025-247.method: POLARIS uses explainable AI (a method that reveals which power patterns are most exploitable to attackers) to guide a masking approach that scrambles these patterns. It automatically builds its own training dataset without requiring security experts to manually label attacks. The framework then trains a model to specifically disguise the power patterns that attackers can most easily exploit, making mitigation efficient by focusing protection exactly where it matters most.
dac-2025-247.key_novelty: It's the first framework to use explainable AI to automatically identify and mask the power patterns most vulnerable to attackers, eliminating the need for manual security expertise.

dac-2025-242.method: Windowed arithmetic pre-computes values to speed up quantum factoring, but quantum computers must erase intermediate results afterward—a cleanup process called uncomputation that wastes quantum resources. This paper reduces the cost of this cleanup by about 50% using specialized techniques. The result is 1.5-3.4% fewer total quantum operations needed, depending on RSA key size, or optionally 16% faster execution with 12% more qubits.
dac-2025-242.key_novelty: In quantum windowed arithmetic, the expensive part isn't fetching pre-computed values but the cleanup (uncomputation) required afterward, which this technique reduces by 50%.

dac-2025-246.method: The approach represents circuit descriptions (SPICE netlists) as 3D point clouds—three-dimensional spatial arrangements—to efficiently handle massive circuits containing hundreds of thousands to millions of connection points. These point cloud representations, combined with circuit images, feed through a large neural network (a machine learning algorithm called a netlist transformer) that learns compact representations from both inputs. A final prediction model combines these learned representations to estimate voltage drop (the unwanted voltage loss that occurs across the circuit).
dac-2025-246.key_novelty: The innovation is representing circuit structure as 3D point clouds and combining this spatial representation with circuit images in a machine learning system to predict voltage drop on large circuits.

dac-2025-248.method: The method uses multiple learning agents (multi-agent reinforcement learning) that each explore different asymmetric ways to place circuit components, abandoning conventional symmetric design. Each placement is tested with simulations of its functional performance (how the circuit behaves) and timing performance (how fast it runs). The agents learn which asymmetric arrangements outperform symmetric placement because asymmetry better accommodates non-linear effects (how physical layout unpredictably impacts performance). Against simulated annealing, a standard optimization baseline, the learning agents produce superior results.
dac-2025-248.key_novelty: This is the first application of multi-agent reinforcement learning to analog circuit layout, discovering that asymmetric component placements work better with the circuits' non-linear physics than conventional symmetric designs.

dac-2025-252.method: The paper uses polynomial encoding—a technique for packing encrypted numbers into polynomials so computation can happen on encrypted data—to perform matrix multiplication under the Brakerski/Fan-Vercauteren homomorphic encryption scheme. It shows how to pack multiple matrix inputs and weights into these polynomials efficiently, regardless of matrix size. To speed this up, it designs custom hardware on an FPGA (the U250 chip) that works together with the main computer, dividing computation so each handles what it does best.
dac-2025-252.key_novelty: It performs encrypted matrix multiplication using polynomial encoding in the Brakerski/Fan-Vercauteren scheme, combined with FPGA hardware (U250) that optimizes work division between the accelerator and host computer.

dac-2025-254.method: InterConFuzz works by combining two complementary testing techniques: fuzzing, which systematically generates random inputs to explore system behavior, and symbolic execution, which analyzes all possible code paths those inputs could take through the system. The tool is built on UVM (Universal Verification Methodology, the industry-standard framework for hardware testing), allowing it to integrate into existing verification workflows. By applying this hybrid approach to NoC systems (the communication networks inside chips that coordinate many parallel operations), InterConFuzz exhaustively searches for security vulnerabilities in high-concurrency scenarios that traditional verification methods typically miss.
dac-2025-254.key_novelty: InterConFuzz combines fuzzing and symbolic execution to comprehensively verify the security of Network-on-Chip systems.

dac-2025-257.method: The attackers reverse-engineer out-of-band management interfaces—administrative channels built into Intel processors that operate separately from normal CPU operations—to access power consumption readings from the Package Configuration Space, a protected area that Intel's MSR filter doesn't defend. They deliberately disable certain CPU monitoring controls to synchronize when code executes inside a secure enclave (SGX or TDX) with simultaneous out-of-band power measurements. Since different operations consume varying amounts of power, analyzing these patterns reveals what the enclave is executing, enabling secret extraction that the existing in-band protections are designed to prevent.
dac-2025-257.key_novelty: This is the first demonstration that out-of-band management interfaces built into Intel processors can be exploited to conduct power side-channel attacks on confidential computing platforms like SGX and TDX, bypassing existing in-band defenses.

dac-2025-245.method: MiniWear creates a hybrid persistent cache—a fast memory layer made of both flash and slower SMR (Shingled Magnetic Recording) storage that survives power loss—with two separate tiers. Fine-grained software scheduling (detailed decision rules) determines which data goes to which tier to balance traffic efficiently. A proactive balancing strategy actively prevents either tier from sitting idle, distributing the mechanical wear evenly across both tiers to extend the flash storage's lifetime.
dac-2025-245.key_novelty: MiniWear introduces a hybrid persistent cache with flash and SMR tiers that actively balances workload between the tiers to distribute wear evenly and extend flash lifetime in EF-SMR systems.

dac-2025-251.method: Generates hypervectors on-the-fly (creating them as needed rather than pre-computing them) using Hadamard binary coefficients, achieving constant-time O(1) generation versus the conventional O(N) iterative search. Uses unary computing—where numbers are represented as counts—and in-memory computing (performing computation where data is stored, not shuttling data around) to reduce operations to addition only. An ASIC (custom hardware chip) implementation exploits Hadamard properties for efficiency.
dac-2025-251.key_novelty: The first hardware implementation to generate hypervectors on-the-fly using Hadamard binary coefficients in constant time O(1), replacing iterative search taking time proportional to vector count O(N).

dac-2025-256.method: An AI agent trained with reinforcement learning generates test programs and runs them in a simulator of a multicore processor—specifically a 16 or 32-core ARM system where multiple cores share memory using the MOESI coherence protocol. After each test, the agent observes what happens and learns to pull out meaningful patterns from those raw observations. Using this learned understanding, the agent gradually improves its test programs to better verify how the multiple cores interact with each other.
dac-2025-256.key_novelty: The main contribution is extracting meaningful state information from raw observations in a multicore simulator, which allows AI agents to automatically learn and generate better tests for verifying core interactions.

dac-2025-258.method: This is a review paper surveying how large language models—AI systems trained on vast amounts of text—can help automate silicon chip design. The authors review existing applications, evaluate which chip design tasks LLMs are ready to tackle, and identify research gaps that must be closed to expand their use.
dac-2025-258.key_novelty: The paper systematically maps where large language models can be applied to chip design automation tasks, evaluates their readiness for practical use, and identifies remaining research gaps.

dac-2025-259.method: The system starts with a fast filter that quickly estimates poses at each moment, then selectively refines them using local graph optimization—checking whether nearby poses fit together correctly. To keep computation manageable, it uses loop sparsification: it identifies representative loops (when the device returns to a location it's seen before) but only checks the ones closest together in time and space, skipping redundant constraints. This selective checking captures the accuracy benefits of graph-based optimization without the computational cost of handling every constraint.
dac-2025-259.key_novelty: Instead of optimizing the entire path at once like traditional graph-based methods, this system locally refines groups of nearby poses and selectively checks loop closures, combining the speed of filters with the accuracy of graphs.

dac-2025-255.method: Replay4NCL compresses stored old knowledge and replays it with fewer processing steps (spikes are electrical signals between neurons; reducing spikes cuts latency and energy). To overcome information loss from compression, the system automatically adjusts two settings: the neuron firing threshold (how easily neurons activate) and the learning rate (how quickly they learn). These adjustments keep the model accurate despite the compression.
dac-2025-255.key_novelty: The core idea is pairing compressed-memory replay with automatic adjustment of neuron firing thresholds and learning rates, allowing fast replay while keeping the model accurate.

dac-2025-253.method: The framework strategically adds or removes glitches (brief electrical pulses that occur unintentionally in circuits) by adjusting the size of logic gates—the small building blocks controlling signal flow in hardware. Adjusting gate sizes changes when electrical signals arrive at different points in the circuit, enabling the framework to control glitch behavior; this timing control is formulated as a geometric programming optimization problem (a mathematical approach that finds the best solution within constraints). Computer simulations validated the approach on three encryption algorithms—AES, CLEFIA, and SM4—ensuring they still work correctly and maintain good performance.
dac-2025-253.key_novelty: This is the first framework to strategically add or remove glitches (brief electrical pulses) to reduce power side-channel leakage—where attackers infer cryptographic keys by observing power consumption patterns—using geometric programming optimization.

dac-2025-261.method: PyraNet is an open-source collection of Verilog code (the language engineers use to describe hardware) organized in layers that progress from simple components to complete designs. When fine-tuning (customizing) large language models with this structured data, the layered organization helps the models learn the systematic patterns of correct hardware code. By training on organized examples rather than random data, the LLMs learn to generate Verilog that is both syntactically correct (follows language rules) and functionally correct (actually works as intended).
dac-2025-261.key_novelty: The core innovation is organizing Verilog code in layers—from simple circuits to complex designs—so that language models can learn to generate correct hardware code more effectively.

dac-2025-263.method: The team tested different types of prediction models (called surrogate models) to see which ones most accurately estimate how fast neural networks run on GPUs. They examined every step of the process—how training data is collected, which model type to choose, and how to train it—to understand what actually matters for accurate predictions. They built the ESM framework as a systematic toolkit that helps you generate reliable training data and automatically pick or build the best prediction model while keeping computational costs in mind.
dac-2025-263.key_novelty: ESM is a systematic approach to building accurate GPU-performance prediction models by identifying which factors actually matter at each stage—from data collection to model selection to training.

dac-2025-249.method: CXL-Interplay investigates how conventional memory and storage systems slow down CXL (Compute Express Link, a standard for memory and storage expansion) by testing on real CXL hardware. The team measures CPU performance metrics and monitors operating-system-level activity to reverse-engineer the specific resource conflicts causing slowdowns. They then test and evaluate solutions that reduce these interference effects.
dac-2025-249.key_novelty: CXL-Interplay is the first systematic characterization of Compute Express Link (a standard for memory and storage expansion) interference on real hardware and the first to reverse-engineer the interference mechanisms using performance metrics.

dac-2025-271.method: ADVISOR uses a fast scoring system called the Approximation Friendliness Index (AFI) to predict which hardware designs will work well with approximation (reducing precision to trade accuracy for speed and power). Instead of fully approximating every design variant—which is computationally expensive—it only applies the full approximation process to designs with high AFI scores. This filtering approach lets the tool explore 68 times faster than exhaustive exploration, because it avoids wasting computation on designs unlikely to benefit from approximation.
dac-2025-271.key_novelty: A static scoring metric (AFI) that quickly identifies which hardware designs will benefit most from approximation, eliminating the need to fully approximate every design variant during exploration.

dac-2025-265.method: PICK puts the k-nearest neighbor search inside SRAM memory itself (processing-in-memory), eliminating trips to slow off-chip storage. It processes distances bit-by-bit to reduce latency, filters out distant points early, and selects the k closest neighbors in constant time regardless of k's value. Two pipelined stages run in parallel—distance calculation and top-k selection—completing the entire search while staying on-chip.
dac-2025-265.key_novelty: Bit-serial processing-in-memory with filtering-and-selection and two-stage pipelining enables constant-time k-nearest neighbor search confined to on-chip SRAM, bypassing off-chip memory entirely.

dac-2025-262.method: The design uses magnetic tunnel junctions (devices exploiting magnetic properties to process information) in a unified circuit serving two functions simultaneously. The circuit acts as a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron—it accumulates electrical signals, gradually leaks them away, and fires when reaching a threshold, mimicking how biological neurons work. The same circuit simultaneously functions as a physically unclonable function, generating a unique security key based on unavoidable random physical variations in the device. This unified approach combines energy-efficient, brain-inspired computing with hardware-based security in a single integrated component.
dac-2025-262.key_novelty: The first single magnetic circuit that simultaneously functions as a spiking neuron and a physically unclonable function, combining brain-inspired computing with hardware-based security in one integrated device.

dac-2025-264.method: Uses specialized hardware features (Micro Trace Buffer and Data Watchpoint and Trace Unit) built into microcontrollers to automatically log program execution paths while code runs, without adding monitoring code or pausing execution. Because logging happens in hardware separate from the running program, it eliminates the performance overhead that made previous approaches too slow. The authors validated the technique on open-source systems.
dac-2025-264.key_novelty: This is the first to use existing hardware debug features (Micro Trace Buffer and Data Watchpoint and Trace Unit) in microcontrollers to track which code runs when (control flow) in parallel, eliminating the performance cost that made previous verification approaches impractical.

dac-2025-272.method: PoP-ECC protects memory using a two-level checksum system. It first computes checksums (Virtual Parities) from the data, then computes checksums of those checksums (Parities of Parities). This hierarchical nesting lets the system pinpoint and fix multiple simultaneous bit errors while adjusting protection strength based on actual error patterns—all with minimal memory and power overhead.
dac-2025-272.key_novelty: Hierarchical checksums—creating checksums from checksums—enable flexible, adjustable correction of multiple simultaneous bit errors.

dac-2025-267.method: The framework uses two neural networks working in parallel. The first (CNN—a network that processes information like images) analyzes power distribution as spatial patterns at multiple scales, blending fine details with broad system-wide effects through modules called LLE and HACG in Power ScaleFusion UNet; the second (GNN—a network designed for graphs and connections) captures how voltage propagates through the power network's topology by gathering information from connected neighbors via a CVA module. Transfer learning enables the model to quickly adapt to new circuits using only a few examples.
dac-2025-267.key_novelty: The innovation is combining spatial power pattern analysis (CNN) with voltage-flow topology analysis (GNN), where each compensates for the other's limitations.

dac-2025-260.method: The system measures quantum states at three distinct energy levels (not just binary on/off). It uses matched filters—tuned signal patterns designed to spot known error types—to detect two specific faults: energy leaking out of qubits (relaxation errors) and unexpected energy jumps (excitation errors). It then applies a modular lightweight neural network that corrects crosstalk—interference from neighboring qubits affecting the measurement. The detection processes data one bit at a time and runs on standard FPGA hardware.
dac-2025-260.key_novelty: Using specialized matched filters and modular lightweight neural networks achieves 60x reduction in FPGA resources and 100x reduction in network size for efficient multi-level quantum readout.

dac-2025-269.method: The approach builds a constraint graph—a network showing how components relate spatially on the circuit board—to arrange them without overlaps or violations. Instead of using simple bounding boxes, it models irregular shapes more accurately by breaking them into rectangles using a slicing technique. It then applies Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP)—a mathematical method for solving optimization problems that mix continuous and discrete choices—to find valid placements that satisfy all constraints. This works even when components have different shapes, rotations, and densities packed together.
dac-2025-269.key_novelty: It combines constraint graphs, slicing-based component modeling, and MILP optimization to enable PCB placement of complex, heterogeneous, irregular-shaped, and any-oriented components in dense designs.

dac-2025-266.method: ReChisel starts by having an AI write code in Chisel, a programming language designed specifically for describing hardware circuits. The generated code is then tested using a compiler and simulator (tools that check if the code works), and any errors or failures are reported back to the AI. The AI takes this feedback and rewrites the code to fix what went wrong, then the cycle repeats—test the new code, get feedback, improve the code. The system keeps doing this until the code works correctly, and it includes a mechanism to escape if it gets stuck repeating the same failed attempts.
dac-2025-266.key_novelty: For the first time, an AI system can automatically generate Chisel hardware code by iteratively refining its output based on feedback from compiler and simulator tests.

dac-2025-268.method: The processor dynamically selects between two instruction variants based on the sensitivity of its data: fast optimized versions for public data, and secure variants that prevent side-channel attacks for sensitive data. This selection happens at the decode stage during runtime. The implementation was built on RISC-V BOOM, an out-of-order processor.
dac-2025-268.key_novelty: The core idea is a data-aware mechanism that automatically selects secure instruction variants for sensitive data and optimized variants for public data—providing protection against microarchitectural attacks (information leaks through processor timing) with zero performance overhead.

dac-2025-278.method: The framework runs different versions of code on simulated computers—programs that mimic exactly how real processors execute instructions—instead of needing actual hardware. Machine learning models trained on statistics from these simulations predict how each code version would perform on real hardware. When tested on simulators for x86, ARM, and RISC-V processors (three common processor types), the models consistently ranked the fastest implementation in the top 3% of all tested versions.
dac-2025-278.key_novelty: Replacing actual hardware execution with simulated computers and machine learning predictions when searching for the fastest way to run ML code.

dac-2025-275.method: The method teaches LLMs to generate hardware test stimuli (test inputs designed to find bugs in chips) using two stages. First, it builds a structured dataset formatted as tables, which teaches the LLM to produce consistent, predictable outputs. Second, it applies reinforcement learning—the LLM receives feedback rewarding tests that achieve good coverage (thoroughly exercise the hardware) and correctness—so the model learns from these rewards and improves over time.
dac-2025-275.key_novelty: It improves LLM test generation by combining table-shaped datasets (which ensure consistent output format) with reinforcement learning feedback (which rewards high-quality tests).

dac-2025-276.method: The traditional approach reserves backside metal layers for power delivery from the start, limiting how signal routing (the data paths between circuits) can optimize and hurting performance. BS-PDN-Last reverses this order: it lets signal routing optimize for speed and performance first by using as much backside space as needed, then fits the power delivery network into the space that remains. This reordering works because signal routing is harder to reroute than power distribution. The method uses vector-based IR-drop analysis—a calculation that predicts voltage drop (power wasted as heat in the wires)—to ensure the final power network still delivers power reliably.
dac-2025-276.key_novelty: Deferring power delivery network design to after signal routing gives performance-critical signal routing priority for the backside metal.

dac-2025-280.method: Creates QUBIKOS, a benchmark test suite with circuit problems where the optimal number of SWAP gates (the minimum hardware rearrangement operations needed to route quantum information between connected qubits) is mathematically proven. Tests four leading QLS tools—LightSabre, ML-QLS, QMAP, and tket—by comparing the SWAP gates each produces against the known-optimal count, revealing substantial performance gaps. Examines specific cases where tools underperformed to extract insights for improving future QLS algorithms.
dac-2025-280.key_novelty: QUBIKOS is the first benchmark set with provably-optimal SWAP counts, enabling direct measurement of how far each QLS tool's solutions fall short of the theoretical best.

dac-2025-270.method: The method searches for better designs by using gradient-based optimization (climbing uphill) in a continuous mathematical space, then uses a diffusion model (trained to convert solutions into valid synthesis sequences) to translate those continuous points back into actual transformations. A separate model predicts how good each design is based on area and delay, guiding the search. The diffusion model ensures every solution remains valid.
dac-2025-270.key_novelty: Using diffusion models to translate continuous optimization into valid synthesis sequences, enabling efficient gradient-based search on a problem with exponentially many possibilities.

dac-2025-277.method: The hardware generates random numbers using quantum tunneling in specially designed transistors, rather than computing them in software. Quantum tunneling is a quantum-mechanical effect where electrons pass through energy barriers they shouldn't classically be able to cross—this inherently random process produces numbers with the bell-curve distribution (Gaussian) that Bayesian neural networks need. This approach is extremely efficient at 200 femtojoules per sample with 0.997 correlation to true randomness, and multiple generators run in parallel for fast inference.
dac-2025-277.key_novelty: Quantum tunneling in transistors directly generates randomness on-chip for Bayesian neural network inference, eliminating software computation overhead.

dac-2025-274.method: RADiT detects redundancy by examining blocks of input features to find when consecutive timesteps repeat the same computation. When redundancy is found, it reuses the previous result instead of recomputing. The Dynamic Threshold Scaling Module adjusts how strict the similarity check is to preserve accuracy, while the Compress and Compare Unit identifies when input blocks are similar enough to reuse.
dac-2025-274.key_novelty: Diffusion transformers repeat computations across consecutive timesteps with similar input blocks; RADiT detects this similarity using adjustable thresholds and reuses results rather than recomputing.

dac-2025-279.method: ARCANE puts a computing unit directly inside the cache memory—the fast storage between your CPU and main memory. A RISC-V controller (a processor using a standard instruction set) takes custom instructions from the main CPU and runs vector operations (calculations on multiple data items at once) on data already stored in cache. Because computation happens where data sits, instead of moving data back and forth to a distant processor, most data stays fast. The architecture automatically handles data placement and synchronization, so programmers never need to manually move data around.
dac-2025-279.key_novelty: Computing moves into the cache using RISC-V instructions, with automatic data placement eliminating manual data movement.

dac-2025-281.method: INSIGHT predicts analog circuit performance by building predictions step-by-step using transformers, neural networks that learn how information flows through sequences. Rather than retraining for each new chip manufacturing technology, it uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation), a technique that updates only a small part of the model to adapt its knowledge. This approach requires 60% less training data for new technologies, while reducing memory usage by 42% and training time by 25%.
dac-2025-281.key_novelty: A neural circuit simulator that predicts performance step-by-step (using transformers) and efficiently adapts to different chip manufacturing technologies through LoRA.

dac-2025-283.method: MHDiff identifies the most important pixels (focal pixels) at the start and keeps them in high precision throughout all steps, while using low precision for other pixels to save memory. A packing module then combines these high and low-precision pixels into complete high-precision matrices, avoiding the expensive memory accesses that mixed-precision methods need to separately load raw data. This lets the PE array process full matrices efficiently without hitting memory bottlenecks.
dac-2025-283.key_novelty: Selective precision based on pixel importance combined with packing into complete high-precision matrices eliminates memory bottlenecks while keeping hardware fully utilized.

dac-2025-285.method: X-SAT combines Conflict-Driven Clause Learning (CDCL)—learning from contradictions found during search to avoid repeating mistakes—with two circuit-specific techniques. First, it simplifies the problem by removing redundant variables and logical statements while preserving the circuit structure. Second, it guides the search with branching heuristics (decision rules) tailored to how arithmetic circuits are organized, so the solver explores the most promising paths first.
dac-2025-285.key_novelty: X-SAT's core idea is that arithmetic circuit solvers should exploit circuit structure in both problem simplification and search decisions, rather than treating circuits as generic logical formulas.

dac-2025-273.method: Precon uses a single processing unit that can switch between 16-bit floating-point (FP16, a decimal number format) and integer arithmetic. By reusing core logic and controlling how data moves through the chip and the sequence of operations, the same hardware can execute three different low-precision combinations: INT4-FP16, INT4-INT4, and INT4-INT8.
dac-2025-273.key_novelty: A single processing unit that can dynamically switch between 16-bit floating-point (FP16) and integer arithmetic, enabling one hardware design to efficiently support various low-precision models without specialized variants.

dac-2025-289.method: The system uses reinforcement learning—an AI technique where an agent learns by taking actions and receiving rewards—to create adversarial (disguised) versions of Linux malware. It does this by adding NOPs (no-operation instructions that do nothing) into the running code in patterns that confuse malware detectors. These extra instructions don't change what the malware does—it keeps its original behavior intact. Over time, the AI learns which NOP placement patterns best hide the malware from detection.
dac-2025-289.key_novelty: Using reinforcement learning to generate Linux malware that evades detection by strategically injecting harmless no-operation instructions while preserving the malware's original functionality.

dac-2025-290.method: Stochastic computing represents numbers as sequences of random bits, where the proportion of 1s encodes the value, and performs arithmetic using only simple logic gates—naturally tolerating electrical noise. Division is implemented inside MTJ (magnetic tunnel junction) memory, a type of emerging non-volatile memory, so the computation occurs where data lives rather than requiring transfers to a distant processor. MTJ substrates have inherent noise and manufacturing variation, so this approach gives you arithmetic that works despite defects that would break traditional binary operations.
dac-2025-290.key_novelty: Stochastic computing performs division directly inside MTJ crossbar memory arrays, making arithmetic robust to the manufacturing defects and electrical noise inherent in emerging memory substrates.

dac-2025-292.method: LA-MTL searches for the best way to share neural network layers across multiple tasks on embedded devices by directly measuring how fast each design will run during the search using an Analytical Latency Factor (ALF). Rather than searching for the best model first and then trying to speed it up afterward, ALF captures both individual layer speeds and full-model speeds as the search happens. This lets the system find designs that simultaneously balance accuracy, parameter efficiency (how many weights to store), and inference latency (how fast predictions run) without needing to redesign solutions after the search completes.
dac-2025-292.key_novelty: The Analytical Latency Factor (ALF) directly measures how fast a model design will run during the search, letting the system find models that are both accurate and efficient without needing to redesign them afterward for speed.

dac-2025-282.method: The SambaNova SN40L uses a reconfigurable dataflow unit (a processing block where data flows through computation stages rather than repeatedly fetching instructions from memory) combined with three levels of memory—on-chip SRAM, intermediate-speed HBM (high-bandwidth memory), and DDR. This dataflow design enables aggressive compute-graph fusion (combining multiple computation steps into single super-fast operations), which maximizes performance during token generation (when the AI produces output). The three-tier memory hierarchy reduces the silicon footprint needed to store trillions of parameters.
dac-2025-282.key_novelty: The core idea is using a dataflow-based, reconfigurable processor (where computation flows through stages rather than fetching instructions) with a three-tier memory system to efficiently generate AI tokens and host multiple models.

dac-2025-294.method: The system automatically customizes tree structures for integrity checking by reshaping the Bonsai Merkle Tree—a hierarchical format where each level holds cryptographic fingerprints to detect data tampering—to match how the specific DNN workload accesses memory. It runs an algorithm to explore different tree shapes and selects whichever one verifies memory fastest while maintaining the cryptographic guarantee that nothing has been changed. By matching the tree shape to actual memory access patterns, it eliminates the normal tradeoff between speed and security.
dac-2025-294.key_novelty: Automatically reshaping the integrity-checking tree to match each workload's memory access patterns eliminates the speed-versus-security bottleneck in DNN accelerator data verification.

dac-2025-287.method: YieldAgent uses multiple AI agents (large language models organized in three layers) to automatically choose the best way to estimate yield—the percentage of working chips from a manufacturing batch. For each circuit, it analyzes the circuit's design and historical manufacturing data to select the right estimation approach. The system retrieves relevant semiconductor knowledge from a database (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) to improve accuracy, and automatically adjusts settings for different chip manufacturing processes using Tree-structured Parzen Estimators.
dac-2025-287.key_novelty: Using AI agents to automatically select the best yield-estimation method (Monte Carlo, importance sampling, or machine learning) for each circuit, with retrieved semiconductor knowledge and automatic parameter tuning.

dac-2025-284.method: CIMFlow provides a complete workflow for designing neural network accelerators using compute-in-memory (CIM)—a technique that calculates data where it's stored, eliminating slow memory access. It works by connecting two usually separate steps: converting neural network code into hardware instructions, and simulating those instructions on hardware. This connection is made through a flexible instruction set—the customizable set of operations the hardware can perform—so designers can quickly test different design options. To handle compute-in-memory's main limitation (limited storage space), the framework automatically splits neural network calculations into smaller pieces and runs them in parallel, ensuring everything fits in available memory.
dac-2025-284.key_novelty: CIMFlow bridges software compilation and hardware simulation for compute-in-memory accelerators, using intelligent partitioning to overcome storage constraints.

dac-2025-288.method: Me-MPK first creates a unified dependency graph—a complete map of all data dependencies and conflicts in the sparse matrix. It then recursively partitions this matrix into independent chunks separated by a buffer zone, each optimized for the CPU's specific architecture. Since the chunks run in a specific parallel order and have no conflicts between them, the CPU can reuse data in its cache while eliminating synchronization delays between processors.
dac-2025-288.key_novelty: A unified dependency graph combined with recursive partitioning solves parallelization conflicts in sparse matrix operations—including symmetric matrices—while maximizing cache reuse.
