dac-2025-300.method: Grasp predicts which mathematical operations in a neural network can be skipped by looking at the size (magnitude) of numbers at each calculation step. It works without any training by grouping numbers together based on how they're distributed throughout a vector, and it specially handles extreme statistical outliers—unusual values that would otherwise confuse the prediction. By correctly predicting which calculations will output zero, Grasp lets computers skip that computation and memory access entirely, saving time and energy.
dac-2025-300.key_novelty: The innovation is grouping numbers by their distribution and explicitly handling statistical outliers to predict which activations will be zero in ReLU-fied LLMs (neural networks where negative values automatically become zero).

dac-2025-296.method: CircuitGPS treats each circuit as a graph—a network where components are nodes and electrical coupling between them are connections. It uses a Transformer model (a machine learning system that learns patterns in networks) to analyze small neighborhoods of this graph. First, it learns to predict which component pairs are electrically coupled; then it learns how strong those couplings are. The system encodes structural information about each neighborhood, allowing it to learn from just a few labeled examples.
dac-2025-296.key_novelty: CircuitGPS learns to predict parasitic capacitance from few labeled examples by treating circuits as graphs with a Transformer model that captures structure, enabling it to work on new circuit designs without retraining.

dac-2025-297.method: VSpGEMM is a specialized accelerator built on Xilinx Versal, a reconfigurable chip combining fixed math units called AI Engines with programmable logic. It introduces BCSX, a storage format that reorganizes sparse matrix data into regular block patterns for both row-major and column-major data layouts, eliminating the random memory access that normally slows sparse computation. The system uses multi-level tiling to decompose the problem into nested layers of chunks, each sized to fit in an AI Engine's local memory. It then partitions the work: AI Engines handle repetitive calculations efficiently, while programmable logic orchestrates combining intermediate results, which reduces data movement between components.
dac-2025-297.key_novelty: BCSX, a block-wise storage format that converts irregular sparse data into regular memory access patterns, enabling efficient hierarchical execution split between fixed and programmable hardware.

dac-2025-286.method: The approach uses special transistors (double-gate ferroelectric FETs) wired for compute-in-memory, where calculations happen directly without repeated data movement. Instead of recalculating total energy each time a variable changes (O(n²) operations), the incremental-E transformation computes only the energy change (O(n) operations). To handle the expensive exponential calculations needed for annealing, it uses simpler fractional approximations. All computation happens inside the hardware itself (in-situ), controlled by adjusting a back-gate voltage.
dac-2025-286.key_novelty: The incremental-E transformation reduces energy computation from O(n²) to O(n) by calculating only energy changes, and when combined with ferroelectric compute-in-memory hardware, it enables in-situ annealing.

dac-2025-302.method: Instead of testing for individual broken transistors (the traditional approach), this methodology designs tests to catch timing slowdowns from random manufacturing variations in transistor threshold voltages—the voltage levels that control when transistors turn on. When multiple performance-critical transistors drift the same way due to manufacturing randomness, the chip becomes just barely too slow to work, even though no single component is defective. The tests target these correlated multi-transistor variations directly, rather than assuming transistors either work perfectly or fail completely.
dac-2025-302.key_novelty: Instead of testing for single broken transistors, the methodology targets timing failures caused by random manufacturing variations in transistor threshold voltages that affect multiple devices together.

dac-2025-295.method: pact approximates how many solutions exist for formulas that combine discrete variables (with specific values like integers) and continuous variables (with values in a range). It uses hash functions—mathematical techniques that divide solution spaces into regions—to make only a logarithmic number of solver queries, meaning the number of queries grows slowly as you add more variables. The method provides theoretical error bounds on how far the approximation can be from correct and handles continuous variables that traditional bit-blasting approaches cannot.
dac-2025-295.key_novelty: Using hash functions to partition solution spaces and efficiently approximate solution counts in hybrid formulas with logarithmic solver query complexity.

dac-2025-303.method: WISEDRAM uses one row of special X-cells to perform bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR—combining data bits) directly in DRAM, while keeping all normal data reads and writes identical to standard DRAM procedures. This separation—computation in special cells, storage in normal cells—preserves DRAM's reliability while enabling parallel in-DRAM computation.
dac-2025-303.key_novelty: WISEDRAM is the first system to enable in-DRAM bitwise operations while keeping the conventional DRAM cell access procedures unchanged, preserving the reliability of standard DRAM.

dac-2025-301.method: EffiCast trains two types of neural networks (LSTMs and Transformers, which learn patterns from sequences of events) on data describing how much power different processor cores consume under varying conditions: different voltage and frequency levels, different application phases, and when cores compete for the same resources. The models predict what the system will need next, enabling the processor to adjust power use dynamically. On real processors, each prediction completes in just 1.82 milliseconds, fast enough to guide real-time power management decisions.
dac-2025-301.key_novelty: EffiCast forecasts energy efficiency in heterogeneous processors (those with different core types) by training neural networks to learn patterns in sequences of system events and resource contention, replacing static prediction models with adaptive deep learning.

dac-2025-291.method: The approach breaks a large quantum graph state into smaller, more manageable pieces and compiles each piece independently to reduce complexity. It then reassembles these pieces while using a graph transformation technique called local complementation, which rearranges how the quantum connections form to reduce overhead. The system schedules the resulting circuits to use the emitter resources (the quantum light sources) as efficiently as possible.
dac-2025-291.key_novelty: The core idea is using graph partitioning with local complementation transforms and hierarchical scheduling to compile quantum states specifically for emitter-photonic hardware.

dac-2025-309.method: The tool simulates metal erosion in stacked chips (2.5D/3D chiplet systems) by running electrical and thermal models together, updating them at each time step. It uses FVM (finite volume method—splitting space into small regions to calculate heat distribution) to map temperature and current in the vertical connections between dies (TSVs), and FDTD (finite difference time domain—a grid-based solver) to track stress buildup and void nucleation and growth. As simulation progresses, these effects reinforce each other: current causes heat (Joule heating), which accelerates metal migration and void growth; voids increase electrical resistance, which changes voltage drop (IR drop) and generates more heat, which shifts mechanical stress—making it possible to catch failure modes that treating each effect separately would miss.
dac-2025-309.key_novelty: This tool is the first to simulate metal erosion in the vertical connections (TSVs) between stacked chips (2.5D/3D chiplets) by jointly modeling electrical flow, heat, stress, and void growth—effects that previous tools treated separately or ignored.

dac-2025-307.method: The approach trains a reinforcement learning agent—a system that learns by trying different options and receiving feedback on results—to select hub nodes (central connection points) that balance two competing goals: keeping wiring cost low and keeping timing differences (clock skew) small. The agent explores different configurations, learning which selections better balance these tradeoffs. By adapting its strategy based on what works, it finds effective hub nodes without evaluating every possible combination.
dac-2025-307.key_novelty: Uses reinforcement learning—a system that learns by experimenting and adjusting its approach based on feedback—to automatically select hub nodes that balance wiring cost and clock timing differences.

dac-2025-299.method: The approach preprocesses circuit satisfiability problems using logic synthesis—techniques to restructure and simplify circuits. It applies lookup-table mapping, which transforms the circuit logic into simplified forms easier for SAT solvers to work with, guided by a reinforcement learning agent that learns which specific transformations produce the fastest solutions. Rather than using the same strategy for all problems, the RL agent customizes its transformation approach for each circuit instance.
dac-2025-299.key_novelty: Reinforcement learning optimizes circuit preprocessing strategies (via lookup-table mapping) for each problem instance, learning which transformations yield the fastest SAT solving.

dac-2025-298.method: ReMaP positions large blocks (macros) around the chip's perimeter using ABPlace—an angle-based analytical placement method with ellipse geometry—which simultaneously minimizes data movement between blocks and prevents overlaps. A rule-based algorithm then refines these positions to align blocks exactly with the chip's physical boundaries, matching how expert chip designers place blocks. The entire process repeats recursively to iteratively improve placement quality, with automatic optimization of the tool's internal settings.
dac-2025-298.key_novelty: Angle-based analytical placement (ABPlace) combined with iterative boundary-guided relocation to match expert macro placement practices.

dac-2025-305.method: The solver uses nested domain decomposition—dividing the massive power grid problem into smaller regions solved in parallel—while computing mathematical summaries (Schur complements) at multiple hierarchical levels. Rather than combining billions or trillions of nodes into one giant summary at the end, it first builds intermediate summaries from groups of regions, then combines those summaries together. This staged approach keeps each computational step manageable and prevents the dense matrix calculations from becoming impractically large, which is the core limitation of traditional domain decomposition at this scale.
dac-2025-305.key_novelty: The innovation is using intermediate Schur complements—mathematical summaries computed at intermediate levels—in the nested decomposition to prevent the global summary from growing too large and dense to solve efficiently when handling billions to trillions of nodes in parallel.

dac-2025-306.method: The method creates a unified verification problem by combining the system being checked with a Büchi automaton (a mathematical machine for checking properties over infinite sequences) that represents the desired property. It then partitions the nested fixpoint calculations—the iterative verification process that finds the stable result satisfying the property—across this combined model-property structure and distributes them across multiple computers. A fairness-aware labeling function tracks states during this distributed computation, ensuring that infinite behaviors are treated impartially and that correctness under fairness constraints is maintained.
dac-2025-306.key_novelty: It is the first parallel symbolic model checking approach for full LTL properties, using fairness-aware state labeling to partition nested fixpoint calculations across the model-property product automaton.

dac-2025-304.method: When one sub-core has an instruction stuck waiting for data, ACRS borrows an idle functional unit from an adjacent sub-core to run it instead. The first module (SF_ISSUE) detects stuck instructions and idle neighboring units, then sends the instruction across; the second module (SF_WriteBack) sends the result back. By always targeting the same adjacent sub-core, ACRS avoids expensive rewiring.
dac-2025-304.key_novelty: ACRS dynamically shares functional units among adjacent sub-cores in partitioned GPUs by offloading instructions waiting for data to idle neighbors.

dac-2025-308.method: HiSpTRSV breaks the sparse triangular solve computation into tiles and identifies opportunities for parallel work across them. It builds a dependency graph—a map showing which calculations depend on each other—to determine which tiles can run simultaneously. To manage data movement between tiles and balance computational load, it applies bidirectional matching and modular indexing techniques that organize memory access and reduce communication costs. Unlike previous FPGA accelerators that only parallelized within tiles, this approach exploits parallelism across multiple tiles.
dac-2025-308.key_novelty: It's the first to parallelize sparse triangular solve across multiple tiles on an FPGA by solving the data communication and workload distribution obstacles that previously blocked this approach.

dac-2025-314.method: The approach automatically constructs a decision tree—a series of conditional tests that identify which instruction a processor is executing—instead of requiring humans to manually design decoders. It uses information theory (math that measures how much each question reduces uncertainty) to decide which tests to include at each level and in what order. The algorithm simultaneously optimizes for correctness and speed, ensuring all instructions are properly identified with minimal decoding time.
dac-2025-314.key_novelty: This is the first decoder-generation approach using information theory and decision trees to handle irregular instruction sets—processors whose instructions follow complex, non-uniform rules—including those with intricate logical conditions and nested special cases.

dac-2025-313.method: ResISC converts images directly to residue number system format (RNS—a remainder-based way of encoding numbers) inside the image sensor itself, which avoids the costly step of moving image data around. A specialized CNN accelerator built from SOT-MRAM cells (magnetic memory devices) then processes this RNS-encoded data, using a mixed-radix unit to efficiently perform activation operations directly in the RNS format. The system also selectively deactivates unused processing channels to further cut power consumption.
dac-2025-313.key_novelty: ResISC is the first integrated sensing-computing system to use residue number system (a remainder-based number format) for both image encoding and CNN processing.

dac-2025-311.method: Local-GS uses order-independent rendering—a method that displays 3D objects made from overlapping Gaussians (mathematical shapes) without requiring front-to-back processing order. Normally, rendering order creates dependencies that force sequential processing, but removing this requirement allows nearby Gaussians to be processed in parallel. The same hardware cores simultaneously handle both rendering (drawing the image) and gradient propagation (the learning process), which makes efficient use of processors in resource-limited edge devices.
dac-2025-311.key_novelty: Local-GS is the first GPU accelerator for training Gaussian Splatting on edge devices, using order-independent rendering to enable parallel processing of nearby shapes.

dac-2025-315.method: This accelerator replaces expensive multiplications in neural networks with lookups into pre-computed tables (lookup tables or LUTs), which is far more power-efficient. Rather than using a central clock signal, it uses self-synchronous pipeline accumulation, where each processing stage signals when it completes and the next stage starts—this eliminates the power and wiring overhead of clock distribution. Tested in 22-nanometer fabrication technology, this design achieved 2.5x better energy efficiency and 5x smaller chip area.
dac-2025-315.key_novelty: This is the first all-digital neural-network accelerator combining lookup-table multiplication with self-synchronous pipeline accumulation (where processing stages coordinate without a central clock), delivering high efficiency and reliability across manufacturing and operating variations.

dac-2025-320.method: Boolean decomposition breaks down logical functions (the mathematical rules that define how digital circuits behave) into simpler building blocks, but the traditional approach is slow because it tests candidate solutions one at a time. EDGE reformulates the problem as a database query: instead of iterating through possibilities sequentially, it asks the database to find all decompositions that satisfy certain criteria and evaluates them together. Database systems are highly optimized for exactly this kind of work—finding patterns in large sets of data and filtering efficiently—which makes generating and evaluating candidates for Gate-Inverter Graph synthesis (converting logic into circuits made of gates and inverters) much faster than the original method.
dac-2025-320.key_novelty: The key innovation is using database query optimization—techniques that efficiently handle large datasets—to speed up finding good Boolean decompositions for circuit synthesis.

dac-2025-317.method: RF circuit simulation requires repeatedly solving a mathematical system using Newton's method. This paper proposes preconditioners—transformations that reshape equations to solve them faster—that operate in the time domain (tracking how signals change over time, rather than just their frequency content). The method works for distributed device circuits and automatically selects the best preconditioner variant by measuring how nonlinear the circuit is through matrix calculations.
dac-2025-317.key_novelty: Time-domain preconditioners that speed up both the linear solver and reduce Newton iterations in RF circuit simulation.

dac-2025-316.method: APSQ treats partial sums (the intermediate values that accumulate during neural-network calculations) as a major compression target, building this directly into the quantization process (the technique of shrinking numbers into smaller storage formats). The method compresses these partial sums down to 8-bit integers (INT8) through strategic grouping and hardware design changes to support it. Testing on AI models like BERT, Segformer, and EfficientViT demonstrated that this compression loses very little information—the models kept their accuracy—when paired with software-level optimizations.
dac-2025-316.key_novelty: This is the first to make partial-sum compression a primary focus in neural-network accelerators, treating it with equal importance as weight and activation compression.

dac-2025-310.method: BPUFuzzer works by creating test programs using control flow graphs—diagrams that show all the different paths a program can execute. It then runs these test programs on the CPU and watches for anomalies (unusual behavior), particularly in how the branch prediction unit handles these complex control flows. The tool deliberately picks promising test cases by measuring two things: how well they explore different code paths and how much they trigger unexpected behavior. Finally, it reads internal CPU state snapshots after each test to understand what happened and guide the selection of even better test cases.
dac-2025-310.key_novelty: BPUFuzzer is the first fuzz testing tool combining control flow graph-based test generation with anomaly detection and fitness-guided selection to find branching transient execution vulnerabilities in RTL (the hardware design level).

dac-2025-312.method: Libra uses filtered bit-group sparsification (removing groups of zero bits from weights) and dynamic bit-group quantization (reducing activation bit-width), which creates irregular computation demands across compute units. The hardware addresses this with a task pool and multi-level workload balancing to keep all units equally busy, plus an adaptive bit-width architecture that lets different parts compute at different precisions simultaneously.
dac-2025-312.key_novelty: It's the first attention accelerator combining weight and bit-level sparsity that solves the load-imbalance problem through multi-level task scheduling and variable bit-width execution.

dac-2025-323.method: ELF uses machine learning to predict which proposed circuit restructurings (called 'cuts') won't help, and skips them before running the expensive rebuilding phase (called 'resynthesis'). Applied to the ABC logic synthesis framework's refactor operator, this filters out most of the 98% of attempts that typically fail, eliminating wasted computation.
dac-2025-323.key_novelty: Predicting and pruning failing circuit restructures with machine learning before expensive resynthesis.

dac-2025-319.method: Normally, GPUs check their L1D cache (the fastest, primary cache closest to the processor) first, then fall back to the victim cache (a smaller backup cache holding data that didn't fit in L1D). HIVE reverses this for latency-critical memory accesses—it checks the victim cache first instead. This works because those requests can be immediately served from data already in the victim cache, bypassing the delay of first checking L1D and discovering the data isn't there. By prioritizing victim cache lookups for time-sensitive accesses, HIVE reduces the delay on the critical path.
dac-2025-319.key_novelty: Reversing the cache hierarchy—checking the victim cache before the L1D cache for latency-critical accesses to reduce critical-path latency (the delay in the time-sensitive execution path).

dac-2025-321.method: SuperFast speeds up supernet training (training a large neural network designed to efficiently run on many different targets) using a two-stage approach. First, it trains a small subnet and captures what works well. Second, it transfers that learned knowledge to the full supernet before the main training begins. This head start helps the large network train faster and achieve better accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs, and it integrates as a plug-and-play component with systems like ElasticViT and NASViT.
dac-2025-321.key_novelty: Instead of warming up the largest model first (the standard approach), it transfers knowledge from a small network to teach the large supernet.

dac-2025-318.method: DAWN compares consecutive video frames and removes redundant point measurements by using detected objects from the previous frame to guide how it divides the 3D space (object-aware partitioning). For scenes with unevenly scattered points, it sorts points along each axis before filtering. It then uses an efficient 3D similarity algorithm to identify and remove duplicate measurements. Adjustable filtering settings let you choose between faster processing and more accurate detection.
dac-2025-318.key_novelty: The key idea is using where objects were detected in the previous frame to guide the current frame's partitioning, enabling similarity-based filtering that removes redundant point measurements between frames.

dac-2025-324.method: The system places components in three stages. First, it positions components globally using Separating Axis Theorem (a collision-detection method that checks whether shapes overlap by testing certain axes) and verifies against exact component shapes and board boundaries. Second, it refines positions using a multi-stage force-directed approach that dynamically adjusts attractive forces (pulling related components together) and repulsive forces (pushing them apart) to maintain clearance for routing. Third, it uses a scanline-based approach to remove remaining overlaps and enforce spacing constraints.
dac-2025-324.key_novelty: Using Separating Axis Theorem to detect collisions between exact, irregular component geometries during global PCB placement.

dac-2025-325.method: The approach uses deduplication metadata (reference counts that track how many copies of each data block exist) to decide where to place data in IMR drives. Since deduplicated data stays unchanged unless its reference count drops to one, this data can be safely placed in overlapped tracks without inducing future rewrites. This replaces traditional frequency-based tracking (which monitors how often data is accessed) with deduplication-informed placement.
dac-2025-325.key_novelty: Deduplication reference counts identify static data that can safely occupy overlapped tracks in IMR drives without triggering rewrites.

dac-2025-326.method: Starting with candidate electrical signals that could fix the chip bug, the framework systematically gathers all possible combinations and tests which ones actually work. A ranking heuristic prioritizes combinations likely to work while keeping the total number of signals minimal. The framework then feeds the validated signal combinations into existing chip-patch generation tools.
dac-2025-326.key_novelty: Instead of manually selecting signals, the approach systematically ranks and validates all candidate signal combinations to find the smallest working fix.

dac-2025-328.method: An AI agent uses a two-stage process to automate post-silicon test engineering tasks. First, it uses a large language model (a neural network trained on text) to understand what the user wants. Second, it connects the model's output to real testing tools and infrastructure, enabling the agent to actually execute tests. A prototype called the Intelligent Engineering Assistant (IEA) demonstrates that this approach can complete tasks autonomously within existing test frameworks.
dac-2025-328.key_novelty: Connecting language models directly to testing infrastructure enables them to understand and execute post-silicon test tasks autonomously.

dac-2025-334.method: Designing analog circuits requires running expensive circuit simulators (SPICE software) many times to test and optimize designs, which is slow and costly. Opera replaces these expensive simulators with fast neural networks (called surrogate models) that predict how a circuit will behave without the computational cost. These neural network substitutes are integrated into a standard reinforcement learning environment (like OpenAI Gym, a training framework for optimization algorithms), so engineers can use existing tools to automatically search for better circuit designs. The entire platform is built on an open-source 45nm semiconductor process, allowing researchers to reproduce the results without paying for access to proprietary manufacturing technology.
dac-2025-334.key_novelty: Opera is the first open platform that replaces expensive circuit simulators with neural network substitutes and integrates them into standard reinforcement learning environments for analog circuit design.

dac-2025-327.method: The attack works by controlling the precise timing of AXI protocol handshakes—the standardized signals (valid, ready, backpressure) that coordinate when data moves in FPGAs. These timing variations get encoded into the spacing of network packets leaving the FPGA, secretly embedding data in packet arrival times. The attack produces minimal traffic signatures, making it hard for cloud providers to detect via normal traffic monitoring.
dac-2025-327.key_novelty: It's the first covert timing channel to exploit AXI protocol handshakes (the data coordination signals in FPGAs) combined with network packet timing in cloud FPGAs.

dac-2025-332.method: Uses reinforcement learning with graph attention networks (neural networks that analyze circuit connections and identify important patterns) to find electrical trade-offs. A graph similarity detector recognizes when different circuits have structurally similar designs, allowing the system to transfer optimization strategies learned on one circuit to other structurally similar circuits, avoiding expensive repeated simulations.
dac-2025-332.key_novelty: Using graph similarity detection to identify when analog circuits have matching structures, enabling transfer of optimization strategies across different circuit architectures.

dac-2025-335.method: TetrisLock splits a quantum circuit into two pieces that interlock like puzzle parts—each one depends on the other to function. Neither piece by itself reveals the complete circuit's behavior or design, making it impossible to steal or reverse-engineer the intellectual property from just one piece. When both pieces are combined, the original circuit works as designed, and this eliminates the need to trust the compiler with the full, unprotected circuit.
dac-2025-335.key_novelty: Splitting quantum circuits with interlocking patterns so that neither individual piece alone can be used to reverse-engineer the original design.

dac-2025-331.method: FPGA-TrustZone creates a protected execution space on FPGAs (programmable logic chips) by replicating ARM TrustZone's security approach—the same feature that protects sensitive CPU code. It does this by inserting security checkpoints at two levels: where the FPGA connects to the rest of the chip (the SoC interconnect), and within the FPGA's programmable logic itself (the fabric). These checkpoints block untrusted code from accessing data and logic marked as trusted, creating the same kind of isolation that TrustZone provides on CPUs.
dac-2025-331.key_novelty: This is the first system to fully extend ARM TrustZone's security model to FPGAs, covering both the SoC interconnect and FPGA fabric layers in chips with both CPUs and FPGAs.

dac-2025-322.method: BlasPart recursively splits a large network into balanced pieces by repeatedly dividing in half at multiple levels of detail in parallel to process data efficiently. At each level, it adjusts the balance constraints (how strictly pieces must be equal-sized), which improves both speed and partition quality. The algorithm produces the same result every single run, even across different computers — this reproducibility is essential for debugging and verification. It scales to partition massive industrial networks into up to 4,096 balanced pieces.
dac-2025-322.key_novelty: A parallel network-partitioner that guarantees reproducible results at massive scale by adjusting balance constraints at each recursion level.

dac-2025-338.method: The approach uses a router that operates at the die level (where each die is an individual chip component) and simultaneously optimizes two things: how signals are physically routed between components, and the timing schedule for time-division multiplexing (where signals share transmission lines by taking turns at different times). By making routing decisions that consider both the physical layout and the transmission timing together, it reduces the need for extremely long wiring connections between distant dies and shortens the longest signal delays in the circuit.
dac-2025-338.key_novelty: This is the first router to jointly optimize both how signals are physically routed and when they're transmitted (using time-sharing) in multi-die FPGA systems.

dac-2025-341.method: DenSparSA augments a standard systolic array—a grid of synchronized processors optimized for dense matrix multiplication—with compact circuits designed to handle unstructured sparse matrices (matrices with zeros scattered randomly). It uses circuit gating (electronically switching off unused portions) to disable these sparsity circuits during dense operations, eliminating their power and area overhead when not needed. The design supports both single-side sparse multiplication (one sparse matrix, one dense) and dual-side sparse multiplication (both matrices sparse).
dac-2025-341.key_novelty: The core idea is decoupling sparsity circuits from the main array and making them gatable (switchable), so the area and power cost only applies when handling sparse data.

dac-2025-337.method: NoiseZO trains neural networks using dual RRAM arrays (resistive RAM—a type of memory that stores data using electrical resistance and can perform calculations during storage). Instead of computing gradients, it leverages the random electrical noise that naturally occurs when writing to RRAM as perturbations for zeroth-order optimization (a training method that updates weights using only function outputs, never computing derivatives). The framework provides fine-grained control over noise levels to improve accuracy, and each training update needs just two forward passes through the network.
dac-2025-337.key_novelty: The core innovation is using RRAM's write noise (the random electrical errors inherent to this memory type) as the perturbation source for gradient-free training, eliminating the expensive gradient computation step.

dac-2025-339.method: FlexStep dynamically allocates processor cores to error detection based on each task's reliability needs, rather than permanently assigning cores like traditional systems do. The hardware can reconfigure to switch cores between computation and error-checking duty on demand, while the OS scheduling system decides how much checking each task requires. Error detection runs asynchronously (independently of the main computation) and can preempt (interrupt) when needed, using lightweight hardware support rather than heavy overhead.
dac-2025-339.key_novelty: Hardware and software work together to enable error detection that dynamically adapts to each task's reliability needs instead of using a static fixed configuration.

dac-2025-329.method: The approach combines algorithm and hardware design to solve inefficient processing of bit-level sparsity (scattered zero values) in neural network weights. On the algorithm side, it identifies recurring bit patterns through pruning (removing non-repeating bits), encodes them compactly, and groups similar patterns to balance workload. On the hardware side, it implements a bit-serial accelerator (a processor that examines one bit at a time) with a pattern decoder and processing elements optimized for these regular patterns, eliminating the random memory access inefficiency caused by scattered zeros.
dac-2025-329.key_novelty: Structured bit-pattern pruning: identifying and keeping only recurring bit patterns in neural network weights to convert random bit sparsity into regular patterns that hardware can efficiently process.

dac-2025-330.method: The system uses three coordinated optimizations to reduce memory and hardware needs. First, it uses a voting mechanism to identify which cached key-value data (information the model stores during text generation) is useful, discarding unimportant data while preserving accuracy. Second, the hardware includes a reconfigurable array of processing elements that adjusts at runtime to efficiently handle multiplication operations of varying sizes, and processes certain mathematical operations (softmax and layernorm) sequentially. This coordination reduces hardware complexity from O(N) to O(1).
dac-2025-330.key_novelty: It pairs adaptive voting to selectively discard cached key-value data (information stored during text generation) with hardware that reconfigures to handle the resulting variable-sized operations.

dac-2025-336.method: Mr.TPL routes multi-pin nets (connections with multiple terminals) across triple patterning's three mask layers by assigning each segment to a mask color that avoids conflicts with segments on different masks. It reduces stitches (connections between different mask layers) which add manufacturing cost and complexity. By optimizing how the path splits across the three masks, it minimizes both conflicts and inter-layer connections.
dac-2025-336.key_novelty: It enables routing of multi-pin nets in triple patterning lithography.

dac-2025-333.method: CiliaGraph adapts hyperdimensional computing—a method that normally requires extremely long vectors (tens of thousands of bits)—to work with short vectors (hundreds of bits) by fixing three core problems: using better encoding to prevent features from distorting when squeezed into fewer bits, applying weighted aggregation (combining neighboring nodes' information with varying importance based on graph structure) to reduce structural bias, and adding expanded supervision to ensure important nodes aren't left unrepresented. The approach succeeds because these neural operations are error-tolerant, allowing the network to learn accurately despite the significant information loss from using far shorter vectors.
dac-2025-333.key_novelty: CiliaGraph is the first graph neural network using hyperdimensional computing that breaks the consensus that you need tens of thousands of bits per vector, proving that hundreds of bits suffice for feature-rich graph learning.

dac-2025-342.method: MOSS combines graph neural networks (GNNs—models of circuit connections) with large language models (LLMs—models trained on circuit code) to overcome their individual weaknesses. It uses an LLM trained on the circuit's source code to create embeddings (numerical representations) for D-type flip-flops (memory components), giving the GNN both structural and code-level understanding. To handle large circuits where distant parts affect each other, it focuses the GNN on fewer critical anchor points and applies adaptive aggregation and two-phase propagation techniques to model signal flow. The LLM's overall circuit understanding also supervises the GNN during training, guiding it toward better representations.
dac-2025-342.key_novelty: MOSS combines GNNs with LLMs by treating LLM embeddings as node features for the GNN and using the LLM's global circuit understanding to supervise training.

dac-2025-344.method: PacTrain removes unnecessary weights from neural networks through pruning, which makes most gradient values zero (sparse). It then applies adaptive compression—adjusting compression levels based on patterns of which weights matter. Since it works with allreduce, the standard mechanism distributed training systems use to combine gradients across machines, it integrates directly into existing frameworks without modification.
dac-2025-344.key_novelty: PacTrain combines weight pruning with adaptive gradient compression to achieve near-optimal compression while remaining compatible with allreduce, the distributed training operation that combines gradients across machines.

dac-2025-348.method: The researchers tested two production Elastic SSDs (cloud storage drives from AWS and Alibaba Cloud that automatically adjust capacity) by running various workloads and measuring performance. They discovered surprising patterns—these cloud drives behaved differently than expected compared to regular local SSDs. From these findings, they identified how cloud software developers can optimize code to take advantage of ESSDs' actual performance characteristics.
dac-2025-348.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive study of Elastic SSDs showing they perform counter-intuitively in ways that differ from local storage drives.

dac-2025-345.method: EPICS speeds up fault simulation by combining loop fusion—compiling simple loops into larger blocks—with event-driven simulation (updating only when signal values actually change). To handle circuits with feedback loops (strongly connected components), it identifies entry points using indegree analysis (counting incoming connections) and selectively compiles larger loops while using lazy propagation (computing internal values only when needed). This hybrid approach—mixing compiled code for speed with event-driven updates for flexibility—enables the parallel execution that traditional methods cannot safely support.
dac-2025-345.key_novelty: EPICS' core innovation is using loop fusion guided by feedback-loop awareness (strongly connected component analysis) to enable safe parallel-pattern fault simulation of sequential circuits.

dac-2025-347.method: MILLION compresses the KV cache (data needed for attention computation) using product quantization with adaptive precision: each chunk gets different compression levels based on its actual values, with special handling for outliers. A custom GPU kernel runs attention computation and compression in parallel, preventing compression from becoming a bottleneck. Sparse computation further reduces overhead by skipping unnecessary decompression.
dac-2025-347.key_novelty: The key contribution is quantization that adapts to the KV cache's actual data distribution (with special handling for outliers) combined with asynchronous processing so decompression never bottlenecks inference.

dac-2025-340.method: Leopard uses a programmable chip on a network card (SmartNIC FPGA) that emulates an NVMe storage device. When the operating system sends storage commands, the FPGA intercepts them and processes each using parallel hardware circuits, communicating directly with remote cloud storage. This completely bypasses the CPU and its software stack. The hardware preserves queue concurrency—the ability to run multiple storage requests in parallel—which the software layers had been unable to maintain.
dac-2025-340.key_novelty: A programmable chip on a network card (SmartNIC FPGA) acts as a direct hardware pass-through for NVMe storage requests to remote cloud storage, preserving queue concurrency by eliminating the CPU-based software stack.

dac-2025-343.method: ZenLeak reverse-engineers how AMD's Zen processors map memory addresses to cache locations (across L2 and L3 cache levels). It then builds eviction sets—groups of memory addresses that force a target address out of cache—by analyzing patterns of which addresses conflict with each other. Finally, it demonstrates the first practical attack on these non-inclusive caches by measuring how long OpenSSL's AES encryption takes to access its lookup table, revealing the encryption key.
dac-2025-343.key_novelty: This is the first practical cache-timing attack on AMD Zen's non-inclusive caches, made possible by reverse-engineering how addresses map to cache locations and a technique for constructing eviction sets on such caches.

dac-2025-352.method: The design stacks special transistors—amorphous oxide semiconductors (AOS) made from materials like W-doped indium oxide and tin oxide—in the back-end-of-line (BEOL) layers above the main logic blocks (CLBs). These AOS transistors store configuration data with less power leakage than conventional silicon SRAM, shrinking the space needed. By placing the FPGA's switch and connection blocks directly above the logic blocks using AOS pass gates (transistors that act as controllable switches), routing distances shrink, reducing interconnect latency.
dac-2025-352.key_novelty: This design replaces silicon SRAM configuration memory with amorphous oxide semiconductor transistors (AOS—materials like W-doped indium oxide and tin oxide) stacked in the upper layers of the chip, positioning configuration storage close to the logic blocks and reducing routing latency.

dac-2025-346.method: ZION protects a virtual machine's memory by combining Physical Memory Protection (a built-in hardware feature controlling which code accesses which memory regions) with paging (dividing memory into chunks) for scalable isolation. It speeds up context switching between virtual CPUs with a faster code path that avoids redundant security checks. It also enables virtio devices to access memory securely using split page tables—where the same page appears at different privilege levels—without modifying the RISC-V processor.
dac-2025-346.key_novelty: ZION achieves confidential virtual machine execution on standard RISC-V processors without hardware modifications, using hierarchical memory isolation and split-page-table mechanisms.

dac-2025-351.method: NVR applies runahead execution to NPU hardware: a lightweight speculative thread runs ahead of the main computation, predicting what data will be needed and fetching it early. This early prefetching fills the cache before data misses occur, eliminating stalls caused by the irregular memory patterns in sparse neural networks. The technique requires no compiler modifications or algorithm changes and adds less than 5% hardware overhead.
dac-2025-351.key_novelty: The core idea is adapting runahead prefetching—where hardware speculatively fetches data before computation needs it—to NPU architecture to eliminate cache misses in sparse neural networks.

dac-2025-349.method: Hypnos simplifies fully homomorphic encryption operations (computation on encrypted data) into memory-efficient commands. It pairs these with a paged memory management system—like how computers use virtual memory—that intelligently stages encrypted data between main memory and on-chip caches based on homomorphic encryption's irregular data access patterns. This approach eliminates the constant data movement and waiting time that slows down older accelerators, which assume all encrypted data must stay on-chip.
dac-2025-349.key_novelty: Hypnos introduces a paged memory management system designed for homomorphic encryption's irregular data access patterns, which stages data between off-chip and on-chip storage only when needed instead of requiring everything on-chip.

dac-2025-353.method: BufferProspector first calculates how much memory each core needs at each stage of the pipeline. Then it redistributes the unused memory sitting idle in some cores to the cores that need it more, timing everything so the memory is available when each stage runs. This solves the fundamental problem of buffer space going to waste because pipeline stages don't all need their memory at the same time.
dac-2025-353.key_novelty: BufferProspector recovers wasted buffer space by redistributing it among cores based on their actual timing requirements in layer-pipeline mapping, instead of letting it sit idle due to pipeline stage timing mismatches.

dac-2025-354.method: SpecASR uses speculative decoding (a small, fast model predicts the next words, then a large model verifies them) to speed up speech-to-text. Because both models hear the same audio, they predict the same words much more often than language tasks without audio. To reduce wasted predictions, SpecASR adjusts how many words the small model predicts based on verification rates, recycles failed predictions, and checks only likely candidates instead of all possibilities during verification.
dac-2025-354.key_novelty: Speculative decoding adapted for speech-to-text that exploits how both models naturally agree when processing the same audio, using adaptive draft length and prediction recycling to minimize wasted work from the fast model.

dac-2025-360.method: BirdMoE reduces communication overhead during training by using bi-random quantization: it randomly converts floating-point numbers (decimals used in computations) to integers while keeping the mathematical average the same, so training quality is preserved despite using fewer bits. It then applies a mixed-precision strategy, meaning it dynamically adjusts how much compression each expert node uses based on how busy it is, which balances the all-to-all communication load (where every expert node sends results to every other expert node).
dac-2025-360.key_novelty: The core idea is load-aware bi-random quantization—a technique that randomly converts data to smaller representations while mathematically preserving accuracy—enabling expert nodes to dynamically adjust compression based on how busy they are.

dac-2025-350.method: Ares pairs a specialized FPGA (reconfigurable hardware chip) with custom software to accelerate Private Set Intersection (finding which elements appear in both encrypted datasets). It introduces Lazy Relinearization—postponing a standard encryption maintenance step that PSI operations normally execute repeatedly until multiple instances can be combined—reducing redundant work without changing the PSI protocol. The system analyzes PSI's computational patterns and implements them as optimized hardware circuits, ensuring the FPGA fully utilizes its bandwidth and processing power.
dac-2025-350.key_novelty: Lazy Relinearization defers a standard encryption operation in Private Set Intersection (finding common elements in encrypted datasets) to enable batching without protocol changes, paired with FPGA hardware architecture tailored to PSI's computational patterns.

dac-2025-357.method: EPIC predicts timing errors in voltage-underscaled processors by analyzing which multiply-accumulate operations are vulnerable, then uses an adjustable clock to add delay so those operations can finish correctly. The system finds the minimum delay needed while keeping hardware costs minimal. This corrects all timing errors and maintains full accuracy, even running at just 74% of normal voltage, while adding only 8% more chip area and 1% extra power.
dac-2025-357.key_novelty: By predicting timing errors and using a clock that can add delay to ensure correct computations, the system achieves full accuracy at 0.74x nominal voltage with only 8% area and 1% power overhead.

dac-2025-359.method: SSDTrain moves intermediate calculation results (activations) from the GPU to ultra-fast solid-state storage (NVMe SSDs), freeing up GPU memory. It overlaps data transfer with GPU computation—while the GPU computes, storage reads and writes happen simultaneously, eliminating idle waiting. The system also deduplicates stored data (keeping one copy instead of many identical blocks) and optimizes the forward calculation pass, integrating with PyTorch, Megatron, and DeepSpeed.
dac-2025-359.key_novelty: SSDTrain's key innovation is perfectly overlapping storage transfers with GPU computation, allowing temporary calculation results (activations) to be stored on fast SSDs rather than GPU memory, enabling larger batches without sacrificing training speed.

dac-2025-361.method: PIMoE pairs a neural processing unit (NPU) with processing-in-memory (PIM) hardware that computes near data storage. Instead of statically dividing work, it monitors each unit's throttling state—how much it's slowing down due to thermal or power constraints—and routes tasks to whichever is currently faster, avoiding bottlenecks. It also includes a near-memory-controller data condenser that translates sparse data formats between the two systems for efficient exchange.
dac-2025-361.key_novelty: The core innovation is routing work to different processors based on their real-time throttling state—how much each is slowing down due to heat or power constraints.

dac-2025-356.method: The approach trains a large vision model—a machine-learning system trained on massive amounts of image data—to optimize chip masks at full-chip scale. It frames mask optimization as a vision task rather than a traditional engineering problem, which lets the model learn from many different mask patterns and understand how different shapes influence each other. The model incorporates knowledge of optical physics (how light behaves through manufacturing) and lithography chemistry (how chemicals etch patterns), so it can work at full-chip scale more accurately than previous approaches that only handled small isolated regions.
dac-2025-356.key_novelty: Using a large pretrained vision model to optimize entire chip masks by learning which patterns work best, with built-in understanding of how light and chemicals affect the manufacturing.

dac-2025-355.method: The approach uses machine learning to predict circuit timing instead of running expensive electrical simulations. It trains neural networks to recognize timing patterns by learning from existing data: one type (generative adversarial network) generates timing predictions, while another type (autoencoder) learns a compact representation of timing characteristics. These models learn how circuit delays vary across operating conditions like temperature, voltage, and manufacturing variations—what chip designers call 'corners.' Once trained, the networks can rapidly predict timing at new corners without expensive simulations.
dac-2025-355.key_novelty: The key idea is using machine learning models to learn timing patterns and generate predictions across different operating conditions, replacing expensive simulations.

dac-2025-362.method: Cayman analyzes the entire application using a hierarchical program representation—a structured view ranging from high-level logic down to detailed operations—to automatically identify computationally intensive sections (kernels) worth converting to hardware, even when those sections involve complex decision-making (control flow). It then optimizes the data pathways between the main processor and accelerators, and merges similar accelerators into reusable designs.
dac-2025-362.key_novelty: Cayman automatically identifies and extracts performance-critical code sections (kernels) from complete applications—including those with complex control flow—using hierarchical program analysis.

dac-2025-363.method: The researchers measured electrical power consumption from an FPGA-based XGBoost accelerator (the FAXID accelerator on a Sakura-X platform) to infer what decisions the model was making. Because different parts of the circuit consume different amounts of power when active, small variations in power patterns reveal which decision tree nodes are being executed and what features the model is checking. They confirmed this power-based attack works through experimental testing.
dac-2025-363.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive demonstration that model parameters can be extracted from hardware-accelerated XGBoost systems by monitoring electrical power consumption.

dac-2025-358.method: GoPTX merges multiple GPU kernels (programs that run on the GPU) into a single program by interleaving their instructions at the PTX level (the GPU's lowest-level instruction format). It uses a latency-aware algorithm—one that tracks how long each instruction takes—to decide which kernel's instruction to run next, and adaptive code slicing to create more scheduling choices. This lets the GPU switch to another kernel's instruction when one stalls (waits for data), keeping the processor busy instead of idle.
dac-2025-358.key_novelty: Interleaving instructions from multiple kernels at the PTX level (GPU's lowest-level code) so the GPU can execute any kernel's next instruction when needed instead of running kernels sequentially, reducing stalls and improving instruction-level parallelism.

dac-2025-365.method: DSPlacer automatically places digital signal processors (specialized arithmetic units on FPGAs) for fast CNN execution, refining the placement iteratively. Each iteration: a graph neural network identifies which processors are needed and how they connect; cost optimization assigns them to physical FPGA locations; and mathematical constraint solving ensures connected processor groups follow layout rules that prevent timing violations.
dac-2025-365.key_novelty: DSPlacer automatically places digital signal processors on FPGAs by combining neural network identification, cost optimization, and constraint solving—a first for CNN accelerator timing optimization.

dac-2025-364.method: The system uses analog circuits (circuits that work with continuous electrical signals rather than discrete 1s and 0s) paired with computing-in-memory technology (performing calculations directly in storage rather than moving data between processor and memory) to execute the matrix operations needed for QMM key generation and encryption. This avoids the digital computing bottleneck where traditional processors repeatedly copy data between CPU and memory. The catch is that analog circuits produce small measurement errors, but the system keeps these errors small enough to preserve cryptographic correctness.
dac-2025-364.key_novelty: This is the first use of analog computing-in-memory (math done directly in storage with continuous electrical signals) to replace the digital multiplication-accumulation steps (repeated multiply-and-add operations) in post-quantum cryptography.

dac-2025-369.method: CMFuzz examines IoT protocol implementations to build a model of how configuration settings (like timeouts or buffer sizes) work together. It identifies relationships among these settings—which ones influence each other and how. Then it uses this configuration relationship map to distribute different configurations across parallel fuzzing processes, ensuring each process focuses on configurations that interact in interesting ways to find more bugs.
dac-2025-369.key_novelty: CMFuzz models configuration relationships within protocols and uses this model to intelligently schedule which configurations each parallel fuzzing process should test.

dac-2025-368.method: Uses speculative decoding, which makes fast guesses about what code comes next and checks multiple guesses in parallel rather than one at a time. Combines this with syntax-aware tokenization—splitting code at points where Verilog's syntax rules matter instead of at arbitrary character boundaries. Because the code is split into meaningful chunks, the model understands Verilog constructs better and generates both faster and higher-quality code.
dac-2025-368.key_novelty: It pairs speculative decoding (fast parallel prediction of code) with syntax-aware tokenization (breaking code at meaningful syntax points) to make Verilog generation both faster and better.

dac-2025-371.method: This approach uses a deep learning model trained without needing labeled examples—instead, a specially designed loss function guides the training by scoring how well the predicted masks work. The model directly outputs the final chip mask patterns and automatically generates tiny supporting features called SRAFs (sub-resolution assist features) that help ensure the design is manufacturable, with adjustable control over manufacturing difficulty. This eliminates the time-consuming physical simulations and iterative refinement previously required.
dac-2025-371.key_novelty: A deep learning model trained without labeled data that automatically generates optimized chip masks and sub-resolution assist features (SRAFs) to avoid iterative physical simulations.

dac-2025-373.method: The paper develops mathematical principles that determine the minimum amount of data that must move through memory for any tensor operation (the theoretical lower bound), regardless of how you arrange the computation. Using these principles, it finds the optimal way to divide work into chunks (tiling), order the computations (scheduling), and assign them to hardware resources (mapping). It then proposes a hardware architecture called FuseCU that combines multiple operations so they pass data directly to each other rather than writing intermediate results back to memory, reducing overall data movement.
dac-2025-373.key_novelty: Using mathematical principles to calculate the theoretical minimum data movement required for any tensor operation, it identifies which operator combinations can be merged to achieve that minimum.

dac-2025-372.method: The method accelerates RF circuit simulation by recycling old calculation results from previous cycles—a technique that normally requires storing everything but threatens memory limits in large designs. Instead, it intelligently trims the stored results using a Floquet-based strategy, keeping only the most valuable ones (Floquet theory mathematically describes systems that repeat periodically). It also selects optimal starting points for each simulation cycle to minimize iterations needed.
dac-2025-372.key_novelty: Using Floquet theory to decide which recycled calculation results to keep and which to discard, reducing memory use in periodic circuit simulations.

dac-2025-370.method: REMU tracks memory addresses through three layers—the abstract addresses programs use, physical chip locations, and actual DRAM storage—so radiation-induced bit flips at the DRAM level map directly to the neural network calculations they corrupt. This dual-addressing mechanism (tracking addresses through multiple memory translation layers) enables efficient error injection: researchers inject simulated radiation faults at the DRAM level and measure how the AI model's predictions fail.
dac-2025-370.key_novelty: The core contribution is dual-addressing (tracking memory addresses from virtual through physical through DRAM layers) to connect radiation-induced memory faults directly to neural network inference behavior.

dac-2025-378.method: MMDFL works by sending multiple model copies between devices, where each device trains its models on its own local data. The system intelligently picks which devices to collaborate with based on how different their data is from others and how much computing power each device has. Instead of requiring every device to share knowledge with all its neighbors (a dense, expensive communication pattern), the knowledge-sharing step works independently from these neighbor connections, which cuts down total communication overhead.
dac-2025-378.key_novelty: Using multiple traveling models that adaptively choose which devices to connect with based on data diversity and available resources, rather than requiring communication with all neighbors.

dac-2025-366.method: ReaLM co-designs the hardware and software to handle faults—errors from aging and variation in semiconductors. It uses algorithm-based fault tolerance (ABFT), mathematical techniques that detect and recover from errors, customized for LLMs by monitoring which computations are naturally robust to errors. By collecting error statistics in real-time, the system learns which error-recovery steps are unnecessary and avoids expensive protection where the model can tolerate mistakes.
dac-2025-366.key_novelty: ReaLM measures how much computational error LLMs naturally tolerate via large-scale error injection testing, then uses this statistical knowledge to focus error-recovery on problems that actually matter.

dac-2025-375.method: SeDA secures neural network accelerators using three hardware-software techniques: bandwidth-aware encryption that encrypts data efficiently based on available throughput, choosing block sizes using intra and inter-layer tiling patterns (how computation breaks up within and between network layers), and multi-level integrity verification—checking whether data has been tampered with at multiple checkpoints—to eliminate expensive memory access. Together, these keep the system secure while maintaining performance.
dac-2025-375.key_novelty: The core innovation is performing integrity verification at multiple levels to catch tampering without incurring the memory access overhead that normally slows down secure accelerators.

dac-2025-367.method: RAGNAR reverse-engineers RDMA network cards by running small test programs to explore their behavior at multiple levels of detail. It identifies vulnerabilities that arise when different programs compete for the same hardware resources, then creates attacks exploiting this competition. The attacks show two capabilities: building hidden communication channels between programs and stealing sensitive data by observing how resource competition affects timing. It demonstrates these attacks work against real distributed database systems.
dac-2025-367.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive demonstration of volatile-channel attacks (exploiting hardware contention on network cards) that work against real distributed database systems.

dac-2025-377.method: MetaDSE addresses the problem of designing CPUs for different types of programs (workloads) by using few-shot meta-learning—training a system to design well from just a few examples. It applies model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML), which finds starting weights that adapt quickly with minimal data. For each workload, a workload-adaptive architectural mask identifies which CPU design properties (like cache organization or instruction pipeline) matter most, preventing overfitting where one design approach excels on some programs but fails on others.
dac-2025-377.key_novelty: The key innovation is combining few-shot meta-learning with workload-adaptive architectural masking to enable rapid CPU design adaptation across different workloads.

dac-2025-376.method: YOCO performs 8-bit multiplication directly inside the memory (rather than moving data out to a separate processor), using electrical charge to encode numbers and accumulating results over time—both techniques are efficient in analog circuits. It combines two types of memory: ReRAM, which packs data densely, and SRAM, which is fast and reliable, to achieve both efficiency and high capacity. For transformer AI models, which rely on an expensive attention mechanism, YOCO includes a specialized pipeline optimized for this calculation, reducing data movement overhead.
dac-2025-376.key_novelty: YOCO performs 8-bit multiplication inside memory cells using electrical charge and accumulation over time, achieving 123.8 TOPS/W (operations per watt).

dac-2025-381.method: PHOENIX represents quantum programs as Pauli strings using binary symplectic form—a mathematical encoding that compactly describes quantum operations. It treats compilation as a simplification problem: using Clifford transformations (a family of quantum operations that preserve certain properties), it rewrites the program into equivalent but simpler forms, measured by reducing the complexity of the representation (column-weight reduction). A heuristic algorithm searches for the most efficient 2-qubit operators (gates affecting two quantum bits at once) and arranges them globally—like Tetris placing blocks optimally—to minimize the overall program structure.
dac-2025-381.key_novelty: By compiling quantum programs at the Pauli level using binary symplectic form representation, it enables systematic optimization across the entire program rather than just individual gates.

dac-2025-380.method: The system builds a 256-by-128 array of dual-8T SRAM bitcells (memory cells containing 8 transistors each, grouped in pairs) that store three-level weights rather than binary, keeping read and write operations separate for better efficiency. To handle multi-bit inputs, it splits them into single bits (a process called bit-slicing) and combines them using a charge-sharing binary weighted accumulator—a circuit where electrical charge flows between weighted components to add values more efficiently than traditional circuits. A reading technique called Read WWL Under Drive lowers the electrical current during reading, which reduces current variation and noise.
dac-2025-380.key_novelty: The key innovation is sharing reference signals across a reconfigurable in-memory converter (ADC), which reduces area overhead by 9 times while achieving 1146 trillion operations per watt.

dac-2025-383.method: GSAcc uses a technique called Gaussian depth speculation—predicting the depth ordering of Gaussian elements (a way of representing 3D objects as blobs) early on to parallelize the initial steps. Instead of processing Gaussian elements through sequential stages one-by-one, it reorganizes the pipeline around Gaussian elements themselves (Gaussian-centric dataflow), allowing preprocessing and rasterization (converting the Gaussian elements into pixels) to happen at the same time rather than one after the other. This avoids storing temporary results between stages, freeing up memory. Dedicated hardware accelerators handle the sorting and rasterization operations faster than the GPU alone.
dac-2025-383.key_novelty: The key innovation is reorganizing the rendering pipeline around Gaussian elements so preprocessing and rasterization can happen simultaneously, eliminating the need to store intermediate results and allowing all stages to run in parallel.

dac-2025-374.method: The processor (UniCAIM) uses FeFET transistors—hardware cells storing multiple values each—with three operating modes: constant-time filtering of key-value pairs through approximate similarity search, applying preset filtering patterns, or performing exact attention calculations through electrical-current operations. Because storage and computation occur directly in the transistor cells, it avoids expensive data transfers between components.
dac-2025-374.key_novelty: First chip design that combines content-searching and in-memory computing to filter AI model caches using both preset patterns and real-time analysis, with transistors storing multiple values for efficient computation without data movement.

dac-2025-379.method: AASD accelerates language model inference through speculative decoding—a technique where multiple tokens are predicted quickly and then verified by the full model. It reuses the cached key-value pairs (reusable intermediate calculations from processing earlier tokens) from the full model to quickly generate draft predictions. A compression layer (KV Projector) reduces the size of this cache while preserving accuracy-critical information. A special attention mechanism (Target-Draft Attention) then aligns the draft predictions with the full model's output, efficiently accepting or rejecting each draft without compromising quality or multimodal understanding.
dac-2025-379.key_novelty: The key novelty is the Target-Draft Attention mechanism, which aligns predictions between fast draft and full target models during speculative decoding (predicting tokens quickly then verifying them) for multimodal language models.

dac-2025-386.method: PARO first identifies that video generation attention patterns follow predictable structures—they're not random. It reorganizes these patterns into block-diagonal form (a matrix layout where data clusters along the diagonal, leaving mostly zeros elsewhere). Using mixed-precision quantization, it assigns different bit depths to different regions based on their precision requirements, achieving lossless compression at 4.80 bits on average. The co-designed hardware processing arrays optimize the query-key multiplication to work efficiently with this mixed-precision data format.
dac-2025-386.key_novelty: By reorganizing attention patterns into block-diagonal structure, mixed-precision quantization compresses attention maps losslessly.

dac-2025-387.method: The approach creates a two-stage transmission schedule for energy-harvesting IoT devices. First, it plans a baseline schedule offline using predictions about how much energy each device will have and when data needs to be fresh. Then it adjusts this plan in real time as actual energy conditions change, shifting which devices transmit to keep the collected data as current as possible within available power.
dac-2025-387.key_novelty: It minimizes data staleness when multiple energy-harvesting devices send sensor readings to a central collector, adapting the transmission schedule in real time to changing energy conditions.

dac-2025-388.method: LiK teaches an existing language model (Deepseek-Coder) to specialize in Verilog hardware design through three training stages. First, continuous pre-training exposes it to more Verilog code to build domain expertise. Second, supervised fine-tuning trains it on examples of actual bugs paired with their exact locations. Finally, reinforcement learning refines its accuracy by rewarding correct predictions and penalizing errors.
dac-2025-388.key_novelty: The core novelty is using three specialized training techniques together—continuous exposure to Verilog code, supervised learning on bug-location pairs, and reinforcement learning on accuracy—to train an LLM that pinpoints exact bugs in hardware designs.

dac-2025-385.method: PISA splits each 16-bit value into a 4-bit portion and a 12-bit portion, exploiting the fact that higher-order bits are often sparse (mostly zeros). An 'early bird' mechanism looks at just the 4-bit portion to predict whether the final result will matter, letting the system skip expensive calculations when they won't affect the answer. This integrates with systolic arrays, the hardware grids that accelerate matrix math in AI accelerators.
dac-2025-385.key_novelty: The innovation is splitting 16-bit values into 4-bit and 12-bit slices, then using the 4-bit portion to predict result importance and skip unnecessary computation.

dac-2025-382.method: Recommendation systems store numerical representations called embeddings for every item, wasting memory on items users rarely interact with. This framework splits embeddings by frequency: frequently-used embeddings go into compact lookup tables; infrequently-used embeddings are computed on-the-fly using deep hash embedding networks (neural networks trained to approximate embeddings via mathematical hash functions). This reduces memory demands significantly while keeping training time and accuracy essentially unchanged.
dac-2025-382.key_novelty: The key innovation is this hybrid approach: direct storage via lookup tables for frequently-accessed embeddings and on-the-fly computation via deep hash embedding networks (neural networks using hash functions) for rare ones.

dac-2025-390.method: The system uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (randomly sampling different options to learn which design improvements are most valuable) guided by circuit rankings that preserve options excelling at different tradeoffs rather than discarding all but one. A machine learning model predicts which local circuit modifications (small changes to improve speed or size) are most promising to try next. This enables systematic exploration of approximate circuits that balance speed, area, and acceptable error without getting stuck at a local optimum.
dac-2025-390.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a ranking approach that preserves competitive designs (not just one 'best' circuit) combined with Monte Carlo Tree Search to systematically explore approximate circuits optimizing for speed, area, and error constraints.

dac-2025-389.method: The system uses an Inter-token Bit-sparsity Awareness algorithm to detect patterns of zero-bits within similar tokens, which previous pruning methods missed. It implements this using a Bit-Serial Tensor Core—specialized GPU hardware that performs the core multiplication-accumulation operations (the basic math that powers transformers) in both fixed-point whole numbers and floating-point decimal numbers in parallel. The technique uses novel data mapping to coordinate CUDA and Tensor Core parallelism, allowing both types of processing to run at full speed simultaneously.
dac-2025-389.key_novelty: The core innovation is a Bit-Serial Tensor Core that combines fixed-point and floating-point computation with exponent alignment, enabling efficient processing of sparse-bit vision transformer data.

dac-2025-391.method: To predict timing before routing while accounting for power delivery effects, the approach creates two AI models: one learning how voltage drops in the power network (IR drop) affect timing, and another learning how routing constraints affect timing. These models process three data sources: the circuit's logical connections (netlist), its physical layout, and its power delivery network structure. Pareto optimization combines them by fairly balancing their contributions so none dominates the prediction. This is tested on TSMC 16nm circuits.
dac-2025-391.key_novelty: A Pareto-optimized combination of voltage-drop, routing-constraint, and circuit-structure models that balance their importance to predict chip timing before routing while accounting for power delivery network effects.

dac-2025-384.method: NSFlow analyzes how data flows through a Neuro-Symbolic AI workload and creates an optimized dataflow (the most efficient path for data to travel through computations). It reconfigures an FPGA array (a reprogrammable hardware chip) to execute that dataflow, adjusting which computing units are active, how memory is organized, and numerical precision (bits per number) to match the workload.
dac-2025-384.key_novelty: NSFlow automatically generates optimized FPGA hardware by analyzing the data flow patterns (what computations depend on what data) in Neuro-Symbolic AI workloads, enabling end-to-end system acceleration.

dac-2025-395.method: BoolE explores all equivalent ways to arrange a circuit's basic building blocks (gate-level netlists) using Boolean transformation rules, storing the equivalent forms in a data structure called an e-graph. It then uses an extraction algorithm to recognize when groups of gates form familiar structures like full adders or datapath blocks—even after the circuit has been optimized—making it easier to reason about what the circuit does and improve it.
dac-2025-395.key_novelty: The key innovation is recognizing high-level circuit patterns (full adders, datapath blocks) from gate-level representations, even when the circuit has been restructured by optimization tools.

dac-2025-392.method: PIMDup tackles deduplication—finding and removing duplicate data—on UPMEM processing-in-memory chips (DPUs), which have processors built directly into memory. It spreads the work across many DPUs in parallel, breaks data into chunks using techniques that don't require multiplication (which these chips can't do efficiently), and minimizes how much data moves between the DPUs and the CPU. The system maintains 100% accuracy in identifying duplicates.
dac-2025-392.key_novelty: PIMDup is the first deduplication system designed from the ground up for processing-in-memory hardware, overcoming the challenge that DPUs can't easily communicate with each other and lack built-in multiplication through parallelization and multiplication-free chunking.

dac-2025-401.method: The framework uses pin-extended cells (standard cells with connection points extended further outward) to improve accessibility to routing pins despite the compressed vertical space in CFET designs. It also strategically places blockages in the circuit layout, preventing circuits from being packed into certain areas to reduce the crowding of routing wires in the limited back-end-of-line resources.
dac-2025-401.key_novelty: Pin-extended cells and placement blockages together solve the specific pin accessibility and routing congestion problems created by CFET technology's compressed standard cell height.

dac-2025-397.method: SimPhony simulates electronic-photonic AI chips across all design levels—from individual devices to complete system architecture—using dataflow models specific to optical components that capture multiple forms of parallelism. It calculates power consumption based on actual data patterns and component behavior, estimates chip area and optical signal quality, and adjusts memory bandwidth to match throughput requirements. It integrates with machine learning frameworks so researchers can test new designs without building physical prototypes.
dac-2025-397.key_novelty: SimPhony is the first tool to simulate all design layers of electronic-photonic AI hardware as one unified system, including optics-specific dataflow that models forms of parallelism beyond spatial and temporal dimensions.

dac-2025-400.method: MacroDiff uses diffusion-based generative modeling (an iterative refinement technique, similar to progressively denoising an image) to place large circuit blocks called macros.
