Instead of directly predicting where each macro should go, it first predicts the wirelength relationships—how far signals need to travel between components. This indirect representation automatically preserves how signals connect through the circuit, reduces the number of placement constraints, and naturally handles rotations and translations (different orientations and positions of the layout).
dac-2025-400.key_novelty: By using wirelength relationships (distances signals need to travel between components) as an intermediate representation instead of direct placement coordinates, diffusion-based macro placement automatically preserves circuit connectivity and handles rotations and translations.

dac-2025-393.method: DataMaestro is a specialized data-fetching unit that speeds up deep learning inference on dataflow accelerators. It fetches data before the processor needs it (called prefetch) and dynamically switches how it accesses memory to avoid conflicts when multiple accesses try to hit the same memory location simultaneously (bank conflicts). It can also reshape data as it fetches it to use less memory. The system integrates with matrix-multiply (GeMM) and quantization accelerators on a RISC-V processor, with an FPGA prototype and silicon synthesis (VLSI) validation.
dac-2025-393.key_novelty: A programmable data-fetching unit separate from the compute core that fetches data before it's needed, avoids memory conflicts dynamically, and reshapes data in real-time.

dac-2025-398.method: TAXI solves Traveling Salesman Problems by breaking them into smaller subproblems with hierarchical clustering, then solving each subproblem in parallel using Ising macros—specialized circuits built from crossbars (grid-like arrangements of switches). The crucial design choice is that each macro works entirely independently without sharing data with other macros, enabling true parallelism. The random numbers used during annealing (gradually cooling down to lock in good solutions) come from SOT-MRAM devices (Spin-Orbit-Torque magnetic memory chips), which produce randomness rapidly while consuming very little power.
dac-2025-398.key_novelty: TAXI's key novelty is co-designing algorithm and hardware so that Ising solver macros built from crossbars and paired with SOT-MRAM devices can solve hierarchically-clustered problems entirely in parallel, with each macro working independently and sharing no data.

dac-2025-399.method: The approach divides DRAM memory into bank groups and lets each group operate independently—loading data from its rows and processing it without waiting for other groups to finish. This independence hides the time overhead of row activation (the delay in accessing stored memory data) that would otherwise slow computation. Within each bank group, however, all banks stay synchronized, which eliminates the need for large accumulator circuits (temporary storage units needed for intermediate results). This hybrid two-level synchronization balances the speed gains from independent group operation with the area efficiency from coordination within groups.
dac-2025-399.key_novelty: The core idea is using bank groups as the synchronization boundary: different groups run asynchronously to hide row-activation overhead, while staying synchronized within groups to eliminate large accumulator storage.

dac-2025-403.method: Sparse fine-tuning skips some calculations to reduce time and memory, but on regular GPUs the random pattern of which calculations to skip causes inefficient, scattered memory access. SSFT solves this by using regular, predictable patterns for which calculations to skip (structured sparsity), making memory access organized and efficient. A custom hardware accelerator (SSFT-Hw) is co-designed with the algorithm (SSFT-Alg) to efficiently handle these patterns without the memory overhead that generic sparse operations cause on standard GPUs.
dac-2025-403.key_novelty: The core idea is designing sparsity patterns to be regular and predictable specifically for hardware accelerators, rather than using generic sparse operations that scatter memory access.

dac-2025-402.method: FPGen-3D automatically creates 3D FPGA designs (reconfigurable chips with logic blocks stacked vertically and connected by programmable wires) based on parameters you specify. It produces the hardware description code and the programming instructions for each design. The framework explores different strategies for connecting components across vertical layers by testing different designs of 3D switch blocks (devices that route signals between layers) and 3D logic blocks (computational units arranged in 3D).
dac-2025-402.key_novelty: It automates the exploration of how to connect 3D FPGA components vertically by systematically trying different switch block and logic block designs.

dac-2025-396.method: CHORD combines fixed optical hardware (built into the chip and unchangeable) with adjustable electronic controls. During training, the system learns the best control settings for each task, optimizing them across the entire system. This allows one physical chip to handle many different AI problems. It pairs the speed advantage of optical computing — which uses light to naturally parallelize operations — with the flexibility of electronically adjustable settings.
dac-2025-396.key_novelty: By combining fixed optical hardware with learnable electronic controls, CHORD enables exponentially more different AI tasks.

dac-2025-394.method: PacQ optimizes three things together at the tile level: how low-precision integer weights are packed in memory, how data flows through the processor, and the design of a multiplier that works directly on packed weights. Normally, weights must be unpacked and converted back to full-precision floating-point numbers before multiplication—a slow process that wastes the efficiency gains of using low-precision weights. Because PacQ's packing, dataflow, and multiplier are designed for each other, no unpacking is needed. This co-optimized design processes multiple weights in parallel and fits into SIMT processors (which run the same instruction across many parallel threads).
dac-2025-394.key_novelty: A specialized multiplier co-designed with optimized weight packing and dataflow strategies to process packed low-precision weights directly without unpacking.

dac-2025-404.method: DuoQ reduces neural networks to 4-bit numbers to accelerate large language models on FPGAs (reconfigurable hardware). The challenge is that some values are extreme outliers that normally require expensive special handling by channel or token. DuoQ solves this using learnable transformations—mathematical adjustments that the system learns during training to eliminate these outliers entirely. This algorithm is co-designed with custom hardware: DSP-aware processing elements (PE units using specialized math circuits) and post-processing components for handling nonlinear operations and accounting for token importance.
dac-2025-404.key_novelty: Learnable transformations automatically eliminate quantization outliers, enabling efficient per-tensor 4-bit quantization without the expensive channel-wise isolation required by other methods, co-designed with DSP-aware processing elements.

dac-2025-408.method: SDM-PEB begins by extracting features at multiple scales using overlapping image patches that are hierarchically merged together—this lets the system recognize both broad patterns and fine details in the 3D resist structure. The core is a Mamba-based attention unit (a neural network layer that learns which parts of the 3D space matter most), which uses customized selective scanning (efficiently focusing computation on relevant data instead of processing everything equally) and structured state space models (a mathematical framework for tracking how chemical concentrations change over time). This combination captures how photoacids and inhibitors spread vertically between layers and how they vary spatially within each layer.
dac-2025-408.key_novelty: Instead of standard convolution or basic attention, SDM-PEB uses a Mamba-based architecture with customized selective scanning to efficiently model both vertical photoacid diffusion between resist layers and spatial concentration variations within each layer.

dac-2025-405.method: Designs a specialized processor using spiking neural networks—artificial neurons that fire discrete signals. The hardware simplifies neuron models, uses optimized convolution operations, and organizes processors in a hierarchical parallel array. A custom data-flow pattern called KCTR (Kernel-Channel-Timestamp-Row) with dual processing pipelines computes results directly from input data, eliminating the need to store intermediate spike values between processing layers.
dac-2025-405.key_novelty: A data-flow pattern called KCTR with dual processing pipelines that lets neuromorphic (brain-inspired) processors handle event streams directly without storing intermediate results between layers.

dac-2025-409.method: HPIM-NoC combines simulation and search to optimize systems where different types of processing cores are connected by a network-on-chip (a grid of communication channels on the chip). It accurately models how long data takes to travel through the network by simulating transmission delays. The system searches for good designs in three stages using a customized simulated annealing algorithm (a method that gradually refines solutions by testing variations), guided by prior knowledge about architecture. To accelerate the search, it pre-calculates performance metrics for each core type, reduces simulation frequency for the network, and applies a customized layout algorithm.
dac-2025-409.key_novelty: The framework enables optimization of heterogeneous Processing-in-Memory systems—chips with different types of cores built in—connected by on-chip networks, using prior architectural knowledge to guide a multi-stage search and custom layout optimization to explore configurations.

dac-2025-410.method: ABC-FHE organizes computation as a stream (continuous flow through the chip) with a customizable Fourier transformation engine—the mathematical core of encryption—that can switch between NTT (Number-Theoretic Transform) and FFT (Fast Fourier Transform) depending on what's most efficient. Rather than fetching random numbers and transformation helper values from slow off-chip memory, it generates them directly on the chip, which is far faster. The design also schedules operations carefully to speed up CKKS encryption calculations on the client side.
dac-2025-410.key_novelty: By combining a dual-mode Fourier engine (switchable between NTT and FFT) with on-chip random number and twiddle factor generation, ABC-FHE removes memory access bottlenecks in bootstrappable fully homomorphic encryption processing while minimizing chip area.

dac-2025-417.method: AutoPower splits a chip's power consumption into independent groups (like the clock, SRAM memory, and logic circuits) and trains a separate machine learning model for each group, based on how that group's power correlates with measurable structural features of the chip design. It then subdivides each power group further into smaller sub-models. This multi-level breakdown lets the models learn accurate power predictions from just a few training examples, rather than requiring extensive data.
dac-2025-417.key_novelty: By splitting power consumption into independent, hierarchical groups that mirror how CPUs actually use power, the method can predict chip power accurately using only 2 known chip designs.

dac-2025-406.method: FeKAN uses a software-hardware co-design approach that pre-computes the B-spline basis functions KAN needs and stores them in specialized FeFET-based memory structures (lookup tables and content-addressable memory that quickly find stored values), converting expensive dynamic calculations into simple static lookups. The system compresses the stored basis functions using sparse-data encoding, groups operations together to reduce memory traffic and power use, and optimizes the processing pipeline to prevent bottlenecks.
dac-2025-406.key_novelty: FeKAN achieves hardware acceleration specialized for KAN by using FeFET-based lookup tables and content-addressable memory to pre-compute B-spline interpolations, eliminating the need for expensive dynamic calculations.

dac-2025-407.method: The approach combines algorithm and hardware design to handle sparse point clouds efficiently. The algorithm skips empty voxels (tiny 3D boxes that partition the point cloud) based on a threshold. The hardware uses a 3-stage hierarchical search engine that progressively narrows which voxels contain data, adapting to the irregular sparsity patterns of each point cloud. This eliminates wasted computation by processing only the voxels with actual data.
dac-2025-407.key_novelty: A hierarchical multi-stage search pipeline that progressively narrows which voxels to process based on sparsity patterns, combined with threshold-based skipping made during processing to eliminate wasted work.

dac-2025-416.method: The Secure Normal Form (SNF) framework lets data owners explicitly specify which data aspects are non-sensitive and how much information those aspects can safely leak—like rough frequency patterns. The system then processes queries on encrypted data in a way that reveals only those pre-approved patterns while protecting the sensitive data completely, so queries can run efficiently without accidentally leaking secret information.
dac-2025-416.key_novelty: A formal system for explicitly defining which information leakages are acceptable in encrypted data systems, rather than relying on ad hoc assumptions about what might leak.

dac-2025-411.method: The approach trains a controller using reinforcement learning (learning through trial-and-error feedback) to decide what actions to take, then uses a neural network to propose safety barriers—mathematical descriptions of regions where the system is guaranteed safe. Rather than requiring perfectly certified barriers upfront, the method verifies each candidate barrier through efficient computation. Importantly, this verification works with constraints in their actual complex form, without needing the simplifying approximations that previous methods required.
dac-2025-411.key_novelty: Vector barrier certificates—safety boundaries using multiple dimensions rather than one, making them more expressive—are generated by neural networks and then verified, while handling constraints without the simplifying approximations previous methods required.

dac-2025-412.method: G-SpNN reformulates passivity enforcement (ensuring electrical models conserve energy) as training a neural network instead of treating it as a traditional optimization problem. The passivity constraints are converted into penalty terms added to the neural network's loss function (the objective being minimized during training). Running this on a GPU (a processor designed for fast parallel math operations) achieves faster convergence and uses less memory than the traditional Domain-Alternated Optimization method.
dac-2025-412.key_novelty: The core idea is reformulating passivity enforcement as a neural network training task, which enables GPU acceleration and overcomes the memory and convergence problems of traditional optimization methods.

dac-2025-414.method: LION tests the Simulink compiler using differential testing—running the same model across different Simulink versions and comparing results to find bugs. It inserts 'store-revert' block pairs (blocks that save and immediately restore state) between existing blocks to preserve the model's data flow. It then uses MCMC sampling (a statistical method that explores many possible block combinations) to generate diverse test cases, ensuring comprehensive compiler testing.
dac-2025-414.key_novelty: The innovation is using MCMC sampling (a statistical method) to systematically generate diverse block mutations that thoroughly test the Simulink compiler while store-revert patterns maintain data flow equivalence.

dac-2025-418.method: DCDiff uses an AI diffusion model to reconstruct missing DC coefficients (key numerical values in JPEG compression) instead of using statistical formulas. The model learns from real images to identify and correct reconstruction errors at specific locations. This stops errors from spreading throughout the image, which is a problem with traditional statistical methods. Since it adds only a diffusion step to standard JPEG processing, it works with existing low-cost camera hardware.
dac-2025-418.key_novelty: A learned AI diffusion model replaces statistical methods for reconstructing missing image data, using knowledge of how real images look to prevent errors from spreading.

dac-2025-415.method: The solution combines software and hardware design: the software creates an encoding (a way of representing numbers and data) tailored to work with FPGA lookup tables—the small memory blocks FPGAs use to implement logic—with adjustable sensitivity to detect zero bits. The hardware handles multiply-accumulate operations that take variable time depending on sparsity. This allows FPGAs to efficiently skip computing with zero bits while keeping results accurate.
dac-2025-415.key_novelty: An encoding scheme designed for FPGA lookup tables with adjustable granularity to detect and exploit bit-level sparsity in multiply-accumulate operations while maintaining accuracy and timing closure.

dac-2025-425.method: Zero-knowledge proofs normally work by encoding computations into vast systems of mathematical constraints, which is expensive to evaluate. zkVC cuts this overhead by introducing Constraint-reduced Polynomial Circuits (CRPC)—a technique that uses far fewer constraints—and Prefix-Sum Query (PSQ), which efficiently aggregates partial results. These optimizations specifically target matrix multiplication, the bottleneck operation in zero-knowledge proof systems.
dac-2025-425.key_novelty: zkVC uses constraint-reduced polynomial circuits to dramatically lower the constraint overhead needed to prove operations like matrix multiplication while keeping the proofs cryptographically secure.

dac-2025-422.method: The system trains a machine learning model to learn where different parts of the graph (vertices and edges) are located in memory, using information about the graph's structure. It then watches how the graph is actually accessed and reorganizes memory by moving frequently used data closer together, so these pieces can be retrieved faster.
dac-2025-422.key_novelty: The system uses a machine learning model that understands graph structure to predict where data is located, combined with continuously rearranging memory based on actual usage patterns.

dac-2025-427.method: The tool uses an AI language model trained with reinforcement learning—where the model learns from reward signals—to generate hardware designs (RTL). After each generated design is converted to a circuit (synthesis), the tool measures the actual power consumption, speed, and chip area (PPA metrics) and feeds these measurements back as rewards to guide the model. This teaches the model to generate designs that hit specific optimization targets instead of discovering mismatches only after costly synthesis runs.
dac-2025-427.key_novelty: The core idea is using measured power, performance, and area results from synthesized designs as direct learning feedback to teach the AI model which designs to generate, rather than treating those measurements as a separate evaluation step.

dac-2025-423.method: CAE-DFKD transfers knowledge from a large model to a smaller one without original training data by working with learned representations (embeddings—abstract patterns the model captures) instead of raw images. It retrains the generator that creates synthetic training data to improve representation quality and transferability to new tasks. This embedding-level approach prioritizes making learned knowledge useful for downstream applications, not just image recognition accuracy.
dac-2025-423.key_novelty: It improves knowledge transfer by focusing on learned representations instead of raw images, making them more useful for new, related tasks.

dac-2025-426.method: LeakyDSP reconfigures DSP blocks—math accelerators built into FPGAs—to measure voltage across the chip. When another tenant's circuit runs on the same FPGA, the voltage fluctuates depending on how much power that circuit's operations consume. By monitoring these voltage patterns, an attacker can infer what the colocated circuit is computing and extract sensitive information.
dac-2025-426.key_novelty: This is the first side-channel attack to repurpose DSP blocks—math accelerators already built into FPGAs—as voltage sensors, rather than requiring custom attack circuits.

dac-2025-420.method: Blaze speeds up attention mechanisms in AI models by exploiting sparsity at two levels: skipping zero values and skipping zero bits within individual numbers. However, these non-zero bits don't spread evenly across the data—some hardware ends up idle while other parts get overloaded. Blaze solves this load imbalance with an Approximate-Computing-Based (ACB) workload orchestration system, which redistributes computations and allows small approximation errors when necessary to keep hardware running at full capacity. It also includes a Leading-Booth mechanism that optimizes bit-serial computation (processing data one bit at a time) and runs all of this on a reconfigurable computing engine that can adapt between different computation strategies.
dac-2025-420.key_novelty: Blaze's core innovation is combining an Approximate-Computing-Based workload orchestration mechanism with a Leading-Booth enhancement for bit-serial processing to solve the load imbalance problem in sparse attention hardware.

dac-2025-419.method: NN-AdderNet reformulates the sum-of-absolute-difference (SAD, a multiplication-free calculation) to make weights nonnegative, eliminating the sign bit per weight and saving 1 bit per weight. It identifies two complementary sparsity patterns in the quantized weights—two different arrangements of mostly-zero values—and uses lossless compression (reducing file size without data loss) with both patterns simultaneously. These changes together drastically reduce the bitwidth needed for ultra-low-bitwidth quantization while keeping the model accurate.
dac-2025-419.key_novelty: Reformulating sum-of-absolute-difference to enable nonnegative weights (eliminating sign bit overhead per weight) while exploiting dual sparsity patterns to compress the quantized model.

dac-2025-413.method: STREAMINGGS replaces tile-centric rendering (loading all Gaussian blob data first, then selecting which tiles need them) with memory-centric rendering (streaming Gaussian groups and loading only the tiles each group affects). The algorithm and hardware work together using fine-grained pipelining—overlapping different tasks so the GPU stays busy while waiting for memory. This dramatically reduces wasted DRAM transfers and lets the mobile GPU's memory system predict and fetch data more efficiently.
dac-2025-413.key_novelty: The core innovation is reversing the rendering paradigm from tile-centric (load all Gaussians first) to memory-centric (stream Gaussian groups, load only affected tiles), which dramatically reduces DRAM bandwidth requirements and enables efficient fine-grained pipelining.

dac-2025-431.method: DCART is a specialized hardware processor that speeds up Adaptive Radix Tree operations by recognizing when the same nodes are accessed repeatedly over time (temporal similarity) or when searches tend to follow predictable sequences (spatial similarity). It combines multiple operations targeting the same tree nodes into single batches, eliminating redundant work. It also automatically adjusts which tree nodes and their search results it keeps in fast-access cache memory, based on which ones are used most frequently.
dac-2025-431.key_novelty: The core technique is batching operations targeting the same tree nodes while automatically tuning which nodes and search results stay in fast cache memory based on real-time access patterns.

dac-2025-430.method: 3D-Flow models the 3D layout (stacked semiconductor dies) as a grid graph—a network of interconnected regions, each with limited capacity. When overcrowding occurs, the algorithm finds the shortest paths to move cells from packed areas to empty spaces, using branch-and-bound (systematically testing the best combinations of moves) to optimize which paths to take. It then applies cycle-canceling (removing unnecessary circular movements) to minimize the total distance cells actually travel.
dac-2025-430.key_novelty: Treats 3D cell placement as a network flow problem across all dies simultaneously, which minimizes cell movement by solving the entire layout as one connected system rather than handling each die separately.

dac-2025-433.method: SRBO improves the search for optimal RISC-V processor designs by using a teacher-student model setup within Bayesian optimization—a method that learns from each design test to guide the next search smartly. One model (the teacher) trains a simpler backup model (the student) to predict and correct errors before they mislead the search. Multiple neural networks (deep ensembles) then vote on whether each design meets practical constraints like power consumption and chip size, ensuring only feasible options move forward.
dac-2025-433.key_novelty: Pairing a teacher model with a simpler student model inside Bayesian optimization simultaneously reduces prediction errors and enforces design constraints.

dac-2025-428.method: SimPicker reduces the computational cost of 3D video attention through three techniques. First, it predicts which data is redundant by comparing tokens (data elements) at two levels: entire frames and individual tokens. Second, a specialized hardware component multiplies floating-point and integer numbers using lookup tables (precomputed values) rather than doing calculations. Third, an adaptive strategy groups similar tokens together despite them being scattered throughout the input, keeping the workload balanced.
dac-2025-428.key_novelty: SimPicker combines speculative similarity detection with a lookup-table multiplier for floating-point and integer operations to accelerate 3D video attention.

dac-2025-424.method: AmpereBleed exploits INA226 current sensors—measurement devices built into ARM-FPGA SoCs (chips combining ARM processors and programmable logic on one die)—in a power side-channel attack (stealing secrets by observing electrical usage patterns). By reading what these sensors measure, attackers can fingerprint (identify by their unique electrical signatures) what encryption and machine-learning programs are executing, then exploit that knowledge to extract their secrets. Unlike earlier power side-channel attacks, this one doesn't require planting malicious circuits on the chip first; it uses only sensors the manufacturer already included.
dac-2025-424.key_novelty: A power side-channel attack—stealing secrets by observing electrical power usage—that uses only the built-in INA226 current sensors to spy on machine-learning and encryption programs, without needing to plant malicious circuits on the chip.

dac-2025-429.method: The architecture stacks 3D memory directly on the logic chip and uses compute-in-memory (doing computations where the data sits) to minimize shuttling data around. Instead of moving token data across the chip, it keeps tokens in place and brings computation to them, reducing data movement and power consumption. This approach optimizes resource allocation for more parallel token predictions during LLM decoding, accelerating the process.
dac-2025-429.key_novelty: Token-stationary compute-in-memory with 3D memory stacking (keeping tokens in place while computation moves to them) to overcome the memory bottleneck in LLM speculative decoding.

dac-2025-434.method: The approach uses a diffusion model—a generative technique starting from noise and iteratively refining toward realistic solutions—to produce high-quality initial floorplans (arrangements of circuit blocks). It employs a heterogeneous graph neural network that learns how different entity types (blocks and pins/connection points) should relate and position relative to each other. A guidance function steers this generation process by optimizing for minimal wirelength (total connecting wire length) and zero block overlaps.
dac-2025-434.key_novelty: The core idea is using a diffusion model paired with heterogeneous graph feature extraction to generate initial floorplans that analytical floorplanners can then optimize.

dac-2025-421.method: The method proposes a bilevel optimization algorithm—a technique that solves two related optimization problems alternately. It builds mathematical models of cache miss rates (cache lookups that fail) and network latency (data transfer time between chiplets) based on cache hierarchy design and how chiplets are connected. It then alternates between optimizing the cache subsystem and the inter-chiplet network, both aiming to minimize concurrent average memory access time (C-AMAT, the average time to fetch data across chiplets working together), within cost and power constraints.
dac-2025-421.key_novelty: This introduces bilevel optimization (a technique for solving two linked design problems) for jointly designing cache hierarchies and chiplet interconnects to minimize concurrent average memory access time (C-AMAT).

dac-2025-435.method: The approach represents curved mask patterns using cardinal splines—mathematical curves defined through a few control points that can be adjusted. It iteratively refines these control points by simulating lithography (the optical printing process used in chip manufacturing) to predict how light will actually render each curve. While optimizing, it continuously verifies that designs meet all mask manufacturing rules for line width, spacing, area, and curve properties, and it reconciles results with inverse lithography techniques (methods that reverse-engineer ideal mask designs from manufacturing constraints) to fix any violations.
dac-2025-435.key_novelty: Using cardinal splines—mathematical curves adjusted through control points—to represent and optimize curved mask patterns while maintaining mask manufacturing rule compliance.

dac-2025-444.method: AssertSolver trains a large language model on synthetic examples of SystemVerilog assertion failures paired with their fixes. The model learns from these examples and improves when its predictions are wrong (error-driven learning). When given an assertion failure, it generates diagnostic code and proposes design fixes to resolve the issue.
dac-2025-444.key_novelty: AssertSolver is the first large language model trained specifically to fix SystemVerilog assertion failures, using artificially generated failure examples and learning from its own mistakes to improve.

dac-2025-432.method: MAGE uses multiple AI agents working together to generate Verilog code. The system generates many diverse candidates by using high-temperature sampling (varying how randomly the AI makes choices to explore more options). It immediately tests each candidate and catches functional errors, providing precise feedback about what broke. Agents then iteratively refine the code based on this feedback until it works correctly.
dac-2025-432.key_novelty: Multiple AI agents with immediate code testing catch bugs in generated Verilog earlier.

dac-2025-441.method: IMCsim simulates complete AI systems by adding tensor operations (specialized instructions for neural network math) to a processor, mapping them onto different memory architectures—embedded flash, SRAM, or in-memory compute circuits—and validating results against actual silicon prototypes built at 22nm and 28nm scales. Researchers can then explore how to trade off performance, power consumption, and chip area for different AI tasks.
dac-2025-441.key_novelty: The first simulator connecting in-memory computing device physics to running AI workloads, verified against actual silicon.

dac-2025-436.method: ChatLS works in two stages. First, it searches a database of past chip designs to find similar examples and the synthesis strategies that succeeded for them (retrieval-augmented generation). Second, it feeds the current design's features and constraints into a language model, asking it to work through the reasoning step-by-step (chain-of-thought prompting) before generating the final TCL script, which is the configuration file that controls chip optimization.
dac-2025-436.key_novelty: This is the first application of step-by-step language-model reasoning combined with database example retrieval for automatically generating logic synthesis scripts, by treating the optimization as a reasoning problem over the design's metadata—its key characteristics.

dac-2025-442.method: FactorHD tags each object with a unique symbolic marker, allowing multiple objects to remain distinguishable when combined together and preventing the information loss that normally occurs in this situation (called superposition catastrophe in hyperdimensional computing). The factorization algorithm uses these markers to identify and eliminate redundant classes without losing any information.
dac-2025-442.key_novelty: Using unique symbolic markers for each object enables lossless extraction of class relationships in multi-object hyperdimensional representations.

dac-2025-445.method: AssertSolver trains an AI language model on synthetic data—artificially created examples from challenging hardware test cases—teaching it to recognize assertion failures (automated checks that verify designs work correctly). The model strengthens itself by learning from its own mistakes through error feedback. When given a failing assertion and its corresponding RTL code (the detailed hardware logic), it predicts the needed bug fix, achieving an 88.54% success rate on the first attempt.
dac-2025-445.key_novelty: AssertSolver is an AI language model trained specifically for fixing hardware assertion failures using artificially created test cases and learning from its own mistakes.

dac-2025-440.method: During language model inference, the system avoids reading all key-value pairs from cache; instead, it predicts which ones will matter for generating the next output. It uses cluster-based associative arrays (lookup tables organized into related groups for rapid matching) to calculate correlation scores between the current query and each cached pair. A prediction engine filters out low-scoring pairs, keeping only the important cache accesses. A custom ASIC chip accelerates this by exploiting sparsity in attention patterns (the fact that most attention weights are near zero).
dac-2025-440.key_novelty: The key insight is using Q-K correlation prediction—measuring how much each cached key-value pair relates to the current query—to selectively access only important pairs, without requiring model retraining.

dac-2025-438.method: During the packing stage (where logic pieces are grouped into blocks), the approach reassigns which lookup tables (LUTs—small memory blocks that implement logic) are paired together within each block to reduce routing congestion (overuse of routing wires). Because lookup tables in MLC-based FPGAs (nonvolatile FPGAs using multi-level-cell memory for higher density) can be functionally equivalent—the same logic can work from different positions—the method can quickly explore different pairings. By re-pairing LUT assignments instead of doing full block re-placement, it keeps wire usage down without completely redesigning block positions.
dac-2025-438.key_novelty: The approach reduces congestion by re-pairing lookup table assignments to match MLC routing topology, avoiding the cost of full block re-placement.

dac-2025-446.method: PatternPaint fine-tunes a pretrained image model for chip layout generation using diffusion-based inpainting, a technique that fills in masked (hidden) parts of images by gradually removing noise. The method treats layout generation as an inpainting problem, handled through template-based denoising. Fine-tuning requires only 20 design-rule-compliant sample layouts, enabling it to work with new technology nodes that lack large training datasets.
dac-2025-446.key_novelty: PatternPaint adapts image-generation techniques (diffusion inpainting) to chip layout design, requiring only 20 example patterns instead of the thousands needed by existing methods.

dac-2025-437.method: The approach works in three stages: first, it breaks transistors into smaller groups while keeping solution quality high, making the problem easier to solve; second, it places transistors using an SMT solver (a constraint-solving tool) that simultaneously checks whether connections can actually be routed, catching routing conflicts before they become expensive to fix; third, it routes the metal connections layer by layer—the bottom layer follows manual routing practices, while upper layers use integer linear programming (mathematical optimization) to handle the vertical stacking's unidirectional routing constraints.
dac-2025-437.key_novelty: The key advance is doing routability checks (verifying whether metal connections can fit) while placing transistors using a constraint solver, rather than after placement, which prevents layouts from becoming unroutable.

dac-2025-453.method: SAPO extends the HHL quantum algorithm (which solves linear equations on quantum computers) by embedding mean-variance financial theory—a technique that balances expected returns and risk—into the quantum circuit design using mathematical transformations that improve scalability. It then applies a min-max eigenvalue model calibrated on historical market data to automatically adjust the quantum circuit's parameters, fine-tuning the trade-off between speed and accuracy.
dac-2025-453.key_novelty: SAPO is the first to simultaneously tune both the quantum circuit structure and its parameter settings by leveraging financial domain knowledge and patterns from historical market data.

dac-2025-449.method: XShift enables efficient binarized LLMs (where weights and activations are 1-bit values) by replacing expensive multiplications with XNOR operations and bit shifts. It adapts to the structure of each neural network layer by detecting outlier values and sparse activations across channels, then exploits these patterns using a systolic array (a grid of simple processing units optimized for matrix math). A specialized XNOR-Shift Systolic Array and base-2 SoftMax converter (using only powers of 2 for the probability conversion) keep computation efficient throughout.
dac-2025-449.key_novelty: XShift maintains precision in binarized LLMs by using XNOR and shift operations instead of multiplications, with adaptive handling of outlier values.

dac-2025-451.method: The system extracts features from bio-signals using spikes—brief pulses that capture meaningful activity while reducing data by over 10-fold compared to traditional frame-based methods. These spikes are computed directly inside RRAM (resistive memory, hardware that stores and processes data in one location), achieving high efficiency at 4.09 trillion operations per watt. To maintain accuracy despite RRAM's gradual performance changes and imperfections, the system uses two techniques: Spike-Activity-Distillation (identifying the most important computations) and Aid-Loser-Only (selectively reinforcing weaker memory cells).
dac-2025-451.key_novelty: Use spike-driven feature extraction from bio-signals processed directly in resistive memory (RRAM), with algorithms that compensate for the hardware's physical degradation over years of use to maintain accuracy.

dac-2025-450.method: The approach splits a circuit's verification problem into smaller, independent pieces by identifying key cutting points (critical nodes), which can then be checked in parallel rather than as one large problem. A dynamic task scheduler distributes these verification tasks across processors, keeping the workload balanced so that difficult pieces don't become a bottleneck for the entire process.
dac-2025-450.key_novelty: Critical-node circuit partitioning combined with dynamic task scheduling enables parallel datapath equivalence checking.

dac-2025-452.method: The method converts the circuit into a graph that includes HLS directives (optimization instructions) and resource reuse information. A Graph Neural Network model—using TransformerConv layers and pooling—learns from this graph to spot timing delays. It then predicts the circuit's critical path delay (how fast it runs), power consumption, and resource utilization.
dac-2025-452.key_novelty: The method predicts post-implementation circuit performance by incorporating resource reuse patterns from HLS directives into the graph representation, which prior approaches didn't do.

dac-2025-447.method: Quantum computers introduce errors during readout measurements. DyREM improves this by exploiting sparsity—the fact that quantum probability distributions contain many zero or near-zero values. Rather than processing large error-correction matrices, DyREM dynamically creates smaller versions. An embedded hardware accelerator performs the required calculations (tensor products), using gating—conditional logic gates—to skip computing certain quantum state values, reducing latency and memory overhead.
dac-2025-447.key_novelty: DyREM's core idea is that quantum probability distributions are sparse (full of zeros), enabling dynamic shrinking of error-correction matrices through gated computation that skips unnecessary calculations.

date-2025-000.method: HiFlex uses multiple identical computing cores (processing elements, or PEs) that perform the main computations, connected by a reconfigurable on-chip network that can change how data flows between them—routing it directly between two cores or broadcasting to multiple cores. Software dynamically decides which cores to activate and how to configure the network by analyzing what each layer of the neural network needs to compute.
date-2025-000.key_novelty: The on-chip network reconfigures itself in real-time to match the different data-movement needs of GCN spatial processing and RNN temporal processing, optimizing data reuse in both cases.

dac-2025-439.method: HybriMoE efficiently runs MoE models (neural networks where different specialized components handle different parts of the task) on CPU-GPU systems. For each layer, it dynamically assigns experts to CPU or GPU based on which ones are actually needed. It also preloads predicted experts for the next layer and prioritizes keeping high-value data in GPU cache.
dac-2025-439.key_novelty: Instead of using fixed processor-expert assignments, it dynamically changes these for each layer based on real-time usage.

dac-2025-454.method: The technique identifies proof obligations (states that need to be proven unreachable) and ranks them by how severely they block verification progress. It focuses computational effort on the critical cases—the ones most preventing completion. For each critical state, it extracts the minimal set of constraints (logical rules restricting which states are possible) that prove it can't reach unsafe behavior, avoiding unnecessary reasoning. It also propagates proven safety properties systematically across related states, speeding up discovery of new verified layers (frames) and reusable proof facts (lemmas).
dac-2025-454.key_novelty: It prioritizes proof obligations by how severely they impede verification progress, using this ranking to guide the extraction of minimal constraint sets and propagation of proven safety facts across verification layers (frames).

dac-2025-443.method: The architecture combines two strategies. First, a Balanced Systolic Array (a processing grid where data flows through connected processors in coordinated waves) redesigns tiling—how computation is divided into memory-sized chunks—so that it can achieve both efficient data reuse AND keep all processors busy, reaching 99.5% utilization compared to conventional systolic arrays. Second, Multi-Row Interleaved operation ordering batches multiple rows of computation together, which keeps more intermediate results in fast cache instead of writing them all to slower memory (SRAM), reducing those writes by 31.7%.
dac-2025-443.key_novelty: Balanced systolic array that achieves high processor utilization and efficient data reuse together, combined with multi-row interleaved operation ordering to reduce SRAM energy.

date-2025-009.method: Neural network data naturally follows a Laplace-like distribution—most values cluster around zero with few large outliers. WinAcc exploits this by using a narrow dynamic-range data format (a restricted range of representable numbers) instead of standard floating-point, since most values fall within this narrow window. This simpler representation uses only narrow shifters and narrow adders (simpler versions of floating-point hardware) for combining values, reducing both register complexity and energy consumption.
date-2025-009.key_novelty: WinAcc's key insight is recognizing that neural network data follows a Laplace-like distribution (values concentrate around zero), which enables building accumulators with a narrow dynamic range instead of expensive floating-point units.

date-2025-014.method: Rather than testing analog neural networks through thousands of simulations with random variations (called Monte Carlo simulation), this work uses formal verification—a mathematical approach that proves correctness by analyzing all possible behaviors at once. The key technique is reachability analysis, which calculates what outputs an analog circuit can produce when its components deviate from ideal values (device mismatch). By mathematically proving the circuit produces correct outputs even under worst-case deviations, the approach avoids the time and computing resources that exhaustive simulation requires.
date-2025-014.key_novelty: Formal verification with reachability analysis can mathematically prove analog neural networks produce correct outputs even when components vary, eliminating the need for extensive simulations.

dac-2025-455.method: OutlierCIM tackles three core problems. First, it groups outliers together (outlier-clustered tiling) to keep memory access and compute load balanced in the CIM array. Second, it uses flexible bit allocation (hybrid-strategy quantization with reconfigurable double-bit CIM macro arrays) so the hardware stores both normal values and outliers efficiently without wasting space or adding delays. Third, it adds a dedicated quantizer and post-processing step that unifies floating-point and integer arithmetic, since outlier handling requires both.
dac-2025-455.key_novelty: It's the first approach that designs the algorithm and hardware together specifically to handle activation outliers in CIM accelerators using hybrid quantization and reconfigurable storage.

date-2025-013.method: The researchers inject random bit-flip errors (transient hardware faults from radiation) into programs using Arm SVE and RISC-V RVV vector instructions, which process multiple data items at once. They measure which errors break the final result and track how two factors influence error damage: register cross-section (how much data sits in the processor's fast storage and is exposed to faults), and workload characteristics (what type of computation is running). This reveals which patterns make errors more likely to cause incorrect results.
date-2025-013.key_novelty: This work characterizes how vulnerable Arm SVE and RISC-V RVV vector instructions are to soft errors (bit-flip faults), showing that vulnerability depends on register cross-section (how much data in fast CPU storage can be hit) and the type of computation being executed.

date-2025-012.method: BOSON-1 approaches nanophotonic inverse design as a discrete optimization problem where each location is either solid material or empty space, respecting real constraints of fabrication and real-world variations. To find reliable designs, it combines three strategies: enhanced gradient flows (strong steering toward the goal) to escape local optima (solutions that are locally best but globally poor), restriction of the search to physically fabricable designs, and adaptive sampling-based robust optimization that tests designs under realistic fabrication conditions.
date-2025-012.key_novelty: BOSON-1 achieves robust photonic inverse design by restricting the search to fabricable structures and using adaptive sampling-based optimization to find designs that work reliably despite fabrication variations.

date-2025-021.method: The authors extended gem5 (a computer chip simulator) with a new model that simulates how separate chips communicate and keep their data consistent within a single system. This model can enforce different data-consistency rules—like Arm's CHI protocol, which ensures that when one chip updates a piece of data, all other chips see that update instead of using stale copies. The authors validated this model by comparing its results to real hardware.
date-2025-021.key_novelty: They added the ability to simulate multiple chips with synchronized memory caches using various data-consistency protocols—a capability gem5 previously lacked.

date-2025-036.method: The paper presents two complementary approaches to push beyond current chip design limits. First, it stacks complementary transistor pairs (CFETs—combining positive and negative transistors) vertically in layers and places memory directly on top of the computing circuits, rather than separating them; this vertical arrangement packs more transistors into the same physical space and reduces the distance data must travel. Second, it operates chips at cryogenic temperatures (near absolute zero), where transistors work faster because parasitic resistance—unwanted electrical friction in wires—decreases significantly.
date-2025-036.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining vertically stacked transistor pairs (Complementary FETs or CFETs) with memory integrated directly above the logic circuits in a monolithic 3D chip, which packs more components per unit area and increases on-chip memory capacity.

date-2025-051.method: The paper proposes a two-level cache system using SLC (single-level-cell, faster but more expensive memory) in front of TLC (triple-level-cell, slower but cheaper memory). The two levels operate at different chunk sizes: L2 (the lower level) works with large chunks of data, while L1 (the upper level) works with small chunks, allowing each level to process data efficiently at its own scale. The system monitors how applications write data and automatically adjusts how much cache space goes to each level based on the typical chunk size each application uses, rather than using a fixed allocation. The design is then compared against existing SLC cache management schemes.
date-2025-051.key_novelty: A two-level SLC cache where each level handles different chunk sizes and the division of cache space automatically adjusts based on how each application actually writes data.

date-2025-047.method: The approach uses genetic algorithms—iterative search methods similar to natural selection—to generate noise patterns that fool image segmentation systems into producing corrupted outputs. It then trains a machine learning model to predict whether a given image will yield corrupted segmentation when exposed to such noise, achieving over 96% accuracy. The method is evaluated on YOLOv8 and DETR segmentation systems.
date-2025-047.key_novelty: This is the first machine learning model to predict whether imperceptible noise will corrupt image segmentation with over 96% accuracy, and it shows that noise causing corruption doesn't need to be located in the same image regions where the corruption appears.

date-2025-052.method: The method combines two levels of simulation working together: gate-level simulation (modeling individual logic gates) to accurately capture how defects behave in arithmetic units, paired with microarchitecture simulation (simulating CPU instruction execution) which runs faster. In stage one, the researchers inject faults into arithmetic units during instruction execution and watch how those faults change the output values. In stage two, they run complete programs to completion and measure whether each fault results in silent data corruption (wrong answer without crashing), a crash, or gets masked (harmlessly absorbed).
date-2025-052.key_novelty: By combining fast microarchitecture simulation with accurate gate-level models, the approach can run long programs to completion and catch rare silent data corruption events that couldn't be observed with a single simulation level.

date-2025-039.method: The researchers used low-cost pulse generator hardware to send electromagnetic pulses (bursts of electromagnetic energy) at an Intel Neural Compute Stick 2, a small AI chip used in edge devices. By systematically testing different pulse configurations—varying things like timing, location, and intensity—they found ways to make the AI classifier output wrong answers, and demonstrated these attacks could be repeated reliably.
date-2025-039.key_novelty: They demonstrated the first practical, repeatable electromagnetic pulse attacks that make a real Intel Neural Compute Stick 2 AI chip misclassify data.

date-2025-048.method: The approach uses model-driven engineering (designing systems through machine-readable specifications) with traceability (tracking how information and changes flow) embedded as the core infrastructure. It creates a framework for coordinating multiple industrial digital twins by solving their main challenges: identifying which twin is which, managing shared information about the data (metadata), enabling direct communication between twins, and establishing rules for how they coordinate. The framework was validated on two real industrial scenarios.
date-2025-048.key_novelty: The core innovation is using traceability—automatic tracking of information and changes—as the central mechanism for coordinating multiple industrial digital twins as a federation.

date-2025-024.method: The approach reformulates SAT problems into multi-level, multi-output Boolean circuits (hierarchical logic diagrams), then applies gradient-based optimization—the learning technique from neural networks—by reinterpreting it as regression. This enables differentiable, parallel bit-wise operations on GPU tensor hardware, allowing many candidate solutions to be processed simultaneously rather than sequentially.
date-2025-024.key_novelty: Finding diverse SAT solutions on GPUs through gradient-based optimization (the learning technique from neural networks) applied to refactored Boolean circuits.

date-2025-023.method: Verification of hardware designs like RISC-V cores uses bounded model checking—testing whether bugs can occur within a limited number of steps—via a SAT solver, a tool that systematically searches for failure scenarios. When a design is modified, PrediCore doesn't restart this search from scratch; instead it saves the logical impossibilities and constraints the SAT solver learned from the previous design and feeds them to the solver for the next version of the SystemVerilog code. This lets the solver skip redundant work and accelerates verification.
date-2025-023.key_novelty: Instead of reverifying from scratch after each design change, it reuses the logical constraints that the SAT solver learned from the previous design version.

date-2025-034.method: The authors extend AUTOSAR Adaptive (an automotive software standard) with System-Level Logical Execution Time (SL-LET), a timing mechanism that ensures tasks execute predictably and deterministically—a requirement for automotive safety systems. They build a prototype of this extension and validate it on realistic automotive applications using the official AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform Demonstrator.
date-2025-034.key_novelty: This is the first extension of SL-LET (a model ensuring deterministic, predictable task execution) from AUTOSAR Classic to AUTOSAR Adaptive's more flexible, service-based architecture.

date-2025-025.method: CONVOLVE protects edge-AI devices by designing specialized hardware that guards against attackers with physical access—preventing them from stealing cryptographic keys (authentication and encryption secrets) or neural network weights (the trained AI model's intellectual property). The system treats security as a fundamental hardware design principle from the start, and carefully manages the device's limited power consumption and computing capacity.
date-2025-025.key_novelty: CONVOLVE's core idea is protecting edge-AI processors from physical attackers by securing both cryptographic keys and neural network weights simultaneously, even under extreme power and computing constraints.

date-2025-079.method: Normally, each process maintains its own page table—a bookkeeping structure that tracks where its data lives in memory. MPFS instead creates one shared page table that all processes use together, eliminating the duplicate memory overhead. To make this sharing efficient, they organize the page table in 512GB-aligned blocks (called PGD alignment), which lets hardware handle address translations faster. A protection mechanism keyed to these alignment boundaries ensures one process's data stays isolated from another's.
date-2025-079.key_novelty: Multiple processes share a single page table structure aligned to 512GB chunks instead of each maintaining their own, reducing memory waste while keeping their data protected from interference.

date-2025-063.method: In STT-MRAM memory, finding the right reference voltage to read a cell is slow when using conventional methods that try values sequentially. To solve this, the paper proposes three algorithms: DRRS (Dual Read Reference Search) determines the optimal reference from two array reads using statistical analysis, TRRS (Triple Read) handles variation across different parts of the array, and SRS (Simultaneous Reference Search) optimizes both magnetic alignment states (Parallel and Anti-Parallel) at the same time. Because these algorithms run on the memory chip itself, the reference can be adjusted quickly if temperature or other conditions change.
date-2025-063.key_novelty: By analyzing statistical patterns in read data, the method finds the optimal reference through minimal array operations, eliminating the need to search through values sequentially.

date-2025-060.method: The framework automatically injects faults (simulated particle impacts) throughout a system by accessing memory and scan chains—built-in testing pathways—to cover 100% of potential failure points. It simulates particle-induced bit flips based on measured cross-sections, the probability of impact at different particle energies, and supports both system-wide and component-level testing. The approach works across any processor architecture and adds only about 2% computational overhead.
date-2025-060.key_novelty: Complete fault injection coverage (100% of all possible bit flips) is achieved through direct hardware access with minimal performance overhead (<2%) while matching real particle irradiation with 98.4% correlation.

date-2025-069.method: The method works in two phases. Phase 1 thoroughly analyzes the circuit to understand where errors occur and how bad they are when approximations are applied. Phase 2 improves the circuit by reusing the analysis from Phase 1, which keeps the computation minimal.
date-2025-069.key_novelty: By reusing results from thorough analysis instead of recomputing during each optimization step, the method achieves fast and efficient improvements.

date-2025-073.method: The system works like a biological reflex: when computing resources are plentiful, it runs complex algorithms, but when resources become scarce, it automatically switches to simpler, resource-efficient ones instead. ReflexLang is a specialized programming tool that automatically generates the code for this switching behavior.
date-2025-073.key_novelty: Instead of pre-planning backups for every possible scenario, the reflex pattern lets systems automatically pick the right algorithm based on current resource availability.

date-2025-064.method: The accelerator implements Quickscorer (a tree-based algorithm for ranking documents) by representing its decisions as bit sequences (bitvectors) and performing logical operations—like AND and OR—directly within racetrack memory rather than moving data elsewhere. To reduce expensive shifting operations needed to access data in racetrack memory, it schedules related decision steps together (interleaving). An optimization algorithm (quadratic assignment problem) determines the best placement of data in memory to minimize total read, write, and shift costs.
date-2025-064.key_novelty: The core innovation is adapting tree-based ranking algorithms to run directly inside racetrack memory using logical operations on bits, avoiding the expensive data movement of traditional ranking systems.

date-2025-089.method: The detection system uses cheap sensors called Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) that measure the voltage changes caused by laser heating of the chip. By combining data from at least two of these sensors instead of just one (multi-sensor fusion), the system can reliably detect laser attacks while avoiding false alarms.
date-2025-089.key_novelty: The key idea is combining measurements from multiple Time-to-Digital Converters (sensors that measure voltage timing) to reliably detect laser attacks on cryptographic chips with minimal false alarms.

date-2025-094.method: During compaction, the system identifies data blocks whose contents haven't changed. Rather than rewriting these blocks to a new location (which wastes SSD write cycles), it uses remapping—a technique that updates pointers to the data instead of moving the data itself. A lightweight tracking system monitors which individual key-value items within each block have been modified. The approach includes a strategy to keep unchanged blocks intact and prevent them from being split when adjacent blocks do change.
date-2025-094.key_novelty: Unchanged data blocks are kept in place using remapping during compaction instead of being rewritten, reducing redundant SSD writes.

date-2025-090.method: This framework helps you design custom hardware accelerators (specialized circuits designed to quickly run algorithms) that predict movement from brain signals using Kalman Filters. Instead of building one fixed design, you can adjust settings to explore different configurations—finding the sweet spot between fast response time and accurate predictions. This tunable approach is essential for embedded brain-computer interfaces that have limited computing power.
date-2025-090.key_novelty: A configurable Kalman Filter hardware accelerator framework that optimizes the tradeoff between response speed and prediction accuracy for embedded brain-computer interfaces.

date-2025-068.method: The MC³ attack sends hidden messages by creating contention in shared DRAM—one program deliberately slows down memory access for another program's memory requests. The attacker varies (modulates) the stress intensity to encode signals, and the receiving program decodes them by measuring how much slower its memory access becomes. This approach works on mobile system-on-chips (SoCs) without a last-level cache (LLC), where previous covert attacks couldn't operate. The technique trades speed of communication against risk of detection—more intense patterns are faster but easier for security monitoring to catch.
date-2025-068.key_novelty: Fast secret communication through shared memory strain (DRAM contention) alone, without the last-level cache, special system access, or irradiation that previous attacks needed.

date-2025-070.method: Each graph node is represented by an artificial neuron with delay mechanisms (dendritic delay lines) that encode the cost of traveling along edges. When a signal originates from a starting node, it propagates through the network with delays proportional to edge costs; a backward-tracing method breaks the problem into sub-problems that are solved iteratively. The shortest path is identified by whichever neuron fires (sends its signal) earliest—since delays accumulate along paths, the first neuron to fire must be closest to the start. The system uses countdown counters to manage signal timing and eligibility traces to track and encode the edge costs into the delay values.
date-2025-070.key_novelty: Using when neurons fire (spike timing) as the direct solution to shortest-path dynamic programming problems.

date-2025-086.method: When automatically searching for the best quantum-dot circuit arrangement, this method identifies regions that can't possibly work and eliminates them during the search. By cutting away these impossible paths before exploring them fully, it avoids wasted computation. This continuous pruning of impossible designs dramatically speeds up finding the optimal arrangement.
date-2025-086.key_novelty: By identifying and removing impossible designs during the search, the method achieves a 33-times speedup in automated SiDB logic design.

date-2025-085.method: The system uses a specialized processor embedded in memory that computes directly on stored data, avoiding the cost of moving data to and from external memory. It compresses the graph structure to reduce space and applies dynamic quantization—adjusting the precision of numbers per layer based on how weights are distributed in that layer. It also tracks weight patterns to identify which connections contribute little and propagates this sparsity (pattern of sparse values) through layers to skip unnecessary computations.
date-2025-085.key_novelty: The system minimizes data movement by using dynamic quantization and sparsity propagation (reducing number precision and skipping unnecessary computations) that adapt to each layer's actual weights.

date-2025-091.method: The researchers measured how much PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances—persistent chemicals used extensively in semiconductor manufacturing) is needed for different computer chip designs. They tested this across chips built with different feature sizes (7nm, 16nm, and 28nm process nodes, where smaller numbers mean denser circuits) and different lithography methods: EUV (extreme ultraviolet light, a more advanced technique) versus DUV immersion (an older approach using deep ultraviolet light with special fluids). By comparing PFAS amounts across all these manufacturing variations, they could see which design and manufacturing choices result in the least environmental chemical usage.
date-2025-091.key_novelty: The work shows that semiconductor manufacturing's PFAS environmental impact can be substantially reduced by optimizing the choice of lithography method and production process node.

date-2025-107.method: The design creates a strong PUF (a hardware security device that generates unique fingerprints from manufacturing variations) using only six minimum-size transistors per unit, arranged in an array. It operates using electrical current rather than voltage, which makes it naturally stable when the power supply varies. Despite this minimal design, it can efficiently generate many different challenge-response pairs (where you ask it a security question and it gives a unique answer based on its physical properties) without consuming much chip space.
date-2025-107.key_novelty: The core innovation is that using minimal transistors in a current-mode design enables a strong PUF to produce many unique challenge-response pairs while taking up almost no additional chip area.

date-2025-121.method: The paper outlines a complete approach to building secure space systems by thinking about cybersecurity from the very start of development, not adding it at the end. It covers secure design practices (building security into how the system is built), thorough testing to find vulnerabilities, strategies to keep systems working even under attack, and industry standards. By weaving cybersecurity into every phase—from figuring out what the system needs to do, through design, testing, and deployment—it prevents security problems from being overlooked.
date-2025-121.key_novelty: The key idea is treating cybersecurity as integral to every stage of space system development, from requirements to deployment, rather than as an afterthought.

date-2025-093.method: The researchers ported a brain-signal decoding algorithm (software that interprets electrical brain patterns for control commands) from high-power laboratory computers to a small battery-powered embedded device. They optimized the algorithm through techniques like streamlining calculations, using more efficient operations, and restructuring the code for lower-power hardware, achieving a 25-fold reduction in power consumption. Crucially, these optimizations preserved the algorithm's ability to process signals instantly in real time and maintain accuracy for spinal stimulation control.
date-2025-093.key_novelty: The core innovation is that brain signal-decoding algorithms can be ported to battery-powered portable devices achieving 25-fold power reduction while preserving real-time responsiveness and accuracy.

date-2025-108.method: The framework ensures consistent testing by running each miner in an isolated Docker container—standardized computing environments that prevent installation differences from affecting results. It provides modular evaluation methods that assess both what a specification means (semantic) and how it's structured (syntactic), so different evaluation approaches can be plugged in as needed. Instead of hunting for consensus on real specifications, the framework automatically generates synthetic benchmarks: artificial specifications with known correct answers that miners should discover. This provides an objective measure of whether miners work correctly.
date-2025-108.key_novelty: The core idea is using automatically generated synthetic specifications as objective ground truth for evaluating miners.

date-2025-143.method: EILID builds on a trusted hardware foundation (CASU Root-of-Trust) that keeps the software locked down and prevents it from being secretly modified. It then adds automatic checkpoints throughout the code to catch attacks when function calls or returns try to jump to unexpected places—checking both where functions are called (forward-edge) and where they return (backward-edge). To make this reliable even on devices with very limited memory, it maintains a secure shadow stack (a hidden backup copy of return addresses) that it compares against actual execution to detect attacks.
date-2025-143.key_novelty: EILID achieves real-time local detection of control-flow attacks on resource-limited IoT devices by layering automatic code checks on top of a trusted hardware foundation, rather than relying on remote verification.

date-2025-148.method: The method uses adaptive gradient quantization that handles both small and large-magnitude gradients by finding optimal thresholds through kernel density estimation (examining how densely gradient values cluster). Rather than generating expensive new random numbers for each rounding operation, it introduces an LFSR-based reusable stochastic rounding unit—a simple shift register that produces repeating pseudo-random patterns—allowing the same random numbers to be reused across many rounding steps and significantly reducing hardware complexity.
date-2025-148.key_novelty: An LFSR-based stochastic rounding unit that reuses the same pseudo-random number patterns instead of generating new ones, eliminating the computational cost of random number generation in low-bit training.

date-2025-106.method: Logarithmic domain computing (representing numbers as logarithms) reduces quantization error and complexity in large language models, but normally requires expensive, high-precision hardware to handle the multiplication and accumulation operations that neural networks depend on. The paper proposes segment-wise accumulation (SWA): dividing the computation into segments that are processed separately and then combined, which reduces errors that build up during computation. A custom processing element allows SWA to integrate into systolic array architectures (the grid-like hardware accelerators used in AI chips) with significantly lower hardware overhead than floating-point precision enhancements.
date-2025-106.key_novelty: Segment-wise accumulation decomposes computation into segments, enabling efficient logarithmic domain computing without requiring expensive, high-precision hardware.

date-2025-170.method: Uses classical deep neural networks—the same type used in computer vision—to predict what parameters should be set in quantum circuits based on input data. Neural networks naturally process batches of many samples at once, avoiding the need to configure quantum circuits one sample at a time. The method employs real-valued circuit parameters and a three-phase training strategy to achieve this efficiency.
date-2025-170.key_novelty: Uses classical neural networks to directly predict quantum circuit parameters from input data, enabling efficient batch quantum data loading.

date-2025-117.method: IR drop is the inevitable voltage sag that occurs in a chip's power distribution network—computing it at full scale is computationally prohibitive. IR-Fusion addresses this by starting with a numerical solver (AMG-PCG, combining algebraic multigrid with conjugate gradient optimization) to quickly generate a rough but accurate foundation. A specialized neural network (Inception Attention U-Net) then refines this foundation by learning power grid patterns across multiple scales—both broad and fine-grained—through hierarchical fusion, which blends the solver's structural information with the network's learned features. The system uses curriculum learning (training progressively on harder design variations) to generalize across different chip designs.
date-2025-117.key_novelty: The core innovation is a hybrid numerical-machine-learning fusion where a traditional solver generates an accurate foundation that a neural network rapidly refines, combining solver precision with machine learning speed.

date-2025-141.method: The approach uses data mining—a technique for finding patterns in data—to extract rules describing how legitimate Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs: unique, unchangeable hardware identifiers) normally behave. It then compares new or suspicious PUFs against these learned patterns to detect anomalies: significant deviations that indicate tampering, manufacturing defects, or counterfeiting. By systematically identifying when a PUF doesn't match expected behavior, the system catches security compromises automatically.
date-2025-141.key_novelty: Using data mining to automatically detect when PUFs deviate from patterns of legitimate chips, catching tampering and defects.

date-2025-129.method: In STT-MRAM, cells far from write drivers become less reliable because connecting wires act as resistors and capacitors, degrading the electrical signals needed for writing data. Instead of using uniform error correction coding (a technique that detects and fixes data corruption) across all cells, this method applies stronger error protection to vulnerable rows and weaker protection to reliable rows nearer the drivers. This zone-based strategy concentrates the overhead of error correction exactly where errors are most likely to occur.
date-2025-129.key_novelty: The innovation is applying variable-strength error correction that matches each location's vulnerability to interconnect effects instead of protecting uniformly.

date-2025-105.method: The paper examines how Logarithmic Number System addition works in large language models, identifying patterns unique to these workloads. It derives the mathematical relationships between lookup table design choices (such as size and precision) and resulting computation errors. Using these insights, it restructures the lookup table to exploit LLM-specific patterns, reducing hardware area while maintaining calculation accuracy.
date-2025-105.key_novelty: Lookup tables for Logarithmic Number System addition become more hardware-efficient when tailored to large language model patterns instead of generic use.

date-2025-192.method: The system uses a signal comparator (a circuit that examines incoming data) to split the work between two paths. Low-precision signals use low-resolution photonic converters, which can process many operations in parallel through photonic circuits. High-precision signals bypass the slow conversion step and go straight to digital circuits instead. By routing each type of signal to the right processor, the system avoids the expensive conversion overhead that normally limits photonic speedup.
date-2025-192.key_novelty: The core innovation is choosing where each signal gets processed—photonic converters for low-precision data, digital circuits for high-precision data—so the expensive signal conversion only happens when photonic processing can actually speed things up.

date-2025-153.method: PS-GS divides the rendering scene into groups of Gaussians (the 3D blob-like primitives used in Gaussian Splatting), adapting each group's composition to the camera viewpoint so that each stage handles simpler work. Preprocessing clusters the data and sorts by depth (distance from camera), and these stages flow through a hardware pipeline where different stages can process different groups simultaneously—while one group renders, the next is being prepared. This parallel processing of groups through multiple stages, combined with reduced complexity at each stage, enables real-time rendering on resource-constrained devices.
date-2025-153.key_novelty: The core idea is to use approximate Gaussian ordering (fast but not perfect) to divide work into groups that can flow through multiple pipeline stages at the same time.

date-2025-152.method: This approach builds Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs (network structures that find similar data points by navigating through connections) with parameters that automatically adapt to your data. Instead of using fixed settings for the number of connections per node and the search depth, it measures how tightly data points cluster together locally and how many dimensions your data has, then adjusts these two settings accordingly. The result is a graph structure optimized for your specific data characteristics, making both construction and searching more efficient.
date-2025-152.key_novelty: Instead of using fixed settings, automatically adjust a Hierarchical Navigable Small World graph's connection count and search depth based on how clustered and high-dimensional your data is.

date-2025-181.method: Instead of simulating the entire 3D structure, the method splits it into a Region of Interest (ROI—where the important thermal components are) and a Region of Fixity (ROF—the rest). It then simulates only the ROI, using a flexible thermal conductance model (TCM) to represent how the ROF region thermally affects the ROI.
