The TCM uses rational expressions (fractions of polynomials)—which encode the steady-state thermal impact as a function of varying boundary conditions like cooling rates—so the model adapts to different scenarios without re-running the full simulation.
date-2025-181.key_novelty: A thermal conductance model using rational expressions (polynomial fractions) predicts how outer regions thermally affect the inner region without full re-simulation, and adapts to changing boundary conditions.

date-2025-217.method: The method uses Genetic Algorithms (a search technique that mimics evolution) to identify which signals flowing through a chip matter most for power prediction, then feeds only those key signals into Spiking Neural Networks (neural networks modeled on how neurons fire in bursts, which efficiently learn patterns over time). By reducing the number of signals needed, the model becomes smaller and faster to run, enabling real-time power management.
date-2025-217.key_novelty: The core idea is combining Genetic Algorithms for signal selection with Spiking Neural Networks—neural networks that efficiently handle time-series patterns by processing discrete events—to achieve a compact, accurate model for predicting power consumption.

date-2025-156.method: MEMHD breaks high-dimensional vectors into multiple smaller pieces, grouped by similarity (clustering). These pieces are shrunk to fit the fixed-size in-memory computing array, and the system learns to compensate for this shrinkage over repeated cycles. This approach enables one-shot and few-shot retrieval while fully utilizing the array.
date-2025-156.key_novelty: Decomposing hyperdimensional vectors into multiple clustered representations enables full utilization of fixed-size in-memory computing arrays.

date-2025-211.method: The approach uses three techniques running on a multi-core CPU (a processor with multiple processing units working together) to speed up the simulation of functional pattern faults. First, it removes faults that can be mathematically proven to not matter, so the simulator doesn't waste time on them. Second, it groups similar faults together so they can share calculations instead of being simulated separately. Third, it distributes the remaining work across the CPU's cores so multiple faults are tested at the same time.
date-2025-211.key_novelty: The key idea is combining fault filtering, grouping, and parallelization into one strategy that's optimized for how functional pattern faults behave.

date-2025-187.method: The approach uses three techniques that work together. First, it predicts when data blocks will no longer be accessed and proactively writes them back to main memory, reducing the number of dirty cachelines (modified data still in cache). Second, it monitors the CXL Memory Module's bandwidth usage and only performs these write-backs during idle periods to avoid slowing down other traffic. Third, Buddy ECC assigns different levels of protection: stronger error correction (ECC, which detects and fixes errors) for the remaining dirty cachelines, and simpler error detection (EDC, which detects but doesn't fix errors) for clean cachelines, since they're safely backed up in main memory.
date-2025-187.key_novelty: Buddy ECC exploits CXL's full-duplex capabilities (simultaneous two-way data transfer) to dynamically adjust error-protection strength based on cacheline state, using strong ECC for dirty cachelines and weak EDC for clean ones.

date-2025-193.method: The circuit uses pairs of magnetic memory cells (STT-MRAM) to perform multiply-accumulate math on data that stays in memory. Since STT-MRAM produces weak signals that become corrupted by manufacturing defects and power supply changes, the design converts voltage readings into timing signals (measuring pulse duration), which are stable and resistant to these variations. The timing is then converted back into the final computation result. The system automatically adjusts its calibration whenever manufacturing differences or power fluctuations occur, keeping computations accurate without requiring a separate analog-to-digital converter.
date-2025-193.key_novelty: It converts analog voltage measurements to timing signals for stable in-memory computing with automatic calibration, avoiding a separate analog-to-digital converter.

date-2025-203.method: The system uses an FPGA (programmable hardware chip) to run thousands of reinforcement learning environments in parallel, using pipelining—arranging stages of work so data transfers and computation overlap. This hides the delay from moving data between the chip and computer, preventing data transfers from becoming the slowest part. Users can define custom environments, and it scales from 1024 to 43,008+ parallel environments.
date-2025-203.key_novelty: Pipelining parallel environments (arranging stages of work so data transfers and computation overlap) to eliminate the I/O bottleneck in multi-environment reinforcement learning.

date-2025-212.method: SBQ enables extreme low-precision quantization (2-4 bits) without accuracy loss by extracting only significant bits—the most critical bits—from high-precision operands. A product-aware method identifies which bits matter by examining multiplication results. Error-compensated computation mathematically corrects for the discarded bits, and a custom inference engine efficiently implements this on hardware.
date-2025-212.key_novelty: Dynamically extracting significant bits (the most critical bits) and mathematically compensating for the discarded bits enables accurate quantization at extreme compression levels (2-4 bits).

date-2025-219.method: GTN represents a standard cell as a graph with transistors as nodes and connections as edges. A transformer neural network (which can process all connections simultaneously) uses positional information about the circuit layout to predict electrical waveforms directly from this structure. This bypasses most SPICE simulations (the traditional verification bottleneck), achieving a 70% reduction while maintaining accuracy.
date-2025-219.key_novelty: The key insight is combining circuit graphs (transistors as nodes, connections as edges) with a transformer neural network using positional encodings (information about how transistors sit and connect in the circuit) to predict electrical behavior directly from circuit structure.

date-2025-223.method: FUSIS merges two techniques that usually involve choosing between them: it trains a Deep Kernel SVM model (a machine-learning classifier that predicts whether a chip design passes or fails), then uses those predictions to guide importance sampling—a statistical method that concentrates computational effort on scenarios most likely to fail, enabling faster convergence to an accurate yield estimate. A correction factor adjusts the final yield prediction to account for any systematic errors the SVM introduces. The approach was tested on SRAM and analog circuits.
date-2025-223.key_novelty: The core idea is using a machine-learning surrogate to decide where importance sampling should concentrate its computational effort, merging the speed of surrogates with the accuracy of importance sampling.

date-2025-232.method: When data is written to overlapping magnetic disk tracks, it can disturb neighbors, requiring expensive read-modify-write fix-ups to keep data correct. EF-IMR minimizes these fix-ups through smart scheduling (reducing disk head movement), write merging (combining multiple writes), and skip detection (avoiding unnecessary operations).
date-2025-232.key_novelty: EF-IMR maintains data safety during crashes on overlapping-track magnetic disks while reducing wasted disk head movement by intelligently scheduling which fix-up operations to perform and skipping those that aren't needed.

date-2025-226.method: The researchers designed an IoT tag (a small device for locating wireless objects) that powers itself from harvested solar energy. They created a simulation combining models of energy generation from the solar panel and energy consumption from the electronics, including the nRF52833 microcontroller and DW3110 ultra-wideband transceiver (a radio module that determines location through wireless signals). They used publicly available simulation tools to optimize the design by testing tradeoffs: larger solar panels provide more power and longer device lifespan but require more physical area, while faster localization uses more energy.
date-2025-226.key_novelty: They developed an integrated simulation that combines models of solar energy harvesting with device electronics power consumption, enabling optimization of energy-autonomous Internet-of-Things devices.

date-2025-244.method: The team evaluates a stochastic calibration protocol—which adjusts quantum gate parameters based on measurement results—to understand how feedback delays affect performance. They synthesize the required classical control logic and simulate it on 28nm CMOS technology, then extend simulations to 14nm FinFET and cryogenic operating temperatures. These simulations demonstrate the protocol is practical and characterize its resource and performance requirements.
date-2025-244.key_novelty: Quantum gate calibration can run inside standard computer chips without specialized control hardware, while keeping feedback fast enough to track quantum system drift.

date-2025-266.method: The project creates tools to manage computing resources spread across edge devices (at network boundaries), fog nodes (in between), and cloud servers (centralized). It uses cognitive orchestration—intelligent algorithms that automatically place tasks where they'll run most efficiently based on current conditions. It provides one unified environment where developers design and manage these distributed systems without separately handling each layer's unique technical requirements.
date-2025-266.key_novelty: Unified design and intelligent orchestration across the entire edge-fog-cloud computing continuum.

date-2025-239.method: The design uses 4-terminal nanoelectromechanical (NEM) relays—mechanical switches with four connection points, controlled by electric signals—instead of transistors to build comparators (circuits that determine if two numbers are equal or which is larger). A single-bit comparator needs only 6 NEM devices versus 9 transistors in traditional silicon designs, and the relays are built on a silicon-on-insulator substrate (a layered semiconductor structure). For larger comparators, a tree-based stacking pattern reduces the total device count by about 47% versus traditional designs when handling 64-bit numbers.
date-2025-239.key_novelty: Using 4-terminal nanoelectromechanical relays instead of transistors to build comparators in silicon eliminates standby power waste and tolerates extreme conditions: temperatures up to 300°C and radiation doses exceeding 1 Mrad.

date-2025-249.method: The technique represents both the specification and implementation of how memory addresses are assigned in a chip using graphs—diagrams where components appear as nodes and their memory connections appear as edges. It then systematically compares these two graphs to detect any discrepancies and pinpoint exactly where they differ. This graph-based approach ensures complete and systematic verification compared to manual inspection.
date-2025-249.key_novelty: A single graph-based representation for both specification and implementation address maps enables systematic verification that they're identical.

date-2025-280.method: HAAN tackles the normalization bottleneck—the step where models stabilize values flowing through the network—by jointly redesigning the computation and the hardware that runs it. Rather than keeping the algorithm fixed and hoping hardware will improve, the approach tweaks the computation itself and designs specialized hardware tailored to run that exact algorithm. This co-design (joint optimization of algorithm and hardware) reduces both latency and energy consumption. Because normalization happens frequently in LLM inference, even small per-operation gains compound into significant overall speedups.
date-2025-280.key_novelty: The core idea is applying co-design (joint algorithm-and-hardware optimization) to normalization in LLM inference.

date-2025-233.method: Slipstream tracks how much each embedding (learned numbers representing different items) changes during training and detects saturation—when it stops learning. When an embedding saturates, Slipstream skips its gradient updates (computationally expensive calculations that adjust the learned numbers), since they no longer provide improvement. Combined with existing techniques that categorize embeddings as popular or non-popular, this delivers greater savings.
date-2025-233.key_novelty: Detecting when embeddings have saturated and skipping their gradient updates reduces training work while maintaining model accuracy.

date-2025-265.method: The researchers tested whether Rowhammer and Rowpress attacks—which exploit repeated memory access to flip bits in nearby rows—could compromise monolithic 3D embedded DRAM with oxide-channel transistors. They examined vulnerabilities across traditional 2D layouts and new 3D stacking arrangements (including memory on logic and memory-on-memory configurations), investigating whether the physical stacking itself introduces new electrical disturbances. They evaluated whether changes to chip design and memory architecture could defend against these attacks.
date-2025-265.key_novelty: This provides the first comprehensive security analysis of monolithic 3D embedded DRAM with oxide-channel transistors, identifying vulnerabilities specific to vertical memory stacking.

date-2025-289.method: CorrectBench takes a hardware design specification (RTL) and uses an LLM to automatically generate test cases. It runs these tests to validate them. When tests fail, the system analyzes the failures and uses that error information to automatically fix the tests. This process repeats until the tests pass.
date-2025-289.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically fixing broken tests using failure information, with no human involvement needed.

date-2025-274.method: The approach trains hard reset spiking neural networks (neural networks that compute using discrete pulses, built into neuromorphic hardware devices) by using gradient clipping—capping the size of weight adjustments during training to keep the learning process stable. Rather than treating device noise (random variations in the physical hardware) as interference to eliminate, the method exploits it to enhance learning performance. The technique is validated across multiple datasets and neural network architectures.
date-2025-274.key_novelty: Device noise in neuromorphic hardware can improve learning in hard reset spiking neural networks, contrary to the standard practice of treating it purely as interference.

date-2025-258.method: By connecting academic AI researchers directly with manufacturers, the project grounds AI solutions in real factory problems rather than lab settings. The resulting AI-driven tools and hardware are designed with two constraints built in from the start: they must keep humans meaningfully involved in decisions (not just executing automated steps), and they must reduce environmental impact. This co-design approach means technical capability and human/sustainability requirements shape each other.
date-2025-258.key_novelty: Industry 5.0 AI systems can integrate automation hardware, digital autonomy (system flexibility and independence), environmental sustainability, and human involvement as mutually reinforcing rather than competing priorities.

date-2025-298.method: The method creates artificial test images and uses entropy—a measure of information diversity—to guide which images reveal the most about how a chip behaves under manufacturing variations. It then selects a compact set of just 10-20 images from these synthetic options that capture all the important testing scenarios. Finally, it uses a machine learning model to detect outlier patterns in how the chip responds to these images, classifying each test result as pass or fail.
date-2025-298.key_novelty: The core idea is using entropy-guided synthetic images to test manufacturing variations without needing the original training data.

date-2025-313.method: SparseInfer predicts which computations in language models can be skipped when using ReLU activation (where negative outputs become zero) without any training. It checks only whether each input and weight value is positive or negative—not the actual numbers—to decide if an activation will be zero and safe to skip. You can tune the predictor to be more or less aggressive, trading off how many operations you actually skip against the risk of incorrectly identifying which ones can be skipped.
date-2025-313.key_novelty: It predicts which computations can be skipped in ReLU language models using only sign comparison of inputs and weights, without training a separate predictor.

date-2025-236.method: The RTL-Breaker framework tests how to poison LLMs that generate hardware designs (HDL/RTL code specifies how chips operate). It hides malicious patterns in training data to make the LLM produce harmful code in hardware designs, then measures which patterns are most effective and whether the poisoned code still works. It also examines whether attacks stay effective over time. The framework and datasets were released publicly.
date-2025-236.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of how LLMs that generate hardware designs can be poisoned by introducing malicious patterns into training data, examining which patterns work best and whether such poisoning can be detected.

date-2025-297.method: BIMAX performs bitwise logic operations (AND, OR, NOT, XOR, NAND, NXOR) and row-copy directly within 6T-SRAM cells using a specially modified sense amplifier—the circuit normally used to read bits from memory. By designing this sense amplifier with intentional asymmetry (making one input path stronger than the other), it can compute logic results when comparing multiple cell values in parallel, instead of just reading them. The computed results are then written back to memory, enabling logic gates and data copying to happen inside the SRAM array itself.
date-2025-297.key_novelty: The core innovation is designing the sense amplifier asymmetrically (with one input path intentionally stronger) so it can reliably compute bitwise logic operations in standard 6T-SRAM cells despite electrical noise.

date-2025-315.method: SAFELOC combines poisoning detection (identifying data deliberately corrupted to sabotage training) with indoor localization in a single neural network deployed across mobile devices using federated learning, so sensitive data never leaves the device. As training happens, it monitors for poisoning attacks, and when one is detected, it uses saliency maps—a technique that shows which parts of the model matter most—to adjust how much it trusts each device's updates. The stronger the detected attack, the more aggressively it filters out suspicious contributions.
date-2025-315.key_novelty: SAFELOC's innovation is using saliency maps to intelligently combine federated learning updates from multiple devices, scaling its poisoning defenses proportional to detected attack severity while maintaining a model compact enough for mobile devices.

date-2025-290.method: The researchers evaluate a prior multiplicative masking design (from De Meyer et al. 2018) using the PROLEAD evaluation tool. This tool searches for side-channel leakage—ways that sensitive information might escape through observable side effects like power consumption or timing—by testing the design under conditions that allow attackers to observe these effects. They find that the Kronecker delta function (which compares values and outputs 1 when they match, 0 otherwise) leaks information this way, particularly at the first-order level (the most direct form of leakage). They then propose a solution by optimizing the randomness used in the masking scheme.
date-2025-290.key_novelty: The Kronecker delta function (a mathematical building block that detects when values match) in multiplicative masking designs has a leakage vulnerability that can be fixed through improved randomness optimization.

date-2025-301.method: The system combines hardware and software to monitor an unmodified RISC-V program as it runs, continuously generating Generalized Path Signature Analysis (GPSA) signatures—fingerprints based on the execution path (the actual sequence of instructions being executed). These signatures check that the program's control flow (which instruction is executed next) remains correct and that the code itself hasn't been corrupted. If a fault attack tries to alter the program's path or code, the signature check catches it.
date-2025-301.key_novelty: This is the first method to protect already-compiled RISC-V programs from fault attacks without compiler or binary modifications, including indirect jumps (jumps where the destination is calculated while the program runs).

date-2025-323.method: CLEAR groups existing users based on their emotion-recognition patterns, finding natural clusters without needing labels (unsupervised clustering). When a new user arrives with minimal labeled data, the system assigns them to the most similar cluster and fine-tunes that cluster's model using just a few of their labeled examples, adapting it to their individual style. The entire system runs on resource-constrained edge devices: Coral Edge TPU and Movidius Neural Compute Stick 2.
date-2025-323.key_novelty: The key idea is using unsupervised clustering to group users, allowing new users to personalize a cluster's model with just a few labeled examples instead of needing either a generic model or full individual labeling.

date-2025-316.method: The method implements two control flow checking algorithms—YACCA and RACFED—using Rust, which has built-in protections against memory errors that are common in C. Because Rust prevents these memory mistakes automatically, the same code can run on any hardware without modification (this is called 'platform-agnostic'). The checks work at the application level, meaning they're built into the program itself rather than requiring special OS or hardware support, and they detect when a program's execution path deviates from its intended course to catch faults in safety-critical systems—those where failures could cause real harm.
date-2025-316.key_novelty: These control flow checking algorithms are the first to be implemented in Rust at the application level, making it possible to detect faults in safety-critical systems using the same code across any hardware platform.

date-2025-331.method: The approach identifies optimization opportunities using two enumeration strategies. A dynamic strategy adapts in real-time as the circuit (represented as an And-Inverter Graph, or AIG—a compact way to store circuit logic) changes during optimization, while a static strategy prioritizes speed for stable circuits. Both search for Maximum Fanout-Free Windows—sub-structures where outputs don't branch—to rewrite and improve circuits and prepare them for specific hardware.
date-2025-331.key_novelty: This is the first systematic exploration of fanout-free windows as multi-output optimization targets, introducing dynamic and static enumeration algorithms for circuit optimization.

date-2025-336.method: The approach splits the mapping problem into two sequential searches instead of solving them together. First, it uses SMT (a logical solver that checks whether constraints can be satisfied) to find the timing schedule—determining when each operation should execute. Then, it uses monomorphism-based graph matching (a structural pattern-matching technique that preserves how operations connect to each other) to assign each operation to a physical location on the array. By solving timing first, it eliminates many impossible spatial arrangements, making the spatial search much faster.
date-2025-336.key_novelty: Solving the timing schedule before choosing spatial locations eliminates impossible option combinations and dramatically speeds up compilation for large arrays.

date-2025-330.method: Amphi predicts which memory addresses the processor will need next from the L1 cache (the processor's smallest, fastest built-in memory) using a binarized temporal convolutional network—a type of neural network that learns patterns from sequences of past memory requests. By binarizing the network (converting its internal values to just 1s and 0s), Amphi shrinks the model from ~27 KB (the size used by previous ML prefetcher Pythia) to 3.4 KB, small enough to fit on a chip, while maintaining the same performance.
date-2025-330.key_novelty: This is the first machine-learning prefetcher designed for the first-level cache, made practical by using binarized neural networks to compress the model small enough to fit on a chip.

date-2025-321.method: The approach uses Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) — an automated reasoning technique that solves complex logical constraints — to design hardware translation logic between restricted and unrestricted codes. Rather than engineers manually designing this logic over weeks, the SMT solver automatically finds designs that minimize both hardware complexity and transmission error effects. This reduces design time from weeks to hours.
date-2025-321.key_novelty: Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) automatically designs hardware that translates constrained codes, eliminating the manual, error-prone design process.

date-2025-302.method: The approach uses caching to speed up software simulation of RISC-V processors. When the processor executes the same instruction sequence multiple times (called a basic block), the simulator caches the results so it doesn't have to re-simulate them—it just looks them up instead. Similarly, it caches memory read and write operations, which are normally slow to simulate. These two optimizations are built into a SystemC-based virtual prototype, achieving high performance while keeping the code understandable and modifiable.
date-2025-302.key_novelty: The core idea is combining instruction-sequence caching (basic blocks) with memory-operation caching to achieve high performance without sacrificing code clarity.

date-2025-310.method: The algorithm breaks the timing graph into cycles (called strongly connected components) and arranges them into layers. It calculates how signals propagate in parallel across different layers, but works through each cycle step-by-step. It also detects divergent loops—cycles where the calculation won't converge—so it can skip those unnecessary iterations.
date-2025-310.key_novelty: By breaking timing feedback loops into independent groups (strongly connected components) and looking ahead for cycles that won't converge, the method cuts computation from quadratic in all pins to quadratic in each group's size.

date-2025-334.method: Instead of manually translating processor instruction specifications into intermediate code (a step prone to errors), this tool uses formal, machine-readable specifications directly for symbolic execution—a technique that tests code by systematically exploring all possible execution paths. The formal specifications precisely define how each instruction in the processor works, and the tool reads them directly rather than requiring researchers to hand-translate them. The approach was prototyped on RISC-V and shown to extend to other processor architectures.
date-2025-334.key_novelty: Using machine-readable formal specifications directly avoids the error-prone manual translation step that traditional symbolic execution requires.

date-2025-347.method: ReRAM-PIM accelerators distribute data across separate memory banks to speed up matrix multiplications, but this creates a problem: softmax normally requires seeing all values at once to compute the correct normalization. The solution breaks softmax computation into independent segments that stay within each memory bank's local data, avoiding the need to copy values between banks. Each segment produces a localized result, then these are carefully recombined to match what a single global softmax would produce. This keeps computation close to the data, eliminating the expensive communication bottleneck that would otherwise appear when the real matrix-math bottleneck is solved.
date-2025-347.key_novelty: Instead of trying to compute softmax across all distributed data, segment it so each memory bank normalizes its own local portion independently, then merge the results—solving the data-movement bottleneck that ReRAM-PIM architectures create.

date-2025-332.method: Cocktail reduces GPU memory by lowering the precision of the KV cache—the data cached from previous tokens that enables fast attention computation. Instead of deciding precision individually for each token (which takes too long to search), it groups tokens into chunks and uses the similarity between the current query and previous context to choose how much precision each chunk needs. It then reorders the chunks by precision level, so the GPU processes all chunks of one precision level together before switching to the next, which lets the hardware run efficiently without constantly switching between different precision formats.
date-2025-332.key_novelty: Cocktail groups tokens into chunks for mixed-precision decisions and explicitly reorders them by precision level so the GPU can process chunks of the same precision together, avoiding the efficiency penalty of constantly switching precisions.

date-2025-358.method: SCALES applies scaling factors (adjustable multipliers) at multiple levels to handle how activation values vary across the network. It scales at three granularities: across network layers (layer-wise), across pixels in an image (pixel-wise), and across information channels (channel-wise). Each scaling factor adjusts based on the specific input image, so it adapts to whatever activation distributions (the ranges and patterns of intermediate values) appear. This multi-level scaling captures how activation distributions differ across the network's depth and across spatial regions of the image.
date-2025-358.key_novelty: Using input-dependent scaling factors at multiple levels (layers, pixels, and channels) allows binary neural networks to accurately capture the varying activation distributions needed for image super-resolution.

date-2025-342.method: A spiking neural network (a type of AI inspired by how brains work, where neurons fire sparsely rather than constantly) embedded in a variational autoencoder (a learning technique that finds patterns in compressed data representations) processes spectral measurements from high-speed electron microscopy at 400 frames per second, predicting material structure as new data arrives. Unlike traditional approaches that require offline training on pre-recorded data first, this system learns continuously from the data stream as it comes in. The entire process runs on an FPGA (field-programmable gate array—customizable hardware), achieving signal clarity of 28.3 dB and processing speeds 25.2 to 93.7 times faster than standard methods.
date-2025-342.key_novelty: This is the first electron energy loss spectroscopy system that learns continuously from incoming data using brain-inspired neural networks combined with a data-compression learning method, all running directly on hardware without needing any pre-recorded training data.

date-2025-368.method: PICBench creates a test suite that measures how well AI language models can generate netlists—detailed specifications describing photonic integrated circuits (optical chips that process information using light). It validates the AI-generated designs by simulating them and comparing the results to expert-written solutions, checking both the correctness of the instructions and whether the circuits work as intended. The framework systematically tests different AI models and different ways of instructing them (prompt engineering strategies) to determine which approaches are most effective.
date-2025-368.key_novelty: PICBench is the first systematic test and evaluation framework specifically designed for measuring how well AI language models can design photonic integrated circuits.

date-2025-374.method: The system starts by guessing labels for incoming data that has no labels—this is called pseudo-labeling. It then uses dataset condensation to compress that data into a small set of synthetic examples, keeping the most useful information while discarding the rest. To make sure each synthetic example clearly represents a single category, the method adds an objective that pulls examples of the same class together while pushing different classes apart, improving class purity.
date-2025-374.key_novelty: The core idea is to use guessed labels to enable dataset condensation—compressing unlabeled streaming data into synthetic examples—so edge devices can learn without needing human-labeled data.

date-2025-349.method: The system audits devices to detect when hardware Trojans (malicious circuits hidden in chips) from different vendors coordinate, then removes infected devices from operation. It employs multi-agent reinforcement learning (multiple AI agents learning through trial and error) to automatically decide which vendor should supply each device, optimizing to keep the maximum number of devices running.
date-2025-349.key_novelty: Using multi-agent reinforcement learning to assign devices to vendors protects cyber-physical systems from hardware Trojans even when only a few vendors are available.

date-2025-394.method: The system watches which experts each input sequence actually uses, then dynamically chooses whether each expert lives on the faster GPU or slower CPU storage. Before the GPU needs an expert, it predicts which one comes next and pre-calculates it on the CPU—so the answer is ready before the GPU requests it. This prediction-and-preparation strategy replaces the expensive CPU-GPU data transfers that normally happen. When GPU memory fills up, the system gracefully switches to using more CPU storage; it runs slower but stays accurate instead of crashing.
date-2025-394.key_novelty: The system predicts which experts each input needs and pre-positions them to avoid the slow CPU-GPU data transfers that normally eliminate the GPU's speed advantage.

date-2025-351.method: ASNPC uses a prediction model to efficiently search through the vast space of SNN-processor design options without needing expensive hardware simulations. It automatically generates hardware code (RTL, which describes exactly how the processor's circuits work) for the most promising designs and feeds their performance results back into the search. Over multiple iterations, this discovers a set of good designs where each makes different trade-offs between competing goals like speed, energy efficiency, and accuracy.
date-2025-351.key_novelty: Combining a prediction model for exploring multiple design trade-offs with automatic hardware code generation enables efficient SNN-processor co-design.

date-2025-396.method: The approach trains a neural network to predict electromagnetic fields (how electricity and magnetism spread through space) while enforcing Maxwell's equations—the fundamental physics laws of electromagnetism—as constraints during training. Instead of using fixed weights to balance physics and data accuracy, the system automatically adjusts these weights at each training step, letting both objectives improve together. This avoids running expensive electromagnetic simulations (called FDTD), achieving over 200 times faster predictions than traditional methods.
date-2025-396.key_novelty: The innovation is an algorithm that automatically adjusts the importance of physics constraints versus data accuracy during training, allowing both objectives to improve together.

date-2025-411.method: The researchers develop an attack methodology by profiling Samsung DRAM chips to capture how RowPress (a memory-based attack that flips targeted bits through repeated access patterns) produces distinct bit-flip patterns compared to RowHammer. They then evaluate how these RowPress-induced bit-flips affect 11 different neural network architectures across multiple standard benchmark datasets to measure the real-world impact.
date-2025-411.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive evaluation showing that RowPress attacks degrade deep neural networks faster than RowHammer attacks.

date-2025-409.method: The method presents Verilog generation problems as a Tree of Thoughts prompt, which branches out into multiple reasoning paths organized hierarchically (like a tree) rather than following a single linear chain. This hierarchical structure explicitly encodes how real hardware breaks down into nested modules, where each module's correctness depends on lower-level components working properly. By matching the prompt structure to hardware's actual organization, the LLM can understand design constraints and dependencies that standard Chain-of-Thought prompting misses.
date-2025-409.key_novelty: The core innovation is organizing prompts as a hierarchical tree (multiple branches layered to reflect hardware design structure) rather than a linear sequence, enabling LLMs to generate correct Verilog code by reasoning about component dependencies.

date-2025-383.method: The accelerator combines a unified data format with specialized hardware that handles two types of sparsity: value-level (skipping computations on zero values) and bit-level (skipping computations on zero bits within values). Normally, exploiting these separately creates multiplexing delays and forces slow bit-by-bit processing. Instead, the hardware is codesigned with the software to work directly with the unified format, eliminating these bottlenecks.
date-2025-383.key_novelty: This is the first accelerator that exploits value-level and bit-level sparsity together through a single unified hardware-software design, rather than handling them separately.

date-2025-378.method: The approach uses an Unsupervised Learning Residual LSTM (ULR_LSTM)—a type of neural network—to learn how to cancel out the nonlinear distortion created by digital power amplifiers. Unlike traditional methods that require expensive iterative training loops, this network is trained once to reverse the amplifier's behavior. The system is implemented as a 15-bit transformer-based quadrature digital power amplifier chip in 28nm CMOS technology, using Class-G power efficiency and IQ-cell-sharing (which efficiently handles in-phase and quadrature signal components).
date-2025-378.key_novelty: This is the first use of unsupervised LSTM training to correct power amplifier nonlinearity without iterative learning loops.

date-2025-384.method: SHWCIM combines SRAM-based computing-in-memory cores—which perform calculations directly within memory rather than shuttling data between storage and a separate processor—with reconfigurable hardware blocks that can be rewired to handle different operations. This combination lets one chip efficiently process diverse workloads instead of being limited to a single type of computation. The design was evaluated using SMIC 55nm process technology.
date-2025-384.key_novelty: It's the first scalable design combining SRAM-based in-memory computing cores (which calculate directly where data is stored) with reconfigurable hardware blocks to handle diverse workloads.

date-2025-376.method: The system combines two token-selection techniques applied at different depths of the Vision Transformer. In early layers, it uses Keypoint-based Token Selection, which identifies and keeps tokens corresponding to visually important features. In later layers, it switches to Attention-based Token Selection, which removes tokens that other parts of the model aren't using. Custom hardware accelerators speed up both the token selection process and the Vision Transformer backbone.
date-2025-376.key_novelty: The key idea is using two different token-selection methods at different network depths—content-based in early layers and attention-based in later layers—with hardware acceleration.

date-2025-417.method: Matrix multiplication normally requires heavy arithmetic, which FPGAs struggle with due to limited memory bandwidth. LUT-MU replaces arithmetic with lookup tables (memory locations storing pre-computed results), which approximates answers much faster on FPGAs. It then rearranges how data sits in local memory and stages the computation in a pipeline (sequential processing steps) so more data moves per cycle and the processor always has work ready, making better use of available bandwidth.
date-2025-417.key_novelty: Structuring LUT-based matrix multiplication as a pipeline specifically designed for how data moves through on-chip memory lets the FPGA overcome bandwidth bottlenecks.

date-2025-404.method: This method breaks the single-ring topology into multiple smaller sub-rings connected by waveguides, greatly reducing the longest distance any light signal must travel. It then uses mathematical optimization—specifically mixed integer linear programming (MILP)—to determine which wavelengths (colors of light) to assign to each connection. This wavelength assignment minimizes the number of optical splitters (devices that distribute light signals) needed in the power distribution network.
date-2025-404.key_novelty: Sub-ring clustering (dividing the ring into smaller interconnected sub-rings) combined with MILP-based wavelength assignment enables customization of optical network design for specific applications.

fccm-2025-002.method: UltraFormer reduces the memory and computation needed for transformers on FPGAs by combining hybrid linear attention—a simplified attention mechanism that works better on FPGAs than standard approaches—with BitNet b1.58, which uses ultra-low-precision arithmetic (roughly 1.58 bits per number instead of standard 32-bit floats) for the linear projection layers. This achieves ~10x compression in model weights and 13.2x compression in the key-value cache (the temporary data needed during inference). High-Level Synthesis tools compile the architecture to hardware, and it runs on Xilinx FPGAs with optimizations tailored to FPGA constraints.
fccm-2025-002.key_novelty: UltraFormer combines hybrid linear attention with BitNet b1.58 ultra-low-precision projections as a transformer design specifically optimized for FPGAs.

fccm-2025-006.method: Compute-in-memory puts processing logic right inside memory blocks rather than having separate memory and processors that swap data back and forth. On FPGAs (reconfigurable chips), engineers modify the memory blocks already built into the chip to also perform calculations. Because computation happens where data lives, it eliminates the slow, energy-expensive data movement that creates a bottleneck in traditional computer designs.
fccm-2025-006.key_novelty: Using existing FPGA memory blocks as the foundation for compute-in-memory, adding computation capability to what's already there instead of requiring entirely new custom hardware.

fccm-2025-000.method: The authors analyze bit patterns in FP8 numbers to identify where approximations—skipping certain calculation steps—still produce results accurate enough for neural networks. They implement this approximate multiplier on AMD and Altera FPGAs using standard hardware building blocks and layout templates, optimized for minimal resource use. They verify the design through accuracy and resource measurements, then test it in actual neural network inference to confirm power efficiency.
fccm-2025-000.key_novelty: This work creates the first FPGA-based multiplier that approximates FP8 math—trading perfect accuracy for faster, lower-power computation—establishing a benchmark for efficient low-precision floating-point arithmetic.

fccm-2025-009.method: The approach shrinks Vision Transformer models through quantization—converting numbers from 32-bit floating point to lower precision to reduce memory and computation needs. It then implements a multi-kernel hardware design on an FPGA (a reconfigurable hardware chip) where processing units share resources by taking turns executing different operations (time-multiplexed scheduling). Custom hardware accelerators are built specifically for the most expensive ViT computations: attention mechanisms (finding important patterns in images) and linear layers (applying learned transformations). This combination lets the complete model fit and run efficiently on memory-limited FPGAs while preserving its accuracy.
fccm-2025-009.key_novelty: The innovation combines quantization, multi-kernel hardware, and time-multiplexed scheduling (where processing units take turns using shared resources) into a unified design that lets Vision Transformer models run efficiently on memory-limited FPGAs.

fccm-2025-003.method: SoftCUDA is a framework that compiles and runs CUDA programs (code written for NVIDIA GPUs) on a Vortex softcore GPU implemented on FPGAs (reconfigurable hardware you can program). The framework automatically translates CUDA instructions into commands that the Vortex architecture understands, so programmers don't need to rewrite their code. This approach works because FPGAs can be customized to support different GPU designs.
fccm-2025-003.key_novelty: SoftCUDA enables unmodified CUDA applications to run on softcore GPU designs built on FPGAs without requiring translation to a different programming model.

fccm-2025-001.method: The design uses on-chip SRAM (fast memory built into the chip) to reorganize data from HBM into better access patterns. Matrix tiles are arranged using a Latin Square-inspired layout (a mathematical pattern where each value appears exactly once per row and column), with scheduling logic that prevents simultaneous accesses to the same memory bank. A fully pipelined architecture (where operations overlap to run concurrently) with multiple processing elements then reads from HBM in parallel using small strides (nearby memory addresses rather than scattered ones).
fccm-2025-001.key_novelty: The core idea pairs a Latin Square-inspired SRAM data layout with scheduling that eliminates bank conflicts (simultaneous accesses overloading the same memory section), while maintaining efficient small-stride HBM access (accessing nearby rather than scattered addresses).

fccm-2025-007.method: The solver runs on specialized hardware (an FPGA) using a spatially-parallel collision algorithm: it divides space into regions and processes collisions region-by-region instead of letting all processors randomly evaluate collisions. This spatial organization eliminates race conditions—conflicts that occur when multiple processors simultaneously update the same data—that normally limit parallel speedup. The FPGA hardware includes custom memory layouts tailored to different particle densities, which is especially valuable for low-particle microscale simulations.
fccm-2025-007.key_novelty: Organizing collision calculations spatially (dividing space into regions) prevents race conditions that normally block parallel speedup.

fccm-2025-004.method: NeuraLUT-Assemble overcomes the fan-in limitation—the constraint that lookup tables can't efficiently handle many inputs—by combining multiple smaller lookup tables into each neuron. It uses mixed-precision quantization, representing some values with fewer bits than others, to keep the total hardware resources manageable while increasing connectivity. Skip-connections allow gradient signals to flow backward across the network during training, which improves learning. The result is competitive accuracy with traditional dense neural networks while fitting within hardware constraints.
fccm-2025-004.key_novelty: Assembling neurons from smaller lookup tables with mixed-precision quantization (representing different values with different bit-widths) to overcome the fan-in limit—the maximum number of inputs a lookup table can handle.

fccm-2025-010.method: The design uses an FPGA—a reconfigurable chip that can be reprogrammed—organized as a pipeline where processing stages work in sequence like an assembly line, allowing multiple operations to overlap. Data accesses from memory happen in parallel for speed, and the hardware performs double-precision arithmetic (64-bit math) for the accuracy required. To handle stiff differential equations—systems with components that change at vastly different rates—it includes adaptive numerical integration that automatically adjusts step sizes. The modular architecture lets researchers swap different Differential Evolution algorithms and integration methods without rebuilding the hardware.
fccm-2025-010.key_novelty: The core innovation is a modular, pipelined FPGA design—a reconfigurable chip that processes data through sequential stages—built specifically for Differential Evolution, an optimization method that evolves candidate solutions, applied to scientific model fitting.

fccm-2025-008.method: DRSA replaces a greedy approach (choosing the best position for each circuit block one at a time without considering future steps) with simulated annealing, an optimization algorithm that explores many different overall arrangements to find ones that work well together. It iteratively adjusts where the macro components (large circuit blocks) are positioned on the FPGA to minimize the drop in operating frequency, discovering combinations that greedy placement would overlook. This keeps DynaRapid's advantage of fast compilation while fixing the frequency loss that was the main bottleneck.
fccm-2025-008.key_novelty: Using simulated annealing instead of greedy placement for macro components in DynaRapid solves the operating-frequency loss without sacrificing compilation speed.

fccm-2025-011.method: The approach uses a compiler—a tool that translates descriptions into hardware designs—with three components. First, a simple language based on scheduling primitives (basic building blocks for describing how to organize computations) lets you specify what the accelerator should do. Second, a two-step mapping process translates how data flows through computations into actual hardware using sparse meta-operations (reusable patterns for efficient sparse operations). Third, an automated search strategy guided by your actual workload explores different hardware designs and picks the fastest.
fccm-2025-011.key_novelty: The key idea is automatically generating sparse tensor hardware accelerators using a compiler that translates from a simple scheduling-based description language (combining basic building blocks) to hardware using reusable sparse computation patterns.

fccm-2025-012.method: BCIM processes cipher operations one bit at a time rather than in parallel, which naturally takes constant time regardless of input—making it inherently resistant to timing-based side-channel attacks where attackers measure operation duration to deduce secrets. To maintain high speed despite this bit-serial approach, it uses column-wise SIMD processing (single-instruction-multiple-data, where one operation processes multiple data columns simultaneously). The design includes circuit-level optimizations that reduce the memory space needed for storing encryption keys and improve the circuit's operating frequency and power efficiency.
fccm-2025-012.key_novelty: Using bit-serial processing (one bit at a time) alongside column-wise SIMD to achieve both constant-time encryption—which resists timing-based attacks—and high throughput in memory.

fccm-2025-014.method: The approach organizes 3D points using an Octree—a tree structure that divides space into nested boxes—grouping nearby points together. Since points in the same region behave similarly, it approximates them with fewer representative points while preserving the overall structure. This filtering logic runs on an FPGA (a hardware chip designed for specific tasks), processing raw sensor data before it's transmitted or stored.
fccm-2025-014.key_novelty: Approximating point cloud reduction using Octree spatial groupings is fast enough to run in custom hardware (FPGA) right at the 3D sensor, filtering data before transmission.

fccm-2025-013.method: They add small computing circuits called Dot Product Engines—built from RRAM (a type of memory that retains data without power) and placed directly in the FPGA fabric so computation happens where data lives. Dot products (which multiply matching pairs and add the results) are a common operation in AI workloads. They design this for 40 nm chips using the Verilog to Routing framework and test it with a custom event-driven simulator that measures how operations perform over time.
fccm-2025-013.key_novelty: Building analog Dot Product Engines from RRAM and embedding them directly in FPGA fabric means computing happens in memory instead of shuttling data between separate compute and storage blocks.

fccm-2025-017.method: The approach works by first scanning the neural network's weights (the parameters that control how the AI model makes decisions) to find which ones are most sensitive to radiation damage. It then protects only those critical weights using Triple Modular Redundancy — a fault-tolerance technique where three copies of each critical component are built and compared, so if one copy gets corrupted by radiation, the other two vote it down. The design includes custom memory blocks that can be reconfigured after the hardware is deployed, allowing tasks to be swapped without rebuilding the entire chip. A specialized synthesis tool then decides how much redundancy to add to each part based on area and power budgets you set.
fccm-2025-017.key_novelty: It uses vulnerability analysis to apply redundancy only where actually needed, rather than everywhere, and keeps the design reconfigurable after deployment.

fccm-2025-019.method: The method uses sub-8-bit quantization—cutting the precision of weights to a few bits, which shrinks the model and speeds up inference but normally destroys accuracy. To recover that accuracy, it applies an iterative tensor decomposition technique (using SVD to break large operations into simpler, lower-rank parts) that reduces computational cost while compensating for the precision loss. It then runs a hardware-aware search (Design Space Exploration) that tries different precision levels and decomposition depths to find the best balance between accuracy, inference speed, and memory use for the target hardware and language model.
fccm-2025-019.key_novelty: The innovation is a hardware-aware integration of sub-8-bit quantization and iterative tensor decomposition to achieve high model compression without accuracy loss.

fccm-2025-016.method: The paper designs a specialized computing chip (FPGA) that speeds up the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT)—a mathematical operation central to homomorphic encryption, which enables computation on encrypted data. Rather than building different hardware for each NTT size, the design reuses the same computational units flexibly across different sizes and different types of homomorphic encryption. This approach is more efficient than traditional designs because it avoids duplicating expensive hardware components.
fccm-2025-016.key_novelty: A single NTT accelerator hardware design that works across different transform sizes and different types of homomorphic encryption, without needing separate hardware for each size.

fccm-2025-005.method: The approach builds neural networks by programming FPGA lookup tables (LUTs)—the basic programmable logic elements that FPGAs are made of—to compute network operations. Rather than using uniform precision, it strategically mixes low-precision lookups (to save hardware space) with high-precision lookups (to maintain accuracy and allow the network to represent complex patterns). Three specific designs—PolyLUT, NeuraLUT, and NeuraLUT-Assemble—each combine these mixed-precision lookups differently to reduce the network's size and speed up inference.
fccm-2025-005.key_novelty: The key innovation is constructing neural networks directly from FPGA lookup tables with multiple precision levels integrated, rather than building networks first and then adapting them to hardware.

fccm-2025-024.method: IceSpy uses reconfigurable circuit chips called FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays) arranged in a parallel-processing pattern called a systolic array to filter sensor data and add privacy protection directly at the monitoring site, before transmitting anything. The system removes unnecessary information from sensor readings, dramatically cutting how much data needs to be sent wirelessly. It also scrambles sensitive readings using local differential privacy (mathematically adding disguising noise to preserve individual privacy while keeping overall patterns intact), so measurements are already hidden before reaching untrusted servers. This parallel arrangement processes large streams of sensor data efficiently.
fccm-2025-024.key_novelty: IceSpy combines on-device data filtering with privacy protection through local differential privacy using reconfigurable chips (FPGAs) arranged for parallel processing, achieving 3× power reduction while preserving privacy in structural health monitoring.

fccm-2025-023.method: Instead of using traditional block RAM—which can only read one row at a time—they replace it with compute-in-memory cells built from a 2T1C structure: two transistors paired with one capacitor per cell. These cells compute using charge redistribution, where electrical charge moves between capacitors to perform calculations. To save space, they reuse the same capacitors that normally convert signals from analog to digital. Because each memory cell now does computation itself, multiple operations can happen in parallel, speeding up neural network inference.
fccm-2025-023.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining ferroelectric transistors (FeFETs), 2T1C cells, charge redistribution computation, and reused analog-to-digital conversion capacitors to replace block RAM and enable parallel processing on FPGAs.

fccm-2025-022.method: The TinyTL framework runs on an AMD RFSoC platform, which combines an ARM processor with an FPGA (field-programmable gate array—a reconfigurable chip that can be optimized for specific tasks). The FPGA handles the computationally intensive training of neural networks, while the ARM processor manages the overall coordination, allowing models to be adapted directly on wireless devices. This approach is applied to Digital PreDistortion (DPD)—a technique for adjusting power amplifier models in real-time as wireless conditions change.
fccm-2025-022.key_novelty: The core idea is combining an ARM processor and an FPGA accelerator on a single chip to enable transfer learning training (adapting pre-trained models to new tasks) efficiently on resource-limited wireless devices.

fccm-2025-015.method: HighWave simulates waves on an FPGA (a computer chip reconfigurable for specific tasks) by coordinating processing cores with High-Bandwidth Memory (memory optimized for rapid data transfer). The design keeps frequently-used data close to processors to reuse it, schedules memory accesses in predictable patterns rather than random jumps, and distributes work evenly across memory channels to prevent bottlenecks. It uses the discontinuous Galerkin method with Gauss-Lobatto-Legendre quadrature (mathematical techniques for solving wave equations) to handle elastic and acoustic waves.
fccm-2025-015.key_novelty: HighWave is the first FPGA wave simulator combining High-Bandwidth Memory with coordinated optimizations—data reuse, predictable access scheduling, and balanced load distribution—to achieve full memory bandwidth utilization for discontinuous Galerkin solvers, which inherently require processing large data volumes despite minimal computation.

fccm-2025-018.method: InTAR automatically switches between two execution patterns based on what each task needs: sequential (doing operations one after another, which efficiently uses the chip's computation resources) and dataflow (where data stays on the chip and moves directly from one processing stage to the next, reducing trips to external memory). Rather than committing the hardware to one pattern, InTAR computes the best pattern sequence ahead of time based on available resources and the sizes of the problems being solved, then encodes this sequence directly into the circuit design, tailoring each neural network model to run optimally. Since the pattern sequence is pre-computed and encoded into the design, the hardware can optimize each model without any runtime delays, using HLS (a code-generation tool) to make implementation practical.
fccm-2025-018.key_novelty: InTAR's main innovation is determining the execution pattern schedule once before building the hardware and encoding it directly into the design, enabling model-specific resource allocation without the runtime computation that traditional reconfigurable accelerators require.

fccm-2025-025.method: The paper develops HLS algorithms (automated tools for converting code into FPGA designs) that maximize how much the FPGA's processing elements—its parallel computational cores—are used simultaneously when running attention layers, the neural network components that weight different inputs. It analyzes how various parameter settings affect latency (time to compute), then applies a tiling technique—breaking the work into appropriately-sized chunks—and provides a methodology for selecting optimal tile sizes that balance high resource utilization against low latency.
fccm-2025-025.key_novelty: Systematically optimizing tile sizes and attention layer parameters for FPGA implementations achieves both maximum processing element utilization and minimum latency.

fccm-2025-029.method: The authors built and tested 9 memory designs on FPGAs: some with multiple ports (simpler, supporting many simultaneous accesses) and others using banks (splitting memory into independent sections). They ran 51 benchmarks combining matrix transposition and FFT algorithms at different data sizes, measuring each design's speed, clock frequency (targeting 770+ MHz), and FPGA memory usage to see which works best when.
fccm-2025-029.key_novelty: Simpler multi-port memories perform better on small datasets despite higher memory overhead, while banked memories become more efficient at larger data sizes.

fccm-2025-027.method: You add one special instruction (#pragma HLS RealProbe) to your code, and RealProbe automatically creates measurement code that tracks everything—the main function, helper functions, and loops. Instead of interfering with your actual computation, it uses separate dedicated measurement hardware alongside your design. This measurement hardware counts clock cycles with high precision to tell you where time is being spent. You can also use it to quickly try different hardware configurations by only rebuilding the parts you changed, rather than rebuilding everything.
fccm-2025-027.key_novelty: It is the first fully automated profiler that measures performance inside running FPGA hardware using only a single pragma instruction, achieving 100% accuracy in counting clock cycles with minimal extra hardware and no interference with the design.

fccm-2025-030.method: TrackGNN runs on FPGA hardware (a programmable circuit optimized for custom computations) and accelerates graph neural networks—AI models that process interconnected data points—by flowing data through multiple parallel processing stages simultaneously. It includes a self-adaptive renaming system that watches how the graph's nodes are structured and reorganizes their processing on the fly to reduce delays. By combining parallel data processing with flexible scheduling that adapts to each computation's needs, it achieves both speed and efficiency.
fccm-2025-030.key_novelty: The core innovation is a self-adaptive renaming system that dynamically reorganizes how graph nodes are processed, reducing overall latency with negligible extra hardware cost compared to earlier FPGA-based graph accelerators like FlowGNN.

fccm-2025-020.method: They updated IRON—a toolkit for programming neural processing units (NPUs, specialized AI hardware you control directly)—by making its programming constructs modular and customizable. Programmers can now plug in custom tools to control how code maps to hardware regions (placement) and how data moves between them (data transformation). They evaluated it three ways: efficiency (measured by code reduction and code-complexity metrics), expressivity (support for all existing IRON features and patterns), and extensibility (whether placement and data-movement tools can be customized).
fccm-2025-020.key_novelty: The core idea is a customizable programming interface for neural processors with modular tools that let programmers control optimization details—how code maps to hardware (placement) and how data moves (transformation)—while making code 26% shorter.

fccm-2025-021.method: FPGAPart divides circuit netlists (descriptions of how components connect) into smaller chunks while minimizing signal propagation delay—the core goal of timing-driven optimization. Built for FPGAs and integrated with VTR 7.0, it starts with grouping hints from VTR, then applies the FP-Growth algorithm to find repeating patterns across timing-critical paths, improving component clustering. To speed up the mathematical solver (ILP—a method for finding optimal solutions), it adds 'neighborhood influences-based cutting planes'—constraints linking nearby sections to narrow the search space.
fccm-2025-021.key_novelty: FPGAPart is the first open-source timing-driven netlist partitioner for FPGAs, using 'neighborhood influences-based cutting planes' (constraints linking nearby circuit sections) to achieve 38× faster optimization with less than 1% quality loss.

fccm-2025-026.method: NoH uses mathematical optimization called integer linear programming (a technique for finding the best arrangement given many constraints) to automatically place communications on a hardened network-on-chip (a pre-built communications system in an FPGA). The algorithm decides which communications use the NoC versus the programmable logic (the flexible parts), handling both time-critical memory access and flexible communication between chip modules. It predicts where the programmable logic will be placed, then positions the NoC connection points based on that prediction, removing the need for manual placement expertise.
fccm-2025-026.key_novelty: NoH is an HLS compiler that automatically handles hard network-on-chip offloading through mathematical optimization, eliminating manual placement expertise requirements.

fccm-2025-031.method: BiKA makes KANs practical for edge hardware by using binarization—converting weights and activations (the numerical parameters a network learns) to just two values instead of decimals. This cuts the hardware complexity of computing the learned nonlinear functions (functions that adapt to the data), since binary arithmetic is far simpler to build into circuits than continuous-number math. The technique preserves what makes KANs work while shrinking the physical chip size and power needed.
fccm-2025-031.key_novelty: The core idea is applying binarization (reducing learned parameters to just two values) to KAN's learnable nonlinear functions to reduce hardware implementation complexity while preserving KAN's benefits.

fccm-2025-034.method: The system distributes 231 types of electron repulsion integral calculations across 2 to 14 AMD AI Engines (specialized processors), with each engine using a vectorization scheme that efficiently uses the AI Engine's floating-point hardware. The engines are arranged both horizontally (side-by-side) and vertically (stacked) in a grid pattern. Vertically stacked engines share time-divided communication channels to stream results between layers, allowing computation to overlap—when one engine sends its result, the next layer immediately processes it while the first engine starts fresh work, nearly eliminating idle waiting time.
fccm-2025-034.key_novelty: Vertically stacked ERI-Engines using time-shared result channels to almost completely eliminate delays from individual engine computations by allowing different layers' work to overlap.

fccm-2025-028.method: AutoNTT is a tool that automatically designs hardware accelerators for NTT (a computational building block in cryptography) by converting high-level code into hardware designs (high-level synthesis). It explores three circuit arrangements—sequential processing (iterative), parallel pipeline processing (dataflow), and mixed approaches (hybrid)—across different polynomial sizes (2^10 to 2^17 elements) and number ranges (28-64 bits). The designs are optimized by reducing memory for temporary values and precomputed factors (twiddle factors), and by simplifying how the circuit's computation modules (butterfly units) connect.
fccm-2025-028.key_novelty: The key innovation is automating the generation and exploration of multiple NTT accelerator architecture patterns to support diverse fully homomorphic encryption parameter ranges.

fccm-2025-032.method: During training, SparseLUT removes weak connections between neurons and tests new ones in their place, continuously searching for the best network structure. This active approach finds good configurations directly, eliminating the computational waste of trying many random seed combinations. The method achieves efficient training with no additional hardware overhead.
fccm-2025-032.key_novelty: SparseLUT optimizes which connections stay by pruning (removing) weak connections and regrowing (testing) new alternatives during training, eliminating random seed optimization.

fccm-2025-036.method: Chronbench records real hardware design work by capturing ordered snapshots (called 'commits') in git repositories, where each snapshot is a complete, compilable design. The researchers built a tool that transforms public code repositories into benchmark test suites. They analyzed these benchmarks by compiling all 170 snapshots through the three main stages—synthesis (converting designs to basic logic gates), placement (arranging components on the chip), and routing (connecting them with wires)—to study how designs evolve, which parts change between versions, and how much work could be reused.
fccm-2025-036.key_novelty: Turning ordered, compilable snapshots of real hardware development from git repositories into standard benchmarks enables researchers to study how to rebuild only the parts that changed, instead of recompiling entire designs from scratch.

fccm-2025-039.method: Instead of using hash tables that cause random, inefficient memory access, this method uses a reconfigurable pipeline—a series of processing stages that automatically adjust themselves based on the aggregation task you're performing (like grouping data or computing time-series values). The pipeline arranges data flow to keep memory access sequential and predictable, so complex queries process quickly without wasting hardware resources.
fccm-2025-039.key_novelty: This approach replaces hash-based aggregation with a reconfigurable pipeline that adapts to different task types, eliminating inefficient random memory access patterns.

fccm-2025-041.method: The circuit performs division using stochastic computing—a technique where calculations work with probabilistic signals instead of exact binary numbers—integrated directly into the memory hardware. By using approximate, probabilistic calculations rather than precise arithmetic, the circuit becomes simpler and uses far fewer transistors than a traditional division unit. This trades numerical precision (results are approximate) for a lightweight, low-power design that can fit inside the memory substrate.
fccm-2025-041.key_novelty: For the first time, division operations can run directly inside memory hardware using stochastic computing (mathematical operations based on probabilistic signals instead of exact binary values).

fccm-2025-040.method: SmartNICs (specialized network cards with their own processors) sit between different computer types—x86 and ARM processors—to enable memory sharing. When any processor reads or writes data, the SmartNIC intercepts the request and applies coherence rules (the protocol that ensures all processors see the same data). The SmartNIC also routes requests to access remote memory across the network, eliminating the need for a separate central system to manage coherence.
fccm-2025-040.key_novelty: The core idea is using SmartNICs—which already connect heterogeneous computer systems—as distributed coherence controllers, rather than building separate centralized coherence hardware.

fccm-2025-038.method: The work implements the complete hardware logic (RTL) for fast Fourier transforms (FFT) and their inverse on an FPGA—a programmable chip—using double-precision floating-point math, specifically designed for FALCON's cryptographic needs. To prevent attackers from learning the signature key by observing power consumption or timing differences (side-channel attacks), the hardware runs in constant time—taking the same amount of time no matter what values it processes. The design optimizes how the hardware handles floating-point arithmetic to keep latency as low as possible.
fccm-2025-038.key_novelty: The core idea is the first hardware implementation of FALCON's floating-point FFT and inverse that runs in constant time—taking the same duration for any input—to prevent side-channel attacks while keeping latency low.

fccm-2025-033.method: EVO-QNN pairs software and hardware to run neural networks efficiently on edge devices. The software identifies which parts of the neural network (like convolution operators) can use lower precision representations (2-8 bit quantization, which stores numbers with fewer bits), while the hardware provides custom instructions and SIMD extensions (which process multiple data points in parallel) on a RISC-V processor so these different precision levels execute fast.
fccm-2025-033.key_novelty: Using specialized RISC-V instructions to automatically select the best precision level (2-8 bits) for each neural network operator.

fccm-2025-046.method: The authors built specially designed routing puzzles where solutions are mathematically guaranteed to exist but resources are limited. This setup let them pinpoint exactly where PathFinder fails. They discovered that PathFinder's approach of routing each connection in isolation and making greedy choices (picking the immediately easiest path without considering the overall picture) creates tangled paths with excess nodes. They designed a better algorithm that avoids this trap by making more coordinated routing decisions.
fccm-2025-046.key_novelty: PathFinder fails because routing each connection greedily in isolation builds paths with unnecessary nodes, even when more efficient solutions are possible.

fccm-2025-043.method: The approach automatically converts C/C++ code into an Extended Task Graph (ETG), breaking the program into individual tasks. It then groups these tasks into clusters for an FPGA (a reconfigurable chip optimized for specific workloads), while simultaneously balancing three objectives: applying the hardware's available optimizations within each cluster, reducing data traffic between the CPU and FPGA, and keeping tasks that access the same data together.
fccm-2025-043.key_novelty: Instead of separately deciding how to split work between CPU and FPGA and then optimizing each piece, this approach handles both simultaneously through source-to-source compilation, allowing partitioning choices to directly influence available optimizations.

fccm-2025-042.method: They write GPT-2 training code using bare-metal programming (code that speaks directly to the hardware without an operating system layer). By carefully mapping each training operation to what the AMD NPU can do natively, they eliminate unnecessary overhead. This tight hardware-software alignment improves both training speed and power efficiency on client devices.
fccm-2025-042.key_novelty: The key idea is using bare-metal programming to map GPT-2 training directly onto AMD NPU hardware, eliminating the operating system layer for maximum efficiency.

fccm-2025-035.method: C2OPU combines two hardware units: computing-in-memory arrays (which perform calculations directly where data is stored) optimized for weight-stationary vector-matrix multiplications (where weights stay fixed during matrix operations), and a coarse-grained reconfigurable architecture or CGRA (a flexible unit that can be rewired to handle different computation patterns and higher precision). An accuracy-bound workload allocation strategy assigns tasks between these units by predicting how analog computing errors will affect results, balancing speed with accuracy. A compiler automatically determines the optimal configuration as different transformer models are processed.
fccm-2025-035.key_novelty: An accuracy-bound workload allocation strategy, implemented through automated compilation, automatically distributes transformer operations between computing-in-memory arrays (which efficiently execute matrix math but with limited precision) and a coarse-grained reconfigurable architecture (which provides flexible, high-precision computation).

fccm-2025-037.method: The system builds an FPGA (a programmable chip) with a reconfigurable processing unit that can perform both dense and sparse matrix operations, plus a pruning unit to trim calculations in Vision Transformers. A compiler translates each AI task into hardware configuration, and the FPGA can reconfigure at runtime without reloading. This allows one chip to efficiently run diverse AI models—vision, graphs, language—without being completely reprogrammed between tasks.
fccm-2025-037.key_novelty: An FPGA that reconfigures itself at runtime without reloading can efficiently support diverse AI workloads on a single chip.

fccm-2025-053.method: LLM-IMC uses a large language model (without requiring special training) to automatically write SPICE netlists—the detailed circuit descriptions needed for simulation—for analog in-memory computing systems (where processing happens inside memory using continuous electrical signals). The Python-based framework systematically generates diverse simulation scripts and uses the LLM to analyze their performance, helping engineers explore different design options. It also provides a roadmap for integrating these designs into neuromorphic crossbar architectures, which are grid-like circuits modeled after how biological brains process information.
fccm-2025-053.key_novelty: Using a large language model without special training to automate SPICE netlist generation and performance analysis for analog in-memory computing system design.

fccm-2025-050.method: TRILLI uses a Versal chip that combines a GPU and FPGA to split image registration work. The GPU handles the computationally heavy geometric transformation and interpolation (moving and resizing images to align them), while the FPGA computes similarity metrics (measurements of how well images match). By using each hardware type where it excels, TRILLI creates an end-to-end system that performs better than making one hardware type handle all the work.
