fccm-2025-050.key_novelty: TRILLI's core idea is using the GPU for image transformation and the FPGA for similarity metric computation, rather than forcing one hardware type to handle both tasks.

fccm-2025-049.method: HBMex is a configurable module placed between an accelerator and its HBM memory. It takes incoming memory requests from the accelerator and distributes them across multiple HBM interfaces so they're processed in parallel instead of backing up in a queue. For workloads with irregular access patterns (like sparse matrix operations or graph analytics), this prevents the interconnect from stalling and allows the accelerator to use the full available bandwidth.
fccm-2025-049.key_novelty: A module that distributes irregular memory requests across multiple HBM interfaces to prevent interconnect stalls.

fccm-2025-054.method: ASTEF runs on a Zynq-7000 chip (a programmable piece of hardware) attached directly to the event camera to filter noise at the sensor itself. Event cameras detect individual pixel changes rather than capturing full frames, but produce noisy, sparse signals in dim light. The system uses adaptive temporal filtering (which learns over time what patterns are noise versus real events) and dynamic thresholding (which adjusts sensor sensitivity based on lighting conditions) to reduce false detections. A Python simulator validated the improvements in dark scenes.
fccm-2025-054.key_novelty: The core idea is processing event data right at the camera using a programmable chip that combines adaptive temporal filtering and dynamic thresholding to eliminate noise in low light.

fccm-2025-044.method: The tool automatically rewrites code to work around limitations of hardware compilers. It flattens structs and arrays (simplifying nested data structures) because hardware compilers can't handle complex data layouts. It moves dynamic memory allocations to the CPU and replaces them with static, compile-time-determined sizes, since hardware needs to know memory requirements before compilation. It also asynchronously executes host-side functions like printf() separately, because hardware can't perform these operations.
fccm-2025-044.key_novelty: A coordinated set of automatic code transformations that overcome C/C++ language feature restrictions, allowing larger code regions to run on hardware accelerators.

fccm-2025-048.method: N-TORC learns how each computation layer performs and uses resources by analyzing real data, then tunes these learned patterns to your constraints. A mathematical optimizer (Mixed Integer Program solver) uses these tuned models to rapidly generate hardware designs meeting your latency targets while minimizing area and maintaining model accuracy.
fccm-2025-048.key_novelty: Instead of slow end-to-end hardware compilation, N-TORC combines data-learned performance and area models for each computation layer with mathematical optimization (Mixed Integer Programming) to rapidly generate hardware designs meeting latency requirements.

fccm-2025-052.method: Designs the hardware accelerator and software together to run Random Forest inference (making predictions using decision-tree ensembles) efficiently on embedded devices by organizing computation around memory access patterns. Tests different configurations: varying the depth of individual decision trees and trying different hardware designs, using a resource estimation model to predict how much computing hardware each option needs. Systematically explores these combinations to find which one delivers the fastest prediction time for a given Random Forest model.
fccm-2025-052.key_novelty: Co-optimizing decision tree structure and hardware architecture using resource estimates to achieve low-latency Random Forest inference on embedded devices.

fccm-2025-055.method: The approach analyzes FFT loop structures to find places where calculations at different levels can run in parallel—called hierarchical parallelism, which means different stages of the algorithm progress simultaneously rather than sequentially. HP-FFT automatically generates hardware designs from this analysis with adjustable parallelism settings. This tuning dial lets designers choose between using less silicon and power or achieving faster data throughput.
fccm-2025-055.key_novelty: The core idea is using automatic hardware generation to systematically find and exploit multiple levels of parallelism within FFT algorithms, balancing high throughput with hardware portability.

fccm-2025-047.method: The approach builds looming-detection computation directly into the image sensor using reconfigurable transistor circuits (CMOS, the switching technology in all modern chips), which mimics how the retina detects approaching objects. The sensor computes results as light arrives rather than collecting raw pixel data for processing later, using only 0.36 picojoules of energy per detection event on a 5×5 pixel area. The circuit was built using GlobalFoundries' 22nm FD-SOI technology and validated against real laboratory footage and hardware-behavior simulations.
fccm-2025-047.key_novelty: The core idea is building looming detection directly into the image sensor using a reconfigurable circuit, so the computation happens as light arrives rather than in separate processing hardware.

fccm-2025-045.method: The framework automatically divides the hardware design into two parts: an ASIC portion that's redacted (security-critical logic removed) and sent to the foundry, and an FPGA portion that stays in-house on a low-cost board (Terasic DE10-SoC). On the FPGA's embedded processor, software APIs let researchers launch and test attacks on the redacted design—simulating threats without actually fabricating chips. The design stays secure because the FPGA's bitstream (the configuration code that makes the FPGA work) is the key; without it, the incomplete redacted ASIC sent to the foundry cannot be completed or reverse-engineered.
fccm-2025-045.key_novelty: The core idea is an open-source FPGA-based emulation platform that tests attacks on hardware redaction systems orders of magnitude faster than simulation.

fccm-2025-051.method: The approach adds a watermark during the pixel-readout stage of a CMOS camera sensor, before the analog signal converts to digital (ADC conversion transforms the continuous signal into numbers). Instead of watermarking the finished image in software, the watermark is injected directly into the sensor's readout electronics, specifically the column amplifier circuit controlled by a secure pattern generator. Because the watermark is embedded at the hardware level during readout, before digitization, it becomes permanently mixed into every pixel's value without adding computational overhead, and cannot be separated or removed.
fccm-2025-051.key_novelty: The innovation is watermarking at the analog readout stage before digital conversion, directly built into the sensor hardware, creating a tamper-resistant mechanism.

fccm-2025-062.method: The system adds custom instructions to the RISC-V processor vocabulary—the set of operations a CPU understands—optimized specifically for sparse convolution (multiplying matrices where most values are zero, common in neural networks). Programs can call these custom instructions directly from C code using inline assembly (raw processor commands embedded in C), making sparse math operations fast without rewriting entire programs. The researchers prototyped this on an FPGA (programmable hardware) and predicted its power consumption and chip area using a 55nm CMOS process (a standard manufacturing specification that estimates real-world performance).
fccm-2025-062.key_novelty: The core idea is adding custom processor instructions specifically optimized for sparse convolution—multiplying large matrices where most values are zero—to enable neural networks to run faster on power-limited edge devices.

fccm-2025-059.method: The system synchronizes multiple FPGAs using a simplified version of Precision Time Protocol (PTP), which keeps their clocks aligned to nanosecond precision. For fast communication between the FPGAs, it uses Aurora protocol, a high-speed serial standard that keeps data transfer delays under hundreds of nanoseconds. These synchronization and communication layers are integrated with QubiC, an open-source quantum control and measurement system, to create a complete, scalable solution for controlling thousands of qubits across multiple FPGA boards.
fccm-2025-059.key_novelty: It combines a simplified Precision Time Protocol for synchronizing multiple FPGA clocks to nanosecond precision with Aurora protocol for low-latency data communication, enabling a practical multi-FPGA quantum control system.

fccm-2025-066.method: The technique processes multiple input channels of a neural network layer at the same time, rather than one after another. When channels run in parallel, the pattern of electrical activity in the chip (which attackers can measure through power consumption or timing) no longer matches what the network is actually computing—instead of a clear signal for each computation step, attackers see a jumbled mix. This works because attackers rely on spotting predictable power spikes or timing delays to figure out what the network is doing. The parallel design can be adjusted to either use minimal extra hardware resources or achieve faster execution.
fccm-2025-066.key_novelty: Processing multiple input channels in parallel simultaneously makes side-channel attacks harder while letting designers choose whether to prioritize using less hardware or running faster.

fccm-2025-057.method: The team designed a small neural network for detecting objects in SAR radar images that uses attention mechanisms (ways to focus computation on important regions). To run fast on constrained hardware, they replaced expensive softmax-based attention with a simpler version and reduced numerical precision (quantization). They then built custom hardware on an FPGA (Xilinx Alveo U280, a reprogrammable chip) using HLS to program processing kernels that implement a streaming dataflow architecture—data flows continuously through these units like an assembly line, avoiding repeated memory accesses.
fccm-2025-057.key_novelty: The approach combines softmax-free attention mechanisms (simplified focus calculations) with streaming dataflow FPGA architecture through joint design of the neural network and hardware for SAR radar image recognition.

fccm-2025-065.method: The implementation splits the MUSIC algorithm into four pipeline stages—QR Decomposition, Singular Value Decomposition, Spectrum Calculation, and Direction of Arrival Identification—that run simultaneously across a 2D grid of specialized processors (SIMD/VLIW chips that execute the same operation on multiple data points at once) on the AMD Versal AI Engine. The loops in QR and SVD stages are unrolled (expanded to remove looping) and distributed across multiple processor tiles to execute in parallel. Data flows directly from DDR4 memory via DMA (Direct Memory Access, which moves data without CPU overhead) to the processors, which handle 128×8 blocks of signal samples, with each processor working on 8 complex numbers simultaneously.
fccm-2025-065.key_novelty: The innovation uses a deep pipeline—where multiple computation steps run simultaneously—distributed across processor tiles, with loops expanded to maximize each processor's throughput per cycle.

fccm-2025-056.method: The approach automatically divides the circuit design into smaller, independent pieces. Each piece then goes through placement and routing (deciding where components sit on the chip and how they connect) in parallel—all pieces processed at the same time instead of waiting for each one to finish. Once each piece is placed and routed, the results merge back into one complete FPGA design. The entire process runs automatically without any manual work needed.
fccm-2025-056.key_novelty: The core idea is automatically dividing the circuit into pieces so that placement and routing can happen in parallel instead of sequentially.

fccm-2025-063.method: LLM4DV automates the creation of test inputs for hardware verification by having multiple large language models (AI systems trained on text) work together using refined prompting techniques—different ways of asking the models to generate tests. Rather than manually creating tests for each chip design, the framework tests six different models and six different prompting strategies across eight hardware designs to discover which combinations work best.
fccm-2025-063.key_novelty: Using coordinated large language models (multiple AI systems working together) with refined prompting to automatically generate hardware test inputs.

fccm-2025-058.method: The team built an FPGA accelerator (a specialized reconfigurable chip) using a compact number format called Microscaling Integer (MXInt) that can handle all Vision Transformer operations while maintaining accuracy, including complex operations like Softmax and LayerNorm. They developed custom hardware circuits that run these complex operations using mathematical approximations designed specifically for the MXInt format. Previous accelerators could only efficiently run multiplication on the FPGA and had to send complex operations to the CPU, creating communication delays; keeping everything on the FPGA eliminates this bottleneck.
fccm-2025-058.key_novelty: This is the first Vision Transformer accelerator to perform all operations—including the complex arithmetic functions normally offloaded to the CPU—directly on an FPGA using Microscaling Integer format.

fccm-2025-060.method: A graph neural network is trained to predict congestion (crowding of signals) and resource consumption for circuit layouts. Since predictions take milliseconds, designers can rapidly explore many layout options instead of iteratively running the slow Vitis design tool. This replaces manual parameter tuning with automated design space exploration.
fccm-2025-060.key_novelty: A graph neural network trained to predict floorplan quality eliminates the need for expensive iterative Vitis design runs.

fccm-2025-067.method: The approach tests different ways to split transformer workloads (deep learning models) across AMD Versal's three processor types: CPUs for logic, FPGAs (reconfigurable custom circuits), and AIEs (specialized AI processors). For each split, they measure speed and data throughput to find the best trade-off. They built ARIES, an automated compilation tool using MLIR (a standard compiler intermediate format), which creates a unified translation that takes application code all the way down to running on the AIEs without manual hardware configuration.
fccm-2025-067.key_novelty: ARIES is the first unified MLIR-based compiler intermediate representation that enables automatic end-to-end deployment of applications on AMD Versal's AIE processors, eliminating manual hardware mapping.

hotchips-2025-005.method: Everactive harvests energy from three ambient sources—radio waves (RF rectifier), heat (thermoelectric), and vibration (piezoelectric)—to power itself. A wakeup receiver detects events while using minimal power, and an energy-aware subsystem dynamically adjusts computing and memory use based on how much harvested power is available.
hotchips-2025-005.key_novelty: A chip that powers itself by harvesting ambient energy and dynamically adjusts its power use, enabling indefinite operation without a battery.

hotchips-2025-000.method: KLIMA solves SAT problems by evaluating Boolean clauses directly in memory using mixed-signal circuits—combining analog logic with digital interfaces. Rather than moving data between memory and a separate processor, current-mode analog circuits stay in memory and compute using electrical current flow, which evaluates expressions faster than digital logic can fetch them. This in-memory computing approach eliminates the traditional von Neumann bottleneck (the slowdown from shuttling data back and forth) and achieves single-digit nanosecond latency for arbitrary-order SAT problems.
hotchips-2025-000.key_novelty: KLIMA embeds analog circuits directly in memory to evaluate Boolean expressions for SAT solving, bypassing the need to move data to a processor.

fccm-2025-064.method: The team built Hfqmamba2 using a reconfigurable FPGA (a chip you can reprogram for specific tasks) instead of a GPU. They employ hybrid-precision quantization, reducing some numbers to fewer bits more aggressively than others to save space and computation. To avoid expensive calculations, they included a segmented lookup table that approximates RMSNorm's inverse square root operation—a normalization step—without computing it fully each time. The design pipelines SSM operations (Mamba-2's state-machine calculations) so different layers run in parallel, all validated on an Alveo U50 FPGA board.
fccm-2025-064.key_novelty: The core idea is combining a reconfigurable FPGA with lookup-table approximations and selective-precision quantization to efficiently run Mamba-2 where GPUs with tensor cores struggle on element-wise operations.

hotchips-2025-002.method: The RTX 5090 combines NVIDIA's latest streaming multiprocessor design (the core processing units, based on their recent Ada and Hopper GPU generations) with enhanced Tensor cores—specialized circuits optimized for low-precision math (approximate calculations that trade some accuracy for speed) that neural networks need. It adds faster data connections between the processor and memory through next-generation interconnects, ensuring information flows quickly enough to keep all processors busy. Dedicated hardware for ray tracing (computing realistic shadows and reflections) and neural network evaluation prevents these operations from competing with each other for the chip's shared resources.
hotchips-2025-002.key_novelty: This GPU architecture gives both classical graphics operations (ray tracing, shadow computation, material simulation) and neural network inference equal performance priority, rather than optimizing mainly for one.

fccm-2025-061.method: Arbitrary-precision multiplication splits into two computational phases: parallel byte-level multiplications and sequential bit-level additions with shifting. The approach uses AMD's Versal ACAP platform—a single chip integrating 400 AI Engine processors (each capable of doing many multiplications at once), an FPGA (reconfigurable logic with DSPs and LUTs—specialized components for arithmetic), and an ARM CPU. It assigns the parallel byte-level phase to the 400 AIEs because they're built for processing many operations simultaneously, and assigns the sequential bit-level phase to the FPGA because its DSPs and LUTs excel at step-by-step arithmetic.
fccm-2025-061.key_novelty: The approach partitions arbitrary-precision multiplication across two hardware types—AI Engines handle parallel byte-level multiplications and FPGAs handle sequential bit-level operations—assigning each phase to the processor optimized for it.

hotchips-2025-001.method: CORSAIR builds AI accelerators from modular chiplets—specialized chips where computation circuits sit inside local memory, eliminating slow data transfers between separate memory and processor. Each chiplet contains analog or mixed-signal circuits (electronics using continuous signals rather than pure digital 0s and 1s) that perform matrix operations directly in the memory. Standard interfaces connect chiplets together, allowing flexible scaling by replicating chiplets or combining different compute types within each one.
hotchips-2025-001.key_novelty: CORSAIR decomposes in-memory computing into modular chiplets—building blocks that can be replicated for scale and mixed with different compute types.

hotchips-2025-008.method: Cuzco implements a RISC-V processor using pipelined execution that divides each instruction's work into stages, allowing multiple instructions to progress simultaneously in an overlapping manner. It reorders instructions dynamically whenever safe to do so, keeping the processor busier and working more efficiently. The design includes cache memory tuned to minimize delays for latency-sensitive operations. It achieves full compliance with RVA23, the standardized RISC-V instruction set.
hotchips-2025-008.key_novelty: Cuzco provides a production-ready, high-performance RISC-V processor implementing the full RVA23 standard, with performance comparable to modern x86 and ARM processors.

hotchips-2025-006.method: Pollara 400 combines a programmable packet processing engine—based on PISA-style architecture, which applies custom rules to network traffic—with multiple compute cores and high-speed memory hierarchies. This allows the network card itself to perform computations and offload AI workloads, rather than requiring the server to handle all processing. An advanced switching fabric (the hardware routing infrastructure) connects these components and enables flexible traffic management.
hotchips-2025-006.key_novelty: A programmable network interface that reaches 400Gbps throughput and performs AI-specific packet processing and computing directly within the card itself.

hotchips-2025-009.method: MEGA.mini runs AI computations through two parallel systems: a large fixed-point unit (fast, simple math) that handles over 95% of operations on normal data values, and a smaller floating-point unit (precise math) that handles less than 5% of operations on unusual outlier values. The hardware automatically detects which system should handle each piece of data and routes it accordingly, switching between the two paths based on the numbers it encounters. Three versions (MEGA, median, mini) scale the design down for different deployment targets from data centers to embedded devices.
hotchips-2025-009.key_novelty: Splitting AI computation between two cores—one fast (fixed-point) for regular data and one precise (floating-point) for unusual values—with automatic selection of which to use.

hotchips-2025-010.method: The PEZY-SC4s packs hundreds of identical processing cores that can each run different instructions on different data simultaneously (MIMD). Each core connects to a high-speed memory system that can move data in and out quickly, and they use cache coherence (a system to keep shared data consistent when multiple cores access the same data). The connections between cores are flexible, allowing the same hardware to run either traditional scientific computing algorithms or AI workloads.
hotchips-2025-010.key_novelty: A many-core MIMD processor (where each core runs different instructions on different data) that balances flexibility and energy efficiency to handle both scientific computing and AI workloads.

hotchips-2025-003.method: Passage M1000 places a 3D optical routing layer—built from silicon photonics (technology that guides light like wires guide electricity)—between AI processor chips to replace or supplement electrical wires. It sends multiple signals at once using wavelength-division multiplexing (assigning each signal a different color of light), enabling far more data to travel between chips using less energy than electrical connections.
hotchips-2025-003.key_novelty: A 3D photonic interposer built from silicon photonics enables all-optical interconnects (light-based connections) between AI chips, replacing electrical wires.

hotchips-2025-004.method: ConnectX-8 works by processing packets in customizable ways directly on the network interface card (NIC — the hardware connecting servers to the network). It performs collective operations (like AllReduce and AllGather, which combine and share data across servers) inside the network hardware itself, rather than sending data back to servers' processors. It also manages network congestion by adjusting traffic flow when links get busy, and uses a high-speed switching infrastructure to move data between servers with minimal delay.
hotchips-2025-004.key_novelty: A network interface card now runs collective operations (AllReduce and AllGather, used to combine and share data across servers in distributed training) directly in its hardware, instead of requiring a server's main processor.

hotchips-2025-007.method: The IPU E2200 is a specialized processor with multiple cores optimized for infrastructure work in data centers—particularly managing network packets and other infrastructure tasks. It includes hardware accelerators for cryptography and telemetry collection, specialized circuits that speed up encryption and system monitoring compared to general-purpose processors. A high-speed fabric connects the IPU to the main CPU and GPU, allowing them to offload all these infrastructure tasks to the IPU.
hotchips-2025-007.key_novelty: Intel's E2200 is a second-generation infrastructure processing unit that improves over the E1100 with more processing cores and better memory organization for data center networking, security, and monitoring tasks.

hotchips-2025-018.method: Rapidus is a government-backed Japanese semiconductor factory that combines cutting-edge manufacturing techniques to produce advanced chips. It uses extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography—a technology for etching extremely fine details onto silicon—along with advanced packaging that densely connects chip components. The factory controls more of its own manufacturing chain rather than outsourcing, and focuses on gradually increasing production while optimizing how many chips work correctly (yield).
hotchips-2025-018.key_novelty: A government-backed Japanese fab integrates extreme ultraviolet lithography and advanced packaging technologies to manufacture semiconductors at advanced nodes.

hotchips-2025-014.method: Tomahawk Ultra is an Ethernet switch with many ports (high-radix means numerous connection points) designed for extreme speed. It uses cut-through forwarding: instead of waiting to receive an entire data packet before sending it on, it starts forwarding the packet immediately upon arrival—cutting down the delay significantly. The switch keeps the waiting lines (queues) for packets very short to prevent data from sitting idle. It also includes smart traffic controls built into the switch itself that detect when the network is congested and automatically prioritize packets from AI collective training operations, ensuring these time-sensitive workloads experience minimal latency.
hotchips-2025-014.key_novelty: An Ethernet switch designed to move data with sub-microsecond latency specifically for AI collective operations and distributed training.

hotchips-2025-012.method: BROCA uses a RISC-V processor with dedicated hardware accelerators for two tasks: one processes speech using parallel vector calculations (like digital signal processors), and another runs compressed neural networks (quantized transformers) that handle language understanding and speech generation. By integrating everything on one chip, including audio connections, BROCA eliminates delays between receiving speech and producing a response.
hotchips-2025-012.key_novelty: A low-power RISC-V chip that combines speech and language accelerators, allowing mobile phones to run voice assistants that respond in real-time.

hotchips-2025-011.method: This technology builds capacitors and inductors (components that store electrical energy and regulate power flow) directly into the processor chip using silicon and specialized manufacturing techniques. These components are packed more densely than traditional external capacitors, fitting more storage capacity into the same space. By integrating them directly on-chip, the electrical pathways carrying current are shorter, which reduces parasitic resistance and inductance—the unwanted losses that occur when electricity flows through connections.
hotchips-2025-011.key_novelty: Integrating high-density silicon capacitors and inductors directly into the processor chip to deliver power efficiently without needing extra circuit board space.

hotchips-2025-021.method: UB-mesh connects GPUs in a mesh topology—a grid-like pattern where each GPU links directly to its neighbors—instead of routing all data through central switches like traditional networks do. This reduces the distance (hop counts) data travels between GPUs and multiplies the total communication bandwidth available since many GPU pairs can communicate simultaneously over their direct connections. The switches and link speeds are optimized specifically for this mesh layout rather than being general-purpose.
hotchips-2025-021.key_novelty: UB-mesh replaces traditional switch-based interconnects with a mesh topology where GPUs connect in a grid pattern, reducing communication latency and increasing bandwidth density.

hotchips-2025-016.method: The processor reduces each neural network weight from 32 bits down to just 1-2 bits—this extreme quantization lets you store many more weights in the same memory. It then runs calculations on these tiny numbers using specialized hardware circuits designed for speed and efficiency. When quantized weights become zero, the custom dataflow automatically skips them, avoiding wasted memory access and computation.
hotchips-2025-016.key_novelty: Running billion-parameter Llama models using 4.69 milliwatts by shrinking weights to 1-2 bits and using hardware built specifically for calculations on these tiny numbers.

hotchips-2025-022.method: Electrochemical additive manufacturing (ECAM—a type of 3D printing) produces custom-shaped copper structures that attach directly to computer chips. Liquid coolant flows through these structures, absorbing heat at the source. The structures are designed to transfer heat efficiently while keeping pressure drop minimal, so the coolant moves freely.
hotchips-2025-022.key_novelty: Using electrochemical 3D printing to create custom-shaped copper cooling structures that attach directly to chips for optimized heat transfer.

hotchips-2025-013.method: Ironwood increases memory bandwidth—the rate at which data flows between the processor and memory—to support reasoning models that work through many intermediate thinking steps before producing an answer. It optimizes matrix multiplication (the core mathematical operation in neural networks) specifically for reasoning model compute patterns. It also improves communication between multiple processors through enhanced interconnect and collective operations (coordinated mathematics across multiple chips), ensuring these components don't become bottlenecks when training or serving reasoning models at scale.
hotchips-2025-013.key_novelty: Ironwood is a processor architecture built specifically for reasoning models rather than adapted from general-purpose AI chips, designed to optimize three priorities simultaneously: performance, cost-efficiency (performance per dollar), and energy-efficiency.

hotchips-2025-019.method: The system uses three techniques. First, it redesigns memory organization and uses high-bandwidth memory (HBM) with vertically stacked chips (3D stacking) to dramatically increase how much data can flow between memory and processors per second. Second, it creates faster communication pathways between memory and compute units by redesigning the wiring and protocols that connect them. Third, it designs memory and processors as one integrated system rather than independent components, so they can optimize for each other's needs.
hotchips-2025-019.key_novelty: Instead of focusing on making processors faster, the work identifies memory bandwidth as what actually limits data center performance, and redesigns the entire system around fixing that bottleneck.

hotchips-2025-023.method: The chip contains specialized circuits for vision processing and graphics rendering that work together. The vision engine analyzes camera images using optical flow (detecting motion through pixel changes) to track the device's position and reconstruct the physical environment in 3D. The graphics engine simultaneously renders virtual objects based on this tracking data. Because tracking, mapping, and rendering all happen on dedicated silicon instead of the general-purpose CPU, the system achieves the low latency required for AR/MR.
hotchips-2025-023.key_novelty: A custom hardware chip combines vision tracking and graphics rendering on the same silicon, enabling real-time world-locked rendering on mobile devices.

hotchips-2025-025.method: When neural networks run inference (make predictions), many of the intermediate values they produce are zero or less important—this is called sparse activations. The accelerator stores these values using bit-separable encoding, which breaks numbers down to their individual bits so that zeros and small values take minimal space instead of full memory slots. It combines this with specialized memory access patterns designed to efficiently read and write these compressed values, which reduces the total amount of data traveling between the processor and main memory.
hotchips-2025-025.key_novelty: Using bit-separable encoding (breaking numbers into individual bits) for sparse activation values reduces the memory bandwidth that transformer inference requires.

hotchips-2025-030.method: The keynote surveyed emerging trends and research opportunities across computing systems, presenting insights on how the field is developing. By covering multiple areas and directions, it provided attendees with a broader view of where computing research and engineering are heading.
hotchips-2025-030.key_novelty: Computing systems research is entering new technical directions that require focused investigation and development.

hotchips-2025-020.method: Presto pairs a RISC-V processor with custom hardware accelerators that perform FHE's expensive mathematical operations. The accelerators handle two core tasks: polynomial transformations (NTT and convolution, mathematical rearrangements central to FHE) and lattice arithmetic (calculations on discrete mathematical structures that form the foundation of FHE encryption). The system supports multiple encryption schemes—BGV and CKKS—through flexible hardware dataflow and custom processor instructions that adapt to each scheme.
hotchips-2025-020.key_novelty: Presto accelerates multiple FHE encryption schemes (BGV and CKKS) using a single chip that combines RISC-V control with hardware optimized for lattice arithmetic.

hotchips-2025-029.method: Instead of placing light-transmission components (waveguides that carry light signals, modulators that convert electrical signals to light, and detectors that convert light back to electricity) far from the electronic switch, they're built together in one package. This eliminates the long wires that would normally connect them, reducing power consumption and latency—the time signals take to travel.
hotchips-2025-029.key_novelty: Putting light-based optical components and electronic switch circuits in the same package reduces power consumption and latency for GPU cluster interconnects.

hotchips-2025-024.method: Adelia is a purpose-built computer chip (an ASIC) made at 4nm—an extremely small manufacturing scale that makes transistors energy-efficient—specifically for running large language models. The chip includes separate optimized hardware for the three core LLM operations: matrix multiplication (fast math on grids of numbers), attention (the mechanism that determines which parts of the input are most relevant), and feed-forward networks (layered mathematical transformations). To manage data efficiently, it uses a two-tier memory system: fast, small on-chip SRAM for active processing and larger external HBM (high-bandwidth memory) for bulk storage. It also supports mixed-precision quantization—storing some numbers with fewer bits than others—to reduce power and memory usage without significantly harming accuracy.
hotchips-2025-024.key_novelty: Adelia achieves fast, power-efficient LLM inference by designing a 4nm chip with a hardware architecture built specifically for attention mechanisms—the operation that selects which input parts matter most.

hotchips-2025-026.method: RDNA 4 builds on RDNA 3 by redesigning three core parts: the compute units (the processor cores that do math), the cache hierarchy (fast memory layers holding frequently-accessed data), and the memory subsystem (how data travels between the processor and main memory). These improvements increase the GPU's computational output per watt of power, making it work well for both gaming and professional compute tasks like AI training.
hotchips-2025-026.key_novelty: RDNA 4 achieves higher performance and efficiency per watt by redesigning its compute units and memory architecture to serve both consumer gaming and professional computing workloads.

hotchips-2025-033.method: The system uses hyperdimensional computing (machine learning based on comparing high-dimensional vectors) to enable fast, gradient-free training on edge devices—avoiding the heavy backpropagation computation that drains power and memory. It combines two efficiency techniques: Kronecker encoding (a structured way to build vectors) and weight clustering feature extraction (grouping similar weights to reduce learning complexity). The core innovation is progressive search, which cuts query complexity by 61% by encoding and comparing only partial query vectors instead of full ones, letting the device learn continuously from new data within its power budget.
hotchips-2025-033.key_novelty: Progressive search reduces hyperdimensional computing query complexity by 61% through partial hypervector encoding, enabling efficient on-device continual learning.

hotchips-2025-031.method: Clearwater Forest adds lower-power 'efficiency cores' alongside high-performance cores in Xeon processors. The processor can direct lightweight workloads to these efficiency cores, while sending demanding computations to the more powerful cores. This flexible assignment reduces overall power consumption because simpler tasks no longer require activating the processor's most energy-hungry components.
hotchips-2025-031.key_novelty: Xeon processors now include efficiency cores alongside performance cores, allowing the processor to use low-power cores for routine tasks instead of always relying on energy-intensive high-performance cores.

hotchips-2025-027.method: This work builds the systems and processes that let university researchers design and submit three full chips for manufacturing per semester (called tapeouts) using Intel 16 technology (a modern manufacturing process at the 7nm scale). It automates the time-consuming steps of placing circuit components and routing connections between them, then optimizes the overall design. By combining this automation with shared access to fabrication facilities, it dramatically speeds up the traditional chip design cycle.
hotchips-2025-027.key_novelty: Academic researchers can achieve three chip tapeouts per semester in modern manufacturing technology by using streamlined, automated design workflows.

hotchips-2025-032.method: IRIS is a specialized chip designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting, a technique that represents 3D scenes as millions of overlapping soft blob shapes. It has dedicated hardware components for three tasks: converting blobs to screen pixels (Gaussian rasterization), mathematically optimizing the rendering quality (differentiable rendering), and detecting solid surfaces in the scene (surface reconstruction). By building the entire chip around these specific tasks, it achieves real-time performance at only 8.55 millijoules per frame.
hotchips-2025-032.key_novelty: IRIS is the first chip designed specifically for 3D Gaussian Splatting, with hardware and software built together to optimize rendering and surface modeling.

hotchips-2025-017.method: EdgeDiff accelerates diffusion image generation with three techniques: mixed-precision arithmetic (lower-precision math in layers where quality doesn't matter), reordered group quantization (compression that groups similar weights to minimize error), and few-step distillation (training the model to produce good results in fewer steps). The hardware exploits temporal coherence—since each step is similar to the previous one—to reuse computation results instead of recalculating them.
hotchips-2025-017.key_novelty: EdgeDiff enables real-time image generation on edge devices by jointly optimizing model compression and hardware execution.

hotchips-2025-028.method: Basilisk uses open-source design tools—Yosys to convert high-level descriptions into logic gates, and OpenROAD to arrange those gates on a chip—to build a Linux-capable 64-bit processor chip in 130nm BiCMOS technology, producing a 34mm² die. The team enhanced these tools by tuning them to work better with the specific manufacturing process, achieving 2.3x improvement in timing (how fast signals travel) and 1.6x reduction in area during logic design, plus 12% die-size reduction during final layout. The result includes a 64-bit core, 124MB/s DRAM controller, USB 1.1, video output, and a 62Mb/s chip-to-chip communication link.
hotchips-2025-028.key_novelty: This is the largest chip ever built using only open-source design tools, proving these tools can now scale to production-grade systems capable of running operating systems.

hotchips-2025-034.method: Power11 improves upon the POWER instruction set—the basic language processors understand—with faster internal circuits for executing instructions and a redesigned cache hierarchy (layered temporary fast memory that helps the processor access data more quickly). It enhances the memory controllers that manage data flow between the processor and main memory, and it includes specialized accelerator circuits designed to speed up specific workloads common in enterprise servers and supercomputing environments.
hotchips-2025-034.key_novelty: Power11 comprehensively improves the POWER processor architecture—with faster cores, better caching, improved memory bandwidth, and specialized accelerators—for high-performance enterprise and supercomputing workloads.

hpca-2025-005.method: Ariadne tracks which memory pages get used frequently when an app relaunches (labeled 'hot'), sometimes ('warm'), or rarely ('cold'), and remembers these labels for future relaunches. It compresses hot and warm memory using small chunks that decompress quickly on the critical launch path, while using large chunks for cold data to save more storage space. It also predicts which pages will be needed next during startup and decompresses them in advance, so this decompression happens in parallel with the app launching.
hpca-2025-005.key_novelty: The core idea is to compress relaunch-critical data into small fast-decompressing chunks while compressing rarely-used data into larger high-compression chunks, and to predict which data is needed next so decompression can happen in the background.

hpca-2025-001.method: When a core requests data from the last-level cache (the shared memory closest to all cores), Push Multicast doesn't just send it to that one core—it also predicts which other cores will need the same data and sends it to them too, using multicast (one transmission to multiple destinations), saving bandwidth. To prevent wasted duplicate deliveries, routers have a coherent filter that recognizes when an incoming request matches data already being pushed and cancels that request. When the network gets congested, a pause/resume mechanism temporarily disables pushing to avoid interfering with regular data requests.
hpca-2025-001.key_novelty: Instead of the last-level cache just responding to requests, it actively predicts which other cores will need the same data and sends it to them at the same time, while routers intelligently cancel any redundant requests for data that's already being delivered.

hotchips-2025-036.method: This work designs a specialized chiplet that follows the UCIe interconnect standard. It uses optical transducers—devices that convert electrical signals to light and back again—to bridge electrical signals (used inside AI chips) and optical signals (light pulses between chips). The chiplet also includes signal conditioning circuits that clean up and re-time the signals to fix degradation that happens during transmission, maintaining reliability across the chip boundary.
hotchips-2025-036.key_novelty: A chiplet that follows the UCIe standard to convert electrical signals to optical signals and clean them up, enabling AI accelerator chips to connect and scale together.

hotchips-2025-037.method: Celestial AI builds light-based communication hardware and regular computing circuits on the same chip. The optical hardware includes components that convert electrical signals into light pulses (modulators), convert light pulses back into electrical signals (detectors), and channels that guide light around the chip (waveguides). Integrating all this onto one die enables direct optical communication between parts of the chip.
hotchips-2025-037.key_novelty: This is the first single-chip computer to integrate optical communication hardware directly on the die itself, without needing external optical equipment.

hpca-2025-000.method: BitMoD divides neural network weights into small groups (128 weights each) and selects the best numerical compression format for each group—choosing from formats like INT4, FP4, or NF4—to minimize information loss. The hardware uses a bit-serial processing design (processing one bit at a time), which naturally handles all these different formats by converting them internally to a unified representation; a specialized unit then rescales each group's results with minimal overhead.
hpca-2025-000.key_novelty: The core insight is that per-group numerical-format assignment becomes practical when paired with bit-serial hardware that processes all formats through a unified internal representation, eliminating the need for separate processing circuits per format.

hotchips-2025-035.method: The 4th Generation CDNA improves on earlier versions through higher compute density (more math operations per unit of chip area) and a redesigned memory hierarchy (how data flows between processing units and memory). It features upgraded tensor cores, which are specialized math units built for matrix operations—the fundamental calculation in large language models. The design includes custom instructions specifically tuned for transformer networks and mixed-precision computing, which uses different number formats to improve speed and efficiency.
hotchips-2025-035.key_novelty: The key innovation is designing both the tensor cores (specialized math units for matrix operations) and the memory system optimized specifically for the data-access and computation patterns of generative AI and large language models.

hpca-2025-004.method: The paper evaluates three defenses against side-channel attacks (information leaking through memory access patterns): linear scan (reading every row of the embedding table—a lookup table for neural network parameters—to hide which row is actually used), ORAM (a technique that encrypts and reshuffles memory accesses to obscure patterns, but is expensive for huge tables), and Deep Hash Embedding (DHE), which computes the embedding through a neural network fed the index directly, eliminating the memory access signature. A hybrid scheme combines DHE for large tables (where computation cost is spread across many lookups) and linear scan for small tables, chosen per table based on measured performance tradeoffs.
hpca-2025-004.key_novelty: The core innovation is replacing embedding table lookups with Deep Hash Embedding (DHE)—a neural network that computes embeddings from indices instead of fetching them from memory—which defends against side-channel attacks by eliminating the telltale memory access pattern rather than merely hiding it, yielding 4x speedup over optimized ORAM and 1116x memory footprint reduction.

hpca-2025-007.method: QuCLEAR uses a two-step process to optimize quantum circuits. First, Clifford Extraction identifies sections of the circuit that are "Clifford" (a special type mathematically easier to handle) and slides them toward the end using logical gate-rearrangement rules (commutation) while simultaneously reducing the harder non-Clifford gates—this reshuffling exposes opportunities to simplify further. Second, Clifford Absorption takes advantage of the fact that Clifford circuits can be computed by classical computers: instead of sending the extracted Clifford gates to run on noisy quantum hardware, it calculates their effect mathematically and bakes that result into the circuit's classical post-processing, removing those quantum gates entirely.
hpca-2025-007.key_novelty: The core idea is Clifford Absorption: using a classical computer to post-process the Clifford part of the circuit after the quantum gates have run, rather than executing it on noisy hardware, which cuts entangling depth by up to 84.1% compared to traditional gate-level optimization.

hpca-2025-003.method: VQ-LLM solves codebook access bottlenecks by placing the most frequently-used codebook entries in each thread's registers (avoiding slow shared-memory collisions), less common entries in shared memory, and rare ones in main memory. Instead of spreading lookups across many parallel paths that duplicate work, it reorganizes computation so each thread block loads exactly one codebook section at a time, then uses register shuffles (shfl.xor instructions) to pass data between threads without returning to shared memory. The system adaptively tunes its memory layout and work division by measuring shuffle overhead versus shared-memory latency for each vector-quantization configuration and GPU type.
hpca-2025-003.key_novelty: VQ-LLM treats the codebook lookup as the center of its computation strategy: it places frequently-accessed codebook entries in registers, reorganizes work to load each codebook together as a unit, and uses register shuffles for inter-thread sharing—converting vector quantization from a speed bottleneck into a practical speedup over element-wise quantization.

hpca-2025-008.method: DPUaudit switches from having the monitored computer push logs to having a DPU (Data Processing Unit, a specialized chip on the network card) pull system events directly from the computer's memory. Because the monitored computer no longer needs a log sender running on it, it doesn't need heavy software protections guarding that sender—eliminating the main source of slowdown. The DPU handles all log collection, processing, and verification itself, isolated on the network card away from the monitored system.
hpca-2025-008.key_novelty: The key idea is reversing the audit data flow—from the monitored computer pushing logs to a DPU pulling them directly, which eliminates the log sender and its protection overhead, achieving 2.1% overhead compared to order-of-magnitude higher overhead in previous approaches.

hpca-2025-006.method: Anaheim adds computing units (processing-in-memory, or PIM) directly into DRAM to perform simple arithmetic operations (addition, multiplication, NTT butterfly transforms) that had become the bottleneck. By running these operations in DRAM instead of moving data to the GPU and back, it eliminates bandwidth congestion. The system partitions work: the GPU handles NTT-heavy computation while PIM units handle arithmetic, and it strategically maps data to match DRAM's internal structure (banks and rows) so operations can complete with minimal data movement.
hpca-2025-006.key_novelty: The core idea is recognizing that FHE's GPU bottleneck comes from simple element-wise arithmetic operations (not NTT transforms), and solving it by placing calculation units directly in DRAM with data mapping that aligns with DRAM's internal bank organization.

hpca-2025-002.method: LEGO represents hardware using mathematical transformation rules (affine transformations, which convert time and space coordinates into computation instructions) that keep computation logic, data paths, and memory completely separate. It solves linear equations to find which processing units should connect to maximize data reuse, uses a tree algorithm (Minimum Spanning Tree via the Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm) to remove unnecessary connections, and applies breadth-first search to plan wiring across combined computation flows (fused dataflows) while organizing memory into banks that avoid access conflicts. Finally, it converts the high-level design (Architecture Description Graph) into a detailed specification (Detailed Architecture Graph), applies mathematical optimization (linear programming) to minimize temporary storage hardware and eliminate unused logic, and outputs synthesizable hardware code.
hpca-2025-002.key_novelty: The core innovation is a unified approach based on affine transformations that completely separates control logic from data flow, enabling automatic generation of working hardware code (synthesizable RTL) for any combination of spatial dataflows without hand-written templates, while reducing control overhead by 2 to 6.5 times compared to prior polyhedral and state-transition-table (STT) approaches.

hpca-2025-009.method: SpecMPK executes the memory permission update instruction (WRPKRU) speculatively—out-of-order, without waiting for earlier instructions to finish. The processor monitors all memory accesses that follow: if any try to access memory whose permissions were temporarily loosened by the speculative update, the processor blocks them from taking effect. These blocked accesses are allowed to proceed only once the permission update itself is guaranteed to happen (past the point where it could be undone). This prevents attackers from reading protected data through speculative execution while the processor gains speed by overlapping the permission update with useful work.
hpca-2025-009.key_novelty: SpecMPK allows the memory permission update instruction (WRPKRU) to execute out-of-order speculatively while preventing speculative access to memory regions whose permissions were temporarily loosened, by blocking such accesses until the update is guaranteed to happen.

hpca-2025-017.method: Mithril uses layer parallelism instead of the traditional approach of splitting the graph across GPUs: each GPU handles a consecutive set of neural network layers and processes all graph nodes for those layers, reducing communication between GPUs by a factor equal to the number of layers. To prevent GPUs from waiting idle, the graph is split into dependent chunks, and embedding speculation — making informed predictions about intermediate values to avoid blocking — is used to keep the pipeline moving across layers. For very large graphs, Mithril combines layer parallelism with graph-splitting to balance GPU utilization and ensure training converges.
hpca-2025-017.key_novelty: Mithril is the first system to apply layer-level model parallelism to full-graph GNN training, using embedding speculation (predictions of intermediate representations) to handle cross-layer data dependencies without stalling the GPU pipeline.

hpca-2025-018.method: NVMePass allows virtual machines to communicate directly with NVMe storage devices, bypassing the hypervisor (the software layer that normally mediates all access). Each VM is assigned exclusive I/O queues (communication channels with the storage) and storage space (logical block address ranges) that cannot overlap. A new hardware component called an NVMe Resource Domain (NRD), built into the storage controller itself, acts as a security guard for storage access—it checks every request and blocks any VM from accessing storage assigned to another VM. Because the hypervisor no longer needs to inspect every storage operation, the system achieves near-native performance without the slowdown that comes from software mediation.
hpca-2025-018.key_novelty: The key innovation is a hardware component (NVMe Resource Domain) embedded in the storage controller that enforces VM isolation and enables full I/O queue passthrough without any hypervisor involvement in the storage data path.

hpca-2025-012.method: The authors build a model that accounts for all costs in satellites with computing systems (space microdatacenters): power consumption, equipment weight, hardware purchase price, and communication. They explore different design approaches: using specialized chips (ASICs and neural processors) that do more floating-point operations per watt, coordinating computing across multiple earth-observation satellites, choosing between one centralized system and many distributed ones, and using more computing capacity than strictly necessary. Analysis reveals that power consumption is the dominant cost factor, though not in a linear relationship, while hardware cost and weight are much less significant.
hpca-2025-012.key_novelty: This is the first framework to use total ownership costs to design space microdatacenters, revealing that extreme heterogeneity—deploying many types of specialized chips (ASICs and neural processors) that do more floating-point operations per watt—cuts total costs by 116 times, despite being expensive per unit of computation.

hpca-2025-014.method: SoMa introduces Tensor-centric Notation (TCN), a formal system that describes all possible ways to schedule when data is fetched from and stored to main memory (DRAM) during execution of multiple fused neural network layers. A scheduling compiler uses this notation to explore trade-offs in when to prefetch data, when to store results, and how to group layers together, optimizing for different accelerators and workloads. The framework has been deployed as a compiler in a commercial accelerator product.
hpca-2025-014.key_novelty: SoMa's Tensor-centric Notation formally defines all possible DRAM data-scheduling strategies when executing multiple fused neural network layers together, enabling a compiler to jointly optimize them instead of tuning each layer separately.

hpca-2025-013.method: ChameleonEC breaks the repair process into small tasks and assigns them to unused network bandwidth, avoiding interference with regular traffic. It dynamically adjusts how data flows across these tasks in real time. When it detects slow nodes (stragglers), it rearranges which repair tasks go where and adapts transmission speeds to bypass them. The system was implemented and evaluated on Amazon EC2.
hpca-2025-013.key_novelty: The key idea is that repair can adapt in real time to network conditions and slow nodes by flexibly rerouting and rescheduling repair tasks, without modifying the erasure code (the redundancy algorithm).

hpca-2025-016.method: They used gem5 (a computer simulator) to deliberately inject faults into arithmetic units (integer and floating-point components) of five modern x86 processor designs, measuring how often these faults cause silent data corruptions—wrong results without crashes. The simulation tested different instruction classes and arithmetic unit types. They combined these results with real defect measurements from large-scale datacenters to estimate how often silent data corruptions actually occur in deployed systems.
hpca-2025-016.key_novelty: This is the first detailed study of silent data corruptions in arithmetic units (the math-doing parts, not memory) across five x86 processor designs, using real defect data from datacenters to estimate actual occurrence rates.

hpca-2025-021.method: Gaze works by analyzing the order and timing of memory accesses within a spatial region to predict what the program will access next. Instead of relying on external signals like the program location (trigger PC) or memory address patterns, it uses these internal ordering patterns, which are more consistent across different workloads. For programs with very dense memory access patterns within a region, Gaze uses a two-stage approach: it first identifies these high-density patterns, then makes targeted decisions about which data to fetch in advance, so it doesn't fetch data that won't be used.
hpca-2025-021.key_novelty: The key idea is using the order of memory accesses within a region (footprint-internal temporal correlation) as the signal for prediction, rather than relying on external context like the program location (trigger PC) or memory address patterns.

hpca-2025-011.method: TDRAM embeds small, fast lookup tables (called tag mats) directly on the HBM3 memory chip, enabling it to check whether requested data is cached internally and send data only on hits—eliminating wasted transfers on misses. Early tag probing begins lookups before the full memory row is ready, reducing latency on both hits and misses. A flush buffer (temporary storage in the DRAM) holds dirty data (modified but not yet saved), avoiding delays from writing old data back before fetching new data.
hpca-2025-011.key_novelty: Adding low-latency tag lookup tables (tag mats) directly to the HBM3 DRAM die enables in-DRAM tag comparison and conditional data response—data transfers to the CPU only on cache hits—matching SRAM cache behavior by eliminating wasted bandwidth on misses.

hpca-2025-020.method: Grad learns how each microservice's response time changes with different CPU and memory allocations, accounting for interference from other services. Using calculus-based optimization to find where performance improves most per additional resource (gradient-based extraction), it automatically selects which microservices—both bottleneck and supporting ones—should get more resources. A real-time simulator predicts overall performance and detects when response-time targets are missed (SLA violations). The approach was tested on real microservice benchmarks and production workloads.
hpca-2025-020.key_novelty: Grad jointly scales both critical and non-critical microservices by measuring how each responds to resources and how they interfere with each other—recognizing that one service's resources can help another service perform better (resource substitutability)—to minimize overall latency.

hpca-2025-010.method: Rush or Wait (RoW) uses a small hardware table (64 entries, each with a 4-bit counter, indexed by hashing the instruction's program counter) to predict whether to execute atomic instructions immediately (eagerly) or wait (lazily) based on how much contention—other threads competing for the same data—is expected. It learns contention patterns by detecting three signals: when other cores interrupt the data while locked, when they request data during instruction preparation (monitored via the Atomic Queue), or when data arrives slowly from another core's cache exceeding 400 cycles. Store-to-load forwarding from older instructions can override lazy predictions to improve locality. The mechanism needs only 64 bytes of total storage.
hpca-2025-010.key_novelty: This work proposes the first hardware predictor that dynamically chooses between eager (immediate) and lazy (delayed) execution of atomic operations by predicting cacheline contention, using only 64 bytes of state.

hpca-2025-026.method: CORDOBA uses a single metric called tCDP (total Carbon Delay Product)—the total lifecycle carbon (manufacturing plus operation) multiplied by execution time—to optimize hardware designs by balancing carbon and performance in one goal. The framework explores different hardware configurations by varying core counts, memory hierarchy, and chip stacking approaches (2D vs. 3D), then eliminates designs that are inferior in all dimensions (Pareto-dominated), discarding up to 98% of candidates. Two case studies demonstrate this on real CPU systems: reducing processor cores from 8 to 4, and adopting 3D memory-logic stacking.
hpca-2025-026.key_novelty: The tCDP metric unites operational carbon, embodied carbon, and performance into a single optimization target, enabling systematic carbon-efficient hardware design exploration.

hpca-2025-023.method: The BADA architecture splits numbers into bit-slices (the individual bit layers within each number) and uses a front-end unit (the first processing stage) to select only non-zero slices before computation. It skips calculations in two ways: when an entire chunk of bits is zero, and when either the input or weight has a zero bit-slice at any position (catching both types of empty space at once). The system represents each bit-slice using 8 bits without needing extra hardware—better than the 6-7 bit limit in earlier designs—and during training it adjusts weight distributions to create more zeros in higher-order bit-slices, amplifying the sparsity gains.
hpca-2025-023.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a front-end selection mechanism to exploit both input and weight sparsity simultaneously at the bit-slice level, paired with training that concentrates zeros into higher-order bit-slices.

hpca-2025-015.method: Chronus mitigates RowHammer attacks (where repeatedly accessing one memory row corrupts adjacent rows) by moving the activation counters (devices that track how many times each row is accessed) to a separate location on the DRAM chip. This separation lets the system update these counters simultaneously with reading or writing data, instead of doing them sequentially, which eliminates the performance delay. To stop 'wave attacks' (where attackers use specific patterns to force the system to exhaust its refresh budget), Chronus dynamically adjusts how many preventive memory refreshes are triggered each time, rather than using one fixed conservative number that degrades performance. The solution requires only in-DRAM modifications and is open-sourced.
hpca-2025-015.key_novelty: Chronus mitigates RowHammer (memory corruption from repeated row access) by decoupling activation counters from data storage, enabling concurrent updates without performance penalty, and by dynamically controlling preventive refresh counts to defeat wave attacks.

hpca-2025-024.method: C4 exploits two key properties of distributed training. First, because training iterations are structured and homogeneous, hardware failures produce detectable anomalies in collective communication patterns (the synchronized messages all GPUs exchange)—C4 monitors these patterns in real time to identify and restart faulty components without waiting for software timeouts. Second, these collective communications consist of a small number of predictable, long-lived network flows, so C4 plans traffic in advance to eliminate bandwidth contention and collision-induced queuing, reducing idle time in GPU clusters.
hpca-2025-024.key_novelty: It diagnoses hardware faults by detecting anomalies in collective communication patterns (synchronized GPU traffic), using the periodic structure of training iterations as a diagnostic signal.

hpca-2025-025.method: The paper derives harmonic mean speedup from two concrete scenarios: equal-work (how much faster one system finishes the same task) and equal-time (how much more work gets done in the same time). It proves that harmonic mean correctly averages performance across multiple workloads, while the currently-used geometric mean does not. Examples show geometric and harmonic mean can rank competing architectures oppositely, so the wrong metric leads to wrong architectural choices.
hpca-2025-025.key_novelty: Equal-work harmonic mean speedup is the mathematically correct metric for summarizing system performance across multiple workloads.

hpca-2025-019.method: AsyncDIMM lets the host CPU and a near-memory accelerator (a specialized processor attached to memory) share the memory bus through three modes: one device alone, both at once, or switching between them seamlessly. It manages concurrent access using an offload-schedule-return mechanism (host sends work, accelerator executes, accelerator returns results) with explicit synchronization (host waits for a signal) and implicit synchronization (timing coordinates handoffs). Three optimizations minimize delays: expedited work offload, reduced mode-switching overhead via locality-aware methods, and improved result throughput through adaptive batching and timing-division multiplexing notifications. The implementation modifies only existing memory controllers and was validated on an FPGA.
hpca-2025-019.key_novelty: AsyncDIMM achieves concurrent host and near-memory accelerator access on existing unmodified memory buses through an offload-schedule-return mechanism with dual synchronization modes (explicit and implicit).

hpca-2025-022.method: Compressing a neural network by clustering weights (grouping similar weights together) requires an algorithm that saves temporary values during backpropagation (the step where weights get updated) to calculate how much each weight should change. eDKM shrinks the memory this requires in two ways: uniquification detects and removes duplicate copies of the same temporary data before offloading it to CPU storage, and sharding splits the remaining large data into smaller pieces that compress better. Together these techniques reduce memory use per decoder layer by 130x, enabling a 7B LLaMA model to be compressed to 3 bits per weight and fine-tuned on a standard GPU.
hpca-2025-022.key_novelty: The core insight is removing duplicate copies of temporary data (uniquification) and breaking large data structures called tensors into smaller partitions (sharding) during CPU offload of the backward pass, reducing memory by 130x per decoder layer and making train-time weight clustering practical for 7B-parameter language models.

hpca-2025-034.method: GSArch fixes the three main slowdowns in 3D Gaussian Splatting training with three targeted hardware techniques. First, it identifies which Gaussian data objects are accessed repeatedly (called 'hot' Gaussians) and stores them in fast on-chip memory rather than fetching them from slower main memory each time—this eliminates the dominant source of redundant memory traffic. Second, it recognizes that many gradients (values used to update the model during training) contribute very little to the final result, so it skips the expensive atomic write operations for these low-value gradients. Third, it reorganizes memory read requests to avoid 'bank conflicts'—a problem where multiple reads hitting the same memory location simultaneously force them to queue up—by bundling conflicting requests into non-conflicting groups. These three changes together speed up the backward pass of 3DGS training.
hpca-2025-034.key_novelty: The core insight is automatically identifying which Gaussians are used repeatedly and caching them in fast on-chip memory instead of constantly fetching them from slower main memory, which eliminates the single biggest bottleneck in 3DGS training.

hpca-2025-027.method: WarpDrive speeds up the NTT operation (a mathematical transform for homomorphic encryption) using three techniques: First, it restructures the calculations to reduce instructions by 73%. Second, it pipelines memory loads to eliminate 86% of pipeline stalls, where the GPU would otherwise sit idle waiting for data. Third, it runs CUDA Cores (general-purpose GPU processors) and Tensor Cores (specialized math accelerators) concurrently within the same kernel—the first to do this for NTT—exploiting both types' complementary strengths. The system also maximizes parallelism at the individual ciphertext level without requiring values to be batched together.
hpca-2025-027.key_novelty: WarpDrive is the first framework to run CUDA Cores and Tensor Cores at the same time within a single NTT kernel for FHE, achieving higher throughput than either processor type alone.

hpca-2025-032.method: The researchers studied multiple machine learning models that Google uses to balance server resources in data centers and documented real cases where these models failed silently on workload patterns they had never seen in training. They tested three categories of approaches to detect these failures: distance-based methods (checking how similar new workloads are to training data), confidence-based methods (checking if the model said it was sure), and ensemble methods (combining predictions from multiple models)—measuring the tradeoff between precision (avoiding false alarms), recall (catching real failures), and inference overhead (the computation cost). They found that Bayesian models, which natively estimate the uncertainty in their predictions, could reliably flag unreliable predictions and allow human operators or fallback systems to intervene before resource balancing went wrong.
hpca-2025-032.key_novelty: Bayesian machine learning models' built-in uncertainty estimates can reliably detect unusual or unfamiliar workload patterns in production data center resource balancing, as proven at Google's fleet scale.

hpca-2025-037.method: EFFACT pairs a specialized compiler with custom hardware design (targeting both FPGA and ASIC) to accelerate Fully Homomorphic Encryption. The key optimizations are: (1) a streaming memory access scheme that continuously feeds data into calculations, achieving high throughput even with limited on-chip memory; (2) function unit reuse at the circuit level, letting the same hardware components handle multiple tasks without performance loss; and (3) custom hardware for Number Theoretic Transform operations (the mathematical calculations central to FHE) and automorphisms (operations that rearrange encrypted data). The compiler supports multiple FHE schemes—CKKS, BGV, BFV—and automatically determines optimal on-chip memory allocation.
hpca-2025-037.key_novelty: EFFACT achieves high Number Theoretic Transform throughput with limited on-chip memory by streaming data sequentially (matching how encryption kernels naturally access information), combined with circuit-level function unit reuse that maintains performance while reducing hardware.

hpca-2025-029.method: Anda compresses floating-point activation data by grouping values with a shared scale (exponent) per group but variable precision (bits) per value, letting different network layers use different precision without retraining. It automatically searches for the best precision per layer by testing accuracy and efficiency after training. The hardware organizes data by individual bits, processes them sequentially in specialized units, and compresses on-the-fly as the model runs. Together, these co-designed software and hardware changes reduce data storage and the floating-point-to-integer calculations that currently bottleneck large language model inference.
hpca-2025-029.key_novelty: Anda uses a grouped data format with a shared scale per group but variable precision per value, automatically tuning precision per layer to simultaneously reduce data storage, bandwidth, and the floating-point-to-integer math that bottlenecks large language model inference.

hpca-2025-039.method: SparseWeaver solves the problem of sparse graph operations causing GPU cores to sit idle unevenly by converting those operations into balanced dense operations that distribute work evenly. A lightweight hardware component called Weaver is added to GPU cores; it identifies patterns in the graph structure (using both compile-time and runtime analysis) where sparse operations can be converted to dense ones, then performs the conversion directly in the execution pipeline without extra memory overhead or synchronization delays. The design is tested on Vortex, an open-source RISC-V GPU.
hpca-2025-039.key_novelty: A dedicated Weaver hardware unit converts sparse graph operations to dense operations by recognizing the underlying graph structure, eliminating memory and synchronization overhead compared to software approaches.

hpca-2025-036.method: MANT uses different number formats (quantization schemes) for different groups within the same tensor, rather than using one format for the entire tensor, because different groups have different value distributions. The system dynamically chooses the right MANT numeric variant for each group. To speed up execution, the hardware combines decoding and computation into single processing elements rather than doing them separately. These elements are arranged in a systolic array (a grid of processors used in ML accelerators), allowing the same hardware to quantize both model weights and dynamically generated KV cache data in real time.
hpca-2025-036.key_novelty: MANT uses a mathematically adaptive numeric type that adapts quantization per group (not per tensor) to simultaneously quantize both model weights and real-time KV cache data with fused decoding-computation.

hpca-2025-033.method: ER-DCIM uses three complementary strategies to prevent errors during math operations in memory. First, it adds mathematical check-information (residue codes) to the computation that lets it catch and fix errors in the results as they happen—the first real-time error correction technique designed for DCIM. Second, it fixes defective SRAM cells gradually without interrupting the calculation. Third, it reuses the error-correction hardware that was built for low-voltage mode (where errors occur more easily) to boost performance at standard voltage instead, preventing wasted chip space.
hpca-2025-033.key_novelty: Using residue codes to correct errors in multiply-accumulate results during DCIM computation, rather than at the SRAM cell level—the first real-time approach of this kind.

hpca-2025-042.method: Zebra works around ZNS SSDs' append-only constraint by using the ZRWA—a small random-write buffer at the front of each zone—to store parity updates instead of separate metadata zones. When RAID needs to recalculate parity bits (called a partial parity update), Zebra writes the updated parity to the ZRWA buffer, which supports random rewrites even though the main zone only allows appends. By keeping parity chunks small enough to fit within this buffer, the approach avoids violating the zone's append-only rule. Complementary techniques maintain performance and reliability across different SSD models and zone sizes.
hpca-2025-042.key_novelty: The key insight is using the zone's built-in random-write buffer (ZRWA)—rather than separate metadata zones—to store repeated parity updates, since the ZRWA's native random-write capability directly matches the parity update workload's I/O pattern.

hpca-2025-030.method: NOVA separates two core operations in graph processing—reduction (combining results from neighbors) and propagation (sending computed values forward)—which allows the entire graph data to stay in off-chip DRAM instead of being split to fit in fast on-chip memory. Rather than storing graph state, the on-chip memory becomes a prefetch buffer that loads data early to mask DRAM access delays. Multiple NOVA chips can be connected to process larger graphs, achieving nearly linear performance scaling as you add more chips. Cycle-accurate simulation with gem5 (architectural modeling software) confirms the design.
hpca-2025-030.key_novelty: Separating reduction and propagation operations eliminates the need to partition graph data, enabling it to stay entirely in DRAM with on-chip memory serving only as a prefetch buffer to hide access delays.

hpca-2025-028.method: EDBP (Enhanced Dead Block Predictor) identifies cache blocks (small fast data storage) that appear 'live' (potentially reusable) to conventional dead-block predictors but will actually be lost before reuse due to an imminent power failure in an energy-harvesting system. It powers down these blocks to eliminate leakage energy (power wasted when keeping idle data), freeing that energy for actual computation. Combined with the Cache Decay predictor, EDBP achieves near-theoretical-minimum cache leakage across 20 Mediabench and MiBench applications.
