hpca-2025-028.key_novelty: Incorporating power-failure prediction into dead-block identification, enabling leakage reduction for cache blocks that appear 'live' but will be unreachable due to imminent energy exhaustion.

hpca-2025-041.method: EIGEN places two layers on the active interposer (the chip connecting other chips). The first layer (AspLayer) sets up an optimized connection pattern based on the application's typical needs; the second layer (DynLayer) adapts in real time, rerouting data around bottlenecks as they form. A machine-learning system (reinforcement learning) learns the best routing paths by trial and error, rewarded for low message delays and high link usage—considering network structure, current traffic, and memory access patterns. The layers work together to move data between chips with fewer relay hops and less congestion.
hpca-2025-041.key_novelty: A two-layer active-interposer design that separates setting up optimized connection patterns from real-time traffic routing, both guided by machine learning trained to balance message speed and link efficiency.

hpca-2025-031.method: PROCA is a specialized hardware processor for MCMC algorithms (Markov Chain Monte Carlo - a statistical method where each sample depends on the previous one). The processor uses processing-in-memory function units to generate samples, and it's programmable to handle any posterior distribution form from software probabilistic programming frameworks. The speed-up comes from a prediction step: PROCA predicts whether a proposed sample will be accepted before the full evaluation completes, starting computation on the next sample while still finalizing the current accept/reject decision. This prediction breaks MCMC's inherent sequential dependency, enabling multiple processor cores to work in parallel on different samples.
hpca-2025-031.key_novelty: PROCA breaks MCMC's sequential dependency by predicting accept/reject decisions before they're fully computed, enabling multiple cores to process samples in parallel using processing-in-memory function units.

hpca-2025-043.method: The system watches upcoming requests and predicts how much temporary storage space for computation will be needed, then uses a machine learning model to estimate how long each computational step will take. Based on these predictions, it adjusts the GPU's speed—running it fast when there's work to do and slow when it can coast—and updates these decisions after every single step. The predictions are highly accurate (R² score exceeding 0.97) with an average error of less than 1 step per second. By tuning both the GPU speed and the number of model instances running in parallel, the system cuts energy use while guaranteeing response times stay within promised limits.
hpca-2025-043.key_novelty: The system predicts upcoming memory and request needs to adjust GPU speed after every computational step, cutting energy proactively instead of waiting and capping power after the system gets overloaded.

hpca-2025-046.method: Modern processors have different sleep levels (C-states: C0 is running, C1/C1E/C6 are increasingly deeper sleeps) that wake up at different speeds. BrokenSleep sends network requests to a victim server and measures response times—deeper sleep states wake up more slowly, so responses arrive slightly later. By analyzing these timing patterns, an attacker can figure out what sleep state the processor is in, then use this to steal data across security boundaries (covert channel) or infer user keystrokes from timing (side-channel). The attack works on both Intel and ARM processors using standard power management, without exploiting any processor design flaws.
hpca-2025-046.key_novelty: This is the first timing attack that works over the network by measuring processor wake-up times, so an attacker doesn't need code running on the target machine.

hpca-2025-035.method: EXION combines software and hardware acceleration to skip redundant calculations in diffusion models. The FFN-Reuse algorithm recognizes that the feedforward network layer (a key component of transformer models) produces similar outputs across neighboring iterations; it computes the first iteration fully, then reuses those outputs in subsequent iterations where values are too small to affect results, achieving 70-97% sparsity in the first layer and reducing feedforward operations by 52-85%. A second algorithm predicts which attention scores (the mathematical weights that determine which input parts matter most) will be negligible using a two-step leading-one detection method, enabling it to skip those computations within each iteration (20-95% sparsity, skipping an average of 26% of query projections and 22% of key-value projections). The ConMerge mechanism converts the scattered sparse outputs into compact dense matrices suitable for efficient execution on the specialized Diffusion-Sparsity Aware Core hardware—a chip with a 16x16 processing array, synthesized at 14nm, 800MHz, 0.8V.
hpca-2025-035.key_novelty: FFN-Reuse exploits output redundancy in feedforward networks across iterations by reusing computation, while ConMerge converts the resulting sparse outputs into compact dense matrices executable at high hardware utilization.

hpca-2025-038.method: The Encoded Ising Model (E-I model) inserts a digital encoding circuit between the solver and the optimization landscape, using combinational logic (circuits that instantly compute outputs from inputs) to map the solver's spin states (output configurations) to legal variable assignments and prevent exploration of infeasible states. Instead of using energy penalties to discourage bad solutions, constraints are enforced as hard logical rules. The Fuse software framework lets researchers describe constrained optimization problems in high-level code and automatically deploy them to p-computer hardware, reducing wasted iterations by orders of magnitude.
hpca-2025-038.key_novelty: A digital encoding circuit inserted into the Ising solver loop structurally prevents exploration of infeasible states by enforcing constraints as hard logical rules instead of energy penalties.

hpca-2025-049.method: The researchers tracked 4 million jobs over 11 months across two large GPU clusters (using A100 GPUs) with over 150 million GPU-hours of data, categorizing the different types of failures and calculating how often jobs fail on average (Mean Time to Failure, or MTTF) based on the number of GPUs each job uses. They built a mathematical model of when and why jobs fail, then created a formula called the Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR) that estimates how much useful training time a job actually gets based on checkpoint frequency (how often you save progress), restart delays, and failure rate. They used this formula to show how strategies like saving progress more often would reduce the impact of failures.
hpca-2025-049.key_novelty: The key idea is the Effective Training Time Ratio (ETTR), a formula that estimates what fraction of a training job's time is spent actually training rather than failing and recovering, enabling engineers to predict the real impact of software improvements like more frequent checkpointing across different cluster sizes.

hpca-2025-047.method: Ditto exploits a simple fact: when a diffusion model removes noise step-by-step, the output from one step to the next barely changes. Instead of recalculating everything each time, the algorithm computes the full result on the first step, then only figures out the tiny differences in each subsequent step (representing them with fewer bits, often as zero). Neural network math lets you do this: you can compute just the difference and add it back instead of recalculating the whole thing. The hardware is specially designed to recognize when there's no difference at all and skip that step, while organizing memory to efficiently handle storing and retrieving these differences.
hpca-2025-047.key_novelty: The core innovation is to exploit nearly identical outputs between diffusion model steps by representing their tiny differences with fewer bits (often zero) and designing hardware that skips these zero-difference operations without sacrificing accuracy.

hpca-2025-053.method: Marching Page Walks scans the queue of pending address translation requests to find groups that can share the same page table lookups—for example, when different threads need to translate nearby addresses that map through the same page table entry (the lookup table mapping virtual to physical memory). It bunches these compatible requests and sends multiple lookup instructions to memory at once instead of one at a time. This batching works because GPU workloads tend to access memory in clusters, with many threads working on nearby addresses simultaneously.
hpca-2025-053.key_novelty: Marching Page Walks lets a single page table walker send multiple address translation requests concurrently by batching requests that share page table lookups, cutting queue waiting times without needing extra hardware.

hpca-2025-050.method: PAISE moves the memory-heavy attention computations (the parts where transformers multiply keys and values together) from an AMD MI100 GPU to HBM-PIM devices (special memory chips located near the GPU). A scheduling algorithm decides which operations to move based on the transformer's structure (layer type, number of attention heads) and the PIM hardware's capabilities (memory bandwidth and floating-point operations per second). The optimized code restructures the key-value cache data by spreading reads across multiple memory banks, so different attention heads can fetch their data simultaneously—this lets the hardware handle more memory requests in parallel.
hpca-2025-050.key_novelty: PAISE's core innovation is moving transformer attention to specialized memory chips (PIM) by reorganizing data so multiple attention heads work in parallel, paired with a scheduling algorithm that picks which layers benefit most from this move.

hpca-2025-056.method: Adyna solves the problem of dynamic neural networks (networks that conditionally skip computation when inputs are easy) by precompiling multiple specialized kernels (hardware-optimized computation versions), each designed for a different workload size. At runtime, instead of using a generic kernel or compiling on demand, the system observes what the actual workload looks like and selects the precompiled version best suited for it. An intelligent algorithm decides which kernel versions to prepare upfront, balancing coverage of different workload sizes against the limited on-chip memory available on the accelerator. This ensures the hardware always runs code optimized for the specific input at hand, unlocking efficiency gains that dynamic networks promise but hardware traditionally cannot deliver.
hpca-2025-056.key_novelty: The core insight is precompiling a small set of specialized kernels (each optimized for a specific workload size) and dynamically selecting which one to execute based on observed input characteristics, so hardware resources are always well-utilized regardless of how much computation the input actually requires.

hpca-2025-051.method: The system aligns GPU memory to power-of-two boundaries (allocations at multiples of 2) and performs static analysis—inspecting the code before it runs—to mark instructions that perform pointer arithmetic (operations that calculate new memory addresses). Instead of storing bounds information in separate tables, it encodes the size and base address of each allocated block directly into the unused upper bits of the 64-bit addresses that GPUs use. Before each memory access executes, hardware logic validates it against the bounds encoded in the pointer itself, all with minimal added latency even when thousands of operations run concurrently.
hpca-2025-051.key_novelty: The core idea is storing each object's bounds information entirely in the unused upper bits of GPU pointers—using power-of-two alignment and static marking of which operations change memory addresses—instead of keeping separate bounds tables.

hpca-2025-048.method: LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) separates quantum memory into Computational Registers (CR), small regions that are very fast to access, and Scan-Access Memory (SAM), much larger regions that are slower with variable access times. The system defines an instruction set for these regions, with two concrete implementations called point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. To hide SAM's access delays without slowing down computation, the design overlaps memory operations with other computation and reorders accesses based on which qubits the program tends to use near each other, identified through static analysis of when each qubit is referenced.
hpca-2025-048.key_novelty: LSQCA achieves nearly double the quantum memory density (from 50% to 100%) by splitting memory into fast Computational Registers and slower Scan-Access Memory, then hiding access delays through instruction scheduling guided by static analysis of memory access patterns.

hpca-2025-058.method: TidalMesh is an AllReduce algorithm (a distributed operation where all computing nodes combine their data and share results) built specifically for 2D mesh networks—grid-shaped topologies where each node connects to neighbors. Instead of adapting generic algorithms to the mesh, it sends data in wave-like patterns that follow the grid lines, using both directions on every link and preventing traffic bottlenecks. A "Sparse" variant cuts bandwidth overhead. To reduce communication delays, it overlaps different operation phases (reduction, scattering, then gathering) so that compute and communication can happen in parallel instead of sequentially.
hpca-2025-058.key_novelty: It builds an AllReduce algorithm natively for 2D mesh networks using wave-like flows aligned to the grid, achieving near-optimal bandwidth usage instead of adapting generic ring or tree algorithms.

hpca-2025-045.method: MVE (Multi-dimensional Vector ISA Extension) enables processors to efficiently handle data arranged in up to 4 dimensions at once (like nested tables), rather than the 1D arrays that conventional processors are limited to. Execution control happens at the dimension level, using a compact mask register to activate or deactivate entire groups of iterations simultaneously, instead of controlling individual processing lanes. A specialized controller in the L2 cache converts multi-dimensional logical accesses into physical storage locations in the SRAM, using a transpose unit (with 8T bit-cells and a crossbar) to route data through all 8192 processing lanes (each 32 bits wide) in the right order, while managing L1 cache interactions to keep data consistent. The compiler supports this through data-lifetime analysis, hybrid instruction scheduling that mixes different strategies, and efficient register allocation to prevent unnecessary spills to main memory.
hpca-2025-045.key_novelty: A vector instruction set that supports up to 4D memory accesses (with various stepping patterns and random access) and dimension-level masked execution (turning entire iteration groups on or off), hiding cache storage details from programmers while raising processing efficiency from 23% to 60% for mobile workloads.

hpca-2025-052.method: VR-Pipe adds two optimizations to GPU hardware for volume rendering. First, it repurposes the depth-test units (specialized hardware that normally checks which objects are in front) to stop ray marching once pixels become fully opaque, avoiding wasted computation. Second, it pre-blends fragments (pixel colors) in the programmable shader cores by grouping them into tiles and merging quads before passing them to the fixed-function blending hardware, which removes the blending bottleneck. The design targets 3D Gaussian Splatting.
hpca-2025-052.key_novelty: VR-Pipe makes volume rendering efficient on fixed-function GPU hardware by repurposing depth-test units for early termination and using multi-granular tile binning with quad merging to pre-blend fragments in shader cores before fixed-function blending.

hpca-2025-054.method: Uni-Render is a specialized computer chip (ASIC) that can reconfigure itself to accelerate different types of neural rendering. It identifies computational operations shared across rendering methods—ray marching (stepping rays through 3D space to find surfaces), Gaussian rasterization (projecting 3D points as pixels), MLP inference (evaluating neural networks), and volume compositing (blending samples into a final image)—and implements a flexible processing engine that dynamically adjusts the dataflow and operations based on the rendering algorithm being used. The chip's processing units and memory layout can be reorganized at runtime to support both typical and hybrid rendering pipelines.
hpca-2025-054.key_novelty: A single reconfigurable hardware accelerator that covers all representative neural rendering pipelines by exploiting their shared computational operations and dynamically adapting data flow for each algorithm.

hpca-2025-055.method: The system converts neural network weights into lookup tables using vector quantization—where similar values are grouped and stored as a table of representatives. Instead of the usual multiply-accumulate operations (the basic math that neural accelerators perform), the hardware simply looks up precomputed results in these tables and adds them. The LUTBoost training algorithm learns, through multiple training stages, which weight patterns (called codebooks) work best with lookup tables. A co-design framework then searches for the best combination of table size, codebook structure, model accuracy, and hardware cost, with the final ASIC accelerator implementing hardware units that fetch results from lookup tables and accumulate them.
hpca-2025-055.key_novelty: The core innovation is replacing multiply-accumulate hardware units with vector quantization lookup-table units, achieving compression below the 1-bit limit that scalar quantization cannot reach.

hpca-2025-057.method: Alecto decides, for each memory access the CPU actually needs, which prefetcher should attempt to fetch that data ahead of time. It evaluates which prefetcher can predict the access most correctly (accuracy), catch all the data the CPU will need (coverage), and deliver it with the right timing (timeliness). Rather than having all prefetchers speculate on every access, it routes each access only to the most suitable prefetcher for that pattern. This focused routing prevents prefetchers from polluting their lookup tables with bad patterns and stops them from wasting bandwidth and memory request slots by competing with each other.
hpca-2025-057.key_novelty: Instead of using all prefetchers for every memory access, Alecto selects the best prefetcher for each individual access, improving accuracy, coverage, and timeliness while reducing energy waste from unnecessary training.

hpca-2025-061.method: HATT converts fermionic quantum systems (particles that behave like fermions) into qubits (quantum bits) using a customized bottom-up tree construction tailored to the specific system's properties. Rather than using generic methods like Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev, the algorithm analyzes the target quantum system and builds a ternary tree (a branching structure where each node has up to three children) that minimizes Pauli weight (the complexity measure of quantum operations needed). This reduces the algorithmic complexity from O(N^4) to O(N^3) while preserving the vacuum state properties (the zero-particle quantum state needed for correct simulation).
hpca-2025-061.key_novelty: The core idea is a bottom-up ternary tree construction that is Hamiltonian-aware—meaning it adapts itself to fit the specific quantum system being studied—thereby reducing computational complexity from O(N^4) to O(N^3).

hpca-2025-062.method: When training neural networks, the weight matrices in the forward pass and backward pass are mathematical transposes of each other—this paper exploits that relationship to find 2D block sparsity patterns that behave more like unstructured sparsity (which keeps accuracy higher) while remaining structured enough for hardware efficiency. The hardware includes an adaptive codec that converts between row-wise and column-wise sparse storage formats on-the-fly, and a scheduler that optimizes sparsity-aware computation. This achieves 1.47x bandwidth utilization and 1.57x computational utilization improvements compared to standard approaches.
hpca-2025-062.key_novelty: Instead of one-dimensional sparsity patterns, this approach derives 2D block patterns from the transpose relationship between forward and backward pass weight matrices, achieving both structured hardware efficiency and near-unstructured neural network accuracy.

hpca-2025-059.method: ZAC (Zoned Architecture Compiler) optimizes quantum circuits for zoned quantum computers by keeping qubits in the entanglement zone when they'll be used there immediately, avoiding wasteful round-trips to and from storage. It also predicts future operations to decide optimal qubit placement and schedules operations more efficiently for zone-specific constraints using ZAIR, an intermediate representation that tracks which zone each qubit needs to be in. The compiler uses a flexible specification language to adapt to different zoned quantum architectures. On real circuits, this approach achieves 22x better signal quality (fidelity) compared to monolithic (non-zoned) quantum computers.
hpca-2025-059.key_novelty: The key insight is that keeping qubits in the entanglement zone when they're about to be used there cuts out wasteful movement between zones, which is the primary source of signal quality loss in zoned quantum computers.

hpca-2025-060.method: CROSS is a compiler that analyzes where nonzero weights cluster together in a neural network (parameter distribution locality) to identify sections where dense computation remains fast. It splits sparse neural network computation into pieces at different sparsity levels and routes each piece to either a specialized sparse kernel or an optimized dense kernel. The framework translates the sparse computation graph into a form that works with high-performance dense GPU routines (BLAS-level operations), avoiding the expensive overhead of sparse index encoding while still skipping zero values. It handles various sparsity patterns: unstructured (random zero distribution), structured (entire rows or columns of zeros), and N:M (exactly M nonzeros per N values).
hpca-2025-060.key_novelty: CROSS exploits weight clustering (parameter distribution locality) and sparse graph translation to run sparse neural networks efficiently on dense GPU kernels, avoiding sparse format overhead while still skipping zero computations.

hpca-2025-044.method: Panacea introduces AQS-GEMM, a hardware design that compresses and skips computation on nonzero bit-slices (individual bit positions across data) created by asymmetric quantization. Two algorithm-hardware co-optimization techniques increase sparsity: zero-point manipulation (shifting the quantization zero-point to push common values toward zero) and distribution-based bit-slicing (selecting bit positions to compute based on how activation values are distributed). The hardware uses a specialized dataflow for mixed sparse and dense computation, with run-length encoding (representing repeated values as a count instead of individually) to reuse data across operations and reduce off-chip memory traffic.
hpca-2025-044.key_novelty: AQS-GEMM is the first bit-slice GEMM (a specialized matrix multiplier) that compresses and skips the nonzero bit-slices produced by asymmetric quantization, rather than only the zero-slices that symmetric quantization creates.

hpca-2025-065.method: The researchers added a tensor core (specialized hardware for matrix multiplications) to the open-source Vortex RISC-V GPU and identified two bottlenecks slowing it down: memory bandwidth (how quickly data can move) and warp contention (multiple thread groups competing for the single tensor core). Their solution lets multiple warps share a single tensor core operation at the same time, which reduces the memory each warp must handle and allows the GPU to overlap data movement with computation. The hardware tensor core control system was enhanced to schedule and manage this sharing between warps.
hpca-2025-065.key_novelty: Multiple warps can share a single tensor core operation simultaneously, reducing each warp's memory requirements and improving tensor core utilization by up to 3x compared to running separately.

hpca-2025-063.method: The system recognizes that LLM neurons (the basic units) aren't equally important—some get used much more than others depending on the input. It keeps the frequently-used 20% of neurons that handle 80% of the work on the consumer GPU for speed, and offloads the rarely-used 80% of neurons that only handle 20% of work to processing units embedded in DRAM chips, so computation happens right at the data instead of moving weights across the slow PCIe link. A lightweight predictor watches each input to identify which neurons will be active, and a scheduler balances work across multiple DRAM modules while the GPU and DRAM chips compute in parallel.
hpca-2025-063.key_novelty: It recognizes that LLMs use some weights much more than others, and stores the rarely-used weights in processing units built into DRAM chips rather than shuttling all weights across the slow PCIe connection, so computation happens right where the data lives.

hpca-2025-066.method: The researchers tested 160 DDR4 and 4 HBM2 memory chips from three manufacturers by repeatedly measuring each row's read disturbance threshold—the number of times a row can be read before it corrupts its neighbors—watching how this threshold changed over time. They discovered that the minimum threshold only appeared after up to 94,467 measurements and could be 3.5 times lower than the highest observed value. They examined how the threshold variability changed based on chip density, manufacturing process, data patterns, how long the attacking row stayed active, and temperature. They evaluated whether guardbanding (reserving safety margins) or ECC error correction methods like SECDED and Chipkill could defend against this varying vulnerability.
hpca-2025-066.key_novelty: This is the first experimental demonstration that DRAM rows' sensitivity to read disturbance (how quickly repeated reads can corrupt neighboring rows) varies dramatically and unpredictably over time—termed Variable Read Disturbance—undermining the assumptions that existing RowHammer protection methods rely on.

hpca-2025-074.method: The system adds two types of value prediction (guessing the result of a computation before it finishes) to an in-order processor pipeline built on a CVA6 RISC-V core. Because instructions execute in strict order, the processor can aggressively guess values without needing complex recovery logic—if a guess is wrong, the real result simply overwrites it when the computation finishes. The cache system is redesigned with a fast first-level cache that can accept these speculative guesses. The core uses a 32-entry scoreboard to track instruction dependencies and issues 4 instructions per cycle, all without traditional register renaming or out-of-order memory hazard detection.
hpca-2025-074.key_novelty: In-order processors can do aggressive value guessing without performance penalties (because wrong guesses get overwritten), matching the speed of complex out-of-order designs without their expensive register renaming or memory hazard detection.

hpca-2025-068.method: InstAttention offloads both the KV cache (the data storing information about previous tokens) and the attention computation to special storage drives with built-in processors (Computational Storage Drives, or CSDs). Because the computation runs inside the drive, it can access the stored data through fast internal flash memory instead of the slow PCIe connection between the GPU and drive. The system is optimized for how flash memory actually works—reading large sequential blocks efficiently—and runs the attention decode phase (where the model calculates which previous tokens matter when generating each new token) directly in the CSD, sending only the final results back to the GPU. The approach targets offline inference of 13B-parameter models on NVIDIA A6000 GPUs.
hpca-2025-068.key_novelty: The key idea is performing attention computation directly inside the storage drive, where it can access the KV cache through fast internal flash pathways instead of sending data back and forth through the slow PCIe cable.

hpca-2025-064.method: Mascot builds on TAGE (a prediction technique that uses instruction history patterns) but extends it to track both when memory accesses depend on each other and when they don't. This dual tracking lets it serve two purposes: preventing loads from starting before their dependencies complete, and speculatively sending values directly from stores to loads without waiting for address resolution. A single shared prediction table handles both, eliminating the need for separate hardware.
hpca-2025-064.key_novelty: A single prediction table that learns when memory accesses are independent (as well as dependent), letting it handle both dependency prediction and speculative value forwarding.

hpca-2025-067.method: ARTEMIS finds efficient chip designs by putting a real-time task scheduler directly into the design-search loop. Normally, exploring chip designs means searching over both chip architectures AND how to assign tasks to different hardware components—a huge search space. By building in an intelligent scheduler, ARTEMIS automatically handles task assignment while the search focuses only on chip architecture, making the problem tractable. The scheduler uses policies like strategically delaying tasks to reduce memory traffic and assigning work based on power requirements, and the method was validated on FPGA hardware using autonomous vehicle and AR/VR benchmarks.
hpca-2025-067.key_novelty: The core idea is embedding a real-time task scheduler directly into the chip-design search process, which eliminates the need to explore task-assignment choices and achieves 5.1-12.8x faster design discovery while guaranteeing 100% real-time deadline compliance.

hpca-2025-073.method: SPARK modifies a CPU's L1 cache, the small, fast memory right next to its processors, to also perform calculations, adding only 1.4% to the CPU's total physical size. It detects which parts of data matrices contain zeros (making them sparse) and skips redundant multiplications on those values, while also identifying and reusing calculation patterns that recur throughout ILP solving steps like simplex pivots and branch-and-bound traversals. The same reconfigurable hardware solves both sparse and dense problems without needing separate accelerators.
hpca-2025-073.key_novelty: Adding sparsity and pattern-reuse hardware to a CPU's L1 cache for just 1.4% extra area lets ILP and LP problems run faster inside the CPU pipeline without separate accelerators.

hpca-2025-070.method: FHENDI places computation inside memory (near-DRAM) to avoid expensive data movement of large encrypted values. It exploits parallelism at four scales—individual elements, data chunks (limbs), frequency components (coefficients), and whole ciphertexts—assigning each to different hardware hierarchy levels. Within individual memory banks, a conflict-free localized permutation network (a specialized reordering method) enables element-wise and butterfly operations without data conflicts or inter-bank movement. The HElayers compiler pipelines parallel bootstrapping (re-encryption) operations, while dual banking and subarray-level parallelism hide memory latency.
hpca-2025-070.key_novelty: The core innovation is a conflict-free localized permutation network (a data-reordering technique contained within each memory bank) that enables efficient element-wise and butterfly NTT operations on encrypted data without requiring inter-bank communication.

hpca-2025-072.method: AutoRFM prevents Rowhammer attacks by using DDR5's Refresh Management command to refresh one small memory section (a subarray) at a time, allowing other sections to continue handling requests. When a request arrives for the subarray being refreshed, the memory chip signals the processor to retry after about 200 nanoseconds. Randomized Memory Mapping prevents repeated targeting of the same subarray by shuffling which addresses map to which locations, and a Fractal Mitigation Algorithm handles sophisticated multi-step attacks like Half-Double without repeatedly refreshing the same subarray. Testing used SPEC, GAP, and stream workloads.
hpca-2025-072.key_novelty: AutoRFM mitigates Rowhammer memory attacks by refreshing one small section (subarray) at a time, keeping all other sections active instead of stalling the entire memory bank.

hpca-2025-079.method: Piccolo puts a scatter-gather operation directly into memory hardware. Scatter-gather means grabbing data from many random locations or writing data there — the access pattern that wastes bandwidth in graph algorithms. Instead of putting full arithmetic units into DRAM (which is expensive and complex), Piccolo only embeds the scatter-gather operation. The accelerator's cache system and miss-handling architecture are redesigned to work with this in-memory scatter-gather, enabling graph tiling (on-chip data reuse) to work alongside the memory-based operations and reducing off-chip data traffic without the expensive overhead of full processing-in-memory.
hpca-2025-079.key_novelty: The core insight is using scatter-gather operations in memory hardware instead of full arithmetic processing, cutting the cost of fine-grained random access while keeping cache and tiling optimizations compatible.

hpca-2025-069.method: EDA is a compiler that prepares neural networks for efficient execution on edge processors with limited on-chip memory. It breaks down the network into smaller parts and uses a cost model—a calculator estimating memory efficiency—to decide how many layers each part should process together, balancing the benefit of keeping intermediate data in fast on-chip memory against the cost of accessing slower main memory. It allocates on-chip memory carefully to prevent overflow and groups computation operations to improve how well the processor's compute units and memory are utilized. The result avoids both excessive main-memory traffic from processing too many layers together and computational waste from processing too few.
hpca-2025-069.key_novelty: The innovation is a cost model—a mathematical calculator—that determines, for each section of a neural network, how many layers should be processed together, balancing how much intermediate data stays in fast on-chip memory against trips to slower main memory, optimized for edge processors with limited on-chip storage.

hpca-2025-078.method: Phelps creates a helper thread for each inner loop containing hard-to-predict branches and runs every such branch unconditionally (without guessing which way it goes first) in every loop iteration, including branches that depend on other branch outcomes. It tracks the results of each branch separately in queues synchronized with loop iterations, so the main thread can use whichever results are needed based on how branches actually execute. Memory writes that both influence a hard-to-predict branch and depend on its outcome are marked as conditional on that branch's outcome within the helper thread. For nested loops where the inner loop's iteration count is short or unpredictable, a dual helper-thread setup handles the inner and outer loops independently.
hpca-2025-078.key_novelty: The key innovation is unconditionally running all hard-to-predict branches—even those dependent on other branches—instead of predicting them in the helper thread, using per-branch queues kept synchronized with loop iterations.

hpca-2025-080.method: PIMnet is a network that lets PIM compute units communicate directly across memory banks, eliminating the need to route messages through the host CPU—a traditional bottleneck for collective operations like all-reduce and broadcast. It uses a multi-tier architecture mirroring DRAM's physical structure: communication within a single chip and across chips happen simultaneously, multiplying available bandwidth. Since PIM logic itself manages this network rather than the host processor, it's optimized for the collective communication patterns that appear in actual PIM workloads.
hpca-2025-080.key_novelty: PIMnet enables direct communication between PIM compute units across memory banks and chips without routing through the host CPU, using a network structure that matches DRAM's physical organization.

hpca-2025-071.method: Rather than computing floating-point and integer multiplication directly, FIGLUT precomputes all possible products of floating-point activation values (intermediate computations flowing through the neural network) with every possible low-bit integer weight pattern, storing these results in lookup tables. During inference, the hardware looks up the answer in these tables using the weight bits as an index. To reduce memory overhead, the design uses a half-size lookup table variant with a dedicated decoding and multiplexing unit (hardware that selects between precomputed results). This single hardware configuration supports multiple bit precisions and quantization methods (different levels of weight compression).
hpca-2025-071.key_novelty: The design uses a half-size lookup table with dedicated decoding to replace floating-point and integer multiplication with table lookups, enabling efficient multi-precision weight-only quantized operations and delivering 59% higher energy efficiency (TOPS/W—computation per watt) than prior lookup-table accelerators.

hpca-2025-076.method: HILP schedules multiple independent applications—each with phases that must run in sequence—across a shared set of heterogeneous cores and accelerators, minimizing total execution time while respecting power and memory bandwidth constraints. To do this, it formulates the scheduling problem as a job-shop scheduling problem (where different types of work must be assigned to different types of machines) and solves it using integer linear programming, a mathematical technique that converts all constraints into equations and finds the best solution. This approach captures the full spectrum of how applications can run in parallel, not just the minimum and maximum extremes, making it suitable for exploring many different hardware configurations during early design.
hpca-2025-076.key_novelty: By formulating heterogeneous SoC workload scheduling as a job-shop scheduling problem (where different applications are assigned to different processor types) solved with integer linear programming, this work enables early exploration of the full spectrum of realistic parallelism instead of just the extreme cases.

hpca-2025-083.method: Lincoln uses a two-phase strategy matched to how large language models work. During the prefill phase (the initial stage, which is compute-heavy), it connects Flash storage to the NPU using LPDDR, which is the same fast interface normally used for RAM, so weights move much faster than standard Flash connections while keeping costs down. During the decode phase (the output stage, which needs lots of memory access), it embeds computing directly on Flash storage using hybrid bonding (a 3D connection technology), so matrix-vector calculations happen at the storage itself and avoid slow data transmission, while speculative decoding predicts future tokens to reduce latency. Flash's internal speed is also improved using tighter array designs that reduce read time and enable more parallel data paths, all built on 3D hybrid bonding already present in consumer Flash chips.
hpca-2025-083.key_novelty: The core idea is to split the LLM workload by phase: use LPDDR's high speed to stream weights from Flash during prefill, and embed compute directly on Flash storage using hybrid bonding (3D connection technology) during decode to handle memory-intensive operations without transmission delays.

hpca-2025-081.method: Concord adapts the cache coherence approach from hardware processors—a system that keeps multiple copies of data synchronized across locations—for serverless computing. It allows data to be replicated across multiple nodes and serves reads from any nearby copy, cutting latency by avoiding slow central-storage accesses. A centralized directory tracks where each data's copies live and coordinates invalidation or update messages on writes to prevent stale reads. The protocol exploits serverless patterns (heavy reads, few concurrent writes) to reduce traffic, tolerates node failures and frequent instance churn (as functions start and stop), and enables transactional storage operations and transparent data-aware function placement.
hpca-2025-081.key_novelty: A directory-based coherence protocol that adapts hardware cache coherence principles to serverless environments, enabling multi-node data replication with efficient invalidation and supporting transactional storage operations and transparent data-aware function placement.

hpca-2025-077.method: FACIL modifies the memory controller to support different DRAM address mappings for different huge pages (large memory regions), so different mappings can convert the same address to different physical bank locations. Software chooses which mapping to use for each tensor, placing weights where both PIM (processing-in-memory hardware that does fast matrix-vector operations) and SoC processors (which do larger matrix-matrix computations) can access them. The same physical weights work for both types of operations without copying or reorganizing the data, eliminating the costly re-layout overhead when switching between the two.
hpca-2025-077.key_novelty: By using per-huge-page configurable DRAM address mapping in the memory controller, FACIL enables both PIM (processing-in-memory hardware) and SoC (system-on-chip) processors to access model weights from the same banks without data reorganization.

hpca-2025-082.method: The system has three management layers that dynamically adjust three key settings to save energy: how many servers run, how the model splits across GPUs (tensor parallelism), and GPU speed. Requests are directed to separate server pools based on their input/output token requirements, with a BERT-based prediction model determining the right pool for each request. When reconfiguring, the system minimizes switching overhead by: pre-warming machines from saved snapshots, moving model weights efficiently over fast GPU-to-GPU connections (NVLink) using a matching algorithm, and keeping the GPU control tool (nvidia-smi) ready in memory for instant speed adjustments.
hpca-2025-082.key_novelty: The system adjusts server count, model-to-GPU distribution, and GPU speed for each request type, while minimizing reconfiguration overhead by efficiently moving model weights over NVLink and reusing pre-warmed machine snapshots.

hpca-2025-075.method: RecMG uses two machine learning models that optimize where embedding vectors (chunks of lookup data for recommendation systems) are stored across tiered memory: a caching model predicts which vectors have long reuse distances or few future reuses and keeps them in fast memory, while a prefetching model predicts upcoming accesses and loads vectors into fast memory ahead of time using a differentiable loss function (a mathematically optimized guide) that narrows which candidates to consider and directly reduces unnecessary memory fetches. Both models train on real access patterns from recommendation systems where data is accessed sparsely and at irregular intervals. At inference time, the models continuously make placement decisions based on these predictions.
hpca-2025-075.key_novelty: The core innovation is a differentiable loss function—a mathematically optimized formula—for the prefetching model that directly reduces on-demand memory fetches from slow tiers by focusing on the highest-value embedding vectors to prefetch into fast memory.

hpca-2025-088.method: The system arranges two different species of atoms into interleaved error-correction groups. Within each group, quantum gates are performed efficiently by exploiting the natural interaction asymmetry—atoms of different species interact over longer distances (1/r^3), while identical atoms interact weakly at short distances (1/r^6)—which eliminates the need to move atoms. Between groups, quantum information is transferred through routing channels created by interleaved lattice surgery. The design was validated through simulations and by compiling real quantum algorithms.
hpca-2025-088.key_novelty: The innovation is leveraging asymmetric interactions between two atom species (1/r^3 for different species, 1/r^6 for identical species) to achieve fault-tolerant quantum computation without moving atoms.

hpca-2025-085.method: MLPerf Power adds standardized power-measurement rules to the existing MLPerf benchmarks, developed by a coalition of over 20 industry organizations. It defines how to measure power consumption at different levels—individual devices, server racks, or entire data center facilities—and tests both inference (running trained models) and training (teaching new models) workloads. Researchers collected 1,841 reproducible measurements from 60 different systems, enabling fair comparisons of energy efficiency across different hardware architectures.
hpca-2025-085.key_novelty: MLPerf Power measures machine learning energy efficiency using standardized methods across all deployment scales—from microwatt-range IoT devices to megawatt-range data centers—bringing together the work of 20+ industry organizations.

hpca-2025-090.method: CogSys uses three coordinated techniques. The algorithm reduces memory and compute demands through tensor factorization (breaking symbolic reasoning calculations into smaller pieces that take less space and processing). The hardware is a custom chip (ASIC) with reconfigurable processing tiles (nsPEs) that switch between neural and symbolic work; a bubble streaming dataflow architecture (using spatial-temporal mapping to spread computation across space and time) lets them execute tasks in parallel without blocking. An adaptive scheduler assigns work to tiles based on demand, keeping all tiles busy and fully utilized, implemented on TSMC 28nm.
hpca-2025-090.key_novelty: Reconfigurable processing tiles (nsPEs) with bubble streaming dataflow enable a single spatial chip design that unifies neural and symbolic reasoning with adaptive kernel scheduling, making real-time abductive reasoning (inferring likely causes from observations) possible.

hpca-2025-089.method: IBM's Telum and Telum II processors use a modular cache design that splits memory into independent slices spread across separate chiplets, connected by high-bandwidth internal pathways. The design includes an adaptive algorithm that learns which cache levels should hold frequently-accessed data during different workload phases, automatically adjusting as access patterns change. The approach shows how memory requests flow through these cache levels and how changing cache sizes impacts overall performance. This design allows Telum II to simultaneously handle both traditional enterprise business workloads and generative AI inference tasks.
hpca-2025-089.key_novelty: IBM's Telum processors achieve 90%+ sustained processor utilization in enterprise and generative AI workloads by combining a modular, distributed cache architecture with an algorithm that adapts which cache levels hold the most frequently-accessed data.

hpca-2025-086.method: The researchers tested 388 real DDR4 memory chips from three manufacturers to see how fast individual refresh operations could run to defend against RowHammer attacks (bit flips caused by repeatedly accessing the same memory row). They discovered that refresh operations can be completed 64% faster while needing only 0.54% more refreshes, revealing an efficiency gap in how these systems are normally tuned. They designed PaCRAM (Partial Charge Restoration for Aggressive Mitigation) to exploit this: it speeds up each refresh but does them slightly more frequently, reducing the performance cost of five leading RowHammer defenses.
hpca-2025-086.key_novelty: The key discovery is that refresh operations can run 64% faster with only 0.54% more refreshes, enabling cheaper defenses against RowHammer attacks.

hpca-2025-094.method: Spiking neural networks transmit information using binary signals where neurons either fire or stay silent at each time step. Product Sparsity recognizes that whenever multiple output neurons receive the same pattern of input firings, they must produce identical outputs—but existing systems compute this result independently for each neuron, wasting computation. Prosperity groups neurons by their input firing patterns using a real-time pattern-matching engine, computes the weighted sum (inner product) once per unique pattern, and reuses that single result for all neurons with matching patterns. This optimization applies to both fully-connected and convolutional layers in SNNs with binary activations.
hpca-2025-094.key_novelty: Product Sparsity reuses inner product results across neurons with matching binary input firing patterns instead of computing them separately for each neuron.

hpca-2025-092.method: LAD is a specialized hardware chip designed to speed up LLM text generation by exploiting a key observation: attention scores (which measure how important past tokens are at each generation step) often stay approximately the same from one generated token to the next. Normally, the system must read the entire key-value cache (the stored history of past tokens) at every single decoding step, and beyond 2048 tokens this becomes the main bottleneck. LAD detects when attention scores remain numerically stable across consecutive steps and caches their corresponding key-value vectors locally on the chip, rather than repeatedly fetching them from main storage, significantly reducing cache accesses while keeping generation accuracy intact.
hpca-2025-092.key_novelty: LAD exploits numerical locality in attention scores—the observation that they remain approximately constant across consecutive decoding steps—to reduce redundant key-value cache reads by detecting stable positions and caching them directly on the hardware.

hpca-2025-093.method: OASIS watches how your data is accessed while the program runs, using hardware counters—essentially tallies of memory reads and writes—to figure out what access patterns each piece of data follows across different execution phases. For each piece of data in each phase, it picks the best handling strategy: on-touch migration (moving data to a GPU only when it's first accessed there), access-counter-based migration (moving data based on observed usage patterns), or duplication (keeping copies on multiple GPUs). The system coordinates between software and hardware to automatically switch strategies when the program moves into a new phase, without requiring any manual programmer annotation.
hpca-2025-093.key_novelty: OASIS automatically picks the best page management approach for each piece of data based on its actual runtime usage patterns and current execution phase in multi-GPU systems, choosing between migration (moving data to GPUs) and duplication (keeping copies across GPUs).

hpca-2025-091.method: CCZNS splits the compression work between the SSD and host: the SSD hardware performs compression, then shares metadata about the compressed chunks (boundaries and offsets) with the host instead of hiding them. The host software (such as RocksDB with ZenFS) uses this information to track data locations and reclaim space freed by compression—responsibilities it already handles. This works around ZNS's sequential write constraint by letting the host work with variable-length chunks instead of having the SSD hide them.
hpca-2025-091.key_novelty: CCZNS revives hardware compression on ZNS SSDs by separating compression (done by the SSD) from index management (done by the host) through a shared interface that exposes compression metadata.

hpca-2025-096.method: DAPPER uses secure hashing—cryptographic randomization that hides patterns—to scramble which DRAM rows map to which access counters, preventing attackers from predicting where to target. DAPPER-S provides a baseline with a single hash function; DAPPER-H extends it with double-hashing (using two lookups to reduce collisions) and reset strategies that avoid predictable reset times. Both versions integrate RowHammer defenses into the system's normal memory-refresh cycles, piggybacking the mitigation to spread performance cost. The design uses just 96KB of SRAM per 32GB of DRAM and was validated on 57 workloads from SPEC2006, SPEC2017, TPC, Hadoop, MediaBench, and YCSB.
hpca-2025-096.key_novelty: DAPPER defends against both RowHammer bit-flip attacks and attacks on shared tracking counters by using secure double-hashing (randomization across two lookup levels) plus adaptive reset strategies, all within under 100KB SRAM per 32GB DRAM.

hpca-2025-098.method: The paper introduces a mathematical notation (bit-weight dimension) that exposes the internal structure of multiply-accumulate (MAC) circuits—the core units that multiply and sum numbers. By systematically transforming how bits flow through these circuits, the authors derive four optimization techniques that improve timing performance, silicon area, or power consumption. The design is implemented in hardware simulation at 28-nanometer scale and tested on four standard tensor processor architectures plus a new bit-slice design.
hpca-2025-098.key_novelty: A mathematical notation for the bit-weight dimension (the bit-level structure of multiply-accumulate circuits) enables four independent processor microarchitecture optimizations in addition to existing dataflow strategies.

hpca-2025-084.method: IRIS adds three lightweight components to the image sensor's preprocessing stage (ISP) to reduce resolution for less-important image regions using existing computations. It calculates importance scores from edge information and motion vectors the ISP already extracts, groups the image into hierarchical blocks at three sizes (16×16, 32×32, and 64×64 pixels), and downsamples blocks that fall below a backend-provided importance threshold, reducing them from 32×32 or 64×64 to 16×16 pixels and recording each block's final resolution as metadata. The backend adapts: Vision Transformers use a Quadformer-style mixed-resolution tokenizer to handle variable-resolution blocks, and localization algorithms (ORB-SLAM3) process regions in order of importance until improvements diminish. The sensor pipeline never stalls during this processing.
hpca-2025-084.key_novelty: The innovation is repurposing edge masks and motion vectors that the image sensor already extracts—data normally discarded—as a zero-extra-computation importance scorer that automatically reduces resolution on less-critical image regions before storage.

hpca-2025-100.method: BOSS groups quantum operations (the instructions given to qubits) into blocks to minimize how many times ions need to be shuttled (moved) across the trap. By batching related operations together, the algorithm reduces the total shuttling overhead that would otherwise happen between every operation. It uses realistic experimental conditions, including sympathetic cooling (a technique where one cooled ion helps cool others nearby), to predict execution time and fidelity more accurately. Testing covers circuits with 4000+ two-qubit gates across 64-78 qubits.
hpca-2025-100.key_novelty: BOSS cuts shuttling operations by up to 96.1% by grouping quantum operations based on which qubits they use, taking advantage of the fact that related operations often cluster on nearby qubits.

hpca-2025-099.method: HSMU-SpGEMM redesigns how GPUs accumulate (collect and combine) partial results in sparse matrix multiplication by separating two competing demands that usually force a compromise: reducing hash collisions (when multiple values map to the same memory address) and efficiently packing data into fast shared memory. Rather than solving both together, the new accumulator tackles each independently, allowing more useful data to fit in shared memory while keeping collisions low. The design also optimizes earlier calculation stages (row counting and product computation) to work better with the new accumulator, with testing on three GPU types (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Turing) showing the improvement.
hpca-2025-099.key_novelty: By decoupling collision reduction from memory packing efficiency, the new accumulator design allows both to be optimized independently rather than forcing a tradeoff between them.

hpca-2025-103.method: I-DGNN avoids reprocessing unchanged parts of the graph by recognizing that the differences between consecutive snapshots can be expressed as chained matrix multiplications (repeated sequences of matrix operations), which can be computed independently rather than routing the entire updated graph through the full neural network pipeline. The system uses a unified accelerator architecture that flexibly reconfigures itself to handle both this independent computation and the main pipeline stages. The dataflow is optimized so data stays locally available rather than moving repeatedly to off-chip memory. Together, these changes reduce the redundant computation and data movement that normally accumulate when processing sequences of similar graphs.
hpca-2025-103.key_novelty: The core insight is that differences between consecutive graph snapshots can be expressed as independent chained matrix multiplications (repeated matrix operations), eliminating the need to route data through the entire neural network pipeline and thus cutting both computational redundancy and expensive memory transfers.

hpca-2025-087.method: MOKA is a filter controlling when an L1D prefetcher issues requests across page boundaries (fixed-size memory divisions). It employs three strategies: machine-learning predictors (hashed perceptrons) trained on program patterns (current instruction, memory access spacing, recent history) to predict when cross-page prefetches help; adjustment based on system state (TLB address-cache pressure and pending-miss queue occupancy); and periodic recalibration across execution phases. The prototype DRIPPER applies this to three prefetchers (Berti, IPCP, BOP) without changing their internals.
hpca-2025-087.key_novelty: The key idea is using machine-learning predictors (hashed perceptrons) to automatically determine which page-crossing prefetch requests to issue, based on program behavior and system state, while continuously adapting as execution phases change.

hpca-2025-107.method: LegoZK uses reusable building blocks called finite field arithmetic units, or FAUs (circuits that perform specialized math for zero-knowledge proofs), connected through a hierarchical on-chip network. Because the FAUs and network can be reconfigured at runtime, the same hardware can handle all stages of proof generation without needing different chips for each stage. For Multi-Scalar Multiplication (MSM)—the slowest stage—it uses a pipelined bucket reduction algorithm based on lookup tables, which speeds up calculations by processing many values in parallel. The network connections and FAU assignments automatically switch between proof stages.
hpca-2025-107.key_novelty: By treating simple arithmetic circuits (FAUs) as universal, reconfigurable building blocks and connecting them with a hierarchical network, one chip design can efficiently handle all stages of zero-knowledge proof generation instead of needing separate specialized chips for each computation type.

hpca-2025-095.method: QPRAC builds a Priority-based Service Queue (PSQ—a queue ordering pending mitigation requests by row activation count, with most-accessed rows handled first) in the memory controller. It uses PRAC's per-row counters to prioritize which rows get protected, serving the most-activated rows immediately to prevent attackers from exploiting less-protected rows. To minimize performance impact, the design uses two tactics: it adds extra protections to Refresh Management (RFM—regular memory refresh cycles) at minimal cost, and it proactively drains the queue during standard DRAM refresh (REF) operations before emergency slowdowns (Alert Back-Off, or ABO) trigger.
hpca-2025-095.key_novelty: A priority-based service queue (PSQ) that orders RowHammer mitigations by row activation count (how many times each row is accessed) within the PRAC/ABO framework, providing principled security while opportunistic and proactive refresh coordination reduces ABO-induced slowdowns to nearly zero.

hpca-2025-101.method: Choco-Q encodes constraints directly into the quantum algorithm by selecting a driver Hamiltonian that commutes (stays mathematically compatible) with the constraint structure, which guarantees that quantum solutions always satisfy all requirements—achieving 100% success. To make this runnable on today's quantum hardware, it applies three optimizations: breaking the constraint structure into independent pieces reduces circuit depth from approximately 4,000 to 24 operations; converting these to basic quantum gates (control-phase and CX gates) takes linear time instead of exponential time, replacing an otherwise expensive standard method; removing variables with redundant solution entries further shrinks qubit count and circuit depth. The approach is tested on IBM quantum processors—Fez (159 qubits), Sherbrooke, and Osaka (127 qubits)—and on an A100 GPU simulator.
hpca-2025-101.key_novelty: The core idea is using the commute Hamiltonian as the driver for QAOA (Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm), which universally encodes any linear constraint exactly and decomposes into deployable circuits in linear time.

hpca-2025-104.method: GoPIM uses machine learning to watch which pipeline stages are lagging and dynamically shifts ReRAM crossbar resources (physical computing elements) to the stage that needs them most at any moment. It also uses interleaved vertex mapping to spread graph nodes across multiple crossbars so that nodes with more connections don't all end up on the same resource. Together, these reduce execution time while maintaining accuracy.
hpca-2025-104.key_novelty: The innovation is a machine-learning policy that dynamically shifts ReRAM crossbar resources to pipeline stages based on real-time bottlenecks, combined with interleaved vertex mapping to distribute graph nodes despite their skewed degree distributions (many nodes have far more connections than others).

hpca-2025-102.method: It creates a unified tree-based representation of Near-DRAM Processing hardware that works across different DRAM types. A simulator counts every clock cycle to precisely track what the memory and processing units are doing moment-by-moment. A compiler then optimizes where data gets stored and how work gets scheduled across the DRAM layers, using a strategy that quickly eliminates bad options by checking the hardware's current behavior. It uses a performance predictor tuned to the specific DRAM's timing characteristics to speed up compilation.
hpca-2025-102.key_novelty: A tree-based (hierarchical) representation of hardware with matching instructions lets a single compiler and simulator handle Near-DRAM Processing architectures across all DRAM technologies.

hpca-2025-097.method: SPASM is a hardware-software co-design framework that analyzes input matrices to understand their data access patterns (how they retrieve values from memory) and creates specialized templates for different matrix types. The system uses reconfigurable hardware (processing units programmed to switch between strategies) to apply the best pattern for each matrix at runtime, rather than being locked into one fixed approach. A global analysis of the input matrix determines how to configure the hardware and distribute computational work across multiple processing units, preventing any unit from being overloaded. This approach optimizes for expected matrices while gracefully handling unexpected structures.
hpca-2025-097.key_novelty: The key novelty is flexible data-access pattern templates combined with adaptable hardware, allowing both optimization for expected matrices and support for unexpected patterns at runtime.

hpca-2025-109.method: Palermo modifies the RingORAM protocol to run multiple memory operations in parallel instead of one at a time—both within a single access request and across concurrent requests—without compromising security. A hardware controller concurrently issues memory requests but selectively enforces only the ordering dependencies necessary to keep the ORAM tree (the structure that hides which data you're accessing) consistent. The hardware also manages temporary storage (stash) and an address-lookup table (position map) on the chip to prevent overflow, which enables back-to-back memory accesses.
hpca-2025-109.key_novelty: Palermo's core innovation is combining protocol and hardware changes to eliminate unnecessary sequential ordering in classical ORAM, enabling concurrent memory requests while maintaining security and correctness.

hpca-2025-110.method: Pegasus maps DRAM errors (detected using ECC memory error-checking) to specific virtual machines by tracking which memory addresses belong to which VM. A predictor analyzes error-correction patterns and spatial-temporal error clusters (where and when errors happen together) to identify which VMs have memory in at-risk DRAM regions. Rather than migrating all VMs on a server when errors occur, it selectively migrates only the at-risk VMs to healthy hardware.
hpca-2025-110.key_novelty: Pegasus is the first system to predict which individual virtual machines will be affected by DRAM failures by mapping memory errors directly to VMs, enabling selective migration of just the at-risk VMs instead of evacuating entire servers.

hpca-2025-108.method: GBU is a hardware module for edge GPUs that accelerates the Gaussian Blending Stage—the calculation of each Gaussian blob's contribution to every pixel. It processes pixels row by row, left to right, using a two-step coordinate transformation that reuses calculation values between adjacent pixels (cutting work by up to 5.5×) and skips Gaussians that contribute minimally (saving up to 93% per pixel). A Gaussian Reuse Cache reduces memory accesses by 44.9%, and a dedicated rendering engine balances workload across Gaussians.
hpca-2025-108.key_novelty: Intra-row sequential shading (IRSS) processes each row left to right, where a two-step coordinate transformation exploits adjacent pixels' similarity to simultaneously reuse intermediate calculations and skip Gaussians that contribute minimally—both optimizations in one unified pass.

hpca-2025-118.method: NearFetch intercepts memory requests as they travel through intermediate GPU modules and checks if any of these modules already store the requested data locally. If one does, the data is forwarded from that nearby module instead of fetching it from the distant main memory partition, saving the extra hops. To support this interception, NearFetch uses a topology-aware Miss Status Handling Register (MSHR) coalescing scheme—a tracking mechanism that records which memory addresses exist in which modules so forwarding decisions can be made intelligently. The system introduces a metric called Inter-Module Bandwidth per Access (IBPA) to measure how much bandwidth is wasted when data travels multiple hops across modules.
hpca-2025-118.key_novelty: NearFetch intercepts memory requests traveling through intermediate GPU modules and forwards data from whichever module along the path already has it, reducing the number of hops needed without restructuring the GPU's physical design.

hpca-2025-111.method: NeuVSA uses Product Quantization (PQ) to unify both the embedding and search stages—PQ compresses vectors by splitting them into parts and looking each part up in a shared codebook. Both the codebook and the search index are trained together in one unified process, learning the optimal setup for both simultaneously. The custom ASIC contains multiple coordinated sub-accelerators that use structured index assignment and an elastic on-chip buffer to prevent data conflicts and maximize throughput, achieving 4.6% better recall and 43.5% better accuracy than LUT-NN.
hpca-2025-111.key_novelty: NeuVSA unifies embedding and vector search into a single system by designing the algorithm and hardware together around Product Quantization, eliminating the traditional separation between these two stages.

hpca-2025-116.method: SkyByte coordinates the host OS and SSD controller through three mechanisms. When the processor detects slow CXL-SSD accesses, the OS switches to running other threads (thread-level parallelism) to hide latency instead of stalling. The SSD controller's DRAM buffers small byte-level writes with a cacheline-level write log and page-level data cache, merging them at log cleanup time to reduce flash I/O traffic. Frequently-accessed pages are automatically promoted from the CXL-SSD to the faster host DRAM based on access frequency, together reducing stall cycles and flash I/O amplification.
hpca-2025-116.key_novelty: SkyByte bridges the mismatch between byte-level CXL access and page-level flash storage by pairing OS-level context switching (the OS runs other threads during slow CXL-SSD waits) with a two-tier SSD controller DRAM buffer (cacheline-level write log and page-level data cache) that merges small writes together before they reach flash.

hpca-2025-105.method: Hydra splits a deep learning model across multiple FPGA cards (specialized computing hardware that can be programmed for specific tasks), with each card handling different layers. A central host computer coordinates the work, routing encrypted data and scheduling operations. Different layers run simultaneously on different cards—one layer processes data while another works on the next—and each card also runs multiple operations internally, creating the parallelism needed to scale across many cards.
hpca-2025-105.key_novelty: Hydra exploits model parallelism—splitting the model across multiple FPGA cards so different layers run simultaneously—rather than just trying to make a single card faster by adding more parallelism to it.

iccad-2025-000.method: The researchers first mapped the pattern of DRAM errors (bit flips caused by rowhammer—repeatedly accessing the same memory row to corrupt adjacent data) on actual hardware platforms (DDR3 and DDR4). They then used this fault pattern information to craft targeted rowhammer attacks designed to flip the specific bits needed to forge digital signatures. Finally, they demonstrated a working forgery attack on SPHINCS+, a post-quantum signature algorithm, using the standard liboqs implementation.
iccad-2025-000.key_novelty: This work demonstrates the first practical rowhammer attack (repeated memory access that flips bits in DRAM) capable of forging digital signatures on SPHINCS+, a hash-based algorithm that NIST standardized for post-quantum cryptography, showing this is a real security threat for cryptographic software in cloud systems.

hpca-2025-119.method: Pivot partitions memory bandwidth by prioritizing latency-critical tasks, but specifically targets only the load instructions that stall the CPU's execution pipeline—rather than all latency-critical accesses. It identifies these critical instructions through two-phase offline profiling: Phase 1 determines which memory loads miss the cache, and Phase 2 marks which of those cache misses actually halt the processor's instruction reordering. These marked loads receive priority at every stage of memory access—L1 and L2 caches (fast on-chip memory), L3 cache (larger on-chip memory), and the DRAM controller (main memory interface)—instead of only at a single bottleneck.
hpca-2025-119.key_novelty: It specifically identifies load instructions that cause CPU pipeline stalls and prioritizes those throughout the entire memory path—L1, L2, L3 caches and DRAM controller—rather than equally protecting all latency-critical accesses at one point.

hpca-2025-120.method: FLACK is an offline algorithm (one with knowledge of all future instruction accesses) that computes optimal micro-op cache evictions by accounting for how these caches differ from regular ones: re-fetching evicted instructions is much more expensive, and instruction groups may be partially cached. This beats standard algorithms like Belady's because it optimizes for these unique costs. FURBYS then implements this strategy for real-world online use (without future knowledge) through three techniques: (1) measuring which instructions hit or miss across a full program run, (2) detecting locally or temporarily hot instruction patterns, and (3) ignoring entries with low hit rates when choosing what to evict.
hpca-2025-120.key_novelty: FLACK is a near-optimal offline replacement algorithm for micro-op caches that accounts for their unique costs—expensive instruction re-fetches and partial instruction caching—and provides a new theoretical bound for practical policy design.

hpca-2025-114.method: RpcNIC combines hardware and software on a Xilinx U280 FPGA (a reprogrammable smart network interface) to speed up RPC messaging by reducing PCIe bottlenecks. It uses three techniques: batching writes to the FPGA's fast memory with compact data structures to cut PCIe transfers, collaborating between the CPU and network interface to keep data on the CPU side instead of copying over PCIe, and automatically reconfiguring RPC message encoding when applications change so unchanged fields avoid crossing PCIe.
hpca-2025-114.key_novelty: Three PCIe-aware optimization strategies enable commodity PCIe-attached SmartNICs to match the performance of specialized RPC accelerators with custom interconnects for datacenter workloads.

iccad-2025-001.method: Multiple AI agents (powered by large language models) analyze the circuit's structure and design goals, then iteratively adjust the parameter values to meet performance targets. They use an adaptive simulation strategy—each design test teaches them something, and they learn from successful and failed attempts to decide which simulations to run next, reducing wasted effort. At each step, the agents explain their reasoning, so engineers can understand and verify each design choice.
iccad-2025-001.key_novelty: AI agents (powered by large language models) design analog circuits efficiently while explaining their choices, by learning from previous design attempts to optimize which simulations to run next.

hpca-2025-113.method: AccelES splits computation into two stages to avoid expensive full-precision math on the entire sparse matrix. Stage 1 uses a low-bit representation (an approximation using fewer bits per number, making it faster to scan) to rapidly identify the top-K most-relevant entries and filter out the rest with minimal data movement. Stage 2 performs exact full-precision calculation only on those selected top-K entries. To handle the irregular memory access patterns of sparse matrix operations, the system uses two new storage formats called Ultra-CSR and Random-CSR, which optimize data flow through memory.
hpca-2025-113.key_novelty: The innovation is a two-stage approach: a fast low-bit pass identifies top-K candidates, then full-precision math is applied only to those candidates, so expensive computation is used only on the ones that actually matter.

hpca-2025-117.method: MeHyper addresses computational redundancy in hypergraph neural networks: when processing vertices and hyperedges separately, systems recalculate the same intermediate feature values. The system introduces microedges—small units that capture shared information—and processes each microedge once using a Read-Process-Activate-Generate cycle, distributing results to all dependent aggregation tasks. The hardware accelerator uses a decoupled pipeline (processing stages that work independently in parallel) and hierarchical feature management (organizing on-chip memory by data granularity) to reduce expensive off-chip DRAM accesses for the large intermediate feature vectors created during microedge aggregation.
hpca-2025-117.key_novelty: MeHyper identifies and exploits implicit dataflow dependencies—hidden patterns in how data flows through computations—in hypergraph neural networks via the microedge abstraction, eliminating redundant calculations across vertex and hyperedge aggregation.

hpca-2025-115.method: Gemina coordinates memory deduplication (removing duplicate pages) and huge pages (larger blocks for faster access) by treating them as separate decisions. Its three components are: (1) a fine-grained detector that classifies pages by redundancy and access frequency, enabling independent deduplication choices; (2) a distributor that carefully processes pages to avoid expensive switches between hot/cold patterns or page sizes; and (3) an adapter that rearranges memory to enable fast conversion from 4KB pages to huge pages. By selectively skipping deduplication on frequently-accessed pages, the system preserves huge-page benefits while retaining most memory savings.
hpca-2025-115.key_novelty: The core idea is coordinating memory deduplication and huge-page management through a three-component system that preserves huge-page performance while retaining nearly all memory savings.

iccad-2025-004.method: SPIMA places the matrix multiplication computation directly inside DRAM (the main computer memory) instead of moving data to a separate processor. The DRAM is organized into independent banks that operate in parallel, and the system uses multiple temporary storage areas (buffers and registers) positioned strategically to keep data close to where it's being used. This arrangement lets the same data be reused multiple times, which is especially valuable for sparse matrices (matrices filled mostly with zeros) where traditional approaches waste bandwidth on unused values. The entire architecture is carefully designed to optimize how data flows between these components.
iccad-2025-004.key_novelty: SPIMA's core innovation is performing sparse matrix multiplication directly inside DRAM using multiple memory banks working in parallel, which enables efficient data reuse and avoids the bandwidth bottlenecks that normally come from processing matrices filled mostly with zeros.

iccad-2025-002.method: When chip designers route wires connecting components, they sometimes can't reach the connection points (pins) on standard cells—the pre-built components used throughout a chip. This system fixes routing failures by adaptively modifying pins on problem cells using three techniques: pin-shift-trim (moving and shortening pins), pin-free (removing pins entirely), and pin-bridge (creating bridges between pins). For each cell that has a routing failure, it tries these modifications and uses maze routing (a pathfinding algorithm that explores paths around obstacles) to find working connections.
