iccad-2025-002.key_novelty: Adaptive pin pattern modifications to individual cells enable late-stage routing changes (ECO) with no impact on performance, power, or area—116x faster than competing multi-commodity flow methods.

iccad-2025-008.method: Instead of just shrinking transistors (which hits physical limits), CMOS 2.0 stacks multiple specialized processing layers vertically by bonding wafers together and processing from the back side. This requires new chip designs and new design software tools (called EDA—electronic design automation) to handle these 3D structures.
iccad-2025-008.key_novelty: The core shift is from making transistors smaller to stacking specialized processing layers vertically in 3D as the new path for scaling.

iccad-2025-009.method: FACAM searches for analog values (continuous numbers rather than binary patterns) using a two-phase process. Each memory cell contains two ferroelectric transistors (FeFETs—transistors that use a ferroelectric layer to store and switch between states) and one regular transistor; the FeFETs are programmed to define both the center point and width of the matching range. During the search, the matchline (the signal that reports whether a match occurred) is prepared and checked simultaneously in the cell, improving efficiency. An adaptive scheme can stop the second search phase early if the result is already confident, which saves energy.
iccad-2025-009.key_novelty: A compact analog-search cell using ferroelectric transistors, with a two-phase search method that can terminate early to reduce energy use.

iccad-2025-007.method: The paper evaluates large-scale chips using silicon photonics—light signals replacing electrical ones—built from tiles connected in different topologies (network layouts). It tests various waveguide implementations (optical paths) and how well they work for different applications. It specifically measures the power-consumption limits of microring resonators (small rings that direct light signals) and evaluates the performance of custom-designed waveguide networks.
iccad-2025-007.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive comparison of silicon photonic versus electrical interconnects for waferscale chips, showing that the benefits and implementation challenges depend on the application and topology.

iccad-2025-006.method: AccelStack analyzes how 3D-stacked LLM accelerators—chips that stack memory directly on top of computing logic to boost performance—can balance speed with manufacturing costs. It examines three die-stacking configurations (die-on-die, die-on-wafer, and wafer-on-wafer) to understand how each performs on LLM workloads compared to NVIDIA's A100 and H100 chips.
iccad-2025-006.key_novelty: AccelStack compares different ways to physically stack 3D LLM accelerators by analyzing both their performance and manufacturing costs.

iccad-2025-003.method: DecoRTL generates multiple versions of code in parallel and compares where they agree. For each token, it adjusts temperature (a parameter controlling the model's conservatism)—setting it low for syntax-critical tokens (rigid rules) and high for design-critical tokens (exploratory choices). Finally, it ranks the candidate codes based on their mutual agreement.
iccad-2025-003.key_novelty: The core insight is using contrastive sampling (comparing multiple generated versions) at test time, with different strategies for syntax-critical tokens (conservative) and design-critical tokens (exploratory), and requiring no model retraining.

iccad-2025-010.method: Decoupling capacitors smooth voltage delivery by storing energy in power distribution networks. Traditional optimization methods get stuck in local optima. This approach models the problem as integer semidefinite programming (SDP—a mathematical optimization framework), then relaxes integer constraints to enable efficient solving and reduces connection points (ports) to improve scalability. An adaptive optimization scheme further refines the result.
iccad-2025-010.key_novelty: The core insight is reformulating the nonlinear decap placement problem as integer semidefinite programming, which enables deterministic global optimization instead of heuristic local search.

iccad-2025-014.method: MIRAGE detects adversarial attacks by monitoring hardware performance counters—measurements that track CPU cache and branch predictor activity—without requiring their reset between inference runs. It trains a CNN classifier to recognize attack patterns in these counter signals. Unlike existing defenses that need to clean the hardware's state between runs (slowing the system down), MIRAGE completes detection in one pass at full performance.
iccad-2025-014.key_novelty: MIRAGE detects adversarial attacks in a single inference using hardware performance counters without resetting cache or branch predictor state, enabling practical deployment on performance-critical systems.

iccad-2025-015.method: The attack monitors how much electrical power the GPU draws and how hot it gets while running the transformer model—these fluctuate naturally as different layers execute. Without needing special admin permissions, the attacker analyzes the statistical patterns in these power and temperature readings to map out the model's structure. Different transformer configurations (with varying numbers of layers and attention heads) produce distinct power signatures, so the architectural details can be reverse-engineered from these leaked power patterns.
iccad-2025-015.key_novelty: This demonstrates that GPU power and temperature readings can reveal a transformer's architecture details without needing special access privileges.

iccad-2025-011.method: Pathfinder constructs taint graphs (maps showing how information flows through a circuit at each clock cycle) by combining two analysis techniques: taint tracking (which follows how data moves) and self-composition (which compares system states to spot differences). The system creates these graphs at cycle-accurate precision, tracking information flow at each step. From violation traces (records of unwanted information flows), it automatically extracts only the relevant signals, eliminating the need to manually analyze hundreds or thousands of signals.
iccad-2025-011.key_novelty: It automatically generates cycle-accurate maps of information flow from violation records, eliminating the manual analysis work that would otherwise require searching through hundreds of signals.

iccad-2025-016.method: Dynamic programming—an optimization technique that builds solutions from smaller pieces—creates a baseline routing solution. A search algorithm then explores different orderings for routing individual signals through the package. It keeps only the promising options, finding an ordering that shortens the longest signal path (called the critical path) without allowing wires to cross on the same metal layer.
iccad-2025-016.key_novelty: It combines dynamic programming baseline routing with search-based signal reordering to minimize the critical path while preventing wire crossings.

iccad-2025-013.method: WROXIM extends the open-source Noxim simulator by adding cycle-accurate modeling of optical components—waveguides (light transmission channels), serializers and deserializers (electrical-to-optical signal converters), and buffers (data storage). This allows the simulator to handle both optical and electrical parts of the network, enabling end-to-end communication simulation at clock-cycle precision.
iccad-2025-013.key_novelty: WROXIM simulates wavelength-routed optical networks at network level by combining optical and electrical component models with realistic task workloads.

iccad-2025-012.method: A deep learning model called U-Net analyzes the chip design layout (treating it like an image analyzed at multiple detail levels) to simultaneously check design rules across all layers. It handles rules for horizontal layers, vertical connections between layers, and non-Manhattan geometries (diagonal and curved shapes) all in one step, rather than running separate sequential checks. The model is trained on design rule sets from different semiconductor manufacturers, allowing it to work across various production processes.
iccad-2025-012.key_novelty: A single U-Net deep learning model performs all design checks simultaneously—for horizontal layers, vertical connections, and diagonal shapes—replacing sequential tool workflows.

iccad-2025-005.method: This framework designs SFQ circuits—a type of extremely fast superconducting circuit technology—by simultaneously optimizing three interconnected design decisions: which clock phase controls each part of the circuit, how to partition computation into pipeline stages, and how the signal distribution network is structured. It works by explicitly modeling the timing of each gate operation (measuring how long signals take to travel), then using efficient algorithms to find area-efficient designs without compromising speed, even for large circuits.
iccad-2025-005.key_novelty: The core idea is using explicit timing information to jointly optimize path balancing (ensuring signals arrive together), clock phase assignment (choosing which clock phase controls each part), and the circuit area-performance tradeoff.

iccad-2025-017.method: The framework treats embodied carbon—carbon emitted during chip manufacturing—as probability distributions (ranges of likely values) rather than single fixed numbers, accounting for where and when a chip is made. It models how four key factors vary by location and time: energy-per-area (factory electricity per unit of chip space), gas-per-area (manufacturing gas emissions per unit of chip space), yield (percentage of working chips produced), and carbon intensity (cleanness of the power source), doing this separately for each technology node (manufacturing scale like 5nm, 7nm, etc.). The team validated the framework by comparing two chip designs—chiplet architectures (multiple smaller chips connected together) and monolithic architectures (one large chip)—to determine which produces lower embodied carbon when accounting for real-world uncertainty.
iccad-2025-017.key_novelty: It's the first embodied carbon model that captures how supply chain uncertainty varies across different manufacturing scales by treating carbon as probability distributions rather than single fixed numbers.

iccad-2025-019.method: The method divides a circuit into smaller pieces, each affecting only certain signals (support-limited subcircuits). For each piece, it builds a truth table—a map showing what output it should produce for every possible input combination. Using this truth table, it finds better ways to rearrange the piece's wiring to use fewer or faster logic connections. All pieces are simultaneously rebuilt together, so improvements in one piece improve the others.
iccad-2025-019.key_novelty: The core contribution is dividing circuits into pieces, rewiring each using its truth table, and rebuilding them all simultaneously so improvements spread through the entire circuit.

iccad-2025-020.method: This approach uses reinforcement learning (a machine learning method where a system learns by trying different actions and receiving feedback) to simultaneously solve two tasks that are usually done separately: constructing Steiner trees (minimum-wire networks connecting multiple circuit points) and inserting buffers (devices that regenerate electrical signals). Rather than first routing connections and then adding buffers, the system learns which combinations of routing and buffer placement decisions work best together by trying many possibilities and improving based on feedback. Harmonic functions (mathematical functions representing optimal balanced solutions) guide the learning process.
iccad-2025-020.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining reinforcement learning with harmonic functions to jointly optimize Steiner tree construction and buffer insertion, rather than solving them as separate sequential tasks.

iccad-2025-022.method: The CRISTAL framework builds choice networks in three steps. First, it searches for representative logic cones—typical patterns in the logic that needs hardware mapping. Second, it uses equality saturation (exploring every mathematically equivalent form of a structure and different ways to reorganize it) to generate diverse alternatives. Third, it ranks candidate choices by quality and keeps only the best ones, discarding the low-quality options that initial simulation and SAT solving would normally retain.
iccad-2025-022.key_novelty: CRISTAL improves choice networks for technology mapping by using equality saturation to explore different structural forms, then selecting only the highest-quality options rather than keeping all simulation results.

iccad-2025-021.method: The system coordinates three strategies to handle the storage hardware's unique design. Zigzag Data Placement arranges data to align with the mechanical stage's side-to-side motion, reducing wasted movement. Z-Axis First Placement prioritizes the fast optical axis before slower mechanical movements. Shortest Moving Time First scheduling selects operations based on predicted movement time, processing those requiring the least motion first.
iccad-2025-021.key_novelty: This is the first I/O middleware designed specifically for glass archival storage systems that combine mechanical and optical movement.

iccad-2025-026.method: Researchers compete over several months on problems provided by companies that make chip-design tools (EDA software—electronic design automation). Each problem includes industrial benchmarks (actual test cases from real chip projects) and automated evaluators that verify whether solutions work. This gives researchers genuine real-world challenges instead of simplified toy problems.
iccad-2025-026.key_novelty: An annual competition (running since 2012) that connects academic researchers with real chip-design problems from industry.

iccad-2025-024.method: The method models the quantum control system as a hypergraph—a graph where edges can connect multiple nodes at once—representing both the quantum circuit and the controllers issuing commands to it. It uses a heuristic algorithm (a practical, rule-of-thumb approach) to partition this graph into groups, placing controllers that command the same circuit parts nearby to minimize the distance signals must travel between them. This reduces communication latency—the delay between when one controller sends a signal and another receives it—cutting the time overhead from controller coordination.
iccad-2025-024.key_novelty: It's the first layout synthesizer to prioritize reducing communication delays between multiple controllers in a distributed quantum system, rather than focusing only on circuit execution depth.

iccad-2025-027.method: The framework uses Mixed-Integer Linear Programming—a mathematical technique for finding the best solution among many options while respecting design constraints—to optimize three things simultaneously: how transistors are connected together (topology), where they're physically positioned (placement), and how the wires between them are routed. To keep computation manageable, the approach uses design space pruning, which eliminates obviously suboptimal combinations before solving, so the optimizer focuses on the most promising possibilities.
iccad-2025-027.key_novelty: This is the first automatic framework to optimize circuit topology, transistor placement, and wiring routes all at the same time using Mixed-Integer Linear Programming.

iccad-2025-028.method: The approach splits the optimization into two connected stages, each modeled as a weighted graph-matching problem. It assigns processor cores to output ports and configures the microring resonators (optical components whose sizes determine which wavelengths they filter) to handle the actual traffic demands between cores. Using strict weight-based rules, it finds solutions quickly; if those rules make a solution impossible, it progressively loosens them until finding a feasible assignment.
iccad-2025-028.key_novelty: A two-stage graph-matching approach that jointly solves core-to-port assignment and microring resonator tuning according to actual bandwidth demands, achieving much faster results than existing methods.

iccad-2025-023.method: The accelerator performs computation directly within memory, exploiting sparsity—areas of zero or near-zero values—in both the weights (model parameters) and activations (data flowing through the network) to skip unnecessary work. Instead of using rigid array structures, it employs set-associative circuits (flexible mapping logic that resembles how cache memory stores data, allowing dynamic routing of sparse values to available compute units). This flexibility enables it to simultaneously support fine-grained pruning (removing unimportant weights identified during training) and outlier-aware quantization (compressing values to lower precision while preserving unusually large numbers that significantly affect results).
iccad-2025-023.key_novelty: The key innovation is a customized set-associative circuit that extracts N:M sparsity patterns (keeping only N non-zero values per M consecutive positions) from both weights and activations simultaneously, creating a unified compression approach.

iccad-2025-018.method: The system combines custom hardware with a compression format that keeps memory access aligned while varying precision levels by data type. It reorders activation outliers (values much larger than others) so memory fetches stay aligned, which makes access faster. It compresses different groups of data to different precision levels—finer for outliers to preserve accuracy, coarser for normal values to save space—adjusting group sizes based on how data varies across neural network layers. The hardware includes three accumulation stages designed to efficiently compute with this mixed-precision compressed data.
iccad-2025-018.key_novelty: A compression format combining outlier reordering, memory-aligned data access, and different precision levels for different data groups.

iccad-2025-025.method: The system uses a log-structured approach—data writes are appended sequentially to the end of storage rather than scattered randomly—paired with Zoned Namespace SSDs, which are designed to handle this sequential writing natively. The hardware and software manage the storage together: frequently-accessed data is kept in faster tiers while the system automatically cleans up old copies from slower storage, reducing unnecessary writes that wear out the SSD. The design includes optimizations to speed up reading data even when it's stored on the SSD.
iccad-2025-025.key_novelty: The core novelty is aligning log-structured writes with Zoned Namespace SSDs—hardware designed for sequential access—to optimize CXL-based memory expansion by reducing wasteful writes and improving both speed and durability.

iccad-2025-030.method: SubtreeLU reshapes the separator tree—the structure that nested dissection creates from circuit equations—by combining or splitting pieces to form a private-pipeline where processors work independently without synchronizing. It supports both pivoting (reordering values for numerical stability) and non-pivoting modes. Supernodal methods batch related operations together to speed up the numerical calculations.
iccad-2025-030.key_novelty: Reorganizing the separator tree into a private-pipeline structure that decouples synchronization constraints, allowing processors to work independently in parallel sparse LU factorization.

iccad-2025-032.method: The paper adds three small modifications to existing CNN accelerators (chips optimized for visual processing) to enable them to run transformer language models. First, it modifies how the accelerator handles multi-head attention (where the same computation runs on different slices of data) to avoid requiring dedicated hardware for data rearrangement. Second, it adds a lightweight processor that performs non-linear operations like Softmax and RMSNorm (functions that squeeze and normalize values during transformer computations). Third, it optimizes power efficiency during the generation phase, when the system is waiting for data from memory rather than performing intensive calculations.
iccad-2025-032.key_novelty: By adding three targeted hardware modifications to handle attention data-rearrangement, non-linear math, and memory efficiency, standard CNN accelerators can efficiently run modern transformer language models.

iccad-2025-031.method: The IEEE CEDA DATC establishes an open-source chip design environment on GitHub using OpenROAD, a free tool that places circuit components and routes connections on chips. It creates formal agreements with commercial vendors that allow public benchmarking of their proprietary place-and-route tools—the software that optimally arranges circuit components. It also launches the ML EDA Commons initiative to apply machine learning to chip design automation.
iccad-2025-031.key_novelty: The core innovation is establishing formal collaboration agreements that enable commercial EDA tool vendors to publicly share benchmarking results with academic researchers.

iccad-2025-033.method: The approach uses a search-tree algorithm that tests different transistor arrangements and eliminates dead-end options, focusing on transistors in the speed-critical path that determine overall chip speed. It then reorganizes transistors using dynamic programming to maximize diffusion sharing—reusing electrical connections between transistors to improve performance. Finally, it optimizes the wiring between transistors by formulating the speed-critical connections as a mathematical constraint-satisfaction problem.
iccad-2025-033.key_novelty: Prioritizing speed (delay) at the cell level over area (size), inverting the traditional synthesis approach.

iccad-2025-034.method: FRESCO uses a two-phase algorithm to organize operations into clusters for heterogeneous CGRAs. In the first phase, it discovers possible cluster configurations using an abstract decision tree strategy—a method that makes systematic yes/no choices to eliminate unpromising options early, avoiding the exponential explosion of checking every combination. In the second phase, it selects the best overall combination of the discovered clusters.
iccad-2025-034.key_novelty: The innovation is using abstract decision trees to enumerate potential cluster configurations while efficiently pruning the search space.

iccad-2025-038.method: STMC breaks quantum circuits into smaller pieces that map onto hardware tiles, then runs multiple copies of each piece simultaneously. When photons are lost or fusion operations fail (when quantum states are combined imperfectly), at least one parallel copy succeeds, avoiding the expensive cost of re-running the entire circuit.
iccad-2025-038.key_novelty: Running multiple copies of small circuit pieces in parallel allows STMC to tolerate photon loss and fusion failures without re-running the entire circuit.

iccad-2025-037.method: The method simulates how heat spreads over time through liquid-cooled stacked chips using random walks on circuit thermal models—imagining heat flow as particles taking random paths through the network, then averaging many paths to find temperature distribution. To make random walks work with liquid cooling, it replaces a problematic circuit element (voltage-controlled current source) with a diode model that's compatible with the random walk algorithm. GPU acceleration and time-domain path reuse (reusing results across time steps) make this fast enough for large systems.
iccad-2025-037.key_novelty: Replacing a circuit element with a diode model adapts random walks to liquid-cooled systems, enabling GPU-accelerated thermal simulation.

iccad-2025-029.method: Tenpura uses FPGA emulation—running the chip design on reconfigurable hardware instead of pure software simulation—to speed up the testing process. It traces which parts of the hardware are actively used by reading scan chains (built-in test circuits that read internal state). Since faults occurring in inactive hardware can't affect the chip's operation, the system only injects faults into active regions. This scope narrowing dramatically reduces the fault-testing workload compared to testing every possible transient fault.
iccad-2025-029.key_novelty: The key innovation is using scan-chain activity data to identify which transient faults could matter, enabling ultra-fast pre-silicon fault injection.

iccad-2025-039.method: Instead of repeatedly solving complex equations for electricity and heat flow (which is computationally expensive), this approach trains neural networks to respect physics laws—called physics-informed neural networks or PINNs. The method works in two stages: a coarse model predicts electrical potential and temperature across the entire 3D chip design, then a fine-grained model focuses on regions that need higher resolution. The training is optimized for fast convergence, combining learned patterns with physical constraints to ensure accuracy.
iccad-2025-039.key_novelty: A two-stage neural network that first predicts electrical and thermal behavior across an entire 3D chip design, then refines specific regions of interest for higher precision.

iccad-2025-042.method: Instead of manually designing each connection between components like pumps and cell cultures, this method automatically generates the routing designs needed for microfluidic chips—systems that move liquids through tiny, precise channels. Researchers use an interactive online tool called the Munich Microfluidic Toolkit to view, adjust, and finalize the automatically generated designs before fabricating the actual chip.
iccad-2025-042.key_novelty: Automatically designing how components connect in microfluidic systems while following ISO standards to ensure all modules work together reliably.

iccad-2025-041.method: The framework automatically adjusts the many configuration settings (parameters) used in high-level physical synthesis—the process of placing hardware components on multi-die FPGAs. It uses smart decision rules (heuristics) that respond to measurements from the actual physical design, like how well signals arrive on time (timing closure). By repeatedly measuring the design's performance and adjusting settings accordingly, it achieves consistent results without requiring engineers to manually tweak settings.
iccad-2025-041.key_novelty: Using measurements from actual physical design performance to automatically optimize configuration settings, creating a feedback loop that eliminates manual tuning.

iccad-2025-040.method: The framework solves gate sizing (resizing logic gates) and buffer insertion (adding intermediate signal copies) together as a unified mathematical problem, rather than separately. It builds a mathematical model where changes in circuit design directly compute their timing effects, using GPU acceleration to speed up the calculations. It strategically places buffers based on timing requirements and simultaneously optimizes both gate sizes and buffer placement using algorithms that respect the fact that circuit components only come in certain fixed sizes. Throughout the optimization, it accurately models the actual physics of the circuit instead of relying on simplified approximations.
iccad-2025-040.key_novelty: It unifies gate sizing and buffer insertion into a single mathematical problem (differentiable—solvable with calculus) with rigorous circuit physics, rather than solving them separately with simplified models.

iccad-2025-046.method: It uses two simulation techniques working together. First, it calculates how many clock cycles the accelerator code will take by analyzing the high-level code directly—this skips the slow step of simulating every hardware detail gate-by-gate. Second, it runs the actual hardware simulation connected to the real host software that will use it, using inter-process communication (direct connections between programs) to pass data between them. This combination lets engineers quickly test accelerator functions, predict their speed accurately, and verify the entire system works correctly without rebuilding hardware repeatedly.
iccad-2025-046.key_novelty: The core idea is combining fast performance prediction from high-level code analysis with complete hardware-software system simulation through inter-process communication.

iccad-2025-044.method: GenEDA aligns circuit encoders (which read circuits as graphs) with text-generation decoders into a shared mathematical space, so they can learn from each other's representations. This bridges graph-based circuit understanding with text-based language models. The framework provides two paradigms: one with a trainable language model and another using a frozen (fixed) commercial LLM.
iccad-2025-044.key_novelty: GenEDA aligns circuit encoders and language models in a shared space, letting language models directly process bit-blasted netlists (circuit descriptions at the bit level) and generate high-level specifications.

iccad-2025-036.method: Adder-DCIM compresses the neural network by breaking operations into simpler forms, removing unnecessary computations (fine-grained sparsity), and using fewer bits where precision isn't critical—with KLD validation ensuring accuracy is preserved. It then runs this on hardware that performs calculations directly in memory with parallel processing instead of serial bit-by-bit operations, supporting different precision levels throughout. A flexible circuit efficiently handles these varying precisions, and the hardware replaces multiplication with addition to reduce power consumption and silicon area.
iccad-2025-036.key_novelty: The core innovation is co-designing the neural network and a parallel in-memory computing accelerator with flexible precision handling so the network replaces multiplication with addition while maintaining accuracy.

iccad-2025-035.method: LEAF uses two coordinated strategies to accelerate FALCON signature verification. First, it organizes data flow through the hardware to help each computational unit reuse work more efficiently (a technique called data dependence flow optimization), shrinking the total hardware needed. Second, it introduces a new method to fetch twiddle factors—coefficients used in FALCON's NTT mathematical engine—that avoids wasted memory access. These strategies together enable efficient verification on resource-constrained hardware.
iccad-2025-035.key_novelty: Organizing data flow and twiddle factor access in a new way enables FALCON signature verification on resource-constrained hardware without sacrificing throughput.

iccad-2025-045.method: The researchers created the first model to estimate the carbon released during manufacturing of photonic chips by studying the energy requirements and production success rates (yield) of these chips compared to traditional semiconductor chips. They built a tool called EPiCarbon that measures both manufacturing carbon and the carbon produced by running Electro-Photonic accelerators during their lifetime. They applied this tool to analyze leading EPiC accelerator designs and identify methods to reduce their overall carbon footprint.
iccad-2025-045.key_novelty: This work introduces the first model to measure the carbon from manufacturing photonic chips, demonstrating these chips use 4.1 times less energy to produce than traditional semiconductor chips.

iccad-2025-048.method: The system uses hybrid sparse attention, which recognizes that different attention heads benefit from different patterns of skipping computations—some heads skip the same token pairs consistently (static sparsity), while others skip adaptively based on what's important in each input (dynamic sparsity). The hardware exploits this by placing compute and memory directly adjacent to each other using hybrid bonding (stacking silicon dies closely to share data locally), eliminating long data transfers that consume power. A load-balancing scheduler breaks the attention computation into tiles and orchestrates parallel execution, ensuring all compute units stay busy and work distributes evenly across the hardware.
iccad-2025-048.key_novelty: The system combines hybrid sparse attention—which adapts each attention head to use static or dynamic sparsity—with hybrid bonding hardware that co-locates compute and memory to efficiently match the varying sparsity patterns across heads.

iccad-2025-043.method: The system uses machine learning (a neural network called an autoencoder) to create two types of camouflage that fool reverse engineers. It modifies the logic gates (basic components that process electrical signals) while keeping the circuit's outputs the same—so an attacker sees fake logic that doesn't explain the outputs. It also inserts fake gates (fake inverters, fake buffers, and universal transmitters) that serve no purpose. Together, these two approaches hide what the circuit really does while keeping it functionally correct.
iccad-2025-043.key_novelty: The innovation is using machine learning to combine two types of deception simultaneously: changing how the circuit works internally while keeping the same results, and adding fake gates that don't do anything.

iccad-2025-047.method: The framework uses a large language model—an AI trained on text—to automatically design circuits for flexible electronics, which bend and flex unlike rigid silicon. It automates the design workflow: writing hardware descriptions (RTL), converting them to working circuits (logic synthesis), and exploring different design options to optimize power consumption, speed, and chip size for machine learning classifier applications while respecting flexible materials' physical constraints. The system handles these trade-offs end-to-end without human intervention at each design step.
iccad-2025-047.key_novelty: It's the first system using large language models to automate circuit design specifically for flexible electronics, which have different constraints than rigid silicon.

iccad-2025-051.method: The approach introduces two new cell designs (TFFDO and TFFDE) that work with two-phase clock signals, reducing the number of D flip-flops (storage elements) needed in the circuit. Clock signals are then distributed across the circuit column-by-column using maximum flow, an algorithm that finds optimal routing paths. The circuit components are arranged vertically using dynamic programming — a systematic optimization technique that minimizes wire length while respecting fixed ordering constraints. Finally, components are reordered based on wire lengths to further reduce total wiring overhead.
iccad-2025-051.key_novelty: A placement framework designed specifically for multiphase-clocked RSFQ circuits that combines new cell designs (TFFDO and TFFDE) with wire-length-aware ordering to reduce D flip-flop overhead.

iccad-2025-055.method: The decoder reformulates quantum error correction as an optimization problem: given sensor measurements (syndromes) revealing where errors occurred, find the errors that most likely caused them. Using One-Hot QUBO—a specific optimization structure—each variable represents a pairing between error locations, and the cost reflects measured error probabilities. The algorithm solves by finding permutation matrices (mathematical structures where each row and column has exactly one 1) that minimize total cost, which directly identifies the most probable errors.
iccad-2025-055.key_novelty: The One-Hot QUBO formulation reduces the number of variables by 99.9x and enables quantum error correction to decode errors in microseconds on commodity CPUs.

iccad-2025-057.method: The approach fuses multiple tensor mathematical operations into single combined steps, keeping intermediate data in the GPU's fast on-chip memory rather than moving it back to slower main memory—this solves the memory bottleneck that was limiting performance. It also restructures the computation to eliminate redundant operations. A specialized hardware architecture is then designed specifically to perform the tensor products that graph neural networks use to calculate molecular forces.
iccad-2025-057.key_novelty: Custom hardware architecture designed specifically for the tensor operations in graph neural network-based molecular force calculations.

iccad-2025-050.method: The system builds a neuromorphic processor (brain-inspired chip) from spintronic devices (circuits based on magnetic spin) and ferroelectric materials (substances that permanently store electrical charge). Spintronic neurons naturally produce the random behavior needed for random-walk methods in solving PDEs; ferroelectric synapses persistently store the numerical weights for computation. This approach generates randomness directly in hardware, bypassing the software randomness generation that typically creates a major performance bottleneck.
iccad-2025-050.key_novelty: Spintronic devices that naturally generate randomness for random-walk PDE solvers, eliminating software randomness generation.

iccad-2025-054.method: The system uses a neural network trained to predict how heat spreads through photonic circuits from heater positions (operator learning). It represents heat sources in a pseudo-3D way that accounts for the circuit's layered structure, and trains using a physics-informed loss function that directly enforces heat-diffusion rules. The network includes attention mechanisms to focus on areas with sharp temperature changes and heat crosstalk effects, and uses zero coordinate shift encoding to make predictions work regardless of circuit position, improving generalization.
iccad-2025-054.key_novelty: A neural network combining operator learning with physics-based training and position-independent representations to quickly predict thermal behavior in stacked photonic circuits.

iccad-2025-052.method: The team tested different techniques for speeding up matrix math on encrypted data. They compared a basic packed-row method against BSGS (Baby-step Giant-step, a technique that breaks large calculations into smaller, faster chunks), finding BSGS 13.7x faster at scale. They also pruned the network's feed-forward layers down to 11.46x smaller and upgraded the Orion compiler to multiply encrypted matrices directly. Using roofline analysis—a method that measures whether computation or memory access limits performance—they discovered that moving data in and out of memory is the bottleneck, not the speed of arithmetic itself.
iccad-2025-052.key_novelty: Optimizing encrypted transformers requires improving both the compiler and the network design, with performance analysis revealing that memory movement—not computation—is the limiting factor.

iccad-2025-049.method: The approach trains the model in four stages. It filters training data to only include compilable code (100% pass rate), then compares code pairs across five hardware design dimensions (RTL: register-transfer level, meaning how hardware state changes), marking which version is better in each dimension—teaching the model to evaluate code across multiple criteria. Finally, it fine-tunes with reasoning examples and uses Verilator simulation (a hardware validation tool) with reinforcement learning to reward code that passes functional validation.
iccad-2025-049.key_novelty: The innovation is comparing hardware code versions across five design dimensions based on functional correctness, combined with training that emphasizes step-by-step reasoning.

iccad-2025-061.method: LimTDD works by splitting quantum states into smaller, connected pieces using tensor networks—a mathematical way to break large states into factors. These pieces are then stored using decision diagrams, a tree-like structure that compactly represents them by skipping redundant branches. Because quantum states grow exponentially in size, this compact factorization allows the method to represent and work with states that would otherwise be too large to fit in memory.
iccad-2025-061.key_novelty: Combining tensor networks with decision diagrams creates a more compact representation for quantum states.

iccad-2025-053.method: The design stacks voltage across multiple circuits to save power, but prevents the resulting voltage ripple and power loss by using clocked differential logic (symmetric circuit pairs) in the datapath to maintain constant current consumption every cycle. The register file uses fully differential latches with symmetrical multiplexers to maintain balance in stored data. Control signals remain standard CMOS, and execution across all parallel lanes stays synchronized to prevent variation from accumulating.
iccad-2025-053.key_novelty: It solves the current imbalance problem that voltage stacking creates by using differential logic (symmetric circuits that draw constant current each cycle) in the datapath.

iccad-2025-056.method: The method models how analog hardware errors affect neural network accuracy by representing different types of errors as variations in the network weights, allowing them to be analyzed together. It develops NIPA (Non-Ideal PIM Accuracy), a model that accounts for how these errors interact with each other using information about how neural networks typically respond to weight changes. Rather than the traditional approach of simulating each bit and crossbar individually, it evaluates the model's accuracy all at once, eliminating the expensive granular simulation.
iccad-2025-056.key_novelty: By evaluating how all errors affect the model at once instead of simulating individual bits and crossbars, it achieves 105.8x speedup.

iccad-2025-062.method: The paper analyzes how to design and train image-recognition neural networks (CNNs) that work on analog camera chips—sensors that process light directly as analog signals before digital conversion. It derives design guidelines by working backward from hardware constraints: which network topologies, training methods, and data-processing strategies let the network handle real-world analog challenges like noise (random signal variations), quantization errors (information loss in the analog-to-digital conversion), and raw unrefined sensor output. The key recommendations cover network architecture choices, training recipes that make the network robust to noise and quantization, and techniques to process raw sensor data directly without special digital image preprocessing (ISP).
iccad-2025-062.key_novelty: The core idea is to design neural networks and their training specifically for the constraints of analog in-sensor hardware—accounting for noise, quantization errors, and raw sensor data—to enable efficient image recognition directly on the chip.

iccad-2025-058.method: The system uses two different types of cores instead of identical ones: a fast, heat-producing core for computation-heavy tasks and an efficient core for memory-intensive operations like attention mechanisms. The fast core handles math work like matrix multiplications, while the efficient core focuses on data access that requires high memory bandwidth. By separating these workloads, the design avoids concentrating heat in one spot. A bandwidth scheduler allocates shared memory access between the cores to prevent waste, and thermal management techniques spread heat evenly across the stacked layers to prevent dangerous hot spots.
iccad-2025-058.key_novelty: A 3D-stacked chip design using two different core types—one fast for computing, one efficient for memory access—that combines thermal management with memory bandwidth sharing to accelerate large language model inference.

iccad-2025-060.method: E-graphs are data structures that represent all mathematically equivalent ways to partition a circuit into LUTs (the logic blocks used in FPGAs). The system systematically explores different partitioning strategies by combining exact SAT-based methods—which find provably optimal arrangements—with faster heuristics that guide the search, producing circuits with fewer LUTs and shorter signal paths.
iccad-2025-060.key_novelty: The core contribution is using e-graphs to systematically explore all equivalent FPGA circuit configurations, combining exact optimization methods with practical heuristics to improve LUT mapping.

iccad-2025-064.method: The approach uses a large language model to generate an optimized buffer tree—the arrangement of signal buffers throughout a circuit—in one pass for all connections that violate timing constraints. The model is then trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, a reinforcement learning technique that updates the model based on how well each solution balances power consumption, circuit speed, and chip area. This allows designers to prioritize whichever trade-off matters most for their specific design.
iccad-2025-064.key_novelty: This is the first formulation of buffer tree generation as a sequence-to-sequence task—translating circuit connection constraints into optimized buffer placement—that large language models can solve directly.

iccad-2025-059.method: The system co-designs both hardware architecture and data flow strategy to efficiently handle speculative inference (where the model guesses ahead to speed up token generation), using intelligent memory controllers that dynamically move data between regular memory and processing-in-memory (PIM) banks—special memory that computes directly where the data sits. A hardware component removes wasteful speculative token predictions to save energy. The system then schedules computations dynamically to maximize processor and memory utilization in parallel.
iccad-2025-059.key_novelty: Jointly designing hardware architecture and data flow to efficiently handle speculative inference on mobile by filtering wasteful draft tokens.

iccad-2025-066.method: The approach speeds up dynamic programming problems by using graphics processors (GPUs), which can perform many calculations simultaneously instead of one at a time. It works by breaking the expensive cost calculations into independent pieces that run in parallel across the GPU's cores, then efficiently combines these results back together. This is demonstrated on the practical problem of optimally arranging electronic components of different sizes on a computer chip.
iccad-2025-066.key_novelty: The main contribution is a general GPU acceleration framework for any dynamic programming algorithm in chip design.

iccad-2025-065.method: The approach splits computation between GPU and PIM hardware: the GPU handles attention operations (which need flexible full-precision computation) using its high-bandwidth memory, while PIM accelerates fully-connected layers by operating on data in simplified number formats. Rather than choosing one precision level for everything, they use mixed-precision quantization—assigning different precision (fewer or more bits per number) to different layers based on both what each layer's math requires to stay accurate and what PIM's internal bandwidth can handle efficiently. A dataflow scheduler coordinates this split, routing each operation to the processor that can execute it best.
iccad-2025-065.key_novelty: Mixed-precision quantization that chooses each layer's precision by balancing the algorithm's accuracy needs against the hardware's bandwidth capabilities.

iccad-2025-068.method: The routing algorithm finds the optimal path for connecting qubits on a silicon spin-qubit chip by combining two search techniques: Dijkstra's algorithm (which prioritizes shorter paths) and breadth-first search (which systematically checks nearby regions first). It uses bit-vector representation—expressing available routing regions as binary numbers—to quickly check if routing paths would overlap without conflicts.
iccad-2025-068.key_novelty: Unlike existing routing methods from other quantum platforms, this approach specifically targets silicon spin-qubits' unique hardware constraints.

iccad-2025-067.method: It divides a 3D circuit into functional sections (partitioning) using gradient-based optimization (calculating the best partition by following slopes of errors), running on GPU with PyTorch. The cost function accounts for snaking — the winding paths signals take through layers — and timing constraints (how quickly signals must travel). It also spaces circuit elements evenly to avoid clustering. This early-stage optimization reduces wasteful winding on speed-critical paths and cuts the number of bond pads (metal connections between layers) needed.
iccad-2025-067.key_novelty: It combines snaking and timing awareness into gradient-based partitioning at the earliest design stage, accelerated on GPU.

iccad-2025-063.method: The strategy identifies weight and input channels by measuring two statistical properties: kurtosis (how much their values cluster at extremes) and saliency (how important they are to the network's output). It groups channels with high kurtosis or high saliency together and assigns them to higher-precision computational units, while grouping less critical channels for lower-precision processing, using reconfigurable hardware tiles that can switch between precision modes. This targeted grouping reduces extreme values in the output and improves signal-to-noise ratio when facing quantization and analog hardware noise. The entire process works without retraining the model.
iccad-2025-063.key_novelty: Group weight and input channels by their statistical properties (kurtosis and saliency) and assign them to hardware with appropriate precision levels, improving noise robustness without retraining.

iccad-2025-070.method: The system automatically selects between two strategies: Tensor Parallelism (dividing mathematical computations among devices) or Expert Parallelism (assigning specialized model components to different devices). As the model runs, it monitors device usage and communication traffic, then dynamically switches between strategies to keep devices equally busy while reducing the time data spends moving between devices.
iccad-2025-070.key_novelty: During execution, the system dynamically switches between Tensor and Expert Parallelism (two ways to distribute a language model across devices) and continuously rebalances work to minimize communication delays in mixture-of-expert models running on distributed near-memory processing accelerators.

iccad-2025-073.method: The method uses Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM), an iterative algorithm that breaks the legalization problem into smaller pieces that can be solved in stages. CPUs and GPUs divide the work: the GPU performs parallel optimization on the continuous math problem, while the CPU handles the discrete constraints that force cells to snap to valid grid positions. This parallel analytical approach avoids the runtime slowdown of pure analytical methods while achieving better results than traditional heuristic cell-by-cell search.
iccad-2025-073.key_novelty: Legalization is solved analytically using ADMM with CPUs and GPUs working in parallel to jointly handle continuous optimization and discrete cell positioning.

iccad-2025-071.method: The researchers tested this question on real quantum hardware: they ran 16 different quantum algorithms on five IBM quantum computers with 127 qubits each. For each algorithm, they compared two approaches—one that constantly updates how the quantum code is translated and optimized based on current noise measurements, and one that uses a simpler random assignment. By measuring how accurately each approach executed the algorithms, they could determine whether the expensive adaptive process was actually necessary.
iccad-2025-071.key_novelty: A simple random approach to executing quantum code performs nearly as well as constantly updating the code-to-hardware conversion based on noise, suggesting the expensive adaptation isn't necessary.

iccad-2025-069.method: DevTrace records the data transfers between computers and connected hardware like GPUs or storage devices. Rather than letting recording interrupt the kernel (the core operating system) constantly—which would create huge overhead—it uses a separate recording framework that runs independently. Because it requires only minimal changes to device driver software, it achieves low overhead while avoiding expensive kernel interrupts.
iccad-2025-069.key_novelty: The breakthrough is a lightweight plug-in design that traces any device type while staying independent from the core system.

iccad-2025-074.method: The solution uses FPGA components—mixed-mode clock managers (MMCMs), phase-locked loops (PLLs), and IDELAY blocks—to filter out timing noise (jitter) from cryptographic circuits. These components smooth out signal timing variations that an attacker could otherwise detect using a time-to-digital converter (hardware that measures precise signal timing). By removing the jitter, the defense eliminates the information needed for a jitter-based side-channel analysis attack.
iccad-2025-074.key_novelty: This is the first defense built specifically to stop jitter-based side-channel analysis attacks on cryptographic hardware.

iccad-2025-079.method: MiCo automates finding the best mixed-precision quantization scheme (using lower bit counts for some neural network layers and higher for others) by running an optimization algorithm that balances accuracy against speed limits. It predicts how fast each scheme will run on specific hardware targets—like GPUs or edge AI accelerators—without physically building and testing each option. Once the best scheme is found, MiCo directly generates optimized C code from the PyTorch model that runs on bare metal, letting you deploy straight from exploration to edge devices.
iccad-2025-079.key_novelty: MiCo combines automated mixed-precision search, hardware-specific latency prediction, and direct C code deployment in a single end-to-end system for edge AI.

iccad-2025-076.method: In analog in-memory computing arrays (specialized chips that perform calculations using memory), stuck-at faults (defects where certain values get stuck and cannot change) corrupt computations. This method adds redundant copies of neural network weights spread across both rows and columns of the array—going beyond existing approaches that only use columns—so faulty cells can be bypassed. A compiler reformulates the problem of fitting weights around faults as an optimization task solved by standard mathematical solvers (Integer Linear Programming, which finds the best solution within constraints). By recognizing fault patterns that have obvious solutions, the approach cuts compilation time sharply while maintaining fault protection.
iccad-2025-076.key_novelty: The key advance is row-column hybrid grouping—a 2D arrangement of redundant weight backups across both rows and columns instead of columns alone—combined with optimization software that automatically finds the best fault-tolerant layout for in-memory computing arrays.

iccad-2025-077.method: DiffCCD solves the problem of adjusting clock and data timing as a mathematical optimization on a GPU, using gradients—mathematical slopes that indicate which way to adjust parameters to improve timing results. The approach has three components: first, it converts the timing problem into smooth mathematical equations with a calibration step to ensure the gradients stay accurate; second, it breaks the large problem into smaller subproblems that are solved in alternating rounds using a technique called ADMM; third, it implements the solution through buffer sizing (adding delays in the clock network) and repositioning components on the chip, while keeping everything within physical design limits.
iccad-2025-077.key_novelty: DiffCCD is the first approach using gradient-based optimization to jointly handle clock skew and data path timing delays during post-CTS timing closure while maintaining physical design constraints.

iccad-2025-072.method: The approach splits a graph into sections small enough to fit on a chip's fast local memory. For boundary nodes (called halo nodes) that would normally require repeated fetches from slow external DRAM, the system uses similar nodes already stored locally instead. Over multiple refinement phases, the partition boundaries improve, and data uses block floating-point format (grouping similarly-sized numbers to save storage and energy).
iccad-2025-072.key_novelty: The key innovation replaces halo nodes (boundary nodes normally fetched from external DRAM) with similar nodes already in the partition's local memory.

iccad-2025-081.method: SPARTA combines algorithm and hardware design to address the scattered, unpredictable spikes that waste power in spiking transformers. On the algorithm side, it uses reinforcement learning (a machine-learning approach that learns through trial-and-error) to intelligently decide which transformer tokens (input chunks) are informative and which can be skipped; it also predicts and eliminates tokens that will be inactive, converting unstructured spikes into organized token-level sparsity. The hardware implements a specialized ReRAM-based architecture (ReRAM is resistive memory that performs calculations in-place) with ReRAM-CIM (computing-in-memory) for linear layers and a dedicated token-spike fusion engine that efficiently routes tokens and computes spike attention operations.
iccad-2025-081.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining reinforcement-learning-based token skipping (a learned algorithm for selecting which tokens matter) with custom ReRAM-CIM hardware, both specifically designed to handle the sparsity patterns that naturally emerge in spiking transformers.

iccad-2025-075.method: OptiRange reduces energy waste in ReRAM-based processing-in-memory accelerators by making ADCs (analog-to-digital converters) do less work. The Split-the-Burden algorithm shifts stored values toward zero so ADCs need less precision to convert them. A second technique adapts each column's ADC range at runtime and skips unnecessary conversions. The third technique uses varying computation times across columns to keep the system busy and boost throughput while maintaining accuracy.
iccad-2025-075.key_novelty: By independently rearranging ReRAM values and adapting each column's ADC range, OptiRange cuts energy waste without changing the underlying computation.

iccad-2025-088.method: LLM-on-the-Palm puts tiny math processors (called multiply-accumulate or MAC units—the basic calculations that neural networks use) directly into NAND flash storage. A 256 GB storage drive gets one of these processors per storage layer, giving 256 total. Instead of hauling data back and forth between storage and the main processor—the speed bottleneck that kills mobile LLM performance—the math happens right in storage where the data already is. This way, mobile phones can run billion-parameter language models fast without slowing down the storage itself.
iccad-2025-088.key_novelty: Running neural-network computations directly in NAND flash storage with one processor per storage layer enables mobile LLM inference with minimal hardware modifications.

iccad-2025-078.method: FabThink combines a language model with document retrieval and step-by-step reasoning to solve complex wafer defect problems in semiconductor manufacturing. It breaks questions into logical steps and retrieves relevant documents at each step, combining information from both text and images. It ranks documents by their relevance to each reasoning step and uses a specialized generator to produce answers based on the most relevant documents.
iccad-2025-078.key_novelty: It uses step-by-step reasoning to improve document retrieval—processing both text and images—for semiconductor manufacturing problems involving wafer defects.

iccad-2025-080.method: CPUs execute code speculatively—running instructions before confirming they're actually needed—and during this time, hardware prefetchers (the parts that guess which memory data you'll need next) accidentally reveal secrets. SpectrePrefetch exploits this by encoding secrets into how the prefetchers behave, then extracting those secrets in two ways: by reading the memory-access patterns the prefetchers leave in the cache, or by reading the confidence levels stored inside the prefetcher. The attacks were tested on Intel processors and a detailed simulator (Gem5), and researchers also proposed a defense using randomized prefetching that maintains normal performance.
iccad-2025-080.key_novelty: This is the first framework to exploit hardware prefetchers as hidden information leaks (covert channels) during speculative execution, showing that cache-based defenses against speculative attacks are insufficient.

iccad-2025-083.method: Instead of duplicating the same hardware logic many times—which wastes FPGA space—CTDM reuses a single copy by running it repeatedly with different data at different time steps (a technique called time-division multiplexing). It chains together the FPGA's built-in shift register primitives (simple hardware components that shift data sequentially) and uses an automated CTDM compiler to translate Verilog, VHDL, HLS, and Chisel code across different FPGA devices. For multi-FPGA systems, block interleaving (strategically ordering which data gets sent when) hides delays in the high-speed serial I/O pipelines between FPGAs and keeps them fully utilized by doing other work while waiting for data to arrive.
iccad-2025-083.key_novelty: Chain-based time-division multiplexing (reusing logic instead of duplicating it) dramatically reduces FPGA resource overhead for large-scale neural processor (NPU) simulation and enables multi-FPGA deployments through an automated compiler supporting multiple hardware description languages.

iccad-2025-082.method: ChronoTE uses a graph neural network—a machine learning model that processes interconnected structures—to estimate how long signals take to travel through chip wiring while accounting for crosstalk (interference between nearby wires). Rather than the traditional pessimistic approach of only considering coupling capacitance, it jointly models the physical wiring layout and timing characteristics, encoding timing-window-aware features (information about when signals arrive) into the connections between nodes. This enables accurate delay prediction early in the design process, before the expensive and time-consuming steps of full routing or parasitic extraction.
iccad-2025-082.key_novelty: The key innovation is using a graph neural network enhanced with timing-window-aware features (information about signal arrival times) to predict crosstalk delays accurately during early routing without expensive parasitic extraction.

iccad-2025-090.method: FlexOn breaks a machine learning model into small, fine-grained segments and then dynamically selects where each segment runs based on available computing resources at that moment. As the device's workload and resource availability change during operation, the framework can run segments locally on the device or offload them to external processors and servers—whichever provides the best performance. This dynamic, fine-grained approach lets the framework adapt rapidly even when multiple programs are competing for the same computing resources.
iccad-2025-090.key_novelty: This is the first work to address resource contention (programs competing for computing resources) in embedded systems, enabling faster and more responsive machine learning predictions.

iccad-2025-093.method: The approach uses computer simulations to test different ways of designing a multi-die chip—a chip made of multiple separate pieces that work together. AI automatically searches through thousands of possible configurations, evaluating each one by simulating how data moves between the pieces, how real software runs on it, and measuring factors like power consumption and speed.
iccad-2025-093.key_novelty: Using AI to automatically explore and evaluate the vast space of possible multi-die chip designs instead of relying on manual design choices.

iccad-2025-085.method: JSA-CIM is a hardware accelerator built with 8-transistor SRAM memory cells that compute neural networks using addition instead of multiplication (AdderNet). It saves energy by exploiting zeros in both activation values and weights—processing them one bit at a time, skipping entire activation values when they're zero at the system level, and skipping individual weight bits that are zero at the circuit level. A robust method reliably selects minimum values during this bit-by-bit processing, which is critical for AdderNet computation.
iccad-2025-085.key_novelty: It exploits zeros in both weight parameters and intermediate values (a property called joint-sparsity) using a specialized 8-transistor memory design, delivering energy-efficient computation for addition-based neural networks (AdderNet).

iccad-2025-086.method: CiFold finds repeated sequences of quantum operations within a circuit and merges them into single building blocks, creating a condensed representation (meta-graph) of the full circuit. Using this smaller map, it can quickly identify where to optimally split the circuit across multiple quantum processors without the computational expense of checking every possible cut location. Two metrics—folding factor and variance—ensure the compression is balanced and the circuit's structural properties are maintained.
iccad-2025-086.key_novelty: By merging repeated patterns in quantum circuits through circuit folding, the method enables efficient, scalable identification of cutting locations that would otherwise require prohibitive exhaustive searching.

iccad-2025-087.method: TOGGLE uses Signal Temporal Logic—a mathematical notation for formally specifying language properties—to define what linguistic behaviors must survive compression. It searches through layer-wise configurations for making the model smaller, including quantization (reducing weight precision) and pruning (removing unimportant connections), using Bayesian optimization (a guided search method favoring configurations that satisfy the constraints). The result is a compressed model mathematically proven to preserve the specified linguistic properties without retraining.
iccad-2025-087.key_novelty: First to add formal verification (Signal Temporal Logic—a mathematical method for specifying and checking what systems do) to large language model compression, mathematically proving that compressed models preserve specified language properties.

iccad-2025-089.method: FLASC saves a device's state (checkpointing) by splitting the work between hardware and software. Normally the hardware tracks which memory changed—expensive when memory is large—but FLASC uses lightweight software tracking instead, keeping hardware cheap and simple. The system saves in the background while the processor keeps working, with safeguards ensuring correctness and no slowdown.
iccad-2025-089.key_novelty: FLASC splits checkpoint work between hardware and software to enable asynchronous saving—storing only memory changes without pausing—while avoiding proportional hardware cost growth as memory increases.

iccad-2025-094.method: When the same memory banks are accessed repeatedly in stacked HBM layers, heat concentrates in one location due to poor thermal conductivity between the layers. The solution remaps (rearranges) which physical banks handle streaming accesses, directing them to banks that are not stacked directly on top of each other so heat spreads across different layers. Rather than installing temperature sensors in each bank, it monitors how frequently each bank is accessed and automatically throttles (slows down) accesses when activity reaches dangerous levels.
iccad-2025-094.key_novelty: It addresses HBM thermal throttling through vertical bank address remapping combined with activity-based throttling instead of temperature sensors.

iccad-2025-097.method: Half-Height Double-Row CFET (stacked transistors in compact rows) lets designers freely adjust standard cell layouts and then optimize cell placement during the final routing stage of chip design. This two-stage approach—flexible cell design followed by block-level optimization—achieves better space efficiency than fixed designs. The technique stays within realistic manufacturing limits for the metal interconnection layers.
iccad-2025-097.key_novelty: First half-height stacked-transistor design enabling area optimization at both cell and block levels of chip design.

iccad-2025-099.method: STAR protects high-capacity SSDs by randomizing how data is stored to avoid patterns vulnerable to lateral charge spreading (charge leaking between neighboring cells in stacked memory layers). It detects errors by reading memory cells with opposite electrical polarities (dual-polarity reads), then corrects them using an analytical model that predicts how each cell's threshold voltage—the electrical level determining whether a bit reads as 0 or 1—drifts over time.
iccad-2025-099.key_novelty: It is the first data randomizer specifically designed to address the weak data patterns caused by lateral charge spreading in high-capacity 3D NAND SSDs.

iccad-2025-095.method: PDGM-IMC merges physics-based understanding with real measurement data to model imperfections in analog in-memory computing systems. It uses normalizing flows—a machine learning technique that transforms simple probability distributions into complex, realistic ones—customized with transformations based on device physics. The framework captures three interconnected problems: the statistical distribution of errors across the chip, how errors correlate in different regions, and natural manufacturing variations between individual chips.
iccad-2025-095.key_novelty: It's the first generative framework combining physics-based principles with machine learning to model imperfections in analog in-memory computing while preserving both interpretability and generalization.

iccad-2025-092.method: The approach uses reinforcement learning—where an algorithm learns by trial and error to reach target goals—to automatically choose component values in analog circuits. It creates an automatic curriculum by sampling training targets from the Pareto frontier (the set of designs where improving one performance metric means sacrificing another), selecting targets based on dominance relationships to prioritize harder problems. During training, it learns from past failed design attempts using Conservative Hindsight Experience Replay (a technique that reuses failed trials carefully to keep training stable), and avoids running expensive simulations that would fail.
iccad-2025-092.key_novelty: This is the first goal-conditioned reinforcement learning framework enabling efficient policy training for analog device sizing with strong generalization across PVT corners (the different combinations of manufacturing process, voltage, and temperature variations).

iccad-2025-096.method: The system uses three coordinated techniques to handle a 3D-stacked chip. It shrinks the model layer-by-layer by removing unnecessary weights (sparsity) and using different numerical precision levels (4-bit to 8-bit integers) tuned to each layer's hardware constraints. It dynamically splits inference work into adaptive batches and adjusts temporary memory usage (the KV-cache) during execution. It also schedules data transfers across the silicon interconnects (Through-Silicon Vias or TSVs) in phases to avoid signal degradation in the densely-packed layers.
iccad-2025-096.key_novelty: The core idea is stacking different processor types (analog and digital compute-in-memory units plus a neural processing unit) in 3D and using dynamic scheduling to balance work across layers instead of using a fixed allocation.

iccad-2025-091.method: The tool creates a single unified design process for multi-layer 3D chips, supporting both identical stacked layers and mixed chip types in one workflow. It starts by compacting the physical footprint while preserving all connections. Then it splits circuits across layers while respecting density limits for the tiny inter-layer connections called 3D vias. Speed-critical circuits are routed to faster layers to improve performance, and finally an algorithm trained by trial and error (reinforcement learning) automatically fixes any resulting connection violations.
iccad-2025-091.key_novelty: This is the first unified design framework that natively handles both identical-chip stacks and mixed-type 3D integration.

iccad-2025-084.method: The work presents an open CGRA ecosystem (a modular set of tools for building flexible reconfigurable hardware). It has three components: HyCUBE, a chip with reconfigurable data-routing wiring that completes all data transfers in a single cycle even when routing through multiple intermediate steps; PACE, which embeds HyCUBE in a complete RISC-V processor system for edge computing devices; and Morpher, an open-source framework that automatically adapts to different hardware designs and provides tools for design exploration, code compilation, simulation, and testing. The entire ecosystem is deliberately open at every layer—from hardware design to software tooling—to remove barriers to innovation.
iccad-2025-084.key_novelty: The key novelty is an open ecosystem for building reconfigurable accelerators, with a design framework that adapts to different hardware architectures, enabling customization and optimization across the entire hardware-software stack without being locked to any specific software implementation.

iccad-2025-104.method: RE-PNRL uses reinforcement learning (an AI technique that learns by trying different solutions and getting feedback) to reconstruct the missing parts of incomplete chip designs (partial netlists) by calculating node-level transition probabilities—the likelihood that different circuit components connect to each other. Once the netlist is complete, the system uses clustering (grouping similar patterns) to identify hardware trojans embedded in the design.
iccad-2025-104.key_novelty: It's the first hardware trojan detection system designed to work with the incomplete netlist information produced by real-world reverse engineering, instead of assuming you have a complete chip design.

iccad-2025-098.method: EarDVFS uses machine learning to automatically adjust mobile device processor speed, monitoring not just the processor itself but also ambient air temperature and heat from other components like battery and display. To prevent damage, it slows down the processor proactively before overheating occurs. The system learns the best strategy for each specific device, so the same approach works well across different phones. By tracking all heat sources instead of just processor temperature, it makes smarter throttling decisions.
iccad-2025-098.key_novelty: EarDVFS is the first machine learning-based system for mobile processor speed adjustment that adapts to its environment by tracking ambient temperature and heat from device components like battery and display.

iccad-2025-101.method: TETRIS is an FPGA accelerator (programmable hardware that speeds up calculations) that trains instance segmentation models on edge devices while reducing computational and memory demands through quantization (converting high-precision numbers to lower-precision). It uses two quantization techniques: channel-aware smoothing quantization, which reduces precision while respecting patterns in the data, and distribution-aware tie quantization, which handles repeated values intelligently. The hardware uses different types of processors: a reconfigurable convolution processing unit (a specialized calculator for neural networks) that adjusts to variable kernel sizes and a fully pipelined auxiliary processing unit that processes operations in parallel stages.
iccad-2025-101.key_novelty: TETRIS is the first FPGA accelerator specifically built to train instance segmentation models on resource-constrained edge devices.

iccad-2025-100.method: They convert photonic designs to electronic form, optimize them with standard chip-design software, and convert back to photonic layouts—reusing proven design methods. They apply this to design an optical clock tree (distributing light-based timing) and optical router (directing light signals), then fabricate and test a photonic interposer in thin-film lithium niobate.
iccad-2025-100.key_novelty: This is the first transformation that lets standard chip-design tools optimize photonic circuits, demonstrated by building a photonic interposer in thin-film lithium niobate.

iccad-2025-109.method: The accelerator uses compute-in-memory (CIM) technology, which processes data directly where it's stored in memory rather than moving it back and forth to a separate processor. It stores data in 256 kilobytes of SOT-MRAM (a fast magnetic memory) and uses adaptive compression that automatically adjusts data packing based on patterns in the sparse matrix. For MIMO precoding (the signal processing needed to send wireless data to multiple users simultaneously), this minimizes storage while keeping parallel calculations fast through CIM's design.
iccad-2025-109.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining compute-in-memory technology with adaptive data compression to efficiently handle the sparse matrix calculations that massive MIMO systems need for wireless precoding.

iccad-2025-103.method: DynVec uses MLIR, an intermediate representation for code, to automatically convert scalar operations into vector operations (where a single operation processes multiple data items simultaneously). It generates execution graphs showing how data flows through these vector operations, using flexible computational units that adapt to different vector sizes. Rather than making all scheduling decisions at compile time when memory access patterns are unknown, DynVec makes both vectorization and scheduling decisions at runtime, based on actual data patterns. This allows it to exploit parallelism opportunities in irregular workloads that traditional tools cannot vectorize.
iccad-2025-103.key_novelty: DynVec couples vectorization and dynamic scheduling in a single framework, allowing both to adapt based on runtime memory access patterns in irregular workloads.

iccad-2025-102.method: The device detects errors by reading each memory cell in two opposite ways (called dual-polarity reads) and comparing the results; when these readings differ, the device knows an error is occurring. To correct the errors, it uses a mathematical model that predicts how threshold voltage (the electrical level needed to read a cell) drifts over time, then automatically adjusts its read settings based on error patterns it observes.
iccad-2025-102.key_novelty: A memory technology called Selector-Only Memory can detect and correct its own errors without external hardware, by using only a dual-polarity read method—reading each cell in opposite directions to spot problems.

iccad-2025-108.method: Discriminate Weight Approximation (DWA) tests how much each weight affects the neural network's accuracy. Weights with little impact get stored with lower precision, saving chip area and LUT resources (hardware memory used to store values). Critical weights stay at full precision. This selective approach cuts hardware costs without the accuracy loss that happens when all weights get approximated indiscriminately.
iccad-2025-108.key_novelty: Selectively approximating only the weights that can tolerate lower precision, based on sensitivity analysis, rather than approximating all weights equally.
