iccad-2025-107.method: Robin compresses model weights using Partial Block Circulant Matrices (PBCM)—a technique that reshapes weights into circular block patterns to reduce memory needs while maintaining accuracy. It implements configurable circulant computing cores (specialized hardware blocks that efficiently perform operations on these circular patterns) that directly map onto DSP48E resources (the FPGA's math units), using a dual DSP packaging strategy to optimize utilization. The entire system is co-designed: software and hardware engineered together so the compressed weights and efficient cores work seamlessly, enabling more efficient inference than GPU-based approaches for this type of linear-attention model.
iccad-2025-107.key_novelty: The central idea is using Partial Block Circulant Matrices to compress weights while designing configurable hardware cores that efficiently execute these patterns on the FPGA's DSP units.

iccad-2025-105.method: SLTarch speeds up neural rendering on mobile GPUs by pairing algorithm changes with custom hardware accelerators. It adds a specialized data structure called SLTree and a hardware accelerator called LTcore to make level-of-detail search faster—the search for how much geometric detail to show in each pixel, which normally creates workload imbalance where some GPU cores get far more work than others. For the splatting step (blending neural network outputs into the final image), it uses an algorithm and hardware component called SPcore that prevents warp divergence—where GPU cores take different computation paths and waste cycles—and efficiently handles irregular memory access patterns.
iccad-2025-105.key_novelty: The core innovation is co-designing specialized hardware accelerators (LTcore and SPcore) with custom algorithms to directly eliminate the two bottlenecks of point-based neural rendering: workload imbalance in level-of-detail search and warp divergence in splatting.

iccad-2025-106.method: Hummingbird overcomes the 4GB memory limit of embedded FPGAs by using memory offloading—storing model data outside the chip and loading pieces in as needed—to run 8-billion-parameter LLMs. The design optimizes the FPGA's computing resources (DSP blocks and lookup tables, which are specialized hardware for math and logic operations) and power consumption on KV260 and ZCU104 embedded FPGAs, achieving 93-94% model bandwidth utilization (efficiently using the available capacity to move data between memory and the processor).
iccad-2025-106.key_novelty: Hummingbird is the first practical FPGA accelerator that runs LLaMA3-8B on embedded FPGAs by using intelligent memory offloading to work around their memory constraints.

iccad-2025-112.method: MMPack partitions an ultra-large chip into smaller sections (chiplets) arranged to minimize communication crossing mask boundaries—the seams where different manufacturing masks connect. Using hierarchical layout planning with alternating optimization (iteratively refining different parts of the design), it respects manufacturing constraints imposed by these seams. Finally, it applies physics models to identify high-stress regions near mask seams and through-silicon vias (vertical connections between layers), then redesigns them to reduce thermal and mechanical stress.
iccad-2025-112.key_novelty: MMPack is the first framework that jointly optimizes for both the manufacturing constraints of splitting chips across multiple production masks and the thermal-mechanical stress (damage from heat-induced material expansion) that concentrates at mask seams in ultra-large wafer-scale integration.

iccad-2025-111.method: STEM defends Vision Transformers against adversarial attacks by identifying and removing malicious image tokens (the discrete pieces the model processes). It combines Block-wise Selective Fusion, which groups tokens into blocks and merges redundant ones while flagging suspicious ones, with Identify-Prune, which removes flagged tokens based on the model's attention patterns (the internal calculations showing which tokens matter most). The defense runs on STEMA, a specialized hardware accelerator with a dedicated Security Core that performs token fusion, selects the top-k highest-priority tokens, and manages token metadata—using just 5% of the chip.
iccad-2025-111.key_novelty: The core innovation is a parallelizable token-removal defense combining selective fusion with statistical adversarial detection, implemented with minimal dedicated hardware.

iccad-2025-114.method: SNO protects FPGA-based network processing using three security components. Secure boot ensures trusted code loads without being tampered with. SNO Manager verifies the right code is running (attestation) and orchestrates the system alongside the CPU's trusted environment. SNO Guard encrypts and authenticates all packets using AES-GCM with a pipelined design—operations overlap to minimize slowdown.
iccad-2025-114.key_novelty: SNO is the first trusted execution environment for FPGA-based SmartNICs that combines secure boot, attestation (proof the right code is running), and encrypted packet protection without major performance overhead.

iccad-2025-113.method: RePM uses adaptable computation units (butterfly units) that eliminate the need for pre-computing values, combined with a memory layout that reduces data shuffling (conflict-free near-memory mapping). It applies two alternating computation strategies (radix-2 and radix-4) that together remove the setup and cleanup steps normally required for polynomial multiplication. This flexible design works with multiple post-quantum cryptography algorithms while meeting strict power budgets.
iccad-2025-113.key_novelty: Adaptive butterfly units with hybrid radix-2/4 computation and conflict-free memory mapping eliminate preprocessing steps in polynomial multiplication for cryptography.

iccad-2025-119.method: The approach combines software and custom hardware to speed up 3D Gaussian rendering on edge devices. A specialized hardware unit (called a pattern-aware rasterization unit) uses flood encoding to compactly represent which screen tiles need rendering, and applies k-means codebook compression (grouping similar patterns to reduce size) to keep the hardware small while maintaining visual accuracy. The GPU then streamlines the process by merging two steps—coverage testing (checking what's visible) and alpha blending (combining colors)—into one continuous pipeline, and processes screen tiles in groups with early depth-sorting (checking closer objects first) to avoid unnecessary work.
iccad-2025-119.key_novelty: Pattern-based tile rasterization using flood encoding and k-means codebook compression enables efficient 3D Gaussian rendering on edge devices.

iccad-2025-115.method: In 3D chip placement, calculating how components distribute across space (density gradients) becomes a bottleneck that worsens as grids grow larger. The approach applies the divergence theorem—a mathematical principle that converts expensive 3D volume calculations into simpler surface calculations—to speed up this computation. Implementations are provided for both CPU and GPU hardware.
iccad-2025-115.key_novelty: Applying the divergence theorem (converting 3D volume calculations to surface calculations) accelerates density gradient computation in 3D chip placement.

iccad-2025-110.method: RTPU is a reconfigurable multi-core hardware design that performs similar underlying operations for both regular unencrypted tensor math (plaintext) and encrypted homomorphic-encryption math (polynomial ring ciphertext), enabling the same hardware to handle both through fine-grained reconfiguration. It uses kernel group-based scheduling to organize and coordinate computations strategically, optimizing how much of the hardware gets used while maintaining consistent performance (quality of service) for multiple simultaneous jobs with different privacy requirements.
iccad-2025-110.key_novelty: A reconfigurable multi-core architecture that seamlessly switches between regular unencrypted tensor math (plaintext) and encrypted polynomial-ring computations, achieving substantial silicon reuse instead of requiring separate specialized accelerators.

iccad-2025-121.method: ComoPy framework lets you simulate and debug hardware designs using familiar software techniques. You can set breakpoints (pausing points to inspect code) and trace execution on hardware description language source lines, then hot-reload changes (recompile and reload without restarting) for quick debug-fix cycles. The framework lets you dynamically switch between fast low-level RTL simulation (register-transfer level, the detailed gate-by-gate logic) and higher-level HDL execution (hardware description language), letting you balance speed against visibility for each debugging task.
iccad-2025-121.key_novelty: The core idea is bringing software debugging techniques (breakpoints, tracing, hot-reloading) to hardware design verification by executing the hardware description language natively in a programming language.

iccad-2025-123.method: The approach uses a Physics-Informed Message Passing Neural Network (PIMNEM)—a neural network that bakes in the physics of Korhonen's equation, which models how electromigration damages interconnects. To handle large, complex interconnect patterns, it uses hierarchical graph partitioning (recursively dividing the interconnect network into smaller subgraphs). Each piece is trained on its own without labeled data, then the full system is fine-tuned using boundary constraints that enforce correct predictions where the pieces meet.
iccad-2025-123.key_novelty: Combining physics-informed graph neural networks with hierarchical adaptive partitioning makes it possible to solve multi-scale electromigration equations on large interconnect networks efficiently.

iccad-2025-120.method: The approach uses differentiable optimization (calculus-based search for better placements) with timing preconditioning that smooths out the optimization landscape, making solutions easier to find. It gradually adjusts the balance between wirelength and timing constraints using a multiplier scheduling scheme. To improve timing prediction accuracy, an XGBoost machine learning model learns to predict net delays from data, replacing manual timing estimates with learned predictions.
iccad-2025-120.key_novelty: It combines smooth calculus-based optimization with machine-learned delay prediction to better optimize both wirelength and timing in FPGA placement.

iccad-2025-116.method: The framework predicts available routing space during the initial global routing phase to enable better early decisions. It then adjusts all connection points (where wires attach to circuit elements) simultaneously across every wire rather than optimizing one at a time, which reduces total wire length. Finally, for each individual wire, it uses dynamic programming (an algorithm that efficiently explores path options) to find the route with the fewest wire segments while respecting I/O alignment constraints.
iccad-2025-116.key_novelty: It enables any-angle routing (wires can route in any direction, not just 90 or 135 degrees) through two-stage optimization of connection points across all wires, while satisfying I/O alignment constraints.

iccad-2025-127.method: The approach trains a neural network operator called DeepONet to learn how manufacturing conditions like temperature patterns create warpage—physical bending—in semiconductor chips. Physics laws are incorporated as constraints during training so the network's predictions respect the actual rules of how materials deform under heat. Once trained, the network instantly predicts warpage for new manufacturing scenarios, replacing expensive finite element method (FEM) simulations that normally require mesh generation and solving enormous systems of equations.
iccad-2025-127.key_novelty: Using a physics-informed neural network operator (DeepONet) to replace expensive computer simulations for predicting semiconductor chip warpage during manufacturing.

iccad-2025-125.method: The approach designs the algorithm and hardware together from the start, allowing them to optimize for each other rather than working independently. It reduces computational overhead by using lightweight math operations (simple calculations), data compression (making data smaller to move around faster), and pruning strategies (skipping branches that won't find results) that especially help with sparse graphs (networks where most possible connections don't exist). The resulting custom FPGA design (programmable circuit built for this specific job) runs on Zynq UltraScale+ hardware with only 4 GB of working memory (DRAM), consuming minimal energy.
iccad-2025-125.key_novelty: The core idea is designing the algorithm and hardware together as one system from the start, rather than separately, to enable efficient graph pattern counting while keeping memory use minimal.

iccad-2025-117.method: The algorithm uses multiple electrostatic systems—treating component placement like a physics problem where components repel each other like electric charges—to prevent overlaps while keeping movement minimal. It applies resistive forces based on non-Newtonian fluid physics (fluids whose thickness changes under stress), which gradually pull components back to their designated boundaries (called fence regions) when they drift out. This gradual restoration improves convergence and handles cases where components are permitted in multiple boundary types.
iccad-2025-117.key_novelty: Resistive forces based on non-Newtonian fluid physics (fluids whose thickness changes under stress) that gradually restore components to fence regions, combined with multi-electrostatic systems to prevent overlaps.

iccad-2025-124.method: The system uses a diffusion model (an AI technique that gradually clears noise to produce structured data) paired with neural networks to automatically create analog circuits at the transistor level. Rather than having engineers manually design each circuit, the system generates both the transistor arrangement and the settings for each device to meet specific performance targets. It measures success using the Circuit Generation Efficiency Index (CGEI), which combines how well the circuit performs (figure of merit) with how quickly it generates the design.
iccad-2025-124.key_novelty: This work uses diffusion models (AI that gradually refines random data into organized structures) to automate the complete generation of transistor-level analog circuits, from overall layout to individual component settings.

iccad-2025-126.method: DIVE avoids the problem of optimizing all transistor sizes at once, which becomes computationally infeasible when there are many parameters (a problem called curse of dimensionality). Instead, it uses information theory to identify which transistor sizes are most critical by calculating which parameters would provide the most useful information if optimized, while respecting design rules. It tunes only these critical transistors first using a machine learning technique called Gaussian process regression, which learns which parameters matter most and guides the search. As optimization progresses, it progressively adds more parameters to tune, mimicking how experienced circuit designers prioritize the most critical components.
iccad-2025-126.key_novelty: Progressive parameter expansion based on information theory, starting with the most critical transistor sizes and adding more as needed, mimicking how experienced circuit designers work.

iccad-2025-129.method: The approach replaces expensive matrix-vector multiplications in hyperdimensional computing's encoding and search phases with fast lookup operations. This is enabled by binary code quantization, which converts data into a discretized form that maps directly to lookup tables. These table lookups run on a custom FPGA (a programmable chip designed for specific applications) with an optimized pipeline.
iccad-2025-129.key_novelty: Replacing matrix-vector multiplications with lookup table operations to speed up hyperdimensional computing while keeping accuracy high.

iccad-2025-118.method: HIPPO estimates how much power an FPGA accelerator will consume by analyzing C/C++ source code directly, without waiting for the full synthesis process. It respects the code's natural structure—nested loops and operations at different levels—and builds power estimates that mirror this structure. The system converts the code into a hardware representation (a control/dataflow graph, tracking how data and operations connect), combines mathematical formulas with machine-learning models trained on real data, and filters out measurement noise through intelligent operation grouping. This multi-level approach lets designers estimate power during early design stages instead of waiting for expensive full synthesis runs.
iccad-2025-118.key_novelty: HIPPO estimates FPGA power consumption from C/C++ code before synthesis using multi-level power models that preserve the code's hierarchical structure.

iccad-2025-122.method: It speeds up timing analysis—predicting signal propagation through circuits—by running on a GPU (graphics processor) instead of a CPU. When designers modify the circuit, instead of recalculating everything from scratch, it updates only the affected paths using dual-CSR data structures (optimized storage formats) and incrementally recalculates dependency levels (how elements depend on each other). This approach efficiently handles both small timing adjustments and major structural changes like rearranging circuit components.
iccad-2025-122.key_novelty: First GPU-accelerated circuit timing analyzer that can efficiently handle both small modifications and major structural changes using dual-CSR data structures.

iccad-2025-132.method: The technique combines aggressive reduction of the thousands of I/O ports with projection-based model order reduction (PRIMA) to create a fast but approximate model. It runs expensive high-fidelity time-domain simulations on a limited set of test cases, then trains a compensation network—a machine-learning model—to learn the gap between the approximation and the accurate results. To efficiently capture how different ports correlate with each other, it uses a tensorized mapping technique, treating port data as multi-dimensional arrays so it doesn't need exponentially more data.
iccad-2025-132.key_novelty: It combines a fast reduced-order model with a learned compensation network that corrects approximation errors, making model reduction practical for systems with tens of thousands of ports.

iccad-2025-130.method: The processor speeds up MoE inference on an FPGA using three coordinated techniques. First, it removes unimportant weights from experts based on how often each expert gets used (keeping 25–75% depending on the usage pattern, expressed as ratios like 1:4 to 8:8), and stores numbers in space-saving formats (16-bit, 8-bit, or 4-bit precision). Second, it predicts which experts the next layer will need with an 83.4% success rate, so the hardware can load them in advance. Third, it uses a reconfigurable grid of processing cores (a systolic array) that can efficiently compute with both sparse weights and mixed-precision numbers in parallel.
iccad-2025-130.key_novelty: It predicts which experts to use next and removes weights from rarely-used experts, both strategies guided by expert activation patterns, so prediction and pruning work as one system.

iccad-2025-131.method: The approach uses two separate analysis paths: a transformer neural network finds timing patterns in the voltage/current waveforms at chip inputs, while a graph neural network analyzes the structural relationships in the hardware design code (RTL). These separate analyses are then aligned through self-supervised contrastive learning (training by comparing different versions of the data) and combined using a lightweight fusion module. Finally, a power prediction layer estimates the power consumption for one clock cycle.
iccad-2025-131.key_novelty: The key insight is processing waveform timing patterns and circuit structure through separate analytical pathways before combining them to predict power consumption.

iccad-2025-134.method: The approach represents each standard cell as a Topology-Geometry Graph (TGG)—a combined representation capturing both the circuit's logical connections and its physical layout. Rather than training on massive datasets, it uses prototype learning: identifying recurring structural patterns in CMOS logic and common routing configurations, then reusing these patterns to predict power, performance, and area for new cells with minimal training data.
iccad-2025-134.key_novelty: The core idea is representing circuits as Topology-Geometry Graphs that combine logic and layout, then using prototype learning to identify and reuse structural patterns across different cells.

iccad-2025-133.method: The approach gathers information about a chip design from two sources: an LLM (language model trained on domain knowledge) reads the written design descriptions, while a graph neural network analyzes the actual circuit structure (Chisel-compiled RTL). A multilayer neural network combines these two perspectives to predict performance, using Monte Carlo dropout—running the prediction multiple times with random variations—to measure prediction confidence. The entire system trains together using Bayesian optimization, which automatically searches for the best settings.
iccad-2025-133.key_novelty: It combines semantic understanding from written descriptions (LLM) with structural understanding from circuit code (graph neural network) to capture richer information about chip designs for design space exploration.

iccad-2025-136.method: Wit-HW generates passing test cases (called witness cases) in addition to analyzing the initial failing test case. It compares which lines of hardware code execute in the passing cases versus the failing case to identify which lines are innocent and cannot contain the bug. To create effective witness cases, it uses mutation-based testing—systematically modifying the code to try different versions—to find passing cases that are especially good at revealing where the actual bug is.
iccad-2025-136.key_novelty: Using passing test cases (witness cases) combined with execution comparison between passing and failing runs to pinpoint bugs in hardware designs.

iccad-2025-128.method: Detailed placement—deciding exactly where each component goes on a chip to minimize wiring—normally requires searching through millions of possibilities, which is slow on CPUs. This approach uses a GPU to speed up the search by running SROA (Simultaneous Row and Order Assignment), a two-step process: first, dynamic programming (systematically evaluating options) assigns each component to a row, then heuristics (practical tricks) fine-tune positions within that row. Since GPUs compute many possibilities in parallel, this method explores far more possible arrangements than CPU methods, finding better placements.
iccad-2025-128.key_novelty: The core innovation is the SROA algorithm, which combines row assignment and cell positioning so that GPUs can accelerate the search for better chip layouts.

iccad-2025-137.method: CoXplorer breaks the combined problem of compressing AI models and designing hardware accelerators into stages, making the search space easier to explore. The AC-Copilot toolchain predicts performance at multiple levels of detail—from hardware simulations through to compiled code. The system identifies performance bottlenecks (the slowest parts) at each level and uses these insights to coordinate decisions about model compression and hardware design together.
iccad-2025-137.key_novelty: CoXplorer stages the algorithm-hardware co-design exploration and uses multi-level performance bottleneck analysis to guide model compression and hardware optimization together.

iccad-2025-138.method: Coflex combines a Sparse Gaussian Process (a model that learns from past accelerator designs to predict which new designs will work well) with multi-objective Bayesian optimization (a search algorithm that balances competing design goals). It simplifies the mathematical calculations from cubic to near-linear complexity, making the model much faster while keeping predictions accurate. This enables efficient exploration of large design spaces that would otherwise require prohibitive computational cost.
iccad-2025-138.key_novelty: Sparse Gaussian Process combined with multi-objective Bayesian optimization reduces accelerator design search complexity from cubic to near-linear, making large-scale exploration practical.

iccad-2025-142.method: R2T-Tiny reconfigures the FPGA hardware while running, dynamically switching between two acceleration types per neural network layer: pipelined designs (which process multiple data items in parallel for speed) and systolic designs (which arrange computations in regular grids for efficiency). Each layer also uses tailored approximations—simplified calculations that sacrifice tiny amounts of accuracy for faster processing and smaller hardware footprint. This combination lets the system use exactly the throughput and resources needed per layer.
iccad-2025-142.key_novelty: The key innovation is the ability to reconfigure the accelerator while running, allowing the system to switch between pipelined and systolic acceleration strategies at the layer level to optimize throughput on resource-constrained FPGAs.

iccad-2025-144.method: Opto-ViT splits computation between photonic (light-based) and electronic processors: the photonic half uses lasers called VCSELs and microring resonators—optical devices that manipulate light—to rapidly multiply large matrices, while the electronic half handles operations that are difficult to implement with light, such as nonlinear functions and normalization. A lightweight network examines the image and identifies which regions matter, then skips processing the irrelevant patches. The vision transformer model is prepared for this hybrid approach through quantization-aware training (learning while simulating the lower precision the photonic hardware will use) and matrix decomposition (splitting large matrices into smaller pieces that fit the photonic constraints).
iccad-2025-144.key_novelty: A photonic hardware accelerator positioned near image sensors that speeds up vision transformers on edge devices by skipping irrelevant patches and splitting computation between photonic and electronic processors.

iccad-2025-141.method: NSTherm combines a neural network—trained to predict heat distribution rapidly—with stochastic methods that use random sampling to solve equations reliably. To handle different chip shapes without retraining, it uses diffeomorphic mapping (a mathematical technique for smoothly transforming one shape into another while preserving structure). The neural network guides the stochastic method to reduce noise in results, while the stochastic calculations verify the neural predictions and prove accuracy bounds.
iccad-2025-141.key_novelty: NSTherm's core idea is pairing a fast neural network with stochastic verification through mathematical shape-deformation (diffeomorphic mapping) to guarantee accurate thermal simulation across varying chip geometries.

iccad-2025-148.method: The framework uses artificial intelligence to predict how signals behave in circuit boards, replacing slow computer simulations. It learns by analyzing 3D structures where traces (copper wires) run on multiple layers and interact electromagnetically—the way electric fields from one trace influence others nearby. By understanding these multi-layer interactions, it predicts S-parameters (measurements of signal behavior) across frequencies from DC to 1 gigahertz.
iccad-2025-148.key_novelty: Using artificial intelligence to model multi-layer electromagnetic interactions in circuit boards, replacing slow computer simulation for S-parameter prediction.

iccad-2025-147.method: M3 uses a machine-learning system called Mamba combined with model-based reinforcement learning (learning through trial-and-error guided by predictions) to design multiple circuits with different topologies (physical layouts) simultaneously. The system includes a dynamic scheduling mechanism that adjusts the balance between exploring new design possibilities and refining promising ones. Because it learns to handle different circuit topologies directly, it works without needing manual adjustments for each circuit type.
iccad-2025-147.key_novelty: A single learning system that optimizes multiple circuits with different physical layouts at once, without needing manual reconfiguration for each circuit type.

iccad-2025-145.method: HyDra accelerates hyperdimensional computing (a computation method using massive high-dimensional vectors) by performing critical operations directly in memory using SOT-MRAM, a fast and energy-efficient magnetic memory technology configured as a CAM—searchable memory that finds matching content rather than retrieving by fixed address. This architecture supports three key operations in-memory: binding (combining vectors through bitwise operations), permutation (rearranging bit order), and similarity search (measuring how closely vectors match). A bit-drop permutation method—which skips certain bit positions during rearrangement—reduces latency by 6x. Additional optimizations for addition operations and four-stage voltage scaling (which reduces power loss in interconnects) further decrease energy consumption and chip area.
iccad-2025-145.key_novelty: HyDra pairs SOT-MRAM based CAM (searchable memory using magnetic storage) with a bit-drop permutation technique that rearranges bits more efficiently, achieving 6x speedup in hyperdimensional computing.

iccad-2025-139.method: CIMWise is an AI compiler built on IREE that automatically finds the best way to run AI models on CIM (computing-in-memory) processors. It improves on existing CIM compilers by tuning both hardware settings (like memory and timing) and dataflow patterns (how data moves through the computation), because a workload's performance depends on how these factors interact. The compiler searches this space systematically using a two-stage simulated annealing algorithm—a technique that gradually explores and refines possibilities—with an adaptable on-chip memory model and operator-level optimizations to fine-tune each part of the model.
iccad-2025-139.key_novelty: CIMWise auto-tunes both hardware parameters and dataflow characteristics to find optimal scheduling strategies for CIM processors.

iccad-2025-143.method: SERA-Float protects the most important bits (sign and exponent, which control a number's sign and magnitude) using error-correcting codes—redundant bits that can automatically fix errors. Rather than discarding the least important precision bits, it keeps 8 valid mantissa bits (the digits representing the number) and intelligently tracks which bits are critical to prevent overflow (when numbers get too large), underflow (when numbers get too small), and NaN exceptions (invalid results). Smaller arithmetic circuits can exploit this format, reducing energy use while maintaining protection against random hardware errors.
iccad-2025-143.key_novelty: SERA-Float combines error-correcting codes with critical bit tracking to protect approximate floating-point computation against both hardware errors and the exceptions they trigger.

iccad-2025-150.method: CROP retrieves similar successful circuit designs from past projects along with their design rules, providing this context to a large language model (LLM) to generate parameter recommendations. The recommended parameters are applied to the circuit, and their performance is measured against the design goals. Based on how well each recommendation worked, the LLM generates improved suggestions for the next iteration, and this cycle repeats until the design meets the performance targets.
iccad-2025-150.key_novelty: The core contribution is using an LLM that learns from past successful circuit designs to automatically generate parameter recommendations, replacing the manual tuning experts normally do.

iccad-2025-152.method: DiSPlace places transistors on a chip by searching for opportunities to combine adjacent diffusion regions—the areas of semiconductor material that transistors are built from—into shared zones that save space and reduce wire lengths. While arranging the transistors, the algorithm identifies which pairs can safely share diffusion without violating electrical constraints or timing requirements, using optimization to find the best overall layout.
iccad-2025-152.key_novelty: It integrates diffusion-sharing optimization directly into transistor placement instead of handling it as a separate step.

iccad-2025-135.method: ScanNow breaks sparse matrices into 'scan windows'—regions it processes in sequence—and automatically adjusts each window's size based on the actual data patterns it encounters, keeping frequently-used data in fast local storage to reduce unpredictable memory access. The architecture dynamically balances how much input versus output data to keep in this local storage based on what's happening in real time, rather than using a fixed ratio. This design lets multiple operations run in parallel, maximizing how busy the hardware stays.
iccad-2025-135.key_novelty: The innovation is a 'scan window' task dispatch method that automatically adjusts window sizes and input/output data buffering based on real sparsity patterns, processing the matrix row by row.

iccad-2025-146.method: The framework simulates how unwanted quantum interactions (called cross-Kerr effects) behave in superconducting Transmon-Tunable Coupler-Transmon (TTT) systems and measures how accurately controlled-phase (CPhase) quantum gates perform between two three-level quantum systems under realistic noise. It then jointly optimizes both the control signals and device design to find the best conditions—specifically the target resonant frequency—that enable these gates to work more reliably using adiabatic schemes, where quantum states are gradually adjusted to maintain their integrity.
iccad-2025-146.key_novelty: A simulation framework that predicts and optimizes the accuracy of quantum gates in three-level quantum systems (called qudits), specifically superconducting Transmon-Tunable Coupler-Transmon (TTT) devices.

iccad-2025-154.method: Mass spectrometry spectral search normally copies gigabytes of data back and forth between storage and processors, creating a bottleneck. FeNOMS solves this by embedding the search algorithm directly in 3D FeNAND storage hardware (stacked layers of ferroelectric storage chips). The algorithm — hyperdimensional computing, which represents each spectrum as a point in high-dimensional space and finds matches by comparing these points — runs fast enough inside the storage hardware itself to complete searches without moving data.
iccad-2025-154.key_novelty: This is the first time hyperdimensional computing has been used for mass spectrometry search by embedding the computation directly inside 3D FeNAND storage hardware.

iccad-2025-157.method: MASIM coordinates computational tasks across multiple SIMD processing arrays—specialized processors that perform the same operation on many data items in parallel and are positioned near memory. It reduces data copying by strategically assigning each task to whichever array already has its input data close by, avoiding wasteful movement of data between the memory system and the different processing arrays.
iccad-2025-157.key_novelty: MASIM optimizes across multiple processing arrays to keep data local, directly reducing the copy instructions typically needed to move data between memory and processing.

iccad-2025-151.method: The system uses MetaSchedule, a probabilistic framework (software that explores possibilities through sampling to find good solutions), to automatically search for effective ways to arrange tensor programs (mathematical operations on arrays) for RISC-V vector extensions (processor instructions for parallel computation). It tests strategies like loop tiling (breaking computations into smaller chunks), vectorization (grouping operations to run in parallel), and memory optimization (arranging data for faster access).
iccad-2025-151.key_novelty: MetaSchedule, which uses probabilistic search (exploring possibilities through sampling), is adapted here to automatically optimize tensor programs for RISC-V vector extensions (processor instructions for parallel computation).

iccad-2025-155.method: MM-GRADE retrieves relevant documentation by searching across both text passages and visual materials like diagrams and screenshots. It combines retrieval-augmented generation (searching a documentation database to find relevant content) with vision language model finetuning (customizing a model that interprets images to specialize in EDA tools). This allows the model to understand and reason across text and images simultaneously when answering questions.
iccad-2025-155.key_novelty: The innovation is making retrieval-augmented generation work across mixed documentation types—text, diagrams, and screenshots—by customizing a vision language model for EDA tools.

iccad-2025-156.method: BIGX takes Van Ginneken's buffer insertion algorithm—which determines where to place buffers (signal-boosting circuit elements) to fix timing violations—and runs it on GPU instead of CPU. Instead of computing sequentially, it breaks the problem into independent subproblems that GPU threads can solve in parallel, while optimizing how data flows through GPU memory to avoid the bottlenecks that slow down CPU versions.
iccad-2025-156.key_novelty: Parallel GPU implementation of Van Ginneken's buffer insertion algorithm for timing-violation recovery.

iccad-2025-159.method: Tiny-Align makes automatic speech recognition and language models work together on tiny devices like Raspberry Pi. It uses three techniques: knowledge distillation (transferring what a large model learned into a small one), quantization (storing numbers using fewer bits to save memory), and cross-modal fusion (efficiently combining speech and language outputs). These techniques are designed to fit within the severe memory and computing limits of edge devices.
iccad-2025-159.key_novelty: Framework for combining automatic speech recognition with language models on tiny devices like Raspberry Pi.

iccad-2025-158.method: COBRA builds a specialized hardware accelerator (using programmable FPGA chips) that runs Transformer models by representing weights and activations as 1-bit values (either 0 or 1 instead of full numbers). This representation converts multiplication operations into much simpler binary logic gates (AND and XOR operations), which require far less energy and silicon area. The FPGA design is optimized to maximize prediction throughput while keeping energy consumption low for edge device deployment.
iccad-2025-158.key_novelty: COBRA's core idea is using 1-bit multiplications in an FPGA-based Transformer to reduce energy use for edge device inference.

iccad-2025-160.method: GeoFA represents 2D layout patterns as a finite automaton—a state machine designed to recognize specific pattern sequences. This automaton can scan through a chip layout and identify matches more efficiently than brute-force geometric search, because it follows predefined recognition paths rather than trying all possible geometric comparisons. The pattern specifications are encoded as states and transitions in the automaton, so the machine knows exactly what to look for and how to recognize it.
iccad-2025-160.key_novelty: GeoFA applies finite automaton theory to 2D layout pattern matching, representing patterns as state machines to efficiently recognize matches in chip layouts.

iccad-2025-162.method: PipeSDFA trains spiking neural networks (SNNs—networks that operate through discrete pulses like biological neurons) using a specialized accelerator built from RRAM, a memory technology that performs arithmetic operations directly at the storage location. The forward pass (computing network outputs) uses analog multiply-accumulate circuits—this avoids the energy cost of moving data between memory and processor. For learning, it applies Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), a method that adjusts weights using direct feedback signals rather than computing gradients through every layer. RRAM's programmable resistance properties enable the hardware to implement both the forward computation and DFA weight updates efficiently.
iccad-2025-162.key_novelty: This is the first system to train spiking neural networks on RRAM hardware using Direct Feedback Alignment, combining analog in-memory computation with a brain-inspired learning algorithm.

iccad-2025-163.method: Orthrus solves the problem of finding the best application settings, hardware architecture, and semiconductor manufacturing choices all at once by using two search strategies together. Bayesian optimization (a technique that learns which settings look promising as it searches) handles refined searching, while differential evolution (which tests variations across many candidate solutions) handles broad exploration across the entire space. This dual approach lets you efficiently navigate the enormous number of possible combinations without having to check every single one.
iccad-2025-163.key_novelty: Orthrus efficiently optimizes application parameters, hardware architecture, and semiconductor technology choices simultaneously by combining Bayesian optimization for refined search with differential evolution for broad exploration.

iccad-2025-153.method: Clay is an open-source toolkit that automates designing ASIPs (application-specific processors—custom chips optimized for a single job). Engineers use it to specify which instructions they want, how those instructions behave in hardware, and how to maintain state (data stored in the processor) across instructions. The toolkit simulates the design and tests different instruction combinations to find the optimal set for the application.
iccad-2025-153.key_novelty: It's an open-source ASIP design toolkit with explicit support for stateful instructions and microarchitecture-aware customization—capabilities existing frameworks lack.

iccad-2025-161.method: 3D-MoE physically stacks memory and compute layers together, placing an LLM's expert networks directly next to DRAM instead of keeping them far apart. It distributes both the data and the experts across these stacked layers—different layers handle different experts while different data flows through others. This keeps data physically close to where computation happens, eliminating the slow bandwidth bottleneck that normally occurs when experts need to access distant memory.
iccad-2025-161.key_novelty: The core idea is using 3D stacking to place memory and compute next to each other, then splitting both experts and data across the layers so information stays close to processors.

iccad-2025-164.method: CIMTester is a compiler that automatically creates self-testing circuits for compute-in-memory (CIM) chips—systems that do calculations within memory instead of using separate processors. It combines reusable templates (blueprints encoding common fault patterns and how to detect them) to generate efficient test circuits matched to each CIM system's memory layout. This enables comprehensive fault detection built directly into the chip.
iccad-2025-164.key_novelty: CIMTester is a compiler that uses reusable fault-test templates to automatically create complete self-testing circuits for compute-in-memory chips.

iccad-2025-166.method: CIDRE automatically finds the most frequently-executed parts of RISC-V programs by measuring where code spends the most time—these critical sections are called hot spots. It suggests custom instructions (new machine operations) tailored to those hot spots and describes them formally in nML, a hardware specification language. The tool then uses EDA (Electronic Design Automation) software to evaluate each instruction's worth: how much it speeds up the program versus how much chip area and power it adds.
iccad-2025-166.key_novelty: It automates the entire process of designing RISC-V processors with custom instructions, from automatically detecting performance-critical code to generating the matching instructions.

iccad-2025-165.method: BARQ adds constraints during training that keep numeric values within the range of the low-precision converter, preventing overflow and clipping errors where values get cut off. It uses a mathematical technique (Euclidean projection) to initialize the model's weights in a way that minimizes quantization error from the beginning. This approach also makes weights sparse (randomly setting some to zero), which reduces computation and helps training converge faster and more reliably.
iccad-2025-165.key_novelty: The core innovation is adding constraints during training based on the low-precision converter's boundary limits to prevent overflow errors during inference.

iccad-2025-171.method: The approach uses a deep learning model (a convolutional neural network or CNN—a type of AI trained to find patterns in data) to detect side-channel leaks in FPGA-based hyperdimensional computing hardware, where side-channels are unintended physical signals like power consumption or electromagnetic emissions that reveal what data is being processed. It improves accuracy by using Grad-CAM (a technique that identifies which parts of the sensor data are most revealing), which iteratively pinpoints the measurement regions most useful for extracting the secret hypervector bits and strengthens the signal-to-noise ratio. The paper also introduces dynamic masking as a protective countermeasure against such attacks.
iccad-2025-171.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining a neural network with automated attention mapping (Grad-CAM) to discover which physical signals are most useful for extracting secrets from hyperdimensional computing accelerators.

iccad-2025-169.method: HyperEF 2.0 coarsens hypergraphs (groups of densely interconnected nodes) by measuring node distances through an expanded mathematical search space — specifically, Krylov subspace expansion using both clique and star connection patterns — to better estimate 'effective resistance' (the structural distance between nodes). It then groups nearby nodes together using this resistance metric (resistance-based local clustering), merging them into larger supergroups while keeping the partition balanced. Finally, it integrates this process into multilevel partitioning, recursively coarsening at multiple scales while adjusting hyperedge weights and applying community detection to maintain solution quality.
iccad-2025-169.key_novelty: The key innovation is using an expanded mathematical search space (Krylov subspace expansion with clique and star patterns) to measure node distances more accurately as 'effective resistance,' then grouping nodes based on this resistance metric to simplify hypergraphs while maintaining solution balance.

iccad-2025-170.method: BAGNet models an SRAM chip as a graph of connected memory cells and uses a neural network to learn patterns in this physical structure, summarizing each cell's characteristics. It builds a fast approximation model that predicts chip performance, adapting to focus on boundaries between column groups where parasitic effects (unwanted electrical interactions in tightly-packed cells) cause failures. Instead of running expensive circuit simulations, it uses targeted sampling to concentrate simulation effort on risky scenarios and estimate overall yield—the percentage of manufactured chips that will work.
iccad-2025-170.key_novelty: BAGNet replaces circuit simulation with a neural network that models SRAM's physical structure and adapts to catch failures at column boundaries where parasitic effects are strongest.

iccad-2025-168.method: ADO-KT uses large language models to extract design knowledge from past analog circuits and organize it into a knowledge graph—a structured map of how design concepts relate. It then verifies this knowledge graph to ensure accuracy. Finally, it applies these insights to new circuit designs in a way that works regardless of circuit type, allowing design knowledge to transfer between fundamentally different circuits.
iccad-2025-168.key_novelty: Large language models can build knowledge graphs that transfer analog circuit design knowledge between different circuit types.

iccad-2025-174.method: The approach uses a feedback loop: measure the ADC, then refine a mathematical model of its behavior in real-time using an Extended Kalman Filter (a statistical technique for tracking systems with uncertainty). Instead of following a fixed test plan, it selects each new measurement based on where the model is least confident, concentrating testing effort where information gain is highest. As the model improves, measurements narrow to progressively tighter intervals in critical regions, and the method directly calculates which capacitor manufacturing imperfections (mismatches) are causing linearity errors.
iccad-2025-174.key_novelty: The method uses the model's uncertainty to decide which measurements to take next, rather than following a predetermined test sequence.

iccad-2025-179.method: The approach uses a Graph Neural Network (an AI trained on interconnected data) to predict which regions of a large circuit netlist (the description of how electronic components connect) are likely to contain the target circuit pattern. It trains using both positive examples of real matches and negative samples (similar-looking non-matches) so the model learns to tell them apart accurately. Rather than running the neural network separately for every possible location in the circuit—which is computationally expensive—the method directly extracts numerical representations of circuit patterns that capture the whole circuit's structure at once. This filters the search down to the most promising regions before doing expensive detailed matching on individual candidates.
iccad-2025-179.key_novelty: It predicts which regions of the circuit likely contain the target pattern first using a neural network, then applies detailed matching only to those regions instead of checking every location.

iccad-2025-167.method: QuickFlow recognizes that convolution mappings with the same data reuse patterns perform similarly, so it groups equivalent mappings together. It quickly selects the best group and uses greedy local search—making locally optimal choices—to fine-tune the mapping within that group. It also applies an analytical model that calculates exact tile sizes (the size of computation chunks) for any convolution, avoiding trial-and-error sizing.
iccad-2025-167.key_novelty: QuickFlow reduces the mapping search space by grouping convolution mappings with equivalent data reuse patterns and only exploring representative solutions from each group rather than trying every possible combination.

iccad-2025-177.method: The approach converts quantum gate matrices to integers, which require less memory to store and compute faster than decimal numbers. Quantum gates have an inherent mathematical structure with real and imaginary parts (the two components that make up the complex numbers representing quantum operations). By splitting these parts and skipping calculations where values are zero, the scheme reduces both the number of arithmetic operations and the memory needed.
iccad-2025-177.key_novelty: Representing quantum gates as integers and using their mathematical structure to skip zero-value calculations reduces the total arithmetic work.

iccad-2025-173.method: TREX-F uses X-ray microscopy (detailed X-ray imaging taken from specific angles) to capture the natural manufacturing defects in circuit boards—solder irregularities, uneven material deposition, and microscopic surface anomalies. It applies computer vision techniques to extract a unique fingerprint from these X-ray images: Canny edge detection and SIFT identify distinctive features and patterns, contour detection traces shapes, and PCA reduces the data to what matters most. Finally, it converts this fingerprint into authentication codes in QR and data-matrix barcode formats that can be scanned to verify the board's authenticity.
iccad-2025-173.key_novelty: Circuit boards are authenticated by creating unique fingerprints from their natural manufacturing defects, captured via X-ray imaging and analyzed with computer vision.

iccad-2025-180.method: The approach uses open-source tools to add custom instructions (new operations) to RISC-V processors (an open-source chip design standard) that handle machine-learning operations. Specifically, it defines instructions for quantized LSTM inference (a compressed type of neural network) and table-based function approximation (using lookup tables instead of calculating functions). These new instructions integrate into the standard RISC-V software toolchain by encoding them as instruction types and creating memory-mapped control registers (special memory addresses that control the accelerator).
iccad-2025-180.key_novelty: An open-source software toolflow that lets designers add custom machine-learning accelerator instructions to RISC-V processors, demonstrated with quantized LSTM inference and table-based function approximation.

iccad-2025-185.method: Build custom circuits on reconfigurable hardware (FPGAs) that accelerate three hash functions designed for zero-knowledge proofs: Griffin, Rescue-Prime, and Concrete. The circuits use specialized calculation paths for modular arithmetic (operations within a finite mathematical field) and pipeline stages so multiple operations overlap in time. Process multiple hashes in parallel while optimizing how the hardware fetches and stores data to reduce delays during proof generation.
iccad-2025-185.key_novelty: Accelerate zero-knowledge proof generation by building customized FPGA circuits that speed up its bottleneck hash functions (Griffin, Rescue-Prime, Concrete) through optimized modular arithmetic and pipelined calculation stages.

iccad-2025-181.method: Merkle trees (tree structures that verify data integrity by detecting any changes) used in DNN accelerators suffer from poor memory locality because fixed storage layouts force distant branches that are accessed together to be far apart in memory. The system uses affine address transformations (mathematical formulas that remap where data sits in memory) to dynamically reorganize the tree layout, keeping frequently-accessed branches closer together in cache and scratchpad storage. By monitoring actual access patterns at runtime in heterogeneous systems with both CPUs and GPUs, it continuously adapts the tree organization to reduce memory latency.
iccad-2025-181.key_novelty: Dynamic affine address transformation of Merkle tree layout based on runtime access patterns in heterogeneous DNN accelerators.

iccad-2025-172.method: PROFUZZ combines two techniques: automatic structural analysis of hardware (ATPG) and directed graybox fuzzing (testing that targets specific hardware parts using partial knowledge of their design). Rather than creating random starting test cases, PROFUZZ leverages ATPG's understanding of hardware structure to generate smarter seeds for each module. This approach enables precise testing of specific hardware components and better scalability for large designs.
iccad-2025-172.key_novelty: The core idea is using ATPG (automatic structural analysis of hardware) to generate smarter starting test cases for directed fuzzing of specific modules.

iccad-2025-182.method: The approach reduces number precision in small language models using low-bit formats (INT8 and INT4—8 or 4 bits per number instead of 32) and tailors this reduction to the model's architecture. It implements this on edge CPUs and microcontrollers using code optimized for SIMD (a CPU feature that processes many numbers in parallel). To maintain accuracy despite this aggressive shrinking, it uses knowledge distillation (training the small model with guidance from a larger one) and activation-aware quantization (cutting precision more aggressively in less-important computational parts). This combination keeps the models accurate while fitting them onto memory-limited edge devices.
iccad-2025-182.key_novelty: The core innovation is a complete quantization system that reduces small language models to run on SIMD-capable edge processors while maintaining accuracy.

iccad-2025-175.method: The attack measures power consumption from a FrodoKEM hardware implementation (FPGA) using ~10,000 power traces from specially crafted test inputs. Statistical analysis called correlation power analysis identifies patterns in the power measurements that correspond to the secret encryption key. The implementation protects certain operations (matrix multiplication and addition) using random noise masking—one layer of noise protection called first-order masking—but leaves other operations unprotected. By analyzing power leakage from the unprotected operations, the attack recovers secret matrix rows and breaks the encryption.
iccad-2025-175.key_novelty: Incomplete masking allows an attack to break first-order masked FrodoKEM through power analysis when protection doesn't cover all operations.

iccad-2025-178.method: Uses a graph transformer (a machine learning model for understanding interconnected structures like circuits) to predict timing problems before a chip is fully wired. It incorporates spatial awareness through distance-aware self-attention and positional encoding tailored to circuit geometry—encoding the fact that nearby signals propagate faster than distant ones. Working at the placement stage (when components are positioned but connections not yet routed), it identifies timing violations that would normally emerge only after routing. When violations are detected, the framework preemptively adjusts required arrival times to resolve them before they occur.
iccad-2025-178.key_novelty: Using a graph transformer with spatial distance encoding to predict and prevent the timing violations caused by routing variations, starting at the chip placement stage.

iccad-2025-184.method: Bounded model checking (formal verification of all possible execution paths up to a fixed depth) identifies the constraints—the rules and limits—that RISC-V instructions must follow. Fuzzing (automated random testing) then uses these constraints to focus on corner cases that the formal method couldn't explore deeply. This creates a feedback loop: formal verification narrows the search space by identifying what matters, and fuzzing scales testing across that narrowed space to catch bugs that either technique alone would miss.
iccad-2025-184.key_novelty: Combining formal verification and fuzzing (automated random testing) with constraints from verification guiding fuzzing's search toward corner cases in RISC-V processors.

iccad-2025-186.method: The team implemented Mamba—a sequence-processing model—on an FPGA, which is reprogrammable hardware that accelerates computation. To overcome memory bottlenecks from processing tokens (smallest input units) one at a time, they merged multiple tokens together, reducing the effective sequence length. They also optimized the hardware circuit to process only selected tokens and built an efficient memory system to store the state vector (the model's running context). These changes eliminate the memory access delays that normally limit FPGA throughput.
iccad-2025-186.key_novelty: Token merging—combining multiple input tokens—eliminates the memory delays that bottleneck Mamba on FPGAs, improving throughput and energy efficiency.

iccad-2025-176.method: The architecture uses Spin-Orbit Torque MRAM (a magnetic memory technology) built into a Computing-In-Memory system—hardware that runs neural network calculations directly in memory. Each memory cell includes two read ports and one write port (a 2R1W configuration): one read port for inference, and the other read port plus the write port for on-chip learning. This dual-access design allows the system to simultaneously read weights for inference and write updated weights for learning without interrupting the network's computation.
iccad-2025-176.key_novelty: Spin-Orbit Torque MRAM (magnetic memory) in a Computing-In-Memory system with simultaneous read-write capability, enabling neural networks to continuously learn without pausing inference.

iccad-2025-183.method: The approach represents a circuit as a network of electrical components and their connections (called a graph), then trains a machine learning model using pairs of similar and different circuits so it learns which connections affect parasitics—the unwanted electrical properties that slow down circuits. Because training data tends to have many examples of common parasitic types but few rare ones, the method rebalances these categories so the model learns to handle all types equally well. With this combination of graph-based learning and balanced data, models trained on one set of circuits can make good predictions on entirely new circuit designs without retraining.
iccad-2025-183.key_novelty: Combining graph-based contrastive learning with label rebalancing enables parasitic element predictions to transfer across different AMS circuit designs.

iccad-2025-190.method: The method predicts routing costs during the placement stage—the step where qubits are assigned to positions—for neutral atom quantum computers. It models zone constraints (regions where qubits can't directly connect) and the overhead of routing signals between zones. It uses simulated annealing (an optimization technique that gradually improves solutions through random trials) or graph-based heuristics (algorithms that treat the problem as a network) to find placements that work reliably and efficiently.
iccad-2025-190.key_novelty: The core idea is combining qubit placement decisions with routing-cost prediction for neutral atom quantum computers with zoned constraints (areas where qubits must route through intermediate zones instead of connecting directly).

iccad-2025-194.method: Train a machine learning model (a graph neural network) on experiments where deliberate errors are injected into circuits to see how they spread through the design. The model learns to predict which errors are most dangerous for safety and uses explainable techniques (like graph attention) to show exactly which circuit connections matter for each prediction. Validate the model against standard fault injection benchmarks.
iccad-2025-194.key_novelty: A machine learning model that verifies automotive chip designs meet ISO 26262 safety standards by predicting which circuit errors are dangerous and explaining how those errors would propagate.

iccad-2025-187.method: The system learns circuit representations without human-labeled examples using contrastive learning—comparing different descriptions of the same circuits to learn what makes them similar or different. It uses two complementary descriptions: AND-inverter graphs (logic gates showing how computation flows) and netlists (component connections showing physical layout). The learning process encourages the system to recognize when these two different views describe the same circuit, while distinguishing it from different circuits. This creates a unified understanding that captures both logical behavior and physical structure, making it robust even when the two views don't perfectly align.
iccad-2025-187.key_novelty: The core contribution is learning unified circuit representations by combining two views—logical structure (AND-inverter graphs) and physical connections (netlists)—through self-supervised contrastive learning.

iccad-2025-191.method: After pruning an LLM, zeros scatter randomly through the weight matrix, but hardware accelerators run fastest when zeros are grouped into blocks. LLM-Barber identifies the most important remaining weights by their magnitude, then restructures the pruning pattern to create contiguous blocks of zeros matching the accelerator's block size. It does this in one pass without retraining, reorganizing which weights get removed to optimize the sparsity mask for hardware execution.
iccad-2025-191.key_novelty: Restructuring a pruned LLM's sparsity pattern into blocks—grouped zeros that hardware can execute efficiently—in one pass without retraining.

iccad-2025-189.method: The work creates computer design tools (CAD software) that automatically generate standardized connectors for microfluidic circuit boards—tiny chips with microscopic fluid channels that simulate living tissues. These tools enforce a single connection standard, so instead of each lab designing custom connectors, the software produces identical designs that can be reliably fabricated. Because all organ-on-chip platforms follow this standard, they can plug together like modular components regardless of which lab created them.
iccad-2025-189.key_novelty: The core idea is using computer design tools to standardize how organ-on-chip platforms connect to each other.

iccad-2025-195.method: PeZO trains neural networks on resource-limited hardware (FPGAs and ASICs) by reusing the same random numbers across multiple training steps rather than generating new ones each time. It also switches from Gaussian-distributed (bell-curve shaped) random numbers to uniform-distributed (evenly spread) ones, which hardware can generate more efficiently. Finally, it uses adaptive scaling that adjusts automatically to each layer, further reducing the total memory and computation demands.
iccad-2025-195.key_novelty: This is the first approach to train neural networks on resource-limited hardware using zeroth-order optimization combined with efficient random perturbation generation.

iccad-2025-188.method: The design embeds XOR logic gates (basic logical operators) directly into an RRAM crossbar array—a grid of resistive memory elements that can perform computations. To handle multi-input operations, it uses a voltage-to-time converter: a circuit that translates voltage signals into time delays (encoding the answer as how quickly a signal crosses a threshold), which are then read out. Careful tuning of timing and voltage settings minimizes the energy wasted on unnecessary switching while maintaining accuracy.
iccad-2025-188.key_novelty: Voltage-to-time conversion (translating voltage signals into time delays) allows XOR-logic RRAM arrays to compute multiple-input operations directly in memory with minimal energy waste.

iccad-2025-199.method: The accelerator runs on an FPGA (a reprogrammable circuit chip) and uses approximated differential attention: instead of fully recomputing attention for each diffusion step, it computes only what's changed. The system ranks which computations matter most using significance scoring, then routes data through the hardware with optimized access patterns to prevent bottlenecks. By splitting the computation workflow based on partial conditioning information, it can use low-bit quantization (representing numbers with fewer bits, like 8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats).
iccad-2025-199.key_novelty: This is the first FPGA accelerator that applies temporal differential computation—where each diffusion step only computes what's changed from the previous step—to enable low-bit Diffusion Transformer inference.

iccad-2025-193.method: K-PACT groups related spectrum processing steps together so they can share data already in fast memory. It watches which steps typically run one after another; when the processor switches between them (a context switch), it prefetches the next step's data. This keeps the data ready in fast memory instead of forcing the step to wait for data from slow storage.
iccad-2025-193.key_novelty: Rather than using a fixed task schedule, dynamically prefetch the next task's data by learning which tasks usually follow each other, allowing related tasks to share data in fast memory.

iccad-2025-197.method: The system combines two forms of parallelism: dividing work across both the circuit's structural layout (structural-level parallelism) and across the different faults being tested (fault-level parallelism). When a processor finishes early, it steals remaining work from busier processors through work-stealing, keeping all processors busy. A unified schedule handles both computation tasks and synchronization points between processors in a single plan, eliminating idle gaps where processors would otherwise wait.
iccad-2025-197.key_novelty: First RTL fault simulation framework using two-dimensional parallelism (structural-level and fault-level) to balance uneven task loads.

iccad-2025-201.method: The system coordinates four specialized AI models—a Planner, Programmer, Reviewer, and Evaluator—that collaborate to write hardware descriptions (Verilog code). Each model receives prompts that explicitly ask it to minimize Power, Performance, and Area (PPA) costs—essentially the electricity usage, speed, and physical chip size. The system feeds actual performance data from hardware synthesis reports back into the models, letting them learn how to write code that performs well when manufactured into real hardware.
iccad-2025-201.key_novelty: This is the first system to combine multiple AI models with specialized roles, all trained to optimize power-performance-area trade-offs using real hardware performance feedback.

iccad-2025-198.method: The system coordinates six specialized AI agents in a hierarchy—higher-level agents guide lower-level ones. They split the work: some describe designs at multiple detail levels, others generate code by learning from working examples (retrieval-augmented generation), others validate whether designs would actually function, and others explore different possible configurations to find better solutions.
iccad-2025-198.key_novelty: This is the first system using multiple AI agents organized hierarchically to automatically generate 2.5D chiplet designs (architectures where smaller chips are arranged horizontally on a shared layer).

iccad-2025-192.method: Rather than placing chip components and routing wires as separate sequential steps, this approach optimizes both together. It uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (a technique that explores many candidate solutions by sampling promising paths and learning which work best) to try different component arrangements. For each arrangement, it predicts whether connections can physically fit using incremental SAT solvers (tools that verify if routing constraints can be satisfied, updated as new constraints arrive). The algorithm then uses routing feasibility results to guide which placements to try next.
iccad-2025-192.key_novelty: The key innovation is jointly optimizing chip placement and routing using Monte Carlo search guided by SAT solver feasibility checks, rather than solving these as separate steps.

iccad-2025-196.method: The system uses a large language model to guide an agent exploring hardware through beam search, which maintains multiple candidate paths simultaneously instead of following a single path. The LLM learns from each test execution which paths are more likely to find corner cases and adjusts the exploration strategy in real-time. This dynamic guidance helps the agent escape the dead ends where traditional heuristics typically get stuck.
iccad-2025-196.key_novelty: COTIA is the first to use large language models with beam search to dynamically guide path exploration in hardware concolic testing.

iccad-2025-200.method: This implements a SAT solver—a tool that checks if logical formulas can be satisfied—as synthesizable hardware (SystemVerilog code compiled into circuits) instead of software. It uses three hardware-optimized operations: linked-list literal-watching for tracking which variables need checking, concurrent constraint propagation in a tree structure, and pipelined clause learning where learning stages execute in parallel instead of sequentially.
iccad-2025-200.key_novelty: Building a SAT solver—a tool that checks if logical formulas can be satisfied—as synthesizable hardware with data structures and processes designed to exploit parallel circuit execution.

iccad-2025-207.method: The approach uses a SAT solver (a constraint-satisfaction engine that finds exact optimal solutions) to design transistor networks. Rather than optimizing one layer of logic gates at a time, it considers multiple layers together, revealing deeper optimization opportunities. Critically, it accounts for physical transistor placement on the chip—not just logical correctness—enabling simultaneous reduction of both transistor count and chip area.
iccad-2025-207.key_novelty: This is the first SAT-based method that optimizes transistor networks across multiple stages while directly accounting for physical transistor placement on the chip.

iccad-2025-205.method: GROOT co-designs the algorithm and GPU implementation together, rather than separately. It extracts node features using a polarized approach that distinguishes high-degree nodes (with many connections) from low-degree nodes (with few). It partitions the graph into smaller sections and re-grows edges between them to reduce memory usage. Two specialized GPU kernels (HD-kernel for high-degree nodes, LD-kernel for low-degree nodes) optimize how each type is processed.
iccad-2025-205.key_novelty: GROOT is the first algorithm-system co-design for circuit verification using graph neural networks, optimizing both the algorithm and GPU implementation for circuit structure.

iccad-2025-202.method: Twill is a real-time scheduler for mobile devices with multiple processor types. It assigns model computations to the processor each one performs best on (task affinity), prioritizes critical work by pausing less important tasks when needed, and adjusts processor speed and voltage (Dynamic Voltage/Frequency Scaling, or DVFS) to reduce power consumption. These strategies minimize total execution time while respecting power budgets.
iccad-2025-202.key_novelty: Twill is the first scheduler that manages multiple AI model types—deep neural networks, transformers, and large language models—running simultaneously on mobile devices with heterogeneous hardware.

iccad-2025-209.method: The approach performs computations directly inside NAND flash memory (where the data lives) rather than moving it to a separate processor. It uses group testing—a technique for testing multiple patterns together—to compare many genome sequences against hundreds of memory pages simultaneously in one read cycle. This allows multiple genomic searches to run in parallel, speeding up the filtering stage.
iccad-2025-209.key_novelty: The core idea is using group testing (simultaneous multi-pattern matching) inside NAND flash memory to compare hundreds of genome sequences in a single read cycle.

iccad-2025-206.method: The framework repeatedly repositions feedthrough pins—internal connection points that pass through the chip's hierarchy levels—using a gradient-based optimization approach (making small adjustments to find the best solution). After each move, it measures how crowded the routing paths become (congestion) based on signal flow patterns, then uses this measurement to guide the next adjustment. This process repeats until congestion stops improving.
iccad-2025-206.key_novelty: The first to reduce routing congestion in hierarchical designs by optimizing feedthrough pin placement (where internal connections pass between hierarchy levels) rather than just minimizing wire length.

iccad-2025-208.method: The approach trains a machine learning model on standard cell layouts—the repeating building blocks of chip designs—to predict capacitance, which measures how much electrical charge connections store. Once trained, this model predicts capacitance in milliseconds for new layouts, replacing commercial tools that require 25+ minutes per change. The predictions are as accurate as traditional 2.5D extraction methods (models that treat geometry as 2.5-dimensional), enabling designers to quickly test many design variations.
iccad-2025-208.key_novelty: Machine learning predicts parasitic capacitance in milliseconds, enabling designers to rapidly test chip design parameter variations during optimization (tasks that previously required 25+ minutes each).

iccad-2025-213.method: Hyle automatically translates Hyperdimensional Computing algorithms (a type of efficient machine learning) into optimized hardware designs for FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays, which can be customized for specific tasks). The tool specifically focuses on speeding up cosine similarity calculations (measuring how similar two high-dimensional vectors are) and binary classification operations (sorting data into two categories), which are computationally expensive in HDC. By using high-level synthesis—a process that converts algorithm descriptions directly into hardware design—Hyle removes the manual work of building accelerators, making it practical to run HDC algorithms on FPGAs instead of slower processors.
iccad-2025-213.key_novelty: Hyle is the first framework to automatically translate Hyperdimensional Computing algorithms (an efficient machine learning approach) into optimized FPGA hardware designs, with special focus on accelerating cosine similarity and binary classification operations.

iccad-2025-214.method: The approach uses a Graph Neural Network—an AI model that understands how things connect together—to predict two outcomes: how good the computed results will be and how much computing power they'll need. Rather than training a fresh model for each new design problem, the team trains one model on multiple approximate computing scenarios and reuses that knowledge to predict performance on new problems (a technique called transfer learning). This saves time because the pre-trained model already understands the general patterns of how design choices affect quality and cost.
iccad-2025-214.key_novelty: This is the first work to use a pre-trained Graph Neural Network that can transfer its knowledge across different approximate computing design problems, eliminating the need to build and train a new model from scratch for each scenario.

iccad-2025-203.method: A machine learning system learns to detect wafers made with untrusted mask-sets (the photomasks that control which patterns get printed onto semiconductor chips) by analyzing inline measurements from manufacturing and electrical tests of finished chips. Trained on 8000 wafers, it learns to recognize how changes to the mask-set causally alter both the physical structures and electrical performance of the resulting chips.
iccad-2025-203.key_novelty: Machine learning authenticates semiconductor mask-sets by detecting process variation signatures—distinctive patterns in how manufacturing variations differ between wafers made with authentic versus untrusted masks.

iccad-2025-210.method: Treats circuit design as a differentiable optimization problem—one where you can compute gradients like neural network training—then applies gradient descent to simultaneously optimize three interconnected choices: logic gate selection (technology mapping), repeater placement (buffer insertion), and transistor sizing (gate sizing).
