Since these choices affect each other—transistor sizes determine circuit speed, which determines where repeaters are needed, which constrains gate selection—optimizing them jointly finds better solutions than sequential tuning. The GPU-accelerated method efficiently explores the design space.
iccad-2025-210.key_novelty: First to simultaneously optimize technology mapping, buffer insertion, and gate sizing using gradient descent on differentiable circuit timing analysis.

iccad-2025-212.method: A Spiking Hopfield Network—a brain-like neural network where neurons fire brief electrical pulses that loop back to each other, allowing the system to store and recognize patterns—is designed to analyze EELS (electron energy loss spectroscopy), which captures energy data from electrons interacting with materials. The network runs on an FPGA (programmable hardware), which consumes much less power than traditional computers and processes data directly at the measurement device. Performance is compared against a Spiking VAE baseline, another spike-based neural network approach.
iccad-2025-212.key_novelty: Spiking Hopfield Networks—neural networks that communicate through electrical spikes like biological neurons—are used to analyze EELS spectroscopy data for the first time.

iccad-2025-211.method: The approach uses a statistical model—heteroscedastic Gaussian processes, which learns when predictions are more or less reliable depending on operating conditions—to capture how manufacturing variations affect circuit behavior. Bayesian optimization then iteratively searches for the best circuit design by testing candidates and learning what to try next across three refinement phases. The method incorporates the learned uncertainty directly into the optimization goal, ensuring final designs work reliably even when manufacturing causes component values to vary.
iccad-2025-211.key_novelty: This is the first application of heteroscedastic Gaussian processes (a statistical technique that learns varying levels of prediction confidence) within Bayesian optimization to design analog circuits that stay robust to manufacturing variation.

iccad-2025-221.method: The approach uses semi-supervised learning (training on a mix of labeled examples and unlabeled data to reduce manual work) combined with Vision Transformers, an AI model designed to understand images by breaking them into visual patches and learning their relationships. It analyzes lithography patterns in two ways at once: by looking at the images directly and by examining their frequency characteristics (which reveal repetitive structures and potential defects). This dual perspective helps identify which patterns are hardest to manufacture reliably.
iccad-2025-221.key_novelty: Instead of manual expert annotation, it combines semi-supervised learning with Vision Transformers and frequency analysis to automatically detect which lithography patterns are critical for manufacturing quality.

iccad-2025-216.method: A coreset is a small, representative subset of data that captures the key properties of a routing problem. The method combines this with transfer learning—reusing knowledge from previously solved routing problems to address new ones. Because routing problems often share common patterns, applying past solutions requires much less training data than solving each problem from scratch, while maintaining high-quality routes that balance competing objectives like timing (delay), power consumption, and wirelength (total length of connecting wires).
iccad-2025-216.key_novelty: It combines coresets and transfer learning—sampling representative data and reusing prior solutions—to speed up circuit routing while optimizing multiple conflicting objectives.

iccad-2025-217.method: The framework trains a large vision model—an AI system that processes and understands images—on 100,000 examples of lithography patterns paired with their simulated results. A vision transformer architecture (a type of neural network designed to understand images) learns to directly map chip design patterns to their expected outputs. Because it learns general principles rather than memorizing specific examples, it can work on advanced technology nodes that weren't part of its original training data.
iccad-2025-217.key_novelty: This is the first approach using a large vision model for lithography simulation, achieving 120 times faster results than commercial simulation tools.

iccad-2025-204.method: The system uses reinforcement learning—training through trial and error with feedback—to improve Verilog code generation. When generated code runs in simulation, the system traces through execution to identify which parts caused problems, providing reliable feedback even when simulation results are sparse or noisy. All training examples are weighted equally to prevent the model from forgetting previous lessons while learning new ones. The code-generation strategy and the model that judges code quality learn together, each improving based on what the other learns.
iccad-2025-204.key_novelty: Verilog code generation improves when the code generator and reward model (which judges code quality) iteratively improve together from simulation traces.

iccad-2025-220.method: Stochastic computing represents numbers using random bit streams, which is naturally resistant to radiation but vulnerable to bit errors. SCArmor uses a genetic algorithm (an optimization technique that tests many candidate solutions mimicking natural selection) to jointly determine which neural network layers to protect from errors and what bit-width (number of bits per value) to assign to each layer. This combined optimization reduces the circuit's total area, power consumption, and processing time by hardening only the layers that matter most.
iccad-2025-220.key_novelty: This is the first genetic algorithm-based approach to jointly choose which layers of a stochastic-computing neural network to harden against radiation and what bit-width to use in each layer.

iccad-2025-219.method: The system trains a language model (an encoder-decoder architecture that converts buggy code into a mathematical representation and back out as fixed code) on 300,000 examples of buggy hardware synthesis code, learning to identify where bugs are located, what type they are, and how to correct them.
iccad-2025-219.key_novelty: A language model specialized for hardware synthesis code debugging achieves 3x better bug correction than GPT-4.

iccad-2025-215.method: LEAP designs a chip that puts processing elements directly at memory (called processing-in-memory) and connects them with an on-chip network, built from scratch for language models. This avoids the common problem where data travels far from memory to a distant processor, wasting time and energy. The system spreads work evenly across many processors so nothing waits for data, and adjusts automatically whether you run a small or large model.
iccad-2025-215.key_novelty: The core innovation is putting processing right at memory with an on-chip network, both designed together specifically for language models, so work distributes evenly and prevents bottlenecks.

iccad-2025-218.method: The tool uses a neural network (an AI trained on examples) to predict circuit timing by analyzing signal paths in both forward and backward directions through the circuit. What makes it different is handling non-uniform input arrival times—accounting for the fact that different signals reach a circuit block at different moments, a common real-world scenario that traditional prediction methods usually ignore. These predictions happen before the circuit design is physically built (pre-synthesis stage), working on hierarchical designs (complex circuits built from smaller building blocks), which is much faster than actually simulating or testing the hardware.
iccad-2025-218.key_novelty: This is the first neural network-based timing predictor that directly accounts for non-uniform input arrival times at the pre-synthesis stage.

iccad-2025-224.method: The toolkit takes specifications for a microfluidic device and automatically generates designs from them. It validates these designs through simulations at multiple levels—first testing individual components, then testing the complete system. As an open-source tool supporting diverse microfluidic design approaches, it can be used and adapted for different research needs.
iccad-2025-224.key_novelty: This toolkit brings together automatic design generation and multi-level simulation validation for microfluidic devices in a single open-source package.

iccad-2025-228.method: The approach has two stages: First, a fast algorithm designs initial paths through the circuit by considering required path lengths, constraints that certain paths must match each other's length, minimizing bends in the paths, and which types of waveguides (channels that guide light through the circuit) can be used together. Second, an optimization technique (MILP — a mathematical method for finding the best solution within constraints) automatically decides where to switch between different waveguide types along each path, placing transitions that reduce signal loss while maintaining the matched-length requirements.
iccad-2025-228.key_novelty: This is the first automatic routing system for optical circuits that can use multiple waveguide types while simultaneously satisfying length-matching requirements and minimizing signal loss.

iccad-2025-222.method: The system searches encrypted databases for patterns without decrypting them, using Fully Homomorphic Encryption (computation directly on encrypted data) combined with Hyperdimensional Computing (representing patterns as high-dimensional vectors for efficient matching). To make this practical, they built a hardware accelerator connected via CXL (a high-speed standard for connecting processors to accelerators) that performs both the encryption and pattern-matching calculations. They demonstrated it on protein spectra databases.
iccad-2025-222.key_novelty: They created a hardware accelerator combining Fully Homomorphic Encryption (computation on encrypted data) and Hyperdimensional Computing (high-dimensional pattern matching) for private database searches.

iccad-2025-225.method: It trains a neural network called DeepONet on physics equations (specifically the heat equation and Maxwell's equations, which describe how electricity and heat behave) to learn the mapping between a 3D chip's geometry, materials, and the resulting electromagnetic and thermal fields. Rather than solving these equations from scratch for each new design—which takes hours in traditional simulation software—the trained network produces predictions instantly. The network learns transfer functions that generalize across different chip configurations with different boundary conditions, so it works on designs it hasn't encountered during training.
iccad-2025-225.key_novelty: It's the first neural-network simulator that combines electromagnetic and thermal field analysis for arbitrary 3D chip configurations, delivering 844–7600× speedup compared to commercial software (COMSOL) while maintaining 97% accuracy on electromagnetic predictions and 99.8% on thermal predictions.

iccad-2025-223.method: The method co-designs the algorithm and custom hardware for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It uses the camera position to identify and eliminate redundant calculations, and builds the hardware to process only what's needed for each frame. By streaming data through the system continuously rather than loading everything into memory, it prevents the processor from stalling while waiting for data.
iccad-2025-223.key_novelty: The core advance is co-designing the algorithm and hardware for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering specifically to eliminate redundant work and prevent memory delays.

iccad-2025-229.method: FPGA-CC creates a secure channel connecting virtualized FPGAs (specialized computing hardware running on shared cloud servers) to a trusted execution environment or TEE (a secure CPU that encrypts code and data from other users). This isolated data path protects information as it flows between the FPGA and the secure CPU, keeping everything confidential from other users on the same cloud. The framework achieves this while maintaining acceptable performance for real applications.
iccad-2025-229.key_novelty: FPGA-CC is the first to make virtualized FPGAs secure for cloud users by connecting them through an encrypted channel to trusted CPU environments that protect the data traveling between them.

iccad-2025-236.method: The paper brings together experts from universities and companies to determine what large AI models can actually accomplish for circuit design and where they fail. It examines three core questions: reliability (can you trust the AI's results?), scalability (does it work for large, complex designs?), and interpretability (can engineers understand why the AI made each choice?). The overarching goal is to assess whether these AI models outperform the traditional computer-aided design tools we already use, or whether they work better when combined with existing methods.
iccad-2025-236.key_novelty: This is an authoritative overview assessing what large language models and AI circuit models can and cannot actually achieve in chip design.

iccad-2025-232.method: ASTRA automatically sizes transistors by connecting AI models, stored engineering knowledge, and Bayesian Optimization (a method that learns from each simulation to make better guesses, requiring fewer tests). It works in two stages: first, it retrieves relevant design rules and uses AI reasoning to narrow down feasible transistor sizes using the gm/ID methodology (which relates transistor gain and current); second, it uses Bayesian Optimization to refine the sizes by focusing on critical transistors the AI identified. The system integrates these components through a messaging protocol that lets them work together seamlessly while fitting into existing design tools.
iccad-2025-232.key_novelty: ASTRA combines AI reasoning, engineering knowledge, and Bayesian Optimization to automatically size transistors, reducing required simulations by up to 4.35×.

iccad-2025-231.method: ExactMap maps digital logic onto ASIC cells—the physical building blocks of a chip—while accounting for electrical load on wires and how that affects how fast signals travel. It identifies the speed-critical parts of the circuit by analyzing this load information, then selects cells that minimize delays using accurate load-aware delay predictions. To balance both speed and chip area, it uses a two-pronged optimization strategy called dual recovery. The algorithm runs in parallel on a GPU, evaluating many different cell selections at once rather than sequentially.
iccad-2025-231.key_novelty: It pairs load-aware delay prediction (accounting for how wire resistance and capacitance affect signal speed) with parallel GPU processing in ASIC mapping, achieving 32% delay reduction and 65.33× speedup.

iccad-2025-238.method: Uranus uses a split encryption strategy: CKKS (a compression-friendly encryption scheme) for linear layers where approximate arithmetic works, and BFV (a scheme preserving exact integer values) for nonlinear activation functions that need precision, both with reduced encryption parameters sized for hardware. The hardware accelerator is highly reconfigurable to handle this mixed workload and maximize utilization by strategically balancing computation speed, memory use, and accuracy.
iccad-2025-238.key_novelty: Uranus is the first accelerator that combines software and hardware design for encrypted graph neural networks (fully homomorphic encryption), achieving 92× speedup versus CKKS-only methods and 3.3–4.2× speedup versus PPGNN, with 119× better energy efficiency.

iccad-2025-234.method: The system stacks memory and processor chips vertically in 3D layers (instead of flat 2D arrangements), with memory sitting directly on logic chips and logic on more logic, reducing the distance data has to travel. It distributes mixture-of-experts (separate specialized neural network branches) and multi-head attention (parallel processing of different aspects) across these 3D layers. Dynamic head pruning automatically turns off attention heads that aren't contributing to the output, cutting computation. This approach lowers energy use and processing time through shorter vertical interconnects.
iccad-2025-234.key_novelty: The key innovation is the first 3D hardware approach using stacked layers of memory and processor chips to support spiking transformers with mixture-of-experts and dynamic attention pruning.

iccad-2025-226.method: Partition and placement are normally optimized sequentially—first deciding which blocks go on which die, then arranging them physically—which locks in partition choices that might not work well with the final placement. This system alternates between refining both decisions together using a data structure called HeteroACG (Abstract Constraint Graph) that captures constraints from both. Each change to partition immediately affects placement optimization, and vice versa. They evolve together until reaching a solution where both decisions work well together.
iccad-2025-226.key_novelty: This is the first framework to optimize partition and placement together by cycling between them, rather than locking in partition first and then optimizing placement around it.

iccad-2025-230.method: BITLUME is a photonic computing unit (a processor that uses light instead of electricity) that can perform multiplications with more than 8-bit precision, overcoming a key limitation of typical light-based systems. To achieve this, it uses a precision-flexible design—meaning you can adjust how precise each calculation needs to be—combined with an optimized round-truncation algorithm that simplifies numbers while keeping them accurate. The system also employs a data-mapping strategy that reduces conversions between light and electrical signals and maximizes data reuse. It integrates photonic components with programmable electronics (FPGA) and RF components into a hybrid architecture.
iccad-2025-230.key_novelty: BITLUME is the first photonic processor that adjusts precision for neural network operations, achieving 3.7× faster dot-product calculations (the fundamental operation in neural networks) than an A100 GPU.

iccad-2025-227.method: The approach uses two parallel schemes (both running on multiple processors or GPUs simultaneously) to speed up node remapping (reassigning circuit nodes to physical gates). The first scheme prioritizes timing-critical nodes by starting with the longest data path, while the second scheme prioritizes paths with the least slack (remaining timing margin before a path becomes too slow). Both schemes greatly reduce the search space by focusing on critical paths rather than exhaustively checking every possible node-to-gate assignment.
iccad-2025-227.key_novelty: This is the first parallel node remapping approach for NIMCH circuits (building blocks with non-integer height multiples), achieving 5.58× speedup while preserving placement quality by prioritizing timing-critical paths.

iccad-2025-235.method: HLSTester uses large language models to automate hardware testing in four coordinated steps. It converts existing C/C++ tests to hardware-compatible testbenches, identifies key variables using backward slicing (tracing code dependencies) and analyzes how they affect program behavior at runtime, generates new test inputs through LLM-guided dynamic mutation (systematically changing test data), and filters redundant tests before execution on real hardware. This automation reduces the manual effort of finding where synthesized circuits behave differently than the original C/C++ programs.
iccad-2025-235.key_novelty: HLSTester uses large language models to automate the testing of synthesized circuits and identify where they behave differently from the original C/C++ code.

iccad-2025-237.method: SparCIM combines two types of computing-in-memory chips (where calculations happen in memory rather than being shuttled to a separate processor): analog chips that quickly approximate patterns with many zeros in attention and feedforward calculations, and digital chips for precise calculations that depend on the input context. A dynamic workload allocator switches the digital chips between storage and compute modes, reducing trips to external memory and the time per generated token. A bit-level alignment unit exploits the fact that individual bits within numbers can often be ignored (bit-level sparsity), packing more useful computation into each memory cell. Built in 28nm process technology.
iccad-2025-237.key_novelty: SparCIM is the first heterogeneous analog-digital computing-in-memory accelerator for large language models that exploits both context-dependent sparsity and bit-level sparsity, achieving 1.27–5.98 times better energy efficiency.

iccad-2025-242.method: The approach uses integer linear programming—a mathematical technique for finding optimal solutions to problems with whole-number constraints—to automatically design multipliers (arithmetic circuits) for Xilinx FPGAs. Rather than manual tuning, it systematically explores the complete range of efficient speed-versus-size combinations (the Pareto frontier, where you cannot improve both dimensions at once). The resulting designs achieve 27.8% faster operation and use 21.4% fewer lookup tables (LUTs—the basic configurable building blocks in FPGAs) compared to hand-designed baselines.
iccad-2025-242.key_novelty: The core idea is using mathematical optimization (integer linear programming) to automatically find the best multiplier designs for FPGAs by balancing speed and chip area.

iccad-2025-241.method: The method combines graph neural networks (AI models that map connections between components) with finite element simulation (dividing the chiplet stack into sections to calculate heat flow). A key technique is adaptive graph learning, which adjusts predictions based on the specific thermal properties at each layer's interface. This hybrid approach achieves 1000× faster predictions than traditional finite difference methods, with 0.05% mean absolute percentage error accuracy.
iccad-2025-241.key_novelty: The innovation is using graph neural networks combined with finite element simulation to automatically adapt thermal predictions for stacked chiplets based on how each interface conducts heat differently.

iccad-2025-240.method: The system uses a transformer (a neural network) to learn how circuit components interact with each other and creates unified numerical representations (embeddings) for all components. Since it learned the fundamental rules of how components work together, it can predict performance for new circuit layouts it has never seen before—without retraining—a capability called zero-shot inference. This approach evaluates circuits 13 times faster than running expensive SPICE simulations.
iccad-2025-240.key_novelty: It learns circuit component interactions using transformer embeddings and applies that knowledge to predict performance on new circuit designs without retraining.

iccad-2025-239.method: The system extracts parasitic effects—unwanted electrical interference that slows down circuits—across an entire chip using four complementary techniques. These include geometric shielding patterns in three designs to isolate wires, a fast data structure to efficiently identify candidate interfering signals, timing simulation to find which interference actually affects circuit behavior (versus just being theoretically possible), and a model of how manufacturing variations alter wire resistance.
iccad-2025-239.key_novelty: The core innovation is being the first methodology to comprehensively extract parasitic effects across an entire chip while realistically accounting for wire shielding, manufacturing variations, and which interference actually occurs.

iccad-2025-244.method: The approach uses an FPGA (a programmable hardware chip) to accelerate KANs by replacing expensive mathematical calculations with fast lookup tables—pre-computed tables that instantly provide answers. To make lookup tables handle KANs' learnable non-linear activation functions (the mathematical transformations neurons apply, which change as the network learns), the design uses two techniques: quantization (representing numbers with fewer bits to save space and power) and adaptive lookup tables that adjust to match what each network learns. This achieves roughly 10,000 times better energy efficiency than running KANs on standard edge CPUs (processors in phones and IoT devices).
iccad-2025-244.key_novelty: The innovation is replacing KANs' learnable non-linear activation functions with adaptive lookup tables implemented on FPGA hardware.

iccad-2025-233.method: Promise figures out what's always true in a circuit by analyzing simulation traces—recordings of how the circuit behaves when you run it. From these traces, it identifies invariants: relationships between signals and registers that are always true across every possible circuit state, like 'if signal A is high, register B always stores value X'. Using fast algorithms (polynomial-time, meaning they stay efficient on large circuits), it removes parts that these invariants prove unnecessary, and integrates with high-level synthesis tools to optimize the final design.
iccad-2025-233.key_novelty: Promise finds circuit-wide invariants (patterns that are always true) from simulation traces using polynomial-time algorithms, making it practical to remove redundancy from circuits created by high-level synthesis.

iccad-2025-243.method: An AI system called UVM2 automatically generates testbenches—code that verifies whether a hardware design works correctly—by reading circuit specifications, replacing the manual process where experts hand-write verification code. It then measures test coverage (which parts of the design were actually tested) and uses this information in a feedback loop to improve the tests iteratively. This addresses the core problems of verification being time-consuming and error-prone. The method achieves a 38.82× reduction in setup time and 87.44% code coverage.
iccad-2025-243.key_novelty: The key idea is combining automatic test generation with coverage feedback, so tests automatically improve based on what parts of the design actually get tested.

iccad-2025-251.method: The system works with fully homomorphic encrypted circuits (TFHE), which let you perform computations directly on encrypted data. When evaluating these circuits, different operations run faster with different ways of representing plaintext numbers—called encoding strategies. Rather than manually choosing a single strategy for the entire circuit, this system automatically picks the best strategy for each operation, achieving a 53.46% reduction in evaluation time.
iccad-2025-251.key_novelty: Automatically choosing the optimal plaintext encoding strategy for each operation during fully homomorphic encrypted circuit evaluation.

iccad-2025-248.method: The accelerator organizes 3D point cloud data into spatial regions (called panels) and assigns computation to these regions, so points that interact are stored near each other in memory. For the attention layers—where the network learns which points are related—it uses locality-based compression, shrinking the data representation based on how close points are to each other in 3D space, since distant points barely interact. This spatial organization and compression reduce memory bandwidth (the amount of data moving between storage and computation units), which is where most energy is consumed in current accelerators.
iccad-2025-248.key_novelty: Using spatial locality to both organize computation into regions and compress attention data, so the hardware only moves data for point interactions that actually matter.

iccad-2025-246.method: Contour tracing identifies the edges of shapes in VLSI chip layouts (patterns in semiconductor designs). The algorithm runs on a GPU (graphics processor with thousands of cores) instead of a CPU (traditional single processor), splitting the work so each GPU core traces contours in a different layout region simultaneously. Results combine to form the complete edge map. This parallelization achieves 90× speedup versus CPU processing.
iccad-2025-246.key_novelty: The core idea is moving contour tracing to GPUs so thousands of cores can process different layout regions in parallel instead of one processor doing it sequentially.

iccad-2025-245.method: The method combines three techniques: parallelized heuristics (fast approximation methods) generate candidate solutions quickly, adaptive pruning (smart elimination of unlikely good options based on what works) narrows the search space, and ILP solving (exact optimization that finds the mathematically best solution) refines the remaining candidates. This hybrid approach achieves a 558× speedup over pure ILP solving and produces circuits that are 7.6-8.1% smaller in area.
iccad-2025-245.key_novelty: The core innovation is using adaptive pruning (smart elimination that learns what works) to focus expensive exact optimization on the most promising circuit candidates generated by parallel approximations.

iccad-2025-247.method: The accelerator is a specialized chip designed specifically for Vision Mamba, a neural network that processes images by sequentially updating internal state. It uses a systolic scan array—a hardware pattern with repeating cells optimized for sequential state calculations—to run these updates efficiently. To fit on edge devices, it applies quantization (reducing number precision from 32-bit to 8-bit values, for example) to compress the model. All components—hardware, compression, and software—integrate into one coordinated system for efficient edge deployment.
iccad-2025-247.key_novelty: This is the first hardware accelerator built specifically for Vision Mamba, using a systolic scan array (repeating hardware cells optimized for sequential state calculations) to efficiently run these image models on edge devices.

iccad-2025-252.method: The approach runs graph sparsification on a GPU (a specialized processor designed for parallel computation), using localized random walks—a technique that samples paths through the graph while staying in nearby regions to identify which edges are critical and can be safely removed. By processing only the affected parts of the graph when edges are added or deleted, rather than recomputing everything, it efficiently handles both operations. This achieves a 10× speedup over the inGRASS algorithm.
iccad-2025-252.key_novelty: Running graph sparsification on a GPU using localized random walks—sampling nearby paths to identify important edges—to efficiently handle both edge additions and removals.

iccad-2025-249.method: The framework automates 3D FPGA design by letting you specify how the vertically stacked layers should connect to each other. It generates the complete hardware description (synthesizable RTL, which is code that hardware tools convert into circuits) and the configuration file (bitstream) needed to program the chip. This lets researchers quickly test many different vertical interconnect designs to find the best trade-offs for their application.
iccad-2025-249.key_novelty: An open-source tool that automates 3D FPGA design with flexible vertical interconnects, eliminating manual effort in the design-to-configuration pipeline.

iccad-2025-254.method: The approach replaces neural network multiplications with addition operations, which are simpler for hardware to implement efficiently. Network weights are encoded in a non-positive format (zero or negative values), and a decoder is built directly into the hardware to detect when bit-flips corrupt data during computation. By designing the algorithm and hardware together for this specific approach, the overhead of the defense mechanism stays minimal.
iccad-2025-254.key_novelty: The innovation is efficiently defending against bit-flip attacks in non-negative addition-based neural networks by encoding weights as non-positive values through hardware-algorithm co-design.

iccad-2025-256.method: GenomeDPU adds simple processing logic directly to the DRAM interface, the point where data moves between the GPU and main memory. Rather than sending genome sequences to the GPU for alignment processing and then back to storage, the processor handles part of the alignment work right at the interface. This keeps data local to memory and eliminates the expensive back-and-forth transfers that were the main source of slowdowns.
iccad-2025-256.key_novelty: GenomeDPU achieves in-memory processing for GPU-accelerated genome analysis by adding simple logic to the DRAM interface instead of embedding costly processors into memory chips.

iccad-2025-250.method: The approach collects Verilog code examples—the language for describing chip hardware designs—from community contributors and uses them to fine-tune language models. Fine-tuning trains the models further on this specialized data to learn patterns of correct Verilog code. Success is measured by testing whether generated code works correctly (pass@1 metric: whether a single generated output passes validation), and fine-tuning improves this by 6.6-13.2% across different models.
iccad-2025-250.key_novelty: Community-sourced Verilog datasets enable language models to generate working hardware-design code, improving generation success rates by 6.6-13.2%.

iccad-2025-260.method: SiST cuts unnecessary work in three places: it predicts which tokens can be skipped before generating QKV matrices (the Query, Key, and Value tensors used by attention), groups similar tokens in the FFN (the feed-forward layer) to share computations, and exploits weight sparsity by skipping calculations on near-zero weights. The FPGA is designed to handle this unstructured sparsity—where zeros are scattered randomly rather than in regular patterns—efficiently.
iccad-2025-260.key_novelty: The core innovation is co-designing the transformer algorithm and FPGA hardware together as a single system to exploit both token similarity and weight sparsity across all three transformer modules (QKV generation, attention, and FFN).

iccad-2025-255.method: PIGen automates ReRAM design using two types of neural networks. A physics-informed neural network learns how ReRAM (resistive memory devices) switch states, constrained to follow real physics laws. A conditional generative network then generates optimized device parameters that meet performance targets for endurance, latency, and energy.
iccad-2025-255.key_novelty: It combines physics-constrained learning with generative design to automatically optimize ReRAM parameters for different materials.

iccad-2025-259.method: Therm-PCT represents the 2.5D IC as a point cloud (scattered 3D points rather than a grid) and processes it with a transformer, a neural network designed to learn patterns in data. It combines three techniques: adaptive multipath-coupled diffusion (AMD) which simulates how heat flows through multiple pathways, wavelet-based fine-grained recovery (WFR) which captures fine-scale temperature variations, and thermal-aware Mixture-of-Material-Experts (TA-MoME) that routes predictions through specialized submodels trained for each material type.
iccad-2025-259.key_novelty: A point-cloud transformer that routes predictions through material-specific expert submodels to predict thermal behavior in geometrically complex 2.5D integrated circuits.

iccad-2025-258.method: CorDBA avoids expensive transistor-level simulations by separating yield improvement from yield measurement. It uses statistical process-variation corners (predicted worst-case manufacturing scenarios) to identify where circuits might fail. Then it optimizes using max-minimum optimization, which focuses on making even the worst-performing chips as robust as possible. This multi-stage approach lets designers refine designs without constantly re-running expensive simulations.
iccad-2025-258.key_novelty: The key idea is decoupling—improving yield without expensive simulations by using statistical process predictions and optimizing for the worst-performing chips.

iccad-2025-257.method: FENIX co-designs the encryption algorithm with specialized hardware. It breaks oblivious transfer (a secure communication protocol) into small pieces that overlap with homomorphic encryption (computation on encrypted data), and uses flexible batch encoding to balance storage and computation speed. Specialized processors placed near memory accelerate the memory-intensive encryption operations.
iccad-2025-257.key_novelty: The core idea is co-designing the encryption algorithm with specialized hardware positioned near memory, enabling fine-grained operation scheduling that overlaps encrypted operations for greater efficiency.

iccad-2025-253.method: The approach builds a detailed cost model for multi-chiplet systems where different chiplets use different manufacturing processes (called technology nodes), accounting for packaging (assembling chips together), yield (manufacturing success rates), and power consumption. It then uses this model to optimize system designs by exploring different arrangements and tradeoffs between these costs. By systematically searching for the best design choices, this optimization achieves 18-31% cost savings compared to baseline configurations.
iccad-2025-253.key_novelty: The work models the total cost of multi-chiplet systems using different manufacturing technologies, accounting for packaging, yield, and power, enabling cost-optimized designs.

iccad-2025-266.method: QUARK exploits the fact that transformers use similar patterns in their mathematical processing operations (called nonlinear operations). It applies quantization—using fewer bits to represent numbers—which makes approximations accurate enough for one hardware circuit to perform multiple different operations instead of needing separate circuits for each. This approach on an FPGA reduces the total hardware needed.
iccad-2025-266.key_novelty: Using quantization to enable a single hardware circuit to handle multiple different nonlinear operations in transformers.

iccad-2025-269.method: The approach uses cross-attention networks—neural mechanisms that learn which design elements affect each other—to understand how a processor's internal structure (microarchitecture) and design tool settings interact. This captures design interdependencies, allowing insights from one processor design to transfer to others despite their different performance characteristics. It then uses uncertainty estimates (confidence in predicted design quality) to guide the search toward solutions matching the designer's preferences for speed, power consumption, and area tradeoffs.
iccad-2025-269.key_novelty: Using attention mechanisms to transfer processor design knowledge across different architectures, guided by uncertainty toward the designer's preferred speed-power-area tradeoffs.

iccad-2025-268.method: GTA accelerates track assignment—the process of placing wires along predefined paths on a chip—by running it on a GPU (graphics processor) instead of a CPU, and uses lightweight lookup tables to quickly detect when placements conflict. Unlike prior GPU approaches, it accounts for design rules (the physical and electrical constraints layouts must satisfy), enabling accurate congestion analysis and high-quality starting solutions for detailed routing.
iccad-2025-268.key_novelty: GTA is the first track assignment system that combines GPU acceleration with design-rule awareness to improve routing quality.

iccad-2025-264.method: H3D creates routing grids—maps of where wires can go and where hybrid bonding terminals (HBTs, the connection points between 3D chip layers) can be placed—then jointly optimizes routing and HBT placement rather than solving them separately. It applies dynamic programming (an algorithm breaking problems into reusable subproblems) with reverse depth-first and breadth-first search to find optimal wire paths and connection placement that form Steiner trees (minimal-cost structures connecting specified points in 3D space).
iccad-2025-264.key_novelty: H3D is the first global router that jointly optimizes wire routing and hybrid bonding terminal placement—the connection points between 3D layers—in face-to-face bonded 3D circuits.

iccad-2025-272.method: The approach uses diffusion models—AI systems that build images by gradually refining noise—to create chip layouts as a series of template-guided image-filling tasks (inpainting). Each task fills in parts of a chip design while respecting the intricate 2D metal interconnect design rules that govern how metal layers can be arranged. It applies a denoising step with templates to clean up residual artifacts. The system then uses minimal labeled examples (few-shot fine-tuning) to quickly adapt to new semiconductor process nodes.
iccad-2025-272.key_novelty: It uses diffusion models—AI systems trained to generate images by refining noise—as a pre-trained foundation for efficiently generating chip layouts at sub-3nm nodes with minimal new training data.

iccad-2025-273.method: Exponential integrator methods (mathematical techniques for simulating circuit behavior over time) normally become numerically unstable when applied to nonlinear circuits. This framework fixes that using two techniques: implicit regularization—adjusting the system's mathematical properties (eigenvalues) to prevent a problematic numerical separation that causes instability—and truncated rational approximation to represent nonlinear behavior as a simplified mathematical function. By solving the linear and nonlinear parts separately rather than nested together, it reduces the three-level iteration structure of earlier methods to a single Newton iteration loop. This makes exponential integration methods as practical to use as conventional circuit simulation techniques.
iccad-2025-273.key_novelty: Combining implicit regularization and truncated rational approximation to stabilize exponential integrator methods for nonlinear circuits.

iccad-2025-274.method: SetupKit accelerates timing characterization through three techniques working together. It uses BEIRA, a search method that applies statistical error modeling to guess and refine solutions more quickly. It estimates good starting points by analyzing the circuit design itself. Most importantly, it employs active learning with a Gaussian Process (machine learning that learns from test results to predict which future tests will be most revealing) to focus simulations on the most informative manufacturing conditions and temperatures, avoiding redundant tests.
iccad-2025-274.key_novelty: SetupKit uses a Gaussian Process (machine learning that learns from test results) to actively predict which manufacturing conditions and temperatures will be most informative to test, reducing the total number of simulations needed for multi-corner characterization.

iccad-2025-261.method: The accelerator stores weights in SOT-MRAM and SRAM memory and performs calculations directly in that memory instead of moving data to a separate processor, which saves time. It automatically skips operations involving numbers with low impact on the result, and reuses data efficiently across repeated calculation steps on floating-point values (decimal numbers). A specialized transpose array then quickly flips the arrangement of weights to efficiently compute the attention mechanism.
iccad-2025-261.key_novelty: The core innovation pairs magnetic RAM (SOT-MRAM) with standard RAM (SRAM) to perform calculations directly in memory, automatically skip low-impact operations, and use a specialized transpose array for efficient transformer attention.

iccad-2025-262.method: PAR-CIM reduces chip area to 0.35× using layer/gate-level approximate computation in its adder trees (circuits that add numbers)—letting some calculations use less precision when exact results aren't critical. It combines this with fractional mixed-bitwidth quantization, which assigns each layer the precision it needs based on Taylor sensitivity analysis (identifying which layers are sensitive to precision loss) and DoReFa-Net (a method for determining optimal precision levels), enabling multi-bit reconfigurable computation mode so the chip dynamically chooses between precise and approximate computation for each operation.
iccad-2025-262.key_novelty: A reconfigurable CIM (computing-in-memory) macro that combines precise and approximate computation with fractional mixed-bitwidth quantization, dynamically adjusting each layer's precision to balance accuracy and chip efficiency.

iccad-2025-271.method: The system uses a fast draft model to generate multiple candidate next words in parallel, then verifies them using a slower but accurate target model—when candidates are wrong, it backtracks to a previous point without storing all intermediate values (hidden states). At the algorithm level, it processes candidates in order rather than exploring all possible branches, and breaks computations into small chunks (tiles) that fit in fast memory to reduce slow memory accesses. The FPGA hardware (AMD VHK158 and VCK190) runs matrix multiplications in parallel while state-space model layers—which depend on prior results—run sequentially, keeping the hardware continuously computing.
iccad-2025-271.key_novelty: It's the first FPGA accelerator that enables speculative decoding for Mamba by coordinating memory backtracking at the system level, candidate verification at the algorithm level, and computation scheduling at the hardware level.

iccad-2025-265.method: The system uses graph neural networks to encode the quantum circuit structure as an interconnected network, then applies deep reinforcement learning—an AI technique that learns through trial and error with rewards—to decide where to insert SWAP gates. Rather than optimizing just the immediate step, it uses look-ahead rewards to account for how each decision affects future steps. It also uses biased exploration, which means it guides its search using practical rules about what tends to work well in quantum computing, rather than trying purely random options.
iccad-2025-265.key_novelty: It applies graph-based deep reinforcement learning that combines forward planning (look-ahead rewards) and guided search (using domain expertise) to solve quantum circuit mapping by finding optimal SWAP gate placements.

iccad-2025-263.method: The method treats voltage regulator placement as an optimization puzzle: deciding which regulators to use, where to place them, and what type—each choice expressed as a yes/no decision in a mathematical system. To handle complexity, it uses macromodeling—breaking the system into smaller, simplified models instead of simulating every detail. The algorithm then searches for the best combination of number, location, and type of switched-capacitor voltage regulators (devices that stabilize electrical power using capacitors) to install on the silicon interposer connecting the chiplets.
iccad-2025-263.key_novelty: The paper automates voltage regulator selection and placement in 2.5D systems with heterogeneous chiplets using binary-choice mathematical optimization and model simplification.

iccad-2025-267.method: MMCircuitEval assembles 3,614 question-answer pairs combining text and circuit diagrams, drawn from textbooks, datasheets, and technical documentation reviewed by experts. These pairs cover both digital and analog circuits across the entire circuit design process—from basic knowledge questions through design specifications, front-end work (initial design), and back-end work (physical layout). Each question is categorized by design stage, circuit type, the skill it tests, and difficulty level.
iccad-2025-267.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive benchmark combining text and circuit diagrams for electronic circuit design, spanning all design stages and both digital and analog circuits.

iccad-2025-270.method: SSHR (Spatial Structure-based Hypercube Reduction) discovers geometric regions called parallelotopes in the hypercube representation of Boolean functions (abstract spaces representing all possible input combinations), then extracts spatial patterns from them to minimize Multi-Control Toffoli gates (expensive quantum operations that conditionally apply a NOT gate based on multiple qubits) in quantum circuits. Two variants handle this differently: SSHR-H uses heuristic functions (quick approximation rules) to speed up the search, while SSHR-I employs Integer Linear Programming (a mathematical optimization solver) to maximize the exploitation of spatial structure.
iccad-2025-270.key_novelty: By using parallelotopes to encode the spatial structure of Boolean functions, it accesses quantum circuit optimizations that conventional methods cannot find.

iccad-2025-280.method: The framework generates synthesizable hardware designs (RTL) that support various architectural configurations. It connects two simulators—Verilator, which simulates the hardware design cycle-by-cycle as it would run, and gem5, which can run realistic software workloads and operating systems. Running both simulators together (called co-simulation) gives you better accuracy than using either alone, because you're testing the actual hardware design against realistic workloads instead of simplified scenarios.
iccad-2025-280.key_novelty: The core innovation is connecting a realistic-workload simulator (gem5) to a cycle-accurate hardware simulator (Verilator) so you can validate memory system designs by testing actual hardware descriptions against realistic software before building chips.

iccad-2025-279.method: The approach replaces computationally expensive differential equations with a simplified electrical circuit made of basic elements (resistors, capacitors, controlled sources—devices that adjust voltage or current based on conditions) that represent electromigration physics. It exploits the fact that electrical current flow and mechanical stress evolution (how atoms move under heat and current) follow equivalent patterns, so a single circuit model captures both simultaneously. Temperature effects are built in through controlled sources that respond to heat distribution. During simulation in standard SPICE tools, the circuit automatically reconfigures between void nucleation (void formation onset) and post-void phases, using adaptive mesh refinement (a grid that's finer where needed) to keep computation fast.
iccad-2025-279.key_novelty: The core idea is an electrical circuit model for electromigration where electrical, mechanical, and thermal effects are all explicitly linked (electro-thermomechanical coupling), enabling direct simulation in standard SPICE tools instead of solving expensive differential equations.

iccad-2025-278.method: The method treats thermal resistance—the opposition to heat flow—like electrical resistance in a circuit, using a resistor network model that naturally captures how heat distributes through interconnects. Unlike previous approaches, it explicitly incorporates the detailed physical layout of vias, the tiny vertical connections between metal layers, using the Woodbury formula to calculate thermal resistance. This inclusion of actual connection geometry, rather than simplified approximations, produces more accurate thermal predictions for 3D chips where via layout significantly affects heat dissipation.
iccad-2025-278.key_novelty: The core contribution is using a resistor network model that accounts for detailed via connectivity—the actual layout of vertical connections between layers—when calculating thermal resistance in 3D integrated circuits.

isca-2025-004.method: FATE assigns different numerical precision (how many bits are used to represent each number) to different dimensions of hypervectors, using lower precision for less-important dimensions and higher precision for important ones. It also skips computations on near-zero values (a technique called sparsity) to reduce the overall computational work. Designed for embedded FPGAs, this approach achieves high accuracy while using fewer bits on average than standard systems that apply the same precision uniformly across all dimensions.
isca-2025-004.key_novelty: FATE breaks from the standard practice of uniform numerical precision by assigning different precision levels to different dimensions of hypervectors, exploiting the fact that some dimensions contribute more than others to enable sparse computation and faster FPGA performance.

iccad-2025-277.method: The tool runs a seven-step design workflow for 3D chips that simulates the physics of vertically stacked silicon: thermal behavior, signal integrity (electrical signal propagation), and through-silicon vias (the tiny holes connecting layers). Language models automate bonding pad placement and script generation for the design tools, and the platform enables face-to-face layer coupling using a custom bonding approach, as demonstrated on a 3D RISC-V CPU with stacked memory built in the GF180 manufacturing process.
iccad-2025-277.key_novelty: The platform is an open-source tool for designing 3D stacked chips that combines language model automation for design decisions with complete physics simulation to verify the design works.

isca-2025-002.method: The system proposes Similarity-based Branch Prediction (SBP), which combines traditional branch predictors (which guess the next instruction based on history or compiler hints) with a new component called CHESS that records the actual control flow (sequence of executed code) from previous requests. When the traditional predictor is cold (lacking recent state due to context switches between services), CHESS identifies similar past requests and replays their execution paths to predict which branches will be taken, without waiting for the predictor to re-learn from scratch. This approach requires only 18.1 KB of additional memory to store reference execution traces from prior requests.
isca-2025-002.key_novelty: CHESS exploits the similarity of control-flow patterns across requests in microservices—rather than trying to preserve the branch predictor's state across service invocations, it stores execution traces from similar past requests and replays them to predict branches for new requests.

isca-2025-006.method: The approach reuses partial products (intermediate computation results from multiplying chunks of matrices) that were already calculated in earlier steps, rather than recomputing them. It tracks which results can be reused using directed acyclic graphs—visual dependency maps showing which calculations depend on others—then finds the best order to execute everything while respecting those dependencies and running operations in parallel. The Transitive Array accelerator implements this without dedicated multiplication hardware, instead spreading the work across multiple parallel lanes to maintain balanced throughput.
isca-2025-006.key_novelty: Transitive sparsity reuses intermediate GEMM results (partial computation fragments from matrix operations) by executing them according to a directed acyclic graph that specifies their dependency order, enabling a multiplication-free hardware accelerator for LLM inference.

iccad-2025-275.method: Apollo uses graphics processors (GPUs) to speed up the layout process. It models distances with an asymmetric bending-aware wirelength function (accounting for how waveguides curve, with different treatment for different directions), and tracks where waveguides would crowd or cross (routing congestion and crossings). It enforces positioning rules (like alignment and spacing) gradually using conditional projection, and optimizes using blockwise adaptive Nesterov acceleration. The system couples placement directly with physical-aware routing, so positioning decisions account for the practical constraints of connecting components.
iccad-2025-275.key_novelty: It automates large-scale photonic circuit layout by coupling component placement with physical-aware routing constraints, using GPU acceleration.

iccad-2025-276.method: CacheGuardian protects the shared last-level cache using a hardware-based detector that monitors cache access patterns to identify various timing attacks in real time (attacks where someone measures how fast the cache responds to steal data). When it detects an attack, the system blocks only that attacker's access to specific cache sections rather than disrupting other users. This cache-set-level access control achieves fine-grained protection with minimal performance impact. The design was implemented and evaluated in gem5, a processor simulator.
iccad-2025-276.key_novelty: CacheGuardian detects timing attacks by monitoring cache access patterns and blocks only the attacker's access to specific cache sections, enabling low-overhead protection.

isca-2025-010.method: Lumina renders 3D scenes by blending thousands of Gaussians (fuzzy 3D spheres). Exploiting temporal coherence—the fact that consecutive video frames look almost identical—S2 (Spatial-temporal Skipping) avoids recalculating Gaussian contributions that haven't changed between frames. RC (Radiance Caching) stores intermediate color calculations to skip redundant rasterization work. LuminCore, a purpose-built mobile accelerator, is co-designed to efficiently support these cache lookups and eliminate bottlenecks in standard 3DGS rendering on mobile SoCs.
isca-2025-010.key_novelty: The core insight is that most computation repeats across consecutive video frames, so Lumina combines S2 (Spatial-temporal Skipping to skip unchanged Gaussians) and RC (Radiance Caching to reuse calculated colors), enabled by a custom mobile accelerator (LuminCore).

isca-2025-017.method: The approach starts with a key observation: while ahead prediction theoretically must consider all 2^N possible combinations of branch outcomes for N intermediate branches, almost all of these combinations never actually happen during program execution—in practice, only one or two patterns ever occur. The authors modify the TAGE predictor (a standard branch prediction mechanism that tracks recent history) to identify which history combinations are real and which never materialize in actual code, then stop evaluating the fake ones. By only predicting down the paths that actually matter, the system uses only 1.5x the normal energy instead of the previously assumed 14.6x, while improving CPU throughput by 4.4%.
isca-2025-017.key_novelty: Most intermediate branch-direction combinations never occur in real programs, reducing the branching factor of ahead prediction from an exponential explosion down to just one or two paths, making practical ahead prediction feasible.

isca-2025-000.method: ANVIL puts the name-matching logic directly into the NAND flash chips of a regular SSD. Normally you'd stream all the key-value data to the host computer to check for name matches, but ANVIL filters inside the storage device instead, throwing away the entries that don't match before they cross the SSD-to-host connection. ANVIL supports different data organization methods (arrays, dictionaries, key-value stores, data mining formats) through one unified approach.
isca-2025-000.key_novelty: ANVIL accelerates name-value data stores by filtering inside the storage device's NAND flash chips instead of at the host, supporting multiple data organization formats.

isca-2025-003.method: RSN treats the hardware as a network of computing units (called functional units) connected by data pipelines, where each computation specifies its own path through the network—multiple paths run in parallel as long as they don't conflict. Programming is streamlined through instruction compression: RSN combines multiple instruction streams into compact packets, using just 1 byte to drive up to 1.6 billion floating-point operations. On the Versal VCK190 prototype (RSN-XNN), the FPGA's memory blocks, arithmetic units, and AI Engine accelerator tiles all connect through the same pipeline interface, treated as compatible computing units. This allows different neural network layers to run at the same time and share memory bandwidth, rather than waiting for each layer to finish before starting the next.
isca-2025-003.key_novelty: RSN introduces a streaming network instruction abstraction where different neural network layers route data through the same FPGA hardware network, enabling simultaneous execution and memory sharing without per-layer reprogramming.

isca-2025-005.method: The system protects memory by storing authentication codes (small checksums that verify data hasn't been corrupted) organized in a tree. Rather than protecting all memory in fixed-size chunks, it dynamically chooses from four different chunk sizes based on how each processor actually accesses memory—CPUs prefer large chunks while GPUs work better with smaller ones. A detection mechanism watches each processing unit's access patterns and selects the best chunk size per memory region. It also incorporates existing tree optimizations to reduce the cost of checking these authentication codes.
isca-2025-005.key_novelty: Instead of using fixed chunk sizes for memory protection, this approach dynamically adjusts both the authentication code and counter chunk sizes at the same time based on each processor's access patterns, making it efficient across CPU, GPU, and NPU workloads.

isca-2025-012.method: TQSim (Tree-Based Quantum Circuit Simulation) breaks a quantum circuit into smaller subcircuits and saves the intermediate quantum states (density matrices or statevectors—the two formats for tracking quantum information) produced by each one. When running the circuit multiple times with different noise, the system reuses the saved states for subcircuits unaffected by the noise, and only recalculates the ones the noise changes. This avoids redundant recomputation—otherwise each noise trial would recalculate all intermediate states from scratch. The system is designed for distributed HPC clusters and maintains tight fidelity bounds, ensuring approximations stay accurate.
isca-2025-012.key_novelty: Tree-based partitioning of quantum circuits enables reuse of intermediate quantum states across noise simulations, reducing total computation proportional to how much can be reused.

isca-2025-016.method: Avalanche keeps both input matrices in a small on-chip cache using three coordinated mechanisms. Mat-Reorder rearranges one input matrix's columns to group frequently-accessed data together, enabling faster computation and early row completion. DP-Evict (Dead-Product Early Eviction) immediately frees cache space by removing fully-computed intermediate results, while RM-Caching (Reuse Distance-Aware Matrix Caching) prioritizes retaining matrix elements with short reuse distance (data needed again soon) in fast on-chip storage (SRAM) rather than slower main memory (DRAM). Together, these keep both matrices in a 6.15 mm² chip with minimal spillover to DRAM.
isca-2025-016.key_novelty: The core innovation is Mat-Reorder, which reorders columns of the sparse input matrix (a matrix with mostly zeros and few actual values) to align the processor's non-zero access patterns with what fits in the small on-chip cache, enabling both input matrices to stay cached simultaneously.

isca-2025-015.method: Caravan groups together multiple neighbor search queries that initially follow the same path through a k-d tree (a tree structure that organizes 3D points to speed up searches), and processes these groups using SIMD instructions (AVX512, which can perform the same operation on many data elements in parallel). As the search goes deeper into the tree, different queries need to take different branches, leaving some processors idle. To keep all processors busy, Caravan adds two new processor instructions: one that reassigns which data each processor is working on, and another that reorganizes the data layout so processors can work efficiently. The entire hardware addition takes up only 0.032 square millimeters of silicon.
isca-2025-015.key_novelty: Two new processor instructions that reassign and reorganize active processors when searches diverge at deep tree levels, eliminating the efficiency loss from unused processing capacity in batched neighbor search without a custom accelerator.

isca-2025-013.method: Folded Banks redistributes DRAM bank subarrays vertically across stacked silicon dies and moves the control logic and sense amplifiers to a dedicated logic layer at the base. Signals travel vertically through tiny connections called through-silicon vias (TSVs) and hybrid bonds instead of along long horizontal paths, dramatically reducing power loss from electrical resistance. Self-timed sense amplifiers (which detect when stored charge is ready to read) eliminate the need for dummy test subarrays, adding further power and area savings.
isca-2025-013.key_novelty: Folding bank subarrays vertically across stacked dies with vertical signal routing and a dedicated logic layer eliminates the power and area penalties of long horizontal wiring, enabling fine-grained random memory access.

isca-2025-020.method: REIS moves the similarity-search computation (called Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search, or ANNS) directly inside the storage device, cutting out the massive data transfer between the computer and storage that normally slows down retrieval. Rather than forcing a generic search algorithm onto the storage hardware, REIS designs the algorithm specifically to match how NAND flash controllers (the chips inside SSDs) naturally work in parallel. To speed up retrieval further, REIS overlaps the vector search with fetching the actual data, so the storage device can work on both tasks at the same time rather than one after another. This design avoids the need for major modifications to the SSD hardware.
isca-2025-020.key_novelty: REIS designs the similarity-search algorithm (ANNS) specifically to match the flash storage controller's internal design, which accelerates both vector search and data retrieval without major hardware modifications.

isca-2025-007.method: Oaken has two stages: offline, it runs about 100 inferences to find data-agnostic breakpoints (thresholds that depend only on the layer, not the input data) in values for each layer. Online during inference, these thresholds partition each token's KV data into three groups: large outliers, small outliers, and normal values. For each group, group-shift quantization subtracts the threshold to narrow the value range, then encodes each value with 4 or 5 bits. Outliers are fused into unused slots of the dense 4-bit matrix using 8 bits total per outlier, and a custom hardware engine with DMA and page-based memory management handles bandwidth-efficient burst access from HBM or LPDDR memory; the system is built on an LPU architecture synthesized in TSMC 28nm.
isca-2025-007.key_novelty: By pre-computing per-layer value thresholds offline, Oaken avoids expensive online sorting and can pack outliers directly into unused slots of the dense 4-bit matrix, reducing storage from 23 to 8 bits per outlier.

isca-2025-018.method: AMALI improves standard GPU models in three ways, all validated on A100 hardware. First, it measures instruction flow through tensor cores and identifies pipeline stalls caused by insufficient queued work—delays that simpler models overlook—instead of guessing at throughput. Second, it measures instruction and constant cache latencies directly via micro-benchmark kernels rather than assuming constant speeds. Third, it tracks heterogeneous warp execution, accounting for the fact that different thread groups execute different numbers of instructions, affecting occupancy and scheduling—details existing models simplify.
isca-2025-018.key_novelty: Explicit measurement of instruction and constant cache latencies combined with tensor-core stall modeling reduces LLM inference prediction error on A100 GPUs from 127.56% to 23%.

isca-2025-021.method: Ecco places compressors/decompressors between a GPU's fast cache and main memory. It compresses weights and KV cache to 1/4 their size by grouping 128 values and replacing each group with the nearest match from 64 learned patterns (k-means: selecting the closest representative value), then applies Huffman coding with 4 codebooks per pattern for further compression (using shorter codes for common values); activations use simpler 2x INT8 compression. The decompressor runs 64 parallel Huffman decoders on overlapping 15-bit chunks of 512-bit blocks, feeding results into a 6-stage tree circuit and 128 parallel mappers. The compressor uses a bitonic sorter to extract outliers and scores 16 candidate patterns to pick the best one, with both components replicated 20x to sustain the cache's 5,120 bytes/cycle throughput, in 28nm silicon (scalable to 7nm).
isca-2025-021.key_novelty: The core innovation is a parallel Huffman decoder with 64 overlapping sub-decoders fused into a tree-combining stage that breaks the sequential bottleneck of normal Huffman decoding, achieving 100x latency reduction while maintaining GPU L2 cache speed for a lossy entropy-aware compression scheme.

isca-2025-019.method: GCStack accurately identifies GPU performance bottlenecks by tracking all the different types of slowdowns (memory delays, synchronization waits, and idle cycles) that happen simultaneously in each cycle, instead of just the most important one. GCScaler predicts how these slowdowns change across different GPU designs using mathematics, without re-running expensive simulations. Together, they enable exploration of 1,000 GPU designs from a single baseline simulation.
isca-2025-019.key_novelty: By tracking all the slowdowns that happen simultaneously and mathematically scaling those patterns to new GPU designs, the method enables accurate performance analysis and rapid exploration of 1,000 design options from a single simulation.

isca-2025-028.method: MagiCache allows each cache array to dynamically switch individual rows between being compute lines or regular cache lines on the fly, rather than dedicating entire arrays to one role. A virtual engine (software running on the chip) monitors what the program needs at each moment—how much storage versus how much computing—and reallocates rows accordingly. To handle sudden bursts of memory requests without stalling, MagiCache uses instruction chaining: it schedules compute operations and memory requests out-of-order and in parallel, so the long wait for data from HBM/DRAM (the main memory) overlaps with ongoing computation.
isca-2025-028.key_novelty: MagiCache dynamically reallocates individual cache rows between compute and storage roles and uses instruction chaining to hide memory latency, eliminating the fixed capacity loss of array-level in-cache architectures.

isca-2025-014.method: Programmers write code once in HDC++, a programming language with 24 built-in operations for hyperdimensional computing (hypervector and hypermatrix operations, Hamming distance, cosine similarity, and loop constructs for encoding, training, and inference). The HPVM-HDC compiler translates this code to multiple hardware targets: CPUs, GPUs (via CUDA, cuBLAS, and Thrust), a 40-nanometer digital HDC ASIC (with a Hamming-distance pipeline achieving 0.78 TOPS per watt), and a ReRAM accelerator simulator. To optimize performance, the compiler exploits HDC's tolerance for approximation using automatic binarization (reducing numbers to 1 bit via taint analysis to identify which values can be safely simplified) and reduction perforation (strided or segmented loop skipping for Hamming distance, cosine similarity, and matrix operations over hypervector dimensions).
isca-2025-014.key_novelty: HDC++'s high-level loop constructs (encoding_loop, training_loop, and inference_loop) can be compiled to different abstraction levels: coarse-grained accelerator instructions for ASICs and ReRAM, or fine-grained CUDA and CPU instructions for GPUs and CPUs, enabling the first execution of complete hyperdimensional computing applications on both a fabricated digital ASIC and a ReRAM accelerator.

isca-2025-032.method: NetCrafter applies three techniques at the network boundary to manage traffic on the lower-bandwidth links connecting GPU groups. It packs together partially-filled packets (network data units called flits) heading to the same destination to maximize bandwidth usage, drops speculative prefetch requests that haven't been requested to eliminate wasted traffic, and reorders packets so time-critical data reaches its destination before bulk data. These techniques reduce delays for critical requests without modifying the GPU compute pipelines.
isca-2025-032.key_novelty: NetCrafter combines three traffic-shaping techniques—packet packing, filtering of unused speculative requests, and priority-based reordering—to exploit the unequal bandwidth structure of hierarchical multi-GPU systems.

isca-2025-026.method: The approach implements partial quantum error correction (a strategy to catch and fix quantum computation errors without excessive hardware overhead) by protecting certain operations (Clifford operations) with lightweight error codes while handling more complex operations (Rz rotations) through magic state injection, which is more efficient than an alternative method called T-state distillation. Architectural optimizations cut circuit latency by 2x and achieve 66% qubit efficiency. It was validated by comparing quantum state fidelity (accuracy) improvements to standard algorithms without error protection, across different Early Fault Tolerance device configurations.
isca-2025-026.key_novelty: This work adapts partial quantum error correction—protecting Clifford operations with lightweight codes and complex operations via magic state injection—to variational quantum algorithms in the Early Fault Tolerance regime, achieving a 9.27x fidelity improvement while avoiding the prohibitive qubit overhead of full surface-code error correction.

isca-2025-027.method: Zettafly is a two-layer network: the bottom layer has small non-blocking groups (regions where data packets flow freely without congestion), and the top layer connects them with global routers. The key structural principle is that any packet moving between groups passes through at most one global router, keeping network distances short. The groups are sized to match typical small-to-medium HPC jobs that dominate production systems, so jobs running within a group achieve non-blocking communication without bottlenecks. The paper develops adaptive routing algorithms (algorithms that adjust paths based on live network conditions) for this topology and evaluates it against fat-tree and dragonfly variants through simulation on HPC workloads with multiple concurrent jobs.
isca-2025-027.key_novelty: Zettafly separates control of non-blocking group size from overall network scale, so you can partition massive networks into smaller non-blocking sub-networks matched to typical HPC and AI job sizes while keeping network paths short and costs reasonable at zettascale.

isca-2025-022.method: CapChecker is a hardware interface between accelerators and memory that intercepts every memory access from the accelerator. It reads permission rules from the CPU—specifying which memory addresses are accessible and what operations (read/write) are allowed—and blocks any request that violates these rules. The accelerator hardware doesn't change; instead, the CPU sends the rules through a lightweight communication mechanism that maps the accelerator's direct memory accesses to CHERI capabilities (the CPU's built-in memory-access labels).
isca-2025-022.key_novelty: CapChecker brings fine-grained memory protection to CHERI-unaware accelerators by enforcing CPU permission rules at the hardware interface, without requiring any accelerator modification.

isca-2025-034.method: WindServe uses a central scheduler that constantly watches how much compute and memory each part of the system is using, then dynamically reassigns jobs between the compute-heavy prefill phase (which prepares input) and the memory-heavy decoding phase (which generates output) to avoid queuing and reduce overhead from moving KV caches (data that stores the model's context) between phases. Its stall-free rescheduling strategy keeps memory constantly busy during these data transfers without creating scheduling pauses. A stream-based pipeline separates prefill and decoding tasks into different execution channels and handles their dependencies asynchronously, preventing interference when both run at the same time.
isca-2025-034.key_novelty: WindServe's key breakthrough is a rescheduling method that keeps memory constantly busy while moving KV caches between phases without scheduling delays, enabling dynamic load balancing that static schedules cannot match.

isca-2025-035.method: Heliostat reuses the ray tracing accelerators (specialized hardware in modern GPUs that finds where light rays hit objects) to perform GPU address translation—the process of converting virtual memory addresses to physical ones. Ray tracing and address translation both work by traversing tree structures with nearly identical logic: ray tracing traverses bounding-volume hierarchy (BVH) trees to find ray-object intersections, while address translation traverses radix trees to map addresses. By mapping address-translation operations onto the existing ray-tracing hardware, Heliostat increases translation bandwidth without requiring dedicated hardware, avoiding the area and power cost of scaling the main translation unit (GMMU). Heliostat+ extends this by predicting which addresses will be needed next and pre-translating them (like memory prefetching), further reducing translation latency.
isca-2025-035.key_novelty: Heliostat is the first design to reuse ray tracing accelerators for address translation by exploiting the identical tree-traversal patterns of ray tracing (bounding-volume hierarchies for finding ray-object intersections) and address translation (radix trees for mapping memory addresses), achieving translation speed at just 1.53% the area and 5.8% the power of a dedicated solution.

isca-2025-029.method: FAST is a hardware accelerator for Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE—computing on encrypted data without decrypting it). It implements two cryptographic optimizations: hoisting (which eliminates redundant number-transformation operations during key-switching) and KLSS gadget decomposition key-switching (an efficient method for processing encryption keys). The accelerator dynamically switches between these methods during execution based on how computationally complex the encrypted data is, using tunable-bit arithmetic (adjustable calculation precision) to match each method's specific requirements. It scales by configuring its array of processing elements to handle varying workload demands.
isca-2025-029.key_novelty: FAST is one FHE accelerator supporting hoisting and both hybrid and KLSS gadget-decomposition key-switching, dynamically switching between methods as the ciphertext level changes (encrypted data's computational complexity) and adjusting calculation precision accordingly.
