isca-2025-033.method: vNPU virtualizes inter-core connected NPUs using three integrated techniques: (1) routing virtualization redirects instructions and data from virtual core IDs to physical cores across the chip's communication highways (NoC); (2) memory virtualization translates addresses intelligently, accounting for where data lives in each core's fast memory (SRAM) and across the network, to reduce stalls and maintain memory bandwidth; (3) topology mapping tests different virtual-to-physical core mappings and selects the one that best balances hardware utilization against program performance. The design was tested on an FPGA (Chipyard+FireSim) and an NPU simulator (DCRA).
isca-2025-033.key_novelty: vNPU is the first virtualization design for inter-core connected neural processing units (NPUs) that handles routing, memory translation, and topology mapping together to preserve how cores communicate within each virtual partition.

isca-2025-041.method: Cassandra adds a hardware Branch Trace Unit (BTU) to the processor that replays predetermined control-flow paths (branching sequences) for cryptographic code instead of using normal branch prediction, which makes speculative guesses that can lead to unintended code paths. The system records and compresses the branching patterns of these code regions—which tend to be repetitive with loop-heavy structures—and stores the compressed traces in the BTU. During execution, the BTU supplies the correct branch decisions directly to the processor, eliminating the speculative paths that enable Spectre-class attacks.
isca-2025-041.key_novelty: Cassandra replaces branch prediction with a hardware record-and-replay system using compressed control-flow traces for cryptographic code, achieving security against Spectre-class attacks without speculation overhead and gaining a net speedup.

isca-2025-038.method: On spatial dataflow architectures (systems where program instructions run on separate processing units, or PEs, distributed across a chip), different PEs sit at different distances from memory. The compiler identifies which load instructions (instructions that read data from memory) are critical using dependence analysis (tracing which instructions depend on others), then maps those loads to the PEs physically nearest to memory, reducing the distance data must travel. This is implemented on the Monaco SDA architecture (from Efficient Computer) with the effcc compiler, which exposes PE-to-memory distances to guide the compiler's placement decisions. This inverts NUMA systems: instead of moving data closer to fixed processors, NUPEA moves the data-reading instructions closer to memory.
isca-2025-038.key_novelty: NUPEA places load instructions near memory instead of moving data near processors—a simpler approach for compilers to analyze and optimize on spatial dataflow architectures.

isca-2025-036.method: Magellan is a compiler-based software prefetcher that analyzes pointer-chasing chains (like A[B[i]], where one result feeds into the next lookup) across nested loops. It builds a map of data dependencies spanning loop boundaries and inserts prefetch instructions scheduled to arrive ahead of when they're needed, based on how many times the loop runs and estimated memory fetch time. This approach covers multi-level indirection patterns that single-level prefetchers miss, prefetching for both current and future loop iterations.
isca-2025-036.key_novelty: Magellan is the first prefetcher to track data dependencies across multiple loop levels and understand how inner and outer loops interact to handle nested pointer-chasing patterns.

isca-2025-040.method: The design treats each weight as a signal delay and each activation magnitude as a signal's arrival time, replacing standard arithmetic operations. These time-based signals flow through a systolic array—a grid of synchronized processors—using proven data patterns that efficiently reuse the same hardware across both space and time cycles. Between layers, the system sums time-shifted signals using noise-tolerant operations and stores results in hybrid circuits combining digital memory with time-based encoding, while maintaining full compatibility with traditional ANN algorithms.
isca-2025-040.key_novelty: Encoding ANN weights as delays and activation magnitudes as signal arrival times enables traditional ANN algorithms to run on biologically inspired circuits with 11× better energy than spiking neural networks.

isca-2025-025.method: zkSpeed is a specialized computer chip with eight processing units that work together to generate zero-knowledge proofs—cryptographic proofs that demonstrate knowledge of information without revealing it. It performs massive multiplication on very large numbers (255-381 bits) using polynomial structures up to degree 2^24 (roughly 16 million); one unit cuts multiplication time by 92% through improved value grouping, and another processes operations in batches of 64 to spread out the cost of expensive calculations. The units communicate through four shared channels; polynomial data is compressed 10-11 times to fit in fast on-chip memory, while large computation streams use high-bandwidth memory at 2 TB/s. The design was optimized by simulating thousands of chip configurations.
isca-2025-025.key_novelty: The core innovation is fitting the complete HyperPlonk proving process into a single chip by reusing hardware—a circuit that performs all three proof checks (ZeroCheck, PermCheck, OpenCheck) using shared multipliers to cut area by 48.9%, combined with a hybrid tree-traversal unit and batched division operations.

isca-2025-037.method: SpecASan extends ARM's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE)—a hardware feature that assigns security tags to memory locations—from normal execution into speculative execution (where the CPU predicts ahead). When the CPU speculatively accesses memory, the hardware checks whether the pointer's security tag matches the memory location's tag; if they don't match, that access is held up until the prediction completes, preventing it from leaving traces in caches and memory translation buffers. This combines with Control-Flow Integrity rules that block gadget sequences (code chains attackers link together), using only the existing MTE tag-checking hardware with minimal new additions.
isca-2025-037.key_novelty: SpecASan is the first to repurpose ARM MTE tag checks on the speculative execution path to selectively delay potentially leaking memory accesses, enforcing security rules without disabling speculation or adding hardware structures to track data access.

isca-2025-044.method: Telos is a specialized chip that exploits regular grid-pattern sparsity in sparse triangular solvers. It divides the problem into parallel "planes" (slices of computation) mapped across processing elements, with each plane keeping its data local to avoid slow memory access. Communication between planes is reorganized into synchronized pipeline flows (systolic flows), allowing dependent computations to execute as soon as their inputs arrive with minimal waiting. The chip overlaps computation with memory fetches to hide data-access delays.
isca-2025-044.key_novelty: Plane-parallel pipelining—breaking computation into parallel planes with synchronized data flow between them—that resolves loop-carried dependencies while preserving data locality by exploiting the regular grid patterns in PDE-derived sparsity.

isca-2025-046.method: SEAL replaces binary pixel encoding with delay-based encoding, where each pixel's brightness is represented as a timing delay—how long a signal takes to arrive encodes the brightness value (analog-to-time conversion). This timing data feeds directly into a processor built into the sensor that performs keypoint detection and tracking using race logic, an ultra-efficient technique where computation is encoded in signal arrival times, using just one wire per variable. Before data leaves the sensor, a quantized frontend processor compresses the timing outputs. By keeping the localization computation on the sensor instead of sending raw pixel data to an external computer, SEAL eliminates both the energy and latency bottleneck of data transfer.
isca-2025-046.key_novelty: SEAL runs the complete keypoint detection and tracking pipeline inside the pixel sensor using timing-based encoding (race logic) instead of binary encoding, all implemented in fully digital CMOS circuits.

isca-2025-030.method: IPEX (Intermittence-aware Prefetching EXtension) is an add-on layer that sits on top of existing prefetchers (hardware that tries to fetch data before it's needed) on batteryless energy-harvesting systems, without replacing them. It tracks which prefetched data blocks actually get used before power fails, then suppresses prefetching of blocks that historically go unused before the next outage (reducing 'useless prefetches'). It also monitors harvested energy levels to predict imminent power failures and, at that moment, throttles (reduces) how aggressively it prefetches, targeting only data blocks the processor is likely to use before power loss. This way, harvested energy is redirected from futile prefetches toward making actual progress on the program.
isca-2025-030.key_novelty: IPEX is the first prefetch extension that actively suppresses prefetches based on tracking data usage and predicting power failures, converting energy that would be wasted on cache lines never accessed into forward progress.

isca-2025-045.method: WarmCache caches data in STT-RAM (magnetic memory that survives power outages but with reduced data retention—it loses accuracy over time but lasts longer than regular SRAM). The compiler breaks the program into regions and checks cache data at each region boundary for retention errors (data corruption from the reduced retention time). If errors are found, that region is re-executed to restore correct cached data. The compiler aligns region boundaries with the STT-RAM's refresh interval by stitching short regions together and splitting long ones, which reduces how often corruption occurs.
isca-2025-045.key_novelty: WarmCache preserves cache across power failures using relaxed-retention STT-RAM (magnetic memory) instead of fully persistent storage, paired with compiler-driven error detection and re-execution to avoid write-back overhead.

isca-2025-050.method: InfiniMind adds a memory controller that reduces wear on non-volatile memory (permanent storage that degrades with each write). The controller uses four complementary techniques: (1) skipping writes for neural signals that repeat or don't change, (2) collecting multiple small changes and batching them into fewer writes, (3) packing several partial updates into single write operations, and (4) compressing neural signal data by using patterns natural to brain signals. Together, these reduce the total writes to storage, extending the chip's lifetime and enabling practical continual learning on implanted brain-computer interfaces.
isca-2025-050.key_novelty: A memory controller that combines four complementary write-reduction techniques, each exploiting a different natural pattern in brain signals: sparse activity, temporal clustering, and regular waveform structure.

isca-2025-049.method: AQB8 shrinks bounding boxes (the 3D bounds that guide ray-tracing searches) from 32-bit floating-point to 8-bit integers at every level of the scene hierarchy tree. Unlike prior compression schemes that expand these integers back to floating-point for ray intersection tests, AQB8 performs all tests directly in 8-bit integer arithmetic. The hardware replaces expensive floating-point math circuits with simpler, lower-power integer units, eliminating both memory bandwidth waste and arithmetic cost. To avoid incorrectly discarding rays due to rounding errors, the design propagates and adjusts quantization bounds across hierarchy levels to prevent false negatives.
isca-2025-049.key_novelty: AQB8's core idea is using 8-bit quantization at every level of the BVH hierarchy tree so ray intersection tests run entirely in integer arithmetic, eliminating the expensive decompression to floating-point that prior work required.

isca-2025-051.method: UPP creates a compact instruction set (a language the hardware understands) specifically built for filtering data in storage hardware. The database recognizes what data needs filtering, translates those operations into UPP instructions, and sends them to an FPGA chip inside the storage device (SmartSSD), which executes them directly on the stored data using bitwise comparisons (bit-by-bit checks) and lightweight metadata (bookkeeping about data structure) without reading data into memory or reformatting it. This separation of the instruction set from individual filter operations allows the database to compile and push arbitrary complex filters to storage while keeping data formats unchanged on disk.
isca-2025-051.key_novelty: UPP's core idea is a compact instruction set for storage hardware that enables flexible filter evaluation, so databases can compile any filter operation into executable code instead of relying on hardwired operator support.

isca-2025-042.method: LightNobel compresses intermediate values in protein structure prediction models using Token-wise Adaptive Activation Quantization (AAQ), which exploits a pattern unique to these models: values vary much more between different amino acid positions (tokens) than between feature channels, making per-position compression more effective. The system identifies three value ranges with different precision needs—using 8-bit, 4-bit, and 4-bit-only compression while keeping outliers at higher precision—and uses custom hardware (a Reconfigurable Matrix Processing Unit with a 128-lane parallel unit) that processes mixed 4-bit/8-bit/16-bit numbers directly without unpacking each element. To prevent memory overflow, attention is computed one position-pair at a time (like FlashAttention) rather than building the full Ns×Ns×Ns score matrix. The design runs at 1 GHz on 28nm silicon with 80 GB of HBM2E memory.
isca-2025-042.key_novelty: The core innovation is token-wise adaptive quantization that exploits how protein structure models have higher variance between positions than between feature channels, combined with hardware that dynamically handles mixed 4-bit/8-bit/16-bit precision without decompressing individual elements.

isca-2025-047.method: Corki replaces per-frame discrete action decisions with trajectory prediction (smooth cubic paths calculated over multiple steps), reducing how often the LLM needs to run by up to 5.1x. A custom dataflow ASIC accelerator runs task-space computed torque control (a method that calculates joint forces and torques), using pipelined stages (breaking the calculation into parallel steps connected by FIFOs and line buffers) and an approximate computing unit that skips matrix recalculation when robot joints move below a threshold (saving >51% of matrix updates). Communication latency is hidden by overlapping image capture and transmission with trajectory execution.
isca-2025-047.key_novelty: Replacing frame-by-frame action prediction with cubic trajectory planning decouples the LLM inference rate from the control rate, enabling an FPGA hardware accelerator with task-space computed torque control and approximate computing to achieve 29x control speedup.

isca-2025-043.method: Fair-CO2 uses the Shapley value—a mathematical principle that fairly divides shared costs by measuring how much each workload contributes under every possible combination—to attribute cloud carbon responsibility. The system captures embodied carbon effects: instead of splitting a server's manufacturing emissions based on flat time allocation, each workload's share is based on its actual utilization rate, so a heavily-used server's manufacturing carbon is proportionally attributed to the workloads that actually used it. It also captures interference effects from colocation, where performance degradation caused by shared resource contention directly reduces the attributed costs of the workloads experiencing that degradation. Because computing the exact Shapley attribution is mathematically intractable (grows exponentially with workload count), Fair-CO2 approximates using two components: demand-aware embodied carbon (adjusting hardware depreciation by real-time utilization) and interference-aware operational costs (accounting for performance loss from co-tenancy), validated through Monte Carlo simulations to confirm the approximations' fidelity to the exact Shapley solution.
isca-2025-043.key_novelty: Fair-CO2 uses Shapley value—a mathematical fairness principle—to attribute cloud carbon, with scalable approximations that account for actual hardware usage (embodied carbon) and performance loss from resource sharing (interference).

isca-2025-048.method: TRACI adds tags to messages that GPUs send when requesting embeddings, marking when multiple requests need the same data (input-reuse) and when data has already been retrieved (output-reuse). Network switches read these tags and recognize duplicate requests, combining them instantly so each unique request is processed just once and the results are sent to all GPUs that need them, rather than routing every request separately to a host.
isca-2025-048.key_novelty: Using metadata tags on embedding requests to mark identical requests (input-reuse) and available results (output-reuse), enabling network switches to combine duplicates on-the-fly instead of routing all requests to a host.

isca-2025-052.method: RAGO creates RAGSchema, a structured template describing the building blocks and data flow of any RAG algorithm (the steps that retrieve context and rerank results before the language model generates answers). Using this template, they measure how different RAG variants actually behave in production—which steps are slow, how much computation each requires—to identify performance bottlenecks. Instead of treating all RAG systems the same way as extended language model inference, RAGO tunes specific optimizations (scheduling policies that decide which requests to process first, resource partitioning that splits compute between GPUs and CPUs, and batching strategies that group requests) to match each variant's particular performance problems.
isca-2025-052.key_novelty: RAGSchema is a structured template that describes any RAG variant, enabling optimization tuned to each variant's specific bottlenecks rather than applying a single strategy to all.

isca-2025-056.method: EOD improves both algorithm and hardware to speed up the preparation stage. The algorithm precomputes training nodes to convert exponential neighborhood growth to linear growth, and compresses the combined features using Zero-Value Compression (ZVC). A processor built directly into memory performs aggregation on the compressed features without decompressing them, bypassing the slow PCIe and host memory bottleneck by exploiting the memory's high internal bandwidth.
isca-2025-056.key_novelty: A compression format for concatenated features paired with a processor built into memory that aggregates directly from compressed storage, eliminating the expensive host memory access.

isca-2025-061.method: AiF solves the data bottleneck in on-device AI inference by putting matrix multiplication compute hardware directly inside flash chips, so calculations happen where the data lives instead of shuttling data through the slow external PCIe connection. It introduces specialized flash read techniques designed for how LLM weights are arranged in memory and streamlines the error-correction process (which normally slows reads) to achieve 4x faster internal data movement with minimal overhead. This allows in-flash matrix operations to run at nearly full speed on the flash chip's internal pathways.
isca-2025-061.key_novelty: AiF embeds matrix multiplication compute directly inside flash chips using flash-read techniques optimized for how LLM weights are stored, achieving a 4x boost to internal data movement speed through a streamlined error-correction scheme.

isca-2025-059.method: LIA runs large language models on a single GPU by offloading heavy math work to matrix units (AMX) built into modern Intel CPUs—specifically 4th-gen Sapphire Rapids and 6th-gen Granite Rapids Xeons. By keeping the model weights in CPU memory instead of shuttling them back and forth over the slow PCIe connection, the system avoids transfer bottlenecks. It also expands memory capacity by combining standard RAM (DDR) with a new high-speed memory protocol (CXL), enabling larger batch inference. The framework automatically distributes each transformer layer's computation between CPU and GPU, optimizing either for low latency (fast answers per question) or high throughput (many answers per second).
isca-2025-059.key_novelty: Single-GPU inference that uses Intel CPUs' matrix units (AMX) as true computational partners to the GPU, with CXL memory taking the place of multi-GPU setups.

isca-2025-054.method: Ruche Networks add long-range shortcut connections (Ruche channels) to a standard 2-D mesh grid of routers, allowing distant routers to communicate through fewer intermediate routers without redesigning individual routers or cores. The researchers implement this at the register-transfer level—the detailed hardware specification that translates directly to circuits—and test it against standard 2-D mesh and torus layouts, measuring throughput (data flow per second), latency (message arrival time), power consumption, area efficiency, and cycle time across workloads that demand high-bandwidth data streaming.
isca-2025-054.key_novelty: Ruche Networks improve network performance while maintaining a mesh's ability to scale efficiently by adding uniform long-range bypass links that don't require changes to router or core designs.

isca-2025-053.method: Neo takes the CKKS encryption scheme (a way to compute on encrypted data without decrypting it) and reformulates its two main computational bottlenecks—the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT, a fast algorithm for multiplying encrypted polynomials) and polynomial multiplication—as matrix operations. GPU Tensor Cores (specialized hardware within GPUs) can then accelerate these operations using 8-bit integer or 16-bit floating-point math. To fit onto Tensor Cores, the design breaks the NTT into smaller stages (butterfly stages) matching the Tensor Core's matrix dimensions and uses residue number system arithmetic (an encoding that prevents overflow in low-precision math). Custom code handles data arrangement, twiddle factor injection (rotation constants used in NTT), and modular reduction to keep everything within precision limits.
isca-2025-053.key_novelty: The core idea is reformulating encrypted polynomial arithmetic (NTT and residue number system multiplication in CKKS) as matrix multiplication, so GPUs' specialized Tensor Core hardware can accelerate cryptographic calculations instead of using general-purpose GPU cores.

isca-2025-063.method: RLGS uses reinforcement learning (an AI approach where an algorithm learns through trial and error) to optimize how graph states (entangled collections of photons) are generated in photonic quantum computers. It creates a structured "map" of the quantum circuit that organizes two-qubit gates (operations on pairs of quantum bits) and their dependencies (which operations must happen first), allowing the RL agent to search for generation sequences that reduce generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions simultaneously. The system balances competing constraints: minimizing the sequential depth of gates while also reducing crosstalk (unwanted interference between qubits).
isca-2025-063.key_novelty: RLGS restructures the quantum circuit into a "map" that the RL agent can navigate, converting what would otherwise be an exponentially difficult search over gate dependencies into a tractable optimization problem that simultaneously minimizes generation time, emitter count, and CZ gate insertions.

isca-2025-055.method: DX100 is a programmable accelerator that CPU cores can share to speed up indirect memory accesses (A[B[i]] patterns) and streaming data operations, with an 8-instruction instruction set supporting loads, stores, atomic read-modify-write operations, and loop control. Its core strategy is using a large hardware reordering buffer—the Row Table with 16K entries made from BCAM (binary content-addressable memory for fast lookups) and SRAM (fast storage memory)—that batches and reorganizes addresses to maximize DRAM row-buffer hits; a Word Table coalesces redundant accesses, and a Request Generator spreads them across DRAM channels and bank groups for parallel execution. Streaming data flows through the L3 cache, while indirect accesses bypass the cache and go directly into DRAM controllers, with a Coherency Agent maintaining cache consistency by monitoring directories. An MLIR-based compiler with Polygeist automatically identifies indirect accesses in C/C++, tiles loops, and generates DX100 code, covering over 99% of graph frontier operations in real benchmarks.
isca-2025-055.key_novelty: DX100's core innovation is a large hardware reordering table (the Row Table with 16K entries) that can see and rearrange 500 times more memory addresses than DRAM controllers' built-in buffers (which hold only 32 addresses), allowing it to achieve near-peak DRAM bandwidth use regardless of how scattered the memory accesses are.

isca-2025-057.method: QR-Map creates a map of the quantum circuit by organizing two-qubit gates (operations affecting two qubits at once) to show which operations depend on each other. From this map, it finds places where qubits can be reused—where a qubit finishes one task and starts another without sitting idle. It simultaneously optimizes two things: keeping the circuit shallow (gate serialization depth, the number of operation layers) and reducing crosstalk (interference between neighboring qubits on the hardware). Because the algorithm is deterministic and runs in polynomial time, it reliably finds the best qubit-reuse solution instead of requiring exhaustive search.
isca-2025-057.key_novelty: Instead of exponential search, QR-Map uses a map-based structure of two-qubit gates to reliably find the optimal qubit-reuse solution in polynomial time.

isca-2025-064.method: Jord co-locates functions in a single memory space but isolates them using hardware memory protection keys—CPU features that mark which memory regions each function can access, with enforcement at nanosecond speed and no OS involvement required. Functions share memory directly without copying, and Jord's scheduler switches between functions within the process instead of triggering OS context switches. The result is microsecond-scale latency instead of the millisecond overhead of container isolation.
isca-2025-064.key_novelty: Jord achieves microsecond-scale function latency by co-locating functions in a single memory space with hardware-enforced isolation at nanosecond granularity, instead of isolating them in separate containers or virtual machines.

isca-2025-067.method: HYTE combines upfront planning with runtime adjustment to tile sparse tensors (breaking multi-dimensional arrays containing mostly zeros into chunks) on specialized hardware accelerators. Before execution, it samples the sparse data to estimate good tile sizes, shapes, and processing order without examining the full dataset. At runtime, it adjusts tile shapes on-the-fly as the actual sparsity (where zeros are located) varies across the data. It also efficiently manages metadata (the structural information about how data is organized) in both main memory and fast on-chip storage, solving an overhead problem that earlier approaches overlooked.
isca-2025-067.key_novelty: HYTE combines simple upfront sampling of the data with runtime adjustment to jointly optimize tile size, shape, iteration order, and memory allocation while adapting to how sparsity varies.

isca-2025-068.method: H2-LLM stacks compute chips directly against memory chips using hybrid bonding—a technology that connects them with thousands of tiny data pathways (through-silicon vias) that move data far faster than traditional side-by-side layouts. Instead of uniform compute, it mixes specialized processors optimized for different tasks: some for math-heavy operations, others for memory-heavy ones. The system assigns each LLM operation—attention heads, feed-forward layers, memory lookups—to whichever compute resource sits closest to where its data lives, whether during prefill (when the model processes your input) or decoding (when it generates output one token at a time). Finally, an automated search finds the best combination of compute count and memory allocation that balances speed and efficiency.
isca-2025-068.key_novelty: H2-LLM jointly explores hardware architecture and dataflow design together—instead of separately—for hybrid-bonded LLM accelerators, so compute placement and data flow can reinforce each other.

isca-2025-076.method: The paper embeds a reconfigurable processor directly inside NVMe storage devices that can reprogram itself to work with different search algorithms (like HNSW or IVF, which organize vectors to speed up matching). This in-storage processor runs the smaller language models that convert search queries into vectors entirely inside the storage—without the main CPU getting involved. It also performs the similarity search to find relevant documents, all without data leaving the storage device. The main GPU (DGX A100) only participates once documents are selected, to generate the final answer.
isca-2025-076.key_novelty: An in-storage processor that reconfigures itself to run both query-to-vector conversion and document search entirely inside the storage device, eliminating slow data transfers between storage and the CPU.

isca-2025-069.method: Prophet helps programs run faster by predicting future memory accesses in advance (called prefetching) when that data follows irregular patterns, like pointers jumping around in a data structure. It profiles the program once using lightweight counters instead of recording every single memory access, then uses that profile to create hints—special instructions embedded in the program—that tell the hardware prefetcher how to best manage its limited storage space at runtime. These hints adapt automatically when the program runs with different data, so you don't need to re-profile. Prophet augments existing prefetching hardware, optimizing the most-used code paths while leaving the standard hardware approach to handle everything else.
isca-2025-069.key_novelty: Prophet combines lightweight instruction counting (instead of expensive full-access tracing) with hints embedded in the program binary to let the hardware automatically adjust its prefetching strategy at runtime, eliminating the need to re-profile for different program inputs.

isca-2025-060.method: Garibaldi maintains a lookup table (16K entries, 194 KB) where each instruction address maps to the hotness of its associated data using a counter that maxes out at 63. At eviction time, it queries this table and protects instructions paired with hot data instead of following the standard eviction policy. When an instruction miss occurs, the system prefetches the related cold data. Every 100K accesses, it measures how often data misses follow instruction misses and adjusts the protection threshold.
isca-2025-060.key_novelty: Garibaldi is the first to measure the cost of instruction misses by the hotness of the data they trigger, using this connection to decide which instructions to protect and which data to prefetch.

isca-2025-058.method: The system places small processors (Processing Elements or PEs) inside DIMM buffer chips at the channel level (a near-memory processing architecture), keeping data right at the computation site instead of shuttling it back to the main CPU. Each processor runs a three-stage pipeline on data chunks called MacroNodes: Invalidation Check (discarding outdated data), TransferNode Extraction (pulling data to transfer), and Routing and Update (directing results and updating state). Within each chip, a crossbar switch routes data between processors; across different chips, a network bridge forwards TransferNodes between DIMMs. Software optimizations enhance efficiency: batching the genome into 10% chunks reduces peak memory by 14 times, pointer deduplication removes redundant MacroNode copies, and large MacroNodes (over 1 KB) are sent to the main CPU rather than overloading the processor buffers.
isca-2025-058.key_novelty: The core idea is placing pipelined processors in DIMM buffer chips (channel-level near-memory processing) and designing them specifically for MacroNode data structures, enabling the Iterative Compaction step to process many pieces in parallel with routing between chips and CPU backup for large outliers.

isca-2025-072.method: HeterRAG uses two different types of processing-in-memory—hardware that does computation directly on the storage itself—to solve two different problems: DIMM-based PIM (affordable, large-capacity standard memory) stores knowledge bases and accelerates the scattered memory access patterns during document retrieval, while HBM-based PIM (specialized high-speed memory) handles the matrix-vector multiplications (GEMV operations) that LLMs repeatedly do during text generation. The system sends each retrieval or generation task to whichever PIM type handles that kind of memory access best, managing the data flow between them.
isca-2025-072.key_novelty: HeterRAG is the first system to combine two types of processing-in-memory (DIMM-based and HBM-based) to simultaneously solve the knowledge-base size problem in retrieval and the data-movement speed problem in LLM generation for RAG.

isca-2025-075.method: The researchers tested Intel's DLB (Dynamic Load Balancer, hardware built into processors to distribute work across cores) against software alternatives using focused performance tests. They then designed AccDirect, which uses a direct hardware-to-hardware communication channel (called PCIe P2P) between the network interface card and the DLB, bypassing the CPU entirely. The network card can now directly send work assignments to the DLB's queues using P2P DMA (direct memory access between devices, without CPU involvement), removing the CPU overhead that normally happens when preparing and enqueuing these assignments. By cutting the CPU out of this frequently-executed operation (the 'hot path'), they eliminated a major bottleneck.
isca-2025-075.key_novelty: AccDirect eliminates host CPU involvement in load balancing by using a direct hardware-to-hardware connection (PCIe P2P) between the network interface card and the processor's built-in load balancer, reducing system-wide CPU power consumption by 10% while maintaining equivalent throughput.

isca-2025-071.method: LightML combines a light-based computing core (photonic crossbar) with a custom memory and buffering system that keeps it 80% utilized for machine learning tasks. The system handles large matrix multiplication, element-wise operations, nonlinear activation functions, and convolutional layers using dedicated photonic and electronic circuits working together. It targets both edge and data-center deployments, achieving 325 trillion operations per second while consuming just 3 watts.
isca-2025-071.key_novelty: The single innovation is a memory and buffer architecture designed to keep a light-based computing core (photonic crossbar) 80% utilized across different machine learning operations.

isca-2025-066.method: ANSMET puts a small processor inside each memory rank (a unit of physical memory) that calculates distances right where data lives, rather than sending all vectors to the main CPU. For each candidate vector, the system quickly estimates the distance using partial data (a subset of dimensions or bits); this estimate is guaranteed to be at most the true distance, so if it already exceeds the target threshold, the fetch stops immediately. Memory is laid out to support these early-stop decisions, and a simple protocol between the host CPU and memory processors handles index traversal and result sorting.
isca-2025-066.key_novelty: ANSMET uses conservative estimates from partial data (partial dimensions and bits) to stop fetching vectors early, with this early-termination logic embedded in memory-rank processors to eliminate wasted bandwidth for far-away candidates.

isca-2025-078.method: Nyx divides the FPGA into reconfigurable regions and adds virtual FIFOs (data buffers between tasks) that let dependent tasks exchange data without running simultaneously. The system's controller tracks the queue state and schedules tasks across regions with high throughput, allowing different pipelines to share the same hardware by running at different times.
isca-2025-078.key_novelty: Virtual FIFOs enable pipelined tasks to stream data between each other and run at different times on shared FPGA regions instead of requiring all pipeline stages to run simultaneously.

isca-2025-074.method: OptiPIM reformulates the challenge of mapping operations to PIM hardware and arranging data—choosing where each computation should run and how data should be laid out—as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem, a mathematical technique for finding the optimal solution when you have many constraints to satisfy. It builds accurate cost models (predictions of runtime efficiency for different choices) that efficiently represent the full design space. Implemented as a compiler pass within MLIR (an open-source framework that transforms high-level code like PyTorch into efficient hardware instructions), OptiPIM exploits the problem's structure to compute optimal mappings for PIM accelerators in just 4 minutes.
isca-2025-074.key_novelty: OptiPIM approaches PIM mapping using Integer Linear Programming (a mathematical method that finds the best solution to complex problems with many constraints) integrated into MLIR, automatically producing the mathematically optimal way to map data-intensive applications onto PIM accelerators in just 4 minutes.

isca-2025-091.method: DReX splits the search into two stages. First, logic built into the DRAM hardware itself quickly filters out far-away candidate vectors by comparing the query to summary points (centroids) without moving all the vector data off the chip. Then a specialized accelerator near the memory performs exact nearest-neighbor search on just the remaining, much smaller set of candidates. This cuts down on expensive data movement between memory and processor while guaranteeing you get the exact top-k closest vectors.
isca-2025-091.key_novelty: DReX uses in-DRAM filtering hardware to eliminate distant candidates, then performs exact nearest-neighbor search on the survivors, removing the speed-versus-accuracy tradeoff without large off-chip data transfers.

isca-2025-081.method: PACIPV (Prefetch-Aware Coarse-grained Insertion and Promotion Vectors) improves cache replacement by making two key decisions configurable rather than hardcoded: where a cache line enters the cache hierarchy when first stored (insertion position) and when it moves to a higher priority level (promotion position). Instead of choosing these rules by hand, the system searches exhaustively through all possible insertion and promotion combinations on test workloads to find the optimal one. Crucially, the policy treats prefetch requests (data speculatively loaded by the processor) differently from regular memory requests by giving them different placement and priority rules, which prevents prefetching from hurting performance by displacing data the processor will actually need soon (called prefetch thrashing). The final hardware implementation uses simple counter logic, adding negligible overhead compared to previous replacement policies.
isca-2025-081.key_novelty: Exhaustive search through prefetch-aware insertion and promotion vectors finds simple RRIP-based cache replacement policies for instruction-heavy workloads that match or exceed complex learned replacement policies.

isca-2025-077.method: In fault-tolerant quantum computers, logical qubits (bits encoded across many physical qubits for error correction) sometimes run at different speeds and must synchronize before merging via Lattice Surgery (a qubit-merging operation). This paper proposes three synchronization strategies: Passive idles the fast qubits for their entire time deficit right before the merge—one long wait that lets decoherence errors build up; Active spreads this idle time into small chunks inserted after each error-correction round, preventing long waits; and Hybrid runs extra error-correction rounds on slower qubits to shrink the time deficit, then applies Active to the remainder. A hardware controller (Patch Counter Table, Phase Calculators, and Synchronization Slack Calculator) tracks when each qubit region finishes its cycles and injects timing directives into the control schedule without adding latency.
isca-2025-077.key_novelty: Active synchronization distributes idle time across multiple error-correction rounds rather than all at once, reducing peak decoherence per round and cutting the logical error rate by up to 3.4x.

isca-2025-083.method: Concorde combines analytical models (mathematical formulas based on how CPUs work) with machine learning to predict CPU performance quickly and accurately. The analytical part separately models major CPU components—pipeline stages (instruction execution steps), cache hierarchy (layered memory), branch prediction (guessing execution paths), and memory access—using structured equations. Machine learning then corrects the remaining errors from complex interactions between components that the math alone can't capture. Each analytical sub-model is tuned independently and combined at prediction time, making it fast to evaluate new CPU designs.
isca-2025-083.key_novelty: The key innovation is composing separate analytical models for each CPU stage that are tuned independently, then combining them with machine learning to fix errors from complex component interactions.

isca-2025-080.method: Hybe assigns the compute-intensive prefill stage (processing the full context once) to GPUs (NVIDIA H100 with vLLM) and the memory-hungry decode stage (generating tokens one at a time) to lightweight NPUs. The key innovation is fine-grained KV streaming: instead of storing all the key-value cache data (what the model learns about each token in the context) in GPU memory, the GPU streams it directly to the NPU's memory (high-bandwidth memory, or HBM) as it's being computed—this dramatically cuts GPU memory usage. A dynamic scheduler assigns incoming requests to whichever hardware is idle, preventing bottlenecks. The NPU is built in a 4nm process with HBM matching the H100's memory specification.
isca-2025-080.key_novelty: Streaming key-value cache data piece-by-piece from the GPU to the NPU as it's generated during prefill, rather than storing it all in GPU memory first, enables million-token contexts while keeping the NPU minimally sized for the decode stage.

isca-2025-085.method: FlexNeRFer is a specialized chip where an internal communication network (called a Network-on-Chip or NoC) reconfigures itself to handle different ways data flows through the computation, allowing the same hardware to adapt to different algorithm styles. Its multiply-accumulate units (the computational cores) can adjust their precision—operating at different bit-widths like 8-bit or 16-bit—based on accuracy needs, and the chip automatically detects sparse data (matrices with lots of zeros) and selects the most efficient storage format at runtime to avoid wasting computation on zero values. Built in 28 nanometer CMOS technology, this combination of flexible routing, adjustable precision, and automatic sparse-data handling enables one chip to efficiently run many different NeRF algorithms.
isca-2025-085.key_novelty: FlexNeRFer uses a flexible internal network that adapts its data routing and compute precision on-the-fly, automatically selecting the right format for sparse data, so a single accelerator chip can efficiently run different NeRF algorithms that would otherwise each require algorithm-specific hardware.

isca-2025-090.method: Chimera examines the data-movement operations each parallelism strategy (tensor, pipeline, data, sequence) requires. When combining multiple strategies, it finds where redundant operations occur—multiple strategies asking for identical data movements. It then merges these into a single operation that accomplishes the combined work at once. This merged operation replaces the original blocking communications (operations that pause computation while syncing data), cutting overhead.
isca-2025-090.key_novelty: Chimera identifies and eliminates redundant data movements that occur when combining multiple parallelism strategies by merging them into a single operation.

isca-2025-088.method: The protocol develops constant-rate entanglement distillation (conversion of noisy quantum pairs to high-fidelity ones at a steady rate) through repeated two-way distillation rounds (cycles where partners exchange information to identify and eliminate errors). It uses quantum error-detecting codes with increasing code rate (starting with strict error-checking, then relaxing rules as pairs improve), combined with standard fault-tolerance techniques (ways to keep systems working reliably even when errors occur) to ensure that a constant fraction of raw entanglement pairs become high-fidelity logical pairs (very-high-quality quantum states for computation). Numerical optimization minimizes practical overhead within finite memory constraints.
isca-2025-088.key_novelty: This is the first constant-rate (in expectation) entanglement distillation protocol for noisy quantum interconnects, achieved by chaining quantum error-detecting codes (methods that identify errors without destroying quantum information) with increasing rate in a two-way distillation ladder (back-and-forth refinement cycles).

isca-2025-093.method: FRED distributes tiny routing switches (microswitches) across a silicon wafer to interconnect processing chips (chiplets), allowing data paths to flexibly adjust without any link becoming a bottleneck. Rather than routing all data to a central processor to combine results, these in-network switches start combining data partway through the network, reducing the total traffic. The network maps different parallelism types—data parallelism (processing different datasets), tensor parallelism (splitting model layers), and pipeline parallelism (sequential training stages)—to separate communication groups, so they don't compete for the same links.
isca-2025-093.key_novelty: Embedding reconfigurable microswitches across the wafer that can combine data in-network lets any arbitrary group of processing chips communicate without interference.

isca-2025-079.method: LUT Tensor Core combines software and hardware optimization to speed up AI inference with low-precision numbers. On the software side, lookup-table precomputation is merged with the preceding operation to eliminate redundant work; weights are rewritten symmetrically (from {0,1} to {-1,+1}), which halves table storage. On the hardware side, a specialized Tensor Core processes bits one at a time and uses an elongated tiling pattern (M=2, N=64, K=4) to reuse the lookup table across calculations; a new instruction (LMMA) integrates with compilers (TVM/Roller/Welder) to automatically generate optimized code.
isca-2025-079.key_novelty: The innovation combines table-lookup software optimization (symmetric weight rewriting and operation merging) with a bit-serial elongated-tiling Tensor Core, achieving 4–6x lower power and area than MAC-based Tensor Cores and 1.44x better efficiency than prior lookup-table designs.

isca-2025-086.method: Finesse uses a three-layer design: an intermediate representation (shared notation) for math operations on finite and extension fields, a RISC-style instruction set that executes multiple instructions per cycle (VLIW extension), and a customizable hardware pipeline model. A specialized compiler optimizes data flow, schedules instructions using issue-slot affinity (aligning long arithmetic operations with short linear ones to prevent conflicts), allocates registers, and generates executable code. A cycle-accurate simulator measures real performance and feeds results back to both the compiler and the hardware design tools (EDA toolchain) for joint optimization. The hardware implements four core arithmetic operations (mmul, madd, mlin, minv) in a multi-core SIMT (single instruction executing on multiple cores with different data) architecture with shared instruction memory, on both 40nm ASIC and Virtex-7 FPGA.
isca-2025-086.key_novelty: The innovation is issue-slot affinity scheduling, which partitions the pipeline's instruction slots into periodic intervals and aligns long modular-multiplication operations with short linear operations to eliminate write-back conflicts, combined with a co-design feedback loop between the compiler and hardware synthesis tools (EDA) that jointly optimizes any pairing curve implementation.

isca-2025-097.method: The authors built a formal mathematical model (an axiomatic model) that defines how exceptions behave in Arm-A processors when memory operations don't always execute in the order they're written. They identified three critical cases the model must handle: what happens at exception boundaries when memory is relaxed, external hardware aborts, and software-generated interrupts. To validate the model, they built a toolchain and a library of litmus tests—small test programs that show exactly which processor behaviors are allowed and which are forbidden. The model extends existing Arm-A specifications by adding formal rules for how exceptions enter and exit.
isca-2025-097.key_novelty: This is the first formal definition of what exception precision means in Arm-A, a processor with relaxed memory, answering a decades-old question in computer architecture.

isca-2025-082.method: MeshSlice trains large neural networks across many computers by breaking communication operations into smaller pieces that can run while computers continue computing. It arranges computers in a 2D grid and schedules these pieces so communication in one direction overlaps with computation in another, hiding most communication delay. An optimizer searches over grid shapes, computation dataflows, and piece sizes to find the best settings for each network layer on TPUv4 hardware with its torus interconnect topology.
isca-2025-082.key_novelty: MeshSlice hides communication delays in 2D tensor parallelism for distributed neural network training by slicing all-reduce operations into smaller pieces that overlap with computation.

isca-2025-094.method: Neoscope defines two quantitative measures—Magnitude and Disruption—that track how a workload changes over time, sorting the churn into four categories: Minimal, Perturbing, Escalating, or Volatile. It then frames finding the best chip design as an integer linear program (a mathematical technique that systematically finds the best combination of discrete design choices) combined with job-shop scheduling principles (concepts from factory scheduling that help arrange complex, competing tasks). This lets it find near-optimal chip designs in a single pass rather than exhaustively testing thousands of design combinations. The framework simultaneously optimizes five objectives: performance, chip area, energy consumption, cost, and carbon emissions.
isca-2025-094.key_novelty: Neoscope is the first pre-silicon chip-design framework that explicitly measures workload churn (how workloads change over time) and uses integer linear programming to find designs resilient to this churn, while simultaneously optimizing for performance, area, energy, cost, and carbon emissions.

isca-2025-101.method: DREAM proposes two approaches to efficiently handle DRFM (Directed Refresh Management, a DRAM command that refreshes rows to mitigate Rowhammer attacks). DREAM-R delays issuing the refresh command after detecting a frequently-accessed row, allowing multiple banks to complete their own row accesses in the same time window and spreading the performance cost across more refresh operations; DREAM-C instead groups 32–256 randomly selected rows from across 32 banks into teams that share a single counter, reducing tracker storage by 8× versus Graphene while avoiding expensive lookup hardware and staying compatible with standard DRFM.
isca-2025-101.key_novelty: DREAM exploits the fact that DRFM already refreshes multiple banks simultaneously, using this multi-bank capability to either amortize performance penalties or compress tracking storage, without requiring new DRAM commands.

isca-2025-096.method: ATiM automatically optimizes tensor programs (matrix calculations) for UPMEM systems, which perform computation inside memory chips rather than in the main processor. It searches different ways of organizing code that runs on the main processor and the code that runs inside the memory chips, using techniques designed for UPMEM's structure where memory is organized into separate banks. The system explores different choices like how many parallel workers to use, how to break up loops, and where to place data in memory, then generates optimized code without requiring manual library engineering.
isca-2025-096.key_novelty: ATiM is the first compiler that automatically searches for and generates optimized tensor program code for UPMEM systems, handling their banked-memory structure without requiring engineers to manually write libraries.

isca-2025-103.method: ARTERY predicts quantum measurement outcomes while they're still happening, using two signals: historical statistics (how often this measurement gave each result) and real-time pulse analysis (the shape of the measurement signal as it arrives). A branch predictor combines these signals into a single prediction that downstream gates can act on immediately. The hardware includes FPGA interconnects for fast communication, a trigger system for precise gate timing, and adaptive sampling to extract maximum information from the measurement pulse.
isca-2025-103.key_novelty: ARTERY brings classical branch prediction to quantum circuits by combining historical measurement statistics with real-time pulse-shape analysis, enabling quantum gates to speculatively start executing before mid-circuit measurement results are complete.

isca-2025-095.method: Hermes distributes a large RAG database across multiple computers. It uses a two-tier system: a fast preliminary index rapidly identifies which data partitions might be relevant to a query, then only those partitions go through full dense retrieval—either exact k-nearest-neighbor search (finding the most similar documents) or approximate k-NN (finding good-enough matches faster). By skipping full retrieval on irrelevant partitions, this approach cuts computation time while preserving retrieval quality.
isca-2025-095.key_novelty: Hermes combines datastore partitioning with intelligent hierarchical routing that directs queries to relevant data partitions (skipping irrelevant ones), cutting computation while preserving recall—the fraction of relevant documents that get found.

isca-2025-108.method: The system combines a deep learning model (POLONet) that tracks where your eyes are looking with a custom processor chip (POLO accelerator) built into VR headsets. Because human eyes can only see sharp detail in a small central area (the foveal region) where you're focused, the system renders that area in full detail while rendering everything else at lower quality, saving computation. The deep learning tracker and the accelerator chip work tightly together, exchanging data efficiently, so the whole system has minimal delay and uses less computing power than rendering everything at full quality.
isca-2025-108.key_novelty: The core insight is designing the hardware and software together—a specialized eye-tracking AI model (POLONet) and a custom processor chip (POLO) built into the VR headset—so they work seamlessly to render images based on where you're looking, without adding noticeable lag.

isca-2025-099.method: HardHarvest moves core harvesting entirely into processor hardware. A hardware scheduler monitors incoming requests, detects idle cores in latency-critical applications (Primary VMs), and assigns them to batch jobs (Harvest VMs) without hypervisor calls—eliminating expensive software overhead. To prevent batch jobs from slowing down the main application, the system partitions memory caches—TLBs (fast caches for memory addresses) and data caches—between workloads using a smart replacement algorithm that keeps the main application's frequently-used data in cache while quickly freeing batch job data when needed. The scheduler continuously reclaims cores before the main application's latency increases.
isca-2025-099.key_novelty: HardHarvest solves the core-harvesting problem for microservices by implementing the entire operation—idle-core detection via request monitoring, cache/TLB partitioning with smart replacement, and preemption—in processor hardware instead of software.

isca-2025-106.method: SWIPER predicts data dependencies between quantum error correction decoding windows (similar to branch prediction in classical CPUs) and launches multiple layers of decoding work in parallel based on these predictions, rather than waiting for earlier windows to complete. If a prediction is wrong, the system rolls back and redecodes with correct information. The system is optimized to maximize prediction opportunities, and performance is measured with a cycle-accurate simulator.
isca-2025-106.key_novelty: SWIPER applies speculative execution—making educated guesses about data dependencies between quantum error correction decoding windows before those dependencies are resolved—to eliminate processing delays at window boundaries.

isca-2025-102.method: Qtenon is a RISC-V chip (a common CPU architecture) that puts quantum and classical processors on the same die to eliminate communication delays. It has three core components: a shared memory accessible to both the classical and quantum sides for fast data exchange (instead of slow round-trip messaging), a dedicated quantum controller with direct data paths for quantum operations, and a multi-stage processing pipeline that runs quantum and classical instructions in parallel. It also adds custom instructions—new commands the processor understands—for coordinating data movement, synchronization, and scheduling between the quantum and classical sides.
isca-2025-102.key_novelty: A unified memory bridging classical and quantum processors, combined with custom RISC-V instructions for synchronization and scheduling, enables tightly coupled hybrid quantum-classical computation on a single chip.

isca-2025-113.method: The paper describes PRACLeak, an attack that exploits timing variations caused by PRAC's ABO protocol and RFM commands (which manage memory refresh) to extract cryptographic keys from AES implementations by measuring how long memory operations take. The authors then propose TPRAC, a defense that eliminates this leak by issuing RFM refresh commands on a fixed schedule regardless of memory activity, breaking the timing pattern attackers rely on. TPRAC uses a single-entry mitigation queue per memory bank and works with existing DRAM standards.
isca-2025-113.key_novelty: PRAC's ABO and RFM commands create a timing side-channel that leaks information tied to memory access patterns, which TPRAC fixes by issuing refresh commands on a regular clock schedule instead of responding to memory activity.

isca-2025-098.method: HyFlexPIM combines specialized hardware with mathematical optimization. The hardware uses three tiers with increasing storage density but decreasing precision: digital memory for time-critical attention calculations, simple analog cells for precision-critical weights, and dense analog cells (2 bits per cell) for error-tolerant weights. A single analog module reconfigures between simple and dense modes with less than 1% area and energy overhead. To decide which weights go where, the software decomposes the weight matrix using singular value decomposition (a mathematical technique that identifies important components), truncates it, and fine-tunes for 1-3 epochs; this automatically concentrates importance into 5-10% of weights while safely placing 90-95% in the denser cells.
isca-2025-098.key_novelty: Through singular value decomposition, truncation, and fine-tuning, the method naturally concentrates critical weight importance into 5-10% of parameters, enabling 90-95% of Transformer weights to be computed in efficient two-bit memory cells with less than 1% accuracy loss.

isca-2025-109.method: Phi handles spike activations by splitting them into two parts with different computation strategies. The first part uses pre-defined patterns found offline via k-means clustering (which groups similar spike structures), whose multiply-accumulate products with weights are pre-computed, so most runtime arithmetic becomes fast table lookups. The second part is a highly sparse residual matrix handling spikes not covered by the patterns, requiring minimal computation since most entries are zero. The network is fine-tuned to maximize residual sparsity, and the hardware has dedicated datapaths for processing each sparsity tier.
isca-2025-109.key_novelty: Phi's insight is that spike activations follow repeating patterns whose multiply-accumulate products can be pre-computed offline, eliminating the majority of calculations needed during network execution.

isca-2025-111.method: Assassyn lets developers write a single program using asynchronous event handling—a way of describing what happens when events occur, rather than requiring everything to move in lockstep. The framework compiles this single program into two versions: a cycle-accurate simulator (software showing exactly what the hardware does, moment by moment) and synthesizable RTL (the hardware description code that becomes an actual chip). Both versions come from the same source code, so they stay synchronized—no divergence between simulation and implementation. This approach works for many types of hardware: pipeline stages, out-of-order CPUs (processors executing instructions flexibly), and application-specific accelerators.
isca-2025-111.key_novelty: A single programming abstraction based on asynchronous event handling that generates both a cycle-accurate simulator and synthesizable RTL from the same code, eliminating the dual-codebase problem by construction.

isca-2025-112.method: The approach uses GPU Work Graphs—a feature in AMD GPUs that lets workgroups schedule and coordinate directly on the device—to fuse preprocessing with per-row sparse-matrix-vector multiplication. Instead of preprocessing on the host and then launching computation, both steps happen together on the GPU: as preprocessing generates metadata about which algorithm suits each row, specialized kernels automatically launch. This keeps more data in the GPU's fast L1 and L2 caches and eliminates expensive CPU-GPU communication. The GPU needs only a fixed 25 MiB of supporting data regardless of matrix size, unlike rocSPARSE LRB which requires more memory as matrices grow.
isca-2025-112.key_novelty: The key innovation is applying GPU Work Graphs—a graphics-world feature for on-device task scheduling—to fuse SpMV preprocessing and per-row computation on the GPU, eliminating host CPU coordination and improving cache locality.

isca-2025-117.method: Bishop groups spike data (individual output signals from spiking neural networks) into containers called Token-Time Bundles that pack information across tokens and time steps together. These bundles are then routed to specialized hardware cores: dense bundles (with many spikes) go to cores optimized for heavy computation, while sparse bundles (with few spikes) go to cores optimized to skip empty work. During training, Bundle Sparsity-Aware methods ensure the bundles stay sparse. Before and after the attention computation, Error-Constrained Pruning removes unnecessary spikes from the query/key/value data while guaranteeing the error stays within acceptable bounds, and the final attention operation runs as AND and accumulate calculations on binary spike signals.
isca-2025-117.key_novelty: Token-Time Bundles pack spike data jointly across tokens and time steps, enabling simultaneous dense/sparse core routing and weight reuse across both dimensions.

isca-2025-107.method: DRAM uses counters to detect Rowhammer attacks—repeated accesses to one row that can corrupt nearby data. Normally counters update on every row access, adding overhead. MoPAC reduces this overhead by updating counters only on randomly selected accesses instead of every one, and maintains security by lowering the attack threshold inversely to compensate (if updates happen half as often, the threshold halves, so attackers are still caught). It can be implemented either at the memory controller (MoPAC-C) by randomly selecting between precharge command variants, or inside the DRAM chip (MoPAC-D) by randomly choosing which accesses trigger counting while hiding the timing cost.
isca-2025-107.key_novelty: The core idea is that randomly selecting which accesses trigger Rowhammer counter updates, while adjusting the security threshold proportionally, reduces DDR5 timing overhead without changing how DRAM hardware works.

isca-2025-114.method: The DS-TPU chip learns continuously on-device by using electric current flowing through the chip as a feedback signal for training—similar to how physical systems naturally settle into lower-energy states—rather than relying on software-based error calculations. To handle complex relationships between graph nodes, it uses Chebyshev polynomial expansions (mathematical functions that approximate smooth curves) for nonlinear node interactions, staying compatible with analog hardware. The design was evaluated with a 5-Watt power envelope across six real-world graph learning benchmarks.
isca-2025-114.key_novelty: An electronic Dynamical System chip that learns continuously on-device using its own electric current as a learning signal, with Chebyshev polynomial expansions (mathematical functions that approximate curves) enabling nonlinear node interactions.

isca-2025-116.method: SpecEE reduces the early-exit predictor's bottleneck by using a small draft model to filter the vocabulary search—instead of checking all ~30,000 possible tokens per layer, the predictor only evaluates likely candidates, cutting the up-to-20% latency overhead. The predictor is redesigned to run in parallel on GPUs and exploit natural data variation to reduce complexity. It profiles which layers are most uncertain and concentrates effort there rather than uniformly. Finally, it adds tree-aware mapping so speculative decoding (generating multiple tokens at once) works efficiently with early exiting, avoiding the exponential complexity that would normally arise.
isca-2025-116.key_novelty: A small draft model shrinks the early-exit predictor's search space, enabling efficient composition of early exiting and speculative decoding.

isca-2025-121.method: ArtMem uses a learning algorithm (reinforcement learning) that watches how often the fast memory tier gets accessed and how data access patterns change during execution. Based on what it observes, the algorithm decides which data to keep in fast memory and which to move to slower tiers, how many pages to migrate at once, and when to stop migrating entirely if the fast tier isn't being heavily used. Instead of using fixed rules set beforehand, it learns what works best for each workload by trial and feedback, adapting its decisions as workload behavior evolves.
isca-2025-121.key_novelty: The innovation is using a learning agent that controls three interconnected decisions about memory migration—which strategy to use, how many pages to move, and whether to pause migrations—adapting them together in real time based on changing workload behavior.

isca-2025-119.method: DiTile-DGNN identifies where the same data appears across different snapshots (the graph's state at different time steps) and eliminates that redundant computation. To keep data flowing efficiently between processors without unnecessary waiting points, it uses a workload-balancer that removes synchronization barriers between snapshots. The system uses a reconfigurable accelerator with a flexible interconnect that can adapt to handle different types of graph neural network computations—including GNN aggregation (combining data from neighboring nodes), RNN recurrence (processing sequences over time), and combinations of both—without hardware redesign.
isca-2025-119.key_novelty: The core innovation is a redundancy-free parallelism strategy that eliminates duplicate data across graph snapshots while simultaneously reducing how much information must pass between processors in distributed graph neural network inference.

isca-2025-104.method: HiPER is a custom semiconductor chip (ASIC) with 1024 processing elements built in 16-nanometer technology, occupying 16.37 square millimeters. It combines a fractal network topology—a self-similar nested pattern—connecting local systolic arrays (grids of pipelined compute units) with hierarchical extensions to efficiently handle both dense machine-learning and sparse optimization computation. A six-level hierarchy of pointer queues manages which operations execute where at runtime, continuously adapting to shifts between neural-network and optimization phases without requiring a complex scheduler.
isca-2025-104.key_novelty: A fractal network topology (a self-similar nested pattern) combined with multi-level pointer queues that dynamically remaps computation across time and space at runtime, enabling one chip to handle both dense neural-network and sparse optimization workloads efficiently without complex scheduling.

isca-2025-124.method: The researchers tested 316 real DDR4 DRAM chips from four major manufacturers to see whether activating multiple memory rows at the same time (an access pattern used by processors that compute inside DRAM) triggers more bitflips (read disturbance errors that flip stored data bits) than activating just one row. They varied the test conditions: temperature, data patterns, timing settings, whether rows activate simultaneously or one-after-another, and different locations on the chip. For each test, they measured how many accesses it took to cause the first bitflip—called the hammer count. They compared this to standard RowHammer, which activates only one row.
isca-2025-124.key_novelty: This is the first study measuring on real DDR4 chips whether the multiple-row activation pattern (used in processing-inside-DRAM) triggers bitflips more easily, finding that it can reduce the access threshold by up to 158.58 times compared to standard RowHammer.

isca-2025-122.method: The work creates a model for a data center that fits in a single cabinet using a single wafer (the silicon base) with chips stacked vertically. The framework, called Titan, automatically explores different hardware designs by tracking dependencies between decisions—how large to make processing tiles, how much fast memory (SRAM) to include, how to connect separate chiplets, and whether to stack them—and verifies each design is physically feasible, won't overheat or fail, and fits within space constraints. By rejecting infeasible designs early, Titan accelerates the search for an optimal configuration.
isca-2025-122.key_novelty: Titan simultaneously optimizes how computation is organized (parallelism and task assignment) and how hardware is built (chiplet layout and vertical memory stacking) for single-wafer data centers, subject to physical space and reliability limits.

isca-2025-127.method: IDEA-GP is an FPGA (a reconfigurable hardware chip that can be reprogrammed after manufacturing) containing an array of general-purpose processing units designed for the 3D math needed in robotics—rotation matrices, quaternions, and coordinate transformations. A compiler watches what computations are happening at runtime and dynamically sends instructions to assign each processing unit sub-problems, like solving linear equations or optimizing pose graphs. Because the assignment happens through instructions rather than being fixed at hardware design time, the same processor array can efficiently handle both SLAM's varied operations (incremental position tracking and loop-closure detection) and Structure from Motion's operations (camera position optimization and point triangulation) without rebuilding the hardware. The system is deployed on a Xilinx ZCU102 evaluation board.
isca-2025-127.key_novelty: A compiler that dynamically assigns different geometric-perception operators to the same processor array at runtime using instructions, rather than requiring hardware reconfiguration for each task type—achieving high resource efficiency despite changing workloads.

isca-2025-128.method: SwitchQNet is a compiler that jointly optimizes quantum computation at two levels: the program layer (how quantum gates and qubits are arranged) and the network layer (when optical switches connecting different quantum processor racks reconfigure). It models the network topology and switch reconfiguration delays, then schedules quantum operations to batch and reorder communications so that one switch reconfiguration spreads its setup cost across multiple operations. The compiler integrates with quantum error correction for fault-tolerant quantum computing and is open-sourced at https://zenodo.org/records/15377656.
isca-2025-128.key_novelty: The core idea is optimizing quantum gate scheduling and optical switch reconfiguration as one problem instead of separately, achieving 8.02x speedup in quantum data centers by sharing the cost of each switch reconfiguration across multiple operations.

isca-2025-123.method: CORD moves the responsibility for enforcing write ordering from the source processor to the last-level cache directory (the central component that keeps track of which caches have copies of data). Instead of the processor sending each write and waiting for directory acknowledgment, the directory accumulates writes and enforces their ordering locally, eliminating this round-trip communication. To keep memory overhead low, the protocol uses metadata compression (a way to store tracking information in less space) for in-flight writes at the directory and scales across multiple directories without serialization bottlenecks.
isca-2025-123.key_novelty: Moving release consistency enforcement from the source processor to the cache directory, eliminating unnecessary round-trip communication.

isca-2025-126.method: AIM reduces voltage drop (IR-drop) by first recognizing that it's directly caused by how often individual bits flip in the data — more bit-flips mean more electrical current and thus more voltage drop. The software side employs two techniques during model training and initial setup: one adds a penalty during training that steers neural network weights toward numbers with fewer '1' bits (Hamming Rate reduction), and the other shifts all weights offline into naturally low-'1'-bit ranges while compensating for the numerical change at runtime. At runtime, embedded voltage sensors near the chip's power regulators continuously monitor for actual voltage drop, and when detected, dynamically adjust the chip's clock speed and voltage based on pre-measured safe operating zones for different computational patterns. Finally, the software optimally assigns computational operations across chip regions to minimize interference between them, based on the actual bit patterns in the data rather than worst-case circuit assumptions.
isca-2025-126.key_novelty: AIM is the first architecture-level approach to voltage drop in SRAM processing-in-memory chips that links the distribution of '1' bits in weights (Hamming Rate) to current draw, then jointly optimizes weight quantization, weight shifting, power-voltage control, and task mapping based on actual workload behavior rather than worst-case circuit signoff.

isca-2025-132.method: The approach breaks down the quantum algorithm (2048-bit factoring as the test case) into specialized building blocks—magic state factories that prepare T-state magic states for 8T-to-CCZ distillation, ripple-carry adders using Cuccaro gadgets with CCZ teleportation, and quantum lookup tables via GHZ-state-assisted CNOT fan-out—each built using surface-code transversal gates (gates where syndrome extraction doesn't require additional rounds beyond the operation itself). Atoms are moved using optical tweezers with pipelined ancilla measurement to keep movement distances bounded (at most √2·d·l per step, where d is code distance). The team calibrated a logical error model against MLE decoder simulations, finding that transversal CNOTs introduce noise requiring a decoding correction factor of roughly 1/6. Finally, space-time trade-offs using bridge qubits and time-optimal scheduling minimize total computation work while keeping syndrome extraction constant per operation.
isca-2025-132.key_novelty: Using transversal gates (gates where syndrome extraction stays constant with code distance) on neutral atom arrays, this work provides the first complete architectural design with detailed subroutine layouts and a calibrated logical error model that achieves 50x speedup for 2048-bit RSA factoring through correlated decoding.

isca-2025-129.method: The key insight is that sparse matrix multiplication and ray tracing actually solve analogous problems: both find intersections (non-zero positions in the matrix case, ray-triangle hits in the graphics case). The authors first implement a straightforward version (SW-RTSpMSpM) by repurposing the ray tracing API (DXR/OptiX) and its specialized intersection hardware to detect where non-zero results occur. Then they improve this by adding two architectural tweaks: computing the actual products at the same time as checking for intersections (rather than in separate steps), and introducing a small row accumulation engine that exploits Gustavson's sparse data processing pattern to eliminate redundant memory operations. This engine takes up only 0.2% of the GPU's physical area.
isca-2025-129.key_novelty: The central idea is that sparse matrix multiplication can map directly onto ray tracing hardware (which finds ray-triangle intersections), and architectural optimizations—simultaneous product computation alongside intersection checks, plus a row accumulation engine—make this mapping efficient with only 0.2% added silicon.

isca-2025-131.method: UGPU dynamically divides a single GPU into unbalanced slices, each with a custom amount of compute resources (SMs, or Streaming Multiprocessors) and memory (HBM, or High Bandwidth Memory), using a demand-aware algorithm that figures out what workloads need without complex mathematical models. When rebalancing memory across slices, instead of using traditional slow page migration, UGPU introduces PageMove, which exploits the fact that all HBM memory channels already share physical TSV connections (vertical wires through the DRAM stack), allowing it to move pages in parallel across different bank groups simultaneously.
