PageMove pairs this parallel channel exploitation with a customized memory address mapping and Parallel Page Migration Mode (PPMM), achieving high-throughput page migration across memory dies without the latency cost.
isca-2025-131.key_novelty: PageMove uses the pre-existing vertical connections (TSVs) through the DRAM stack that link HBM memory channels to execute parallel page migrations simultaneously across memory bank groups, eliminating the latency overhead that blocks dynamic GPU slice reconfiguration.

isca-2025-133.method: The protocol operates in two stages. First, it tests how different control signals affect each qubit pair individually, then selects the best tuning approach for that pair rather than using one approach for all. Second, it uses a graph algorithm to identify which tuning tasks don't interfere with each other, allowing them to run in parallel instead of sequentially. The approach was tested on real IBM quantum hardware with up to 127 qubits.
isca-2025-133.key_novelty: Profiling each qubit pair to find its optimal tuning method, then running those tuning tasks in parallel, simultaneously reduces calibration time and two-qubit gate error.

isscc-2025-000.method: The team builds temperature sensors at micron-scale resolution (about 1/100th the width of a human hair) using low-voltage 16nm CMOS. These sensors measure temperature in real time at spatial scales as fine as 100 micrometers, detecting localized thermal hotspots before they degrade performance. They validate this approach on a 16nm buck converter (a switching power supply) and an SoC load-current emulator (a test circuit mimicking realistic power workloads), showing the sensors accurately track temperature across different operating conditions.
isscc-2025-000.key_novelty: Micron-scale temperature sensors built in low-voltage CMOS can detect thermal hotspots at 100-micrometer resolution in real time, making fine-grained thermal monitoring of high-power SoCs feasible.

isca-2025-134.method: S-SYNC is a compiler that simultaneously optimizes two competing goals: reducing qubit shuttles (moving qubits across a segmented electrode array) and reducing SWAP gates (quantum operations that exchange qubit positions). Normally designs shuttle qubits first and then add SWAPs to fix connectivity problems; instead, S-SYNC treats both as equally important choices from the start. It applies optimization rules tailored to the specific QCCD chip topology, weighing the thermal cost of shuttling (heat that harms qubits) against the time cost of extra SWAPs. The compiler is tested on different QCCD topologies and initial qubit configurations.
isca-2025-134.key_novelty: By treating shuttle and SWAP operations as equally important, jointly-optimized decisions (rather than choosing shuttles first then SWAPs sequentially), S-SYNC reduces shuttle counts by 3.69x on average.

isscc-2025-001.method: Nebula replaces the slow sequential farthest-point sampling (FPS—repeatedly finding the farthest point from previously selected ones) with adaptive block-wise partitioning, which divides the point cloud into balanced segments instead. It then uses multi-skipping dataflow (skipping redundant calculations on points that won't contribute to the output) to reduce operations during grouping, convolution, and aggregation. Finally, it aggregates in blocks with predictable memory access patterns (fetching data sequentially rather than randomly), eliminating irregular memory accesses.
isscc-2025-001.key_novelty: Nebula eliminates redundant point-cloud neural network operations (farthest-point sampling, grouping, convolution, aggregation) while maintaining balanced computation across varying point cloud distributions.

isscc-2025-005.method: The device shifts the phase (timing) of radio signals across the D-band (110-170 GHz range for 6G). Using a frequency/switching-staggering technique (adjusting when different parts activate based on the signal frequency), the phase shifts work equally well across a 24% range of frequencies without needing manual calibration. It achieves less than 2.38° phase error and less than 0.63dB gain error (signal strength error), and the same device handles both transmit and receive signals.
isscc-2025-005.key_novelty: The frequency/switching-staggering technique (adjusting when different parts activate based on the signal frequency) enables phase adjustment codes that work across a 24% bandwidth without manual tuning, achieving phase errors below 2.38° and gain errors below 0.63dB.

isscc-2025-002.method: IBM Telum II designs the processor and manufacturing process together, jointly optimizing both rather than designing first and fitting to the process later. The team created custom standard cells (basic circuit building blocks) and pre-made functional modules specifically tuned to a modified 5nm Samsung process. They designed different parts of the chip—memory arrays, storage registers, analog circuits, input/output interfaces, and custom logic—simultaneously instead of sequentially, surfacing conflicts early so everything can be optimized together. To handle the massive complexity of a 43-billion-transistor design, they built abstraction layers that organize design information at different levels of detail.
isscc-2025-002.key_novelty: Concurrent hierarchical design lets teams simultaneously develop standard cell libraries (basic building blocks), IP blocks (pre-made functional modules), and gate-level logic (individual circuit elements), which manages the complexity of 43 billion transistors.

isscc-2025-008.method: A chip outside the display measures each pixel's transistor characteristics using a two-point detection method (testing the transistor at two signal levels to reveal its unique properties), then uses those measurements to dynamically adjust the voltage sent to each pixel, correcting its brightness. A single corrector circuit handles this for all pixels by processing them one at a time in rapid sequence (time-multiplexing), and because the correction occurs outside the pixel rather than inside it, the pixel preserves its full light-producing area.
isscc-2025-008.key_novelty: Two-point error detection paired with time-shared voltage correction enables external per-pixel brightness compensation without modifying the pixel structure.

isscc-2025-006.method: The device is a 4×4 active reflective relay array at D-band frequencies, with transmit/receive antennas on-chip using orthogonal (perpendicular) polarizations to separate signals. It detects both horizontal (azimuth) and vertical (elevation) angles of incoming beams using a spatially balanced receiver circuit (common-centroid design) positioned early in the signal path before degradation. This enables real-time adaptive beam steering without lossy frequency converters (which waste power) or unstable phase shifter feedback loops.
isscc-2025-006.key_novelty: A spatially balanced angle detector (common-centroid design) at the receiver front-end enables sub-THz relays to track beam angles in real-time without the power loss from frequency conversion.

isca-2025-130.method: DeepSeek-V3 handles 671-billion-parameter training through five coordinated techniques: compressing attention cache 7-fold (516 KB to 70 KB per token) by projecting keys and values to lower rank, restricting expert routing to 4 of 8 nodes to exploit the 4:1 bandwidth difference between fast GPU-to-GPU links (NVLink) and network links (InfiniBand), and training with FP8 numbers (8-bit floating-point for speed) using tile-wise and block-wise quantization through DeepGEMM to work around accumulation precision limits (FP22). DualPipe overlaps attention and expert computation with coordinated expert dispatch via InfiniBand GPUDirect Async, while a Multi-Plane Fat-Tree topology with 8 independent InfiniBand planes per node eliminates bandwidth bottlenecks. These techniques scale to 16,384 GPUs at the same per-endpoint cost as simpler topologies, achieving 272.8 billion tokens per day at 43.7% GPU utilization with expert-parallelism bandwidth over 40 GB/s per GPU.
isca-2025-130.key_novelty: The Multi-Plane Fat-Tree network topology with 8 independent InfiniBand planes per node enables 8× scaling of 671-billion-parameter expert-based models to 16,384 GPUs while maintaining per-endpoint costs equivalent to conventional two-layer designs.

isscc-2025-004.method: The receiver uses an analog phase detector—a circuit that measures the timing offset between the incoming optical signal and an internal reference light source (running at the same frequency on the chip)—to keep them synchronized. Instead of using power-hungry digital processing to recover the carrier phase (synchronize to the incoming signal's exact timing), this analog circuit does it with simple electronics. The design decodes 16-QAM signals (which encode information in 16 distinct signal states) at 64 gigabits per second.
isscc-2025-004.key_novelty: An analog phase detector that synchronizes the receiver's internal light source with the incoming signal enables 16-QAM decoding at 1.54 picojoules per bit without requiring high-power digital processing.

isscc-2025-009.method: The chip detects spikes (sudden electrical pulses from neurons) only when they actually occur—event-driven detection—rather than continuously reading all raw data, which saves memory and power. Instead of using spike timing to sort them (which fails with many channels), it uses waveform shape—the electrical fingerprint of each neuron—to group similar spikes, which is spatial spike-sorting. It organizes these groupings using a self-organizing map, a technique that learns from each new spike without storing all previous data in memory. Processing only real events, sorting by fingerprint shape, and avoiding per-spike full-memory access lets the chip handle 1024 channels with sub-50-microsecond latency.
isscc-2025-009.key_novelty: Combining event-driven spike detection (processing only real neural signals), spatial spike-sorting (grouping by waveform fingerprint), and self-organizing map clustering enables a chip to handle 1024 neural signal channels with low power consumption and sub-50-microsecond response time.

isscc-2025-003.method: This design uses a series-resonance topology (connecting an inductor and capacitor in series to peak at one frequency) and a pole-convergence technique (aligning electrical response peaks) in pure CMOS transistor technology. Differential signaling (using paired opposite signals to cancel noise) reduces phase noise (timing jitter) while avoiding the area and complexity of multicore VCOs (multiple oscillator copies).
isscc-2025-003.key_novelty: The pole-convergence technique (which aligns electrical response peaks) makes it possible to build a differential series-resonance VCO in pure CMOS transistor technology, achieving 202.1 dBc/Hz phase noise at 10MHz offset without the area and complexity of multicore approaches.

isscc-2025-012.method: The system uses a reconfigurable voltage-regulator fabric—a power-delivery circuit that can reprogram its connections while the chip is running—to adapt to changing power demands. As processor domains shift between active and idle states, the fabric dynamically reassigns which regulators service which domains, and when peak current isn't needed, it simplifies multi-stage buck converters (voltage step-down circuits) down to fewer stages. It also switches simpler voltage regulators called LDOs (which waste less power when the voltage difference is small) into the configuration to reduce losses further. This continuous adaptation to real-time conditions makes the overall power delivery more efficient than fixed designs.
isscc-2025-012.key_novelty: The core innovation is a voltage-regulator system that dynamically reconfigures itself while running—reorganizing which processor domains it powers and adapting which regulator types it uses—to improve efficiency across changing power demands.

isscc-2025-007.method: kNOT embeds two tiny computer chips directly into braided textile yarns: a 0.6×2.15mm² system-on-chip (SoC) with configurable connection points, fault-tolerant startup, clock synchronization, and dynamic network adjustment; and a bySPI chiplet (a communication protocol that lets one sender talk to multiple receivers using just 3 wires). The chips attach to yarn using selective laser ablation (targeted laser burning) and solder reflow (heating metal solder to form electrical joints), avoiding the need for bulky circuit-board interposers.
isscc-2025-007.key_novelty: Embedding computer chips directly into textile yarns with bySPI networking eliminates the need for circuit boards and interposers, making miniaturized multi-chip textile systems with distributed memory possible.

isscc-2025-010.method: The 200-pixel imager at 200GHz uses four integrated techniques: (1) Q-boosted Active Split-Ring Resonators (resonant structures that amplify incoming signals while adding minimal electrical load) enable individual pixel activation, (2) all pixels share a single transmitter/receiver rather than having separate ones per pixel, (3) phase detection measures the timing-shift of waves rather than their power or frequency, eliminating noise from free-running oscillators, and (4) correlated-doubling sampling (comparing measurements at different times) suppresses slow variations in noise. These techniques work together to maintain high sensitivity when imaging lossy biological samples.
isscc-2025-010.key_novelty: Combining Q-boosted resonators with phase-based detection enables scalable 200GHz near-field imaging arrays with a shared source/detector, maintaining high sensitivity in lossy biological samples.

isscc-2025-013.method: A 16-gigabit LPDDR5X test chip implements two techniques to reach 12.7 gigabits per second per pin at 1.05V in a 5th-generation 10nm process. First, a 4-phase self-calibration system reduces clock phase skew (timing signal misalignment from different sources) through four adjustment stages, performing better than prior methods. Second, three AC-coupled equalization schemes (signal-strengthening circuits using alternating-current connections) combat signal loss on lossy interconnects—connections that normally degrade the signal.
isscc-2025-013.key_novelty: A 4-phase self-calibration system combined with three AC-coupled equalization schemes enables 12.7 gigabits per second per pin operation on advanced DRAM.

isscc-2025-014.method: This system tracks power at the symbol level—each discrete packet of data—rather than following a smooth envelope, enabling much faster response. A 400MHz supply modulator adjusts the voltage delivered to the 5G FR2 CMOS PA based on each symbol's power needs, while an adaptive-biasing network automatically tunes transistor bias in real time to maintain efficiency across varying power demands.
isscc-2025-014.key_novelty: Tracking power at the symbol level instead of the overall envelope enables 400MHz supply modulation for 5G FR2 CMOS power amplifiers.

isscc-2025-011.method: A compact 10-bit source-driver IC (a chip controlling voltage levels for each pixel column) uses delta-sigma pulse-width-modulation—a digital technique that rapidly switches between voltage reference levels at varying ratios to create intermediate output voltages—to interpolate between gamma voltages (the standard brightness reference levels). While traditional analog methods like Gm-adjustment and switched-capacitor circuits suffer from nonlinearity issues or require many capacitors and high-voltage transistors, this digital approach maintains voltage accuracy using only low-voltage components, significantly reducing the silicon area needed per channel.
isscc-2025-011.key_novelty: Using delta-sigma pulse-width-modulation (a digital switching technique) for voltage interpolation instead of analog circuits eliminates the capacitors and high-voltage devices required by conventional methods, achieving 1884 square micrometers of silicon per display channel.

isscc-2025-016.method: The design connects four oscillator cores in a circular pattern using transformer-based resonant tanks (transformers that enable oscillation at target frequencies) to maintain high signal quality even with very small inductors. Across the entire frequency range, it automatically aligns the fundamental frequency with its second and third harmonics (multiples of the base frequency) by leveraging properties built into the Class-F₂₃ topology. This eliminates the need for separate harmonic tuning circuits that would normally degrade performance.
isscc-2025-016.key_novelty: This is the first four-core Class-F₂₃ oscillator to automatically align harmonic frequencies (second and third multiples) without separate tuning circuits, eliminating the performance loss those circuits normally cause while operating across a 5.1GHz frequency range.

isscc-2025-019.method: The design leverages 2nm nanosheet transistors' improved on/off-current ratio (transistors that switch more dramatically between fully off and fully on) to double the bit-line loading capacity (how much current the memory lines can handle). This enables packing more memory cells around each peripheral circuit. The team then optimized the physical placement of both cells and supporting circuits to minimize area while preserving reliability margins.
isscc-2025-019.key_novelty: This is the first production SRAM design that uses nanosheet transistors' improved on/off-current ratio to double bit-line loading capacity, paired with layout optimizations that shrink the memory cells and supporting circuits.

isscc-2025-015.method: The design harvests energy from electromagnetic waves using parity-time-symmetry (a balanced configuration that prevents energy loss) operating at sub-GHz frequencies. This harvested energy directly powers traveling-wave electroosmosis actuators—electrodes arranged in channels that create rippling electric fields, pushing fluid to generate motion. Everything is built on a single standard 180nm CMOS chip, eliminating inefficiencies from magnetic coupling or the need for specialized fabrication processes.
isscc-2025-015.key_novelty: This is the first microrobot powered by combining sub-GHz parity-time-symmetry energy harvesting and electroosmotic propulsion all on a single standard 180nm CMOS chip.

isscc-2025-017.method: This 14-bit, 1-gigahertz analog-to-digital converter runs amplification and quantization (precision measurement) in parallel within a pipeline. While one stage performs successive approximation—testing increasingly accurate guesses to convert an analog signal to a digital value—the residual amplifier for the next stage simultaneously amplifies the prior measurement's error. This parallelization eliminates the timing pressure that normally forces amplifiers to be fast and power-hungry. The amplifier uses a ring topology with dynamic-deadzone biasing (self-adjusting circuitry for temperature and voltage variations), avoiding manual per-chip tuning.
isscc-2025-017.key_novelty: Overlapping successive-approximation conversion (testing increasingly precise guesses) with residual amplification to eliminate timing constraints, enabling lower-power amplifier design without sacrificing signal quality or input range.

isscc-2025-024.method: The oscillator uses a cross-coupled pair of CMOS transistors to create current-controlled negative resistance, which actively cancels losses in the circuit. This stage drives an LC tank circuit (an inductor-capacitor pair that acts as a natural resonator), generating low-noise oscillations. The 'pseudo-series-resonance' approach achieves the phase-noise benefits of series-resonance oscillators—which normally require expensive bipolar transistors or four-stage inverter chains consuming over 300 milliwatts—but delivers this performance at 8.1–9.9 GHz in standard CMOS technology with less power.
isscc-2025-024.key_novelty: A single-core CMOS oscillator using pseudo-series-resonance to achieve −128.7 dBc/Hz phase noise at 1 MHz offset with under 300 milliwatts of power, eliminating the area and core-mismatch overhead of multi-core designs.

isscc-2025-022.method: Built in 4nm FinFET, the transceiver handles 212.5 Gb/s PAM-4 signals (2 bits encoded per voltage level) through three stages: a high-bandwidth, low-noise analog receiver operating at doubled signal rates to preserve full signal detail, digital equalization filters (FFE) with adjustable reflection-cancellation taps to undo distortion, and maximum-likelihood sequence detection (MLSD) that recovers data by determining the most probable original sequence through noise. These stages together compensate for over 50 dB of signal loss, enabling high-speed links in packaged AI systems.
isscc-2025-022.key_novelty: By integrating analog-frontend bandwidth enhancement with digital equalization (FFE) and maximum-likelihood detection (MLSD), the transceiver achieves 50+ dB loss compensation at 212.5 Gb/s for packaged AI systems.

isscc-2025-020.method: The solution creates a specialized hardware chip that performs speech decoding from brain signals. It works by first running a neural network to infer which individual speech sounds (phones) are present in the brain signal, then using a beam-search decoder (a search method that tracks the most likely word sequences) guided by a language model (which knows which words commonly follow each other in speech) to produce decoded words. This optimized pipeline achieves 200 words per minute.
isscc-2025-020.key_novelty: This is the first specialized hardware processor that accelerates neural-network inference (AI computation) specifically for speech decoding from brain signals, achieving 200 words per minute at 3.9 milliwatts—the power level that makes implantable brain-machine interfaces practical.

isscc-2025-026.method: The circuit uses transmission lines (specially designed wires that guide signals with controlled timing) arranged in a cross-folded pattern, paired with cross-coupled amplifier cells, to drive high-voltage signals (4 Vppd) for fiber optics. These transmission lines serve two purposes simultaneously: they passively extend the signal bandwidth by reshaping its frequency content, and they act as a built-in 5-tap equalizer (a delay-based filter with tunable stages) to correct signal distortion. This dual functionality eliminates the design trade-off between high amplification and large output voltage that constrained earlier approaches.
isscc-2025-026.key_novelty: A distributed driver using cross-folded transmission lines achieves both high signal gain and large output voltage (4 Vppd) with a built-in 5-tap equalizer for 100 Gbaud fiber optics.

isscc-2025-023.method: The system places a current sensor directly on the same chip as the GaN transistor driver—the circuit that controls when a power semiconductor switches on and off. It measures current by monitoring the electrical charge flowing into the transistor's control terminal (the gate), which correlates directly to the power current. The electrical configuration isolates the control circuit from the main power circuit, preventing noise while enabling precise switching timing. This on-chip approach minimizes wasted energy during the transitions between on and off states (dead-time losses) and achieves current measurement accuracy below 1% error without needing external sensors.
isscc-2025-023.key_novelty: The innovation is using gate-charge monitoring to achieve on-chip current sensing with sub-1% accuracy in a GaN driver circuit, eliminating external sensing components.

isscc-2025-021.method: The design uses a 64 kilobyte hybrid compute-in-memory block (hardware that stores and processes data in the same place) that feeds input features one bit at a time in a rotating pattern (bit-rotated). It processes the sign bit (the +/−) right at the first multiply-and-add step, avoiding the accuracy loss that occurs when other approaches handle signs separately—whether processing all bits at once or one at a time. An embedded sign-bit-processing array efficiently handles compression between positive and negative numbers. A multi-bit-fusion dual-granularity cooperative quantizer then dynamically allocates precision between fast analog hardware and precise digital hardware, based on each bit's significance (how much it contributes to accuracy).
isscc-2025-021.key_novelty: The core innovation is integrating sign-bit processing into the first computation step and using bit-significance to dynamically balance precision between analog and digital, eliminating wasted energy on low-significance bits.

isscc-2025-018.method: The design uses a bang-bang phase detector (a device that measures whether the clock is too fast or too slow) to directly correct quantization errors—the rounding mistakes made by the delta-sigma modulator that divides the frequency. Normally, a digital-to-time converter would fix these errors, but it consumes a lot of power and adds thermal noise that degrades clock quality; this approach avoids that tradeoff. The chip uses orthogonal-polynomial LMS calibration—an adaptive algorithm—to keep the correction working across manufacturing variations, voltage changes, and temperature swings.
isscc-2025-018.key_novelty: A bang-bang phase detector directly corrects delta-sigma quantization errors without needing a power-hungry converter (which would create thermal noise), and orthogonal-polynomial LMS calibration automatically adapts this correction across manufacturing, voltage, and temperature variations.

isscc-2025-025.method: The technique uses transconductor circuits (active amplifiers that convert voltage to current) to generate orthogonal I and Q signals directly from the RF input, replacing passive switches. Because transconductors are active components, they're much less affected by parasitic capacitances and impedances (unwanted reactive effects from wiring and components) that distort passive switches. This keeps the I and Q signals properly balanced in phase and amplitude, enabling strong image rejection.
isscc-2025-025.key_novelty: Using active transconductor circuits (Gm-C) instead of passive switches for quadrature signal generation achieves 40 dB image-rejection ratio (suppression of unwanted frequencies) and eliminates phase/amplitude imbalance problems.

isscc-2025-032.method: The chip has 384 reaction sites, each with its own heating element and temperature sensor. Heat spreads between neighboring sites through the silicon substrate (which conducts heat easily), making independent temperature control nearly impossible. To fix this, they engineered the substrate with thermal barriers—physical structures that block heat spread—giving each site the thermal isolation needed to maintain its target temperature independently.
isscc-2025-032.key_novelty: Substrate engineering that blocks heat spread between sites, enabling independent temperature control at all 384 locations.

isscc-2025-031.method: The sensor shoots light pulses and measures how long they take to bounce back to calculate distance (direct time-of-flight). It uses ultra-sensitive light detectors called single-photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) that can count individual photons. The sensor uses a 'chopped analog counter'—a circuit that suppresses background-light interference by rapidly toggling the measurement on and off—to work in extremely bright conditions (120,000 lux). It builds a histogram of photon arrival times to create a depth map at 76 meters' range at high frame rates.
isscc-2025-031.key_novelty: The chopped analog counter design—which suppresses background-light interference by alternating measurements on and off—enables robust depth sensing at 76-meter range under extreme brightness (120,000 lux).

isscc-2025-029.method: The oscillator's sustaining amplifier (the circuit that maintains the crystal's oscillations) uses analog regulation—electronic control without a separate voltage regulator—to prevent cross-currents, which are unwanted currents that waste power in the inverter (the core switching circuit). Unlike typical designs that reduce power by lowering the supply voltage, this approach keeps losses low by controlling when the inverter switches, eliminating cross-currents during switching transitions. Because power loss suppression happens through timing control rather than voltage reduction, no separate regulation circuit is needed, allowing the oscillator to run directly from standard battery voltages between 0.9 and 2 volts.
isscc-2025-029.key_novelty: This 32 kHz oscillator is the first to achieve below-0.5-nanowatt power consumption from a 0.9-volt battery supply using analog regulation—control of switching timing to prevent power-wasting cross-currents—without a separate voltage regulator.

isscc-2025-030.method: The chip uses 3D NAND-Flash, stacking 321 layers of memory cells vertically to pack far more data into the same space than a flat layout. Each cell stores 4 bits of data instead of 1, boosting capacity to 2Tb. Optimized programming algorithms (controlling how data is written to each cell) achieve 75MB/s write speed despite this extreme density.
isscc-2025-030.key_novelty: The core achievement is maintaining fast write speed (75MB/s) while using extremely high layer stacking (321 layers) and high data density (4 bits per cell)—factors that normally force tradeoffs.

isscc-2025-028.method: The design combines a single integrated GaN transistor with a control system that can route its input signal through either of two paths. When the switch turns off, the device automatically selects the path that keeps the control voltage within safe limits, preventing damage. It also includes built-in circuits for inrush current protection (limiting the sudden surge when turning on) and spike attenuation (smoothing voltage transients during switching).
isscc-2025-028.key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically choosing between control paths to prevent device damage during turn-off, with all the protection built into a single GaN chip instead of relying on external control circuits.

isscc-2025-027.method: A 16 megasamples-per-second (MS/s) analog-to-digital converter that splits input sampling into two phases—coarse and fine—to reduce electrical stress, enabling operation from 1.8 and 0.9 volt supplies without external driver circuits. While converting signals, a background calibration system continuously corrects amplifier gain variations across manufacturing, temperature, and voltage conditions using offset cancellation (measuring and removing systematic errors), a metastability detector (sensing amplifier instability), probability control (keeping corrections stable), and 2-bit input dithering (small noise that prevents calibration from locking onto wrong values).
isscc-2025-027.key_novelty: The core innovation is a split-phase input-sampling scheme eliminating the need for external drivers and high supply voltages, paired with a fast, robust background calibration using a metastability detector (sensing amplifier instability) to correct gain variations across manufacturing, temperature, and voltage conditions.

isscc-2025-036.method: A 16nm processor detects small objects in high-resolution video using three techniques: OICP (orientation-interleaved-causally-processed) bi-FPN, which reduces feature-map memory by reusing data; RARC scheduling, which minimizes bandwidth by choosing whether to recompute or refetch features; and a reconfigurable tensor engine supporting diverse operations. Together they achieve 5.7TOPS throughput.
isscc-2025-036.key_novelty: OICP bi-FPN and RARC backbone scheduling are co-designed to reduce external-memory access during high-resolution multi-scale feature extraction.

isscc-2025-035.method: The engine uses coupled oscillators—electronic devices that swing back and forth and naturally synchronize with each other—to solve Boolean satisfiability problems (finding values for multiple true-or-false variables that satisfy a set of logical rules). Each variable and rule maps to an oscillator; the oscillators all interact at once in a continuous physical system, and their synchronized state naturally encodes which variable values satisfy all rules. This all-at-once approach, driven by physics rather than step-by-step logic, is much faster than traditional search. The hardware achieves 100% success on 50-variable, 218-clause problems in 31.7 microseconds.
isscc-2025-035.key_novelty: All-to-all coupled oscillators directly solve Boolean satisfiability problems without complex preprocessing, achieving 50-variable solvability.

isscc-2025-037.method: Instead of running a separate clock all the time, this receiver pulls timing information directly from the incoming radio signal—a technique called in-band clock recovery. With this recovered timing, the receiver can detect incoming signals by comparing them to a stored pattern (digital correlation) without needing a clock generator. The design responds to signals as they arrive, rather than on a fixed schedule, and runs on leakage power—the tiny bit of current that flows through a sleeping chip—so it needs no external crystal or oscillator.
isscc-2025-037.key_novelty: By extracting timing directly from the incoming signal rather than using a separate clock, the receiver operates entirely on leakage power—the natural current of dormant silicon—without requiring batteries, oscillators, or external crystals.

isscc-2025-040.method: The processor uses a number format called pseudo-FP6 that stores values in fewer bits while maintaining the full numerical range needed for image quality, saving power. It combines multiple neural-network layers in a memory-efficient way, minimizing temporary storage of overlapping pixel regions to further reduce energy use. It also optimizes the deconvolution step (which enlarges images using learned patterns) to avoid redundant calculations. These techniques achieve image enlargement at 107 frames per second while consuming only 0.52 millijoules per frame.
isscc-2025-040.key_novelty: Pseudo-FP6 is the core innovation—a number format that enables low bit-width encoding (using fewer bits per value to save power) while maintaining high dynamic range (the numerical precision needed for image quality) in neural-network-based image enlargement.

isscc-2025-043.method: The oscillator tunes its frequency by using electronic switches to selectively activate inductors (magnetic coils) within a coupled-line resonator—a transmission line structure that naturally oscillates at specific frequencies. By switching different inductors in or out of the circuit, the resonant frequency shifts across a 19.9% range. This design replaces varactors (voltage-controlled capacitors), which perform poorly above 100GHz and suffer from low signal quality; the switched-inductor approach maintains high signal quality (Q-factor) throughout the tuning range at 224GHz.
isscc-2025-043.key_novelty: Using electronically switchable inductors instead of varactors to tune a coupled-line resonator, enabling wide-range frequency tuning with high signal quality at sub-THz frequencies.

isscc-2025-039.method: The circuit uses a race between two electrical signals—an arbiter—to detect tiny manufacturing variations in the silicon, creating a unique fingerprint for each chip. It includes built-in error detection that identifies unstable bit readings when voltage, temperature, or the chip ages over time (variations known as PVT changes), and automatically corrects those bits to keep the fingerprint steady. This on-chip correction achieves an extremely low error rate of just 2 in 100 million readings using 28nm-size transistors, without requiring large external error-correction hardware.
isscc-2025-039.key_novelty: Automatic error detection built into the chip allows it to stabilize the fingerprint across voltage and temperature changes without needing external error-correction hardware.

isscc-2025-044.method: The chip uses a single external capacitor pre-charged to high voltage as its energy reservoir. During a power burst, an on-chip switched-capacitor converter (a circuit that adjusts voltage levels by moving charge between capacitors) steps the voltage up or down to match what the device needs. This approach achieves 91.25% energy-extraction efficiency and delivers up to 5.68mJ per burst—40 times more than prior methods that stored all power on the chip itself.
isscc-2025-044.key_novelty: Pre-charging a single external capacitor to high voltage and extracting that energy with an on-chip switched-capacitor converter (a circuit that converts voltage levels) delivers over 35 times more burst energy than prior methods.

isscc-2025-033.method: The amplifier combines three techniques in a single power stage: a buck-boost converter (a circuit that can increase or decrease voltage to boost power output), a noise-reduction circuit using capacitor feedback (the chopper-amplifier technique), and just one external inductor. This integrated single-stage design achieves a 121.3dB dynamic range—ability to accurately reproduce very quiet and very loud sounds together—at 87% efficiency, with only 13% power loss. By combining voltage conversion, noise reduction, and power delivery in one stage instead of separating them, the design is both smaller and more efficient than previous approaches that required multiple conversion stages.
isscc-2025-033.key_novelty: The core innovation is a single-inductor circuit using flexible voltage boosting (DSVB) and capacitor-feedback noise reduction in one power stage to achieve both high sound quality (121.3dB dynamic range) and high efficiency (87%).

isscc-2025-034.method: The design uses a digital phase-locked loop with a digitally controlled oscillator, or DCO—an oscillator whose frequency you adjust with digital signals. By tracking how the DCO's frequency responds to its control inputs (dynamic-tuning-curve tracking), it encodes data via frequency shifts (GFSK modulation) and hops quickly between Bluetooth channels (2.402-2.480GHz) in under 20 microseconds while adapting to manufacturing and operating variations. It cuts power by using fewer switched-capacitor banks—circuits that switch capacitors on and off to tune frequency—which reduces the energy spent on capacitor switching. The result is 380 microwatts of power consumption with -242.8dB efficiency.
isscc-2025-034.key_novelty: The key innovation is achieving fast frequency hopping with fewer tuning capacitors in the oscillator (a shrunk switched-capacitor bank) by reliably tracking how the oscillator's frequency responds to its control inputs.

isscc-2025-042.method: The power amplifier uses a multi-stage circuit architecture with inductors and capacitors arranged to actively cancel impedance mismatches (called LC-neutralized complex-cascode topology). In large phased arrays, antennas electromagnetically interfere with each other, producing severe impedance variations represented as 4:1 VSWR. This design makes the amplifier resilient to these variations, maintaining stable gain, stable 1-dB compression output power, and stable efficiency across different frequencies and scanning angles beyond 60°, all in a compact form.
isscc-2025-042.key_novelty: The core idea is using an LC-neutralized complex-cascode topology—where inductors and capacitors cancel impedance mismatches in a multi-stage design—to achieve 4:1-VSWR resilience without varactors (electronically-tuned capacitors) or switched impedance-matching networks.

isscc-2025-038.method: The 28nm chip uses three techniques to process hybrid CNN-Transformer models efficiently. It schedules computation to balance memory access and computing demands (memory-compute-intensity-aware dataflow) and merges attention layers with a hybrid approach (hybrid-attention-based layer-fusion) that avoids redundant reloads of Key/Value cache and model weights from external memory. It also removes unimportant weights across the backbone and segmentation head (cascaded pruning), even where sparsity is naturally low. These techniques achieve 0.22μJ per token.
isscc-2025-038.key_novelty: Hybrid-attention layer-fusion eliminates redundant Key/Value cache and weight reloads across fused layers, combined with cascaded pruning that targets the low-sparsity segmentation head.

isscc-2025-049.method: This is an analog-to-digital converter (a device that converts continuous voltage signals into digital numbers) that processes signals in multiple stages and automatically corrects two types of errors—unequal gain across stages and component-to-component variations—without requiring calibration after manufacturing. Instead of using multi-bit feedback signals that would introduce additional errors, it combines both error corrections through single-bit feedback. It uses a specialized circuit called a negative-resistance-assisted residue integrator to efficiently handle the error signals at each stage.
isscc-2025-049.key_novelty: The key innovation is a single-bit feedback technique that corrects both gain and component mismatches simultaneously without introducing the extra errors that multi-bit feedback approaches require.

isscc-2025-041.method: The design cascades ring oscillators in a fractional-N digital phase-locked loop—a circuit that synchronizes to frequencies by using flexible dividers instead of fixed integer ones. It converts time delays to voltages and digitizes them to suppress quantization noise while remaining reliable across manufacturing processes, voltages, and temperatures. A voltage-domain feedforward noise cancellation technique (measuring and subtracting noise before it accumulates) eliminates the need for complex gain calibration. This achieves 290.8 femtoseconds of jitter at 5.5GHz, with less than 7.5% variation across PVT conditions.
isscc-2025-041.key_novelty: Voltage-domain feedforward noise cancellation eliminates the need for correlation-based gain calibration while suppressing phase noise robustly across process, voltage, and temperature variations, reducing power and design complexity.

isscc-2025-046.method: The chip uses separate power supply voltages for different regions: memory cells run at one level (VDDM) while surrounding circuits use another (VDI), so each part gets the right voltage for its job. To keep writes working reliably—especially at the far edges of the memory array where electrical signals degrade—the design adds an extra circuit that boosts write signal strength at those weak points. The design also redesigns the wake-up circuitry to correctly manage the voltage hierarchy (where main power VDD is higher than cell power VDDM, which is higher than ground VSS), keeping writes reliable even as temperature and voltage change.
isscc-2025-046.key_novelty: Pairing a write-assist circuit placed at electrically weak points in the memory array with region-specific power management using different voltage levels enables dual-port SRAM to work reliably at 3-nanometer scales.

isscc-2025-045.method: The processor examines the shape of each Gaussian (the 3D blob of light being rendered) and determines which computations will actually affect the final image. When a calculation's result gets too small to be visible, the processor stops early instead of completing it. A scheduler keeps the most-needed Gaussian data (spherical-harmonic coefficients—numbers describing each blob's appearance) in fast on-chip memory to avoid slow off-chip access.
isscc-2025-045.key_novelty: Instead of treating all Gaussians the same way, the processor adapts its work based on each one's shape—skipping computations that won't show up in the image and keeping only the essential data in fast memory.

isscc-2025-056.method: Dense magnetic memory arrays (cross-point layouts where each magnetic cell connects through a transistor) face a fundamental tradeoff: the read signal must be strong enough to reliably detect what's stored, but weak enough that it doesn't accidentally flip the stored data. This approach uses time-controlled discharge—releasing electrical charge at precisely-timed moments—combined with local-capacitance mode—collecting charge responses right at each cell—to sense the magnetic state. By carefully calibrating when the discharge happens, it balances these competing demands: extracting a strong enough read signal to work reliably while keeping disturbance margins tight enough that stored values stay intact, enabling safe read/write operations in high-density 1S1M arrays.
isscc-2025-056.key_novelty: Pairing time-controlled electrical discharge with local-capacitance sensing allows magnetic storage cells in dense cross-point arrays to be read reliably without accidentally erasing the stored data.

isscc-2025-055.method: MEGA.mini splits processing between two types of cores: large cores handle complex, single-pass computations in transformers and CNNs, while smaller cores are optimized for the repetitive steps that diffusion models need to run many times (25–100x iterations). This heterogeneous architecture (mixing different core types) lets the processor assign each model type to the cores that work best for it, improving speed and energy efficiency.
isscc-2025-055.key_novelty: The processor combines two core types in one chip—large cores optimized for transformers and CNNs, small cores for diffusion models' iterative steps—to efficiently handle both model families without the 25–100x efficiency penalty of a single-type design.

isscc-2025-048.method: A voltage-biased digitally-controlled oscillator with harmonic-shaping minimizes noise by automatically tuning its common-mode resonance (the resonant frequency of the shared signal path) based on second-harmonic amplitude (the strength of oscillations at twice the main frequency), eliminating manual calibration across different process conditions, supply voltages, and temperatures. The adaptive tuning works both during active operation and in the background, continuously adjusting to changing conditions. A transformer expands the common-mode impedance range, maintaining low noise across its entire frequency tuning range.
isscc-2025-048.key_novelty: The circuit automatically tunes its common-mode resonance (shared signal resonance) by monitoring the second-harmonic amplitude (oscillations at twice the main frequency), eliminating manual calibration and improving robustness across process, voltage, and temperature variations.

isscc-2025-047.method: The amplifier includes an all-passive (unpowered) cancellation circuit that removes interference signals by creating an inverted copy that cancels them out before the signal enters the active amplifier stages. Since interference is removed before amplification, strong unwanted signals don't get amplified and can't cause the distortion that would otherwise mix them with wanted signals and create noise. This approach uses only unpowered passive components, so it adds no extra power consumption.
isscc-2025-047.key_novelty: The single core idea is an all-passive interference-cancellation path built directly into the amplifier that removes interference before amplification, solving the three-way trade-off between achieving low noise, high linearity, and sharp filtering simultaneously.

isscc-2025-051.method: A single inductor (an electromagnetic coil that stores energy) resonates to pulse groups of transducers at staggered times, controlling the ultrasound beam direction—this is called beamforming. The shared inductor recycles energy that would otherwise be wasted in the semiconductor switches controlling each element, which normally cause heating losses called body-diode losses. This energy recycling reduces the power spent charging and discharging the transducers by 88%.
isscc-2025-051.key_novelty: Pulsing element groups at different times allows a single inductor to perform beamforming for the entire array, replacing the multiple separate inductors required in previous designs.

isscc-2025-052.method: This oscillator (a circuit that generates radio signals) covers frequencies from 9.05 to 37.0 GHz—an extremely wide range—by automatically switching between different magnetic operating modes instead of requiring manual adjustments. It uses a tuning-free common-mode resonator (a circuit element that naturally adjusts to the operating frequency without external tuning) to maintain performance across the entire range. This automatic approach eliminates the complex manual mode transitions that typically burden wide-bandwidth oscillator designs.
isscc-2025-052.key_novelty: Automatic magnetic-mode switching with a tuning-free common-mode resonator eliminates the complex manual control required to cover 9.05–37.0 GHz.

isscc-2025-054.method: A 4-lane 212.5Gb/s/lane retimer sends data using PAM-4 encoding (four signal levels) and puts the laser driver directly on the transmitter chip instead of using a separate external module. It handles the severe 40dB signal loss in the chip-to-module connection using receiver-side equalization—the same principle as noise canceling, which counteracts distortion from the lossy path. The design meets the power and thermal requirements of AI/ML systems.
isscc-2025-054.key_novelty: Integrating a high-swing (high-voltage) laser driver directly on the transmitter chip eliminates the external driver module while preserving full equalization across the 40dB lossy chip-to-module path.

isscc-2025-059.method: The converter uses 6 inductors (coils that store energy in magnetic fields) arranged in parallel phases, each handling part of the 12V-to-<1V voltage drop. Flying capacitors (capacitors that shuttle charge between voltage stages) work at each step, improving efficiency. This approach keeps all components compact and reduces resistive losses compared to using fewer, larger inductors. The result is exceptionally high current density—868 amps per cubic centimeter—in a small footprint.
isscc-2025-059.key_novelty: The core innovation is merging hybrid and multi-phase topologies: parallel inductors split the 60:1 voltage conversion across phases, with flying capacitors positioned for maximum efficiency, enabling 868A/cm³ current density.

isscc-2025-050.method: The ADC corrects errors from its amplifiers by continuously learning correction factors in the background (while operating normally) instead of stopping for calibration. It uses an adaptive filter that learns piecewise-linear corrections—breaking the error curve into straight-line segments instead of using complex polynomial formulas—with threshold values that adjust based on observed patterns. A dual-path amplification design further improves settling speed and power efficiency.
isscc-2025-050.key_novelty: Continuously learning piecewise-linear corrections with adaptive thresholds in the background eliminates both polynomial computation and calibration downtime.

isscc-2025-058.method: HuMoniX generates 3D motion by iteratively refining noisy predictions into clear motion—a process called diffusion denoising. It exploits two opportunities to reduce computation: pruning denoising computations that barely affect the output across iterations, and reusing joint calculations across frames since joints move gradually between frames. The hardware dataflow and scheduling are specialized to efficiently handle these sparse patterns.
isscc-2025-058.key_novelty: It accelerates text-to-motion generation by identifying and exploiting two forms of redundant computation: denoising steps that barely matter across iterations and joint calculations that repeat across frames.

isscc-2025-061.method: The system integrates a millimeter-scale CMOS chip (computer circuit) with vacuum-based microfluidics (channels that transport fluid using suction pressure) in a single compact package, eliminating the need for external syringe pumps. It detects biomarkers (disease indicators in blood or saliva) using multimode sensing—measuring electrical current (electrochemical), light signals (optical), or electrical resistance (impedance)—tailored to each target molecule. Vacuum microfluidics passively moves samples through the channels by creating pressure differences, requiring no external mechanical actuation.
isscc-2025-061.key_novelty: The core innovation is merging a CMOS chip with vacuum microfluidics in an RFID-inspired single package that eliminates external pumps and complex bonding techniques, achieving a pocket-sized diagnostic device.

isscc-2025-057.method: The circuit samples radio frequency signals up to 38 gigahertz using sub-sampling—taking measurements at only 12.8 billion samples per second, much slower than conventional sampling would require. This works because the sampling windows are carefully timed and paired with anti-aliasing filters (which block interfering frequencies), preventing signal loss despite the lower rate. The design achieves 6.4 gigahertz of usable bandwidth for flexible multi-channel reception across 1 to 32 gigahertz while maintaining high signal quality (over 39dB SNDR), using FDSOI technology (fully depleted silicon-on-insulator, a low-noise semiconductor process) in a 22-nanometer fabrication.
isscc-2025-057.key_novelty: A sub-sampling circuit achieving 38 gigahertz input bandwidth with 6.4 gigahertz usable bandwidth for flexible reception across 1 to 32 gigahertz.

isscc-2025-053.method: NeuroPilot implements dual-direction searching (exploring paths from both start and goal simultaneously) to use full search time without idle cycles, uses a dynamic-logic pilot processing element with an outspread pre-charge circuit to reduce power consumption, area, and leakage compared to traditional flip-flop storage, and applies a three-step coarse-fine path flow (TsCFP) to efficiently handle large maps.
isscc-2025-053.key_novelty: NeuroPilot combines dual-direction path searching with a dynamic-logic pilot processing element and an automated coarse-fine path flow to accelerate path-finding in CIM architecture.

isscc-2025-060.method: The charger uses a circuit design with three voltage levels and two separate input switches—one for plugged-in charging and one for wireless charging. When charging the battery, the circuit steps down the input voltage (called buck conversion); when the battery powers an external device, it steps up the voltage (called boost conversion); and when idle, it does nothing. The charger keeps current stable across all these modes by adjusting the switching frequency, using both coarse (rough) and fine (precise) tuning. Because the circuit handles a very wide range of input voltages, it doesn't need separate circuit designs for high or low voltage inputs—a single design works for both wired and wireless charging.
isscc-2025-060.key_novelty: The circuit smoothly switches between charging and power-sharing modes without needing extra helper circuits, by using coordinated switching of the three voltage levels and automatic frequency adjustment.

isscc-2025-064.method: The design combines digital and analog filtering working together to eliminate unwanted signal copies that appear at the output of high-speed transmitters. A digital polyphase filter (multiple parallel signal paths that are individually filtered and then combined) reduces the internal data rate for each channel while keeping the final output speed high. Then analog filtering built directly into the power amplifier circuit (which amplifies the weak signal for broadcast) further removes these unwanted replicas. A single unified architecture handles both low-band and high-band standards without requiring separate circuits for each band, reducing chip area and complexity.
isscc-2025-064.key_novelty: The key innovation is combining digital polyphase filtering with analog interpolation inside the power amplifier to suppress unwanted signal replicas, eliminating the need for expensive external RF filtering.

isscc-2025-068.method: This design embeds anti-aliasing filtering (the sharp frequency cutoff needed before digitization) directly into the analog-to-digital converter's core circuit, eliminating a separate bulky filter. A staged conversion approach overlaps multiple conversion steps so the filtering operations don't slow things down. Between these overlapped stages, a floating-charge-transfer amplifier efficiently amplifies and reshapes the signal at high speed without needing extra buffering circuitry. The design is fabricated in 28nm CMOS.
isscc-2025-068.key_novelty: Staging the conversion process together with a floating-charge-transfer amplifier lets filter-embedded analog-to-digital converters operate at 80 MHz bandwidth—4 to 5 times faster than previous approaches that combined filtering with analog-to-digital conversion.

isscc-2025-065.method: The system uses different radio frequencies to simultaneously deliver power and transmit data wirelessly without interfering with each other (called frequency-splitting). The implant sends neural signals back using backscatter—reflecting external radio waves with minimal power—at 200 megabits per second using just 0.67 trillionths of a joule per bit. A processor inside the implant automatically identifies and groups neuron firing patterns (spike sorting) without needing training data, so it only transmits categorized signals instead of raw data. A circuit filters out electrical noise from stimulation pulses during simultaneous recording, preventing false feedback loops.
isscc-2025-065.key_novelty: Frequency-splitting—using separate radio frequencies for wireless power and data (200 Mb/s backscatter)—enables the implant to run without a large battery by receiving power and sending neural signals simultaneously without interference.

isscc-2025-063.method: MAE is a tiny specialized processor built in 3nm technology, integrating 576 MAC units (the multiply-accumulate operations that form the basis of neural networks) into just 0.168 mm². Instead of processing each layer completely before moving to the next, it uses a line-based depth-first approach: processing thin horizontal slices of data all the way through the computation pipeline, which keeps related data in fast on-chip memory much longer and avoids repetitive trips to slow external DRAM. The design includes local caching to hold frequently reused data, and an optimization system that jointly minimizes memory access while keeping the computation units busy—addressing the problem where tiny chips normally sit idle waiting for data from memory.
isscc-2025-063.key_novelty: The innovation combines line-based depth-first scheduling (processing thin horizontal slices through the entire network before moving to the next slice) with local data caching, reducing external memory access by 40–80% compared to traditional layer-by-layer processing.

isscc-2025-066.method: The converter uses two feedback loops running at different speeds (20 MHz and 1 MHz) to rapidly detect and respond to sudden changes in power demand. Instead of one large inductor, it uses multiple inductors of different sizes that can all be activated at the same time, with a current allocation strategy that decides how much current should flow through each one. By controlling when each inductor's switches turn on and off, the system can quickly increase current levels, responding to power demand changes while maintaining the efficiency benefits of series-capacitor buck converters.
isscc-2025-066.key_novelty: This converter enables simultaneous activation of multiple inductors of different sizes using dual-speed feedback control (20 MHz and 1 MHz) with intelligent current allocation, achieving 2x faster load step response compared to single-loop designs while maintaining the efficiency benefits of series-capacitor buck converters.

isscc-2025-062.method: Multiple sampling circuits take turns at staggered times (hierarchical time-interleaving), sharing the sampling workload across stages to achieve high-speed sampling with simpler individual circuits. Despite being designed identically, manufacturing imperfections make each circuit slightly different, causing mismatched measurement results. The chip automatically corrects these mismatches using progressive digital calibration — measuring and adjusting for errors stage-by-stage without any external manual tuning. Everything runs on-chip using 4nm FinFET transistors, eliminating external components and saving space and power.
isscc-2025-062.key_novelty: Automatic self-calibration integrated into a hierarchical time-interleaved sampling architecture eliminates the need for external manual tuning, achieving 70+ dB SNDR (signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio) with spurious signals below -68 dBFS at 16 GS/s in 4nm.

isscc-2025-073.method: The circuit uses a direct-to-digital approach with delta amplification—a circuit design that extends the input range—in the first stage, breaking the traditional tradeoff between low noise and artifact rejection. Instead of amplifying first and saturating under large artifacts, this keeps the signal linear across a wide range while a VCO-based delta-sigma modulator (an analog-to-digital converter) digitizes it. This enables the front-end to reject 100+ millivolt artifact spikes while maintaining 50-60 nanovolts per square root Hertz noise, and achieves a 3.47 NEF (noise efficiency factor).
isscc-2025-073.key_novelty: Delta amplification in an ADC-first VCO-based converter simultaneously achieves low noise (3.47 NEF) and high dynamic range (handling 100+ millivolt artifacts) for bio-signal recording.

isscc-2025-070.method: The system uses a low-power electronic nose front-end (67 microwatts per channel) with gas sensors and analog signal conditioning (preparing the raw sensor signals for processing). Instead of sending data to a cloud server for analysis, a lightweight neural network runs directly on the chip and learns from each patient's individual breath signature in real time, using just 0.13 nanowatts per synapse (neural connection) per bit. This on-chip learning allows the sensor to automatically calibrate itself and adapt to each specific patient without needing external connectivity.
isscc-2025-070.key_novelty: The system uses on-chip incremental learning—where the neural network continuously learns and adapts—to calibrate itself specifically for each patient using only 0.13 nanowatts per synapse per bit, which lets it maintain accuracy even as environments change.

isscc-2025-072.method: The design replaces the standard current-mirror buffer (which changes resistance based on load) with a pseudo-impedance buffer that maintains constant resistance. A frequency-compensation strategy then improves phase margin (the regulator's stability buffer) across all loads without requiring complex high-order compensation. The regulator combines a single-stage error amplifier, the pseudo-impedance buffer, and a pass transistor, avoiding Miller compensation to maintain stability even below 1 volt.
isscc-2025-072.key_novelty: The pseudo-impedance buffer decouples the sub-1-volt regulator's phase margin from load current, enabling reliable operation across both light and heavy loads.

isscc-2025-074.method: The accelerator reduces energy by using different precision levels at different stages of GPS acquisition. In early stages—Doppler and code-delay estimation, where you're narrowing down which satellite and at what timing the signal is—lower precision is acceptable. The chip skips expensive calculations by using ROM-assisted computing: precomputed lookup tables stored in read-only memory. It combines a dual numerically controlled oscillator (NCO, which generates reference signals), a mixed-radix FFT engine (a signal transformer that breaks down complex calculations), and a correlator (which matches received signals to references), all built at 28nm in CMOS technology with adaptive word-widths.
isscc-2025-074.key_novelty: The accelerator exploits the fact that GPS acquisition stages don't all need the same precision, using lower precision early on and precomputed lookup tables to cut energy while still detecting satellites as accurately as existing methods.

isscc-2025-069.method: The design uses multipath feedback—routing the output signal back through multiple parallel paths instead of a single path—in an analog phase-locked loop (a circuit that synchronizes an output signal to an input reference clock). The parallel paths reduce the dead-zone (where the charge pump circuit stops responding) and reference spurs (unwanted frequency spikes from the reference clock), improving loop stability. This yields very low jitter—timing noise in the output signal—while using just an 80 MHz reference frequency, 7.5 times lower than previous low-jitter designs. The circuit produces output from 7.3 to 9.5 GHz.
isscc-2025-069.key_novelty: Multipath feedback in an analog phase-locked loop achieves 34 femtoseconds (trillionths of a second) of RMS jitter with just an 80 MHz reference frequency, eliminating the expensive 150–500 MHz references that previous low-jitter designs required.

isscc-2025-076.method: The system removes the traditional rectifier that converts piezoelectric vibrations into electrical power, eliminating the energy wasted in that conversion step. Instead, it uses a sense-and-track algorithm that continuously measures the vibration and adjusts the electrical impedance (the load resistance) in analog electronics to match the current vibration amplitude. This adjustment completes in a single vibration cycle—fast enough to keep up with sudden shock impacts where the amplitude changes rapidly. By skipping the rectifier and adapting this quickly, it extracts more power than traditional systems, especially under shock conditions.
isscc-2025-076.key_novelty: Single-cycle maximum power point convergence using a rectifier-free design and sense-and-track algorithm allows instant adaptation to fast-changing shock vibrations.

isscc-2025-077.method: The converter uses a single shared magnetic core (a passive transformer) that connects to all power domains, instead of requiring separate connections for each domain. Power distribution is controlled by sensing what the receiving circuits actually demand, and using that information to adjust the converter's switching. Since all adjustments happen on the receiver side and information only flows one way through the isolation barrier (the electrical separation between input and output), the system doesn't need digital isolators—chips that would normally relay control signals across isolated sections.
isscc-2025-077.key_novelty: A single shared magnetic core, combined with receiver-side power modulation based on sensing actual power demands, eliminates the need for control signals to cross the isolation barrier.

isscc-2025-075.method: A boost converter steps up voltage by rapidly switching a transistor on and off to pump energy through an inductor. Traditional designs place the inductor at the input, which concentrates voltage stress on a single component and creates a right-half-plane zero—an electrical property that slows the circuit's response to sudden load changes. This design instead places the inductor in the middle (between input and output stages), spreading voltage stress across multiple components and eliminating the RHP zero. With continuous current flow on both sides, this achieves 93% peak efficiency and faster transient response.
isscc-2025-075.key_novelty: Moving the inductor to the middle of the circuit eliminates the right-half-plane zero and spreads voltage stress across multiple components instead of concentrating it on one.

isscc-2025-067.method: The circuit uses two LC resonators (coil-capacitor circuits tuned to vibrate at a set frequency), optimized separately for the input and output sides. The input side drives oscillation through an optimized LC circuit, while the output side converts this to DC power using resonant rectification—a rectifier tuned to that frequency—instead of a traditional full-bridge rectifier that wastes energy across multiple diodes. The output side provides voltage regulation by modulating how much current it draws, which modulates the input resonator through backscattering (a technique where load changes couple back through the resonator), eliminating the need for an expensive digital isolator.
isscc-2025-067.key_novelty: The dual-LC-resonant topology with inherent backscatter feedback achieves 65.4% peak efficiency and eliminates the need for digital isolators—a 6–13% efficiency gain compared to conventional isolated DC-DC converters.

isscc-2025-078.method: SHINSAI is a programmable physical layer (called an interposer) that connects stacked computer chips together, built in 28nm CMOS with through-silicon vias (tiny wires threaded through the silicon). Inside, it has two routing layers: horizontal 2.5D paths (H-Link) that route connections within the interposer, and vertical 3D paths (V-Link) that connect upward to the stacked chips. It includes 512Mb of on-board SRAM to manage data between chips. Because the routing is programmable rather than hardwired, you can reconfigure how different chips connect without changing the physical hardware, letting the same interposer work with many different chip combinations.
isscc-2025-078.key_novelty: The core innovation is making the interposer's routing programmable so it works with different chip combinations instead of being locked into one configuration.

isscc-2025-079.method: The design connects a boost bridge (a circuit stage that increases voltage) and a buck bridge (a circuit stage that decreases voltage) in series. A flying capacitor (a capacitor that moves charge around the circuit to balance electrical stress) enables continuous current flow across the full voltage range. By operating in a single fixed configuration rather than switching between multiple operating modes, this eliminates the voltage spikes and output ripple that plague conventional multi-mode converters.
isscc-2025-079.key_novelty: A single-mode cascaded buck-boost converter using a flying capacitor to maintain continuous current delivery, which eliminates voltage glitches and ripple by avoiding mode transitions.

isscc-2025-083.method: The design combines a power supply (voltage regulator) directly integrated into a 3nm chip that automatically switches its operating mode based on power demand. When the chip draws heavy current, it uses hard-switching—rapidly flipping transistors on and off to transfer power efficiently. At lower power levels, the system automatically switches to soft-switching (transistor transitions with less electrical noise) and then discontinuous conduction mode (where the inductor fully discharges each cycle, reducing noise further). This three-mode approach keeps voltage stable while achieving 86% efficiency when running at light load.
isscc-2025-083.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically switching between three operating modes—hard-switching at high load, soft-switching at medium load, and discontinuous conduction mode at light load—to maintain efficiency across the full power range.

isscc-2025-071.method: A frequency management module puts an RC-based frequency reference (a resistor-capacitor oscillator with stability improvements) and a frequency synthesizer (a circuit that generates different output frequencies) on the same CMOS chip. The oscillator stays accurate within ±47/±42 parts per million across -40 to +95°C. The synthesizer generates frequencies from 1.8 to 3.0 GHz with this accuracy; after accelerated aging tests, accuracy drops to ±150/±70 parts per million.
isscc-2025-071.key_novelty: An RC frequency reference (resistor-capacitor oscillator) and synthesizer (frequency-generation circuit) are integrated on a single CMOS chip for the first time, achieving frequency stability matching external crystal oscillators and eliminating off-chip frequency trim (tuning).

isscc-2025-084.method: The detector spreads tiny voltage-sensing circuits (called remote droop detectors, or RDD) across the chip that continuously sample at up to 4GHz. A central control circuit (droop detection controller, or DDC) coordinates all these distributed sensors and automatically adjusts for manufacturing variations and environmental conditions (PVT tolerance), keeping them synchronized. Together, they detect voltage droop in under 2 clock cycles with 0.69% accuracy, implemented in 2nm transistor technology.
isscc-2025-084.key_novelty: Instead of a single bulky centralized detector, this design distributes tiny voltage sensors across the chip with centralized coordination that adapts to manufacturing and temperature variations, enabling high-speed detection everywhere without routing problems.

isscc-2025-080.method: The 22nm accelerator performs calculations directly in memory (compute-in-memory or CIM) instead of moving data back and forth, saving power. It splits memory into sections that match each layer's actual data needs (bandwidth-aware partitioning) and divides memory access paths using bit-line segmentation, keeping data local and reducing movement. These optimizations especially help tasks requiring multi-view or temporal attention—comparing multiple camera angles or frames over time—which are common in 3D and video generation.
isscc-2025-080.key_novelty: It solves the problem of varying data needs across layers by using bandwidth-aware memory partitioning and bit-line segmentation in compute-in-memory, which cuts data-access power without sacrificing computational efficiency.

isscc-2025-087.method: The receiver uses 256 antenna elements arranged in a phased array—a technique where multiple antennas work together and their signal timing is adjusted to focus reception in particular directions. It operates in the Ka-band microwave frequencies. The design positions switches and quadrature hybrids (circuits that split signals into two versions shifted 90 degrees apart) early in the signal chain, allowing the same hardware to flexibly switch between receiving single circular-polarized waves (where the wave rotates in one direction), dual circular-polarized waves (receiving two circular rotations simultaneously), or linear-polarized waves (where the wave vibrates in a fixed plane)—different encoding schemes satellites use depending on their mission.
isscc-2025-087.key_novelty: The switch-type quadrature-hybrid-first design enables flexible polarization switching without duplicating hardware, reducing power consumption by 50% when operating in single-polarization mode.

isscc-2025-085.method: The sensor places a separate analog-to-digital converter (ADC — a circuit that converts light signals to digital numbers) directly on each pixel in a stacked 3D structure. Because every pixel converts its signal simultaneously (a "pixel-parallel" architecture), all 25.2 million pixels digitize at the same instant rather than row-by-row, creating a "global shutter" that eliminates the rolling-shutter distortion of conventional cameras. This design maintains high dynamic range (visible detail in bright and dark areas) and low random noise even at 120 frames per second.
isscc-2025-085.key_novelty: Stacking an analog-to-digital converter on each pixel in a 3D structure enables 25 million-pixel global-shutter imaging with high dynamic range and minimal noise.

isscc-2025-082.method: The transmitter sends data as PAM-4 (four signal levels spaced closely together, making them noise-prone). To keep the signal clean across the channel, it uses a feed-forward equalizer (FFE) that adjusts the signal before sending it, calibrated automatically (ZQ-based) to the actual circuit's electrical properties. To save power, it adds PAM-4 LSB DBI-DC encoding (selective bit-flipping to reduce power-bus activity) built directly into the four signal levels, avoiding extra circuitry.
isscc-2025-082.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining a self-adjusting signal recovery circuit (ZQ-based FFE) with power-saving bit-encoding (PAM-4 LSB DBI-DC) in a single PAM-4 transmitter.

isscc-2025-081.method: BROCA is a single integrated circuit that runs conversational AI directly on mobile devices. It processes conversation through five stages: perceiving user input (with multimodal encoding for speech and vision), retrieving relevant context, generating a response using a transformer language model, generating emotional tone, and converting to speech via a vocoder. To reduce power consumption, the chip uses adaptive bit-truncation and acoustic-cluster bit grouping—techniques that adjust the numerical precision (number of bits) used in each stage based on what that stage actually needs.
isscc-2025-081.key_novelty: The core innovation is using an adaptive bit-truncate unit and acoustic-cluster bit grouping to optimize numerical precision in each stage of the conversational AI pipeline, reducing power consumption.

isscc-2025-088.method: Tomahawk5 is a monolithic chip—meaning all the network switching logic fits on one 5-nanometer piece of silicon—achieving 51.2 trillion bits per second switching capacity in a single integrated design. The chip uses Peregrine SerDes cores, which are high-speed circuits that translate signals between the chip's internal architecture and external cables, enabling it to work with multiple physical connection formats. These cores support direct copper cables, front-panel optics, pluggable optical modules, and fiber optics built directly into the chip's package, allowing data centers to use whichever connection method they already have deployed.
isscc-2025-088.key_novelty: Embedding Peregrine SerDes cores into the monolithic switch enables a single 51.2Tb/s chip to natively support multiple connection types—copper and various optical formats—without needing separate interface cards.

isscc-2025-089.method: The design combines a 16-nanometer chip with 216 kilobytes of gain-cell memory that supports three formats: microscaling (a compact format), integer, and floating-point. It converts floating-point data to microscaling format inside the computation rather than beforehand, using a specialized unit that tracks signal variance to maintain accuracy. The adder tree—which sums partial results—is optimized for high-probability operations, reducing wasted work in common cases. The chip dynamically reconfigures how it accumulates results based on the precision needed at each step.
isscc-2025-089.key_novelty: The core contribution is enabling a single CIM chip to support microscaling, integer, and floating-point formats by performing format conversion inside the computation and using a pattern-aware adder tree optimized for high-probability operations.

isscc-2025-095.method: Slim-Llama compresses model weights to 1-2 bit values (binary or ternary quantization) instead of full precision, cutting the data that must be loaded from external memory—the primary energy bottleneck for large models. Custom hardware logic accelerates token processing while working with these compressed weights. This achieves 9 picojoules of energy per parameter—a 3x to 25x improvement over prior approaches that required 26-222 picojoules—while keeping total power below 5 milliwatts for billion-parameter Llama models.
isscc-2025-095.key_novelty: Extreme weight compression (binary or ternary quantization: 1-2 bits per parameter) combined with hardware designed specifically for this format achieves 9 picojoules per parameter for billion-parameter model inference.

isscc-2025-097.method: A clock-referenced PAM3 transceiver (a timing-synchronized 3-level signal receiver) tracks voltage reference changes from the transmitter, which eliminates reference mismatches between them.
