The receiver includes circuits that reject supply-noise-induced jitter (random timing errors from power-supply voltage fluctuations), and the signal design reduces crosstalk (interference between neighboring signal wires, which is twice as bad in PAM3 as in standard two-level signals). The transceiver achieves 0.275pJ/b efficiency at 42Gb/s per pin.
isscc-2025-097.key_novelty: A timing-synchronized receiver that dynamically tracks the transmitter's voltage reference instead of using a fixed reference voltage, eliminating the reference mismatch problem in single-ended PAM3 signals.

isscc-2025-093.method: The design distributes control signals to power transistors using noise-resistant techniques that prevent on-chip electrical interference from disrupting the signals. This ensures even current distribution across all transistors despite high electrical noise throughout the chip. It delivers 2 amps of output current while maintaining stable voltage output.
isscc-2025-093.key_novelty: Making control signals resistant to electrical noise enables distributed analog voltage regulators to work reliably in noisy modern chips.

isscc-2025-092.method: When a write command arrives at the memory interface, the voltage regulator gets advance warning and predicts that the write buffers (WDQS) will soon draw a sudden surge of current. To prevent the voltage from dropping too far, the regulator proactively pumps extra current into the circuit just before the surge hits. This prediction-based approach achieves voltage stability within 10mV and settles within 400 picoseconds, while using only 20pF of on-chip energy storage and 150μA of idle power.
isscc-2025-092.key_novelty: By predicting voltage droop from command signals and acting proactively, the regulator maintains sub-10mV stability in 400ps without large on-chip capacitors.

isscc-2025-091.method: The receiver detects 42 billion bits per second on graphics memory (GDDR7) using three signal levels (PAM-3). Because each bit's signal is distorted by previous bits (inter-symbol interference), it uses a decision feedback equalizer — subtracting out the known interference from already-detected bits. To do this fast enough, the design combines two approaches: direct-feedback, which uses only the immediately previous bit for fast response, and loop-unrolled detection (calculating several future bits in parallel instead of one at a time). This hybrid approach delivers fast feedback timing without the silicon and power cost of fully parallel detection.
isscc-2025-091.key_novelty: It combines fast single-bit feedback with partial parallel detection of future bits to achieve 42Gb/s without the full area and power cost of detecting all bits at once.

isscc-2025-098.method: The system connects a laser with four-level modulation (VCSEL-PAM-4) directly to a receiver amplifier without adding digital processing delays. It uses an analog equalizer circuit (CZ-CTIE, which uses coupled inductors) embedded in the laser driver to fix signal distortion from the laser's frequency response, and a high-linearity amplifier that converts optical to electrical signals while another equalizer stage in the amplifier's feedback corrects remaining distortion. This approach lets the receiver decode data at 108 Gb/s with minimal power overhead by avoiding digital re-timing.
isscc-2025-098.key_novelty: Using a continuous-time analog equalizer circuit (CZ-CTIE) embedded in the optical driver and receiver to fix signal distortion eliminates the power-hungry digital re-processing step normally required for direct-drive optical signals.

isscc-2025-090.method: The design reduces power through three techniques: optimizing the write-clock distribution to minimize losses, using an optimized dual-emphasis transmitter (a circuit that sends data using two complementary signal techniques), and allowing circuits to operate within relaxed voltage and timing tolerances. Together, these maintain 42.5Gb/s data transmission—required for AI systems—while consuming less power.
isscc-2025-090.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining an optimized dual-emphasis transmitter (using two complementary signal techniques) with relaxed voltage and timing tolerances to achieve 42.5Gb/s GDDR7 memory transmission with reduced power consumption.

isscc-2025-086.method: The device extracts a unique fingerprint from tiny manufacturing variations in how much voltage transistors need to turn on (threshold-voltage mismatches) in simple inverter circuits. It uses a technique called Vth-tilting — adjusting the measurement method for these threshold voltages — to streamline enrollment by testing only at standard operating conditions instead of across temperature and voltage extremes. The design adds three protections: power-gating (disabling power during idle to prevent aging), a balanced sampler (symmetrically measuring signals to resist eavesdropping), and laser-attack detection.
isscc-2025-086.key_novelty: The core innovation is the Vth-tilting measurement scheme, which cuts enrollment test time by requiring screening only at standard voltage and temperature.

isscc-2025-094.method: The receiver uses a small 3D-shaped coil (0.904 cubic centimeters) with electrical circuits tuned to resonate at a specific frequency, which improves how efficiently wireless power transfers through tissue. It automatically adjusts this tuning in real time as the surrounding tissue's electrical resistance changes, keeping power transfer efficient while using low power—all without any manual intervention or programming.
isscc-2025-094.key_novelty: The receiver adjusts itself automatically and continuously as tissue changes, without needing any programming, all in a tiny 3D-shaped coil (0.904 cubic centimeters).

isscc-2025-096.method: EdgeDiff compresses few-step diffusion models using two quantization techniques applied across the encoder, UNet, and decoder: mixed-precision quantization, which stores different model parts with different numbers of bits (giving more bits to sensitive components like the encoder and decoder), and reordered group quantization, which groups similar weights and finds the best grouping order for efficient compression. Unlike standard diffusion models, few-step models lack redundancy between denoising steps, so this approach focuses on optimizing each component's compression tolerance directly rather than exploiting temporal patterns. The result is efficient mobile inference while preserving accuracy in the sensitive multi-modal components.
isscc-2025-096.key_novelty: EdgeDiff accelerates few-step diffusion inference by combining mixed-precision quantization (using different bit-widths for different model parts) with reordered group quantization (optimizing weight groupings), without relying on inter-timestep redundancy.

isscc-2025-104.method: RNGD uses tensor contraction—a generalized operation that multiplies and sums arrays along specific dimensions—as its core computational unit instead of traditional matrix multiplication, which exposes far more opportunities for parallel work. Execution pipelines like a vector processor: each processing stage finishes and immediately passes its results to the next stage while earlier stages keep working, rather than waiting for entire operations to complete. The hardware's processing elements can split dynamically into smaller independent slices with adjustable data-fetch networks, letting the accelerator adapt to different tensor shapes and sizes without losing parallelism.
isscc-2025-104.key_novelty: The core idea is using tensor contraction—with dynamically split processing elements and pipelined data flow—as the fundamental building block instead of matrix multiplication, enabling efficient and flexible LLM inference.

isscc-2025-102.method: This receiver divides the incoming signal into many frequency bands (discrete multitone or DMT) and equalizes each band separately. A time-based ADC converts the analog signal to digital form by measuring how fast signals cross a threshold, rather than measuring voltage directly. Within each band, the receiver applies equalization and uses MLSE—an algorithm that picks the most likely transmitted sequence given what was actually received—to decode the data. This design sidesteps the fundamental problem with traditional PAM-4 approaches: they require massive numbers of equalizer stages (FFE taps) and face timing constraints in feedback paths (DFE), both of which become impractical above 100 Gb/s.
isscc-2025-102.key_novelty: Discrete multitone (DMT) modulation with time-based ADC avoids the exponentially growing complexity of large equalizer stages (FFE and DFE) that traditional PAM-4 designs require at high speeds above 100 Gb/s.

isscc-2025-106.method: DustNet uses ultrasound—sound frequencies around 1-9 MHz that pass through body tissue without getting absorbed—to send data to and from tiny implants placed several centimeters deep. Each implant takes its turn transmitting (time-division multiplexing) so they don't interfere with each other. When receiving, implants send data back by reflecting the ultrasound at one of 16 different signal strengths (16-level ASK backscatter modulation), allowing each implant to transmit at 50kb/s.
isscc-2025-106.key_novelty: DustNet achieves multi-implant wireless neural recording at clinical tissue depths using ultrasound implants with time-division multiplexing (taking turns) and 16-level signal strength modulation (16-level ASK backscatter).

isscc-2025-105.method: The design uses three power amplifier stages stacked in 22nm FDSOI CMOS (a compact silicon technology) arranged in a Doherty configuration with stacked operational-amplifier-based biasing. In a Doherty topology, the peak and auxiliary amplifier stages dynamically adjust their electrical impedance to maintain high power efficiency across different output power levels. The stacked operational-amplifier biasing further improves efficiency at back-off (reduced power) conditions, which matters for 5G signals that have high peak-to-average power ratios.
isscc-2025-105.key_novelty: Stacked operational-amplifier biasing that enables high efficiency in compact three-stage Doherty power amplifiers for 5G millimeter-wave integration.

isscc-2025-110.method: p-circuits avoid the power and area costs of converting between analog and digital by using a hybrid approach: inputs and outputs look digital, but the actual computation happens through probability. Each output is a random 0 or 1, where how often it outputs 1 (versus 0) is controlled by an analog function that smoothly responds to the inputs. By manipulating these probabilities, the circuit performs calculations without ever converting signals between analog and digital domains.
isscc-2025-110.key_novelty: p-circuits use probability as the fundamental computational substrate, with analog functions directly controlling output probabilities instead of requiring costly digital-analog conversions.

isscc-2025-099.method: This 3nm FinFET design reduces power in TCAM (ternary content-addressable memory—a device that searches memory entries against patterns) by using dynamically gated search lines, which selectively activate only the entries that need searching rather than all entries at once. Asymmetric-split architecture further reduces power by adjusting consumption based on the number of bits being searched. Together they achieve 37.4% power savings and 46.6% lower peak current.
isscc-2025-099.key_novelty: Dynamically gating search lines—turning them on selectively to search only the needed entries instead of searching all at once—reduces power consumption in TCAM.

isscc-2025-111.method: Instead of conventional I-Q mixing (multiplying the signal by two reference signals), this IC uses time-to-digital demodulation, which converts signal timing into digital information for measurement. It achieves high phase accuracy through co-prime delay-locked sampling (a technique where precisely timed delays stack to simulate a much faster sampling rate), reaching 21.6GHz effective sampling from a 240MHz clock. A phase comparator-based delay-locked loop generates these accurate delays, while an optimized wideband current generator and front-end design handle frequencies up to 30MHz. This design eliminates the distortion caused by analog multiplication in conventional systems.
isscc-2025-111.key_novelty: The core idea is using time-to-digital demodulation with co-prime delay-locked sampling to measure phase accurately across a wide frequency range without the distortion that traditional analog I-Q multiplication causes.

isscc-2025-108.method: The converter uses a hybrid design that reduces the maximum current in its energy-storage inductor coil to half what conventional designs allow, cutting resistive power losses since they increase dramatically with current. It operates as a voltage booster (charging from USB) in one direction and as a voltage reducer (supplying power) in the other, both with reduced stress on the inductor. An adaptive system continuously measures power demand and adjusts the converter's operating point to maintain efficiency as conditions change.
isscc-2025-108.key_novelty: The key innovation is a hybrid converter design that keeps inductor current at half-levels (reducing resistive losses since they grow with the square of current) and automatically adjusts its operating point based on power demand, cutting stress on both the inductor and transistors.

isscc-2025-100.method: Neural networks need to repeatedly perform matrix multiplications, which normally requires fetching weights from distant storage—a power-hungry process for always-on sensors. This microprocessor integrates magnetic memory (MRAM) directly on-chip to store 1.1 megabits of weights right next to the compute hardware. The MRAM cells form crossbar arrays (grids where current flows through magnetic cells), performing multiply-and-add operations directly in the hardware using analog electrical signals. Because weights are stored co-located with the math, the entire neural network can run without fetching data from external memory, eliminating a major source of power consumption.
isscc-2025-100.key_novelty: First microprocessor to demonstrate end-to-end deep neural network inference with all weights stored on-chip in MRAM-embedded 28nm CMOS technology.

isscc-2025-103.method: The system combines a specialized circuit (biased-SECE, which combines switch-harvesting-on-inductor-peak or SHIP with parallel SECE) with an algorithm using geometric mean calculations to track the optimal electrical load. Rather than stopping energy extraction to measure and adjust—like traditional methods—this approach continuously adapts based on recent voltage readings. It responds to voltage changes in 8.75 cycles and achieves 99.9% efficiency, meaning it wastes almost none of the harvested energy on the tracking process itself.
isscc-2025-103.key_novelty: A geometric-mean-based tracking algorithm continuously finds the optimal electrical load without pausing energy extraction, responding in just 8.75 cycles per voltage change.

isscc-2025-109.method: The receiver uses a five-stage filter (fifth-order filtering) at the input with steep roll-off exceeding 20dB per decade of frequency, which sharply rejects signals from nearby channels before they can interfere. It employs a mixer-first architecture where the incoming radio signal passes through this front-end filter before being converted to baseband (the low-frequency signal containing the data). To keep power consumption low while maintaining the low noise figure needed for weak-signal reception, the design uses stacked capacitors for passive gain—amplifying the signal without drawing extra current.
isscc-2025-109.key_novelty: Five-stage filter architecture that steeply suppresses adjacent-channel interference while using less power than previous mixer-first designs.

isscc-2025-101.method: A 3x3.3mm semiconductor chip manufactured using 180nm CMOS technology (an advanced process that efficiently packs millions of components into tiny spaces) contains individual gamma-ray sensors. Each sensor independently adjusts its sensitivity based on the incoming radiation intensity and environmental conditions like temperature. The chip measures the energy of each detected gamma ray to determine the lesion's depth and size during surgery.
isscc-2025-101.key_novelty: Configurable pixels that measure gamma-ray energy let surgeons distinguish lesion depth and size during cancer surgery.

isscc-2025-115.method: The system combines spatial compressive sensing (acquiring measurements of an image space rather than measuring every point separately) with a specialized converter (SAR ADC) that performs matrix multiplication during analog-to-digital conversion. The hardware simultaneously compresses and converts the photoacoustic signal measurements at the sensor itself, avoiding the need for separate compression steps later. Since photoacoustic signals are inherently weak—about 10 times fainter than ultrasound—the converter is optimized with tuned gain, bandwidth, and noise characteristics to reliably capture these faint signals.
isscc-2025-115.key_novelty: A matrix-multiplying SAR ADC integrates compressive sensing directly into analog-to-digital conversion, compressing photoacoustic images at the moment of sensing rather than in a separate step.

isscc-2025-107.method: The system uses a tiny AI model (a convolutional neural network, or CNN) small enough to fit on a single chip. It learns directly from each person's voice on-chip—not on external servers—which enables personalization while saving power. To minimize power consumption to 13.5 microwatts, it uses two techniques: a simplified approach to identifying important sound patterns (called feature extraction) using sine waves and approximate logarithms, and quantization (using lower-precision numbers to reduce power and space needs). This enables accurate recognition of 35 keywords, even with accented speakers, while adapting to each user's unique speech patterns.
isscc-2025-107.key_novelty: The core idea is personalizing the system by training it directly on-chip—using simplified math based on sine waves and approximate logarithms—to achieve ultra-low power recognition of 35 keywords even with accented speech, consuming just 13.5 microwatts.

isscc-2025-114.method: Xiling co-integrates (combines on the same chip) two independent ultra-precise voltage generators (18-bit dual-DAC—circuits that convert digital numbers into exact analog voltages) directly with the single-electron transistor at cryogenic temperatures (60mK). Normally, quantum chips require long cables to distant room-temperature electronics (300K), which introduces noise and signal degradation; this design keeps the voltage generators cold and on-chip to eliminate those problems. Special low-power circuits designed for extreme-cold operation deliver 4.6µV precision (18-bit level control) and 4.1nV/√Hz noise floor—the precision required for reliable quantum gate control.
isscc-2025-114.key_novelty: Xiling places voltage control circuits directly on the quantum chip at cryogenic temperatures (60mK), eliminating the long cables and noise from remote room-temperature electronics, and achieving 4.6µV precision with 4.1nV/√Hz noise floor.

isscc-2025-112.method: This sub-sampling PLL uses a phase detector that samples both rising and falling edges of the oscillator—this doubles the timing information, shrinking the tuning range without prescaler circuits (which traditionally reduce frequency but widen the tuning range). To lock quickly in fractional-N mode (where non-integer frequency ratios slow normal feedback), the design measures remaining frequency errors with a Time-to-Digital Converter and corrects them beyond what the reference clock can reach, settling in under 2 microseconds.
isscc-2025-112.key_novelty: The design combines polarity-reversible phase detection (sampling both clock edges) with a Time-to-Digital Converter frequency loop to achieve both tuning range reduction without prescalers and fast fractional-N locking.

isscc-2025-116.method: This design creates a stable voltage reference that works at just 0.8V power supply—a challenge because traditional approaches using BJTs (bipolar transistors) need significant voltage overhead to function, and existing solutions required either special non-standard transistor structures or large filtering circuits. Instead, it uses charge-pump and switched-capacitor circuits (transistor-based switching techniques that manage voltage with minimal overhead rather than pushing steady current through components). The result is exceptional: the voltage drifts only 31 parts per million per degree Celsius as temperature changes, and it rejects power-supply noise across DC-to-GHz frequencies by -40dB (meaning interference is reduced to roughly 1/10,000th of its original strength), all within just 294µm² using only standard core transistors.
isscc-2025-116.key_novelty: Standard-transistor voltage references can now operate at ultra-low 0.8V power levels with 31ppm/°C temperature stability and -40dB power-supply-noise rejection in 294µm² by using charge-pump and switched-capacitor switching instead of traditional BJT or special-structure approaches.

isscc-2025-119.method: A 32Gb/s, 64-lane UCIe interface uses matched-delay architecture (internal pathways with identical timing characteristics) to maintain synchronized clock and data signals during dynamic power gating. When power switches on or off, voltage droops (temporary dips in supply voltage) normally cause timing delays to shift unpredictably, misaligning clock and data at the sampling point. The matched-delay design ensures both signals experience the same delay shifts, keeping them aligned and preventing bit errors from voltage variations.
isscc-2025-119.key_novelty: Matched-delay architecture that prevents data sampling misalignment caused by voltage droops when power is dynamically switched in chiplet interfaces.

isscc-2025-113.method: The circuit measures capacitance in two stages: a fast rough estimate using SAR (successive approximation register, a binary-search measurement technique), then precise refinement based on oscillator timing (VCO). To reduce thermal noise that worsens at low measurement speeds, it uses chopping—repeatedly flipping the signal to shuffle noise away—requiring only minimal signal amplification, unlike conventional methods that need power-hungry amplifiers. It stabilizes the feedback loop using phase-domain lead-compensation (an 'add-then-subtract' technique for timing adjustments), enabling a stable high-order loop without reducing measurement accuracy and eliminating the need for separate amplifier circuits (OTAs).
isscc-2025-113.key_novelty: Combining chopping for thermal noise cancellation with efficient phase-domain lead-compensation enables high-order oscillator-based measurement without separate amplifier circuits.

isscc-2025-121.method: The system uses solid-state batteries (compact, integrated energy sources with no liquid electrolyte) built into the microrobot to convert its low-voltage battery power (3-5V) into high voltages (tens of volts) for the electrostatic and piezoelectric actuators. The design optimizes how efficiently this conversion happens and manages energy delivery to the capacitive loads (electrical charges that power the actuators).
isscc-2025-121.key_novelty: Solid-state batteries integrated into flying microrobots enable lightweight, efficient power conversion from low to high voltage for driving microactuators.

isscc-2025-120.method: The processor improves low-quality video in both spatial detail (pixels) and temporal smoothness (between frames) using space-time video super-resolution. To run on edge devices, it combines multiple processing operations using layer-fusion, which drastically cuts the temporary data stored on the chip. It uses deformable convolution — filters that adapt their shape to follow motion between frames — to align frames precisely across time. Custom processing-element hardware is built specifically for 8K resolution at 60 frames per second with minimal power draw.
isscc-2025-120.key_novelty: The key innovation is layer-fusion: fusing multiple motion-tracking layers into a single operation to eliminate the intermediate data storage overhead from deformable convolution.

isscc-2025-118.method: Instead of treating each frame as a standalone image, this processor uses the structure built into video codecs. Modern video codecs already compute motion vectors (which direction pixels moved) and residuals (the pixel differences they don't need to store) to compress efficiently—this processor feeds those directly into its super-resolution pipeline instead of starting from scratch. It processes multiple frames together through alignment and refinement stages, reusing information across frames and using pre-computed codec data. This approach achieves 210fps performance at 4K resolution with lower energy than conventional super-resolution.
isscc-2025-118.key_novelty: The key innovation is directly feeding motion vectors and residuals from the video codec into super-resolution processing, rather than re-analyzing raw pixel data independently.

isscc-2025-126.method: The circuit uses an internal reference copy to detect and cancel two major sources of frequency drift: signal propagation delay (time for signals to travel through the circuit) and comparator offset (built-in errors in the voltage-comparison stage). Correction circuits integrated into the design automatically compensate for these effects without needing adjustable resistors or complex mathematical calibration. This achieves ±9.83ppm/°C frequency stability (less than 10 parts per million drift per degree Celsius) across -40°C to 125°C while using only 0.4µW/MHz of power.
isscc-2025-126.key_novelty: An open-loop oscillator that internally cancels propagation delay and comparator errors, matching the stability of closed-loop designs while avoiding their circuit complexity.

isscc-2025-127.method: This 10-bit, 3-billion-sample-per-second ADC detects and corrects for ambiguous comparator outputs (metastability — when a comparator gets a marginal input and oscillates between 0 and 1) by pipelining extra decision stages. Instead of trying to resolve the ambiguity within the main conversion path, it separates detection into additional latches that work in parallel, giving more time for diagnosis. Mutually exclusive correction logic (only one error path can fire at a time) then fixes the error, keeping the overall conversion speed intact.
isscc-2025-127.key_novelty: Adding detection stages across the conversion pipeline lets the circuit catch and fix ambiguous comparator readings, reducing bit errors while keeping the overall conversion speed unchanged.

isscc-2025-124.method: The chip has four transmit and four receive channels. It generates D-band signals using a frequency quadrupler (a circuit that multiplies the signal frequency by 4 and amplifies it), then amplifies them further with a power amplifier built from low-loss slow-wave coplanar waveguide (special interconnects designed to reduce signal loss) and LC-ladder power combiners (circuits that merge multiple signals into a single stronger output). Finally, it uses an antenna integrated into the chip package with a cavity backing (which focuses the radiation to boost antenna gain). Together, these components achieve 28.7 dBm EIRP (effective radiated power).
isscc-2025-124.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining a cavity-backed antenna integrated into the chip package with LC-ladder power-combining circuits to achieve 28.7 dBm EIRP for D-band radar transceiver arrays.

isscc-2025-122.method: The processor handles encrypted computation (where each party uses their own encryption key) through three hierarchical operation levels: task-level configurations that specify what to compute (linear or nonlinear transformations), encrypted-number operations (multiplication, key-switching which changes the encryption key, and rescaling which adjusts precision), and polynomial-level mathematics (NTT which transforms data representation, base conversion which changes number formats, and permutations which rearrange data). By flexibly combining these levels, it efficiently computes any task while scaling to unlimited parties.
isscc-2025-122.key_novelty: It's the first hardware processor that enables unlimited parties to compute on encrypted data (each using their own encryption key) by flexibly integrating operations at multiple hierarchical levels.

isscc-2025-129.method: The system integrates power sensors (tiny current-measuring devices) directly onto the 3nm octa-core processor chip and uses machine learning algorithms that continuously improve their accuracy by learning from real chip behavior. Every 50 millionths of a second or faster, it measures instantaneous electrical current and compares it to the power budget (the maximum current the power supply can safely deliver). When current approaches the safety limit, the system automatically distributes computational work across the eight cores to keep peak current below this threshold, preventing power-supply overload and system crashes.
isscc-2025-129.key_novelty: On-die power sensors with silicon machine learning calibration (algorithms embedded in the hardware that stay accurate by learning from actual chip conditions) enable real-time peak-current management across the eight processor cores.

isscc-2025-117.method: The receiver uses three tunable signal-processing stages (3-tap RX FFE, which adaptively cancel channel distortion) to create a target pulse pattern (1+0.50: main signal plus a half-strength echo) for a one-tap speculative decision-feedback stage (which predicts bits ahead of time to reduce delay). This recovers from 21.2dB of signal loss without requiring the transmitter to pre-process the signal (no TX FFE). The design separates the cancellation stages from the feedback stage to avoid timing conflicts, eliminates the first intersymbol interference (h1: the strongest echo from prior bits), and maintains power efficiency using mostly-analog circuits.
isscc-2025-117.key_novelty: The core idea is using three receiver-side processing stages to generate a 1+0.50 pulse response for a speculative decision-feedback stage, which eliminates transmitter-side processing while maintaining power efficiency.

isscc-2025-123.method: The chip detects irregular heartbeats using a Bayesian neural network—a type of AI that measures confidence in its predictions. Normally this incurs huge power overhead from generating random numbers and running multiple iterations. This 65nm accelerator uses three techniques: analog circuits to generate random numbers in parallel (simpler than digital), in-memory analog computation that does math where data already sits (avoiding expensive data movement), and partial sampling to reduce iterations. Together, these cut the energy overhead from over 6× to practical levels for battery-powered implants.
isscc-2025-123.key_novelty: Using parallel analog circuits for random-number generation and in-memory math, plus sampling shortcuts, makes Bayesian neural networks practical for battery-powered heart devices.

isscc-2025-125.method: The 161nW detector combines two techniques to minimize power use. First, information-aware compression removes unnecessary audio data, keeping only features relevant to detecting speech. Second, spiking neural networks—brain-inspired processors using electrical pulses—identify patterns in how audio changes over time and frequency. This produces far fewer pulses than level-crossing coding methods, reducing power consumption.
isscc-2025-125.key_novelty: Combining information-aware compression (filtering to keep only speech-relevant features) with spiking neural networks (brain-inspired processors that communicate through electrical pulses) achieves 161nW voice detection that works reliably at 0-5dB signal-to-noise ratio.

isscc-2025-131.method: The design puts amplification directly into the sampling stage using a bootstrapped sampler—a circuit that automatically lowers its resistance when needed to reduce current draw. This cuts settling time (the delay for signals to reach their final stable value) and power wasted in resistors and capacitors. The resulting 12.2µW discrete-time zoom PPD delta-sigma modulator achieves 99.6dB SNDR and 184.8dB FOM.
isscc-2025-131.key_novelty: By embedding amplification into the sampling stage via a bootstrapped design, the circuit cuts power waste at the input stage of high-resolution discrete-time delta-sigma modulators.

isscc-2025-132.method: The power amplifier combines two techniques: series-load conducting Gallium Nitride (SLCG), which efficiently uses the GaN semiconductor's properties, and Doherty-Continuum architecture, which automatically engages different amplification stages depending on the output power needed. This combination maintains efficiency above 38% across 1.35–7.6 GHz, even at partial power levels (back-off conditions) where conventional amplifiers waste significant energy.
isscc-2025-132.key_novelty: Combining SLCG and Doherty-Continuum architectures achieves over 38% efficiency at 6dB back-off across 1.35–7.6 GHz.

isscc-2025-128.method: Typically, engineers design the PLL (phase-locked loop—a circuit that locks to a reference frequency) and XO (crystal oscillator—the reference clock source) separately, leading to inefficiencies. This approach co-designs both, using a self-aligned pulse-injection driver (a component that automatically synchronizes them without manual adjustment) to coordinate their interaction. The result is 4.6GHz operation with 63.3fs integrated jitter (timing uncertainty summed across all frequencies) and a -255.2dB figure-of-merit—a combined score of power consumption and timing noise across the entire system.
isscc-2025-128.key_novelty: Using a self-aligned pulse-injection driver to co-design (jointly optimize) the PLL and crystal oscillator as one system, rather than optimizing them separately.

isscc-2025-138.method: The team designed a standardized chip-to-chip data link following the UCIe standard (a universal format for connecting modular computer chips), capable of transferring 4 to 16 billion bits per second through each connection pin. They implemented this using 3nm FinFET transistors—extremely small, efficient transistors—and packaged the design using 2.5D CoWoS-S technology, which arranges and connects chips on a substrate. The result achieves 5.27 terabits per second of bandwidth density and consumes only 0.29 picojoules of energy per bit transmitted.
isscc-2025-138.key_novelty: This work proves for the first time that standardized chip-to-chip links (UCIe) using 2.5D CoWoS packaging can match or exceed the efficiency and bandwidth of custom proprietary designs.

isscc-2025-133.method: The receiver uses cascaded allpass filters (circuits that pass all frequencies but shift their phase response differently)—starting with a low-noise first-order filter in the RF canceller stage for flat frequency response, followed by a second-order filter using delay-peaking (a phase adjustment technique) to extend the cancellation bandwidth. These stages are combined with multi-domain Hilbert-transform-equalization, which applies phase-shifting operations across multiple frequency domains to cancel self-interference—the unwanted signal from the transmitter leaking into the receiver. The system achieves 65 decibels of self-interference cancellation across 120 megahertz of bandwidth, with the RF delay varying by less than 10%.
isscc-2025-133.key_novelty: The approach combines multiple allpass filter stages with Hilbert-transform equalization—a technique that uses phase adjustment across multiple frequency domains to cancel interference—achieving wideband self-interference cancellation without the noise and power drawbacks of traditional high-Q filters.

isscc-2025-136.method: Each battery cell gets its own small monitoring chip (CM) that talks wirelessly to a central control unit (system hub, or SH) using serial communication—meaning data travels one bit at a time without physical wires. The chips measure each cell's voltage and charge state, then can rebalance charge across cells when needed. The wireless network adapts dynamically to reliably connect up to 216 monitoring chips to a single hub, eliminating the physical wiring normally required for large battery packs.
isscc-2025-136.key_novelty: Wireless (contactless) serial communication for per-cell monitoring eliminates wiring while supporting the same monitoring chip design across different battery pack sizes.

isscc-2025-130.method: The processor is built on 28-nanometer technology and can be reconfigured to run three encryption schemes (BGV, BFV, CKKS) that allow computation directly on encrypted data—a property called homomorphic encryption. It optimizes circuits for both the client side (requesting encrypted computation) and server side (performing computation on encrypted data). The design reduces overhead from expensive operations like NTT transforms (mathematical operations essential to these encryption schemes) and polynomial automorphisms (rearrangements of encrypted values), and optimizes how data moves within the chip to reduce memory bottlenecks.
isscc-2025-130.key_novelty: First chip supporting reconfigurable encryption schemes for computation on encrypted data across both client and server roles.

isscc-2025-135.method: The transmitter uses multiphase subharmonic switching—combining multiple time-delayed versions of a reference oscillator to distribute the transmit signal power across many paths. It has three main components: a phase-shifted subharmonic divider (a circuit that creates a lower-frequency reference and rotates the signal timing to suppress unwanted frequency spikes called spurs), a phase-interpolator multiplexer that selects between different phase-shifted versions, and a dual-rate digital-to-analog converter with noise shaping (which directs unwanted noise into frequency bands where it causes less harm). This design enables 3.2Gb/s data transmission at 24GHz while maintaining efficiency across peak and reduced-power operation.
isscc-2025-135.key_novelty: Multiphase subharmonic switching overcomes two key limitations of prior transmitters: it eliminates the 3dB power loss inherent to two-path (IQ) signal combining by splitting across multiple paths, and it suppresses spurs (unwanted frequency spikes) using phase-shifted subharmonic dividers, maintaining efficiency across peak and reduced-power operation.

isscc-2025-141.method: T-REX reduces external memory access—the main power drain in transformer chips—by keeping more data on the chip and reorganizing the memory hierarchy. It also keeps processing units busier through smarter scheduling of computation and data movement. This achieves 68–567 microseconds latency and 0.41–3.95 microjoules per token, depending on model size and batch size.
isscc-2025-141.key_novelty: T-REX demonstrates that improving external memory efficiency can deliver bigger performance gains than the traditional focus on speeding up on-chip computation.

isscc-2025-139.method: They built a microscopic probe using micromachining techniques and integrated it with a radio-frequency (RF) sense amplifier built directly into the probe. The probe is designed with high electrical impedance (drawing minimal current from the signal), which prevents capacitive and inductive loading—the unwanted electrical interference that normally distorts measurements at tiny interfaces. The integrated amplifier captures low-noise signals from DC to 50GHz without requiring external 50Ω test equipment.
isscc-2025-139.key_novelty: By putting the RF sense amplifier directly onto the micromachined probe instead of using external 50Ω test equipment, they eliminate the loading effects that distort measurements, enabling non-disruptive high-impedance probing at microsystem interfaces.

isscc-2025-140.method: The analog front-end (AFE) chip applies two signal-shaping techniques to the driving signal: sine2 waveform shaping (which smooths the signal to reduce sharp edges) and pipelined dual-frequency modulation (which drives at two interleaved frequencies instead of one). These techniques prevent the 200-500kHz driving signal from producing excessive electromagnetic radiation (EMI) in the form of unwanted harmonics. By shaping the signal before transmission rather than filtering afterward, the design avoids the computational overhead of FFT-based filtering, saving chip area and power while maintaining signal quality and touch-detection speed.
isscc-2025-140.key_novelty: Combining sine2 waveform shaping with pipelined dual-frequency modulation reduces electromagnetic radiation enough to meet CISPR 25 standards without FFT-based filtering, saving the chip area and power overhead of previous methods.

isscc-2025-134.method: The system packs 16 organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs—devices that detect biomarkers by responding to chemical binding) onto a millimeter-sized chip and sends measurements wirelessly, replacing older three-electrode and ion-selective field-effect transistor designs that could only handle one or two channels. The circuit interface between each OECT and the measurement system is optimized to manage the high idle current these transistors demand.
isscc-2025-134.key_novelty: A millimeter-sized wireless chip integrates 16 organic electrochemical transistors (devices that detect biomarkers by changing electrical conductivity) to achieve 0.1 picomolar sensitivity—the ability to measure 0.1 trillionths of a mole per liter.

isscc-2025-144.method: The transmitter converts digital baseband signals directly to radio frequency using eight separate phases arranged at different time offsets. To prevent timing errors during this rapid switching, the system dynamically retimes when gates activate and uses a glitch-free phase-mapper to ensure smooth transitions between phases without unwanted signal spikes. The output stage uses custom low-threshold LDMOS transistors—a semiconductor type that conducts more easily at lower voltages—arranged into banks where each transistor is subdivided into fine segments (in-finger gate segmentation) for precise power control. All the orchestration logic is integrated densely on the same chip through flip-chip DTX controller integration.
isscc-2025-144.key_novelty: This is the first all-digital transmitter to achieve the 20W power levels and wideband modulation needed for base-station multiple-antenna systems, using dynamic retiming and glitch-free phase mapping to enable practical all-digital transmission at scale.

isscc-2025-149.method: The design combines two sensors measuring temperature and power supply voltage (the electricity level flowing into the chip) through sensor fusion, a technique where multiple measurements are merged to improve accuracy. Built into a 65nm CMOS chip, it achieves temperature accuracy of ±2.4°C and voltage accuracy of ±9mV (measured at ±3σ, a statistical confidence level) without external calibration. The sensors maintain accuracy even when power supply voltage varies across different regions of the chip or electrical noise interferes with measurements.
isscc-2025-149.key_novelty: A single on-chip device that simultaneously measures temperature and power supply voltage via sensor fusion, eliminating the need for external calibration.

isscc-2025-145.method: The sensor works by stacking two components: thin membranes (Membrane-type Surface-stress Sensors, or MSS) on top that bend when exposed to different gases, sitting directly on standard chip electronics (CMOS) below that measure and process these physical deformations into electrical signals. By stacking the components instead of wiring them together, the design eliminates the bulky connections and packaging, shrinking to just 3.5×3.5mm2. The 16-channel architecture allows simultaneous detection of multiple gases, consuming only 1.47 milliwatts per channel.
isscc-2025-145.key_novelty: The core idea is stacking gas-sensing membranes (MSS) on top of standard chip electronics (CMOS) to detect multiple gases simultaneously across 16 channels at 1.47mW per channel on a 3.5×3.5mm2 chip.

isscc-2025-137.method: The design uses an RC oscillator (a timing circuit made from resistors and capacitors) built using 3nm FinFET technology (advanced transistor design). It generates a stable 100MHz clock through self-calibration, which means the circuit automatically adjusts itself to maintain accuracy. It also includes a glitch-detection circuit that identifies when attackers attempt fault injection—deliberately disrupting the clock to break security.
isscc-2025-137.key_novelty: This is the first RC oscillator providing both stable on-chip clock generation and integrated clock-glitch detection in a single chip, enabling boot-up independence and real-time attack monitoring.

isscc-2025-152.method: Instead of reading all pixels simultaneously at fixed intervals, this sensor reads pixels only when they detect changes—an event-driven strategy. Each pixel independently measures time-of-flight (the time for light to bounce back from an object) and automatically adjusts its detection threshold based on the local light level, avoiding the bulky on-chip histogramming circuits that constrain other designs. By filtering data directly on the chip and adapting to scene lighting, the sensor achieves variable frame rates between 5 and 250 frames per second.
isscc-2025-152.key_novelty: Each pixel independently adapts its detection threshold to ambient light conditions, enabling asynchronous, variable-frame-rate 3D imaging (5–250fps).

isscc-2025-147.method: The circuit uses a 60GHz local oscillator based on single-sideband mixer technology (using only half the frequency spectrum) combined with an integrated LC filter (made of inductors and capacitors). It achieves sub-nanosecond frequency switching (less than a billionth of a second) through a rapid frequency-hopping architecture that quickly jumps between frequencies. I/Q calibration—a technique that balances the two perpendicular components of the radio signal—suppresses spurious tones to -56dBc (56 decibels below the main signal).
isscc-2025-147.key_novelty: This design combines single-sideband mixer technology, integrated LC filtering, and I/Q calibration to create a 60GHz oscillator that achieves both sub-nanosecond frequency switching and -56dBc spurious suppression—two performance goals that traditional radio oscillators struggle to meet together.

isscc-2025-146.method: The system transfers 50 watts of power wirelessly using the Qi standard. To communicate between transmitter and receiver, it uses ASK modulation—a technique where the signal's strength is varied to encode information—but with modifications that reduce the vibrations this normally causes in the receiver's coil. The receiver decodes these signals using a hybrid method: simultaneously measuring both voltage (electrical potential) and current (electrical flow) to reliably extract the transmitted information. This approach achieves 98% power transfer efficiency while eliminating acoustic noise.
isscc-2025-146.key_novelty: The innovation combines a noise-reducing signal technique in the transmitter with simultaneous voltage-and-current measurement in the receiver, enabling 50W Qi wireless charging at 98% efficiency without receiver coil vibration.

isscc-2025-151.method: The circuit converts measured capacitance into a phase shift using a resistor-capacitor filter that passes low frequencies, then digitizes this phase shift using a phase-domain delta-sigma modulator—a type of analog-to-digital converter that repeatedly samples and integrates differences to achieve high precision. The filtering in the front-end and modulator together eliminate common-mode noise (signals that appear equally on both measurement paths) by 119dB at low frequencies and 97dB at 100MHz. This enables measurement of capacitances from 35.2aF to 500pF within a 143dB dynamic range without requiring manual range switching.
isscc-2025-151.key_novelty: A phase-domain delta-sigma architecture achieves simultaneously high dynamic range (143dB, measuring from 35.2aF to 500pF), dual-band noise rejection (119dB at DC and 97dB at 100MHz), and elimination of sub-ranging complexity.

isscc-2025-143.method: The sensor uses voltage-biasing (applying a fixed voltage across the sensor rather than driving current through it) instead of the traditional current-biased approach, with a circuit designed to minimize measurement errors. Two sensing elements output their signals as currents rather than voltages, which allows them to be easily subtracted from each other to cancel fixed systematic errors (offset) and reduce noise. The design is built in standard 0.18-micrometer CMOS technology.
isscc-2025-143.key_novelty: This voltage-biased architecture achieves 3 times lower offset error (1.0 microTesla) and 5 times lower noise (60 nanoTesla per root-hertz) than current-biased sensors, demonstrating that this architectural change substantially improves precision magnetic field measurement.

isscc-2025-142.method: The chip uses four-level signal encoding (PAM-4) to transmit data at 212.5 billion bits per second while compensating for signal degradation from cables and connectors. Built in 5-nanometer transistor technology, it includes specialized analog electronics that restore weakened signals, handling over 46 decibels of loss. This signal restoration happens efficiently, consuming only 2.2 picojoules of energy per bit transmitted.
isscc-2025-142.key_novelty: This transceiver achieves long-reach performance (>46dB loss compensation) and low power consumption (2.2pJ/b) at 212.5Gb/s simultaneously, making dense 200-gigabit-per-lane data center interconnects practical.

isscc-2025-150.method: The converter uses a symmetrical multi-core design with an embedded transformer to suppress common-mode current (electrical noise that leaks through the transformer's internal capacitance). A high-speed switching converter using pulse-width modulation (PWM—rapid on-off switching at tens of MHz) regulated by a slower feedback loop (~1 MHz) manages the voltage conversion while the transformer architecture actively reduces electromagnetic noise and output ripple. The result is less than 5mV output ripple and CISPR-32 Class-B electromagnetic compliance without external filters.
isscc-2025-150.key_novelty: A multi-core isolated converter with an embedded magnetic transformer achieves electromagnetic noise suppression and efficiency in a single integrated chip.

isscc-2025-154.method: Instead of receiving power as voltage (the standard approach), the system receives power directly as current from the wireless coil, which maintains high efficiency even when the electrical resistance between electrode and tissue (electrode-tissue impedance) changes—no separate voltage regulation needed. A feedback loop continuously monitors the current flowing into the tissue and adjusts it to stay constant, ensuring precise delivery of charge regardless of how this resistance varies. This design works with different electrode sizes because it can maintain steady output current while tolerating high voltages.
isscc-2025-154.key_novelty: The core innovation combines current-mode power reception (receiving wireless power as current instead of voltage) with built-in feedback control of the stimulus current, enabling high power efficiency and precise charge delivery across varying electrode-tissue impedances without requiring impedance-sensing or adaptive tuning.

isscc-2025-148.method: This chip drives each pixel's brightness using a 10-bit signal (1024 brightness levels) on OLED-on-Silicon displays. It automatically corrects voltage drift in each pixel column and uses an amplifier designed for fast voltage switching. The design achieves an extremely compact footprint—2273pm² of silicon per pixel column—with voltage errors down to 1.9 millivolts, enabling ultra-high-resolution (6285-PPI) AR/VR displays.
isscc-2025-148.key_novelty: Automatic per-channel voltage calibration—without external manual trimming—packed into a 2273pm² footprint, enabling ultra-high-resolution (6285 PPI) OLED-on-Silicon displays.

isscc-2025-159.method: It's a single-chip device made from gallium nitride (GaN) that delivers power to 5G base-station transmitters by splitting the job into two stages: voltage generation, which slowly produces multiple voltage levels efficiently, and tracking, which quickly adjusts the output voltage to match what the transmitter needs at any moment. Using multiple voltage levels instead of just two reduces energy waste and electrical noise compared to simpler binary designs. The device handles up to 48 volts and delivers 74 watts of power, achieving high efficiency and good heat management on a single integrated chip.
isscc-2025-159.key_novelty: A single-chip GaN device that powers 5G base-station transmitters by separating slow, efficient voltage generation from fast voltage tracking using multiple voltage levels.

isscc-2025-161.method: The phase shifter uses outphasing, a technique that splits the signal into two constant-amplitude paths—this allows the device to handle amplitude and phase changes without wasting power in traditional amplifiers. Built-in gain and phase adjustments compensate for manufacturing variations and temperature changes. The design uses SiGe BiCMOS (a silicon-germanium process combining bipolar and CMOS transistors), which can operate reliably at 125–170GHz while keeping multiple components on a single chip.
isscc-2025-161.key_novelty: This design combines outphasing (splitting the signal into two constant-amplitude paths) with automatic gain and phase adjustments to efficiently shift signals at sub-THz frequencies from 125–170GHz.

isscc-2025-155.method: This 3D-NAND design bonds wafers together at the manufacturing level (WF-bonding) and structures voltage signals through stacked layers to prevent interference. It removes or optimizes dummy holes (non-data structural spaces) that would consume power, redesigns cell packing to reduce wear from unavoidable stray voltages on inactive cells, and maintains clean signal patterns on high-speed data pins (5.6 gigabits per second per pin) with sufficient electrical margin. The result: 28 gigabits per square millimeter of density, with 3 bits per memory cell.
isscc-2025-155.key_novelty: The core idea is combining wafer-level bonding (bonding whole wafers of memory together), optimized voltage-signal routing through stacked layers, and careful electrical signal management on high-speed data pins to let 3D-NAND scale to hundreds of layers while staying fast and reliable.

isscc-2025-160.method: Conventional SRAM designs force the entire chip to operate at the voltage the memory cells need, even if logic around it could run lower and save power. This design decouples that using Interface Dual-Rail (IDR): the SRAM interface runs at ultra-low voltage (380mV minimum—the lowest reported for this memory type), while internal cells stay at their required higher voltage. An extended-range level shifter (a converter with built-in latches) and a bypass path on the clock signal handle the voltage conversion with minimal overhead. The chip's main logic can now operate independently of memory voltage needs, achieving 38 megabits per square millimeter density—the highest reported for single-port SRAM.
isscc-2025-160.key_novelty: Decoupling SRAM interface voltage from internal cell voltage using an extended-range level shifter to enable 380mV ultra-low-voltage operation.

isscc-2025-158.method: A 112Gb/s receiver uses an LC-resonator CTLE (continuous-time linear equalizer: a circuit using inductors and capacitors to compensate for signal loss over long channels) combined with a digital signal processor to recover signals weakened by over 52dB of loss. The LC-resonator front-end boosts weakened frequencies without excessive power consumption, while the digital processor performs adaptive equalization and decodes PAM-4 symbols (a 4-level encoding that packs more data per signal pulse). Built in 4nm FinFET (advanced transistor manufacturing process), the design minimizes latency through analog path optimization and achieves the energy efficiency needed for data-center interconnect deployment.
isscc-2025-158.key_novelty: The core innovation is using an LC-resonator (inductor-capacitor circuit) for the CTLE to achieve over 52dB of channel loss compensation in a DSP-based PAM-4 receiver while maintaining energy efficiency.

isscc-2025-153.method: The system uses a receiver circuit made of a capacitor and inductor (an LC tank) with switchable resistance. By switching this resistance, it implements link-load isolation—reducing the load that the power transfer link must drive, which decreases the critical coupling coefficient (the minimum magnetic connection needed between coils). The system operates at two frequencies (f_H and f_L) using frequency-shift keying (data encoding by switching between frequencies) to transmit both power and data, with efficiency remaining flat across this frequency range, enabling receiver coils smaller than a centimeter.
isscc-2025-153.key_novelty: The key innovation is a switchable receiver circuit that dynamically isolates power transfer from data transmission, achieving a 10-fold reduction in receiver coil size while preserving the efficiency of frequency-splitting wireless power transfer.

isscc-2025-156.method: The chip includes two specialized tensor engines: one optimized for language models that need to continuously read large weights from memory, another for vision models that require intensive matrix calculations. A multi-level memory system with on-chip storage and DRAM tiling efficiently caches weights to reduce repeated memory fetches. Fan-out wafer-level packaging improves heat dissipation for sustained high performance. Built at 4nm in Samsung's Exynos 2400, it supports traditional image processing (CNNs), language models (LLMs), and image generation models.
isscc-2025-156.key_novelty: Two specialized tensor engines on a mobile chip, each optimized for different AI workloads: one for language models that need fast memory access, one for vision models that need fast computation.

isscc-2025-157.method: The amplifier uses a ground-isolated circuit that explicitly accounts for interference entering through two paths: parasitic coupling to the body and parasitic coupling to the ground. Instead of ignoring the ground-coupling path (as traditional designs do), this circuit lets the interference split between both paths, which allows it to tolerate extremely large interference signals of 133 volts peak-to-peak. The result is excellent interference rejection with a common-mode rejection ratio of 102dB, achieved at ultra-low power consumption of 4.6 microwatts with a noise efficiency factor of 3.3.
isscc-2025-157.key_novelty: The design accounts for parasitic ground capacitance by splitting interference between body and ground paths, achieving 133V_PP tolerance and 102dB common-mode rejection ratio at 4.6μW.

isscc-2025-169.method: This paper identifies the semiconductor components and system designs required to transform vehicles into software-controlled platforms. It describes three essential layers: a central processor that coordinates vehicle functions, remote software updates delivered over networks, and local processors at key vehicle systems that make rapid decisions. The paper maps what new semiconductor capabilities and architectural choices are needed at each layer, and why current technologies fall short.
isscc-2025-169.key_novelty: Semiconductors are not just components in software-defined vehicles—they are the foundational technology that makes such vehicles possible.

isscc-2025-171.method: The system uses injection-locking (locking one oscillator to match another's frequency) to build a quadrature-clock generator operating at 2-5GHz. Instead of sending four pre-made clocks across long distances (which causes timing errors), it sends a single reference signal (WDQS) to each data group, where a local generator creates all four clocks on-site. This approach filters out timing jitter (unwanted variations in clock edges) through the locking mechanism and can instantly switch between clock phases when needed.
isscc-2025-171.key_novelty: The injection-locking approach with instant-toggling eliminates the need for separate circuits to fix quadrature errors, instead handling jitter filtering, error correction, and power savings in a single design.

isscc-2025-163.method: This millimeter-wave converter operates from 21 to 31 GHz and maintains linear signal output without software correction by using two design techniques. First, it keeps the output impedance constant regardless of the input signal, preventing impedance variations from distorting the signal. Second, it automatically suppresses the local oscillator signal (the reference frequency) from leaking into the output, adapting to temperature and voltage variations without requiring feedback loops.
isscc-2025-163.key_novelty: A millimeter-wave converter that delivers natural linearity from 21 to 31 GHz through constant output impedance and adaptive local oscillator leakage suppression, eliminating the need for digital signal correction.

isscc-2025-166.method: The platform uses densely packed tactile sensors (many touch sensors positioned close together) to capture fine-grained pressure and touch patterns. These sensor signals are processed by neuromorphic encoding circuits—circuits that work like the brain's nervous system, converting raw sensor data into neural-like signals. A neuromodulator component adjusts these signals in real time based on feedback. Since sensing and signal processing both happen together in one integrated system, it can be embedded directly into prosthetics, wearables, or implanted devices without needing external computation.
isscc-2025-166.key_novelty: The key innovation combines dense touch sensors with neuromorphic encoding (brain-mimicking signal processing) and integrated neuromodulation to enable prosthetics and wearables to locally sense and interpret tactile feedback.

isscc-2025-162.method: The design pairs three memory tiers—on-chip SRAM (fastest, smallest), on-package HBM (fast and large), and off-package DRAM (largest but slower)—with a reconfigurable dataflow unit that rearranges computations to match where data sits. Two identical processor dies (each 600mm² in size, built at 5nm) are vertically stacked with a connector layer between them (called an interposer), with each die containing 102 billion transistors and delivering 640 BF16 TFLOPs. The dies share memory bandwidth through a direct peer-to-peer connection, avoiding the memory bandwidth bottleneck that prevents single-die accelerators from handling trillion-parameter models.
isscc-2025-162.key_novelty: The design uses two processor dies vertically stacked together with three tiers of memory, giving trillion-parameter AI models the bandwidth they need from fast memory layers and the total storage from slower capacity layers, all within acceptable thermal and size limits.

isscc-2025-170.method: The chip measures the charge state of multiple spin qubits simultaneously using a single radio-frequency carrier wave, with QAM multiplexing (encoding different signals by varying the wave's amplitude and phase) allowing each qubit's signal to be distinguished on the same frequency. This approach shares the RF generation and amplification resources across multiple qubits, reducing per-qubit power consumption compared to designs that need a separate carrier for each qubit. Instead of the bulky inductors (coils) that earlier readout designs used, this circuit achieves amplification through a capacitive-feedback architecture (which couples signals through a capacitor), saving chip area and power; the result is 18.5 microwatts per qubit operating in CMOS at cryogenic temperatures.
isscc-2025-170.key_novelty: This design enables reading multiple spin qubits using a single radio-frequency carrier with QAM multiplexing (varying amplitude and phase), instead of requiring one carrier per qubit like earlier on-off-keying schemes.

isscc-2025-164.method: The accelerator tackles all three challenges with three core techniques. First, it stores model weights in compressed form (using fewer bits) and performs matrix multiplication directly on these compressed weights combined with normal-precision activations—avoiding the expensive decompression that typically wastes 4.6x extra power. Second, it organizes the compressed weights into aligned data clusters so that data moves efficiently and processing happens in uniform chunks. Third, it decouples the processing timeline so matrix operations and special functions (softmax, trigonometry) run on separate independent paths simultaneously, allowing processors to keep working instead of idling while waiting for non-linear operations to finish.
isscc-2025-164.key_novelty: The key innovation combines matrix operations on aligned bit-compressed weights using mixed-precision (integer and floating-point) arithmetic with parallel independent execution of special functions, to eliminate processor stalls in language model inference.

isscc-2025-167.method: The approach redesigns chips and system power management so robots can run large AI models directly on their hardware. It achieves this by integrating the AI tightly with sensors and motors—so sensor data flows immediately to the AI, which produces motor commands in real time—and by powering down unused components at each moment instead of running everything constantly.
isscc-2025-167.key_novelty: Designing hardware so robots can run large generative AI models directly with integrated sensor-motor control, solving the energy-efficiency problem that prevents edge deployment.

isscc-2025-165.method: A two-stage system supplies 12A at sub-1 volt output voltages. First, an intermediate bus converter (a voltage-stepping device) efficiently converts 12V to an intermediate voltage. Second, a switched-capacitor converter at the chip (using capacitor-based circuits with controlled natural-frequency oscillations instead of inductors) delivers the final voltage with 89.3% peak efficiency and voltage drops of just 26 millivolts during power demand spikes.
isscc-2025-165.key_novelty: The innovation combines regulated resonant switched-capacitor power conversion (capacitor-based circuits with controlled natural-frequency oscillations) at the chip's power input, achieving both high efficiency and rapid response to sudden power demand changes—capabilities that typically require design trade-offs.

isscc-2025-175.method: The chip uses 16 parallel SAR ADC channels (successive approximation converters that build up each measurement bit by bit) working in interleaved time slices to reach 12 billion samples per second. It's manufactured in 16nm FinFET technology (a modern process that densely packs transistors), and instead of requiring custom voltage levels, it runs on just two standard supplies—1.8V and 0.8V—which simplifies integration into larger systems while keeping the circuit small and power-efficient.
isscc-2025-175.key_novelty: The key innovation is using standard power supply voltages from the chip's manufacturing process rather than custom ones, which simplifies integration into larger transceiver systems while maintaining a 48.1dB SNDR (signal-to-noise and distortion ratio).

isscc-2025-172.method: The chip includes two integrated transceivers (receiver-transmitter pairs) for impulse radio ultra-wideband (IR-UWB)—a communication technique using short radio pulses across a wide frequency range—supporting channels 5 through 12 to operate in the crowded 6GHz spectrum without interfering with each other. Both transceivers share transmit and receive antennas through integrated RF switches (electronic gates that route signals), designed to minimize insertion loss—the weakening of signal strength as it passes through. By keeping insertion loss low, the receivers maintain their sensitivity despite signal routing, and the entire system is built as a single integrated circuit using CMOS technology in compliance with IEEE 802.15.4/4z standards.
isscc-2025-172.key_novelty: The core innovation is designing integrated RF switches that reduce both insertion loss and noise figure degradation compared to prior CMOS designs, enabling two transceivers to reliably share antennas without sacrificing receiver sensitivity.

isscc-2025-173.method: The paper maps enabling technologies across four interconnected areas: chip design and manufacturing, multi-chip packaging with thermal management, system architecture, and software/networking. By treating these areas as one system rather than separate domains, it shows which combinations of advances in each area work together to support AI systems that scale from small edge devices to massive cloud computers.
isscc-2025-173.key_novelty: The key idea is that AI system scaling requires coordinating improvements across silicon, packaging, architecture, and software together, not optimizing each separately.

isscc-2025-174.method: The circuit matches voltage to each transmitted signal pulse (symbol-by-symbol power tracking) rather than only adjusting between longer time blocks. It uses a split capacitor—a capacitor divided into sections that can be charged independently—with a direct switching converter to rapidly transition between voltage levels in just 102 nanoseconds per volt. This speed fits within the 1.17-microsecond cyclic prefix (guard interval between 5G symbols) while achieving 94.3% efficiency, with 94.3% of input power reaching the amplifier rather than being wasted as heat.
isscc-2025-174.key_novelty: A pre-charged split-capacitor architecture enables sub-microsecond voltage transitions for 5G symbol-level power tracking.

isscc-2025-176.method: The transmitter uses a free-running LC oscillator (an electronic circuit that generates oscillations without needing a crystal reference) rather than complex circuits that require crystals. Because LC oscillators naturally drift in frequency and produce noise, a neural network learns to automatically adjust both how the data shapes the signal (modulation) and how the data is encoded (coding) in response, compensating for these imperfections and maintaining signal strength. By optimizing modulation and coding together as a single problem instead of separately, the system finds better compensation strategies than conventional approaches.
isscc-2025-176.key_novelty: The core idea is that a neural network can jointly compensate for oscillator drift and noise by adjusting modulation (how data shapes the signal) and coding (how data is encoded), eliminating the need for a crystal reference and its cost and power overhead.

isscc-2025-168.method: The chip uses standard semiconductor manufacturing (CMOS) to pack 4096 sensors on a single piece of silicon. Each sensor is coated with a metal-organic framework—a porous molecular material that selectively absorbs specific gases. Built into each sensor is a heating element that can rapidly warm the coating and force absorbed gases to escape (desorb), regenerating the sensor for the next measurement. The chip also includes readout and digitization circuits right at each sensor to process the detection signal.
isscc-2025-168.key_novelty: Temperature-controlled heaters built into each sensor rapidly force absorbed gases to escape (desorb), enabling fast sensor regeneration.

isscc-2025-179.method: The sensor consists of three layers stacked vertically, with the top layer containing tightly-spaced pixels (1.2 micrometers apart) that read out one row at a time for high resolution (50 megapixels), while a middle layer holds larger pixels (2.4 micrometers apart) that capture all at once to eliminate flicker (12.5 megapixels). A hybrid shutter design lets the sensor switch between these two capture modes depending on whether you need maximum resolution or flicker-free images. Advanced stacking techniques keep all layers thin enough to fit within a single package.
isscc-2025-179.key_novelty: A single sensor with switchable modes can operate in high-resolution rolling-shutter (50 megapixels, 1.2-micrometer pixel pitch) or global-shutter (12.5 megapixels, 2.4-micrometer pixel pitch) on demand, instead of forcing a choice between dense pixels and flicker-free capture.

isscc-2025-180.method: The approach uses a reusable base chip design called a via-programmable neuron array (VPNA), where vias (the metal connections between circuit elements) can be selectively placed in different patterns to configure different neural-network layers without needing new photomasks (production templates). To make this work efficiently, it combines two techniques: (1) a Bit- and Neuron-Serial Circuit (BNSC) that reduces the wiring area by 1/1024, and (2) Sparse Binary Neural Networks (FS-NNN) that compress the neural network to fit on fewer VPNA tiles.
isscc-2025-180.key_novelty: A single-mask design can be customized for different neural networks by changing only the via placement (the metal routing connections within the chip), reducing the cost per customization to 1/40th of what it would be with separate masks for each design.

isscc-2025-184.method: Memory companies have developed multiple technologies—some that increase speed, others that pack more data per chip (denser storage), and still others that use less power—to solve a core problem: AI chips compute faster than memory can deliver data to them (the 'memory wall'). Rather than seeking one perfect solution, companies are gradually integrating these different technologies into products. Each approach helps close the gap between computing speed and data delivery speed.
isscc-2025-184.key_novelty: The industry is shifting from trying to make processors faster to prioritizing memory speed and capacity, recognizing memory as AI's real performance bottleneck.

isscc-2025-177.method: This is a fractional-N sampling PLL (a frequency-locking circuit that divides by fractional amounts and measures phase at specific moments) designed to operate at 0.65V. It uses a two-stage converter approach: a coarse digital-to-time converter paired with a fine resistor-based DAC, allowing precise frequency tuning across a wide range. The circuit applies hybrid cascaded digital predistortion—a technique where it inverts the hardware's own distortion patterns in two stages—to cancel out nonlinearity from both the timing converter and the phase detector. The phase detector uses a negative-level-inverter topology, a specialized circuit design that reduces noise specifically at low voltages where power supply headroom is limited.
isscc-2025-177.key_novelty: Combining hybrid cascaded digital predistortion (which cancels hardware distortion to reduce correction overhead and minimize noise folding) with a negative-level-inverter phase detector (designed to operate with minimal voltage headroom) enables the fractional-N sampling PLL to achieve 73.8fs jitter at 0.65V supply voltage.

isscc-2025-183.method: The equalizer uses capacitive feedback—capacitors in a feedback loop—to clean up PAM-4 signals (which encode data using 4 different voltage levels) without adding pipeline delay. When signals travel through a channel, they blur together (inter-symbol interference), but the capacitors sense this distortion and feed it back to compensate in real-time. Implemented in 28nm CMOS, the circuit achieves this compensation at the receiver's input stage, so the signal reaches the decision circuitry already corrected, avoiding the latency that traditional multi-stage equalizers introduce.
isscc-2025-183.key_novelty: Capacitive-feedback equalization without pipeline delay for PAM-4 receivers.

isscc-2025-181.method: This amplifier uses a passive switched-capacitor design—capacitors that rapidly switch on and off to amplify signals—operating in multiple modes to handle signals across a wide dynamic range. By processing signals at discrete time intervals rather than continuously, the circuit naturally resists temperature-induced drift that plagues traditional logarithmic and low-drift amplifiers. The design maintains its logarithmic output characteristics (0.75% conformity error, meaning it stays very close to the ideal logarithmic curve) across extreme temperatures from -25 to 200°C.
isscc-2025-181.key_novelty: The core innovation is achieving precise logarithmic amplification (0.75% conformity error) across -25 to 200°C using a simple passive switched-capacitor design, eliminating the need for manual tuning and temperature-compensation circuits.

isscc-2025-185.method: The device divides the high AC input voltage (85–230V) using a series stack of capacitors—a capacitor-drop topology that protects the internal converter stages. This sigma-floating switched-capacitor architecture uses a three-mode active rectifier (a circuit converting AC to DC with three distinct operating states) to adjust current flow, keeping the output voltage steady at 3.3–4.6V. Compared to earlier two-mode designs, the three-mode approach significantly reduces power wasted during idle periods.
isscc-2025-185.key_novelty: This sigma-floating switched-capacitor architecture delivers regulated output power above 1 watt from AC mains with 81.3% efficiency, outperforming prior passive capacitor-based and hybrid switched-capacitor-linear-regulator designs.

isscc-2025-182.method: Zen 5 packs 8 processor cores into a 55mm² area using TSMC's 4nm FinFET technology (which builds extremely dense transistors). Each core has 1MB of fast memory (L2 cache) while all cores share 32MB of slower shared memory (L3 cache). The design uses adjustable vector processing that can handle either 256-bit or 512-bit data operations to adapt to different computational needs, and improves instruction prediction, code fetching, and memory operations through additional temporary slots (rename registers) and faster address translation (TLB). A Zen 5c variant prioritizes power efficiency and density for mobile and embedded devices.
isscc-2025-182.key_novelty: The core innovation is configurable vector processing that switches between 256-bit (FP256) and 512-bit (FP512) modes to balance speed and power consumption based on what type of program is running.

isscc-2025-178.method: The sensor uses a wire-metal resistor as the temperature-sensing element—as temperature changes, the resistor's resistance changes in a predictable way. A fractional-discharge FLL converts these resistance changes into changes in timing signals (by precisely controlling how long it takes to discharge a capacitor). These timing changes are then amplified by a time-domain amplifier, which detects delays instead of voltage swings, making small temperature changes measurable. This approach eliminates active biasing requirements, since passive resistors don't need the careful voltage and current control that transistor-based sensors require.
isscc-2025-178.key_novelty: The key innovation is using time-domain amplification (measuring timing differences instead of voltages) combined with a fractional-discharge frequency-locking circuit and passive resistors, which achieves high accuracy without the active transistor biasing that traditional sensors require.
