isscc-2025-186.method: IRIS compresses the 3D Gaussian parameters using Single-Embedding-Multi-MLP (a single compact data representation fed to multiple small neural networks), reducing the over 50MB of data while maintaining visual quality. It features custom processor circuits specifically designed for surface-aware 3D modeling and interactive photorealistic rendering, keeping data in the fast on-chip cache (4MB) instead of requiring slow external memory access, and reuses hardware components during backpropagation (the computationally expensive training step that consumed 55.8% of the work in older approaches). Scheduling and memory orchestration keep all processing within the 15-millisecond latency budget required for real-time interaction.
isscc-2025-186.key_novelty: IRIS is the first processor chip built specifically for real-time mixed-reality rendering using 3D Gaussian Splatting, achieving 8.55 millijoules per frame through neural-network data compression and hardware that jointly optimizes surface modeling, rendering, and training.

isscc-2025-197.method: HOOP arranges multiple hybrid DC-DC converters (each using multiple power stages) in a ring topology—connecting them in a closed loop. Within this ring, a power path circulates electricity to naturally spread the current load evenly across all converters, while a separate control path allows individual stages to be switched off when unneeded. This works because capacitors (energy-storage components) inherently share electrical charge when connected together, a principle that simple single-stage converters rely on, but here it extends across multiple parallel converters connected via the ring.
isscc-2025-197.key_novelty: Connecting hybrid converters in a ring topology allows them to automatically balance current without a separate digital controller.

isscc-2025-188.method: The radio chip, built in 28nm CMOS technology, uses two integrated filtering strategies to eliminate the need for external components: a harmonic-rejection transmitter that prevents generating duplicate frequencies (harmonics), and a spur-avoidance receiver that prevents generating unwanted signals (spurs). The receiver's amplifier, mixer, and signal-conditioning stages are combined on one chip with tunable circuits that support multiple frequency bands. This design supports LTE Cat1bis wireless protocols while minimizing external parts and die area.
isscc-2025-188.key_novelty: A single radio chip integrates harmonic-rejection in the transmitter (preventing duplicate frequencies) and spur-avoidance in the receiver (preventing unwanted signals), eliminating external filters and reducing component count and die area for cost-sensitive IoT devices.

isscc-2025-196.method: The circuit uses two feedback loops working together: a delay-locked loop (a timing-synchronization circuit that creates eight aligned clock phases from a single input) and a ring oscillator (an oscillator made from chained inverters that pulse back and forth) that locks onto these phases and reinforces them. The ring oscillator's internal feedback simultaneously reduces jitter (small unwanted timing variations) and phase error (misalignment between intended and actual clock timing) across the wide 8–28GHz frequency range. This dual-feedback approach achieves the low jitter and accurate timing needed for high-speed data transmission without requiring the expensive divider circuits that traditional phase-locked loops need.
isscc-2025-196.key_novelty: The core innovation combines a delay-locked loop with a ring oscillator's self-regulating feedback to achieve both low timing error and low jitter across 8–28GHz without needing the expensive dividers of traditional phase-locked loops.

isscc-2025-187.method: The design starts with a quasi-class-E Colpitts oscillator—a circuit that generates oscillating signals using capacitors and inductors while minimizing wasted energy—and adds a transformer-based two-port resonance structure (a transformer with two connection points tuned to create strong feedback at specific frequencies). This combination achieves very high-frequency operation across 47.3–58.4GHz while reducing phase noise—unwanted random timing variations in the signal—directly within the circuit through careful waveform shaping. Implemented in 40-nanometer CMOS technology, it achieves phase noise of -124.9 to -119.8dBc/Hz at 10MHz offset.
isscc-2025-187.key_novelty: The core innovation is a transformer-based two-port resonance structure in a quasi-class-E Colpitts oscillator that surpasses previous designs using harmonic extraction (frequency multiples) or coupled oscillators, achieving a figure-of-merit score of 198.8dBc/Hz.

isscc-2025-189.method: The system stacks 20 small chips (chiplets) in layers connected by extremely fast data highways (20Tb/s, meaning 20 trillion bits per second). All chips share 300MB of high-speed memory (SRAM) split across the stack. Before assembly finishes, engineers customize each chip's computing power, memory allotment, and bandwidth based on the AI inference tasks the system will handle. The chips can come from different manufacturers and technology generations, so each can be optimized for its specific job in the overall system.
isscc-2025-189.key_novelty: This reconfigurable 2.5D chiplet system allocates its memory, computing power, and bandwidth differently depending on each AI inference workload.

isscc-2025-198.method: The controller operates at 4K by combining bipolar transistors—which maintain good electrical performance at cryogenic temperatures—with CMOS technology for miniaturization and integration. It uses QCCD (quantum-charge-coupled-device) control to manage two key operations: shuttling trapped ions between different trap regions and entangling qubits for quantum computation.
isscc-2025-198.key_novelty: Integrating bipolar and CMOS circuits that work at cryogenic temperatures with QCCD control architecture unlocks the ability to scale up trapped-ion quantum computers.

isscc-2025-193.method: The power amplifier uses a radial power combiner to merge outputs from multiple transistor cores, arranging them in a circular geometry that reduces parasitic losses compared to linear routing. It employs matched-zone expansion—a technique that maintains constant electrical impedance across combining stages, preventing the efficiency losses that normally occur when scaling to more cores. Electromagnetic optimization and parasitic minimization further reduce losses. The design delivers 30.2dBm output power at 23.5% peak power-added efficiency, measuring how much input power converts to useful output versus waste heat.
isscc-2025-193.key_novelty: A radial power combiner with matched-zone expansion—maintaining constant electrical impedance as you scale up the design—enables high-power, high-efficiency amplifiers at millimeter-wave V-band frequencies without the efficiency loss that has constrained prior designs.

isscc-2025-200.method: The sensor stacks three layers of light-detecting semiconductors into each pixel, with 10-bit memory (SRAM) built into each pixel to store measurements. To capture both bright and dark details in one shot, each pixel independently controls how long it measures light—a technique called per-pixel exposure time control. The chip includes image processing circuits that average frames to reduce noise and correct fixed pattern noise (systematic errors that repeat in every image). It transmits only important pixel data to AI processors, reducing power use.
isscc-2025-200.key_novelty: The core innovation is stacking three semiconductor layers in each pixel with built-in memory (SRAM) and image processing (ISP), achieving a tiny 3.24μm pixel that captures an extremely wide brightness range (117dB dynamic range) in a single photograph.

isscc-2025-195.method: In a pipelined ADC, each stage must amplify the leftover signal (residue) from the previous stage before it can be quantized (converted to digital)—this amplification step becomes the speed bottleneck at high conversion rates. This design makes residue transfer (passing the leftover signal between stages) and quantization happen concurrently (at the same time) by using differential sampling (measuring both a signal and its complement) and a source-follower inter-stage amplifier (a simple, linear, wideband, low-power circuit that replaces the traditional residue amplifier). The chip also uses automatic common-mode-regulated power-gating to shut off unused buffer circuits without adding extra switching overhead.
isscc-2025-195.key_novelty: The core innovation is concurrent residue transfer and quantization, which eliminates the residue amplifier bottleneck using only a simple source-follower circuit for inter-stage gain.

isscc-2025-199.method: The sensor uses an NPN transistor—a type of semiconductor—to generate two currents that change with temperature: one increasing (PTAT, proportional to absolute temperature) and one decreasing (CTAT, complementary to absolute temperature). A continuous-time delta-sigma modulator digitizes the ratio of these currents, converting analog signals to digital form for precise temperature measurement. A current-assisted amplifier strengthens this ratio without adding noise, reducing the energy needed for accurate conversion.
isscc-2025-199.key_novelty: By combining charge-balancing in the delta-sigma modulator (which keeps charge flow stable to reduce noise) with a current-assisted amplifier, the sensor uses 2.5 times less energy than previous designs.

isscc-2025-203.method: The design uses a charge-injection SAR ADC (successive approximation register, a converter that finds the digital output by testing bits one at a time) built from 40nm CMOS transistors operating at cryogenic temperature (6.5K). A charge-injection digital-to-analog converter keeps the input capacitance at just 4 femtofarads by storing charge in microscopic capacitors. At such cold temperatures, kT/C noise (thermal noise that limits precision in normal electronics) becomes negligible, making these tiny capacitors reliable for accurate conversion. It achieves 7-bit resolution at 800 million samples per second with 64.1dB spurious-free dynamic range (the strongest unwanted signal is 64.1dB weaker than the desired signal).
isscc-2025-203.key_novelty: The chip exploits the fact that thermal noise becomes negligible at cryogenic temperature (6.5K) to use a charge-injection DAC that achieves a record-low input capacitance of just 4 femtofarads.

isscc-2025-192.method: The transceiver transmits 200G per lane using two semiconductor technologies on the same chip: an older 0.13µm SiGe (silicon-germanium) analog front-end that conditions the signal directly in analog form, and modern 28nm CMOS digital logic for clock recovery and network functions. Instead of converting the weak incoming signal to digital and cleaning it up with DSP (digital signal processing, which adds processing delay), the analog side directly filters out the -14dB insertion loss from the fiber channel. This non-ADC receiver approach keeps latency near zero while achieving competitive energy efficiency.
isscc-2025-192.key_novelty: A non-ADC receiver design combining 0.13µm SiGe and 28nm CMOS that eliminates DSP delay for 200G/lane transmission by filtering signals directly in analog form, enabling low-latency AI networks.

isscc-2025-204.method: The design uses a standard 6-transistor memory cell built with Intel's new RibbonFET transistors (ultra-thin transistors that wrap around a silicon fin) with adjustable widths to fine-tune performance. Power delivery moves to the back of the chip (PowerVia) instead of routing through the front, reducing power supply noise (voltage droop) that normally forces higher operating voltages. By redesigning the core memory cell and its surrounding circuits together, they fit more memory into the same space while maintaining a low minimum operating voltage, without needing extra circuit assist features.
isscc-2025-204.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining backside power delivery (PowerVia) with RibbonFET transistors to eliminate voltage droop, achieving a record 38.1 megabits per square millimeter of memory density while reducing the minimum operating voltage and eliminating the need for assist circuits.

isscc-2025-190.method: Telum II is a 600mm² chip made with Samsung 5nm technology containing 43 billion transistors, with 8 cores running at 5.5GHz. To handle data-intensive work better, it makes three key changes: it adds a Data Processing Unit (a specialized accelerator for AI and data processing), expands both the fast L2 cache (10 copies of 36MB each, 40% larger than Telum) and the L3 cache (360MB versus 256MB before), and shrinks the processor cores themselves to make room for more cache while improving how they work — better branch prediction, smarter instruction prefetching, more registers to track operations, and faster memory address translation. All of this fits on the same die, and up to 32 chips can be linked together through interconnects to share memory coherently.
isscc-2025-190.key_novelty: The key innovation is combining a Data Processing Unit (hardware for AI acceleration) with expanded cache and improved processor cores to handle both traditional computing and AI workloads on a single chip.

isscc-2025-194.method: Edge detectors in each unit cell identify switching delays, and a slope-to-phase tuner adjusts signal edges in real-time to cancel the resulting phase distortion. Since the self-calibration responds within one modulation period, it can handle signals across a wide frequency range. An asymmetrical 4-to-1 differential power-combining transformer balances impedance and efficiency, and this built-in calibration eliminates the need for separate digital pre-distortion.
isscc-2025-194.key_novelty: Real-time in-cell slope-to-phase self-calibration corrects AM-PM distortion (phase shift changing with signal amplitude) in high-frequency switched-capacitor amplifiers without external digital pre-distortion, enabling direct support for complex modulation formats.

isscc-2025-191.method: This charge-pump phase-locked loop (a circuit using controlled currents to synchronize an oscillator to a reference clock) uses a dual-path design combining three refinements: a resistive-discharge phase detector that improves linearity (eliminating distortion) and provides higher gain, a series-resonance oscillator with tuned LC circuitry and overvoltage protection that suppresses jitter (timing noise), and a sampling-based filter providing sharp filtering without large capacitors. The dual-path architecture—using two parallel signal paths working together—allows the high-gain phase detector to suppress timing noise while maintaining stable lock.
isscc-2025-191.key_novelty: A dual-path charge-pump phase-locked loop architecture combining a resistive-discharge phase detector and series-resonance oscillator achieves 15.8 femtoseconds of integrated jitter and -98.5dBc reference spur at 13GHz.

isscc-2025-202.method: Granite Rapids-D is Intel's Xeon 6 processor in two specialized versions. One prioritizes computational performance—both sequential and parallel—using PCIe5 connections and low-latency memory for cloud data centers and vRAN (virtualized radio access networks). The other is built rugged: it operates from -40°C to 85°C with dynamic temperature management for harsh field conditions. Both include a secure processing area for confidential data (TEE—a protected zone where sensitive information can be processed securely) and support for ethernet and accelerators.
isscc-2025-202.key_novelty: One processor family with two versions: one optimized for high-performance cloud work and one built to withstand extreme field temperatures.

isscc-2025-201.method: The design performs cross-correlation entirely in analog circuits, avoiding the power cost of converting to digital. A 256×256 grid of four-transistor cells computes correlations by propagating signal differences (margin-propagation), with each column handling a different time-lag. Instead of building dedicated delay lines to create different lags, the design uses sampling to create these timing variations directly within the analog computation, saving chip area. All 256 correlation results are collected in a single readout pass.
isscc-2025-201.key_novelty: Margin-propagation analog compute cells achieve 256-lag cross-correlation at 996–1060 TOPS/W (trillion operations per watt, far exceeding digital's 5–20 TOPS/W) and 1.3 TOPS/mm² density.

isscc-2025-205.method: The transceiver simultaneously sends and receives data on the same wire (doubling the data rate), using three types of analog filtering to remove interference. Echo cancellation suppresses reflections of the transceiver's own transmitted signal bouncing back on the wire. Near-end and far-end crosstalk cancellation remove unwanted signal leakage from neighboring wires—near-end crosstalk from wires close by, far-end from wires farther away. To maximize wire density, the design eliminates ground shielding (the protective grounded wires that normally isolate signals), making effective crosstalk cancellation essential.
isscc-2025-205.key_novelty: The novelty is combining echo and crosstalk cancellation (near-end and far-end) in a single transceiver to enable simultaneous two-way signaling on unshielded wires.

isscc-2025-210.method: The system protects the implanted device using two separate authentication steps: a doctor enters their password and then provides a second verification (such as a code from their phone). During emergencies—when the authentication server is unreachable, a doctor's account is compromised, or no one knows the account password—authorized responders can use a special key stored directly on the device itself to access it immediately, without needing to reach the central server or retrieve the backup security keys stored there.
isscc-2025-210.key_novelty: Emergency responders can access the implant even when the central authentication server is offline or breached, because the emergency authorization key is stored on the device itself rather than only on the server.

isscc-2025-207.method: The design uses gallium nitride transistors (semiconductors that handle higher power and voltage than traditional options) to build a power amplifier for signals in the 216–226 GHz range. These transistors have unwanted electrical side effects that interfere with output power, so the design applies multiband impedance correction—adjusting the output's electrical properties (resistance and reactance) to match the target across the full frequency band. The circuit and its physical package are designed together as one system, enabling efficient power transfer to the antenna while managing heat and parasitic effects.
isscc-2025-207.key_novelty: A gallium nitride power amplifier combining multiband impedance correction with co-designed circuit-package integration, delivering watt-level power at 220 GHz.

isscc-2025-206.method: The design broadcasts a single input value across many processing locations and performs floating-point alignment (matching up decimal points before arithmetic) inside each multiply-accumulate unit rather than in separate circuits. A lightweight converter lets the same macro use both BF16 (a compact 16-bit floating-point format) and INT8 (8-bit integers). Instead of using 2's-complement (the standard way to represent negative numbers), the design uses a non-2's-complement format that reduces unnecessary circuit switching and better handles negative-weight sparsity—the fact that many neural network weights are negative and clustered.
isscc-2025-206.key_novelty: The key innovation is a broadcast-alignment architecture that shifts floating-point alignment from separate peripheral circuits into each multiply-accumulate unit, combined with a non-2's-complement encoding that reduces sign-bit overhead and exploits negative-weight sparsity.

isscc-2025-214.method: The platform combines two types of energy harvesters—piezoelectric (which converts vibration into electricity through material deformation) and electromagnetic (which converts motion into electricity using a coil in a magnetic field). Rather than using separate inductors and capacitors (electronic components that store and regulate electrical energy) at each power-conversion stage, it reuses the electromagnetic coil as a shared inductor for all three stages: rectification (converting AC to DC power), DC-DC conversion (adjusting voltage levels), and regulation (stabilizing the output voltage). This coil-sharing synchronous rectification scheme means one component does multiple jobs, eliminating the need for external inductors and capacitors.
isscc-2025-214.key_novelty: A coil-sharing scheme that eliminates external inductors and capacitors by reusing the electromagnetic harvester's coil across all power-conversion stages.

isscc-2025-208.method: The converter combines coarse and fine quantization (precision measurement at two levels simultaneously) to digitize signals. It removes thermal noise in capacitors (kT/C noise) using an amplifier that operates only during the cancellation phase, not throughout conversion—drastically reducing power compared to designs that keep the amplifier always active. By processing both measurement levels concurrently and activating the amplifier only when needed, the design avoids repeated sampling overhead that slowed earlier incremental converters.
isscc-2025-208.key_novelty: The core innovation is a gated amplifier (one that activates only during noise cancellation) enabling simultaneous coarse and fine measurements without repeated sampling.

isscc-2025-211.method: The crystal oscillator, built in 28nm CMOS, injects tiny pulses of energy at adaptively timed moments in the oscillation cycle (Class-C-like operation, where transistors conduct only during a narrow window). The timing of these conduction-angle pulses adjusts automatically to match the oscillator's state, allowing it to start itself without a separate start-up circuit. This eliminates the need for added control logic while providing robust oscillation that resists interference.
isscc-2025-211.key_novelty: By automatically adjusting the conduction angle (the phase when transistors are active in each cycle), the oscillator starts itself without needing a separate start-up circuit.

isscc-2025-212.method: Processors normally add a fixed voltage safety margin (guard band) to handle worst-case conditions like power droops, temperature swings, and aging. The IBM zNext system instead continuously monitors actual conditions with on-chip sensors and firmware to dynamically reduce this margin in real-time. It simultaneously uses two techniques: on-chip power delivery management (which prevents voltage droops) and error recovery mechanisms like voltage-independent correction codes or timeout-based recovery (which let the processor tolerate lower voltages when droops do occur). By combining droop prevention with error tolerance, the system reduces the required safety margin without sacrificing reliability.
isscc-2025-212.key_novelty: The system dynamically adjusts guard bands by combining voltage droop prevention with error tolerance, rather than using a fixed margin to cover all worst-case scenarios.

isscc-2025-217.method: This K-SAT solver is built as a specialized 28nm chip that uses fast memory blocks (SRAM) in two simultaneous paths: one deduces variable values from problem clauses, while the other deduces new clauses from known variables. Rather than recomputing everything when the problem changes, the chip tracks variable assignments incrementally and maintains clauses at multiple levels of detail, ensuring it can correctly handle both satisfiable and unsatisfiable problems without the accuracy loss of analog methods.
isscc-2025-217.key_novelty: It's the first K-SAT solver chip that can prove problems unsolvable, using fast memory to simultaneously track both clause-to-variable and variable-to-clause deductions.

isscc-2025-218.method: The design uses a simplified switching amplifier (Class-D power amplifier with Q-downsize technique) that naturally prevents shoot-through current—the dangerous short circuit when both transistors conduct simultaneously—which eliminates the need for artificial delays that normally reduce efficiency. The transmitter is built with perfectly symmetrical circuits on both sides of the isolation barrier, and the coils wind in opposite directions so their magnetic fields cancel each other; this symmetry automatically suppresses the electromagnetic interference that normally leaks across isolated converters. The circuit operates at 180MHz and achieves 45.3% peak efficiency, with stable performance even when the switching frequency varies from its target.
isscc-2025-218.key_novelty: A simplified Class-D switching amplifier (the Q-downsize technique) that naturally blocks shoot-through current surges without needing efficiency-stealing delays, while maintaining stable performance despite frequency variations.

isscc-2025-209.method: The chip contains an amplifier-multiplier chain operating at 232–260 GHz in CMOS technology. It radiates the signal out the back using a patterned dielectric matching sheet instead of expensive silicon lenses—this thin layer transitions waves from silicon's high permittivity (εr=11.9) to air's low permittivity (εr=1), preventing the signal from bouncing back and improving radiation efficiency and bandwidth. The circuit uses high-power FinFET transistors and broadband power amplifiers designed for strong gain across the frequency range.
isscc-2025-209.key_novelty: A patterned dielectric matching sheet replaces expensive silicon lenses for efficient terahertz radiation out the back of a CMOS chip, enabling low-cost packaging.

isscc-2025-215.method: The analyzer uses two pulse-based measurement techniques: time-domain reflectometry (sending a pulse down a wire and measuring echoes to detect impedance mismatches) and time-domain transmission (measuring the signal that reaches the far end) to measure signal degradation on high-speed electrical connections. Both techniques are integrated into a single application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) using 28-nanometer CMOS process technology, allowing four measurement ports to fit on one device. The system covers frequencies from DC (direct current) to 40GHz with a 9.1 picosecond response time, consuming only 99.5 milliwatts per port.
isscc-2025-215.key_novelty: A single application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) with four measurement ports characterizes signal degradation on high-speed data links from DC to 40GHz while consuming only 99.5 milliwatts per port.

isscc-2025-216.method: The circuit reads analog signals continuously without sampling (avoiding kT/C thermal noise, which is measurement error from discrete sampling), using a frequency-controlled current source whose power and operating speed vary with frequency. Tuning this frequency lets applications choose any point across a 225× range of bandwidth-to-power trade-offs, from power-efficient low-bandwidth operation to fast high-bandwidth modes.
isscc-2025-216.key_novelty: A frequency-controlled current source enables continuous-time (non-sampling) sensor interfaces to scale their bandwidth and power consumption together across a 225× range.

isscc-2025-219.method: A 6.78MHz Class-E power amplifier (a highly efficient power circuit) solves wireless charging efficiency by separately controlling how the circuit adapts to changing loads. It adjusts the real part of load impedance (the resistive load) using a dynamic matching network, and adjusts the imaginary part (the phase shift) using adaptive capacitance, specifically using tunable elements instead of nonlinear MOS capacitors. This dual control keeps the circuit operating efficiently across changing charge states, achieving 94.2% peak efficiency.
isscc-2025-219.key_novelty: Separately controlling the real and imaginary parts of load impedance with adaptive tuning elements instead of using nonlinear MOS capacitors.

isscc-2025-213.method: A 60-gigabit-per-second burst-mode clock-and-data recovery circuit recovers timing from arriving data bursts using cross-injection-locking—a technique where oscillators stabilize each other to reduce jitter (unwanted timing variations). It combines this with a flash phase detector (a fast circuit using parallel comparators that measures timing offset between data and clock within 2 bit periods). Implemented in 28nm CMOS, it achieves 0.13 nanosecond reconfiguration time.
isscc-2025-213.key_novelty: The key idea is using cross-injection-locking—where oscillators mutually stabilize each other's frequency—to suppress jitter (unwanted timing variations) in burst-mode clock and data recovery.

isscc-2025-221.method: The approach designs circuits using analog or mixed-signal electronics, arranging their physical properties to match the constraints of the optimization problem. Instead of running computational steps, the circuit naturally evolves toward solutions that satisfy these constraints. This works because the problem's constraints are translated into physical rules in the circuit, allowing the physics to automatically find the solution.
isscc-2025-221.key_novelty: The approach solves optimization problems by building their constraints directly into circuits as physical rules, so physics automatically finds the solution without needing algorithms.

isscc-2025-220.method: The system exploits sparse, intermittent neural firing to hit the 10nW-per-input power target. It uses event-driven activation (reading only during spikes) and spatially-selective zooming (focusing on active electrode clusters), paired with an ultra-low-power analog-to-digital converter (ADC) using a reconfigurable-inverter fabric. Each electrode also adaptively compresses its signal (input-adaptive quantization), using fewer bits for less-informative channels, which reduces data rates and power while preserving critical neural information.
isscc-2025-220.key_novelty: The innovation combines input-adaptive quantization (varying precision per electrode) with spatially-selective event-based recording (capturing only from active regions during spikes) to achieve 10nW-per-input power consumption while preserving neural information.

isscc-2025-226.method: The converter automatically balances current across its inductors by using segmented-interlacing (staggered activation of inductor groups) with duty-cycle compensation (timing adjustments per phase), eliminating the need for per-phase current sensors. During sudden load increases, all inductors are energized simultaneously, which dramatically speeds up the slew rate (how fast current can rise), preventing the large voltage dip that normally occurs at the output. This design achieves current balancing passively through circuit structure rather than active feedback control.
isscc-2025-226.key_novelty: Automatic inductor current balancing without per-phase current sensing, achieved through segmented-interlacing and synchronized inductor energization during load transients.

isscc-2025-224.method: The approach calculates light patterns that compensate for tissue scattering (mean scattering length ~100 microns) and sends this pre-patterned light through the tissue. The tissue's scattering process then reverses the distortion, refocusing the light at depths beyond 1mm for high-resolution imaging. This requires optoelectronic integrated circuits—specialized chips combining light-processing and electronics—to rapidly calculate these patterns and modulate (adjust) the signal in real-time during detection.
isscc-2025-224.key_novelty: Reversing light scattering in tissue enables high-resolution biochemical imaging at depths beyond 1mm.

isscc-2025-223.method: The chip stores 1 terabyte using 3D Flash memory (vertically stacked silicon), with each cell holding 3 bits. It cuts read power consumption by 29% through small-voltage-swing word-line control (applying smaller electrical pulses to activate memory rows instead of large ones, which wastes less energy). Data moves at 4.8 gigabits per second via power-isolated low-tapped-termination I/Os (data connections that keep support circuits tightly bundled), minimizing the extra area needed beyond the memory array.
isscc-2025-223.key_novelty: The key innovation is reducing the voltage pulse for memory row activation (small-voltage-swing word-line control), achieving 29% lower read energy while keeping support circuits tightly integrated with the memory in 3D stacking.

isscc-2025-222.method: This system uses a digital phase-locked loop (a feedback circuit that automatically adjusts an oscillator to match a target frequency) to generate frequency sweeps called chirps from 11 to 16.4 GHz. It applies digital predistortion specifically to the final segment of each sweep to pre-correct for hardware distortions, allowing the system to converge—reaching stable operation—within just 5 chirp cycles. The resulting chirps sweep upward at 3.4 GHz per microsecond, cover 5.32 GHz of bandwidth, and maintain 0.043% RMS frequency accuracy despite the hardware's inherent nonlinearities.
isscc-2025-222.key_novelty: Posterior-segment digital predistortion (applying correction only to the end of each frequency sweep rather than throughout) enables convergence within 5 chirp cycles, supporting rapid frequency-switching and multi-mode operation when multiple vehicles share radar spectrum.

isscc-2025-225.method: The chip combines three usually-conflicting functions in a single 65-nanometer CMOS chip: a sensitive receiver (adding only 3.3dB of noise—a measure where lower means cleaner signals), a powerful transmitter (reaching 20.2dBm output power), and isolation circuitry that prevents the transmitted signal from interfering with the received signal. It covers frequencies from 17.7 to 29.5 GHz by electronically tuning to whichever frequency is needed.
isscc-2025-225.key_novelty: The key innovation is doing low-noise receiving, high-power transmitting, and transmit-receive isolation all in one wideband transceiver, rather than requiring separate narrowband designs.

isscc-2025-230.method: This 36V circuit uses current-balancing—a design where identical electrical currents flowing through symmetric paths cancel measurement errors—to precisely measure sensor signals despite large noise offsets. It accepts sensor signals up to ±24V apart while ignoring up to ±10V of noise appearing equally on both wires. The amplifier uses direct coupling (no blocking capacitors) and carefully tuned stages to keep its common-mode rejection ratio at 140dB—a measure of how well it eliminates signals appearing identically on both inputs—across all gain settings.
isscc-2025-230.key_novelty: By using current-balancing, the circuit achieves 140dB common-mode rejection (suppressing signals that appear equally on both wires) at all gain settings without needing a separate higher-voltage power supply.

isscc-2025-233.method: This converter combines period modulation (which measures capacitance by timing oscillations, achieving a wide input range to 18.5nF) with SAR conversion (a rapid binary-search technique that refines the measurement). Instead of slowly counting oscillation cycles like traditional period-modulation designs, the SAR stage efficiently processes those cycles to complete the measurement in under 10µs. By merging both methods, it eliminates the analog saturation limitations that prevent standard SAR and ΔΣM converters from handling large capacitances.
isscc-2025-233.key_novelty: It combines period modulation (measuring capacitance via oscillation timing) with SAR conversion (a fast binary-search technique) to overcome the traditional range-versus-speed tradeoff.

isscc-2025-235.method: An mm-wave low-noise amplifier applies Doherty active load modulation—a technique that dynamically adjusts how power flows through the circuit—to handle both weak signals and strong interfering blockers. The Doherty architecture works by shifting the gain-linearity trade-off in real time: when weak signals arrive it optimizes for low noise, and when strong blockers arrive it optimizes for linearity to prevent distortion. This dynamic adjustment maintains efficient power output across the entire range of input signal strengths.
isscc-2025-235.key_novelty: This work applies Doherty active load modulation—a technique that dynamically adjusts power-flow in the circuit—to mm-wave low-noise amplifier design, achieving simultaneous high linearity and low noise in the presence of strong interfering signals.

isscc-2025-234.method: A fractional divider uses two paired digital-to-time converters—circuits that convert digital signals into precise timing delays—to generate a divided clock. These converters normally suffer from gain errors (wrong conversion ratio) and integral nonlinearity (INL—where the conversion is inconsistent across different input ranges). The system measures both error types by comparing the two converters against each other during normal operation (a process called background calibration), then automatically adjusts for them in real-time. The result achieves a worst-case jitter of 257 femtoseconds in a chip area of just 0.024 square millimeters.
isscc-2025-234.key_novelty: Using two paired digital-to-time converters to simultaneously calibrate each other's gain and integral nonlinearity errors during normal operation, eliminating the need for external reference circuits.

isscc-2025-229.method: A SAR analog-to-digital converter that uses the full available voltage range incorporates continuous-time correlated level shifting (continuously adjusting its reference level in real-time) in the input buffer to maintain signal accuracy while driving large capacitor arrays. This level-shifting technique is built directly into the noise-shaping feedback loop (which shifts unwanted electronic noise to frequencies that don't affect accuracy). By combining these techniques, the design avoids needing a higher power supply voltage.
isscc-2025-229.key_novelty: Continuous-time correlated level shifting (adjusting the reference level in real-time) enables the input buffer to integrate directly into the SAR noise-shaping loop while maintaining rail-to-rail voltage swing and avoiding higher power supply requirements.

isscc-2025-228.method: The robot's centralized battery must power actuators spread throughout its limbs via long cables, which waste energy as resistive heat (heat proportional to current squared). The converter reduces this waste using two stages: a boost stage raises the 48V battery voltage higher, which reduces transmission current and therefore heat loss; a buck stage then lowers voltage back to what the motors need. Both stages are optimized to work efficiently with power flowing in both directions.
isscc-2025-228.key_novelty: Using high-voltage transmission with separate direction-optimized converter stages—stepping voltage up to reduce current losses, then down to motor levels—efficiently powers distributed robot limbs from a centralized battery.

isscc-2025-227.method: Out-of-band and alias-band blockers—strong interfering signals from nearby frequencies—corrupt the signal quality after it's converted to digital form. This receiver prevents that using a mixer-first architecture followed by three filtering techniques: multilevel time-approximation filtering (sampling at irregular, precisely chosen intervals rather than uniform clock ticks), a VCO-based integrator with embedded digitalization (which simultaneously collects and converts signal energy), and non-uniform N-path filtering. Time-gated integration patterns—which change when signal collection occurs—allow it to suppress multiple types of blockers at once. The result is 65dB of blocker rejection while maintaining reconfigurability and low implementation cost in 28nm CMOS.
isscc-2025-227.key_novelty: Combining multilevel time-approximation filtering with a VCO-based integrator (which simultaneously collects signal energy and converts it to digital form) achieves 65dB of blocker rejection while keeping the receiver reconfigurable and inexpensive.

isscc-2025-232.method: Bayesian neural networks need to track two properties for each weight: its mean (central value) and its deviation (how much uncertainty there is around that value). This chip processes these two properties using two separate paths—one optimized for mean calculations and one for deviation calculations—letting each circuit be tuned for its specific job. It stores weights using STT-MRAM (magnetic memory that consumes less power), and performs calculations directly in the memory rather than shuttling data back and forth to a separate processor.
isscc-2025-232.key_novelty: A chip architecture that processes Bayesian neural network weights using two separate computation paths—one optimized for mean values and one for deviations—rather than forcing both through a single general-purpose circuit.

isscc-2025-231.method: The receiver uses a slice-based continuous-time linear equalizer (CTLE—a signal-cleaning filter that divides work across multiple stages instead of one). It generates eight sampling clock phases using a phase-interpolator, enabling 8x faster sampling. By distributing the filtering work, the design achieves 224Gb/s operation at 1.11pJ per bit in 12nm CMOS while meeting power and area constraints.
isscc-2025-231.key_novelty: The core innovation is a slice-based continuous-time linear equalizer that divides signal-cleaning work across multiple stages, achieving 224Gb/s at 1.11pJ per bit power efficiency.

isscc-2025-237.method: The design uses a hardware block that computes directly in memory (CIM macro) to process different types of data distributions, not just the bell-curve patterns (Gaussian distribution) that typical designs assume. It keeps intermediate calculation results in the memory block itself—called partial-sum and residual accumulation—which drastically cuts down on how much data needs to be moved between the processor and memory, reducing the power cost from currently 26-72% of total power to minimal. It also flexibly detects when data is sparse (contains lots of zeros) rather than assuming fixed sparsity patterns, letting it adapt to different compound AI models. This achieves speedups approaching the theoretical maximum possible from exploiting sparsity.
isscc-2025-237.key_novelty: The key innovation is integrating partial-sum accumulation and flexible sparsity detection into a full-datapath CIM hardware block, enabling it to handle any data distribution while reducing data-movement power from 26-72% to minimal and approaching theoretical maximum sparsity speedup.

isscc-2025-238.method: The converter measures capacitance using successive approximation (SAR)—repeatedly comparing the signal to reference values and refining the estimate. It operates continuously instead of waiting for clock pulses, which eliminates timing errors that reduce accuracy. Noise-shaping (mathematically redirecting unwanted electrical noise to high frequencies where it can be filtered) combined with oversampling (taking many measurements) produces a high-resolution digital output.
isscc-2025-238.key_novelty: The core idea is using continuous-time noise-shaping in a successive-approximation (SAR) capacitance-to-digital converter to achieve high resolution while consuming just 14.5 femtojoules per measurement.

isscc-2025-240.method: When a laser probes chip voltages from the back, it creates extra electrical current (photocurrent injection) in the transistors it hits. The circuit detects this by monitoring the chip's power leakage—electricity wasted as heat in transistors—which shifts noticeably during laser injection. The design triggers protective actions using these existing measurements with minimal overhead (4.35% additional silicon area), requiring no separate attack sensors.
isscc-2025-240.key_novelty: The circuit detects laser attacks by monitoring shifts in power leakage during normal operation, without requiring dedicated sensors.

isscc-2025-242.method: The transmit/receive module uses an asymmetric Doherty power amplifier, which dynamically adjusts its operating point as signal strength changes—improving efficiency when broadcasting signals like OFDM that have varying peak and average power. Normally, standard power amplifiers waste significant power when handling these varying-strength signals. The entire module, including the power amplifier, low-noise receiver, and transmit/receive switch, fits into 0.22mm² of silicon and operates across 24-29GHz.
isscc-2025-242.key_novelty: The core innovation is an asymmetric Doherty power amplifier design that achieves high efficiency on varying-strength wireless signals (OFDM) while integrating the entire 24-29GHz front-end module into just 0.22mm².

isscc-2025-239.method: The transmitter uses a 1-bit power amplifier controlled by delta-sigma modulation (DSM—converting signals into rapid on-off pulses). Phase angles are encoded through edge-selection (the timing of transitions) rather than using CORDIC (an algorithm that converts angles but adds distortion). The 1-bit design naturally maintains signal linearity without distortion-correction circuits while avoiding the power losses of switched-capacitor amplifiers.
isscc-2025-239.key_novelty: Edge-selection-based phase modulation in a 1-bit DSM power amplifier replaces CORDIC, achieving signal linearity without digital pre-distortion.

isscc-2025-248.method: The chip combines 64 parallel converter units (each running at 1.125 gigasamples per second at different times) to achieve 72 gigasamples per second through time interleaving. Each unit uses a pipeline-SAR architecture (a hybrid of two conversion methods that balances signal accuracy with conversion speed), equipped with linearized input buffers to handle 20GHz signals without distortion, dual-path bootstrapped switches for consistent performance, and a simple resistor-based amplifier. These design choices eliminate the complex calibration between stages that conventionally limits time-interleaved converters at high frequencies.
isscc-2025-248.key_novelty: The core innovation is a time-interleaved pipeline-SAR architecture using linearized input buffers and bootstrapped switches that achieves 55dB signal-to-distortion ratio at 20GHz wideband inputs without inter-stage gain calibration.

isscc-2025-241.method: This radar chip uses 8 transmitting antennas and 8 receiving antennas arranged in a 2×4 grid, all operating at 77GHz. It transmits frequency-swept radio signals (chirps) and listens for their reflections; by switching between different signal patterns, it adapts to detect objects at three different distances: long range (186m away), medium range (3-30m), and short range (under 10m), with 3-centimeter measurement precision. The transmitters take turns sending signals (a technique called time-division multiplexing, or TDMA), and the receiver antennas work together to focus and steer the signal electronically (MIMO beamforming), which allows the chip to find both distant objects and measure their precise angle from the radar.
isscc-2025-241.key_novelty: The hybrid architecture combines time-division transmission (TDMA) with multi-antenna reception (MIMO) and adapts its signal patterns to simultaneously achieve all three detection ranges—long, medium, and short—from a single integrated chip.

isscc-2025-244.method: A transimpedance amplifier (TIA—a device converting optical currents into usable voltages) handles four signal levels per bit (PAM-4) at 112 gigabits per second across 4 channels. It solves long-interconnect problems in two ways: active-input-termination (AIT-TIA) suppresses signal reflections that degrade performance, and a signal-interpolation-based converter transforms the signal from single-ended (one wire) to differential form (two complementary wires), recovering lost bandwidth. Together these allow the photodiode to sit 0.2 inches from the TIA—compared to 0.03 inches before—while using just 0.61 picojoules per bit in 28nm CMOS.
isscc-2025-244.key_novelty: An amplifier design combining active-input-termination (which suppresses signal reflections) with signal-interpolation-based conversion to differential signals (transforming single wires into pairs of complementary signals) enables photodiodes to sit 0.2 inches from the amplifier—versus 0.03 inches in prior work—while using 0.61 picojoules per bit.

isscc-2025-246.method: A heater built into the chip performs automatic calibration at room temperature to correct the operational amplifier's offset (the baseline error in output voltage) and its temperature-dependent drift. During trim calibration, the heater creates thermal changes that reveal exactly how much correction is needed—without requiring expensive external test equipment. This approach reduces offset from ±45µV to ±5.8µV (3σ) and drift from ±330nV/°C to ±88nV/°C (3σ).
isscc-2025-246.key_novelty: An on-chip heater enables room-temperature self-trimming to correct the amplifier's offset and drift, eliminating the need for expensive external equipment or complex electronic cancellation techniques.

isscc-2025-243.method: For burst-mode fiber communications, this 28nm chip integrates two signal filters: a 5-stage feed-forward equalizer (with 3 stages looking back and 1 looking forward) and a 7-stage decision-feedback equalizer (4 of which reach back 16 symbols) that uses confirmed symbols to correct future ones. Together they cancel inter-symbol interference—the signal smearing where old symbols bleed into new ones—that would otherwise corrupt 50G signals. The receiver locks onto the signal's timing edges in just 15 nanoseconds using specialized fast-lock circuitry, while an integrated high-gain photodiode captures incoming light.
isscc-2025-243.key_novelty: A burst-mode receiver that combines deep signal filtering (5-tap feed-forward and 7-tap decision-feedback equalizers) with 15-nanosecond lock time through edge-based fast-lock design.

isscc-2025-247.method: A cascaded phase-locked loop uses two variable-frequency dividers sharing a single delta-sigma modulator (the circuit that introduces quantization errors during signal conversion). The shared modulator operates at an elevated frequency, which pushes the quantization noise—the conversion errors—out of the useful frequency range, where it is then naturally filtered out. This two-divider structure also suppresses fractional spurs (unwanted frequency components) that would otherwise pollute the useful band. It does this through noise subtraction (feeding back and subtracting the error signal) rather than requiring intensive digital recalibration.
isscc-2025-247.key_novelty: A cascaded PLL sharing a single delta-sigma modulator (the circuit that creates conversion errors) between two multi-modulus dividers automatically eliminates quantization noise and fractional spurs through noise subtraction, eliminating the need for calibration.

isscc-2025-245.method: The platform harvests energy from the environment (battery-free at 94.8nW) and uses multiple sensor types that only activate on demand (event-driven multimodal sensing). It pairs these with an ultra-low-power neural network accelerator—a specialized chip for running AI models efficiently. The system adjusts its AI models when data characteristics change (model adaptation for data distribution shifts) and enables different sensor nodes to share information and coordinate decisions together (collaborative sensing), all within strict power budgets.
isscc-2025-245.key_novelty: A network of distributed sensors using different measurement types (multimodal) that fuse their data and run adaptive AI models, all powered by harvested environmental energy at 94.8nW instead of batteries.

isscc-2025-236.method: This 28-nanometer design integrates multiply-accumulate circuits directly into SRAM memory, enabling dual-mode-transpose architecture. One mode performs forward passes with weights directly; the other performs backward passes with transposed weights. Floating-point numbers preserve training precision. An optional approximate computing mode trades some accuracy for faster, more efficient operation.
isscc-2025-236.key_novelty: This design builds multiply-accumulate circuits into SRAM memory and reuses a single set for both forward and backward training by switching between normal and transposed weight modes in floating-point format, eliminating separate circuits.

isscc-2025-255.method: The chip combines automatic gain control (AGC — circuitry that automatically adjusts microphone sensitivity to handle different speech volumes) on each audio channel to process inputs ranging from quiet whispers to loud speech (>60dB range). A neural network processes the audio sequentially, recognizing that speech contains significant silence and repetition — it skips unnecessary analysis moments, reducing power consumption. The entire pipeline, from audio front-end to language recognition, runs on a single chip.
isscc-2025-255.key_novelty: A neural network that saves power by exploiting natural pauses and repetition in speech, enabling end-to-end voice recognition on a single ultra-low-power chip with integrated audio level adjustment.

isscc-2025-252.method: The converter uses a special oscillator called a gated cyclic coupled ring-oscillator—a circuit that oscillates by feeding back signals through logic gates—as a shared measurement device for both channels and both conversion steps. This single oscillator is more efficient than separate ones because it automatically provides fine-grained measurements by sampling different points in its oscillation cycle, and it measures signals the same way regardless of their size. Rather than modifying the input signal, the circuit applies the reference signal to the measurement path instead, which keeps the input impedance constant and prevents signal reflections that would degrade the measurement.
isscc-2025-252.key_novelty: The core innovation is sharing a single gated cyclic coupled ring-oscillator across both channels and conversion steps, which reduces chip area through interleaving while naturally providing fine-grained measurements and maintaining constant input impedance.

isscc-2025-254.method: The system uses reinforcement learning (machine learning that learns by trying different options and evaluating results) to automatically discover circuit architectures without relying on manual template selection. It uses inverse EM synthesis to calculate what passive networks—inductors and capacitors for signal matching and combining—are needed based on the desired electrical performance, bypassing iterative simulation. Together, these methods automate the entire process from specifications to layout generation without requiring designer intervention.
isscc-2025-254.key_novelty: Automated RF circuit design using machine learning that simultaneously optimizes transistor arrangements and passive networks, rather than starting from predefined human templates.

micro-2025-011.method: HiPACK reorganizes numbers compressed below 8 bits into standard 8-bit chunks before multiplication begins, sidestepping the conflict between unpacking and parallel processing. It improves how the fast cache near the processor (L1/L2) serves this packed data and selects how to divide it so that ultra-fast registers don't overflow while still reusing data from cache effectively. The core technique, Dual Interleaved Register (DIR), interleaves two data streams across alternating register slots, enabling a single SIMD (parallel) multiply instruction to handle both streams at full width without resorting to slower single-value fallback operations.
micro-2025-011.key_novelty: The Dual Interleaved Register (DIR) mechanism interleaves two sub-8-bit data streams in registers so a single SIMD multiply instruction processes both at full width without stalls from width mismatch.

isscc-2025-256.method: A rectifier (circuit that converts wireless AC power to direct current) operating at 6.78MHz produces two independent voltages in a single stage. One output voltage (V_OUT2) is kept tightly stable for the recording front-end (biopotential measurement electronics), while the other (V_OUT1) responds quickly to changes needed by the stimulation circuits. Both voltages are regulated and charged simultaneously during each half-cycle, rather than cascading multiple converters or compromising either voltage's performance.
isscc-2025-256.key_novelty: A single rectifier stage can simultaneously charge and independently regulate two voltages with opposite needs (stability and responsiveness) in one half-cycle, replacing the multiple converters implants normally require.

isscc-2025-250.method: This circuit recovers timing and data from incoming signals without an external reference clock. A successive-approximation register (SAR—a circuit that uses binary search, repeatedly halving the frequency range to find the target) locks onto the correct frequency band in a constant 55 nanoseconds. A charge pump with positive net current then accelerates the final frequency tuning. These combined SAR band-switching and tuning steps complete frequency acquisition in under 150 nanoseconds.
isscc-2025-250.key_novelty: Using successive-approximation register (SAR) for frequency-band selection in reference-less clock-recovery circuits guarantees constant-time frequency acquisition.

isscc-2025-249.method: The ST-BPA combines beamforming (steering and shaping signals across antenna arrays using amplitude and phase control) with power back-off efficiency (managing how much power the amplifier uses when transmitting high-demand signals) in a single mm-wave integrated circuit. Instead of using separate circuits for signal steering and power efficiency, this unified design handles both simultaneously. The chip can additionally use efficiency-enhancement techniques—such as Doherty (combining two amplifiers), envelope tracking (dynamically adjusting power supply), or outphasing (offsetting signal phases)—to further improve performance across the phased array.
isscc-2025-249.key_novelty: A mm-wave power amplifier that directly combines antenna-array beamforming and power efficiency in a single chip using amplitude and phase control, eliminating the need for separate baseband or RF circuits.

isscc-2025-251.method: A fully dynamic noise-shaping SAR ADC (successive approximation register — a type of chip that converts analog signals to digital) reshapes electrical noise into higher frequencies that can be filtered out more easily, while powering down components between measurements using fast comparators and on-demand voltage references. Unlike earlier designs, it avoids the power-draining requirements of amplifying remaining errors, recalibrating settings, or using large filters — so power consumption scales directly with sampling frequency.
isscc-2025-251.key_novelty: This fully dynamic noise-shaping SAR achieves 120dB SNDR (signal-to-noise-and-distortion ratio — how accurately it converts analog signals to digital) without static power loss or needing external amplifiers, enabling duty-cycle scaling (power consumption that scales with how often it samples).

micro-2025-014.method: CryptoBTB uses a two-level Branch Target Buffer (a cache that predicts where a program's control flow jumps next) where encryption—which hides which storage location is accessed—happens separately from the prediction calculation to avoid slowing things down. The hierarchical design avoids the collision problem (multiple branches mapping to the same storage) that plagued prior flat designs like HyBP, recovering wasted capacity for programs with large instruction footprints and reducing conflicts when a single thread accesses many branches.
micro-2025-014.key_novelty: Decoupling encryption from the prediction path enables fast secure access, while the two-level hierarchical design recovers the BTB capacity that prior approaches only partially used.

micro-2025-019.method: MAMA divides control into two layers. Each processor core runs a simple decision agent (a multi-armed bandit—it tries different options and learns which works best) to choose how aggressively to prefetch memory into the cache. A central supervisor watches overall bandwidth and sends feedback to each local agent about global load, encouraging them to back off when the system is congested. The supervisor then coordinates these local choices to maximize system-wide speed or fair sharing—avoiding the exponential explosion that would occur if the center had to individually control every core.
micro-2025-019.key_novelty: A central supervisor shows each core's prefetcher how much memory bandwidth the entire system is using, enabling them to coordinate their prefetching instead of each core competing blindly for resources.

micro-2025-018.method: Chasoñ is a specialized processor (built on an FPGA, which is reconfigurable hardware) that accelerates sparse matrix multiplication on AMD Alveo U55C hardware running at 301 MHz. Sparse matrices have mostly zeros and only scattered non-zero values; when accessing these in irregular patterns, some processing units sit idle while others are overloaded. To solve this, Chasoñ dynamically moves non-zero values between memory channels during execution — when processors on one channel have no work, the scheduler finds and migrates data from other channels, enabling out-of-order execution that crosses channel boundaries. The design targets real matrices from the SuiteSparse and SNAP collections.
micro-2025-018.key_novelty: The core innovation is that non-zero data can migrate between memory channels during execution, eliminating processing bottlenecks by dynamically redistributing work based on actual demand.

isscc-2025-253.method: The chip uses a technique called DAO (duty-cycle-automatic-optimization) to suppress unwanted oscillations. It works by automatically adjusting the on/off timing of the drive signal in response to temperature changes, keeping the circuit stable while consuming just 1.5µW of always-on power. When activated, the sensor wakes up to full measurement mode in 2.8 milliseconds with reliable performance (±5% stability) across temperatures from −40°C to +85°C.
isscc-2025-253.key_novelty: The key innovation is duty-cycle-automatic-optimization (DAO)—a technique that automatically adjusts the drive signal's on/off ratio to suppress unwanted oscillations in always-on MEMS gyroscope drive loops.

micro-2025-021.method: LLMulator fine-tunes a pre-trained language model (LLaMA-3.2-1B using LoRA, a parameter-efficient training method) to predict hardware performance through three techniques. First, instead of predicting performance as a single number, it predicts digit-by-digit, treating each digit as a discrete category rather than a continuous value—this works across any performance range and enables error correction via beam search (testing multiple digit sequences and keeping the best). Second, it continuously updates from live hardware simulations (Verilator), learning to adapt when loop sizes or branching patterns change during execution. Third, it builds training data by analyzing code structure (AST parsing), systematically varying loops, augmenting with an LLM, and using compiler tools (SiliconCompiler, OpenROAD) to show how code becomes hardware.
micro-2025-021.key_novelty: By treating performance numbers as digit-wise category predictions instead of single continuous values, LLMulator can generalize to any performance scale and combine this with online learning from hardware feedback to adapt to varying loop bounds and control flow.

micro-2025-007.method: Distributed-HISQ combines two mechanisms. HISQ is a hardware instruction set extending RISC-V 32I that represents quantum operations as timed commands: 'send codeword X to port Y at time T'—this separation lets the same instructions work across different quantum hardware and electronics implementations. BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol) eliminates synchronization overhead by letting controllers reserve their sync points in advance instead of requesting sync on demand; since quantum gates run for a fixed, known duration, the system can send synchronization messages during this execution time, achieving zero-cycle overhead when the preceding operations are long enough to hide communication delays. The system connects controllers using a hybrid tree-and-mesh network topology: a balanced tree handles region-level synchronization, while mesh-like links mirroring the physical qubit layout handle nearest-neighbor synchronization, with only 13 LUTs per SyncU hardware cost on an FPGA.
micro-2025-007.key_novelty: BISP (Booking-based Instruction Synchronization Protocol) lets controllers pre-announce their synchronization points in advance, hiding the communication delay under the fixed-duration execution of preceding quantum gates and enabling zero-cycle synchronization overhead in the common case.

micro-2025-020.method: LeakyHammer exploits RowHammer defenses (PRAC and RFM) by measuring the timing delays that occur when their protective memory refreshes block DRAM access. A spy process observes these timing delays to steal victim behavior information—a weakness called a side channel—or to send secret messages by modulating the patterns—a covert channel. The attack demonstrates this by fingerprinting websites: when a victim browses, the timing patterns created by defense refreshes reveal which sites they visited. Three countermeasures are evaluated: randomizing refresh timing, hiding memory access patterns, and injecting timing noise to obscure the real delays.
micro-2025-020.key_novelty: RowHammer defense mechanisms (PRAC and RFM) become vulnerabilities themselves: their timing delays leak both what victims access (side channel) and enable secret communication (covert channel).

micro-2025-030.method: SMX combines two components orchestrated by a processor: a new instruction set extension (SMX-1D) that handles variable-length sequences and alignment edge cases, and a specialized hardware accelerator (SMX-2D) that rapidly computes the repetitive core math using systolic-style wavefront computation (a technique where data flows through in parallel waves). Together they support DNA, protein, and text sequences with weighted gap penalties and custom scoring matrices. The design is physically compact—just 0.34mm² at 22nm technology, consuming 30% the silicon area of a standard single-issue CPU core.
micro-2025-030.key_novelty: A unified heterogeneous architecture pairing a flexible instruction extension (for irregular alignment tasks) with a dedicated 2D wavefront accelerator (for regular computation) achieves 18x better performance per silicon area than specialized accelerators.

micro-2025-033.method: The paper fuses all the pattern-matching instructions into a single loop that processes one data block at a time, so each block gets loaded once from memory and processed by all instructions before moving to the next block. To handle the fact that later instructions depend on results from earlier blocks, they use selective recomputation—recalculating parts of the dependency chain when needed rather than having threads communicate with each other. They also restructure these dependency chains to reduce the depth of synchronization barriers between groups of GPU threads (warps), and skip computation entirely on data blocks that are all zeros, since sparse patterns often produce zero results.
micro-2025-033.key_novelty: Instead of running one pattern-matching instruction across all data blocks before running the next instruction, this approach fuses all instructions into a single loop that processes one block at a time, improving data reuse and avoiding intermediate storage, while resolving dependencies through selective recalculation rather than inter-thread communication.

isscc-2025-257.method: The design places a light-driven oscillator at each pixel—a circuit powered by the infrared light itself to produce oscillations at a fixed frequency, eliminating external power supplies. A phase-reconstruction circuit reads the timing of these oscillations and extracts fine details to recover weak signals and reduce quantization noise (rounding error), while each pixel's 20-bit counter uses gray-code format (where adjacent values differ by one bit) and counts asynchronously (without a shared global clock). The 320×256 array of 30μm-pitch quantum-well infrared photodetectors (QWIP—infrared sensors using quantum-physics properties), built in 0.18μm CMOS technology (a standard semiconductor process), transfers data via a low-swing bus with minimal voltage to reduce power consumption and signal crosstalk.
isscc-2025-257.key_novelty: A light-powered modulator at each pixel converts infrared current to oscillations (current-to-phase conversion) without external power, enabling analog-to-digital conversion to happen independently at every pixel rather than through centralized circuits.

micro-2025-054.method: A compiler analyzes code execution frequency and marks each piece as hot, warm, or cold, grouping them in separate program sections. The operating system reads these markings and encodes them as 2-bit temperature values into existing ARM PBHA bits in page table entries—reusing unused hardware fields with zero additional storage cost. When the L2 cache needs to decide what instruction to evict, the memory management unit sends these temperature bits along with the memory request; the cache prioritizes keeping hot code (RRPV=0), then warm code (RRPV=1), then cold code (RRPV=2), following the existing RRIP replacement mechanism. This strategy works because the compiler has information about code importance that hardware-only caches cannot access.
micro-2025-054.key_novelty: The innovation is using existing, unused ARM PBHA bits in page tables as a zero-cost communication channel to pass compiler-derived code temperature (hot/warm/cold) to the cache replacement policy, eliminating the need for additional hardware storage or ISA modifications.

micro-2025-025.method: ρHammer reverse-engineers the computer's DRAM layout by timing memory access patterns to identify which addresses map to the same bank. It exploits asynchronous prefetch instructions (PREFETCHT2/PREFETCHNTA—commands that pre-load data from memory without blocking the CPU), spreading them across multiple banks to maximize row activations while avoiding out-of-order execution reordering by the processor. Finally, it uses indirect addressing and dummy operations to confuse the CPU's branch prediction, maintaining the attack sequence without memory barriers (which don't constrain prefetch instructions anyway).
micro-2025-025.key_novelty: ρHammer uses asynchronous prefetch instructions (which don't block the CPU) instead of regular loads to hammer DRAM rows faster, enabling successful RowHammer attacks on Raptor Lake where traditional load-based methods produce zero bit flips.

micro-2025-061.method: ShadowBinding builds hardware designs for two security schemes—Speculative Taint Tracking (STT, which marks data that might leak through speculation) and Non-Speculative Data Access (NDA)—implemented on a RISC-V processor called BOOM. For STT, it proposes a variant called STT-Issue that moves the tagging step from the rename stage (where the processor first decodes instructions) to the issue stage (where it decides to execute them), eliminating a bottleneck where each instruction waits for the previous one's tag to be computed. The team uses RTL synthesis and cycle-accurate simulation to measure the real performance cost, including both instruction-throughput loss (IPC) and clock-speed reduction.
micro-2025-061.key_novelty: STT-Issue moves the step of marking unsafe data from the rename stage to the issue stage, removing the bottleneck that slows down wide processors, and provides the first real-hardware measurement showing that the combined instruction-throughput and speed loss from in-core security schemes reaches 35% or more on fast processors.

micro-2025-038.method: Quartz is a specialized computer chip (ASIC) that can reconfigure itself while it's running—meaning its dataflow (how data moves through it) can be reprogrammed to match the access patterns of a sparse application. Instead of one large central memory, it uses multiple small memory banks spread across the chip close to the processing units, allowing data to travel short distances instead of getting stuck in traffic. A flexible routing system inside the chip directs data between the memory banks and processing elements based on the reconfigured dataflow.
micro-2025-038.key_novelty: Combining runtime-reconfigurable dataflow—the ability to adjust how data moves through the chip while running—with distributed memory banks allows one chip to efficiently adapt to the different access patterns of various sparse applications.

micro-2025-059.method: CrossBit adds communication pathways to NAND flash memory so different bitlines (columns of storage cells) can exchange data during in-flash computation. Normally, flash can only operate on data within a single bitline, but these pathways break that barrier. This enables error correction (ECC) to work directly on multi-level cells (MLC, which store multiple bits per cell), and it accelerates database operations like filtering and joins that need to combine data from multiple bitlines.
micro-2025-059.key_novelty: CrossBit is the first in-flash processor to enable data from different bitlines to interact during computation, making it possible to run error correction on multi-level cells and a wider range of database operations entirely within the flash chip.

micro-2025-035.method: DECA is a hardware accelerator integrated next to each CPU core that unpacks compressed weights (quantized down to 1-8 bits and sparsified with zeros removed). It has three stages: lookup tables convert quantized values to full size (BF16), parallel prefix sum computes where zeros should go from a bitmask and controls a crossbar to restore them, and per-group scale factors are applied. Crucially, the CPU speculatively invokes DECA (via a TEPL instruction) without blocking—like requesting data speculatively from a cache—and since DECA never writes to memory, abandoned speculations are safe. Two register pairs buffer outputs so DECA can work on the next batch while the CPU reads the current one.
micro-2025-035.key_novelty: A 3D roofline model (adding a vector-throughput axis to the traditional 2D roofline) that correctly identified decompression—not memory bandwidth or compute—as the bottleneck for highly compressed models, directly enabling the design of DECA and its TEPL ISA extension, which speculatively invoke decompression without per-iteration memory fences.

micro-2025-067.method: ORCHES splits reasoning work between a GPU and PIM units (Processing-in-Memory chips that process data where it's stored). It addresses three bottlenecks with coordinated mechanisms: (1) it monitors branching patterns in real-time and dynamically shifts computation between the GPU and PIM units to balance the load; (2) it uses speculative execution (computing multiple possible next steps in parallel) to pipeline reasoning steps together and reduce delays from branch dependencies; (3) it reorganizes memory layout and caching to keep related data physically close, preventing fragmented, irregular memory access caused by branch pruning.
micro-2025-067.key_novelty: The innovation is combining speculative execution (computing multiple possible next steps in parallel) to pipeline reasoning steps, with adaptive GPU-PIM work splitting based on real-time branching patterns during test-time reasoning.

micro-2025-012.method: Stratum integrates specialized DRAM (Mono3D) with a processor chip via copper-to-copper bonding, connecting both to a GPU through a 2.5D silicon interposer. Expert weights are stored in two DRAM tiers: fast (faster access time) and slow—before processing each batch, a topic classifier predicts which experts will be used and remaps hot experts to fast tiers via a row-swap buffer, avoiding expensive off-chip data transfers. The processor contains tensor cores (matrix multiplication hardware) positioned near the DRAM, connected by a ring network, plus engines for Softmax/SiLU computation; the GPU handles prefill (first token), while Stratum handles decoding (remaining tokens).
micro-2025-012.key_novelty: The core innovation is exploiting Mono3D DRAM's inherent speed differences between its layers, combined with predicting which experts each batch will use, to keep hot expert weights in fast tiers without off-chip data movement.

micro-2025-057.method: Pimba places a specialized processor (SPU) directly in memory to handle math-heavy operations that become bottlenecks during AI model generation. It shares this single processor between two memory banks using interleaved access—while one bank reads data, the other writes results simultaneously, keeping the processor constantly busy without needing separate hardware per bank. The processor contains custom MX8 math units (floating-point format with 8-bit shared exponent and 1-bit microexponents per element group, using stochastic rounding) and processes data through four pipeline stages: state fetch, state decay and outer product in parallel, accumulation, and GEMV output with write-back. The system offloads state updates and attention operations to the PIM accelerator during the generation phase while the GPU handles the initial data pass (prefill).
micro-2025-057.key_novelty: Sharing a single pipelined processor between two memory banks via interleaved access (reading from one bank while the other writes simultaneously) halves the chip area needed for processing-in-memory acceleration compared to per-bank designs, while maintaining the same throughput.

micro-2025-043.method: The authors reverse-engineered NVIDIA Ampere GPU cores (RTX A6000) using hand-written test programs that measure exactly how many clock cycles each instruction takes. They discovered that dependency management—coordinating when instructions can safely run—is handled by the compiler inserting special control bits (Stall and Dependence counters) into instructions rather than using hardware scoreboards. They also found a compiler-guided warp scheduling policy, a two-bank register file without collector units, a 6-entry register file cache, an L0 instruction cache with a 16-entry prefetcher, and specific queue sizes and latencies in the memory pipeline. They rebuilt the Accel-sim simulator with all these findings and validated it against real hardware.
micro-2025-043.key_novelty: Reverse-engineering revealed that NVIDIA Ampere GPUs handle all instruction dependency management through compiler-inserted control bits (Stall and Dependence counters), eliminating traditional hardware scoreboards and collector units.

micro-2025-068.method: SeaCache uses three techniques to make sparse caches more efficient. First, it reorganizes variable-length sparse data (rows or columns of nonzero values) by splitting long fibers across multiple cache blocks and grouping short fibers together, reducing wasted space. Second, instead of using an expensive way to decide which data to keep when the cache is full, it uses a practical approximation that exploits access patterns in sparse computations.
