Third, it dynamically adjusts how much cache space is reserved for data versus the metadata needed for these decisions, measuring the optimal split at runtime.
micro-2025-068.key_novelty: The core idea is a two-phase process that dynamically adjusts how the on-chip SRAM is split between sparse data and the metadata used to decide which data to keep, tuning their ratio at runtime to maximize space for variable-length fibers.

micro-2025-071.method: AIORE speeds up encrypted access to CXL memory expansion devices by using two different encryption methods depending on how often data is accessed. Frequently accessed pages (hot pages) use CTR encryption, which is fast and can run in parallel, while rarely accessed pages (cold pages) use XTS encryption, which is required by the CXL IDE security standard. When a page's usage pattern changes, AIORE re-encrypts only that single page, doing the work using compute resources inside the CXL memory device itself so the re-encryption happens in parallel with regular memory traffic. This approach is tested using gem5 full-system simulation across diverse workloads.
micro-2025-071.key_novelty: The key advance is offloading incremental page re-encryption to the CXL memory device's own compute, enabling dynamic switching between CTR and XTS encryption modes based on access frequency.

micro-2025-072.method: LEGOSim wraps each chiplet simulator as an independent parallel process (simlet) that runs on its own schedule rather than waiting at every cycle. Synchronization is on-demand: each simlet advances through adaptable time windows (time quanta) and only stops to exchange messages when one chiplet actually needs to communicate with another, eliminating expensive global synchronization barriers. A separate simulator handles the network connecting the chiplets, tracking message latency, bandwidth, and routing. Testing on SIMBA (a multi-chiplet neural network accelerator) and a CiM-based accelerator showed simulation errors of 3.79% and 3.94% respectively.
micro-2025-072.key_novelty: The core idea is using on-demand synchronization with adaptive time windows: chiplet simulators advance independently and only pause to exchange messages when cross-chiplet communication actually occurs, eliminating the global synchronization barriers that were consuming up to 99.9% of simulation time.

micro-2025-090.method: Citadel is a software memory allocator that prevents Rowhammer attacks (exploits where repeated memory access corrupts nearby DRAM rows) by physically isolating different security domains—separate applications or users—in distant memory regions so they never occupy adjacent rows. It works by tracking the physical layout of rows in DRAM and partitioning the address space (the mapping of memory addresses to physical locations) so domain boundaries are always separated by guard rows or page-aligned gaps. The system supports thousands of simultaneous security domains with only 7.2% additional memory overhead and no measurable performance loss, while working on any DRAM platform without requiring hardware modifications.
micro-2025-090.key_novelty: Citadel prevents cross-domain Rowhammer attacks using a software memory allocator that physically isolates security domains in separate DRAM regions, providing protection without hardware modifications, performance loss, or the excessive overhead of earlier approaches.

micro-2025-084.method: When the hardware task scheduler queues a task, the Task-Seeded Prefetcher (TSP) uses the task descriptor (the instruction packet identifying the task type) to load the required memory addresses into the cache before the task runs. The Memory Response Task Scheduler (MRS) monitors which tasks have completed prefetching and prioritizes assigning those tasks to available cores, ensuring their data is cached before execution starts. Together they create a feedback loop: the scheduler queue signals TSP to prefetch early, and TSP's prefetch completion status guides MRS's scheduling decisions.
micro-2025-084.key_novelty: A task-descriptor-triggered prefetcher paired with a prefetch-status-aware task scheduler creates a feedback loop that hides memory latency in fine-grained task parallelism.

micro-2025-077.method: Task-LP adds a hardware accelerator that clusters up to 128 in-flight tasks using label propagation—an algorithm where each task adopts the most common group label among dependent tasks. For speed, it stores task dependencies as compact binary data and uses bitwise operations, converging in under 300 cycles for typical task graphs. The Task Placement Engine then uses these clusters to assign tasks to cores, tuning the balance between keeping related tasks on the same core (so they share cached data) and spreading work evenly across available cores. The system runs on a 24-core RISC-V processor (Rocket Chip) prototyped on an FPGA (Alveo U55C).
micro-2025-077.key_novelty: A dedicated hardware accelerator that runs label propagation to cluster task dependencies in under 300 cycles—up to 581x faster than software—enabling locality-aware task placement without slowing down scheduling.

micro-2025-063.method: The core problem is that Block Max outliers in MXFP4 have only 1 mantissa bit (precision bits) for their value, causing large rounding errors that corrupt the entire 32-element block. MX+ solves this by repurposing the Block Max's exponent bits—which are always set to maximum and unused—as extra mantissa bits instead, changing the encoding from E2M1 (2 exponent bits, 1 mantissa bit) to E0M3 (3 mantissa bits) and tripling precision. To locate the Block Max within each 32-element block, an 8-bit index is added (5 bits for position, 3 bits reserved). MX+ supports both software and hardware paths: on regular GPUs it decomposes the Block Max into high and low halves (BMH, BML) and runs a standard matrix multiply plus one sparse matrix multiply; on NVIDIA Blackwell it adds dedicated hardware units (BM Detector, Forward and Swap Units, BM Compute Unit) to compute Block Max operations in parallel with the main pipeline, adding 0.020mm² at 28nm.
micro-2025-063.key_novelty: MX+ repurposes the Block Max element's exponent bits as additional mantissa (precision) bits, since the Block Max's exponent is always at maximum (a fixed property of the format), enabling outlier precision improvements without changing block structure, adding storage overhead, or requiring software modifications.

micro-2025-087.method: The approach analyzes an application to identify which instructions from the full RISC-V instruction set (RV32E) it needs—typically 24-86% of the total—then assembles pre-built, formally verified hardware blocks for those instructions from a library into a Modular Execution Unit (ModularEX) using a switch statement. The combined hardware is synthesized (converted to a physical chip layout) with commercial tools (Synopsys ICC2 or Cadence Innovus) on Pragmatic Semiconductor's 0.6-micron IGZO FlexIC process (a technology for making low-area, flexible chips), and the synthesis automatically eliminates unused logic gates. A single-cycle, non-pipelined microarchitecture (where each instruction completes in one clock step, rather than overlapping multiple instructions) suffices for the kilohertz performance requirements of extreme-edge devices. For applications that need firmware updates later, an AI tool rewrites any instructions outside the chosen subset using equivalent instructions from within it.
micro-2025-087.key_novelty: The core idea is using a library of formally pre-verified instruction-sized hardware blocks that can be automatically assembled into minimal-area processors on the FlexIC process, eliminating per-application design and verification cycles.

micro-2025-080.method: CAMP introduces a specialized multiplier that breaks down quantized integer multiplication (operations using reduced-precision 4-bit and 8-bit integers) through a two-level nested approach using Cartesian products—decomposing each multiplication into smaller sub-multiplications. This design efficiently handles multiple precision levels (4-bit and 8-bit integers) within the same circuit by recognizing and exploiting the mathematical patterns in quantized matrix operations. CAMP was integrated into the ARM A64FX processor (using ARMv8 SVE, fabricated at TSMC 7 nm) and RISC-V edge SoCs (fabricated at GlobalFoundries 22 nm), increasing chip area by 1% and 4% respectively.
micro-2025-080.key_novelty: CAMP, a hierarchical multiplier that uses Cartesian products (breaking large multiplications into smaller nested operations), enables vector architectures to efficiently execute multiple precision levels (4-bit and 8-bit) of quantized neural network matrix multiplication with just 1-4% chip area overhead.

micro-2025-078.method: GLADIATOR detects qubit leakage (when qubits jump to unwanted higher energy states) using a probabilistic graph where nodes are syndrome patterns (error-checking readouts) and edges show how likely each pattern is under leakage versus regular errors, calibrated to the actual device. Offline, it labels patterns dominated by leakage-induced transitions and stores them in a lookup table. Online, each quantum error-correction cycle observes a 5-bit syndrome per qubit and uses a tiny classifier (at most 10 LUTs per qubit—the basic logic building blocks on a chip) to recognize it in under 1 nanosecond, triggering recovery only for flagged patterns; GLADIATOR-D extends this with two cycles of syndrome history and works across surface, color, and qLDPC codes.
micro-2025-078.key_novelty: GLADIATOR uses a probabilistic graph-labeling framework with calibrated transition probabilities to distinguish leakage-induced syndrome patterns from regular-error patterns while reducing hardware overhead to 10 LUTs per qubit—versus 177–5393 for prior work—across different quantum error-correction codes.

micro-2025-093.method: Drishti improves how computer processors decide which data to keep in their largest caches (LLCs), which are split into slices per core. Today's best methods (Hawkeye and Mockingjay) only look within each slice separately, but Drishti adds two fixes: First, each core learns to predict data reuse by watching all its accesses across all slices—getting a complete view without needing extra communication between slices. Second, each slice automatically monitors more cache entries to ensure it sees enough misses to make good decisions. The improvements were tested on systems with 4, 16, and 32 cores, using caches of 8, 32, and 64 MB.
micro-2025-093.key_novelty: The core contribution is separating the reuse predictor (one per core, looking globally at all its accesses) from the cache monitoring (local to each slice), so policies can infer global reuse patterns without adding extra messages between slices.

micro-2025-091.method: When doing math with sparse tensors (large arrays where most values are zero), you organize the computation into smaller blocks called 'tiles' that fit in the computer's fast memory (cache). The best tile size depends on where the non-zero values are scattered, which varies for each input and isn't known when the code is written. This paper uses probability and statistics—building a model of typical sparsity patterns—to predict how the cache will perform with different tile sizes, then automatically selects the best one.
micro-2025-091.key_novelty: Using statistical models of sparsity patterns to predict cache behavior and automatically select the best tile size.

micro-2025-069.method: RTGS combines algorithm optimization with custom hardware to speed up SLAM rendering. On the software side, it removes unimportant Gaussians (3D point blobs) by reusing gradient calculations from training, and dynamically lowers image resolution for non-keyframe images from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on their distance to the nearest keyframe. The hardware is an 8.11-watt ASIC chip with three units: a Workload Scheduling Unit that reuses task patterns across frames for efficient load balancing, a Rendering & Backpropagation buffer that stores intermediate rendering values to avoid recomputation during training (cutting gradient time from 20 to 4 cycles), and a Gradient Merging Unit with a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree that efficiently aggregates gradient updates instead of using slower atomic operations. The chip operates at 500 MHz in 28 nm technology and occupies 28.41 mm².
micro-2025-069.key_novelty: Since SLAM's Gaussians remain fixed between tracking iterations, the system can reuse scheduling patterns (pixel-level pairwise scheduling) to achieve near-optimal load balancing with minimal hardware overhead.

micro-2025-089.method: OmniSim is a multi-threaded simulator running on intermediate code (LLVM IR) that solves a core mismatch: software threads are scheduled unpredictably by the operating system, but hardware runs on precise clock cycles. It classifies dataflow designs into three types (A: blocking-only; B: non-blocking or circular but single-behavior; C: non-blocking with behavior depending on FIFO access outcome) and applies different strategies to each. The key approach splits the simulator into Func Sim threads (one per dataflow module, running the program) and a dedicated Perf Sim thread (tracking when FIFO events occur in hardware cycles); when Func Sim threads encounter a non-blocking FIFO access, they consult FIFO timing tables for exact hardware-cycle timing rather than waiting for OS scheduling, and both thread types run concurrently for speed. An LLVM compiler pass instruments the code to track execution traces and rewrites dataflow functions to launch these concurrent threads, with incremental simulation supported so FIFO size changes don't require full restarts.
micro-2025-089.key_novelty: OmniSim's core idea is to synchronize non-blocking FIFO operations (reads/writes that don't wait for data) across functional and performance simulation threads using exact hardware-cycle timestamps from lookup tables, enabling correct simulation of previously unsupported Type B and C HLS dataflow designs (those with non-blocking accesses or circular dependencies) at near-C speed.

micro-2025-099.method: The system represents the quantum circuit as a dependency graph and uses a memory-management strategy to schedule qubit operations: storage zones act like slow disk, operation zones like fast memory, and optical zones like the CPU. It prioritizes gates that are immediately ready to execute, assigns each qubit to the nearest available zone, and when zones fill up, evicts the least-recently-used qubit to a lower zone—the same page-replacement strategy classical computers use. To reduce qubit movements across hardware modules, it looks eight circuit layers ahead and strategically inserts SWAP operations (which exchange two qubits' positions) to move qubits closer together. A bidirectional initial placement algorithm inspired by the standard SABRE method further reduces shuffling overhead.
micro-2025-099.key_novelty: It adapts classical computer cache management (specifically LRU replacement, which keeps frequently-used data fast and evicts rarely-used data to slower storage) to trapped-ion quantum systems by treating the three functional zones as a multi-level memory hierarchy.

micro-2025-103.method: LLM.265 repurposes the video codec hardware built into modern GPUs (H.265/HEVC engines) to compress neural network data. Neural network tensors—weights, activations, gradients, and KV cache (stored attention query/key vectors)—naturally contain redundancy similar to video: smooth regions, gradual changes, and correlated values. The system treats these tensors as video frames and applies the codec's standard compression stages to this structure: intra/inter prediction identifies patterns between neighbors, transform coding reorganizes data to expose structure, scalar quantization rounds values, and context-adaptive arithmetic coding encodes common patterns efficiently. Small hardware extensions to the existing video engine improve throughput without major GPU architectural changes.
micro-2025-103.key_novelty: It unifies compression of all neural network data types (weights, activations, gradients, KV cache) using existing GPU video codec hardware, eliminating the need for specialized compression accelerators.

micro-2025-113.method: The researchers tested 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips from three major manufacturers, systematically varying temperature, data patterns, and memory timing parameters (tRCD, tRAS, tRP—specific delays between memory operations) to trigger bitflips (bit errors). They measured how quickly the first bitflip occurred and how many rows were affected under normal 63.6-millisecond refresh intervals (the time window when memory refreshes stored data). By simulating the detailed circuit behavior and comparing against normal data-loss rates, they demonstrated how this disturbance could undermine power-saving strategies that skip refreshes for cells known to retain data reliably.
micro-2025-113.key_novelty: This is the first detailed experimental study of ColumnDisturb, a disturbance where a single activated memory row can damage cells across up to 3 subarrays (sections of a chip) through shared electrical paths (bitlines/columns), affecting far more rows at once than RowHammer.

micro-2025-097.method: REACT3D accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting through two algorithmic optimizations and a hardware buffer design. First, it identifies fully-trained 3D point clouds (Gaussians) by checking their spatial spread and training convergence, skipping redundant rendering passes, and merges loss calculation (the measure of prediction error) into the rendering pipeline through a pixel block-wise dataflow instead of storing it separately. The hardware uses content-addressable memory (special silicon that retrieves data by matching its contents rather than using addresses) with two parallel index tables to resolve memory conflicts when combining training updates across scattered point-to-pixel mappings.
micro-2025-097.key_novelty: The dual-index Gaussian Buffer, built with content-addressable memory hardware that retrieves data by content rather than address, that resolves irregular memory access and gradient-merging conflicts when training 3D point clouds from streaming camera feeds.

micro-2025-105.method: Bootes reorders rows of the input matrix so that rows needing the same data sit next to each other in memory. It uses spectral clustering (a technique that groups similar items based on structural patterns) guided by a map of which data each row needs; placing similar rows together lets the accelerator reuse data already loaded from memory, cutting wasteful traffic. The clustering algorithm is optimized to run 11.61x faster than previous reordering methods. Before rearranging anything, a decision tree trained on real-world matrices checks whether the reordering will actually help; if not, it skips the preprocessing to avoid wasting time on an optimization that wouldn't improve performance.
micro-2025-105.key_novelty: Applying spectral clustering to reorder sparse matrix rows based on which data they share in common, combined with a decision tree that automatically skips reordering when it wouldn't improve memory efficiency.

micro-2025-081.method: For atomic operations (read-modify-write instructions used for synchronization) on distant data, Delegated AMOs execute the operation at the current data owner without moving data, while Migrating AMOs transfer ownership to the requester (useful if the requester will access it again). Six static policies (All-Central, All-Migrate, Present-Central, Pinned-Owner, Unowned-Central, Chiplet-Aware) determine which approach fits based on data location. Delegato improves this by tracking a one-bit reuse flag that the directory's Predictor Table uses to learn access patterns and adapt between three strategies (Pinned-Owner, Present-Central, Chiplet-Aware). Testing used gem5 23.1, AMBA 5 CHI protocol, 32 out-of-order cores across two 16-core chiplets, and HeteroGarnet.
micro-2025-081.key_novelty: Delegated and Migrating AMO coherence transactions that allow operations to execute at the cache-line owner without moving data, paired with Delegato—a one-bit reuse tracker that feeds access patterns to the directory's predictor to enable adaptive strategy selection.

micro-2025-106.method: Misam uses a lightweight machine learning classifier to predict the optimal dataflow—the computation strategy—for sparse matrices by analyzing sparsity characteristics like density and distribution patterns. Rather than building a single fixed accelerator, it runs on FPGAs, which are programmable chips that can be reconfigured, and selectively loads specialized hardware designs optimized for each sparsity regime. Before reconfiguring, the system checks whether the predicted performance gain justifies the overhead of loading the new design.
micro-2025-106.key_novelty: Misam's core idea is dynamic hardware specialization: machine learning predicts the best computation strategy for each sparse matrix, and FPGA partial reconfiguration loads specialized hardware for that strategy instead of simultaneously supporting all approaches.

micro-2025-109.method: StreamTensor is an MLIR-based compiler that represents tensor data flow through kernels using iterative tensor types (itensors), which encode element shape, iteration space, and data-access order—capturing exactly how each kernel reads and writes data. It converts high-level tensor operations into a dataflow graph via Linalg tiling, automatically fuses kernels with matching itensor types directly via FIFOs, and inserts minimal data-format converters (ping-pong buffers) where types mismatch; it then merges adjacent buffers and aligns FIFO bandwidth with kernel parallelism through vectorization. The compiler analytically sizes buffers from itensor patterns and solves a scheduling problem via linear programming to prevent deadlocks while minimizing depth. Finally, it searches across kernel tiling, fusion, and resource-allocation choices using blackbox optimization (Optuna), intensity-aware unrolling, and permutation heuristics.
micro-2025-109.key_novelty: StreamTensor's iterative tensor (itensor) type system captures each kernel's streaming data-access order, enabling a compiler to automatically fuse kernels via FIFOs, generate minimal data converters, and mathematically size buffers to prevent deadlocks on dataflow accelerators.

micro-2025-096.method: MCBP operates at bit-granularity, breaking weights into individual bit layers to find structure that coarser approaches miss. First, it identifies repeated bit patterns within groups of weights using a special memory unit (CAM) and reuses their computations (achieving 12.1x speedup), while also compressing high-order bits (3-7 in INT8 format) that are over 65% sparse into a two-state code, leaving lower bits uncompressed. Second, it filters the cache of computed values by progressively estimating attention scores bit-by-bit from most to least significant, eliminating entries that won't help the final answer after each step and reducing cache accesses by up to 50%.
micro-2025-096.key_novelty: MCBP's novelty is working at bit-layer granularity to jointly address all three LLM inference bottlenecks with a single design by exploiting fine-grained structure: repeated bit patterns (12.1x computation reduction), high-order bits in INT8 (bits 3-7 over 65% sparse, enabling two-state compression), and progressive bit-by-bit attention scoring (50% KV cache reduction) that value-granular accelerators cannot access.

micro-2025-115.method: The researchers built optimized x86-64 CPU code for NTT and large-integer BLAS (which perform arithmetic on very large numbers), then applied SIMD vectorization—a technique where the CPU processes multiple data points in parallel using AVX2 and AVX-512 instructions—to reach 38x and 62x speedups respectively over the previous best CPU implementations. They found that specialized cryptographic chips (ASICs) still outperform CPUs because they have hardware built-in for multi-precision modular arithmetic (the core mathematical operations in these algorithms), so they designed MQX: a small x86 extension that adds three instructions targeting these operations. MQX reduces the per-core gap to 35x, and their analysis shows that when large server CPUs with MQX use multiple cores, they can approach ASIC-level performance.
micro-2025-115.key_novelty: MQX, an x86 extension adding three AVX-512 instructions for multi-precision modular arithmetic (the large-number mathematical operations at the core of cryptographic algorithms), closes most of the remaining performance gap between standard CPUs and specialized cryptographic chips for NTT and large-integer BLAS.

micro-2025-092.method: FALA combines two processing approaches: a CPU with its cache, and processing-in-memory (PIM—computing hardware built into DRAM banks). It uses fine-grained column access to let the system fetch only the specific columns (graph vertices) it actually needs, rather than full DRAM rows, which eliminates bandwidth waste from pulling data you don't actually use. A locality-aware policy routes frequently-used vertex data through the CPU cache, while irregular accesses get processed directly near-memory via PIM. This combined strategy cuts unnecessary memory traffic while fully utilizing both DRAM bandwidth and CPU cache.
micro-2025-092.key_novelty: The core innovation is a fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM banks (allowing selective access to individual vertices instead of full rows) combined with a locality-aware policy that routes frequently-accessed vertex data through the host CPU cache and irregular accesses through processing-in-memory.

mlsys-2025-000.method: FlashInfer unifies different KV-cache layouts—ragged, paged, and tree-structured—through a single Block-Sparse Row (BSR) format, allowing all layouts to use the same computation path. It decomposes attention calculations into shared-prefix and unique-suffix portions, combining partial softmax results to reuse work across requests. For each attention variant (GQA, MLA, sliding-window), a JIT compiler generates optimized CUDA code templates once on first request, then reuses the compiled binaries for all subsequent requests. Finally, a load-balanced scheduler distributes computation work to GPU thread blocks using a priority queue, wrapped in a static layer to remain compatible with CUDAGraph (static CUDA execution graphs).
mlsys-2025-000.key_novelty: FlashInfer solves the problem of diverse KV-cache layouts by introducing a single Block-Sparse Row format that represents ragged, paged, and tree-structured layouts uniformly, while maintaining compatibility with CUDAGraph (static GPU execution graphs) through a static priority queue wrapper that enables dynamic load balancing.

mlsys-2025-001.method: FLStore builds a cache that sits between applications and data storage, placing computation right next to the cached data to avoid latency. A hash-table-based Cache Engine spreads data across cache nodes and sends requests to whichever node holds the needed data using locality-aware key hashing (a method that keeps related data together). A Request Tracker watches how each client accesses data over time to spot frequently-used data ('hot data'). The system uses four caching policies, each designed for a different type of federated learning workload: P1 stores each client's model updates by round, P2 caches the aggregated (combined) models, P3 saves derived information like gradients and loss values across rounds, and P4 pre-loads data it predicts will be requested next.
mlsys-2025-001.key_novelty: FLStore avoids the bottleneck of a central aggregator by analyzing how federated learning workloads access data, deriving four specialized caching policies, and running computation directly on cache nodes that hold the relevant data.

micro-2025-114.method: TransFusion represents the entire Transformer layer stack as Einsum Cascades—a structured graph of mathematical operations that captures which data each operation needs and when it runs. The DPipe scheduler divides this graph and runs different layers in parallel (pipelining), using dynamic programming to find the arrangement that makes FFN and attention stages as fast as possible together. TileSeek, using Monte Carlo Tree Search to explore many random solutions and find good ones, determines how to break computations into chunks on cloud and edge hardware, balancing on-chip memory constraints against data reuse.
micro-2025-114.key_novelty: Representing the entire Transformer encoder/decoder stack as Einsum Cascades—one mathematical graph—and optimizing inter-layer data movement, intra-layer pipelining, and scheduling end-to-end through dynamic programming (DPipe) and Monte Carlo Tree Search (TileSeek), instead of optimizing each component in isolation.

micro-2025-118.method: The paper tests a commercial GSI APU—a processor with 2 million 1-bit processors, 500 MHz speed, 25 TOPS compute power, 26 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, and a memory hierarchy (12MB L1, 64KB L2, 1MB L3, 16GB main memory)—using realistic AI workloads (Phoenix benchmark suite) and matrix tests. The researchers built a Python tool to identify where data movement creates bottlenecks across the memory hierarchy, then validated three optimizations on real hardware: (1) rerouting expensive data through cheaper scalar-vector operations (multiplying a single value by many values) instead of slow parallel reductions, (2) eliminating redundant data copies that accumulate across loop iterations, and (3) shrinking broadcast lookup table sizes from K×N to N entries to reduce latency. All three were demonstrated on information retrieval tasks over 10-200GB datasets.
micro-2025-118.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive real-hardware evaluation of a commercial compute-in-SRAM processor (processors that compute directly with stored data: GSI APU) on realistic AI workloads, showing that even with this architecture, data movement becomes the bottleneck without optimization, and demonstrating three optimizations reaching maximum performance.

mlsys-2025-010.method: In pipeline-parallel training, GPUs process data in stages that sometimes pause, leaving compute time wasted—these idle gaps are called bubbles. PipeFill uses this wasted time to run secondary work: batch inference or small model training that can complete during the pause. It introduces three components to make this work: a Pipeline Bubble Instruction (PBI, a description of what fill work is allowed), a Fill Job Executor (which assigns fill work to idle GPU moments), and a Fill Job Scheduler (which tracks when bubbles occur and sends work to them). The implementation uses DeepSpeed with GPipe and 1F1B schedule strategies.
mlsys-2025-010.key_novelty: PipeFill is the first system to systematically exploit pipeline bubbles (idle GPU time in pipeline-parallel training) for secondary workloads by introducing the Pipeline Bubble Instruction abstraction, which describes secondary work independently of the primary training schedule.

micro-2025-104.method: ReGate cuts energy waste in NPU chips (neural processing units) by powering off unused components using hardware and software controls adapted to each type. In the systolic array (a grid of processors performing neural-network multiplications), it detects which rows and columns have zero weights (multiply-by-zero operations) and powers them off; the power-on signal propagates diagonally, matching how data naturally flows through the array, so processors wake up at exactly the right moment with only single-processor latency. For memory controllers—ICI (inter-chip interconnect) and HBM (high-bandwidth memory)—a hardware detector recognizes idle periods between collective operations like AllReduce and AllGather and gates them off. For vector units and SRAM scratchpad (on-chip memory), the compiler uses a new ISA extension with setpm instructions in three modes (on/auto/off) to insert power-management commands at statically-known idle points determined from instruction scheduling and memory analysis.
micro-2025-104.key_novelty: The key innovation is exploiting the natural diagonal data flow of weight-stationary neural-network computation—where weights stay fixed in the array while data flows diagonally—to synchronize individual processor power-on signals in the systolic array, achieving processor-level power-gating with only single-processor wake-up latency.

mlsys-2025-008.method: DiffServe routes requests through a lightweight model first, then uses a classifier (EfficientNet-V2) to decide if the result is good enough or should be redone by the heavyweight model; the classifier was trained on real photographs (MSCOCO) and generated images, with the counterintuitive finding that training with only real photos as 'good' works better than also using heavyweight outputs. A controller periodically solves an optimization equation (Mixed Integer Linear Program) that adjusts device counts, batch sizes, and the classifier's confidence threshold to meet latency and throughput targets as demand fluctuates (tracked via exponential smoothing with 5% safety margin), solving asynchronously in ~10ms outside the serving path.
mlsys-2025-008.key_novelty: DiffServe combines a real-or-fake image classifier (EfficientNet-V2) trained on real photographs versus generated images to intelligently route queries between lightweight and heavyweight diffusion models, paired with an optimization algorithm that jointly adjusts confidence thresholds, batch sizes, and device allocation to meet quality and throughput targets under changing demand.

mlsys-2025-002.method: TileLink provides tile-level operations—high-level building blocks like 'notify when tile is ready' or 'move tile between GPUs'—so you don't have to write complex GPU code by hand. The system automatically compiles these operations by deciding tile sizes, assigning tiles to GPU ranks (using formulas or runtime lookups), and selecting communication channels (NVLink or InfiniBand). It generates GPU code where compute and communication threads run side-by-side in the same kernel, overlapping data movement and calculations to reduce network delays.
mlsys-2025-002.key_novelty: TileLink's core idea is a tile-level primitive abstraction that separates compute and communication concerns, automatically compiles to overlapping kernels via shape/rank/channel mappings, and achieves expert-level performance with ~10 times less code than hand-written CUDA.

mlsys-2025-009.method: Instead of using inefficient scattered operations to extract embeddings one-by-one, SparseTransX reformulates training as a single sparse matrix multiplication. It encodes each training fact as a row in a sparse matrix with +1 and -1 markers showing which embeddings to add or subtract, then multiplies this sparse matrix against the dense embedding table to compute all predictions at once for both forward prediction and backward gradient phases. The approach supports four translation-based embedding models (TransE, TransR, TransH, TorusE) and uses optimized sparse libraries: iSpLib with SIMD vectorization for CPUs and DGL's g-SpMM for GPUs, including support for distributed training via PyTorch's DDP and FSDP.
mlsys-2025-009.key_novelty: SparseTransX replaces the scattered embedding lookups that bottleneck knowledge graph embedding training with a single sparse matrix multiplication, by encoding all training facts into one sparse matrix that extracts the needed embeddings in one unified operation.

mlsys-2025-005.method: The paper exploits Python's shared global variables to demonstrate supply-chain attacks on machine learning systems. A malicious package can rewrite PyTorch or TorchVision settings (interpolation modes, softmax functions, model forward methods) at import time, or use Python's inspect module and a low-level C API to modify function variables, enabling three attack types: backdoor injection via model hijacking, pipeline breaking via interpolation swaps, and model weight theft via steganography. The authors measure security awareness using GPT-3.5 (97.8% recall) then GPT-4 (78.9% precision, 0.85 Cohen's kappa) to analyze 549,635 GitHub issues/PRs from the 50 largest ML repositories, compared against the 50 largest Linux repositories.
mlsys-2025-005.key_novelty: Python's shared memory—where packages can modify each other's code—enables attackers to build supply-chain attacks that secretly change machine learning models without triggering existing security tools, confirmed by LLM-assisted analysis of 549,635 GitHub issues.

mlsys-2025-007.method: This study tests four KV cache compression methods (ways to shrink memory storing past conversation data): KIVI and GEAR both reduce number precision, with GEAR adding error correction; StreamingLLM keeps only certain data; H2O discards less-important data based on attention scores. It measures their performance on three production scenarios standard benchmarks miss: (1) speed when running through serving systems like LMDeploy with PagedAttention and FlashAttention optimizations, across different batch sizes and model sizes (LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-70B); (2) how response length changes, measured across 1000 real conversations; and (3) cases where compression reduces accuracy by more than 10%, grouped by task type (summarization, question-answering, code, few-shot, synthetic). It provides three practical deployment tools: a throughput predictor, a response-length predictor (a BERT-based classifier), and a benchmark dataset of compression failures.
mlsys-2025-007.key_novelty: The study identifies three overlooked dimensions for evaluating KV compression in production: speed under real serving systems, changes in response length, and which specific inputs lose accuracy—and provides tools to measure each one.

mlsys-2025-006.method: ProtoRAIL encodes CPU usage sequences using a neural network (LSTM or Transformer) into embeddings, then groups them into K prototypes representing typical VM behavior; oversubscription decisions are made by comparing how similar current usage is to each prototype. It learns from expert decisions via imitation learning (behavior cloning or adversarial training) while pursuing four goals: keeping prototypes close to real data, far apart from each other, grounded in actual trajectories for interpretability, and good at predicting actual demand. When it encounters uncertain situations (mixed or overlapping prototypes) or risky predictions (predicted oversubscription below actual usage), it asks domain experts to vote on prototypes, suggest actions, or restructure clusters (merge/split), then automatically adjusts how strongly each training goal is weighted to apply this feedback—only requesting help when genuinely uncertain or risky.
mlsys-2025-006.key_novelty: Interpretable prototype-based imitation learning where experts can minimize risk by voting on and restructuring pattern clusters, requiring minimal feedback queries.

mlsys-2025-004.method: Marconi maintains a tree structure (a radix tree) that stores cached data for attention layers (KV-cache blocks) and SSM layers (state checkpoints). Before processing the input, it speculatively identifies points in the tree where SSM state checkpoints are needed. It only keeps two types of cached prefixes: those shared unchanged across conversations (system prompts, shared context) and those varying per conversation (multi-turn history). When cache fills, eviction uses a score combining recency with FLOP-efficiency (computing power saved per byte stored), prioritizing high-return entries and only deleting leaves or single-child nodes to avoid invalidating subtrees.
mlsys-2025-004.key_novelty: Marconi caches prefixes in hybrid Attention+SSM LLMs using a FLOP-efficiency eviction metric that measures computing power saved per byte stored and speculatively identifies SSM checkpointing points before prefill.

mlsys-2025-013.method: AIOpsLab sets up a standard way for AI agents to interact with a realistic cloud system: it uses DeathStarBench, a microservice testbed that deliberately breaks services using ChaosMesh, measures what happens through Prometheus (a metrics collector), and tracks requests across services with Jaeger (distributed tracing). The system tests agents on 100 problems organized into four levels: detecting that a fault occurred, pinpointing where it happened, analyzing why it happened (root-cause analysis), and applying a fix. Faults come in two types—symptomatic ones where you can observe the problem but don't know its source, and functional ones where the root cause is specified. The best-performing agent, FLASH, achieves 59.32% accuracy on these tasks.
mlsys-2025-013.key_novelty: This provides the first comprehensive system for evaluating AI agents in cloud operations, combining a standardized Agent-Cloud Interface, realistic fault injection in microservices, and a four-level task taxonomy (detect, localize, analyze root cause, mitigate) spanning the full incident response workflow.

mlsys-2025-014.method: A new RISC-V machine instruction called xDecimate accelerates N:M sparse operations (patterns where every M numbers contain exactly N non-zeros) in a single hardware step. The method uses Decimate Im2col to reformulate convolution (the core operation in neural networks) so that xDecimate can process the reshaped feature maps, with the MATCH compiler automatically generating the optimized code. The design was synthesized at 22nm technology for the Vega PULP system-on-chip (the basis for commercial GAP9 chips), and evaluated on ResNet-18 and ViT networks at 1:4, 1:8, and 1:16 sparsity ratios.
mlsys-2025-014.key_novelty: xDecimate is the first RISC-V instruction specifically designed to accelerate N:M sparse patterns (1:4 to 1:16 sparsity where only a fraction of each group is non-zero) at just 5% area overhead on commercial chips.

mlsys-2025-011.method: Conformal prediction creates calibrated prediction sets for multimodal inputs, measuring uncertainty from noisy or ambiguous sensor data. Decision uncertainty is modeled using Formally-specified Markov Decision Processes (FMDP)—mathematical decision models that map possible states (using Kripke structures) and verify behavior follows formal rules via temporal logic specifications. When sensor uncertainty is high, the system automatically requests additional observations; when decision uncertainty is high, it automatically refines its model. The approach was tested on LLaVA-1.5-7B and CLIP models using the Carla driving simulator and real-world driving data.
mlsys-2025-011.key_novelty: This is the first framework to separately measure and address perception uncertainty (sensor and input noise via conformal prediction) and decision uncertainty (model reasoning via Formally-specified Markov Decision Processes with Kripke structures and temporal logic), enabling targeted fixes for each type in multimodal robotic systems.

mlsys-2025-012.method: The algorithm distributes the dataset across many computers (workers). Each worker independently estimates how valuable each remaining data point would be to add to the selection (called marginal gains), using upper and lower bound estimates that tighten through grow and shrink steps based on each point's minimum and maximum potential value—without workers needing to send data to each other. Over multiple rounds, the algorithm redistributes data across workers and combines their selections into a global result, running on Apache Beam for large-scale distributed execution.
mlsys-2025-012.key_novelty: The algorithm computes provably tight bounds on marginal gains (how much each data point would improve the selection) distributed across many computers rather than centralizing everything, enabling selection quality nearly matching a centralized greedy algorithm without requiring one machine to hold all billion data points in memory.

mlsys-2025-021.method: The approach combines HQQ-based INT3 quantization (storing weights as 3-bit integers without calibration data) with adaptive low-rank compensators that use SVD (a matrix decomposition) to recover lost accuracy. For each layer, the compensator's complexity is chosen based on three factors: dense vs sparse layer type, weight distribution (kurtosis), and expert activation frequency. Both the quantized weights and compensators are jointly optimized and packed into INT3 format. The method includes a custom GPU kernel (W3A16 Tensor Core GeMM) that efficiently runs these 3-bit weights with multiple inputs at once through zero-bit-waste INT3 packing, fast binary-manipulation integer-to-float conversion, and asynchronous weight loading.
mlsys-2025-021.key_novelty: It provides the first GPU kernel proven to speed up mixture-of-experts models when processing multiple inputs at once using 3-bit weights, while recovering accuracy through calibration-free adaptive weight correction.

mlsys-2025-017.method: Dynamic Input Pruning (DIP) saves DRAM bandwidth by selecting only the K largest input values entering the MLP layer—a process called top-K selection based on input magnitude (the size of the numbers)—and ignoring the rest, which means you don't need to load weight columns for inputs you're skipping. Instead of using a separate predictor network to decide what to keep, DIP simply looks at input magnitudes directly. A cache-aware variant called DIP-CA goes further: it uses a gamma multiplier (gamma=0.2) to prefer keeping weight columns that are already in the device's fast cache, reducing how often the device needs to fetch data from DRAM. Testing on Apple A18 processors (60 GB/s DRAM, 1 GB/s Flash) with Phi-3-Medium and LLaMA models showed the approach works, and LoRA fine-tuning can recover any accuracy lost.
mlsys-2025-017.key_novelty: Predictor-free pruning based on input magnitude (the size of incoming values) that simultaneously removes weights from all three MLP matrices, plus a cache-aware variant (DIP-CA) that prioritizes keeping already-cached weights to reduce DRAM fetches.

mlsys-2025-019.method: Bio-FO trains networks layer-by-layer using only forward passes, without any backward error propagation. At each hidden layer, an auxiliary classifier (a small neural network attached to that layer) uses the layer's output and a fixed random matrix to estimate how well that layer is performing, computing a local error and updating weights based only on adjacent layer activations. This prevents needing error signals from deeper layers and simultaneously eliminates four biological implausibilities: it doesn't require symmetric feedback weights (weight transport), error signals stay local (non-locality), layers update immediately as data arrives (update locking), and activations don't pile up in memory (frozen activities). The method supports locally-connected and convolutional networks through sparsity masking.
mlsys-2025-019.key_novelty: This is the first forward-only training algorithm to simultaneously solve all four biological implausibility problems of backpropagation (weight transport, non-locality, update locking, and frozen activities) while outperforming prior forward-only methods (FF, PEPITA, DRTP) and achieving 3x memory reduction and up to 19.8x energy reduction.

mlsys-2025-020.method: Pitot uses a pair of neural networks that together apply matrix factorization—a technique for estimating missing values by decomposing data—to predict runtime. The networks take two types of information as input: features describing the workload's instructions (opcode counts) and specifications of the hardware platform. The system adds a low-rank bilinear interference term (a compact mathematical component modeling how multiple simultaneous workloads slow each other by competing for resources) directly into the learned representation. It's trained by minimizing log-scale prediction errors and provides confidence intervals via conformalized quantile regression with optimal quantile selection, calibrated separately for each platform type.
mlsys-2025-020.key_novelty: Pitot integrates the interference model—the mathematical component capturing how concurrent workloads slow each other—directly into the matrix factorization embedding space via a low-rank bilinear term, enabling joint estimation of missing runtime values and interference effects from sparse observations.

mlsys-2025-015.method: Instead of hand-writing separate kernels for each attention variant, users write two simple Python functions: one that modifies attention scores (like adding ALiBi bias) and one that specifies which token pairs should attend to each other. A BlockMask structure precomputes which blocks of computation can be skipped (called sparsity), enabling a sparse version of FlashAttention. PyTorch's compiler then converts these functions into a single optimized Triton kernel by combining them into one tiled operation—matrix multiply, softmax, matrix multiply—that skips any fully-masked blocks.
mlsys-2025-015.key_novelty: A composable Python API combining BlockMask and two modifier functions lets the compiler automatically generate optimized Triton kernels for any attention variant, achieving near-FlashAttention-2 performance for standard cases and major speedups for unsupported ones—paged-attention overhead drops to under 1% versus 20-26% in vLLM.

mlsys-2025-016.method: The system groups tokens into two categories: those whose validity depends only on grammar (precomputed offline before inference) and those that depend on where the parser currently is (checked during decoding). For Llama-3.1 generating JSON, only 1,134 out of 128,000 tokens need runtime checking—under 1%. The system tracks parsing progress using a state machine (technically a persistent pushdown automaton, the standard technique for tracking nested structures) and shrinks runtime-checked tokens to about 120 through context expansion (a 90% reduction). Token masks are cached per parser state using just 0.2% extra memory, with remaining runtime checks hidden behind GPU work.
mlsys-2025-016.key_novelty: By splitting tokens into grammar-determined (>99% precomputable offline) and context-determined types, and handling context-dependent tokens with a persistent pushdown automaton (state machine for parse tracking) and adaptive token mask caching, XGrammar eliminates nearly all constrained decoding overhead.

mlsys-2025-023.method: ThunderServe uses two optimization levels to split LLM serving across heterogeneous GPUs: tabu search (an algorithm that explores solutions while avoiding previous dead-ends) partitions the GPU pool and assigns groups to prefill-phase (processing input) or decode-phase (generating output), while linear programming determines how to split the model within each group and route requests. Compute-heavy prefill work goes to fast GPUs like A40s, while decode work needing fast memory access goes to high-bandwidth GPUs like 3090Tis. The system compresses intermediate data to 4 bits during inter-phase transfer to reduce network congestion and adjusts assignments dynamically when traffic changes.
mlsys-2025-023.key_novelty: It's the first system to split LLM serving between prefill and decode phases and assign each phase to different GPU types optimized for that phase in cloud environments with low-bandwidth interconnects between GPUs.

mlsys-2025-022.method: TASD (Tensor Approximation via Structured Decomposition) breaks any randomly-scattered sparse weights down into a series of structured patterns (where exactly N out of M values are non-zero) that can run efficiently on GPU accelerators. For weights, an offline greedy search (trying combinations and keeping the best) finds the decomposition minimizing dropped values while maintaining 99% model accuracy. For activations (data flowing through during inference), the system picks the right pattern dynamically based on how sparse the data is. Custom hardware (TTC) extends existing accelerators to support multiple N:M patterns simultaneously, while optimizations keep data blocks stationary to spread the decomposition cost across many operations.
mlsys-2025-022.key_novelty: This is the first method that enables unstructured sparse neural networks to run on structured sparse hardware without retraining, by decomposing weights into a series of structured patterns using the distributive property of matrix algebra.

mlsys-2025-027.method: LAVA uses a machine learning model (gradient boosted decision tree) trained on VM features (zone, family, shape, SSD, project metadata) to continuously estimate remaining VM lifetime based on how long it's already run—updating its guess as time passes instead of guessing once at startup. The model compiles into the Borg scheduler to run in <10 microseconds (780x faster than previous systems). Three algorithms use these predictions: NILAS picks hosts where running VMs are predicted to exit soonest; LAVA marks each host as open or recycling and switches modes when predictions are wrong; and LARS defragments by migrating longest-lived VMs first, letting shorter ones exit naturally.
mlsys-2025-027.key_novelty: LAVA is the first production system to continuously update VM lifetime predictions as they run and adapt scheduling decisions when predictions are wrong, showing that this approach works better than guessing once at startup.

mlsys-2025-026.method: Lumos records detailed execution traces from LLM training runs using PyTorch's Kineto profiler (about 10 lines of instrumentation code), capturing CPU operations, GPU kernels, and CUDA runtime events. It builds a task dependency graph that maps what must happen in sequence: CPU-to-CPU work (cudaLaunchKernel), CPU-to-GPU (correlation IDs), GPU-to-CPU synchronization (cudaStreamSync), and GPU-to-GPU coordination across parallel streams (cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent). The graph can be modified to simulate parallelism strategy, architecture, or layer configuration changes, then replayed to estimate performance under those new conditions.
mlsys-2025-026.key_novelty: Lumos is the first to accurately model how GPU operations on parallel streams overlap computation and communication (via cudaEventRecord/cudaStreamWaitEvent), achieving 3.3% average error and enabling what-if analysis for parallelism and architecture changes.

mlsys-2025-024.method: NEO overlaps GPU and CPU execution by splitting each inference iteration into two request groups that run simultaneously. The GPU group processes prefill requests and most decode requests through a linear projection stage, while the CPU group handles attention (reviewing previous context tokens) on the same requests using optimized parallel kernels. The key-value cache — data from prior computation — is split across GPU memory (fast) and main memory, with transfers timed to overlap with GPU computation. A scheduler pre-measures operation durations, uses linear interpolation to estimate costs, and greedily assigns requests per iteration to maximize throughput.
mlsys-2025-024.key_novelty: The innovation is asymmetric sub-batching: combining prefill and most decode on the GPU to lengthen its work phase, allowing the CPU's attention phase to run simultaneously without creating pipeline gaps.

mlsys-2025-018.method: SOLA treats LLM request scheduling as a constrained optimization problem solved at each serving step, dynamically deciding which requests to serve, how many to bundle, and how many tokens to generate. Unlike systems with fixed priorities, SOLA continuously monitors actual performance—how long until the first response token arrives (TTFT) and how long between subsequent tokens (TPOT)—and picks the right strategy for each step: either minimize the longest gap between tokens while keeping first-token latency acceptable, or minimize the longest first-token latency while keeping between-token time acceptable. It executes this strategy through hierarchical prioritization (first among processing phases—prefill for input processing, decode for token generation—then among requests) using polynomial latency models that refine from real measurements, implemented in vLLM v0.4.2.
mlsys-2025-018.key_novelty: Rather than using fixed scheduling priorities, SOLA formulates LLM request scheduling as a constrained optimization problem that it solves fresh at each serving step, dynamically choosing whether to prioritize minimizing first-token latency or per-token latency based on real-time feedback about request states and system resources.

mlsys-2025-025.method: TurboAttention shrinks memory and computation by using smaller numbers instead of full-precision floats. FlashQ quantizes the query/key/value matrices to 8-bit integers for matrix multiplication, then compresses the key/value cache down to 2-4 bits—assigning 2-bit precision to the least important attention heads and 4-bit to the rest based on variability metrics—compressing every 64 steps. SAS (Sparse Activated Softmax) approximates the expensive exponential calculation using a lookup table for the integer part and a degree-3 polynomial for the decimal part. This runs on Tensor Cores in half-precision and treats near-zero attention scores as exactly zero, so the entire attention operation can stay in 8-bit integers and half-precision.
mlsys-2025-025.key_novelty: TurboAttention is the first to combine FlashAttention's efficient tiling method with low-precision quantization, letting both the matrix multiplication and softmax of attention run entirely on GPU Tensor Cores in 8-bit and half-precision, avoiding slow full-precision computation.

mlsys-2025-029.method: The method reorders rows and fields to maximize KV cache prefix hits—reusing previously computed results when the same data patterns repeat. It uses two algorithms: OPHR (Optimal Prefix Hit Recursion) recursively splits the table by distinct field values for the mathematically optimal ordering but is exponentially slow, while GGR (Greedy Group Recursion) approximates this by greedily selecting the highest-impact field and value at each step. GGR further optimizes by using functional dependencies to group related fields and value statistics to skip unnecessary work, processing tables up to 30K rows with 57 fields in under 15 seconds via PySpark and vLLM.
mlsys-2025-029.key_novelty: The key contribution is using relational database structure—how fields depend on each other, and value distributions—to reorder rows and fields, so language models can reuse more previously computed results when processing data in batches.

mlsys-2025-030.method: In RLHF training, the model serves four different roles (actor, critic, reference model, and reward model) with different GPU and memory needs. Instead of using one fixed GPU arrangement for all, this system moves the model's parameters between GPUs between stages—each role can use the GPU layout optimized for it. The system uses MCMC (a statistical method that efficiently explores configuration options) to automatically find the best way to arrange GPUs for each stage and the order to run them.
mlsys-2025-030.key_novelty: Instead of keeping model parameters in one fixed GPU arrangement throughout the training pipeline, this redistributes them between RLHF stages to match each stage's needs, using MCMC to find the optimal redistribution and execution order.

mlsys-2025-031.method: The system fits LLM inference on power-constrained FPGAs by reorganizing attention calculations and compressing weights. It processes attention by handling multiple tokens (input pieces) in parallel while sequencing through heads (sub-units of attention) one at a time, which keeps all needed data in the chip's fast on-board cache instead of repeatedly fetching from slow external memory. For weight tensors, it identifies repeating chunks and compresses them based on frequency—high-frequency chunks stay lightly compressed for speed, low-frequency ones get aggressively compressed to reduce memory traffic to external storage. All numbers are also stored as 8-bit integers (W8A8 quantization) to minimize the overall memory footprint.
mlsys-2025-031.key_novelty: The core contribution is combining token-parallel head-sequential attention processing with frequency-based weight compression (compressing rarely-used weight patterns more aggressively than frequently-used ones) to enable LLM inference on sub-10W FPGAs, achieving 1.5-2.5x speedup over conventional matrix-multiply approaches.

mlsys-2025-032.method: For each state, it maintains a sorted ranking (max-heap) of upper-bound reward estimates for each possible action, and discards actions whose upper bounds fall below the current best lower bound after each update. It provides four variants combining different optimizations: VIH (heap only), VIAE (updating states one at a time rather than all together), VIAEH (combining both approaches), and VIAEHL (with a look-ahead step). All exploit the monotone nature of value estimates—they improve or stay constant across iterations—which ensures the action pruning is always correct.
mlsys-2025-032.key_novelty: It eliminates dominated actions using a sorted list of upper bounds during value iteration, relying on value estimates that only improve (never decrease) over iterations to avoid pre-analyzing the action space.

mlsys-2025-036.method: Photon trains large language models across separate data centers by having each training site perform multiple local gradient steps before sending parameter updates to a central Aggregator server, rather than synchronizing after every step. This works because federated averaging—averaging updates from many sites—is naturally robust to local changes, enabling each site to use smaller batches with higher learning rates; this combination improves learning through noise injection that helps generalization. The system automatically adapts its communication method (centralized parameter server, AllReduce, or Ring-AllReduce) and local parallelization strategy (DDP, FSDP, or sub-federation) based on network connectivity between data centers.
mlsys-2025-036.key_novelty: Photon successfully trains billion-parameter language models across multiple data centers at the same quality as single-datacenter training by using federated averaging's robustness to combine small batch sizes with high learning rates, reaching 2x faster convergence than DiLoCo.

mlsys-2025-028.method: Venn is a centralized scheduler for federated learning that uses two algorithms. Intersection Resource Scheduling (IRS) groups jobs by device type, sorts jobs within each group by remaining work (shortest first), and allocates devices to the group with the most waiting jobs relative to available resources, prioritizing groups needing scarce hardware (O(max(m log m, n^2)) complexity). A tier-based matcher then partitions devices into V capability levels and randomly assigns jobs to tiers, only engaging tier-matching when it reduces job completion time (1 + c > V + c*g). Fairness logic adjusts job priorities to prevent starvation.
mlsys-2025-028.key_novelty: It formalizes and solves the Intersection Resource Scheduling problem for federated learning—where job device needs can overlap, contain, or nest within each other—using a strategy aware of device contention (how often multiple jobs need the same hardware) that jointly reduces job startup delays and response collection time.

mlsys-2025-035.method: GSplit pre-computes an optimal GPU assignment for graph vertices during an offline phase by sampling graph patterns to estimate which vertices and edges are used together frequently, then using METIS (a graph partitioning algorithm that minimizes edges crossing between groups) to assign vertices to GPUs accordingly. At training time, each sampled mini-batch is instantly partitioned by looking up each vertex's pre-assigned GPU in a table—a constant-time operation that replaces expensive per-batch optimization. During each GNN layer, GPUs exchange only the features that cross their boundaries, eliminating the redundant loading that occurs when the same vertices appear in multiple GPU batches.
mlsys-2025-035.key_novelty: The core idea is pre-computing a global GPU assignment from sampled graph patterns using METIS, reducing per-batch graph partitioning from an NP-hard optimization problem to a constant-time lookup while provably minimizing inter-GPU communication.

mlsys-2025-041.method: FedProphet breaks the full neural network into small sequential modules (cascade learning), with each module trained on devices of a particular capability level. To ensure all modules pull toward the same training goals despite working separately, the system applies a mathematical constraint called strong convexity regularization to each module. A central server then orchestrates using two mechanisms: Adaptive Perturbation Adjustment (APA), which dynamically adjusts the strength of adversarial attacks to balance accuracy and robustness trade-offs, and Differentiated Module Assignment (DMA), which assigns each module to device types based on their memory and compute capabilities.
mlsys-2025-041.key_novelty: The core insight is that cascade learning combined with strong convexity regularization (mathematical constraints ensuring consistent training goals) allows neural networks to be both memory-efficient and adversarially robust in federated settings.

mlsys-2025-034.method: The algorithm uses a greedy approach to partition the KV-cache radix tree (a tree structure representing shared prefixes in the cache) into two groups: shared context and query-specific parts. A specialized attention kernel based on FlashAttention processes the shared context once and reuses it across all queries in a group by processing them together. This transforms slow individual matrix-vector operations (GEMV) into a single fast batched matrix-matrix operation (GEMM) that hardware can efficiently execute.
mlsys-2025-034.key_novelty: The algorithm greedily assigns edges in the KV-cache tree to identify query groups that can share computation, converting slow per-query matrix-vector operations into fast batched matrix-matrix operations.

mlsys-2025-040.method: Seesaw switches the model's parallelization strategy during inference based on the current phase: using tensor parallelism (splitting layers across GPUs) for prefill (processing prompts) and pipeline parallelism (distributing layers sequentially across GPUs) for decode (generating tokens). To manage memory efficiently, the key-value cache—intermediate results needed for fast computation—is stored in fast GPU VRAM for active batches and slower CPU DRAM as overflow storage, with asynchronous background transfers between them. A scheduler batches requests together to reduce how often resharding occurs, spreading the switching cost across multiple requests.
mlsys-2025-040.key_novelty: The core idea is dynamically resharding the model between different parallelization strategies mid-inference, combined with tiered KV cache management and request batching to minimize resharding overhead.

mlsys-2025-039.method: AdaParse routes PDFs through a three-stage classifier to pick the right parser: first, a rule-based check of PyMuPDF-extracted text features to reject broken files; second, a prediction of whether expensive high-quality parsers are worth running on a particular document; third, a SciBERT-based ML model trained on preferences from 23 domain experts to select the best parser. The model is fine-tuned using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which teaches it to predict what experts prefer. To handle massive scale, Parsl orchestrates execution on the Polaris supercomputer, batching PDFs together, warming up parser models, and distributing tasks across nodes.
mlsys-2025-039.key_novelty: The core idea is using Direct Preference Optimization to align an ML router to expert preferences, enabling it to skip expensive parsers when faster ones will work—achieving 17x throughput improvement over Nougat with 0.2% better BLEU accuracy.

mlsys-2025-046.method: AI Metropolis uses out-of-order execution instead of waiting for all agents to finish each step before proceeding. It tracks which agents actually depend on which others by calculating whether they're close enough to interact: agent A is blocked by agent B only if their spatial distance is within interaction reach given the time difference and maximum possible speed (using the formula: radius_p + |StepA - StepB - 1| * max_vel). Agents within interaction range at the same time step are grouped into clusters, which a controller dispatches to parallel workers via a priority queue ordered by step number (earlier steps run first). Workers update the dependency graph in parallel using Redis, an in-memory database with transactional safety, with critical controller logic written in C++ for low latency.
mlsys-2025-046.key_novelty: Spatial-temporal dependency tracking enables out-of-order execution for multi-agent simulation, eliminating false blocking between distant agents while preserving true causality.

mlsys-2025-038.method: The approach breaks attention computation into small tiles and runs two separate processing streams in parallel: matrix multiplication (MatMul) on the multiply-accumulate (MAC) units and softmax (the normalization step) on the vector (VEC) units. Instead of running one after the other—which leaves one unit idle—these streams run overlapped in a semi-synchronized pipeline to keep both compute units busy simultaneously. The tile sizes (sub-matrices for MatMul and row-level chunks for softmax) are optimized offline using MCTS (Monte-Carlo Tree Search) and Genetic Algorithm to find the best configuration for the device. To prevent running out of on-chip memory during processing, the system proactively overwrites and reloads intermediate matrices (the K and V tiles) as needed, prioritizing softmax completion to avoid stalling the pipeline.
mlsys-2025-038.key_novelty: It's the first attention acceleration method to exploit edge devices' separate compute units (MAC and VEC) by running matrix multiplication and softmax in parallel semi-synchronized pipelines, combined with a proactive strategy that overwrites intermediate data to prevent cache overflow without stalling either stream.

mlsys-2025-033.method: When large AI models run on limited GPU hardware, each layer must decide where to execute. FlexInfer uses a mathematical model, checking three things in real time (free GPU memory, PCIe bandwidth between CPU and GPU, CPU compute capacity), to pick the best strategy for each layer: CPU-only, GPU-offload, or SplitGen (split computation between CPU and GPU). It makes these decisions while the model runs, not beforehand, which avoids profiling overhead.
mlsys-2025-033.key_novelty: FlexInfer dynamically selects per-layer execution strategy among CPU-only, GPU-offload, and SplitGen based on real-time hardware state, using a mathematical model rather than static policies or machine learning.

mlsys-2025-037.method: LeanAttention divides attention work equally across GPU cores using Stream-K, a parallel-processing technique: it breaks the key-value sequence into fixed-size chunks called LeanTiles (each sized optimally for the GPU hardware), distributing them regardless of how attention heads (separate computation paths) are organized. When LeanTiles span head boundaries, their partial results are combined using softmax re-scaling, which is associative—you can compute pieces separately and combine them to get the exact same answer as one complete computation. This keeps GPU cores busy for any sequence length.
mlsys-2025-037.key_novelty: LeanAttention proves that softmax re-scaling (the normalization step in attention) is associative, meaning you can compute attention work in arbitrary split pieces and combine them perfectly, enabling full GPU utilization for any context length or batch size.

mlsys-2025-043.method: HyC-LoRA compresses activations using two coordinated strategies. Within individual operations, it identifies data channels with extreme outliers and keeps those in full precision (FP16) while compressing the rest to 2-bit (INT2); for attention queries/keys, it compresses before the rotation step (RoPE) where values are smoother. Across operations, it reorders quantization and LoRA adapter application so the activation-times-adapter product (XA) stays in memory while the main branch is compressed separately, enabling backward passes to regenerate results instead of storing them; it also fuses quantization with adjacent operations using Triton kernels to reduce processing overhead.
mlsys-2025-043.key_novelty: It combines outlier preservation within operations (keeping extreme values at full precision, compressing others to 2-bit) with LoRA-aware compression reordering that enables backward passes to regenerate data instead of storing it.

mlsys-2025-044.method: VoLUT uses a two-stage super-resolution process for 3D point clouds. Stage 1 uses dilated k-nearest neighbor search (finding nearby points using a wider search pattern to provide context), accelerated via octree parallelism (organizing 3D space into a tree structure for parallel processing), with neighbor relationships reused across steps. Stage 2 normalizes coordinates to [0,1], quantizes them into 128 bins per axis, and looks them up in a precomputed 3D table (built from a neural network, 1.6GB, with a 4-pixel receptive field) that provides position offsets; an adaptive bitrate algorithm (Model Predictive Control) dynamically adjusts downsampling based on network conditions.
mlsys-2025-044.key_novelty: VoLUT achieves real-time 3D point cloud super-resolution on mobile devices by converting trained neural networks to a precomputed 3D lookup table (1.6GB, 128 bins per axis) for position refinement, combined with dilated k-nearest neighbor interpolation and adaptive bitrate streaming.

mlsys-2025-047.method: LServe accelerates attention on long sequences by strategically reducing required computations. During prefill, half the attention heads are predetermined to only look at sink tokens (the very beginning) plus recent tokens in a sliding window, while other heads compute normally—both run together in one optimized GPU kernel. During decode, LServe uses a two-level page system: fine-grained logical pages score which key-value memories matter most using query dot products with statistics, while larger physical pages store the actual compressed data; it reuses these scores across consecutive decode steps instead of recalculating them. All key-value data is quantized to 4 bits (W4A8KV4) to minimize memory usage.
mlsys-2025-047.key_novelty: LServe's core contribution is unifying static sparse attention heads (predetermined during prefill) with dynamic hierarchical page pruning (during decode) into one fused GPU kernel using quantized key-value storage, speeding up both stages of long-sequence LLM serving.

mlsys-2025-050.method: The system splits a massive input sequence across multiple GPUs instead of fitting it all on one. It uses two complementary ring strategies: pass-KV circulates Key/Value tensors (cached representations) across GPUs while each GPU keeps its own query block; pass-Q does the opposite, circulating queries while GPUs hold fixed Key/Value data. To keep all GPUs equally busy, each sequence is split into 2N chunks across N GPUs. The system automatically switches between pass-KV and pass-Q based on how often cached data must be fetched, optimizing for all three inference phases: prefill (encoding the input), persistent KV prefill (caching intermediate results), and decode (generating one token at a time).
mlsys-2025-050.key_novelty: The core idea is load-balancing a massive sequence by splitting it into 2N chunks across N GPUs using two complementary ring-attention methods—pass-KV and pass-Q—that automatically switch based on how much cached data needs to be fetched.

mlsys-2025-054.method: Negativa-ML hooks into CUDA's cuModuleGetFunction API—a checkpoint where GPU kernels load before execution—to detect which GPU functions actually run on each workload. It removes bloat at two levels: individual functions and entire cubin files (compiled GPU binaries). CPU code bloat is identified using standard call-graph analysis. The method was tested on 4 ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, MXNet), 10 real workloads, and 300+ shared libraries.
mlsys-2025-054.key_novelty: This is the first tool to locate and remove GPU code bloat from ML libraries by observing which kernels are actually used, revealing that GPU waste (not CPU waste) is the primary source of bloat due to hardware-architecture mismatch.

mlsys-2025-042.method: The method identifies redundant layers by measuring angular cosine distance (how similar the outputs from adjacent layers are in their directional orientation) — the most similar outputs mark the best layers to remove. The original unpruned model regenerates the training dataset by creating high-quality responses that preserve semantic meaning, while selectively keeping original responses for prompts where the pruned model already performs well. The pruned model and the version trained on these regenerated responses are merged using SLERP merging (spherical linear interpolation, which blends model weights along the shortest path), and the pruned model can also function as a draft generator in speculative decoding paired with the full model as verifier.
mlsys-2025-042.key_novelty: Using the unpruned model to regenerate a semantically-aligned fine-tuning dataset prevents catastrophic forgetting in depth-pruned models, while also enabling SLERP model merging (a method to blend two model versions) and speculative decoding.

mlsys-2025-045.method: JaxPP lets you mark where one processing stage ends and another begins with simple annotations; it automatically infers the data flow between stages from your model code. Unlike systems that force a single execution pattern, JaxPP supports flexible gradient accumulation schedules—like 1F1B (one forward pass, one backward pass) and Interleaved 1F1B—that use memory more efficiently and improve throughput. A central controller orchestrates execution by converting your model to a task graph, distributing tasks to processing units (SPMD actors, each managing one or more devices), determining data movement through topological ordering to avoid deadlocks, freeing memory buffers once they're no longer needed, and bundling all data transfers into single efficient messages.
mlsys-2025-045.key_novelty: JaxPP is the first system that lets JAX users define any pipeline schedule they want—like 1F1B or Interleaved 1F1B—using simple code annotations, without requiring model rewrites.

mlsys-2025-052.method: Vocabulary Parallelism distributes embedding and output layers (which handle vocabulary processing—the complete set of tokens the model can work with) evenly across pipeline devices instead of concentrating them on one device. The method reduces communication overhead between devices, measured in all-reduce barriers (device synchronization points), through two strategies: Algorithm 1 cuts these from 3 to 2, and Algorithm 2 reduces to 1 by computing softmax outputs online (incrementally rather than storing intermediate values) and using pre-computed gradients. This integrates with existing pipeline scheduling methods like 1F1B and V-Half.
