mlsys-2025-052.key_novelty: Computing softmax outputs incrementally (online softmax) combined with pre-computed gradients reduces inter-device communication barriers from 3 to 1, enabling vocabulary computation to integrate into existing pipeline schedules with minimal extra memory cost.

mlsys-2025-049.method: ScaleFusion exploits spatial-temporal independence: spatial attention (comparing pixels across the image) is independent from different time frames, and temporal attention is independent from different spatial regions. This enables splitting each layer into 4 temporal or 4 spatial slices without breaking dependencies. Within a layer, it overlaps computation and communication: while computing slice i, it prepares the all-to-all data exchange for slice i+1. Between layers, it eliminates additional idle time by overlapping 2/3 of the next layer's data exchange with the previous layer's final slice, using two parallel execution streams with default parameters: 4 temporal slices, 4 spatial slices, 1 temporal sub-partition, and 3 spatial sub-partitions.
mlsys-2025-049.key_novelty: ScaleFusion eliminates cross-machine all-to-all communication overhead in spatial-temporal video transformers by overlapping these data exchanges with computation both within layers and between consecutive layers, exploiting the independence of spatial and temporal attention.

mlsys-2025-053.method: To reduce data loading bottlenecks, the approach optimizes how data moves from storage to the GPU. It uses chunk reshuffling—organizing data in larger blocks instead of individual rows—which lets the GPU prepare its own training batches. It overlaps reading from storage with GPU computation by prefetching the next batch while the current one processes, and uses GPU Direct Storage (GDS) to connect the GPU directly to fast storage for very large graphs. Additionally, it adjusts the training process using mini-batch gradient descent and chunk-based sampling strategies to handle the expanded input sizes.
mlsys-2025-053.key_novelty: The key finding is that data loading, not computation, is the bottleneck in pre-propagation GNN training, and chunk reshuffling—organizing data in larger blocks instead of individual rows—lets the GPU prepare training batches without fine-grained per-row shuffling.

mlsys-2025-055.method: COMET combines two techniques. First, it analyzes shared memory buffers, breaks tensors (multi-dimensional arrays) into pieces along independent dimensions like the M-axis for matrix operations or N-axis for ranking, and reschedules computation to start as soon as local data is available. Second, it isolates communication and computation into separate groups of GPU cores (thread blocks) within a single merged kernel, then dynamically adjusts how many cores go to each task based on input size and parallelism strategy.
mlsys-2025-055.key_novelty: COMET solves the mismatch between communication work (which processes whole tokens) and computation work (which works on matrix tiles) by using fused GPU kernels that decompose data into independent parts, reschedule the work for better overlap, and dynamically allocate computing resources between communication and computation.

osdi-2025-001.method: Tintin systematically measures how hardware performance changes when you run the same code multiple times and across different platforms, then tracks down what causes these variations (like temperature shifts or processor states). It quantifies the uncertainty in these performance measurements by analyzing the variability data. This lets you understand how reliable your performance predictions are and catch cases where they're likely to be wrong.
osdi-2025-001.key_novelty: Tintin unifies hardware performance profiling across different platforms to measure variability and manage uncertainty in a single system.

osdi-2025-000.method: Tigon stores database records in a shared CXL memory pool accessible to all servers, using CXL's cache coherency feature (where all processors automatically see the same latest version of data) to maintain consistency without extra synchronization. Rather than having each server maintain its own copy and send updates across the network, Tigon optimizes data placement and update handling within the pool to take advantage of the hardware-enforced coherency. This approach reduces both access latency and the synchronization overhead of traditional distributed databases.
osdi-2025-000.key_novelty: Tigon redesigns distributed database architecture to exploit CXL's shared memory pool and hardware-enforced consistency, eliminating the copying and network synchronization overhead of traditional approaches.

mlsys-2025-048.method: Each workload trains its own lightweight gradient-boosted trees model (a machine learning method combining multiple decision trees) at the application layer to rank shuffle jobs by importance. The model learns from application-level information: job execution details, allocated resources, disk read/write patterns, and timestamps, assigning each job an importance category—category 0 for jobs that lose money on fast SSD, categories 1 through N for increasingly disk-intensive workloads. At the storage layer, an Adaptive Category Selection algorithm monitors SSD usage, including overflow events (spillover), and cost metrics (TCIO feedback), dynamically adjusting an admission threshold to decide which categories go to SSD. Because the application model is independent of the storage system, it doesn't need retraining when SSD capacity or costs change—only the threshold needs adjustment.
mlsys-2025-048.key_novelty: Each workload trains its own gradient-boosted trees model to predict job importance independent of the storage system, while an Adaptive Category Selection algorithm translates those importance levels into SSD or HDD placement using real-time feedback, separating machine learning from storage decisions.

mlsys-2025-059.method: APOLLO realizes that AdamW's per-element learning rate adjustment—where each weight gets its own learning rate—can be simplified to per-channel or per-tensor adjustment without hurting training quality. To avoid expensive SVD calculations, APOLLO uses a shortcut: randomly project the gradient into a smaller space using a Gaussian random matrix, apply AdamW's momentum-tracking to the compressed gradient, extract scaling factors, then apply those factors to the full gradient. The Gaussian random matrix is resampled every 200 steps. APOLLO-Mini uses rank-1 (tensor-wise) scaling to match SGD's memory footprint, and a Norm-growth Limiter stabilizes training.
mlsys-2025-059.key_novelty: APOLLO proves using the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma that randomly projecting gradients preserves their scaling factors to within a bounded ratio, enabling low-rank approximation without expensive SVD while achieving SGD-level memory and AdamW-level training quality.

mlsys-2025-056.method: Rubick learns how each training job's speed depends on the computational resources it receives and the strategy it uses. It builds a performance model from 7 trial profiling runs that predicts speed based on GPU, CPU, and bandwidth constraints across the compute phases (forward pass, backward pass, parameter updates) and their potential overlap, and updates this model continuously as jobs run. For each job, it calculates a sensitivity curve showing how throughput changes with different resource allocations, then uses these curves to decide which job should give up resources to which: it shrinks the job least sensitive to resource reduction to feed more resources to the job that benefits most, while guaranteeing each job meets its deadline.
mlsys-2025-056.key_novelty: Rubick is the first deep learning cluster scheduler that dynamically adjusts both each job's execution strategy and its resource allocation as a single decision, rather than using fixed strategies.

osdi-2025-006.method: EMT creates a flexible translation layer in the operating system that maps virtual addresses (the addresses programs use) to physical memory addresses (actual RAM locations). It supports both traditional page tables—fixed-size memory blocks managed by the OS—and alternative translation schemes. By abstracting away the specific translation method, the same OS can work with different architectural approaches without needing separate implementations.
osdi-2025-006.key_novelty: EMT is an operating system framework that supports multiple memory translation architectures (different hardware mechanisms for mapping virtual to physical addresses) instead of being locked into a single translation approach.

mlsys-2025-051.method: Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer (FPDT) trains large language models by splitting the work across multiple GPUs, storing pieces of the input in the computer's main memory when GPU memory fills up. It breaks the long sequence into 64,000-token chunks and uses a double-buffer strategy—keeping one chunk ready to copy while the GPU processes the current chunk—which hides the delay of transferring data from main memory to GPU. The system redistributes intermediate results across GPUs in a coordinated pattern and synchronizes the final output layer (vocabulary computation) with this chunking process.
mlsys-2025-051.key_novelty: A double-buffer design that keeps one data chunk ready while the GPU processes another hides the delays of copying data from main computer memory to GPU, enabling training on sequences 16 times longer than previous methods—specifically, 8-billion-parameter models on 2-million-token sequences using just 4 GPUs while maintaining 55% of the GPU's theoretical peak performance.

osdi-2025-003.method: Paralegal scans code without running it (static analysis) to find where private data might leak or be accessed by people who shouldn't have it. It works by tracking how sensitive information flows through your code—where it originates, where it travels, and who can access it at each point—to catch when data leaks out or is used improperly. The system is designed to scale across large, real-world codebases, not just small examples.
osdi-2025-003.key_novelty: Paralegal uses static analysis—scanning code without running it—to find privacy bugs in real-world software at scale.

mlsys-2025-057.method: Radius observes that the most important gradients (top-k, the largest ones) stabilize after 15-20% of training, so it computes which ones matter once and reuses that selection for 200 steps rather than recomputing every step. Since all workers compute this same selection from combined gradient data independently, they only need to send the values of selected gradients using standard combining (allreduce) without exchanging index information, avoiding the expensive allgather step. Before computing selections, Radius applies AdamW's optimizer adjustments so that selections reflect genuine model changes. It accumulates non-selected gradients and periodically adds them back to prevent permanent information loss.
mlsys-2025-057.key_novelty: Leverages the fact that important gradients (top-k indices) stay mostly the same across training steps to reuse the same selection for 200 steps, replacing expensive index-sharing (allgather) with efficient combining (allreduce) while enabling compatibility with AdamW optimizers.

osdi-2025-002.method: Large language model training distributes work across four dimensions: splitting data samples (data parallelism), dividing network weights (tensor parallelism), breaking computation into stages (pipeline parallelism), and splitting text sequences (sequence parallelism). WLB-LLM continuously rebalances load across these dimensions based on your hardware layout and the cost of moving data between processors, rather than using a fixed strategy. This keeps all processors equally busy instead of having some wait idle for others to finish.
osdi-2025-002.key_novelty: It dynamically adjusts how the four parallelism dimensions (data, tensor, pipeline, sequence) share the workload, based on actual conditions instead of a fixed strategy.

mlsys-2025-058.method: Youmu breaks data into small chunks called pages (kilobytes to megabytes) instead of huge blocks, and at startup builds an index from Parquet file metadata; when training needs a random page, layered binary search (a fast multi-level lookup) finds its exact location on disk. The system reads compressed pages directly from SSDs and decodes them using metadata, avoiding the need to load everything into memory first. It feeds pages into a fixed-size buffer that continuously shuffles data as it's consumed, maintaining high randomization for training. The implementation is about 500 lines of Rust with Python bindings.
mlsys-2025-058.key_novelty: Youmu's core idea is using small pages (kilobytes to megabytes) as the unit of direct access to Parquet columnar data, eliminating format conversion while enabling global shuffling across billions of pages in terabyte-scale datasets.

mlsys-2025-060.method: SampleAttention speeds up attention computation by sparsifying (keeping only important) connections in the attention matrix. Stage 1 partitions queries into chunks and computes full attention only for representative blocks at chunk boundaries, then aggregates scores by blocks (128 tokens) in column and diagonal directions to identify important regions. Stage 2 independently selects the minimum blocks in each direction needed to preserve a target fraction of attention probability per query (measured by Cumulative Residual Attention, or CRA), builds a sparse mask, and runs the efficient FlashAttention2 kernel, with efficiency boosted by fusing operations together and precomputing patterns per model and sequence-length range.
mlsys-2025-060.key_novelty: The core innovation is the Cumulative Residual Attention (CRA) metric—the minimum fraction of attention probability to retain per query—which can be computed at runtime and reliably predicts downstream task accuracy, enabling fully adaptive sparsity patterns that vary per query and per input without requiring model retraining.

osdi-2025-007.method: When a serverless function hasn't run recently, the system must start from scratch—preparing a container (the isolated environment where code runs), starting the runtime (the system that executes the code), and loading the application. The paper identifies which of these three steps causes the most delay and proposes specific optimizations to speed each one up.
osdi-2025-007.key_novelty: Cold start latency isn't a single problem but three distinct bottlenecks in container initialization, runtime startup, and application loading that can each be optimized separately.

osdi-2025-004.method: Cluster file systems normally couple data striping (spreading data across machines) and redundancy grouping (placing backup copies) with a single unified strategy, which constrains both. Okapi decouples these concerns: first, it optimizes data placement across machines purely for speed, then separately optimizes where copies go purely for reliability. Because these decisions can now vary independently, each can be tuned perfectly for its actual purpose.
osdi-2025-004.key_novelty: Okapi decouples data distribution for speed from copy distribution for fault tolerance, enabling independent optimization of each strategy.

osdi-2025-008.method: PipeThreader replaces fixed hardware pipelines with software control over how deep neural networks (DNNs—large models built from many computational layers) are divided into processing stages. The key mechanism is dynamic adjustment: as the neural network runs, the software can change both how many pipeline stages exist and how work is distributed across processors based on what the computation needs. This orchestration (coordination) enables the system to optimize for whatever hardware and workload it encounters. Instead of being locked into one design, the parallelism strategy—how many independent data paths run in parallel—adjusts on the fly.
osdi-2025-008.key_novelty: PipeThreader's core idea is using software to dynamically define and adjust neural network pipelines instead of relying on fixed hardware designs.

osdi-2025-005.method: The system pre-assigns the sequence of database operations using 'Fix-Ante' ordering, eliminating the slow coordination normally needed with a shared log (a record all nodes check to stay synchronized). Servers then speculatively execute these pre-ordered operations (running them before full coordination completes). Each server independently verifies whether its speculative execution matched the pre-assigned order, correcting any conflicts. This delivers the speed of speculation while maintaining the consistency guarantees that distributed databases require.
osdi-2025-005.key_novelty: Fix-Ante ordering lets servers speculatively execute database operations without coordination overhead by pre-assigning their order, achieving low latency while guaranteeing correctness.

osdi-2025-016.method: The system uses best-first search—an algorithm that prioritizes the most promising candidates—and structures the search to align with how SSDs (solid-state drives) prefer to fetch data in sequential chunks rather than random access. It traverses the graph in patterns that minimize costly disk jumps and adds prefetching, which loads data before it's needed, to hide the latency of disk operations.
osdi-2025-016.key_novelty: By organizing the graph structure and search algorithm around how SSDs actually behave, graph-based nearest-neighbor search on disk performs as fast as keeping everything in memory.

osdi-2025-010.method: Kamino places virtual machines across data center servers by considering two often-overlooked factors: cache affinity (when two workloads share frequently-accessed data, keeping them on nearby processors lets the shared data stay in fast cache memory rather than requiring slow repeated trips to main memory) and latency sensitivity (how quickly certain workloads must respond). For each virtual machine, it evaluates whether a particular server placement would preserve cache efficiency through proximity to related machines, and whether that server can meet the workload's latency needs. It then selects placements that reduce both cache misses and response delays.
osdi-2025-010.key_novelty: The core idea is to optimize virtual machine placement by jointly considering cache efficiency and latency sensitivity together, rather than optimizing each independently.

osdi-2025-012.method: PICSOU introduces C3B, a communication method for replicated state machines (systems maintaining identical data copies across many servers) in different data centers. Based on how TCP makes internet connections reliable, C3B keeps bookkeeping overhead constant as systems grow and only retransmits messages that actually failed. It achieves this through QUACKs—quorum acknowledgments where nodes ask a voting majority of other nodes "did you get this message?"—giving precise knowledge of what safely arrived.
osdi-2025-012.key_novelty: C3B, using quorum acknowledgments (a voting mechanism for servers to confirm message arrival), enables replicated state machines to communicate reliably across distant data centers while maintaining strong consistency.

osdi-2025-019.method: The approach automatically optimizes deep learning programs by iteratively applying small transformations to code, guided by a diffusion model (a technique that gradually transforms one representation into another). Instead of randomly trying changes, it uses Bayesian uncertainty estimation—probability distributions that measure confidence in different optimization choices—to decide which transformations are most promising. This probabilistic guidance makes the search much more efficient than blind exploration.
osdi-2025-019.key_novelty: It applies diffusion models to automatic deep learning program optimization for the first time, using Bayesian uncertainty to guide the search.

osdi-2025-013.method: The paper proposes stripeless data placement for erasure-coded in-memory storage (a technique storing data in RAM with built-in redundancy so you can recover lost pieces). Unlike traditional striping—dividing data into uniform chunks distributed across locations—stripeless placement adapts the layout to match actual data sizes and access patterns. This removes the rigid alignment requirements that striping imposes, eliminating both the alignment overhead and the performance inefficiencies that come with striped storage.
osdi-2025-013.key_novelty: Stripeless placement—using flexible, adaptive layouts instead of striped patterns—eliminates alignment overhead in erasure-coded in-memory storage.

osdi-2025-014.method: QOS works like a classical operating system but for quantum hardware: it manages qubits (the basic units of quantum information) to prevent programs from interfering with each other, schedules when quantum programs run, and coordinates error correction (the techniques that fix errors as quantum systems process information). It also bridges classical computers and quantum processors, enabling instructions to flow from classical to quantum and results to flow back.
osdi-2025-014.key_novelty: QOS is an operating system designed specifically for quantum computers, managing quantum resources and coordinating program execution—functions that classical operating systems are not designed to handle.

osdi-2025-011.method: QiMeng-Xpiler converts deep learning tensor programs from one hardware platform to another by having an LLM generate candidate code transformations, then using symbolic program synthesis (automated verification) to check and fix them. An automatic tuning system explores different transformation sequences and parameter settings to optimize performance. The system works with four hardware platforms: Intel DL Boost (VNNI), NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA), AMD MI accelerators (HIP), and Cambricon MLU chips (BANG).
osdi-2025-011.key_novelty: The core idea is pairing LLM code generation (for exploring possible solutions) with symbolic program synthesis (for guaranteeing correctness), enabling practical automated transcompilation across different hardware platforms.

osdi-2025-009.method: Instead of funneling all file system changes through a single journal (creating a bottleneck), this spreads the journaling across multiple independent journals organized by epochs—fixed time windows. When a crash occurs, the system recovers individual transactions within epochs rather than replaying entire epochs. This lets multiple processes simultaneously write to different journals without queuing at a central point, improving performance on multi-core systems.
osdi-2025-009.key_novelty: The core innovation is decentralized journaling organized into epochs (time windows) with fine-grained recovery, enabling concurrent writes without central bottlenecking.

osdi-2025-018.method: Standard GPU profilers measure only a fixed set of metrics, limiting your ability to debug performance. This system lets you write custom measurement code and inject it directly into running GPU computations. Since your code runs during actual kernel execution, it captures exactly what you need to debug, without limitations of preset measurements. This programmable approach lets different users customize their profiling to specific performance questions.
osdi-2025-018.key_novelty: It's the first GPU profiler to support programmable probing—letting you inject custom measurement code to observe what happens inside running computations.

osdi-2025-015.method: The system integrates performance measurement directly into Triton, a GPU compiler (a tool that translates code into instructions GPUs can execute). Rather than measuring performance while the program runs, it adds instrumentation at compile time—embedding measurement logic directly into the compiled code. This approach captures detailed performance data about GPU kernels, the small parallel computation units, with minimal runtime overhead.
osdi-2025-015.key_novelty: This is the first profiling system integrated directly into the Triton compiler, achieving only 8.2% slowdown from measurement and keeping measurement error within 2%, enabling the compiler to automatically improve its optimizations based on real performance data.

osdi-2025-022.method: When training large AI models across multiple computers, the slowest worker (a straggler) forces everyone to wait, significantly slowing the entire system. This work uses what-if analysis—testing different parameter scenarios like batch size, network bandwidth, or hardware configuration to predict their effects—to understand which workers will become stragglers and why. By simulating these scenarios in advance, you can identify the root causes of slowdowns (like insufficient network bandwidth or imbalanced computation) and make better decisions about how to distribute the training work.
osdi-2025-022.key_novelty: What-if analysis can predict which workers will slow down distributed model training and identify the root causes of those slowdowns.

osdi-2025-021.method: File systems and storage systems must survive crashes without losing or corrupting data (crash consistency) and must be able to detect if corruption has happened anyway. This framework verifies both of these properties using a single approach that works with different storage systems and verification tools, rather than requiring a separate custom verification method built for each one.
osdi-2025-021.key_novelty: The first method for verifying crash consistency and corruption detection that works across different storage systems and tools instead of being tied to a specific one.

osdi-2025-017.method: The method introduces a new programming model (PLMR) and specialized collective operations (MeshGEMM for matrix multiplication and MeshGEMV for matrix-vector multiplication) designed for wafer-scale hardware like Cerebras WSE2. These break neural network calculations into pipeline stages—continuous operations running in sequence—where processing units arranged in a mesh grid can combine intermediate results locally before sending them along the network, reducing data movement.
osdi-2025-017.key_novelty: The innovation is enabling large language model inference on wafer-scale hardware by designing matrix multiplication operations (GEMM and GEMV) that exploit the mesh-grid topology of the processing units.

osdi-2025-020.method: The system analyzes the training code to automatically determine what rules (invariants) should always hold true during training—for example, that numerical values stay within expected ranges or that data doesn't get corrupted. As training runs, it continuously monitors whether these rules are violated by tracking the actual numbers being computed and how data flows through the network. When it detects a violation, it alerts you before the faulty model completes training.
osdi-2025-020.key_novelty: It automatically infers what should be true during training, then catches silent errors by checking those rules while training runs.

osdi-2025-023.method: Memory tiering systems place data across fast, expensive storage and slow, cheap storage. Traditional systems decide placement using one simple factor: how often data is accessed (hotness). This system improves placement by considering additional factors alongside access frequency. By weighing multiple decision factors, it achieves better data placement and system performance.
osdi-2025-023.key_novelty: Memory placement decisions consider multiple factors beyond access frequency.

osdi-2025-028.method: Instead of modifying file metadata in place, the system writes new versions to fresh disk locations, never overwriting the old data. This means a crash can only leave you with the previous complete version or the new complete version—never a partially written, corrupted mixture. The system waits for each write to physically reach disk before confirming it's done (synchronous writes), ensuring consistency without traditional journaling (backup logs used for recovery).
osdi-2025-028.key_novelty: This file system achieves synchronous crash consistency for file metadata by using a write-once approach (writing metadata to new locations instead of overwriting it), eliminating the need for traditional recovery journals.

osdi-2025-027.method: The system splits vectors into multiple partition levels and uses a learned cost model (a machine-learned prediction system that estimates how expensive different index arrangements will be) to continuously monitor how the workload changes—which vectors are being queried, updated, and how often. When access patterns shift, it restructures the index automatically to keep performance high. It also accounts for NUMA locality (the fact that data sits in physically distributed memory banks at different distances from CPU cores), placing frequently accessed data closer to reduce latency.
osdi-2025-027.key_novelty: It learns which access patterns matter most in your workload and restructures the index automatically, with parallelism that respects NUMA locality so parallel tasks access data physically close to the CPU cores executing them.

osdi-2025-026.method: The researchers implemented container technology on microkernel operating systems (kernels where only essential functions run in the core, with other services layered on top) and measured their performance. They compared containers running on microkernels to containers on traditional monolithic kernels (where all core functions are integrated into one program) by testing performance overhead, resource usage, and isolation strength. This comparison quantifies the exact tradeoffs involved in choosing microkernel-based containers.
osdi-2025-026.key_novelty: This is the first systematic cost-benefit analysis of containers on microkernel operating systems, measuring performance costs against isolation and modularity benefits.

osdi-2025-030.method: DecDEC stores the lost precision as residuals—the differences between original full-precision weights and their quantized low-precision versions—on the CPU. As the model runs inference, it monitors for activation outliers (unusual spikes in intermediate values flowing through the network) to identify which channels (processing pathways) are most sensitive to precision loss at that moment. For these sensitive channels, it fetches the stored residuals from the CPU and adds them back to recover some precision. This lets the model adapt its precision correction to what's actually happening during inference instead of using a fixed strategy.
osdi-2025-030.key_novelty: The key idea is detecting activation outliers as the model runs to identify which channels need precision correction in real-time, rather than deciding this upfront.

osdi-2025-032.method: When a network interface gets too busy, FuseLink uses the GPU as a relay point to forward traffic to a less busy interface through the high-speed connections inside the server. This balances the network load across all available connections instead of letting one interface become a bottleneck. The system integrates into NCCL (the standard communication library that machine learning frameworks use), so existing applications work without requiring any code changes.
osdi-2025-032.key_novelty: GPUs dynamically redirect network traffic to less busy connections instead of being permanently bound to a single interface.

osdi-2025-031.method: The paper analyzes how network interface cards' receive rings—the hardware buffers that hold incoming network packets—currently perform two conflicting jobs: buffering packet data and managing control metadata. By measuring the architectural tensions this creates, the researchers demonstrate why these functions should be separated. They propose splitting them into independent hardware structures so that packet buffering and control management can each be independently optimized.
osdi-2025-031.key_novelty: The core insight is that NIC receive rings force two incompatible functions (packet buffering and control metadata) to share hardware, when they should be separated for better performance.

osdi-2025-025.method: The system stores frequently-used data across multiple computers. Instead of requiring all machines to always use the newest data (strict consistency—which is slow to coordinate) or allowing them to serve arbitrarily old data (eventual consistency—which is unpredictable), it offers a middle ground: you set a maximum age for how old cached data can get, and the system automatically enforces that limit. This enables quick data access while guaranteeing nothing is older than your specified bound.
osdi-2025-025.key_novelty: The key idea is explicitly and practically controlling data staleness—you set a maximum age that the system enforces for cached data, rather than choosing between always-fresh data (slow) or unpredictably stale data.

osdi-2025-033.method: Omniglot acts as a controlled translator when one programming language calls code written in another. It automatically converts data from one language's format to another's (a process called marshalling) and ensures data types match exactly across the language boundary (type checking). It enforces these checks either at runtime (while the code runs) or through static analysis (checking before the code runs), preventing the security and correctness problems that commonly occur when languages interact at their boundaries.
osdi-2025-033.key_novelty: Omniglot provides safe cross-language function calls by automatically converting and type-checking data at language boundaries to prevent the common vulnerabilities that occur there.

osdi-2025-024.method: The approach automatically extracts rules about correct system behavior from existing test cases and packages them as semantic checkers (tools that validate whether the system is behaving correctly). These checkers are deployed to production where they run continuously, comparing the actual system behavior to the expected behavior defined in the tests. When the system violates these rules, the checker flags a failure—including silent failures that don't crash the system or show obvious errors. By reusing tests this way, the system gains production monitoring without needing to manually write separate validation rules.
osdi-2025-024.key_novelty: Automatically extracting semantic checkers from test cases to detect silent failures in production.

osdi-2025-029.method: The researchers systematically studied how to speed up code running on a single processor core, separate from parallelization (spreading work across multiple cores). For each optimization technique, they documented the underlying principle: what change actually causes the speedup and under what conditions it works best. They organized these findings into a coherent framework, showing how serial optimization principles differ from and operate independently of parallelization principles.
osdi-2025-029.key_novelty: This paper documents and organizes all the principles governing single-threaded performance optimization in one unified framework.

osdi-2025-035.method: XSched schedules tasks across multiple types of accelerators (called XPUs) that have different hardware designs. It can pause running tasks and move them between accelerators (preemption and task migration), and it chooses where to place each task based on what the task does. It knows the safe points to pause each accelerator type and adjusts its scheduling decisions based on how fast each accelerator actually performs.
osdi-2025-035.key_novelty: The core contribution is a unified scheduler that efficiently handles diverse accelerators with different hardware designs by pausing and moving tasks between them.

osdi-2025-037.method: Scalio uses specialized processor chips called DPUs (Data Processing Units) instead of the main CPU to handle storage network operations. When a key-value store reads or writes data across multiple storage boxes, the DPU manages the storage protocol work (NVMe-oF, which sends storage data over a network), data movement, and storage-specific tasks. This frees the main CPU to focus entirely on running the key-value store application. By using hardware built specifically for I/O-intensive work, Scalio reduces CPU overhead that normally limits throughput in large-scale JBOF systems.
osdi-2025-037.key_novelty: Scalio eliminates CPU bottlenecks by moving storage network processing (NVMe-oF target operations) from the main CPU to specialized DPU chips.

osdi-2025-038.method: A quantum virtual machine acts as a translator between high-level quantum programs and actual quantum hardware, converting the program into an intermediate representation (a format that any quantum backend can understand). The system's runtime layer assigns physical qubits from available hardware, schedules operations to avoid conflicts across different quantum systems, coordinates switching between classical and quantum operations, and applies error mitigation techniques to reduce quantum errors.
osdi-2025-038.key_novelty: A quantum virtual machine that enables the same program to run on any quantum hardware by using intelligent scheduling and allocation to overcome scarce qubit availability.

osdi-2025-036.method: Weave optimizes privacy-preserving queries by grouping multiple queries together and mixing their execution order (shuffling), which spreads the overhead of hiding data access patterns across more work—making it cheaper per query. It runs computation across multiple computers and uses specialized data structures to reduce how much data must be transferred between storage and processors. It also uses processor-specific optimizations and vectorization (parallel processing of multiple operations) to speed up the core privacy operations.
osdi-2025-036.key_novelty: Weave achieves both speed and flexibility in privacy-preserving analytics by grouping queries together to distribute the overhead of hiding data access patterns.

osdi-2025-039.method: FineMem adapts memory chunk size based on how the program actually allocates and uses memory—choosing smaller chunks when allocations are frequent (to waste less space) and larger chunks when they're sparse (to reduce bookkeeping overhead). It uses historical patterns to predict needs, stores allocation metadata (bookkeeping information) in a layered structure to minimize tracking costs, and automatically combines free chunks back together to prevent fragmentation.
osdi-2025-039.key_novelty: FineMem adapts memory chunk size in real-time based on allocation patterns, eliminating the choice between allocation speed and memory waste in disaggregated memory systems.

osdi-2025-034.method: The system speculatively executes transactions (starts them running before getting final approval) at different server locations that hold copies of the data, which cuts down the time spent waiting for all servers to agree. If a transaction's tentative results turn out to conflict with others, the system aborts it without applying the changes. Read-only transactions (queries) and transactions that change data use different strategies, with coordination checks to ensure everything stays correct.
osdi-2025-034.key_novelty: Mako reduces latency in geo-replicated systems (databases across geographically distant locations) by starting transactions at local copies before waiting for all locations to approve, catching conflicts to ensure consistency.

osdi-2025-040.method: The researchers compared computer systems both with and without PRI enabled, running various realistic workloads on each version to measure the results. They tracked how performance changed — whether it improved, by how much, and what the overhead or resource cost was. By examining these comparisons across different types of work, they identified the specific conditions where enabling PRI actually helps versus where it hurts performance or wastes resources.
osdi-2025-040.key_novelty: The research provides a framework for deciding when to enable PRI: activate it if your specific workload and system constraints justify the cost, disable it otherwise.

osdi-2025-042.method: ZEN notices that gradient updates—the adjustments computers share during distributed training—mostly contain tiny or zero values that don't actually help the model. Instead of sending every gradient value, ZEN only transmits the large, important ones. It adapts how aggressive this filtering is based on observed patterns, ensuring the model still trains to a good solution while cutting the data sent between computers.
osdi-2025-042.key_novelty: ZEN reduces inter-computer communication during distributed training by only sending gradients that are large enough to matter, exploiting the sparsity (the fact that most gradient values are small or zero) in the updates.

osdi-2025-041.method: Söze collects simple traffic information from standard network switches—the equipment routing data in cloud networks. Each data flow is assigned a weight indicating its bandwidth priority; the system uses only these switch-level metrics and weights to calculate how much bandwidth each flow should get, without needing to know the network's full topology, which servers are involved, or which paths the data takes. These calculations happen in a decentralized way (no central controller needed), and the allocations are then enforced throughout the network.
osdi-2025-041.key_novelty: Weighted bandwidth allocation can be achieved using only simple traffic information from standard switches, without needing to track individual flows, know the network's layout, or understand routing paths.

osdi-2025-045.method: DeDe starts by recognizing that resource allocation problems (the challenge of distributing resources to meet competing demands) have a natural separation: the constraints governing resources are independent from the constraints governing demands. It breaks the optimization into alternating subproblems for each resource and each demand, which can be solved both efficiently and in parallel. The framework is provided as a Python package with an intuitive modeling interface.
osdi-2025-045.key_novelty: The key insight is that resource and demand constraints in allocation problems are naturally separable, making it possible to decompose them into parallelizable subproblems.

osdi-2025-046.method: The system intercepts untrusted machine code and takes strict control of three normally-variable aspects: when instructions execute (timing), the order memory accesses happen, and how tasks are scheduled. By fixing these values, the code runs in the exact same way every time—making it deterministic. This control happens on your computer (client-side) rather than requiring special hardware, so performance is maintained.
osdi-2025-046.key_novelty: The core idea is using controls on your computer to make untrusted code run in the exact same way every time, without needing special hardware or losing speed.

osdi-2025-048.method: Basilisk tracks where data originates and how it flows through a distributed protocol—this data-origin tracking (provenance invariants) serves as a foundation for automated proof generation. The system translates the protocol's rules and tracking properties into a constraint-satisfaction problem: a set of logical requirements that must all be satisfied simultaneously. Automated solvers then search for solutions that satisfy every constraint, which effectively constructs a valid proof, even for protocols that no traditional proof algorithm could handle.
osdi-2025-048.key_novelty: Using provenance tracking (data-origin tracking) to automatically prove the correctness of theoretically undecidable protocols.

osdi-2025-047.method: KRR records only the critical kernel events that determine a program's behavior, not every single operation, to avoid the massive slowdown that recording typically causes. It compresses this recorded information so it takes little space. To replay the program later, KRR runs the execution across multiple processor cores simultaneously, but carefully coordinates when each event happens so the result is always the same.
osdi-2025-047.key_novelty: KRR is the first system to record kernel events with minimal performance slowdown while also replaying them efficiently across many processors simultaneously.

sc-2025-002.method: The Protego framework first explores different inputs to find that distinct groups of inputs require different patterns of instruction duplication—the practice of running certain instructions twice to detect transient hardware faults (temporary glitches). At runtime, it rapidly extracts features from the input data to classify which group the current input belongs to. Based on this classification, it selectively enables the appropriate instruction duplication strategy for that input group, adapting which instructions are protected without needing to re-profile the entire application.
sc-2025-002.key_novelty: Selective instruction duplication (running certain instructions twice to catch transient hardware faults) should adapt which instructions to protect based on analyzing runtime input data, rather than using a fixed protection strategy determined in advance.

osdi-2025-052.method: Compass enables encrypted semantic search by using special encryption that allows mathematical operations on encrypted data (homomorphic or functional encryption) combined with approximate nearest-neighbor search—a technique that quickly finds similar vectors without checking all of them. To reduce computational cost, the system compresses vector precision (quantization) and reduces the number of dimensions while maintaining accurate results. Query processing then uses secure comparison protocols to find which encrypted vectors are most similar to the query without decrypting anything.
osdi-2025-052.key_novelty: Compass achieves high-accuracy encrypted semantic search by optimizing approximate nearest-neighbor search and vector quantization specifically for encrypted operations.

osdi-2025-049.method: BlitzScale sends model parameters through the direct network between GPUs, which is typically underutilized, instead of slower storage paths. It maintains a constant-sized cache on each host that doesn't grow as models get larger, providing efficient memory usage. Rather than scaling entire computing instances at once (which must pause while parameters load), it scales individual model layers, allowing computational work to start on newly added GPUs before parameters fully finish loading. The system uses network broadcast sending (multicast) to efficiently deliver parameters to multiple instances without excessive caching overhead.
osdi-2025-049.key_novelty: BlitzScale eliminates autoscaling delays by loading parameters through the GPU-to-GPU network with a constant-sized cache, and scaling individual layers so computing instances never block waiting for parameters to arrive.

osdi-2025-044.method: Rendering normally happens one task at a time, but many tasks don't actually depend on each other—wasting potential for parallelism. This system executes multiple rendering tasks in parallel (out of order), checking as they run which operations actually affect each other. Once all work completes, an in-order commit stage finalizes results in sequence, ensuring correctness even though execution was parallel.
osdi-2025-044.key_novelty: This applies a CPU technique to OS rendering: execute independent operations in parallel (out-of-order), then finalize them in sequence (in-order commit) for the correct output.

sc-2025-000.method: The approach works by tracking when data gets evicted (pushed out) from the cache and measuring how often the program reuses the same data (temporal locality) or accesses nearby memory locations together (spatial locality). It categorizes each cache miss—a failed lookup—by its root cause, whether the data was evicted too soon or accessed in a pattern mismatched to the cache structure. It then visualizes these interactions in a Cache Interaction Graph diagram and extends Cachegrind (an existing memory profiler) to analyze this down to individual variables.
sc-2025-000.key_novelty: The Cache Interaction Graph visualizes which pieces of data compete with each other in the cache, revealing the root cause of performance slowdowns.

osdi-2025-051.method: NanoFlow improves GPU utilization by running multiple copies of the same operations on a single GPU at the same time—by splitting the input into smaller nano-batches. This works because while one batch is computing, the GPU can simultaneously fetch data for the next batch and transmit the previous result over the network, so compute, memory transfer, and networking overlap instead of happening one after another. The system automatically figures out how many nano-batches to create, their size, the order to process them, and how to split the GPU's resources among them, all while managing interference between concurrent operations to minimize total execution time.
osdi-2025-051.key_novelty: Nano-batches enable intra-device parallelism (concurrent operations on one GPU) by overlapping compute, memory transfer, and networking instead of sequential execution.

sc-2025-003.method: The researchers tested HPL (a benchmark that measures supercomputer performance using large matrix operations) on Frontier, a supercomputer combining GPUs and CPUs. They built performance models to understand different strategies for panel factorization, which decomposes matrices by breaking them into manageable sections. They developed two approaches: one using dedicated CPU threads to manage work, and another running the factorization directly on GPU hardware using HIP cooperative groups (parallel programming tools that let GPU threads coordinate and share work).
sc-2025-003.key_novelty: Running panel factorization (the matrix decomposition step) directly on GPUs using HIP cooperative groups outperforms running it on CPUs on Frontier.

osdi-2025-043.method: The system creates a unified blueprint (μGraphs) representing tensor programs at three levels of GPU organization: kernels (whole programs), thread blocks (groups of threads), and threads (individual execution units). This lets it explore improvements across all levels simultaneously rather than one level at a time, using smart shortcuts (abstraction-based pruning) that discard unpromising options early while guaranteeing the final answer is optimal. The system finds improvements in three forms: rearranging the math operations, changing how computation is scheduled across hardware, and writing new optimized code. Finally, it uses a probabilistic equivalence verification procedure—a mathematically-proven method to check that the optimized program produces identical results—to ensure correctness.
osdi-2025-043.key_novelty: μGraphs provide a unified representation of tensor programs across GPU hierarchy levels (kernels, thread blocks, and threads), enabling optimizations across all levels simultaneously with guaranteed optimality.

sc-2025-001.method: Split containerization into five separate layers: building environments with Spack (a tool for managing software dependencies) and CI/CD pipelines (automated deployment workflows), enabling user sessions with authentication (PAM) and Kubernetes for container orchestration, connecting to Slurm (HPC's standard job scheduler), and handling system integration and security. Rather than one monolithic system, each layer uses standard open-source tools. Build and evaluate prototypes to validate this modular approach.
sc-2025-001.key_novelty: By breaking HPC containerization into five modular layers using open-standard tools, the framework eliminates the traditional tradeoff between stability, customization, and reproducibility.

sc-2025-009.method: The paper implements CountSketch—a dimensionality reduction technique that uses randomized hash functions to compress matrix data—to run efficiently on GPUs (graphics processors designed for parallel computation). It demonstrates how multisketching (applying the sketch multiple times and combining results) works with this GPU implementation. The method is applied to solve least squares problems (finding the best-fit solution when there are more equations than variables) and compared against the standard normal equations approach for both speed and numerical accuracy.
sc-2025-009.key_novelty: Implementing CountSketch to run efficiently on GPUs makes multisketching practical, and when applied to least squares it delivers a 77% speedup and better numerical stability than normal equations.

sc-2025-008.method: The researchers ran high-performance computing workloads on the Sophon SG2044 RISC-V chip and measured how fast it ran compared to the earlier SG2042 and other manufacturers' chips. They focused on two key components: RVV v1.0 (RISC-V's vector processing system that handles many numbers simultaneously) and an upgraded memory subsystem. This benchmarking approach revealed whether the newer RISC-V design could match the performance of established HPC architectures.
sc-2025-008.key_novelty: This is the first evaluation of whether RISC-V's SG2044 chip can compete in high-performance computing, showing that improvements to vector processing (RVV v1.0) and memory systems are successfully closing the performance gap with established HPC processors.

sc-2025-007.method: Helix compiles tensor code (numerical arrays) without requiring specific shape information beforehand by decomposing the compilation task across the computer's architectural layers—from high-level programming abstractions down to low-level machine operations. It uses a bidirectional strategy: applying optimization rules top-down while building concrete machine kernels (instruction sequences) bottom-up. At lower architectural levels it measures performance directly, and at higher levels it estimates performance to avoid expensive measurement.
sc-2025-007.key_novelty: Helix eliminates the expensive shape-sampling step in dynamic tensor compilation by organizing the compiler around the computer's architectural hierarchy instead.

sc-2025-004.method: They built an HPX backend for FleCSI to make it work with HPX's parallel execution model. Task dependencies—where one task must wait for another to finish—are represented as HPX futures, which are promises of results. The key optimization reduces the overhead of creating communicators, which are the data channels between tasks, by streamlining expensive setup work. They validated the approach on two physics simulation applications.
sc-2025-004.key_novelty: The key idea is reducing the overhead of creating communicators, the data channels between tasks, when translating Legion-like task graphs to HPX's execution model.

sc-2025-010.method: Hypertron explores seven different ways to distribute model training work across multiple Ascend NPU accelerators, including approaches like splitting the model across devices, splitting training data across devices, and their combinations. It intelligently combines these seven dimensions and uses a performance model to predict which combination runs fastest while using the least memory and communication bandwidth. This approach supports both dense and sparse models with different context lengths.
sc-2025-010.key_novelty: By exploring all seven parallelization dimensions together, Hypertron finds optimal training strategies that existing frameworks cannot support, significantly reducing memory usage and communication overhead.

sc-2025-006.method: TraceFlow performs static program analysis on the source code beforehand to identify interaction patterns—which parts of the program communicate with each other. Based on this understanding, it partitions trace events so that events from interacting parts are assigned to the same analysis process. This strategy eliminates the inter-process communication that normally bottlenecks large-scale trace analysis.
sc-2025-006.key_novelty: Static program analysis enables communication-free trace analysis by directing related trace events to the same process based on code interaction patterns.

sc-2025-005.method: The approach uses AI agents powered by large language models to accept natural language questions and convert them into structured queries for workflow provenance data—records showing what processes executed and what data they created. It uses a metadata-driven design where the system understands the structure of the provenance data, combined with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG—giving the LLM access to relevant metadata records to ground its answers in real data). The prompts feeding the system are tuned for accuracy, and the approach was tested on LLaMA, GPT, Gemini, and Claude models across diverse query types.
sc-2025-005.key_novelty: The innovation is using large language model agents with retrieval-augmented generation to enable natural language queries of workflow provenance data.

sc-2025-011.method: They created LLMFI, a tool that injects simulated hardware faults into LLM training to observe resulting failures. Running over 300,000 of these experiments across 5,000+ GPU hours revealed distinct failure patterns. They then developed LLMFT, an ML-based framework that continuously monitors for these failures (using extracted system features and a fault detector) and automatically applies recovery strategies to resume training.
sc-2025-011.key_novelty: They identified six distinct failure modes in LLM training on HPC systems and built an ML-based closed-loop control system (continuous monitoring with automatic targeted recovery) to handle each one.

sc-2025-013.method: The framework tracks water usage with three complementary metrics tailored to each region: WUE (water usage effectiveness—how much water is consumed per unit of computing work), PUE (power usage effectiveness—the ratio of total facility power to the computing portion), and EWF (embodied water footprint—water embedded in electricity generation and cooling). The team measured these metrics on four real supercomputers—Marconi, Fugaku, Polaris, and Frontier—using actual operational data. They then assessed how regional conditions like water scarcity and power sources (including nuclear energy) affect whether these systems operate sustainably.
sc-2025-013.key_novelty: ThirstyFLOPS measures supercomputer water consumption—including cooling and electricity—in ways that adapt to each region's water availability and power sources, to guide water-conscious infrastructure design.

sc-2025-012.method: gParaKV is a key-value store using key-value separation (storing keys and values in separate locations to save space) that accelerates its two biggest bottlenecks—compaction and garbage collection—by offloading them to a GPGPU (a graphics processor used for general computing, with many parallel cores). During compaction, the GPU parallelizes merge-sorting (combining multiple sorted data blocks), running hundreds of operations simultaneously instead of sequentially as CPUs do. For garbage collection, it uses a GPU-optimized bitmap (a compact structure tracking which records are still alive) and parallel marking (examining many records simultaneously) to rapidly identify and remove obsolete data.
sc-2025-012.key_novelty: GPU acceleration of compaction merge-sorting and garbage collection using bitmap and parallel marking structures for efficient parallel execution.

osdi-2025-050.method: Instead of forcing a choice between unsafe unrestricted code execution or slow heavy isolation, the system assigns capabilities to each extension—specific access to the memory regions and system features it's allowed to use. Before executing dynamically loaded code, the system verifies it respects these constraints, catching unsafe operations upfront rather than repeatedly at runtime. This lightweight verification and control approach avoids the overhead of virtual machines or heavyweight sandboxes, letting extensions run at nearly native speed while still being confined.
osdi-2025-050.key_novelty: A system that runs dynamic extensions safely at full speed by controlling what each one can access and verifying code before it executes, without virtualization.

sc-2025-015.method: Instead of using a single language model to handle all decisions, the system breaks the research workflow into specific specialized tasks—simulation setup, particle tracking, data analysis, literature research, and hypothesis generation—with a dedicated LLM agent for each. Each agent receives custom instructions tailored to its job and access to the software tools it needs, and they're coordinated to work together. Humans remain in control by validating the agents' work at each step before results are used.
sc-2025-015.key_novelty: The core idea is using multiple specialized LLM agents, each handling one research task with humans validating results, rather than having a single model try to handle everything—allowing the same approach to work across different research domains.

sc-2025-021.method: Seq2ParDiff compares the actual behavior of parallelized code (OpenMP) against the original sequential version by running both on diverse test inputs and checking whether their execution produces identical results in three key areas: program outputs, data stored in memory, and which code branches execute. When the parallel and sequential versions diverge, it identifies a transformation error—such as data races (when multiple threads unsafely access the same data) or incorrect results. By testing real execution rather than analyzing code statically, it catches bugs that static validation alone cannot find.
sc-2025-021.key_novelty: Seq2ParDiff detects sequential-to-parallel transformation errors by running both versions and comparing their actual execution behavior, catching bugs that static validation misses.

sc-2025-024.method: The researchers adapted astrophysical N-body simulation code (software that calculates gravitational forces between many objects like stars or planets) to run on a Tenstorrent Wormhole n300 accelerator card—a specialized piece of hardware based on RISC-V architecture (a simple, open instruction set for chips) instead of traditional CPUs. They then benchmarked the accelerator against a highly optimized CPU baseline to measure how much faster it could perform the same calculations.
sc-2025-024.key_novelty: This work shows that the RISC-V-based Tenstorrent Wormhole accelerator can handle scientific computing workloads, demonstrated through astrophysical N-body simulations.

sc-2025-023.method: The paper presents three parallel computing assignments that have been tested with students and designed for other instructors to adopt easily. The assignments span different domains: a biological simulation (cellular automata, where cells on a grid evolve by following rules), a physics model of water flowing downhill with rainfall on uneven terrain, and a machine learning operation called softmax (which converts raw numbers into probabilities). Each teaches parallelization by tackling a problem that naturally breaks into independent pieces that can run simultaneously across multiple processors.
sc-2025-023.key_novelty: The contribution is curating parallel assignments across diverse motivations—biology, physics simulation, and machine learning—so students see parallelization as practical and broadly useful, not just theoretical.

sc-2025-017.method: EDDE redesigns how container images are loaded on-demand at the edge by reducing communication delays with the central image repository. It switches from FUSE (where file operations run in user-space programs and add overhead) to kernel-based file operations, which are much faster. It also delivers images more efficiently to avoid overwhelming the limited storage available on edge devices.
sc-2025-017.key_novelty: EDDE optimizes container deployment for edge devices by cutting communication with the central image repository, switching to fast kernel file operations instead of slow FUSE, and reducing storage footprint on resource-limited hardware.

sc-2025-018.method: gLLM uses token throttling—controlling how many input and output tokens flow through each pipeline stage—to independently regulate the prefill phase (processing input) and decode phase (generating output). The decode phase has relatively consistent computational cost, so keeping it balanced prevents GPU idle time; prefill has variable cost depending on input size, so it adjusts dynamically based on queue depth (how many requests are waiting) and available KV cache memory (storage for precomputed values). This independent regulation, coordinated via asynchronous message passing, prevents the computation imbalances that occur with fixed token budgets.
sc-2025-018.key_novelty: gLLM independently throttles prefill and decode token quantities, dynamically adjusting based on queue depth and KV cache memory instead of using a fixed token budget across the pipeline.

sc-2025-020.method: AMD Flang implements OpenMP target directives—special code annotations that tell the compiler which Fortran code sections to run on GPUs. It uses map clauses to specify which data must be transferred to GPU memory. The compiler transforms Fortran code through multiple processing stages: converting it to an internal representation, handling loop constructs like DO CONCURRENT through the OpenMP intermediate representation, and generating GPU machine instructions.
sc-2025-020.key_novelty: AMD Flang adds GPU offload support to Fortran using OpenMP target directives.

sc-2025-022.method: The workshop runs for one week and teaches biologists three practical skills: navigating command-line file systems (typing commands instead of clicking), submitting computing jobs to HPC systems using SLURM (a job scheduler that queues and runs tasks), and applying machine learning and deep learning to real biological datasets. To make this accessible, it uses Jupyter Notebooks (interactive documents where you write and run code), graphical remote-desktop access via DCV (so you see a familiar desktop interface), and software containers (pre-configured computing environments), all running on HPC systems.
sc-2025-022.key_novelty: A reusable workshop framework teaches domain scientists HPC and machine learning using accessible technologies—Jupyter Notebooks for interactive coding, graphical interfaces (DCV) for familiar interaction, and software containers to eliminate setup complexity—with survey data confirming it works.

sc-2025-014.method: The system uses MLIR (an intermediate language compilers use to translate between human-readable source code and hardware instructions) to automatically identify Fortran intrinsics—built-in mathematical functions in Fortran—and redirect them to AMD AIEs, which are specialized hardware accelerators built into Ryzen AI processors. The compiler translates these high-level operations into low-level instructions specifically optimized for the accelerators. Programmers don't need to modify their existing code at all; the compiler handles the entire offloading automatically.
sc-2025-014.key_novelty: The compiler automatically routes Fortran's mathematical functions to specialized hardware accelerators without requiring code changes.

sc-2025-026.method: They simulated a molten chloride small modular reactor using MOOSE (a software tool for modeling how heat, fluid flow, and materials behave together in complex systems). The reactor ran at partial capacity with control rods held at 60% open, and they analyzed the steady thermal and fluid-flow behavior—how heat and coolant flow stabilize—under these below-maximum-power conditions.
sc-2025-026.key_novelty: First simulation of how a molten chloride small modular reactor behaves when running below full capacity, as it would need to in real data center operation.

sc-2025-027.method: The paper takes the syscall_intercept library, which catches system calls (requests from programs to the operating system kernel) before they execute, and makes it work on RISC-V Linux. The library operates in user-space without needing superuser access by inserting interception code into running programs. The authors adapt this approach to RISC-V's specific processor architecture and test it on actual RISC-V systems.
sc-2025-027.key_novelty: This work provides the first high-performance syscall_intercept implementation for RISC-V processors.

sc-2025-025.method: ROSE is a framework that coordinates expensive physics simulations and machine learning model training across multiple supercomputers (Polaris, Perlmutter, Delta). Instead of guessing which simulations to run next, it uses active learning—an algorithm that selects new simulations based on what would most improve the model's predictions. The system can run analysis alongside the simulations (in-situ) or afterward (ex-situ), and it updates its predictive model either continuously as new data arrives (online) or in batches (offline). By handling all this coordination asynchronously and adapting which simulations to run based on what it learns, ROSE efficiently builds and refines surrogate models—learned predictors that mimic expensive simulations.
sc-2025-025.key_novelty: The framework orchestrates active learning (intelligently selecting which simulations to run) and asynchronous parallel execution across multiple supercomputers to manage the entire surrogate modeling pipeline, reducing orchestration overhead.

sc-2025-029.method: We created a reusable energy model by running small diagnostic programs (microbenchmarks) on GPUs to measure exactly where energy is consumed. The model breaks down energy use by specific hardware components (floating-point units, tensor cores, integer arithmetic units), memory tiers (L1 cache, L2 cache, and HBM high-bandwidth memory), and separates energy spent on control logic from energy spent on actual computation. We tested this approach across four GPU generations and validated it against real supercomputing and AI workloads.
sc-2025-029.key_novelty: The key idea is using small test programs to measure GPU energy in fine detail—identifying which specific hardware component (floating-point unit, tensor core, or integer arithmetic unit), which memory tier (L1, L2, or HBM high-bandwidth memory), and whether it's for control logic or computation—in a way that extends to new GPU generations.

sc-2025-019.method: The system connects the Advanced Light Source (ALS) synchrotron to high-performance computing centers (NERSC and ALCF) via ESnet, a high-speed research network. It uses two parallel pipelines: one streams data directly to NERSC where GPU and CPU algorithms immediately perform 3D reconstruction for instant scientist feedback; the other automatically transfers complete datasets to both facilities for more intensive reconstruction that prioritizes quality. This gives scientists rapid preliminary results while thorough analysis proceeds in parallel.
sc-2025-019.key_novelty: The innovation is a dual-pipeline architecture that transparently streams synchrotron data to HPC facilities for rapid 3D reconstruction while batching complete datasets for intensive analysis, eliminating the need to choose between speed and quality.

sc-2025-031.method: The researchers test different strategies for rearranging rows and columns of sparse matrices (mostly-zero matrices) to speed up sparse matrix-vector multiplication—the operation of multiplying such a matrix by a vector. They measure performance on various multicore CPUs, testing both single-core and multi-core execution. The goal is to see if reordering reduces data movement between the CPU and memory, and distributes computational work evenly across cores so none become bottlenecks.
sc-2025-031.key_novelty: The work systematically evaluates matrix reordering strategies across different CPU platforms, revealing that load imbalance—how unevenly work distributes across cores—determines whether reordering actually improves performance.

sc-2025-036.method: Umpire provides a single, unified interface for managing memory across different types in HPC systems—whether it's CPU memory, GPU memory, or high-bandwidth memory. Instead of allocating and freeing memory piece-by-piece, Umpire uses memory pools, which pre-allocate memory in large blocks and reuse them efficiently, avoiding the overhead of constant allocation. It integrates with RAJA, a portability framework, so the same code can run across different architectures without rewriting memory management.
sc-2025-036.key_novelty: Umpire combines memory pooling (reusing pre-allocated memory blocks instead of constant allocation/deallocation) with a portable API to achieve 15x+ speedups across different HPC architectures.

sc-2025-035.method: The researchers built a new module for MLIR (a compiler's intermediate representation—the format compilers use internally before generating machine code) that treats OpenSHMEM communications (direct messages between processors) as visible language features instead of hiding them in opaque function calls. This allows the compiler's optimization algorithms to see and understand the communication patterns. They integrated it with existing LLVM optimizations and demonstrated four specific improvements: tracking which processor initiates each communication (PE recording), combining multiple atomic operations into fewer ones, switching code from waiting-for-completion mode (blocking) to continuing-without-waiting mode (non-blocking), and bundling multiple messages into larger batches.
sc-2025-035.key_novelty: The first compiler that makes OpenSHMEM's one-sided communications visible to optimization algorithms, enabling four transformations: processor tracking (PE recording), operation fusion, blocking-to-non-blocking conversion, and message aggregation.

sc-2025-016.method: ORBIT-2 combines two techniques to efficiently process long climate sequences at scale. First, it uses Reslim, a lightweight neural network (based on Vision Transformers) with skip connections (residual learning—adding the input directly to the output to improve training) and Bayesian regularization (which quantifies uncertainty to prevent overfitting). Second, it uses the TILES algorithm to speed up attention (the mechanism that finds relationships between all data points): instead of checking every possible relationship in quadratic time, it processes data in tiles, reducing cost to linear time; this scales to 10 billion parameters across 65,536 GPUs.
sc-2025-016.key_novelty: ORBIT-2 reduces transformer attention complexity from quadratic to linear using the TILES algorithm, enabling billion-token climate sequences with Reslim's efficient residual architecture and Bayesian uncertainty estimates, achieving 74-98% scaling efficiency at 10 billion parameters on 65,536 exascale GPUs.

sc-2025-034.method: The researchers built simulations of two real RISC-V computers—a commercial single-board computer called MILK-V Pioneer and a desktop RISC-V CPU—using FireSim. They ran the same performance benchmarks on both the real hardware and in the simulation to compare results. They tested both single-core and four-core configurations using different workloads, including small test applications and LAMMPS (molecular dynamics simulation software).
sc-2025-034.key_novelty: This work provides the first systematic validation of FireSim's accuracy by comparing its simulations directly to real RISC-V hardware.

sc-2025-033.method: The approach uses two complementary techniques to enforce computational limits on reasoning models while preserving safety. First, they fine-tune the models using length-controlled policy optimization (LCPO—a machine-learning method that trains models to keep reasoning chains within a specified length). Second, they apply quantization (reducing numerical precision to make the model smaller and faster) to fit more chain-of-thought reasoning into a fixed compute budget. They then measure how these constraints affect safety performance.
sc-2025-033.key_novelty: The core finding is that compute constraints significantly impact reasoning model safety, requiring careful management of length limits and quantization to preserve safety performance.

sc-2025-038.method: A Kubernetes operator (automated software that manages applications) controls Charm++ parallel programs and automatically adjusts how many computing resources each gets based on what's available in the cluster. The scheduler prioritizes jobs by importance level, giving high-priority work more resources when they're scarce. As resources become available, it expands job allocations; as demand drops, it shrinks them—reducing wasted compute nodes while keeping important jobs on track.
sc-2025-038.key_novelty: The core idea is elastic, priority-aware scheduling for HPC on Kubernetes—automatically scaling job resource allocation based on cluster availability while ensuring high-priority work gets resources first.

sc-2025-039.method: The team implemented the C++26 Senders API—a standard way to describe sequences of computations—in the pika parallel tasking runtime (software that schedules work across processor cores). They represented asynchronous MPI messaging calls (which send data across networked computers) as individual nodes in a computation graph, treating network I/O the same way the runtime treats regular computation. Then they tested different strategies for polling (checking when messages arrive) and dispatching (routing completed messages to the right task).
sc-2025-039.key_novelty: This is the first implementation of the C++26 Senders API in an HPC tasking runtime, which makes network communication via MPI a first-class scheduling primitive (treated the same as regular computation tasks) instead of an afterthought.

sc-2025-030.method: They built a distributed FFT layer using kokkos-fft (built on Kokkos, a programming abstraction that runs code on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA and AMD without rewriting). The layer introduces batched-distributed FFT, enabling multiple transforms to run simultaneously across distributed systems. It automatically routes to each hardware's vendor-optimized library (cuFFT for NVIDIA, rocFFT for AMD) for optimal performance without user configuration.
sc-2025-030.key_novelty: Batched-distributed FFT that automatically selects vendor-optimized libraries (cuFFT, rocFFT) through a unified Kokkos interface.

sc-2025-041.method: The authors built a dedicated hardware accelerator in the Chipyard chip-design framework that performs SZx compression—a technique for squeezing down data as it streams from scientific detectors (like those generating petabytes per second in physics experiments). The accelerator processes multiple data elements in parallel across several pipeline stages, which is more efficient than a general-purpose CPU because every circuit is built specifically for this compression task. By optimizing how data moves between stages, it reduces the expensive bottleneck of shuffling massive amounts of data to storage. They then directly compared how much faster this hardware version was compared to software compression on a CPU.
sc-2025-041.key_novelty: First hardware accelerator built specifically for SZx streaming compression, demonstrating how specialized hardware can overcome the data-movement bottleneck that limits software approaches.

sc-2025-043.method: Uno treats all network traffic—whether within a data center or between distant ones—with a single unified system. It uses a transport protocol that quickly detects congestion and fairly adjusts each application's send rate to avoid starvation.
