It also spreads traffic across multiple paths using erasure coding (splitting data into redundant pieces so you can recover the original from fewer than all pieces) and adaptive routing that continuously selects the best path based on real-time network conditions.
sc-2025-043.key_novelty: A single unified congestion control system handles both intra- and inter-datacenter traffic fairly despite different round-trip times, using integrated erasure coding and adaptive routing.

sc-2025-045.method: The approach breaks workforce training into small, stackable microcredentials (bite-sized certifications) that can be updated quickly as technology evolves, with curricula co-designed by educators and industry partners. It focuses on RISC-V architectures (an open-source chip instruction set) and full-stack HPC system design—meaning students learn both the hardware fundamentals and how to write software that runs efficiently across complete computing systems.
sc-2025-045.key_novelty: The innovation is using microcredentials aligned with TCPP curriculum standards to teach open hardware and HPC at scale, so training can update rapidly and stay current with technology.

sc-2025-047.method: The algorithm separates subgraph counting—finding how many times a graph pattern appears—into two steps: identifying instances of the core subgraph pattern, then computing occurrences by examining the fringe vertices (the adjacent vertices and edges around each match) using set operations to efficiently determine which connections belong to which instance.
sc-2025-047.key_novelty: By decomposing subgraph counting into core-pattern identification and separate fringe-vertex occurrence computation, the algorithm can exactly count larger patterns than previously possible, with GPU acceleration for patterns where fringe computation is the bottleneck.

sc-2025-040.method: The approach dynamically reduces processor speed on supercomputer nodes to lower operating temperature and slow aging, accepting reduced computational performance as the tradeoff. A scheduling algorithm assigns jobs to nodes and selects their running speed, trying to complete all work before hardware fails while minimizing performance loss. This aging-aware scheduler is compared to a baseline that runs everything at constant speed, and tested to confirm it works even when the device-aging model isn't perfectly accurate.
sc-2025-040.key_novelty: A job scheduler that extends supercomputer device lifetime by adjusting processor speed based on each computer's remaining lifespan and heat output, rather than running everything at constant speed.

sc-2025-046.method: They integrated Proteus (a runtime compiler based on LLVM) with RAJA, a layer that lets parallel code run across different hardware platforms. At runtime, Proteus applies dimension specialization: it replaces generic variables for loop sizes with the specific numbers determined when code starts executing, enabling highly optimized code tailored to those exact dimensions.
sc-2025-046.key_novelty: Using a runtime compiler to optimize portable parallel code by specializing loops for the actual dimensions available when code executes.

sc-2025-048.method: The reproducibility evaluation independently tests the DRIM-ANN approximate nearest neighbor search engine by re-running its experiments following SC25 Artifact Description and Evaluation standards. Researchers verify that the code, datasets, and experimental procedures match what was published, checking whether others can achieve the same performance results. The process documents what reproduces correctly, where results differ, and what information was missing or unclear in the original paper. This systematic verification confirms whether DRIM-ANN's claimed speedups and accuracy on DRAM-PIMs (memory chips with built-in processors) hold up under independent testing.
sc-2025-048.key_novelty: This work validates whether the DRIM-ANN approximate nearest neighbor search engine's results can be independently reproduced by other researchers.

sc-2025-032.method: SmartIO predicts upcoming I/O operations while the system runs, using context-free grammars (a pattern-matching technique for recognizing operation sequences). It learns the characteristics of those predicted operations. Then it applies rules-based optimization created from research literature and empirical testing to improve the I/O before execution.
sc-2025-032.key_novelty: SmartIO uses runtime I/O pattern prediction with context-free grammars (a pattern-matching technique) and rules-based optimization to replace offline tuning and machine learning training, with negligible performance overhead.

sc-2025-049.method: The SICKLE framework uses maximum entropy sampling, a technique that selects the most diverse and informative data points from the dataset—instead of random selection, it prioritizes examples that represent the full range of system conditions. The approach is evaluated against two alternatives: purely random sampling and phase-space sampling (selecting from specific regions of possible states). By intelligently curating which data the model trains on, this method reduces both the dataset size needed and the computational energy required.
sc-2025-049.key_novelty: Maximum entropy sampling intelligently selects the most representative training data, reducing both dataset size and computational energy costs, as validated on the Frontier supercomputer.

sc-2025-042.method: The work extends the LLVM Flang compiler to translate Fortran 2023 code containing multi-image parallelism (running the same program across multiple processors simultaneously) into PRIF, a standard intermediate form called the Parallel Runtime Interface for Fortran. The Caffeine parallel runtime is built to execute PRIF instructions. Finally, an MLIR dialect—a standardized notation used in compilers to represent code—is designed specifically for Fortran's multi-image features so different compiler tools can reuse the same representation.
sc-2025-042.key_novelty: The work provides a complete implementation pipeline for Fortran 2023's multi-image parallelism (where the same program runs on many processors at once): LLVM Flang compiler, PRIF (Parallel Runtime Interface for Fortran) as the intermediate representation, and Caffeine runtime.

sc-2025-037.method: The approach packages GenAI software—specifically a vLLM inference server for running Llama models—into containers (portable bundles containing all code and dependencies). These same containers are deployed on both traditional HPC systems and Kubernetes (cloud-style infrastructure management) using multiple container runtimes (software that executes containers). By testing which runtimes work on both platforms, they show their containerized GenAI workloads can run on either HPC or Kubernetes infrastructure.
sc-2025-037.key_novelty: This is the first practical demonstration that containerized GenAI workloads can run on both Kubernetes and HPC systems using container runtimes compatible with both platforms.

sc-2025-052.method: The team ran the Implicitly Restarted Arnoldi Method—an algorithm that finds eigenvalues of large matrices—using four alternative numeric formats (OFP8, Bfloat16, Posit, and Takum, which are different systems for how computers store decimal numbers). They executed the same computations described in the original paper and verified whether the reported numerical results could be reproduced. This checks whether the code actually works and produces the claimed performance.
sc-2025-052.key_novelty: The work validates whether the Implicitly Restarted Arnoldi Method's numerical results can be independently reproduced across alternative numeric formats (OFP8, Bfloat16, Posit, and Takum).

sc-2025-053.method: The researchers tested 107,632 different compression algorithms (methods for shrinking data size) across three compilers (NVCC, Clang, HIPCC) and two GPU platforms (NVIDIA, AMD). For each algorithm-compiler-platform combination, they measured how fast the compression ran. By gathering this data at scale, they could identify which compiler-and-platform pairings produced the fastest compression for different algorithms.
sc-2025-053.key_novelty: The key finding is that compiler and GPU platform interact: the best-performing compiler depends on your GPU, and the best GPU depends on your compiler choice.

sc-2025-044.method: The system is an AI chatbot that helps answer HPC questions by combining a curated knowledge base with retrieval-augmented generation—a technique where relevant documents are retrieved and paired with AI-generated explanations, keeping answers grounded in actual sources. It can read and understand different types of HPC documents (code, text, diagrams, etc.) and their structure, since HPC information is scattered across multiple formats. When answering, the system shows both the retrieved source material and the AI-generated explanation, providing users with factual references and clear, understandable answers.
sc-2025-044.key_novelty: The system combines modality-aware parsing (understanding different document types and formats) with dual-context retrieval-augmented generation that pairs retrieved HPC information with AI-generated explanations.

sc-2025-054.method: Progressive compression organizes floating-point data into n-dimensional trees—hierarchical structures spanning multiple data dimensions—where traversing deeper into the tree adds accuracy to the data. Users can stop at any depth to get a version with just enough precision for their needs, rather than being forced to download full-precision data that may be wastefully large. This approach trades off file size against data quality based on what accuracy each user actually requires.
sc-2025-054.key_novelty: Using hierarchical trees lets users choose their needed accuracy level when loading compressed data, rather than requiring full-precision compression in all cases.

sc-2025-060.method: The system assigns computational tasks to machines in a distributed system without knowing what tasks will arrive next. Instead of planning everything in advance, it adapts proven scheduling strategies from the past (HEFT and CPoP heuristics, which identify which machine each task should run on) to make decisions in real-time. As new information arrives—like how busy each machine currently is—the scheduler adjusts its choices dynamically to keep things running efficiently.
sc-2025-060.key_novelty: Classic offline scheduling strategies (HEFT and CPoP) can be adapted to work online with incomplete future knowledge, achieving 3–5% performance overhead compared to perfect scheduling versus 10% for naive approaches.

sc-2025-050.method: MLP-Offload moves computations and intermediate data values from GPU memory to CPU or storage during language model training. It uses multi-level offloading to choose the granularity at which to move data and multi-path offloading to direct data to the most appropriate destination based on memory and speed constraints. This combination reduces peak GPU memory requirements, allowing training of models larger than GPU memory alone would support.
sc-2025-050.key_novelty: Multi-level, multi-path offloading—moving computations and intermediate values from GPU at variable granularities to multiple possible storage locations—reduces GPU memory requirements during large language model training.

sc-2025-058.method: The researchers tested whether RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet—a technique for efficiently moving data using regular network cables) could match the performance of the more expensive InfiniBand networking standard when training large language models at scale. They systematically benchmarked different training configurations: splitting the workload across multiple computers (data sharding), representing numbers with fewer bits (quantization), recalculating values instead of storing them (recomputation), and adjusting how many examples are processed together (batch sizing). By measuring how well these approaches worked on both RoCE and InfiniBand, they identified the settings where RoCE achieves similar scaling efficiency.
sc-2025-058.key_novelty: RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet, a cheaper networking approach using regular cables) achieves near-linear scaling—where speed improves proportionally as you add more computers—matching the performance of InfiniBand when properly configured.

sc-2025-051.method: The algorithm divides matrices into tiles and uses index arithmetic—calculations based on position—to identify which overlapping sections from different tiles must be combined. It runs on graphics processors using a PGAS C++ framework that creates a shared virtual memory space, allowing GPUs on the same machine to send data directly to each other. Because the algorithm calculates overlaps using position-based arithmetic rather than assuming a fixed partitioning pattern, it works with any way of dividing matrices without requiring data to be shuffled around.
sc-2025-051.key_novelty: Unlike existing algorithms that work only with specific partitioning patterns and require data redistribution, this algorithm uses index arithmetic to support any matrix partitioning scheme directly.

sc-2025-062.method: HPK is a compatibility framework that allows cloud-native workloads (applications built to run in containers with orchestration, like Kubernetes) to execute on Slurm (a job scheduler for HPC clusters) without any code changes. Instead of needing separate physical clusters for the two workload types, HPK translates cloud-native requests into Slurm jobs, so both run on the same shared cluster infrastructure.
sc-2025-062.key_novelty: Instead of partitioning expensive computing resources into separate cloud and HPC clusters, you can run both workload types together on a single Slurm cluster.

sc-2025-059.method: The framework builds a decision tool called the Streaming Speed Score that figures out whether to send data directly to a remote computer (streaming) or save it to files first. It does this by measuring four things: how fast data arrives (data rate), how well it travels across the network (transfer efficiency), how quickly the remote computer can handle it (processing power), and how much time gets lost reading and writing files (I/O overhead). By comparing these measurements, the model tells you which approach—streaming the data live or storing it as files—will finish your analysis faster.
sc-2025-059.key_novelty: The innovation is a mathematical model (Tpct) that determines when streaming outperforms the file-based approach by considering data rate, network transfer efficiency, and processing power.

sc-2025-057.method: The framework uses SYCL (a programming language for GPUs) to write code that runs on AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA hardware. It narrows down candidate matches through multiple filtering stages using neighborhood signatures—fingerprints encoding the local graph structure around each node—which eliminates most non-matches before expensive computation. Once filtered, it runs a depth-first search on the GPU to find actual matching subgraphs, using parallel processing to explore candidate paths efficiently.
sc-2025-057.key_novelty: It combines multi-level signature-based filtering with GPU-accelerated depth-first search for subgraph matching, all in portable SYCL that works on AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA GPUs.

sc-2025-055.method: The system monitors real network traffic on the supercomputer using factor graphs—mathematical models that show how different security signals relate to each other and might indicate an attack. When alerts come in, the system uses these dynamic models to distinguish real attacks from false alarms, letting it identify threats before they cause damage. Visualization tools help security teams understand what attacks are being detected and respond accordingly.
sc-2025-055.key_novelty: The system uses factor graphs to detect attacks in petascale production supercomputers—systems operating at the scale of millions of trillions of calculations per second.

sc-2025-061.method: The solver uses the finite difference method—which breaks a complex mathematical problem into calculations on a grid of small points—and converts these calculations into quantum operations using the C2Q compiler. It provides two algorithm variants: one directly converts the grid calculations into a quantum circuit, while the other breaks the work into column-by-column operations to improve accuracy and performance on larger problems. This design allows the solver to run on both quantum computer simulators and real quantum hardware.
sc-2025-061.key_novelty: The solver uses direct conversion of grid-based calculations to quantum operations instead of variational quantum algorithms (which adjust quantum circuits through repeated trial-and-error), achieving better results on quantum simulators and real quantum devices.

sc-2025-064.method: The Calder toolkit compares a proxy application to its parent using similarity algorithms (methods that measure behavioral similarity) and Laplacian scores (a technique for ranking feature importance). It uses correlation filters to identify which HPC application features are essential for the proxy to accurately reproduce the parent's behavior.
sc-2025-064.key_novelty: The toolkit enables researchers to quantify how faithfully a proxy application reproduces its parent by identifying which HPC features are essential for matching behavior.

sc-2025-068.method: The Extended Quantum Framework provides a single programming interface to five quantum computing backends: Qiskit Aer, NWQ-Sim, QTensor, and TN-QVM (which run on local machines) and IonQ (which runs on remote cloud hardware). When you submit a quantum circuit, you can explicitly choose which backend to use, or let the system select based on circuit characteristics. The payoff is that different simulators use different internal strategies and perform better on different types of circuits, so having easy access to all of them lets you pick the best one for your specific problem.
sc-2025-068.key_novelty: The framework lets users swap between different quantum simulators and cloud providers without rewriting code, revealing which backend is best for different circuit types.

sc-2025-072.method: We obtained the ATLAHS toolchain (a simulator for modeling how AI, HPC, and storage systems send data across networks) and followed the authors' instructions to build and run it. We then tested whether the code produces the same results the paper claims and verified that other researchers can reliably use it by checking that the code builds without errors, runs successfully, and generates consistent outputs.
sc-2025-072.key_novelty: This report verifies whether the ATLAHS network simulator actually works as described when independent researchers attempt to use it.

sc-2025-065.method: DRAM-PIM (processing-in-memory) integrates small processors into DRAM itself, eliminating the usual bottleneck of moving data between memory and a separate CPU or GPU. DRIM-ANN optimizes approximate nearest-neighbor search (finding items similar to a query, not necessarily the closest match) for UPMEM's commercial DRAM-PIM hardware through tuning approximation levels to balance speed and accuracy, replacing expensive squaring math with pre-computed lookup tables, distributing work evenly across embedded processors (load-balancing), and minimizing data transfers (I/O optimization). This keeps computation and data together, avoiding the memory bottlenecks that slow CPUs and the capacity limits that constrain GPUs.
sc-2025-065.key_novelty: DRIM-ANN is the first approximate nearest-neighbor search system built for commercial DRAM-PIM hardware, with optimizations targeting the low-power embedded processors inside DRAM banks.

sc-2025-071.method: The evaluation process involves running the code and data from the original research to see if someone else can reproduce the same results. The team attempts to execute the implementation of high-performance branch-free algorithms for extended-precision floating-point arithmetic (computation using special high-accuracy math without conditional jumps in the code), documenting what functionality was tested and whether it produced the expected outputs. They check which components worked, which failed, and whether the original performance measurements held up under independent verification.
sc-2025-071.key_novelty: This report verifies whether the prior research on high-performance branch-free algorithms for extended-precision floating-point arithmetic can be independently reproduced and validated.

sc-2025-066.method: UpANNS positions data intelligently within a Processing-In-Memory chip (where processors are built into the memory itself to eliminate slow data movement) to speed up similarity searches across billions of entries. It dynamically adjusts computational resources based on real-time needs, and encodes data so similar items sit near each other (called co-occurrence optimization), making lookups faster. Finally, it eliminates weak candidate matches early on, so the system only fully computes scores for the most promising results.
sc-2025-066.key_novelty: UpANNS achieves near-linear performance scaling for billion-entry similarity search on Processing-In-Memory chips, delivering 4.3 times higher query throughput than the standard Faiss system and 2.3 times better energy efficiency than GPU approaches.

sc-2025-069.method: The reproducibility team examined the code, data, and experiment configurations that the authors submitted, checking whether their descriptions matched what was actually implemented. They then ran the experiments themselves to verify they could reproduce the same results reported in the paper.
sc-2025-069.key_novelty: This report verifies that the TensorMD paper's results can be independently reproduced using the authors' submitted code and data.

sc-2025-067.method: They created a benchmark that measures how Mixture of Experts models—systems that automatically route data to different expert subnetworks—perform on H100 GPUs under different configurations. They varied parameters like batch size (how many examples at once), sequence length (how long the input is), number of experts, and feed-forward network size. The benchmark tests optimization techniques including pruning (removing unused experts), fused operations (combining multiple computational steps into one), speculative decoding (predicting outputs early), quantization (using lower precision), and parallelization (distributing work across processors).
sc-2025-067.key_novelty: By testing Mixture of Experts models from different sources (Mixtral, DeepSeek, OLMoE, Qwen) under various configurations, they showed that the best way to run these models depends on factors like batch size and sequence length.

sc-2025-056.method: The researchers surveyed 9 supercomputing domains. For each, they documented three things: the data the application processes (its workload), what compression it specifically needs, and what current compressors can actually provide. This revealed the gaps—where applications need compression features that current tools don't offer.
sc-2025-056.key_novelty: The paper identifies where compression tools fall short in meeting scientific application needs and provides 24 actionable recommendations to address the gaps.

sc-2025-073.method: The evaluators reviewed the artifact description from the original paper—how the authors documented the Spack software implementation. They then independently ran the code to verify that it actually produced the claimed results about binary and source-based package management. This involved comparing what the paper claimed would happen with what actually occurred when the software ran.
sc-2025-073.key_novelty: This report verifies whether the original paper's findings on Spack package management can be independently reproduced from its artifacts.

sc-2025-063.method: PEAK uses Dynamic Binary Instrumentation—inserting measurement code into a running program—to profile its performance. Static mode caps overhead at a fixed amount. Heartbeat mode dynamically adjusts how much measuring happens using regular timing pulses, maintaining the user-specified overhead ratio in real-time.
sc-2025-063.key_novelty: The core novelty is heartbeat-based dynamic adjustment that maintains a constant overhead ratio in real-time, enabling better profiling accuracy for changing workloads.

sc-2025-075.method: The approach packages code in two flexible forms—source code (human-readable) and intermediate representation (a half-compiled form)—inside containers. Rather than making hardware-specific optimization choices when building the container, it waits until deployment time. When the container lands on a specific machine, AI models automatically discover which optimizations work best for that hardware and compile the code accordingly, keeping everything inside the container.
sc-2025-075.key_novelty: The system keeps code in flexible form inside containers and delays hardware-specific optimization decisions until deployment time, when AI automatically discovers the best optimizations for the target hardware.

sc-2025-070.method: The team obtained and evaluated the Moment paper's code and documentation describing a technique for optimizing two aspects together: the physical communication pathways between GPUs and where data is stored when training graph neural networks (neural networks designed for graph-structured data) on multiple GPUs with some data on disk because it exceeds GPU memory. They recreated the experimental environment and ran the training jobs as described, comparing their reproduced results against the original paper's reported performance to verify whether the work is reproducible.
sc-2025-070.key_novelty: This report verifies whether the Moment paper's approach of jointly optimizing GPU communication topology and data placement actually produces its claimed performance improvements for training graph neural networks across multiple GPUs with disk-based storage.

sc-2025-074.method: They built a streaming interface—continuous data pipelines created through hardware synthesis tools—that enables communication between a host computer and a dataflow accelerator (a processor optimized for routing data through operations). The interface uses MPI (the standard multi-computer communication protocol) and allows the accelerator itself to initiate collective operations, which are coordinated data exchanges involving multiple processors. They validated the design using an enhanced version of the HPL benchmark from the HPCC_FPGA suite.
sc-2025-074.key_novelty: A collective communication interface using data streaming for dataflow accelerators that reduces hardware resource consumption.

sc-2025-078.method: Wasp computes shortest paths (fastest routes from one starting point to all others) on multiple processor cores using work stealing—when one thread runs out of tasks, it borrows work from a busier thread. Unlike older methods like Δ-stepping that create redundant computations upfront, Wasp only produces redundancy when threads actually need more work. Threads operate asynchronously (without waiting for synchronization), which handles the irregular work patterns that shortest-path algorithms naturally create.
sc-2025-078.key_novelty: Using priority-aware work stealing (where idle threads take high-priority tasks from busy ones), Wasp ensures redundant computation in shortest-path algorithms only occurs when threads need more work, not by design upfront.

sc-2025-080.method: The framework automatically selects which optimization algorithm to use for a network by having an LLM (a language model) analyze three types of information: the available algorithms, the current network's operating conditions, and incoming service requests. The LLM converts this information into numerical patterns (called embeddings) that capture their key characteristics. It then matches the network's current situation to the algorithm from a pool of candidates that will perform best—working like a triage system to pick the right solution for each specific scenario.
sc-2025-080.key_novelty: An LLM automatically selects the best optimization algorithm for a network by analyzing embeddings of available algorithms and current network conditions, without relying on hardcoded rules.

sc-2025-087.method: The Vernier system monitors application communication using histograms—buckets that count message frequencies in different categories—rather than recording every individual message. You annotate points in your code where communication happens, and Vernier collects statistical summaries for each annotated region. This approach is fast enough to run during actual execution (online) or afterward from logs (offline), and the compact statistics can feed directly into benchmarking and network simulations.
sc-2025-087.key_novelty: Vernier uses statistical histograms to track application communication patterns instead of detailed message traces, making monitoring fast enough to run during execution and scalable enough for network simulation and optimization.

sc-2025-082.method: The HashBrick library organizes data into rectangular blocks called bricks and uses hashing to quickly find neighboring blocks that need to exchange data. Instead of the usual message-passing approach that requires copying data into buffers, it uses NVIDIA NVSHMEM, a method where one GPU can directly read data from another GPU's memory without needing the other GPU to actively participate in sending it. This avoids the packing overhead and complex neighbor lookups that slow down traditional approaches. The approach is tested on an NVIDIA GH200 cluster using a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) application and a Jacobi iteration benchmark.
sc-2025-082.key_novelty: Hash-based indexing of irregularly distributed bricks combined with one-sided NVSHMEM communication enables efficient ghost-zone (boundary-data) exchange between GPUs without buffer-packing overhead.

sc-2025-079.method: FT-Transformer treats the entire attention module as a single protected unit rather than protecting individual operations, which reduces the computational overhead. For linear layers (matrix multiplications), it uses algorithm-based fault tolerance (ABFT)—a mathematical technique that detects errors by checking properties of the computation—applied in a strided way so that parallel threads don't need to wait for each other to synchronize. This approach protects all the computational steps that make up the attention module.
sc-2025-079.key_novelty: FT-Transformer protects the attention module as a single unit instead of protecting individual operations, using algorithm-based fault tolerance with strided processing to eliminate thread synchronization, achieving 7.56x speedup.

sc-2025-084.method: The approach improves LLM training by focusing on communication—the data transfers between processors that often become the bottleneck. It finds good tuning settings by using performance portability, a metric that measures how efficiently training runs across different hardware systems rather than optimizing for just one machine. The method was tested on real production LLM training using DeepSpeed, a framework that distributes training across multiple GPUs.
sc-2025-084.key_novelty: The core idea is tuning LLM training to reduce communication between processors, using performance portability (how efficiently settings work across different hardware) as the measure, which achieves 1.6x faster training than default settings.

sc-2025-081.method: A committee member independently ran the MANS paper's code to verify its experimental results. They tested whether ANS encoding (Asymmetric Numeral Systems—a compression technique for multi-byte integers) actually achieved the efficiency gains reported on both CPUs and GPUs. They verified the code was truly portable, working correctly on both hardware types.
sc-2025-081.key_novelty: Independent verification confirmed that the MANS paper's ANS encoding achieves its claimed efficiency and portability across CPUs and GPUs.

sc-2025-083.method: When adding edges to a graph on multicore computers, processor cores interfere with each other accessing shared cache memory, and work becomes unbalanced between cores, which slows the system down. Bubble fixes this by sorting incoming edges in small batches (mini-batches) before adding them to the graph — this sorting groups related edges together so each core accesses only its own private L3 cache without interfering with others. As a result, adding new edges to the graph scales nearly linearly with more cores (gets faster proportionally), and the system still performs well when analyzing the graph afterward.
sc-2025-083.key_novelty: Mini-batch sorting arranges incoming edges so each processor core works only with its private L3 cache (built-in fast processor memory), eliminating the cache interference that limits multicore graph processing.

sc-2025-085.method: The system combines three layers: a language model (an AI system trained on text) that holds general knowledge, specialized models for different types of data (text, sequences, structures, images), and external databases and tools. When given a research question, it automatically selects one of eleven reasoning methods by identifying keywords and analyzing the question with the language model.
sc-2025-085.key_novelty: The system automatically selects from eleven specialized reasoning methods instead of using a single approach for all biological research problems.

sc-2025-077.method: The researchers analyzed 2.5 years of actual error data from the Delta supercomputer to understand failures as they happened in production. They compared memory error rates (measured by MTBE — mean time between errors, which indicates how reliable the memory is) and studied which hardware components failed most frequently and why. They then projected how these failure patterns would affect system availability when scaled to thousands of GPUs.
sc-2025-077.key_novelty: This is the first real-world measurement of H100 and A100 GPU reliability at exascale (systems with thousands of GPUs), showing that H100 has worse memory errors and identifying shortcomings in its recovery mechanisms.

sc-2025-076.method: The researchers tested various HPC applications on Frontier, a supercomputer with AMD MI250X GPUs. They systematically restricted GPU frequency (how fast it runs) and power consumption at different levels, running identical tests on both single nodes and 32-node clusters. They measured the trade-off between computing speed lost and energy saved for each combination of constraints and application type.
sc-2025-076.key_novelty: Frequency and power capping save energy through different mechanisms on exascale GPU systems, with effectiveness depending on workload and system scale.

sc-2025-086.method: The design moves communication from the CPU to the GPU itself, so the GPU can directly exchange data with other GPUs via NVSHMEM (a library that lets GPUs access each other's memory). Instead of packing data first and then sending it, the GPU kernels combine both steps in a single operation. This leverages NVLink's asynchronous copy engine (dedicated hardware for memory transfers) to hide latency: while data moves between GPUs, the GPU keeps computing other work instead of waiting idle.
sc-2025-086.key_novelty: The innovation is having the GPU itself initiate and manage data exchanges with other GPUs via asynchronous memory transfers, rather than the CPU coordinating this, yielding 1.5x speedup within a single node, 2x speedup across multiple nodes with NVLink, and 1.3x speedup across multiple nodes with InfiniBand.

sc-2025-090.method: MP-SpMM converts unstructured sparse matrices into patterns that specialized hardware (Sparse Tensor Cores) can process efficiently. It uses a matching algorithm from graph theory to identify how to best rearrange the non-zero elements, then adds strategically-placed zeros to form 2:4 or 1:2 sparsity patterns—the specific structured formats the hardware requires. The approach includes a custom storage format and an optimized GPU kernel designed to exploit the Sparse Tensor Cores' capabilities.
sc-2025-090.key_novelty: By applying a graph-theory-inspired matching algorithm, the method transforms unstructured sparse matrices into the 2:4 and 1:2 sparsity patterns that Sparse Tensor Cores require, enabling efficient hardware processing of real-world sparse data.

sc-2025-091.method: ZeroSpec profiles program executions to identify where zero-values (variables equal to zero) frequently cause wasted computation. It uses static analysis—specifically control data flow analysis, which traces how values flow and change through the code—to pinpoint exactly where these zero-values propagate. For each optimization opportunity, a fine-grained cost model calculates whether specializing the code would save enough time to justify the effort. For the most valuable opportunities, it automatically generates specialized fast-path versions of the code that skip redundant operations when zero-values are detected.
sc-2025-091.key_novelty: It combines runtime profiling with static control data flow analysis to automatically identify and eliminate redundant operations caused by zero-values through code specialization.

sc-2025-093.method: The researchers design processors that tightly integrate analog accelerators (specialized circuits using continuous electrical signals) as coprocessors embedded inside processor cores, using the RISC-V open-source processor design as the foundation. They model this hybrid system using SST (Structural Simulation Toolkit), a software tool that simulates how computer hardware behaves. They test the design by running two iterative linear solvers—computational methods that repeatedly refine solutions to systems of equations—to measure how well the analog and digital parts work together.
sc-2025-093.key_novelty: The key contribution is using simulation to show where digital components become the limiting factor in hybrid analog-digital RISC-V systems, guiding optimization of the analog-digital balance.

sc-2025-094.method: The study examines foundation models (large AI models pre-trained on massive data) across five biological domains: genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, chemistry, and biomedical literature. For each domain, researchers identify computational bottlenecks (slow points), measure memory and data storage requirements, and characterize the mathematical operations the models perform.
sc-2025-094.key_novelty: First systematic cross-domain study establishing which high-performance computing infrastructure and design principles work best for biological foundation models.

sc-2025-095.method: The researchers examined errors that actually occurred in the PanDA workflow management system, which coordinates computational work across computing sites distributed globally. They collected data on failures across all these different sites and organized them into categories based on type (network problems, resource shortages, software bugs, etc.). By analyzing which types of errors happened most frequently and where, they identified patterns in how large-scale distributed systems fail. This systematic error mapping is essential for designing defenses against future failures.
sc-2025-095.key_novelty: This analysis systematically characterizes the types of errors and failure patterns that occur in production-scale distributed workflow systems across heterogeneous computing sites.

sc-2025-092.method: SWDOCKP2 works by first organizing the molecule database—grouping similar molecular shapes through conformational sorting and merging—to enable faster screening. It then aligns search grids for multiple protein targets and screens them in parallel, testing many targets simultaneously rather than sequentially. To accelerate the core calculations, it uses SIMD (single-instruction multiple-data, where a processor performs the same operation on many data points at once) to speed up trilinear interpolation, a mathematical technique for estimating values between known points. Finally, it uses an emulator for the Sunway processor architecture, allowing the code to run efficiently across different hardware platforms.
sc-2025-092.key_novelty: The core idea is organizing the molecule database by conformational shape and screening multiple protein targets in parallel, enabling trillion-ligand drug screening.

sc-2025-088.method: eIM reduces the memory overhead of influence maximization on GPU by storing reverse reachable (RRR) sets—the random path samples used to estimate influence spread—more efficiently. The approach cuts memory requirements for the network data and RRR sets by 54% while maintaining accuracy compared to baseline GPU implementations. This frees up GPU memory, allowing the algorithm to handle much larger networks.
sc-2025-088.key_novelty: eIM's core insight is that reverse reachable sets can be stored more efficiently on GPU, reducing memory requirements by 54% while achieving 1-3 order-of-magnitude speedups in influence maximization compared to prior GPU implementations.

sc-2025-089.method: RL4Sys embeds a lightweight client in the target system that watches behavior and runs a cached machine-learning policy, keeping overhead below 6%. Separately, remote trainers asynchronously improve the policy from the recorded observations—communicating through zero-copy gRPC (sending data without duplicating it) with adaptive batching that groups updates for efficiency. This split between a minimal local client and powerful remote trainers avoids the heavy integration overhead of traditional RL frameworks.
sc-2025-089.key_novelty: The innovation is achieving practical system-level reinforcement learning with under 6% overhead by pairing a lightweight embedded client with remote asynchronous trainers using zero-copy communication.

sc-2025-098.method: AMRaCut divides meshes across multiple computers for parallel processing using parallel label propagation (where region assignments spread through the mesh structure) combined with graph diffusion (information flowing through connections). It operates mostly on each partition locally, exchanging information only with neighboring partitions, avoiding expensive global coordination. This is efficient for adaptive mesh refinement (where meshes automatically refine in important regions and coarsen elsewhere) because changes are mostly localized, making local decisions sufficient.
sc-2025-098.key_novelty: Using parallel label propagation to partition adaptive meshes efficiently through local-only communication between neighboring regions.

sc-2025-103.method: KVMSR+UDWeave works by separating three programming decisions that are usually tangled together: how many tasks run in parallel, which processor handles which task, and where data gets stored. The UpDown supercomputer makes this possible through two built-in features: you can name specific processor locations for computations to run on, and every processor can see the same addresses in memory (shared global address space). This separation allows programmers to write code that takes full advantage of the hardware's parallelism, even for irregular graph algorithms where some parts have far more work than others.
sc-2025-103.key_novelty: The innovation is separating how many things run in parallel from where they run and where their data lives, which unlocks extreme-scale performance for irregular graph algorithms on the UpDown supercomputer.

sc-2025-101.method: Students in this 3-day Toledo EXCEL workshop built a custom IoT sensor system (hardware that collects real measurements like soil moisture and light) and used MakeCode (a visual block-based programming tool) to write code that processes that sensor data. They then used Teachable Machine (a tool that lets you train a machine learning classifier by showing it examples) to teach the system to recognize plant health conditions from the sensor readings. Working through this full pipeline, they created a functional smart plant care assistant that could make predictions based on live sensor inputs.
sc-2025-101.key_novelty: The workshop made machine learning training accessible to high school students by combining real sensor hardware, visual block programming, and hands-on classifier training in one integrated project.

sc-2025-099.method: STELLAR uses an LLM (a large language model that acts as an autonomous reasoning system) to automatically tune parallel file systems. It starts by extracting tunable parameters from system manuals and analyzing I/O traces (recordings of how data moves through the system), then proposes tuning strategies and runs test applications to measure their effectiveness. Based on the results, it refines its strategies and learns from each attempt. The system combines retrieval-augmented generation (looking up specific parameter knowledge when reasoning), tool execution, LLM-based reasoning, and a multiagent design (multiple specialized agents that work together and verify each other's thinking).
sc-2025-099.key_novelty: STELLAR introduces LLM-based autonomous reasoning to automatically tune parallel file systems, combining multiagent design to make the reasoning more reliable and retrieval-augmented generation to access parameter knowledge from documentation.

sc-2025-100.method: mpitofino moves MPI collective operations—where multiple computers coordinate to combine or share data—from running in software on individual computers to running directly on the network switch hardware (an Intel Tofino ASIC). The system uses P4, a programming language for network chips, to specify what operations the switch should perform, and leverages existing RoCEv2 and RDMA capabilities on network cards to enable direct memory access. By integrating into Open MPI, the system lets existing parallel computing applications automatically benefit from network-level coordination without requiring code changes.
sc-2025-100.key_novelty: mpitofino is the first practical implementation of MPI collective operations on a programmable Ethernet switch (Intel Tofino), using P4 with RoCEv2 and RDMA support.

sc-2025-105.method: Ran distributed radix sort—an algorithm that constantly moves data between computers, making it a tough test for any framework—on five programming frameworks (Chapel, MPI, OpenSHMEM, Conveyors, Lamellar) on HPE Cray systems. For each framework, they measured three things: raw speed, how well it scaled to more computers, and how much code was needed to implement it. By testing all five on the exact same demanding problem, they could see which frameworks handled communication overhead best and which were easiest to program.
sc-2025-105.key_novelty: This benchmark directly compares five distributed-memory programming frameworks on identical communication-intensive tasks, measuring practical trade-offs in performance, scalability, and code complexity.

sc-2025-102.method: An independent evaluator (Roberto R. Exposito) attempted to reproduce the MXBLAS paper's results by running its code on real hardware, following the artifact evaluation standards of SC25 (a major supercomputing conference). They examined the complete artifact—software, source code, and test data—and reviewed the Artifact Description and Evaluation appendix, which documented what tests were run and how.
sc-2025-102.key_novelty: Independent validation that MXBLAS's results for accelerating 8-bit deep learning can be reproduced using the paper's released code.

sc-2025-107.method: CRK-HACC handles a trillion particles by splitting the calculation into separate size scales (separation-of-scale techniques) and running tree-based gravity solvers (algorithms that hierarchically organize calculations) on GPUs to accelerate them. It analyzes results as the simulation progresses (in situ analysis pipelines) rather than storing all raw data, saving storage overhead. A multi-tiered approach optimizes how data moves to and from storage, allowing the Frontier supercomputer to process the full trillion-particle scale.
sc-2025-107.key_novelty: This presents the first trillion-particle cosmological hydrodynamics simulation at full-sky scale on Frontier (Frontier-E), advancing roughly ten times beyond prior work through hierarchical algorithm design and GPU acceleration.

sc-2025-097.method: MQSS Pulse extends the Munich Quantum Software Stack with a compiled C/C++ API for pulse-level control—the ability to directly specify fine-grained hardware commands that control quantum gates, running faster than Python because it's compiled rather than interpreted. It extends LLVM (a compiler framework) to generate and optimize pulse instructions. A C-based backend interface adapts these instructions to each quantum hardware's specific constraints. The system defines a portable pulse exchange format, a standardized way to represent pulse code that works across different quantum computers.
sc-2025-097.key_novelty: MQSS Pulse enables end-to-end compiled pulse-level control in heterogeneous quantum computing using C/C++ APIs, LLVM integration, and a portable pulse exchange format.

sc-2025-106.method: The researchers set up a hybrid system that streams X-ray detector data directly to a Groq accelerator, a specialized processor designed for fast, predictable computation. Using a supporting software stack, the Groq processor performs image analysis with minimal delay (low-latency inference), which is critical since X-ray detectors generate data faster than traditional approaches can handle. The system integrates these results back into photon science workflows, giving scientists real-time feedback from their experiments.
sc-2025-106.key_novelty: Streaming X-ray image analysis using a deterministic tensor processor (Groq) at the edge achieves microsecond-level latency, matching high-speed detector data rates.

sc-2025-109.method: The course teaches students how to run machine learning systems in production by having them practice on Chameleon Cloud, a research computing platform where they rent computing resources. Students work on real infrastructure tasks: setting up servers, training models across multiple machines, deploying those models to run as services, monitoring their performance, and automating routine operations. The course used 186,692 compute instance hours.
sc-2025-109.key_novelty: This work is the first to measure and report the true computational costs of teaching operational ML systems, including what it would cost on commercial cloud platforms.

sc-2025-096.method: IDS lets scientists write a single query that retrieves data and runs AI models (like AlphaFold or AutoDock Vina) together, avoiding manual shuffling between separate tools. The system stores data in multiple formats—organized tables in a feature store, numerical vectors used by AI algorithms in a vector store, and relationship networks in a knowledge graph—and caches results at different levels across machines for faster repeated queries. Scientists can search using keywords, combine datasets with set operations (union, intersection), or use vector and matrix math to navigate the data, while the Cray Graph Engine determines which data to fetch and which models to run.
sc-2025-096.key_novelty: IDS combines data retrieval and model execution—using simulations (AutoDock Vina), AI prediction (AlphaFold), and sequence analysis (Smith-Waterman)—in one query, with results cached at different levels across machines so scientists get faster results and avoid manual data movement.

sc-2025-114.method: They tested three different architectures for moving data between facilities: Direct (straightforward connection), Proxied (routed through an intermediate server), and Managed Service (using a cloud service). They ran this evaluation on real HPC infrastructure—OLCF's Advanced Computing Ecosystem—using the DS2HPC framework and SciStream toolkit. They used synthetic workloads designed to mimic real scientific workflows to measure how each architecture performed.
sc-2025-114.key_novelty: This is the first time anyone has systematically measured how different cross-facility data-streaming designs (Direct, Proxied, and Managed Service approaches) perform on real production HPC systems.

sc-2025-104.method: The method breaks the electron-dynamics calculation into local regions that mostly operate independently, drastically reducing communication between processors. It uses basis functions (mathematical building blocks) that only affect nearby atoms, so each region can work mostly with local data. To avoid redundant calculations, especially in hybrid functionals (which blend different ways of modeling electron interactions), it compresses and reuses intermediate mathematical results. Finally, it uses a fused operation combining matrix multiplication and summation into a single step to maximize hardware efficiency.
sc-2025-104.key_novelty: It uses basis functions that only affect nearby atoms (discontinuous Galerkin), eliminating the inter-processor communication bottleneck that previously limited electron-dynamics simulations to thousands of atoms and enabling scale to million atoms.

sc-2025-110.method: DALIA speeds up inference for multivariate Gaussian processes (systems with many interconnected variables where predictions are correlated) using graphics processors (GPUs) and a mathematical shortcut called integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA), which trades some accuracy for much faster calculation. The method stores model relationships as sparse inverse covariance matrices—keeping only important connections rather than dense full matrices—and organizes these into block-dense chunks for efficient GPU processing. Work is distributed across multiple computers in a hierarchy using distributed-memory parallelism, so different machines can solve different pieces of the problem simultaneously.
sc-2025-110.key_novelty: Combining GPU acceleration with hierarchical distributed parallelism enables INLA to handle multivariate Gaussian processes efficiently across hundreds of supercomputer nodes.

sc-2025-108.method: The approach accelerates RELION using three core strategies: task-level parallelism (dividing work into independent tasks that run simultaneously), three-phase GPU memory management (organizing data flow in stages to avoid delays), and Tensor Core acceleration (using specialized fast-math hardware to speed up the core difference calculations). It overlaps operations to keep the GPU busy while data transfers occur, and reuses data multiple times within the GPU to minimize memory transfers.
sc-2025-108.key_novelty: This is the first to apply task parallelism and specialized GPU math acceleration (Tensor Cores) to RELION, optimizing how data flows through GPU and CPU memory for better efficiency.

sc-2025-113.method: The researchers compared two ways of processing genetic data from millions of cells: traditional computer processors (CPUs) and graphics processors (GPUs, using libraries like RAPIDS and CuPy that speed up calculations). They took a dataset of 1.3 million cells and deliberately reduced its size in controlled steps, running both methods on each version. By comparing whether the results stayed consistent across smaller and larger datasets, they could tell whether the speedup from using GPUs came at the cost of changing the biological conclusions.
sc-2025-113.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study showing that graphics processors can speed up cell analysis significantly but produce different biological results than traditional methods.

sc-2025-115.method: Packets are labeled at the source computer with priority markers (DSCP—Differentiated Services Code Point, a standard way to identify traffic type) that indicate whether they carry real-time streams or bulk data. Existing network switches read these labels and queue packets separately by priority class. At the edge gateway to the high-speed network, the system controls how fast each priority class of packets can be transmitted—real-time traffic goes through immediately while bulk transfers are rate-limited.
sc-2025-115.key_novelty: This is the first deployment of DSCP-based traffic prioritization in an HPC datacenter's local network, achieving performance guarantees without requiring new hardware or custom software.

sc-2025-111.method: TianheEngine divides a trillion-scale graph across thousands of computers while accounting for hierarchical communication costs—the fact that communication speed varies depending on distance within the system. It analyzes which parts of the graph are densely connected and which are sparse, then arranges the division to keep densely-connected regions on fast communication paths (like between cores on the same server) while spreading sparse regions to slower paths (like between distant servers). By matching graph structure to the actual communication hierarchy, it reduces wasted time on expensive cross-system communication.
sc-2025-111.key_novelty: This is the first system to systematically account for hierarchical communication costs—how communication speed differs across system levels—when dividing trillion-scale graphs, validated on 79,024 computing nodes.

sc-2025-116.method: Qonductor provides a universal programming interface that doesn't depend on specific quantum hardware brands (hardware-agnostic). It estimates how much quantum processing and classical computing each job needs. Then a smart scheduler assigns jobs across both quantum and classical resources, balancing speed against resource efficiency.
sc-2025-116.key_novelty: Qonductor is the first cloud orchestrator designed for jobs mixing quantum and classical computing, combining resource estimation with smart scheduling across different types of hardware.

sc-2025-119.method: When saving a checkpoint of a PDE simulation, the method compresses the data using lossy compression—a technique that discards some precision to reduce file size—while actively controlling how much kinetic and potential energy are allowed to change during that compression. By constraining these energy perturbations, the approach prevents the simulation from becoming unstable—avoiding divergence and oscillations—when it restarts from the compressed checkpoint. The technique was validated across diverse PDE configurations on the Frontier supercomputer.
sc-2025-119.key_novelty: This is the first lossy compression method for PDE checkpointing that explicitly controls physical invariants like energy, ensuring simulations remain stable even across multiple save-and-restart cycles.

sc-2025-117.method: Mojo is a programming language that compiles Python-like code to run on GPUs using MLIR, an intermediate compiler format that translates the same code to work on different GPU types without rewriting. It uses syntax similar to CUDA (the standard GPU programming language) so experienced GPU programmers can learn it quickly. The researchers tested this on four scientific computing tasks: stencil and BabelStream (where moving data between memory and processors is the limiting factor) and miniBUDE and Hartree-Fock (where actual computation is the bottleneck, with Hartree-Fock also using atomic operations to safely coordinate multiple processors updating shared data).
sc-2025-117.key_novelty: Mojo shows that MLIR-based compilation can give the Python scientific ecosystem portable, high-performance GPU code that works across different vendors.

sc-2025-112.method: X-ray ptychography requires repeating mathematical steps to rebuild detailed images from the data collected. The problem is that modern microscopes generate data much faster than traditional reconstruction methods can process it. The solution uses graphics processors—chips that excel at performing many calculations simultaneously—installed directly at the microscope instead of at a distant computer. This allows images to be reconstructed immediately as data arrives, rather than being stored and processed later.
sc-2025-112.key_novelty: Graphics processors positioned at the microscope enable real-time image reconstruction during high-speed X-ray ptychography, making autonomous experimental control possible.

sc-2025-118.method: The system automates the creation of multiple-choice exam questions from a large collection of scientific papers. It reads PDF papers, breaks them into meaningful sections, automatically generates questions from those sections, and tests whether small language models—AI systems with 1.1 billion to 14 billion parameters—can answer correctly. The key experiment compares two retrieval strategies: giving the models the actual paper text to search through versus giving them reasoning explanations from a much larger model (GPT-4). The case study generated over 16,000 questions from 22,000 papers focused on radiation and cancer biology.
sc-2025-118.key_novelty: This automated system generates large-scale exam benchmarks from scientific papers and shows that reasoning traces from a larger model work better as retrieval sources than paper chunks for improving small language model performance on domain-specific expert exams.

sc-2025-124.method: We ran the code and experiments from the original paper ourselves, following SC25's official standards for reproducibility evaluation. We used the same hardware setup and workloads they described, measured whether we got similar performance results, and documented any differences. This process checks if someone else can get the same results when they follow the original paper's instructions.
sc-2025-124.key_novelty: This paper verifies whether another paper's claimed performance improvements actually happen when you run their code yourself.

sc-2025-120.method: Spack is an HPC package manager that normally forces you to choose between pre-compiled packages (fast but inflexible) or source-code compilation (flexible but slow). This extension adds a 'binary compatibility model'—rules that determine which pre-compiled packages can safely work together without conflicts. With this model, Spack can intelligently mix pre-compiled binaries and source-compiled packages in the same system, choosing which to use based on speed and flexibility needs. The system still tracks dependencies automatically, so it always knows what depends on what.
sc-2025-120.key_novelty: It creates a binary compatibility model—rules determining which pre-compiled packages (especially ABI-sensitive ones like MPI) can safely work together—letting HPC package managers mix fast pre-built binaries with flexible source compilations.

sc-2025-121.method: Rather than generating all permutations on a single processor, the approach distributes the work across many GPUs in a cluster, where each GPU computes permutations for its assigned portion of the data in parallel. By splitting the computation across multiple processors instead of relying on a single machine, this method keeps resource demands proportional to the dataset size. This enables efficient processing of datasets containing billions of elements, which would be infeasible on a single GPU.
sc-2025-121.key_novelty: Permutation generation is scaled across GPU clusters so billion-element datasets can be rearranged efficiently without overwhelming any single machine.

sc-2025-122.method: coMtainer saves build-time metadata (information about how the code was originally compiled) in the container. When deployed on a remote supercomputing system, that system can recompile the container using its native compilers and apply LTO (Link Time Optimization) and PGO (Profile Guided Optimization, which uses performance data to make code faster). This allows containers to remain portable across systems while still being optimized for each system's specific hardware.
sc-2025-122.key_novelty: coMtainer embeds build-time metadata in containers, enabling remote HPC systems to automatically optimize them for local hardware without losing portability.

sc-2025-125.method: BLAZE accelerates BLASTP (a tool for comparing DNA or protein sequences) on GPUs by using hybrid parallelism, which means it switches between fine-grained parallelism (many small parallel tasks) and coarse-grained parallelism (fewer large tasks) based on what works best for each piece of data. Instead of using one kernel (a GPU program) for all sequences, BLAZE creates specialized kernel versions tuned for different sequence lengths, since a single kernel wastes GPU resources when sequences don't match its optimized size. The approach also applies additional GPU-specific optimizations. This combination allows BLAZE to outperform hand-optimized CPU implementations.
sc-2025-125.key_novelty: BLAZE combines adaptive parallelism—switching between fine-grained and coarse-grained work distribution—with kernels customized for different sequence lengths to make GPUs faster than CPUs at sequence comparison.

sc-2025-127.method: The workflow standardizes drug response measurements to a consistent scale, then analyzes how prediction errors are distributed across different drug types to identify which errors matter most in an imbalanced dataset. It was tested on the Aurora exascale supercomputer.
sc-2025-127.key_novelty: The core contribution is a step-by-step workflow that uses data standardization and error distribution analysis together to understand failures in drug response prediction when promising drugs are rare.

sc-2025-123.method: RESILIO builds tomographic reconstruction (assembling a 3D image from many 2D slices taken at different angles) as a pipeline of independent, pluggable components using Mofka (a persistent data streaming system from the Mochi middleware). Because data flows through the pipeline continuously as it arrives rather than waiting to batch, latency stays low. The persistent streaming (data recorded at each step) lets the system recover from failures by restarting at the last checkpoint rather than from the beginning.
sc-2025-123.key_novelty: RESILIO treats tomographic reconstruction as a composable pipeline of components that continuously stream and persist data, enabling automatic failure recovery without reprocessing.

sc-2025-134.method: They built a GitHub Action—a tool that automatically runs when code changes—that securely connects to and runs tests on remote HPC machines. This solves the problem that HPC researchers can't easily test their code on the specialized hardware they need without manual work. The tool includes security controls so only trusted code can access expensive HPC systems. They also surveyed existing reproducibility efforts and identified the main barriers preventing HPC research from being more reproducible.
sc-2025-134.key_novelty: They enabled GitHub Actions to automatically run tests on remote HPC machines with security protections, allowing HPC research to be reproduced without manual intervention on specialized hardware.

sc-2025-126.method: They created DeepFlame, a flame simulator that replaces expensive physics calculations with trained neural networks, dramatically reducing computational time. To leverage this speedup at trillion-cell scale, they optimized three critical areas: parallel computing (coordinating work across thousands of processors simultaneously), computational efficiency (streamlining calculations per processor), and data I/O (faster reading/writing of simulation results). The complete system was tuned specifically for Sunway and Fugaku supercomputers.
sc-2025-126.key_novelty: Deep learning can accelerate supercritical flame simulation to trillion-cell scale while preserving real-fluid physics accuracy on leadership supercomputers.

sc-2025-131.method: Researchers independently tested AMD's MI300X and MI325X GPUs using focused tests (microbenchmarks) that measure specific capabilities—compute speed, memory access speed, and data throughput—plus real AI and scientific computing applications. This approach reveals both peak performance and real-world behavior while tracking speed, power consumption, and energy efficiency.
sc-2025-131.key_novelty: This provides the first comprehensive independent testing of AMD's MI300X and MI325X GPUs to measure their speed, power consumption, and energy efficiency.

sc-2025-128.method: The approach runs three interconnected climate models—which simulate the atmosphere, oceans, ice sheets, and other systems working together—to project decades of future climate worldwide. These simulations run on two of Europe's most powerful supercomputers (LUMI and MareNostrum5) to handle the enormous calculation needed to model the planet at 5-kilometer resolution (fine enough to capture details like mountain valleys and coastal features). The team also demonstrated that scaling to 1-kilometer resolution is technically feasible.
sc-2025-128.key_novelty: The first fully working digital twin of Earth's climate, simulating decades-long global changes at kilometer-scale resolution on European supercomputers.

sc-2025-133.method: The system watches code as it runs and uses spectral analysis (a technique that identifies repeating computational patterns) to detect which patterns recur during execution. For each pattern, it measures the GPU's energy consumption, then uses gradient-descent optimization (systematically testing frequency adjustments to find the best setting) to determine the ideal GPU frequency for that pattern. This saves energy because different computation patterns achieve different power-efficiency tradeoffs at different GPU speeds.
sc-2025-133.key_novelty: The innovation is optimizing GPU power consumption at runtime for any application—without needing to know its internal details—by detecting repeating patterns and tuning the GPU frequency separately for each one.

sc-2025-130.method: Mako transforms quantum chemistry calculations into matrix operations—the computations that GPUs are optimized to handle. It has three components: KernelMako converts the mathematical core (electron repulsion integrals, or ERI) into matrix multiplications using CUTLASS, an NVIDIA library for efficient matrix operations; QuantMako applies physics-aware compression to reduce data size while preserving accuracy; and CompilerMako combines operations together and customizes them for specific hardware. This restructuring allows GPUs to execute quantum chemistry workloads efficiently instead of leaving them underutilized.
sc-2025-130.key_novelty: The core idea is restructuring quantum chemistry's irregular computation patterns into regular matrix operations that AI accelerators like GPUs are optimized to handle efficiently.

sc-2025-129.method: The OLCF Test Harness (testing framework for Oak Ridge's leadership-class supercomputers) connects four specialized database tools to work together. Apache Kafka shuttles test data between systems quickly, InfluxDB stores timestamped measurements (like temperature or performance readings), Apache Druid analyzes large datasets efficiently, and Grafana creates interactive dashboards. This setup lets engineers watch tests run in real time and dig through historical results afterward.
sc-2025-129.key_novelty: It uses integrated database systems instead of flat files to collect, store, and analyze testing data from leadership-class supercomputers.

sc-2025-136.method: The method runs sparse-dense matrix multiplications on GPUs using Strassen's algorithm, which reduces the number of required multiplications through mathematical rearrangement. It applies three improvements: (1) fusing related GPU operations so the fast on-chip memory holds more data at once, (2) reusing intermediate calculation results because the adjacency matrix doesn't change between iterations, and (3) splitting the computation across two stages to distribute the irregular workload from sparse matrices evenly across processing cores.
sc-2025-136.key_novelty: It combines Strassen's algorithm (which reduces multiplications) with GPU-specific optimizations tailored to the sparse-dense matrix multiplications that GCN training requires.

sc-2025-140.method: The challenge is that simulating hundreds of billions of individual stars requires extremely small computational timesteps when supernovae (stellar explosions) occur, which makes the simulation run very slowly. To overcome this, the method pairs a physics simulator with a machine learning surrogate model—essentially a neural network trained to predict the effects of supernova explosions without running the full physics calculation. Instead of simulating every supernova event in detail, the surrogate model predicts how each explosion affects nearby stars on short timescales, letting the main simulation use much larger timesteps. This avoids the bottleneck of computing short-timescale physics explicitly, making it possible to simulate the full galaxy of hundreds of billions of stars.
sc-2025-140.key_novelty: A machine-learning surrogate model coupled to the physics simulator predicts supernova effects instead of computing them explicitly, enabling the first star-by-star simulation of the Milky Way (300 billion particles), up from the previous computational limit of 1 billion.

sc-2025-141.method: RAPTOR is an LLVM-based tool (a compiler framework) that automatically substitutes lower-precision number formats (like 16-bit floats) for higher-precision ones in your code, then profiles the results to measure numerical accuracy and how errors accumulate through calculations. It lets you test custom precision formats across different code regions to find where precision can be safely reduced without breaking numerical correctness.
sc-2025-141.key_novelty: RAPTOR is the first LLVM-based tool to systematically test which regions of HPC code can safely use lower-precision arithmetic without losing numerical accuracy.

sc-2025-138.method: The system uses a digital twin—a computer model that mimics real behavior—to figure out what happened on the seafloor by running Bayesian inversion (mathematically working backward from sensor measurements to find the cause). To make this real-time feasible with a billion parameters, the method exploits shift-invariance: the physics equations are identical across all seafloor locations, so the expensive calculations happen once (offline) and are reused for fast real-time answers (online). The offline phase uses MFEM—software for solving wave equations—scaled to 43,520 GPUs, while the online phase runs parallel algorithms to deliver results instantly.
sc-2025-138.key_novelty: Shift-invariance decomposition—reusing physics calculations that are identical across the seafloor—enables real-time Bayesian inference on billion-parameter problems, achieving a ten-billion-fold speedup with 92% parallel efficiency on the El Capitan supercomputer.

sc-2025-135.method: The team adapted Dyninst (a tool that modifies and analyzes executable programs without needing their source code) to support RISC-V processors. They solved three architecture-specific challenges: correctly parsing RISC-V instructions in binary files, modifying those instructions while the program runs, and updating memory addresses when instrumented code is relocated. By solving these problems, Dyninst now works on RISC-V the same way it does on other processors like x86 and ARM.
sc-2025-135.key_novelty: This shows that Dyninst can be extended to new processor architectures like RISC-V while keeping the same core design.

sc-2025-143.method: The approach assembles Schur complement matrices—matrices that capture how sub-problems interact when a large problem is decomposed into smaller pieces—directly on the GPU to avoid expensive data transfers to the CPU. It systematically exploits sparsity, meaning it only computes and stores the non-zero elements of these matrices, thereby reducing both memory usage and computation time. This strategy is applied to FETI (Finite Element Tearing and Interconnecting), a technique for solving large engineering problems by dividing them into smaller interconnected sub-domains.
sc-2025-143.key_novelty: Systematically exploiting sparsity—the prevalence of zero values—when assembling Schur complement matrices on the GPU delivers significant speedup compared to treating these matrices as entirely dense.

sc-2025-139.method: The researchers connected C++26's execution control patterns (a standard way to coordinate asynchronous work on different computer types) with Qthreads, a library using software-managed lightweight threads instead of operating system threads. By doing this, they extended C++26's patterns to work with systems that discover and create work dynamically during execution, solving a limitation of traditional frameworks that require all work to be specified upfront.
sc-2025-139.key_novelty: C++26's execution control patterns work with dynamic parallel runtimes like Qthreads that create work during execution, not just static frameworks that require upfront work specification.

sc-2025-146.method: The approach works by matching computing jobs (from PanDA) to their corresponding data files (in Rucio) using metadata—information about what data is stored where and what each job needs. It then identifies wasteful data transfer patterns across the global system that violate data-centric principles, such as moving the same file repeatedly when it could stay in place. Finally, it proposes coordination strategies to improve how the two systems work together and reduce unnecessary transfers.
sc-2025-146.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of how a job scheduler (PanDA) and data management system (Rucio) interact globally, discovered by precisely matching individual computing jobs to their specific data files.

sc-2025-132.method: AERIS generates weather predictions using a diffusion transformer—a neural network that creates output by progressively refining random noise—scaled to 1.3 to 80 billion parameters at pixel-level resolution. The model uses Swin transformer blocks (which apply attention within local windows to reduce computation) combined with SWiPe, a parallelism technique that distributes computation via window-based, sequence-based, and pipeline-based splits across processors without extra communication overhead.
sc-2025-132.key_novelty: AERIS combines billion-parameter diffusion transformers for Earth systems weather prediction with SWiPe composable parallelism, a technique that coordinates three processor-split methods (window-based, sequence-based, and pipeline-based) without extra communication.

sc-2025-142.method: They extended an open-source testing harness that had been used at ALCF for previous systems, adapting it specifically for Aurora. The harness validates both individual components and the complete system working together, simulates real-world workloads to test actual performance, and tracks regressions—automatically detecting when something that previously worked breaks. Multiple testing modes allow comprehensive verification of system stability and correctness across the exascale supercomputer.
sc-2025-142.key_novelty: A reusable testing framework developed through vendor-facility collaboration successfully enabled Aurora's deployment and can serve as a model for future exascale systems.

sc-2025-144.method: QoSlicer breaks inference computations (kernels—tasks run on the GPU) into flexible pieces. Before running (at compile time), the system pre-computes multiple slicing plans and uses heuristic search to find which plan best meets each inference's latency target (maximum completion time).
