Performance estimation (test-run measurement) validates each plan will work. At runtime, the scheduler simply activates the right pre-computed plan, keeping decisions fast.
sc-2025-144.key_novelty: By pre-computing how to slice inference computations at compile time, QoSlicer guarantees latency targets without runtime scheduling overhead.

sc-2025-150.method: lsCOMP runs a single processing kernel on a GPU to compress X-ray data from light sources, supporting both lossless compression (keeping all original data) and lossy compression with adjustable precision (trading quality for smaller file size). It achieves 380-509 gigabytes per second throughput in lossless mode and can randomly access compressed data at terabyte-per-second speeds, making it practical for near-real-time data handling. The system works with multiple types of light source data formats.
sc-2025-150.key_novelty: A GPU compressor built for light source data that can sustain 250+ gigabytes per second processing rates today and 1+ terabytes per second in the future while maintaining data quality.

sc-2025-149.method: VGC (Versatile GPU Compression) is a framework that compresses data from scientific simulations using graphics processors (GPUs) and three different compression algorithms. It understands the dimensional structure of the data, which helps it apply compression more effectively, and uses GPU processing routines that are specially optimized to achieve ultra-fast compression speeds while controlling how much accuracy is lost. It works in two operational modes: one optimized for memory efficiency during compression, and another that decompresses only the specific parts of data you need.
sc-2025-149.key_novelty: VGC combines versatility—supporting multiple data types and compression algorithms—with ultra-fast compression speeds by using GPU processing routines that are optimized for the GPU's architecture.

sc-2025-147.method: When a gamma-ray detector spots a burst, it produces increasingly accurate location estimates over time. The framework decides when to send each estimate to an optical telescope—too early wastes its effort on an inaccurate location, too late wastes time. It finds the optimal send schedule to minimize the time from burst detection to when the optical telescope begins observing the target.
sc-2025-147.key_novelty: It optimizes the timing of progressive location updates to accelerate multi-telescope coordination for burst discovery.

sc-2025-153.method: Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) is a high-compression-ratio algorithm, but it doesn't work efficiently with multi-byte integers—data that comes in chunks larger than a single byte, like 2, 4, or 8 byte numbers. MANS introduces Adaptive Data Mapping (ADM), which converts multi-byte integers to single-byte space based on the data's actual characteristics, allowing ANS to compress them efficiently. The system combines separate optimizations tuned to CPU and GPU architectures into a single portable pipeline.
sc-2025-153.key_novelty: Adaptive Data Mapping extends Asymmetric Numeral Systems to handle multi-byte integers while maintaining efficiency across CPUs and GPUs through architecture-specific optimizations.

sc-2025-145.method: Uses a conditional normalizing flow—a machine learning model trained to reverse the simulation process. Instead of starting with initial conditions and predicting outcomes (as typical simulations do), this model takes a target outcome and generates multiple different initial conditions that could produce it. Demonstrated on two physics problems—electrostatic potential (electric field behavior) and heat diffusion (temperature spreading)—showing it can rapidly generate diverse starting conditions for complex simulations.
sc-2025-145.key_novelty: Applying conditional normalizing flows to inverse design enables efficient generation of initial conditions from target simulation outputs.

sc-2025-157.method: Extend Vessim, a tool that simulates computing workloads and energy together, with realistic renewable energy models from NREL's System Advisor Model. Automatically test many different microgrid designs (different mixes of solar, wind, batteries, and other storage) by simulating how they'd behave with real data center workloads. Track both operational carbon (emissions from daily running) and embodied carbon (emissions built into the equipment itself).
sc-2025-157.key_novelty: Simultaneously optimize data center workloads and renewable microgrid composition to account for both operational emissions (from running) and embodied emissions (from manufacturing equipment).

sc-2025-148.method: LiquidGEMM accelerates 4-bit weight, 8-bit activation matrix operations using two techniques. LiquidQuant converts compressed 4-bit weights back into usable form using just 2 operations per 4 elements while preventing overflow. The kernel then overlaps three tasks—loading weights, converting them, and performing matrix multiplication—across parallel thread groups without pausing any threads or repeating data from memory.
sc-2025-148.key_novelty: LiquidQuant converts 4-bit weights in just 2 operations per 4 elements, fast enough that W4A8 matrix operations run all computation stages in parallel on Tensor Cores without needing thread synchronization.

sc-2025-154.method: They run MPI-BugBench's tests through three MPI correctness tools (MUST, PARCOACH, and clang-tidy) and measure which parts of each tool's code get executed. This reveals the code coverage—a map of what was tested and what wasn't. By analyzing these coverage gaps, they identify missing MPI features and code structures, particularly varying-count collectives (operations on different-sized message groups), loops, and array-based handles. They then design and write 34 new tests to cover these previously untested scenarios.
sc-2025-154.key_novelty: Using code coverage to identify missing MPI features and code structures in correctness test benchmarks, then generating new tests to cover them.

sc-2025-156.method: This study tests Implicitly Restarted Arnoldi (ARPACK), a standard method for finding eigenvalues and eigenvectors—special numbers and vectors that reveal fundamental properties of large sparse matrices—when using different numerical storage formats (OFP8 with variants E4M3 and E5M2, bfloat16, posit, and takum). Researchers tested this method on real matrices from two major collections—the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection and the Network Repository—to measure how well the solver performs with each numerical format.
sc-2025-156.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive test of eigenvalue-finding methods across multiple emerging floating-point formats using real-world matrices, without customizing the solver for each format.

sc-2025-152.method: HStencil combines three optimizations. Microkernels (small code blocks) run matrix and vector operations together so both processor units work in parallel instead of one sitting idle. Fine-grained instruction scheduling interleaves operations—while one processor unit computes, another fetches data—maximizing parallel execution. Spatial prefetching (pulling nearby data proactively) sustains performance when working sets exceed cache capacity.
sc-2025-152.key_novelty: The core idea is using matrix and vector compute units together for stencil operations by interleaving outer-product calculations (multiplying vector pairs to build matrix values), with fine-grained scheduling to keep both units constantly busy.

sc-2025-151.method: Workload Intelligence sets up a two-way communication channel between workloads (the programs running on VMs) and the cloud platform. Workloads send the platform information about what kind of work they're doing and what resources they need, while the platform sends back information about available resources and platform events. This lets workloads adjust their behavior based on what the platform tells them, and lets the platform make smarter decisions about how to allocate resources across all workloads.
sc-2025-151.key_novelty: Cloud workloads and platforms can now directly communicate about their needs and conditions, allowing workloads to adapt and platforms to optimize resource allocation.

sc-2025-155.method: The approach converts C/Fortran+OpenMP programs into Go code using an AI language model following natural-language instructions (vibe coding). The translated Go code is then checked with Go's built-in data race detector, which monitors the program as it runs to catch conflicts where multiple threads access the same memory simultaneously. The team compares how well this method catches data races against existing tools like ThreadSanitizer and Archer that analyze the original code.
sc-2025-155.key_novelty: The approach translates code to Go using an AI model and checks it with Go's built-in data race detector, providing a complementary detection method that catches races existing tools miss.

sc-2025-158.method: The method reorders the rows of one matrix and organizes the other into hierarchical clusters (nested groups of data), which reduces irregular memory access and improves data reuse. A new row-clustered matrix format allows clustering to work independently from reordering. The researchers tested 10 reordering algorithms and 3 clustering patterns on 110 sparse matrices to identify the most effective combinations.
sc-2025-158.key_novelty: This is the first to systematically combine row reordering and hierarchical clustering for sparse matrix multiplication, introducing a row-clustered format that decouples the two techniques.

sc-2025-160.method: The system automatically tunes machine learning code using large language models (AI trained on text) and reinforcement learning (AI that learns through trial and reward). It represents code in a form humans can read that follows mathematical principles, and validates that any changes it makes are mathematically correct. The framework optimizes computation kernels (core routines) for different hardware—CPUs, GPUs, accelerators—without needing you to specify the hardware details beforehand. This keeps the optimized code understandable to humans while letting the AI learn and improve.
sc-2025-160.key_novelty: This is the first system to use large language models and reinforcement learning to automatically optimize code for different computers while keeping the code human-readable and mathematically valid, instead of relying on complicated hand-coded optimization rules.

sc-2025-161.method: The system uses an LLM that reasons through decisions step-by-step using the ReAct framework (Reason + Act combined). It has three components: a memory scratchpad tracking past scheduling decisions, natural-language refinement where you give feedback in plain words, and a constraint checker ensuring decisions are actually feasible. Testing used real HPC workloads across 7 scenarios (including heterogeneous, bursty, and adversarial cases), with OpenAI O4-Mini and Anthropic Claude 3.7, compared against traditional methods (FCFS, SJF) and Google OR-Tools on 10-100 job batches.
sc-2025-161.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive study of using reasoning-capable language models (the ReAct framework) to optimize HPC job scheduling across multiple competing objectives, with explanations you can read in plain English.

sc-2025-165.method: The team implemented low-bit fused matrix-vector multiplication kernels (combining matrix-vector operations using fewer bits to run faster and use less memory) in three programming frameworks: CUDA and HIP (vendor-specific) and SYCL (designed to work across vendors). They tested these implementations on GPUs ranging from datacenter chips (A100, MI100) to desktop cards (RTX3090, MI250) to laptop chips (RTX4050, MI28). Using profiling tools, they identified why performance varied by examining three key factors: how well the compiler unrolled loops to avoid overhead, the cost of sending work to the GPU, and how efficiently the GPU could sum intermediate results.
sc-2025-165.key_novelty: This research systematically tests how SYCL's portable code performs across different GPUs for low-bit matrix-vector operations, uncovering what prevents better performance.

sc-2025-162.method: SIREN watches running programs and creates fingerprints of their code (called fuzzy hashes) that stay similar even when the program is updated or compiled differently. It collects basic information about each running process along with these fingerprints to recognize when the same program runs again, even if it looks different on the surface. The approach was tested on LUMI, a real supercomputer, with users able to opt in or out of sharing their data.
sc-2025-162.key_novelty: SIREN uses fuzzy hashing (fingerprints that stay similar across program versions) to identify running software at the process level in supercomputers, while letting users opt in to preserve privacy.

sc-2025-159.method: The approach bundles multiple threads together for efficiency (thread coarsening) and creates two versions of the code: one optimized for bundling and one for normal execution. At runtime, it checks whether all threads will execute the same instructions (thread uniformity); if yes, it runs the optimized version, otherwise it runs the regular version when threads diverge to different code paths. It applies this to OpenMP code for both CPUs and GPUs using LLVM IR transformations (the intermediate form that compilers work with), evaluated on HecBench and LULESH benchmarks.
sc-2025-159.key_novelty: The core innovation is deferring the uniformity check—determining whether all threads follow the same code path—from compile-time to runtime, which lets it handle divergent control flow.

sc-2025-171.method: The system takes support tickets and filters them to focus on the most frequent and recent problems. It then uses an AI language model to summarize the tickets, groups similar problems together by understanding their meaning (semantic clustering), and generates FAQ entries from these groups. Finally, domain experts review the results.
sc-2025-171.key_novelty: The system uses AI language models to create FAQ entries automatically from support tickets by grouping similar problems, summarizing them, and generating questions and answers.

sc-2025-167.method: They trained 19 open-source language models (ranging from 500 million to 34 billion parameters—the weights that define what each model knows) on pairs of CUDA and SYCL kernel code, two languages for programming graphics processors and specialized hardware. The training examples came from heterogeneous computing benchmarks—standard test suites for code that runs across mixed CPU and GPU systems. They used parameter-efficient fine-tuning, which adjusts only a small subset of weights rather than retraining everything, making the process faster and cheaper.
sc-2025-167.key_novelty: ChatPORT uses language models fine-tuned on paired CUDA-to-SYCL code examples to translate parallel computation kernels (the core functions that run on graphics processors), achieving 19.9-81.7% correctness compared to the near-0% baseline of unfine-tuned models.

sc-2025-166.method: The system uses multiple AI agents, where each agent pairs a large language model (AI trained to understand text) with a deterministic engineering solver (a specialized program that calculates exact answers). These agents coordinate two key power-grid tasks: AC Optimal Power Flow—finding the best way to route electricity through the grid—and N-1 contingency analysis, which tests what happens if one component fails. The agents communicate through natural language (human words) combined with function calls (explicit coded instructions), allowing the AI to understand the problem while the solvers calculate precise answers.
sc-2025-166.key_novelty: Smaller language models achieve comparable accuracy to larger models when paired with engineering solvers, while responding faster.

sc-2025-175.method: Each tenant gets their own isolated Kubernetes control plane (a virtual control plane or vCluster) that manages only their containers, preventing one tenant from interfering with another. Containers run inside virtual machines (like Azure Container Instances) rather than on shared infrastructure, adding a hardware boundary for stronger isolation. A policy engine (Kyverno) automatically applies security rules across all tenants.
sc-2025-175.key_novelty: The core idea is combining per-tenant virtual control planes with VM-backed container isolation to achieve hostile multi-tenancy in Kubernetes while keeping it compatible with standard Kubernetes tools and maintaining negligible performance overhead.

sc-2025-170.method: HELM collects data from the Unified Memory driver—the GPU's automatic memory-management system—to understand how programs access memory. By analyzing these access patterns, it determines which data should stay on the GPU and which can be moved back to main memory. HELM then uses this analysis to automatically select the data-migration policy that works best for each program, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all default.
sc-2025-170.key_novelty: HELM introduces metrics that reveal what programs actually do with GPU memory, enabling automatic optimization of data-migration policies and achieving an average 3.5x speedup.

sc-2025-168.method: The approach uses ant colony optimization (an algorithm inspired by how ants find efficient paths by marking promising routes) initialized with a good starting solution from the queue. It represents job scheduling constraints as disjunctive graphs (networks showing which jobs can run simultaneously and which must wait). It then refines the solution through parallel local search on subgraphs (testing small schedule variations across different parts of the network at the same time) while OR-Tools (an optimization library) handles the complex mathematical optimization.
sc-2025-168.key_novelty: The core idea is combining fast heuristic scheduling with rigorous optimization techniques, achieving 5-10x speedup while solutions remain only 3-5% worse than the theoretical optimal.

sc-2025-174.method: The approach combines neural networks—which learn patterns in quantum system behavior—with a filtering technique called Selected Configuration Interaction (SCI, which selects only the most important quantum states to simulate). Instead of calculating all possible states for large systems (which is infeasible), the system automatically chooses which ones to include based on their importance. It runs the Slater-Condon rules (the mathematical calculations for quantum interactions) in parallel across multiple processors and uses memory compression to efficiently handle the vast space of quantum states.
sc-2025-174.key_novelty: NNQS-SCI scales to 152 spin orbitals (representing over 10^14 possible quantum states) through adaptive configuration selection, which maintains accuracy without arbitrary limits.

sc-2025-169.method: They integrated Kokkos—a library that lets code run efficiently on different hardware—into LAMMPS, a molecular dynamics simulator. They then optimized this combination to handle three types of atomic force calculations: pairwise interactions between atoms, many-body reactive forces in complex chemical reactions, and machine learning-based models that predict atomic behavior.
sc-2025-169.key_novelty: They proved Kokkos integration works reliably in production LAMMPS, maintaining efficient performance across three exascale supercomputers and the Alps system with different force field types.

sc-2025-163.method: EMLIO places a lightweight helper program (daemon) on storage nodes that serializes (converts to transmission format) and batches (groups) raw data samples, streaming them over TCP. It supports out-of-order prefetching (requesting data before it's needed, even when packets arrive out of sequence) and integrates with NVIDIA DALI to do preprocessing on the GPU as data loads. The system was tested on local disk, local area networks with round-trip delays of 0.05–10 milliseconds, and wide-area networks with 30 millisecond delays.
sc-2025-163.key_novelty: EMLIO is the first system to jointly minimize I/O latency and energy consumption, maintaining constant performance and power efficiency whether data transfers happen locally or over long distances.

sc-2025-173.method: The researchers surveyed 300 HPC users to understand their energy awareness. They created two billing approaches—one charging based on direct energy consumption, another based on carbon emissions—to test whether charging users for computing resources would motivate them to choose more efficient options. Both approaches were evaluated through computer simulations and with actual user studies.
sc-2025-173.key_novelty: Directly charging users for their energy consumption—rather than just showing them feedback—reduced energy use by 40%.

sc-2025-164.method: The method uses a lightweight 3D neural network to remove distortions left by lossy compression. Training uses fixed-scale batch normalization—a technique that standardizes input data at each layer using a consistent scale—to keep training stable and inference fast. The researchers measured how network size affects output quality (minimum MSE loss, or average squared error from correct values) and validated the approach across five compressors (SZ1, SZ2, SZP, SZX, ZFP) and multiple scientific domains.
sc-2025-164.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of using neural networks to remove compression distortions from scientific data, with demonstrated success across five compressors (SZ1, SZ2, SZP, SZX, ZFP) and multiple scientific domains.

sc-2025-183.method: Students implement a task-based parallel programming model (where work is broken into independent tasks and launched asynchronously with finish points to synchronize when they complete), then build a dynamic load-balancing runtime that distributes these tasks across processor cores. They iteratively improve both to handle real processor challenges like uneven task execution time and keeping data in fast cache memory.
sc-2025-183.key_novelty: The course teaches programming abstraction and runtime systems together—students implement both the task-based language construct and the runtime scheduler that makes it run efficiently, so they see how one depends on the other.

sc-2025-176.method: The approach implements mixed-precision computation (strategically using both 64-bit double and 32-bit single precision within the same calculation) on exascale GPU supercomputers to reduce memory bandwidth bottlenecks in scientific simulations. By applying lower precision where accuracy isn't critical and higher precision where it is, the method cuts the volume of data moving between GPU memory and processors—the fundamental bottleneck in these workloads. The HPG-MxP benchmark includes algorithm optimization to efficiently implement this precision mixing for sparse matrices (matrices with mostly zero values) across thousands of GPUs.
sc-2025-176.key_novelty: This is the first large-scale validation that mixed-precision arithmetic (combining double and single precision) improves performance for sparse matrix computations on exascale GPU supercomputers, demonstrating a 1.6x speedup.

sc-2025-179.method: These algorithms optimize all-to-all communication, where every parallel process sends data to all the others simultaneously—a common bottleneck on modern supercomputers with many cores per processor. Instead of using a fixed strategy, the algorithms adapt based on the message size and number of processes involved, since different communication patterns work better at different scales. By aligning the algorithm choice with many-core processor characteristics, they avoid performance losses that generic implementations suffer from.
sc-2025-179.key_novelty: Tailoring all-to-all algorithms to many-core processor characteristics instead of using generic implementations yields 3x speedup on Sapphire Rapids at 32 nodes.

sc-2025-181.method: This report evaluates whether the FaSTCC code—which performs sparse tensor contractions, a mathematical operation that efficiently combines multi-dimensional arrays when most values are zero—produces the same performance results as the original paper reported. The researchers ran the implementation on CPUs following the SC25 Reproducibility Initiative's systematic testing approach, checking performance across different systems and comparing actual speedups to those claimed in the original work. They verified whether the optimization approach actually works and whether the performance improvements hold up in practice.
sc-2025-181.key_novelty: This work independently tests whether FaSTCC's sparse tensor contraction implementation on CPUs actually achieves the performance improvements claimed in the original paper.

sc-2025-178.method: RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) needs error recovery when data travels long distances, but traditional Selective Repeat doesn't work well at millisecond-scale latencies. SDR-RDMA solves this with a software-defined approach that lets you customize the error-recovery strategy. It tracks received packets using a receive buffer bitmap and offloads the high-speed work to a Data Path Accelerator (DPA), specialized hardware that maintains line-rate (full network speed) performance without slowing anything down.
sc-2025-178.key_novelty: SDR-RDMA enables software-defined error recovery for remote memory transfers, letting you choose strategies beyond Selective Repeat while maintaining line-rate performance and zero-copy semantics.

sc-2025-177.method: The researchers tested a genome alignment tool (BWA-MEM2) on AMD processors under three security configurations: no security features (SMP), memory encryption alone (SME), and both memory encryption plus virtualization-layer encryption (SEV+SME). They tested each setup with different numbers of processor threads and measured how runtime and memory bandwidth changed. This quantified the performance overhead that security features add to real genomic data processing.
sc-2025-177.key_novelty: This is the first measurement of how AMD's security features—memory encryption (SME) and virtualization-layer encryption (SEV)—affect real genome alignment, showing a 50% reduction in memory bandwidth and 10.4-20.9% increase in runtime.

sc-2025-184.method: The AMD MI300A combines CPU and GPU on one chip with shared memory, which differs from traditional systems where CPU and GPU are separate. The researchers tested how four MPI libraries—MVAPICH-Plus, Open MPI, MPICH, and Cray MPICH—perform on MI300A nodes by running microbenchmarks that measure simple message-passing, multi-node coordinated operations, and scaling behavior. They validated their findings with real applications: OpenFOAM for computational fluid dynamics and LLM distributed training.
sc-2025-184.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive measurement of how MPI communication performs on AMD MI300A chips, which integrate CPU and GPU with shared memory.

sc-2025-186.method: The system (called xGFabric) physically connects three things: distributed sensors that gather data, a private 5G wireless network serving as a bridge, and a high-performance computing center. The 5G network uses network slicing (a technique that carves out dedicated communication channels) to move sensor data to the computer center quickly and without loss. By putting a fast, reliable 5G network between unreliable sensors and a distant computing center, the system creates an end-to-end link that is both responsive and trustworthy.
sc-2025-186.key_novelty: The core insight is that a private 5G network can serve as the reliable, fast link between unreliable sensor networks at the edge and distant computing centers, enabling real-time scientific applications.

sc-2025-185.method: The approach trains task-specific expert adapters using tensor-train decomposition (a compression technique that factorizes matrices into sequences of smaller operations), keeping each expert compact for efficient deployment. Then it trains a separate router that evaluates each input using base model representations and picks exactly one expert to apply, reducing computational overhead by only running the selected expert rather than combining multiple experts.
sc-2025-185.key_novelty: It trains compact expert adapters using tensor-train compression, then trains a separate router to select which expert to use, while keeping the experts frozen so that different tasks don't interfere with each other's learned representations.

sc-2025-180.method: The researchers used NVIDIA's GH200 superchip, which combines Grace CPUs (general-purpose processors) and Hopper GPUs (graphics processors optimized for heavy computation). They split the Earth system simulation work between these two processor types, letting each handle what it does best rather than forcing one type to do everything. They also optimized the ICON codebase (the Earth system simulation software) to run efficiently on this mixed setup.
sc-2025-180.key_novelty: For the first time, they simulated the entire global Earth system (atmosphere, oceans, and land simultaneously) at 1.25km resolution, achieving 145.7 simulated days per real day—faster than previous atmosphere-only simulations.

sc-2025-182.method: Drona provides a graphical interface where researchers describe HPC (high-performance computing) workflows by clicking through options, automatically generating the underlying scripts. Before execution, users see an editable preview of the generated script and can modify it directly. This combines the ease of a point-and-click tool with the control of hand-written code. The system can import, create, and share workflows, making them reusable across projects.
sc-2025-182.key_novelty: It generates HPC (high-performance computing) scripts through a graphical interface but displays them in an editable preview, combining automated assistance with full manual control.

sc-2025-191.method: They tested the RAPTOR numerical profiling framework—a tool that monitors how numbers behave during calculations in scientific code—by following the official SC25 Reproducibility Initiative checklist. They obtained the code, examined how it was built, and ran the same experiments as the original paper to check if the reported results matched. They documented what worked, what didn't, and whether independent researchers could reproduce the original findings.
sc-2025-191.key_novelty: This work independently verifies that RAPTOR's implementation is reproducible and produces the results the original paper claimed.

sc-2025-172.method: The system embeds implicit sequence numbers (ISN)—packet identifiers that take up no extra header space—to detect when individual data units called flits get dropped during transmission and restore in-order delivery. These sequence numbers are packaged in a new protocol called RXL that extends the CXL interconnect standard to handle multi-node configurations reliably. Error handling operates in multiple layers: at the transport layer, checksums (CRC) catch transmission errors; at the physical link layer, forward error correction (FEC) can actually repair corrupted data rather than just detecting problems.
sc-2025-172.key_novelty: The core innovation is implicit sequence numbers—numbering packets without adding header space—which detect lost data and ensure in-order delivery across multi-node chip interconnects.

sc-2025-192.method: The team followed the SC25 Reproducibility Initiative guidelines to systematically evaluate continuous integration systems used in HPC (high-performance computing—the large-scale clusters that run parallel calculations). They took the code, data, and setup instructions researchers had provided, then tried to rebuild and re-run these systems themselves to see if they could reproduce the published results. They documented what succeeded, what failed, and what crucial information was missing, creating a practical assessment of which continuous integration practices actually work reliably in practice.
sc-2025-192.key_novelty: This work documents which continuous integration practices for HPC systems are actually reproducible—meaning others can rebuild and rerun them using only the provided code and instructions.

sc-2025-188.method: The researchers compiled HPC benchmark programs using two major compilers—GNU and LLVM—testing both variable-length vector mode (VLA, where width adapts) and fixed-length vector mode (VLS, where width is fixed). They measured which vectorization instructions each compiler actually generated and categorized all vectorization failures into three types: compiler backend limitations, missed optimization opportunities (patterns the compiler doesn't recognize), and unsupported instruction patterns.
sc-2025-188.key_novelty: This work comprehensively analyzes which RISC-V vector instructions GNU and LLVM compilers actually generate when vectorizing HPC workloads.

sc-2025-187.method: They built a biophysical neuron simulator—software that models how neurons work at the cellular level with electrical and chemical detail—and optimized it for Fugaku supercomputer. They proved it scales efficiently (maintains performance gains) across up to 152,064 compute nodes, then ran a complete simulation of the entire mouse cerebral cortex (9 million neurons, 26 billion synapses) using 145,728 Fugaku nodes.
sc-2025-187.key_novelty: This work achieved the first whole-cortex biophysical simulation of a mammalian brain by optimizing neural simulation software for exascale supercomputers.

sc-2025-197.method: The system wraps multiple GPU FFT libraries (fast algorithms for specific math operations) with a lightweight machine-learning predictor that learns to estimate result accuracy. When you run an FFT operation, it samples characteristics of your input, predicts the error that each library-precision combination would produce, then automatically selects the fastest and most energy-efficient option that still meets your accuracy threshold.
sc-2025-197.key_novelty: It's the first system to use machine learning to simultaneously select both the GPU library and floating-point precision (how many bits to use for numbers), rather than optimizing each choice separately.

sc-2025-189.method: The researchers extended RISC-V Vector—an instruction set for processing multiple operations in parallel—to directly support arithmetic on large numbers (those exceeding a single processor word). They built mathematical performance models to predict how well this extension would work across different processor designs. They validated their approach by testing it on two important algorithm families: number theoretic transforms and post-quantum cryptography.
sc-2025-189.key_novelty: The core innovation is adding native multi-word arithmetic support to RISC-V Vector, which speeds up carry-propagation (the arithmetic dependency between parts of a large number) that currently limits performance.

sc-2025-190.method: The model predicts execution time by accounting for the fact that different cores access shared memory at unequal rates (per-core traffic inhomogeneity)—a reality that traditional models ignore by assuming uniform traffic. It uses three hardware parameters to calculate how cores compete for limited memory bandwidth when access patterns are unbalanced. This approach produces accurate time predictions even when cores have very different memory demands, whereas bandwidth-based models with their uniform-traffic assumption fail in these cases.
sc-2025-190.key_novelty: The core idea is building a performance model that accounts for per-core memory traffic inhomogeneity—unequal memory access across cores—in shared memory systems.

sc-2025-198.method: The approach uses two complementary strategies. First, it isolates system services from applications using cgroup and systemd (Linux tools that control which CPU and memory resources each process can use), preventing them from interfering with each other. Second, it tunes the operating system itself—adjusting task scheduling and resource management—to reduce noise (unexpected delays and interruptions caused by system tasks). These tuning steps work on any Linux distribution, making them widely applicable.
sc-2025-198.key_novelty: This work is the first to document how system noise (interruptions from OS services) limits exascale systems like El Capitan (1M+ CPU cores, 10K+ GPUs), and provides tuning solutions that work on any Linux distribution.

sc-2025-193.method: Bine Trees optimizes collective operations (communications between multiple processes, such as broadcasting across a computing cluster) by arranging them to minimize the distance data travels. This reproducibility evaluation tested the technique's claimed speedups by running it on multiple hardware systems following SC25's reproducibility standards, measuring whether the performance improvements actually occur in practice.
sc-2025-193.key_novelty: This report confirms that Bine Trees' optimization of collective communications achieves the claimed performance improvements when independently tested.

sc-2025-196.method: SlimIO avoids expensive system call overhead by writing directly to storage hardware (passthru I/O). It uses Flexible Data Placement (FDP) SSDs, which allow the database to control exactly which regions of flash storage receive writes, rather than letting the SSD firmware decide. By isolating each process's writes, it prevents different processes' write patterns from creating performance interference through the SSD's garbage collection and wear-leveling.
sc-2025-196.key_novelty: SlimIO controls database writes directly to Flexible Data Placement SSDs with process isolation and passthru I/O, ensuring each database write maps to exactly one SSD write and achieving a write amplification factor of 1.0.

sc-2025-200.method: SparStencil takes scientific stencil computations—which typically have irregular sparse patterns—and transforms them into a format that GPU sparse tensor cores can efficiently process. It does this in three stages: first, adaptive layout morphing (a flatten-crush pipeline) restructures how the data is organized, second, it converts the irregular sparsity into structured 2:4 sparsity (where every 4 values must have at least 2 zeros) using graph matching, and third, it automatically generates optimized GPU code by searching for the best memory layout and data mapping.
sc-2025-200.key_novelty: This is the first system to use GPU sparse tensor cores for scientific stencil computations, achieving this by introducing adaptive layout morphing to transform irregular sparse patterns into 2:4 sparsity (where every 4 values has at least 2 zeros).

sc-2025-194.method: The framework trains a graph neural network surrogate—a learned model that predicts how quickly different MCMC preconditioner parameters will make a Krylov solver converge on ill-conditioned linear systems (matrices where small changes cause huge changes in the result). A Bayesian acquisition function then intelligently selects which parameter sets to test next, balancing exploration of new options against refinement of known good ones, with the goal of minimizing solver iterations. Since the neural network provides fast predictions without running the full solver each time, this approach replaces expensive manual parameter tuning and grid search.
sc-2025-194.key_novelty: The core innovation is training a graph neural network surrogate to automatically predict and optimize MCMC preconditioner parameters, using Bayesian optimization to guide the search instead of manual tuning.

sc-2025-201.method: They obtained the GPU sparse linear solver code from the paper and ran it on their own hardware, following the SC25 Reproducibility Committee's standard verification procedures. They measured whether the code actually achieved the speedups and produced the numerical results that the paper claimed, and documented how their independent results compared.
sc-2025-201.key_novelty: This independently verifies that the Sparsified Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient Solver on GPUs actually achieves the performance improvements reported in the original paper.

sc-2025-205.method: The method breaks the long input sequence into equal-sized chunks and feeds them through multiple GPU devices in parallel using a pipeline (new data starts processing while previous data is still computing). It uses a 1F1B schedule—each device performs one forward pass and one backward pass in sequence—to keep the pipeline full and reduce idle waiting time. Since causal attention (where each token can only reference previous tokens, not future ones) creates unequal work across devices, the system redistributes computation to balance the load and prevent bottlenecks.
sc-2025-205.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining uniform sequence slicing with intelligent workload redistribution to enable pipeline parallelism on extreme-length contexts up to 2 million tokens.

sc-2025-195.method: They designed a specialized hardware accelerator based on RISC-V architecture, integrated with Chipyard's RocketCore processor design. The accelerator uses a pipelined design—where calculation stages overlap like an assembly line—combined with a Humlidek 8th-order rational approximation (a mathematical formula using polynomial ratios) to quickly compute the Faddeeva function for Doppler broadening (the temperature-dependent effects on particle collisions). They tested performance against software implementations on RISC-V and an Intel Core i5 Tiger Lake-U processor.
sc-2025-195.key_novelty: A specialized RISC-V hardware accelerator can speed up the cross-section calculations that bottleneck neutron transport simulations, demonstrating RISC-V's potential for high-performance computing.

sc-2025-203.method: The system moves data compression from CPUs to GPUs, which can process many calculations in parallel. It combines two compression techniques—bitplane encoding (breaking numbers into individual bit layers) and lossless encoding (preserving all original data)—arranged in a pipeline so different stages run together for speed. Instead of always retrieving complete data, users retrieve it progressively, stopping when they have 'good enough' quality. Users specify their acceptable level of error, and the system delivers compressed data meeting that quality threshold.
sc-2025-203.key_novelty: GPU-accelerated progressive compression of scientific data where users control precision during retrieval.

sc-2025-210.method: The evaluation independently runs the experiments and code from the XaaS Containers paper following the SC25 Reproducibility Committee's standardized guidelines, without access to the authors' original setup. Evaluators recreate the published results to verify whether other researchers can obtain the same outcomes. If successful, this confirms that the paper's experimental claims are reproducible and its conclusions are based on sound, repeatable evidence.
sc-2025-210.key_novelty: This is a reproducibility verification confirming that the XaaS Containers paper's experimental results can be independently reproduced, not a new technical method.

sc-2025-206.method: The simulation runs on multiple GPUs working together in a cluster. To fit massive atomic systems in GPUs' limited memory, they compress the lattice—the three-dimensional grid structure where atoms sit—and selectively decompress vacancy data (information about empty atomic sites) as needed. A multi-level computation pipeline with intelligent communication merging minimizes data transfer between GPUs.
sc-2025-206.key_novelty: This is the first Kinetic Monte Carlo simulation to reach micrometer scale—simulating 20 quadrillion atoms—on GPU clusters, made possible by data compression strategies that work within GPUs' memory constraints.

sc-2025-202.method: The approach uses a priority-ranked cache system to manage where different experts are stored based on usage patterns. Experts that are used frequently across the entire model stay in high-priority caches at each layer, where they're fastest to access. Experts used frequently within specific layers sit in medium-priority caches managed by least-recently-used (LRU) replacement—a strategy that removes the oldest unused item when space is needed—combined with predictive prefetching (loading experts before they're requested, based on patterns). The least frequently-used experts are loaded into cache only when needed, on-demand.
sc-2025-202.key_novelty: The key innovation is organizing expert caches into different priority levels based on both overall popularity and recent usage—the first approach to jointly optimize for both global and temporal patterns in MoE inference.

sc-2025-208.method: This method combines two neural network techniques: a VAE (which compresses data into a compact 'latent space' representation) and a conditional diffusion model (which reconstructs images by gradually reducing noise, guided by specific conditions). Instead of compressing every frame of video, it stores only keyframes—the key visual moments—in their compressed latent form. The diffusion model then fills in all the frames between keyframes by learning to predict what they should look like based on those stored keyframes. By storing only compressed keyframes rather than compressing every single frame, this achieves much higher compression ratios.
sc-2025-208.key_novelty: Combining VAE and diffusion models to store only compressed keyframes and reconstruct the rest, achieving better compression than generative methods that compress every frame separately.

sc-2025-211.method: The system uses a software layer called distributed shared memory (DSM)—a unified memory view across multiple networked computers—customized for graph pattern matching problems. This layer automatically adapts the same code to run efficiently on different supercomputer configurations, whether they have different processors, GPUs, or memory systems. It handles the complexity of coordinating work across many computers while hiding the specific details of each machine's hardware.
sc-2025-211.key_novelty: A software layer (distributed shared memory) designed for graph pattern matching that lets the same code run across different supercomputers while matching the speed of hand-tuned versions built for each specific machine.

sc-2025-204.method: In parallel I/O libraries, multiple processes creating data must normally synchronize and check that their metadata (the information describing the data structure) matches—a verification step that slows down with more processes. This work splits the metadata into separate blocks in the file header, each assigned to a different process. Each process can now create data independently without waiting for other processes, eliminating this synchronization overhead.
sc-2025-204.key_novelty: By partitioning metadata into separate blocks in the file, each process can independently create data objects without synchronizing with other processes.

sc-2025-213.method: To understand how Linux decides which data to move to disk when memory is tight, researchers built a lightweight measurement tool that doesn't significantly slow down the system. This tool tracks two critical aspects of Linux's Two-Queue LRU (2QLRU) and Multi-Generational LRU (MGLRU) policies: the decision overhead (how much time it takes to decide which data to move) and reclamation effectiveness (how well the decisions actually free up memory). The researchers tested both policies across seven different applications under various memory constraints, from generous to severely limited.
sc-2025-213.key_novelty: This research uses lightweight profiling to comprehensively measure both the decision overhead and reclamation effectiveness of two Linux page reclamation policies (2QLRU and MGLRU).

sc-2025-215.method: They developed HybridCloudSim, a simulation tool that models hybrid quantum-HPC cloud systems—environments where classical computers work alongside quantum computers to handle computational tasks. The tool lets researchers test different scheduling and resource allocation strategies (methods for deciding which tasks run on which computer and when) without needing actual hardware. They also surveyed existing scheduling and orchestration techniques and organized them by their underlying strategy, resource allocation approach, how they coordinate work across distributed systems, and the metrics they use to measure performance.
sc-2025-215.key_novelty: HybridCloudSim combines a survey of scheduling techniques with a simulation framework for hybrid quantum-HPC systems that models real-world challenges: quantum processor noise, device variability, and distributed coordination.

sc-2025-199.method: It maintains a central database recording all hardware events in the GPU system and analyzes patterns to identify which failures correlate with each other and which components repeatedly break. Based on these patterns, it automatically applies different repair strategies depending on failure history using multi-strike policies (repair strategies that treat a component's first failure differently from repeated failures). This automated recovery system was deployed on the Aurora supercomputer.
sc-2025-199.key_novelty: It's the first automated system for managing hardware failures in exascale GPU supercomputers by analyzing failure patterns and applying multi-strike policies (different repair strategies based on failure history).

sc-2025-209.method: The system tests a small proxy version of the LLM across several different parallelism and compression configurations, creating a fingerprint of its performance. It then uses analytical extrapolation—mathematical prediction—to determine how the full LLM would perform under those same settings. Finally, it places the model's layers across the cluster while accounting for fragmentation, the scattered and uneven distribution of available hardware resources, rather than assuming uniform resources everywhere.
sc-2025-209.key_novelty: It predicts full LLM performance through fingerprinting a small proxy model instead of expensive full-model testing, and intelligently deploys layers across fragmented cluster resources by accounting for their uneven distribution.

sc-2025-214.method: The system combines a compiler and runtime. The compiler figures out the best way to execute each query across a mix of hardware types—CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs—and generates specific code for each. The runtime then executes these queries using pipelined stages (running different parts in parallel) while minimizing data movement between machines and ensuring no machine runs out of memory.
sc-2025-214.key_novelty: This is the first system to handle analytics workloads across disaggregated resources (computing machines spread across a network) paired with diverse hardware accelerators (different types like GPUs and FPGAs).

sc-2025-220.method: The system extends OpenMP's variants mechanism (alternative optimized code paths you can write for different hardware conditions) with a runtime engine that decides which version to use as your program executes. It measures the power consumption and heat of each variant, then selects the one that best fits within current power budgets and temperature limits. Built into LLVM, the system runs lightweight monitoring code that collects these measurements and applies a balanced strategy that respects power caps, thermal headroom, and performance.
sc-2025-220.key_novelty: The first runtime system to automatically select between code variants during program execution based on real-time power and temperature measurements, while maintaining performance.

sc-2025-216.method: The approach removes some values from the preconditioner—a helper matrix that reshapes a problem to speed up solving—making it sparser. Sparsifying it reduces how much each iteration depends on the previous one, so many can run simultaneously on GPUs. The method uses ILU(0) and ILU(K) preconditioners (incomplete factorization techniques) on symmetric positive definite matrices while maintaining reliable convergence.
sc-2025-216.key_novelty: Sparsifying preconditioners—removing values from the helper matrix—breaks dependencies between iterations, enabling GPU parallelism without sacrificing convergence.

sc-2025-212.method: Instead of just testing whether models get scientific questions right or wrong, the researchers broke down the task into smaller steps—like identifying coordinates on an image or calculating exact pixel locations—to see exactly where models fail. They evaluated two multimodal language models, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct, on high-resolution visual data using this decomposed approach.
sc-2025-212.key_novelty: Breaking scientific question-answering into small subtasks shows where multimodal language models—AI systems that interpret images and text—get stuck in their reasoning or fail to integrate their components properly.

sc-2025-207.method: ROSfs is a user-level filesystem (a software layer that runs above the operating system) that organizes sensor data from multiple robots by timestamp. Instead of searching through nested folders, one robot can query another robot's data by time—for example, 'send me all camera images from the last 30 seconds'—and get instant access. The system works with ROS (Robot Operating System), the standard software used in robotics, and was tested on real UAV (drone) and UGV (ground robot) systems to confirm it handles real-world scenarios.
sc-2025-207.key_novelty: The core idea is time-indexed queries—organizing data by timestamp so robot teams can instantly access each other's recent information instead of searching through files.

sc-2025-221.method: They use multiple job-scheduling simulators to test different scheduler configurations and observe how each handles workloads that mix urgent and standard jobs. They built a lightweight framework that mimics how jobs get submitted to the system, along with tools to analyze and visualize the results. This lets them measure three competing goals: how quickly urgent jobs complete, how fairly standard jobs are treated, and how efficiently the system uses its computing resources. By comparing these results, they identify which configurations work best for mixed-urgency workloads.
sc-2025-221.key_novelty: The work evaluates how HPC job schedulers like Slurm should be configured to handle workloads with mixed urgency levels, using a practical testing framework.

sc-2025-218.method: The algorithm reconstructs 3D laminography images using an iterative method called ADMM-FFT, which repeatedly performs expensive mathematical transformations (FFTs, which convert data between different frequency representations). The key insight is that many of these FFT operations are similar, so instead of recalculating them each time, the system saves the results in memory and reuses them—a technique called memoization. To avoid overflowing CPU memory, intermediate data is moved to graphics processors (GPUs), a technique called variable offloading. The computation is then distributed across multiple GPUs on the same machine and across different machines in a cluster.
sc-2025-218.key_novelty: Memoization of repeated FFT operations in the ADMM-FFT iterative algorithm, combined with variable offloading to GPUs to reduce CPU memory usage and enable multi-GPU scaling.

sc-2025-222.method: A reviewer tested whether the quantum circuit mapping code and data actually produce the results the authors claimed. The evaluation examined both the artifact description (what authors said was provided) and the evaluation appendix (detailed test results) to verify the work can be independently reproduced. This is part of SC25's reproducibility initiative, which systematically checks whether published research can be replicated.
sc-2025-222.key_novelty: A report verifying that quantum circuit mapping optimization code produces reproducible results.

sc-2025-219.method: When serving Mixture of Experts models on GPUs with memory constraints, unused experts must be transferred between GPU and main memory frequently, creating a data transfer bottleneck. To reduce this, the approach uses error-bounded lossy compression—specifically the SZ3 and CuSZp algorithms, which shrink data by accepting a controlled amount of intentional information loss. The researchers then systematically measure how these compression errors affect the model's inference accuracy across different layers of the network.
sc-2025-219.key_novelty: Different layers in Mixture of Experts models tolerate compression errors with varying robustness—some can withstand aggressive compression while others are highly sensitive.

sc-2025-225.method: The researchers took a two-part approach to moving Gysela (a turbulence simulation code) to GPU: first, they used OpenMP offloading (a standard technique that tells the compiler to run code on the GPU) across most of the code for broad coverage. Then, for the performance-critical collision operator—the part where the simulation spent most of its time—they rewrote that section in Kokkos (a C++ library designed to write code once but run efficiently on different hardware). They tested this on AMD hardware including the Genoa CPU, MI250X GPU, and MI300A APU (an all-in-one processor combining CPU and GPU) on the Adastra supercomputer.
sc-2025-225.key_novelty: The core finding is that you can efficiently port legacy Fortran code to GPU by first using OpenMP offloading for broad coverage, then surgically rewriting only the performance-critical collision operator in Kokkos.

sc-2025-223.method: A reviewer obtained the C.A.T.S. tool (which traces memory access patterns and program execution flow to analyze whole-program performance), along with its artifact description and evaluation instructions. The reviewer ran the tool following the paper's procedures to check whether it produced the expected results and worked when executed independently.
sc-2025-223.key_novelty: An independent evaluation confirmed that the C.A.T.S. performance tracing tool produces reproducible results when others follow the paper's experimental procedures.

sc-2025-224.method: The researchers created a digital twin—a computer simulation that accurately mimics real high-performance computing (HPC) systems—and extended it to evaluate different scheduling policies (the rules that decide which jobs run when). Using real operational data from actual supercomputers as input, the simulation can predict how changes to scheduling would affect power consumption and cooling needs. The framework connects to external scheduling simulators and can test scenarios with financial incentive structures and machine-learning-based scheduling algorithms.
sc-2025-224.key_novelty: The core innovation is pairing HPC scheduling simulators with digital twins to predict how scheduling changes affect power and cooling before deploying them to real systems.

sc-2025-227.method: The approach creates a translation layer between quantum programs and different quantum hardware types. It works by splitting the problem into two parts: intent (the computation you want to perform) stays separate from context (the description tailored for a specific quantum backend type, like gate-based Qiskit or annealing D-Wave systems). A working example built with Qiskit and D-Wave demonstrates that programs written in this middle layer can run on different quantum hardware types without being rewritten.
sc-2025-227.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a backend-neutral middle layer that separates intent from context with a descriptor pattern (borrowed from high-performance computing design), so quantum code only needs to be written once regardless of which quantum hardware it runs on.

sc-2025-228.method: The system uses AVX-512 instructions (the CPU's high-speed data operation set) to directly control data flow over PCIe, rather than relying on DMA hardware controllers. It enables peer-to-peer memory mapping so that GPUs can access each other's memory directly, without data routing through the main CPU. By keeping communication paths short and direct, this design achieves sub-2-microsecond latencies while using simpler software.
sc-2025-228.key_novelty: Ultra-low sub-2-microsecond latency between GPUs and FPGAs is achieved using AVX-512-driven direct PCIe I/O and peer-to-peer GPU memory mapping, eliminating traditional DMA controllers.

sc-2025-217.method: LangChain is a framework for building AI agents that can use tools; Parsl is a system for managing parallel computations on supercomputers. The work integrates these by converting LangChain tool calls into Parsl functions that are then queued to worker computers for parallel execution. Two implementations were tested: (1) automatically converting LangChain tool calls into Parsl tasks, and (2) creating a Parsl ensemble (a coordinated group of parallel jobs) that the LLM can directly invoke as a tool. The system was demonstrated on both a local Nvidia GPU workstation and the Polaris supercomputer at Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF), executing molecular dynamics simulations (calculations of how molecules behave).
sc-2025-217.key_novelty: The first integration of large language model agents (LangChain) with high-performance computing job schedulers (Parsl) enables AI systems to directly manage large-scale computational simulations on supercomputers.

sc-2025-230.method: The system stores training data and model parameters across multiple memory tiers—GPU memory for speed, CPU memory for capacity, disk for storage—moving data strategically between them to keep the GPU working without waiting. It uses multiple independent data-transfer paths instead of a single bottleneck, with intelligent scheduling that prevents these transfers from disrupting the backward pass (where the network computes how to adjust each weight based on errors). The optimizer state—statistics that control weight adjustments—is spread across these memory tiers and managed with caching (keeping frequently-needed data nearby) and contention-awareness (detecting when different parts are competing for resources).
sc-2025-230.key_novelty: The core innovation combines multiple memory tiers with multiple parallel data-transfer paths coordinated through smart scheduling to avoid conflicts, plus optimizes data movement specifically for the backward pass (where error signals update weights) and weight updates (where model parameters change), achieving 2.5x faster training than conventional offloading.

sc-2025-229.method: Three complementary frameworks handle different serving patterns: AI-Flux processes requests in batches for efficiency, Ray Serve responds to dynamically arriving requests, and Illinois Chat maintains always-on availability. They provide OpenAI-compatible APIs and hierarchical resource management (making resource allocation decisions at multiple levels) so users can pick the best approach for their workload type.
sc-2025-229.key_novelty: The work integrates three complementary LLM serving frameworks—batch (AI-Flux), dynamic (Ray Serve), and always-on (Illinois Chat)—using OpenAI-compatible APIs and hierarchical resource management for high-performance computing environments.

sc-2025-234.method: Slurm divides all work into short time periods instead of letting any single job run to completion, cycling through different tasks rapidly. Interactive and AI workloads receive high priority and guaranteed resource allocations (specific portions of the computer reserved exclusively for them), ensuring they get quick response times, while batch jobs run during the unused capacity in between.
sc-2025-234.key_novelty: The approach reserves dedicated computing resources with high priority for interactive and AI work, allowing these responsive workloads to coexist with traditional batch jobs on the same scheduling system without conflicting demands.

sc-2025-226.method: The researchers connected a real 20-qubit superconducting quantum computer (where quantum bits are stored in circuits cooled to near absolute zero) with a traditional supercomputer at Germany's Leibniz Supercomputing Centre. Rather than simulate or theorize, they documented what actually had to work: power delivery and cooling systems, software connections between the quantum and classical computers, and operator training. This hands-on integration revealed practical challenges that isolated lab experiments don't show.
sc-2025-226.key_novelty: This work shows what actually must happen in practice when combining a quantum computer and a supercomputer in a real computing facility.

sc-2025-233.method: The method automates the traditionally manual task of tuning a simulator: it tests the simulator with different detail levels and parameter settings, measures how each matches real-world behavior, and automatically identifies the best trade-off between accuracy and speed. A framework then systematically determines which simulator components require high detail and which can be safely simplified. Two case studies demonstrate the approach on different types of parallel and distributed systems.
sc-2025-233.key_novelty: The core innovation is an automated framework that determines the right level of detail for simulators, working across different parallel and distributed computing domains.

sc-2025-232.method: The approach designs a Dynamic Programming Accelerator (DPA)—custom hardware built specifically for dynamic programming, which is a technique where you solve complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and reusing results instead of recomputing. The hardware is optimized to find optimal network routes when links fail, a computationally expensive problem for general processors. The method shows that this specialized hardware outperforms GPU and CPU solutions on the same task.
sc-2025-232.key_novelty: Specialized hardware built for dynamic programming finds optimal network routes faster when links fail than general-purpose processors.

sc-2025-237.method: The approach trains a large language model (LLM) to predict how much power each computing job will consume by analyzing its characteristics. Based on these predictions, a lightweight scheduling strategy shifts when jobs run to align with grid conditions or renewable energy availability. The system integrates into Slurm, the job scheduler widely used in data centers, without modifying its core code, making deployment straightforward.
sc-2025-237.key_novelty: Using learned representations from a language model (LLM embeddings), the approach predicts job power with 15% lower error than prior methods, enabling a 4.0 MWh shift of computing load to solar-peak hours without reducing throughput.

sc-2025-231.method: The method extends s-step PCG—a fast linear equation solver that groups computation steps to reduce how often processors must synchronize—to work with any mathematical basis (the underlying set of foundation vectors used in calculations). By supporting flexible basis selection, different bases can be tuned to maintain numerical accuracy while retaining the speed benefit. The researchers comprehensively analyze different bases to identify which provide the best balance between synchronization reduction and numerical stability.
sc-2025-231.key_novelty: The key insight is that s-step PCG's numerical stability can be controlled through basis selection—enabling methods that are both fast (low synchronization) and numerically accurate.

sc-2025-238.method: The researchers integrated RADICAL-Pilot, Flux, and Dragon runtime systems to manage compute resources through layered decision-making rather than a single scheduling point like Slurm's srun. In this approach, upper layers allocate resources across machines while lower layers handle task scheduling to individual processors, enabling rapid scheduling of diverse AI and HPC workloads. By distributing scheduling decisions across multiple components instead of routing everything through one bottleneck, they overcame Slurm's throughput limitation.
sc-2025-238.key_novelty: Combining RADICAL-Pilot, Flux, and Dragon runtime systems solves Slurm's throughput bottleneck, achieving over 1,500 task launches per second and reducing hybrid AI-HPC workflow completion time by 30–60%.

sc-2025-235.method: The system embeds monitoring code directly into the Linux kernel using eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a framework that lets programs run in kernel space with minimal overhead. It categorizes incoming network packets by IP address and protocol type (TCP, UDP, etc.) and records traffic counts at millisecond-scale resolution. Because the monitoring runs at kernel level rather than as a separate application, it captures detailed per-IP network behavior with very little CPU consumption—crucial for scientific experiments that need accurate, real-time network performance data.
sc-2025-235.key_novelty: By running network monitoring directly in the Linux kernel via eBPF, the system achieves per-IP telemetry at sub-millisecond resolution with only 4% CPU overhead and no need for special hardware.

sc-2025-239.method: CAMEO breaks the energy system design problem into smaller, pluggable pieces that can run in any order as long as dependencies are met (using a DAG—a dependency graph where each node runs after its inputs are ready). Each component is containerized (packaged with its own software environment) and described using JSON specifications, so they can communicate with each other and be reused across different problems. Nextflow orchestrates these containers—it manages scheduling, data flow, and parallel execution—so designers can mix and match components without rewriting them.
sc-2025-239.key_novelty: CAMEO lets energy system designers solve different optimization problems by mixing and matching components with standardized interfaces, rather than building a custom solver for each problem.

sc-2025-243.method: The system dynamically breaks work into smaller pieces and assigns them to GPUs in real time based on what each GPU can handle. For the most compute-heavy operations, it spreads the work across multiple GPUs to reduce latency. For the Attention computation (which calculates how different parts of the input relate to each other), it specifically distributes the workload across lower-end GPUs by dividing it into smaller attention heads. A real-time routing system decides which GPU gets which work by weighing the time data takes to travel between GPUs, how much computation each GPU must do, and how much memory each operation requires.
sc-2025-243.key_novelty: Unlike systems that use a fixed strategy for all operations, this one dynamically adjusts how it splits work across mixed-strength GPUs based on what each part of the model actually needs.

sc-2025-245.method: The researchers built fluid-simulation solvers for 2D and 3D problems on Intel Agilex 7 FPGAs (reconfigurable chips customized for specific tasks) using the Intel oneAPI framework. They sped things up by using the FPGA's large on-chip cache to keep data close and avoid repeatedly fetching from slower main memory. They also split the simulation into independent regions (domain decomposition), which let them duplicate the processing pipeline across multiple FPGAs and scale the work up.
sc-2025-245.key_novelty: This demonstrates that fluid simulations can run at practical scale across multiple FPGAs while achieving energy efficiency competitive with GPUs, despite individual FPGAs having lower throughput.

sc-2025-241.method: The evaluation ran the published GPU code for subgraph matching—finding whether smaller molecular structures exist within larger ones—on test cases by combining multiple queries into batches to maximize the GPU's parallel processing efficiency. Measurements were taken and compared against the original paper's reported results to confirm the batching approach delivered the claimed speedups.
sc-2025-241.key_novelty: Independent confirmation that batch-processing multiple subgraph matching queries on a GPU for molecular analysis produces the speedups the original paper reported.

sc-2025-242.method: The researchers measured the Cerebras WSE-2 chip by running tests that measure its computational speed, memory bandwidth (how fast data moves in and out), and communication latency (how long messages take between processing elements on the chip). They also measured bisection bandwidth—the maximum amount of data that can flow across the entire chip at once—to understand communication bottlenecks. These measurements were combined into a roofline model, a graph that shows the theoretical performance ceiling based on the chip's computing power and memory speed.
sc-2025-242.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive benchmark of the Cerebras WSE-2 chip that measures how processing elements communicate with each other and what performance it achieves in practice.

sc-2025-240.method: The study tests oversubscribing—running more jobs simultaneously than there are physical processors—on actual server hardware using real workloads instead of simulations. Oversubscribing works because the operating system's scheduler can rapidly switch between jobs, letting quick interactive tasks complete without waiting for long-running batch jobs to finish. By measuring actual memory usage during these experiments, the researchers identified the real constraints on when this strategy is effective.
sc-2025-240.key_novelty: Oversubscribing proves to be an effective and simpler alternative to complex multi-queue schedulers for balancing interactive and batch jobs.

sc-2025-236.method: ILAN is a task scheduler for LLVM OpenMP on NUMA systems—computers where different processors have varying-speed access to different memory regions. It uses moldability (changing how many parallel tasks run based on the situation) to reduce interference, the slowdown when too many tasks fight over the same memory and cache. It also organizes tasks hierarchically—scheduling at different levels from processor sockets down to individual cores—so each task runs near the memory it needs to access.
sc-2025-236.key_novelty: ILAN reduces task interference and improves data locality on NUMA systems through hierarchical task scheduling that's aware of the hardware's memory topology (how different processors connect to different memory at different speeds).

sc-2025-246.method: A web application built on the Open OnDemand platform that makes it easy to submit jobs (computational tasks) to supercomputers without learning Linux commands. When users access the application, they fill out a form specifying their needs—like how many computers to use and how long the job should run—and the application generates the shell script (the command sequence) required for submission. Users can view the generated script, edit it directly for more control, submit the job, track its progress, and save parameters from previous jobs to reuse later.
sc-2025-246.key_novelty: The key innovation is providing both automatic script generation and manual editing in one tool, so beginners can get started easily while advanced users can customize fully.

sc-2025-244.method: SENSE uses software-controlled networking (Software-Defined Networking) to let scientists request guaranteed bandwidth for their data transfers by declaring their needs upfront—rather than hoping the network has spare capacity. When a request comes in, the system automatically coordinates resources across multiple independently-managed networks (like booking time across different facilities) to ensure the bandwidth is reserved end-to-end. The researchers tested this approach on a comprehensive testbed that includes real production networks: GNA-G AutoGOLE, NRP, FABRIC, and LHC CMS infrastructure.
sc-2025-244.key_novelty: SENSE is the first system to show that networks can be treated as first-class scheduled resources through intent-based reservations across multiple independent administrative domains.

sc-2025-252.method: The researchers took MPI-BugBench, an existing test suite that checks for bugs in C implementations of MPI (a standard library that lets programs run in parallel across multiple computers), and adapted it to work with Fortran code. They documented the challenges that came up during the conversion, since Fortran has different language features than C. They then used MUST—a tool that automatically finds bugs in MPI code—to test both the C and Fortran versions side by side, comparing how well it caught bugs in each language.
sc-2025-252.key_novelty: This is the first MPI correctness test suite adapted to Fortran, and it revealed that bug-detection tools don't catch errors equally well across both languages.

sc-2025-249.method: The researchers tested Qdrant, a distributed vector database (a system for finding similar data across multiple computers), by running it on the Polaris supercomputer at Argonne National Laboratory. They used real biological text from the BV-BRC project, converting it to numerical embeddings (mathematical representations capturing text meaning) using the Qwen3-Embedding-4B model. They measured insertion speed, index construction time (building the lookup structure), and query latency (response time for similarity searches), scaling from 1 to 32 worker processes.
sc-2025-249.key_novelty: This is the first performance study of vector databases (software for finding similar numerical data across multiple computers) on supercomputers, using realistic biological text and extracting practical deployment lessons.

sc-2025-247.method: The work adds a sampling plugin to THAPI, a framework that records detailed traces of what high-performance computers are doing. This plugin periodically reads hardware counters from CXI network cards (Cassini Interconnect) — essentially built-in meters that measure network congestion, retries, and other low-level network metrics. The iprof tool weaves these periodic measurements into the main trace timeline, and Perfetto visualizes everything together so you can see when network problems happen and what the application was doing at that moment.
sc-2025-247.key_novelty: This work is the first to combine measurements from network hardware (NIC hardware counters tracking congestion and retries) with an HPC tracing system, showing network problems and application behavior in a single timeline.

sc-2025-250.method: The researchers taught 19 computer science students (both undergraduates and graduate students) GPU programming in two ways: using Python paired with Numba, a compiler that converts Python code to run on graphics processors, and using C++ with CUDA, the standard programming framework for GPUs. They checked what students knew beforehand, measured how each approach performed, and analyzed what specific mistakes students made in each language.
sc-2025-250.key_novelty: This study measured specific mistakes students make in Python GPU programming and their impact on learning outcomes compared to C++.

sc-2025-251.method: The method uses three load-balancing techniques all written in SYCL (a programming framework that runs on any GPU): grouping related data to speed up memory access, distributing work evenly to keep all GPU processors busy, and using a strided pattern (skipping through memory in a regular way) to assign work fairly. A single codebase using these techniques runs efficiently on AMD MI300X, Intel Max 1550, and NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
