sc-2025-251.key_novelty: The core idea is that load-balancing strategies tailored to SYCL let a single BFS codebase run efficiently on AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA GPUs.

sc-2025-248.method: PGT-I extends PyTorch Geometric Temporal (a library for graph neural networks on spatiotemporal data—events with both location and time patterns) to use distributed data parallel training, where computation is split across multiple GPUs or machines. It employs two strategies: index-batching and distributed-index-batching, which exploit the spatiotemporal structure by building graph snapshots (versions of the graph at specific moments in time) on-the-fly during training instead of pre-computing all of them in advance. This dynamic snapshot construction saves memory because snapshots are built only as needed during training.
sc-2025-248.key_novelty: PGT-I is the first framework to train graph neural networks on spatiotemporal data (events with both location and time patterns) on full-scale real datasets like PeMS without partitioning the graph, by dynamically building graph snapshots during training instead of pre-computing them all upfront.

sc-2025-258.method: ASCRIBE-XR is a VR headset application built on the Godot game engine that lets scientists immersively explore 3D scientific data. It combines three capabilities: local VR rendering that creates the sensation of being inside the data, remote processing on supercomputers (HPC systems) that stream large-scale calculations to your headset, and internet communication protocols (WebRTC and MQTT) that let multiple scientists view and work with the same data in real time.
sc-2025-258.key_novelty: The innovation is bringing together virtual-reality headsets, supercomputers, and AI-driven 3D object modeling into one unified system where multiple scientists can collaborate on scientific visualization.

sc-2025-260.method: A member of the SC25 conference's reproducibility committee independently tested the code and data that the lsCOMP paper made publicly available. The evaluator followed detailed instructions in the paper's Artifact Description and Evaluation appendix (the section where researchers explain what materials they're sharing and how to verify the work) to check whether the results could be reproduced correctly.
sc-2025-260.key_novelty: This report assesses whether the lsCOMP paper's results can be reproduced by running its code and data, rather than contributing new research ideas itself.

sc-2025-254.method: The team tested MetoHash—a data-structure index for hybrid memory systems combining persistent memory (PMem, which survives power loss) with DRAM—by running it on actual hardware. They measured two things: how much memory MetoHash used and how efficiently it moved data between the PMem and DRAM layers. They followed SC25 reproducibility standards, meaning they documented every test step, reported all results transparently, and ensured that other researchers could independently run the same tests and get the same answers.
sc-2025-254.key_novelty: This work independently confirms that MetoHash's hybrid memory hashing design achieves its claimed improvements in memory efficiency and data-traffic optimization on real hardware.

sc-2025-259.method: A member of SC25's reproducibility committee took the TurboFNO paper's code and data (the artifact—all materials the authors provided) and tried to run the experiments themselves, following the instructions the authors gave. They checked whether the code ran without errors and whether the results matched what the paper reported. This validates that the paper's findings are reliable and that other researchers could independently recreate them.
sc-2025-259.key_novelty: This is a reproducibility check—verifying whether published work can be independently repeated—rather than a paper that introduces new research.

sc-2025-256.method: TensorMD builds its own molecular dynamics calculator based on machine learning interatomic potentials (learned models that predict how atoms interact), instead of using general ML frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch. This independence lets engineers optimize for the specific computational patterns that molecular dynamics requires—patterns that general frameworks can't address because they're designed to handle many different types of work. The result is faster simulations through hardware-aware optimizations tuned to this specific workload.
sc-2025-256.key_novelty: A custom machine learning interatomic potential built for molecular dynamics instead of general ML frameworks, enabling workload-specific optimizations.

sc-2025-264.method: The framework captures real system traces—the actual OS interrupts, cache contention, and memory access delays that happen in production—and replays them as controlled disturbances to test how different parallel programming models (OpenMP and SYCL) perform under stress. They evaluated each workload both with normal system behavior and with injected noise, trying three mitigation tactics: thread pinning (locking threads to specific processor cores), dedicating certain cores to housekeeping tasks only, and toggling SMT (simultaneous multithreading, where one core runs multiple threads) on or off. They measured performance using two standard benchmarks—N-body and Babelstream—plus a smaller test application called MiniFE. Testing happened on two different processor platforms to see how resilience varied across hardware.
sc-2025-264.key_novelty: This is the first systematic, reproducible method for measuring how well parallel programming models maintain performance when faced with controlled system noise injection.

sc-2025-255.method: The tool integrates into AMD's GPU compiler (ROCm/HIP) using LLVM passes—a standard compiler technique for injecting monitoring code. It instruments both CPU and GPU code to record every write, read, and synchronization operation that touches the shared memory space. After the program runs, it analyzes these traces offline to find data races: situations where CPU and GPU access the same memory without proper coordination, causing unpredictable behavior.
sc-2025-255.key_novelty: It's the first tool to detect data races in CPU/GPU unified memory systems—where both processors can access the same memory.

sc-2025-261.method: Ceph's communication system is moved to a specialized processor called a DPU (Data Processing Unit), keeping the actual storage work on the main CPU. For metadata operations, it uses lightweight RPC (a way to invoke functions remotely), and for data movement, it uses DMA—a hardware feature that moves data between computers without the main CPU handling it. To work around limits on how much data hardware can move at once, it pipelines operations by overlapping data transmission with buffer preparation, so the system doesn't stall waiting for either to finish.
sc-2025-261.key_novelty: Offloading Ceph's communication to a specialized processor (a DPU) and pipelining data transfers—sending while preparing space—to reduce CPU work.

sc-2025-265.method: Instead of randomly initializing embeddings and training them from scratch, this approach analyzes the underlying data structure to provide smarter starting values. It uses MIRA (an efficient algorithm for finding the most important directions in large sparse data) to identify these principal directions by examining the data's correlations and word-pair patterns, then projects embeddings onto these directions. Because MIRA operates naturally in parallel and requires few tunable parameters, it scales to large datasets while reducing memory and computation costs.
sc-2025-265.key_novelty: Using MIRA spectral methods to initialize embeddings along the data's principal directions rather than random values.

sc-2025-257.method: The researchers built a detailed computer simulation (using gem5, a widely-used architecture simulator) that models a complete computer system using RISC-V instructions, with superconducting cores running at 100 GHz (superconductors that operate at extreme cold temperatures) and cryogenic semiconductor cores running at 4 GHz. The simulation includes multilevel cache memory, a superconducting interconnect called SRNoC that connects components, and a hardware accelerator called NOVA for processing graphs. They evaluated the simulation using standard benchmark programs (SPEC CPU2006) and compute-intensive workloads.
sc-2025-257.key_novelty: This is the first time a complete computer system combining superconducting cores, caches, realistic interconnects, and memory has been modeled in a simulator that researchers widely use.

sc-2025-269.method: PACE starts by grouping datacenter sensor readings into related patterns without needing labeled examples (unsupervised), then applies a time-aware causality detector called Granger causality to identify which measurements actually predict others—revealing genuine cause-and-effect relationships rather than just coincidental overlap. It produces visual maps (causal graphs and heatmaps) structured to match how the physical cooling, power, and network systems actually work and how their controls interact. These maps feed into digital twin models—computer replicas of the datacenter—enabling what-if analysis: predicting what happens if you adjust cooling by a certain amount or add more network capacity.
sc-2025-269.key_novelty: The core idea is pairing unsupervised pattern discovery with time-aware causal detection to automatically isolate root causes by tracing which sensor readings actually forecast others, rather than just detecting correlated symptoms.

sc-2025-267.method: A member of the SC25 Reproducibility Committee tested whether the lsCOMP paper by Franck Cappello et al. can be reproduced—meaning the researchers' code actually runs and produces the same results as published. The committee member reviewed the Artifact Description (documentation of the code and data provided) and the Evaluation appendix (the testing process used to verify those results).
sc-2025-267.key_novelty: This assesses whether published research can be reproduced, rather than introducing new research ideas.

sc-2025-253.method: The approach chains two different types of analysis. Static tools (CoVer and SPMD IR) examine the code without running it to find regions that might cause MPI data races—situations where multiple processes simultaneously access the same memory, causing corruption. These suspicious regions are forwarded to a dynamic tool (MUST) through a generic exchange format that lets different tools share information. The dynamic tool then instruments (monitors the execution of) only those regions, letting it verify which problems are real, combining the speed of static analysis with the accuracy of real-time observation.
sc-2025-253.key_novelty: This is the first system that couples static and dynamic MPI correctness tools through a generic exchange format, enabling them to work together and achieve improvements in both accuracy and speed that neither could accomplish alone.

sc-2025-270.method: The approach extends PolKA (source routing — a technique where the sending computer picks each packet's path through the network) by adding traffic classification at the network edge, the boundary where data enters the network. It develops traffic patterns and fair queuing methods to allocate network capacity fairly across different applications based on their type. The system uses in-band network telemetry (INT — measurement that happens inside the network as packets flow) and P4 programmable switches to identify what application each packet comes from and decide which path to send it on.
sc-2025-270.key_novelty: The core contribution is combining traffic classification at the network edge with source routing (path selection by the sending computer), so the network can allocate paths based on what application each packet belongs to rather than treating all traffic the same.

sc-2025-266.method: This approach modifies HOOI (Higher Order Orthogonal Iteration, an algorithm that compresses large multi-dimensional arrays) to automatically determine how much to compress—measured by the 'rank'—instead of requiring you to specify it beforehand. You set a tolerance for acceptable error, and the algorithm adjusts the rank automatically to stay within that error budget. To handle massive datasets, the researchers optimized each algorithm step and implemented it to run in parallel across thousands of processor cores.
sc-2025-266.key_novelty: The core idea is making HOOI both rank-adaptive (automatically selecting compression level) and parallel (running across thousands of cores), achieving compression quality that matches or exceeds fixed-rank methods like STHOSVD.

sc-2025-268.method: The approach automatically determines how to assign multi-dimensional Fourier transform computations and surrounding numerical operations to different computers in a cluster. It uses Z3, an automated constraint solver, to explore different arrangements by finding configurations that satisfy logical constraints. The solver jointly optimizes how Fourier operations and numerical computations are distributed across computers, while selecting the optimal grid shape for arranging them. By considering these operations together, it minimizes the data communication needed during coordinated cluster operations (MPI collectives).
sc-2025-268.key_novelty: The core idea is using automated constraint solving to jointly schedule Fourier operations and numerical computations across distributed computers to minimize inter-computer communication.

sc-2025-262.method: Pre-Trajectory Sampling improves quantum trajectory simulation (tracking individual quantum paths under noise) by matching error types to real hardware instead of generic ones, batching multiple trajectories to eliminate redundant work, and collecting error information efficiently during computation. Tests reached a 35-qubit quantum error-correction code using statevector simulation and an 85-qubit system using tensor network simulation.
sc-2025-262.key_novelty: Pre-Trajectory Sampling selects which quantum trajectories to compute before simulation begins, enabling batched processing and efficient error collection.

sc-2025-273.method: They tested seven different compression programs on six real scientific datasets. For each one, they checked quality five different ways: PSNR (measuring average error), SSIM (checking if patterns look preserved) in two settings, Error Autocorrelation (whether errors bunch up in one place or spread randomly), and Pearson Coefficient (whether relationships between data points held up). This shows which compressor works best depending on what quality aspect matters most for your science.
sc-2025-273.key_novelty: This is the first benchmark to measure compression quality using correlation-based metrics—like structural similarity and error spread patterns—alongside traditional error-value metrics, revealing that the best compressor depends on which quality metric matters most.

sc-2025-275.method: An independent member of the SC25 reproducibility committee systematically tests whether the published GPU lossy compression artifacts actually work as described. They run the code and data, evaluate the results against the official SC25 Artifact Description and Evaluation criteria, and document their findings. This process checks whether other researchers can actually reproduce the original paper's work.
sc-2025-275.key_novelty: This report independently verifies whether a published GPU lossy compression artifact actually works and can be reproduced, following established evaluation standards.

sc-2025-263.method: The system uses multiple AI helpers, each doing one job: one writes lesson plans, one explains concepts, one scaffolds code (provides step-by-step code guidance), and one runs the code. These helpers run directly on the world's most powerful supercomputers, not external cloud services. They coordinate their work using carefully written instructions to complete complex teaching sequences. To prevent each helper from being overwhelmed with history, the system regularly summarizes what each one has learned.
sc-2025-263.key_novelty: The core innovation is using prompts (text instructions) to coordinate multiple AI tutors that run directly on supercomputers, rather than depending on external cloud services, enabling personalized HPC education.

sc-2025-271.method: DPAR adds privacy directly into AllReduce (how many computers combine their data together) by injecting noise—randomness—into each machine's contribution before combining, which blocks collusion attacks without key exchanges. A scalable noise mechanism adjusts the privacy cost as aggregation happens across machines while preserving accuracy, and noise pooling spreads this cost across multiple computations to minimize performance overhead. The result works as a drop-in replacement for standard MPI AllReduce.
sc-2025-271.key_novelty: DPAR achieves collusion-resistant AllReduce using differential privacy and noise pooling, avoiding the key exchange overhead required by encryption-based approaches.

sc-2025-274.method: FaSTCC analyzes how much data each possible loop order must access from memory and how much storage it requires, using this knowledge to design a 2D tiling strategy (breaking the computation into rectangular blocks). To handle the unpredictable sparsity of real-world tensors, it uses statistical prediction to automatically decide whether each block's intermediate results should be stored densely (as a continuous array) or sparsely (only keeping non-zero values), and to choose block sizes that minimize memory traffic. These blocks execute in parallel using hash-based data structures to efficiently manage and access the sparse data.
sc-2025-274.key_novelty: FaSTCC uses a 2D contraction-index-outer tiling scheme combined with probabilistic modeling to automatically select whether each tile's results are stored densely or sparsely and to optimize tile sizes based on predicted memory access costs.

sc-2025-272.method: The DynaChain framework optimizes GEMM-like matrix operations by separating two concerns: how to compute (arithmetic operations) and how to move data (from memory to processors), allowing each to be optimized independently. It uses constraint dependency chains—rules based on MT-3000's hardware capabilities—to automatically skip invalid scheduling options during the search, making it much faster to find good solutions. For matrix operations with irregular dimensions, it applies integer linear programming (mathematical optimization) to break down the problem efficiently. Finally, the actual computation kernels are custom-designed for MT-3000's VLIW+SIMD architecture (which executes multiple instructions at once and processes multiple data elements in parallel), with optimized register allocation and instruction pipelining for better throughput.
sc-2025-272.key_novelty: The innovation combines constraint dependency chains to automatically eliminate invalid search options, ILP-based decomposition for irregular matrix dimensions, and VLIW+SIMD-aware micro-kernel design with optimized register allocation and pipelining on MT-3000.

sc-2025-276.method: The workflow automatically records GPU kernel execution using an intercept layer (a middleman that captures GPU calls), then replays it on a CPU where tools like PoCL and Verificarlo analyze exactly where floating-point errors occur. It tests both standard IEEE floating-point and reduced-precision formats (FP16, TF32, BF16—compact number types that trade some accuracy for memory savings), and uses stochastic arithmetic (testing with random rounding via MCA and PRISM) to measure how compiler optimizations like -ffast-math (which prioritize speed over precision) affect numerical accuracy.
sc-2025-276.key_novelty: It enables automated, standardized floating-point error analysis of GPU kernels without manual source code modification—supporting reduced-precision modes and compiler optimizations.

sc-2025-277.method: A thin wrapper layer in C++ keeps your original CUDA kernel code (the GPU commands written for NVIDIA) readable and runnable while making it work with SYCL (a portable GPU framework that runs on multiple brands). The approach mechanically converts kernels into function objects—a process called 'functorization'—without forcing you to rewrite the source code by hand. The team tested it on CRK-HACC, an N-body cosmology simulation (a program that models how gravity pulls many objects around), running the same code on both Polaris (NVIDIA GPUs) and Aurora (Intel GPUs). The system preserves architecture-specific optimizations, so you keep the speed tweaks you've made for each GPU type.
sc-2025-277.key_novelty: The innovation is a wrapper that lets you keep your CUDA code exactly as-is and compile it for both NVIDIA and Intel GPUs, avoiding code duplication and automated translation while preserving your kernel structure and performance optimizations.

sc-2025-280.method: An independent evaluator runs the KAMI GPU GEMM code to verify it produces the same results the authors published, checking against SC25's standard criteria for research artifacts. The evaluation confirms the code works as described, has no hidden dependencies, and achieves the claimed speedups on GPU hardware. This independent verification demonstrates that the research can be reproduced and validated by others.
sc-2025-280.key_novelty: Independent confirmation that KAMI's GPU GEMM code successfully reproduces its published results when evaluated according to SC25 standards.

sc-2025-281.method: The researchers tested two cloud supercomputers—Azure Eagle (ranked 3rd globally with 14,400 H100 graphics processors) and Reindeer (ranked 32nd with 960 H200 graphics processors)—using targeted performance tests and real scientific computing workloads like HPL (a standard supercomputer benchmark). They measured computational efficiency, how the systems scale with more processors, data transfer speeds, network delays, and the performance cost of cloud virtualization (the software layer that manages shared hardware). They compared all results to identical systems running on dedicated on-premises hardware to isolate the true impact of the cloud environment.
sc-2025-281.key_novelty: This work provides the first direct performance comparison between cloud supercomputers and bare-metal systems, measuring the actual impact of cloud virtualization on high-performance computing.

sc-2025-285.method: The researchers built two versions of task-management systems that do the same job but use different approaches: one with traditional stackful coroutines (where each task gets its own memory stack) and one with C++20 stackless coroutines (a lighter approach that doesn't allocate full stacks). They tested both systems on work where tasks steal work from each other across a network (using RDMA, a fast way to access memory on other computers), running lots of small tasks that themselves spawn more tasks. They measured how fast each system could create new tasks, switch between them, how much memory each approach needs, and how long it takes to send work between computers.
sc-2025-285.key_novelty: This is the first head-to-head comparison of traditional stackful coroutines versus lightweight stackless coroutines in a distributed task system that uses RDMA networking, with detailed measurements of what each approach costs.

sc-2025-286.method: The solver splits the work into two levels: large blocks processed sequentially, and small blocks that run in parallel across multiple GPU processing streams. It caches frequently accessed data in memory to minimize repeated retrieval. The matrix is distributed across GPUs using a 1D block-cyclic pattern (blocks repeat cyclically across GPUs), optimized for NVLink, which is the direct high-speed connection between GPUs.
sc-2025-286.key_novelty: The key innovation is a lightweight static scheduler (one that's fast and pre-determined rather than dynamic) enabling fine-grained parallel work across GPU streams, combined with intelligent data caching and 1D block-cyclic matrix distribution optimized for NVLink.

sc-2025-279.method: Develops EasyC, a tool for measuring greenhouse gas emissions from HPC systems using only public Top 500 data. It tracks both operational carbon—emissions from energy use—and embodied carbon—emissions from manufacturing—covering 391 and 283 systems respectively. The tool fills gaps through interpolation, estimating values between known data points, then projects how carbon emissions will evolve through 2030.
sc-2025-279.key_novelty: EasyC enables the first comprehensive carbon footprint assessment of the Top 500 HPC supercomputers using minimal public data.

sc-2025-284.method: ChatEED retrieves relevant entries from decades of electronic logbooks (ELOGs) and uses them to generate clear answers to operator questions, solving the problem that ELOG entries are often fragmented, jargon-heavy, and hard to search. To address operator needs, the system automatically summarizes shift reports, retrieves ELOG information in real-time as operators ask questions, and makes its reasoning transparent. It was built by interviewing accelerator facility operators and analyzing their actual workflows, which shaped its focus on security, efficiency, and modularity.
sc-2025-284.key_novelty: ChatEED brings human-centered design to AI-powered search for electronic logbooks by building the system directly from accelerator facility operators' workflows.

sc-2025-289.method: We compared a traditional machine learning autotuner against LoopGen-AI, an agent system powered by three large language models (GPT-4.1, Claude 4.0, Gemini 2.5), on loop reordering (rearranging the order of computational loops to speed them up). We used prompt engineering techniques—Persona patterns (which assign the AI a specific role) and Context Manager patterns (which provide it relevant background information)—to guide both systems' decisions. We then measured how quickly each system converged to good solutions, how many actual program runs each required, and the quality of the final optimization choices.
sc-2025-289.key_novelty: This is the first systematic comparison of AI agents (systems powered by large language models) against traditional machine learning autotuning for HPC, showing that AI agents achieve competitive performance with substantially fewer actual program runs.

sc-2025-291.method: When multiple processes write data to storage simultaneously, some produce far more data than others, causing performance bottlenecks where slower writers make faster ones wait. This method uses ADIOS2's BP5 engine (a parallel I/O system that coordinates multiple writers) to dynamically adjust how data gets distributed across processes based on each process's actual output volume, rather than using fixed groupings by compute node. This prevents processes with heavy data loads from bottlenecking the rest. The approach was tested on simulated workloads with both mild and severe load imbalance.
sc-2025-291.key_novelty: This is the first parallel I/O strategy for ADIOS2 that dynamically adjusts workload distribution based on each process's actual data volume, enabling efficient in situ data extraction (live-simulation analytics) from severely unbalanced workloads.

sc-2025-283.method: The approach breaks down the complex simulation into smaller pieces: spatial subproblems (different locations) and physical subproblems (different physical processes), each with values that don't vary wildly and minimal dependencies on other pieces. Each piece is assigned to the hardware that's best suited for it—CPUs, GPUs, or specialized units. A mathematical technique called metamodel-space algebra combines the solutions while reducing communication overhead and precision requirements. The entire calculation runs across 60,000 Aurora GPUs using XS-NNQMD—neural-network quantum molecular dynamics that uses trained neural networks to predict quantum behavior for excited energy states.
sc-2025-283.key_novelty: The work combines three strategies: dividing multiphysics problems into pieces suited for different hardware (CPUs, GPUs, specialized units), using mathematical techniques to minimize communication and precision loss between pieces, and applying neural-network quantum dynamics at exascale across 60,000 GPUs.

sc-2025-292.method: Serverless systems running on processors with mixed core types—fast 'big' cores and power-efficient 'LITTLE' cores (asymmetric multi-cores)—must decide which functions run on which cores. GreenMix solves this using randomized sketching, a technique that rapidly finds approximate optimal assignments. It minimizes energy consumption and the cost of keeping functions ready to run, while maintaining performance standards (QoS). The system was tested on ARM big.LITTLE and Intel Alder Lake architectures.
sc-2025-292.key_novelty: It uses randomized sketching (an approximation technique) to decide which serverless functions run on which core type in asymmetric multi-cores, minimizing both energy use and the cost of keeping functions ready.

sc-2025-290.method: The system uses a team of AI agents (software that makes autonomous decisions) to coordinate experiments by translating plain English descriptions into instructions via an AI language model. These agents communicate with equipment and supercomputers through standard software interfaces (APIs), while maintaining a complete workflow record so results can be reproduced and understood. The approach was tested on additive manufacturing (3D printing) experiments requiring real-time coordination with supercomputers.
sc-2025-290.key_novelty: AI agents automatically coordinate between supercomputers and manufacturing equipment, making adjustments based on real-time feedback instead of waiting for manual decisions.

sc-2025-287.method: This compiler pipeline is built on MLIR (a flexible compiler framework that can work with multiple 'dialects' or specialized instruction sets). It takes Fortran code parsed by the Flang frontend and transforms it using MLIR at multiple levels, combining the OpenMP dialect (for multi-core parallel computing) with the HLS dialect (High-Level Synthesis—tools that turn code into hardware descriptions). The HLS backend then generates the actual hardware logic for FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays, chips that can be reconfigured to perform different computational tasks). Programmers mark which code sections run on the FPGA using OpenMP target directives (standard annotations for parallel computing), and can manually optimize individual kernels for performance.
sc-2025-287.key_novelty: This is the first compiler to selectively offload Fortran code to FPGAs using standard OpenMP target directives, by combining hardware-synthesis and parallel-computing tools within MLIR (a compiler platform built to work with multiple target hardware platforms).

sc-2025-288.method: They tested 5 commonly-used lossless compressors (bzip2, XZ, and others) plus new algorithms automatically designed by an LC framework. They took 14 single-precision scientific datasets (32-bit floating-point numbers) from the SDR-Bench collection and encoded each in both IEEE 754 format (the standard) and posit format (an alternative). For each dataset and compressor pair, they measured the compression ratio (how much the file shrank) and the speed.
sc-2025-288.key_novelty: This is the first empirical comparison of how well posit numbers compress compared to IEEE 754 across multiple compression algorithms.

sc-2025-282.method: Dori is JGI's supercomputer cluster designed to serve both production and research work on data-intensive tasks. It combines three components: governance and communication systems that manage resources fairly, software tools that different research teams can customize, and operational learning from processing petabytes of genomic data in practice since 2022.
sc-2025-282.key_novelty: Dori's core idea is user-centered design for HPC clusters—building the system based on what researchers actually need for data-intensive work, rather than forcing them to adapt to standard solutions.

sc-2025-278.method: The approach trains graph neural networks using all data at once (full-graph training) by splitting the computational work across GPUs in three dimensions: spatially (dividing the graph), temporally (dividing the training steps), and along a third dimension. It uses a double permutation scheme (reordering the data twice in a specific way) to ensure work is distributed evenly across GPUs even with irregular graph structure. A performance model automatically determines the optimal configuration of these three dimensions for any hardware setup. The method was evaluated on six graph datasets using up to 2048 GPUs on Perlmutter and 1024 GPUs on Frontier.
sc-2025-278.key_novelty: Three-dimensional parallelism combining spatial and temporal work division with a double permutation load-balancing scheme enables full-graph training of graph neural networks on billion-edge irregular graphs.

sc-2025-295.method: We independently tested Caracal, a GPU-resident sparse LU solver that uses lightweight fine-grained scheduling, following SC25's artifact evaluation guidelines. We ran the implementation, reproduced the reported results, and verified whether the claimed speedups over existing solvers actually matched the original claims.
sc-2025-295.key_novelty: Independent testing to verify that Caracal's claimed performance improvements for solving sparse linear systems on GPUs actually work.

sc-2025-297.method: Following SC25's artifact evaluation guidelines, the team independently tested whether the quantum transport simulation (calculations showing how particles move through materials using the GW approximation method) works correctly. They reproduced the exascale performance results—confirming the code runs at supercomputer-scale speeds—and assessed code quality and documentation to ensure others can reproduce the work.
sc-2025-297.key_novelty: This work independently verified that quantum transport simulations using the GW approximation method achieve their claimed exascale performance and produce reproducible results.

sc-2025-299.method: DAGonStore stores workflow data across edge-to-cloud systems by splitting it into redundant pieces using erasure codes—a technique where you break data into fragments so the full data can be recovered even if some storage nodes fail. It distributes these pieces using utilization-aware load-balancing, which watches how full each storage node is and spreads the load to prevent any single node from getting overwhelmed. The system was tested for scalability across many nodes, fault tolerance when storage nodes fail, and how little manual work users need to do.
sc-2025-299.key_novelty: The core idea is combining erasure codes with utilization-aware load-balancing so workflow data stays available even when storage nodes fail across edge-to-cloud systems.

sc-2025-296.method: The approach builds a parser—a tool that breaks down data into usable pieces—for DUNE's custom packet format directly into a Tofino programmable network switch, which is reconfigurable hardware in the network itself. Rather than sending all raw data to computers for processing, the switch performs the parsing as packets flow through the network. The team tested this setup using real network traffic from the ICEBERG DUNE prototype detector on the FABRIC testbed, measuring the switch's processing speed and identifying performance bottlenecks.
sc-2025-296.key_novelty: This shows that programmable network switches can handle parsing High-Energy Physics experiment data directly, instead of relying on computers to do it after the data arrives.

sc-2025-294.method: The Presto-OCS connector analyzes SQL query execution plans to find operations that can run inside the object storage system. Instead of executing expensive operations like aggregations (summing rows into groups), top-N queries (finding the top or bottom values), and joins (combining tables) on a separate compute layer, it pushes these operations into object storage where the data already sits, avoiding massive data transfers across the network. The system was tested on real-world analytics workloads and the TPC-H benchmark.
sc-2025-294.key_novelty: For the first time, a distributed SQL engine (Presto) can run complex query operations directly in object storage, substantially reducing data movement and improving query speed.

sc-2025-300.method: CASSE is a threat-modeling approach—a systematic way to identify potential security threats—designed specifically for data management libraries like HDF5, Zarr, and NetCDF. Unlike existing frameworks like STRIDE (which identify generic threat types), CASSE creates an attack taxonomy tailored to these libraries' unique file formats and data structures, and includes file-structure diagrams to show where attackers could intervene. The method was evaluated on HDF5, NetCDF, and Zarr.
sc-2025-300.key_novelty: CASSE is the first threat-modeling framework specifically designed for data management libraries, incorporating their file formats and data structures into a tailored attack taxonomy.

sc-2025-293.method: FZModules is a framework for building custom compression pipelines by connecting reusable modules that run on CPUs, GPUs, or both. Its execution system figures out the right order to run compression stages in based on what data each stage needs, moves data efficiently between CPU and GPU memory, and enables different parts of the pipeline to run in parallel—both along alternative branches and across sequential stages simultaneously. The framework was evaluated on four representative scientific datasets.
sc-2025-293.key_novelty: By using CPUs and GPUs together, the framework enables rapid design of custom error-bounded compression pipelines (you set the maximum acceptable data loss) where you control the trade-off between compression quality and speed.

sc-2025-301.method: Instead of waiting for one stage to finish completely before the next stage starts, this approach enables continuous streaming of data between stages. It uses two complementary strategies: dispel4py manages the workflow execution logic (which tasks run when and in what order), while CAPIO handles the actual data movement. The key technical contribution is adding a new rule to CAPIO that allows streaming even when files are created dynamically—you don't need to specify all files upfront. This hybrid approach keeps some data in memory for speed while using disk storage when needed.
sc-2025-301.key_novelty: The key innovation is a new commit rule that enables streaming over dynamically generated files without rewriting existing workflow code.

sc-2025-305.method: To verify the X-MoE paper's results, researchers downloaded and ran the authors' code on HPC systems (supercomputers), testing how efficiently mixture-of-experts training—a technique that routes different data to multiple specialized neural network sub-components—scales as computing power increases. They repeated the original experiments and measured whether they achieved the same performance improvements reported in the paper. This independent verification was part of the SC25 Supercomputing Conference's official Reproducibility Committee review process.
sc-2025-305.key_novelty: This report independently confirms that X-MoE's published results for training mixture-of-experts models (networks that route data to multiple specialized sub-components) on supercomputers are reproducible by following the authors' methodology.

sc-2025-298.method: PerfAnalyzer is an interactive dashboard that tracks how a program's performance changes as its code changes. It automatically gathers input parameters, hardware/software settings, and performance results at each code version stored in Git (the version control system), then displays this data visually so you can identify which code changes affected performance. The system was tested on CloverLeaf, a scientific computing mini-application, across multiple versions.
sc-2025-298.key_novelty: The core idea is displaying program performance alongside code changes across versions (tracked in Git), revealing which code modifications affect performance.

sc-2025-307.method: The method reformulates symbolic factorization—predicting which values will be zero and non-zero during matrix decomposition—using standard graph operations from GraphBLAS, a widely-available library. It applies optimization techniques including masks (filters that specify which computations to perform) and elimination trees (structures that track dependencies in the factorization order). The approach is then tested on both multi-core CPUs and many-core accelerators (such as GPUs) across various sparse matrix types to confirm it runs efficiently on different hardware.
sc-2025-307.key_novelty: Standard graph operations can express symbolic factorization in a way that achieves good performance across CPUs, GPUs, and other hardware without needing specialized algorithms for each architecture.

sc-2025-308.method: Bine trees—structures based on binomial negabinary trees—reorganize collective operations (coordinations where all computers send data) to route messages through local network links rather than scarce global connections, keeping traffic flowing within dense clusters instead of bottlenecking. The authors built eight Bine-based collective operations and evaluated them on four network topologies: Dragonfly, Dragonfly+, oversubscribed fat-tree, and torus.
sc-2025-308.key_novelty: Bine trees reduce the global-link traffic created by collective operations by up to 33% by routing messages through local connections, while maintaining the design flexibility of binomial trees and butterfly network structures.

sc-2025-311.method: The researchers added custom monitoring code—called instrumentation—to five high-performance GPU graph analysis programs, rather than relying solely on standard profiling tools like NVIDIA Nsight Compute. They inserted counters tracking two levels: overall GPU statistics and individual measurements from each thread. By analyzing these counters, they could see exactly how the code behaves in practice, verify whether their assumptions were correct, and identify specific parts needing optimization.
sc-2025-311.key_novelty: Custom instrumentation with global and per-thread counters reveals insights about irregular GPU workloads like graph algorithms that standard profilers cannot.

sc-2025-304.method: C.A.T.S. creates a unified trace that records two things: the program's control flow (the actual sequence of decisions and loops during execution) and every memory access. A compiler analysis automatically extracts these traces from the program's code without running it. Interactive visualizations display this data as timelines, data flow diagrams, and memory access patterns to help engineers identify optimization opportunities in data layout, allocation, and algorithm design.
sc-2025-304.key_novelty: C.A.T.S. traces control flow (the actual sequence of program decisions and loops) and memory accesses together—rather than just tracking function calls—using static compiler analysis.

sc-2025-310.method: DiOMP-Offloading unifies OpenMP target offloading with PGAS—Partitioned Global Address Space, a programming model that makes distributed GPU memory appear as one shared pool, so you program multiple GPUs as if they share memory. It's built on LLVM-OpenMP (the compiler) and GASNet-EX (a communication layer), with OMPCCL adding collective operations like broadcasts and reductions across GPUs from any vendor without vendor-specific code. The system handles both symmetric and asymmetric GPU memory allocations (different memory layouts across GPUs) and supports moving data between GPUs via remote put/get operations.
sc-2025-310.key_novelty: DiOMP-Offloading combines OpenMP with PGAS (Partitioned Global Address Space, treating distributed GPU memory as one shared space), introduces OMPCCL for vendor-neutral collective GPU operations, and provides centralized global memory management for multi-GPU systems.

sc-2025-306.method: The approach introduces new programming directives (annotations developers add to guide optimization) specifically built for tensor computations with many reductions—operations where values across multi-dimensional arrays get combined repeatedly into fewer results. These directives are grounded in Multi-Dimensional Homomorphisms (MDH), a mathematical framework that preserves structural properties through transformations, and designed for data-parallel operations (calculations running in parallel on many data elements). The implementation is a Python-based framework that compiles code for both CPUs and GPUs using OMPCCL (a portable library managing collective communication between processors), ensuring the same code runs efficiently on either hardware without requiring manual optimization.
sc-2025-306.key_novelty: The innovation applies Multi-Dimensional Homomorphisms—a mathematical framework that preserves structural properties—to directive design, enabling efficient reduction-heavy tensor computations with portable performance across CPUs and GPUs.

sc-2025-309.method: TEGRA separates compute from memory into independent, separately-scalable components connected via a standard called CXL, with processors communicating through message-passing—sending messages to request data and coordinate work. This setup allows the number of active compute resources to adapt to each workload's needs, avoiding the fixed compute-to-memory imbalance that limits traditional accelerators. The researchers simulate the system with gem5 (a detailed computer architecture simulator) to measure memory bandwidth efficiency and performance across diverse graph problems.
sc-2025-309.key_novelty: TEGRA uses CXL to separate compute from memory in graph processing, and automatically scales compute resources based on each workload's arithmetic intensity (the ratio of computation to memory access).

sc-2025-316.method: The SC25 Reproducibility Committee independently ran the ThirstyFLOPS code and experiments to check whether its water usage models for high-performance computing (HPC) systems produce the same results as reported in the original paper. They tested whether the work's findings and calculations were reproducible when someone else followed the authors' methodology.
sc-2025-316.key_novelty: Independent verification confirms that water footprint modeling for high-performance computing systems is reproducible.

sc-2025-302.method: We built a PyTorch tool that simulates neural networks performing their activation functions (the steps between layers) in ultra-low precision: FP8, FP6, FP4, FP3, and FP2, which use 2 to 8 bits instead of the standard 32. We then trained and tested these models across different architectures and datasets to measure how much accuracy they lost at each precision level.
sc-2025-302.key_novelty: Activation functions can work reliably at ultra-low 2-4 bit precision, with FP4 as the practical lower bound, but different activation types—smooth ones like sigmoid versus piecewise-linear ones like ReLU—degrade at different rates.

sc-2025-303.method: The framework uses specialized hardware on network cards (called SmartNICs) to gather and move data between distributed supercomputer nodes, supporting three different exchange methods. Rather than the main computer handling this work, the SmartNIC processes data directly—reducing system overhead. The researchers tested the framework on real supercomputer hardware, measuring transfer speed (latency), data volume per second (throughput), and how performance scales as systems grow larger.
sc-2025-303.key_novelty: Using specialized network hardware (SmartNICs) to exchange any type of data between distributed nodes, reducing what the main computer must do.

sc-2025-315.method: Scientists today are bottlenecked by manually coordinating distributed labs and equipment instead of doing research. The work addresses this by creating a framework that visualizes how scientific workflows can evolve in two dimensions: how they get smarter (from fixed procedures to adaptive decision-making) and how they scale (from isolated labs to collaborative networks of labs and AI agents). Building on this framework, the authors then specify an actual architecture for autonomous, distributed laboratories—systems where AI agents manage equipment coordination and run experiments without needing constant human intervention.
sc-2025-315.key_novelty: The framework maps how scientific workflows can evolve from manual coordination to full autonomy as AI agents progressively take over coordination and execution tasks.

sc-2025-318.method: They tested 11 standard supercomputing benchmark programs on three cloud platforms—AWS, Azure, and GCP—comparing results against dedicated supercomputers at Lawrence Livermore National Lab. The tests used different combinations of CPUs and GPUs across 6 environment configurations, scaling up to 28,672 CPUs and 256 GPUs. By running identical workloads on both cloud and traditional systems, they could directly measure whether clouds delivered equivalent performance and usability.
sc-2025-318.key_novelty: Testing whether AWS, Azure, and GCP can match traditional supercomputers for scientific computing by running 11 benchmarks at scale—up to 28,672 CPUs and 256 GPUs.

sc-2025-321.method: When GPUs in the same computer send data to each other, they can use multiple communication paths simultaneously. This model predicts how fast data will actually move by accounting for the speed of each communication link (link bandwidth), the delay cost of managing multiple data flows (pipeline overhead), and the need to coordinate different data streams so they don't interfere with each other (stream synchronization). By understanding these factors, it determines the best way to split up the data transfer across available paths to minimize total transfer time.
sc-2025-321.key_novelty: The key insight is a mathematical model that accurately predicts the fastest way to split GPU data transfers across multiple paths—within 6% accuracy.

sc-2025-313.method: Moment jointly optimizes the physical GPU connections and data distribution for efficient multi-GPU graph neural network training. It models GPU connections as directed graphs with capacity limits, uses max-flow optimization to find efficient data routing paths, and applies a data-distribution-aware knapsack algorithm to place training data on each GPU.
sc-2025-313.key_novelty: Moment jointly optimizes physical GPU topology and data placement using max-flow routing and distribution-aware placement to enable efficient out-of-core graph neural network training.

sc-2025-322.method: Tensor Cores are specialized GPU accelerators optimized for fast matrix multiplication. The authors speed up sum reduction operations—a computational bottleneck in molecular docking where you repeatedly add up numbers—by using Tensor Cores on NVIDIA GPUs (A100, H100, B200). Since Tensor Cores prioritize speed over precision, the team applies numerical error correction techniques to detect and fix small inaccuracies, keeping results accurate despite the acceleration.
sc-2025-322.key_novelty: This work accelerates irregular molecular docking by offloading its sum reduction bottleneck to Tensor Cores on NVIDIA GPUs (A100, H100, B200), then using numerical error correction to maintain accuracy.

sc-2025-317.method: Attention breaks its batch into smaller independent blocks (called tiling) and processes B examples at a time, which reduces memory usage. The attention outputs are then concatenated back into a larger batch of size B_tilde=G*B. This larger batch feeds into the MLP experts (computational units that handle calculations beyond attention). By decoupling batch size between these layer types, attention can operate at the small batch size B it needs for memory efficiency, while MLPs receive the large batch they need for compute efficiency on wafer-scale processors.
sc-2025-317.key_novelty: Dynamic batch tiling applied to attention layers addresses the architectural mismatch between attention's need for small batches and MLPs' need for large batches on wafer-scale processors.

sc-2025-319.method: They took MuMMI, an ensemble workflow (a coordinated set of computational tasks), and redesigned it to run on Kubernetes, a cloud platform for managing containerized software. The redesign transformed it from traditional HPC (where tasks run tightly coupled on a supercomputer) to a cloud-native architecture where components can be independently deployed and scaled. They tested two coordination methods: service-based orchestration that uses shared filesystems to pass data between tasks, and event-driven orchestration where each completed task sends a message to trigger the next step.
sc-2025-319.key_novelty: Event-driven orchestration—where completed tasks automatically trigger the next step via messages—achieves better performance and lower cloud costs for HPC workflows compared to service-based coordination.

sc-2025-328.method: The researchers implemented stencil algorithms (patterns where the same computation applies repeatedly across a grid of data points) in SYCL, a language designed to work across different hardware types. They created optimized versions for both AMD CPUs and Intel Stratix 10 FPGAs—specialized hardware accelerators—and ran the same algorithms on both systems, measuring execution time and how much of the FPGA's hardware resources they consumed.
sc-2025-328.key_novelty: The paper tests whether SYCL can practically move code from CPUs to FPGAs, and finds that algorithms with low arithmetic intensity (few calculations relative to memory accessed) hit fundamental performance limits on FPGAs.

sc-2025-324.method: They implemented island detection—an algorithm that groups neighboring particle signals together—using high-level synthesis (HLS), a tool that converts high-level code into FPGA hardware. They tested different data layouts (1D and 2D) and neighbor-detection rules (4-way or 8-way connectivity, where 8-way includes diagonal neighbors). They then measured resource usage, throughput, and identified which code optimizations were necessary for high-speed operation.
sc-2025-324.key_novelty: This work shows whether high-level synthesis is actually practical for the complex, high-speed signal processing required in particle physics experiments, and identifies which code optimizations are essential.

sc-2025-323.method: Plugins receive a digital signature—cryptographic proof of authenticity and integrity—when created. Before the system loads any plugin, it verifies this signature to ensure the plugin hasn't been modified. The team evaluates different implementation strategies and measures the tradeoff between performance overhead and security assurance.
sc-2025-323.key_novelty: The approach verifies HDF5 plugins with digital signatures before they load, ensuring they're authentic and unmodified.

sc-2025-326.method: A progressive one-year course (Fall 2024-Spring 2025) teaches GPU programming in three stages: GPU architecture fundamentals, hands-on GPU coding, then building AI agents that retrieve information to answer questions (called RAG) on AWS SageMaker. Students learn on real cloud infrastructure and track progress through assignments, surveys, and profiling tools (TensorBoard and HPC profilers that measure performance).
sc-2025-326.key_novelty: A course that teaches GPU hardware, parallel programming, and real AI agent deployment all together as one learning path.

sc-2025-332.method: The researchers injected random single-bit errors into the numerical weights that make up a language model, then had it generate text and measured what happened in two ways: standard accuracy metrics and actual text quality degradation. This revealed whether the model was truly resilient or just appeared okay on traditional measures. They tested across different task complexities to see whether harder tasks broke down more easily under bit-level faults.
sc-2025-332.key_novelty: Language models appear resilient based on standard accuracy measurements, but actually generate degraded and meaningless text when hit by random bit-flips, with the damage severity depending on how complex the task is.

sc-2025-329.method: SwapServeLLM saves model checkpoints to GPU, enabling hot-swapping (moving models in and out without stopping service) between fast GPU memory and slower host memory as requests arrive. It analyzes incoming request patterns to decide which models should stay on GPU, and directs requests to minimize response delays. The same checkpointing approach works across different serving engines like vLLM and Ollama without needing engine-specific code, letting providers pause underutilized models and reactivate them when demand increases.
sc-2025-329.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a single checkpointing technique to swap models between GPU and host memory identically across any serving engine, eliminating engine-specific engineering.

sc-2025-325.method: ASaP is an automatic software prefetching system in MLIR (a compiler framework) that works with sparse tensors—arrays stored in specialized compressed formats where most values are zero. It analyzes the tensor storage format and the loop structure that accesses the data, then calculates which memory regions need to be prefetched. It automatically inserts prefetch instructions—software requests to load data into the cache in advance—in both inner and outer loops, so memory is ready at multiple nesting levels.
sc-2025-325.key_novelty: The breakthrough is semantic-aware prefetching—intelligently using MLIR's understanding of sparse tensor structure to inject prefetches in both outer and inner loops, rather than the single-loop prefetching of earlier systems.

sc-2025-331.method: They created a custom batched linear-system solver (a tool solving many sets of equations together) using Kokkos, a framework that runs the same code efficiently on different GPU types. The solver reduces data movement between the GPU's fast and slow memory and performs as much mathematical work as possible at compile time—when the code is being prepared to run. They tested it on NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI300A GPUs.
sc-2025-331.key_novelty: A Kokkos-based batched linear-system solver outperforms existing libraries while running efficiently on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

sc-2025-327.method: The research team converted an existing quantum circuit simulator (a program that mimics quantum computer behavior) to use QIR—a standardized format for describing quantum operations. They tested several different adoption strategies and measured whether the new QIR-based version ran as fast as the original. They also demonstrated that using QIR enables classical control flow, meaning you can write regular programming logic (like if-statements or loops) mixed together with quantum instructions.
sc-2025-327.key_novelty: The paper demonstrates that quantum simulators can adopt QIR format without any performance loss while gaining the ability to mix regular programming logic with quantum operations (classical control flow).

sc-2025-312.method: ATLAHS records the actual network communication from real AI, HPC, and storage applications and represents it in a format called GOAL (Group Operation Assembly Language). The toolchain can then simulate these workloads using multiple simulation engines that understand the GOAL format. It supports multiple jobs or users running at the same time.
sc-2025-312.key_novelty: ATLAHS uses GOAL, a portable trace format for capturing real application workloads, to enable application-centric simulation of AI, HPC, and storage systems with under 5% error, outperforming AstraSim in runtime and efficiency.

sc-2025-330.method: The framework provides a C++ library for simulating the compute graph (the sequence of operations performed on hardware) and an automatic code translator that converts your C++ code into AMD's AIE format. You write your application in standard C++, and the translator automatically generates the host and accelerator code, eliminating the need to manually maintain separate codebases.
sc-2025-330.key_novelty: The framework automatically translates a single C++ program into separate host and accelerator components using compile-time code execution, eliminating manual code separation.

sc-2025-320.method: MPPI uses C++20 language features—concepts (rules defining what operations a type supports), ranges (sequences of elements), and reflection (inspecting a type's internal structure)—to automatically examine your C++ data types at compile-time (when the code is being prepared to run). It generates the correct MPI datatypes describing how your data should be communicated, eliminating the error-prone manual work of describing memory layouts.
sc-2025-320.key_novelty: The tool automatically extracts MPI datatype information from C++ types at compile-time using C++20 features, removing the need for manual specification.

sc-2025-334.method: BurstEngine trains transformers on million-token sequences by organizing computation across GPUs in four complementary ways. First, it arranges GPUs in a ring topology where each GPU sends data to its neighbor, and overlaps data transmission with computation so no GPU sits idle waiting; it also selectively saves intermediate values during training to manage memory usage, merges the final prediction layer with loss calculation into one operation, and balances attention work across GPUs since masking (blocking irrelevant attention calculations) causes uneven computational load. These techniques together keep GPUs busy and productive throughout training on extremely long sequences.
sc-2025-334.key_novelty: BurstAttention reduces the network communication needed for transformer attention across GPUs compared to RingAttention by understanding the physical GPU network layout and performing useful computation while data travels between GPUs.

sc-2025-343.method: They created a web-based dashboard—a visual control panel you access through your browser—built on Open OnDemand (a framework that brings supercomputer access to the web instead of requiring complex command-line tools). The dashboard displays key information through separate pages: announcements about the system, its current status, details about your computing jobs, and real-time resource usage, all designed to work well on any screen size (phones, tablets, desktops) and built with accessibility standards so non-experts can navigate them without special technical training.
sc-2025-343.key_novelty: The core innovation is making HPC system interfaces usable for non-experts by redesigning dashboard pages to be responsive (adaptable to any screen size), modular (each section works independently), and accessible to people without command-line experience.

sc-2025-338.method: The authors tested whether the results from a published study on GPU reliability could be independently verified. They obtained H100 Hopper and A100 Ampere GPUs and recreated the experiments exactly as described in the original paper 'Story of Two GPUs' by Cui et al., documenting their experimental setup and comparing results. This independent verification—called artifact evaluation—confirms whether published conclusions about GPU resilience are trustworthy when others follow the same steps.
sc-2025-338.key_novelty: Independent verification of GPU resilience findings for H100 and A100 GPUs by reproducing the original experiments.

sc-2025-335.method: ModuLair automates Python virtual environment setup (containers that isolate different Python package versions) using metadata (configuration files) on HPC systems. It works with both EasyBuild (software used to automate software installation on HPC systems) and other module systems. It provides command-line and graphical interfaces—including Jupyter, Drona Composer, and the HPRC Dashboard—so users can manage environments however they prefer.
sc-2025-335.key_novelty: ModuLair is the first virtual environment framework that automatically detects an HPC's module system and manages Python environments through configuration files, accessible via both command-line and graphical interfaces.

sc-2025-333.method: LLMTailor solves checkpoint bloat—the massive storage and compute waste from periodically saving the entire model's weights and optimizer state (values like momentum that the optimizer tracks). Instead of complete checkpoints, it combines layers from different checkpoint snapshots to form smaller, custom checkpoints. This gives you precise control over exactly which model parameters and optimizer internals you save at each step.
sc-2025-333.key_novelty: LLMTailor is the first tool to enable selective layer-wise checkpointing by combining layers from different checkpoint snapshots into smaller checkpoints, letting checkpoint storage happen independently from training.

sc-2025-340.method: This processor extends RISC-V with custom neuromorphic instructions (brain-mimicking operations designed for neural computation) that compute Izhikevich neuron state updates directly. Instead of requiring many basic arithmetic steps per neuron update, each custom instruction handles the entire Izhikevich calculation in a single operation. These instructions are implemented by expanding the ALU (the arithmetic logic unit) to natively execute these specialized operations.
sc-2025-340.key_novelty: This is the first RISC-V processor to include custom neuromorphic instructions designed specifically for Izhikevich neuron computations.

sc-2025-336.method: The method combines two iterative algorithms—FGMRES and Richardson—in a nested structure where the outer solver repeatedly uses the inner solver as part of its calculations. It starts with high-precision (64-bit) arithmetic and progressively reduces to half-precision (16-bit) arithmetic as it goes deeper into the nesting, gaining speed and reducing memory use. The inner solver runs for only a limited number of iterations each time—just enough to improve the solution without the rounding errors that normally break low-precision calculations. Since the inner solver repeats many times within the outer solver's work, these small improvements compound, and the nested feedback ensures the overall answer converges correctly.
sc-2025-336.key_novelty: This is the first nested solver to effectively use half-precision arithmetic—it keeps the low-precision inner solver's iterations deliberately limited so they don't accumulate rounding errors, while the nested repetition ensures the overall solution still converges correctly.

sc-2025-344.method: VPIC 2.0 uses Kokkos, a library that lets code run on both CPUs and GPUs, to solve the portability problem. It then removes the performance overhead through three techniques: rearranging particles based on the target hardware for efficient access (platform-targeted particle sorting), processing multiple particles at once (vectorization), and optimizing memory layout so processors don't waste time waiting for data.
sc-2025-344.key_novelty: Kokkos-based particle-in-cell code can match the performance of hand-written CPU code while simultaneously achieving superlinear scaling on GPUs—where doubling processors yields more than double the speedup.

sc-2025-339.method: The researchers independently ran the HP-MDR code on GPUs using the authors' original experimental setup to check if they got the same results. This process—called artifact evaluation—verifies that the reported speedups for data refactoring (reorganizing data structures for faster access on GPUs) actually occur when others run the experiments. The evaluation confirms both that the experimental conditions were set up correctly and that the measured performance matches what was originally published.
sc-2025-339.key_novelty: This work independently verifies whether the reported HP-MDR results for GPU data refactoring are reproducible.

sc-2025-337.method: AutoMDT breaks data transfer into three separate, independently-optimizable stages—reading, network transfer, and writing—and uses machine learning (specifically reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trying actions and getting rewarded for good results) to find the optimal number of simultaneous operations for each stage. The learning method, called PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization), is designed to be stable and efficient. To avoid slowing production networks, the system trains this learning offline using a lightweight simulator that accurately mimics real network and system behavior—this training takes about 45 minutes.
sc-2025-337.key_novelty: AutoMDT is the first modular data-transfer framework using reinforcement learning (PPO) to automatically optimize how many operations run in parallel at each stage, learning this from a lightweight network simulator offline.

sc-2025-341.method: Machine learning models predict execution time for CCSD calculations—chemistry simulations that model how electrons behave in molecules—based on problem size and parameter choices. The system uses Gradient Boosting (combining many simple predictors into a stronger one) and Active Learning (strategically selecting which expensive experiments to run when data is limited) to train these models efficiently. With accurate runtime predictions, users can optimize their resource submissions on supercomputers like Frontier and Aurora, avoiding suboptimal requests and wasted allocations.
sc-2025-341.key_novelty: Active learning combined with gradient boosting enables accurate prediction of chemistry simulation resource requirements from limited experimental training data.

sc-2025-349.method: The tool automatically sets up and runs the same performance test repeatedly, measuring results from hardware performance counters—numeric readings that track what's happening in the CPU/GPU during execution. It analyzes how much each counter's results vary from run to run, identifying which ones stay stable despite system noise (interference from background processes and unpredictable system behavior). Finally, it ranks all available counters by their resilience, showing which ones reliably give consistent measurements even when other things are happening on the system.
sc-2025-349.key_novelty: It automatically identifies which hardware performance counters remain stable by running experiments repeatedly and selecting the ones that produce consistent results every time.

sc-2025-346.method: The approach brings computation closer to the data to avoid expensive data movement. It uses a specialized programming language (called a domain-specific language) to describe how to filter and update data iteratively. The team designs processing-in-memory hardware, where computation happens at the memory itself, optimized for these patterns. The design is validated using the PIMEval simulator.
sc-2025-346.key_novelty: This is the first framework to co-design hardware and software for filter-update computational patterns on processing-in-memory, achieving 83% data sparsification (processing just 17% of the original data) with minimal convergence overhead.

sc-2025-348.method: The system connects multiple university supercomputing centers together as one federated network, letting researchers share access to AI model-serving capacity. When scientists submit requests, the system uses Globus—a secure authentication service—to verify who they are and what they can access, then automatically distributes work across available computers. If demand grows, the system wakes up standby machines while keeping some warmed up for instant response. It supports multiple AI model serving backends like vLLM, so each institution can choose their preferred software.
sc-2025-348.key_novelty: It brings cloud-like AI inference services to federated research computing centers by using OpenAI's standard API and automatically distributing requests across multiple institutions' supercomputers.

sc-2025-342.method: InferA uses large language models (AI systems trained on vast text data to understand and solve problems) to power multiple data-analysis agents that work together. A supervisor component directs the work by assigning some agents to retrieve data and others to analyze it. The system asks users questions during the analysis to clarify their goals rather than working blindly.
sc-2025-342.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a supervisor to direct multiple AI agents to analyze large scientific datasets through specific queries without loading all data into memory.

sc-2025-345.method: Researchers interact with a conversational AI agent by asking questions in plain English instead of writing code. The system retrieves matching data from questions, uses image recognition to find similar waveforms (wave patterns shown as pictures), and automatically retrieves scientific papers on related topics. This combination lets researchers without programming skills or domain expertise explore massive earthquake simulation datasets.
sc-2025-345.key_novelty: This is the first AI system built specifically for earthquake simulation data, combining text-based querying, visual waveform search, and automatic scientific literature retrieval in a single conversational interface.

sc-2025-347.method: They apply the roofline model—a performance technique that reveals whether a system is limited by computation speed or data-transfer bandwidth—to analyze three ways of accessing AWS S3 cloud storage from high-performance computers: NFS-mounted Storage Gateway, data migration through Storage Gateway, or direct S3 API calls. By measuring how much computational work happens per byte of data (operational intensity) for each method and comparing it against available bandwidth, they identify which approach performs best and whether its bottleneck is compute, network bandwidth, or latency.
sc-2025-347.key_novelty: The work extends roofline modeling to cloud storage systems by measuring operational intensity and bandwidth ceilings across different S3 access methods to identify performance limits.

sc-2025-350.method: The compiler analyzes code to identify data structures (organized chunks of data) that are candidates for movement to slower, far memory. At runtime, the system monitors actual memory conditions and dynamically decides for each data structure whether to move it ('remoting'), load it ahead of time ('prefetch' to hide delays), or clear it out ('evacuation' to free space), rather than following a fixed compile-time decision. By operating at the data structure level instead of byte-by-byte, the system makes decisions efficiently.
sc-2025-350.key_novelty: The key innovation is adapting far-memory placement decisions at runtime at the data structure level, guided by compile-time analysis, instead of locking in decisions at compile time.

sc-2025-353.method: Qdislib breaks large quantum computations into smaller pieces that individual quantum computers can execute. It maps the circuit using graphs (networks of nodes representing each operation), then uses two techniques to split it: wire cutting breaks the quantum connections between qubits, and gate cutting replaces complex multi-qubit operations with simpler single-qubit operations plus classical post-processing. These pieces are distributed across multiple quantum processors, with classical computing coordinating results between them. The library integrates with quantum programming frameworks Qiskit and Qibo.
sc-2025-353.key_novelty: Qdislib enables large quantum circuits to run on current quantum computers by splitting them across multiple quantum processors while automatically coordinating the classical computation needed between them.

sc-2025-356.method: They tested Ceph, a distributed storage system, by systematically changing how much CPU, memory, and disk bandwidth it could access. Using Linux hotplug (which dynamically enables or disables CPU cores) and Cgroups (which constrains how many resources a process can use), they created different hardware configurations. They then measured I/O performance—how fast the system could read and write data—under each configuration.
sc-2025-356.key_novelty: Adding more CPU, memory, or disk bandwidth to a distributed filesystem doesn't speed up I/O performance proportionally; the relationship is non-linear and depends on which resource is increased.

sc-2025-355.method: CIRE analyzes floating-point rounding error—the inaccuracies that accumulate when calculations are rounded to fit limited precision—by reading LLVM code (the compiler's intermediate representation) without running it. It breaks the code into basic blocks (straight-line sections between branches) and calculates accumulated rounding error through up to 10^5 floating-point operations per block. The analysis tracks how compiler optimizations interact with precision settings to change where and how rounding errors occur.
sc-2025-355.key_novelty: CIRE statically measures floating-point rounding error in LLVM code while accounting for how both compiler optimizations and precision settings affect the error.

sc-2025-358.method: They develop iterative solvers (like Conjugate Gradient, which solve equations by successive approximations) that overlap computation with data movement across large GPU clusters. Instead of routing all GPU-to-GPU data through the CPU, they use direct communication libraries (NCCL/RCCL for collective operations, NVSHMEM for direct memory access) that let GPUs exchange data efficiently. They test two variants: one where the CPU initiates data transfers, and one where GPUs initiate them directly.
sc-2025-358.key_novelty: The core idea is letting GPUs directly initiate data transfers using NVSHMEM, removing the CPU bottleneck that had to coordinate all communication in the cluster.

sc-2025-359.method: D-CHAG processes multi-channel image data in hierarchical stages, combining channels progressively rather than all at once. Each stage is designed to work with distributed computing techniques like tensor parallelism (splitting model layers across GPUs) and model sharding (dividing computation across multiple processors). This alignment between the hierarchical processing and distributed computing reduces memory overhead and communication costs between devices.
sc-2025-359.key_novelty: Distributing the stage-by-stage channel aggregation across multiple processors for multi-channel vision transformers reduces memory use by 75% and doubles processing speed.

sc-2025-363.method: The method creates a mathematical model that calculates the maximum possible speed for all-to-all communication—where every GPU in a multi-GPU system sends data to every other GPU. The model accounts for the system's hierarchy, recognizing that some communication pathways (like between GPUs on the same computer) are faster than others (like between separate computers). By analyzing these different communication speeds mathematically, it derives what the theoretical performance limit should be, which lets you evaluate whether an actual implementation is performing well.
sc-2025-363.key_novelty: This is the first mathematical model to predict the peak performance specifically for all-to-all communication patterns in hierarchical multi-GPU systems.

sc-2025-351.method: EAS-Sim is a simulation-based tool for designing job schedulers that handle multiple competing objectives in AI clusters.
