The methodology guides the design of different scheduler variants: Zeus for minimizing energy, Hades for ensuring fairness, AuraChronos for meeting service-level agreements, and Charon for respecting power budget limits.
sc-2025-351.key_novelty: The framework enables systematic design of job schedulers that optimize energy efficiency alongside fairness, service-level agreements, and power constraints.

sc-2025-362.method: Modern GPUs and accelerators have INT8 matrix engines—special-purpose hardware designed to multiply many small numbers very quickly while using minimal power. The approach emulates higher-precision matrix multiplication by breaking it down into smaller operations that these INT8 engines can handle, then combining the results back together. This works because matrix multiplication is mathematically decomposable without losing accuracy. By reusing the fastest, most efficient hardware for this decomposed computation, the approach gains significant speedup and power efficiency compared to general-purpose processors.
sc-2025-362.key_novelty: The core insight is that decomposing higher-precision matrix multiplication into INT8 operations lets you reuse specialized INT8 matrix engines, yielding 2-3x speedup and significant power savings.

sc-2025-360.method: SimAI-Bench is a benchmarking tool that tests data movement between AI systems and simulations running together, addressing a gap in tools for analyzing performance in these coupled workflows. It evaluates two patterns: one-to-one setups where an AI system and simulation share the same hardware (colocated), and many-to-one (ensemble) setups where multiple simulations send data to a single AI system. By measuring how efficiently data transports between these components on the Aurora supercomputer, the tool helps researchers identify and prototype solutions for performance bottlenecks.
sc-2025-360.key_novelty: SimAI-Bench enables performance testing of data transport in coupled AI-simulation workflows and demonstrates the performance advantage of DragonHPC for this purpose.

sc-2025-361.method: OmniFed is a federated learning framework—where multiple computers train together while keeping data private—built from components you can mix and match. You configure how the computers connect (topology) and communicate (protocols), then select your privacy method: differential privacy (mathematically obscures individual data), homomorphic encryption (computes on encrypted numbers), or secure aggregation (combines results without revealing individual entries). The framework includes data compression to reduce network traffic and supports multiple training algorithms, working across edge devices and supercomputers.
sc-2025-361.key_novelty: OmniFed's core innovation is making federated learning modular—you can configure and swap different privacy protections, compression methods, and communication protocols rather than committing to a single fixed design.

sc-2025-364.method: The approach extends OpenMP with new pragmas—compiler directives that programmers add to their code—to automatically offload MPI operations (Message Passing Interface, how connected computers exchange data in HPC systems) to SmartNICs (specialized network processor cards). This keeps the main CPU free for computation while the SmartNIC handles communication in multi-GPU clusters, reducing performance bottlenecks in hierarchical systems.
sc-2025-364.key_novelty: The first OpenMP pragmas designed to enable offloading of Message Passing Interface communication to SmartNICs.

sc-2025-352.method: They used pointer-chasing microbenchmarks—small focused tests where each memory access points to the next location, forcing the system to wait rather than parallelize requests—to measure data-retrieval speed from each GPU memory layer: sL1, L2, MALL (Infinity Cache), and HBM. They tested different configurations to understand how memory performance varies.
sc-2025-352.key_novelty: It characterizes memory access latency in AMD CDNA 3 GPUs, focusing on the MALL (Memory Attached Last Level cache) and revealing how NUMA effects—the variation in access speed based on data location—influence performance.

sc-2025-357.method: Reproducibility means independently running a paper's experiments to verify whether similar results occur. The team obtained the Uno paper's code and test setup for its datacenter congestion control (a traffic management system for both between-datacenter and within-datacenter networks) and its reliability mechanisms. By re-running these experiments, the report documents what results they achieved, where they matched the original paper's claims, and what problems they encountered.
sc-2025-357.key_novelty: Validation that Uno's datacenter congestion control and reliable connectivity mechanisms work as the original paper claimed.

sc-2025-354.method: The system collects real-time data about network conditions between servers (like how fast data travels and how busy the connections are). It uses machine learning (AI trained on this data) to predict how long each job would take to finish on different servers. Then it ranks these predictions and places each job on the server predicted to finish it fastest.
sc-2025-354.key_novelty: It learns from real-time measurements of network performance across multiple data centers to predict which server will finish each job fastest, then places jobs there instead of ignoring network conditions.

sc-2025-369.method: The tool runs 50+ microbenchmarks—small programs that test specific hardware behaviors—to automatically discover how a GPU is structured internally (its cores, memory levels, and how data flows between them). By observing how the GPU responds to these tests, the tool figures out the topology without needing documentation or special knowledge from the GPU manufacturer. This approach works across different vendors because it relies on testing the hardware itself, not vendor-specific APIs or information.
sc-2025-369.key_novelty: This is the first tool to automatically discover GPU topology across different vendors (NVIDIA and AMD) and 10+ GPU models by observing how the actual hardware behaves.

sc-2025-367.method: They converted graph algorithm implementations from CUDA (NVIDIA's GPU programming language) to HIP, a compatibility layer that allows code to run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs. The conversion involves translating the GPU kernels—the specialized computational code that executes directly on the GPU—to use HIP's standardized interface instead of CUDA-specific features. After porting, they ran performance benchmarks on both NVIDIA and AMD hardware to measure how efficiently the algorithms execute on each platform.
sc-2025-367.key_novelty: Using HIP, they enabled the same graph algorithms to run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and measured the performance difference between the two platforms.

sc-2025-366.method: The team takes an existing AI language model and provides additional training using data specific to HPC (High Performance Computing — systems built to run massive computational problems). This specialized training teaches the model to understand HPC components like parallel computing frameworks and performance optimization techniques. Because the model learns from HPC-specific examples rather than just general internet text, it becomes more reliable at generating answers to HPC questions.
sc-2025-366.key_novelty: Training the model on HPC-specific examples instead of general internet text boosts its trustworthiness by 90% compared to ChatGPT-4o, because domain knowledge helps it avoid false claims about HPC systems.

sc-2025-368.method: Post-variational quantum neural networks use a hybrid classical-quantum approach to avoid repeatedly running the quantum circuit. Instead of the variational method's approach of measuring the quantum circuit many times to estimate parameter updates, this method uses the classical computer to compute how to improve parameters differently—handling expensive calculations that would normally require repeated quantum measurements. This reduces the demand on the quantum hardware, making training feasible on small, noisy quantum devices (NISQ devices).
sc-2025-368.key_novelty: It trains quantum neural networks on resource-limited quantum computers with better accuracy than variational methods, without needing to repeatedly evaluate the quantum circuit.

sc-2025-371.method: StreamHub transfers scientific data securely by verifying each packet (zero-trust security—checking that nothing is tampered with or sent from an untrusted source) instead of trusting the network. It integrates Globus Compute, which runs analysis code on remote facilities, so data flows directly into computational pipelines at the destination. Encryption and cryptographic checks protect every packet during transit.
sc-2025-371.key_novelty: StreamHub is the first zero-trust streaming system—one that verifies every packet for security—with less than 2% performance overhead.

sc-2025-365.method: They created a new MLIR dialect—a custom language within the MLIR compiler framework—specifically for distributed sparse tensor computations. Sparse tensors are arrays containing mostly zeros, and this dialect lets the compiler handle operations on these tensors efficiently across multiple machines. This fills a gap where compiler support for distributed sparse tensor operations was previously missing.
sc-2025-365.key_novelty: An MLIR dialect that enables compiler support for distributed sparse tensor computations.

sc-2025-375.method: The system uses an FPGA (specialized hardware that can be quickly customized to handle specific tasks) to rapidly move X-ray detector data across the network. It integrates this transport layer with EPICS, a widely-used framework that controls and monitors scientific experiments. The FPGA accelerates the data transfer, while EPICS coordinates everything and ensures detector data flows continuously in real time to remote facilities, letting scientists analyze results as soon as they arrive.
sc-2025-375.key_novelty: This is the first integration of EJFAT (a detector data transport system) with EPICS (the standard experiment control framework) for real-time streaming of X-ray detector data to remote facilities.

sc-2025-370.method: The framework is built on SimGrid, a simulation tool that models how distributed computer systems work. It adds plugin mechanisms—extensible components researchers can customize—to configure simulations of large-scale distributed computing environments. This lets researchers test ideas about these systems without needing access to actual large-scale infrastructure.
sc-2025-370.key_novelty: It is the first simulation framework capable of operating at WLCG scale while automatically generating datasets using machine learning.

sc-2025-372.method: This approach treats the training job as independent tasks that each GPU can run on its own portion of data without constant coordination. At the end of each epoch—after each GPU has processed all of its assigned data once—the GPUs synchronize to share results, rather than syncing after every single training step. This drastically reduces communication between GPUs, which is especially critical in hierarchical systems where some GPUs are farther from each other than others.
sc-2025-372.key_novelty: Synchronizing GPUs only at epoch boundaries instead of after every training step reduces training time by 95%.

sc-2025-374.method: HIP is a framework that lets the same GPU code run on different hardware vendors (NVIDIA, AMD, etc.) instead of being locked to one brand. The researchers rewrote GPU operations originally optimized for CUDA (NVIDIA's framework) to use HIP instead. They incorporated mixed precision—strategically combining different numeric precision levels (like 32-bit and 16-bit floating point) to balance speed and accuracy. They then tested these operations across different GPU architectures to verify that porting to HIP actually preserves performance.
sc-2025-374.key_novelty: CUDA graph kernels maintain efficient performance across different GPU vendors when ported to HIP with mixed precision.

sc-2025-377.method: The framework uses an FPGA (a programmable hardware chip) to connect incoming network data directly to storage drives (NVMe SSDs) without going through the CPU. The FPGA acts as a bridge that moves data and performs processing tasks—like classifying images from the stream—without the main processor getting involved. This works because FPGAs can handle the sustained high-speed data flow that would slow down a general-purpose CPU.
sc-2025-377.key_novelty: It connects 100G Ethernet directly to SSD storage via FPGA, allowing both the network and storage to hit their maximum speed limits simultaneously without the CPU getting in the way.

sc-2025-378.method: Dynamic LLM techniques like mixture-of-experts create workload imbalance—some workers do far more computation than others, slowing training as fast workers wait for slow ones. DynMo solves this by continuously measuring each worker's load and automatically reassigning tasks to balance the work. It consolidates computation onto fewer workers when efficient and operates across multiple GPUs and machine clusters.
sc-2025-378.key_novelty: DynMo guarantees the maximum possible reduction in workload imbalance while consolidating workers without slowing down training.

sc-2025-383.method: LLM4FP uses language models to generate test programs that expose how different compilers handle floating-point arithmetic (decimal math) differently. It works in two stages: Grammar-Based Generation creates syntactically correct programs, then Feedback-Based Mutation observes which ones trigger compiler differences and modifies them to find more inconsistencies. By combining systematic generation with learning from prior results, the approach discovers compiler mismatches that traditional testing tools miss.
sc-2025-383.key_novelty: It's the first framework to use language models to hunt for floating-point inconsistencies across compilers, uncovering numerical differences that occur in normal calculations rather than only at extreme values.

sc-2025-380.method: The STZ framework divides scientific data into hierarchical levels of partitions, and at each level uses prediction to reduce storage by forecasting what data comes next. This enables progressive decompression—reading from start to finish—and random-access decompression—jumping to any chunk without reading everything. The hierarchical structure allows both access modes to work efficiently from the same compressed data.
sc-2025-380.key_novelty: This is the first compression framework that simultaneously supports both progressive decompression (streaming from start to finish) and random-access decompression (jumping to any chunk), using hierarchical partitioning to overcome the quality and speed degradation that normally occurs when supporting both modes.

sc-2025-382.method: Normally, computers send data across networks by bundling it into packets using protocols like TCP or RoCE. Instead, cMPI lets computers directly access each other's memory using CXL (Compute Express Link), a new interconnect standard that treats memory as shared between machines. To make this work, the system handles three key challenges: managing where data objects live across machines, keeping copies consistent between different computers' caches (cache coherence), and making sure atomic operations (single indivisible actions) happen correctly without conflicts. The authors proved their approach works on actual CXL hardware.
sc-2025-382.key_novelty: This is the first to implement MPI communication using CXL memory sharing—a paradigm where machines directly access each other's memory instead of exchanging network packets—and demonstrate it on real hardware.

sc-2025-376.method: The method pairs NEGF (non-equilibrium Green's functions, a quantum technique for tracking electron flow) with the GW approximation (a more accurate way to account for how electrons interact with each other). It handles the enormous computational burden by using spatial domain decomposition—splitting the system into smaller regions, solving each separately, then combining the results. This let them maintain full quantum accuracy while simulating 42,240 atoms at exascale speed.
sc-2025-376.key_novelty: First successful demonstration of GW-approximation NEGF for NRFET-scale quantum transport simulations at exascale performance.

sc-2025-385.method: MXBLAS speeds up matrix multiplication (the core computation in deep learning) using templates that generate optimized code at runtime for each specific problem, rather than relying on one fixed approach. It coordinates computation and memory access together and embeds the quantization step (reducing numbers to 8-bit precision) directly into the final calculation stage instead of handling it separately.
sc-2025-385.key_novelty: It's the first system to handle all MX format variations (different representations of 8-bit numbers) with a unified library while actually delivering the full speed benefits of 8-bit computing.

sc-2025-389.method: The study measured large reasoning model training across four stages on NERSC Perlmutter, a top-500 supercomputer: supervised fine-tuning (teaching the model with labeled examples), group relative policy optimization (reinforcement learning that rewards better outputs), generation, and distillation (compressing the model). Researchers tracked processor utilization, memory efficiency, and speed through each stage to identify performance bottlenecks and system inefficiencies.
sc-2025-389.key_novelty: For the first time, researchers comprehensively measured how large reasoning models train on a top-500 supercomputer and identified 19 key performance insights across all training stages.

sc-2025-381.method: During bulge-chasing (the phase where computation shifts along the matrix diagonal), replace BLAS3 operations—which work on entire matrix blocks—with BLAS2 operations, which work on single vectors. Reorganize the workflow from a fixed backward sequence to a pattern that maximizes GPU parallelism, which hides the latency introduced by the divide-and-conquer decomposition.
sc-2025-381.key_novelty: The core insight is switching to BLAS2 operations and reorganizing the workflow for GPU parallelism during back transformation (computing the eigenvectors from the decomposition).

sc-2025-391.method: They designed a software intermediary (middleware) that improves hybrid HPC-quantum systems by adding a second scheduling stage after the main HPC scheduler. This second stage uses QRMI—a manufacturer-independent standard interface—to optimize when and how quantum processors (QPUs) run their tasks. The system includes monitoring and observability tools to show what's happening and help developers diagnose issues.
sc-2025-391.key_novelty: A second scheduling layer using vendor-neutral standards (QRMI) to optimize quantum processor use in hybrid HPC systems.

sc-2025-386.method: Smurfs runs multiple smaller, faster models (called SSMs, or State Space Models) that each try to predict what tokens the full LLM would generate next. Instead of relying on any single prediction, it collects all their guesses and uses majority voting—only accepting tokens that most SSMs predict. These voted tokens are then verified by the full LLM in a pipelined fashion, where each new batch of predictions starts before the previous batch finishes verification, eliminating idle waiting time.
sc-2025-386.key_novelty: Using multiple smaller models that vote on predicted tokens instead of trusting a single model increases accuracy and reduces verification overhead in LLM inference.

sc-2025-390.method: BISQIT uses a block-diagram framework (visual representations of how components connect and exchange data) to make quantum network design more intuitive and manageable. The framework creates a documented migration path that allows designs to transition from BISQIT into SeQUeNCe, a production quantum network simulator. Scalability is validated through testing on Frontier, a supercomputer, demonstrating the approach can handle realistic simulation scales.
sc-2025-390.key_novelty: The key novelty is a block-diagram design framework for quantum networks that provides a practical migration path to production simulators, demonstrated through integration with SeQUeNCe.

sc-2025-392.method: The approach uses GPU-aware Message Passing Interface (a communication system that lets GPUs exchange data directly, without going through the CPU). On 8,192 computers, it optimizes all-to-all communication (where every computer sends data to every other one) by handling small and large messages as separate problems, using different strategies for each. Instead of just maximizing throughput (how much data moves per second), it cuts latency—the time it takes to initiate communication—which is the critical bottleneck when thousands of nodes coordinate.
sc-2025-392.key_novelty: The central insight is that optimizing for latency (communication startup time) rather than throughput matters most for all-to-all communication at exascale, and this approach outperforms the hardware vendor's implementations with 65,536 parallel tasks on Frontier.

sc-2025-379.method: KAMI reduces data movement during matrix multiplication on GPUs using three communication-avoiding approaches (1D, 2D, and 3D thread block configurations). For each approach, it stores intermediate results in different memory levels—thread registers (ultra-fast, one per core) and shared memory (fast, shared across a block)—and uses specialized tensor cores (hardware built into GPUs for fast matrix math). The framework also supports sparse variants called SpMM and SpGEMM for matrices with many zeros.
sc-2025-379.key_novelty: KAMI is the first to analyze communication-avoiding matrix multiplication at the GPU clock cycle level (counting individual GPU processing steps), providing a unified framework for dense, sparse, batched, and low-rank matrices.

sc-2025-388.method: The team obtained the RedSan tool, which uses redundant checking to catch problematic memory instructions in GPU programs. They ran this tool on the test cases from the original paper and followed SC25's standard procedures to verify the results matched the original findings.
sc-2025-388.key_novelty: This work confirms that RedSan's method for detecting memory instruction problems in GPU programs is reproducible and reliable.

sc-2025-387.method: The approach uses ESIMD (Intel's tool for writing code that directly harnesses the GPU's 512-bit wide registers) to restructure the solver into block-sparse vector operations—calculations on chunks of the matrix of varying sizes that skip zeros efficiently. This efficient packing reaches memory speeds within 10% of the theoretical maximum, overcoming the bandwidth bottleneck despite variable row lengths and irregular memory access patterns.
sc-2025-387.key_novelty: Using ESIMD vectorization, Intel GPUs can match NVIDIA GPU performance on unstructured-grid solvers.

sc-2025-384.method: WAGES lets multiple requests share a single GPU using NVIDIA MPS (a technique that allows multiple processes to use one GPU simultaneously). It dynamically adjusts the GPU's streaming multiprocessors (compute cores) and clock speed based on what each request actually needs—allocating more resources and faster speeds for demanding workloads, less for lighter ones. A two-tier scheduling framework manages which requests run together and how resources are distributed.
sc-2025-384.key_novelty: By dynamically partitioning GPU streaming multiprocessors (compute cores) and adjusting clock speeds to match each request's workload needs, WAGES achieves both improved response-time targets and reduced energy consumption for serverless LLM serving.

sc-2025-398.method: cuSZ-Hi compresses scientific data on GPUs while keeping errors within a user-set bound. It uses interpolation-based prediction (estimating each value from nearby values) to find the error between the estimate and the actual data, then applies lossless compression to shrink those errors further. Running fully on GPU hardware, this approach compresses large data streams quickly while guaranteeing the data stays within the specified error limit.
sc-2025-398.key_novelty: cuSZ-Hi achieves a 249% compression ratio improvement over existing methods at the same error bound using fully GPU-optimized adaptive prediction.

sc-2025-403.method: DQTetris works in stages to assign qubits to separate quantum modules, starting with a global pass that tries to arrange qubits so that operations stay within a single module and avoid costly messages between modules. It then prunes (removes) unnecessary gates layer-by-layer within each subcircuit. For operations that must cross module boundaries, it uses adaptive teleportation—selectively moving qubits between modules based on the circuit structure—to minimize the expensive inter-module communication that would otherwise slow execution.
sc-2025-403.key_novelty: The core innovation is a smart strategy for splitting circuits across modules and adaptively deciding when to teleport qubits, reducing inter-module communication overhead by 28-75% compared to existing methods.

sc-2025-402.method: NodeSentry detects when individual nodes in a high-performance computer (HPC) system are failing or misbehaving by first grouping similar nodes together (coarse-grained clustering), which reduces the complexity of handling systems with thousands or millions of nodes. Instead of training a separate detection model for each node, it shares models across nodes in the same group (fine-grained model sharing), cutting training time and computational cost. This combination allows the system to monitor each node independently despite the massive scale, frequent job transitions, and complex performance patterns in modern HPC systems.
sc-2025-402.key_novelty: By sharing a single detection model across multiple similar nodes instead of training separate models for each node, the system cuts training overhead by 45.69% while reaching F1-score >0.876—an average 0.560 improvement over baseline approaches.

sc-2025-401.method: Following the Supercomputing conference's standards for reproducibility, the authors tested whether the original paper's claims hold up in practice. They ran the code on GPU clusters with two communication strategies—CPU-initiated (where the main processor manages message transfers between CPUs and GPUs) and GPU-initiated (where GPUs transfer data directly)—to verify the claimed performance gains for conjugate gradient methods, which are iterative algorithms for solving large systems of equations.
sc-2025-401.key_novelty: The paper confirms that choosing between CPU-initiated and GPU-initiated communication strategies produces real performance improvements for conjugate gradient computations on large GPU clusters.

sc-2025-395.method: The approach applies Information Geometric Regularization (IGR—a technique that shapes the solution space using principles from information theory to favor more stable, efficient forms). It combines this with unified memory that allows CPUs and GPUs to work on shared data without copying, mixed-precision arithmetic (16-bit for less-critical data, 32-bit for precision-sensitive parts) to reduce memory and computation time, and adaptive algorithms that adjust to the specific hardware available, such as CPU-GPU systems or APUs.
sc-2025-395.key_novelty: It achieves 1 quadrillion degrees of freedom (20 times the prior record) while maintaining strong scaling and near-ideal efficiency, overcoming traditional scalability limits in ultra-high-resolution spacecraft CFD.

sc-2025-404.method: AP3ESM uses Kokkos, a software framework that lets the same code run efficiently on different supercomputers like Sunway and GPU systems, solving the challenge of writing code that works portably across different hardware. It improves weather prediction by replacing traditional approximations (called parameterizations) with AI-learned versions that better capture small-scale weather patterns. The model accelerates computation through adaptive algorithms that adjust the level of detail based on local conditions, and mixed-precision arithmetic that uses lower-precision calculations in less sensitive parts while keeping high precision where it matters.
sc-2025-404.key_novelty: This is the first kilometer-scale Earth system model to run year-scale simulations (0.85-0.54 years simulated per computation day), achieving accurate predictions of extreme events like Super Typhoon Doksuri's rainfall.

sc-2025-394.method: Multicomponent Flow Code (MFC) is a simulation tool for complex fluids, paired with an automated system that performs three tasks: compiling the code for different supercomputers, checking that results stay consistent when the code or compilers change (regression testing), and measuring how fast the code runs. By automating these steps across diverse hardware, researchers can verify whether newly built supercomputers work correctly and efficiently without setting up tests manually for each machine.
sc-2025-394.key_novelty: A portable testing framework that automatically detects compiler bugs and performance regressions (when code runs slower than it should) when running fluid-dynamics simulations on emerging supercomputers.

sc-2025-396.method: Choir records real network traffic and plays it back at 100 Gbps on ordinary computers, allowing researchers to recreate the exact same network conditions repeatedly. This accurate replay eliminates the randomness (jitter and packet loss) that normally makes results unpredictable on shared lab networks (called testbeds). Choir includes a consistency metric—a measurement showing whether different testbeds behave identically when given the same traffic—so researchers can assess testbed reliability.
sc-2025-396.key_novelty: Choir is the first tool to replay network traffic at 100 Gbps on commodity hardware while quantitatively measuring whether different testbeds produce consistent results.

sc-2025-397.method: The framework evaluates optical circuit switching (light-based routing that can be reconfigured dynamically) in AI systems using two strategies that adjust the network during job execution. The system uses a multi-dimensional all-to-all topology (where each component can reach every other through multiple independent paths), enabling hybrid parallelism by allowing different parallelization strategies to work together in the same system.
sc-2025-397.key_novelty: The first quantitative framework for optical circuit switching in AI networks, showing that OCS-enabled multi-dimensional topologies achieve 1.75x better performance-per-watt compared to static topologies like Fat-Tree and 3D-Torus.

sc-2025-399.method: Normally, Fourier Neural Operators split computation into four separate GPU operations (FFT, filtering, matrix multiplication, and inverse-FFT), with each launch moving data between fast and slow memory. TurboFNO fuses all four into a single continuous kernel that keeps data in fast GPU memory throughout. The implementation uses custom-written FFT and matrix multiplication code, strategically arranges data in memory (called "memory swizzling") to avoid slowdowns, and removes unnecessary zero-padding during computation.
sc-2025-399.key_novelty: This is the first implementation to fully fuse the three core operations (FFT, matrix multiplication, inverse-FFT) into a single GPU kernel, achieving 100% utilization of the GPU's shared memory and matching or exceeding NVIDIA's hand-optimized libraries cuBLAS and cuFFT.

sc-2025-406.method: The approach trains a predictive model on data collected during the early stages of a simulation run. This model learns to approximate what the full simulation would compute, so analysis tasks can run independently rather than waiting for each simulation timestep. By decoupling analysis from simulation, the system avoids the performance slowdown that comes from tightly synchronizing these two operations.
sc-2025-406.key_novelty: A predictive model trained from early simulation data decouples in-situ analysis from simulation steps, achieving 1.20-3.51x speedup while maintaining 83.33-99.60% accuracy.

sc-2025-405.method: Graphago preprocesses the graph before processing starts by predicting which vertices will be accessed frequently, then storing those vertices and their nearby neighbors close together on the SSD (activity-neighborhood ordering). It partitions the graph into chunks so frequently-accessed data is evenly distributed (active-data-balanced partitioning). This way, when the SSD reads a 4KB chunk to fetch one vertex, it brings along nearby vertices that the program actually needs, reducing wasted reads.
sc-2025-405.key_novelty: Activity-aware preprocessing—organizing the graph to place frequently-accessed vertices close together—reduces wasted disk reads and achieves a 4.8x speedup with reasonable preprocessing overhead.

sc-2025-400.method: The method converts complex physics equations (PDEs, or partial differential equations describing how quantities change over space and time) into N-body simulations—models where individual particles interact with each other. Graphics processors (GPUs) found in gaming desktops are built to efficiently calculate thousands of these particle interactions in parallel, making the simulation run far faster than a regular computer. This lets undergraduates run real physics research without first mastering years of mathematical theory.
sc-2025-400.key_novelty: The key contribution is using N-body simulations (where many particles interact with each other) running on GPUs in gaming desktops to make advanced physics research accessible to undergraduates, without requiring years of mathematical training.

sc-2025-410.method: UltraAttn organizes the input sequence into hierarchical tiles at three levels: across multiple computers (nodes), across processing units within each computer (devices), and at the kernel level where individual computations run. Tile sizes are adjusted to balance how much computation overlaps and how well each processor is utilized. A mathematical optimization algorithm (Integer Linear Programming) then determines the most efficient schedule for distributing attention computations across all these levels, reducing overall latency.
sc-2025-410.key_novelty: The core idea is hierarchical tiling of the input sequence combined with mathematical optimization to schedule distributed attention computations most efficiently.

sc-2025-414.method: The researchers tested open-source and commercial large language models on three scientific workflow tasks: configuring (setting up which operations run in what order), annotating (adding metadata and descriptions), and translating (converting between workflow formats). They used current workflow systems to measure how well each model performed on these tasks.
sc-2025-414.key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of whether large language models can perform scientific workflow tasks, revealing which abilities they lack and how performance varies by model and system.

sc-2025-409.method: LCI is a communication library that helps multiple threads exchange messages efficiently without blocking (making threads wait). It achieves this by using atomic data structures (data that multiple threads can safely update simultaneously), fine-grained non-blocking locks (small locks that let threads keep working instead of waiting), and deep understanding of how networks operate at a low level. The library provides simple point-to-point messaging (direct communication between two threads), multiple ways for threads to know when a message has arrived, and flexible control over resource usage.
sc-2025-409.key_novelty: LCI is a communication library specifically optimized for asynchronous multithreaded patterns (where multiple threads work independently without waiting), achieving this through low-overhead synchronization (minimal-cost coordination between threads) and fine-grained resource control (detailed control of what resources are used).

sc-2025-416.method: TaGNN speeds up dynamic graph neural networks by running multiple computations at the same time based on the graph's structure. Instead of recalculating everything each time step, it updates only the vertices (nodes) that actually change, while loading the unchanged ones just once per layer. The data is organized by the graph's topology and timestamps so the computer's fast memory cache works efficiently. When the RNN (recurrent neural network, which processes sequences) outputs are nearly identical between steps, it skips those redundant calculations.
sc-2025-416.key_novelty: TaGNN speeds up dynamic graph neural networks on FPGA by using the graph's structure to run multiple computations at once, organize data efficiently for the memory cache, and skip redundant neural network steps when outputs barely change.

sc-2025-407.method: The system implements a shared-memory driver inspired by XPMEM. It batches and parallelizes pinning operations (locking memory pages in place) instead of handling them one at a time, reducing synchronization overhead. When mapping to physical frame numbers—the actual memory addresses—it skips unnecessary cache-policy lookups. Through dynamic re-registration, it can expand the registered memory region without resetting existing mappings.
sc-2025-407.key_novelty: The key idea is combining parallel batched pinning (locking multiple memory pages together) with dynamic re-registration that preserves existing mappings, which eliminates redundant translation work and enables memory sharing to scale efficiently.

sc-2025-413.method: It converts atomic coordinates into connectivity maps—simplified text representations showing only atomic bonding, not exact positions—then applies three automated filters: rule-based screening, a language model trained on correct and artificially-corrupted molecular examples, and deduplication of identical structures.
sc-2025-413.key_novelty: A language model trained on correct and artificially-corrupted molecules can automatically classify which 3D electron diffraction structures are accurate using only their connectivity patterns.

sc-2025-408.method: Phoenix makes GPU memory directly visible to the Linux kernel using ZONE_DEVICE (a kernel feature from version 4.3 onward that lets the system designate device memory regions). A kernel module allocates virtual memory addresses that point directly to GPU memory, mapping these into the kernel's page table—the system's directory for where memory is located. This eliminates phony buffers (dummy memory locations in system RAM that were previously required to communicate with the kernel), allowing I/O operations to access GPU memory directly.
sc-2025-408.key_novelty: Phoenix directly connects GPU memory to the Linux kernel using ZONE_DEVICE, eliminating the dummy buffer intermediaries of previous approaches.

sc-2025-415.method: RingX improves ring attention (splitting attention across GPUs by chaining data through them) by redesigning workload distribution and communication patterns. Ring attention's point-to-point communication (GPU-to-GPU in a chain) doesn't match modern supercomputer network topologies, causing inefficiencies. RingX optimizes the communication pattern to match how supercomputers like Frontier are actually wired, reducing bottlenecks and balancing the workload. It supports both bi-directional and causal attention mechanisms.
sc-2025-415.key_novelty: RingX optimizes ring attention for supercomputer network topologies like Frontier, achieving 3.4x speedup over conventional ring attention.

sc-2025-411.method: AGILE is a library that lets GPUs request data from SSDs without pausing computation—instead of waiting for data to arrive, it fetches it in the background while computations continue. It uses a temporary high-speed memory cache on the GPU to hold frequently-used data. To coordinate between computation and data fetching without creating deadlock situations (where tasks wait forever for each other), it uses special data structures that don't require traditional locks.
sc-2025-411.key_novelty: Combining asynchronous I/O with an integrated GPU-based high-speed memory cache and deadlock-free coordination lets GPUs fetch data from SSDs without stalling computation.

sc-2025-412.method: LowDiff uses the compressed gradients (calculation records that training produces) as checkpoint snapshots, recording only what changed between training steps rather than saving entire model copies. It bundles multiple gradient writes together to reduce disk overhead and automatically adjusts checkpoint frequency and batch sizes based on system performance.
sc-2025-412.key_novelty: LowDiff reuses gradient compression from distributed training as differential checkpoint snapshots, dynamically tuning checkpoint frequency and batch sizes for efficiency.

sc-2025-420.method: InferCT breaks large CT scans into smaller cube-shaped chunks that fit inside GPU memory, then processes them in parallel across multiple GPUs. To maximize speed on any vendor's hardware, it uses: a lock-free shared memory data structure (letting multiple processors safely access data without waiting), pipelined execution that overlaps data loading with processing, and a parallel data loader that feeds data to all GPUs simultaneously.
sc-2025-420.key_novelty: InferCT makes 3D CT inference practical by combining three techniques—breaking volumes into GPU-sized chunks, lock-free data synchronization (eliminating waits between processors), and pipelined execution—that work on any GPU vendor's hardware.

sc-2025-417.method: MetoHash spreads an index (data lookup table) across three memory levels: fast CPU caches, intermediate DRAM, and persistent memory (PMem) for permanent storage. It batches items together in the cache before moving them down to DRAM and eventually to PMem, reducing how many trips to slow storage are needed. It uses fingerprinting (a compact summary of each item) to avoid checking PMem unnecessarily, and removes duplicate copies when reorganizing how data is stored in buckets (storage containers).
sc-2025-417.key_novelty: It stages insertions through three memory levels and uses fingerprint shortcuts to reduce unnecessary persistent memory traffic.

sc-2025-418.method: X-MoE scales mixture-of-experts training (a neural network approach where different experts activate based on input) through three optimizations: memory-efficient code that runs on different hardware platforms, direct expert routing that eliminates redundant data copying, and hybrid parallelization that splits both the data and model across machines. Together, these reduce memory overhead and communication bottlenecks that normally limit the size of models you can train.
sc-2025-418.key_novelty: X-MoE is a mixture-of-experts training system that eliminates wasted memory space and redundant data routing, enabling models 10x larger than existing methods across diverse hardware including AMD GPUs.

sc-2025-422.method: The GW method (a quantum simulation of electron interactions) is implemented in the BerkeleyGW package to run efficiently on different GPU types—the AMD MI250X on Frontier and Intel Xe on Aurora. The approach splits the calculation into two levels and optimizes how computing nodes communicate with each other to minimize data-transfer delays.
sc-2025-422.key_novelty: The GW implementation scales nearly linearly to 9,408+ nodes on Frontier with 59.45% of peak performance, and the same code runs efficiently on both AMD MI250X and Intel Xe GPUs without modification.

sc-2025-421.method: The algorithms eliminate conditional branches—if-statements that interrupt CPU instruction pipelines—from floating-point arithmetic operations. They handle double, triple, and quadruple precision numbers for all standard IEEE floating-point inputs, within overflow and underflow limits. To ensure the branch-free operations are correct across all these cases, a computer automatically verified each algorithm against a formal proof, rather than relying on testing alone.
sc-2025-421.key_novelty: Branch-free floating-point algorithms with computer-verified correctness, delivering order-of-magnitude speedups over existing libraries.

sc-2025-428.method: Instead of moving terabytes of data across the network to a client, the system runs the data analysis directly on the storage servers where the data lives. It executes VTK's data pipeline stages—reading and filtering files—right on the servers, then sends only the filtered results back to the client. A FUSE interface (a software layer that lets the client transparently communicate with the storage servers) enables this coordination. The system uses pNFS's knowledge of where data is physically stored and Linux storage features to access files efficiently on the servers, while enforcing user credentials and access permissions.
sc-2025-428.key_novelty: The first practical system that runs VTK analysis directly on pNFS storage servers via a FUSE interface, achieving 6–7× speedup by filtering data at its source instead of transmitting it across the network.

sc-2025-426.method: They used superconducting quantum processors (specialized computers that perform calculations by harnessing quantum mechanics) to generate 55 protein fragments over the course of roughly tens of hours. They then compared these quantum-generated structures to predictions from AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 (the leading AI models for predicting protein shapes) using two metrics: RMSD to measure how closely the predicted shapes matched, and docking affinity to measure how strongly small molecules would bind to the proteins. This represents the first dataset of protein structures created by quantum computers at this scale.
sc-2025-426.key_novelty: This work creates the first large-scale dataset of protein structures made by quantum computers, showing they predict protein binding regions more accurately than AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 (the leading AI protein prediction methods) based on both shape accuracy (RMSD) and binding strength (docking affinity).

sc-2025-423.method: The system runs multiple AI models on a single GPU by splitting it into logical sections using MIG (Multi-Instance GPU partitioning), then further sharing each section using MPS (Multi-Process Service), which lets multiple model processes run simultaneously on the same partition. It automatically decides which models to run together, how to split the GPU into partitions, how to distribute the workload across processes, and where to map the GPU's computing threads (thread blocks) to each process. Rather than trying to predict exactly how models will interfere with each other when sharing resources—which often leads to inaccurate guesses—it uses Bayesian optimization (a method that learns from past experiments to intelligently suggest new configurations to try) to explore different MPS settings and find what actually works best in practice.
sc-2025-423.key_novelty: This system combines MPS (letting multiple processes share sections of the GPU) with MIG (dividing the GPU into partitions), then uses Bayesian optimization to automatically find the best MPS settings by trying different configurations and measuring performance, avoiding the inaccuracy of trying to predict interference mathematically.

sc-2025-430.method: Phoenix works by keeping the original sparse pre-trained weights (with many zeros placed strategically) and adding small task-specific layers called low-rank adapters on top during fine-tuning. Instead of retraining all the original weights and filling in the zeros, only these small adapters are updated, which preserves the sparsity pattern throughout. The approach takes advantage of Cerebras CS-2 hardware, which efficiently handles unstructured sparsity—weights that can be zero in any irregular pattern, not just regular grids—to make inference fast without computing through the zero values.
sc-2025-430.key_novelty: This is the first method to maintain weight sparsity during fine-tuning by combining sparse pre-trained weights with low-rank adapters, enabling 50–60% sparsity on Cerebras without accuracy loss.

sc-2025-427.method: The tool works by inserting monitoring code into compiled CUDA programs to track every memory operation—both loads (reading data) and stores (writing data)—as the program runs, without requiring access to the original source code. It identifies when the same data is loaded multiple times unnecessarily or when data is stored but never used, marking these as redundant operations. The method was validated on standard performance benchmarks: PolybenchGPU, Rodinia, PASTA, DARKNET, and LULESH.
sc-2025-427.key_novelty: It's the first tool to use binary instrumentation (monitoring how compiled CUDA code actually runs, without source files) to find and eliminate redundant memory operations, achieving over 6× speedup by catching inefficiencies that existing profilers miss.

sc-2025-429.method: MAGUS monitors memory access patterns to predict memory bandwidth demand (memory intensity) and identifies execution phases in GPU workloads. It automatically scales down the uncore components—memory, cache, and interconnect hardware—when those phases don't need full speed, handling transitions between phases smoothly. The system integrates with vendor power management (NVIDIA DCGM, Intel RAS) and runs transparently without code changes.
sc-2025-429.key_novelty: MAGUS is the first uncore scaling system to adapt to GPU-dominant workload phases, delivering 27% energy savings while maintaining less than 5% performance loss.

sc-2025-424.method: HyTiS uses two-level hybrid tile scheduling: the first level uses standard tile sizes to keep all GPU processing waves (groups of threads running together) fully utilized, while the second level switches to fine-grained adaptive tiles for leftover work that doesn't fill complete waves, reducing partial-wave latency. It pre-profiles different tile combinations offline and stores the most efficient ones as a library. Finally, it selects tile layouts using an analytical model that predicts data movement between main GPU memory and L2 cache, optimizing to minimize this movement.
sc-2025-424.key_novelty: The first framework to jointly address wave quantization and L2 cache efficiency in GPU matrix multiplication by using fine-grained adaptive tiling for partial waves and an analytical model to select tile layouts based on cache behavior.

sc-2025-419.method: DAS-ILU breaks a large computation into two types of data: interior nodes (pieces each processor handles independently) and separator nodes (shared boundaries between processors). It processes all interior nodes first in parallel, then asynchronously updates separator nodes, meaning each processor updates its boundaries when ready rather than waiting for synchronization. This cuts separator size in half and reduces communication. The method extends to block-structured matrices, where data is arranged in rectangular blocks.
sc-2025-419.key_novelty: The core insight is splitting computation into independent pieces and asynchronously updating boundaries between pieces, which halves separator size and reduces communication.

sc-2025-425.method: The key insight is decoupling how sparse matrices are stored from how algorithms use them. A new abstract layer automatically handles data partitioning across multiple computers by tracking three things in parallel: the problem domain, the output space, and the locations of non-zero values. Universal operators co-partition matrices and vectors together, and a multi-operator approach lets algorithms work with data scattered non-contiguously across memory. The implementation targets Legion, a task-based runtime that breaks work into independent chunks.
sc-2025-425.key_novelty: The first abstraction decoupling sparse matrix storage format from Krylov algorithm implementation, so partitioning changes automatically propagate without code rewrites.

sc-2025-431.method: The framework speeds up updates to erasure-coded storage (where data is split across multiple drives with built-in redundancy) by combining three strategies. It groups updates targeting the same stripe—the set of drives holding related data—together to reduce network traffic. It selects an efficient node to collect the updates and designs a routing structure that balances the work across the network, avoiding bottlenecks. It also adjusts routing in real time based on network speeds, favoring faster connections.
sc-2025-431.key_novelty: It jointly optimizes three strategies—data locality, load balancing, and adaptive scheduling—for storage updates in erasure-coded systems for the first time, achieving 16–88% throughput gains.

usenix-2025-004.method: The system uses temporary ownership agreements (called leases) to ensure only one function can modify a piece of data at a time, keeping it consistent. To avoid slowdowns from moving data across the network, it places functions close to the data they need (called affinity-aware placement). By combining these two strategies—leasing for consistency and colocated placement for speed—the system handles many concurrent tasks without corruption or major performance loss.
usenix-2025-004.key_novelty: Use temporary-access leases combined with placing functions near their data to achieve both consistency and speed in serverless systems.

usenix-2025-000.method: SpaceExit designs neural networks (AI systems trained to recognize patterns) that can stop calculating early. Normally they run through all their layers (stages of computation), but SpaceExit lets them stop partway when they're confident enough in their answer. The system adjusts how confident they need to be before stopping based on the current power and cooling available in space—tighter constraints mean earlier stopping and lower energy use. Hardware optimizations reduce the overhead from checking when to stop.
usenix-2025-000.key_novelty: Neural networks that automatically adjust when they stop calculating based on available power and cooling in space.

usenix-2025-003.method: KATZ separates ControlNets (specialized networks that guide image generation) from the main model and runs them on dedicated GPUs where results can be cached and reused across requests. For LoRA adapters (lightweight model customizations), it loads them in the background while the base model executes, overlapping up to K steps of computation with loading time without losing image quality. The base model runs faster across multiple GPUs using latent parallelism—processing different parts of the image's compressed representation simultaneously.
usenix-2025-003.key_novelty: KATZ removes ControlNets (image-guidance networks) from the main computation pipeline by running them on dedicated GPUs as an independent, separately scalable service.

usenix-2025-008.method: Swift uses two competing neural networks (a Generative Adversarial Network, or GAN) to explore performance configurations efficiently. One network proposes candidate settings, while the other evaluates their quality; through this adversarial process, they iteratively find good configurations. This approach is faster than trying every possible combination because the generator learns to focus on promising areas rather than searching blindly.
usenix-2025-008.key_novelty: Swift uses two competing neural networks—one generating candidate system configurations and one judging their quality—instead of traditional exhaustive search methods to find optimal performance settings.

usenix-2025-002.method: Toppings delegates scheduling and memory management to the CPU while GPUs focus purely on inference computation. The CPU uses rank-aware prioritization—scoring adapters by request characteristics or importance—to decide which adapter to use, batch requests efficiently, and move data between CPU and GPU memory. This keeps GPUs busy with compute work instead of wasting cycles on scheduling and overhead, enabling them to handle more adapters concurrently.
usenix-2025-002.key_novelty: Using CPU-based rank-aware prioritization (dynamically scoring adapters by request characteristics or importance) to handle adapter scheduling and memory overhead, freeing GPUs to focus entirely on inference for multiple adapters.

usenix-2025-010.method: The system watches how much CPU, memory, and network bandwidth each container actually uses during training. When one container needs more resources while another has spare capacity, it automatically shifts resources between them without pausing the job. These adjustments happen continuously based on what the workload demands at each moment.
usenix-2025-010.key_novelty: The system automatically shifts CPU, memory, and network resources between containers while training is running, adjusting in real-time to match what each container actually needs rather than using pre-set allocations.

usenix-2025-001.method: PMR reclaims memory by spreading the work across multiple processor cores simultaneously, using lock-free mechanisms (coordinated approaches that don't require cores to wait for each other) to minimize overhead. The system prioritizes freeing memory that's accessed least frequently, allowing efficient cleanup without disrupting active parts of the app.
usenix-2025-001.key_novelty: PMR coordinates multiple processor cores to reclaim memory in parallel instead of sequentially, eliminating the garbage collection slowdown.

usenix-2025-009.method: The researchers compared six different TCP network stacks—both kernel-bypass versions (which skip the operating system for faster data sending) and traditional in-kernel ones—by running them on representative workloads: bulk data transfers over multi-hundred gigabit Ethernet and small request-response messages. They measured throughput (how much data flows per second) and latency (response time) to understand which design choices work best for each workload type.
usenix-2025-009.key_novelty: This is the first systematic comparison of kernel-bypass TCP stacks across representative workloads, showing that no single design excels at both bulk data transfers and low-latency request handling.

usenix-2025-005.method: This system lets training and serving share a single GPU by dynamically dividing its resources—memory, computing power, and bandwidth—either by taking turns (time-sharing) or reserving separate regions (spatial partitioning). A scheduler continuously decides how to allocate resources based on each task's priority: how quickly the serving needs to respond (latency) and how fast training should progress (throughput). Kernel-level isolation (controls built into the operating system) or virtualization (creating isolated execution spaces) keeps the tasks from interfering with each other despite sharing hardware.
usenix-2025-005.key_novelty: A single GPU can run both training and serving at the same time through dynamic arbitration of resources—constantly deciding which task gets access based on their different performance needs.

usenix-2025-007.method: DDLumos tests database structure-change operations (called DDL, or Data Definition Language) by generating command sequences designed to expose failures. It combines dynamic analysis—observing how code actually behaves—with transaction state monitoring to track the database state as operations run. By comparing actual behavior against the database specification, it detects atomic violations: cases where structure-change operations don't complete fully or leave the database inconsistent when running alongside other operations.
usenix-2025-007.key_novelty: A single unified testing framework can systematically find atomic consistency bugs in database structure-change operations across different database systems.

sc-2025-432.method: The system moves DAOS client logic from the CPU to a specialized network processor card (NVIDIA BlueField-3 DPU). It splits the work into two paths: control commands use lightweight gRPC messaging, while high-speed data transfers use RDMA and UCX (network techniques that let the network processor directly access memory without burdening the CPU). This way, GPUs can pull data directly without CPU overhead or kernel context switches. The storage server side needs no changes, and the network processor handles encryption and multi-tenant isolation.
sc-2025-432.key_novelty: This is the first practical demonstration that offloading DAOS storage logic to a SmartNIC (specialized network card) using RDMA can achieve host-comparable performance, proving that network processors (DPUs) are viable for object storage in AI training workloads.

usenix-2025-015.method: μEFI restructures UEFI from a monolithic design—where all drivers run in shared memory—into a microkernel architecture with a minimal trusted core and isolated driver domains. Drivers communicate through capability-based message passing (permission tokens that grant specific access rights) instead of directly accessing shared memory. All inter-domain interactions are monitored and logged, creating an auditable record of firmware operations.
usenix-2025-015.key_novelty: μEFI applies microkernel isolation principles to firmware design, simultaneously achieving strong isolation between drivers and full transparency of firmware operations.

usenix-2025-012.method: Poby uses SmartNICs—specialized hardware cards positioned in the network between storage and compute nodes—to handle image decompression and transfer. The SmartNIC's hardware acceleration decompresses the VM image and moves it from storage to the compute node, work that would otherwise use the compute node's CPU. By offloading this work, Poby frees the CPU for other tasks, reducing contention and speeding up image provisioning.
usenix-2025-012.key_novelty: The innovation is using a SmartNIC (a specialized network acceleration card) to handle VM image decompression and transfer instead of relying on the compute node's CPU.

usenix-2025-016.method: DShuffle moves shuffle logic to specialized hardware called Data Processing Units (DPUs) positioned at the network edge, right next to network interfaces and with direct access to local memory where incoming packets are stored. The framework optimizes how data packets are routed and reorganized to reduce network congestion and the overhead of communication between CPUs and DPUs. It connects to existing distributed processing systems through a transparent abstraction layer that doesn't require changes to applications.
usenix-2025-016.key_novelty: DShuffle eliminates the shuffle bottleneck in large-scale data processing by offloading data reorganization work from CPUs to specialized hardware units (DPUs) positioned at the network edge.

usenix-2025-018.method: The researchers performed an empirical case study on Open CAS, an open-source storage system that caches data at the block level (storing frequently-accessed chunks in fast memory). They examined how Open CAS maintains crash consistency—where data doesn't get corrupted or lost if the system suddenly crashes—by analyzing transaction ordering (the sequence of operations), write-ahead logging (recording changes before making them permanent), and recovery procedures. Through failure scenarios, they identified vulnerabilities in how these mechanisms protect cached data.
usenix-2025-018.key_novelty: This empirical study reveals crash consistency vulnerabilities in a production block-level caching system (Open CAS) and characterizes how its recovery mechanisms actually work during failures.

usenix-2025-022.method: SNARY moves database searches from the CPU to a SmartNIC—a network card with its own processor that can run custom code. It stores lookup tables and search logic directly on this hardware, using programmable packet processing (custom instructions for handling network data) to run searches while data passes through. Because the search happens on the network card itself rather than the CPU, it avoids the bottleneck of shipping data back and forth. The system exposes a simple, flexible interface so many different types of searches can run on the same hardware without needing to redesign it.
usenix-2025-022.key_novelty: SNARY lets many different types of database searches run on the same SmartNIC hardware without having to build custom versions for each one.

usenix-2025-006.method: TGW directs incoming requests to servers efficiently and spreads them evenly across servers to prevent overload. When a server fails, the system automatically detects it and redirects traffic to working servers. By combining intelligent routing with automatic recovery, the gateway efficiently handles large-scale traffic.
usenix-2025-006.key_novelty: TGW operates cloud gateways at scale by distributing requests intelligently and automatically recovering when servers fail.

usenix-2025-014.method: CAFault creates system configurations (settings that determine how a system behaves) specifically tailored to each fault type being tested. Rather than using the same configuration for all tests, it adapts the settings based on what fault is being injected—for example, changing timing parameters or network constraints based on whether you're testing crash faults, delay faults, or resource exhaustion. By systematically trying these targeted configurations, it discovers which combinations of settings and faults cause distributed systems to actually fail.
usenix-2025-014.key_novelty: CAFault generates many system configurations customized to each fault type rather than using fixed or random configurations for all tests.

usenix-2025-020.method: GPU preemption means pausing a task running on a graphics processor so you can run a more urgent task instead. GPREEMPT saves the paused task's state (called a checkpoint) so it can resume from that exact point later. The system uses smart scheduling rules to decide when to pause or resume tasks, and it works across different GPU types (NVIDIA, AMD, etc.) by hiding their technical differences behind a common layer of abstraction. This approach keeps the performance cost low.
usenix-2025-020.key_novelty: A common abstraction layer enables a single preemption system that pauses and resumes GPU tasks efficiently on any hardware.

usenix-2025-017.method: The researchers continuously measure cloud hardware by tracking its performance and diagnostic signals to identify fail-slow states—when components gradually slow down but keep running. They develop detection methods that look for patterns in these measurements to identify hardware degradation and predict when components will become fail-slow.
usenix-2025-017.key_novelty: The work detects fail-slow hardware—components that gradually slow down while still operating—rather than hardware that stops working completely.

usenix-2025-021.method: Optimus works by finding idle GPU time that occurs when different parts of a multimodal LLM (processing both images and text) finish computing at different times. It creates separate execution plans for the image encoder and language model, then uses a scheduling algorithm to fit encoder work into GPU idle gaps. The system breaks encoder operations into small units (kernels), identifies idle moments in the parallel GPU setup (called 3D parallelism), and schedules encoder tasks into those gaps at sub-millisecond precision while maintaining correct data flow between components.
usenix-2025-021.key_novelty: Because multimodal LLMs have idle GPU time while the language model runs, you can fill that time by scheduling encoder work, and this works across all GPUs without disrupting data flow.

usenix-2025-024.method: The paper tests real Graph Neural Network systems to measure their performance and identify bottlenecks—the operations that consume the most time. The researchers systematically compare different GNN frameworks and analyze where computation time is spent in each. This reveals common design inefficiencies that repeatedly appear across multiple implementations.
usenix-2025-024.key_novelty: This work systematically identifies and categorizes design flaws in production Graph Neural Network systems.

usenix-2025-019.method: The approach embeds machine learning models into programmable network switches and SmartNICs (specialized network cards) to speed up pattern matching. The ML model learns which patterns are most likely to appear in traffic, allowing the hardware to prioritize checking those patterns first or skip comparisons that won't match. This prioritization maintains accuracy while handling terabit-scale traffic volumes by exploiting the parallel processing power built into switches and SmartNICs.
usenix-2025-019.key_novelty: Machine learning is applied for the first time to speed up pattern matching in programmable network switches and SmartNICs.

usenix-2025-023.method: When serving multiple large language models simultaneously, GPUs hit a bottleneck: attention operations (the computational step where the model decides what to focus on) consume massive amounts of GPU memory and processing power. Weaver fixes this by moving these attention calculations to the CPU or auxiliary memory instead, freeing up GPU resources. By scheduling attention operations separately and managing data movement between the GPU and these alternative resources, the system can serve more models concurrently.
usenix-2025-023.key_novelty: The key insight is treating attention operations (the memory-intensive step where the model decides what words to focus on) as a separate offloading problem—instead of serving the entire model together—so more language models can run on the same GPU.

usenix-2025-027.method: Fast ACS minimizes message delivery time by choosing different communication strategies based on whether the destination is nearby or far away. For machines within the same cluster, it uses RMA (one-sided communication: the sender directly writes to the receiver's memory without waiting for permission), which is fast. For distant machines across different clusters, it uses RPC (request-response messaging: the sender asks and waits for a reply), which is slower but more reliable over long distances. The system stores all messages in files to guarantee they arrive in the correct order.
usenix-2025-027.key_novelty: The system uses fast direct-memory delivery for nearby machines and slower request-response delivery for distant clusters, automatically choosing which method to use based on message distance.

usenix-2025-028.method: HypeReca creates a database that lives in memory across multiple computers, designed for embedding tables (lookup tables that map IDs to learned values) that recommender systems need. It arranges data in memory layouts optimized for how embeddings get accessed, making lookups fast, and splits data across machines so work happens in parallel. The system uses custom communication to keep embeddings synchronized when multiple processors work together, and hardware-aware scheduling that runs each task on the device type (GPU, CPU, etc.) best suited for it.
usenix-2025-028.key_novelty: The core idea is an in-memory database optimized for embedding access patterns that works across different hardware types in distributed recommender training.

usenix-2025-026.method: The approach breaks the input into sections and uses binary search to identify which ones are necessary to trigger the crash (a technique called delta-debugging). Rather than running the kernel repeatedly from scratch, it predicts which input changes won't affect the crash by reusing information from previous runs, skipping unnecessary kernel executions. It also parallelizes multiple minimization attempts to speed up the overall process.
usenix-2025-026.key_novelty: It skips redundant kernel executions during minimization by predicting which parts of the input are unnecessary for the crash, based on observations from previous runs.

usenix-2025-031.method: DEEPSERVE organizes work into three nested levels—requests, jobs, and tasks—to simplify management. It uses FLOWSERVE, a lightweight serving engine built around NPUs (specialized AI processing chips), which runs copies of the model in parallel across multiple machines using SPMD (running the same code on different inputs across processors). To handle traffic surges, it keeps containers ready to launch, pre-loads model data into memory, and uses NPU-fork (a technique to quickly duplicate a running model instance) to scale from one machine to 64 machines in just seconds.
usenix-2025-031.key_novelty: Combining NPU-fork (a fast technique to duplicate running AI models on specialized chips) with automatic serverless scaling enables large language models to start handling requests in under a second on a cluster of separate Ascend NPUs.

usenix-2025-029.method: STORM monitors how each network path performs—tracking latency (how long packets take to arrive) and loss rates (how many packets disappear)—then sends each packet on whichever path is performing best at that moment. Using acknowledgments (delivery confirmations) as feedback, the scheduler continuously updates its understanding of each path's quality and shifts packet assignments between paths to maximize throughput (total data arriving per second) while keeping buffering delays minimal.
usenix-2025-029.key_novelty: The core insight is continuously measuring performance on each available network path and dynamically routing each packet to whichever path will deliver it most reliably, adapting instantly as mobile network conditions change.

usenix-2025-035.method: mTuner introduces Elastic Tensor, a technique that dynamically reshapes and repositions training data (tensors) based on each GPU's memory structure and how the GPUs are connected to each other. It packs these tensors efficiently to reduce wasted memory space (fragmentation). The system overlaps communication—sending data between GPUs—with computation on each GPU, so processors don't sit idle waiting for data. A workload-aware scheduler balances gradient calculations and weight updates across all GPUs to prevent any single GPU from becoming a bottleneck.
usenix-2025-035.key_novelty: Elastic Tensor dynamically resizes and reorganizes trainable tensors during parameter-efficient fine-tuning to optimize how they fit in GPU memory and reduce communication overhead between GPUs.

usenix-2025-033.method: When training large language models with pipeline parallelism (splitting computation into stages running in parallel), idle periods called bubbles naturally occur as stages wait for each other. Gradient checkpointing normally requires expensive recomputation that adds to training time, but Obscura schedules this work to run during the bubble periods where hardware would otherwise sit idle. By overlapping recomputation with the waiting time, the extra work becomes hidden and doesn't extend the total training duration.
usenix-2025-033.key_novelty: Scheduling gradient recomputation to run during the idle waiting periods (bubbles) in pipeline-parallel training.

usenix-2025-013.method: CrossPipe models real-world network delays and bandwidth limits that slow distributed training. It then finds optimal schedules by jointly optimizing two training strategies: running the model across a sequence of machines (pipeline parallelism) and overlapping gradient synchronization between model copies with other computation (data parallelism). The system can use mathematical solvers to find perfect schedules or faster approximations for practical use. Its flexible execution engine keeps scheduling decisions separate from how communication is actually implemented.
usenix-2025-013.key_novelty: CrossPipe jointly optimizes pipeline parallelism (running model stages across machines), overlapping data parallelism updates (sharing gradients during other computations), and explicit accounting for network latency and bandwidth limits to find optimal training schedules across distant datacenters.

usenix-2025-034.method: Chitu improves Byzantine consensus by distinguishing between temporary network delays and actual Byzantine faults (faulty or malicious nodes), preventing unnecessary fallback to slower restart modes. It uses three techniques to make this distinction: better leader election signaling (how leader nodes report their status to others), timeout adjustment (tuning how long to wait before assuming failure), and view-change optimization (streamlining how the protocol switches between consensus rounds). By staying in fast normal mode when only transient delays occur, Chitu maintains high throughput and low latency while preserving safety and liveness.
usenix-2025-034.key_novelty: Chitu avoids unnecessary fallback in Byzantine consensus by accurately detecting whether network problems are temporary or represent genuine Byzantine faults (faulty or malicious nodes), thereby reducing expensive mode switches while maintaining safety and liveness guarantees.

usenix-2025-032.method: SwCC adds a programmable layer inside RDMA engines (specialized network hardware for fast data transfers) that lets you upload custom congestion control algorithms at runtime. These algorithms inspect each packet individually and dynamically decide whether to forward, slow it down, or mark it—rather than making one decision per data flow. The key advantage is that this control logic is separate from the hardware, so you never need to modify the underlying chips.
usenix-2025-032.key_novelty: SwCC moves programmable congestion control into the RDMA engine itself, making decisions per-packet instead of per-flow, rather than relying on hardcoded hardware rules or host-based software.

usenix-2025-039.method: Rex is a specialized programming language and compiler designed for kernel extensions (code that runs at the system's most privileged level). Developers write in this high-level language, and the compiler automatically translates their code into a form that can be mathematically proven correct (formal verification), handling the complex translation that would normally require manual, error-prone work. The language uses type checking (rules about what data types can flow where) to prevent whole categories of safety bugs before verification even begins. This means programmers get an easy-to-use language while still getting mathematical proof that their kernel code won't crash or be exploited.
usenix-2025-039.key_novelty: A compiler infrastructure that automatically translates high-level, programmer-friendly code into kernel extensions with formal safety guarantees, eliminating the need for manual verification.

usenix-2025-025.method: Cuckoo hashing resolves collisions (when multiple keys hash to the same location) by displacing one key to an alternative slot—if that slot is occupied, the old item also moves elsewhere, cascading until all items find slots (like musical chairs where people keep moving to find seats). In disaggregated systems where the hash table sits on a remote server and clients query it over a network, each displacement step requires a server round-trip, creating bottlenecks. This paper reduces those round-trips by letting clients batch operations together, cache metadata locally, and perform more work locally before contacting the server.
usenix-2025-025.key_novelty: This work adapts cuckoo hashing for disaggregated systems by optimizing how collision resolution works across network boundaries, reducing server round-trips and coordination overhead while preserving the fast, guaranteed lookup times that make cuckoo hashing efficient.
