usenix-2025-037.method: HyCache speeds up DNN input preprocessing (the data-loading stage in AI models) by coordinating fast-memory caches on both the CPU and GPU. The system tracks which data is used repeatedly and keeps it in the fastest available storage, avoiding slow main-memory delays. It also predicts which data will be needed next and loads it ahead of time (prefetching), continuously adjusting its storage strategy based on the actual data access patterns it observes.
usenix-2025-037.key_novelty: Coordinating CPU and GPU fast-memory caches as one integrated system for the data-preparation stage of AI models, rather than treating them separately.

usenix-2025-038.method: Para-ksm moves memory deduplication work from the CPU to a specialized hardware accelerator (a data streaming accelerator) that processes many pages simultaneously. The accelerator computes a unique identifier (hash) for each page and identifies duplicates by comparing these identifiers in parallel. This offloads the repetitive work from the CPU, reducing overhead and dramatically increasing the speed of finding duplicate pages.
usenix-2025-038.key_novelty: Using a specialized hardware accelerator (a data streaming accelerator) to parallelize memory page deduplication, eliminating the CPU bottleneck of processing pages one at a time.

usenix-2025-042.method: Koala creates a standard set of test tasks that researchers run on different shell systems to measure performance. The tests measure how fast each shell executes commands, how much CPU and memory it uses, and how it behaves under different conditions. By comparing results across different shells and different types of workloads, researchers can identify which design choices and optimizations actually improve shell performance.
usenix-2025-042.key_novelty: Koala is the first standardized benchmark suite that measures shell performance across different shell types and different kinds of command patterns.

usenix-2025-041.method: PPipe measures how fast each layer of the model runs on different GPU types. It uses pool-based pipeline parallelism to assign layers to GPU classes based on these per-layer latency measurements. An optimization algorithm (MILP) in the control plane decides the assignments, while the data plane implements adaptive batching with resource reservations to maintain consistent throughput and meet response-time deadlines.
usenix-2025-041.key_novelty: Pipeline parallelism—traditionally used for training throughput—is applied to time-critical inference serving by exploiting how many layers run at comparable speeds across different GPU types.

usenix-2025-036.method: Z-LFS organizes data writes to align with the SSD's zones (limited storage blocks), preventing writes from crossing zone boundaries and triggering expensive resets. The system segments both the temporary write buffer and the file system's address space into zone-sized chunks, so data stays within zone limits by design. When reclaiming space (garbage collection), it prioritizes resetting individual zones rather than the entire drive, reducing the total reset burden. Adaptive zone mapping lets the system adjust zone assignments while maintaining sequential writes (ordered writing), which SSDs require for performance despite small zone boundaries.
usenix-2025-036.key_novelty: Z-LFS is the first production-ready file system optimized for commodity SSDs with small zones (limited-size storage regions), using a log-structured design that appends all writes sequentially.

usenix-2025-045.method: When training large neural networks on distributed computers, systems normally save snapshots of training progress (called checkpoints) in a format locked to the current setup—specifically how the model is distributed across devices and what hardware you're using. UCP stores checkpoints in an abstract format that doesn't depend on any particular hardware or parallelization strategy instead. Using pattern-based rules, it automatically remaps the checkpoint data to work with different ways of splitting the model or different hardware configurations, without needing to rebuild the checkpoint from scratch.
usenix-2025-045.key_novelty: The core idea is storing training checkpoints in a format independent of how you distribute the model across computers or which hardware you use, so you can change your training setup without repeating previous work.

usenix-2025-050.method: LITESHIELD protects containers by running security functions as small, isolated programs in user space (where applications normally run, rather than in the kernel—the core of the operating system). Each security function handles one job, like controlling file access or network permissions, and they work together through a coordinator. Because these functions run outside the kernel, they add less overhead to container performance. You can also pick which security functions to use based on what your specific container needs, rather than being locked into an all-or-nothing approach.
usenix-2025-050.key_novelty: Instead of building container security into the kernel, LITESHIELD lets each security function run as a separate, swappable program in user space, so you only pay for the protections you actually need.

usenix-2025-040.method: PathWeaver uses three coordinated techniques on multiple GPUs: pipelining-based path extension (connecting GPUs to share search progress and eliminate duplicate work), ghost staging (using representative datasets to find optimal starting points), and direction-guided selection (filtering irrelevant points to reduce calculations and memory transfers). These techniques make GPUs collaborate on searches instead of working independently.
usenix-2025-040.key_novelty: Pipelining-based path extension using GPU-to-GPU communication (connecting GPUs to share search progress) to eliminate redundant search iterations in multi-GPU systems.

usenix-2025-030.method: FLB reroutes traffic dynamically without preset thresholds to spread the load evenly and use network links better during normal operation. When congestion occurs, it quickly isolates the heaviest flows onto separate paths so they don't block other flows in the queue—a head-of-line blocking problem that worsens congestion in Priority Flow Control (PFC) systems, which pause flows to prevent data loss. The system works with RDMA and RoCE (network protocols for fast data transfer) and coordinates with PFC to avoid pathological rerouting patterns where traffic bounces unproductively between the same paths.
usenix-2025-030.key_novelty: It combines threshold-free rerouting with congested flow isolation to prevent head-of-line blocking in Priority Flow Control systems while maintaining load balancing.

usenix-2025-043.method: IRHash compares code at the intermediate representation level—the standardized form that all compilers use between source code and machine code—rather than comparing the original source. It normalizes this intermediate form and computes a stable checksum (hash) for it. When the same checksum appears (whether from Python, Java, or another language), the cache retrieves and reuses the previously compiled result. This works because semantically equivalent code in different languages produces identical intermediate representations.
usenix-2025-043.key_novelty: Instead of matching source code, it matches the intermediate representation that all compilers use, so different languages can share compilation results.

usenix-2025-048.method: The system uses RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access), which lets computers directly read and write each other's memory without CPU involvement, to minimize transaction coordination overhead. Instead of locking data to prevent conflicts, it relies on optimistic concurrency control (checking whether data changed after reading rather than preventing changes upfront) paired with RDMA atomic operations—actions that either fully complete or have no effect. By using RDMA's one-sided operations, where the remote computer doesn't need to respond or participate, most transaction work completes in a single message round-trip instead of requiring back-and-forth coordination steps.
usenix-2025-048.key_novelty: The core idea is replacing traditional request-response coordination with RDMA's one-sided operations, so distributed transactions can commit across multiple computers in fewer network round-trips.

usenix-2025-046.method: Pallas uses information about each request's CPU needs to sort them at network switches into groups (shards) with similar computational demands. By routing these CPU-similar requests to appropriate servers using a simple rule (CPU affinity), the system avoids complex optimization and keeps load balanced. Each server then schedules incoming requests with full knowledge of what's coming, making better decisions than scheduling blindly.
usenix-2025-046.key_novelty: Sorting requests by CPU demand at the network level rather than at individual servers, which enables simpler and more efficient rack-scale scheduling.

usenix-2025-053.method: XRT is software that runs alongside your programs and keeps track of what different hardware accelerators (specialized chip units optimized for specific tasks like graphics, AI, or encryption) can and can't do. When your program has work to do, XRT decides which accelerator to send each piece to, managing the coordination—preventing multiple tasks from using the same accelerator at once and ensuring all pieces finish in the right order. It does this by continuously monitoring what the hardware is doing and intelligently scheduling incoming work to the accelerator that can handle it best.
usenix-2025-053.key_novelty: Instead of requiring separate, incompatible software for each accelerator type, XRT provides one unified layer that understands all accelerators and coordinates work across them.

usenix-2025-044.method: When multiple computers train together on graph data (distributed graph learning), they need to combine results from all computers—a process called aggregation that normally happens at the endpoint computers, creating a bottleneck. This method offloads that work to programmable network hardware (specialized adapter cards called SmartNICs or programmable switches). The network hardware collects results from all computers and combines them in the network as data flows through, eliminating both the computational load on endpoints and the need to send all raw data to one location.
usenix-2025-044.key_novelty: This approach performs result aggregation (combining data from multiple sources) directly in programmable network hardware (SmartNICs or switches) instead of at endpoint computers.

usenix-2025-047.method: DSA-2LM uses Intel's Data Streaming Accelerator (DSA)—a specialized hardware chip designed to move data—to automatically manage data across a two-level memory hierarchy without the main CPU being involved. The system uses DSA to make three key decisions: where to place each piece of data (in faster or slower memory), when to prefetch it (bringing data into faster memory before it's needed), and how to keep all copies of data matching each other across the two memory tiers. By offloading these management tasks to DSA, the CPU is freed from the overhead of constantly deciding how to move data around.
usenix-2025-047.key_novelty: DSA-2LM is the first system to use Intel's Data Streaming Accelerator to handle all tiered-memory management—data placement, prefetching, and coherence management (keeping all copies of data matching each other)—without CPU involvement.

usenix-2025-058.method: FiDe monitors machines by running multiple independent checks: regular status signals between machines (heartbeats), direct network tests, and requiring agreement from a majority of monitoring nodes (quorum-based verification) before declaring a machine dead. Rather than using a fixed timeout that works poorly under varying network conditions, it adjusts how long to wait before declaring a machine failed based on current network delays. This approach reduces false alarms when networks are congested while maintaining fast detection of genuine crashes.
usenix-2025-058.key_novelty: FiDe separates the speed-versus-reliability tradeoff into independent tuning dimensions rather than trying to optimize both simultaneously.

usenix-2025-049.method: MemoryTrap marks sensitive memory regions with special hardware tags so the processor can track which data is protected. When an attacker tries to read this protected memory, the hardware detects the unauthorized access and immediately responds by blocking the read, corrupting the data, or sending an alert. The defense uses memory tagging (hardware labels on sensitive bytes), access monitoring (hardware watching all reads), or specialized memory-controller logic to intercept disclosure attempts at the hardware boundary before data leaves the chip.
usenix-2025-049.key_novelty: MemoryTrap detects and blocks memory disclosure attacks at the moment someone tries to read sensitive data, using hardware mechanisms instead of software checks or encrypted data.

usenix-2025-051.method: AnchorNet is a single system that handles both live broadcasting (one source streaming to many viewers) and collaborative streaming (multiple people streaming to each other in real-time). It works by identifying what both types need—when to send data, how much to temporarily store in buffers, and where to direct computing resources—and uses these same solutions for both broadcast and peer-to-peer delivery. This shared approach lets the system efficiently manage data flows whether they're one-to-many or many-to-many.
usenix-2025-051.key_novelty: A single unified architecture that handles both live broadcast and collaborative peer-to-peer streaming together, eliminating the need for separate specialized systems.

usenix-2025-052.method: SolFS records which parts of files get written to—specifically their position and size in data structures called per-file extent trees—instead of computing expensive hash values on entire files. It permanently stores these operation logs and versions them so multiple apps can share the same backup system. To keep overhead minimal, it compresses the logs and adjusts how finely it tracks operations (this dynamic granularity adapts to the situation). On the server, shadow files are quickly reconstructed from these operation records.
usenix-2025-052.key_novelty: It identifies changed data without computing hashes by recording write operations at the filesystem level.

usenix-2025-064.method: Minos hides network traffic patterns (the timing and size of packets that reveal who is communicating) by using simple scrambling techniques in programmable network switches—special hardware devices that can be reconfigured to process packets in custom ways. Rather than relying on heavy cryptographic protection that would slow the network down, it adapts these obfuscation techniques to match current threat levels and network conditions. All of this happens at line rate, meaning the network operates at full speed without any performance penalty.
usenix-2025-064.key_novelty: The core idea is implementing traffic pattern obfuscation as lightweight, self-adapting logic within programmable network switches, rather than using computationally expensive defenses elsewhere.

usenix-2025-061.method: Converos automatically tests all possible orderings of thread operations in concurrent kernel code to find bugs. To prevent this from taking forever, it uses abstraction (simplifying the code to just the essential parts) and reduction techniques (eliminating redundant checks) to cut down the number of execution paths that need checking. This makes automatic verification practical for real Rust OS kernels.
usenix-2025-061.key_novelty: Using targeted simplification to manage the explosion of possible execution paths makes automatic verification practical for real Rust OS kernels.

usenix-2025-057.method: HotRAP, built on RocksDB, continuously tracks which records are accessed most frequently using an on-disk index organized as an LSM-tree (a structure that efficiently handles data updates). When frequently accessed records end up on slower storage after the system reorganizes data (compaction), the system promotes them back to fast storage using one of three different methods, selected based on access patterns. This ensures frequently accessed data stays fast while less-accessed data can remain on cheaper, slower storage.
usenix-2025-057.key_novelty: Using an LSM-tree to track which records are accessed most frequently, combined with three distinct promotion strategies that efficiently move hot data between storage tiers.

usenix-2025-055.method: Barre simplifies congestion control policy writing by providing higher-level building blocks instead of requiring deep networking expertise. Users compose these blocks to create policies tailored to their specific cluster. The policies run either within network switches (in-network) or on end systems like GPUs and network cards (end-host).
usenix-2025-055.key_novelty: Barre lets you quickly develop and deploy custom congestion-control strategies across different hardware vendors without modifying switch or NIC firmware.

usenix-2025-056.method: When a sudden burst of parallel work arrives, the system starts many serverless functions in parallel. It coordinates these functions so each waits for its dependencies to finish, and schedules the work to maximize parallel execution while minimizing idle time.
usenix-2025-056.key_novelty: Coordinating serverless functions when massively parallel workloads arrive in bursts, instead of invoking each function independently.

usenix-2025-060.method: Primus is a training system that works with different types of recommendation models (systems that predict what users will like) without requiring separate custom training code for each. It uses standardized processes for loading data and running training, automatically optimizing how work gets scheduled and distributed across computers and GPUs based on how recommendation models use memory and computation. This allows one unified system to efficiently train diverse recommendation models at production scale.
usenix-2025-060.key_novelty: Primus provides a unified training system that standardizes training across different recommendation models at production scale.

usenix-2025-063.method: NetKeeper continuously watches network traffic and automatically detects anomalies—unexpected shifts in how data flows. When an anomaly is spotted, it reconfigures the network on its own (adjusting routing rules, queue management, and resource allocation) to handle the new conditions without manual intervention.
usenix-2025-063.key_novelty: The system automatically adjusts network settings when traffic patterns change unexpectedly, without human intervention.

usenix-2025-069.method: The researchers analyzed real-world data from a major AI company to understand how KVCache (data stored from language model computations) actually gets reused in practice. They examined which cached data gets accessed again and how often, comparing short single-turn requests with long multi-turn conversations, and found these patterns are predictable within each category. They built a cache eviction policy (the rule for deciding what to delete when storage fills up) that automatically adjusts itself based on what type of requests are happening.
usenix-2025-069.key_novelty: First study of real production data showing that cache reuse patterns are heavily skewed and that short single-turn requests need as much attention as long multi-turn conversations—contradicting what prior work assumed from artificial test workloads.

usenix-2025-062.method: CLONE takes a paired approach: it designs both the AI model and the hardware accelerator together rather than treating them as separate components to optimize independently. The hardware uses 28nm technology and dynamically adjusts power consumption during inference using real-time energy monitoring. The language model itself is customized—compressed and optimized—to run efficiently on this specialized hardware. Together, these changes ensure the system meets strict latency (response time) targets while minimizing power usage, whether on always-on devices or intermediate edge systems.
usenix-2025-062.key_novelty: CLONE jointly designs the language model and specialized hardware accelerator as a single system to meet latency and power requirements together, rather than optimizing them independently.

usenix-2025-054.method: Asterinas uses a framekernel architecture—an OS design where the kernel has different privilege levels, similar to building zones with restricted access—to isolate risky code. All unsafe operations (code that bypasses memory-safety checks) are confined to a single, carefully audited section, while the rest of the kernel uses safe Rust that the compiler automatically verifies. OSTD provides a framework and tools for this safe OS development. The system implements kernel functionality through safe Rust abstractions (clean, memory-safe-by-design interfaces), supports 210+ Linux syscalls, and keeps the unsafe code portion minimal and auditable.
usenix-2025-054.key_novelty: The framekernel architecture confines all memory-unsafe code to a small, audited section while the rest uses safe Rust, reducing the memory-safety code that must be manually verified.

usenix-2025-059.method: The work enhances a Bluetooth Low Energy fuzzing framework with Combinatorial Security Testing, a method that systematically explores all combinations of protocol inputs and device states instead of random sampling. Because it tests all meaningful cases, this approach is more reliable at finding security bugs than traditional fuzzing. The researchers evaluate it on 10 real Bluetooth devices across multiple firmware versions and measure how many bugs it finds and execution time compared to traditional fuzzing.
usenix-2025-059.key_novelty: Combinatorial Security Testing with guaranteed input space coverage—systematically testing all input combinations—overcomes the probabilistic limitations of traditional fuzzing for finding Bluetooth Low Energy security bugs.

usenix-2025-065.method: RHONE uses a two-stage process. First, it builds models of satellite behavior—power consumption, heat, orbits, networking, and computation—by combining real satellite data with real chip code running in a simulator. Then it runs containerized applications (self-contained software packages) through these integrated models to simulate how entire satellite networks would function.
usenix-2025-065.key_novelty: The core innovation is using real satellite data together with real chip code in a simulator to accurately model how satellites and constellations operate while remaining practical to use.

usenix-2025-066.method: JENGA identifies which tokens (pieces of text like words or subwords) matter most for learning by looking at where the model's attention goes or which tokens contribute most to fixing errors. It then does full computation on important tokens but skips or speeds up computation on unimportant ones. Fine-tuning requires two passes—forward (making predictions) and backward (updating weights)—so this selective approach cuts computation in both directions, making fine-tuning faster and cheaper without hurting how well the model learns.
usenix-2025-066.key_novelty: Instead of processing all tokens equally, JENGA does less computational work on tokens that don't matter much for learning during fine-tuning, cutting costs substantially while keeping learning quality.

usenix-2025-072.method: The approach modifies the TLS handshake—the initial security exchange when connecting to a server—to include hardware attestation credentials (proof from a TPM security chip or CPU that the hardware is legitimate and unmodified). Rather than sending attestation evidence in separate messages, it's bundled directly into the certificate exchange that already occurs during TLS setup. This allows clients to verify both the server's identity and its hardware integrity in one integrated verification, eliminating the need for separate attestation workflows.
usenix-2025-072.key_novelty: The single core idea is embedding remote attestation—verification that hardware hasn't been tampered with—directly into the TLS handshake instead of requiring it as a separate verification mechanism.

usenix-2025-067.method: GMI-DRL monitors the workload and switches its parallelization strategy in real time between two approaches: for bursty, irregular computation, it uses fine-grained task parallelism (breaking work into many small parallel tasks so every GPU stays active), and for more uniform workloads, it uses coarse-grained pipeline parallelism (feeding work sequentially through GPU stages to reduce communication overhead).
usenix-2025-067.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically switching between fine-grained task parallelism and coarse-grained pipeline parallelism based on real-time GPU workload patterns.

usenix-2025-077.method: Voltrix lets different processing tasks run independently without waiting for each other, eliminating the delay that normally happens when all tasks must pause together. To handle the irregular patterns in sparse matrices—where some parts have many zeros and others have fewer—it automatically rebalances work across processing elements to keep all of them busy. The whole system is designed around how Tensor Cores specifically access memory and perform calculations.
usenix-2025-077.key_novelty: The core idea is using independent, non-blocking task execution paired with dynamic workload rebalancing so that Tensor Cores can efficiently handle sparse matrix multiplication even though the irregular sparsity patterns would normally underutilize them.

usenix-2025-075.method: The approach tests a compiler by systematically trying different compilation settings. It uses attributes of the program being compiled (structure, patterns, characteristics) to guide which settings to try first, prioritizing combinations likely to trigger bugs. It then checks whether the compiled code is correct, catching mistakes the compiler made.
usenix-2025-075.key_novelty: It uses program attributes to systematically search for compiler bugs instead of randomly testing.

usenix-2025-074.method: Instead of assigning work to groups of cores, the scheduler gives tasks to individual PIM cores based on each one's available memory bandwidth (how fast data flows in and out) and computing capacity. It dynamically adjusts which cores get which tasks to prevent multiple cores from competing for memory access at the same time. This keeps cores from sitting idle and ensures efficient use of the available computing power.
usenix-2025-074.key_novelty: It brings ANNS scheduling down to individual PIM cores, dynamically matching each core's workload to its actual memory bandwidth and computing capacity.

usenix-2025-070.method: When a GPU runs both inference (applying a trained model to new data) and training (improving a model) at the same time, they both compete for GPU memory. Instead of copying data between them, this approach lets them hand off and reuse memory blocks directly. Optimized scheduling coordinates which workload accesses which memory regions and when, preventing conflicts, minimizing handoff delays, and reducing fragmentation.
usenix-2025-070.key_novelty: The key idea is a fast way to hand off memory blocks between inference and training workloads on the same GPU, enabling them to reuse the same memory with minimal delay.

usenix-2025-068.method: GeneralSparse builds an efficient sparse matrix multiplication (SpMM) system that handles pruned neural networks, where weights are zeroed to compress the model. Rather than assuming all networks have the same sparsity pattern, it analyzes the specific pattern during inference and automatically selects the fastest computation method, arranges data efficiently in GPU memory, and compiles the calculation on-the-fly to maintain speed across varying sparsity densities and granularities.
usenix-2025-068.key_novelty: A sparse multiplication engine that adapts to any irregular pattern from pruning without requiring fixed structure types or reverting to dense computation.

usenix-2025-079.method: MP2 tracks the user's movements in real-time and predicts where they will be a moment later, sending this prediction across the network to all the servers managing different parts of the VR world. Because network signals and rendering both take time, sending a prediction ahead compensates for this delay and keeps the lag low. The system also synchronizes all the distributed computers to render at the exact same moment through an optimized network protocol, so the user sees seamless motion without seeing inconsistencies between what different systems are displaying.
usenix-2025-079.key_novelty: MP2 enables unconstrained roaming in distributed VR by predicting user motion ahead of time and synchronizing rendering across multiple networked computers.

usenix-2025-080.method: Bin2Wrong generates random test binaries and passes them to target decompilers to produce C code versions. It then compares the original binary and decompiled C code to see if they behave identically when executed. To find where they diverge, it analyzes the control flow (the sequence and branching of operations) and data dependencies (which values depend on which other values) in both versions to spot semantic errors—cases where the decompiled C runs differently than the original.
usenix-2025-080.key_novelty: An automated framework that generates test binaries to systematically find semantic errors—cases where decompiled C code behaves differently than the original—across multiple decompilers.

usenix-2025-073.method: GREYHOUND automatically detects when GPUs or network links slow down during hybrid-parallel training by continuously monitoring performance, achieving over 99% accuracy. When slowdowns occur due to device degradation, system contention, or network congestion, GREYHOUND automatically applies multiple corrective strategies that adapt to the specific slowdown, without requiring engineers to pause training and restart from a checkpoint. The system responds on-the-fly during training, eliminating manual intervention and the downtime of checkpoint-restart failover.
usenix-2025-073.key_novelty: GREYHOUND automatically fixes GPU and network slowdowns using multiple strategies without manual intervention or checkpoint-restart.

usenix-2025-071.method: LogCrisp extracts patterns directly from compressed logs without decompressing them first. It works in two stages: the first stage pulls raw patterns from the compressed data, and the second stage refines them for accuracy. Then it runs queries on those patterns using SIMD operations—a technique where one instruction processes multiple pieces of data at once—enabling rapid analysis of large datasets.
usenix-2025-071.key_novelty: Instead of decompressing logs first, it extracts patterns directly from compressed data in two stages and queries those patterns using SIMD (fast parallel processing) to eliminate the decompression bottleneck.

usenix-2025-082.method: The system automatically decides where each 3D printing job should run—whether on a local printer or processed in the cloud—and coordinates the work to minimize data transfer and computing resources used. It predicts what each job will need and uses coordination protocols that reduce communication overhead (the repetitive back-and-forth messages between the cloud and printer) while respecting both the printer's capabilities and the job's constraints.
usenix-2025-082.key_novelty: The key innovation is a scheduling system that considers cloud computing costs and 3D printing job placement together as a single optimization problem, rather than optimizing them separately, to achieve near-optimal total cost of operation.

usenix-2025-081.method: ShieldReduce reduces how much space data takes up inside a trusted execution environment (TEE)—a secure, isolated area of the processor with limited memory. It does this by compressing data, removing duplicate copies, or trimming unnecessary information, while using careful memory management to keep everything encrypted and isolated from outside access.
usenix-2025-081.key_novelty: ShieldReduce shrinks data size at a detailed, selective level—through compression and deduplication—inside encrypted execution environments while keeping all security intact.

usenix-2025-085.method: Torpor stores inference models in regular memory, then loads them onto the GPU only when needed (late binding), minimizing the slowdown from moving models around. It speeds up this loading through four techniques: asynchronously handling incoming requests while models load in the background, sharing GPU runtime across multiple functions, executing predictions in a pipelined sequence, and managing GPU memory efficiently. It then schedules requests intelligently, using high-speed GPU interconnects to avoid conflicts and meet each function's performance targets.
usenix-2025-085.key_novelty: Late binding (loading models only when needed) with dynamic model swapping allows hundreds of concurrent inference functions to share GPUs while maintaining performance as good as if each function had its own GPU.

usenix-2025-078.method: FPRev reveals the accumulation order (the order in which a system adds floating-point numbers—decimal numbers represented in computers) without modifying code or hardware. It tests the system with carefully chosen numerical inputs and observes the output differences, since different addition orders produce different results. By analyzing these output patterns, FPRev determines which order was used, and the efficient test design makes this faster than checking all possible sequences.
usenix-2025-078.key_novelty: It reveals the accumulation order (the sequence of additions) by analyzing how outputs vary with carefully chosen numerical tests, rather than requiring inspection of the implementation code or hardware.

usenix-2025-087.method: AssyLLM breaks a language model into pre-trained blocks (self-contained components trained beforehand) and selectively fine-tunes only the critical ones across multiple distributed computers. Instead of synchronizing the entire model's weights between computers, it sends only block-level updates, which cuts communication and computation costs. This parameter-efficient approach works because not all model components need retraining—focusing on the essential blocks is enough.
usenix-2025-087.key_novelty: The core contribution is selective fine-tuning of pre-trained blocks in a federated setting, which reduces communication by synchronizing only block updates instead of full model weights.

usenix-2025-084.method: HEC verifies that code transformations (like those in compiler optimizations) produce results identical to the original code. It works by building e-graphs (data structures that compactly represent all mathematically equivalent forms of code) and integrating them with MLIR (a compiler framework that represents code in intermediate form). The system applies two verification strategies—dynamic rewriting tests actual transformations, while static rewriting verifies they're mathematically equivalent—to check loop unrolling (repeating loop bodies to reduce overhead), tiling (dividing loops into smaller blocks), and fusion (merging separate loops). On standard PolyBenchC benchmarks, it validated transformations across over 100,000 lines of code in 40 minutes.
usenix-2025-084.key_novelty: HEC verifies code transformations by combining e-graphs (data structures for tracking equivalent code) with MLIR (a compiler framework) and using both dynamic execution testing and static mathematical verification.

usenix-2025-089.method: DRack uses CXL (a high-speed hardware protocol for direct machine-to-machine connections, bypassing software routing layers) to let one rack access another rack's memory and processing power directly. Instead of sending requests through multiple network software layers—which adds latency—DRack redesigns the physical connections so that one rack can treat another's resources almost as if they were local. This eliminates the software routing overhead that normally slows down inter-rack access.
usenix-2025-089.key_novelty: DRack's core insight is using CXL (a direct hardware connection protocol) at the rack level to skip the traditional network software layers when one rack accesses another's memory or processing power.

usenix-2025-092.method: The technique analyzes your code without running it, examining how counting operations (like incrementing values) depend on each other and access memory. It automatically determines which operations need to be atomic—completing entirely or not at all—so that your data stays consistent if the system crashes. This matters especially for persistent memory systems, where memory survives crashes and partial updates can corrupt accumulated data.
usenix-2025-092.key_novelty: The tool automatically infers which counting operations need atomic guarantees in crash-proof memory systems, rather than having programmers manually specify them.

usenix-2025-083.method: PageFlex lets applications customize how the operating system frees up memory without modifying the OS itself. It uses eBPF (a secure way to run custom code inside the OS kernel) to intercept the moment when the OS needs to free up memory. When this happens, programs running outside the kernel can step in and decide which data to delete based on how the application uses memory. The OS automatically verifies this application-written code to make sure it won't crash the system.
usenix-2025-083.key_novelty: PageFlex uses eBPF to safely delegate paging policy decisions to user-space, allowing applications to customize memory management at runtime for their specific workloads without modifying the OS.

usenix-2025-090.method: The system decouples operations by giving compaction (the background process that reorganizes data in LSM-tree structures), writes, and reads their own separate memory pools so they don't fight over DRAM cache. It also assigns each operation type distinct I/O scheduling rules—separate policies controlling which operation gets to transfer data between memory and hybrid storage (the mix of different-speed storage devices) at any moment. This works because when operations aren't competing for the same resources, each can run efficiently without being blocked or slowed down by the others.
usenix-2025-090.key_novelty: The core innovation is isolating background data reorganization (compaction) from foreground reads and writes by giving each operation type its own memory pool and I/O scheduling in LSM-tree key-value stores on hybrid storage.

usenix-2025-086.method: The system distributes data across multiple available network paths simultaneously, using classical load-balancing techniques that send entire conversations down one path or spread packets across all paths. It maintains packet ordering and respects network congestion. By applying these techniques transparently—without requiring applications to change—systems fully utilize the multi-path capabilities of modern data centers.
usenix-2025-086.key_novelty: Transparent, automatic splitting of network connections across multiple paths, extending classical load-balancing to modern multi-path data centers.

usenix-2025-076.method: PluS is an ML compiler with pluggable scheduling strategies—the rules for arranging computations efficiently can be swapped or combined for different hardware. The system separates scheduling logic from the core compiler framework, enabling different optimization strategies to be applied independently. This lets the same compiler efficiently work with different hardware platforms (like GPUs or CPUs) by plugging in the right schedule.
usenix-2025-076.key_novelty: The core idea is pluggable scheduling: you can swap optimization rules for different hardware targets without modifying the compiler itself.

usenix-2025-088.method: In typical GPU programs, producers and consumers pause at synchronization barriers until everyone reaches the same point—wasting time waiting. WIC uses interrupt signals directed at thread groups (called warps) so producers can notify consumers asynchronously, without waiting for confirmation. Instead of repeatedly checking (polling) or pausing to synchronize, consumers continue other work until an interrupt wakes them when data arrives. This decouples their timing, hiding synchronization delays so they don't reduce overall GPU throughput.
usenix-2025-088.key_novelty: Interrupt signals to thread groups let producers notify waiting consumers automatically, eliminating the need for synchronized pause-point barriers.

usenix-2025-093.method: When multiple applications request GPU resources, the system intercepts these requests at the kernel level—the lowest software layer where the OS directly controls hardware. Based on each workload's priority, it schedules GPU compute and memory access across the applications while enforcing isolation boundaries so one app's GPU use doesn't affect another. This kernel-level approach means existing applications don't need to be modified and you don't need to create virtual GPUs.
usenix-2025-093.key_novelty: Intercepting GPU requests at the kernel level enables transparent, priority-aware GPU sharing and isolation without modifying applications or requiring virtual GPUs.

vlsid-2025-000.method: It uses a single resonant circuit (an electrical circuit tuned to specific frequencies) that matches impedances—aligning the power source and receiver for efficient energy transfer—at two different RF frequency bands without requiring electronic switches. By eliminating switches, the design stays compact and avoids the power losses that switches would introduce.
vlsid-2025-000.key_novelty: A single resonant circuit achieves switchless dual-band impedance matching for RF power harvesting systems.

usenix-2025-094.method: QFactory creates a specialized diagram called Qtile Graphs that maps how quantized operations (reduced-precision math that runs faster) flow through the hardware. The compiler then uses this diagram to apply three key optimizations: combining related operations into single instructions (kernel fusion) to cut overhead, choosing the best order to run operations while moving the least data possible between memory and processors (memory-aware scheduling), and grouping operations into blocks sized for the hardware (operation tiling). These optimizations work together to use more of the hardware's computing power and reduce the time spent moving data during inference.
usenix-2025-094.key_novelty: Qtile Graphs are a specialized diagram format for quantized operations that automatically exposes where the compiler can combine operations, minimize data movement, and organize work into hardware-efficient blocks.

usenix-2025-097.method: SAVE detects bit flips in GPU memory during model inference by checking for corruption in the data being used (applying error detection codes—mathematical checksums that reveal when bits have flipped). When corruption is found, it recovers either by re-running the affected computation or using backup data, all through software running on the GPU or CPU. This protects against bit flips without requiring special error-correcting hardware or keeping duplicate copies of the entire model in memory.
usenix-2025-097.key_novelty: Software-only protection against GPU memory bit flips during model inference, without special error-correcting hardware or data duplication.

usenix-2025-096.method: MARC detects motion in each video frame using optical flow (which tracks how pixels shift between frames) or frame differencing (which compares consecutive frames). Based on the detected motion, it dynamically adjusts how much data the cloud encoder sends (bitrate and resolution)—more for high-motion scenes and less for low-motion ones. The encoder uses this motion information to prioritize bandwidth for complex, fast-moving parts instead of wasting it on static scenes.
usenix-2025-096.key_novelty: The system continuously detects motion in video frames and automatically adjusts how much data (bitrate) gets sent based on that—allocating more bandwidth to motion-heavy scenes and less to static ones.

usenix-2025-091.method: PopFetcher predicts which experts will be heavily used by tracking recent activity patterns, then loads them into memory early—while the system is working on other tasks—so they're ready when needed. It treats the total training time as a math problem, figuring out exactly which experts are worth prefetching by eliminating unnecessary ones. During the backward pass—when the network learns by updating its weights—the system prioritizes communication across all processors, preventing bottlenecks.
usenix-2025-091.key_novelty: It predicts which experts will be needed from recent usage patterns, then mathematically determines which ones should be loaded in advance to minimize training time.

usenix-2025-098.method: The system watches how Ascend hardware behaves during training and gathers detailed performance measurements (a process called profiling). It analyzes these measurements to identify bottlenecks—the slow components that limit overall speed. Then it optimizes at two levels: adjusting low-level hardware settings using performance counters (built-in sensors that measure chip activity), and speeding up the training code itself.
usenix-2025-098.key_novelty: It combines hardware monitoring, bottleneck detection, and optimization into a single system designed specifically for model training on Ascend chips.

usenix-2025-095.method: FlexPipe groups sequences by actual length instead of padding them to uniform length. It then dynamically reconfigures the pipeline—the parallel stages that process data on the GPU—to match these groups. This eliminates wasted computation from padding while keeping all pipeline stages active and busy.
usenix-2025-095.key_novelty: Dynamically adjust the pipeline to match how input lengths are actually distributed, rather than enforcing fixed-length batching and padding.

vlsid-2025-003.method: A buck converter reduces voltage by rapidly switching transistors on and off in a controlled pattern. This design is fully autonomous, meaning internal feedback circuits continuously monitor the load's current demand and adjust the switching automatically without external commands. When the load suddenly demands more current (a transient spike), the converter detects this and instantly increases output to supply up to 1.2 amps, then returns to baseline when demand drops.
vlsid-2025-003.key_novelty: An auxiliary converter that automatically detects and supplies current (up to 1.2 amps) when the load suddenly demands power, without needing external control signals.

vlsid-2025-002.method: The approach uses a hardware circuit design (VLSI) implemented on an FPGA—a reconfigurable chip—to speed up Kaliski's Montgomery domain modular inversion algorithm. Bit-slicing is the key technique: each bit of the data is processed through parallel hardware paths, allowing many computations to run simultaneously. Montgomery domain is a number representation that trades one-time conversion work for much faster repeated multiplications during the algorithm's execution. This hardware-software combination significantly accelerates modular inversion, a crucial operation in elliptic curve cryptography.
vlsid-2025-002.key_novelty: The core contribution is using bit-sliced parallel hardware design on FPGAs to accelerate Kaliski's Montgomery domain modular inversion.

usenix-2025-099.method: HyperTurtle uses hardware acceleration to speed up nested virtual machines (VMs running inside other VMs). Nested VMs are slow because they repeatedly trigger 'exits'—expensive pauses when the inner VM needs to request something from the outer VM. By optimizing how these exits are handled at the hardware level, HyperTurtle cuts the overhead and makes nested VMs practical.
usenix-2025-099.key_novelty: Specialized hardware that accelerates nested virtual machines specifically, rather than just making regular VMs faster.

vlsid-2025-004.method: The approach trains a Convolutional Autoencoder (CAE)—a neural network that learns to compress and reconstruct images—on real silicon test data from various post-silicon validation projects. During training, the autoencoder learns to replicate normal oscilloscope images seen during testing. When presented with new test images, the autoencoder attempts to reconstruct them; if the reconstruction significantly differs from the original, that difference indicates an anomaly requiring investigation.
vlsid-2025-004.key_novelty: Using reconstruction error in a Convolutional Autoencoder to identify anomalies in post-silicon validation oscilloscope images.

vlsid-2025-005.method: The accelerator performs computations directly inside SRAM memory cells using analog electrical currents rather than digital signals. Instead of using voltage levels to encode data, it uses time-domain encoding—information is represented by how long or short electrical pulses last—allowing transistors to operate in the subthreshold regime (at voltages below where they would normally switch on, which dramatically reduces power consumption). Each computation cycle executes a multiply-and-accumulate operation (multiplying values and adding results to a running sum) by controlling these analog currents. The outcome is determined using differential current sensing, which compares currents flowing in opposite directions to produce the final result.
vlsid-2025-005.key_novelty: The core idea is combining time-domain encoding with subthreshold transistor operation and analog current-domain multiply-and-accumulate directly in SRAM cells to achieve energy-efficient in-memory computing.

vlsid-2025-008.method: They fabricated a two-dimensional tin sulfide (SnS) memristor, a device whose electrical resistance changes based on the history of voltages applied to it. The memristor was designed to follow an integrate-and-fire model: it accumulates electrical charge over time until reaching a threshold, then rapidly fires an electrical spike, just like a neuron's cell body (soma) does. Testing showed the memristor's electrical behavior matches experimentally observed neuronal somatic responses. This creates a hardware component that can be used directly in neuromorphic circuits (computing systems that mimic biological neural networks).
vlsid-2025-008.key_novelty: Using a 2D tin sulfide memristor's switching behavior to hardware-implement the integrate-and-fire model of biological neurons.

vlsid-2025-009.method: The transmitter sends data through inductive coupling links (electromagnetic connections between stacked chip layers) using differential signaling, which transmits both a signal and its inverse to cancel electrical noise. Instead of using two voltage levels like conventional systems, this design encodes information with three levels, fitting more data into each transmission cycle. The tri-level differential approach achieves a 5× improvement in signal-to-noise ratio while maintaining the same number of pins per unit area, making each connection point more efficient for densely stacked 3D circuits.
vlsid-2025-009.key_novelty: This design combines three-level voltage encoding with differential signaling in inductive-coupling links for 3D stacked chips, achieving a 5× improvement in signal-to-noise ratio without requiring additional pins.

vlsid-2025-007.method: Cond-FWC compresses memory blocks by analyzing cache lines—the fixed-size chunks of data moved between main memory and CPU—to identify which multi-byte words (values) appear most frequently. It eliminates these redundant words by storing them only once and replacing each occurrence with a short reference, shrinking the data size. This compression reduces the bandwidth required to transfer data between main memory and processor, lowering energy consumption.
vlsid-2025-007.key_novelty: The technique compresses cache lines by identifying frequently repeated words and storing them once with references instead of repeated copies.

vlsid-2025-020.method: The system uses Q-learning (a machine learning technique where a routing agent learns which paths work best through repeated trials and feedback) to manage data routing on a ZMesh NoC—a network topology that combines a regular mesh grid with zigzag routing patterns. When faults occur and damage parts of the network, the routing algorithm dynamically adapts its decisions based on what it has learned about which paths remain functional. This allows messages to automatically find alternate routes around broken connections without manual reconfiguration.
vlsid-2025-020.key_novelty: The core innovation is using Q-learning (machine learning that learns by trial and reward) to automatically adapt routing around network faults in a ZMesh NoC's mesh-zigzag topology.

vlsid-2025-012.method: The approach uses NSGA-II, a genetic algorithm that explores many potential designs and identifies the best combinations across competing objectives. It automatically tunes the number of basic logic blocks (CLBs), signal-processing units (DSPs), and memory blocks (BRAMs) in an FPGA design. By evaluating multiple configurations, it finds architectures that minimize both critical path delay—the time electrical signals take to traverse the circuit—and power consumption, tailored to the specific workload.
vlsid-2025-012.key_novelty: A genetic algorithm optimizes heterogeneous FPGA building blocks (CLBs, DSPs, BRAMs) to balance critical path delay and power consumption for specific workloads.

vlsid-2025-013.method: A central control system called the Resource Arbiter receives service requests that need fast responses and decides which edge server should handle each one. Since the servers are different types with different capabilities, the system continuously adapts these routing decisions based on real-time conditions to efficiently distribute work across the servers stationed at 5G network nodes.
vlsid-2025-013.key_novelty: The innovation is a centralized control system (Resource Arbiter) that adjusts request routing in real-time based on changing conditions across servers of different types.

vlsid-2025-017.method: The researchers built LESCA—a stream cipher (a type of encryption)—to run on quantum computers. They then tested how it would fare against Grover's search algorithm, a quantum attack that tries encryption keys much faster than traditional computers could. They verified that LESCA still meets the security standards set by NIST even under this quantum attack.
vlsid-2025-017.key_novelty: This is the first quantum implementation of LESCA, including analysis of how it resists Grover's search algorithm and compliance with NIST security standards.

vlsid-2025-019.method: The approach clusters (groups) incoming memory requests based on which memory rows they need to access. Modern DRAM uses a row buffer—a temporary holding area that keeps one row of data readily available. When requests keep asking for different rows, the buffer must constantly close the current row and load a new one; these switches are slow and waste memory bandwidth. By bundling requests that target the same row together, the system can process many requests from that row before switching—reducing the number of expensive row switches and making better use of available bandwidth.
vlsid-2025-019.key_novelty: Clustering memory requests by their target rows reduces DRAM row buffer switching overhead in manycore systems.

vlsid-2025-018.method: Creating patterned regions of N-well material (a semiconductor region type) in a p-type substrate shields spiral inductors from electrical losses at millimeter-wave frequencies. The patterns act as barriers that reduce eddy currents (unwanted circular electrical currents induced in the substrate) and capacitive coupling (unwanted electrical connections through the substrate). Two specific patterning structures suppress both types of losses simultaneously, improving inductor efficiency at high frequencies.
vlsid-2025-018.key_novelty: N-well patterning reduces substrate losses in millimeter-wave inductors without degrading their self-resonant frequency.

vlsid-2025-016.method: The approach models splitting a neural network between device and server as a mathematical optimization problem (Mixed Integer Linear Programming, or MILP). To solve this, they use an algorithm based on the knapsack problem—the classic technique for fitting different-sized items into a limited container—adapted to handle multiple constraints (like memory and computation speed limits) while respecting which network components must execute in order. This finds a way to keep the entire neural network running on just the edge device.
vlsid-2025-016.key_novelty: Local-Only Split Computing (LO-SC) runs the complete neural network on the edge device, preserving accuracy without any need for server communication.

vlsid-2025-022.method: The approach exploits symmetries—patterns where certain inputs behave the same way—to make Boolean function synthesis practical. Inspired by Edward's theory, it recursively breaks large problems into smaller subproblems with the same structure, synthesizing solutions for each piece. By reusing solutions across symmetrical parts, the method can handle Boolean functions with up to 20 inputs, whereas earlier approaches got stuck at 6.
vlsid-2025-022.key_novelty: By exploiting symmetries in Boolean functions and breaking them into recursive, interpretable structures, this method scales synthesis from 6 to 20 inputs.

vlsid-2025-006.method: The paper analyzes a multi-stage analog-to-digital converter (ADC) where each stage uses a successive approximation register (SAR) converter with noise shaping—pushing unwanted quantization noise to higher frequencies for the next stage to handle. The residue (leftover signal) from each stage is amplified and fed to the next stage in sequence. The paper examines how real-world imperfections in this residue amplifier degrade performance and identifies the critical design decisions needed to build these converters.
vlsid-2025-006.key_novelty: The paper shows how real-world imperfections in the residue amplifier affect multi-stage noise-shaped SAR converter performance and design choices.

vlsid-2025-015.method: The researchers design ternary logic cells (circuits using three operating states instead of the two used in standard transistors) using CNFETs (carbon nanotube transistors) and MOSFETs (standard silicon transistors), testing designs named NTI, PTI, and STI at 45nm technology. They exploit a key difference: CNFETs' threshold voltage—the electrical point where they turn on—can be tuned and adjusted, whereas MOSFETs cannot. This tunable property lets them optimize the ternary cells for both lower power consumption and superior performance.
vlsid-2025-015.key_novelty: Ternary logic cells built with carbon nanotube transistors (CNFETs) that have tunable threshold voltage achieve better power efficiency than those using standard silicon transistors (MOSFETs).

vlsid-2025-014.method: LAMA works by providing a configurable design that lets engineers adjust how much hardware resources the accelerator uses versus how fast it executes CNNs. Different applications have different priorities—some need maximum speed while others have tight limits on chip size or power consumption—so this tunability lets each designer optimize for their situation. Rather than buying a fixed accelerator, they can configure it to balance performance and resource use according to their specific constraints.
vlsid-2025-014.key_novelty: The innovation is providing an accelerator where designers can adjust the balance between hardware size and execution speed to match their application's specific needs.

vlsid-2025-026.method: Lichen watches a program as it runs and dynamically morphs (switches) between different processor cores, each supporting a different instruction set (the language a processor understands), and different execution modes—in-order (executing instructions strictly in sequence) versus out-of-order (reordering instructions for efficiency). Before each switch, a machine learning algorithm called CART predicts which combination will run the next code section fastest based on the program's current behavior. This continuous fine-grained optimization across cores and execution modes replaces older systems that could only switch at coarse program phases, missing many opportunities for improvement.
vlsid-2025-026.key_novelty: Instead of switching at coarse program phases, Lichen continuously morphs between heterogeneous processor cores and execution modes based on machine learning predictions, achieving 85.44%/91.35% accuracy.

vlsid-2025-023.method: The researchers tested how quantum pulses—the electromagnetic signals that control quantum gates—resist bit-flip errors (random bit changes in memory) when represented using two different number formats. They compared floating-point representation, which uses scientific notation, against fixed-point representation, where the decimal point is always in the same position. Using IBM quantum simulators, they measured which format better preserved the accuracy of the control signals when bit-flips occurred in the FPGA memory.
vlsid-2025-023.key_novelty: Fixed-point representation—where the decimal point is always in the same place—resists bit-flip errors (random bit changes in memory) better than floating-point representation (scientific notation) when storing quantum control signals.

vlsid-2025-029.method: TimeFloats performs floating-point arithmetic directly within memory, where data is stored, bypassing expensive analog-to-digital converters that translate continuous signals to numbers. It represents floating-point values using timing—the duration of electrical pulses—instead of voltage levels. The system uses purely digital logic, built using 15nm CMOS technology (a modern chip manufacturing process), to compute scalar products (multiplying pairs of numbers and summing them up).
vlsid-2025-029.key_novelty: The core innovation is encoding floating-point numbers through pulse timing rather than voltage level representation, enabling compute-in-memory training without requiring expensive analog-to-digital converters and achieving 22.1 TOPS/W.

vlsid-2025-021.method: The system uses bidirectional spiking neurons—artificial neurons that communicate through discrete electrical pulses and can send and receive signals simultaneously—to sense incoming signals. The design includes two switchable modes: surveillance mode for ultra-low-power operation, and precision modes for high-quality measurement. It is built using 65-nanometer TSMC technology, a commercial manufacturing process.
vlsid-2025-021.key_novelty: A signal sensor using bidirectional spiking neurons that switches between ultra-low-power surveillance mode (under 250 nanoWatts) and precision modes with signal-to-noise-and-distortion performance of 38, 49, and 53.6 decibels.

vlsid-2025-032.method: During random verification, a machine learning model predicts which test inputs (called stimulus) will exercise new parts of the chip design (provide incremental coverage). The system simulates only those inputs the model predicts will be productive, rather than running all random tests. This avoids wasting simulation time on test inputs that won't add new coverage.
vlsid-2025-032.key_novelty: Machine learning predicts which random test inputs will add new coverage, filtering out wasteful simulations before they run.

vlsid-2025-030.method: It uses a differential drive rectifier (comparing opposite-phase inputs) built in 65-nanometer CMOS technology. The circuit self-biases itself—automatically adjusting its internal voltage levels without needing external bias circuits—to minimize wasted power when current tries to flow backward (reverse conduction) while keeping normal power losses low. This automatic adaptation lets the rectifier maintain efficiency across a wide range of input power levels.
vlsid-2025-030.key_novelty: The self-bias scheme is the core innovation—it automatically adapts the rectifier to handle inputs spanning a 14 dB dynamic range (about 25 times variation in power) while converting RF energy at 60.5% peak efficiency, delivering a 74% improvement in dynamic range compared to cross-coupled rectifier designs.

vlsid-2025-025.method: The amplifier splits the input signal into two parallel paths and amplifies each using AlGaN/GaN HEMT transistors (gallium nitride devices that efficiently handle high power). When the amplified signals are recombined, this balanced configuration cancels out distortion that would otherwise occur, resulting in cleaner output and higher efficiency. To manage the heat from high-power operation and support high-frequency performance, all components are integrated on a single silicon carbide (SiC) substrate using UMS's 0.15-micrometer manufacturing process, which creates transistor gates small enough to operate at the required frequencies.
vlsid-2025-025.key_novelty: This balanced power amplifier design delivers 38dBm (about 6 watts) of output power with 32% power-added efficiency (the portion of input power converted to useful output) and 23.6dB gain (amplification factor) across the 18-22 GHz K-band frequency range.

vlsid-2025-028.method: The paper presents circuit modifications to 3nm GPU SRAM bit cells—the tiny storage units in graphics processors—to solve two problems that arise at ultra-low voltage (reduced power for energy efficiency): write failures and leakage current (power wasted through unwanted electrical flow). By adjusting how transistors are sized and connected within each cell, the approach improves the cell's ability to reliably store new data while reducing power loss.
vlsid-2025-028.key_novelty: The innovation is applying circuit design changes to 3nm GPU SRAM bit cells to enable reliable writes and reduce power leakage when operating at ultra-low voltage.

vlsid-2025-024.method: The approach expands the hardware design's behavior step-by-step and reorganizes what needs to be proven. Rather than proving each property from scratch, it reuses proof artifacts (frames—stored proof results) from earlier properties to speed up later ones. It uses statistics to choose the order in which to prove properties—solving simpler ones first to build up proof fragments that help with harder ones.
vlsid-2025-024.key_novelty: Strategic property ordering and proof-clause reuse solve 2461 additional properties.

vlsid-2025-027.method: SHAKTI protects hardware by inserting cascaded gated multiplexers (logic gates that route signals differently based on a secret key) connected in a daisy-chain, where each gate's output feeds the next. The entire chain is controlled by a 64-128 bit secret key. Because each gate depends on the previous gate's output, cracking one gate doesn't reveal the complete key—an attacker would need to understand how all the gates work together.
vlsid-2025-027.key_novelty: Linking gated multiplexers in a daisy-chain—where each logic gate routes signals based on a secret key and feeds the next—creates a hardware lock resistant to SAT solver and structural learning attacks, with only 19.32-19.45% additional chip area.

vlsid-2025-037.method: The researchers tested whether denormalized numbers—extremely small floating-point values that are expensive for hardware to handle—actually matter for neural network accuracy by running vision and speech recognition tasks. They then designed two versions of the hardware multiplier that performs matrix math: one supporting denormalized numbers and one without. They measured both designs on three key metrics: chip area required, execution speed, and power consumption.
vlsid-2025-037.key_novelty: You can remove denormalized number support from neural network hardware multipliers without affecting accuracy, while achieving significant efficiency gains in chip area, power, and speed.

vlsid-2025-036.method: E-DOSA processes spiking neural networks by grouping operations into time-batches—keeping computations for each time step together—and distributing kernel processing across a 2D grid of processing elements (a checkerboard of identical mini-processors working in sync). This layout keeps data in fast cache memory longer, allowing the processor to reuse the same values instead of repeatedly fetching them from slower main memory, which reduces bottlenecks and improves data efficiency.
vlsid-2025-036.key_novelty: Splitting computations into time-batches and distributing them across a 2D grid of processing elements achieves 1.2x average and 6.6x peak speedups by keeping data in fast cache memory.

vlsid-2025-033.method: The approach groups cells that handle critical datapath operations—the signal paths carrying computations—into clusters based on their connections. It then uses where these clusters will be physically placed to guide joint optimization of both the power grid and signal routing, rather than optimizing them separately. By combining manual design guidance with automated tools (a semi-custom strategy), designers can better manage competing demands: delivering sufficient power, routing signals efficiently, meeting area constraints, and preventing voltage drop and electromigration (metal degradation from high current flow).
vlsid-2025-033.key_novelty: By clustering datapath cells and optimizing their placement, the approach enables simultaneous power grid and signal routing improvements while meeting voltage stability and reliability requirements.

vlsid-2025-043.method: The converter transforms BCD numbers (where each decimal digit is stored separately in binary) into pure binary format using multiple parallel processing paths combined with pipelining (breaking the conversion into stages that process different numbers at the same time to improve throughput). It uses FPGA-specific dual-output lookup tables (small memory blocks that can produce two results per access) and carry chains (specialized circuits for efficiently combining arithmetic signals). The designers instantiate these hardware primitives directly rather than relying on a compiler to discover them, ensuring efficient use of the FPGA's resources.
vlsid-2025-043.key_novelty: Combining dual-output lookup tables with pipelined stages achieves better speed-area tradeoffs for BCD-to-binary conversion than traditional FPGA implementations.

vlsid-2025-035.method: Secure memory systems protect data using Merkle trees—hierarchical structures where each node verifies the ones below it, creating a chain of trust from individual memory locations to a single root node. Normally, verifying or updating any data requires traversing this entire chain, from the leaf to the root. This approach identifies intermediate nodes (nodes partway up the tree) as additional roots and stores them in the secure processor alongside the main root. By allowing updates to stop at the nearest intermediate root instead of traversing to the top, the method reduces verification latency while preserving security.
vlsid-2025-035.key_novelty: The key innovation is a multi-root forest structure that promotes intermediate tree nodes to root status, reducing the path length needed for security verification.

vlsid-2025-040.method: A 3:2 compressor (a circuit combining three input bits into two) is structured using two-stage stacking—organizing it in two layers to shrink its size. Smaller circuits use less power and operate faster. The design is tested in 4-bit, 8-bit, and 16-bit multipliers.
vlsid-2025-040.key_novelty: Two-stage stacking of the 3:2 compressor improves the power-delay product (power consumption times response time) by 47.30% on average compared to existing 3:2 compressor designs.

vlsid-2025-031.method: A Siamese neural network (two identical networks that compare image pairs to detect differences) learns to estimate camera pan and tilt angles. The inference runs on Raspberry Pi's CPU at ~17 frames per second through optimization, avoiding the need for external hardware.
vlsid-2025-031.key_novelty: A Siamese network optimized for CPU enables real-time camera angle tracking on Raspberry Pi (17 Hz), achieving 18.45x faster inference and 3x better accuracy than ResNet-18.

vlsid-2025-038.method: The system builds a neural network with two parts: an encoder that compresses audio and a decoder that expands it while filtering out noise. To minimize power and silicon area, it uses quantization—representing numbers with fewer bits instead of full precision—throughout the network. The design also includes a specialized routing scheme that reduces how often the processing elements need to access the fast on-chip memory by 5-9x, which significantly cuts power consumption.
vlsid-2025-038.key_novelty: The core innovation combines quantized neural networks (saving 75% memory) with specialized memory routing (cutting on-chip access 5-9x) to achieve a real-time speech denoiser in just 0.75mm² at 407 microwatts on 28nm silicon.

vlsid-2025-046.method: First, the researchers used first-principles density functional theory (DFT, a computational method that predicts how electrons behave in molecules and materials) with Gaussian 09W and GaussView 6.0 software to simulate acetaldehyde molecules sticking to pristine graphene and graphene doped with gold atoms. They then analyzed the electronic structure using frontier molecular orbitals (the electron clouds that participate in reactions), electrostatic potential (how electrical charge distributes), electron localization function (where electrons actually spend time), density of states (how many energy levels are available), band structure (pathways for electron movement), and Mulliken charges (calculated electron distributions). These measurements revealed why gold-doping strengthens acetaldehyde detection.
vlsid-2025-046.key_novelty: Gold-doped graphene detects acetaldehyde gas better than pristine graphene because gold atoms enhance the electronic properties and create stronger molecular attachment points.

vlsid-2025-045.method: The researchers used TCAD simulations (a tool that models how semiconductors work electrically) to test how manufacturing variations affect 3D NAND memory cells. They changed key dimensions—cell spacing, oxide layer thicknesses, channel thickness, and plug depth—and measured how each change affected the string current (the electrical current flowing through the memory cell) and related electrical properties such as voltage thresholds and gain. This reveals which manufacturing imperfections have the biggest impact on memory performance and reliability.
vlsid-2025-045.key_novelty: This work systematically analyzes how manufacturing process variations affect 3D NAND string current and related electrical properties (ion current, threshold voltage, gain, and subthreshold swing) using TCAD simulation.

vlsid-2025-041.method: The approach uses a Virtex-7 FPGA (a reconfigurable chip that can be customized to perform specific computational tasks) to implement two consecutive SHA-256 hash operations. The hardware circuits within the FPGA are optimized to efficiently process both hash operations. Performance is then compared against purpose-built chips called ASICs built at 180-nanometer and 90-nanometer process technology scales.
vlsid-2025-041.key_novelty: An FPGA design for dual SHA-256 hashing that runs 6.09% faster and achieves 13.40% better computational efficiency than standard SHA-256.

vlsid-2025-042.method: This voltage regulator stabilizes input voltage and outputs your choice of voltage from 5V to 55V using high-voltage CMOS circuitry (transistors at 0.18-micrometer scale designed to handle high voltages). It can sink 550mA of current—meaning it can pull that much current from circuits connected to it. It's designed as the low-side (ground-side) supply for gate drivers, which are circuits that control high-voltage power switches in cryo-cooler electronics.
vlsid-2025-042.key_novelty: The key advance is achieving 550mA current-sinking capability (pulling current from downstream circuits) in a tiny 0.09mm² chip built with high-voltage CMOS, while keeping output voltage stable as input voltage and current demands vary.

vlsid-2025-034.method: A re-convergent clock mesh distributes the timing signal throughout a large AI processor through paths that branch out and then reconverge (rejoin), reducing power consumption and electrical noise compared to traditional designs like flex-H trees and forwarded spines. This was verified using HSPICE electrical simulation and PrimeTime timing analysis.
vlsid-2025-034.key_novelty: A re-convergent clock mesh (where timing-signal paths branch out and then rejoin) achieves 20% lower power consumption at a given clock speed, or runs 20% faster at the same power level.

vlsid-2025-044.method: Harmony measures how different static/dynamic memory allocations affect application performance by running the application and monitoring its behavior. Based on these measurements, it identifies which memory should be allocated upfront (static, avoiding runtime overhead) versus allocated on-demand (dynamic, more flexible but slower). It then recommends a near-optimal split between these two approaches.
vlsid-2025-044.key_novelty: Using runtime measurements to optimize the balance between static and dynamic memory allocation achieves 68% latency improvement over purely dynamic allocation and 29% over purely static allocation.

vlsid-2025-047.method: The approach watches an application run and automatically divides its code into two groups: the parts the CPU handles efficiently and the parts that would run faster on near-memory processors (specialized cores positioned closer to where data is stored). Unlike previous methods that need a large set of labeled examples to learn from, this approach figures out these groups on its own. It then offloads only the memory-intensive portions—the parts where the application spends most time waiting for data—so the overall performance improves without wasting computing power on unnecessary offloading.
vlsid-2025-047.key_novelty: This is the first approach to use unsupervised machine learning—learning without labeled training data—to automatically decide which parts of an application should run on near-memory processing, skipping the time-consuming step of creating labeled datasets while achieving selective offloading of only the beneficial code regions.

vlsid-2025-055.method: The method combines two machine learning techniques—a multilayer perceptron (a neural network with multiple layers) and a random forest (an algorithm that builds many decision trees and averages their predictions)—to forecast three electrical properties of double-gate MOSFETs: drain current (how much current flows through), gate-source capacitance (electrical storage between gate and source), and drain-gate capacitance (electrical storage between drain and gate), based on device dimensions and manufacturing variations. A separate classification model predicts channel length from devices with unknown specifications. Accuracy is measured using MSE (mean squared error), RMSE (root mean squared error), and R² (proportion of variation explained).
