vlsid-2025-055.key_novelty: This is the first approach combining a multilayer perceptron and random forest to predict double-gate MOSFET electrical behavior across manufacturing process variations.

vlsid-2025-050.method: CRIS-b algorithm solves a critical efficiency problem in the Barrett method, which computes remainders after division (modulo reduction)—the standard approach produces intermediate values that grow too large, slowing down hardware implementations. It uses conditional switching to choose between different calculation methods at each step, keeping intermediate results smaller and enabling faster execution. Unlike conventional approaches, CRIS-b handles both positive and negative numbers in a single unified process, which is necessary for the mathematical transformations (NTT butterfly operations) used in CRYSTALS-Kyber post-quantum encryption. The algorithm was implemented on an Artix-7 FPGA (a reprogrammable hardware processor).
vlsid-2025-050.key_novelty: CRIS-b eliminates the size-expansion bottleneck of modulo reduction by conditionally switching between calculation methods, enabling unified handling of both positive and negative numbers needed for post-quantum encryption.

vlsid-2025-053.method: The method shrinks memory by splitting full images into smaller patches before processing—smaller data requires less space for intermediate results. It uses a unified architecture handling both standard convolution (filtering to compress information) and transpose convolution (expanding information back), eliminating separate pathways' memory overhead. Quantization reduces memory further by storing weights with fewer bits. Testing on resource-constrained edge hardware confirms the practical benefit.
vlsid-2025-053.key_novelty: Combining patch-based processing with a unified architecture for both standard and transpose convolutions (the compression and expansion operations in U-Net's skip connections) and quantization enables efficient training on edge devices.

vlsid-2025-048.method: The method assigns physical wires to electrodes on a biochip—a device that manipulates tiny liquid droplets for laboratory testing. It optimizes this wire assignment to achieve three goals together: detecting hard-to-notice tampering attempts, ensuring wires can be physically routed without conflicts, and reducing electrode wear by minimizing switching. By addressing all three goals in a single optimization rather than separately, the method achieves better security, feasible wiring, and long-term reliability.
vlsid-2025-048.key_novelty: This is the first pin-mapping method that simultaneously detects tampering, ensures physical routing feasibility, and reduces electrode wear.

vlsid-2025-057.method: The approach trains neural networks—specifically convolutional neural networks and variational autoencoders (machine learning models that learn patterns from image-like data)—on thousands of thermal simulations generated by Synopsys TCAD for 14 nm SOI FinFET chips. These trained networks predict heat distribution in silicon much faster than running Finite Element Method simulations. Accuracy is evaluated using image-comparison metrics: mean squared error (the average difference between predicted and actual values), structural similarity (how visually similar predicted heat maps are to real ones), and intersection over union (how much predicted hot zones overlap with actual hot zones).
vlsid-2025-057.key_novelty: This is the first application of convolutional neural networks and variational autoencoders (machine learning models trained on examples) to predict thermal patterns in SOI FinFET chips, combining the precision of detailed Finite Element simulations with the speed of machine learning.

vlsid-2025-052.method: The researchers optimized the PRESENT cipher (a lightweight encryption method) by redesigning its Substitution Permutation Network module—the component that scrambles data through substitution and permutation steps. They used three strategies: rewiring the data pathways, routing input data through substitution and permutation layers via multiplexers (electronic switches that intelligently direct signals), and adding hardware units to reduce power consumption. The design was tested on a NEXYS4 DDR FPGA operating at 13.56 MHz, the frequency used in RFID systems.
vlsid-2025-052.key_novelty: The design comprehensively optimizes the substitution-permutation network module of the PRESENT cipher to reduce power consumption while maintaining high encryption speed and efficient use of FPGA circuitry.

vlsid-2025-049.method: The wearable encrypts health data (such as ECG signals) using a secret key and broadcasts the encrypted data wirelessly over RF channels like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. Simultaneously, it sends the unencrypted key through the wearer's body tissue using a human body communication channel—electrical signals that only travel through direct skin contact when touched. Only a receiver in direct physical contact captures the key this way, while the encrypted data broadcasts to anyone in RF range. The intended receiver combines the key received through body contact with the wireless-received data to decrypt the health information.
vlsid-2025-049.key_novelty: The innovation is using human body tissue as the encryption-key distribution channel while sending encrypted health data wirelessly, so only an authorized person touching the device can decrypt the transmitted data.

vlsid-2025-054.method: DNA sequences are converted to binary numbers (0s and 1s) and compared using fast bitwise logic operations (XOR and AND operations, which identify matching and different bits) performed directly inside resistive memory rather than the CPU. Specialized circuits detect the results in-memory without moving data, and mutation classification—identifying where sequences differ—happens at the memory level. The architecture was designed and verified through simulation at 65-nanometer technology.
vlsid-2025-054.key_novelty: This is the first system combining in-memory bitwise DNA comparisons (using resistive memory to perform logical operations on individual bits) with nearby mutation classification, avoiding the slow data transfers to the processor that limit conventional approaches.

vlsid-2025-056.method: The algorithm schedules biological sample preparation on a digital microfluidic biochip—a tiny device that moves and mixes liquid droplets using electrical fields. It divides the preparation process into time intervals and plans which mixing operations to do when, minimizing six resource constraints: the number of input pipes (entry points for samples), mixer units (blending zones), storage units (holding spaces), total mixing steps, storage steps, and fluid-shifting moves. The method was compared against an existing baseline called Reservoir Minimizing Scheduling to measure improvements.
vlsid-2025-056.key_novelty: Using time-interval scheduling to jointly minimize all resource needs—input pipes, mixer units, storage units, mixing operations, storage operations, and fluid movements—instead of optimizing each constraint separately.

vlsid-2025-059.method: Uses reconfigurable transistors (RFETs—transistors that can be switched between positive-channel and negative-channel types) embedded in logic cells designed to sense small ripples in the power supply. Upon detecting an LLSI attack, the RFETs automatically corrupt the circuit's internal state by applying a biased voltage to their control pins, scrambling the data an attacker is trying to read via optical imaging. A biasing circuit holds these control pins at a steady voltage during the attack to ensure reliable state destruction. The approach was tested on combinational logic and D-latch cells.
vlsid-2025-059.key_novelty: First defense against LLSI attacks using RFET transistors, which reconfigure themselves during an attack to automatically destroy stored state, eliminating the need for external laser sensors or large power-supply changes.

vlsid-2025-060.method: Instead of using separate electronics and bulky physical wires to connect distributed controllers, the system puts all control functions into a single integrated circuit (ASIC—a custom-designed chip). Inside this chip, a pattern generator creates the signals that would normally travel through cables: telecommand signals (instructions sent to equipment), telemetry signals (sensor readings), and radar timing signals. By generating signals directly on the chip rather than transmitting them through external cables, the system eliminates the need for bulky differential interconnect lines (high-quality shielded cables that prevent signal distortion between distant control units).
vlsid-2025-060.key_novelty: The core innovation is consolidating distributed controller functions into a single integrated circuit that uses an internal pattern generator to create control signals on-chip, eliminating the bulky external interconnect harness.

vlsid-2025-058.method: The researchers measured how HZO ferroelectric memory devices behave at different temperatures and simulated their performance in 3D stacked memory systems for neural network accelerators. They discovered that higher temperatures make the ferroelectric material switch (flip its polarization, which stores data) more easily, requiring less electrical energy. They exploited this by developing a voltage adjustment strategy that reduces write power when the device is hot, cutting energy use without sacrificing reliability.
vlsid-2025-058.key_novelty: This is the first approach to reduce ferroelectric RAM write energy in 3D memory by exploiting temperature-dependent switching behavior in neural network accelerators.

vlsid-2025-062.method: The researchers train and test quantum machine learning models on several different quantum computers, each with different qubit types, connection patterns between qubits, and noise levels (errors in computation). They measure both how well the models work and how long users have to wait to access each machine, then analyze which hardware choice completes the training job fastest overall.
vlsid-2025-062.key_novelty: By switching between multiple quantum computers based on queue wait times, you can train quantum machine learning models with nearly the same accuracy but significantly faster than waiting for a single machine.

vlsid-2025-051.method: The design uses Intel 4 technology with EMIB packaging (connecting separate silicon components through embedded copper links) to build the memory PHY. It replaces standard transmitters with unterminated, low-swing versions (simpler senders that use less power by skipping termination resistors) and uses unmatched receiver paths (receivers that skip impedance-matching circuitry to save power). To maintain timing accuracy across temperature changes, it includes a linear voltage regulator (which removes electrical noise to reduce timing jitter), a per-bit deskew training algorithm (which adjusts the arrival time of each data line), and periodic sampling-point updates (which continuously check and shift when signals should be read).
vlsid-2025-051.key_novelty: The core idea is using simpler, unterminated transmitter and receiver designs combined with dynamic per-bit calibration and adaptive sampling-point updates to achieve both ultra-low power consumption and reliable high-speed operation.

vlsid-2025-071.method: The approach uses a neural network (GNN) trained to understand hardware circuit structure—creating mathematical embeddings via the DeepGate2 tool—to predict which formal verification engine will perform best at each depth of checking. Rather than using a single engine for the entire verification process, it learns to switch between different engines as it digs deeper into the circuit, based on what the neural network discovers about the circuit's structural properties.
vlsid-2025-071.key_novelty: Using neural circuit embeddings to automatically select which formal verification engine to use and when, replacing fixed strategies with machine-learned decisions.

vlsid-2025-069.method: This approach combines two sorting techniques to assign tasks to cores in a Network-on-Chip efficiently. First, Bitonic sorting—a high-throughput parallel sorting method—quickly places tasks across cores as a starting point. Second, Selection sorting (which picks the best option one at a time) refines these placements, switching between two modes to optimize for either reliability or energy efficiency depending on system needs. The method was tested on an FPGA with both real workloads and synthetic benchmarks.
vlsid-2025-069.key_novelty: The core idea is a two-stage hybrid sorting approach for assigning tasks to Network-on-Chip cores: fast Bitonic sorting provides an initial placement, and then Selection sorting refines it using dual-mode adaptation that prioritizes either reliability or energy efficiency.

vlsid-2025-068.method: The team tested many combinations of pooling methods—techniques that reduce the amount of data in neural networks while preserving important information—across different layers of three real neural networks: AlexNet, UNet, and VGG-16. They combined max pooling (which keeps the largest value in each region) with deviation-based methods such as AAD, BWAD, and AMD (which keep values that stand out significantly from the average). They then built this design twice: once as an FPGA (field-programmable gate array—reconfigurable hardware) on a Xilinx Zedboard, and once as a custom integrated circuit using Cadence tools at 45-nanometer scale.
vlsid-2025-068.key_novelty: Using different pooling methods—mixing max pooling with deviation-based techniques—tailored to each layer of a neural network accelerator outperforms applying the same pooling method throughout.

vlsid-2025-061.method: The design builds a specialized helper processor using the open-source RISC-V instruction set to handle vector operations—processing multiple measurements at once—offloading this work from the main processor. The heart-rate-variability algorithm is optimized for edge devices by processing data in small chunks, allowing it to run on memory-constrained wearables without requiring large data buffers.
vlsid-2025-061.key_novelty: A vector coprocessor—a helper processor that calculates multiple heart measurements in parallel—built on the open-source RISC-V standard enables efficient heart-rate-variability monitoring on memory-constrained wearables.

vlsid-2025-065.method: The design chains frequency multipliers to reach ×18 total multiplication: two triplers (each ×3) and one doubler (×2). The first tripler uses a tail inductor—a coiled circuit element in the power supply—to amplify the 3rd harmonic (a naturally occurring higher-frequency component). The second tripler uses capacitive neutralization (adding capacitors to suppress specific frequencies) to eliminate the fundamental frequency while boosting the 135 GHz output. Buffer circuits between stages are optimized to amplify harmonics before passing the signal forward, and a final push-push doubler (using symmetric transistor pairs) efficiently multiplies by 2 to reach the 0.27 THz target.
vlsid-2025-065.key_novelty: The design uses two different tripler techniques (inductor-boosted harmonic amplification and capacitive fundamental rejection) with optimized harmonic buffering to efficiently achieve ×18 frequency multiplication at 0.27 THz.

vlsid-2025-064.method: The solution works in two stages: First, an automated Failure Mode Analysis system that systematically identifies all the ways an electronic system could fail, ensuring consistency and reducing manual effort. Second, the system uses GCNII (a machine learning model that learns from how circuit components connect together) to automatically identify which parts are most critical to safety and predict how damaging faults in each would be, accelerating the fault injection testing process.
vlsid-2025-064.key_novelty: The key innovation is applying GCNII (a graph neural network that, unlike earlier models, can handle the depth and complexity of modern electronic designs) to automatically identify safety-critical components and predict their vulnerability to faults.

vlsid-2025-063.method: The approach combines standard CMOS transistors with memristors (programmable resistance components), which can be more power-efficient when a circuit is allowed to make small computational errors—a strategy called approximate computing. It starts with an approximate subtractor (a circuit that performs subtraction with intentional small errors to save power), then uses this as a building block for a divider circuit (which performs division) at the 28nm manufacturing node. The hybrid CMOS-memristor topology lets the memristor handle certain operations more efficiently than CMOS alone, reducing overall power consumption.
vlsid-2025-063.key_novelty: This work is the first to combine memristors with standard CMOS transistors in an approximate divider circuit, demonstrating that memristors can successfully improve power efficiency in division operations.

vlsid-2025-073.method: When adding numbers in a circuit, carry propagation—where each bit must wait for the previous bit's result—creates the main delay bottleneck. This design speeds it up by combining two techniques: Carry-Look-Ahead predicts what each carry bit will be without sequential waiting, while Carry-Select pre-computes results assuming both possible carry values and instantly selects the right one. The implementation uses Domino Logic (a fast circuit style that trades increased power for lower delay) and routes carry signals through a Manchester Carry Chain (an optimized pathway design). It includes a low-power partially static flip-flop (a hybrid between fully dynamic and fully static logic) that samples the result on the falling clock edge.
vlsid-2025-073.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining Carry-Look-Ahead and Carry-Select in a Manchester Carry Chain topology using Domino Logic.

vlsid-2025-076.method: The approach automatically scans the signal interconnect (the wires connecting different parts of a chip) using a multi-variate cost function (a formula balancing multiple factors like speed and power consumption) to find routes that aren't optimally designed. For each poorly routed connection, the system recommends better track assignments (alternative routing paths) and incrementally re-routes the interconnect step-by-step, allowing the process to scale efficiently across large designs.
vlsid-2025-076.key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically detecting suboptimal signal routes in completed designs and recommending incremental re-routing improvements to gain timing and power efficiency, regardless of which tool originally created the design.

vlsid-2025-070.method: The design implements a voltage-controlled oscillator using eight cascaded delay stages arranged in a ring (a pseudo-differential ring oscillator, which compares complementary signals to reduce noise) built with 6nm FinFET transistors. It operates at 0.8V supply voltage (with ±5% tolerance) and maintains operation across -40 to +125°C. Two different delay cell architectures (BDC-1 and BDC-2) are designed and compared to find which achieves the wide frequency tuning range needed for high-speed data link applications.
vlsid-2025-070.key_novelty: An 8-phase ring oscillator that achieves wide frequency tuning through comparison of two delay cell architectures (BDC-1 and BDC-2) optimized for 6nm FinFET.

vlsid-2025-067.method: FPUGen automatically generates custom floating-point multiply-add hardware for FPGAs, letting you set the precision (number of bits) for the mantissa and exponent—the two parts of any floating-point number. The generated accelerator can run multiple operations simultaneously at different precisions—you can choose: one 32-bit, two 32-bit tensor operations, two 16-bit, or three 16-bit bfloat operations per cycle (1×SP32, 2×TF32, 2×HP16, or 3×BF16). It includes dynamic precision rounding during computation and lets you choose between pipelined (staged for speed) and non-pipelined architectures.
vlsid-2025-067.key_novelty: Automatically generates floating-point hardware where multiple parallel operations each use only the precision they need.

vlsid-2025-074.method: The approach trains a conditional GAN (a machine learning system that transforms images) on pictures of optimally-wired nets. Each training image shows connection points paired with the shortest routing connecting them, teaching the GAN to recognize efficient wiring patterns. Once trained, the system generates new routings by presenting an unrouted net to the GAN, which outputs the predicted optimal wiring pattern.
vlsid-2025-074.key_novelty: The key idea is treating RSMT construction as an image-to-image translation problem, using conditional GANs instead of traditional routing algorithms.

vlsid-2025-072.method: The system trains neural networks at the interfaces between chip components, using real performance data from complete SOC designs to teach them how different design parameters affect performance. Instead of building an expensive full-chip model, it composes these interface-level networks—combining them according to how the components connect—into a single system-level performance predictor. This composed predictor then guides a search algorithm to efficiently find the best parameter configurations.
vlsid-2025-072.key_novelty: By composing neural networks trained at component interfaces, the method builds a system-level performance predictor that avoids expensive full-chip modeling.

vlsid-2025-075.method: The approach trains a machine learning model on real data from thousands of previous chip designs at sub-10nm scale (an extremely advanced manufacturing process), typically running at 1 GHz clock speeds. The model learns to predict the final power consumption, speed, and physical area of a new chip directly from intermediate design data—avoiding the need to run complete engineering tool simulations. With 6-10% accuracy, this early prediction can happen in parallel with other design work or even before the simulation tools start.
vlsid-2025-075.key_novelty: Machine learning trained on past chip designs can directly predict a new chip's power consumption, performance, and area early in the process with 6-10% accuracy, eliminating the need to wait for slow tool simulations.

vlsid-2025-077.method: An electronic multiplexer (switch) selects between the host computer's clock and an internal relaxation oscillator—a simple oscillator that doesn't need a crystal. Control circuits automatically detect when the host's clock stops and switch to the internal clock without any glitches or need for external signals. The timing circuit maintains high precision while data flows from the host, then accepts lower precision from the internal oscillator as it completes the final memory writes.
vlsid-2025-077.key_novelty: An SSD generates a crystal-free reference clock by automatically switching between a host-provided clock and an internal oscillator, with seamless operation requiring no external control signals and graceful acceptance of lower timing precision when needed.

vlsid-2025-066.method: The system converts ECG heart signals into spike patterns using an Adaptive Exponential (AdEx) neuron model—an artificial neuron that mimics how brain cells work by firing discrete electrical pulses (spikes) and adjusting its firing threshold. This conversion runs on an FPGA (reprogrammable hardware) for real-time processing. From the spike patterns, the system extracts two measurements—Individual Flutter Width (duration of each irregular heartbeat) and Atrial Cycle Length (time between beats)—to detect and classify atrial flutter.
vlsid-2025-066.key_novelty: It applies the AdEx spiking neuron model to detect atrial flutter from ECG signals.

vlsid-2025-080.method: The chip uses a modified 9-transistor SRAM cell (a memory storage unit) with separate wires for reading data and separate wires for writing data—instead of sharing the same wires. This lets the peripheral circuitry (supporting logic around the memory) perform multi-operand Boolean operations (logical AND, OR, NOT combinations on multiple inputs) using compute blocks, equality checkers, and product-line circuits that apply DeMorgan's theorem—a mathematical rule for converting AND operations into OR operations and vice versa.
vlsid-2025-080.key_novelty: The core idea is to separate read and write paths in SRAM cells so that peripheral compute blocks can directly execute any arbitrary Boolean operation—including XOR (exclusive OR, true when inputs are different)—on multiple data inputs simultaneously, within the memory system.

vlsid-2025-078.method: The method automatically transforms circuit designs at the register-transfer level (RTL—the design stage before physical hardware is built) by combining three techniques: duplicating circuit components that process secrets, balancing register operations to equalize timing patterns, and using clock gating (selectively disabling clocks to hide active elements). These transformations randomize the power consumption so it no longer correlates with secret data, defeating power-based attacks on cryptographic keys. The hardened design is validated with TVLA (Test Vector Leakage Assessment), which verifies that power consumption no longer leaks information.
vlsid-2025-078.key_novelty: The core innovation is an automated RTL-level technique combining register duplication, balancing, and clock gating to randomize power consumption and reduce dynamic power draw, preventing power side-channel attacks on cryptographic hardware.

vlsid-2025-086.method: The system uses PYNQ (a programmable system-on-chip platform) to process millimeter-wave radar signals in real-time. The signal processing pipeline has four steps: converting distance measurements into a frequency spectrum using Range FFT, extracting and unwrapping the phase (angle) to track how the signal changes over time, filtering out noise with an FIR filter, and computing respiratory rate using multiple different estimation techniques. Finally, it combines these estimates using weighted averages calculated by a quadratic cost function, which mathematically determines how much weight each technique should contribute to maximize overall accuracy.
vlsid-2025-086.key_novelty: The system combines multiple respiratory rate estimation methods using weights optimized by a quadratic cost function on the PYNQ embedded platform, achieving higher accuracy than any single technique alone.

vlsid-2025-083.method: The system uses a Return Address Stack (RAS)—a small piece of hardware that remembers where a program should jump back to after a function call—to catch buffer overflow attacks targeting control flow. When an attacker tries to overwrite this return address through a buffer overflow, the RAS detects the mismatch and blocks it. The solution reuses existing processor hardware with minimal new circuitry, keeping performance and chip area overhead low. The protection was validated using buffer-intensive benchmarks and the RIPE benchmark (a standard test for overflow attack vulnerabilities).
vlsid-2025-083.key_novelty: RISC-V processors can defend against buffer overflow and Spectre attacks targeting the return address stack by reusing existing hardware with minimal added chip area or processing delay.

vlsid-2025-079.method: DuRTL tracks information flow through hardware designs by attaching unique labels—called tags—to signals in Verilog and VHDL code. Each tag records where the signal originated and when, then stays attached as the signal moves through logic gates and connections. By following the tagged signals, the tool creates a complete record of how information propagates from inputs to outputs.
vlsid-2025-079.key_novelty: DuRTL is an open-source tool that automatically tracks how data flows through Verilog and VHDL hardware designs at the register-transfer level—the layer where individual signals and logic gates are visible—even in unfamiliar or legacy designs.

vlsid-2025-085.method: They used computational models to simulate how an iron-gold magnetic tunnel junction (two magnetic layers separated by a thin insulating barrier) responds to physical stress. The simulations combined two mathematical techniques: one that maps how electrons distribute in the material (density functional theory), and another that calculates electron flow through the barrier when conditions are changing (non-equilibrium Green's function method). They tested both stretching and squeezing the material, measuring how these deformations affected tunnel magnetoresistance (the resistance difference based on whether the magnetic layers align or oppose each other) by examining the energy states that favor electrons spinning one direction.
vlsid-2025-085.key_novelty: This analysis combines density functional theory and non-equilibrium Green's function calculations to show that physical stress reduces tunnel magnetoresistance in iron-gold magnetic tunnel junctions by changing the electron energy bands.

vlsid-2025-087.method: They used 2D computer simulations (calibrated to real measurements) to study how current leaks in these ultra-small transistors, focusing on three pathways: gate-induced drain leakage (where the gate's electric field causes electrons to tunnel through an energy barrier they normally can't cross, a quantum effect), direct tunneling through the gate's insulating layer, and inefficient current spreading through the bulk material instead of the intended path. They compared how these leakage mechanisms differ between conventional silicon and 4H-SiC, a semiconductor that withstands higher voltages and temperatures.
vlsid-2025-087.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive analysis of current leakage in sub-10nm 4H-SiC junctionless transistors, showing that direct gate tunneling and volume depletion—rather than the mechanisms that dominate in silicon—are the key sources of current loss.

vlsid-2025-081.method: We designed adder circuits using MAGIC logic—a method that performs calculations by moving electrical charges through memristors (tiny variable-resistance components arranged in a grid). A single full adder (the circuit unit that adds two bits and a carry bit) requires just 10 computational steps on a 3×7 memristor grid. We tested two designs using different levels of parallelism, and both ran 2× faster than existing memristor-based adders.
vlsid-2025-081.key_novelty: The key innovation is using parallel row-and-column processing in the memristor-based adder circuit to reduce computational steps and double the calculation speed compared to earlier sequential designs.

vlsid-2025-082.method: The method uses YOLOv8, a computer vision system that detects and segments objects frame-by-frame in video. To fit this on the resource-constrained Intel Nezha embedded platform, it applies quantization—a compression technique that represents the model's numbers using fewer bits in formats like INT8, FP32, or Fixed-Posit—reducing memory and computation demands. It includes brightness verification preprocessing to handle low-light conditions before processing each frame. Asynchronous FIFO pipelining—processing data without waiting for previous operations to complete—increases throughput by overlapping computations.
vlsid-2025-082.key_novelty: This is the first real-time system for low-light video that detects and outlines each individual object, running on embedded RGB cameras, by using Fixed-Posit—a number-compression technique in the EQyTorch framework—which consumes less power and runs faster than existing INT8 and FP32 approaches.

vlsid-2025-091.method: The startup works in two stages: first, it charges the ring oscillator—a chain of logic gates that creates oscillations—by directly injecting current into its internal nodes while running in open-loop mode (without feedback control). Once the oscillation frequency stabilizes, the circuit switches to closed-loop operation (where feedback maintains stable frequency). This two-stage approach uses current mirrors (circuits that copy currents) and simple digital logic to control the transition, keeping total area overhead minimal.
vlsid-2025-091.key_novelty: The core idea is using an open-loop startup phase with injected current, then switching to closed-loop feedback once the oscillator settles, which achieves 3x faster startup time (from 466 microseconds down to 150 microseconds) without increasing the circuit's continuous power draw and with minimal additional chip area.

vlsid-2025-093.method: The technique works in two stages. First, it studies the patterns in data already stored in memory to create reusable templates called affine masks. Then, before writing new data, it transforms the incoming data using XOR operations (a basic bitwise operation) with these masks, making it match the stored data as closely as possible. By reducing the difference between what's stored and what's coming in—the bit disparity—it cuts down how many write operations are needed, which slows down memory wear.
vlsid-2025-093.key_novelty: The core idea is pre-processing incoming data with position-affine masks (templates based on existing memory patterns) using XOR operations to minimize how many bits actually need to be flipped when writing, extending memory lifetime.

vlsid-2025-089.method: Sensors detect your finger movements and the device instantly processes this data to provide real-time feedback. A motor system (adaptive actuation) amplifies your hand's movements, adjusting its support based on what you're trying to do. A mobile app guides you through therapeutic exercises and interactive games using three control modes: manual assistance, cyclic training, and task-specific routines.
vlsid-2025-089.key_novelty: A lightweight hand assistant that gives instant feedback on your movements, automatically adjusts its support while you're using it, and pairs with a mobile app to guide your rehabilitation exercises.

vlsid-2025-088.method: The work develops a design framework for building ReLU activation circuits from p-bits—stochastic computing elements that encode information as probabilistic bit states and operate bidirectionally. It uses the Hamiltonian method (an optimization technique from physics) to design these circuits, with two alternative implementations: AND-gate-based or non-imply logic gate-based, each with different performance and complexity trade-offs. The framework also specifies designs for supporting components: a 2x1 multiplexer (a two-input selector) and an AB non-imply logic gate.
vlsid-2025-088.key_novelty: The work implements ReLU in p-bit circuits using a Hamiltonian design method with AND-gate and non-imply variants, achieving invertible (bidirectional) operation and circuit density optimization.

vlsid-2025-084.method: We use a genetic algorithm called NSGA-II (which mimics evolution by testing thousands of designs and breeding the best ones together) to search through different ways to build polynomial multipliers. The algorithm explores various configurations of two existing multiplier designs, MNHKA and MNHOKA, testing different ways to combine them. Each candidate design is tested using Cadence Genus (a chip design tool) with GPDK 45nm silicon technology.
vlsid-2025-084.key_novelty: The core contribution is using NSGA-II, a genetic algorithm, to automatically design non-homogeneous recursive polynomial multipliers (where not all pieces are built the same way), finding all Pareto-optimal designs (where improving speed requires sacrificing power efficiency, or vice versa).

vlsid-2025-092.method: The researchers used a genetic algorithm called SPEA-2 (a method that mimics evolution to explore multiple competing design goals) to automatically determine the best transistor sizes for a library of standard cells optimized to work efficiently at very low voltages (subthreshold, under 500mV). They validated this custom library by running it on RISC-V processors and circuit benchmarks from EPFL, comparing the results against foundry libraries optimized for standard voltage (1.2V) and near-threshold voltage (600mV).
vlsid-2025-092.key_novelty: They used a genetic algorithm (exploring multiple design options to find the best balance between competing goals) to optimize subthreshold standard cells, achieving 44% average energy efficiency improvement and validating the approach on RISC-V processors and benchmark circuits.

vlsid-2025-090.method: When a student touches a 15×15 grid made from Velostat pressure sensors and copper strips, the cloud system instantly detects that touch location. The cloud maps the touch position to a specific vibration pattern and sends it to five coin vibration motors embedded in a wearable glove. As the motors vibrate against the student's fingers, they provide real-time tactile feedback that lets the student feel the spatial relationships and shapes.
vlsid-2025-090.key_novelty: The core idea is to pair a touch-sensitive grid with vibration feedback that's coordinated through the cloud in real-time, letting visually impaired students learn geometry interactively through their fingers.

asplos-2024-002.method: The approach designs the hardware processor and software model together (called co-design) to run deep neural networks efficiently on resource-limited edge devices. It uses two techniques: quantization, which represents numbers using fewer bits to reduce memory and computation (similar to reducing decimal places), and pruning, which removes weights—the connections in the network—that contribute little to results. By optimizing both the custom hardware accelerator and these compression techniques simultaneously rather than separately, it achieves better efficiency overall.
asplos-2024-002.key_novelty: The core idea is to design the hardware accelerator and compression techniques jointly so they work optimally together, rather than optimizing them in isolation.

asplos-2024-000.method: The system learns a single model that handles two types of information at the same time: spatial (where things appear in the image) and temporal (how things change or sequence over time). These two types of information are combined into one unified representation. To answer a visual question, the model uses attention — a mechanism that learns which parts of the image and which time steps are most important — to reason toward the answer.
asplos-2024-000.key_novelty: The key idea is jointly processing spatial layout and temporal information in a single unified model for visual reasoning, instead of handling them separately.

vlsid-2025-097.method: The system tests different possible interpretations of an incoming signal across multiple candidate locations to find which one contains the needed control information (blind decoding). Rather than checking each possibility in software—which would be too slow—they built dedicated hardware using a Xilinx Zynq Ultrascale+ RFSoC ZCU111 FPGA board to test multiple candidates in parallel, guaranteeing results within 0.25 milliseconds. The hardware was integrated into an existing 5G receiver and validated using a real 5G testbed.
vlsid-2025-097.key_novelty: An FPGA-based decoder that performs blind DCI decoding in 0.25 milliseconds while using only 65% of the hardware's available computational resources.

vlsid-2025-095.method: The chip uses two different memory designs in CMOSP18 FD-SOI technology, which is a manufacturing process for low-power chips. Memory placed close to the processor core uses standard timing optimization to achieve 1.2GHz performance. Memory placed farther away uses lower voltage (reduced VDD) and optimized logic gates to cut power leakage. Both designs use high-density memory cells to shrink the chip area and reduce electrical signal delays (RC delay).
vlsid-2025-095.key_novelty: The key idea is optimizing tightly-coupled memory (high-speed memory built into the processor) differently depending on location: using performance-optimized designs for memory close to the core and power-efficient designs for memory placed farther away within the same chip, both with compact memory cells.

asplos-2024-003.method: This paper proposes using gradient checkpointing to train large models more efficiently: instead of storing all intermediate mathematical results (called activations) in GPU memory during the forward pass, the model forgets them immediately and recalculates them during the backward pass (when learning from mistakes). This strategy trades extra computation for substantial memory savings. The approach further optimizes by selectively deciding which intermediate results are worth saving and which to recalculate, plus scheduling the recalculation to minimize computational overhead.
asplos-2024-003.key_novelty: The key innovation is selective gradient checkpointing that strategically chooses which intermediate results to save or recalculate by balancing memory savings against extra computational cost.

asplos-2024-004.method: The compiler automatically splits computational work between CPUs and GPUs (two types of processors with different speeds) by analyzing the dataflow graph—the map of which tasks depend on each other. It measures how fast each device actually performs and continuously adjusts which tasks run where to keep both busy without either becoming a bottleneck. This happens automatically during compilation with no manual tuning needed.
asplos-2024-004.key_novelty: The innovation is a compiler that automatically balances dataflow computation across CPUs and GPUs by adapting to each device's actual performance.

asplos-2024-007.method: AttAcc builds a processing-in-memory (PIM) architecture—computation placed directly in the memory system to reduce data travel delays. The system pairs PIM with a GPU: PIM handles attention layers (the calculation steps requiring massive data reads) by leveraging high memory bandwidth, while the GPU executes fully-connected layers where raw computing power matters most. System-level optimizations coordinate the two components to accelerate batched transformer inference end-to-end.
asplos-2024-007.key_novelty: AttAcc splits transformer inference between specialized memory-compute hardware for memory-hungry attention layers and GPUs for compute-heavy fully-connected layers, matching each type of work to the hardware built for it.

vlsid-2025-094.method: Toggle6.0 delivers 4.8 Gbps data transfer on flash memory interfaces using four coordinated techniques: thin-oxide transistors to reduce parasitic capacitance, elevated ground voltage to reduce driver stress, multi-tap equalization (adjusting signal strength at multiple points) to correct transmission-line distortion, and per-receiver voltage tuning to optimize timing margins. Together, they minimize chip area and power consumption.
vlsid-2025-094.key_novelty: The key insight is combining thin-oxide transistors, elevated ground voltage, multi-tap equalization, and per-receiver voltage tuning to achieve 4.8 Gbps flash memory transfer with significantly less chip area and power than existing approaches.

vlsid-2025-096.method: YOLO object detection models are trained iteratively across different environmental conditions—nighttime, crowds, sunny weather, and small objects—using gradient descent optimization. Transfer learning helps the model reuse features learned from one scenario to speed up learning in another. By going through all environmental conditions repeatedly, the model learns features that work across all of them instead of specializing in just one. The researchers test different YOLO model configurations and use both public datasets and custom datasets built for UAV surveillance.
vlsid-2025-096.key_novelty: Meta-training YOLO object detectors across diverse environmental conditions—nighttime, crowds, sunny weather, and small objects—enables them to work reliably in real-world UAV surveillance without overfitting to any single scenario.

asplos-2024-009.method: Proteus increases request throughput without adding hardware by deploying multiple versions of each AI model—each tuned for different accuracy and speed trade-offs. It automatically selects the right model version for current conditions, places it on whichever devices are available (like GPUs, CPUs, or TPUs), and groups requests into batches whose size adapts to how fast new requests arrive. This adaptive batching (adjusting batch size based on request rate) ensures the system meets its throughput targets while keeping response times and model accuracy within acceptable limits.
asplos-2024-009.key_novelty: The core idea is to handle higher request throughput without buying additional hardware by trading off model accuracy for speed, while jointly optimizing which model version to use, where to place it, and how to batch incoming requests.

asplos-2024-008.method: Red-QAOA uses simulated annealing (a classical optimization technique) to reduce the problem by removing unimportant parts of the graph, shrinking the problem size. Smaller problems need fewer qubits, so the quantum computer experiences less noise. The reduction also concentrates the parameter search space—narrowing down where good parameter settings are likely to be. This keeps the solution quality while making the parameter tuning more reliable despite quantum noise.
asplos-2024-008.key_novelty: Shrinking the optimization problem via simulated annealing-based graph reduction to focus parameter tuning and reduce noise sensitivity.

asplos-2024-001.method: Attention mechanisms in transformers compute weighted interactions between all token pairs, creating bottlenecks in both speed and memory. The paper analyzes these computational patterns and proposes optimizations at three levels: improving how GPUs execute these operations (kernel optimization), improving how data moves through memory, and reducing the computation itself through algorithmic changes like sparse or selective attention.
asplos-2024-001.key_novelty: Diagnosing where attention mechanisms bottleneck on speed and memory, then proposing optimizations that address both together.

asplos-2024-010.method: Promatch adds a preprocessing step called adaptive predecoding that takes error patterns (called syndromes, which is the fingerprint of where errors occurred in the quantum system) and simplifies them by reducing the number of individual errors in each pattern. Once simplified, these patterns can be handled by existing fast decoders called real-time MWPM decoders (which find the most likely way to correct errors), which normally fail when patterns have too many errors. This lets quantum error correction work on larger systems while keeping everything fast—decision time stays under a microsecond.
asplos-2024-010.key_novelty: Using adaptive predecoding (a preprocessing step that reduces the number of errors in error patterns) as a first step allows existing real-time quantum error decoders to handle larger systems, extending beyond distance 9.

asplos-2024-011.method: Elivagar searches for quantum circuits that are good at classification tasks by using a framework specifically designed for quantum hardware. Instead of copying circuit design methods from classical computers, it accounts for quantum-specific limitations like noise (errors in quantum operations) upfront in the search process. This steers the search away from designs that look good in theory but won't work in real quantum hardware, reducing the search space from exponentially large to manageable.
asplos-2024-011.key_novelty: It accounts for quantum hardware constraints directly in the search process, rather than adapting methods from classical computers.

asplos-2024-013.method: TorchDynamo watches Python code as it runs and automatically captures the mathematical operations PyTorch performs, converting them into a compact representation called graphs that optimizers can work with. These graphs are then compiled into fast machine code by TorchInductor: Triton code for GPUs or C++ for CPUs. The key trick is that all this happens automatically while Python code executes normally—no need to rewrite code or manually tell the system what to optimize.
asplos-2024-013.key_novelty: Intercepting Python's execution at the bytecode level (the low-level instructions Python uses internally) enables automatic extraction and compilation of math operations without requiring code changes or sacrificing Python's dynamic capabilities.

asplos-2024-006.method: GMLake intercepts GPU memory requests and uses virtual memory mapping—the GPU's system for translating program addresses to physical memory locations—to combine fragmented physical memory blocks into a contiguous virtual address space. This makes scattered pieces of physical memory appear as one continuous block to the program, eliminating fragmentation waste without requiring changes to the DNN model or memory reduction techniques.
asplos-2024-006.key_novelty: Virtual memory stitching combines fragmented physical GPU memory blocks into a contiguous virtual address space using the GPU's virtual memory mapping system, eliminating fragmentation transparently.

asplos-2024-005.method: DMT (Direct Memory Translation) stores page table entries—the mappings that tell the CPU where memory physically lives—in contiguous memory blocks called Translation Entry Areas (TEAs). Instead of searching through a hierarchy of page tables, the system maintains direct mappings from virtual addresses to these PTEs using dedicated CPU registers, organized per virtual memory region (VMA). When the guest OS and host cooperate, the guest's TEAs can be placed in physical memory, bypassing the virtualization layers that normally add overhead. This cuts translation lookups to one, two, or three memory accesses for native, virtualized, and nested virtualized systems respectively—compared to the original 24 sequential page table fetches.
asplos-2024-005.key_novelty: Storing page table entries (memory-address mappings) in contiguous Translation Entry Areas and mapping them directly per memory region—instead of through nested hierarchy searches—enables nested virtualization without lookup overhead while maintaining x86 compatibility.

asplos-2024-016.method: The authors took MLIR, a compiler framework, and customized it for high-performance computing by adding abstractions for message passing—the coordination mechanism that lets distributed computers work together when running stencil computations (calculations on grids where each point depends on neighboring points, solved in parallel). They integrated this customized MLIR with three stencil DSLs (Devito, PSyclone, and Open Earth Compiler), enabling all three to generate high-performance code by sharing one compiler infrastructure rather than each building and maintaining separate compilation systems.
asplos-2024-016.key_novelty: By customizing the MLIR compiler framework for high-performance computing and adding message-passing abstractions, multiple stencil DSLs can share one compiler instead of building separate ones.

asplos-2024-015.method: SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping—tracking your position while building a map from camera and motion sensors) must be fast enough for real-time AR/VR and robotics, but accurate algorithms are computationally expensive on resource-constrained devices. SlimSLAM solves this by having a runtime that monitors available computing resources and automatically adjusts the algorithm's complexity—using full-featured processing when resources allow and simpler approximations when resources are tight. This maintains accurate pose estimation (precise positioning) in real-time, regardless of the device's computational power.
asplos-2024-015.key_novelty: SlimSLAM maintains accurate SLAM performance in real-time across resource-constrained devices by dynamically adjusting algorithm complexity based on available computational resources.

asplos-2024-019.method: Core-gapped confidential VMs dedicate each CPU core exclusively to a single virtual machine instead of having multiple VMs take turns using the same cores. Normally when cores are time-shared, traces of data get left behind in the core's internal structures (like caches and branch predictors — the circuitry that remembers recent operations) — information that another VM running on the same core can later detect and read. By giving each VM its own cores, these structures remain isolated, so one VM cannot extract information about what another VM has done. This blocks transient-execution attacks, which work by detecting these leftover traces.
asplos-2024-019.key_novelty: Preventing transient-execution attacks by dedicating each CPU core exclusively to one virtual machine instead of time-sharing cores among multiple virtual machines.

asplos-2024-012.method: The paper adds extensions to a CPU that let programs control when cached data is written back to main memory (the slower, larger memory storage). It introduces "Skip It," a filter that detects and blocks redundant writebacks—situations where the same data is being unnecessarily written multiple times. The design was implemented on BOOM, an open-source out-of-order RISC-V processor, and achieved approximately 100-cycle latency for these operations.
asplos-2024-012.key_novelty: Skip It filters out redundant cache writebacks, substantially reducing memory transfer overhead.

asplos-2024-021.method: The work introduces a set of quantum operations (called CRISC—a compact yet comprehensive quantum instruction set) for qubits connected by XX+YY coupling (a specific type of interaction between qubits). These operations can create any possible two-qubit gate by combining single-qubit operations. The scheme manages decoherence—the gradual loss of quantum information over time—to maintain high accuracy while simultaneously minimizing the number of operations needed to run quantum algorithms.
asplos-2024-021.key_novelty: The scheme achieves the seemingly contradictory goal of a minimal yet complete instruction set by exploiting fundamental differences between quantum and classical computer architectures.

asplos-2024-024.method: Centauri breaks up communication tasks (operations where GPUs exchange data during training) into smaller, independent chunks. It then schedules these chunks and computation work together so they overlap—while some data is being transferred between GPUs, other GPUs can simultaneously run computations. This approach works with different types of communication operations and in heterogeneous training environments where GPUs have varying computational resources.
asplos-2024-024.key_novelty: Breaking communication tasks into smaller pieces enables GPUs to better interleave (mix) data transfers with actual computation.

asplos-2024-023.method: EVT enables efficient training by using a tree-shaped map of how forward operations (computing results) connect to backward operations (computing gradients). A systematic procedure (a 'visitor') walks this tree to find groups of operations that can be fused (combined into a single, faster operation). This enables different fusion strategies for complex training operations like normalization and loss functions, allowing the compiler to maintain fast execution on modern GPUs.
asplos-2024-023.key_novelty: EVT's core innovation is using a tree-based structure (the Epilogue Visitor Tree) to map how forward and backward operations connect, making it possible to efficiently combine complex training operations.

asplos-2024-025.method: Slapo is a programming language built specifically for expressing optimization strategies for deep learning training. Developers write instructions declaring what optimizations to apply, and the system applies these progressively—each pass improving training speed. This approach lets developers keep the flexibility of dynamic frameworks like PyTorch while having precise control over performance tuning.
asplos-2024-025.key_novelty: Slapo is a scheduling language that lets developers write optimization instructions for deep learning training, getting the performance improvements of static optimizers without losing the flexibility of frameworks like PyTorch.

asplos-2024-020.method: GMT creates a three-tier memory system with GPU memory, host memory, and SSDs. Unlike previous systems where the host CPU manages data movement (which becomes a bottleneck), GMT lets the GPU itself orchestrate when and where data moves between tiers. The system uses reuse prediction—anticipating which data pages will be used again soon—to decide which pages deserve faster host memory, while leaving others on SSD to avoid wastefully moving everything through host memory.
asplos-2024-020.key_novelty: The GPU directly orchestrates memory tiering across its own memory, host memory, and SSDs, rather than relying on the host CPU to manage these transfers.

asplos-2024-014.method: The technique finds bugs in robot programs by systematically testing them with many varied inputs, a process called fuzzing. It does this in two ways: first, by using knowledge of how the Robot Operating System (ROS) sends messages between components to guide which test cases to try (message-guided fuzzing), and second, by exploring many different dimensions of the input space simultaneously (multi-dimensional fuzzing). This approach generates test cases more likely to find bugs and collects richer feedback about how the program responds.
asplos-2024-014.key_novelty: The core contribution is combining multi-dimensional fuzzing with guidance from the Robot Operating System's message-passing patterns to generate better test cases for robot programs.

asplos-2024-017.method: Two-Face identifies which parts of the matrix contain lots of data (dense) and which are mostly empty (sparse), then adapts its communication strategy: broadcasting to all processors for dense parts, or sending data directly between only needed processors for sparse parts. Broadcasting sends redundant data but requires no coordination; direct communication avoids redundancy but requires careful scheduling. By choosing the strategy based on each part's density, Two-Face minimizes the combined cost of wasted data and coordination overhead.
asplos-2024-017.key_novelty: Dynamically switching between broadcast and point-to-point communication based on whether each region is dense or sparse, to simultaneously minimize redundant data transfers and scheduling overhead.

asplos-2024-029.method: The approach uses formal verification—mathematically proving that code behaves as intended—to check Rust-based page table implementations (the data structures controlling which programs can access which memory locations) in software enclave hypervisors (software that creates isolated execution sandboxes). It verifies that page tables correctly enforce isolation boundaries between different trust domains so they cannot access each other's memory. Unlike Rust's built-in memory safety checks that prevent crashes, this detects logic errors in how isolation rules are written.
asplos-2024-029.key_novelty: Using formal verification to detect logic errors in page table implementations that violate isolation, catching problems that Rust's memory safety guarantees alone cannot find.

asplos-2024-022.method: MAGIS combines two optimization techniques: graph transformation, which modifies tensor shapes and computation structure, and graph scheduling, which determines when operations execute and when data moves between memory. By coordinating these techniques, it discovers memory-performance trade-offs created by shape changes—opportunities that applying each technique separately would never find.
asplos-2024-022.key_novelty: The core insight is coordinating graph transformation and scheduling to jointly optimize memory and performance by exploiting the opportunities that tensor shape changes create.

asplos-2024-031.method: Instead of checking memory versions through Merkle trees (a structure that becomes impractically expensive to maintain at large scales), Toleo puts a trusted smart memory chip directly in the memory system. This chip acts as the authoritative keeper of version numbers—when the CPU needs to access memory, the chip confirms the current version through a secure CXL connection (a protected high-speed link). To reduce the storage required for version tracking, Toleo uses stealth versions with version confidentiality, which cuts the memory overhead in half.
asplos-2024-031.key_novelty: Instead of checking data versions through Merkle trees, use a trusted smart memory chip connected via secure CXL to serve as the authoritative keeper of version numbers.

asplos-2024-027.method: EagleEye uses a two-part system: a leader satellite with a low-resolution camera scans wide areas and detects targets onboard, then commands follower satellites with high-resolution cameras to photograph the detected targets. An optimization algorithm (integer linear programming, which finds the best assignment of satellites to targets) decides which followers should image which targets, ensuring camera movements complete quickly and all scheduling happens within strict time windows. This mixed-resolution approach lets each satellite specialize—the leader finds targets across a wide area, and followers provide high-quality images of those specific targets.
asplos-2024-027.key_novelty: A mixed-resolution satellite constellation where a low-resolution leader detects targets and an optimization algorithm coordinates high-resolution followers to image them.

asplos-2024-034.method: Instead of building general-purpose processors, specialized hardware focuses every component on specific computational tasks—like chips designed purely for AI training or image processing. When you don't need to handle arbitrary jobs, you can eliminate inefficiencies and waste power that would otherwise go to unused features. This matters because Dennard scaling (the historical trend of making chips faster and more power-efficient together) has stopped, so specialization is now one of the main ways left to reduce energy use.
asplos-2024-034.key_novelty: Specialized chips are now the main solution for energy efficiency, since we can no longer rely on making general-purpose processors simultaneously faster and more power-efficient.

asplos-2024-018.method: AWS built the entire system as one unit—chip, servers, network infrastructure, compilers (software that translates code for hardware), and runtime software (what executes that code). Because one organization owned all these layers, designers could make changes and immediately coordinate across teams rather than each group working in isolation. They prioritized simplicity and usability over maximum performance in any single component. Through three product generations, they made design tradeoffs with full-system context—accepting a cost in one layer if it meant better efficiency across the whole system.
asplos-2024-018.key_novelty: AWS unified ownership of all system layers—chip, servers, networks, compilers (code translation software), and runtime—enabling each design decision to account for full-system impacts rather than optimizing each part independently.

asplos-2024-036.method: MaxEmbed arranges embedding tables more efficiently on SSDs by allowing multiple embeddings to overlap across pages (fixed-size chunks of data that SSDs read together). Traditional approaches partition embeddings into completely separate clusters to avoid conflicts, but this wastes storage space and creates read amplification—inefficient disk reads when you need one embedding but have to load an entire page containing unrelated data. MaxEmbed instead finds flexible combinations of embeddings that fit tightly on each page, reducing those wasted reads and extracting more value from each disk access.
asplos-2024-036.key_novelty: MaxEmbed allows embeddings to overlap across SSD pages instead of forcing them into completely separate clusters, reducing wasted disk reads.

asplos-2024-026.method: SEER explores different ways to rewrite a program that will be converted to hardware (called high-level synthesis), keeping only versions that compute the same result. It uses an equivalence graph—a data structure that efficiently stores many mathematically equivalent program variants at once. By compiling each variant to hardware and measuring the result, SEER identifies which rewrite produces the best design.
asplos-2024-026.key_novelty: SEER uses e-graph rewriting to systematically explore mathematically equivalent program variants and select the version that produces the best hardware design through high-level synthesis.

asplos-2024-028.method: AERO runs a 1-millisecond test erase on each block to measure fail bits—the bits that weren't fully cleared. It then predicts the minimum erase time that cell actually needs based on how many bits failed, rather than always applying the standard 3.5+ milliseconds. Modern SSDs have built-in reliability margins, so AERO can safely reduce the voltage duration to what's necessary, speeding up I/O without risking data loss.
asplos-2024-028.key_novelty: AERO measures how many bits fail to clear during a quick 1-millisecond test, then uses that measurement to predict the minimum erase time needed, eliminating the standard worst-case overhead without sacrificing reliability.

asplos-2024-038.method: sIOPMP uses a hardware-based system to control which devices can access protected memory in TEEs. It has three parts working together: first, a Multi-stage-Tree-based checker (a hierarchical structure that efficiently tracks memory regions) supporting over 1000 regions to grant or block access quickly; second, a classification system that divides devices into 'hot' (frequently accessed) or 'cold' (rarely accessed) categories with mountable entries to handle unlimited devices; third, a dynamic remapping mechanism that automatically moves devices between hot and cold groups based on how the workload actually uses them.
asplos-2024-038.key_novelty: The system combines a Multi-stage-Tree-based checker (a hierarchical structure for fast memory protection lookups) with dynamic hot/cold device classification to support over 1000 memory regions and unlimited devices while adding almost no performance overhead.

asplos-2024-032.method: Transistors in FPGAs accumulate damage (called bias temperature instability) as they process data, and this damage pattern encodes information about past computation. Attackers use time-to-digital converters—sensors that measure tiny timing differences in transistor behavior—to detect these patterns. These measurements reveal data that was previously processed, similar to how infrared imaging reveals old paintings hidden beneath new paint.
asplos-2024-032.key_novelty: Transistor aging (bias temperature instability) in shared cloud FPGAs creates a side-channel—a hidden leak of information—that reveals previously processed data through timing measurements.

asplos-2024-040.method: The approach uses load barriers—checks inserted when the program reads from memory—to track which heap objects are still in use. When an object is freed, CHERI capabilities (hardware features that restrict what memory code can access) mark it invalid, so any later attempts to use it are caught. Unlike prior approaches that pause the entire program periodically to reclaim memory, load barriers enable cleanup to happen gradually in the background, keeping pause times short and practical.
asplos-2024-040.key_novelty: Load barriers enable CHERI heap temporal safety with pause times practical enough for real systems, solving the performance limitation that made earlier approaches impractical.

asplos-2024-035.method: DTC-SpMM makes sparse matrix multiplication run fast on Tensor Cores (GPU units designed for high-speed math) using three coordinated techniques. First, it compresses sparse matrices to skip zeros and save memory. Second, it reorders matrix elements so frequently-used pieces sit close together in memory, speeding retrieval. Third, it optimizes the runtime pipeline—how work flows through the Tensor Cores—to keep them constantly busy. Testing on modern GPUs shows measurable performance improvements across diverse matrix types.
asplos-2024-035.key_novelty: A unified framework for Tensor Cores that combines data compression, matrix reordering, and pipeline tuning for sparse multiplication.

asplos-2024-043.method: CrossPrefetch splits prefetching (loading data into fast memory before it's needed) between two layers: the OS kernel handles the actual data loading, while a user-level program running alongside applications collects feedback on how well the prefetching works and manages which data to load. This two-layer split avoids the lock contention (performance slowdowns from many programs fighting over the same shared resource) and synchronization delays that bottleneck traditional approaches where everything goes through the kernel.
asplos-2024-043.key_novelty: A two-layer prefetching system that separates data loading in the kernel from feedback and coordination at the application level, eliminating the synchronization bottlenecks of single-layer kernel-based approaches.

asplos-2024-041.method: The solution modifies compiled binary code (the machine instructions a CPU executes) to break up the patterns that leak timing information. By reshuffling these patterns, it prevents sensitive computations from aligning with the CPU's optimizations that create observable timing variations. This works where source-code fixes fail because the leaks originate from hardware optimization strategies that are only visible in the compiled binary.
asplos-2024-041.key_novelty: Binary-code modifications can eliminate timing side channels that leak information through CPU optimizations—a problem that source-code changes alone cannot fix.

asplos-2024-030.method: The study tracked six types of AI tasks (image recognition, physics simulation, image generation, text processing, audio, and data tables) on a test suite called CaSiO across three generations of GPUs. To understand how the AI software and GPU hardware work together, they measured performance at three layers: how the high-level AI software runs, how software communicates with the GPU, and how the GPU's internal design affects speed. They tracked how this relationship has changed as GPU technology evolved.
asplos-2024-030.key_novelty: CaSiO is a test suite that measures diverse AI workloads across multiple GPU generations and system levels (software, GPU communication, and hardware) to reveal how software-hardware interactions affect speed.

asplos-2024-046.method: Modern neural networks need two kinds of operations: GEMM (matrix multiplication, the fast core operation) and diverse emerging operators (like attention and normalization, especially critical in language models). Traditional NPU designs either build isolated dedicated hardware for these emerging operators or make you fall back to slow general-purpose processors. The Tandem Processor instead integrates both operation types into a single unified architecture that can handle them efficiently together.
asplos-2024-046.key_novelty: The Tandem Processor handles diverse emerging neural operators (like attention and normalization) natively within a single unified architecture, rather than using isolated dedicated blocks or forcing fallback to general-purpose processors.

asplos-2024-042.method: Prior hardware accelerators for data compression either used CAM (Content-Addressable Memory—special hardware that instantly finds matching patterns) or kept redundant copies of data to speed up compression. Both approaches sacrifice compression quality and waste memory when dealing with large sliding windows (the window of historical data used to find repeated patterns). BeeZip addresses this by proposing an organized hardware architecture that enables fast compression while maintaining compression quality and using less memory even with large sliding windows.
asplos-2024-042.key_novelty: A hardware acceleration architecture that achieves fast compression while maintaining compression quality and reducing memory overhead, even for large sliding windows.

asplos-2024-044.method: Instead of processing one input symbol at a time and waiting for it to complete, the system processes multiple symbols in parallel. It prefetches results and stores previously calculated results in lookup tables to avoid redundant computations. By keeping each thread's work isolated, the thread consistently accesses the same data, keeping it in fast local cache rather than requiring slower memory accesses.
asplos-2024-044.key_novelty: The core idea is processing multiple input symbols in parallel instead of one at a time, which enables optimizations like prefetching results and reusing previous calculations.

asplos-2024-045.method: GUST separates the multiplier and adder hardware components so they can be reused across different rows and columns of the matrix, rather than having each dedicated to a single row or column. When multiple operations need the same hardware at the same time, resource conflicts occur. GUST uses an edge-coloring scheduling algorithm (which assigns colors to operations so that no two operations needing the same hardware run simultaneously) to resolve these conflicts. This approach keeps the hardware productive and fully utilized even when processing sparse matrices with irregular patterns.
asplos-2024-045.key_novelty: Using edge-coloring scheduling to share multipliers and adders across sparse matrix rows and columns without resource conflicts.

asplos-2024-049.method: Instead of manually writing formal models describing how hardware behaves, this approach automatically extracts simplified models from the RTL specification (a detailed register-level description of the hardware). The extraction process is designed so that any security property proven in the simplified model is guaranteed to hold in the actual hardware. This enables practical checking for microarchitectural vulnerabilities—attacks exploiting low-level details of CPU execution—without the complexity of verifying full hardware.
asplos-2024-049.key_novelty: Automatically extracting formal security models directly from hardware RTL specifications, eliminating manual model construction.

asplos-2024-039.method: ZENO captures two types of information about the neural network: its privacy requirements and data structure (called 'privacy-types' and 'tensor-types'). It uses this understanding to reduce dependencies between individual number calculations—the key bottleneck in zero-knowledge proofs—and to identify operations that can run in parallel. Additional optimizations tailored to neural network computation further accelerate circuit evaluation.
asplos-2024-039.key_novelty: Using type information about privacy requirements and data structure to guide automatic circuit optimization for zero-knowledge neural networks.

asplos-2024-047.method: TinyForge combines memory and computing into a single chip layout using custom latch arrays (small, power-efficient memory units), achieving 8 square micrometers of area per byte and using just 11 femtojoules of energy per data read. To reduce power consumption, it processes data one bit at a time instead of many bits in parallel, and it tests two different compute arrangements—a pipeline-style pattern where data flows through in stages (systolic) and a fully parallel pattern—to find which uses less energy and area for each workload. The system includes customizable design templates, power and area calculators, an operation scheduler, and a genetic algorithm that tests thousands of combinations to discover the best architectural trade-offs.
asplos-2024-047.key_novelty: By integrating memory and compute in custom latch arrays, the design enables computation patterns that skip temporary storage buffers for intermediate neural network results, reducing chip area and power.

asplos-2024-048.method: PDIP works by first identifying which instruction-cache misses actually slow down the processor—distinguishing them from misses that the existing FDIP prefetching system already handles. Then it selectively prefetches (loads into cache in advance) only the slowdown-causing misses instead of every miss. By coordinating this way with FDIP, PDIP avoids wasting prefetch effort on misses already hidden by the processor.
asplos-2024-048.key_novelty: Effective instruction prefetching targets only the I-Cache misses that impact performance, coordinating with FDIP rather than trying to hide every miss.

asplos-2024-050.method: The paper uses hardware that speculatively executes code—trying to run threads in parallel and checking afterward if conflicts occurred over shared data. When conflicts are detected, the system retries just once. If the second attempt also conflicts, it falls back to mutual exclusion locks (software locks that ensure only one thread runs at a time). This bounds the retry cost: instead of potentially retrying forever and wasting resources on repeated failures, you give up after one retry and let locks handle it safely.
asplos-2024-050.key_novelty: The paper shows that one retry before using locks works better than many retries, because beyond one attempt, each additional retry wastes more resources resolving conflicts than it gains.

asplos-2024-037.method: C4CAM takes high-level Torch-Script code and converts it to hardware instructions step-by-step through multiple layers, where optimizations can happen. At each layer, the compiler automatically tries different ways to configure the CAM hardware and measures how each choice affects speed and power consumption, accounting for the differences in latency (response time) and power profiles across different CAM chip types.
asplos-2024-037.key_novelty: The first compiler to automatically generate optimized code for CAM-based accelerators from high-level Torch-Script specifications.

asplos-2024-055.method: TensorTEE uses a unified memory block size across both CPU and NPU, eliminating the mismatches that waste storage and memory. Instead of sending secure data through unprotected parts of the system and re-encrypting it on the other side, the system keeps data protected throughout its transfer between CPU and NPU, cutting out expensive re-encryption and scheduling overhead.
asplos-2024-055.key_novelty: Matching memory granularity (block size) between CPUs and NPUs to enable secure data transfers that stay protected throughout, eliminating the need for unsafe transit through non-secure regions.

asplos-2024-033.method: FOCAL is a simplified carbon calculation method that measures environmental impact by looking at processor size, energy consumption, and power usage, then combines these into a single score called normalized carbon footprint (NCF)—normalized means you can fairly compare different chips. The model ranks typical processor design features as strongly, weakly, or less sustainable choices. Architects use this to understand which design decisions have the biggest impact on environmental footprint.
asplos-2024-033.key_novelty: FOCAL is a simplified carbon model that combines chip area, energy, and power consumption using a normalized metric (NCF, or normalized carbon footprint) to holistically assess processor sustainability.

asplos-2024-056.method: GAIA is a scheduler that decides when to run batch computing jobs based on when the electrical grid is cleanest—that is, when it relies most on renewable energy and has lowest carbon intensity.
