Running jobs immediately is fast but uses dirtier power; delaying them to clean periods reduces emissions but makes jobs take longer and wastes reserved instances (servers you've prepaid for that now sit idle). The scheduler explicitly weighs all three concerns—carbon, speed, and cost—to pick the best timing for each job.
asplos-2024-056.key_novelty: A batch scheduler that explicitly balances carbon emissions, job speed, and infrastructure costs when deciding when to run cloud workloads.

asplos-2024-053.method: Fractal breaks the problem of optimizing sparse neural networks into layers: rather than choosing one pattern for which calculations to skip, it organizes the decision into nested chunks at multiple scales. It introduces PatternIR, a standard format that can describe any multi-level combination of these calculation-skipping decisions. An auto-tuning engine tests different combinations to find what works best for each neural network—balancing speed gains against accuracy loss—and compiles these patterns into machine instructions using techniques from optimizing dense computations.
asplos-2024-053.key_novelty: The key technique is breaking down sparse pattern design—deciding which calculations to skip—into multiple nested levels, rather than using a single global pattern.

asplos-2024-057.method: ORIANNA automates the design of hardware accelerators by analyzing robotic optimization algorithms to find sparse structures—computations that can be skipped or simplified. Rather than requiring engineers to manually design each accelerator, the framework automatically generates hardware architectures optimized for these patterns, reducing both design time and engineering costs. This works because the sparse structures in robotic algorithms are predictable, allowing the system to generate effective hardware designs systematically instead of requiring expensive custom design for each algorithm.
asplos-2024-057.key_novelty: ORIANNA automatically synthesizes hardware accelerators that exploit the sparse computational structures (patterns where many operations can be skipped) found in optimization-based robotic algorithms.

asplos-2024-051.method: The paper shows how to perform multiply-accumulate operations (the core arithmetic of convolutions: multiply two numbers and add to a running sum) directly on time-encoded signals, without converting them to digital form first. Time encoding represents data as time delays rather than voltage levels, which consumes far less power than full analog-to-digital conversion. By doing arithmetic directly on these time delays, convolutions—which are made of multiply-accumulate chains—can run efficiently on temporal signals while keeping their energy-saving advantages.
asplos-2024-051.key_novelty: Complex arithmetic operations like convolution can now happen directly on time-encoded analog signals, not just the simple operations (min, max) that were possible before.

asplos-2024-059.method: When running deep neural network operations on GPUs, greedy operator fusion combines operations one-by-one without considering how they might be organized together later, missing optimization opportunities. Korch systematically explores different ways to map and schedule groups of operations onto GPU kernels, rather than making locally optimal fusion choices. By considering the full space of orchestration strategies—how kernels should be organized and when they should run—Korch finds execution plans that run faster than greedy fusion would.
asplos-2024-059.key_novelty: Optimal kernel orchestration by exploring the full space of possible mapping and scheduling strategies instead of greedily fusing operators.

asplos-2024-052.method: Amanda provides two layers of tools for analyzing and optimizing neural networks. The user-facing layer lets developers easily add measurement points (instrumentation) at each operation level—the individual steps that make up neural networks—while the internal layer uses callbacks (functions triggered by events) to efficiently run both the original code and the measurement-enhanced version. This design works with deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, supporting both graph mode (code compiled before running) and eager mode (code runs line-by-line as written).
asplos-2024-052.key_novelty: Amanda unifies neural network analysis and optimization through operation-level measurement (instrumentation), using a two-layer tool design that balances ease-of-use with efficiency across deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.

asplos-2024-054.method: NetRen uses three stages to generate network configurations. First, sketch extraction converts the network into a graph showing all devices and connections. Second, a GraphTrans synthesizer combines this graph representation with Transformers—a machine learning technique that examines many relationships simultaneously to recognize patterns—to generate routing configurations (OSPF and BGP are protocols that direct how network traffic flows) by learning from examples showing how different configurations perform. Third, a stepwise repairer fixes violations to ensure the configuration works.
asplos-2024-054.key_novelty: The core innovation is the GraphTrans synthesizer, which learns to generate routing instructions by combining graph representations with Transformers (machine learning that learns patterns) and training on examples that show how network performance relates to different configurations.

asplos-2024-060.method: After deduplication removes exact duplicates, Palantir finds nearly identical blocks by analyzing their detailed characteristics (fine-grained features) and grouping these characteristics for faster matching (super-features). When two blocks share characteristics, the system stores only their differences (delta compression) instead of both full blocks, which further reduces storage.
asplos-2024-060.key_novelty: It uses hierarchical organization of block characteristics to detect and compress similarity between blocks that remain after deduplication.

asplos-2024-058.method: NeuPIMs splits the work of running an AI language model across two types of hardware. Matrix-to-matrix math operations (GEMM—multiplying two tables together), which appear in query-key-value generation and feed-forward networks, go to NPUs (neural processing units). Matrix-to-vector math operations (GEMV—multiplying a table by a column of numbers), which appear in multi-head attention, go to PIM (processing-in-memory) instead. The system coordinates both accelerators so they work together, handling multiple requests at the same time.
asplos-2024-058.key_novelty: Routing each type of math operation in a language model to the hardware that handles it best: matrix-to-matrix (GEMM) to neural processing units, and matrix-to-vector (GEMV) to processing-in-memory hardware.

asplos-2024-061.method: Fleet is a garbage collector that distinguishes between active and cached app data. It only cleans up cached-app data, leaving active-app data untouched for fast performance. It predicts which data each cached app will need upon launch and uses this to guide how the operating system arranges disk-based memory (called swap). Finally, it groups small data objects with similar access patterns into the same memory pages, improving swap efficiency.
asplos-2024-061.key_novelty: Fleet coordinates garbage collection and memory swapping (disk-based overflow) with active and cached app awareness, simultaneously improving both app caching capacity and hot-launch performance.

asplos-2024-065.method: DistMSM applies Pippenger's algorithm (a technique for efficiently computing multiple scalar multiplications at once) across multiple GPUs working together, identifying performance bottlenecks at scale and fixing them. At the GPU level, it uses a specialized math kernel for elliptic curve operations that employs two techniques to fit more data into the GPU's ultra-fast register memory, and leverages tensor cores (specialized hardware units optimized for fast multiplication) to speed up big integer multiplication.
asplos-2024-065.key_novelty: DistMSM adapts Pippenger's algorithm for multi-GPU systems by identifying bottlenecks (performance slowdowns) and fixing them with a specialized elliptic curve kernel.

asplos-2024-062.method: The system adds runtime monitoring to C/C++ programs that checks every pointer access as the code executes. Each time a pointer is used, the monitor verifies that it's being accessed as its declared data type and stays within its original scope (the authorized region of memory where it's allowed to operate). By catching both type violations and scope violations before they can be exploited, the system prevents data-oriented attacks that attackers would otherwise use to leak sensitive information like encryption keys.
asplos-2024-062.key_novelty: The system prevents data-oriented attacks on C/C++ programs by monitoring both pointer type and scope constraints at runtime as a single unified system.

asplos-2024-067.method: Modern CPUs run at conservative voltage levels to prevent rare errors, wasting energy—SUIT lets them run at lower voltages by catching and fixing errors when they actually occur. When voltage drops too low, special interrupt handlers (CPU interrupts that pause execution to inspect what went wrong) detect the problem and fix it by re-running the failed instruction, boosting voltage, or enabling error-correction hardware. This lets the CPU safely operate at its minimum viable voltage, saving substantial energy without risking crashes or data corruption.
asplos-2024-067.key_novelty: Replace fixed voltage safety margins with dynamic error detection: instead of preventing errors upfront through conservative settings, catch and fix voltage errors as they happen.

asplos-2024-064.method: AUDIBLE predicts how much resources each burstable virtual machine needs using a convolution-based statistical model—a mathematical technique that combines probability distributions without assuming a specific shape. Because it's non-parametric (requires no parameter tuning), it avoids the computational overhead of training machine learning models. The method works regardless of the workload pattern and was validated through extensive simulations using real production data from a major cloud provider.
asplos-2024-064.key_novelty: Instead of machine learning, it uses a convolution-based statistical model (a technique that combines probability distributions) to predict resources for burstable virtual machines without requiring model training.

asplos-2024-070.method: A million-qubit quantum computer requires qubits distributed across multiple dilution refrigerators (extreme cooling systems that keep quantum bits functional). Since connecting qubits between refrigerators is slow and error-prone, standard error correction (detecting and fixing quantum failures) breaks down due to communication delays and extra gate operations. The paper redesigns error-correction for this distributed setup using a fault-tolerant approach (continuing to work even when some operations fail) that keeps error-detection local to each refrigerator and minimizes data sent across slow inter-refrigerator links.
asplos-2024-070.key_novelty: Error-correction redesigned for distributed million-qubit systems to keep most error-checking local to each refrigerator and minimize inter-refrigerator communication.

asplos-2024-071.method: NDPipe places inexpensive GPUs directly into photo storage servers so that inference and training happen on images right where they're stored, rather than moving data to separate computers. It splits neural network models across storage servers, with each server processing its portion of the model on its local image data. By running different image batches in parallel across servers and coordinating only when necessary, the system achieves high training throughput while keeping synchronization overhead low. Each storage server is tuned to maximize the efficiency of its GPU and data utilization.
asplos-2024-071.key_novelty: NDPipe's core idea is embedding inexpensive GPUs in photo storage servers to run inference and training directly on images, eliminating the overhead of moving data to separate computers.

asplos-2024-069.method: CINM builds a compilation system that translates programs into efficient code for compute-in-memory (CIM) and compute-near-memory (CNM) systems—hardware that processes data right where it's stored to avoid bandwidth bottlenecks. It uses hierarchical abstraction layers that work across different CIM and CNM designs, enabling optimizations that either work on any device (device-agnostic) or are customized for specific hardware (device-aware). The system progressively rewrites programs through multiple compilation steps, optimizing at each stage. It was tested on UPMEM (a real CNM system) and memristor-based CIM accelerators.
asplos-2024-069.key_novelty: This is the first compiler using abstraction layers to create optimizations that work across different compute-in-memory and compute-near-memory hardware, rather than requiring hardware-specific optimization for each device.

asplos-2024-068.method: Pythia works by having the compiler add monitoring code to your program that guards the data values used in branching decisions (the points where a program chooses between different execution paths). An attacker using a control-flow bending attack tries to corrupt this data to make the program execute incorrectly. Pythia's protective code detects when someone attempts to modify this critical data and blocks the modification before it takes effect. This stops attacks that traditional control-flow integrity measures miss, since those tools only protect where a program can jump to, not the conditions that decide whether to jump in the first place.
asplos-2024-068.key_novelty: The single core idea is having the compiler automatically add protective monitoring of the data that controls program branches, catching corruption attempts before they can misdirect execution.

asplos-2024-072.method: TCCL uses a custom profiler to measure how fast GPUs can send data to each other across PCIe when multiple transfers happen simultaneously. It then applies a pathfinding algorithm to discover the optimal ring-based communication pattern, where data flows in sequence through each GPU in a circle to reach all of them efficiently. Once found, these communication paths are built into NCCL (the standard library for coordinating GPU operations) to speed up collective operations like AllReduce (collecting and combining results from all GPUs) and AllGather (gathering results from all GPUs into one place).
asplos-2024-072.key_novelty: Automatically discovering optimal ring-based communication paths for PCIe GPU clusters by measuring actual performance instead of relying on generic one-size-fits-all designs.

asplos-2024-063.method: Limoncello monitors memory bandwidth utilization and disables hardware prefetchers—the built-in mechanisms that predict and pre-load future data—when utilization is high to reduce the contention and latency they cause. When hardware prefetchers are off, the system deploys targeted software-based prefetching in critical library functions (widely-used core routines) to maintain cache efficiency. All of this runs in software without hardware changes.
asplos-2024-063.key_novelty: The core idea is dynamically switching between hardware prefetchers and targeted software prefetching based on real-time memory bandwidth utilization.

asplos-2024-074.method: The paper redesigns how cache memory is organized to handle unpredictable memory accesses that happen when traversing indexes in domain-specific architectures—where you follow pointers through an index to find data. Instead of using a one-size-fits-all cache strategy, it uses specialized caching that anticipates which data you'll need next during index traversal and groups related pieces together in cache. This shrinks the working set (the total memory the index needs) and dramatically increases cache hits—so the data you need is already in the fast cache instead of slow memory.
asplos-2024-074.key_novelty: The key insight is that cache organization—not the index algorithm—is the real bottleneck for index performance in domain-specific architectures.

asplos-2024-066.method: PATHFINDER enables neural prefetchers—machine learning models that predict which data a processor will need next—to learn from actual data patterns while running, instead of requiring training beforehand. Because the model continues learning during operation, it stays small and fast while also working well on new data patterns.
asplos-2024-066.key_novelty: Neural prefetchers can learn from actual data patterns while the system runs, instead of requiring offline pre-training.

asplos-2024-075.method: The paper tests Intel's Data Streaming Accelerator (a chip built into Sapphire Rapids processors that moves and processes data faster than the CPU alone) using both controlled microbenchmarks and real datacenter workloads. They measured its performance at data movement, error-checking (CRC32), finding differences between datasets (delta computations), and verifying data hasn't been corrupted. Based on these tests, they created practical guidelines for programmers on how to use it, validated using DPDK Vhost (a virtualization platform).
asplos-2024-075.key_novelty: Through systematic testing with real workloads, they created practical guidelines for programmers to effectively use Intel's data streaming accelerator.

asplos-2024-076.method: RTL-Repair automatically fixes bugs in RTL code—circuit descriptions written at the register transfer level. It uses an SMT solver (a tool that identifies logical inconsistencies and generates fixes) to both locate and repair bugs in a single pass, keeping code changes minimal. Instead of analyzing entire test cases, it uses adaptive windowing: it focuses on just the most relevant parts of each test, which prevents the slowdowns that plagued earlier tools. The result is repair times under a second.
asplos-2024-076.key_novelty: Adaptive windowing—focusing the repair search on only the most relevant parts of test cases—enables sub-second hardware bug repairs while keeping solutions correct.

asplos-2024-082.method: UBFuzz takes valid programs and uses Shadow Statement Insertion (a method to automatically introduce undefined behavior—bugs that violate language rules—into code). It runs these modified programs through multiple different sanitizers—tools that detect undefined behavior—and compares what each one reports to find disagreements. A key innovation is crash-site mapping, which examines where in the program a crash occurs to determine whether discrepancies stem from a bug in the sanitizer itself or from a compiler optimization.
asplos-2024-082.key_novelty: By analyzing where a crash happens in a program, crash-site mapping can tell whether a bug comes from a sanitizer or from a compiler optimization.

asplos-2024-079.method: Existing distributed graph systems only allow nodes to update properties using data from neighboring nodes. Kimbap introduces a 'Node-Property Map' abstraction that removes this restriction, letting nodes access and modify any properties during iterative computation. This enables previously impossible algorithms like Louvain (which identifies communities) and Shiloach-Vishkin (which finds connected components). The system maintains efficient parallel execution across multiple machines.
asplos-2024-079.key_novelty: Kimbap's Node-Property Map abstraction lets graph algorithms freely access any node properties, instead of limiting them to neighboring nodes' data.

asplos-2024-081.method: Loupe is a tool that measures which operating system features applications actually need when developers are building a compatibility layer (a layer that translates between different operating systems so software from one OS can run on another). It tracks which system requests (syscalls—the way applications ask the OS for services) and OS functions each application uses. By measuring this actual usage rather than guessing, developers can prioritize their work and implement only the features that applications truly need.
asplos-2024-081.key_novelty: The core contribution is a precise way to measure which operating system features applications actually need, letting developers build compatibility layers with only the required features.

asplos-2024-077.method: The system uses Private Information Retrieval—a technique for fetching data from a server without revealing what you're asking for—to retrieve embedding tables from remote servers. It accelerates the PIR calculations using GPUs, which perform the mathematical operations significantly faster than CPUs would. The system is also co-designed with the downstream machine learning application in mind: the retrieval protocol is tuned to match the specific needs of the ML model, which jointly improves both throughput (data transferred per second) and latency (response time).
asplos-2024-077.key_novelty: The core idea is jointly optimizing the private retrieval protocol, GPU acceleration strategy, and machine learning application needs as one system to achieve practical production-scale private embedding access.

asplos-2024-078.method: Atalanta uses hardware and software together to add a lossless compression stage right before the off-die memory controller—the interface connecting the chip to external memory. This layer squeezes both the weights (learned parameters) and activations (intermediate values created during inference), achieving compression efficiency comparable to Arithmetic Coding (a gold-standard compression method) while using minimal hardware overhead (less than 50 bytes of storage per unit). The technique compresses weights to 60% of their original size and activations to 48%, and it works transparently so the rest of the accelerator needs no changes.
asplos-2024-078.key_novelty: The key innovation is a simple hardware layer that compresses tensors (multi-dimensional arrays of numbers) as efficiently as Arithmetic Coding but without the bandwidth and complexity costs of implementing Arithmetic Coding on the chip.

asplos-2024-084.method: The system co-designs both the algorithm and memory hardware together. Normally the specialized memory can only do simple per-number operations and basic matrix multiplication, leaving heavy lifting to the main processor. By tailoring algorithms to match what this memory does well, the system expands which calculation types it can handle, reducing main processor dependency.
asplos-2024-084.key_novelty: Co-designing the algorithm and hardware system together lets the specialized memory handle more types of deep learning calculations.

asplos-2024-080.method: GSCore is a custom ASIC chip manufactured at 28 nanometers that speeds up 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering by combining three techniques in hardware. Shape-aware intersection testing figures out which Gaussians (blurry spheres) affect each pixel based on their shape, hierarchical sorting orders the Gaussians for correct blending, and subtile skipping avoids processing empty screen regions. These three techniques run together as an integrated pipeline.
asplos-2024-080.key_novelty: A specialized ASIC that combines shape-aware intersection testing (determining which blurry spheres affect each pixel), hierarchical sorting (ordering them correctly), and subtile skipping (avoiding empty regions) into a single accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting.

asplos-2024-083.method: FMCC is a compiler that figures out the best order for measurements on a photonic cluster state (a 2-D mesh of entangled photons). It uses dynamic programming (breaking the problem into pieces and building up solutions) with heuristics (practical rules of thumb) to explore different measurement sequences. By smartly ordering these one-way measurements, it reduces the cluster state depth—how many measurement layers the computation needs—while maintaining quantum circuit correctness.
asplos-2024-083.key_novelty: The innovation is using dynamic programming (a technique that explores many possible solutions efficiently) with heuristics to minimize cluster state depth in measurement-based quantum computing on photonic systems.

asplos-2024-086.method: LazyDP trains recommendation systems with privacy protection by fixing two major performance bottlenecks. It speeds up noise sampling (adding random noise to protect privacy) through algorithmic improvements, and speeds up gradient updates (where the system learns) through software optimizations that reduce memory bandwidth constraints. Rather than optimizing the algorithm and software separately, LazyDP co-designs them together, with each accounting for the other's limitations. This integrated approach achieves 119× speedup while maintaining the same mathematical guarantees as standard private training.
asplos-2024-086.key_novelty: Jointly designing the algorithm and software implementation together eliminates the compute and memory bottlenecks that slow down privacy-preserving recommendation systems.

asplos-2024-089.method: The method transforms the problem of choosing the best fermion-to-qubit encoding into a Boolean Satisfiability problem (finding true/false assignments that satisfy constraints), using Pauli algebra—the mathematical framework that describes quantum operations—to express the encoding constraints and objectives. Since the resulting constraints number exponentially, two approximation strategies help find good solutions without needing to evaluate every possibility.
asplos-2024-089.key_novelty: The core contribution is reformulating fermion-to-qubit encoding selection as a Boolean Satisfiability problem (finding true/false values that make logical constraints true), enabling highly-optimized SAT solvers to solve it efficiently.

asplos-2024-073.method: Hydride takes processor manufacturer pseudocode and automatically converts it into AutoLLVM IR, a formally-defined internal representation (one with precise rules) that works across any processor architecture. It then automatically generates instruction-selection rules that decide which processor instruction to use for each operation. Finally, it uses formal definitions of schedule-based languages like Halide—where you explicitly specify how computation is organized—to automatically synthesize optimal code generation for each target processor.
asplos-2024-073.key_novelty: Instead of manually building compiler infrastructure for each new processor architecture, Hydride automatically synthesizes it—including the intermediate representation and instruction-selection rules—from processor manufacturer pseudocode.

asplos-2024-088.method: GIANTSAN groups multiple memory segments together and packs their safety-check metadata into fewer entries. This means the processor fetches metadata less often during program execution, reducing the slowdown from repeated safety checks. It preserves the strong detection accuracy and compatibility of location-based methods by carefully tracking which segments are grouped together.
asplos-2024-088.key_novelty: Segment folding—combining multiple memory segments into shared metadata entries—eliminates repeated metadata fetches during execution, making memory safety checks fast without sacrificing detection accuracy.

asplos-2024-085.method: Speculative inference speeds up LLM text generation by quickly guessing multiple future words and then verifying them, but guessing and verification need very different amounts of computation. SpecPIM addresses this through co-exploration—jointly optimizing hardware design and computational workflow—on processing-in-memory (PIM) systems, where computation happens inside memory rather than in a separate processor. This approach allocates lighter resources to the draft-generation stage using a small model and heavier resources to verification using a large model, keeping both efficient within the PIM architecture.
asplos-2024-085.key_novelty: Jointly optimizing hardware design and computational workflow enables PIM systems to adapt to the drastically different resource demands of draft-token generation versus verification in speculative inference.

asplos-2024-092.method: FUYAO uses Data Processing Units (DPUs) — specialized hardware chips designed to handle data movement — to transfer data directly between serverless functions. Normally, a central control system both decides which functions run AND routes all their data, creating a bottleneck. FUYAO separates these tasks by offloading data movement to the DPU hardware: the control system now only manages which functions run, while the DPU hardware handles moving data between them. This separation allows data to transfer quickly without slowing down control decisions.
asplos-2024-092.key_novelty: The key insight is using specialized hardware (DPUs) to move data directly between serverless functions, instead of routing all data through a central control system.

asplos-2024-093.method: The system adds Software Transactional Memory—a coordination mechanism for simultaneous operations—by running all transaction management (tracking which operations access what data) inside the Processing-In-Memory chip itself, avoiding expensive messages to the host computer. It uses optimistic concurrency control, letting transactions run simultaneously without locks (access restrictions), then checking for conflicts; if conflicts occurred, the system rolls back and retries the affected transaction.
asplos-2024-093.key_novelty: This work implements Software Transactional Memory (a system for coordinating multiple simultaneous operations) directly on Processing-In-Memory chips, allowing concurrent access without the expensive synchronization overhead that normally limits these systems.

asplos-2024-090.method: JUNO reduces wasted computation by skipping distance calculations to vectors that cannot be nearest neighbors (sparsity-aware processing). It organizes related data close together in memory (locality-aware) so the GPU can efficiently check many candidates. The system maps this algorithm to GPU hardware, using ray tracing cores—specialized hardware normally built for graphics rendering—alongside pipelined tensor cores to process searches in parallel.
asplos-2024-090.key_novelty: JUNO repurposes GPU ray tracing cores—hardware built for graphics rendering—to accelerate nearest neighbor search, efficiently processing millions of high-dimensional vectors.

asplos-2024-091.method: FaaSGraph co-designs a graph processing framework with serverless computing by making data flow—not computation scheduling—the primary design concern. Instead of fitting traditional graph algorithms into serverless functions (which have limited memory, short run times, and execute across many machines in parallel), it restructures the graph algorithms themselves to match these constraints. By carefully organizing data movement between functions and optimizing for computation-heavy workloads, it reduces the overhead that normally makes serverless graph processing inefficient.
asplos-2024-091.key_novelty: The innovation is a serverless execution model centered on data flow—rather than computation scheduling—that enables efficient graph processing by restructuring algorithms to work within serverless constraints (limited memory and runtime per function) while automatically scaling with demand.

asplos-2024-094.method: ACES adapts its execution pattern on-the-fly to match whatever sparsity pattern the matrix has, juggling between running many small parallel operations versus keeping data close to where it's needed. When data needs to be removed from the cache (a replacement decision), ACES makes that choice based on both how often data is reused locally and how many concurrent operations need it at the same time. A special buffer that doesn't require operations to wait (a non-blocking buffer) works alongside the main cache, enabling more concurrent operations to proceed without stalling.
asplos-2024-094.key_novelty: The key innovation is a cache management policy that balances data locality—keeping data close to where it's used—against supporting many simultaneous operations for sparse matrix multiplication.

asplos-2024-087.method: Quantum computers need error correction to protect quantum data from noise. This approach designs the error-correcting code and chiplet layout (how separate quantum hardware pieces are arranged) together, not separately. Because each chiplet has its own manufacturing defects, the method observes each chip's defect pattern and tailors the error-correcting strategy to it. Joint design reduces overhead compared to using one fixed error-correction approach for all chips.
asplos-2024-087.key_novelty: Jointly design quantum error-correcting codes (strategies to protect quantum information) and modular chiplets (separate quantum hardware pieces) to handle manufacturing defects, instead of designing them separately.

asplos-2024-097.method: DSCS-Serverless places a programmable accelerator (hardware customized for specific tasks) directly inside the storage device with a 25-watt power budget. In disaggregated systems where compute and storage are separate, accessing remote storage creates latency overhead that overwhelms accelerator benefits—but by co-locating the accelerator with storage instead of using conventional approaches like ARM cores or FPGAs, this design eliminates the access delay that normally dominates performance.
asplos-2024-097.key_novelty: A programmable accelerator embedded within the storage device itself lets serverless functions use acceleration without the latency penalty of accessing remote storage.

asplos-2024-099.method: SpecInfer works by using small, fast models to predict ahead—generating guesses for multiple possible token sequences (the words the LLM will produce next) and organizing these guesses into a tree structure to show the branching possibilities. The main LLM then checks all these predicted branches simultaneously to see which predictions are correct, rather than generating tokens one by one as usual. By verifying many predictions in parallel, the system reduces both the time needed and the computation required.
asplos-2024-099.key_novelty: The main LLM verifies multiple predicted token sequences organized in a tree structure all at once, rather than generating tokens one at a time.

asplos-2024-096.method: During inference (when the neural network is making predictions), Dr. DNA monitors the output values produced by the network's computational units (neurons). Normally, these values follow a consistent pattern or distribution. Silent data corruptions—undetected hardware errors—cause these outputs to deviate noticeably from their normal pattern. By detecting these deviations in real-time, Dr. DNA identifies corruptions and applies corrections to restore the model's accuracy without requiring significant additional computation.
asplos-2024-096.key_novelty: Dr. DNA detects and corrects silent data corruptions in neural networks by spotting anomalies in neuron output patterns during inference.

asplos-2024-102.method: MicroVSA applies Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA), which represents each pattern as a very-high-dimensional vector—a list with thousands of numbers. To classify new input, it compares the input vector against stored pattern vectors to find the closest match. VSA's key advantage is its approximate computing model: instead of performing exact mathematical operations, it uses fast approximate comparisons that dramatically reduce both the computational work and memory needed to run on tiny microcontrollers.
asplos-2024-102.key_novelty: The core contribution is using Vector Symbolic Architecture to enable classification inference on ultra-tiny, resource-constrained microcontrollers where traditional machine learning is too expensive to run.

asplos-2024-095.method: TQ preempts jobs—pauses them and switches to another one—at microsecond timescales (millionths of a second). To prevent starvation (a situation where some jobs never get to run), it forces these switches frequently, even if jobs would prefer to keep running. It uses a two-level scheduling hierarchy to avoid bottlenecking: instead of all scheduling decisions flowing through one point, they're distributed across the two levels.
asplos-2024-095.key_novelty: Using forced task switching combined with hierarchical two-level scheduling makes microsecond-scale blind scheduling scalable without creating a scheduling bottleneck.

asplos-2024-105.method: The system analyzes how many tokens arrive and leave (sequence length distributions) to find the best batch size (how many requests to process together) and partial tensor parallelism configuration (how to split GPU computation across multiple chips). It uses two strategies: Round-Robin Allocation for uniform requests and Workload-Aware Allocation for heterogeneous NLP tasks, continuously adjusting how work is scheduled to keep response times fast (within latency constraints) while processing as many requests as possible.
asplos-2024-105.key_novelty: It schedules work by simultaneously tuning batch size and partial tensor parallelism (splitting GPU computation across chips) to maximize throughput while guaranteeing latency bounds are met.

asplos-2024-098.method: Merlin optimizes eBPF programs (which run in the Linux kernel under strict instruction count limits) by transforming their code after initial compilation but before kernel verification. It uses two optimization techniques: instruction merging, which combines multiple operations into fewer, more efficient ones; and strength reduction, which replaces expensive operations with cheaper equivalents that produce the same result.
asplos-2024-098.key_novelty: The core idea is using compiler techniques specifically tailored to eBPF (custom compiler passes and bytecode rewriting) to discover optimization opportunities that general-purpose compilers overlook.

asplos-2024-104.method: SmartMem classifies operators into four groups and optimizes how data flows between them, allowing operators to share the same memory layouts. It designs efficient memory arrangements for the 2.5D memory structures found in mobile devices, then systematically searches for layout configurations that eliminate the expensive data rearrangements (called layout transformations) that normally occur between operators.
asplos-2024-104.key_novelty: Instead of optimizing each operator's memory layout separately, it coordinates all operators across the entire network so they can share the same memory layouts without needing expensive transformation steps between them.

asplos-2024-100.method: SpotServe runs large language models on cheap preemptible GPU instances that can be turned off without warning. When an instance gets terminated, the system automatically moves the inference work (the process of generating responses) to another available instance and restores the model's state (its stored memory and computation progress), so processing continues uninterrupted. This migration strategy lets the system keep serving requests despite instances being taken away.
asplos-2024-100.key_novelty: Automatically moving inference work between instances and preserving the model's state during transfers enables practical LLM serving on cheap preemptible instances that are frequently interrupted.

asplos-2024-106.method: Longnail automates the creation of custom processor instructions for RISC-V. You describe the instructions you want in CoreDSL, a specialized language, and Longnail generates the hardware needed to add them to any RISC-V processor. Because it automatically handles the differences between different RISC-V cores, one CoreDSL description works across all of them, letting you quickly explore and compare different processor configurations.
asplos-2024-106.key_novelty: One CoreDSL description automatically generates custom RISC-V instruction extensions for any processor core, so you can explore different hardware designs without rewriting the specification each time.

asplos-2024-103.method: SoD2 uses Rank and Dimension Propagation (RDP—a method that traces how tensor dimensions flow through operations) to determine tensor shapes at compile time, even when those shapes depend on input data. It represents each dimension as either a fixed value, an input-dependent expression, or a calculation based on other dimensions, enabling the system to fuse operations into efficient code blocks, plan execution order, and allocate memory in advance rather than at runtime.
asplos-2024-103.key_novelty: Rank and Dimension Propagation statically determines tensor shapes in neural networks with input-dependent operations, enabling compile-time optimization that would normally require shapes to be known in advance.

asplos-2024-110.method: The paper measures the electricity use and heat generated by large language models when running on GPUs (graphics processors) in datacenters, covering both inference (using existing models) and training (building new ones). It then reviews the power management techniques datacenters currently use and identifies specific opportunities to reduce how much electricity these models consume.
asplos-2024-110.key_novelty: By studying large language models specifically in cloud datacenters, it identifies which power optimizations would have the greatest impact.

asplos-2024-107.method: MetaMut feeds compiler knowledge into an LLM to automatically create mutation operators—targeted code variations designed to expose compiler bugs. These operators understand code meaning (semantic-aware) rather than making random edits, so they produce realistic test cases. The system deploys these operators to automatically test the compiler and uncover bugs by exploring how it handles diverse code patterns.
asplos-2024-107.key_novelty: An LLM automatically creates mutation operators for compiler testing, replacing manual expert implementation.

asplos-2024-108.method: Kaleidoscope performs static analysis by making optimistic assumptions: it predicts that pointers point to a narrower set of locations than standard analysis would allow. During program execution, it validates these predictions by checking if pointers actually behave as assumed. When validation succeeds, the precise predictions are used; when validation fails, it falls back to a conservative standard analysis that guarantees correctness.
asplos-2024-108.key_novelty: Verifying optimistic pointer predictions at runtime and falling back to guaranteed-correct analysis when predictions prove wrong.

asplos-2024-109.method: When the program runs, this approach records what happens to the stack—the memory area where local variables get stored temporarily. By examining this recording, it learns exactly how the stack is organized without having to guess. It then uses this runtime information when translating the binary into a new format that can be optimized, ensuring local variables are identified correctly.
asplos-2024-109.key_novelty: It records the program's execution to discover where local variables live, instead of guessing from analyzing the code.

asplos-2024-101.method: Heet measures how different the machines in the cluster are—both in how fast they compute and in how fast data travels between them. Using these measurements, it makes smarter decisions about where to place each training job and which machines to add or remove when scaling. This strategy reduces the harm that mismatched fast and slow machines would otherwise cause to training speed and job completion time.
asplos-2024-101.key_novelty: Heet is the first elastic training scheduler (one that dynamically adds/removes machines during training) to account for both how fast different machines compute and how fast they communicate with each other.

asplos-2024-114.method: MaxK-GNN designs specialized GPU programs (kernels) that tackle the two main performance problems in GNN training: uneven work distribution and unpredictable memory access. It automatically balances the workload across GPU processing units and restructures how data is fetched from memory to make access patterns regular and predictable. This matters because GNN training involves Sparse-Dense Matrix Multiplication (SpMM)—computing with matrices that mix mostly-zero sparse data with full matrices—which normally generates unpredictable memory traffic that slows everything down.
asplos-2024-114.key_novelty: GPU kernels specially designed to handle the workload imbalance and unpredictable memory access patterns of sparse-dense matrix operations in GNN training.

asplos-2024-111.method: T3 tracks what data each computation step needs and automatically starts sending it before earlier computations finish, overlapping data transfer with ongoing work to hide communication delays. It triggers transfers at a fine-grained level (many small transfers at the right moments) rather than waiting for batches. At the same time, it manages which hardware resources (GPU memory, bandwidth) each task uses, preventing data transfer and computation from competing for the same resources.
asplos-2024-111.key_novelty: The system automatically finds opportunities to overlap data transfers with computation without requiring programmers to manually write overlapping code.

asplos-2024-113.method: Litmus watches how long your function takes to run and compares it to how long it would take if the server was empty. The difference is slowdown from other functions using the same CPU and memory. Litmus charges you for the empty-server time instead of the actual time, removing the penalty for system congestion you didn't cause.
asplos-2024-113.key_novelty: Litmus charges you for the execution time your function would have used on an empty server, not the actual time it took with other functions present.

asplos-2024-116.method: To handle sudden traffic surges, datacenters can boost the computing power of existing servers by temporarily speeding them up using DVFS (Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling)—a technique that works by adjusting the voltage and clock frequency of each processor. Running servers at higher speeds generates more heat and power consumption, so the system includes continuous safety checks that monitor temperature, power use, and performance to prevent damage. These safeguards are validated thoroughly across the entire datacenter before DVFS boosting is deployed during peak demand periods.
asplos-2024-116.key_novelty: DVFS boosting—temporarily increasing a server's speed by adjusting voltage and frequency—can safely and reliably expand a datacenter's capacity without buying new hardware.

asplos-2024-112.method: QRCC combines multiple techniques to run larger quantum circuits on smaller quantum computers. Wire cutting splits circuits into smaller pieces that each fit on available qubits, while qubit reuse runs different parts of the computation sequentially on the same physical qubits, reducing total hardware needs. The system also explores gate cutting, which breaks circuits at individual gates rather than at wires and is particularly effective for calculating expectation values—the predicted measurement outcomes of quantum states.
asplos-2024-112.key_novelty: QRCC's key contribution is showing that combining qubit reuse and circuit cutting outperforms either technique in isolation, with gate cutting emerging as especially effective for expectation value calculations.

asplos-2024-115.method: Thesios reconstructs complete disk-operation records from partial samples (down-sampled traces—recordings that capture only some operations) collected from multiple storage devices and servers. The reconstruction infers missing operations and their exact timing by analyzing patterns in the partial data, producing complete sequences that accurately reflect actual disk behavior. This enables efficient what-if testing—simulating changes to storage policies, hardware configurations, or system adjustments—without costly production experiments.
asplos-2024-115.key_novelty: Accurately reconstructing complete disk-operation records from partial samples across multiple servers enables efficient what-if testing of storage scenarios without production experiments.

asplos-2024-121.method: When many cores simultaneously request data from remote memory, each request competes for limited network bandwidth, creating a bottleneck that prevents scaling beyond about 32 cores. SMART addresses this by bundling multiple memory requests into single network packets (request batching), overlapping the sending and receiving of data so the network stays constantly busy (pipelining), and timing when requests go out based on current network conditions (network-aware scheduling). These techniques multiply how many requests the same network can handle per second, enabling efficient operation with dozens of cores.
asplos-2024-121.key_novelty: Batching and pipelining memory requests to match network bandwidth can overcome the bottleneck that prevents disaggregated memory systems from scaling across many cores.

asplos-2024-122.method: CodeCrunch reduces the memory footprint of warm function instances (functions kept running to avoid startup delays) using compression. It then uses a cost-aware algorithm that examines each server's capabilities and costs to decide which ones should maintain warm copies, weighing whether avoiding a cold start is worth the ongoing memory and cost. This lets you reduce startup delays while managing the expense of keeping functions warm during traffic spikes.
asplos-2024-122.key_novelty: CodeCrunch pairs function compression with an algorithm that uses server cost differences to decide where to keep warm copies, reducing cold starts while managing memory and ongoing costs.

asplos-2024-118.method: WASP automatically profiles how an application accesses memory and monitors interference from other running applications to decide whether to enable page-table self-replication—storing copies of the memory-mapping table across processor cores instead of keeping just one. Based on these observations, it turns PTSR on when it improves performance and off when it creates overhead. This eliminates the need for users to manually configure PTSR.
asplos-2024-118.key_novelty: WASP automatically decides whether to enable page-table self-replication by observing application memory access and interference from co-running applications, instead of requiring manual configuration.

asplos-2024-119.method: CIM-MLC is a multi-level compilation stack—a series of translation layers that convert neural networks to hardware operations—built to work with many different computing-in-memory (CIM) accelerator architectures. Each level uses flexible abstractions to handle variable device precision (how many bits store each number), different crossbar sizes and counts (the computing grids), and different computing granularities (the scale at which computations execute). This way, the same compiler works across diverse CIM designs instead of requiring a custom compiler for each architecture.
asplos-2024-119.key_novelty: A multi-level compilation abstraction that works across different computing-in-memory accelerators with different configurations, instead of being locked to one design.

asplos-2024-120.method: ProxiML incorporates multiple design elements that are aware of noise (which is unavoidable when using photonic quantum devices—machines that process information using light particles). These techniques make the system robust—meaning it works well during both training and actual use, even with imperfect hardware. The classifier is tested on Xanadu's X8 photonic quantum machine using circuits specifically tuned for how photonic hardware works.
asplos-2024-120.key_novelty: ProxiML is the first systematic study of machine learning classifiers designed specifically for photonic quantum platforms (quantum computers that use light to process information) with integrated noise mitigation.

asplos-2024-123.method: CKKS encryption uses integers that vary widely in size, typically 30-60 bits each. When hardware multiplies these encrypted integers, they must fit into fixed-size registers, leaving many unused bits that waste silicon and power. BitPacker solves this by packing multiple encrypted integers together into the same arithmetic unit (the hardware that performs calculations), so fewer bits are wasted during each multiplication. This improves both the area efficiency and energy consumption of CKKS accelerators.
asplos-2024-123.key_novelty: BitPacker efficiently packs variable-sized CKKS encrypted integers into arithmetic units to reduce wasted bits during multiplication operations.

asplos-2024-128.method: Marple splits the work into two stages. First, a fixed hardware piece (the frontend) filters noise from incoming electrical signals from brain electrodes in real-time. Next, a flexible software component (the backend) uses machine learning to determine which neuron created each electrical spike, rather than comparing each spike to stored reference patterns. The system compresses how it stores these patterns by 8-11x, which frees up enough memory to handle thousands of channels instead of being limited to 128.
asplos-2024-128.key_novelty: A compression technique for stored reference patterns that reduces memory use by 8-11x, enabling spike sorting on thousands of electrode channels rather than 128.

asplos-2024-125.method: CC-NIC redesigns the interface between a processor and network card in systems where they share the same cache memory (a cache-coherent interconnect). Instead of using PCIe interfaces designed when network cards didn't share caches, it rethinks how the two components signal each other and reorganizes how data is arranged in memory to reduce the work needed to keep their caches in sync. Implemented on Intel's Ice Lake and Sapphire Rapids processors with UPI interconnects, this approach aligns the design to how shared caches actually work.
asplos-2024-125.key_novelty: The innovation is building the processor-NIC interface specifically for shared caches instead of adapting existing PCIe designs.

asplos-2024-127.method: IANUS combines a Neural Processing Unit (a processor specialized for AI inference) with Processing-in-Memory (computation that happens directly inside memory to avoid data movement) into one unified memory system. The PIM hardware serves double duty: it both runs computations and stores the data the NPU needs. Since memory can't simultaneously handle both data accesses and computations, a scheduling system coordinates between these competing demands, optimizing for the diverse needs of LLM inference.
asplos-2024-127.key_novelty: The core idea is using the same memory hardware for both computation and data storage, with scheduling that coordinates them since they cannot happen at the same time.

asplos-2024-126.method: Clapton reformulates the quantum problem's energy equation (the Hamiltonian) using Clifford quantum gates, guided by good quantum solutions computed on a regular computer and models of the device's quantum noise. It applies the variational principle—testing different quantum parameter settings to find the lowest energy reading—to get better energy estimates for these known good solutions even when the quantum device makes errors, which reduces how much noise affects the final ground state (the system's lowest-energy solution). The system handles everything from problem to device, incorporating realistic noise simulation during the problem reformulation.
asplos-2024-126.key_novelty: Clapton cuts quantum noise by reshaping how the quantum problem is formulated (the Hamiltonian), guided by good quantum solutions calculated beforehand on a regular computer.

asplos-2024-117.method: TAPA-CS automatically divides large accelerator programs across a cluster of FPGAs with high-bandwidth memory, spreading the workload to prevent bottlenecks and balance resource use. It carefully plans where components should go (floor-planning) and speeds up communication paths within and between FPGAs (through interconnect pipelining) to maintain high-frequency operation. The FPGAs connect through 100Gbps Ethernet, and the system overlaps communication with computation—while data is sent between chips, they simultaneously process other data.
asplos-2024-117.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically splitting accelerator designs across multiple HBM-FPGAs using layout planning and pipelined communication to enable both scalability and high-frequency operation.

asplos-2024-130.method: Lakeroad automates FPGA technology mapping using sketch-guided program synthesis—a technique that starts with incomplete template patterns (the 'sketch') and automatically fills in the details. It employs architecture-independent sketch templates that work across different FPGA types, completing them by extracting the meaning of hardware descriptions to discover which circuit patterns can map to efficient hardware building blocks like DSPs. This systematic approach replaces handwritten mapping rules, which are error-prone and miss optimization opportunities.
asplos-2024-130.key_novelty: Combining architecture-independent sketch templates with sketch-guided program synthesis to automate FPGA technology mapping.

asplos-2024-124.method: Rubix randomizes how cache lines (chunks of data stored temporarily for fast access) map to physical rows in main memory, so attackers' accesses get spread across different rows instead of hammering a single one. This disrupts Rowhammer attacks, where attackers exploit memory by repeatedly targeting specific addresses to corrupt nearby data. The technique works with existing protections like row-migration (moving threatened data to safe rows) and access-control (limiting row access frequency), reducing their typical performance overhead while maintaining security against sophisticated attacks like Half-Double.
asplos-2024-124.key_novelty: Randomizing how cache lines map to memory rows reduces the performance overhead of existing Rowhammer protections without weakening their security.

asplos-2024-129.method: The approach automatically generates control logic by analyzing three interconnected design layers: architectural specifications (the high-level blueprint), microarchitectural datapath components (the actual hardware devices like functional units), and the control signals needed to coordinate them. Instead of designers hand-writing this coordination logic, an automated process reasons about the dependencies between these layers and automatically generates control logic that orchestrates them correctly. By treating specifications, hardware, and control signals as one unified design problem rather than separate design stages, the tool produces control logic that integrates properly with the hardware.
asplos-2024-129.key_novelty: It automatically generates control logic by treating architecture specifications, hardware components, and control signals as one unified design problem.

asplos-2024-139.method: Isaria automatically finds the best way to write code that processes multiple data items at once (called vectorization) for specialized signal-processing chips (DSPs). Instead of engineers hand-writing transformation rules, the system generates correct transformation rules automatically from the processor's instruction manual. It then groups related transformation rules together to speed up compilation and removes unnecessary intermediate forms during the search to keep the process fast. This lets companies quickly create optimized compilers for new or customized DSP designs.
asplos-2024-139.key_novelty: It automatically creates correct code transformation rules by reading the processor's instruction manual, eliminating the need for engineers to hand-craft them.

asplos-2024-137.method: Cocco explores different ways to distribute neural network computations across the hardware while simultaneously deciding how much on-chip memory to use. For each configuration, it applies data reuse optimization (avoiding repeated fetches of the same data) and layer fusion (combining multiple neural network layers into fewer computation steps) to reduce overall data movement. By trying these combinations together rather than separately, it finds hardware mappings and memory configurations that better balance memory capacity against data-movement costs.
asplos-2024-137.key_novelty: Rather than deciding separately how to map computations and allocate on-chip memory, it explores both choices together to find configurations that balance memory capacity against data-movement costs.

asplos-2024-132.method: Video frames are naturally similar across time—a property called temporal redundancy. The approach compresses the matrix data representing this video using a technique called CODEC-assisted matrix condensing, which shrinks the data before the transformer processes it. This reduces both the raw computation needed and the costly overhead from trying to predict which parts of the transformer's attention mechanism actually matter.
asplos-2024-132.key_novelty: The core idea is using CODEC-assisted matrix condensing to exploit temporal redundancy (the similarity between consecutive video frames), which reduces the overhead of predicting which parts of the transformer's attention mechanism matter.

asplos-2024-142.method: The approach formalizes Nvidia PTX and Khronos Vulkan consistency models—the rules governing how GPUs handle memory operations across parallel threads—and analyzes both to identify which rules they share and which differ between vendors. It then develops tools and frameworks based on this analysis, enabling developers to verify their GPU code will behave correctly under these different consistency rules without requiring deep GPU architecture expertise.
asplos-2024-142.key_novelty: A unified framework for analyzing Nvidia PTX and Khronos Vulkan consistency models together, revealing which memory rules they share and where they diverge.

asplos-2024-136.method: The core challenge in quantum program verification is that measuring quantum states destroys them, making repeated testing impossible. MorphQPV uses tracepoint pragmas—labeled checkpoints marking verified states—and assume-guarantee primitives, which are contracts specifying that if input states have property X, then output states must have property Y. It then applies isomorphism, a mathematical principle where different structures share the same underlying relationships, to infer correct state relationships without re-executing the program. Finally, verification is solved as a constraint optimization problem, finding values that satisfy all contracts and computing a confidence score for correctness.
asplos-2024-136.key_novelty: The core innovation is leveraging isomorphism—the preservation of structural relationships in quantum program states—to enable verification without re-execution, which is necessary since quantum measurement destroys states.

asplos-2024-141.method: Wizard tracks code execution by injecting measurement points—called probes—at the bytecode level (the low-level code the engine processes) without permanently modifying the original code. It reuses the WebAssembly engine's existing just-in-time compiler, interpreter, and optimization-reversal mechanisms to minimize the impact of adding these probes. You can add and remove these measurement points while code is running, and the system guarantees that measurements stay accurate and don't interfere with each other, even when performing multiple simultaneous analyses.
asplos-2024-141.key_novelty: Wizard is the first WebAssembly system that injects measurement points at the bytecode level without modifying the original code, supports adding and removing them on-the-fly, and maintains consistent measurements across multiple simultaneous analyses.

asplos-2024-134.method: When training large language models across multiple devices (like GPUs or TPUs) in parallel, different pipeline stages run on different devices simultaneously. AdaPipe automatically decides for each intermediate value (temporary data computed during processing) whether to save it to memory or discard and recalculate it later, picking whichever is more efficient. It also automatically partitions the pipeline stages across devices to balance memory usage—preventing some devices from running out of memory while others have spare capacity—and reduces waiting time when devices need to synchronize.
asplos-2024-134.key_novelty: AdaPipe jointly optimizes two normally separate decisions—which intermediate values to recompute (versus store) and how to partition pipeline stages across devices—to balance memory consumption against computation overhead.

asplos-2024-131.method: The system identifies which DRAM addresses are vulnerable to Row Hammer attacks through 3-week experiments on real DRAM modules. Starting at boot, it periodically accesses these vulnerable addresses to prevent the bit flips that cause uncorrectable errors. Instead of using the main CPU for this task, it offloads the periodic accesses to a separate processor (a CXL SmartNIC—a specialized chip with its own CPU, connected via CXL, a high-speed connection standard).
asplos-2024-131.key_novelty: The core innovation is handling Row Hammer defense on a separate CXL SmartNIC instead of the main CPU, eliminating performance overhead.

asplos-2024-138.method: TrackFM uses a compiler—the software that converts code to machine instructions—to figure out what data a program needs and where it should be stored across a network of computers (some memory on the local machine, some on remote machines). The compiler automatically inserts instructions to move data between local and remote memory while keeping copies consistent (a task called coherence), and a runtime system handles the actual data movement. Programs automatically get these far-memory capabilities after recompilation, without any code changes.
asplos-2024-138.key_novelty: TrackFM's core idea is using the compiler to automatically manage memory across networked machines, solving the tradeoff where fast systems need programmer changes but simple systems are slow.

asplos-2024-135.method: QuFEM breaks quantum readout noise calibration into smaller pieces, representing each as a noise matrix—a table describing how measurements get corrupted. It learns these matrices through experiments, iteratively refining them with measured probability data while exploiting locality: each qubit primarily affects its neighbors, not all other qubits. The speedup comes from exploiting mathematical sparsity: when combining these matrices (tensor products), most intermediate values are zero; the algorithm skips these unnecessary calculations using a technique inspired by finite element methods.
asplos-2024-135.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a sparse tensor-product engine inspired by finite element methods—skipping zero-valued calculations when combining quantum noise matrices to achieve orders-of-magnitude speedup.

asplos-2024-143.method: MemSnap creates 'micro-checkpoints'—small, frequent snapshots of only the data that changed—built directly into the storage layer. Older systems like EROS, Aurora, and TreeSLS could only save entire snapshots at once, and they still needed both a write-ahead log (a record of every write) and external file backups for safety. MemSnap's approach eliminates these separate mechanisms by integrating checkpoint management directly into the memory and storage system, keeping all data protection unified in one place.
asplos-2024-143.key_novelty: Micro-checkpoints that save only changed data directly in the storage system, eliminating the need for separate write-ahead logs while preserving data consistency.

asplos-2024-133.method: HBC is a compiler that translates C/C++ programs written with fork-join parallelism (instructions that let different code sections run simultaneously, like OpenMP) into optimized machine code. It uses Heartbeat Scheduling to automatically control task granularity—how much work each parallel task completes before yielding—with formal performance guarantees, meaning we can mathematically prove that management overhead won't eliminate parallelism benefits. The compiler adjusts task granularity dynamically based on actual runtime data patterns, so irregular, input-sensitive workloads (where performance depends on what data the program receives) can benefit from parallelism without requiring programmers to manually tune the code.
asplos-2024-133.key_novelty: HBC is the first compiler to automatically translate fork-join parallelism (parallel code sections, including those nested within other parallel sections) into machine code that adjusts task granularity (work per parallel piece) with formal performance guarantees, eliminating manual tuning for irregular workloads.

asplos-2024-140.method: AMNT uses a nested 'tree within a tree' structure — organizing one tree hierarchy inside another — to keep integrity metadata safe even through sudden power failures. To save on-chip space, the design shifts bookkeeping work from hardware (the silicon chip) to software (the running program). Updates to this metadata are fine-tuned to remain fast while making good use of limited on-chip cache space.
asplos-2024-140.key_novelty: A nested 'tree within a tree' structure that preserves file integrity tracking through power failures while saving on-chip area by shifting work from hardware to software.

asplos-2024-146.method: The paper proposes building AI infrastructure by coupling hardware and software design across all layers—networks, accelerators (specialized chips for AI), and servers—rather than trying to squeeze more speed out of general-purpose computers. Each infrastructure piece is optimized specifically for AI algorithm demands through co-design, where hardware and software are developed together so they work perfectly with each other. Security and sustainability are integrated into this approach from the start.
asplos-2024-146.key_novelty: Instead of making general-purpose computers faster, the strategy is to design AI hardware and software together as optimized pairs, each tailored to work specifically with the other.

asplos-2024-145.method: The algorithm uses research on human vision showing that our eyes can't distinguish between very similar colors—especially in our peripheral vision (the edges of what we're looking at). It takes advantage of this by intentionally shifting pixel colors to look identical to the eye but using fewer bits to represent them in memory, saving both storage space and power (since accessing memory is one of the biggest energy drains in VR systems). Lightweight hardware support in the graphics pipeline makes this compression fast enough to happen in real time.
asplos-2024-145.key_novelty: The core idea is to exploit human color perception limitations—our inability to distinguish between similar colors in both central and peripheral vision—to achieve numerically-lossy (less exact) but perceptually-lossless (looks identical to the eye) image compression.

asplos-2024-154.method: PrimePar splits the training work two ways: across hardware devices (spatial dimension) and across time steps (temporal dimension). By splitting both ways instead of just spatially, it avoids forcing all devices to pause and sync their data, and instead overlaps data transfer between devices with ongoing computation. An optimization algorithm efficiently searches this expanded set of configurations to find the fastest one.
asplos-2024-154.key_novelty: Using both temporal and spatial dimensions for partitioning—instead of just spatial—opens up more ways to divide the work, which reduces inter-device communication overhead and memory usage during training.

asplos-2024-150.method: TGLite provides modular, composable components that practitioners can combine to build neural networks for graphs that evolve through timestamped events (continuous-time directed graphs, or CTDGs). It includes optimizations specifically tailored to this problem, enabling efficient execution without manual performance tuning. This composable design allows practitioners to experiment with new model architectures and improvements by combining existing pieces in new ways, rather than rebuilding from scratch each time.
asplos-2024-150.key_novelty: TGLite is a composable framework for building neural networks on graphs that change through timestamped events, designed specifically to support efficient model exploration.

asplos-2024-152.method: MPC-Pipe overlaps computation and communication steps rather than doing them one after another—while data is being computed at one machine, it's simultaneously being sent to other machines, keeping both processing and network active. This pipelined approach is applied to both CNNs (convolutional networks for image processing) and Transformers (models for language tasks), eliminating idle time where the system would otherwise wait between stages.
asplos-2024-152.key_novelty: MPC-Pipe overlaps computation and communication steps in encrypted multi-party machine learning so data flows continuously instead of waiting between stages.

asplos-2024-149.method: Ark is a programming language for designing specialized analog circuits—circuits that use continuous electrical signals instead of digital 1s and 0s to do computations. It includes an automated checker (validator) to ensure designs work and a simulator (dynamical system compiler) that models the circuit's real-time behavior while accounting for imperfections like noise and component variation. This lets designers systematically explore different design choices and predict how manufacturing variations and environmental factors affect performance.
asplos-2024-149.key_novelty: Ark is a programming language that enables systematic exploration of specialized reconfigurable analog circuit designs by automatically verifying correctness and simulating how real-world imperfections like noise and component variation affect performance.

asplos-2024-156.method: DNA storage encodes data into DNA sequences that are synthesized and later read back using 'primers' (starter sequences that identify each data segment) and 'payloads' (the actual data sequences). The problem is that primers often collide with payloads—they overlap or interfere with the data sequences, making parts of the DNA unusable or error-prone. This encoding scheme prevents those collisions by arranging sequences so primers and payloads don't interfere with each other. Because fewer sequences are wasted on collisions, more of each strand can actually store data, increasing practical capacity without needing to pack information more densely.
asplos-2024-156.key_novelty: Preventing primer-payload collisions through careful encoding design is more effective for increasing practical DNA storage capacity than simply increasing encoding density.

asplos-2024-151.method: RTL simulation (register-level circuit testing) is slow for complex hardware designs. The approach identifies circuit modules that appear multiple times and deduplicates them at a coarse-grained level—treating each module as a whole unit instead of examining its internal structure. Across parallel test runs, this allows identical modules to be simulated once and their results reused for all copies, rather than each copy being recalculated separately.
asplos-2024-151.key_novelty: The innovation is to deduplicate replicated hardware components across parallel simulations—treating each component as a single unit (coarse-grained deduplication)—so identical components are simulated once instead of redundantly for each copy.

asplos-2024-147.method: Crocus verifies the correctness of instruction-lowering rules—the translation steps where high-level operations are converted to native CPU instructions—in Cranelift, a WebAssembly compiler for ARM aarch64 processors. It tests these translation rules against WebAssembly 1.0 integer operations to find bugs where the translation produces incorrect results and to uncover assumptions the compiler makes but never explicitly states.
asplos-2024-147.key_novelty: It provides practical verification of instruction-lowering rules—where compilers translate high-level operations to native CPU instructions—in production WebAssembly compilers.

asplos-2024-144.method: CSSTs are a data structure for tracking the order of events in concurrent execution. They replace Vector Clocks, which require O(n) time to add each ordering (where n is trace size) and cannot remove orderings. CSSTs can both add and remove orderings much more efficiently, making it practical to analyze large concurrent execution traces.
asplos-2024-144.key_novelty: Unlike Vector Clocks, CSSTs efficiently handle both insertion and deletion of event orderings in concurrent execution.

asplos-2024-157.method: Zoomie adapts familiar software debugging workflows to FPGA development by letting you pause hardware execution at breakpoints, inspect your circuit's internal state in real-time, and watch data flowing through it. The debugging actions themselves (pause, inspect, continue) are the same for both software and hardware; Zoomie just creates an interface that makes them work with FPGAs. This eliminates the need for developers to learn specialized tools—if you know how to debug software, you can debug hardware.
asplos-2024-157.key_novelty: Zoomie closes the usability gap between software and FPGA development by letting developers debug hardware using the same pause-and-inspect workflows they already know from software.

asplos-2024-148.method: Reducing a chip's voltage saves power but causes random bit errors—flipped 0s and 1s in calculations. MulBERRY adds protections that catch and fix these bit errors in the reinforcement learning AI (where AI learns by trial and error) that coordinates multi-agent drone swarms. This lets the swarms keep operating safely even with power turned down to the minimum.
asplos-2024-148.key_novelty: The key idea is making multi-agent reinforcement learning robust to bit errors—random corrupted calculations caused by low electrical power.

asplos-2024-153.method: RAP consolidates two jobs on the same GPU instead of separate machines: training a recommendation model (predicting what users want) and preparing the input data that feeds into it. The system automatically allocates GPU time between the two tasks based on how much work each requires at any moment. This eliminates the need for hundreds of dedicated CPU nodes currently used just for data preparation—which consume more power than the GPU training itself.
asplos-2024-153.key_novelty: Instead of requiring separate CPU infrastructure for data preparation, this system lets a single GPU handle both model training and data preparation by automatically splitting its time based on what each task needs at any moment.

asplos-2024-158.method: BVAP pairs a compiler with specialized hardware to efficiently process regular expressions. The compiler translates text-search patterns (including bounded repetitions—repeats with limits, like 'match between 1 and 5 times') into hardware-specific instructions. The hardware then uses bit vectors (where each bit represents whether a pattern is actively matching at that point) to run pattern matching directly in memory, cutting energy use and chip size.
