asplos-2024-158.key_novelty: The Action-Homogeneous Non-deterministic Bit Vector Automata (AH-NBVA) model enables hardware to efficiently support regular expression patterns with bounded repetitions (repeats capped at specific counts, like 1 to 5 times).

asplos-2024-162.method: The paper studies CXL 3.0, a hardware standard that lets multiple physical host computers dynamically share a pool of memory without copying data between them. It examines CXL pods—configurations where several hosts connect to shared memory through CXL—as a middle ground between traditional distributed systems (where each computer has isolated memory) and shared-memory multiprocessors (where all computers instantly see all memory). The analysis traces the implications across three layers: computer architecture, operating system design, and programming language abstractions.
asplos-2024-162.key_novelty: CXL pods represent a middle ground between traditional distributed systems (where each computer has its own isolated memory) and shared-memory multiprocessors (where all computers instantly see shared memory), with distinct challenges and opportunities that differ from both.

asplos-2024-164.method: Hector uses a two-level intermediate representation (a middle format between high-level code and GPU instructions) and a code generator that understands relational graph neural networks and identifies opportunities to reorder operations for efficiency. It generates flexible ways to access data in memory that avoid unnecessary duplication, and it separates the network's logic from how data is arranged in memory and how each operation is tuned for performance. The framework builds on proven components like general matrix multiplication and templates for traversing graph nodes and edges, using linear operator reordering and compact storage techniques.
asplos-2024-164.key_novelty: A two-level intermediate representation that separates what the network computes from how data is stored and how each operation is optimized, which allows efficient compilation of relational graph neural networks and reduces what programmers must write from thousands of lines to 51 lines.

asplos-2024-155.method: Alaska puts a middleman (called a handle) between your code's pointers and memory objects, allowing objects to be moved around without breaking the code. A compiler automatically rewrites your code to use handles instead of direct pointers, and optimizes lookups so the extra indirection doesn't slow things down much. The runtime system controls the handles and provides customizable services for memory management features like defragmentation.
asplos-2024-155.key_novelty: Alaska replaces malloc with compiler-generated handles (intermediate pointers), enabling garbage collectors to move heap objects and defragment memory in unmanaged languages like C/C++.

asplos-2024-166.method: MopFuzzer tests JVM compilers using 13 different mutation tools that make targeted changes to trigger specific optimization behaviors. It records profile data—detailed logs of what optimizations the compiler actually performed—and uses this feedback to steer which mutations to test next, focusing on cases where multiple optimizations interact in the same compilation. Correctness is verified through differential testing, comparing results across different compiler versions to catch errors.
asplos-2024-166.key_novelty: Rather than random testing, the approach systematically steers fuzzing toward triggering multiple compiler optimizations that interact with each other in the same run, guided by profile data from actual compilations.

asplos-2024-159.method: ARM-Dedup moves deduplication (finding and removing duplicate data) from the host computer into SSD controllers. Normally, the host's deduplication software maintains one address map while each SSD's internal firmware (the Flash Translation Layer, or FTL) maintains a separate address map, creating redundant work. ARM-Dedup eliminates this by making SSD firmware deduplication-oriented and array-aware—aware of duplicate data and of multiple drives working together—so the SSD controllers handle deduplication storage management directly. The system was built by modifying Linux deduplication software (Dmdedup and mdraid) to work with custom SSD firmware, tested using FEMU SSD emulators.
asplos-2024-159.key_novelty: Making SSD firmware deduplication-oriented and array-aware eliminates the inefficiency of managing array-wide deduplication separately from per-SSD storage management.

asplos-2024-165.method: Souffle maps out how tensors (multi-dimensional data arrays) depend on each other by analyzing the math expressions that create them. It then breaks the large computation into smaller subprograms based on how data flows through the system and what hardware resources are available. Within each subprogram, it rearranges the operations to keep the math identical while letting more instructions run simultaneously, improving data reuse in the processor cache, and optimizing the overall execution schedule.
asplos-2024-165.key_novelty: It optimizes across operators by mapping tensor dependencies through the entire program and splitting the work into subprograms based on this dataflow analysis.

asplos-2024-160.method: The system monitors the harvested power coming in and automatically adjusts how much energy it stores. When power input is high, it shrinks the buffer to prevent overflow—energy being wasted as heat when the storage is full. When power input is low, it grows the buffer to prevent underflow—stored energy slowly leaking away unused. By adjusting storage capacity to match the current power level, the system stays able to handle short bursts of work, even as environmental power fluctuates.
asplos-2024-160.key_novelty: The storage buffer automatically resizes based on how much power is available, instead of using a fixed capacity.

asplos-2024-168.method: FaaSMem works by moving unused memory from idle serverless containers to a shared remote pool (network storage) instead of keeping it all locally. Rather than moving memory in large blocks—which would slow down applications—it uses fine-grained offloading policies (precise rules about which data to move and when). This lets the system recover wasted memory from idle containers while keeping response times fast.
asplos-2024-168.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a remote memory pool with fine-grained offloading policies specifically for serverless computing, enabling memory recovery without sacrificing application response times.

asplos-2024-163.method: The approach tests concurrent programs by exploring different orderings of thread operations, but guides this exploration using data-flow information rather than random sampling: specifically, tracking which thread's reads get their values from which thread's writes (the 'reads-from' relation). By focusing on orderings where this data-flow pattern changes, it identifies orders more likely to expose bugs and achieves more thorough exploration than purely random testing.
asplos-2024-163.key_novelty: The core idea is using the 'reads-from' relation—which thread's read operations get values from which thread's writes—to guide randomized testing of different thread operation orderings.

asplos-2024-167.method: VertexSurge efficiently searches massive graphs (with billions of edges) for patterns where nodes connect through a variable number of intermediate edges. Most existing graph databases are optimized only for direct connections between nodes (called single-hop matching), but this design doesn't work well when connection paths have different lengths. VertexSurge instead specializes its entire architecture around variable-length pattern matching, allowing it to efficiently handle complex, real-world network patterns.
asplos-2024-167.key_novelty: The key idea is building a system specifically designed for variable-length graph pattern matching on billion-edge graphs, rather than adapting single-hop search systems.

asplos-2024-176.method: LFI runs tens of thousands of isolated environments (4GiB sandboxes) within a single address space by rewriting compiled machine code directly (binary instrumentation), without needing a compiler. It ensures all memory reads and writes (loads and stores) and program jumps stay within sandbox boundaries by checking the code once before it runs (static verification), using a small verification program to minimize the amount of code you have to trust. The system also includes defenses against Spectre attacks and supports programming language features like exception handling and SIMD (single instruction, multiple data — a hardware feature for processing many values at once).
asplos-2024-176.key_novelty: LFI is the first practical system that isolates tens of thousands of sandboxes on ARM64 processors (used in cloud computing) with just 7% performance overhead and a minimal amount of code you have to trust.

asplos-2024-161.method: The paper presents a software caching layer for microcontrollers equipped with NVRAM (non-volatile RAM—memory that keeps data even when powered off). The runtime works like a smart traffic controller, automatically moving data between the microcontroller's limited fast memory and the larger NVRAM storage based on what the program needs. By taking advantage of NVRAM's ability to save program state without draining power, the system enables memory-limited devices to handle large-scale data storage and processing while maintaining ultra-low-power operation.
asplos-2024-161.key_novelty: This paper introduces a software caching system designed for microcontrollers with NVRAM, using the memory's non-volatility (ability to keep data when powered off) to enable large-scale storage and processing on memory-limited devices.

asplos-2024-170.method: Normally, programs access storage through the kernel, the core system software that routes all disk requests, which adds latency overhead. BypassD lets programs directly access an SSD, and when multiple programs use the same SSD, they coordinate their accesses through mechanisms in userspace (instead of having the kernel do it), without requiring changes to the kernel, filesystem, or hardware.
asplos-2024-170.key_novelty: BypassD is the first system that lets multiple programs directly access the same SSD from userspace (the programs themselves rather than through the kernel), without requiring changes to the kernel, filesystem, or hardware.

asplos-2024-173.method: Manta recovers the type information that's removed from stripped binaries by using data-flow analysis—tracking how values flow through code—at multiple sensitivity levels (different degrees of strictness), which together catch type constraints that any single approach would miss. The inferred types then eliminate impossible function call targets and help find bugs more accurately.
asplos-2024-173.key_novelty: It combines multiple sensitivity levels in data-flow analysis to infer types and find bugs in stripped binaries.

asplos-2024-181.method: SIRO breaks down IR translation into smaller pieces using a divide-and-conquer approach (splitting a hard problem into easier subproblems). For each piece, it uses program synthesis—automatic code generation that tries different ways to implement each translation—to generate translators for individual IR instructions. These auto-generated instruction translators are then combined to build complete converters that transform LLVM IR from one version to another.
asplos-2024-181.key_novelty: SIRO uses automatic code generation (program synthesis) to build IR version translators, removing the need to manually write them.

asplos-2024-171.method: Grafu reduces disk accesses when processing graphs too large for memory by predicting which data will be needed in future iterations and computing it ahead of time. The system overlaps computation across iteration boundaries—calculating future vertex values while the current round runs—but stays synchronized so each iteration completes before the next begins. It coordinates prefetching (loading data early), computation scheduling, and memory allocation to maximize these lookahead benefits without breaking the ordered execution model.
asplos-2024-171.key_novelty: Grafu reduces disk accesses in synchronous out-of-core graph processing by using future-value computation (computing vertex data ahead of time), something prior systems couldn't do without breaking iteration-order semantics.

asplos-2024-179.method: RainbowCake caches individual layers of Docker container images—the stacked building blocks that make up a complete image—rather than storing entire containers. When a function starts, it can reuse these cached layers instead of rebuilding from scratch, speeding up startup time. Multiple functions can also share the same running container, reducing wasted memory from underutilized containers.
asplos-2024-179.key_novelty: RainbowCake combines layer-wise container caching with container sharing to achieve both the cold-start speed of traditional full caching and the memory efficiency of standalone sharing.

asplos-2024-172.method: The attack exploits the conditional branch predictor—the CPU component that predicts which direction conditional branches in code will go. Read operations extract the path history register (recording which branches were taken) and prediction history tables (storing predictions for each branch), revealing the exact sequence of branches the victim program executed. Write operations modify the predictor state to force speculative execution (running code speculatively to save time) of unintended code, allowing attackers to leak secrets. Practical attacks recover control flow from libjpeg image processing routines and extract cryptographic keys from AES implementations.
asplos-2024-172.key_novelty: First exploitation of branch predictor read and write operations to leak control flow history and enable high-resolution transient execution attacks.

asplos-2024-175.method: The approach measures how different NAND flash chips fail and degrade over time, then builds mathematical models to predict the ideal voltage levels (the electronic signals used to read data) needed for each memory location. From these predictions, it creates a custom lookup table for each chip type—essentially a database pairing operating conditions to the best voltage to use. When reading, the system consults the lookup table to get a starting voltage, then searches nearby values to fine-tune the exact best setting, dramatically reducing the number of failed reads that need error correction.
asplos-2024-175.key_novelty: Instead of using generic read-retry tables, the approach generates chip-specific tables by measuring how each NAND model actually behaves under aging.

asplos-2024-174.method: HIDA organizes how data flows through a system in layers (hierarchical dataflow) and automatically optimizes each layer, breaking down the design problem based on this natural structure. By working layer-by-layer instead of trying every possibility at once, it makes the search manageable instead of overwhelming. The framework takes a high-level algorithm and converts it into a detailed, optimized plan showing which operations run and when, for FPGAs (programmable hardware chips). Testing was done on neural network models from PyTorch.
asplos-2024-174.key_novelty: Using how data naturally flows through a system to automatically break down the design optimization, making it possible to efficiently explore many possible designs.

asplos-2024-169.method: SoCFlow runs AI model training in the background on mobile processor clusters, using the idle computing time between busy periods of user app activity. The system adapts its training schedule to match user demand and distributes the work across different processor types while maintaining performance for active users. It uses compiler-based optimization to make training run efficiently.
asplos-2024-169.key_novelty: Using idle computing time on clustered mobile processors for AI model training without degrading the performance of active user applications.

asplos-2024-183.method: The framework optimizes photonic quantum programs in two stages: first before execution (offline), then during execution (online). It uses a special intermediate representation that explicitly captures which quantum operations are random and how much randomness they introduce. This shared format lets the compiler make better optimization decisions at both stages—choosing safer operations upfront and adapting them dynamically as the program runs.
asplos-2024-183.key_novelty: An intermediate representation that explicitly captures the randomness in photonic quantum fusion operations, enabling optimization both before and during program execution.

asplos-2024-186.method: MECH creates multiple parallel communication pathways between qubits by using spare qubits as intermediaries—trading some qubits that could do computation for the ability to send multiple signals simultaneously. A compilation framework (automatic planning software) then decides how to route each signal through available pathways, reducing the physical distance each signal travels and speeding up quantum program execution.
asplos-2024-186.key_novelty: Trading spare qubits to create multiple simultaneous communication pathways, so quantum operations run in parallel rather than bottlenecking on one slow connection.

asplos-2024-189.method: The researchers created a practical attack that measures tiny differences in how long it takes to access a shared memory cache — the pool of fast memory that all programs on a server use. By observing these timing variations, they can figure out what other programs are doing. They adapted this cache-watching technique to filter out noise from other programs running simultaneously and to work within the extremely tight time limits of cloud serverless functions, where they might have only milliseconds to run.
asplos-2024-189.key_novelty: This work shows for the first time that attackers can actually exploit shared-cache timing attacks in real production cloud servers, even when many programs share the hardware and execution time is severely limited—proving that multi-tenancy and timing constraints do not provide the protection that was assumed.

asplos-2024-188.method: The attacker exploits how the cloud platform schedules functions and allocates resources to place their own functions on the same physical machine as a target victim—bypassing the VPC isolation that should keep them separate. Once co-located, both functions share the CPU cache (fast memory that multiple processes access). The attacker observes timing patterns in this shared cache, using them as a side-channel (an indirect way to leak information) to figure out what sensitive data the victim function is processing.
asplos-2024-188.key_novelty: This is the first practical demonstration that an attacker can force their function onto the same physical machine as a victim function in public cloud FaaS platforms, defeating both VPC isolation and dynamic instance placement.

asplos-2024-185.method: Hassert speeds up hardware verification by running automated checks (called assertions) on FPGA hardware instead of in slow software simulation. FPGA is a reconfigurable chip that can be configured to match the hardware design being tested, so these checks run much faster than simulating everything in software. The framework preserves detailed debugging information throughout, so when a check fails, engineers can pinpoint exactly which microarchitecture behavior was incorrect.
asplos-2024-185.key_novelty: Hassert combines assertion-based verification checks with FPGA acceleration while maintaining the debugging visibility that software simulation provides.

asplos-2024-182.method: Harp works by recognizing that sequence-to-graph mapping—the process of aligning long genomic reads to a reference graph (a network of genetic sequences)—tends to access the graph in a quasi-sequential pattern, mostly moving forward with occasional deviations rather than random jumps. The system exploits this pattern through optimized dataflow and scheduling that arrange computations to match these natural access patterns. This reduces graph processing overhead compared to approaches that treat all accesses as random.
asplos-2024-182.key_novelty: Harp identifies and exploits quasi-sequential (mostly-forward with occasional jumps) access patterns in graph-based long-read mapping to reduce graph processing overhead.

asplos-2024-177.method: MikPoly pre-generates small, optimized code pieces (micro-kernels) for many different shapes of tensors (the multi-dimensional arrays that neural networks use). At runtime, when actual shapes become known, MikPoly uses a lightweight cost model—a simple formula that estimates which combination would run fastest—to select the best pre-made pieces for your network. This approach avoids expensive on-the-fly compilation while still adapting to each network's actual shapes.
asplos-2024-177.key_novelty: Use a lightweight cost model to dynamically select and combine pre-compiled micro-kernels (small code pieces) at runtime for each different tensor shape.

asplos-2024-180.method: The paper defines a formal rulebook for CHERI C by specifying how capabilities (unforgeable security tokens) operate, derive from existing capabilities, and interact with undefined behavior (code that violates normal C rules) and pointer provenance (where memory addresses come from). This rulebook is machine-verifiable, meaning a computer can automatically check its consistency and correctness. Compiler developers can use this verified rulebook to prove their implementations (Clang/LLVM, GCC) are secure.
asplos-2024-180.key_novelty: First machine-verifiable formal specification for a capability-based C dialect, defining how security tokens work, how undefined behavior (code that violates normal C rules) is handled, and pointer provenance (where memory addresses come from).

asplos-2024-178.method: Transformer models demand significant memory and computation, especially on small edge devices. This work compresses models using 8-bit floating-point (FP8) quantization—representing each number with just 8 bits instead of the standard 32 or 64 bits. Previous approaches only quantized matrix multiplication inputs while leaving other operations at full precision; this method quantizes all transformer operations. The result enables both inference and fine-tuning on edge accelerators while maintaining sufficient numerical precision for accuracy.
asplos-2024-178.key_novelty: This work's single core idea is compressing all transformer operations into 8-bit floating-point for both inference and fine-tuning, whereas previous approaches only compressed matrix multiplication.

asplos-2024-192.method: FEASTA works in three layers. First, it represents sparse tensor operations (math on data that's mostly zeros) as a series of combine-and-merge steps on fiber tree structures, using Einstein Summation notation to describe the combination rules. Second, it has a general instruction set with separate instructions optimized for dense (fully-filled) data versus sparse (mostly-zero) data. Third, configurable processing units in the hardware follow these instructions and adapt to different types of computations.
asplos-2024-192.key_novelty: A single unified method—Einstein Summation on fiber tree structures—describes all different sparse tensor operations (math on data with different patterns of zeros), so one flexible hardware architecture can handle any sparsity pattern or computational flow.

asplos-2024-184.method: RPG2 learns from watching a program's actual memory accesses, then makes prefetch decisions (deciding what data to load into fast cache ahead of time) customized to that program and processor. Instead of using the same prefetch rules for all programs, it adapts its strategy based on each program's specific memory patterns and the processor's design. The approach carefully balances timing—prefetching early enough to prevent cache misses (when the processor needs data that isn't readily available in fast memory), but not so early that prefetched data gets discarded unused—while managing how much of the memory connection is used for prefetches versus regular memory requests.
asplos-2024-184.key_novelty: Prefetch strategies need to adapt to how a specific program behaves on a specific processor, rather than using prefetch rules that stay the same for everything.

asplos-2024-193.method: The researchers measured how memory allocators actually perform by profiling production datacenter workloads. They tracked memory request patterns, identified bottlenecks from processes competing for resources (contention), measured memory fragmentation (wasted gaps between allocated blocks), and quantified the performance impact across different applications.
asplos-2024-193.key_novelty: The paper reveals how memory allocators actually behave in real production datacenters by systematically measuring warehouse-scale workloads and identifying their performance impact.

asplos-2024-187.method: LazyBarrier redesigns how write ordering is enforced using an Order-Preserving Write Model—a state machine (Finite Automata) that tracks which operations must remain ordered—to identify which barrier write commands are actually required. The Lazy Issue algorithm cuts the number of barrier write commands by delaying their issuance rather than sending one per thread; F2FS (Android's file system) is modified to support this, and Barrier Scheduling in the multi-queue storage layer ensures ordering is maintained correctly.
asplos-2024-187.key_novelty: The Lazy Issue algorithm delays barrier write command issuance, eliminating the linear scaling where more barrier commands were needed for each additional thread.

asplos-2024-191.method: NetPack schedules training jobs repeatedly in batches using three components: first, it measures which cluster resources are currently available; second, it scores each server based on its spare GPU capacity and network bandwidth; and third, it applies a dynamic programming algorithm to optimally match each job to its best-fitting server.
asplos-2024-191.key_novelty: NetPack jointly optimizes computing and networking resources during job placement using dynamic programming, specifically designed for clusters where gradient data is aggregated in network switches rather than servers.

asplos-2024-196.method: FastGL improves training speed by fixing three bottlenecks simultaneously. First, it reorders how data is accessed during sampling to match natural patterns already in the graph structure, so the GPU's fast cache (tiny, super-fast memory) gets reused and doesn't waste time fetching the same data repeatedly from slow memory. Second, it arranges computations to better exploit the GPU's memory hierarchy—its tiered system of fast and slow storage—even when data is accessed randomly. Third, it fuses sampling and computation steps together so they run without pausing to synchronize, eliminating wasted GPU idle time.
asplos-2024-196.key_novelty: By reordering data access to match patterns already in the graph, it cuts memory traffic without using extra GPU memory for reorganization.

asplos-2024-190.method: Felix uses gradient descent instead of exhaustive search to find high-performance tensor programs faster. Rather than trying millions of different optimization combinations one-by-one, Felix calculates which direction improves performance most and adjusts the program accordingly. This works by treating program optimization as a mathematically smooth problem where you can calculate improvement directions (a property called differentiability), rather than as a discrete set of isolated options to search through.
asplos-2024-190.key_novelty: Felix applies gradient descent (continuous optimization that calculates improvement directions) to tensor program optimization instead of exhaustively searching discrete options.

asplos-2024-195.method: Plankton reads debug information (metadata like variable names and types) that compilers embed in binaries. It uses two reconciliation algorithms to identify and fix mismatches between what the compiled code shows and what the debug information claims, making them consistent. This produces clean LLVM intermediate representations (the standard format analysis tools use), which enables thorough static analysis of binaries without any changes to the build process.
asplos-2024-195.key_novelty: The core innovation is using debug metadata combined with reconciliation algorithms to precisely lift binaries (translate them into analysis-ready code) without modifying the build system.

asplos-2024-194.method: The paper improves the pattern recognition in an auto-vectorizer (the compiler tool that converts regular code into fast vector instructions) so it can identify VNNI patterns in linear algebra operations. It does this with more sophisticated matching techniques than traditional approaches, which only look at small code snippets. Because the auto-vectorizer can now spot these patterns, it generates well-optimized code immediately, reducing the need for auto-tuning (the expensive trial-and-error process of testing many code variations to find the fastest one).
asplos-2024-194.key_novelty: The key idea is teaching auto-vectorizers to spot VNNI computation patterns directly, so they generate fast code without needing expensive auto-tuning.

asplos-2024-197.method: Salus uses a protected area on the host CPU (called a security enclave) to verify and protect the code running on the FPGA accelerator—specifically the bitstreams, or binary files that configure the FPGA's circuits. Rather than requiring entirely new tools, it reuses and enhances existing off-the-shelf FPGA software, allowing it to work with commercial cloud FPGA services without major infrastructure changes.
asplos-2024-197.key_novelty: Salus protects and verifies FPGA code by using the host CPU's security enclave and reusing existing off-the-shelf FPGA tools instead of building separate infrastructure.

dac-2024-008.method: The circuit speeds up calculations by using less precision, which saves power but creates errors. The system watches these errors as the circuit runs; when errors grow too large, it automatically increases the power settings (voltage and frequency) to restore accuracy, and when errors stay small, it reduces these settings to save more energy. This creates a continuous feedback loop where the circuit adjusts itself to keep errors within acceptable limits while minimizing power waste.
dac-2024-008.key_novelty: It automatically adjusts the circuit's power settings (voltage and frequency) based on error measurements taken in real time, rather than using fixed settings, to keep errors within safe bounds.

dac-2024-007.method: The system replaces electronic circuits with silicon photonics (light-based circuits built into silicon), routing data as pulses of light through parallel optical paths instead of moving electrons. It uses wavelength-division multiplexing, where different colors of light simultaneously carry different data, enabling many calculations in parallel. Because light propagates faster through these paths than electrons move in traditional circuits, matrix multiplication completes in sub-nanosecond time.
dac-2024-007.key_novelty: Using integrated silicon photonics with parallel light paths achieves sub-nanosecond latency neural network matrix multiplications while consuming 50x less power than electronic accelerators.

dac-2024-002.method: The approach trains ResNet-50 (a type of neural network) to work with reduced-precision numbers (fewer bits) rather than standard high-precision calculations—a process called quantization-aware training that lets the model learn to compensate for this constraint. Instead of building a general-purpose circuit, the hardware uses specialized arithmetic units designed specifically for these reduced-precision operations, which consume far less power. The dataflow (path data takes through the circuit) is optimized for these reduced-precision operations to avoid wasted computation.
dac-2024-002.key_novelty: The key insight is building the circuit hardware and training the neural network together, rather than separately, so the network learns to work with the simplified arithmetic operations the circuit is designed for.

dac-2024-009.method: The system uses an FPGA (field-programmable gate array—hardware that can be electronically reconfigured to change how it processes information) to physically adapt itself for each different neural network design being tested. Rather than running calculations one at a time through software, the reconfigured hardware performs many calculations simultaneously in parallel and efficiently coordinates the flow of data between them. Compared to testing all designs entirely in software, this approach achieves a 10x speedup.
dac-2024-009.key_novelty: Instead of using fixed software or fixed hardware to test all network designs, this approach dynamically reconfigures an FPGA's internal circuits for each different architecture being tested.

dac-2024-005.method: The system uses phase-change memory—a material that changes its physical structure to store and retrieve data—to perform matrix calculations (the mathematical operations that power machine learning) directly inside the memory instead of shuttling data back and forth between separate storage and processors. Rather than reading data from memory, sending it to a processor, doing the calculation, and storing results back, the computations happen where the data already lives. This eliminates the expensive data movement that slows down and drains power from machine learning systems.
dac-2024-005.key_novelty: The key idea is running machine learning calculations directly inside phase-change memory instead of moving data between separate memory and processors.

dac-2024-013.method: Instead of using expensive matrix multiplication, this approach replaces it with XOR (a bitwise logical operation where you compare bits directly). The paper provides mathematical analysis showing that XOR-based attention approximately preserves the "entropy" of the input—essentially, the randomness and information content—even as correlations between elements change. The method is tested on three types of tasks: arithmetic, sorting, and text generation, using scaled versions of GPT models.
dac-2024-013.key_novelty: Using bitwise XOR operations instead of matrix multiplication in transformer attention mechanisms while mathematically preserving approximate information content of the input.

dac-2024-001.method: The accelerator has two levels of fast on-chip memory, and it watches how data actually flows during CNN inference. When one memory level gets overloaded while another sits idle, the system adjusts bandwidth allocation—how much data can move between levels—to rebalance the flow. This avoids bottlenecks and moves data faster than traditional accelerators that use the same bandwidth allocation regardless of what the network is doing.
dac-2024-001.key_novelty: The memory hierarchy adjusts how much data can flow between levels based on the actual dataflow of the neural network computation, rather than using a fixed design for all cases.

dac-2024-006.method: The algorithm continuously monitors the temperature of each CPU and GPU core, then assigns tasks to cores based on what each task needs and which cores still have capacity before overheating. When a core gets too hot, the system moves its tasks to cooler cores. By treating heat management as equally important as performance in its scheduling decisions, the system keeps all cores productive while staying within a fixed power budget (the total electrical power available).
dac-2024-006.key_novelty: The system makes keeping cores cool a primary scheduling goal—treated with the same importance as performance—and actively balances the two by moving tasks between CPU and GPU cores in real time.

dac-2024-011.method: Planaria detects patterns in how your program accesses memory—specifically patterns that jump between different pages—without needing to know where in the program you are (program counter information). Using these patterns, it predicts when data will be requested and prefetches it into cache before the program needs it. To handle mobile power constraints, it's selective about which prefetches to send, avoiding requests that would waste power.
dac-2024-011.key_novelty: The key innovation is predicting when data across different memory pages will be needed without knowing what part of the program is running, while using little enough power for mobile devices.

dac-2024-003.method: The system combines multiple specialized chips (a GPU for graphics-heavy tasks, an NPU for AI-specific operations, and a CPU for general computing) connected through a flexible network. This network dynamically watches what the AI workload is doing and routes computation to the right chip for each part of the job. It also adjusts how much computing power each chip is using, ensuring resources match the workload's requirements moment-to-moment.
dac-2024-003.key_novelty: A system with multiple different specialized chips (GPU, NPU, CPU) that automatically adjusts which chip does what work based on the AI workload's requirements.

dac-2024-012.method: SMORE uses hyperdimensional computing—a technique that represents data in very high-dimensional spaces where similarity matching becomes computationally cheap—to adapt models at test time. When encountering multi-sensor time series data (measurements from many sensors over time) from a different distribution, the algorithm matches each sample to similar training examples in this hyperdimensional space and customizes the model's behavior for that sample. By avoiding expensive neural network retraining and exploiting efficient parallel operations, it becomes practical for resource-constrained edge devices to handle domain shift (when the data distribution changes from what the model was trained on).
dac-2024-012.key_novelty: The core innovation is using hyperdimensional computing (a technique for fast similarity matching in very high-dimensional space) to adapt models individually for each multi-sensor time series sample at test time, without retraining.

dac-2024-014.method: TrafficHD converts network traffic data into very high-dimensional binary vectors (long lists of 1s and 0s that represent the original features). It classifies these vectors using hyperdimensional computing, a method that's both power-efficient and naturally parallel, allowing it to process many features simultaneously. This enables real-time traffic classification.
dac-2024-014.key_novelty: Hyperdimensional computing applied to network traffic classification achieves significant speedups while remaining robust to noise in the network data.

dac-2024-010.method: The framework catches supply-chain attacks—unauthorized hardware modifications—using formal verification and lightweight runtime monitoring together. Formal verification mathematically proves the hardware design is correct against threat models that describe potential attacks, catching hidden vulnerabilities before manufacturing. Lightweight runtime monitoring watches the actual running hardware to detect any unauthorized modifications introduced during manufacturing or deployment, maintaining minimal performance overhead through selective instrumentation of only the most critical hardware components.
dac-2024-010.key_novelty: Combining formal verification of hardware designs with lightweight runtime monitoring to detect supply-chain attacks in AI systems while preserving performance.

dac-2024-016.method: PathFuzz takes two complementary approaches to generate test inputs that expose CPU design flaws. First, it uses footprint memory—a compact input format tailored to CPU architecture—combined with real-world software examples as seed inputs. Second, it applies coverage-guided fuzzing (a technique that mutates test inputs while tracking which CPU behaviors each input exercises) with improved mutation strategies to automatically discover high-impact test cases.
dac-2024-016.key_novelty: Footprint memory is a compact, CPU-specific input format that replaces inefficient generic test-generation methods used in standard fuzzing.

dac-2024-004.method: The system generates specialized code for sparse tensor operations (math on matrices where most values are zero) by identifying patterns in the code and analyzing how data flows to find optimization opportunities for your specific hardware. It applies two main techniques: combining multiple operations into one (kernel fusion) and arranging computations to skip over zeros (sparsity-aware scheduling). These automatic optimizations reduce compilation time while maintaining near-optimal execution performance.
dac-2024-004.key_novelty: It achieves 60% compilation time reduction while maintaining near-optimal performance, through automatic, hardware-aware optimization of sparse tensor operations (math on matrices where most values are zero).

dac-2024-017.method: The system quantizes intermediate layer values (activations) into a compact floating-point format with shared exponents across blocks (called microscaling) while preserving 4 uncompressed values per 128-element chunk to maintain accuracy where it matters most. It applies different compression depths based on layer sensitivity: 5-bit encoding for the critical decoder input layers and 3-bit for the rest. Custom hardware handles the preserved values with dedicated floating-point units, processes the bulk of compressed values with vectorized integer multipliers for speed, and optimizes the softmax operation (a mathematical step in language models that normalizes values) by approximating it with only bit-shift and subtraction instead of full computation.
dac-2024-017.key_novelty: It combines microscaling quantization of activations with selective outlier preservation and compression levels tuned to how much each layer affects the final model accuracy.

dac-2024-020.method: ReFree watches which embedding data (lookup tables that update during training) gets reused in both the forward pass (when calculating predictions) and backward pass (when calculating updates), identifying these patterns in real-time as training happens. It places lightweight computation directly near the memory rather than separate from it, exploiting data locality (keeping frequently-used information nearby) to spot repeated accesses. This eliminates redundant memory operations and transfers throughout the entire training pipeline.
dac-2024-020.key_novelty: ReFree identifies which embedding data can be reused during training in real-time by using lightweight near-memory processing (computation located close to where data is stored) to eliminate redundant memory operations.

dac-2024-018.method: Q-Pilot is a compiler for quantum circuits on neutral atom arrays—systems where atoms stay in fixed positions. It uses movable helper qubits, called flying ancillas, to enable operations between the fixed data qubits. These moving helpers implement 2-qubit gates (operations connecting pairs of qubits) by strategically positioning themselves throughout the array. The compiler uses FPGA-inspired routing techniques to decide where and when to move these flying ancillas, reducing the total number of operations needed (circuit depth).
dac-2024-018.key_novelty: Q-Pilot uses flying ancillas (movable helper qubits) to enable 2-qubit gates between data qubits fixed in neutral atom arrays.

dac-2024-019.method: IG-CRM combines a hierarchical circuit design with IGZO transistors (a power-efficient semiconductor material). At the cell level, 3T0C or 4T0C cells (configurations with 3 or 4 transistors and no capacitors) enable both CIM operations (multiply-accumulate calculations for neural networks) and CAM operations (pattern-based content searching). At higher levels, IGZO transistors placed in back-end wiring layers reduce adder tree area (circuits that sum numbers together), and reconfigurable macro-based modules—multiple swappable circuit structures—allow the same chip to handle different AI workloads: deep neural networks, transformers, recommendation systems, and graph neural networks.
dac-2024-019.key_novelty: IG-CRM's reconfigurable IGZO-based design lets a single chip perform both multiply-accumulate operations (CIM, used in neural networks) and content searching (CAM, used to find data by pattern matching) efficiently across diverse AI tasks.

dac-2024-026.method: Multi-precision integer arithmetic—calculations with numbers too large to fit in a single 64-bit register—is slow because processors lack specialized instructions for it. The paper tests two ways of representing these large numbers (full-radix and reduced-radix) on 64-bit RISC-V to identify which is faster, then designs custom processor instructions that directly execute the specific arithmetic operations (multiplication and modular reduction) used in CSIDH-512 cryptography. These custom instructions are built into a Rocket processor core and tested to measure performance gains.
dac-2024-026.key_novelty: The core idea is adding processor instructions optimized for the multi-precision arithmetic that post-quantum cryptography requires.

dac-2024-015.method: MAFin assigns tasks to processor cores on FinFET chips and schedules them to meet deadlines, exploiting Temperature Effect Inversion (TEI)—a property where hotter processors run faster, opposite to typical chips. During execution, it actively manages processor frequency based on temperature. The faster execution time gained from heat can be redirected either to run optional, accuracy-improving parts of tasks to enhance results, or to power off cores to save energy.
dac-2024-015.key_novelty: The approach leverages Temperature Effect Inversion in FinFET chips—where higher temperature increases processor speed—to simultaneously enhance task quality and reduce energy consumption in real-time systems.

dac-2024-025.method: The authors develop a systematic method to mathematically find timing side channels — attacks that steal information by measuring how long operations take — in microcontroller chips. They apply this to the RISC-V Pulpissimo SoC and discover a previously unknown attack exploiting memory access timing. They then implement an architectural fix and mathematically verify the chip is now secure against this class of attacks.
dac-2024-025.key_novelty: The paper introduces a formal method for systematically finding timing side channels (attacks that leak information by measuring operation timings) in microcontroller chips that lack shared hardware and were previously thought to be immune.

dac-2024-024.method: CFTCG converts Simulink models (the visual blocks used to design embedded controllers) into code, then applies fuzzing—a technique that feeds random and semi-random inputs to code to explore its behavior—rather than using mathematical constraint solving or step-by-step model simulation. This approach explores complex control paths and internal state combinations that traditional constraint-solving methods often miss.
dac-2024-024.key_novelty: The core idea is applying code-based fuzzing (testing by feeding random inputs to code) to Simulink-generated code for test case generation, instead of constraint solving or simulation.

dac-2024-021.method: Leanor trains a machine learning model to learn patterns in the data distribution. This model predicts which vectors in IVFPQ—a technique used for nearest-neighbor search—are candidates for being nearest neighbors, letting the accelerator skip over irrelevant vectors. By reducing these redundant memory accesses, the approach maintains accuracy while reducing memory overhead, even for high-dimensional data.
dac-2024-021.key_novelty: The core idea is training a machine learning model to predict which vectors to check, so the accelerator can skip redundant memory accesses during high-dimensional nearest-neighbor search.

dac-2024-031.method: The researchers tested a computer vision serving system (designed for high throughput) to quantify performance losses from three sources of overhead: data movement between storage and processing, preprocessing work (decompression, resizing, normalization), and message routing between neural networks. They measured how much latency and throughput impact each caused across different vision tasks (classification, segmentation, detection, depth-estimation), image sizes, and complex pipelines running multiple neural networks at different speeds.
dac-2024-031.key_novelty: Server overhead work—data movement and preparation—dominates performance (56% of latency, approximately 80% of throughput loss) in end-to-end vision inference systems, not the neural networks themselves.

dac-2024-028.method: FDCA reduces precision and circuit complexity through hybrid quantization guided by hessian trace (a mathematical measure of which parameters matter most) and approximation schemes that balance computation speed against storage time. It generates approximate shift-and-accumulate circuits (simplified arithmetic operations) using Cartesian Genetic Programming (an algorithm that evolves optimal circuit designs), then pairs them with error-compensating adder trees that correct for the approximation errors. Finally, it uses weight-stationary dataflow (keeping weights fixed in place while input activations flow through the hardware) to maximize digital-CIM utilization and eliminate idle computation cycles.
dac-2024-028.key_novelty: FDCA's core advance is combining hessian-based hybrid quantization with Cartesian Genetic Programming-designed approximate arithmetic specifically optimized for fine-grained digital-CIM operations.

dac-2024-022.method: They build an L1.5 cache (an intermediate cache between processors' private caches and the shared main cache) that can isolate data to individual processors or make it shareable across multiple processors, with control at the granularity of individual cache lines. A scheduling algorithm for parallel tasks (structured as directed acyclic graphs representing task dependencies) exploits this cache design to arrange which tasks run when, minimizing data movement between processors and total completion time. The approach integrates cache hardware architecture, processor instruction set design, and programming models.
dac-2024-022.key_novelty: An L1.5 cache that controls data isolation and sharing per cache line, combined with task scheduling that exploits these storage choices, to prevent processor interference and reduce data movement in parallel real-time systems.

dac-2024-023.method: Lotus uses a machine-learning agent that learns through trial and error to jointly adjust CPU and GPU processor speeds in real-time. The agent monitors the system's current heat and processing delays, then decides what speeds will prevent overheating while maintaining consistent performance. By continuously adapting to the varying demands of different video frames, the system avoids the thermal and latency issues common in two-stage object detection on mobile devices like the NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and Mi 11 Lite.
dac-2024-023.key_novelty: The core idea is applying machine learning (trained through trial and error) to jointly adjust CPU and GPU speeds in real-time, preventing thermal issues and unpredictable processing delays in two-stage object detectors on edge devices.

dac-2024-027.method: ChatCPU trains a language model on CPU design knowledge, then uses it to automatically generate RTL code (the detailed hardware blueprint) directly from written specifications. The system applies specialized hardware-design techniques to guide the design through manufacturing and verification steps, which speeds up iteration cycles and shortens total development time.
dac-2024-027.key_novelty: The system used a language model to automate the entire CPU design workflow from specifications to taping out (manufacturing), successfully producing a production-ready 6-stage RISC-V CPU.

dac-2024-032.method: inGRASS breaks a graph into clusters of nodes based on electrical resistance (a measure of how well-connected nodes are through the network). During setup, it quickly identifies which edges are critical for keeping the graph connected and removes redundant ones—this takes nearly-linear time, scaling efficiently with graph size. When a new edge arrives, the algorithm uses compact numerical summaries of each node to rapidly decide whether that edge is important; each new edge can be processed in logarithmic time (proportional to the logarithm of the number of nodes), keeping updates fast as the graph grows.
dac-2024-032.key_novelty: A low-resistance-diameter decomposition (grouping nodes by their electrical resistance distance) enables each new edge to be processed in logarithmic time.

dac-2024-030.method: DGR converts the circuit routing problem by representing all possible routes as a directed acyclic graph forest (a data structure encoding wiring patterns) and reformulating it as continuous optimization instead of discrete yes/no choices. It then uses GPU-accelerated deep learning methods—specifically gradient-based optimization techniques—to efficiently find good routing solutions. It simultaneously selects routing paths for all hundreds of thousands of circuit connections by choosing between 2-pin direct connections and Steiner trees (branching routes connecting multiple points), considering all interdependencies globally.
dac-2024-030.key_novelty: DGR solves circuit routing by reformulating it as a differentiable continuous optimization (solvable via calculus on GPUs) rather than discrete yes/no choices, enabling simultaneous optimization of hundreds of thousands of connections.

dac-2024-038.method: The approach builds a dependency map of training samples—a probabilistic graphical model showing which samples relate to each other. It groups samples into clusters based on these dependencies and determines which clusters will help most during training. Rather than sampling randomly, it focuses on high-value clusters and uses error metrics to identify regions that need more coverage.
dac-2024-038.key_novelty: Using probabilistic graphical model decomposition to identify training-sample dependencies and create importance-weighted sampling clusters.

dac-2024-029.method: FeBiM uses ferroelectric field-effect transistors (FeFETs—special transistors that can hold multiple stable states instead of just on/off) arranged in a crossbar grid to build a Bayesian inference engine. It converts probabilities to logarithmic form, where multiplying probabilities becomes adding numbers, and the crossbar grid naturally adds electrical signals. The system encodes log-scale probabilities as different stable transistor states, so when the crossbar adds these signals up, it directly computes the final probabilities without extra circuits.
dac-2024-029.key_novelty: FeBiM maps the logarithmic probabilities Bayesian models need to ferroelectric transistor states, so the hardware computes final probabilities without additional circuits.

dac-2024-039.method: DiffSampler treats finding diverse SAT solutions as a machine-learning prediction problem, where a model uses gradient descent (adjusting weights to minimize prediction errors) to learn multiple solutions at once. The process runs on GPUs, which parallelize calculations across many processors for speed. The result is a collection of diverse solutions with statistical properties comparable to conventional SAT samplers.
dac-2024-039.key_novelty: It uses gradient descent and GPU parallelization to learn SAT solutions directly as a machine-learning task, rather than with traditional sequential search.

dac-2024-041.method: TriSC computes trigonometric functions (like sine and cosine) using stochastic computing, which performs calculations through random bit patterns instead of traditional arithmetic. It integrates the calculation circuit and bit-stream generator as one unit, using carefully controlled randomness—quasi-random bit-streams—to keep data streams independent (decorrelated) without needing hardware delay elements. This approach maintains high accuracy while reducing hardware complexity compared to earlier designs.
dac-2024-041.key_novelty: TriSC's core innovation is co-optimizing the calculation circuit with a quasi-random bit-stream generator to decorrelate data streams in trigonometric functions without delay elements, while maintaining high accuracy.

dac-2024-033.method: The approach searches for learned shortcuts—fast approximations that replace full model training—which drastically reduce benchmark construction costs. It builds a benchmark that optimizes two goals simultaneously: achieving high accuracy on ImageNet2012 and running efficiently on actual hardware accelerators (GPUs, TPUs, and FPGAs). Unlike prior benchmarks using simplified synthetic data, this works with large-scale realistic datasets. The approach is validated through experiments with multiple neural architecture search algorithms (automated methods for finding good network designs).
dac-2024-033.key_novelty: First to create fast benchmarks for finding efficient neural networks on real hardware (GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs) by using shortcuts learned from data instead of simplified, synthetic datasets.

dac-2024-036.method: The approach starts with a black-box thermal dynamics model that predicts temperature responses to heating and cooling inputs. Importance sampling (a technique focusing on critical variables while filtering out minor ones) is used to extract decision trees (if-then rules) from this model, reducing its high dimensionality to a manageable set of variables. Finally, a verification criterion based on domain expertise about HVAC systems, combined with an offline verification algorithm (safety checks run on the model rather than the actual building), mathematically guarantees the control policy is reliable before deployment.
dac-2024-036.key_novelty: The core contribution is extracting interpretable decision trees from black-box thermal dynamics models and combining them with domain-knowledge-based verification to mathematically guarantee HVAC control policy reliability.

dac-2024-034.method: The approach combines two reinforcement learning techniques (Model-Based Policy Optimization and Twin Delayed DDPG) into a single algorithm called MBTD3. It trains an ensemble of probabilistic models—multiple predictive models that output probability distributions rather than single predictions—on data from actual circuit simulations. These models then generate synthetic "rollouts" (simulated design explorations) without running the expensive real circuit simulations at each step. For larger circuits, a multi-agent variant simultaneously sizes different circuit sub-blocks (sections of the circuit) using the same shared probabilistic models, reducing the total number of real simulations needed.
dac-2024-034.key_novelty: The core idea is training multiple predictive models on real simulation data, then using them to generate synthetic simulations, so reinforcement learning can explore circuit designs using far fewer actual circuit simulations.

dac-2024-043.method: SWAT is a specialized hardware accelerator built on FPGA (a flexible chip programmable for specific tasks) to run window attention efficiently — where each token only looks at nearby tokens instead of all tokens. It achieves better performance by reusing data across multiple calculations (row-wise dataflow), combining separate processing steps into single operations (kernel fusion), and keeping input data positioned close to where computations happen (input-stationary architecture), all designed around how FPGAs physically organize their memory and computing resources.
dac-2024-043.key_novelty: The core contribution is matching the hardware's data flow patterns to how window attention naturally accesses data, rather than forcing window attention to fit standard hardware designs.

dac-2024-037.method: Conclave protects shared perception data by running three checks in sequence—like an assembly line—to catch both attacks and sensing errors. The system first verifies each message comes from a trusted vehicle (authentication), then checks that multiple vehicles see the same thing (consensus), and finally rates how trustworthy each vehicle's information is based on its track record (trust scoring). By catching problems early in this pipeline, the system detects faults faster while keeping computational costs down.
dac-2024-037.key_novelty: The core idea is combining three checks—authentication (verifying trusted sources), consensus (confirming agreement across vehicles), and trust scoring (rating reliability)—into a single connected pipeline that handles both security attacks and sensing errors together.

dac-2024-042.method: VVIP is a SIMD processor (hardware that processes multiple data items simultaneously) enhanced with vertical indexing instructions—commands that efficiently select and reorder data elements. These instructions use data-steering hardware and registers to move data around the processor. The processor reuses its register storage as lookup tables (storing precomputed values) and accumulators (running totals) to support bit-by-bit multiplication and sparse data operations (calculations on data where many values are zero or missing). The design was tested on a vector processor implementation.
dac-2024-042.key_novelty: VVIP's core innovation is vertical indexing instructions—commands that enable SIMD processors to efficiently select and reorder data elements, supporting sparse operations with minimal hardware overhead.

dac-2024-035.method: Adversarial examples are specially crafted inputs designed to fool neural networks. When these inputs flow through a network, they cause the CPU to access memory and execute code in unusual ways—creating distinctive patterns. AdvHunter detects these patterns using hardware performance counters (measurements of how the CPU behaves) and Gaussian Mixture Models (a statistical method that identifies data clusters) to flag anomalies. This works without needing to inspect or modify the network's internals.
dac-2024-035.key_novelty: Detecting adversarial examples by measuring the CPU's behavior (through hardware performance counters) without needing access to the network's internals.

dac-2024-044.method: SecPaging protects an enclave's page tables (the OS's record of where code and data are stored in memory) using hardware barriers that block even privileged OS code from tampering. It adds Eager-Allocation to pre-reserve pages and prevent allocation-observation attacks, and Record-Reload to hide page swaps and prevent swap-observation attacks. These mechanisms work by keeping the OS from seeing enclave memory management decisions—the exact information attackers exploit in controlled-channel attacks (where they spy on page table activity to deduce secrets). The design is validated on real Intel SGX hardware.
dac-2024-044.key_novelty: SecPaging prevents attacks that spy on page table activity by having hardware hide the enclave's allocation and swapping decisions from the operating system through Eager-Allocation and Record-Reload mechanisms.

dac-2024-048.method: The approach uses two strategies to transfer cause-and-effect understanding (called causal models—knowledge of what actions cause what outcomes) across objects. One-to-one transfer applies a learned causal model from one object directly to another similar object. Many-to-one transfer combines cause-and-effect patterns learned from multiple objects or users to understand an entirely new object. Researchers collected human-demonstrated causal models for light-producing objects, tested whether these patterns could transfer to new objects, and used the transferred understanding to guide robot tasks.
dac-2024-048.key_novelty: Robots can automatically transfer cause-and-effect understanding learned from human examples to unfamiliar objects and tasks, avoiding the need for experts to reprogram each new scenario.

dac-2024-040.method: The paper uses Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG), a machine learning algorithm that learns what test inputs work best for exposing chip behaviors, enhanced with Prioritized Experience Replay to focus more on the most informative past test runs. The goal is to maximize the average FIFO queue depth—a measure of how fully the data buffer is used—in a MESI cache controller managing four CPUs. Results are compared against DDPG with uniform experience replay and Bayesian Optimization.
dac-2024-040.key_novelty: Combining prioritized experience replay with DDPG to automatically generate hardware verification tests that find rare, hard-to-reach states in complex chip designs.

dac-2024-046.method: CSTrans-OPU uses an FPGA with a processor array where each element contains packed digital signal processors (DSPs—specialized arithmetic units) designed to handle different precision levels through a single unified computation format, ensuring full hardware utilization. The system includes modules that identify sparse tokens—data units where computation can be efficiently skipped—and select appropriate computation modes based on this analysis. A compiler automates the full workflow from model files to hardware instructions, handling model parsing, operation fusion (combining operations), and quantization (reducing precision).
dac-2024-046.key_novelty: The first overlay processor for transformer networks that systematically explores sparsity (identifying which computations can be skipped) using a single unified architecture instead of separate parts.

dac-2024-045.method: The framework tackles AQFP circuits' buffer problem by using entanglement entropy (a measure of how circuit components interconnect) to guide the initial layout design toward circuits that naturally need fewer buffers. It then uses projection-based techniques (straightforward math instead of expensive Lagrangian optimization) to finalize placement decisions while keeping data synchronized across AC-powered clock phases.
dac-2024-045.key_novelty: Applying entanglement entropy (a measure of circuit interconnection) to design AQFP layouts needing fewer buffers, then using projection-based techniques instead of expensive optimization to finalize placement.

dac-2024-049.method: The system uses a Graph Neural Network (a machine learning model designed for analyzing network structures) to automatically decide which clock signals should use the traditional front-side metal layers versus a new back-side layer. The back-side layer has lower parasitic effects—unwanted electrical delays and power loss—but requires special buffer components to work. The GNN learns to optimize this routing decision while respecting the constraint that both layers share the same power delivery network, exploiting the back-side's better properties to achieve superior overall performance.
dac-2024-049.key_novelty: A Graph Neural Network automatically routes clock signals across both front and back metal layers, exploiting the back-side's lower parasitic effects.

dac-2024-056.method: MTL-Split determines the optimal way to split a neural network between an edge device and a remote server by testing different split points and selecting the one that minimizes total response time, accounting for both local computation and communication between device and server. The network uses shared computation layers for all tasks and maintains separate prediction branches for each specific task.
dac-2024-056.key_novelty: MTL-Split is the first systematic approach to finding the optimal way to split a neural network that performs multiple tasks between edge devices and remote servers.

dac-2024-051.method: The approach splits the CPU simulation across multiple processor cores instead of running it single-threaded, while keeping full compatibility with the SystemC TLM-2.0 standard. To avoid slowing down the coordination between parallel cores when accessing shared memory, they cache memory pointers asynchronously (Direct Memory Interface pointer caching) — each core remembers which memory locations it needs without constantly waiting for synchronization. They also add a tunable parameter called async_rate that controls how often the CPU reports timing information to the simulator: more frequent reporting gives accurate timing but slower simulation; less frequent reporting speeds up simulation but sacrifices timing precision.
dac-2024-051.key_novelty: The key idea is parallelizing CPU simulations across multiple cores while maintaining SystemC TLM-2.0 standard compliance by using asynchronous memory pointer caching to reduce coordination overhead and making timing synchronization frequency adjustable.

dac-2024-057.method: ALVEARE designs a specialized language for regular expressions and a custom processor tailored to run it. The regex patterns are converted into a small set of simple, flexible instructions (called a RISC-based instruction set architecture) that can express everything from basic to complex matching rules. The processor uses prediction and speculative execution—making educated guesses about what comes next and executing ahead of time—to run these patterns fast.
dac-2024-057.key_novelty: ALVEARE combines a flexible RISC-based instruction set designed for regex matching with a prediction-based processor to achieve high performance across all regex operators without sacrificing flexibility.

dac-2024-047.method: T1-cells are specialized circuit building blocks for Rapid Single Flux Quantum (RSFQ, a type of superconducting logic) arithmetic circuits. They reduce the extra circuitry overhead that comes with pipelining—splitting computation into stages so multiple operations run in parallel—which normally requires synchronizing signal timing across different paths. T1-cells achieve this by optimizing the circuit layout to pack components more tightly, a particularly important consideration in RSFQ systems where layout density is limited.
dac-2024-047.key_novelty: T1-cells are circuit primitives that reduce pipelining overhead in RSFQ arithmetic circuits by enabling tighter component packing.

dac-2024-055.method: The paper breaks floating-point multiplication into two operations: adding mantissas (the significant digits) and multiplying mantissas. It observes that mantissa addition happens frequently but is computationally simple, while mantissa multiplication happens rarely but is expensive. The system uses two different technologies: traditional digital circuits (which compute using 0s and 1s) handle the frequent mantissa additions accurately; analog circuits (which compute using continuous physical signals) handle the rare mantissa multiplications with far less energy. By matching each operation to the best technology for it, the system achieves both accuracy and energy efficiency.
dac-2024-055.key_novelty: The key insight is that floating-point multiplication splits into frequent simple operations (adding mantissas) and rare expensive operations (multiplying mantissas), enabling you to optimize each separately using the right technology—digital circuits for the common operations and analog circuits for the expensive ones.

dac-2024-052.method: The approach uses a diffusion model—a neural network trained to gradually remove noise—to clean up inaccurate pose predictions. To work efficiently on phones and embedded devices with limited power, the researchers test different noise levels to find the best settings. They then validate the approach on readily available edge hardware using both artificially generated noise and real-world errors from existing pose estimation systems.
dac-2024-052.key_novelty: Using diffusion models to filter human pose estimation errors on phones and embedded devices, efficiently enough for real-time video.

dac-2024-050.method: RELMAS uses deep reinforcement learning—an AI trained through trial and error to improve decisions—to assign incoming neural network processing requests to different accelerators in real time. The algorithm explicitly models how different accelerators like Simba and Eyeriss process computations in different ways and compete for shared memory bandwidth. It learns to balance keeping response times within promised limits (SLA satisfaction) with efficient hardware utilization.
dac-2024-050.key_novelty: The framework uses reinforcement learning to efficiently schedule neural network computations in real time across multiple shared accelerators, explicitly modeling both how they process data differently and the memory bandwidth they share.

dac-2024-054.method: The method uses a Physics-Informed Neural Network (a neural network trained with physical equations built in), specifically a multi-order differential neural network (MDNN). Rather than learning from pre-computed simulations, it encodes the Poisson and drift-diffusion equations—the physics describing charge behavior in semiconductors—directly as constraints the network must satisfy. The network solves for steady-state conditions (where values become constant) by finding values that satisfy both these physical equations and boundary conditions (edge constraints), using physics knowledge instead of training data.
dac-2024-054.key_novelty: The innovation is using a neural network with physics equations built into it to directly solve semiconductor device simulations, without any pre-computed training data.

dac-2024-058.method: When a circuit is modified, Ink avoids recomputing all the critical paths (the longest signal routes that determine maximum circuit speed) from scratch. Instead, it examines paths from the previous calculation and identifies which ones remain similar or still valid. By reusing these existing paths, Ink skips searching most of the possible path combinations. It maintains previous results across changes, so only the affected parts need new calculations.
dac-2024-058.key_novelty: The core innovation is recognizing that critical path traces (the sequences of signal delays through circuits) stay similar between consecutive modifications, allowing previously found paths to be reused instead of recalculated.

dac-2024-061.method: The researchers exploit Apple's System Management Controller—a chip component that monitors power consumption—to measure electrical power drawn by the processor from ordinary user-mode software. As the processor runs encryption operations, different data causes it to consume different amounts of power (data-dependent consumption); by analyzing these power fluctuations, the researchers can infer the cryptographic keys being used. They demonstrate extracting actual AES encryption key bytes from secure kernel cryptography services this way, and they also explore whether frequency throttling (slowing the processor's clock) reveals similar patterns.
dac-2024-061.key_novelty: This is the first demonstration that software-based power side-channel attacks—techniques previously shown to work on x86 platforms—can also extract real cryptographic keys from Apple M1/M2 processors through their System Management Controller interface.

dac-2024-062.method: Instead of testing every voltage combination (which is experimentally expensive and impractical), the method focuses on the voltage ranges where quantum dots transition between different charge states. It uses efficient voltage sweeping to pinpoint these transition boundaries and filters out measurement errors. This targeted approach requires far fewer experiments because it measures only the critical operating regions where independent dot control is established, rather than mapping the entire voltage space.
dac-2024-062.key_novelty: The key insight is that establishing independent quantum dot control only requires measuring where dots change their charge state, not scanning every possible voltage combination.

dac-2024-053.method: Pruning transformers (removing weights to shrink the model) normally scatters remaining weights randomly in memory, causing frequent stalls—pauses where the processor waits for data. This approach prevents stalls by constraining how many correction patches each weight can store in XOR-gate compression, combined with partially-structured pruning (removing weights in patterns) to keep remaining weights organized. This constraint ensures smooth, continuous data flow, allowing faster model execution while maintaining accuracy.
dac-2024-053.key_novelty: Sparse transformer models achieve stall-free memory access by limiting correction patches per weight in XOR-gate compression and using partially-structured pruning patterns.

dac-2024-060.method: DefensiveDR reduces image complexity by projecting them into a lower-dimensional space using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD, which identifies and keeps only the most important patterns) and t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE, which arranges data in fewer dimensions while preserving similarity). A tunable hyperparameter controls how much information to retain, balancing preservation of classification-critical details against filtering of adversarial perturbations. This preprocessing step substantially mitigates patch-based attacks before images reach any ML model, maintaining accuracy across different architectures.
dac-2024-060.key_novelty: The defense uses preprocessing that works with any ML model without access to its architecture or outputs, protecting against attackers whether they know the model's internals or not.

dac-2024-065.method: Sharry puts all processes into one shared memory address space, eliminating the expensive overhead of switching between separate memory views. It carefully manages far memory (memory stored elsewhere) by dividing it into small chunks and moving them around to keep storage utilization high. It also assigns memory blocks using dedicated CPU cores, allowing multiple processes to share memory without slowing down the main processors.
dac-2024-065.key_novelty: Instead of isolating each process's memory separately, Sharry lets multiple processes share a single far memory system by putting them in one unified address space.

dac-2024-063.method: The accelerator places data and calculations in the same fast memory (SRAM embedded in the chip), eliminating the slow journeys of moving data elsewhere and back. It uses digital circuits (reliable 1s and 0s, not analog voltages which pick up electrical noise) for the math. Its processing units and data paths can be reconfigured—rearranged on the fly—to efficiently run both convolution operations (standard math for image processing) and multi-head attention operations (how Transformers focus on different parts of an image).
dac-2024-063.key_novelty: A digital in-memory accelerator with reconfigurable data pathways that efficiently runs both the convolution and multi-head attention operations that hybrid vision transformers need.

dac-2024-059.method: The framework automatically creates training datasets in three ways: translating Verilog (chip design code) into descriptions of how it's structured and what each part does, using templates; deliberately introducing errors into working code and pairing them with feedback from design tools to create repair examples; and using GPT-3.5 to generate descriptions of design automation scripts. These synthetic training pairs teach Llama2 models (13B and 7B parameter versions) how to generate Verilog code.
