dac-2024-059.key_novelty: The framework automatically generates abundant training data by pairing Verilog code with natural language explanations and repair examples, using code-structure analysis and design tool feedback.

dac-2024-068.method: In semiconductor manufacturing, creating precise chip patterns requires optimizing both the light source and the mask, but adjusting them together directly is slow and unreliable. This work reformulates the problem as bilevel (nested) optimization: alternately optimize the source while keeping the mask fixed, then optimize the mask while the source stays fixed. It uses fast forward imaging simulation—specifically accelerated Abbe imaging, which predicts how light patterns form through the mask—to quickly calculate gradients (slopes showing which direction to improve). Three different gradient-based approaches efficiently solve this nested problem.
dac-2024-068.key_novelty: The core novelty is reformulating Source Mask Optimization as a bilevel (nested) optimization problem solved with gradient-based methods.

dac-2024-067.method: The framework splits the circuit netlist into two stacked layers (dies) and simultaneously optimizes placement of large functional blocks (macros), millions of tiny cells, and the physical connection points (hybrid bonding terminals) between layers. It uses special scoring functions (objective functions) tailored to each manufacturing technology's constraints, along with density penalties that prevent overcrowding.
dac-2024-067.key_novelty: The core innovation is a scoring-and-penalty framework specifically designed for 3D placement of mixed-size components when dies use different manufacturing process nodes.

dac-2024-073.method: H3 solves the memory bottleneck by physically stacking memory chips directly on top of the computing chip using 3D hybrid bonding, so data travels a much shorter distance. It adjusts how it breaks down the polynomial calculations (the complex math operations encrypted data requires) on the fly, decomposing them dynamically to minimize data movement. An efficient broadcast mechanism routes the encrypted data directly to the processing arrays that need it, significantly reducing memory traffic and delays.
dac-2024-073.key_novelty: H3 stacks memory chips on top of the processor die using 3D hybrid bonding and dynamically decomposes polynomial calculations to eliminate the memory bottleneck that limits encrypted neural network inference.

dac-2024-072.method: The router learns to select Steiner points (intermediate routing waypoints) using reinforcement learning, where a neural network gets trained via combinatorial Monte-Carlo tree search—an algorithm that explores placement options by simulating routing outcomes. A 3D U-Net neural network processes the chip layout using a Hanan-grid representation (a standard discretized grid for routing), and can handle layouts of any size and routing configuration in a single forward pass, accounting for varying routing costs across layers.
dac-2024-072.key_novelty: The core idea is combining combinatorial Monte-Carlo tree search training with a 3D U-Net neural network to select Steiner points for chip routing of any size, all in a single forward pass.

dac-2024-070.method: E-Syn uses an e-graph—a data structure that stores multiple equivalent ways to represent the same circuit—to explore many different but logically equivalent designs. It evaluates each design using cost functions tailored to the specific hardware technology being targeted, optimizing for either faster execution speed (lower delay) or smaller chip area. By maintaining all these equivalent options throughout optimization rather than greedily committing to each local choice, E-Syn discovers significantly better overall designs.
dac-2024-070.key_novelty: Combining e-graphs—data structures that store equivalent circuit representations—with technology-specific cost functions enables exploration of a much wider set of circuit designs than traditional greedy optimization approaches.

dac-2024-066.method: Artisan trains a specialized language model on high-quality operational amplifier designs, teaching it to connect circuit layouts with both their structural organization and functional behavior. It explores designs using two reasoning methods: branching out to consider multiple possible paths (Tree-of-Thoughts) and reasoning through them step-by-step (Chain-of-Thoughts), with multiple AI agents interacting to refine each design. This bidirectional alignment between circuit topology and function enables the system to generate better amplifier designs without requiring expert input.
dac-2024-066.key_novelty: A specialized language model that bidirectionally connects circuit layouts to their functional properties, combined with multi-step reasoning and agent collaboration, automates operational amplifier design.

dac-2024-069.method: The sensor uses charge-domain convolution (detecting edges by measuring electrical charge patterns) to identify depth-changing regions on the chip, then applies in-memory denoising to remove noise from those pixels. By doing edge detection directly on the sensor, the system activates the time-to-digital converters (the power-hungry circuits that measure how long light takes to return) only in edge regions, slashing power consumption and data volume. A U-Net neural network then fills in the missing depth values across the entire image, reconstructing the full-resolution picture from just the sparse edge pixel data.
dac-2024-069.key_novelty: This is the first SPAD-based dToF sensor combining in-pixel edge detection with sparse reconstruction, achieving 512×512 resolution using only 3.5% sparse edge pixels and improving pixel format by 16×.

dac-2024-064.method: MoteNN reduces peak memory by breaking neural networks into smaller pieces (called operators) and carefully scheduling when they run—since operations don't all need to be in memory at once, this cuts peak memory use overall. It introduces an Axis Connecting Graph (ACG), a graph structure that helps find the optimal way to partition and reschedule operations by focusing on memory bottlenecks, the parts of the network where memory is used up fastest. This achieves substantial memory reduction while keeping computation time nearly unchanged.
dac-2024-064.key_novelty: The Axis Connecting Graph (ACG) is a graph representation that enables fine-grained operator partitioning—splitting neural networks into smaller, optimally-scheduled pieces—to reduce peak memory while keeping computation time nearly the same.

dac-2024-074.method: UpDLRM uses the UPMEM DPU, a real processing-in-memory chip where thousands of small processors sit next to memory instead of far from it on a CPU. This provides high bandwidth for irregular memory accesses—unpredictable lookups that jump randomly through memory rather than reading sequentially. The system splits embedding tables (feature lookup tables for recommendations) so each processor gets roughly equal work, and uses multiple cache levels to keep frequently-accessed data fast. By handling many irregular lookups in parallel within the DPU's memory architecture, it avoids the usual bottleneck where data has to travel far between CPU and memory.
dac-2024-074.key_novelty: UpDLRM is the first practical use of real processing-in-memory hardware (UPMEM DPU) for recommendation inference, handling irregular embedding lookups with high bandwidth.

dac-2024-071.method: Develops algorithms to test if two reversible logic circuits are equivalent when inputs and outputs are flipped or rearranged. For the case where inputs are flipped and rearranged, the work provides a quantum algorithm (for quantum computers) that runs in polynomial time—time that grows reasonably with problem size—while proving classical algorithms need exponential time—time that becomes impractically long. For other variants, the work establishes hardness results.
dac-2024-071.key_novelty: This is the first study of Boolean matching—determining when two reversible circuits are equivalent under input/output transformations—establishing a case where quantum computers solve the problem exponentially faster than classical computers for design automation.

dac-2024-076.method: Traditional cache management removes the least recently used data when space runs out, but this oversimplifies how real data is actually accessed. ICGMM instead uses a Gaussian Mixture Model (a statistical approach that identifies patterns in data) to learn which pieces are likely to be accessed next, then removes the least likely candidates when the cache fills up. The system is prototyped on an FPGA (field-programmable hardware chip), allowing engineers to test whether this learning-based policy works better in real hardware.
dac-2024-076.key_novelty: A Gaussian Mixture Model learns data access patterns to improve cache eviction decisions, outperforming traditional LRU eviction and more complex LSTM approaches while requiring less hardware to implement.

dac-2024-082.method: The approach builds tiny analog circuits (10 transistors each) that exploit natural manufacturing variations in transistors to create a physically-unclonable entropy source — a way to generate high-dimensional computing vectors that can't be copied or reverse-engineered. Custom low-power circuits perform all necessary operations (entropy storage, distribution, binding, permutation, and bundling) entirely in analog form rather than converting to digital, which saves power while keeping sensitive basis vectors protected from data leakage.
dac-2024-082.key_novelty: Using natural transistor manufacturing variations as an uncopyable analog entropy source that securely encodes hyperdimensional computing vectors without ever storing them in digital form.

dac-2024-077.method: Instead of converting chip layouts to images (which loses important details), this method reads the raw GDSII file—a binary format that describes chip layouts—directly as a semantic representation (a structured description of how design elements relate). A pre-trained language model then processes this as a sequence, like analyzing text. This preserves all the metal polygon details and eliminates the noise from image conversion.
dac-2024-077.key_novelty: For the first time, layout hotspots are detected by processing the hierarchical chip layout format directly as semantic sequences for language models, rather than converting it to images for vision models.

dac-2024-075.method: The framework uses a Naive Bayes model (a probability-based approach) instead of the traditional associative memory in hyperdimensional computing, which provides confidence estimates for predictions. An adaptive early termination algorithm monitors this confidence during bit-serial processing (computing one bit at a time) and stops once confidence is high enough. This avoids unnecessary bit processing, substantially reducing energy use and computation time.
dac-2024-075.key_novelty: Using a Naive Bayes model's confidence scores to enable early termination in bit-serial hyperdimensional computing, reducing bit operations by over 70% while maintaining accuracy.

dac-2024-078.method: The approach frames inter-tier via placement—positioning vertical electrical connections between layers in 3D circuits—as an optimal transport problem. Optimal transport is a mathematical method that finds the most efficient way to move or arrange objects by minimizing total distance or cost. This formulation naturally breaks into thousands of independent calculations, each handling a small part of the problem. By running these calculations simultaneously on GPUs (graphics processors), the method solves high-density via-placement problems much faster than traditional single-processor approaches.
dac-2024-078.key_novelty: Optimal transport theory enables GPU-parallelizable solutions to inter-tier via placement.

dac-2024-079.method: CDS works by measuring timing delays in a chain of logic gates within a chip, detecting when those delays change unexpectedly—a sign that an attacker is trying to inject faults via voltage spikes or laser glitches. As chips naturally age over time, their timing characteristics degrade, so CDS includes a calibration module that regularly resets its detection thresholds to stay accurate. It also includes a dynamic adjustment module that adapts in real time as the chip's power supply voltage and clock speed vary during normal operation, ensuring fault detection stays reliable even under these changing conditions. The sensor was tested in simulation protecting a PRESENT cryptographic algorithm accelerator against voltage and laser glitching attacks.
dac-2024-079.key_novelty: CDS keeps delay-chain fault sensors reliable by adding automatic compensation for chip aging and real-time adaptation to voltage and frequency variations.

dac-2024-080.method: The system filters data blocks before fingerprinting to save work and memory. It uses a random forest classifier (a decision tool combining simple rules) and Bloom filters (compact structures for fast membership checks) to predict which blocks might be duplicates, without computing full fingerprints. Only predicted duplicates get actual fingerprints created, while likely non-duplicates skip fingerprinting entirely. Since mobile devices typically have only 10-30% actual duplicates, this cuts memory overhead by avoiding fingerprints for the majority of blocks.
dac-2024-080.key_novelty: Using a random forest and Bloom filter to predict duplicates before fingerprinting, avoiding unnecessary fingerprints for non-duplicates.

dac-2024-084.method: AccMoS speeds up Simulink simulations by converting models into compiled code rather than using an interpreter that processes the model step-by-step during each simulation run. Compiled code runs much faster than interpretation, allowing many more simulation cycles to complete in the time previously needed for just a few—critical for finding errors that only surface after extended runs. The approach maintains model correctness while making comprehensive error detection feasible.
dac-2024-084.key_novelty: Using compiled code generation instead of interpretation to speed up Simulink simulation and make detection of long-running accumulative errors practical.

dac-2024-089.method: The method builds a routing graph supporting 90- and 135-degree connections, then searches for optimal paths while inserting vertical connectors (called vias) between layers on-the-fly instead of pre-planning their locations. This keeps vias flexible during the search—allowing the algorithm to place them wherever needed as it explores different routes—which opens up more possibilities than if via positions were locked in before routing started.
dac-2024-089.key_novelty: Placing vertical connectors between layers (vias) during the routing search itself, rather than pre-planning them before routing begins.

dac-2024-081.method: This approach looks at the detailed hardware circuit designs (gate-level netlist) instead of just analyzing how data flows between instructions. By examining these circuit patterns, it discovers additional opportunities to forward data between pipeline stages or predict future values before they're computed. These two techniques—forwarding and speculation—reduce the waiting periods (stalls) that occur when one instruction depends on another's result, making the automatic pipeline much more efficient.
dac-2024-081.key_novelty: The approach achieves more efficient pipelining by examining actual circuit structures (gate-level) to identify additional opportunities for data forwarding and prediction (speculation), rather than relying solely on high-level data flow analysis.

dac-2024-083.method: The researchers used actual alpha particle irradiation (radiation that causes random bit flips in silicon) on a 22nm AI chip as their reference point. They then tested two simulation approaches: white-box simulation, where they could inject faults anywhere in the chip, and black-box simulation, where they could only inject faults in accessible parts like memory and registers. Finally, they compared both simulations against each other and against the actual irradiation data to see which approach most accurately predicted the chip's behavior.
dac-2024-083.key_novelty: Simulating faults predicts how reliably an AI chip will handle alpha particle radiation before manufacturing, even without full design access, if the memory-to-register failure ratio matches reality.

dac-2024-085.method: Transformers normally calculate attention scores for each token individually, but many scores within the same row are similar—wasted computation. SpARC groups tokens by similarity within rows and calculates attention scores once per cluster instead of per token, achieving an approximate form of attention. The system uses a dedicated accelerator architecture with pipelined stages (processing steps overlapping in parallel) and an optimized memory hierarchy to run this clustering-based computation efficiently.
dac-2024-085.key_novelty: Clustering tokens by similarity within each row of the attention matrix, so attention scores are calculated once per cluster instead of per token.

dac-2024-092.method: G2PM builds a layered artificial-intelligence model (called a hierarchical graph neural network) that learns about two types of programs used on Versal ACAP chips: kernel programs (individual computation tasks) and dataflow programs (how data flows between tasks). The model organizes this information around the AIE array—the accelerator's main processing engine—to understand both the hardware structure and how software runs on it. This lets the model predict system performance without needing to run expensive full simulations.
dac-2024-092.key_novelty: Tailoring hierarchical graph representation to both levels of the ACAP's dual programming model (kernel and dataflow) enables accurate performance prediction without simulation.

dac-2024-091.method: The approach uses gradient ascent—an algorithm that climbs toward better solutions—to search through the space of states both analog circuits can occupy. It handles nonlinear behavior by using local linear approximations and Kronecker Canonical Form, a mathematical transformation that puts both circuit designs into a standard comparable format. A custom-designed scoring function guides the search toward regions where the circuits differ most, while geometric filtering techniques eliminate impossible states the circuits could never physically reach.
dac-2024-091.key_novelty: The key advance combines gradient-ascent search with Kronecker Canonical Form—a transformation that standardizes state spaces—to efficiently find where nonlinear analog circuits diverge.

dac-2024-090.method: RexBDDs represent logical operations using simplified diagrams by combining three techniques: marking outputs to flip when beneficial (complement flags), marking inputs to reorder when beneficial (swap flags), and eliminating unnecessary connections between nodes (reduction-on-edge rules). When used together, these three techniques amplify each other: applying one often creates opportunities for applying another, removing far more redundancy than any single technique could achieve alone. The method establishes a canonical (standard) form that guarantees every logically equivalent function reduces to the same compact diagram.
dac-2024-090.key_novelty: Combining output-flip markers, input-reordering markers, and connection-elimination rules achieves up to four times greater reduction in node count than traditional BDD methods.

dac-2024-086.method: Nona trains a lightweight neural network on performance monitoring counters (hardware measurements showing how the CPU is running), selecting only the most relevant ones through system analysis. The model uses a custom loss function (a technique that helps the network focus specifically on accurate power prediction), and was validated on a Google Pixel 6 phone.
dac-2024-086.key_novelty: Nona achieves 3.4% average error by analyzing the system to choose the right hardware measurements, then using a neural network with a loss function specifically designed for power prediction.

dac-2024-096.method: GQA-LUT uses a genetic algorithm (an automated search that tests many options and keeps the best, like natural selection) to design a lookup table—a pre-computed table of answers—that breaks down non-linear functions into simple line segments. Unlike earlier methods that need high-precision floating-point or 32-bit integer math (FP/INT32), this algorithm designs the lookup table to work specifically with low-precision 8-bit integers (INT8), making hardware implementations much cheaper and faster. The approach is tested on semantic segmentation using both standard and linear Transformer models.
dac-2024-096.key_novelty: A genetic algorithm framework that automatically optimizes lookup-table approximations while accounting for quantization constraints, enabling them to run efficiently on cheap 8-bit integer hardware.

dac-2024-088.method: TITAN improves distributed quantum computers in two coordinated ways. First, it redesigns the photonic switches (optical connections) linking multiple quantum chips (QCCDs) to reduce entanglement latency—the delay for quantum information to spread across the system. Second, it uses a compiler that understands the physical layout, enabling it to optimally place qubits and efficiently route communications through the quantum matter-links connecting the chips. Together, these changes cut latency and improve qubit mapping, accelerating the overall system.
dac-2024-088.key_novelty: TITAN combines a compiler aware of the physical structure with optimized optical connections to cut the delay in quantum information spreading across distributed trapped-ion quantum computers.

dac-2024-093.method: The hardware system is represented as a graph structure where components become nodes and their connections become edges. A machine learning model called a Graph Convolutional Network learns from this graph—studying component properties, labels, and connections—to identify which components would cause functional failures if they malfunction. Regression analysis then assigns each component a numerical criticality score reflecting how severe such failures would be, and explainability analysis reveals which factors determine criticality.
dac-2024-093.key_novelty: This is the first to use regression analysis to put a numerical score on each hardware component's criticality, enabling engineers to focus their safety testing on the parts most likely to cause system failures.

dac-2024-098.method: Chiplever extends chiplet-based systems (packages of multiple specialized chips) to support FHE polynomial operations by reusing existing accelerators (specialized hardware pieces designed for specific tasks) rather than building new ones from scratch. The framework includes compiler-based mechanisms that translate FHE polynomial operations into instructions the existing accelerators can execute. This approach is more efficient than the traditional method of designing entirely new dedicated accelerators whenever you need to support a new computational task.
dac-2024-098.key_novelty: Rather than designing new accelerators every time you need FHE support, Chiplever reuses and extends the diverse accelerator resources already built into chiplet systems through compiler adaptation.

dac-2024-095.method: The system uses hardware performance counters (built-in CPU tools that track memory accesses) to observe traffic patterns in real time. It models the computer's memory system as a tree structure with multiple levels, where each level becomes slower and further from the processor. Based on these traffic observations, it automatically moves frequently-accessed memory pages to the nearest locations, reducing access delays and improving bandwidth efficiency.
dac-2024-095.key_novelty: Using real-time traffic patterns tracked by hardware performance counters, it automatically relocates frequently-accessed memory pages to reduce access delays in multi-level NUMA systems.

dac-2024-097.method: The approach uses a Bayesian Neural Network—a neural network that represents uncertainty through probability—to build a surrogate model (a simplified stand-in for expensive chip simulations). It integrates prior knowledge (information we already have) with new data to avoid overfitting, where the model would just memorize training cases rather than learn general patterns. To optimize yield (the percentage of working chips), the method replaces the sharp on/off behavior of yield thresholds with a smooth mathematical approximation, enabling gradient-based optimization (using calculus to find the best design changes). This avoids expensive Monte Carlo simulation (random sampling to estimate outcomes).
dac-2024-097.key_novelty: The key innovation is enabling gradient-based yield optimization (using calculus to improve designs) by smoothing sharp yield decision boundaries into continuous curves, while using a Bayesian Neural Network that integrates prior knowledge to prevent overfitting.

dac-2024-094.method: HOGA pre-computes features for each circuit node at different neighborhood distances (hops—1 step away, 2 steps away, etc.). A gated attention mechanism then learns which distances are most important for each feature, making these decisions independent of how the circuit graph is wired. This independence allows the model to work on new circuit designs it has never seen and enables efficient training across multiple computers.
dac-2024-094.key_novelty: Gated attention on hop-wise features that learns what matters independent of the circuit's structure.

dac-2024-099.method: The model predicts power consumption at the placement stage (when component positions are assigned). It has a dedicated model for the clock tree (the network distributing timing signals throughout the chip). To handle circuits that change during optimization—like restructuring connections or gate sizing—it learns power patterns from training data and adapts based on physical layout and how components connect.
dac-2024-099.key_novelty: This is the first power prediction model at the placement stage that stays accurate when circuits are modified during optimization (such as restructuring or gate sizing).

dac-2024-087.method: LIVAK combines a trie (a structure for prefix matching), a learned index (which uses machine learning to predict where keys are stored), and a B+-tree (a data structure optimized for lookups on sorted data), where each processes 8-byte chunks of keys. It chooses which to use based on node size: learned indexes for large nodes where they're faster, B+-trees for small nodes. It includes character re-encoding (a technique that prevents slowdown when keys have different lengths).
dac-2024-087.key_novelty: LIVAK efficiently handles variable-length keys in learned indexes by using learned indexes selectively—only for large nodes where they provide speed benefits—while using B+-trees for small nodes and character re-encoding to prevent slowdown.

dac-2024-100.method: Instead of using locks to coordinate cores—forcing them to take turns and creating bottlenecks—PipeSSD treats storage request handling like an assembly line with multiple stages. Different processor cores handle different stages (one receives NVMe requests, another manages the cache, a third writes to flash memory), so many requests flow through the pipeline in parallel. Since each stage is independent, there's no need for locks, and cores can work at full speed without waiting for each other.
dac-2024-100.key_novelty: A lock-free pipeline design where different processor cores process different stages of storage requests, eliminating the synchronization delays that normally limit multi-core systems.

dac-2024-102.method: TIGA's approach uses an adaptive allocator that dynamically distributes the processing cores built into the SmartNIC among its near-data processing engines (specialized processors that sit close to data to avoid moving it over the network) for the best possible utilization. It pairs this with a coordination mechanism that schedules tasks between the SmartNIC and the main CPU, deciding which tasks run where based on what's most efficient. The system is built using FPGAs (reconfigurable hardware) and tested on typical application workloads.
dac-2024-102.key_novelty: The core innovation is a SmartNIC-CPU cooperation mechanism that uses intelligent task scheduling and dynamic resource reallocation to improve performance when memory and compute are physically separated.

dac-2024-105.method: The model represents a circuit as a graph showing how components connect. It converts voltage changes in electrical loops and current flows between parts into numerical representations. A graph-transformer (an algorithm for understanding connected networks) uses these to predict circuit performance without expensive simulation. The approach accurately predicts how circuits behave even when facing designs it has never seen before.
dac-2024-105.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a graph-transformer—an algorithm that reasons about connected systems using voltage and current flow information—to accurately predict circuit performance on designs it has never seen before.

dac-2024-107.method: The approach uses Fuzzy Neural Networks to extract simple, human-readable rules that explain what the system learned about good micro-architecture designs. It combines this with multi-fidelity reinforcement learning, which uses cheap, quick but less-precise simulations to explore broadly, and saves expensive, accurate simulations for verifying the most promising options. Together, this makes the design process both faster (requiring fewer expensive simulations) and more transparent (designers understand why certain designs are recommended).
dac-2024-107.key_novelty: The core idea is combining Fuzzy Neural Networks with multi-fidelity reinforcement learning so designers can understand why certain micro-architecture designs are recommended while exploring the design space with fewer expensive simulations.

dac-2024-104.method: This approach uses ReRAM (resistive memory that performs calculations) to compute directly where data is stored, eliminating the traditional separation between memory and processors. Rather than constantly moving sparse matrix data back and forth between separate memory and computation units—which is slow—the matrix operations and conjugate gradient iterations happen directly within the ReRAM. This both reduces costly data transfers and naturally handles the irregular access patterns of sparse solvers.
dac-2024-104.key_novelty: Using ReRAM compute-in-memory to accelerate sparse conjugate gradient solvers by eliminating data transfers between separate memory and processors.

dac-2024-101.method: DB-PIM combines software optimization with custom hardware to skip wasted computations on scattered zeros (bit-level sparsity) in neural network weights. It uses a dyadic block pattern—a way to organize these zeros that keeps them randomly distributed but limits how many appear per weight—making the pattern structured enough for hardware to reliably detect and skip. Specialized multiplication units (DBMUs) and efficient adders (using Canonical Signed Digit encoding) perform the calculations, while an input preprocessing unit applies similar zero-skipping to incoming data.
dac-2024-101.key_novelty: The dyadic block sparsity pattern—keeping zeros randomly distributed while constraining their count—paired with custom hardware units (DBMUs and CSD-based adders) designed specifically to exploit it.

dac-2024-108.method: The approach works in two stages. First, it assigns each electrical trace to its own non-overlapping region on the circuit board. Then, it winds (meanders) each trace back and forth within its region to reach the exact target length needed while steering around physical obstacles. For pairs of traces that must stay perfectly synchronized (called differential pairs in high-speed electronics), it uses Multi-Scale Dynamic Time Warping—a technique that keeps both traces at the same length as they navigate the board together.
dac-2024-108.key_novelty: The core innovation is using Multi-Scale Dynamic Time Warping to keep paired electrical traces at exactly the same length as they both navigate obstacles and wind through available space on the board.

dac-2024-106.method: Co-Via reuses temporal information (motion and how things change between frames) that's already extracted by the video codec (the compression method) in its bitstream. FPGA and ASIC accelerators extract and use this temporal data to guide frame interpolation, eliminating redundant computation in the neural network. By coordinating the codec layer and accelerator hardware layer, Co-Via reduces overall computation while easing hardware pressure.
dac-2024-106.key_novelty: Using motion information (how things change between video frames) already stored in the compressed video codec to reduce neural network computation for frame interpolation.

dac-2024-109.method: RTL-Timer trains a machine learning model on multiple structural representations of chip designs to predict timing slack (available buffer time) for individual registers. The model uses specialized training objectives designed to capture the latest moment signals can arrive at each register endpoint without exceeding the timing deadline. These predictions then guide standard chip design tools to optimize the circuit in register-aware ways, enabling timing optimization at the early code stage when designs are most flexible to change.
dac-2024-109.key_novelty: RTL-Timer is the first to predict per-register timing slack (available buffer time before timing failures) at the code design stage, making fine-grained timing optimization possible where design changes are cheapest.

dac-2024-103.method: The approach stores more data by using multi-level-cell RRAM (resistive memory where each cell holds multiple values by encoding them at different voltage levels), increasing storage capacity by 3x. Instead of shuttling data between memory and processors—which is slow—it performs calculations directly on the memory. It uses hyperdimensional computing, which represents data in very high-dimensional space and tolerates errors (working correctly even when up to 10% of memory values are wrong), enabling massive hardware parallelism. The design was validated on a fabricated MLC RRAM chip.
dac-2024-103.key_novelty: Combining multi-level-cell RRAM with error-tolerant hyperdimensional computing to speed up Open Modification Search by performing calculations directly in memory.

dac-2024-110.method: Instead of simulating the circuit multiple times, this approach represents quantum errors (called Pauli faults) as symbolic formulas with variables, stored in a data structure called the stabilizer tableau using bit-vector encoding (arrays of 0s and 1s). The method reorganizes how this table is stored in memory to speed up data access. Measurement results are then computed once as formulas, with different outcomes generated by substituting the variables with concrete values.
dac-2024-110.key_novelty: Representing measurement results as symbolic formulas instead of running the circuit multiple times.

dac-2024-114.method: The approach trains multiple simple models by repeatedly querying the quantum network and learning from its responses—without knowing its internal structure. These models are then combined together, like averaging independent guesses, to recreate the original quantum network. This works because quantum computers produce random errors, and the ensemble approach handles these errors the same way machine learning handles noisy training data.
dac-2024-114.key_novelty: Using ensemble learning (training multiple simple models and combining their predictions) to extract quantum neural networks by treating quantum errors the same way as training-data noise.

dac-2024-120.method: Duet splits a recommendation model into two pieces: a user model (which learns from your history and profile) that runs on your local edge device, and an item model (which learns about products or content) that runs in the cloud. These two parts run at the same time. The user part is optimized to use less computing power so it fits on edge hardware with its limited resources, and then their outputs are combined to make the final recommendation.
dac-2024-120.key_novelty: The core idea is splitting a recommendation model into user and item parts that run simultaneously on edge devices and the cloud, combining their results, instead of keeping the entire model in one place.

dac-2024-119.method: The CONVOLVE project optimizes energy across the full computing stack for edge AI. It uses Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)—brain-inspired models that use sparse events instead of continuous values—combined with compute-in-memory (CIM) architectures that process data where it's stored, reducing power-hungry data movement. The hardware uses memristor-based devices (components that perform analog computation) and approximation techniques (low-precision math to save energy). To handle hardware imperfections, it employs online continuous learning—adapting weights during operation to compensate for noise and variations.
dac-2024-119.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining online continuous learning with compute-in-memory architectures, enabling edge AI systems to self-adapt and tolerate imperfections in analog hardware.

dac-2024-113.method: The system learns which optimization settings (called HLS directives) work best by analyzing over 100 example programs tested on real Xilinx ZCU104 FPGA hardware. Rather than trying to predict good settings or search through possibilities, it applies the patterns that have proven successful in the past to new code. It generates optimization recommendations in just 38 milliseconds on average while ensuring the final design remains feasible to build.
dac-2024-113.key_novelty: It learns FPGA optimization settings directly from real examples instead of using search methods or predictive models, achieving 100 to 1,000 times faster results than genetic algorithm approaches.

dac-2024-111.method: Sherlock finds the best way to run bulk bitwise operations—like AND, OR, and XOR—directly on special memory chips that can compute data where it sits, rather than shuttling it to a separate processor. It makes two decisions at the same time: where to store data in the memory and what order to execute the operations. By solving these two decisions as one combined problem instead of separately, Sherlock minimizes unnecessary data movement, which reduces both energy consumption and execution time.
dac-2024-111.key_novelty: Sherlock's core idea is treating data placement and operation scheduling as a single joint problem, rather than two independent ones, for bitwise operations on compute-in-memory hardware.

dac-2024-115.method: RCGP uses Cartesian genetic programming (an evolutionary algorithm that combines modular building blocks) to automatically design reversible quantum-flux-parametron (RQFP) logic circuits. The algorithm creates many circuit variations and keeps designs that minimize gate count (total logic operations) and garbage outputs (extra qubits produced as byproducts). To ensure correctness, it uses simulation and formal verification to confirm that each new circuit variant functions identically to its parent.
dac-2024-115.key_novelty: The framework uses Cartesian genetic programming — an evolutionary algorithm combining modular building blocks — to automatically design large-scale reversible quantum-flux-parametron logic circuits.

dac-2024-112.method: The approach converts Chisel arithmetic hardware designs into Scala software that performs the same operations, then applies Stainless (which mathematically proves whether software works correctly) to verify it. The proof works on the general algorithm rather than specific bit widths, so one verification covers all possible widths instead of requiring separate checks for 8-bit, 16-bit, 32-bit versions, and so on.
dac-2024-112.key_novelty: The innovation is that transforming Chisel to Scala enables a single mathematical proof for the general algorithm to cover all possible bit widths instead of verifying each width separately.

dac-2024-118.method: PowerLens identifies which parts of a neural network consume power similarly and groups them together to find optimal points for processor speed adjustment. For each group, it automatically selects the ideal processor frequency using an algorithm, without needing historical processor activity data. The method is then carefully trained and tested to work across different hardware platforms.
dac-2024-118.key_novelty: PowerLens automatically identifies where to optimize power by grouping neural network components that behave similarly in power consumption, rather than relying on historical processor activity data.

dac-2024-117.method: QUQ compresses vision transformers by splitting the data into at most four ranges, then compressing each range separately with its own scale factor (controlling the compression strength). Since different parts of the network have different data patterns, tailoring the compression strength to each range—rather than using the same compression everywhere—lets each part compress more aggressively while maintaining accuracy. An algorithm finds the optimal partition points and compression settings, with specialized encoding and decoding methods designed to run on hardware accelerators.
dac-2024-117.key_novelty: The central idea is splitting the data into up to four zones, each with its own scale factor (compression strength) that's tuned to that zone's data patterns.

dac-2024-116.method: Estimating rare circuit failures is impractical through direct simulation because failures are so infrequent you'd need billions of runs to observe even one. NOFIS addresses this by using normalizing flows (machine learning models that learn to transform simple random distributions into complex ones) to automatically learn a proposal distribution—a specialized probability distribution designed to concentrate sampling in the rare failure regions. It learns this distribution by minimizing KL divergence (a measure of how different two probability distributions are), then uses importance sampling (a technique that weights rare samples more heavily) to accurately estimate the overall failure probability.
dac-2024-116.key_novelty: The innovation is using normalizing flows to learn proposal distributions for importance sampling in rare circuit failure probability estimation.

dac-2024-122.method: HiMOSS uses Bayesian optimization—learning from past design attempts to predict promising regions—to balance multiple competing objectives. To manage high-dimensional design spaces, it performs adaptive subspace sampling by constructing a smaller search space from gradient information (which direction improves performance) and previous successful designs, with older successes mattering less as the search progresses. Instead of running expensive circuit simulations, it estimates gradients quickly using sparse regression.
dac-2024-122.key_novelty: The innovation is using gradient approximations and success history—with earlier attempts weighted less over time—to adaptively reduce the search to the most important dimensions.

dac-2024-121.method: The approach works through four stages: mathematical distribution across the chip respecting cascade shape constraints (layout rules for how interconnected blocks must physically arrange), region constraints (allowed placement zones), and signal routability (connection feasibility without conflicts); fixing cascade shape violations using optimization; eliminating overlaps while maintaining region boundaries; and refining macro positions for optimal routability. Early stages use analytical optimization to place all pieces at once, while later stages progressively refine placement and resolve remaining violations.
dac-2024-121.key_novelty: It manages cascade shape constraints, region constraints, and signal routability together as integrated concerns throughout all four placement stages instead of handling them separately.

dac-2024-124.method: HTAG is a hardware block that protects embedded neural networks from radiation-induced bit flips, called Single-Event Upsets. It targets the most damaging fault pattern: bits flipping from 0 to 1 in the hidden layers—the intermediate processing stages where the network performs its computations. AND gates, simple logic components, are positioned strategically throughout the network to prevent these specific bit flips from propagating and corrupting the final classification results.
dac-2024-124.key_novelty: The dominant failure mode in embedded neural networks is 0-to-1 bit flips in hidden layers, which can be reliably protected against using AND-gate-based hardware.

dac-2024-125.method: SMILE converts part of the last-level cache into shared memory (memory that GPU threads can simultaneously access) while keeping the rest as a normal data cache. To find the right split for each application, it tries different partition sizes and measures actual performance while the application runs (online profiling). This approach increases the shared memory available to threads, which removes the scheduling bottleneck that currently limits how many threads can run in parallel.
dac-2024-125.key_novelty: The key idea is expanding shared memory by partitioning the last-level cache, with the partition automatically tuned to each application.

dac-2024-133.method: TraiNDSim simulates neuromorphic device training by constraining weight ranges in each layer based on their initial distribution, keeping weights realistic during training. It improves three conductance models—methods of simulating how the device physically changes weights—by better handling non-linear effects, where small changes don't always produce proportional results. The simulator represents weights in both forward and backward directions and compensates for conductance variations (shifts in how well the device conducts and adjusts weights) that accumulate during training.
dac-2024-133.key_novelty: The core advance is layer-wise normalization that accounts for each layer's initial weight distribution, enabling accurate simulation of conductance behavior (how neuromorphic devices change weights) during on-chip training.

dac-2024-127.method: GATE-SiP protects sensitive test data through two complementary techniques: authentication and selective encryption. The system verifies that each chiplet is trustworthy before granting it access to test data, then encrypts only the sensitive portions of that data rather than everything. This approach stops untrusted chiplets from eavesdropping on test information while keeping the performance overhead minimal.
dac-2024-127.key_novelty: The core idea is using identity verification paired with selective encryption to enable secure chiplet testing without the performance cost of encrypting everything.

dac-2024-128.method: Levioso combines the compiler (the program that turns code into CPU instructions) with the CPU hardware itself to stop Spectre attacks more efficiently. The compiler reads through code and identifies which instructions could leak secrets through side channels—invisible escape routes where data seeps out via timing clues or CPU cache behavior—then gives this list to the hardware. The hardware uses this list to selectively block speculative execution (the CPU's practice of guessing which code path to take and running ahead) only at those risky points, instead of blocking all guessing. This prevents both leaks that happen during speculation and leaks that occur even when the CPU isn't speculating.
dac-2024-128.key_novelty: The core idea is using the compiler to identify exactly which instructions leak secrets, so hardware can selectively block speculative execution only at those points rather than applying conservative blanket restrictions that harm performance.

dac-2024-123.method: APTQ compresses neural network layers unevenly by assigning lower precision to less sensitive layers and higher precision to sensitive ones. It measures sensitivity using Hessians—which capture how much each weight affects the model's output—and also accounts for how attention mechanisms nonlinearly influence predictions. By combining these two signals, it can shrink the model while keeping accuracy intact.
dac-2024-123.key_novelty: APTQ is the first to combine layer sensitivity analysis (via Hessian metrics) with how attention nonlinearly affects predictions to decide which layers to compress.

dac-2024-135.method: The algorithm takes a finished circuit layout and minimizes wire segments—a critical goal because in field-coupled nanocomputing (a type of nanoscale computing), wires consume as much area and delay as logic gates do, unlike conventional chips. It works by treating wires as expensive resources and actively seeking ways to reduce them. The method runs fast enough to handle massive designs with millions of basic tiles, and produces circuits that are both physically smaller and faster to operate.
dac-2024-135.key_novelty: An algorithm that minimizes wires in field-coupled nanocomputing by treating them as expensive resources comparable to logic gates—a strategy that works because this technology makes wires costlier than in regular computer chips.

dac-2024-130.method: The paper collects perspectives from quantum optimization researchers to understand what's blocking progress. It identifies the specific barriers and spotlights the most promising research areas, with a focus on finance.
dac-2024-130.key_novelty: The paper brings together expert views on the main obstacles to quantum optimization in finance and the most promising research directions.

dac-2024-126.method: The framework uses two hardware techniques optimized for speed: specialized hardware hashing (computing fingerprints directly in silicon for rapid lookups) and a pruned bitonic sorting network (a circuit that sorts data by removing unnecessary comparisons). These techniques are implemented on a Xilinx XCZU15EG FPGA—a programmable chip—to enable fast watermark verification even on devices with limited computing power.
dac-2024-126.key_novelty: The core contribution is combining hardware hashing and pruned bitonic sorting network acceleration to enable efficient watermark verification on resource-constrained edge FPGAs.

dac-2024-131.method: The framework first generates adversarial attacks (intentional fake malware) to test whether standard ML detectors can be bypassed. It then trains a Deep Reinforcement Learning system (RL: a technique where systems learn to make decisions by receiving rewards for good choices and penalties for bad ones) using an Advantage Actor Critic algorithm to detect these attacks in real-time. The ML detectors themselves are strengthened through adversarial training—exposing them to intentional fake attacks so they learn to recognize similar real threats. Finally, the system automatically decides which defenses should activate at each moment using Upper Confidence Bounds (an algorithm for allocating limited resources intelligently), balancing protection with available computing power.
dac-2024-131.key_novelty: The system predicts adversarial attacks (fake malware attempts) targeting ML-based malware detectors in real-time using Deep Reinforcement Learning, automatically adjusting which specialized defenses activate based on available computing power.

dac-2024-137.method: Instead of searching for a single correct key, the attack looks for ANY valid keys—since multiple key combinations produce correct circuit output. The search tasks are split across multiple processor cores and run simultaneously. This parallel approach is dramatically faster than checking keys one-by-one.
dac-2024-137.key_novelty: Multiple valid keys can unlock a logic-locked circuit, enabling attackers to run key searches in parallel across processor cores for dramatic speedup.

dac-2024-136.method: The approach uses machine learning to automatically select and optimize the settings that control how a 3D integrated circuit (vertically stacked silicon layers) is physically designed, eliminating manual trial-and-error by designers. It was tested against five existing optimization methods on six real 3D designs using TSMC's 28-nanometer manufacturing process, with optimization targeting three different design objectives.
dac-2024-136.key_novelty: The innovation is automating both parameter selection and optimization together in one machine-learning process for 3D chip design.

dac-2024-132.method: The team builds energy-efficient neuromorphic accelerators by combining light-based computing (photonics) with standard semiconductor manufacturing. They integrate phase-change materials—substances that switch between states to store and process information—and III-V semiconductors (optical compounds like gallium arsenide) on a CMOS-compatible platform. To predict system performance, they use gem5 (a processor simulator) that connects the photonic accelerator to a RISC-V processor, measuring speed, energy consumption, and physical size.
dac-2024-132.key_novelty: The core contribution is integrating phase-change and III-V photonic materials into CMOS-compatible manufacturing while using gem5-based system simulation to model the complete neuromorphic accelerator.

dac-2024-140.method: RWriC programs RRAM cells (tiny memory elements that use electrical resistance to store data) sequentially from the most important bits to the least important ones. After programming each cell, it adjusts the next cell's programming target based on errors that accumulated so far, enabling less-important bits to correct errors in more-important bits. The approach uses two techniques: shifting the target for important bits to create more room for less-important bits to compensate, and scaling up less-important bits when variation (unpredictable changes in how cells behave) is large to extend their correction range.
dac-2024-140.key_novelty: Less-important RRAM cells dynamically adjust their programming targets to compensate for errors in more-important cells through adaptive shifting and scaling.

dac-2024-144.method: Instead of guessing what happens at the boundaries between different materials, the paper derives the exact mathematical formulas (analytic surface Green's functions) that describe how electric fields behave when moving through transition regions with multiple layers of different insulators. Rather than pre-computing these formulas with approximations for a fixed set of cases, the team computes them exactly on-the-fly during the simulation itself. These exact formulas replace the old pre-made lookup tables in the floating random walk algorithm, so when the simulation hits a complex transition zone, it gets the correct field behavior instead of an approximation that only worked for certain material stacks. The approach maintains the ability to run calculations in parallel, so accuracy doesn't come at the cost of speed.
dac-2024-144.key_novelty: Instead of using pre-computed approximation tables, the paper derives the exact mathematical formulas (analytic surface Green's functions) that describe electric field behavior in transition cubes with arbitrary layered materials, eliminating approximation errors.

dac-2024-134.method: MERSIT is an 8-bit number format designed to compress neural networks while preserving accuracy. It works by flexibly dividing bits between the exponent (the "scale") and fraction (the "precision") portions, adapting an idea from the Posit number format. To make this work efficiently in hardware, it combines the decoding steps into a single optimized process, called a "merged decoding scheme," which reduces the chip area and power needed compared to previous approaches. This format is tested across different types of neural networks to measure both accuracy and hardware performance.
dac-2024-134.key_novelty: MERSIT is an 8-bit compression format with dynamic exponent/fraction-bit configuration (inspired by Posit) and a merged hardware-efficient decoding scheme.

dac-2024-141.method: The method systematically tests neuromorphic chips by creating test inputs that activate faults—making defective neurons behave differently from working ones. These faulty signals then propagate through the network layers, amplifying their effects so they can be detected at the network's output. For spiking neural networks with L layers, this approach achieves complete fault detection (100% coverage) using only L test configurations (meaning the number of tests scales linearly with network depth), while requiring minimal weight changes and tolerating 4-bit quantization (reduced numerical precision).
dac-2024-141.key_novelty: A scalable, systematic method for finding all faults in neuromorphic chips using only a linear number of tests, without requiring special design-for-testability features.

dac-2024-129.method: CPUs use a Pattern History Table (PHT—a hardware memory recording branch predictions to guess what instructions to fetch). When the CPU speculatively guesses which way a branch (decision point in code) will go, it updates the PHT; Conjuring observes these updates to figure out what control flow path the victim program actually took. Because this happens naturally during normal execution, no special setup or interference with the victim is needed. Improved branch predictor designs actually amplify this leak.
dac-2024-129.key_novelty: First practical side-channel attack that extracts victim control flow through the Pattern History Table without any special setup or victim interference, executable with unprivileged code.

dac-2024-142.method: Hynify is a custom piece of hardware designed specifically to run multiple types of nonparametric statistics—methods for analyzing data without assuming it follows a specific pattern. Because these calculations need lots of processing power and fast memory access, Hynify tackles both problems by reorganizing how data moves through the system and how it's stored at different speed levels in memory.
dac-2024-142.key_novelty: Hynify is the first high-throughput hardware accelerator designed for multiple types of nonparametric statistics in a unified system.

dac-2024-146.method: The approach shrinks the neural network that powers SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping — the process robots use to map their surroundings and track their location) through compression techniques, then designs specialized hardware architecture to efficiently run this smaller network. The hardware is optimized in two ways: at the micro-architectural level (how the chip's internal components are structured and connected) and the dataflow level (how data moves through the chip). By tightly coupling the compressed algorithm to the custom hardware design, the system achieves far greater energy efficiency than running full neural networks on standard GPUs.
dac-2024-146.key_novelty: The key idea is jointly designing the neural network compression and the specialized hardware together from the start, so they optimize each other rather than being developed separately.

dac-2024-139.method: The chip stores weights and performs calculations in magnetic memory cells on the same piece of silicon—a computing-in-memory approach that eliminates the energy waste of shuttling data between memory and processors. The design uses a weight group architecture made of 6 transistors paired with 4 magnetic junctions that can operate in either series mode (junctions stacked end-to-end for efficiency) or parallel mode (junctions side-by-side for flexibility), with a hybrid layout supporting both. A configurable modulation scheme lets you adjust the precision per operation (2, 4, 6, or 8 bits) depending on what accuracy you need, optimizing power consumption. The design was built and validated in both 180-nanometer and 28-nanometer process technologies.
dac-2024-139.key_novelty: The innovation is a hybrid architecture that combines series and parallel magnetic junction configurations in one structure, achieving the energy efficiency of pure series designs and the architectural flexibility of pure parallel designs.

dac-2024-145.method: SpaHet uses a dual-adaptive sliding window—a technique that slides differently across each input matrix based on where its sparse data actually is—to efficiently handle cases where both matrices have different sparsity patterns. Instead of applying one fixed tiling strategy, an exploration algorithm automatically tests different ways of organizing the computation and picks the most efficient approach. A sparsity-aware merge tree then combines all partial result calculations to form the final output matrix, reusing computations wherever possible.
dac-2024-145.key_novelty: Dual-adaptive sliding window mechanism that independently adjusts to each input matrix's sparsity pattern, enabling automatic discovery of optimal tiling strategies for both matrices.

dac-2024-143.method: The paper addresses LLM efficiency by improving four interconnected areas: speeding up the algorithms themselves, designing hardware specifically optimized for LLMs (called co-design), automatically translating code for custom accelerators using compilers, and using LLMs to verify that hardware designs work correctly before building them. By optimizing all layers together rather than separately, the approach reduces bottlenecks from algorithm design all the way through to hardware execution.
dac-2024-143.key_novelty: The paper's distinctive contribution is using LLMs to verify hardware designs work correctly (HLS functional verification), integrated with simultaneous optimization across algorithms, hardware co-design, and compiler techniques.

dac-2024-147.method: This design embeds computation directly into the memory chip, avoiding the energy-wasting delays of shuffling data between separate memory and processors. Multiple read pathways work at the same time, allowing data to be fetched from many locations simultaneously, boosting how much work the system can do per second. The memory ports can read, write, and rearrange data patterns on the fly, letting the hardware update its learning in real-time while still running inference. An arbiter circuit controls traffic between operations and ports, and everything is built using 3nm FinFET transistors—the smallest transistors currently available.
dac-2024-147.key_novelty: The key innovation is pairing multiple memory pathways with flexible read-write ports that rearrange data, controlled by an arbiter circuit, so the chip can run fast neural network inference and learn from new data simultaneously.

dac-2024-151.method: They created a compiler that coordinates work between processing-in-memory units (which compute right where data sits, cutting data movement) and GPUs (which handle math-intensive tasks). At the core is an algorithm that decides optimal data placement and task scheduling for inputs that vary in size. This approach breaks the memory bandwidth bottleneck by reducing how much data needs to travel between storage and processors.
dac-2024-151.key_novelty: A compiler that splits multimodal transformer work between processing-in-memory units (which reduce data movement) and GPUs (which handle computation), using an algorithm tailored for inputs that vary in size.

dac-2024-154.method: QuGeo uses a quantum circuit with 576 adjustable parameters, specifically designed for Full-Waveform Inversion (the process of determining underground rock properties by analyzing seismic waves). Instead of learning purely from raw data, it uses physics principles to prepare and scale the data first, which helps guide the learning process toward more accurate velocity maps. The system was tested on the OpenFWI FlatVelA dataset.
dac-2024-154.key_novelty: The core idea is that quantum circuits designed specifically for Full-Waveform Inversion, combined with physics-guided data preparation, substantially outperform quantum approaches without built-in physics knowledge.

dac-2024-148.method: SkyPlace groups components based on how they're connected and their size—a macro-aware clustering approach—to provide a good starting point for placing them. It applies semidefinite programming relaxation (a mathematical technique that solves hard problems by loosening constraints) to handle large blocks in an analytical placement framework while maintaining solution quality. The method extends electrostatics-based placement (which treats components like charged particles repelling each other) with specialized handling for mixed-size components.
dac-2024-148.key_novelty: The core innovation pairs macro-aware clustering (grouping components by their connections and size) with semidefinite programming to solve both placement initialization and large-block handling in mixed-size chip design.

dac-2024-153.method: The system dynamically re-examines pin access routes (connection points where signals enter and leave the chip) during the routing process instead of locking them in at design time. For each I/O pin, it guarantees at least one usable connection path while freeing up other predetermined paths for competing signals to use. This flexibility reduces routing congestion and improves the overall ability to successfully connect all signals across the chip.
dac-2024-153.key_novelty: First system to dynamically adjust pin access routes during routing instead of using predetermined paths fixed during initial design.

dac-2024-152.method: The system creates smaller versions of the AI model by removing unimportant connections (called width-wise pruning), producing different model sizes for different devices. It uses reinforcement learning—a machine learning technique that learns by trying different options and improving—to automatically choose which model size each device should use based on its processing power and available memory. Each device then trains its assigned model locally on its own data.
dac-2024-152.key_novelty: The core insight is using neural network pruning combined with reinforcement learning to automatically assign right-sized models to each resource-constrained device in a federated learning system.

dac-2024-138.method: The approach jointly trains an audio circuit (source-follower bandpass filter that selects certain sound frequencies) and a Depthwise Separable CNN (a lightweight neural network classifier) as a single system. During training, it uses a combined measurement called Lbpf that weighs both classification accuracy and signal quality (signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR—how much actual signal versus random noise). This shared optimization uses end-to-end backpropagation, which is the standard method for training neural networks but here extended to also adjust the analog circuit parameters, so every component of the system improves together.
dac-2024-138.key_novelty: The key innovation is jointly optimizing the audio circuit (source-follower bandpass filter) and neural network classifier using SNR-aware training, instead of designing them separately.

dac-2024-155.method: FHE-CGRA uses a coarse-grained reconfigurable architecture (CGRA) — hardware whose processing units can be rewired to perform different computational tasks — that changes its configuration while running. Since each stage of ML inference uses different encryption methods with different optimization requirements, the hardware execution units reconfigure themselves to match each stage's specific operations. An MLIR compiler toolchain (software that converts ML code into hardware-level instructions) automatically coordinates this reconfiguration and optimizes resource use across all stages.
dac-2024-155.key_novelty: The core idea is using a CGRA whose execution units reconfigure themselves during operation to match whatever FHE encryption method and operation each stage of ML inference requires.

dac-2024-150.method: The approach uses design-technology co-optimization—jointly optimizing design and manufacturing—to select which multi-bit flip-flop cell variant each instance uses. First, after placement, it explores different cell layouts with different input/output pin positions and selects variants that minimize total wire length. Second, after routing, it uses non-rectangular L- and T-shaped cell layouts that enable selective control of each internal flip-flop's driving strength (how much current it can push), and selects these for timing-critical instances to meet speed requirements.
dac-2024-150.key_novelty: Using design-technology co-optimization to selectively assign multi-bit flip-flop cells to non-rectangular layouts that simultaneously address wiring distance and timing constraints.

dac-2024-158.method: AIG-CIM uses compute-in-memory—placing calculations right alongside stored data to avoid slow data movement—with three different types of compute-in-memory units, each optimized for different parts of diffusion model inference. These units are distributed across scalable chiplets (separate mini-chips that can be connected together), allowing flexible data reuse because data stays near the computation. The entire system was built in TSMC 22nm technology, with careful optimization spanning from individual circuit design to how the multiple chiplets coordinate as a complete system.
dac-2024-158.key_novelty: Three different types of compute-in-memory units that scale across chiplets to enable flexible data-reuse patterns for diffusion model inference.

dac-2024-149.method: The NimbleAI architecture uses 3D silicon stacking (stacking silicon layers vertically) to integrate a vision sensor, spiking neural circuits, and memory in one compact chip. The vision sensor captures sparse events (sudden changes in light) using light-field event-driven sensing (recording from multiple angles to infer 3D depth) combined with selective foveated attention (focusing computation on important regions), encoding data across four dimensions: horizontal position, vertical position, depth, and time. This sparse 4D encoding enables the architecture to efficiently execute standard computer vision algorithms on neuromorphic (event-based) inputs.
dac-2024-149.key_novelty: Combining light-field event-driven vision (capturing 3D depth from light-ray angles), selective foveated attention (focusing on important regions), and neuromorphic processing in a single 3D-stacked chip creates a compact, efficient architecture for 3D scene understanding.

dac-2024-162.method: The approach combines magnetic domain wall MTJs (specialized memory devices using moving magnetic patterns to store information) with CMOS neuromorphic pixels that sense light, so the sensor can perform convolution operations (mathematical pattern matching) directly on the chip instead of sending data elsewhere. These magnetic memory devices have the advantage that they retain their state without power and can be reprogrammed many times, enabling many independent calculations to happen simultaneously on the sensor. The team designed everything together—accounting for device limitations (low tunnel-magnetoresistance and limited dynamic range), circuit challenges (non-linearity and manufacturing variation), and algorithm requirements—using simulations based on 22-nanometer process technology to predict the design's behavior.
dac-2024-162.key_novelty: The core innovation is using programmable magnetic domain wall MTJ devices (which store information through moving magnetic patterns) to perform convolution operations directly in neuromorphic vision sensor pixels.

dac-2024-161.method: The method groups related circuit components together (clustering) to reduce the complexity of placing millions of components on a chip, while accounting for timing performance, power consumption, and the circuit's logical structure. Machine learning predicts the best shape for each cluster—specifically, its width-to-height proportions and density. The approach is validated on both the open-source OpenROAD and commercial Cadence Innovus placement tools.
dac-2024-161.key_novelty: The core idea combines machine learning prediction of the best cluster shapes (width-to-height proportions and how densely packed they should be) with clustering that accounts for power consumption and signal timing, to make chip placement both faster and produce better results.

dac-2024-164.method: RT-MDM breaks deep neural networks (AI models) into segments and determines which segments must run in a specific order to produce correct results. It groups these segments and manages memory by assigning separate memory space to each group, while allowing groups to reuse each other's memory once they finish. A specialized scheduler optimizes how to split the networks into segments and arrange them into groups, aiming to run as many concurrent tasks as possible while ensuring all meet their deadlines.
dac-2024-164.key_novelty: The first real-time scheduler that runs multiple deep neural networks (AI models) on microcontroller units (MCUs) by managing the sequence in which each model segment must run and efficiently sharing memory across segments to meet timing deadlines.

dac-2024-160.method: SAS approximates Boolean circuits (functions with multiple 0/1 outputs) to reduce chip size and power by replacing them with symmetric functions—functions whose output depends only on how many input bits are 1, not which specific inputs are 1. It selects the symmetric function with the smallest Hamming distance from the original (fewest positions where output bits differ). The framework applies a configurable error metric to control exactly how much inaccuracy you introduce, letting you adjust the efficiency-versus-accuracy tradeoff for your specific needs.
dac-2024-160.key_novelty: Symmetric functions with minimal Hamming distance provide an efficient mechanism for controlled approximate Boolean circuit synthesis.

dac-2024-159.method: When hardware faults corrupt CNN calculations, this method detects and fixes errors at the algorithm level using hamming codes—math tools that spot and correct errors in individual data values. It focuses protection on critical computation paths and results rather than protecting everything equally, and uses checkpointing (periodically saving the computation state) to recover from severe faults. This targeted approach keeps runtime overhead to around 72% while correcting over 99.6% of critical faults—substantially better than traditional triple modular redundancy, which runs the entire computation three times.
dac-2024-159.key_novelty: Algorithm-based fault correction tailored to CNN-specific computations—using hamming codes (error-correcting math) and checkpointing (state-saving)—achieves over 99.6% critical fault correction at ~72% runtime overhead, substantially outperforming traditional triple modular redundancy.

dac-2024-166.method: The authors implement order-preserving encryption—a technique that keeps data encrypted while allowing comparisons without decrypting—on an Intel DE10 Standard FPGA, a programmable hardware chip. They systematically test different configurations to understand how the number of trees in the forest, encryption strength, classification accuracy, and available hardware resources interact with each other. Using the MNIST dataset (handwritten digit images), they identify which combinations of settings work best within the constraints of the available FPGA hardware.
dac-2024-166.key_novelty: They show how to implement order-preserving encryption on programmable hardware (FPGA) for random forests, systematically measuring how encryption strength, accuracy, and hardware resources trade against each other.

dac-2024-165.method: The paper introduces micro-fat pointer, which uses TT instructions—specialized hardware in ARMv8-M processors that check memory bounds—to catch buffer overflows efficiently. Each pointer carries metadata (extra information) describing where memory access is allowed; when memory is accessed, a TT instruction checks that the access respects these boundaries. By combining metadata with hardware support, the method achieves safety without the excessive performance or memory overhead of previous approaches, making it practical for embedded systems with limited resources.
dac-2024-165.key_novelty: Using TT instructions (a new hardware feature in ARMv8-M for checking memory bounds) to enable efficient fat pointer bounds-checking for heap memory in embedded systems.

dac-2024-156.method: PDRC speeds up design rule checking by using a graphics processor to run calculations in parallel. It organizes overlapping regions into nested groups (hierarchical interval lists), then applies a sweepline algorithm—which checks where shapes overlap or touch—running many scans simultaneously on the GPU rather than one at a time. This efficiently handles entire package designs including shapes with curved and diagonal edges.
dac-2024-156.key_novelty: The innovation is using a graphics processor to parallelize design rule checking through a sweepline algorithm organized with nested groups, handling packages with curved and diagonal edges.

dac-2024-157.method: Whisper exploits timing differences in CPU transient execution (speculatively-run instructions that might be discarded)—an approach called Transient Execution Timing or TET. Using the Performance Monitor Unit (PMU), hardware counters in CPUs that track execution metrics, the authors measure these timing differences at the architectural level (without needing physical access) to infer secrets. They adapt three known attack techniques (Meltdown, Zombieload, and Spectre-RSB) to use TET, showing how to break KASLR (the security feature that randomizes kernel memory locations). Because existing kernel and hardware protections focus on blocking other types of information leakage, they don't adequately defend against TET-based attacks.
dac-2024-157.key_novelty: Whisper's core innovation is using execution timing differences in transient execution as an architectural-level covert channel (hidden extraction path) that reliably bypasses existing kernel and hardware security protections.

dac-2024-168.method: The approach explores different ways to fold transistors and arrange them using a search tree structure (a branching framework for systematically trying options), finding the configuration that minimizes chip area. It accelerates this search using dynamic programming — calculating solutions for small problem pieces once and reusing those results instead of recalculating. It verifies that electrical connections can be routed by formulating the vertical space check as a network flow problem (like confirming water can flow through a pipe network without bottlenecks), ensuring the final layout is buildable.
dac-2024-168.key_novelty: The core idea is optimizing transistor folding and placement together as one problem, using dynamic programming to reuse calculations and network flow verification to guarantee connections can be routed.

dac-2024-163.method: STING processes graphs by moving the filtering and sorting work onto NVMe storage drives using callback functions (functions that automatically trigger when data is ready). These callbacks coordinate with the storage layer, which filters and sorts the data and sends only results back to RAM—dramatically reducing the data that has to travel across the slow storage-to-memory connection.
