Since all this coordination happens through callbacks without requiring special code changes, existing applications can use STING without modification.
dac-2024-163.key_novelty: STING uses asynchronous callback functions (functions called when data is ready) to transparently shift graph filtering and sorting to storage drives without moving data to RAM or rewriting applications.

dac-2024-171.method: A neural network learns to convert images into DNA sequences using triplet loss, a training method where three images at a time (a target image, one similar to it, and one different) are compared. The network is penalized if the similar image's encoding isn't closer to the target than the different image's is, teaching it to arrange similar images near each other in encoding space. Training uses CIFAR-100, a dataset of 100 types of objects. Once trained, similar images are retrieved efficiently by comparing how close their DNA sequence encodings are to a query.
dac-2024-171.key_novelty: Triplet neural networks can learn DNA-based image encodings where similar images produce similar sequences, enabling efficient similarity-based retrieval.

dac-2024-172.method: PVTSizing combines two optimization methods: TuRBO (trust region Bayesian optimization—a technique that intelligently samples promising circuit designs) provides strong initial designs, while multi-task reinforcement learning (a system that learns which designs work best across different operating scenarios) refines them across all variations in voltage, temperature, and manufacturing. Both methods process multiple designs in parallel batches to speed up execution. Additionally, a critic model (a helper that scores designs) prunes away weak candidates, and focused metrics narrow the search to the most promising designs, while simultaneously handling random variations in component behavior.
dac-2024-172.key_novelty: The innovation is combining Bayesian optimization, multi-task reinforcement learning, and critic-assisted filtering to efficiently design circuits in parallel that stay reliable across all process, voltage, temperature, and manufacturing variations.

dac-2024-167.method: MoNDE divides experts (specialized neural network components) into two groups—frequently-used ones on the GPU, rarely-used ones in main computer memory. During inference, instead of transferring massive expert parameters between GPU and memory, it only moves small intermediate results called activations. Since activations are far smaller than full expert parameters, computing cold experts in place (near-data processing) eliminates unnecessary transfers, substantially reducing communication overhead while keeping computation efficient.
dac-2024-167.key_novelty: MoNDE's key innovation is splitting experts between GPU and main memory by usage frequency, then moving only small activations between them instead of massive expert parameters, substantially reducing communication overhead.

dac-2024-173.method: ModSRAM puts computation circuits directly inside SRAM memory chips, so data doesn't need to shuttle back and forth between memory and a separate processor. Instead of computing carries (the numbers you carry over when doing arithmetic), it uses an algorithm called R4CSA-LUT with pre-calculated lookup tables to perform modular multiplication much faster. Because the algorithm and hardware design work together, the same data can be reused multiple times while staying in memory, eliminating wasted trips.
dac-2024-173.key_novelty: It's the first processor-in-memory architecture using 8T SRAM that speeds up large-number modular multiplication for cryptography.

dac-2024-178.method: Majority-inverter graphs are logic circuits that need optimization to reduce their size. The paper takes three established optimization techniques—rewriting (restructuring the circuit), resubstitution (replacing parts with simpler equivalents), and graph mapping (reorganizing how the circuit is arranged)—and systematically tests different orderings and combinations of them to discover which sequence produces the smallest circuit.
dac-2024-178.key_novelty: Systematically exploring different orderings and combinations of existing optimization techniques achieves better results than any single fixed sequence.

dac-2024-175.method: RL-PTQ compresses neural networks after training by automatically choosing bit-widths (how many bits to represent numbers in each layer) and observer configurations (how to measure each layer's behavior) using reinforcement learning—a machine learning technique where software learns by trying different choices and keeping the ones that work better. The method groups similar layers together in hybrid models (those that mix convolutional and transformer components) and trains an RL agent to discover the optimal quantization settings for each group. This targeted approach handles the unique challenges of mixed architectures better than simpler quantization methods that use the same settings everywhere.
dac-2024-175.key_novelty: Using reinforcement learning to automatically find optimal bit-widths and observer configurations tailored to each layer group in hybrid models that combine convolution and transformers.

dac-2024-174.method: MENDNet detects hardware faults by watching the neural network's confidence at multiple checkpoints—intermediate points where the network could provide an answer—rather than waiting for the final result. It uses an energy-based uncertainty metric (a math-based measure of prediction confidence) at each checkpoint. When confidence suddenly drops, the system knows a hardware fault has corrupted the data and automatically switches to an earlier checkpoint that's still reliable. This catches errors without stopping the system or adding major delays.
dac-2024-174.key_novelty: The core idea is detecting hardware faults by monitoring neural network confidence at multiple intermediate points, then automatically switching to earlier checkpoints to avoid errors without system disruption.

dac-2024-169.method: The design vertically stacks two different materials in a 4-transistor cell: InGaZnO write transistors that retain data longer, and single-crystal silicon read transistors for faster access. Vertical stacking fits the entire cell into the footprint normally needed for one transistor. A self-clamped searching scheme (SC2S—controlling signal behavior during searches) optimizes how search signals propagate through the cell. The design was validated using 3D-TCAD simulation, which models the three-dimensional transistor structure.
dac-2024-169.key_novelty: The core innovation is a vertically stacked design using InGaZnO write transistors (for longer data retention) and single-crystal silicon read transistors (for faster reading) together in a 4-transistor cell.

dac-2024-177.method: The approach constructs a quantum circuit that performs a walk search on Johnson graphs—a mathematical structure where possible subsets sit as nodes and quantum states hop between nearby ones to find solutions. It designs each component of the circuit with specific gate sequences, then measures implementation cost three ways: total number of quantum gates (operations), circuit depth (sequential layers), and qubit width (number of quantum bits needed). The design is compared against Grover's algorithm, showing it uses fewer and shallower T-gates—expensive operations on current quantum hardware—for practically solvable subset-sum instances.
dac-2024-177.key_novelty: The main contribution is a complete, implementable quantum circuit for quantum walk search on Johnson graphs with precise costs for gates, depth, and qubit count—closing the gap between theoretical algorithms and circuits that can run on actual quantum hardware.

dac-2024-183.method: The approach provides a unified programming model for different 3D reconstruction tasks and redesigns how data flows through the algorithm (the dataflow) to improve data locality—keeping frequently accessed data close together in memory rather than scattered across distant locations. It removes unnecessary coordination points (synchronization) by analyzing which computations actually depend on each other. It then introduces Waffle, a specialized chip architecture that places processing closer to memory (near-memory acceleration), which eliminates the slow data movement that was the original bottleneck.
dac-2024-183.key_novelty: Waffle is a specialized architecture that accelerates 3D reconstruction by placing processing closer to memory, solving the data locality and synchronization bottlenecks in the algorithm.

dac-2024-170.method: TraceFormer converts a printed circuit board (PCB) trace—the electrical wires on computer chips—into a graph representing its shape and connectivity, breaking each segment into a token (a data unit) containing geometric and topological information. A transformer machine learning model processes these tokens by learning patterns in sequences, creating a complete PCB representation. Extraction networks (specialized prediction components) then predict four types of S-parameters—complex-valued electrical measurements (with magnitude and phase) that describe how signals scatter and reflect—achieving R² >0.99 accuracy up to 15 GHz for 4-port designs.
dac-2024-170.key_novelty: Graph transformers that tokenize PCB trace geometry and connectivity predict electrical signal scattering measurements (S-parameters) directly, replacing expensive numerical simulation.

dac-2024-180.method: Geneva combines the two buffers that store instructions at different execution stages—one tracking speculative execution, one queuing pending instructions—into a single buffer that dynamically adjusts its allocation between them based on runtime needs. If the workload has many memory operations in-flight, it allocates more space to track them; if instructions pile up waiting to dispatch, it allocates more to queue them. This eliminates wasted buffer capacity and reduces power consumption and silicon area.
dac-2024-180.key_novelty: A buffer that automatically reallocates space between tracking speculative execution and queuing pending instructions based on workload demand.

dac-2024-176.method: The TREND model speeds up thermal simulation of chips and packages by computing heat flow in detail only in thermally critical regions—the hot spots where thermal design is essential—and simplifying calculations in cooler areas. It uses thermal resistance derivatives (measurements of how heat resistance changes through a device) to automatically identify which regions need detailed calculation and which can be approximated, dramatically reducing design time without losing accuracy.
dac-2024-176.key_novelty: By using thermal resistance derivatives to identify thermally critical regions, the model focuses detailed computation only on hot spots, cutting design time without sacrificing accuracy.

dac-2024-181.method: HAIL-DIMM disguises NDP operations (which combine data movement with computation happening at the memory) as standard DDR READ/WRITE commands so the memory controller sees them as regular requests. The controller's built-in interleaving logic (which spreads requests across memory banks to balance load) naturally schedules them fairly with host access, without needing dedicated hardware. Meanwhile, the DIMM recognizes which commands are NDP work based on their address and executes them as computation. This dual interpretation—same request looks like DDR to the controller but NDP to the DIMM—enables fair interleaving using only existing system hardware.
dac-2024-181.key_novelty: HAIL-DIMM's key innovation is using the same request format for two different purposes: the memory controller reads it as a standard DDR operation while the DIMM interprets it as near-data processing (computation happening at the memory), enabling fair interleaving without extra hardware.

dac-2024-188.method: The approach generates alternative instruction sequences that should produce the same result as the original instruction—a process called semantically-equivalent program synthesis. It then runs both the original and alternative versions and compares their actual behaviors. To efficiently explore the vast space of possible alternatives, it uses a CEGIS framework (a structured search method that prioritizes the most likely candidates first). If the original and alternative sequences produce different results, it has found an instruction-level bug that self-consistency checking alone would miss.
dac-2024-188.key_novelty: Instead of just checking if an instruction is consistent with itself, the method detects single-instruction bugs by generating semantically-equivalent alternatives (different ways to produce the same result) and comparing how they actually behave.

dac-2024-191.method: SPARK uses two acceleration units that work together: one standalone accelerator and another integrated directly into the CPU pipeline, allowing forward and backward propagation (the two computation passes needed for training) to run at the same time. A scheduler monitors where the computation is sparse (where many values are zero) and dynamically directs more work to whichever accelerator is free, keeping both units busy. To reduce memory bottlenecks, the system uses a shared memory architecture where data can be fetched in different orientations to match what each computation needs.
dac-2024-191.key_novelty: SPARK combines an acceleration unit built into the CPU pipeline with a scheduler that watches for sparse computation patterns in real-time to route workloads efficiently and enable simultaneous forward and backward propagation.

dac-2024-185.method: SmartATPG represents the circuit as a network graph and uses a graph convolutional network (a machine learning technique that learns patterns from connected structures) to extract important features. It then applies reinforcement learning (learning by trial and error to make better decisions) to select test patterns while minimizing backtracking—the expensive process of undoing choices and trying alternative paths.
dac-2024-185.key_novelty: SmartATPG applies graph convolutional networks (which extract patterns from circuit structures) and reinforcement learning (which learns through trial and error) to reduce backtracking in test pattern generation.

dac-2024-179.method: G-kway speeds up graph partitioning using a multilevel approach on a GPU. It shrinks the graph using union find (a technique that groups connected pieces together while preserving their connections), then partitions this smaller version. During uncoarsening (expanding back to the original size), it refines the partition by rearranging independent sets of nodes (groups of unconnected nodes that can move together). Running all these steps on a GPU makes the entire process much faster than using a regular processor.
dac-2024-179.key_novelty: The key technique is using union find-based coarsening and independent set-based refinement algorithms on a GPU instead of a regular processor, which makes multilevel graph partitioning much faster.

dac-2024-182.method: SLLT (Skew-Latency-Load Tree) addresses a core challenge in chip design: clock signals need to arrive nearly simultaneously everywhere (tight skew), reach destinations quickly (low latency), and consume minimal power (low load), but traditional methods force you to pick which priority matters most. It solves this by combining skew-focused and speed-efficiency-focused tree construction methods into a unified hierarchical structure that uses partition schemes to divide the design into manageable regions and buffering optimization to strategically place signal amplifiers. The method was validated on chips manufactured at 28nm scale.
dac-2024-182.key_novelty: SLLT unifies three design goals—skew control (timing uniformity), latency minimization (signal speed), and load optimization (power efficiency)—into a single clock tree instead of requiring a trade-off between them.

dac-2024-192.method: The attack extracts the secret key that protects a neural network by observing how the network responds to different inputs and outputs—a technique called an I/O attack. It combines two mathematical approaches: algebraic methods (solving systems of equations for the key) and learning-based methods (training a model to infer the key from input-output patterns). The attack reconstructs the key piece by piece, minimizing how many test inputs are needed, and verifies each piece to ensure correctness. This approach was successfully demonstrated on large neural networks with complex architectures.
dac-2024-192.key_novelty: An incremental I/O attack combining algebraic and learning-based methods can extract logic-locking keys from neural networks with minimal test inputs.

dac-2024-184.method: The approach models control channels as a graph (nodes are channels, edges show connections) and uses this structure to minimize tests. For blockages, it needs just 1 test instead of testing every combination. For leaks, it colors the channel graph so connected channels always have different colors, then groups same-colored channels to test together. This reduces leak tests from ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉ to ⌈log2(χ(G) + 1)⌉ patterns, where χ(G) is the chromatic number (fewest colors needed).
dac-2024-184.key_novelty: Graph coloring reveals which control channels can be batch-tested together, reducing leakage tests from ⌈log2(n + 1)⌉ to ⌈log2(χ(G) + 1)⌉ patterns.

dac-2024-190.method: The method reduces memory use by learning that Jacobian matrices (mathematical tables showing how circuit outputs respond to input changes) follow predictable patterns across time and space. It combines three techniques: sparse tensor representation using shared indices (storing only non-zero entries compactly), a spatiotemporal prediction model (forecasting future matrices based on learned time and space patterns), and residual encoding (recording only the small prediction errors). This keeps matrices in memory throughout forward transient analysis, eliminating the need for expensive disk I/O.
dac-2024-190.key_novelty: A spatiotemporal prediction model that learns how Jacobian matrices evolve across time steps and circuit regions, enabling compression by storing only prediction errors instead of complete matrices.

dac-2024-187.method: The framework searches for neural network designs and AQFP hardware configurations together. AQFP (adiabatic quantum-flux-parametron) is a type of superconducting chip logic with specific parameters that affect performance. By exploring both the network design and hardware settings simultaneously, rather than designing them separately, the framework finds implementations where network and hardware choices reinforce each other.
dac-2024-187.key_novelty: The core innovation is optimizing the neural network architecture and AQFP hardware configuration together as one design problem, rather than separately.

dac-2024-196.method: The approach designs a new gate structure for the multiplexer (the control switch that routes fluids) and combines it with mixed coding—using different encoding strategies together to represent more control options in the same physical space. This gate-and-coding combination reduces overhead: you can control more microfluidic valves without needing extra input connections. The authors created LaMUX, an automated tool that designs these mixed-coding multiplexers for pneumatically-driven microfluidic systems (systems using compressed air to push fluids through channels).
dac-2024-196.key_novelty: Pairing a new gate structure with mixed coding (combining different encoding strategies) to pack more microfluidic-valve control into fewer pneumatic connections and valves.

dac-2024-194.method: SpacePulse combines parameterized quantum pulses—adjustable quantum operations that can explore regions of the quantum state space unreachable with traditional gates—with the contextual subspace method, which computes corrections using only a subset of qubits and measurements rather than simulating the full system. This combination enables flexible quantum operations beyond gate-based decomposition. A Pauli grouping strategy (organizing measurements by grouping related quantum properties) optimizes measurement efficiency.
dac-2024-194.key_novelty: The core idea is combining parameterized quantum pulses (adjustable quantum operations) with the contextual subspace method (computing corrections using only a subset of qubits and measurements) to dramatically reduce quantum resource requirements while maintaining solution accuracy.

dac-2024-193.method: Before running the QAOA quantum algorithm, Graph Neural Networks—machine learning models trained on graph patterns—predict good initial parameter values. The approach evaluates multiple neural network designs to find the best one for this task. These predictions provide a warm-start (an educated starting point) that eliminates the expensive parameter-tuning optimization that would normally run on the quantum computer. By moving this optimization work to a classical computer beforehand, the approach reduces the quantum resources required during algorithm execution.
dac-2024-193.key_novelty: Using Graph Neural Networks to predict QAOA parameters classically in advance, eliminating the optimization that would otherwise require quantum resources.

dac-2024-189.method: ElasticZRAM watches what the application is doing and what kind of storage device the phone has, then automatically decides how much to compress data into ZRAM—a compressed memory layer between regular RAM and disk storage. It adjusts compression levels dynamically: using more compression when the CPU has spare capacity or when the storage device is slow, and less compression when the CPU is busy or storage is fast. This adaptation optimizes the tradeoff between how much CPU work is spent compressing data versus how much data gets written to storage.
dac-2024-189.key_novelty: ZRAM management that adapts compression and allocation policies dynamically based on application behavior and storage device speed, rather than using fixed settings.

dac-2024-201.method: The method uses Voronoi diagrams—a technique that divides space into regions where each region is closest to one assigned point—to automatically partition the redistribution layer (the routing layer in 3D chips) into sections for each power supply. For each section, the algorithm finds the optimal shape and size that maximizes usable area while avoiding signal wire routes and satisfying power integrity requirements and manufacturing design rules. This automates what is currently a manual process, allowing all power supplies to be optimized simultaneously instead of one at a time.
dac-2024-201.key_novelty: Voronoi diagrams enable automatic, simultaneous optimization of multiple power planes on redistribution layers, replacing manual single-plane design.

dac-2024-195.method: CAMO applies reinforcement learning—a technique where a system learns by testing actions and getting rewarded for good results—to optical proximity correction, a step in chip manufacturing where masks are adjusted so printed patterns match the design despite optical distortion. Unlike pure data-driven methods, CAMO explicitly models spatial correlation: how adjustments to one mask segment affect neighboring segments. It uses OPC-based manufacturing rules to guide which mask adjustments the system tries. The system trains on metal layer patterns from VLSI chip design.
dac-2024-195.key_novelty: CAMO adds optical proximity correction expertise—how neighboring mask adjustments interact and which adjustments follow manufacturing rules—directly into reinforcement learning rather than relying purely on data patterns.

dac-2024-197.method: PHD speeds up decoding of Huffman-compressed data (a compression technique that shrinks file sizes) by working around a key constraint: each decoded symbol depends on the previous one, which normally prevents parallelization. It uses self-synchronization to identify parallelizable work at three levels—individual bits, groups of symbols (subsequences), and larger data blocks (tiles)—and stores the decoding rule table (codebook) using a two-tier memory design optimized for the FPGA's limited memory. An optimization called ONCE MORE further speeds decoding by reducing loop iterations.
dac-2024-197.key_novelty: PHD is the first FPGA Huffman decoder that enables parallel work despite each decoded symbol depending on the previous one, by using self-synchronization at three scales (bits, subsequences, and tiles), along with smart memory management and loop optimization.

dac-2024-186.method: Winograd convolution speeds up neural network operations by mathematically transforming the computation to require fewer multiplications. This technique is reformulated here into a "Structured Direct" form that naturally separates into hardware-friendly building blocks, making it straightforward to implement on FPGAs. WinoGen automatically generates these optimized FPGA designs: you specify arbitrary input/output tile sizes and kernel sizes, and it produces the hardware implementation using Chisel (a hardware description language)—eliminating manual redesign for each configuration.
dac-2024-186.key_novelty: Structured Direct Winograd Convolution breaks the technique into regular, parameterizable hardware building blocks, enabling a generator to automatically produce efficient FPGA designs for any combination of kernel sizes and tile sizes.

dac-2024-200.method: FLAME exploits two characteristics of Mixture of Experts (MoE) models: expert weights (the neural network parameters) consume enormous memory but many are rarely used, and the model tends to repeatedly activate the same experts. It applies N:M pruning—removing unused connections in a pattern that keeps the hardware efficient—to reduce memory consumption. Since expert usage is predictable and repetitive, FLAME guesses which experts will be needed next and preloads their weights into the chip's fast local cache before the model actually decides which experts to use, using a Circular Expert Prediction and Prefetching strategy (CEPR). A Pruning-Aware Expert Buffering mechanism (PA-BUF) orchestrates this preloading while accounting for both weight sparsity and usage patterns.
dac-2024-200.key_novelty: FLAME predicts which experts a model will need before it actually makes its selection—possible because experts are used in predictable, repetitive patterns—then preloads their weights into fast on-chip cache to avoid delays from fetching slower external storage, using a technique called Circular Expert Prediction and Prefetching (CEPR).

dac-2024-198.method: Static timing analysis predicts chip speed by simulating how transistors behave in detail, using CCS models (Composite Current Source models). Normally this detailed simulation requires so many calculations it becomes impractical. GCS-Timer solves this by offloading the simulation to a GPU with thousands of parallel cores that work simultaneously. This maintains detailed accuracy while achieving much faster results—without simplifying the model, which is how other methods usually trade speed for accuracy.
dac-2024-198.key_novelty: Using GPU parallel processing to accelerate detailed CCS-based circuit timing analysis while maintaining accuracy—without simplifying the model.

dac-2024-204.method: The approach uses a tool called JACO (Jointly Optimize aggregation Cycle and flows' Offsets) that adjusts two interconnected settings: how long each aggregation cycle runs and when individual network flows start relative to that cycle. It uses an incremental heuristic algorithm—a step-by-step method that builds up solutions efficiently—to find good values for both settings simultaneously. The results are tested using OMNet++ simulation software across different network scenarios to verify that this reduces latency (delay) while making better use of network resources.
dac-2024-204.key_novelty: Optimizing aggregation cycle lengths and flow offsets together (instead of one at a time) makes ECQF practical with lower latency and better network resource use.

dac-2024-202.method: The approach combines hardware and software by taking advantage of device aging—the natural, gradual slowdown and efficiency loss that computer chips experience over time. Instead of designing new security circuits, the method trains the neural network using Differential Orientation Fine-tuning (DOFT) to work correctly only on hardware with specific aging patterns. As the chip naturally degrades, the network's performance adapts to match, making the protected model functional only on aged hardware with the expected degradation characteristics. Since this protection uses degradation that happens automatically anyway, it costs essentially nothing to implement compared to traditional security circuits.
dac-2024-202.key_novelty: The single core idea is using the natural aging of computer chips—which happens automatically and costs nothing—as the IP protection mechanism for neural networks, combined with Differential Orientation Fine-tuning so the network only works on aged hardware with expected degradation patterns.

dac-2024-205.method: TBNet uses a Two-Branch approach that splits neural network execution between two places: a regular processor (the untrusted REE—Rich Execution Environment) and a physically-isolated secure zone (the TEE—Trusted Execution Environment). Non-sensitive layers run on the regular processor to maintain speed, while sensitive layers run in the secure zone to prevent the model from being copied or stolen. The system analyzes the neural network structure to automatically determine which layers are sensitive and where to split them.
dac-2024-205.key_novelty: TBNet's Two-Branch approach partitions neural network layers between a regular processor and a secure protected zone to simultaneously protect the model from theft and maintain system performance.

dac-2024-203.method: FastQuery cuts the cost of querying encrypted embedding tables in private AI inference by combining two strategies. First, it uses communication-aware quantization - reducing the precision of numbers while accounting for how much data must be transmitted - and second, it exploits that embedding lookups are naturally one-hot (selecting just one row from a table, represented as mostly zeros with a single 1). This structure enables both aggressive precision reduction and dense packing of operations, simultaneously lowering both computation time and data volume.
dac-2024-203.key_novelty: FastQuery exploits embedding queries' naturally one-hot structure (selecting exactly one row, represented as mostly zeros with a single 1) to enable both aggressive quantization (precision reduction) and efficient packing, simultaneously reducing computation and communication costs.

dac-2024-199.method: The algorithm designs adders (circuits that add numbers) where the input bits arrive at different times—a common hardware challenge. It breaks the design problem into a divide-and-conquer approach: at each level, combining pairs of bit-groups into larger groups. As it builds, it uses dynamic programming—storing the best partial designs and discarding others that won't lead to better final circuits.
dac-2024-199.key_novelty: The key insight is treating adder design as a divide-and-conquer problem that naturally lets dynamic programming select the best partial designs at each step.

dac-2024-209.method: PMP reshapes how data is accessed in memory—a technique called pattern morphing—to reduce the number of separate memory banks the hardware needs. Rather than being stuck with one fixed access pattern, it transforms the pattern into different mathematically equivalent shapes using reduced hyperplane families, giving it flexibility that older methods lacked. The approach then solves an optimization problem (integer linear programming) to find the reshaping that minimizes wasted space (data padding overhead). This adaptive strategy replaces the rigid, one-size-fits-all patterns that previous hyperplane-based methods required.
dac-2024-209.key_novelty: By combining pattern morphing with integer linear programming optimization, the approach automatically finds the minimum number of memory banks needed for any data access pattern, rather than being constrained by the pattern's original shape.

dac-2024-206.method: The paper optimizes individual MSM processing elements using bucket methods (grouping similar operations to reduce conflicts) combined with greedy scheduling (choosing the best next step at each point). To scale to multiple processing elements, the computation flows through three stages—bucket classification, bucket aggregation, and result aggregation—that balance the work. The key is sharing hardware: instead of each processing element having its own input channel and output handler, multiple elements share a single universal input channel and one post-processing unit. This sharing works because the processing elements have different data access patterns that don't interfere with each other, so one shared path can efficiently feed all of them while cutting both the hardware needed and the data traffic congestion.
dac-2024-206.key_novelty: Multiple MSM processing elements can operate efficiently in parallel by sharing a single universal input channel and post-processing unit, which eliminates redundant hardware and prevents bandwidth bottlenecks that would otherwise limit scaling.

dac-2024-208.method: The framework uses machine learning (specifically support vector machines—a pattern-recognition algorithm trained on examples of radiation damage) to automatically identify which parts of a chip are vulnerable to radiation. It automates soft-error analysis across the entire system from hardware through software, building databases that track single-event upsets (bit flips caused by radiation) and single-event transients (timing disruptions) for each circuit component. The approach is validated on RISC-V processors, testing processor cores, interconnects, and memory subsystems.
dac-2024-208.key_novelty: The framework automatically identifies radiation-sensitive circuit nodes using machine learning, enabling efficient soft-error simulation across the entire system.

dac-2024-207.method: The system uses a three-step optimization process built into custom hardware to automatically adjust image signal processor (ISP) settings in real-time as it processes camera feeds. Unlike traditional systems that require humans to pre-configure settings or need offline training on predefined scenes, this framework adapts on-the-fly to new situations. By designing the hardware and software together, it processes 1080P video at 75 frames per second on an FPGA (field-programmable chip) or 240 frames per second on an ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit).
dac-2024-207.key_novelty: Automatic real-time tuning of image signal processor settings that adapt to unforeseen camera scenes without requiring offline training on predefined examples.

dac-2024-213.method: The system uses a dynamic precision quantization algorithm that changes how precisely numbers are represented based on the actual data flowing through each part of the neural network, rather than using the same precision everywhere. The Drift accelerator uses online scheduling to make these precision-switching decisions in real-time as data flows through the network. This works across both CNN and Transformer architectures, the two main types of deep neural networks.
dac-2024-213.key_novelty: The core idea is to dynamically adjust how many bits represent each number in the network based on the actual statistics (the distribution and range of values) flowing through, rather than using fixed precision for the entire model.

dac-2024-211.method: Sanitizers are monitoring tools that watch code as it runs and catch bugs that normal testing misses—like when software reads or writes the wrong memory location, or uses a variable before setting it to a value. The work adds these monitoring tools into embedded operating system code so that during testing, the OS automatically detects these hidden bugs. This reveals problems that don't crash the system obviously but could cause failures later in security-critical deployments.
dac-2024-211.key_novelty: The work applies real-time bug-detection monitors (sanitizers) to embedded operating systems to catch problems that standard testing misses.

dac-2024-210.method: MoC groups nearby 3D points using Morton codes—a spatial sorting method that naturally clusters similar points together. Each feature is split into a precise main part (called a base) and a small remainder (called an offset) that only needs low precision since it's numerically small. The system applies two levels of precision reduction: first shrinking the remainders to low precision, then tuning the precision format for each region based on the actual patterns in that region's remainders. The hardware and algorithm are designed together so the Morton code sorting and main computation can run in parallel, avoiding bottlenecks.
dac-2024-210.key_novelty: The core idea is applying spatial grouping via Morton codes, then using region-aware precision reduction that adapts to each region's actual feature patterns.

dac-2024-214.method: SAT solvers (programs that solve logic puzzles) learn new clauses (logical rules) from mistakes during their search, but must delete less valuable ones to stay efficient. NeuroSelect proposes new ways to measure which clauses are valuable and uses machine learning to automatically choose which measurement approach works best for each specific problem. When tested on Kissat, it achieved runtime improvements on large industrial benchmarks.
dac-2024-214.key_novelty: Machine learning adaptively selects which clause-deletion policy works best for each problem instead of using one fixed policy.

dac-2024-216.method: INSPIRE uses index-pair encoding, a method where values are stored with different amounts of precision depending on how unusual they are. Outlier values—ones that fall far outside the normal range—are stored with high precision, while typical values use lower precision to save space. The method uses index pairs to efficiently map between the original values and their compressed representations, which cuts down the computational cost of encoding (compressing) and decoding (decompressing) the data. It works for both neural network activations (the outputs of neurons) and weight values (the learned parameters).
dac-2024-216.key_novelty: Index-pair encoding that reduces the computational overhead of compressing and decompressing neural network values by automatically assigning high precision to outliers and low precision to normal values.

dac-2024-212.method: The system integrates processing circuits (a ROM-based compute-in-memory scheme using lookup tables for calculations) directly adjacent to the light sensors, enabling massively parallel image preprocessing. Differential-frame computing (comparing successive frames to detect changes) provides robustness and naturally creates data sparsity (abundance of zeros). A bio-inspired compression technique using residual recovery caches and zero-skip circuits further reduces data size without accumulated errors. The entire design uses LTPS TFT technology (low-temperature polysilicon thin-film transistors for large-area integration) with optimizations coordinated across all chip layers.
dac-2024-212.key_novelty: Differential-frame ROM-based compute-in-memory (a processing scheme that compares frames and uses lookup tables) integrated directly into image sensors built from thin-film transistors, combined with bio-inspired compression for data reduction without errors.

dac-2024-219.method: The method uses automated search (called neural architecture search, or NAS) to find network designs that can switch between two operating modes: a deep version with many layers that achieves higher accuracy, and a shallow version with fewer layers that consumes less power and computation for better hardware efficiency. These switchable designs are tested on NVIDIA Jetson embedded systems to validate that they provide both accuracy and efficiency improvements.
dac-2024-219.key_novelty: Networks that can dynamically adapt between deep and shallow versions, combining high accuracy from deep architectures with power and speed efficiency from shallow ones.

dac-2024-217.method: This system uses a memory-based processor (where computation happens directly in storage, saving time), organized in nested groups to skip over empty spaces in the input data and zeros in the weight values (the parameters controlling the calculation). To generate the randomness needed for annealing, it exploits a quirk: SRAM chips running at below-normal power produce random bit errors from manufacturing imperfections during read operations—turning the chip's own noise into a feature. Engineers explored different cluster sizes and programmability levels to balance how well it solves problems against how much hardware it needs.
dac-2024-217.key_novelty: Instead of building a separate random-number generator, the system uses natural manufacturing imperfections in SRAM chips running at low power to create the randomness needed for the annealing algorithm.

dac-2024-218.method: The accelerator uses a conflict-free memory mapping algorithm—a technique that stores data so different computational steps can access what they need simultaneously without waiting. This eliminates the memory bandwidth constraint that normally limits NTT/INTT performance. The design pairs this with a hardware/software pipeline that operates continuously without pausing, achieving 48,543+ operations per second on large transforms where N=2^16 (65,536 data points).
dac-2024-218.key_novelty: The core idea is conflict-free memory mapping—storing data so different computational operations don't interfere when accessing it—which breaks the memory bandwidth bottleneck and enables nonstop NTT/INTT pipeline execution.

dac-2024-215.method: PowerRChol uses a randomized Cholesky factorization (a way to break down matrices that uses randomness to speed things up) with linear-time complexity to create a preconditioner—a transformed version of the problem designed to be faster to solve. It reorders the matrix elements to improve how the computer accesses memory and speeds up how quickly the solution converges. The preconditioned problem is then solved using Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient solvers (iterative solvers that repeatedly improve the answer), efficiently handling the sparse linear systems with millions of equations that power grids generate.
dac-2024-215.key_novelty: Randomized Cholesky factorization with linear-time complexity that delivers both fast preconditioner construction and fast solver convergence, overcoming the tradeoff where existing approaches force you to choose between one or the other.

dac-2024-220.method: The system uses a transformed Gaussian process model—a statistical predictor modified to enforce specified performance targets as hard constraints that guide its predictions. It pairs this with a customized EHRM acquisition function, which is a method for choosing which untested designs to evaluate next while balancing different design trade-offs. The system searches through possible RISC-V SoC architectures for LLM workloads including Transformer, BERT, and GPT-1.
dac-2024-220.key_novelty: This framework incorporates design specifications as hard constraints in Bayesian optimization, ensuring the search finds only chip designs that meet specified performance targets.

dac-2024-223.method: Moctopus stores and processes graph data directly in memory hardware (PIM, for processing-in-memory) by splitting the graph into chunks that adjust dynamically as data changes. The algorithm keeps related data close together (preserving locality) while handling cases where some nodes have far more connections than others (tackling graph skewness). Rather than making the host CPU handle all updates, it spreads the update work across PIM modules. The system then processes multiple path queries in batches, using PIM hardware's parallel processing to handle many queries at once.
dac-2024-223.key_novelty: Moctopus's key innovation is a graph partitioning algorithm designed specifically for PIM hardware that handles uneven data distribution while keeping related data close together, all without making graph updates expensive.

dac-2024-222.method: TensorSSA converts imperative tensor programs—code that modifies data in place, like PyTorch—into functional form, where new data is created instead of mutating existing tensors. Mutations (direct changes to existing data) prevent compilers from fusing operations together (combining multiple operations into one efficient operation), which is a key optimization technique. By eliminating mutations, TensorSSA enables operator fusion across control flow boundaries (if statements, loops, etc.), an optimization scope that previous approaches couldn't achieve.
dac-2024-222.key_novelty: TensorSSA automatically transforms tensor programs from imperative form (code that modifies data in place) to functional form (code that creates new data), enabling operator fusion optimizations across control flow structures that previous methods couldn't handle.

dac-2024-224.method: The solution pairs specialized hardware with smart scheduling. Content Addressable Memory (CAM)—a search technique that works directly on data without moving it—first narrows down which graph vertices must be counted. Processing-In-Memory (PIM)—computation done inside memory chips rather than at a separate processor—then counts the cliques in parallel using repeated Boolean AND operations (finding which vertices appear in multiple sets). Dynamic scheduling distributes the counting work evenly across all PIM chips, ensuring none sits idle.
dac-2024-224.key_novelty: Combining CAM (a search technique that doesn't move data) and PIM (in-memory computation) with dynamic scheduling eliminates the data transfer bottleneck by doing both search-space reduction and parallel k-clique counting right where the data lives.

dac-2024-228.method: VARADE detects anomalies by running a predictive model directly on edge devices instead of sending data to the cloud. It learns patterns from past measurements to predict what the next measurement should be — if actual data deviates significantly from the prediction, it flags an anomaly. To work within the memory and power limits of edge devices, it uses variational inference, a mathematical technique that approximates probability distributions efficiently, enabling real-time detection without expensive calculations.
dac-2024-228.key_novelty: Combining variational inference with autoregressive prediction enables real-time anomaly detection on resource-limited edge devices.

dac-2024-226.method: CDLS uses generative AI to automatically learn which design constraints (rules for where to place components and how to connect them) work best, instead of requiring engineers to write them manually. These learned constraints guide an automated placement and routing tool to produce simulation-ready circuit layouts. The framework was evaluated on real industrial analog circuit designs using Intel's sub-10nm process technology.
dac-2024-226.key_novelty: The key innovation is using generative AI to automatically learn design constraints (rules for where components go and how they're connected) in analog circuits, rather than having engineers manually write them.

dac-2024-221.method: The framework uses a type of AI called Graph Neural Networks—which learns patterns in interconnected data—to speed up two time-consuming parts of chip design: TCAD simulations (detailed physics-based simulations of how semiconductor devices behave) and cell library characterization (measuring how individual logic gates perform under different conditions). By using a unified model that handles both processes, the GNN approach achieves over 100X speedup at the technology simulation level, which cuts overall design iteration time by 1.9X to 14.1X across both emerging and established semiconductor technologies.
dac-2024-221.key_novelty: The core idea is using Graph Neural Networks (AI trained on patterns in interconnected data) to jointly speed up both semiconductor device simulation and logic gate characterization through a unified model.

dac-2024-231.method: DERO rearranges how residual connections (shortcuts that add input values back to outputs in neural networks) execute while a model is running. It analyzes which operations happen inside each residual and how they depend on each other, then reorganizes the timing and storage location of data processing. This shrinks the peak memory needed at any one moment—matching the memory footprint of networks without residuals. The accuracy benefits of residuals are preserved because the final computation stays identical; only the storage order changes.
dac-2024-231.key_novelty: By rearranging when and where data is stored in residual connections based on analyzing their operations, you achieve the memory efficiency of networks without residuals while preserving the accuracy benefits that residuals provide.

dac-2024-229.method: The approach uses a Transformer neural network (a machine learning architecture designed to understand code structures) trained on High-Level Synthesis source code paired with synthesis directives called pragmas—special annotations that tell the compiler how to optimize. The model learns to recognize how different code patterns and pragma choices affect the final hardware's speed and resource usage, then predicts these outcomes for new code.
dac-2024-229.key_novelty: Using a Transformer neural network to predict hardware speed and resource requirements by analyzing source code and synthesis pragmas at the language level (examining the code itself, not its compiled form).

dac-2024-235.method: FCM splits quantum circuits into smaller subcircuits by cutting wires at strategically chosen points. Instead of cutting randomly, it considers the cost and error rate of fusion operations (the connections needed to stitch measurements together in photonic quantum circuits) when deciding where to cut. By optimizing cut placement based on fusion costs, FCM reduces the total number of fusions required, improving circuit reliability.
dac-2024-235.key_novelty: FCM's core contribution is fusion-aware wire cutting: it accounts for the specific error costs of fusion operations when deciding where to cut circuits, rather than applying generic cutting strategies.

dac-2024-239.method: The attack deliberately slows down the processor's clock speed (frequency throttling) while the model executes, which makes invisible power consumption variations appear as measurable timing delays. Software at the processor's lowest privilege level (Ring 0) controls this throttling and records how long execution takes. A machine learning classifier trained on timing patterns learns to recognize which model architecture is running by identifying the distinctive time signature each design produces. The method achieves 96% accuracy in identifying the model architecture family across multiple platforms.
dac-2024-239.key_novelty: Frequency throttling converts power consumption patterns into measurable timing delays that uniquely identify ML model architectures.

dac-2024-225.method: Conventional suppression of reference voltage ripple (fluctuations in the converter's reference signal) requires large capacitors and fast amplifiers. A machine learning model learns to predict ripple errors by analyzing a slow SAR ADC (10MHz), then corrects them in real-time in a faster SAR ADC (200MHz), eliminating the need for these bulky components. The design was validated through 28nm CMOS simulation.
dac-2024-225.key_novelty: A machine learning model trained on a low-speed SAR ADC (10MHz) predicts and corrects reference voltage ripple errors in a high-speed SAR ADC (200MHz) in real-time, eliminating conventional bulk capacitors and high-speed amplifiers.

dac-2024-232.method: The system analyzes hardware documentation using HS-BERT, a language model (software trained to understand text patterns) built specifically for hardware security tasks, to automatically identify security properties—rules about what the hardware should and shouldn't do. The extracted security properties can then be directly converted into assertions (automated checks that verify the hardware design), replacing the manual engineering work that was previously required.
dac-2024-232.key_novelty: HS-BERT is the first language model designed specifically for hardware security, automatically identifying security properties from hardware documentation.

dac-2024-227.method: HyCaMi automatically converts block cipher implementations (encryption algorithms that process fixed blocks of data) into hardware designs using Lookup Tables—memory arrays storing pre-calculated values. Because table lookups always follow the same memory access pattern regardless of input data, they prevent cache side-channel attacks (where attackers infer encryption secrets by observing which memory locations get accessed). HyCaMi then uses quantitative analysis (mathematical measurement) to determine how much security leakage remains and lets you adjust table sizes to balance speed and security.
dac-2024-227.key_novelty: The core idea is quantifying cache leakage to automatically balance security and performance through adjustable lookup tables in block cipher hardening.

dac-2024-236.method: PIVOT examines each input image to assess how much computational effort is needed, then skips some of the attention operations (calculations that find important relationships between different image regions) when the input is simple enough. It discovers which operations to skip by testing different skip strategies directly on the target hardware—a ZCU102 FPGA—rather than relying on theory alone. By skipping unnecessary computation for simple inputs while doing full calculations only when the input demands them, PIVOT reduces energy consumption during inference.
dac-2024-236.key_novelty: PIVOT selects which attention operations to skip for each input based on the input's complexity, discovering which selections work best by testing different strategies directly on the target hardware.

dac-2024-237.method: Lightator processes images right at the camera sensor using light-based devices, before data leaves the hardware. First, it compresses the raw image data at the sensor (keeping only essential information to reduce volume), then it performs the core image-processing math—convolutions—using light instead of electricity. This near-sensor, light-based approach eliminates two expensive steps: converting signals between light and electricity, and transmitting data to a distant processor.
dac-2024-237.key_novelty: Combining compressed image acquisition and fine-grained optical convolutions at the camera sensor in one light-based device, eliminating the need to send data to the cloud for processing.

dac-2024-233.method: The placement algorithm tackles congestion locally and globally. Locally, it adds padding around cells based on their actual routing connections to prevent crowding in specific areas. Globally, it uses Coulomb forces—physics-inspired repulsion (like magnets pushing apart)—where crowded regions naturally push cells into less-congested zones.
dac-2024-233.key_novelty: The core innovation is using virtual Coulomb forces—a physics-inspired repulsion model like magnets pushing apart—to fix routing congestion at both the chip-wide level and in crowded hotspots.

dac-2024-230.method: The approach uses edge-weighted decision diagrams—tree structures with numerical weights on the edges—to represent the target quantum state, handling qudits (quantum bits) of different sizes efficiently. It automatically generates the quantum circuit (the sequence of gate operations) needed to build that state on a quantum computer directly from this representation. To manage quantum hardware's time constraints, the method allows tunable approximation, letting you balance between perfect accuracy, fewer gate operations, or less memory as needed.
dac-2024-230.key_novelty: The innovation is using edge-weighted decision diagrams with integrated approximation to automate the generation of circuits that prepare quantum states with qudits of different sizes.

dac-2024-240.method: The paper reviews lessons learned from building custom hardware accelerators (computer chips designed for specific tasks) in different fields. It uses autonomous systems as a detailed example to identify seven problems that recur whenever engineers design these specialized chips for new applications. These same pitfalls keep appearing in machine learning, genomics, and other domains, explaining why accelerator design is difficult and suggesting what challenges to anticipate.
dac-2024-240.key_novelty: The paper identifies seven recurring problems that appear whenever engineers design custom hardware accelerators—the same pitfalls show up across machine learning, genomics, and autonomous systems.

dac-2024-238.method: Alchemist introduces Meta-OP, a low-level operator that can handle many different types of polynomial operations (the mathematical building blocks of FHE encryption) while staying hardware-friendly and avoiding complex routing logic. To make this work efficiently, it adds a slot-based data management system that organizes data to match how the hardware accesses memory. This combination lets a single accelerator handle both arithmetic operations (additions, multiplications) and logic operations across different FHE encryption schemes.
dac-2024-238.key_novelty: Meta-OP is a low-level operator that unifies different polynomial operations across FHE encryption schemes while being hardware-efficient and avoiding complex routing logic.

dac-2024-234.method: The root cause of DVFS attacks is that Intel processors allow independent control of frequency and voltage. The countermeasure uses switching circuit theory (a mathematical method to predict circuit failures under different electrical and timing conditions) to partition all frequency-voltage combinations into safe and unsafe states. It enforces only safe combinations, preventing attacks while maintaining normal power adjustments. The fix deploys via microcode updates or model-specific registers.
dac-2024-234.key_novelty: The innovation uses switching circuit theory to formally partition frequency-voltage combinations into provably safe and unsafe states, creating a defense that stops attacks without blocking normal power management.

dac-2024-243.method: A branch prediction network (a system that forecasts which code branches each thread will take) runs on the GPU's tensor cores (specialized hardware units) in parallel with the main computation on CUDA cores. Based on these predictions, a thread reorganization algorithm rearranges threads in memory so that threads taking the same branch execute together, reducing the inefficiency of control flow divergence. This approach keeps the overhead minimal because prediction happens concurrently with the main kernel instead of pausing execution to fix divergence after it occurs.
dac-2024-243.key_novelty: The core idea is running branch prediction on tensor cores in parallel with the main kernel execution, so threads can be reorganized efficiently with minimal overhead to mitigate control flow divergence.

dac-2024-244.method: The method uses High-Level Synthesis (HLS—a tool that automatically translates high-level behavioral descriptions into hardware designs) to generate a reference implementation from the original specification. It then compares this automatically generated hardware against the manually written RTL; since HLS produces correct implementations from the spec, any differences point to bugs in the manual design. This avoids the tedious work of manually searching through massive simulation waveforms.
dac-2024-244.key_novelty: Use HLS-generated hardware as a reference point; bugs in manual designs appear as comparison differences, making them visible without extensive simulation analysis.

dac-2024-241.method: S2RAM-PUF operates SRAM cells (memory storage elements) at very low voltages—0.5V to 0.8V—where the natural variation in transistor behavior becomes more stable. Fabricated in a 65-nanometer process, this approach achieves zero bit errors across -40°C to 120°C temperatures because the low voltage keeps the randomness from SRAM startup steady and reliable—this randomness is what generates each chip's unique security key.
dac-2024-241.key_novelty: Subthreshold SRAM operation (running at very low 0.5V-0.8V voltages) achieves zero-error reliability with ultra-low power consumption (3.12 femtojoules per bit), eliminating the traditional tradeoff between dependability and energy use.

dac-2024-242.method: The first strategy uses mid-circuit measurements (checking qubit states during computation) and resets to identify unnecessary qubits, then applies gate-dependency rules (analyzing operation order constraints) to remove them—reducing qubit count by 61.6% on average, or 45.3% when also minimizing circuit depth. The second strategy applies numerical instantiation (finding concrete parameter values), synthesis (building operations), and dependency rules to discover resizing opportunities in circuits the first strategy cannot handle, achieving 20.7% average qubit reduction. Both are implemented in BQSKit.
dac-2024-242.key_novelty: Using mid-circuit measurements and resets combined with gate-dependency analysis makes it possible to shrink quantum circuits that couldn't be reduced before.

dac-2024-245.method: Token-Picker estimates attention probabilities (the calculation of how much each token matters) before softmax to identify tokens with near-zero attention. It then skips reading those tokens from memory, saving computation without retraining. Specialized hardware automates this efficiently, achieving a 12.1x pruning ratio and reducing off-chip memory accesses by 2.6x.
dac-2024-245.key_novelty: The method estimates attention probabilities before softmax to identify and skip low-attention tokens without retraining the model.

dac-2024-248.method: The method chooses which standard-cell height variant to use for each gate after the initial placement phase, without moving gates to different positions. Standard cells come in multiple physical heights; the approach selects variants such that neighboring gates have compatible heights, satisfying the NIMCH constraint that layout regions must contain only gates of the same height. This preserves the original gate positions and avoids the performance loss that occurs when conventional design flows relocate gates to satisfy these height constraints.
dac-2024-248.key_novelty: Selecting standard-cell height variants after placement to satisfy NIMCH constraints without relocating gates.

dac-2024-252.method: GNNavigator creates a unified description of both the software—the graph neural network training algorithm—and the hardware it runs on, so it can predict how they interact. It builds a model that forecasts the training's runtime and memory requirements. Then it automatically searches through different training configurations to find the combination that best balances execution speed, memory use, and accuracy for your specific task.
dac-2024-252.key_novelty: It treats software and hardware as a unified system, then automatically searches for the best training configuration of graph neural networks for each task.

dac-2024-251.method: HyCiM combines three working parts in a memory-based computing system. First, it directly encodes inequality constraints (conditions like 'x must be less than 10') into the optimization problem without adding extra dummy variables, keeping the problem smaller and cheaper to solve on hardware. Second, it uses ferroelectric FET transistors—transistors that store information using a ferroelectric material—in a computing-in-memory circuit to rapidly check whether solutions satisfy these constraints and automatically filter out invalid ones. Third, it applies iterative refinement using the same ferroelectric transistors to gradually improve solutions through simulated annealing, a method that explores many possibilities and progressively focuses on better ones.
dac-2024-251.key_novelty: This method directly transforms optimization problems with inequality constraints into QUBO form without requiring auxiliary variables, which substantially reduces the hardware cost of solving them.

dac-2024-255.method: The system automatically identifies and stores only the most representative training examples from incoming data, reducing memory usage. It then uses the model itself to generate multiple variations of questions and answers from the sparse user feedback, expanding what it can learn from. Finally, it tunes the model directly on your device using this curated dataset, asking the user for more feedback only when needed.
dac-2024-255.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining automatic selection of the most useful training examples with having the model generate its own training variations, making it practical to personalize language models on devices with very limited memory and user feedback.

dac-2024-254.method: TPDA-DRAM embeds detectors directly into the chip to measure voltage differences between bitline pairs (the complementary storage lines for each bit), revealing how much timing margin currently exists—the safety buffer between when data is actually ready and when the system assumes it is. It dynamically adjusts DRAM timing in two complementary ways: one scheme (PVA) recognizes that some cells are naturally weaker due to manufacturing variation and allows faster access when conditions are favorable, while another (TVA) adjusts timing parameters in real-time based on the chip's current temperature.
dac-2024-254.key_novelty: The core idea is to sense real conditions on the chip (how manufacturing variations and temperature affect timing) and adjust DRAM access timing accordingly, rather than using conservative margins that assume the absolute worst case.

dac-2024-258.method: DACPara breaks a circuit's logic network (called an And-Inverter Graph) into independent chunks arranged hierarchically, then processes these chunks through three parallel stages. Each stage works on its chunks independently, but all stages share live information about the overall circuit structure, preventing conflicts in their decisions. This divide-and-conquer approach lets it handle large circuits in parallel without sacrificing result quality.
dac-2024-258.key_novelty: Combining live circuit-wide information with divide-and-conquer parallelization enables high-quality logic rewriting to scale to large circuits.

dac-2024-253.method: The system uses a two-stage process: first locating and cropping to a defective region, then precisely outlining its exact boundaries. Weak supervision—learning from partially labeled images instead of fully annotated ones—cuts the labeling work needed while keeping accuracy equal to fully supervised methods. Testing on 1,328 real SEM images from a semiconductor manufacturing facility confirmed this approach.
dac-2024-253.key_novelty: A two-stage approach using weak supervision (learning from images with partial labels) achieves the same accuracy as fully labeled approaches while requiring only 10% of the labeling effort for nanoscale SEM defects.

dac-2024-250.method: C-Nash combines ferroelectric transistors (special transistors that hold their state) with computing-in-memory to find Nash equilibrium solutions. The system converts the optimization problem into MAX-QUBO form (maximizing quadratic binary functions) without needing extra helper variables, uses a grid of ferroelectric transistors to store and directly compute on the game payoff matrices, and applies a winner-takes-all circuit with two-phase simulated annealing—a search method that explores solutions probabilistically before gradually narrowing the search—to find all equilibrium solutions.
dac-2024-250.key_novelty: A ferroelectric transistor architecture that solves both pure and mixed strategy Nash equilibrium without helper variables, enabling discovery of all equilibrium solutions.

dac-2024-247.method: The framework uses active learning—strategically picking simulations rather than running them randomly. It ranks candidate simulations by three factors: model uncertainty (measured using the neural tangent kernel, a mathematical tool for estimating confidence in predictions), simulation time, and I-V curve complexity (how variable the device's behavior is). By prioritizing highly uncertain simulations where the model has the most to learn, the framework reduces the total number of expensive TCAD simulations while maintaining accuracy.
dac-2024-247.key_novelty: Using neural tangent kernel-based uncertainty to select which TCAD device simulations to run reduces the total number of simulations needed to train accurate device models.

dac-2024-246.method: HiLight reduces circuit latency by preventing braiding paths (the routes taken during quantum operations that move qubits around) from intersecting. The framework uses two approaches: layout-aware compilation that plans operations based on the physical arrangement of qubits, and scheduling that coordinates when operations occur to prevent path collisions. By eliminating these path intersections, the system reduces communication bottlenecks while maintaining practical efficiency.
dac-2024-246.key_novelty: Preventing braiding path intersections through routing and scheduling eliminates surface code communication bottlenecks.

dac-2024-249.method: The system uses an LLM to break a hardware design into basic building blocks and prove each correct incrementally. For each block, the LLM writes invariants (rules about what must always be true, like 'this adder won't overflow') and verifies them using Z3 (an automated theorem prover). As blocks combine, the LLM also verifies that boundaries between them connect correctly. The system was tested on arithmetic circuits including Ripple Carry Adders and Dadda Tree Multipliers.
dac-2024-249.key_novelty: LLMs automate proof generation for hardware verification for the first time by working incrementally—each module gets correctness rules written by the LLM and verified by Z3, a logic verification tool.

dac-2024-257.method: DeepRIoT trains a robotic controller in simulation using reinforcement learning (trial-and-error training toward multiple objectives), then automatically collects data from real robots to refine its model of actual behavior. It adapts the controller to work with the improved model (transfer learning), and deploys new versions through automated CI/CD systems (continuous integration and deployment pipelines), eliminating manual testing and rollout steps.
dac-2024-257.key_novelty: DeepRIoT closes the simulation-to-reality gap by automatically collecting real-world data, improving its model of how the robot actually behaves, retraining the controller to work with the updated model, and deploying the result without manual intervention.

dac-2024-259.method: The technique harnesses processor exceptions—events triggered when the CPU encounters special conditions like invalid instructions or memory protection violations—to intercept code execution. When an exception occurs, the instrumentation code's exception handler activates, observes what's happening, then lets the original code continue. This works on bare-metal devices with no operating system, and correctly handles edge cases like nested exceptions that break existing tools.
dac-2024-259.key_novelty: This work shows that processor exceptions—events the CPU triggers when encountering special conditions—can be the foundation for monitoring binary code on bare-metal systems without an operating system.

dac-2024-260.method: CLUMAP solves the problem of placing and connecting operations on CGRAs (programmable chips that can reconfigure for different tasks) by grouping related operations into clusters first, which makes the placement problem simpler to solve. It uses a cost function (a scoring system that evaluates how good a placement is) specifically tuned for simulated annealing (a search technique that explores alternatives and occasionally accepts worse solutions to avoid getting stuck). The approach separates placement (deciding where clusters go on the chip) from routing (deciding how to connect them with wires), making each step more efficient.
dac-2024-260.key_novelty: The key innovation is that clustering operations with a specialized simulated-annealing cost function lets you map code to any CGRA design without architecture-specific modifications.

dac-2024-256.method: MSMAC uses an FPGA accelerator (a reprogrammable computer chip optimized for specific tasks) with a custom instruction set designed specifically for multi-scalar multiplication. It combines pipelined execution—where new calculations begin before previous ones finish—with special multiplication techniques called hybrid Karatsuba multipliers (which decompose large multiplications into faster smaller ones) to efficiently perform the elliptic curve arithmetic. A runtime system breaks the overall task into optimal sub-tasks and orchestrates them across multiple processing elements to execute in parallel.
dac-2024-256.key_novelty: The core innovation is a custom instruction set combined with a pipelined Point Addition Unit and hybrid Karatsuba multipliers (specialized multiplication techniques) specifically tailored for multi-scalar multiplication.

dac-2024-264.method: The paper uses a machine learning model (a Seq2Seq Transformer, a neural network designed to learn patterns in instruction sequences) to predict optimal qubit routing. The model learns from examples of quantum gate operations and SWAP instructions—operations that rearrange which physical qubits represent which logical qubits to fit the processor's connectivity constraints—then predicts where each logical qubit should map onto the actual physical qubits of a quantum processor. Unlike routing strategies hand-written for each specific processor design, this learned approach works across different quantum hardware backends without requiring manual tuning.
dac-2024-264.key_novelty: Using a machine learning model (a Seq2Seq Transformer: a neural network that learns patterns in instruction sequences) to automatically discover qubit routing eliminates hand-written hardware-specific routing rules and enables one model to work across different quantum processor designs.

dac-2024-263.method: The system shrinks images directly inside the camera sensor using its analog circuits (the continuous electrical signals from the sensor, before they're converted to numbers), rather than capturing full-resolution images first. It can select specific regions to keep at full detail while compressing the rest, further reducing data size. Only the already-compressed image reaches the microcontroller, so nothing ever needs to fit in the device's limited 512kB memory.
dac-2024-263.key_novelty: The key idea is doing high-resolution image compression at the camera sensor (using its analog circuits and selective region focusing) instead of on the memory-constrained edge device itself.

dac-2024-262.method: PREP delays preparing memory columns until all their data has been consumed. Rather than preparing each column immediately when it becomes empty, PREP collects all pending preparation tasks and executes them together in parallel, freeing memory much faster. By exploring different orderings for these preparations, the system balances the amount of chip area used against execution speed.
dac-2024-262.key_novelty: By waiting to prepare memory columns, multiple preparations can run in parallel instead of one-by-one.

dac-2024-267.method: The system encodes knowledge of physiological signals' natural harmonic patterns (repeating frequency signatures, like those of heartbeats and breathing) directly into a neural network designed to analyze spectrograms—visual maps showing which frequencies are present over time. It improves these spectrograms by masking overlapping regions and filling them in using its built-in harmonic knowledge. A preprocessing step aligns incoming sensor signals to match the network's expected format. Because this harmonic knowledge is embedded rather than learned purely from training data, the system can separate mixed vital signs effectively even with minimal data.
dac-2024-267.key_novelty: The innovation is embedding harmonic priors—built-in knowledge of the repeating frequency patterns in physiological signals—into the neural network's architecture, enabling effective signal separation with minimal training data.

dac-2024-261.method: The approach uses Logarithmic Posits (LP)—a flexible number format that reshapes itself based on the actual values it stores, rather than using fixed formats like integers or floats. A genetic algorithm (a search method inspired by evolution) finds the optimal LP settings for each layer, while also comparing how different parts of the network represent data to reduce inconsistencies. Specialized hardware called the LP Accelerator implements this with mixed-precision processing, allowing different layers to use different formats for efficient execution.
dac-2024-261.key_novelty: The key innovation is Logarithmic Posits, an adaptive number format that automatically adjusts to each layer's actual data distribution and is optimized layer-by-layer using a genetic algorithm.

dac-2024-271.method: This paper examines how multiple wearable devices—watches, rings, glasses—can work together to run AI, despite each having limited power and computing ability. It draws inspiration from how humans distribute thinking: we don't try to do everything ourselves, but delegate based on capability and constraints. The approach divides AI work across heterogeneous wearable devices (devices with different capabilities and power budgets) while minimizing power consumption to remain practical for battery-powered hardware.
dac-2024-271.key_novelty: The core idea is that wearable devices can run AI collaboratively by distributing the work among themselves, inspired by how humans delegate tasks, rather than each device working alone or relying entirely on the cloud.

dac-2024-266.method: Specure detects information leaks caused by speculative execution—where the processor guesses which code to run next and executes it before confirming the guess is correct—by running systematic hardware tests that try different hardware configurations while tracking where sensitive information flows. Instead of comparing results against a perfect reference design (called a golden model), it uses a Leakage Path coverage metric to guide the systematic exploration for vulnerabilities.
dac-2024-266.key_novelty: The core idea is combining information flow tracking with hardware fuzzing—guided by a Leakage Path metric—to find speculative execution information leaks without comparing against a reference design.

dac-2024-272.method: OPTIMA is a computer program that quickly predicts how much power a math operation uses inside specialized computer memory (6T-SRAM—a type of memory chip built from six transistors).
