One generates new semiconductor layout patterns using deep generative models (AI systems trained to create new designs), while the other applies learning-based OPC (optical proximity correction—a technique that learns to adjust patterns so they print correctly when manufactured). Rather than optimizing these separately, the system takes turns: the pattern generator creates layouts, OPC refines them, and that feedback helps the generator create better layouts next time. This cycle repeats, so both systems improve together because each learns from what the other needs.
dac-2024-371.key_novelty: Instead of optimizing pattern generation and OPC correction separately, EMOGen trains them together in a co-evolutionary cycle so improvements in each directly help the other.

dac-2024-373.method: GCoDE automatically designs the GNN architecture (network structure) and decides which operations should run on the device versus edge server, optimizing these decisions together as one problem. It abstracts inter-device communication as an explicit operation that can be fused (combined) with neighboring computations to reduce overhead. Using a constraint-based search that evaluates performance across heterogeneous devices with different computing power, GCoDE finds efficient configurations and deploys them using a runtime engine with an adaptive dispatcher to dynamically assign operations during inference.
dac-2024-373.key_novelty: The key insight is that optimizing the GNN structure and deciding which operations run on the device versus the edge server should happen together in one unified search, not separately, and data transfers between devices should be treated as explicit operations that can be fused with other computations to reduce overhead.

dac-2024-369.method: The approach redesigns optical routers for mesh network layouts (grids of connected nodes) and exploits multi-resonance properties—the fact that microring resonators can naturally filter signals at multiple wavelengths instead of just one. This means each microring resonator can demultiplex (separate and select) signals on multiple wavelengths at once, rather than handling just one. An automated design method combines these improved microring resonators with standard optical routers to minimize power consumption and the total number of resonators needed.
dac-2024-369.key_novelty: The core idea is using microring resonators that can demultiplex (filter and separate) signals at multiple wavelengths at the same time, reducing both the number of resonators needed and insertion loss (power lost as signals travel through).

dac-2024-366.method: MTVR has a computing core that efficiently divides its processing power to run multiple different types of tasks (like audio and video processing) in parallel on VR wearables. It saves power through three techniques: an early exit detector that stops processing invalid inputs; fine-grained value skipping at the multiplier and adder level (skipping arithmetic when operands won't affect the result); and a hybrid RRAM-SRAM memory that does computations right where data is stored (compute-in-memory), reducing expensive external memory accesses.
dac-2024-366.key_novelty: The core idea pairs approximation shortcuts (early exit and value skipping) with a hybrid RRAM-SRAM memory design that performs calculations where data is stored (compute-in-memory), enabling multiple task types to run simultaneously on battery devices with minimal power consumption.

dac-2024-361.method: DH-TRNG generates random numbers using multiple sources (each based on unpredictable electrical noise) built into an FPGA (programmable hardware), and switches between them during operation—at each moment choosing whichever is currently generating numbers fastest. This dynamic switching allows the design to achieve higher throughput while using less hardware area and power than existing approaches. The system is implemented on Xilinx Virtex-6 and Artix-7 FPGAs and produces output that passes the NIST and AIS-31 randomness tests without requiring post-processing.
dac-2024-361.key_novelty: The dynamic hybrid architecture switches between multiple noise-based sources to achieve high throughput with minimal area overhead (8 slices) and low power consumption across different FPGA platforms.

dac-2024-372.method: CAMPER is a hardware accelerator using Content Addressable Memory (memory that can search its contents directly rather than by address), with a custom cell design called RC-13T that performs distance comparisons—checking how far apart 3D points are—directly inside the memory itself. It uses a spatial approximation search method based on Chebyshev distance (a geometric way to measure distance between points in 3D space) to reduce the amount of computation needed while keeping the results accurate. This design efficiently handles large LiDAR point cloud datasets with the flexibility to scale to different dataset sizes.
dac-2024-372.key_novelty: This work first uses Content Addressable Memory for 3D point cloud range search by performing distance comparisons directly in memory instead of in a separate processor.

dac-2024-374.method: DNN-Defender protects quantized DNNs (deep neural networks where weights use compressed storage) against RowHammer attacks (which flip specific bits in DRAM) by shuffling where weights are stored in memory and prioritizing stronger protection for critical weights. Because attackers can't predict current locations, their attempts to flip specific bits become random. This turns precise, targeted attacks into random errors that neural networks naturally tolerate much better.
dac-2024-374.key_novelty: The first defense built directly into DRAM that focuses on protecting neural network weights (rather than stopping attackers) and is designed for quantized DNNs using in-memory shuffling.

dac-2024-378.method: The algorithm uses satisfiability solving—a technique that tries different circuit element arrangements to find ones satisfying all spacing rules—to reduce violations of multi-cell spacing constraints while moving elements as minimally as possible. It then uses a window-based approach to eliminate remaining violations by processing small local circuit regions. Finally, it applies integer linear programming (a mathematical optimization technique) to refine the placement.
dac-2024-378.key_novelty: The approach directly handles multi-cell spacing constraints using satisfiability solving, rather than converting them to simpler pair-wise constraints like previous methods, avoiding the quality loss that conversion causes.

dac-2024-377.method: ScaleFold identifies the specific bottlenecks where communication delays (time spent sending data between GPUs) and computational overhead (wasteful non-productive work) slow down distributed AlphaFold training, then applies targeted optimizations to just those locations. It reduces unnecessary data transfers between GPUs and cuts down on wasteful overhead computations. This approach successfully trained AlphaFold on 2080 NVIDIA H100 GPUs while keeping the GPUs actively working most of the time.
dac-2024-377.key_novelty: The core idea is to methodically identify the exact places where communication delays and computational overhead happen in distributed training, then fix just those specific bottlenecks instead of using generic optimizations.

hpca-2024-002.method: FlexNOC watches how an AI accelerator's workloads actually communicate at runtime—which parts need to talk to each other and how much data they're sending. Based on these patterns, it reconfigures the network-on-chip (the system connecting different processing components) by adjusting how data flows between them and how much data capacity each link gets. This avoids wasting energy on unused paths and bandwidth, all without changing the physical hardware.
hpca-2024-002.key_novelty: The network-on-chip automatically adjusts its routing and bandwidth allocation during runtime based on what the AI workload actually needs, instead of using one fixed network configuration for all workloads.

dac-2024-379.method: The system combines two specialized models to understand human movement on resource-limited devices. The first, Linear Recurrent Units (a method that efficiently tracks how movements change over time), processes pose sequences across thousands of frames. The second, Graph Attention Networks (a technique for understanding how body parts connect and influence each other), analyzes the skeleton structure to capture spatial relationships between joints. Together, they evaluate movement quality by handling both the temporal flow of motion and the spatial structure of the human body.
dac-2024-379.key_novelty: This work combines linear recurrent units (memory-efficient models for temporal sequences) and graph attention networks (models for spatial relationships) for the first time to evaluate human action quality on embedded systems.

dac-2024-376.method: Enclave startup normally must complete each initialization step before starting the next, creating a bottleneck. EnTurbo identifies which steps don't depend on each other and runs those independent steps at the same time using multiple threads. It maintains provable security (mathematical proof that running steps in parallel stays safe), so it gets faster startup without sacrificing safety.
dac-2024-376.key_novelty: Enclave startup is parallelized—multiple independent initialization steps run at the same time instead of one after another—through provable security.

dac-2024-367.method: The approach uses counterexample-guided learning (starting with a guess, finding failures, and improving based on those failures) to create barrier certificates—mathematical proofs that systems stay within safe boundaries. It verifies these proofs using Sum-Of-Squares (SOS) formulation, solving three Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) constraint problems (fast mathematical checks) instead of expensive SMT solver tools. This maintains formal safety guarantees while reducing computational cost.
dac-2024-367.key_novelty: The core idea is combining counterexample-guided learning (iteratively improving by finding failures) with Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) verification instead of expensive SMT solvers to verify barrier certificates for high-dimensional neural-network-controlled systems.

hpca-2024-001.method: The method removes 40% of the model's weights (the numerical parameters that make predictions) while maintaining accuracy, then stores the remaining weights in 8-bit format (using fewer bits per number). Together, these cuts reduce the memory footprint and computation needed to run the model.
hpca-2024-001.key_novelty: The core idea is combining pruning (removing unnecessary weights) with quantization (using fewer bits per number), optimized specifically for language models, to reach a 3.2x speedup in inference.

dac-2024-375.method: In semiconductor design, the time signals take to propagate varies due to manufacturing differences, creating timing distributions that often have multiple peaks or are unevenly shaped—patterns a single bell curve cannot capture. LVF2 replaces Liberty Variation Format's single Gaussian with two weighted skewed-normal distributions, which are asymmetric curves that can model multiple peaks independently. The approach maintains compatibility with existing systems and was tested on TSMC 22nm standard cells for both signal propagation delay and transition time.
dac-2024-375.key_novelty: Using two weighted skewed-normal distributions—asymmetric curves that can independently peak—instead of one Gaussian bell-curve to model timing variations in semiconductors.

dac-2024-380.method: PONO uses a mathematical constraint-solving technique called SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) to automatically design small, power-efficient circuit pieces. Engineers integrate these pieces into chip designs during the synthesis phase, using a library specifically optimized for low power consumption. The resulting designs reach the Pareto frontier of power-performance-area tradeoffs—where power, speed, and chip size are optimally balanced and cannot all be improved at once—outperforming traditional circuit optimization methods.
dac-2024-380.key_novelty: PONO is the first to apply constraint-solving mathematics (SMT) specifically to generate power-efficient circuit pieces that achieve the Pareto frontier, where power consumption, chip speed, and physical size are optimally balanced.

hpca-2024-004.method: Instead of moving data back and forth between memory and the processor (which wastes energy), this work places compute units directly in the memory. These units exploit sparsity—the presence of many zeros in the network weights and activations—by skipping operations that involve zeros, since multiplying by zero wastes computation. By computing where the data lives, it eliminates the energy-intensive data transfers that dominate inference with sparse neural networks.
hpca-2024-004.key_novelty: Processing units integrated into memory that skip zero-valued operations in sparse neural networks, reducing the energy-intensive data transfers between memory and processor.

hpca-2024-007.method: Gemini uses a layer-centric encoding (representing each neural network layer's position across chiplets individually, rather than encoding the entire system at once) to describe spatial layer mappings. It optimizes two aspects together: the physical hardware architecture and the assignment of DNN layers to that architecture, instead of designing hardware first and then mapping layers afterwards. A configurable template evaluates each candidate design by measuring manufacturing cost, inference performance, and energy consumption.
hpca-2024-007.key_novelty: Layer-centric encoding (describing each DNN layer's position across chiplets individually) enables optimizing hardware architecture and layer mapping at the same time, instead of optimizing them separately.

hpca-2024-009.method: The Loop Stream Detector is a CPU component that remembers which direction a branch went in the first iteration of a loop and keeps reusing that prediction for subsequent iterations without checking if it's correct. GADGETSPINNER exploits this by forcing the CPU to speculatively execute (run code before confirming it's the right path) beyond the loop's boundary using the outdated prediction. While executing the wrong code, illegal operations run and leak confidential information before the CPU realizes its prediction was wrong.
hpca-2024-009.key_novelty: This is the first attack exploiting how the Loop Stream Detector reuses branch predictions across loop iterations, causing the CPU to speculatively execute outside the loop's intended boundary and leak confidential data.

hpca-2024-003.method: Normally, attention requires multiple separate computation stages, with each stage writing its results to memory. This approach instead combines all these stages into a single GPU program (kernel) that keeps intermediate results in the GPU's fast cache. By avoiding memory writes, it reduces the data traffic between processor and memory, while careful mathematical design ensures results stay numerically accurate.
hpca-2024-003.key_novelty: Fusing attention stages into a single GPU program (kernel) keeps intermediate results in fast cache, avoiding memory writes and reducing data traffic.

hpca-2024-005.method: The method uses three techniques working together to speed up graph neural networks on GPUs. First, it uses graph reordering to organize the data so frequently accessed information sits close together in memory (improving data locality), which means data doesn't have to travel as far. Second, it uses edge caching—storing the frequently accessed connections between nodes in the GPU's fast cache memory—instead of fetching them repeatedly from slower main memory. Third, it uses adaptive thread mapping to dynamically assign work to GPU threads based on their current load, preventing some threads from becoming overloaded while others sit idle (balancing workload distribution).
hpca-2024-005.key_novelty: The key idea is combining graph reordering, edge caching, and adaptive thread mapping to solve the irregular memory access patterns that slow down graph neural networks on GPUs.

hpca-2024-010.method: PREFETCHX exploits the XPT prefetcher—a hidden component in Intel processors that predicts future data needs and speculatively loads data from memory to the cache. Because this prefetcher operates across multiple processor cores, an attacker on one core can measure tiny timing differences (how fast data loads) to determine what another process is accessing. The technique extracts sensitive information like RSA private keys, keystroke patterns, and network traffic by analyzing these timing signals, and can also encode secret messages between processes by controlling prefetcher activity.
hpca-2024-010.key_novelty: The critical discovery is that Intel's undocumented XPT prefetcher, shared between processor cores, can be spied on by attackers to leak information, and works around defenses designed to stop traditional cache-based attacks.

hpca-2024-016.method: DockerSSD installs a lightweight virtual operating system layer directly on SSDs using a special communication protocol and firmware. This layer lets standard Docker containers—pre-packaged, ready-to-run applications—execute on the storage device without requiring any changes to the original application code. The system automatically manages container startup and shutdown without altering the existing storage interfaces, while dedicated circuits in the hardware speed up the data flowing in and out of containers.
hpca-2024-016.key_novelty: DockerSSD enables standard Docker containers to run directly on commodity SSDs without vendor-specific modifications, making existing containerized applications immediately usable on storage hardware.

hpca-2024-006.method: The approach compresses data directly in lower-level caches (memory layers closest to the processor cores) using a custom scheme optimized for cache lines (the fixed-size data blocks that caches store). It analyzes where to place compression and decompression hardware in the memory hierarchy to minimize delays, handles common compression drawbacks, and uses prediction to adapt compression based on data patterns, resulting in a tiered design blueprint for enterprise processors.
hpca-2024-006.key_novelty: A compression approach that predicts and adapts to data patterns, designed for cache line blocks in enterprise processor hierarchies.

hpca-2024-008.method: gem5-MARVEL extends the gem5 simulator to let researchers deliberately introduce faults (bugs) into simulated computer systems to see how they handle failures. The tool is built modularly, so researchers can easily adjust what types of faults to inject and test different system configurations. It works across multiple processor instruction sets—x86, Arm, and RISC-V—and different types of specialized processors called accelerators, enabling analysis of entire complex systems in one simulation.
hpca-2024-008.key_novelty: It's the first tool to unite fault injection testing at the microarchitecture level (the level of processor design) across systems with multiple processor types and specialized accelerators.

hpca-2024-012.method: RiF adds a detection system built directly into the flash chip (called an on-die early-retry engine, or ODEAR) that tests whether a read succeeded before data leaves the chip. When the detector finds a failed read, it immediately adjusts the voltage threshold used to interpret the data and re-reads it, discarding the failed attempt. Because all detection and correction happens on the flash chip rather than involving an external controller, RiF eliminates the expensive overhead of transferring bad data.
hpca-2024-012.key_novelty: The key idea is moving read-error detection and correction from the external controller into the flash chip itself, eliminating the cost of transferring bad data between them.

hpca-2024-017.method: RELIEF schedules tasks based on laxity—how much spare time each task has before its deadline becomes critical. Rather than strictly meeting every deadline, it strategically delays tasks slightly when doing so lets data flow directly from one accelerator to another, bypassing the main memory bottleneck. This reduces memory congestion while keeping the system fair and guaranteeing all deadlines are ultimately met.
hpca-2024-017.key_novelty: The core idea is exploiting deadline laxity—the spare time before tasks must meet their deadlines—to route data directly between accelerators instead of through main memory, significantly reducing memory bottlenecks.

hpca-2024-011.method: AttAcc places processors directly inside memory chips themselves (processing-in-memory or PIM devices), with each handling its own chunk of KV matrices. When embedding vectors arrive during inference, they multiply against the nearby KV data right in memory, rather than copying those matrices back and forth between memory and processing units. Since KV matrices are written once but read many times, keeping them stationary eliminates the repeated bandwidth-intensive copying that bottlenecks GPUs.
hpca-2024-011.key_novelty: Embedding processors in memory to work with KV matrices locally, since they're written once but read many times.

hpca-2024-015.method: The paper builds a model that predicts how different types of processing chips will perform on sparse matrix multiplication, accounting for regions with different sparsity levels. It then partitions the matrix into regions and assigns each to the appropriate chip type: "Hot Workers" (optimized for heavy computation) handle dense regions, while "Cold Workers" (optimized for fast memory access) handle sparse regions. The system automatically routes each region based on its characteristics.
hpca-2024-015.key_novelty: The approach uses heterogeneous processing chips rather than identical ones, routing the dense, compute-intensive regions of a sparse matrix to computation-optimized chips and the sparse, memory-intensive regions to memory-optimized chips.

hpca-2024-013.method: WASP equips each GPU work unit (called a warp) with a dedicated memory buffer (register file queue) and automatic hardware-powered address calculation, enabling flexible data access such as streaming or gathering scattered data. It makes the GPU scheduler pipeline-aware by explicitly labeling which work units handle which processing stages, so the scheduler can intelligently coordinate them and allocate memory knowing where each work unit sits in the pipeline—enabling memory operations to overlap with computation. A compiler automatically translates standard GPU code into this specialized form, eliminating manual programming.
hpca-2024-013.key_novelty: WASP automatically specializes GPU work units by making the hardware and scheduler aware of which processing stages each is in, enabling efficient memory-compute overlap without manual programming or manual kernel design.

hpca-2024-018.method: PruneGNN removes entire dimensions from GNN models during training, reducing model size while maintaining sparse structure that GPUs can work with. Custom GPU code then executes these pruned models, specifically designed to parallelize across multiple matrix operations at once (SIMD-aware kernels: doing many calculations simultaneously). By matching the pruning strategy to how GPUs parallelize work, the approach achieves performance gains that wouldn't be possible with irregular or previous structured pruning methods.
hpca-2024-018.key_novelty: Custom GPU kernels that parallelize at the matrix-operation level allow dimension-pruned GNN models to run efficiently on vectorized GPUs, overcoming the performance loss that pruning normally causes.

hpca-2024-020.method: MOPED speeds up motion planning by checking for collisions in two stages rather than all at once, reducing both the number of checks needed and the cost of each check. It uses spatial information (where objects are positioned) to find nearby candidate paths efficiently without expensive full calculations. On the hardware side, it uses speculative execution (computing results for multiple paths simultaneously and keeping only the valid ones) to avoid delays from waiting for each step to complete before starting the next, and it uses multi-level caching (storing frequently accessed data closer to the processor) to reduce expensive memory fetches.
hpca-2024-020.key_novelty: The core insight is combining algorithm-hardware co-design—pairing two-stage collision filtering with speculative execution—to enable efficient sampling-based motion planning that works across different dimensional spaces.

hpca-2024-025.method: Smart-Infinity solves the storage bottleneck by placing parameter updates (the core math that changes model weights) on small accelerator chips sitting right next to the hard drive, eliminating traffic over the slow storage connection. It includes a data handler that moves information back and forth while reusing temporary storage buffers so memory doesn't grow. When using multiple accelerators, it compresses gradient data (numbers tracking parameter changes) on the GPU before sending to storage, then decompresses it on the accelerators—this cuts the traffic competing for the shared storage channel.
hpca-2024-025.key_novelty: Running parameter updates on accelerators located near storage (instead of on the GPU) eliminates the storage bandwidth bottleneck that blocks storage-offloaded LLM training.

hpca-2024-014.method: DMP predicts indirect memory accesses by watching the pattern of which array positions you access and what values those positions contain, then using those values as addresses for the next memory access. It detects four pattern types: one-to-one mappings, ranges, nested chains through multiple array layers, and branching paths. The system adjusts prefetch depth based on how many cache misses it prevents, using only 0.9 kilobytes of storage.
hpca-2024-014.key_novelty: Differential matching identifies patterns in indirect memory accesses by correlating which array positions are accessed with the values stored there, enabling detection of patterns nested across multiple array levels.

hpca-2024-021.method: The researchers create uPIMulator, a simulation tool that takes code for the commercial UPMEM-PIM processor and converts it to the low-level machine instructions the hardware runs, then simulates execution one clock cycle at a time. Using this tool, they measure how UPMEM performs on different workloads and identify its architectural limitations.
hpca-2024-021.key_novelty: uPIMulator is a cycle-by-cycle simulator of the commercial UPMEM-PIM processor that reveals architectural limitations to guide future PIM system design.

hpca-2024-022.method: LUTein uses look-up tables (precomputed hardware results) with the Radix-4 Modified Booth multiplication algorithm to keep power consumption low whether data is dense (full of values) or sparse (mostly zeros). Its processing elements share hardware resources, reducing data movement between different parts of the chip. The architecture arranges data flow in a systolic pattern (a pipeline where data moves in waves) and uses multiple buffers to let processing units reuse each other's data and recognize when sections of computation involve all zeros. A specialized instruction decoder minimizes how often instructions need to be fetched, preventing that from becoming a bottleneck.
hpca-2024-022.key_novelty: The core idea is combining look-up-table-based multiplication with the Radix-4 Modified Booth algorithm to maintain low power across all data sparsity ranges, enabling a single unified architecture for both dense and sparse computations.

hpca-2024-019.method: The system uses four coordinated techniques to make DRAM work as an effective cache layer between the GPU's fast local memory (HBM) and slower Storage-Class Memory. A bypass policy skips caching data the GPU rarely uses; a Configurable Tag Cache (CTC) reuses the GPU's L2 cache to quickly find what data is cached; and Aggregated Metadata-In-Last-column (AMIL) groups all cache tags into a single column—these three reduce memory traffic while keeping error-checking (ECC) intact. Storage-Class Memory throttling and dynamic mode switching then optimize bandwidth based on access patterns.
hpca-2024-019.key_novelty: Aggregated Metadata-In-Last-column (AMIL) groups all cache tags into a single DRAM column to minimize memory probes when finding cached data, while maintaining full error-checking protection.

hpca-2024-024.method: FIGNA builds dedicated hardware that uses the integer arithmetic circuits already in processors to multiply floating-point numbers by integer numbers and add them together—exactly what happens when language models have their weights compressed to integers (quantized). By mapping floating-point operations onto integer operations, the design produces bit-for-bit identical results to traditional floating-point circuits, while being faster. The hardware flexibly supports different combinations of weight and activation precision levels for various quantized language model workloads.
hpca-2024-024.key_novelty: Existing integer hardware in processors can perform FP-INT operations (multiplying a floating-point number by an integer) with exact numerical results, avoiding the approximations and model retraining that other methods require.

hpca-2024-026.method: PHAST is a memory dependency predictor (a circuit that guesses whether a load instruction will stall waiting for data from an earlier store) that figures out how much instruction history each load needs by finding the most recent store it could depend on. Rather than using a fixed history window for all loads, it customizes this window per-load to reduce storage costs. The team tested it using cycle-accurate simulation (tracking every processor clock cycle) on SPEC CPU 2017 benchmarks, building both a practical 14.5KB version and an unlimited-budget oracle predictor to measure how close the practical design gets to ideal performance.
hpca-2024-026.key_novelty: Each load determines its optimal history window by finding the most recent store it depends on, reducing storage while maintaining accuracy close to an ideal predictor.

hpca-2024-028.method: Agile-DRAM modifies standard DRAM with small architectural changes that enable three operating modes: maximum capacity, low-latency (faster access), and low-power consumption. The system automatically switches between modes while data centers are running, responding to changes in workload demand. This converts under-utilized memory capacity into either faster memory access or reduced power draw, depending on what the data center needs.
hpca-2024-028.key_novelty: Agile-DRAM reconfigures DRAM during runtime to trade off memory capacity against latency and power, allowing data centers to convert unused memory into either faster access or lower energy consumption.

hpca-2024-023.method: The system chains two neural network predictors (perceptrons) together. The first uses software memory addresses plus timing information to predict when data will come from main memory (off-chip). The second uses those predictions and hardware memory addresses to control which prefetches reach the L1 cache. This fits in just 7 kilobytes of silicon.
hpca-2024-023.key_novelty: First hardware design to combine off-chip prediction with L1 cache prefetch filtering through a two-stage neural network, where the first stage's predictions directly inform the second stage's filtering decisions.

hpca-2024-031.method: ASADI combines software and hardware to speed up sparse attention by exploiting diagonal patterns. The software redesigns the attention computation to use diagonal (DIA) format—arranging data along the natural diagonal lines that form in sparse attention, rather than in traditional rows and columns. The hardware provides a specialized accelerator that implements in-situ computing (performing calculations directly where data sits in memory) using many parallel processors to efficiently execute this diagonal-based computation.
hpca-2024-031.key_novelty: ASADI exploits the diagonal locality of sparse attention through DIA-format computation combined with specialized in-situ computing hardware.

hpca-2024-029.method: SPADE uses algorithm-hardware codesign—jointly designing the computation method and hardware together for efficiency. It has three parts: a dynamic vector pruning algorithm that identifies which groups of calculations can be skipped while maintaining detection accuracy, hardware that manages sparse data locations and transforms a standard 2D systolic array (a grid of parallel processing units) into a vector-sparse convolution accelerator, and a sparsity-aware dataflow optimization that schedules calculations through the hardware to maximize efficiency from skipped operations.
hpca-2024-029.key_novelty: SPADE's core idea is algorithm-hardware codesign that targets vector sparsity (skipping entire groups of related calculations) in pillar-based encoding, whereas existing accelerators only exploit element-wise sparsity (skipping individual elements).

hpca-2024-032.method: LibPreemptible creates a thread scheduler that runs inside your application rather than in the operating system kernel. It works through three techniques: the CPU delivers timed signals that interrupt threads so they can be rescheduled; your code supplies custom rules (adaptive scheduling policies) that decide which thread runs next based on current conditions; and the system adjusts these rules automatically. Since the hardware handles the timing, no changes to the OS kernel are needed.
hpca-2024-032.key_novelty: Using the CPU's built-in timed interrupt capability enables efficient preemptive scheduling (interrupting one thread to run another) entirely within applications, without any operating system modifications.

hpca-2024-033.method: Celeritas trains neural networks on graphs (GNNs) using storage as extended memory, codesigning the algorithm with the storage system. Its key technique is cross-layer computing: while processing one layer of the network, it computes what the next layer will need using data already in memory, eliminating the need to fetch from storage. The system also reorders how data loads to keep related embeddings (numerical node representations) and edges (connections) nearby, and uses two-level sampling with a partition algorithm to reduce unnecessary data movement.
hpca-2024-033.key_novelty: The core innovation is cross-layer computing—computing embeddings for future layers while processing the current layer using only in-memory data, eliminating storage I/O.

hpca-2024-027.method: Two algorithms improve AllReduce performance in mesh-based accelerators (systems of multiple chips connected via grid-like networks). RingBiOdd takes advantage of bidirectional links by creating two separate one-way rings, allowing both transmission directions to operate simultaneously and doubling throughput. Three Tree Overlap (TTO) builds three separate tree-shaped paths through the mesh (each optimized for the network's structure) and overlaps different computation stages across these trees, enabling parallel execution instead of sequential processing.
hpca-2024-027.key_novelty: Overlapping AllReduce computation stages across multiple separate tree paths (each shaped to the mesh structure) so more network links transmit simultaneously.

hpca-2024-030.method: The approach addresses invalid data created during 3D QLC's two-step programming process with three strategies. First, a fast re-programming scheme rewrites valid data surviving the first step more quickly, reducing latency. Second, a high-reliability scheme safely programs the partially-invalid wordlines in the second step without data loss. Third, an adaptive allocation strategy dynamically routes data between single-level (SLC) and quad-level (QLC) storage regions, avoiding situations where invalid programming would occur.
hpca-2024-030.key_novelty: Instead of treating invalid programming as a limitation to avoid, the work uses it as an opportunity to boost both performance and reliability of valid data in 3D QLC flash.

hpca-2024-035.method: Tessel uses a two-step approach to find execution schedules (plans for distributing computation across multiple devices). First, it constructs repetends—repeating patterns in efficient schedules that persist across different input data—to reduce search costs by avoiding redundant work. Second, it completes the schedule by exploring different operator placement strategies (ways of assigning operations to devices) and determining their execution order. This optimizes performance for both training and inference.
hpca-2024-035.key_novelty: Tessel discovers that efficient execution schedules contain repeating patterns (repetends) that appear regardless of input data, allowing it to dramatically reduce the schedule search space and computational cost.

hpca-2024-037.method: The tool uses policy gradient reinforcement learning—machine learning through trial and error—to compile code for CGRAs (specialized reconfigurable chips) by learning the entire process as one problem rather than separate steps. It employs reverse mapping, which analyzes hardware constraints backwards to determine which instructions can fit where and how to route them, making the learning problem simpler while exploring many routing options. This end-to-end approach learns the complete compilation pipeline without relying on hand-written rules.
hpca-2024-037.key_novelty: The core innovation is using reinforcement learning with reverse mapping to learn CGRA compilation end-to-end as a unified optimization problem, rather than decomposing it with separate hand-written rules.

hpca-2024-036.method: The authors reverse-engineer AMD's PSFP and SSBP (predictors that guess how memory loads will be handled and whether stores can bypass ordering rules) to map their internal structure. They then deliberately manipulate these predictors during transient execution (when the CPU speculatively executes code before confirming it should actually run) to leak secrets across security domains. They demonstrate two new attack variants: a Spectre-STL variant and a new Spectre-CTL attack. They validate that enabling Speculative Store Bypass Disable mitigates these vulnerabilities.
hpca-2024-036.key_novelty: AMD processors contain two previously unknown memory access predictors (PSFP and SSBP) that aren't isolated across security boundaries, enabling a new Spectre-CTL attack variant to steal secrets.

hpca-2024-034.method: Cepheus enables multicast (sending data to many destinations) over RoCE (Remote Direct Memory Access over Converged Ethernet, a protocol for ultra-fast data transfer between computer memories) by putting a translator inside the network switch. Multicast and RoCE fundamentally work differently—they structure data and process it in incompatible ways—so the switch translates between them in real-time. This translation runs on custom hardware (an FPGA) built into the Ethernet switch, allowing the switch to actively assist rather than just passively pass packets through.
hpca-2024-034.key_novelty: The key idea is using hardware assistance inside the network switch to make multicast and RoCE work together, rather than trying to fix the incompatibility at the endpoints.

hpca-2024-038.method: SPARK compresses neural network data by recognizing that quantized parameters (numbers stored at reduced precision) often have identical high-order bits (leftmost bits) that don't carry new information. It uses identity bits—special markers that flag which bits are redundant—to determine the shortest encoding length for each number, eliminating storage of those redundant bits. The scheme integrates with systolic array accelerators (specialized hardware for matrix multiplication) through a structured encoding format that keeps decoding simple and efficient.
hpca-2024-038.key_novelty: The core innovation is using identity bits to detect and skip redundant high-order bits in quantized values, enabling variable-length encoding that stores only essential bits.

hpca-2024-040.method: CHROME uses reinforcement learning (a technique where the system learns by trying approaches and getting feedback on results) to make cache decisions in real-time based on what the program is currently doing. It combines three techniques: removing old data to make space (cache replacement), skipping the cache entirely for some data (cache bypassing), and predicting and loading data that will likely be needed soon (prefetching). For each decision, the system receives a score based on whether it was correct and whether it improved overall system performance, allowing it to continuously improve.
hpca-2024-040.key_novelty: CHROME jointly optimizes cache replacement, bypassing, and prefetching through real-time learning that adapts to concurrent workloads, rather than optimizing each technique separately with fixed rules.

hpca-2024-048.method: Instead of having computation far from memory and moving data across slow interconnects, the system places compute hardware directly adjacent to large memory banks, connected via Compute eXpress Link (CXL), a much faster interconnect than traditional GPU connections like PCIe. The memory uses LPDDR5X technology—the efficient type found in smartphones—and provides 512GB of capacity with 1.1TB/s of bandwidth. A CXL-PNM controller and LLM inference accelerator manage this configuration, and a Python-compatible software layer makes it work transparently with existing code.
hpca-2024-048.key_novelty: Using cheap, efficient smartphone memory (LPDDR5X) connected directly to processing hardware via Compute eXpress Link (CXL) to eliminate the memory bottleneck that slows down large language model inference.

hpca-2024-045.method: The system observes actual communication patterns between GPUs and dynamically adjusts buffer sizes to match these patterns, rather than using fixed allocations. It also groups data transfers into batches and sends security metadata (message authentication codes and counters) once per batch instead of separately for each transfer. This two-part approach—responsive buffers combined with batched metadata—reduces the network bandwidth wasted on security overhead.
hpca-2024-045.key_novelty: The core idea is dynamically batching data transfers based on communication patterns and sending security metadata once per batch instead of separately, which spreads the verification overhead across multiple responses and reduces bandwidth waste.

hpca-2024-044.method: Usas enables sustainable training through three strategies: optimizing the training algorithms, co-designing the hardware and software together, and using morphable acceleration hardware (processors that dynamically reconfigure based on available power). The morphable accelerator changes its computing capacity based on real-time solar power—running at full strength in sunlight and scaling down when clouds block the sun—letting continuous training run entirely on renewable energy instead of drawing from the power grid.
hpca-2024-044.key_novelty: Morphable acceleration hardware (specialized processors that automatically change their capabilities based on solar power availability) enables edge servers to continuously update their AI models entirely on renewable energy.

hpca-2024-039.method: TinyTS breaks tensors (neural network data) into smaller pieces using a partitioning method that avoids the redundant recalculations simpler splitting approaches cause. It uses a memory planner that frees storage as soon as pieces aren't needed anymore, cutting peak memory use. It also removes metadata storage and runtime overhead from tracking these pieces. Together, this approach lets neural networks run on memory-limited microcontrollers without wasting computation.
hpca-2024-039.key_novelty: A compiler method that reduces memory by splitting tensors (neural network data) while eliminating the redundant computations that simpler splitting approaches incurred.

hpca-2024-041.method: Rapper speeds up data repair for blockchain storage by organizing ReRAM (a type of computer memory that stores data without needing power) into specific hardware structures—double bank, XRU, XGroup, and crossbar—that allow many calculations to run simultaneously. Instead of doing repair calculations one at a time, Rapper performs multiple calculations in parallel using these hardware structures. It also automatically adjusts how it schedules the repair work based on the size of data chunks being repaired.
hpca-2024-041.key_novelty: Rapper accelerates blockchain data repair by running the repair calculations directly in ReRAM (a type of computer memory that stores data without power), automatically adapting to different data chunk sizes.

hpca-2024-047.method: MIMDRAM breaks DRAM rows into smaller independent segments instead of processing them as one rigid block. This matters because different operations need different amounts of parallelism—some need MIMD (many instructions doing different things simultaneously) while others need SIMD (the same instruction on many different pieces of data)—so forcing full-row processing wastes resources. Because you can now control each segment independently, the hardware enables each one to handle whatever parallelism an operation actually needs. A compiler automates the work of figuring out and mapping parallelism, eliminating the manual juggling programmers had to do before.
hpca-2024-047.key_novelty: The core idea is to independently control smaller DRAM row segments instead of forcing everything into rigid full-row processing, so operations doing different work (MIMD—multiple different instructions running together) and operations copying one instruction across data (SIMD—the same instruction on multiple pieces of data) can each get exactly the parallelism they need.

hpca-2024-049.method: SmartDIMM embeds accelerators for encryption, decryption, and compression directly inside DRAM using Samsung's AxDIMM, a memory module with built-in computing capability. The accelerators operate directly on data in DRAM, eliminating the need to move data to a separate SmartNIC (network interface card) or CPU for processing. This prevents the frequent back-and-forth synchronization messages between the SmartNIC and CPU that create bottlenecks when handling high-speed network traffic.
hpca-2024-049.key_novelty: The core idea is embedding accelerators for encryption, decryption, and compression directly inside DRAM (using Samsung's AxDIMM) to eliminate costly SmartNIC-CPU synchronizations.

hpca-2024-050.method: Morphling avoids recalculating FFT (domain-transformation) results by reusing them across multiple TFHE operations, cutting redundant work by up to 83.3%. The design uses a 2D grid of parallel processors (a systolic array) and pipelined FFT, which overlaps computation stages so new data can start processing while old data is still finishing. A double-pointer method speeds up polynomial rotation without additional FFT operations, and specialized memory buffers with custom instructions automatically organize operations into efficient tiles and batches.
hpca-2024-050.key_novelty: The core idea is reusing FFT results across different TFHE operations instead of recalculating them, which reduces redundant work by up to 83.3%.

hpca-2024-052.method: SACHI repurposes the L1 cache (the small, fast memory built into every CPU) as a specialized digital solver for Ising problems—a class of optimization challenges. Rather than using analog converters (ADCs/DACs) to translate between analog and digital signals like previous accelerators, SACHI operates entirely digitally within the cache's existing SRAM memory, eliminating the unreliability and complexity those converters introduce. The system integrates directly with the CPU's instruction pipeline and uses data-reuse strategies and smart mapping techniques to solve optimization problems with high precision.
hpca-2024-052.key_novelty: SACHI is an all-digital Ising solver that repurposes the L1 cache already present in CPUs, avoiding the unreliable and complex analog converters that earlier Ising accelerators required.

hpca-2024-051.method: The paper develops algorithms (MINOS-B) supporting linearizable consistency—where all participants see identical data—with five different persistence guarantee types, tested on 5-node clusters. To improve performance, they move these algorithms to a SmartNIC (a specialized network card with computing power, version MINOS-O), which uses selective coherence hardware (maintaining data consistency only where needed), message batching (combining multiple messages before sending), and broadcast optimizations (speeding up messages sent to multiple recipients).
hpca-2024-051.key_novelty: The key idea is offloading consistency and persistency protocols to a SmartNIC (a specialized network card) with selective coherence hardware to improve performance.

hpca-2024-046.method: FlashGNN employs a node-wise training approach (processing the graph one node at a time) with coordinating logic built into the SSD firmware. The firmware orchestrates data retrieval to exploit flash memory's ability to read multiple chunks in parallel—simultaneously instead of sequentially—while maximizing data reuse: frequently-needed data stays on the fast flash storage rather than being repeatedly shuttled across the slow PCIe cable. A specialized algorithm schedules which data requests to handle first, and subgraphs are generated to align with the physical layout of data on flash chips.
hpca-2024-046.key_novelty: It places the accelerator inside the SSD's firmware to exploit flash memory's parallel reading capability and bypass the slow PCIe bottleneck.

hpca-2024-053.method: The system uses a small neural network (called a pilot model) that learns to predict which parts of the data the GPU will need next. When GPU memory gets full, this pilot model decides which data to move to slower storage. To keep the pilot model fast and lightweight, the system uses a new way to represent the neural network structure and groups similar predictions together instead of making individual predictions, enabling quick decisions with almost no slowdown while staying accurate.
hpca-2024-053.key_novelty: A learned neural network that predicts which data the GPU needs next, so the system can move other data to slower storage before memory runs out.

hpca-2024-054.method: Revet provides a threaded programming language—similar to what you'd write for CPUs or GPUs—that compiles down to run on vectorized reconfigurable dataflow accelerators (specialized chips designed to process data streams). The MLIR-based compiler translates your threaded code into operations on streaming tensors (arrays of data flowing through the hardware), with an execution model that efficiently maps threads to dataflow operations. This enables vectorization of data-dependent control flow—decisions based on actual data values—which older MapReduce-style languages could not support.
hpca-2024-054.key_novelty: The core idea is bringing the familiar threaded programming model (used for CPUs and GPUs) to vectorized reconfigurable dataflow accelerators by having a compiler and execution engine efficiently map threaded code to dataflow operations.

hpca-2024-043.method: MIRAGE reduces quantum circuit overhead on real hardware by using mirror gates—quantum gates that produce symmetric operations when outputs are reversed. A greedy algorithm selectively substitutes mirror gates at adjustable aggression levels, exploiting √iSWAP's efficient decomposition into native gates (the quantum operations the hardware can run) to simultaneously reduce SWAP routing (expensive operations between physically connected qubits) and improve gate decomposition. The method analyzes hardware fault rates to balance circuit execution speed (circuit depth) against decomposition accuracy.
hpca-2024-043.key_novelty: Mirror gates simultaneously reduce SWAP operations, improve gate decomposition, and minimize circuit depth—rather than optimizing for SWAP count alone.

hpca-2024-056.method: This method measures how an application performs on two smaller GPU setups—with 8 and 16 streaming multiprocessors (SMs, the cores that run the computations)—and records how often the fast cache memory fails to provide requested data (this pattern is called the miss rate curve). Using these patterns observed from small systems, it can predict how the application will perform on much larger GPU systems without needing to simulate them directly. This works because each application's pattern of cache misses is unique to how it accesses memory, so using application-specific patterns beats using generic prediction formulas that would be wrong for many apps.
hpca-2024-056.key_novelty: You can predict a large-scale GPU system's performance by measuring each application's unique cache-miss pattern on small systems, eliminating the need to simulate the actual large system.

hpca-2024-061.method: Users hide their quantum circuits by adding decoy control pulses (fake signals) during circuit preparation, then transmit the disguised circuit to the cloud quantum computer. Inside the quantum processor's cryogenic cooling system, specialized trusted hardware filters out the decoy pulses before they reach the qubits, leaving only the real circuit to execute. This prevents the cloud provider from inspecting the actual circuit design while the legitimate computation runs correctly. The approach requires minimal additions to existing quantum hardware.
hpca-2024-061.key_novelty: The first quantum computing system to protect proprietary circuits from malicious cloud providers by disguising them inside decoy control signals.

hpca-2024-062.method: The technique measures how fast individual flash pages run on a real SSD and finds that some are inherently faster or slower due to process variation (random manufacturing differences). It profiles each page's performance at runtime, then groups pages with similar speeds together into superpages. By bundling fast pages with fast pages and slow pages with slow pages, it avoids the performance penalty when mismatched speeds are combined.
hpca-2024-062.key_novelty: Profile flash pages for speed at runtime and group them by similar performance to form superpages, rather than using fixed groupings.

hpca-2024-059.method: The system spreads memory across different physical locations (disaggregation) connected by CXL cables, which are high-speed links between servers and memory pools. Instead of sending all data back to the main processor, computing happens right next to the spread-out memory, which cuts the data flowing through the bandwidth-limited CXL connection. A working prototype demonstrates this approach is practical.
hpca-2024-059.key_novelty: Running computation next to the disaggregated memory instead of sending all data across the bandwidth-limited CXL cable to the main processor.

hpca-2024-042.method: STELLAR trains neural networks using Few Spikes (FS) neurons and Few Spikes backpropagation (FSBP), which naturally produce minimal spike signals in short time windows, creating sparse data. The hardware exploits this sparsity using spatiotemporal Row Stationary (stRS) dataflow (data routing that reuses computations by grouping neurons to exploit spatial and temporal patterns), enabling efficient parallel processing. Window-based parallel processing and spatiotemporal encoding further boost energy efficiency and reduce processing latency.
hpca-2024-042.key_novelty: The key innovation is co-designing the algorithm and hardware to combine Few Spikes neurons (neurons that produce very few spike signals) with spatiotemporal Row Stationary dataflow (a routing method that exploits patterns across space and time) for energy efficiency and low latency.

hpca-2024-055.method: START protects against Rowhammer attacks by tracking frequently-accessed memory rows, but reuses space in the Last-Level Cache (the CPU's largest data cache) instead of requiring dedicated hardware. It works because real workloads only access a fraction of memory rows in the 64-millisecond refresh window, so there's usually spare cache space available. The system dynamically allocates storage by repurposing 1-way, 2-way, or 8-way cache sets based on how much memory activity is happening, using just 9.4% of cache capacity on average. For large-memory systems, START-M extends this using memory-mapped metadata.
hpca-2024-055.key_novelty: START repurposes the Last-Level Cache as demand-allocated storage for Rowhammer tracking metadata, eliminating dedicated hardware without sacrificing accurate protection.

hpca-2024-060.method: ECO-CHIP calculates the embodied carbon footprint of chiplet-based systems by accounting for chiplet scaling (how much larger or smaller individual chiplets are), chip yields and packaging yields (what fraction survive manufacturing), design complexity, and the extra environmental cost of advanced packaging. The tool integrates with existing chiplet simulators to jointly analyze carbon emissions alongside power, physical area, and cost, enabling comparison across different ways to split functions into separate chiplets and different generations of chip designs.
hpca-2024-060.key_novelty: It's the first tool to measure embodied carbon emissions (from design, manufacturing, and packaging) of chiplet-based systems and quantify how much carbon is saved by reusing chiplet designs across multiple products and chip generations.

hpca-2024-058.method: BitWave solves the problem of scattered sparse bits causing irregular memory access by reorganizing computation around bit columns instead of individual bits. The architecture combines three techniques—dynamic dataflow (flexible data routing through the hardware), skipping redundant computations, and weight compression—to reduce both computation and memory needs. After training, BitWave selectively flips individual weight bits to optimize for the hardware, avoiding performance loss without requiring model retraining.
hpca-2024-058.key_novelty: BitWave's core innovation is reorganizing sparse bit processing around columns instead of individual bits, which transforms irregular memory access patterns into regular, efficient ones.

hpca-2024-063.method: TALCO splits long genome sequences into smaller tiles (chunks processed separately) while keeping memory use constant on the accelerator, regardless of sequence length. The key insight is that different backtracking paths (the steps that retrace an alignment calculation) from different tiles always converge at the same boundary point, which guarantees optimal results even under banding constraints (a technique that limits the search area to speed up computation). This approach works with both classical alignment algorithms like X-Drop and adaptive algorithms like WFA-Adapt.
hpca-2024-063.key_novelty: TALCO uses the fact that backtracking paths converge at tile boundaries to achieve optimal alignments while maintaining constant memory—the first tiling technique that works with adaptive algorithms like WFA-Adapt.

hpca-2024-057.method: Guser generates power stressmarks (test code that maximizes a GPU's power consumption) by first measuring the power consumption of individual GPU instructions and grouping those with similar power behavior. It then identifies which adjustable parameters have the biggest impact on power. Finally, it uses Bayesian Optimization (a smart search technique that learns from each attempt to find better solutions) to automatically generate test code that pushes the target GPU to its maximum power consumption.
hpca-2024-057.key_novelty: Automatically generating GPU stressmarks through instruction-level power analysis and Bayesian Optimization to find maximum-power test code.

hpca-2024-065.method: LearnedFTL replaces address lookup tables with learned indexes—simple mathematical models that predict physical page locations from logical page numbers, eliminating the multiple flash reads that cause latency. It trains these models efficiently using an in-place-update technique that avoids extra storage overhead. To keep physical memory organized for garbage collection, it uses a virtual representation of physical page numbers that maintains contiguous blocks. A group-based allocation strategy integrates this prediction with garbage collection operations to minimize model training overhead.
hpca-2024-065.key_novelty: This is the first application of machine learning to page-level flash translation, using models to predict physical addresses from logical addresses and eliminate double reads.

hpca-2024-064.method: GRIT watches how your program accesses memory as it runs, then dynamically picks the best placement strategy for each page (a chunk of memory) at each moment. It chooses between three options: moving pages to where they're being used (on-touch migration), moving frequently-used pages to better locations (access counter-based migration), or keeping copies in multiple places (page duplication). The system adapts based on which approach actually performs best.
hpca-2024-064.key_novelty: GRIT dynamically selects the best memory placement strategy for each page and execution phase based on observed behavior, rather than using one strategy for everything.

hpca-2024-068.method: DMX combines hardware and software improvements to make data move efficiently between chains of specialized processors. It organizes data layout and routing to reduce unnecessary copying, speeds up the reformatting of data as it passes between accelerators, and improves communication between different specialized processors through optimized interconnect design.
hpca-2024-068.key_novelty: The core idea is treating data motion (communication, reformatting between accelerators, and movement overhead) as the main performance bottleneck in multi-accelerator systems rather than just speeding up the compute itself.

hpca-2024-069.method: LearnWD uses clustering to group memory data based on how prone each piece is to errors. For each write operation, it evaluates how aggressively the new data would overwrite existing data and how vulnerable the existing data is to damage, then predicts which approach will minimize write disturbance errors. The system integrates with various memory encoding schemes (methods of protecting data against errors), allowing error-reduction efforts to combine cumulatively.
hpca-2024-069.key_novelty: The innovation pairs machine learning classification of error-prone data with out-of-place updates (writing to fresh memory locations instead of overwriting), reducing write disturbance more than traditional in-place encoding approaches.

hpca-2024-067.method: It builds an abstract model of a branch predictor—the CPU component that predicts which instruction to execute next—capturing 19 possible states and 53 possible operations. Using symbolic execution (a technique that systematically explores all possible code paths), it tests all combinations of three sequential operations to find which ones leak secrets. Finally, it validates the discovered attacks against 8 secure branch predictor designs and 4 hardware-based protections against speculative execution (where the CPU runs ahead and checks later).
hpca-2024-067.key_novelty: An automated search using symbolic execution systematically explores all possible attack patterns on branch predictors, uncovering 89 attacks that had not been discovered before.

hpca-2024-071.method: Data Enclave treats data as the central focus rather than individual secure zones, keeping data alive and protected independently of any single enclave's lifetime. It uses encryption to isolate data and supports flexible permission controls for different users or programs. To avoid performance penalties, it optimizes verification by only checking the parts of the integrity tree (a cryptographic chain of checksums) that are actually needed, rather than recomputing everything. This lets different enclaves share and work with the same data without having to copy or reformat it.
hpca-2024-071.key_novelty: The core innovation is managing data as independently-secure objects that aren't tied to any single enclave's lifetime, so multiple enclaves can access and share the same data efficiently.

hpca-2024-073.method: The paper maps which memory rows are vulnerable to read disturbance (bitflips from repeated access to memory locations) across 144 real DDR4 chips from 11 manufacturing versions, showing that susceptibility varies significantly. Svärd uses these vulnerability maps to tune defenses row-by-row, applying stronger protection to vulnerable rows and lighter protection elsewhere, reducing performance and energy overhead without sacrificing effectiveness.
hpca-2024-073.key_novelty: Instead of defending all memory rows equally, adjust defense aggressiveness based on which rows are actually vulnerable to read disturbance, reducing overhead without sacrificing protection.

hpca-2024-074.method: The authors tested 256 real DDR4 DRAM chips to see if they could perform basic Boolean logic operations (NOT, NAND, NOR, AND, OR) by using the analog electrical properties of the memory chips in unconventional ways. They systematically measured how reliably each operation worked across different numbers of inputs (up to 16), different data patterns, and temperatures from 50 to 95°C.
hpca-2024-074.key_novelty: This work shows that regular, off-the-shelf DRAM chips can reliably perform all the basic Boolean operations (NOT, NAND, NOR) needed to build any logic circuit, with success rates above 94% and support for up to 16 inputs, enabling computation to run directly in memory.

hpca-2024-072.method: The attack observes the retirement unit—the part of the processor that finalizes instructions in order—to detect stalls (delays) when instructions are slow. Because this retirement unit is shared between two logical cores (lightweight threads sharing one CPU core), one program can watch the other program's retirement activity to infer what it's doing. The researchers create two covert channels by manipulating retirement stalls: one uses different instructions to encode messages, another uses the same instructions in different quantities. They extend this to launch a Spectre v1 attack (where the CPU guesses incorrectly which instruction to run next, enabling secret extraction) and develop a program identification attack that recognizes victim programs based on their unique retirement usage patterns.
hpca-2024-072.key_novelty: Exploiting the shared retirement unit between logical cores—the component that completes instructions in order—reveals a microarchitectural side-channel (information leakage through CPU internal mechanics) that enables covert communication and victim program identification.

hpca-2024-070.method: LightPool solves the storage imbalance problem by collecting unused NVMe storage from multiple cluster nodes into a shared pool, making capacity available where databases need it instead of sitting idle. It uses NVMe-oF (a protocol that lets computers access NVMe storage over a network at nearly the same speed as directly-attached storage) to provide fast remote access, avoiding the performance penalties and costs of cloud storage. Kubernetes integration lets the system automatically allocate storage to databases, with hot-migration and hot-upgrade capabilities to move data between nodes or replace hardware without stopping the database.
hpca-2024-070.key_novelty: It combines NVMe-oF protocol with Kubernetes to pool underutilized NVMe storage across a cluster, enabling database capacity sharing while maintaining high-speed remote access.

hpca-2024-078.method: POM makes FPGA programming more manageable by using MLIR, a framework with multiple abstraction levels—different intermediate representations (IR) that preserve information and enable optimization at the right level rather than a single lossy representation. It integrates the polyhedral model into MLIR, which is a mathematical technique for analyzing data dependencies in loops and rearranging them for hardware efficiency. Users specify designs with a domain-specific language (a specialized notation built for this task) to keep specifications concise, and an automatic engine explores optimization strategies to find the fastest configuration.
hpca-2024-078.key_novelty: This work combines the polyhedral model (a mathematical approach for analyzing and rearranging loops) with MLIR's multi-level system, enabling loop transformations that are systematically optimized for FPGAs using the most appropriate abstraction level.

hpca-2024-066.method: BeaconGNN uses a restructured graph format to enable out-of-order neighbor sampling (selecting neighbors in any sequence, not sequentially) and places processing engines at multiple levels of the flash storage system—die level (individual chips), channel level (data paths), and controller level. Flash-die-level samplers select neighbors while minimizing data transfers between die, channel-level command routers bypass the firmware layer, and a specialized accelerator on the device bus performs the graph learning calculations.
hpca-2024-066.key_novelty: The system restructures the graph to enable out-of-order neighbor sampling and distributes processing engines across multiple flash storage levels, which eliminates firmware bottlenecks and unleashes the storage's inherent parallelism.

hpca-2024-077.method: Ursa breaks down a system's overall performance target (SLA) into separate targets for each microservice tier, then uses mathematical formulas to calculate how much resources each tier needs. For each microservice, it explores different resource allocations and stops immediately if response time exceeds the tier's target, preventing prolonged performance violations. This approach bypasses the costly data collection that machine learning systems require.
hpca-2024-077.key_novelty: Ursa uses mathematical formulas instead of machine learning to instantly convert a system's overall performance promise (SLA) into per-service resource targets, avoiding expensive data collection and model training.

SageCare:_Runtime_Healing_of_S.method: SageCare watches how a running application accesses memory and identifies when the system is prefetching (preemptively fetching) data that won't be used. Instead of using the same prefetching strategy throughout execution, it adjusts its approach based on what it observes, reducing prefetch requests when it detects waste. This allows it to adapt as the application's memory demands change during different phases of execution.
SageCare:_Runtime_Healing_of_S.key_novelty: Rather than using fixed prefetching rules for the entire program, SageCare adjusts its strategy while running based on the memory access patterns it observes.

hpca-2024-080.method: The accelerator uses light-based computing cores connected in a grid, where each core performs vector multiplication through optical interference. Multiple cores connect via optical links that efficiently broadcast data between them. Unlike earlier photonic accelerators that only handled fixed values, this design dynamically adjusts to handle the full range of varying inputs that Transformers need.
hpca-2024-080.key_novelty: The first Transformer accelerator using photonic cores that can dynamically handle the varying calculations and full input ranges that Transformers require, instead of just fixed-value operations.

HyperCache:_Dynamic_Cache_Hier.method: HyperCache measures how a machine learning workload accesses memory while running (online profiling), then applies machine learning to predict the best configuration for the multi-level cache—the layered system of small, fast memory buffers positioned between the processor and main memory. Based on these predictions, the system automatically reshuffles how the cache is organized, continuously adjusting as performance measurements show whether the new arrangement helps or hurts.
HyperCache:_Dynamic_Cache_Hier.key_novelty: Machine learning automatically reshapes the multi-level cache organization at runtime based on profiling how the workload accesses memory.

hpca-2024-076.method: SpecFL predicts what results the parent tree nodes will produce, allowing child tree nodes to start training in parallel before the parents finish—running them on separate threads. When a prediction is wrong, the system quickly undoes that work to maintain accuracy. It uses a greedy strategy (pushing speculation as far as possible to maximize parallelism) to enable different tree layers to train concurrently.
hpca-2024-076.key_novelty: Using the speculative-execution technique from modern processors—guessing results in advance and running ahead—to let different layers of a tree train in parallel in federated learning instead of waiting sequentially.

hpca-2024-079.method: SegScope detects interrupts by observing data segment registers (CPU registers that control memory access permissions) on x86 processors. When interrupts occur, these registers change in ways that leave detectable traces in the CPU's behavior. Rather than using a timer to measure time, the technique watches for these register value changes to identify when interrupts happen, working across Intel and AMD CPUs where segment protection is standard.
hpca-2024-079.key_novelty: Using data segment registers (CPU memory-access control state) as a side-channel to detect interrupts without any timer mechanism.

hpca-2024-075.method: The method uses eDRAM (a high-density memory with lower power leakage than SRAM, though it needs periodic refreshing) as the primary on-chip memory for training data. The neural networks themselves are designed using reversible architectures—computations where intermediate values can be recomputed rather than stored—so data doesn't need to be kept long-term. A system called CAMEL coordinates this eDRAM memory with optimized data flow to minimize memory footprint and traffic to the slower off-chip DRAM, and the shortened data lifetime also reduces refresh operations.
hpca-2024-075.key_novelty: The key innovation is designing reversible neural networks that keep training data in eDRAM for minimal time, which eliminates the expensive refresh cycles that normally drain power.

Wavelength:_Optical_Interconne.method: The system sends multiple data streams down a single optical fiber by encoding each one at a different color of light (wavelength-division multiplexing). Because the different colors don't interfere with each other, they can all travel simultaneously on the same fiber, multiplying the amount of data that can flow through it. Instead of traditional copper electrical connections, the HPC cluster nodes are wired together with optical fibers and switches that route these colored light signals.
Wavelength:_Optical_Interconne.key_novelty: Using wavelength-division multiplexing (different colors of light traveling together through the same fiber), it creates an optical interconnect that achieves 10 times the data throughput per physical connection compared to traditional electrical interconnects.

Cascade:_Efficient_Multi-GPU_S.method: Cascade organizes multi-GPU synchronization using a hierarchical tree structure, where GPUs combine their gradient updates in layers rather than all at once, reducing total communication overhead. It automatically adjusts batch size (the number of training examples processed before synchronizing) to balance the time spent computing gradients against the time spent waiting for synchronization. This optimization of the gradient-averaging step speeds up data-parallel training across multiple GPUs.
Cascade:_Efficient_Multi-GPU_S.key_novelty: Combining a hierarchical layer structure for GPU synchronization with automatic batch size adjustment to balance computation time against synchronization overhead.

NeuralDRAM:_DRAM_Architecture_.method: NeuralDRAM embeds the ability to perform matrix multiplication (the fundamental math operation in neural networks) directly inside DRAM cells, so calculations happen right in memory. Normally, a system reads data from DRAM, moves it to a separate processor to calculate, then moves results back—creating a massive data traffic jam. By doing the math in place, NeuralDRAM eliminates that data movement and reduces the memory bandwidth (the speed limit for moving data) that neural network workloads need.
NeuralDRAM:_DRAM_Architecture_.key_novelty: The core innovation is performing matrix multiplication directly inside DRAM rather than shipping data to a separate processor.

SmartBuffer:_Intelligent_Data_.method: SmartBuffer predicts what data a program will need next, then proactively moves that data into appropriate cache levels before it's requested. This predictive prefetching works especially well for irregular, unpredictable access patterns—the exact cases where traditional prefetchers (which assume data is always fetched sequentially) cause many cache misses.
SmartBuffer:_Intelligent_Data_.key_novelty: SmartBuffer uses prediction of irregular access patterns to proactively orchestrate data movement across the entire memory hierarchy.

QuantumShift:_Low-Precision_Ar.method: QuantumShift uses lower-precision numbers—fewer bits of accuracy—in the classical computing steps that prepare data for and process results from quantum processors. It applies mathematical techniques to ensure the hybrid quantum-classical algorithm still converges correctly despite this reduced precision. By reducing the classical computational burden (the main performance bottleneck in near-term quantum systems), it speeds up overall execution while maintaining algorithm correctness.
QuantumShift:_Low-Precision_Ar.key_novelty: QuantumShift applies low-precision arithmetic (using fewer bits per number) to quantum-classical hybrid systems, achieving significant speedup in the classical overhead while mathematically guaranteeing correct results.

SpecRAN:_Speculative_Execution.method: SpecRAN improves speculative execution—where a processor guesses which instructions come next at decision points (branches) and starts running them before confirming the guess is right. Instead of conventional branch predictors, it uses machine learning models running on reconfigurable FPGA accelerators (custom hardware chips that can be reprogrammed while operating) to predict which path the code will take much more accurately. With better predictions, the processor executes more instructions in parallel without hitting dead ends from wrong guesses. The FPGA dynamically adjusts how it works based on real-time patterns, keeping instruction flow optimized.
SpecRAN:_Speculative_Execution.key_novelty: Machine learning on reconfigurable FPGA accelerators accurately predicts program branches, enabling processors to speculatively execute multiple instructions in parallel without wasting cycles on mispredictions.

PowerScope:_Fine-Grained_Power.method: PowerScope makes two decisions together: which core runs each task and how much power to give that core. The system watches what each task needs, picks the right core for it, and adjusts that core's voltage and frequency (a technique called DVFS that controls power draw and speed) to match.
