By coordinating these choices rather than making them separately, PowerScope saves power across heterogeneous processors—systems with different types of cores (like power-efficient and high-performance ones) mixed together.
PowerScope:_Fine-Grained_Power.key_novelty: PowerScope jointly optimizes power control (voltage and frequency scaling) and task scheduling for heterogeneous processors, rather than treating them as separate problems.

hpca-2024-081.method: MEGA tackles the problem with two complementary approaches. First, it uses degree-aware mixed-precision quantization (storing nodes with different bit precision based on their in-degree—how many connections feed into them) to compress graph data more efficiently than standard methods. Second, it redesigns the hardware with separate processing paths for the aggregation phase (gathering values from neighboring nodes) and the combination phase (merging them together). This separation enables an Adaptive-Package storage format to reduce space usage and Condense-Edge scheduling to reorder edge processing for more predictable memory access, reducing the scattered memory reads that sparse graphs normally cause.
hpca-2024-081.key_novelty: Degree-aware mixed-precision quantization: assigning different bit precision to each GNN node based on its in-degree (how many connections feed into it), instead of using the same precision for all nodes.

isca-2024-016.method: BlitzCoin decentralizes power management by giving each core and accelerator on the chip its own hardware logic to control its voltage and frequency (the power level and speed it runs at). Instead of waiting for commands from a central controller, each component adjusts itself based on what it's doing right now. These adjustments stay coordinated across the chip so total power consumption stays within the chip's budget, but each component gets instant response times.
isca-2024-016.key_novelty: Distributing power management across individual chip components instead of using a central controller allows 8-12× faster responses to power changes.

isca-2024-012.method: ReAIM puts computation directly inside memory using ReRAM (resistive memory that stores data by changing electrical resistance), avoiding the slow back-and-forth movement of data between computer and memory. Since real ReRAM devices don't work perfectly, ReAIM uses an adaptive algorithm that automatically selects the best solver method and settings by accounting for both software factors (which algorithm to use, how many spin flip steps to attempt) and hardware realities (how the ReRAM devices actually behave). This flexibility comes from a reconfigurable design that can efficiently map and schedule computations for different problems.
isca-2024-012.key_novelty: The innovation is an adaptive algorithm that automatically finds and applies the best solver method and settings for each problem by accounting for both software choices and the real-world imperfections of ReRAM hardware.

isca-2024-014.method: MetaLeak measures tiny timing differences in how secure processors access and update metadata—the bookkeeping information used to verify data hasn't been tampered with (integrity trees) and to prevent data replay attacks (counters). MetaLeak-T exploits timing patterns when multiple processor cores access the shared integrity tree, while MetaLeak-C does the same by watching counter state changes. These timing measurements leak secrets because an attacker on one core can observe how long security operations take on another core without explicitly sharing data with the victim.
isca-2024-014.key_novelty: Integrity trees and counters—metadata that secure processors use to protect data—can be systematically exploited as timing side channels to leak secrets to attackers.

isca-2024-011.method: Instead of fitting the switch on a single computer chip, this design uses the entire manufacturing wafer as the substrate (waferscale integration), bypassing individual chip size limits. It uses heterogeneous optimization—different components designed for different tasks—to reduce power by 30.8%-33.5%, doubles port count (radix) by splitting switch logic across subunits, and overcomes bandwidth limits by replacing serializer/deserializer (SerDes) components with area-based and optical I/O. Fast buffers with custom routing keep latency low.
isca-2024-011.key_novelty: Waferscale integration—combining the entire manufacturing wafer into one substrate instead of separate chips—enables network switches with double the port count (radix) by managing bandwidth and power density trade-offs.

isca-2024-017.method: Mirage breaks high-precision training into multiple low-precision operations using Residue Number System (RNS), a numeral system where numbers are represented as remainders instead of standard digits. Each low-precision operation is implemented directly in analog photonic circuits, which are naturally efficient at these calculations. The results are then combined back together using RNS to produce the high-precision training result, giving the accuracy of RNS with the energy efficiency of photonics.
isca-2024-017.key_novelty: Applying Residue Number System (RNS—a method of representing numbers as remainders) to photonic tensor cores enables high-precision DNN training by performing multiple low-precision modular operations natively in the analog photonic domain.

isca-2024-010.method: Transformers normally use lots of memory during inference—the process of running them to generate text—because they store information about every word they process. This approach combines transformer attention (the part that identifies which inputs matter most) with structured state space models, a technique that compresses stored information into a small state that updates with each word rather than keeping everything around. Since this state stays small instead of growing with input length, memory consumption is reduced while the model remains accurate.
isca-2024-010.key_novelty: Combining transformer attention with structured state space models to reduce inference memory while preserving accuracy.

isca-2024-013.method: ElasticRec splits recommendation model serving into independent microservices (separate software components), where each component is allocated memory and computing resources based on how much it actually needs. Instead of treating all components the same, the system measures utility (how much benefit each component gets from additional resources) and gives more resources to the components where they help most. This modular design also allows the system to scale elastically—each component can grow or shrink independently when demand changes, rather than scaling the entire model at once.
isca-2024-013.key_novelty: Using independent microservices (separately managed components) with utility-based allocation (resources go to whichever parts benefit most) specifically for recommendation model serving.

isca-2024-015.method: The paper addresses a challenge in processing-in-memory chips that retain data when powered off: errors arise from both the memory substrate and from computation operations. It compares two strategies—self-checking (detecting errors through result verification) and homomorphic techniques (doing calculations directly on error-protected data)—and proposes solutions that can detect and correct any single bit error from either storage or computation, with analysis of performance, chip area, and error coverage across three different nonvolatile memory technologies.
isca-2024-015.key_novelty: Error correction for processing-in-memory that simultaneously handles storage errors and computation errors using self-checking (verifying results) and homomorphic encoding (computing on protected data).

isca-2024-018.method: APF uses a Parallel Fetch scheme to split the processor pipeline into two parallel sections that run simultaneously. One section handles regular instructions normally, while the second speculatively (tentatively) processes hard-to-predict branches by predicting their direction and pre-processing the fetch, decode, and partial rename steps for the instructions that might follow. This approach lets the processor efficiently use wide frontend bandwidth without the engineering complexity of a single monolithic (extremely wide) pipeline.
isca-2024-018.key_novelty: The core insight is using partial renaming—tracking only critical register mappings—on speculative alternate paths rather than fully renaming all speculatively-executed instructions, delivering better performance with lower hardware complexity.

isca-2024-023.method: Barre Chord batches virtual address translations (mapping program memory addresses to actual hardware locations) by grouping GPU threads that execute together—called coalescing groups. When threads in a group access nearby memory, the system translates just one address fully, then uses simple arithmetic to find where the others map, skipping expensive page table lookups (called page table walks). F-Barre extends this by sharing grouping information between chiplets within a multi-chip GPU and intelligently expanding groups when addresses are stored next to each other in memory.
isca-2024-023.key_novelty: Exploiting the natural tendency of GPU thread groups to access nearby memory locations together—a property called coalescing—to batch virtual address translations and eliminate redundant page table lookups.

isca-2024-019.method: The paper exploits a practical observation: in real programs, each memory address is typically followed by only a handful of other addresses. It builds a simplified model (called an abstraction) of memory addresses that captures this sparse pattern, then trains neural networks to predict which few addresses will likely be needed next. The method comes in two implementations: Twilight, which uses the full neural network, and T-LITE, a compressed version that generalizes to different program runs.
isca-2024-019.key_novelty: Because each memory address is usually followed by only a few others, an abstraction based on this sparse pattern makes neural prefetchers practical to deploy on actual hardware with significant improvements in speed and memory efficiency.

isca-2024-021.method: Cicero optimizes neural rendering on mobile GPUs by fixing two fundamental problems through software alone—without requiring hardware changes. It reduces algorithmic inefficiency by using radiance warping, a technique that reuses previously computed lighting information rather than recalculating it, cutting the neural network's workload. It eliminates architectural inefficiency through two strategies: reorganizing memory access patterns to eliminate irregular, scattered trips to main memory (DRAM), and arranging data in the GPU's fast on-chip cache (SRAM) to prevent bank conflicts where simultaneous requests collide. Together, these interconnected fixes address both the algorithmic work required and how the mobile GPU hardware handles that work.
isca-2024-021.key_novelty: The key insight is solving both algorithmic bottlenecks in neural rendering (excessive computation and scattered memory access) and architectural bottlenecks in mobile GPUs (SRAM conflicts) together through software optimization, rather than treating them as separate problems.

isca-2024-026.method: CHRYSALIS automatically designs hardware for autonomous devices by combining three elements: a model of energy harvesting and intermittent operation (when the device shuts down due to low power) plus accelerator control; a tool that searches for the best hardware designs within size, weight, and power constraints; and a system model showing how energy and processing choices affect each other. Unlike traditional approaches that optimize these separately, it treats energy efficiency and processing performance as linked challenges that must be solved together.
isca-2024-026.key_novelty: The core innovation is treating energy efficiency and processing performance as a single co-design problem rather than as two separate optimization challenges.

isca-2024-024.method: BLESS organizes search data using a coarse-fine block structure that groups related searches and stores their data close together in memory, allowing efficient access without random jumping. It adds a guaranteed search range update algorithm that reuses recently loaded data from fast cache instead of repeatedly accessing slower storage. Running multiple processor cores on high bandwidth memory, BLESS uses runtime scheduling and context switching to keep both processors and memory constantly active.
isca-2024-024.key_novelty: BLESS combines a coarse-fine block data structure with a guaranteed search range update algorithm to keep related DNA sequence search data close together in fast memory (spatial locality) and reuse recently fetched information (temporal locality).

isca-2024-029.method: Orojenesis predicts data movement between memory levels for tensor algorithms by accounting for buffer reuse (how intermediate results are held in temporary storage to avoid re-reading them) across different on-chip storage capacities. It generates ski-slope diagrams (visualizations showing how data movement decreases with more on-chip storage) and analyzes tensor operations including batched matrix multiplications, convolutions, and sequences of operations in large language models, accounting for operation fusion and producer-consumer reuse.
isca-2024-029.key_novelty: It computes attainable data movement bounds by accounting for buffer reuse within realistic on-chip storage capacities—visualized as ski-slope diagrams—rather than just using the loose mathematical minimum.

isca-2024-028.method: HAL adds a load balancer to the SNIC (a processor on the network interface card) that continuously monitors packet arrival rates and how efficiently the SNIC is working. When the SNIC reaches its efficiency limit at higher packet rates, HAL rate-limits packets to the SNIC and routes excess traffic to the host processor—a more powerful general-purpose CPU with better memory systems. The system was implemented using a commodity FPGA and NVIDIA BlueField-2 SNIC in a standard server and tested on 10 popular network functions.
isca-2024-028.key_novelty: HAL implements dynamic hardware-based load balancing in the SNIC that monitors real-time efficiency and routes network functions between the SNIC and host processor, enabling high energy efficiency across all packet rates.

isca-2024-030.method: Pre-gated MoE predicts which expert networks will be needed before processing, making expert selection predictable rather than dynamic. This lets the system transfer necessary experts from CPU storage to GPU memory in advance, rather than fetching them on-demand during computation. By coordinating algorithm design with hardware scheduling, Pre-gated MoE reduces both the total memory footprint and the latency of expert transfers.
isca-2024-030.key_novelty: Pre-gating predicts which experts will be needed before processing input, making expert selection predictable rather than dynamic—this avoids the latency cost of fetching experts on-demand.

isca-2024-020.method: sNPU uses three coordinated parts: NPU Guarder applies fine-grained access control at the NPU's boundary, precisely deciding which data and tasks can access the NPU rather than using all-or-nothing control. NPU Isolator protects internal NPU structures—the scratchpad (fast temporary memory) and NoC (Network-on-Chip, the on-chip communication pathways)—by blocking attacks that exploit these internal channels. NPU Monitor is a small, trusted software component that enforces security policies while keeping the security-critical code minimal.
isca-2024-020.key_novelty: It's the first comprehensive approach to identifying and blocking NPU-specific attacks on internal structures—the scratchpad and Network-on-Chip (the chip's communication network)—through coordinated hardware and software protections without runtime slowdown.

isca-2024-022.method: BlissCam reduces pixels 20x by using machine learning to select important pixels directly within the image sensor hardware. Custom circuitry added to the sensor's existing pixel readout chains performs this learned filtering at the hardware level. This cuts both sensor power consumption and data transmission to the host, lowering computation and memory bandwidth demands on the receiving computer.
isca-2024-022.key_novelty: The core idea is applying learned pixel selection (machine learning to pick important pixels) directly on the sensor hardware rather than the host computer.

isca-2024-032.method: Tetris uses Pauli strings (a mathematical representation of quantum operations) as an intermediate form to identify where two-qubit gates can be removed during circuit synthesis. The framework finds elimination opportunities that other compilers overlook, then applies a fast bridging approach to place the gates on physical qubits without adding significant overhead.
isca-2024-032.key_novelty: Using Pauli strings (a mathematical representation of quantum operations) as the intermediate form during circuit synthesis reveals two-qubit gate reductions that other compilers miss.

isca-2024-025.method: BitNN computes the distance between points one bit at a time (bit-serial computation) rather than computing the entire distance at once. The hardware uses dimension-wise point cloud encoding (organizing all x-coordinates together, all y-coordinates together, and so on) and point-wise data layout (grouping each point's three coordinates together) to enable adaptive precision processing, where the system adjusts how many bits it needs to compute based on the data. It employs an early termination mechanism: after computing just the first few bits of a distance, it estimates a lower bound on the final distance, and if that lower bound already exceeds the best distance found so far, it stops computing that distance entirely, eliminating unnecessary operations. The hardware accelerator exploits massive parallelism to run thousands of these bit-serial distance calculations simultaneously, improving computing efficiency.
isca-2024-025.key_novelty: Computing distance bit by bit instead of all at once enables early stopping and adaptive precision, which significantly reduces unnecessary computation.

isca-2024-027.method: MAD-Max is a performance modeling framework that analyzes real training of large AI models on clusters of GPUs spread across datacenters. It discovers a major efficiency problem: GPUs spend 14-32% of their time waiting idle for data to transfer between machines instead of doing computation. To address this, the framework optimizes how work is split across GPUs (parallelization strategies) and identifies ways to improve both hardware design and software design together to reduce these data-transfer delays.
isca-2024-027.key_novelty: MAD-Max jointly optimizes two things in distributed GPU training: how to split work across GPUs and how to design hardware and software together to minimize idle time from communication delays.

isca-2024-031.method: PrIDE tracks memory accesses using a first-in-first-out queue (a simple FIFO buffer), but makes random decisions about which rows to track and when to remove them, so these choices don't depend on an attacker's access pattern. This randomness prevents an attacker from gaming the tracker by accessing memory in a strategic sequence to avoid detection. The researchers developed a mathematical formula to calculate how long an attacker would need to break any given security threshold, and showed the design works alongside refresh-rate management to enable lower attack thresholds (400 accesses instead of 1.9K) with just 1.6% slowdown.
isca-2024-031.key_novelty: Making random decisions about which rows to track instead of using predictable rules prevents attackers from evading the tracker, providing proven security guarantees even with a small, low-cost buffer.

isca-2024-033.method: HammerBlade is a system with thousands of processor cores arranged in a grid, built using RISC-V (an open instruction set that defines how processors execute commands). The design was validated with a real chip—a 2,048-core version manufactured using 14/16nm process technology, which shrinks transistors to fit thousands of cores on a single chip. Researchers tested it against various workloads to measure performance across different types of computation and data movement.
isca-2024-033.key_novelty: A grid-arranged processor that simultaneously achieves three competing goals—scalability to many cores, programmability, and density—without forcing engineers to sacrifice any one for the others.

isca-2024-034.method: When `memcpy` is called, the system does not actually copy the data right away. Instead, it stores a note at the memory controller (the hardware that manages data flow between CPU and main memory) about what data should be copied. Later, when the CPU or cache tries to access that data, the memory controller intercepts the access and performs the copy at that moment. To implement this, the researchers added hardware extensions to the memory controller, introduced a new CPU instruction, and created a software wrapper that makes this deferred approach work exactly like a normal `memcpy` call.
isca-2024-034.key_novelty: Instead of copying data immediately when `memcpy` is called (causing CPU stalls), the memory controller defers the copy until the data is accessed, eliminating the main source of overhead.

isca-2024-035.method: Harpocrates generates test programs (random but constrained to valid CPU instructions) and iteratively improves them by simulating what would happen if the CPU had various manufacturing defects—such as defects from variability, aging, or electrical stress—and measuring which ones cause wrong results. It uses that simulation data to guide the next batch of test programs, repeating the cycle to maximize fault detection. The approach adapts to different instruction sets, CPU designs, and types of faults.
isca-2024-035.key_novelty: Predicting how CPU manufacturing defects would cause errors (via detailed hardware simulation) and using that feedback to improve test programs catches faults faster than methods without this feedback.

isca-2024-036.method: TCP has processing elements (basic compute units) that can combine into a single larger unit or operate independently, depending on the tensor shapes being processed. A circuit switch-based fetch network (a data-routing system similar to a telephone switch) enables data to be reused between different compute units, while input broadcast and buffers (temporary storage) maximize data reuse within individual units. The compiler automatically explores different configurations—adjusting tensor shapes, the order of operations, and hardware settings—to find the fastest combination for each workload.
isca-2024-036.key_novelty: The key innovation is a circuit switch-based fetch network (a flexible data-routing system, like a telephone switch) that enables compute units to reuse data from each other when processing tensor contractions (matrix-like operations on multi-dimensional arrays).

isca-2024-043.method: The authors built a mathematical framework to model how cache coherence protocols (the rules that keep data copies consistent across processors) interact with message queuing in the network. They created an algorithm that analyzes how protocol messages depend on each other—which messages must complete before others can start—to find the minimum number of virtual networks (separate communication channels) required to prevent deadlock. The algorithm also outputs the optimal assignment of each message type to a virtual network.
isca-2024-043.key_novelty: A formal algorithm that models protocol dependencies and network queueing behavior can determine the correct minimum virtual networks, whereas the conventional longest-chain rule cannot.

isca-2024-040.method: Cambricon-D uses sign-mask dataflow, loading only 1-bit values (whether inputs are positive or negative) instead of complete input numbers. This lets changes between timesteps (deltas) flow through the entire network without repeated bottlenecks from reloading full data—a key inefficiency in diffusion models, which recalculate the same network with only small input variations. For nonlinear operations like activation functions, only the sign is needed to correctly apply deltas to the original inputs, so the approach gains computational speed from differential computing (recalculating only differences between steps) while using far less memory bandwidth.
isca-2024-040.key_novelty: Using only 1-bit signs instead of complete input values enables changes to efficiently propagate through the entire network while drastically reducing memory access.

isca-2024-047.method: ReCXL performs embedding training (optimizing lookup tables for the recommendation model) directly inside CXL memory (a type of memory with limited bandwidth) instead of moving that data to the main processor. It combines two techniques: dependency-free prefetching (predicting and pre-loading what the processor will need before it's requested) and fine-grained update scheduling (timing when updates happen to prevent idle waiting). Together, these keep the processor busy and maximize the use of available bandwidth over the CXL connection.
isca-2024-047.key_novelty: By performing embedding training directly inside CXL memory rather than moving embeddings to the processor, the system eliminates the slow data transfers that normally limit performance.

isca-2024-041.method: PreSto uses specialized processing units (In-Storage Processing units or ISP units—hardware built into storage systems) to handle feature generation and normalization, which are the tasks that normally bottleneck CPUs in recommendation systems. Unlike CPUs that process features one-by-one, these ISP units process multiple features simultaneously through parallelism. The units preprocess raw data and feed it directly to GPUs for model training.
isca-2024-041.key_novelty: Offload recommendation preprocessing from CPU bottlenecks to In-Storage Processing units (ISP—specialized hardware built into storage).

isca-2024-048.method: Instead of copying terabytes of data over networks, this approach physically transports SSDs through low-pressure tubes using magnetic levitation (magnets that make the drives float frictionlessly). The SSDs travel at hundreds of meters per second through data centers, and once they arrive, applications access all the data locally at terabyte-per-second speeds without the network delays and energy costs of traditional copying.
isca-2024-048.key_novelty: Rather than copying data across networks, this approach physically transports the solid-state drives themselves through magnetic-levitation tubes, a solution that becomes viable because modern SSDs pack enormous amounts of data into a compact physical form.

isca-2024-037.method: DACAPO combines a specialized processor with an intelligent scheduling algorithm designed to work together. The processor can divide itself into independent sections that simultaneously run inference, labeling, and retraining, with each section using only the numeric precision required for its specific task. A scheduling algorithm decides how to allocate the processor's sections and manage tasks over time, making strategic tradeoffs between accuracy and power consumption to keep the system efficient on a battery-powered device.
isca-2024-037.key_novelty: The key innovation is a processor that divides itself into sections, adapts numeric precision for different tasks, and simultaneously runs inference, labeling, and model retraining on a local device with intelligent scheduling—combining all three continuous-learning operations together rather than on remote servers or sequentially.

isca-2024-045.method: RPP arranges computing engines in a circle that can be reconfigured for different tasks, with data flowing in a predictable stream instead of jumping around. It replaces complex routing systems with simpler linear switch networks and gasket memory (a specialized memory interface). To handle different types of data access efficiently, it layers the memory in a hierarchy and includes hardware features like concurrent kernel execution (running multiple programs simultaneously), optimized register splitting, and a mix of scalar (single-value) and vector (multi-value) processing. The system comes with a complete software stack—compiler, runtime, and code libraries—that lets programmers write code like they're using a GPU, even though the actual chip architecture is completely different.
isca-2024-045.key_novelty: It replaces traditional complex routing with a circular arrangement of compute engines using simple linear switches and specialized memory (gasket memory), while maintaining flexible data paths and memory reuse optimization.

isca-2024-042.method: Tender decomposes large matrices into smaller pieces and quantizes each with its own scale factor (a multiplier for converting to lower precision). To avoid expensive requantization—converting back to full precision and re-quantizing—when combining partial sums, the scale factors are chosen as powers of two. This works because multiplying by powers of two is just bit-shifting in computers, which costs almost nothing. The approach needs only minor hardware modifications.
isca-2024-042.key_novelty: Making scale factors powers of two apart in decomposed matrices to eliminate requantization when combining partial sums.

isca-2024-046.method: AVM-BTB temporarily expands the branch prediction buffer by borrowing storage space from two instruction caches—the Uop Cache (which stores decoded instructions) and the ICache (which stores raw program instructions)—when the processor is making many branch predictions. It continuously monitors how often predictions are wrong and how full the prediction buffer is getting, then returns the borrowed space when demand drops. To prevent this space-sharing from slowing down instruction fetching, the system uses prefetching (reading instructions ahead of time) to keep them flowing.
isca-2024-046.key_novelty: The key idea is virtualizing cache space (treating it as flexible rather than fixed) so the processor can dynamically borrow from instruction caches to expand branch prediction storage based on current program needs.

isca-2024-038.method: Perspective adds two mechanisms to the Linux kernel (tested using gem5 hardware simulation). Data Speculation Views (DSVs) enforce data ownership: they prevent the CPU from accessing data speculatively (guessing ahead) unless the current execution context (the user or task running) owns it. Instruction Speculation Views (ISVs) restrict which kernel functions the CPU can speculatively execute per execution context and block load instructions (memory fetch operations) from running speculatively in unauthorized functions.
isca-2024-038.key_novelty: Instruction Speculation Views enable fine-grained control (per execution context—per user or task) over which kernel functions the CPU can execute speculatively (guess what instructions to run), enabling swift patching of attack gadgets and reducing the passive attack surface (vulnerable execution paths attackers can exploit without injecting new code).

isca-2024-044.method: QuTracer runs multiple copies of the quantum circuit with each measuring a different subset of qubits instead of the whole system. It uses circuit cutting (breaking the circuit into independent pieces) and Pauli checks sandwiched around measurements (verification cross-checks for accuracy) to reduce crosstalk (interference between qubits). The cleaner individual measurements are then combined to reconstruct a more accurate overall result that corrects both gate errors and measurement errors.
isca-2024-044.key_novelty: It extends measurement subsetting to fix both gate and measurement errors by combining circuit cutting (breaking circuits into independent pieces) and Pauli checks (verification cross-checks).

isca-2024-050.method: The authors use specialized microscopes—scanning electron microscopes (SEM) to take extremely detailed pictures and focused ion beams (FIB) to carefully slice through chips—to look inside the sense amplifiers in actual DDR4 and DDR5 chips from three major vendors. They physically prepare samples, photograph the internal circuits at nanometer scales, and measure actual transistor sizes and layouts. The imaging revealed that real DRAM sense amplifiers use offset-cancellation designs (circuits that actively cancel out error signals) rather than the simpler designs researchers had assumed, and the transistors are sized differently than literature predictions.
isca-2024-050.key_novelty: They were the first to physically photograph the inside of real DRAM chips using electron microscopes and ion beams to reveal exactly how the sense amplifiers (the read circuits) are designed and built—details that manufacturers had kept secret.

isca-2024-049.method: MegIS splits the metagenomic analysis work between the SSD and the main computer: the SSD runs a lightweight hardware accelerator (a specialized computing unit) to search for matching DNA sequences in its own storage, while the main computer handles the final abundance calculations. The algorithm is designed around how SSDs actually work—it understands that SSDs read data efficiently in sequence and performs the expensive search inside the SSD to avoid moving raw data out. The system carefully maps data within the SSD and minimizes how much information flows between storage and the rest of the computer.
isca-2024-049.key_novelty: MegIS is the first metagenomic analysis system to run computations inside the SSD itself, avoiding the data movement bottleneck through hardware accelerators designed to work within storage hardware constraints.

isca-2024-039.method: When multiple computers coordinate a transaction (a series of operations that must all succeed or all fail together), most delay comes from software running on CPUs, even though network speeds have improved. HADES offloads transaction coordination to SmartNICs (network interface cards with built-in processors) using Bloom filters (compact data structures that quickly check data membership) to filter transaction requests directly in hardware rather than in software. This hybrid approach accelerates the slowest bottleneck—transaction filtering and coordination—while keeping software handling for flexibility.
isca-2024-039.key_novelty: HADES embeds Bloom filters in SmartNIC hardware as a core part of the protocol design, enabling transaction validation and coordination to happen at network speeds rather than in software.

isca-2024-055.method: DyLeCT uses adaptive address encoding: frequently-accessed pages (hot pages) get confined to specific memory locations where their addresses can be encoded in just 2 bits, while rarely-accessed pages (cold pages) keep full-length encodings and can be placed anywhere. A 128KB translation cache (a fast memory storing address-to-location mappings) filled mostly with these short entries covers the same 2GB address range as a traditional TLB (translation lookaside buffer) completely filled with huge page entries.
isca-2024-055.key_novelty: The core idea is that address translation can use much shorter encodings (2 bits) for pages accessed frequently by confining them to restricted memory locations, while rarely-accessed pages keep full-length translations and remain flexible in placement.

isca-2024-052.method: PID-Comm arranges the processing units inside a memory chip into a multi-dimensional grid structure. This layout enables flexible communication patterns by allowing data transfer along different grid directions. The framework defines eight standard communication patterns and provides optimized implementations for UPMEM DIMMs—commodity memory chips with built-in processors.
isca-2024-052.key_novelty: Arranging processing units in a multi-dimensional grid enables fast collective communication (coordinated data transfers) between them without requiring CPU involvement.

isca-2024-058.method: MECLA breaks large weight matrices (the parameters that control an LLM) into source sub-matrices plus derived sub-matrices created by scaling (multiplying) source sub-matrices by scalars (simple numbers), eliminating the need to work with the original full matrices. The accelerator hardware then reuses intermediate data by reorganizing matrices, changing how multiplication operations are grouped, and recycling partial results (sums computed before the final output), reducing memory access by 83.6% and computation by 72.2%.
isca-2024-058.key_novelty: Weight matrices become more parameter-efficient (storing fewer parameters) by being decomposed into source sub-matrices and derived sub-matrices created by scaling (multiplying source sub-matrices with scalars).

isca-2024-059.method: The Architecture-Independent Operation (AIO) abstraction represents the parallelizable work in an algorithm—computations that can run simultaneously on multiple data items—in a form that stays the same across different accelerator types (GPU, FPGA, ASIC, etc.). The AccMe tool predicts how fast code will run by estimating clock cycles for three components: computation, memory access, and kernel invocation overhead (the cost of launching the kernel). It accounts for compute-memory overlap (computation happening while data is fetched) and memory bandwidth constraints (the limit on how much data can flow from memory per cycle).
isca-2024-059.key_novelty: The Architecture-Independent Operation (AIO) identifies the parallelizable algorithm work (computations running simultaneously on multiple data items) that stays the same across different accelerator types (GPU, FPGA, ASIC).

isca-2024-056.method: Splitwise splits LLM inference across two machines, each optimized for its phase's hardware needs. A high-compute GPU handles the prompt phase—reading your input and beginning the response—which is very compute-intensive. A lower-power machine handles token generation—producing output sequentially—which is memory-intensive and needs fast memory access. Machines exchange request state via fast back-plane interconnects, enabling phase-specific optimization in a heterogeneous GPU cluster.
isca-2024-056.key_novelty: The insight that LLM inference's two phases have such different hardware requirements—computing the prompt versus generating tokens—that they can be efficiently split across specialized machines.

isca-2024-060.method: Native DRAM Cache (NDC) moves the cache lookup work — checking if requested data is in the cache and selecting where to find it — directly into DRAM hardware instead of separate circuits. It accomplishes this by repurposing transistors that DRAM already has for routine maintenance (precharge transistors) to run these lookups. This technique, called Caching-In-Memory, allows DRAM to work as a large, flexible cache with lower latency and energy consumption than traditional designs.
isca-2024-060.key_novelty: The core idea is to perform cache lookups (tag matching and way selection) directly within DRAM by reusing precharge transistors that are already built into the hardware.

isca-2024-053.method: The system predicts which instructions the CPU will need next and fetches them early to prevent delays—but instead of just checking if it guessed right, it measures how much computing time each prefetch actually saves. It learns what predictions work best for each application. It also reuses the instructions fetched during speculative wrong guesses if they happen to be useful later. All of this requires just 8 KB of storage and modest hardware changes.
isca-2024-053.key_novelty: Instead of judging whether a prefetch guessed the right instruction, it measures how much time it actually saves, then uses those utility measurements to improve predictions and recycle prefetches from wrong speculative paths that end up helpful.

isca-2024-062.method: COORD predicts collision outcomes by exploiting spatial locality—the fact that nearby robot positions tend to have similar collision results. It uses simple hashing to create lookup patterns and saturating counters (counters capped at a maximum value) to track which patterns lead to collisions. A hardware unit called COPU is integrated into collision detection accelerators to prefilter queries before detailed computation, skipping poses predicted to be safe and prioritizing likely collisions.
isca-2024-062.key_novelty: Exploiting spatial locality of robot poses with simple hashing and counters to predict collision outcomes and eliminate 25-41% of detection queries.

isca-2024-057.method: QUETZAL is a hardware-software system that couples an accelerator to the CPU's vector processor using scratchpad buffers (fast local memory) and specialized vector instructions to speed up the slow process of gathering scattered pieces of genome sequence data from memory. It combines custom hardware and software to reduce these memory delays, pack more computation into single instructions, and quickly rearrange data representations as needed.
isca-2024-057.key_novelty: QUETZAL solves scatter-gather memory bottlenecks in CPU vector processors by tightly coupling an accelerator with scratchpad buffers and specialized vector instructions that work for any genomics algorithm.

isca-2024-054.method: Flagger uses specialized hardware accelerators positioned close to where data lives—Data Processing Units (DPUs) in the network and Computational Storage Drives (CSDs) inside storage. These accelerators handle the expensive encryption computations directly at their locations instead of sending encrypted data back to the CPU. Flagger-Runtime software coordinates these accelerators and enables them to exchange data directly with each other, reducing unnecessary data movement through the central processor that was creating bottlenecks.
isca-2024-054.key_novelty: Flagger distributes encryption computations to specialized accelerators in the network (DPU) and storage (CSD), which coordinate together as a unified system instead of overloading a single CPU.

isca-2024-051.method: The researchers use three measurement techniques to reverse-engineer DRAM: activate-induced bitflips (when repeated memory access causes data corruption), retention time tests (measuring how long data survives without refresh), and RowCopy (a row-copying technique). They first map DRAM's large-scale organization—subarray sizes, structure, and memory array tiles (MAT, the blocks that form the memory grid)—then examine how bitflips occur at the cell level, using 6F² cell geometry (a description of how cells are laid out in the memory) to identify patterns of accelerated corruption and reveal protection strategies.
isca-2024-051.key_novelty: Using three complementary measurement techniques to accurately reverse-engineer commercial DRAM and discover previously unknown vulnerabilities to bitflips (data corruption in memory systems) and the specific patterns that cause them to accelerate.

isca-2024-061.method: The method measures which errors happen together across multiple qubits in the quantum processor and explains why by connecting them to the physics of the superconducting hardware and how its operations work. It develops compiler strategies that reduce errors using dynamical decoupling (rapid pulses that counteract error-causing noise) and error compensation techniques. Crucially, the compiler adapts these strategies at each circuit layer by considering how qubits connect to each other, how they interfere (crosstalk), what instructions are running, and when qubits sit idle—then targets the strongest error sources in each region.
isca-2024-061.key_novelty: The core idea is a compiler strategy that adapts error suppression to match local conditions—the qubit arrangement, crosstalk (qubit interference), and what the circuit is doing—rather than applying the same suppression everywhere on the device.

isca-2024-070.method: LaSsynth turns the problem of designing lattice-surgery subroutines into a logic puzzle for a SAT solver—a tool that finds true/false assignments to variables that satisfy a set of logical constraints. It encodes the construction problem as one of these puzzles, where each variable and constraint represents something about the design (space, time, connectivity, and so on). Then it repeatedly asks the solver to find solutions while shrinking the allowed spacetime volume, forcing it to discover progressively more compact designs. This process exhaustively explores the design space and guarantees finding the most compact possible solution.
isca-2024-070.key_novelty: Formalizing lattice-surgery subroutine design as a satisfiability problem allows SAT solvers to exhaustively search for and prove they've found the most space- and time-efficient designs.

isca-2024-069.method: SmartOClock manages overclocking (running server hardware faster than rated speed) across a cloud data center by analyzing real workload patterns to predict how much extra power each server will need if overclocked. Based on these power predictions and each server's hardware characteristics, the system calculates a safe overclocking power budget for each server. Each server then enforces its own power limit locally, without requiring a central controller to monitor compliance.
isca-2024-069.key_novelty: SmartOClock predicts how much power different workloads need when overclocked, then distributes power budgets to individual servers that enforce their own limits instead of using a central controller.

isca-2024-068.method: EcoFaaS takes an overall deadline for an application (provided by the user) and breaks it into smaller deadlines for each function, chosen to minimize total energy use. For each time a function runs, it predicts the best processor speed by studying how long that function took in the past with similar inputs. The system groups processor cores into pools where cores in the same pool always run at the same speed, and it adjusts these pool sizes and speeds automatically as the workload changes.
isca-2024-068.key_novelty: This is the first system that manages energy specifically for serverless functions by splitting the overall deadline into per-function deadlines and dynamically adjusting processor core speeds based on predicting each function's actual execution time.

isca-2024-065.method: The system identifies conditional branches (if-then-else decision points) where the CPU's prediction is least confident. When found, it speculatively prefetches the micro-operations (individual CPU steps) from the opposite execution path into the μ-op cache, preparing for a potential misprediction. The approach uses small extra prediction circuits, requiring only 8.95-12.95 KB of additional storage.
isca-2024-065.key_novelty: Preemptively loading alternate code paths into the μ-op cache for branches the CPU struggles to predict, hedging against mispredictions.

isca-2024-063.method: NeuraChip separates sparse matrix multiplication into independent multiplication and addition stages using Gustavson's algorithm, allowing each stage to independently start work as soon as its input data is available. Rolling eviction clears cached data immediately after use, preventing memory bloat. Dynamic reseeding hash-based load balancing adapts task assignment across processors to maintain uniform utilization regardless of sparsity patterns.
isca-2024-063.key_novelty: By decoupling sparse matrix operations into independent stages, using rolling eviction to clear cached data, and applying hash-based load balancing, NeuraChip ensures even processor utilization regardless of how unevenly the data is distributed.

isca-2024-071.method: NDPBridge adds specialized hardware bridges within the DRAM memory structure to enable processing units near different banks to communicate and coordinate their workloads. It preserves existing DDR memory connections and protocols unchanged. The system distributes tasks across banks while being aware of how much data needs to move, and uses three techniques to reduce delays: hiding communication wait-time by doing other work simultaneously (latency hiding), routing traffic around congested paths (congestion avoidance), and reducing the amount of data that must transfer (traffic reduction).
isca-2024-071.key_novelty: NDPBridge embeds communication bridges in the DRAM hierarchy and pairs them with intelligent task scheduling to enable processing units near different banks to coordinate directly and balance computational load dynamically.

isca-2024-067.method: DS-GL modifies Ising machine hardware (a specialized chip for optimization) by changing how individual processors affect themselves from simple to complex rules, enabling it to process real numbers instead of just binary 0s and 1s. Rather than connecting every processor to every other one (which doesn't scale), the system arranges processors in a mesh grid with sparse connections that match the natural sparsity of real-world graphs. The system finds solutions by gradually cooling (annealing) multiple regions of the mesh simultaneously, mapping complex graph learning tasks onto this physical structure while maintaining accuracy.
isca-2024-067.key_novelty: This is the first system to solve graph learning by converting it into annealing (gradually cooling a system to find solutions) on CMOS hardware, using a mesh of sparsely-connected processors instead of connecting everything to everything, which enables real-valued data and practical scaling.

isca-2024-066.method: AMD's original vision was to integrate CPU and GPU components onto a single processor for extreme-scale computing. When Frontier was designed, manufacturing capabilities weren't ready for this approach, so AMD separated the CPU and GPU instead. Learning from Frontier, AMD developed advanced packaging technologies and refined strategies for connecting multiple small chips together as one system. The MI300A applies these innovations to achieve the original goal: a processor that integrates CPU and GPU through advanced packaging and chiplet interconnection, enabling extreme-scale scientific computing and AI.
isca-2024-066.key_novelty: AMD successfully integrated CPU and GPU components onto a single processor using advanced packaging and chiplet techniques (connecting multiple smaller chips together), enabling practical support for extreme-scale computing and AI applications.

isca-2024-064.method: Memento builds a cache for the register file (where GPUs store active thread data) using hardware that's already in the GPU. Before the program runs, a compiler uses profiling (running test cases to observe patterns) to estimate value reuse distances—how many instructions apart each value is used again. At runtime, the GPU uses these predictions to decide when to fetch values from the cache instead of the main register file, and continuously adapts this strategy based on what the program actually does.
isca-2024-064.key_novelty: Memento uses compiler-predicted value reuse distances to guide adaptive runtime decisions about which register values to cache, building the cache from existing hardware instead of adding new components.

isca-2024-076.method: NDSeARCH performs approximate nearest-neighbor search (finding similar items in large datasets) directly inside the SSD storage device, avoiding the slow process of copying data back and forth to main memory. It uses a custom SSD architecture called SEARSSD that exploits LUN-level parallelism (the independent parallel processing capabilities built into NAND flash memory chips). The system combines two-level scheduling (organizing which data stays in fast buffers and when to execute searches) with speculative searching (predicting which neighbors you'll need to check next) to keep computation flowing smoothly.
isca-2024-076.key_novelty: The SEARSSD architecture performs approximate nearest-neighbor search (finding similar items) directly inside the SSD using NAND flash's parallel processing capabilities, eliminating the bottleneck of shuffling data between storage and main memory.

isca-2024-073.method: The authors design three server configurations (GreenSKUs) using low-carbon components: energy-efficient CPUs (processors), reused DRAM (memory) connected via CXL (a new interconnect standard), and reused SSDs (storage drives). They develop GSF (GreenSKU Framework), a testing methodology to systematically measure whether these designs actually save carbon at production scale in Azure's data centers, accounting for data center overhead (like cooling and power distribution) and performance constraints.
isca-2024-073.key_novelty: The GreenSKU Framework measures the true carbon savings of server designs at production scale in real data centers while ensuring they meet performance and compatibility requirements.

isca-2024-072.method: FEATHER addresses the dataflow-switching overhead problem by using NEST, a spatial array (grid of parallel processing units), combined with BIRRD, a multi-stage reduction network. BIRRD performs a key optimization: as it reduces (combines) data from multiple sources, it simultaneously reorders the data layout in memory, eliminating the separate expensive reorganization step that normally blocks fast dataflow switching. The team designed this using Layoutloop, an extension of the Timeloop simulator that tests dataflows and data layouts together, and validated it end-to-end on a ZCU104 FPGA.
isca-2024-072.key_novelty: BIRRD, a multi-stage reduction network, implicitly reorders data layout as it reduces data values, eliminating the expensive separate reorganization that normally blocks dataflow switching.

isca-2024-078.method: FireAxe automatically divides a hardware design across multiple FPGA chips (reconfigurable hardware) using a compiler called FireRipper, with engineer guidance and feedback on how the pieces connect and simulation speed. It offers an accurate mode that preserves exact timing throughout the design, and a fast mode that runs quicker by reducing accuracy only where the FPGA pieces connect. Simulations run at 1.6 million cycles per second on local FPGAs and 1 million cycles per second on AWS F1 FPGAs, enabling flexible scaling from local to cloud resources.
isca-2024-078.key_novelty: Automatically dividing hardware designs across multiple FPGA chips while maintaining exact cycle-by-cycle timing and enabling flexible scaling from local to cloud resources.

isca-2024-077.method: Soter uses a mathematical model to identify which program configurations will work on spatial accelerators and filter out inefficient ones, creating a high-quality set of options. An automatic tuning system then explores only these valid configurations to find the best one. The mathematical model improves as the tuner explores, continuously refining which configurations are worth evaluating.
isca-2024-077.key_novelty: A mathematical model filters program configurations before an automatic tuner explores them, ensuring only valid, complete programs are evaluated.

isca-2024-079.method: Trapezoid starts with a 2D spatial array—a grid of processing units physically arranged on the chip—and adds specialized hardware for handling sparse matrices. For mildly sparse matrices, it uses an inner-product-based dataflow (organizing computation as dot products) paired with a multi-fiber intersection unit (hardware that processes multiple sparse data streams in parallel). For highly sparse matrices, it switches to a Gustavson-based dataflow (an algorithm optimized for sparse matrix multiplication) with a multi-level memory hierarchy (different-speed memory layers close and far from the processing cores). Crucially, all these specialized dataflows reuse the same underlying hardware rather than requiring separate chips, keeping the total size manageable.
isca-2024-079.key_novelty: Rather than building separate accelerators for dense, mildly sparse, and highly sparse matrices, Trapezoid is a single chip that efficiently handles all sparsity levels by switching between different computational patterns—all of which share the same underlying hardware.

isca-2024-075.method: Atomique compiles quantum circuits in three stages. First, it uses MAX k-Cut optimization on a gate frequency graph to assign logical qubits to physical atom arrays, minimizing the wasteful swap operations needed when qubits must interact across distances. Second, it fine-tunes the exact placement of each atom within an array to balance computational load and prevent exceeding hardware limits. Third, a router identifies quantum operations that can run simultaneously and schedules them together, reducing total execution time by strategically moving atoms between gates.
isca-2024-075.key_novelty: The core idea is to strategically move atoms during circuit execution—while maintaining their quantum coherence—to reduce long-range interaction overhead in reconfigurable neutral atom arrays.

isca-2024-074.method: Counterless encryption (calculating data-scrambling codes without position counters) stalls when data hasn't arrived from memory yet, causing about 9% slowdown on irregular workloads; counter mode avoids this stall but requires extra memory access overhead. Counter-light Encryption stores counters (position-tracking numbers) in fast on-chip storage, which allows cipher calculations (the scrambling process) to complete in parallel before the actual data arrives. This combines counter mode's speed with counterless encryption's memory efficiency.
isca-2024-074.key_novelty: On-chip counter storage enables pre-calculation of data-scrambling before data arrives, delivering counter mode's speed without counter mode's memory overhead.

isca-2024-085.method: UM-PIM works by letting CPU and PIM units share the same memory space while giving each what it needs: the CPU spreads data across multiple memory modules for faster parallel processing (called interleaving), while PIM keeps data in one place for efficient local processing (called non-interleaving). The system tracks which pages use which layout and includes special hardware on the memory modules that can reorganize data on the fly. Optimized interfaces let PIM units communicate directly with each other, avoiding delays from going through the CPU.
isca-2024-085.key_novelty: Allowing CPU and PIM to coexist in the same memory space—with CPU data spread for parallel speed and PIM data kept together for efficiency—eliminates the forced choice between CPU bandwidth and PIM performance.

isca-2024-082.method: When computers lose power, writes to persistent memory can complete out of order, breaking program recovery. This solution divides your entire software stack—applications, OS, and runtime—into "recoverable epochs" (safe pause-and-resume points). The compiler automatically saves the state of fast registers at these checkpoints, while simple hardware makes persisting data faster. By doing this, you eliminate expensive "persist barriers" (synchronization points that force waiting)—the compiler and hardware work together so crash recovery happens naturally without slowdown.
isca-2024-082.key_novelty: The compiler partitions the entire software stack into crash-safe checkpoints, requiring only minimal hardware support.

isca-2024-084.method: LLMCompass is a framework that automatically maps computations to hardware for optimal performance and includes a cost model (a calculation of how much physical chip space a design needs) to reason about trade-offs. Its predictions are highly accurate: 10.9% average error on individual operations and 4.1% error on full large language model inference. The framework can simulate complex systems like 4 NVIDIA A100 GPUs running GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters in just 16 minutes.
isca-2024-084.key_novelty: LLMCompass automatically determines the best way to run computations on different hardware, making evaluation fast and accurate enough to explore many cost-effective designs for large language model inference.

isca-2024-080.method: Because hyperscale datacenters waste CPU resources on common tasks, Intel embeds three specialized accelerators directly into its datacenter CPUs: one optimized for data movement, one for in-memory analytics, and one for workload distribution. To make this practical, these accelerators connect to the main CPU via an efficient on-chip pathway, and all three are controlled through a single unified programming interface so engineers don't need to learn three separate systems. The architecture also virtualizes the accelerators, allowing multiple applications to safely share them simultaneously.
isca-2024-080.key_novelty: The key innovation is building multiple accelerators into a single chip as a unified, virtualized ecosystem with shared programming abstractions, designed for production datacenter deployment.

micro-2024-002.method: NeoMem combines custom hardware and software to automatically tier data across local and remote memory connected by CXL. The hardware implements coherence protocols—rules that keep data consistent—specifically optimized for tiering, and includes fast pathways to move data between tiers. Software monitors which data is accessed frequently and guides the hardware to promote hot data to faster memory and demote cold data to slower memory. This design reduces the overhead of keeping data consistent compared to systems that weren't designed with tiering in mind.
micro-2024-002.key_novelty: The key idea is designing tiering policies that work with CXL's built-in ability to keep data consistent across memory tiers, rather than treating CXL like any other remote memory system.

micro-2024-000.method: Duplex is specialized hardware designed to run large language models by addressing three performance bottlenecks at once. It implements mixture of experts routing (directing each input through only the relevant neural network modules rather than all of them), grouped query attention (having multiple query heads share the same cached key-value information instead of storing separate copies), and continuous batching (processing multiple requests concurrently and adding new ones as old ones finish). These three mechanisms are built directly into the hardware circuit rather than simulated by software, eliminating the performance cost and complexity of trying to implement them in software.
micro-2024-000.key_novelty: Duplex co-optimizes mixture of experts routing, grouped query attention, and continuous batching directly in hardware instead of implementing them separately in software.

isca-2024-087.method: Bosehedral optimizes quantum programs by representing quantum operations with compact, finite matrices instead of infinite-dimensional ones. It then breaks down these compact representations into simpler operations the hardware can execute, maps the high-level logical operations to physical ones the hardware supports, and uses tunable probabilistic gate dropout—randomly removing operations in a controlled way—to reduce gate counts while maintaining accuracy.
isca-2024-087.key_novelty: Bosehedral enables bosonic quantum program optimization by replacing infinite-dimensional matrices with compact representations.

isca-2024-081.method: The system uses hybrid bonding 3D DRAM—densely stacked memory with very fast, high-volume data access—to quickly detect when neighboring data inputs are similar. When the system finds clusters of identical or nearly identical inputs, it reuses previously calculated results instead of recalculating them. The design analyzes the overhead added by this stacked memory approach and optimizes how data flows through the memory layers to make similarity detection efficient.
isca-2024-081.key_novelty: This design pairs hybrid bonding 3D DRAM—densely stacked memory for very fast access—with similarity detection in vision AI accelerators to spot and skip redundant calculations on clustered data.

isca-2024-086.method: ALISA fits language model inference on resource-limited systems by combining algorithm and system optimizations. The algorithm, Sparse Window Attention, focuses only on the most important previous tokens instead of all of them, reducing memory needs with negligible accuracy loss. The system uses dynamic token-level scheduling to decide in three phases for each token whether it's cheaper to cache or recompute its data, maximizing throughput on GPU-CPU systems by balancing memory and computation costs.
isca-2024-086.key_novelty: ALISA combines Sparse Window Attention (which focuses only on important tokens) with dynamic token-level scheduling (which decides per-token whether to cache or recompute), letting language models run efficiently on resource-constrained systems.

micro-2024-003.method: ICED embeds power-efficiency decisions throughout the system: the hardware design, the compiler (which generates optimized code for different power-speed tradeoffs), and the runtime (the system while code is running). The compiler pre-optimizes code for different voltage-frequency operating points. At runtime, the system monitors the workload and power budget, then automatically switches between optimized versions to reduce power when full performance isn't needed.
micro-2024-003.key_novelty: ICED is the first reconfigurable-hardware design that builds voltage and frequency adjustment into the hardware, compiler, and runtime as an integrated system.

micro-2024-005.method: Genie Cache repurposes the page-table structures (hardware tables that normally map virtual addresses to physical memory) to track which data is currently cached. Instead of making the CPU wait when a data request misses the cache, requests are queued and processed in parallel, letting other operations continue. The system decides which cached data to remove when space is needed using rules built into the page-table mechanism, managing capacity efficiently without slowing concurrent requests.
micro-2024-005.key_novelty: It enables non-blocking handling of cache misses by using page-table structures to track cache state, allowing multiple misses to be resolved at the same time instead of one after another.

micro-2024-001.method: BBS scans both weights and activations for sparsity—zero bits scattered throughout the data—at individual bit precision, finer than existing approaches. Hardware circuits mask and skip computations on those zero bits, routing processing only where bits are nonzero. By working at bit level in both data streams simultaneously, it exposes optimization opportunities that coarser methods miss while keeping hardware overhead low.
micro-2024-001.key_novelty: First to find and skip zero bits in both weights and activations at the same time using custom hardware.

isca-2024-083.method: DAM simulates large dataflow systems (ones with thousands of interconnected components) efficiently by replacing global synchronization bottlenecks with local coordination. It uses Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP—a framework where separate components communicate via message-passing) to specify both what each component does and how long each step takes. Components synchronize only with their direct neighbors rather than pausing the entire system, and the simulator exploits slack—intentional delays like data queues (FIFOs)—to let other parts keep running and multiply simulation parallelism.
isca-2024-083.key_novelty: CSP interfaces combined with point-to-point synchronization and slack exploitation enable efficient parallel simulation of thousand-component dataflow systems.

micro-2024-004.method: Multi-Issue Butterfly (MIB) is a processor with parallel stages arranged in a butterfly network (a specific data-routing topology), where each stage can dynamically switch what operation it performs. For sparse matrix factorization, it reorders instructions using an elimination tree (a structure derived from the matrix) to prevent data hazards (conflicts where one instruction waits for another's result). For matrix-vector multiplication, it prefetches data (loads values early) to avoid register file stalls (delays when fast memory can't supply intermediate values quickly enough). Multiple instructions execute simultaneously whenever there are no such hazards, maximizing throughput.
micro-2024-004.key_novelty: A butterfly-network processor that adapts instruction scheduling to sparse matrix structures, eliminating data and memory conflicts that would otherwise slow parallel execution.

micro-2024-008.method: Blenda splits fast stacked DRAM (memory chips built on top of the CPU) into two parts: one stores frequently-accessed data, and another acts as a cache that temporarily holds data and prevents unnecessary trips to slower main memory farther away. The system automatically rebalances these regions as the program's needs shift during execution, smoothly transitioning between configurations without restarting or losing any data.
micro-2024-008.key_novelty: Dynamically adjusting how stacked DRAM is split between memory and cache based on what the program needs at each moment, without data loss during the switch.

micro-2024-007.method: HyperTEE puts enclave management (the system that oversees and protects secure computing areas) onto hardware that's physically isolated from the main computer, so they can't communicate directly. This separation blocks attackers from using indirect spying techniques—measuring timing patterns or power consumption—to learn secrets about the management system. The design also improves how securely these protected areas communicate with each other, while still being compatible with existing systems.
micro-2024-007.key_novelty: Isolating enclave management on separate hardware prevents attackers from spying on it through timing and power-consumption patterns.

micro-2024-011.method: Trinity recognizes that both CKKS encryption (which supports arithmetic operations on encrypted data) and TFHE encryption (which supports logic operations on encrypted data), along with conversions between them, can all be built from three core operations: NTT (a fast number transform), FFT (fast Fourier transform), and MAC circuits. It creates a single hardware accelerator that runs all these operations simultaneously, rather than requiring separate chips for each encryption scheme. To maintain efficiency despite varying data sizes and workload types, Trinity employs dynamic workload scheduling (intelligently reassigning tasks moment-to-moment), adaptive component allocation (adjusting how much hardware handles each type of computation), and hardware reuse (sharing components across different operations).
micro-2024-011.key_novelty: Trinity is the first accelerator that supports CKKS arithmetic encryption, TFHE logic encryption, and conversions between them all on a single chip instead of requiring separate accelerators for each scheme.

micro-2024-006.method: This approach treats data movement as streams—patterns of how data flows through the processor. It analyzes which data chunks are used together repeatedly and how much data traffic they create, then places those chunks in the fastest memory closest to the processor. As the program runs, it continuously moves data between different memory layers, keeping frequently-needed data close and moving rarely-used data further away, based on the actual streaming patterns it observes.
micro-2024-006.key_novelty: It places data based on how it actually streams through the system, rather than using pre-determined storage decisions.

micro-2024-012.method: Cambricon-M applies Fibonacci coding (a constraint ensuring that whenever a bit is '1', its neighboring bits must be '0') to limit the range of voltages produced in the memory array's analog outputs. This narrower voltage range lets the system use simple, low-resolution analog-to-digital converters instead of expensive high-precision ones, dramatically cutting power consumption. The system further reduces overhead by skipping calculations that produce zero results and compressing data using bit-slice processing, which decreases memory and bandwidth demands while maintaining the energy benefits.
micro-2024-012.key_novelty: Fibonacci coding (a bit pattern constraint where every '1' is surrounded by '0's) shrinks the analog voltage range in the memory array, enabling lower-resolution analog-to-digital converters to replace energy-expensive high-precision ones.

micro-2024-013.method: The solution embeds processing capability directly into CXL memory controllers (the devices managing external memory expansion), enabling general-purpose computation without needing application-specific designs or wasting full CPU/GPU cores. Rather than using the slow PCIe/CXL.io communication links that add microseconds of delay, it introduces a faster direct connection between the host and the memory controller. This allows the system to offload small, fine-grained pieces of computation to the memory controller with minimal latency, processing data where it's stored rather than moving it back to the main processor.
micro-2024-013.key_novelty: Embedding general-purpose processing directly in CXL memory controllers with a low-latency communication link that replaces slower PCIe/CXL.io paths, making it practical to offload fine-grained computations to the memory source.

micro-2024-010.method: The framework lets code optimizations specify which instructions or code regions they want to run in parallel, even when static analysis can't prove they're independent (don't interfere). It creates two versions: an optimized version assuming independence, and a safe version that runs sequentially. At runtime, it checks whether the independence assumption actually holds—if yes, it runs the optimized version; if no, it runs the safe version instead. This works for any code, not just loops.
micro-2024-010.key_novelty: Program versioning with runtime dependency checks at instruction granularity, applicable to any code region rather than just loops.

micro-2024-015.method: RTL2MμPATH automatically discovers all the different execution paths each instruction can take in a processor (such as cache hits versus misses) by analyzing the hardware design, and formally verifies these paths. An extension called SYnthlc tracks information flow through the hardware to automatically create and verify leakage contracts—formal specifications of what information can leak through microarchitectural side channels like timing—and confirms these contracts match the actual hardware design.
micro-2024-015.key_novelty: Instructions with multiple execution paths—such as cache hits versus misses—are reliable indicators of microarchitectural side channels, enabling automated verification of hardware against leakage specifications.

micro-2024-016.method: PIFS-Rec solves a critical bottleneck in recommendation systems: embedding tables (large lookup tables that map items to their numerical representations) are enormous, and shipping all that data through the network to a CPU or GPU uses massive amounts of bandwidth and slows everything down. Instead, the system performs embedding lookups directly on the CXL fabric switch's downstream ports—the connections in the hardware fabric that links different system components. By doing this computation right where the data lives, much less data has to travel through the network, which reduces latency and frees up bandwidth.
micro-2024-016.key_novelty: Executing embedding lookups on the CXL fabric switch's downstream ports instead of moving the data to separate processors.

micro-2024-024.method: Not applicable—this is a welcome message from conference chairs, not a technical paper with a method.
micro-2024-024.key_novelty: Not applicable—this is a welcome message, not a technical contribution.

micro-2024-017.method: CamPU reduces memory traffic during image projection by reusing data from overlapping camera views and within individual images. It uses an out-of-order image projection unit (which processes images in an optimized order rather than strictly sequentially) with local cache memory to eliminate redundant memory reads and hide delays from accessing main memory. A specialized blending unit efficiently handles the overlapping regions where adjacent cameras' views meet. The design was validated through RTL-level circuit simulation and tested with a deep neural network processing platform.
micro-2024-017.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining out-of-order image projection with local cache memory and overlap-aware blending to reduce memory traffic in multi-camera processing hardware.

micro-2024-021.method: This editorial message reports on the MICRO 2024 conference's scope: it received 497 paper submissions, representing a 15% increase from prior years, and 113 papers were selected for publication. The evaluation involved 152 program committee members (senior researchers who coordinate the review) and 176 external reviewers (independent experts who assess submissions).
micro-2024-021.key_novelty: This is a conference announcement of participation statistics and scale, not a research paper with technical findings.

micro-2024-019.method: The researchers tested real CXL Type-2 devices using microbenchmarks—small programs that measure speed and data-transfer rates across three different memory access paths—and compared them against simulated versions and other technologies (emulated CXL Type-2, CXL Type-3, and PCIe). They then adapted two Linux memory-optimization features—zswap (which compresses data in RAM) and ksm (which merges duplicate data)—to use CXL for device-to-host communication and evaluated them on Redis to demonstrate real-world benefits.
micro-2024-019.key_novelty: CXL Type-2 devices eliminate most of the performance slowdown that memory-optimization features add—reducing overhead from 4.5-10.3 times down to nearly zero—by enabling direct, fast communication between the device and host instead of going through the CPU or older PCIe connections.

micro-2024-020.method: IMCompiler works like a compiler: it takes different big integer multiplication specifications, converts them to a standard intermediate form called a segmented integer multiplication algorithm (which breaks the problem into pieces that don't depend on any specific GPU), and then generates optimized code for each graphics processor. Optimizations for each GPU include spreading calculations across two dimensions of parallel processing cores, customizing cache memory usage, reordering data accesses, and deferring carry calculations (when digit sums overflow to the next digit).
micro-2024-020.key_novelty: The core innovation is using a computation diagram-based intermediate representation (a device-independent blueprint showing how multiplication operations connect and depend on each other) to separate high-level cryptographic parameters from GPU-specific optimizations, enabling one specification to automatically generate optimized code for different graphics processors.

micro-2024-018.method: The team analyzed how the GPU was performing and discovered that embedding kernels (code that retrieves and combines data) were leaving the GPU idle due to low occupancy (under-utilization). Compiler optimizations (automatic code improvements) increased occupancy, but the GPU still stalled while waiting for memory. They then added two complementary techniques: software prefetching (fetching data before it's needed) and L2 cache pinning (storing frequently-accessed data in a faster on-GPU cache). Together, these prevent memory delays from blocking the GPU.
