micro-2024-018.key_novelty: Software prefetching and L2 cache pinning work together to prevent the GPU from stalling while waiting for memory in embedding operations.

micro-2024-025.method: CARS repurposes segments of the GPU's register file (fast memory where computations store intermediate values) as software-controlled stacks for function calls. It exploits the fact that function prologues and epilogues (the setup and cleanup code at function boundaries) follow predictable patterns, enabling registers to be renamed using simple base-plus-offset addressing. The system analyzes the call graph (which functions call which others) and monitors runtime behavior to decide how many stacks to create, balancing stack capacity against the need for enough parallel computations to hide processing latencies.
micro-2024-025.key_novelty: The core idea is to dynamically allocate sections of the GPU's register file as stacks for function calls, sized to maintain high occupancy (keeping enough parallel computations running to hide processing delays).

micro-2024-014.method: Self-Managing DRAM (SMD) gives the DRAM chip itself control over maintenance operations—like refreshing memory cells and protecting against RowHammer attacks—instead of having the memory controller outside the chip do it. To make this work with only a tiny change to the interface, DRAM chips can reject requests to parts of themselves that are currently under maintenance, while still serving requests to other parts. This speeds things up by overlapping maintenance work in one region with data access in another region at the same time.
micro-2024-014.key_novelty: DRAM chips directly manage their own maintenance operations instead of having the memory controller do it, using only a minimal change to the DRAM interface.

micro-2024-009.method: The Hierarchical Search Unit takes the specialized circuitry that GPUs use for ray-tracing (following light paths through 3D graphics) and redesigns it for hierarchical search—the branching, tree-like exploration in recommendation systems and point cloud registration. Rather than rebuild from scratch, the authors reuse the existing datapath (circuits that process data) and add support for more flexible commands (instruction set) and new computations that search algorithms need. This keeps the hardware compatible with GPUs' general computing interface instead of limiting it to graphics APIs.
micro-2024-009.key_novelty: GPU ray-tracing hardware can be generalized to accelerate hierarchical search algorithms (used in recommendation systems and point cloud registration) by reusing its functional units (specialized processing components) with a more flexible datapath (the circuits and connections that route data).

micro-2024-023.method: The researchers measured latency (how long data takes to travel) and bandwidth (how much data moves per unit time) between GPU cores and memory partitions in real NVIDIA GPUs, testing multiple generations and finding variations up to 70% based on physical location. They analyzed how GPUs with multiple memory sections exhibit this non-uniform behavior. Finally, they showed how attackers could exploit these timing differences to steal information through side-channel attacks (measuring operation timing to infer secrets).
micro-2024-023.key_novelty: This is the first comprehensive measurement of non-uniform latency in real NVIDIA GPUs across generations and demonstrates that attackers can perform timing side-channel attacks (stealing secrets by measuring operation timing) by exploiting these latency differences.

micro-2024-028.method: Terminus adds a programmable specialized circuit—a dataflow engine—next to each processor core that can be configured to speed up different types of sparse data operations, like hash table and tree updates, by efficiently managing how data moves. Multiple cores can safely update the same sparse structure at the same time through address-range-based coordination: cores check which memory addresses they need to access, and if those ranges don't overlap, they proceed in parallel without conflicts. Very complex operations that don't fit this approach are delegated to the regular processor cores.
micro-2024-028.key_novelty: A programmable circuit that speeds up both reading and fine-grained updating of diverse sparse data structures while letting multiple cores work safely through memory-address coordination.

micro-2024-029.method: VGA adds specialized compute units (CCUs) designed for complex-number math, which FFT-based convolution requires. These units are built to fully use the bandwidth of fast on-chip SRAM memory by moving data efficiently between storage and computation. Instead of storing all parameters in fast memory beforehand, the hardware calculates them during computation, freeing up memory for data. The design is optimized for global convolution operators from state-space models like H3, achieving high throughput.
micro-2024-029.key_novelty: Specialized compute units that generate parameters on-the-fly free up fast memory for data movement in FFT-based convolution, eliminating memory bandwidth bottlenecks in state-space model inference.

micro-2024-034.method: LUCIE provides a standardized middle layer (an interposer) that sits between separate computer chips and handles their communication directly, rather than requiring custom designs. The interposer arranges chips in a 2D grid pattern (like a checkerboard) where each chip connects to its neighbors. A placement algorithm (using graph theory—a mathematical way of mapping connections) automatically figures out where each chip should sit for efficient communication. The framework supports different connection patterns, like grids (2D mesh) or hub-and-spoke arrangements (star topology), all without requiring new engineering for each design.
micro-2024-034.key_novelty: LUCIE is a reusable grid-based interposer system with automatic chip placement that lets you connect different chips together without designing each connection by hand.

micro-2024-022.method: The GPU interconnect's arbitration system decides which request sends data each cycle, and attackers can observe timing gaps when nodes don't need bandwidth—using these gaps to leak RSA key information and fingerprint kernel execution. Ghost arbitration prevents this by inserting "phantom requests" (fake requests that don't actually send data) into empty slots, keeping the arbitration schedule constant regardless of actual bandwidth demand. A weighted variant further obscures patterns by modulating phantom requests based on observed traffic, making it harder for attackers who've reverse-engineered the scheme to extract information.
micro-2024-022.key_novelty: Ghost arbitration masks contention timing from attackers using phantom requests, hiding side-channels while avoiding the severe performance penalties of strict time-division multiplexing.

micro-2024-026.method: DPT distributes page table entries (records that map virtual memory addresses to physical ones) throughout the entire physical memory instead of keeping them in a separate table, eliminating the need to resize the table. When a page table entry would occupy a memory location already holding data (an address collision), three techniques resolve it: Strided Open Addressing (SOA) probes for open space using fixed-size jumps, Collision-Aware Virtual Address Allocation (CVA) guides how data is initially placed to avoid collisions, and Collided Page Displacement (CPD) moves conflicting pages elsewhere in memory.
micro-2024-026.key_novelty: DPT stores page table entries across the entire physical memory as a distributed hash table, eliminating the need for separate table resizing and reducing collisions.

micro-2024-037.method: Beehive is a network processing system built on an FPGA (a programmable hardware chip). It breaks down network tasks into modular pieces called tiles that connect through a network-on-chip substrate—essentially a small internal network linking different processing units on the same chip. You can add new tiles or scale existing ones to match what your applications need, without disrupting other parts. It includes built-in diagnostic tools and safety checks to prevent deadlock (where components wait on each other forever), and it works seamlessly with standard Linux TCP and UDP applications.
micro-2024-037.key_novelty: Using modular tiles on a network-on-chip substrate enables flexible, adaptable network processing in hardware.

micro-2024-027.method: Hardware compression lets the system store data more densely in DRAM, but the operating system doesn't know how densely each page compresses. The authors add a specialized allocation system—similar to a memory management unit (MMU)—inside the memory controller that adjusts how much real DRAM each page gets based on its compressibility. They test this approach with an FPGA (a reconfigurable hardware chip) running multiple jobs simultaneously.
micro-2024-027.key_novelty: They introduce the first specialized allocation system in the memory controller that manages actual DRAM based on per-page compressibility, rather than using the operating system's generic memory allocation that doesn't account for compression.

micro-2024-033.method: TMiner is a combined software and hardware system designed to speed up graph pattern mining—the process of finding repeated patterns in networks of connected data points—by fixing the main bottleneck: redundant and inefficient memory access. It combines three techniques: splitting tasks so different processors handle non-overlapping sets of neighboring nodes to eliminate duplicate memory fetches; organizing shared data at compile time to keep related information close in memory; and watching which tasks have similar memory access patterns at runtime, then automatically moving and combining them to maximize data reuse. The system includes a DIMM-based near-memory architecture that exploits DRAM's internal bandwidth by placing compute and storage close together.
micro-2024-033.key_novelty: At runtime, the system identifies which tasks access memory in similar patterns and automatically moves or merges them to maximize data reuse.

micro-2024-036.method: Fusion-3D is a specialized computer chip that processes all three stages of converting images into 3D models (NeRF—Neural Radiance Fields). It uses dynamic scheduling that adapts to the workload, and hardware-aware sampling that strategically collects data based on what the hardware handles efficiently during the reconstruction stage. For training and rendering, a shared pipeline uses mixed-precision arithmetic—using lower precision (fewer digits) for fast operations and higher precision where accuracy matters—to run faster. For large scenes, multiple 28nm CMOS chips are connected using a three-level hierarchical tiling scheme that breaks the scene into nested tiles, minimizing communication between chips and balancing work across them.
micro-2024-036.key_novelty: The first end-to-end 3D reconstruction accelerator that handles the complete pipeline in specialized hardware, reconstructing 3D models in under 2 seconds and displaying them at 30+ frames per second, while using only the bandwidth of a USB port (0.625 GB/s).

micro-2024-038.method: ActiveN builds a neuromorphic computer out of many standard RISC-V processors, each designed to handle messages that trigger computations instantly when neural spikes arrive. Instead of storing all synaptic connections (the weights between neurons) on the chip itself, the system keeps them in external memory like DRAM or HBM, which costs less and holds more data. A memory controller watches for sparse data (when connections are mostly zero or unused) and sends only the useful pieces directly to each processor, cutting down the delay. The instruction set includes efficient operations for both whole-number and decimal math, so different brain-inspired algorithms can all run on the same hardware without needing custom circuits.
micro-2024-038.key_novelty: ActiveN achieves scalable, flexible neuromorphic computing by replacing custom circuits with standard RISC-V processors that detect sparse patterns and store synaptic connections in external memory instead of on-chip storage.

micro-2024-031.method: NeuroLobe redesigns a neuromorphic processor—specialized hardware that naturally processes spike signals from the brain—to efficiently handle brain-computer interface signal processing. It extends the processor's instruction set so programmers can deploy different algorithms flexibly. The design speeds up data movement between components, adds a synchronization unit to coordinate large numbers of spikes from electrode arrays, includes software for load balancing, and uses a multitask controller to run multiple algorithms simultaneously.
micro-2024-031.key_novelty: NeuroLobe adapts a neuromorphic processor's spike-handling ability for brain-computer interfaces, combining hardware and software design to enable flexible algorithm deployment.

micro-2024-032.method: PyPIM works as a three-level bridge from Python code to hardware: a Python library translates tensor operations into low-level processor instructions, specialized hardware with an instruction set performs processing-in-memory (calculations happening directly in memory rather than requiring data transfers), and a driver converts processor instructions into actual hardware operations. The system was evaluated using cycle-accurate simulation (running through the hardware design at every clock cycle) across diverse benchmarks to measure performance versus the theoretical maximum.
micro-2024-032.key_novelty: PyPIM closes the gap between Python programming and hardware design by creating an end-to-end pipeline connecting them for memristive processing-in-memory systems.

micro-2024-039.method: The system uses the same error-correction check bits to fix multiple types of memory faults: single-bit errors, double-bit errors, and ChipKill faults (where an entire memory chip fails). A cryptographic fingerprint called a MAC (message authentication code) of up to 60 bits is embedded with each 64-byte data block in the cache to verify the data hasn't been corrupted. When an error occurs, the system iteratively (repeatedly) tests the data against each supported fault pattern using these same check bits, attempting to locate and correct the error. This approach fits within DDR5 memory's standard 40-bit error-correction channel, avoiding the need for additional storage overhead.
micro-2024-039.key_novelty: The same check bits can correct single-bit, double-bit, and ChipKill faults rather than requiring separate check bits for each fault type.

micro-2024-030.method: PIM-MMU combines specialized hardware and coordinating software to speed up data transfers between main memory (DRAM) and PIM chips (memory chips with built-in processors). The system has three main parts: a dedicated hardware engine that copies data without using the CPU, a memory scheduler that coordinates accesses between DRAM and PIM, and an address-mapping function that accounts for differences between the two memory types. The software orchestrates these components to enable efficient transfers.
micro-2024-030.key_novelty: A hardware and software combination with a dedicated copy engine, optimized scheduler, and address mapping that accounts for differences between DRAM and PIM eliminates transfer bottlenecks in commercial PIM systems.

micro-2024-041.method: SegWU divides the instruction queue into segments based on partial tag bits—identifiers that track which previous results an instruction depends on. When instructions arrive, each is placed in a segment based on its tag bits. During wakeup, when checking if an instruction can execute, the system compares tags only within the matched segment rather than across the entire queue, eliminating unnecessary comparisons and cutting power consumption.
micro-2024-041.key_novelty: Divide the wakeup logic into segments based on partial tag bits so tag comparisons happen only within each segment instead of across the entire queue.

micro-2024-040.method: The researchers found four information leaks in GPU support hardware: changes in memory speed (DRAM frequency scaling), and activity levels of the video encoder (NVENC), video decoder (NVDEC), and JPEG processor (NVJPEG). When multiple programs share a GPU through MPS mode, an attacker can observe these leaks by monitoring the data flowing between the CPU and GPU (over PCI-e connections) or between multiple GPUs (over inter-GPU links). They demonstrated attacks using these observations to bypass NVIDIA's GPU MIG isolation system (which normally keeps different programs' work separate) without needing administrator access.
micro-2024-040.key_novelty: The first systematic way to exploit information leaks (side channels) in GPU support components—DRAM, NVENC, NVDEC, NVJPEG—to circumvent NVIDIA's GPU MIG isolation without requiring administrator access.

micro-2024-043.method: The authors study how hardware prefetchers (circuits that predict and load data before the processor needs it) conflict with GhostMinion, a secure cache system that only fetches data after instructions are confirmed safe to execute. They propose two microarchitectural fixes: a redundant traffic filter that stops duplicate cache requests (the same data being fetched twice), and a modified prefetcher that compensates for the delay caused by waiting until commit time to issue fetch requests, restoring timeliness (the ability to deliver data when needed).
micro-2024-043.key_novelty: Combining redundant traffic filtering with commit-time prefetch compensation to maintain prefetcher timeliness while defending against speculative execution attacks.

micro-2024-044.method: ScopeAdvice reads GPU programs written in CUDA and finds places where they're synchronizing too much. It spots three different types of over-synchronization by comparing what synchronization the code actually needs versus what it's currently doing. The tool flags global barrier calls (instructions making all GPU threads pause together) and suggests replacing them with scope-based synchronization (making only relevant threads pause), which runs faster.
micro-2024-044.key_novelty: The key idea is recognizing over-synchronization—GPU threads pausing unnecessarily—as a distinct, automatically detectable performance problem.

micro-2024-045.method: The paper uses a mathematical framework called Einsum cascades (notation for chaining tensor operations) to map out the landscape of attention algorithms and calculate the minimum on-chip buffer (processor memory) and bandwidth they require. FuseMax then implements attention on a spatial array—a 2D grid of processors—using new assignment strategies that keep every processor busy, independent of sequence length.
micro-2024-045.key_novelty: The core insight is using Einsum cascades (a formal way to notate chained tensor operations) to derive the absolute minimum on-chip buffer (processor memory) or bandwidth that any attention implementation would need.

micro-2024-047.method: SCAR finds practical scheduling solutions by using shortcuts (heuristics) rather than searching through the 10^56 impossible combinations possible on 6×6 chiplet grids. It coordinates different chiplets by having them pass data between each other in sequence (inter-chiplet pipelining), optimizing where each model's operations run. The scheduler was tested on ten multi-model workloads for datacenter and AR/VR scenarios.
micro-2024-047.key_novelty: It combines heterogeneous dataflow (different chiplets specializing in different operations) with inter-chiplet pipelining (data moving between chiplets in sequence) to adapt scheduling to any multi-model workload.

micro-2024-049.method: BABOL uses basic, reusable hardware building blocks that software can arrange in different ways to match each flash chip's specific needs. Instead of designing a new controller for each flash package, software reconfigures these same pieces to optimize for that package. The approach was tested on two FPGA implementations (field-programmable gate arrays—chips that can be reconfigured by software) with real commercial flash packages.
micro-2024-049.key_novelty: A flash controller that uses software to mix and match reusable hardware pieces, adapting to different packages instead of requiring a new custom design each time.

micro-2024-035.method: STAR monitors how many of the 16 sub-entries in each L3 TLB entry are actively being used at any moment. When an entry is under-utilized, STAR allows different GPU instances to share it, with each instance using separate sub-entries for its memory address translations. When usage becomes heavy, STAR reserves the entry for one instance to prevent slowdowns from conflicting access attempts. The system continuously adjusts between shared and exclusive modes based on workload patterns.
micro-2024-035.key_novelty: STAR dynamically decides whether to share each TLB entry among GPU instances or reserve it for one, based on how many of its 16 sub-entries are actively used.

micro-2024-046.method: CHATS allows conflicting transactions to read each other's uncommitted data instead of restarting, which normally wastes work. To prevent deadlocks (circular waits between transactions), it tracks which transaction depends on which and requires transactions to finalize in a controlled order that respects these dependencies. This dependency tracking uses less than 280 bytes of extra storage.
micro-2024-046.key_novelty: CHATS makes the requester-speculates policy (where transactions share uncommitted data) work in real commercial hardware by preventing deadlocks through controlled commit ordering.

micro-2024-042.method: AkitaRTM is an interactive web-based tool designed after studying what slows down computer architects in their work. It shows you what's happening in a simulator in real time and lets you control how it runs through a simple, easy-to-use interface. The tool was tested with two case studies (one actually found a simulator bug that got fixed) and a user study where computer architects confirmed it was helpful.
micro-2024-042.key_novelty: An interactive web-based tool that lets you watch and control computer architecture simulations in real time, revealing hidden execution so you can debug.

micro-2024-051.method: The FSDetect protocol extends standard cache coherence rules (specifically MESI, which keeps data consistent across processor caches) to detect harmful false sharing by counting how often different processors access the same cache block, all with negligible performance cost. FSLite extends FSDetect to automatically isolate falsely shared data on-the-fly, maintaining synchronization by updating the affected bytes back at the last-level cache when the isolation ends.
micro-2024-051.key_novelty: By extending standard cache coherence rules to track processor conflicts over cache blocks and automatically create isolated data copies, the system detects and fixes false sharing with minimal performance cost.

micro-2024-048.method: Avatar speeds up GPU memory requests by speculatively translating addresses (predicting which physical memory location each virtual address maps to) before the translation is official. It uses CAST (Contiguity-Aware Speculative Translation) to predict translations by monitoring which pages are adjacent in memory, allowing the GPU to fetch data immediately while the real translation happens in parallel. CAVA (In-Cache Validation) validates these predictions by storing page-mapping information in 32-byte sectors within 128-byte cache lines, enabling near-instantaneous verification at the sector level.
micro-2024-048.key_novelty: By validating speculative address translations through metadata embedded in cache sectors, Avatar lets GPUs fetch data and do address translation at the same time—without special hardware support.

micro-2024-052.method: The system uses composition of experts (deploying 150 separate expert models totaling 1 trillion parameters instead of one giant model) on the SambaNova SN40L Reconfigurable Dataflow Unit. The hardware uses streaming dataflow execution, where data continuously flows through operations without repeatedly loading from and storing to memory, combined with three memory levels: on-chip SRAM (fastest), on-package HBM (medium speed), and off-package DDR DRAM (slowest). Operations are fused together (combined into single steps) to increase the ratio of computation to memory access. Multiple units connect through a dedicated network for scaling across processors.
micro-2024-052.key_novelty: Combining composition of experts (splitting a model into 150 smaller expert models) with streaming dataflow hardware and three-tier memory (on-chip SRAM, on-package HBM, off-package DDR DRAM) solves the memory bottleneck that prevents efficient trillion-parameter language model deployment.

micro-2024-050.method: CacheCraft rearranges each 128-byte memory chunk into four 30-byte sections and one 8-byte section (instead of the standard four equal 32-byte sections), creating 2 bytes per section to store ECC (error-correcting code that catches and fixes memory bit errors) alongside the actual data. By packing the ECC with the data in the same memory chunk, a GPU retrieves both the information and its protection bits in one memory request—avoiding the sequential back-and-forth that traditional systems require, where they fetch data first and then fetch the error-protection information separately.
micro-2024-050.key_novelty: Integrate error-correcting code into cache line sections so that data and its error protection travel together in a single memory request, instead of requiring separate sequential accesses.

micro-2024-055.method: SVR works by predicting which irregular memory addresses (addresses that don't follow a regular pattern) an in-order processor will need next. Instead of waiting for each memory access to complete before starting the next, SVR launches multiple temporary copies of these predicted accesses in parallel, each using a different predicted loop counter value (the numbers that typically control how many times a loop repeats). These parallel memory requests fetch data while the main program continues computing, hiding the stalls (waiting periods) that normally slow down simple processors. By overlapping independent memory accesses, SVR exposes memory-level parallelism (the ability to have many memory requests active simultaneously) even on simple in-order processors.
micro-2024-055.key_novelty: Using temporary parallel execution of predicted irregular memory accesses—each from a different predicted loop counter value—to extract memory parallelism on simple in-order processors.

micro-2024-058.method: The system adds extra memory storage behind the standard TAGE branch predictor (a chip component that predicts which direction a branch instruction will take). It recognizes that branches needing longer histories typically appear together in the same program contexts—sequences of nested function calls. The system predicts which contexts will run next and pre-loads the relevant branch data into a small, fast buffer built into the chip. When making a prediction, the processor checks both the standard predictor and the prefetched data in parallel, eliminating wait time.
micro-2024-058.key_novelty: The key idea is exploiting program context locality—the fact that branches needing long histories appear together in function call sequences—to organize branch data hierarchically and predictively load it into a fast on-chip buffer before it's needed.

micro-2024-061.method: Mosaic works by dividing up the CPU's performance-boosting hardware—caches (fast memory that stores frequently used data), TLBs (hardware that translates memory addresses), and branch predictors (hardware that guesses which direction code will jump)—into separate partitions assigned to individual functions. When the CPU switches between functions, each function's partition stays intact instead of being overwritten, so it keeps the benefit of cached data and correct predictions. Inactive partitions are put into low-power mode to save energy. A scheduler then smartly adjusts how much of each resource each function gets based on what it actually needs.
micro-2024-061.key_novelty: The core idea is to partition the CPU's performance-boosting hardware per function instead of sharing it globally, so each function preserves its hardware state when the CPU switches to another task.

micro-2024-056.method: NoCap combines hash-based Zero-Knowledge Proof algorithms (Orion and Spartan) with a specialized hardware processor designed to run many similar operations at the same time, equipped with custom components for ZKP-specific tasks. The hardware organization matches how these algorithms work, so it can run calculations in parallel and move less data between components. It trades off bigger proofs for faster overall results.
micro-2024-056.key_novelty: The core idea is co-designing hardware and algorithms specifically for hash-based Zero-Knowledge Proofs (Orion and Spartan) using specialized vector processors.

micro-2024-059.method: Leviathan creates a unified system for near-data computing—performing calculations where data is stored instead of moving data to a processor. It uses reactive programming (responding automatically to data events) to determine what to compute, where in the memory system to compute it (caches, memory levels), and when to execute—decisions that normally require manual optimization by programmers. By combining multiple near-data computing approaches into one integrated platform with cache-integrated execution, the system adapts to different computational strategies without needing separate custom designs.
micro-2024-059.key_novelty: Leviathan provides a single unified system with reactive programming that automatically adapts to multiple near-data computing strategies, eliminating the need for separate custom architectures for each approach.

micro-2024-054.method: Instead of tracking which rows were recently accessed, MINT predicts at each refresh cycle which row activation is likely to face a Rowhammer attack (repeated accesses that cause bit flips in neighboring rows) in the next interval. It probabilistically selects that predicted row for protection, and when the next refresh happens, it preemptively refreshes that row's neighbors to block bit flips. By predicting one row ahead instead of maintaining a full history of accesses, MINT achieves Rowhammer mitigation using only one tracking entry per bank, fitting within the tight SRAM budget.
micro-2024-054.key_novelty: MINT's key insight is that if Rowhammer mitigation can only protect one row per refresh, tracking just one row suffices—selected through forward-looking prediction instead of recording access history.

micro-2024-053.method: Elastic Translations watches which page lookups fail in the hardware's translation table and uses that information to automatically select the right page size as the program runs. When frequent lookups reveal that certain memory regions are heavily used, it combines smaller pages into larger ones (4KiB pages merge into 64KiB or 32MiB), reducing lookup overhead. This adaptation happens continuously without manual setup. The system was implemented for ARMv8-A in Linux and KVM.
micro-2024-053.key_novelty: By monitoring page lookup failures in the hardware, the system automatically picks the best page size at runtime, adapting to each program without requiring manual configuration.

micro-2024-062.method: LIBRA accelerates GPU rendering by processing multiple screen regions (tiles) in parallel. It predicts how much memory each tile needs by comparing it to the previous frame—since consecutive video frames share similar memory access patterns (frame-to-frame coherence)—without reducing memory-cache effectiveness. Then it schedules tiles in an order that distributes memory requests evenly across the GPU's raster units (the hardware that converts geometry into pixels), preventing memory congestion from becoming a bottleneck.
micro-2024-062.key_novelty: Use frame-to-frame coherence (the pattern similarity between consecutive frames) to predict tile memory pressure, then schedule tiles to distribute requests evenly and prevent congestion.

micro-2024-060.method: SRender identifies which rays (light paths used in rendering) and points (3D locations in the scene) matter most for image quality using a fast, approximate encoding method called low-precision hash encoding. It then devotes expensive, accurate high-precision computation to these important rays and points, while using cheaper low-precision approximations for the rest. The hardware is specifically designed for this: it includes a sensitivity prediction engine to identify importance, encoding engines optimized to reuse data in fast on-chip cache, and a recovery engine that converts computational savings into actual speedup.
micro-2024-060.key_novelty: Dynamically assigning different precision levels to individual rays and points based on how much each affects the final image enables efficient mixed-precision rendering.

micro-2024-066.method: COMPASS works by predicting which neurons will fire (spike speculation) based on patterns in recent spike activity, so the hardware can skip unnecessary computation during quiet periods. The system uses SRAM memory that performs neural calculations directly within itself (computing-in-memory), modified with minimal additional circuits to detect and exploit these spike patterns. It reorganizes how data flows through the chip to represent spikes as time-stamped events rather than full arrays, which uses less memory and allows many accumulate-and-compare operations (adding up signals and deciding if neurons fire) to run in parallel.
micro-2024-066.key_novelty: The core idea is adaptive spike prediction—forecasting which neurons will fire based on patterns—to skip unnecessary calculations in memory-based neural chips while adding almost no hardware cost.

micro-2024-064.method: GraDMM solves the memory allocation problem by treating it as a graph problem—like finding paths through connected blocks of memory—and using the FPGA's specialized graph-processing hardware to solve it fast. It uses a minimal pipeline design that doesn't require extra hardware resources as memory sizes grow. To find free memory faster, it searches multiple paths at once (concurrent traversal) and uses shortcuts to jump to promising locations. Finally, it incorporates an adaptive defragmenter that reorganizes memory to prevent fragmentation from causing allocation failures.
micro-2024-064.key_novelty: The core idea is treating dynamic memory management as a graph-solving problem and using FPGA hardware specialized for graphs so that it can simultaneously achieve all three goals: scaling to large memory sizes, answering allocation requests quickly, and preventing allocation failures.

micro-2024-065.method: SOFA uses three coordinated techniques to optimize sparse neural network processing: (1) predicting where attention will be sparse using simple log-based math (adding only, no subtraction) to detect patterns with minimal overhead, (2) sorting data within stages and passing sorted results forward to enable fine-grained coordination between stages using FlashAttention, and (3) a dedicated SOFA hardware accelerator that exploits this cross-stage coordination to reduce redundant memory fetches and processing time. The key is coordinating decisions across pipeline stages instead of optimizing each stage independently, which avoids redundant computation and excessive memory access.
micro-2024-065.key_novelty: The core innovation is enabling lightweight, fine-grained coordination of data flow across pipeline stages in dynamic sparse computation to avoid the excessive memory access that occurs when each stage optimizes independently.

micro-2024-063.method: The method uses helper qubits (flag and proxy qubits) that reduce the number of connections each qubit needs while still supporting better error-correction codes (hyperbolic surface and color codes). A greedy scheduling algorithm determines the order of error checks to maintain reliability even if some checks fail. Two specialized decoding algorithms then read the flag qubit measurements to identify which errors occurred and correct them.
micro-2024-063.key_novelty: Flag-Proxy Networks reduce the number of connections needed in quantum LDPC error-correction codes by using helper qubits called flag and proxy qubits.

micro-2024-068.method: TACOS automatically designs communication algorithms customized to each cluster's specific network layout and communication patterns. Instead of using generic algorithms that work the same for all systems, it analyzes how the computers are connected (network topology) and what data needs to flow between them, then synthesizes an optimized algorithm for that exact configuration. The key advantage is that the design process itself is polynomial time—meaning it stays computationally feasible even for massive systems—rather than NP-hard approaches that become prohibitively slow at that scale, enabling practical scaling to systems with tens of thousands of processors.
micro-2024-068.key_novelty: It automatically creates communication algorithms tailored to each specific network layout using polynomial-time computation, making customization practical for systems with tens of thousands of processors.

micro-2024-073.method: FloatAP speeds up floating-point math on associative processors by aligning multiple floating-point numbers in parallel—simultaneously adjusting the decimal points of several numbers so they can be added correctly. Rather than computing multiplication bit-by-bit like traditional systems, it reuses the processor's existing hardware for adding (called adder trees) to handle multiplication and dot product operations. The approach supports standard vector programming through the RISC-V 'V' extension and works with different floating-point formats and integer operations.
micro-2024-073.key_novelty: This is the first programmable associative processor that enables efficient floating-point arithmetic through parallel alignment of multiple floating-point numbers (handling multiple bits and components simultaneously) and by repurposing the processor's existing addition hardware for multiplication.

micro-2024-067.method: ENTROPyINDEX observes which bits of the memory address change most during cache misses—a measurement called entropy, or degree of variation. It then selects the address bits that vary the most, since these will distribute cached data more evenly across the cache storage. Because different programs access memory differently, the scheme adapts its bit selection to match each program's unique patterns.
micro-2024-067.key_novelty: The innovation is using entropy (degree of variation) in address bits during cache misses to dynamically determine which bits index the cache.

micro-2024-057.method: ImPress unifies Rowhammer and Row-Press protection by tracking charge loss (wear on memory cells) with a single model that treats damage from repeated access and row-open-time equivalently. Because charge loss is the underlying cause of both threats, the system can protect against both with one mechanism. The approach works with existing protections (Graphene, PARA, Mithril, MINT), allows rows to stay open as long as needed, and doesn't lower the safety threshold.
micro-2024-057.key_novelty: ImPress unifies Row-Press and Rowhammer defense through a charge-loss model that treats row-open-time as repeated access, extending existing Rowhammer protections without additional cost or tightened safety thresholds.

micro-2024-069.method: The system focuses computation on important image regions through sparse sampling. A ray recursion unit accelerates volume rendering by recognizing irregular data sparsity and processing small sub-tiles with threads scheduled via Morton ordering—a space-filling pattern that keeps memory access efficient. A backpropagation engine with gradient buffers and pose backward units eliminates atomic operations through coalescing and pipeline fusion.
micro-2024-069.key_novelty: A sparsity-adaptive ray recursion unit that uses Morton ordering (a space-filling scheduling pattern) and sub-tile-wise execution to efficiently handle irregular data sparsity in volume rendering.

micro-2024-072.method: SOPHIE breaks large Ising problems into smaller independent tiles that work together. Architecturally, it uses multiple stacked chips with optically addressed phase-change memory arrays (OPCM—memory controlled by light) arranged symmetrically to reduce the memory footprint by roughly 50%, and these arrays efficiently perform matrix multiplication. Algorithmically, each tile solves its own piece using symmetric local updates while coordinating through stochastic global synchronization (random-timed coordination), which minimizes wasted computation and communication. Device-level optimizations include bi-directional memory arrays and dual-precision converters.
micro-2024-072.key_novelty: Breaking large Ising problems into independent tiles with symmetric local updates and stochastic global synchronization (random-timed coordination) allows the machine to solve problems larger than its physical hardware capacity.

micro-2024-074.method: HyFiSS builds a detailed model of how a GPU's computing units execute code, tracking when and why they stall (pause waiting for memory or other resources). It uses actual scheduling logs to replay the thread scheduler's real decisions—how it ordered thread blocks (groups of threads) to run—rather than guessing them. To stay fast, it samples results at the thread-block level instead of simulating every cycle, and compresses instruction traces to reduce storage overhead while keeping simulation accurate.
micro-2024-074.key_novelty: By mixing precise tracking of GPU stalls with coarse thread-block-level sampling, it delivers cycle-accurate simulation precision with cycle-approximate simulation speed.

micro-2024-077.method: LoAS replaces the standard approach of processing timesteps one-by-one with parallel processing—having all timesteps work at the same time instead. This reduces the amount of data that needs to move back and forth between timesteps. The system uses a spike compression method that efficiently encodes neural signals as single bits with memory-access patterns that keep data close together, and a specialized inner-join circuit (a piece of hardware that combines data quickly) that merges data from all timesteps without slowing down overall performance.
micro-2024-077.key_novelty: Converting timestep processing from sequential to parallel to reduce data movement and latency.

micro-2024-071.method: Neu10 creates a virtual NPU (vNPU) — a software layer that divides a physical neural processor into slices that can be shared across multiple jobs. It includes a resource allocator that maps these virtual NPUs to physical hardware using pay-as-you-go billing, where each job pays only for the resources it actually uses. It extends the NPU instruction set (the set of operations the processor can execute) to enable dynamic scheduling of individual tensor operations (calculations on multi-dimensional numerical arrays) across multiple virtual NPUs, deciding in real-time which operation runs on which slice.
micro-2024-071.key_novelty: The core innovation is an NPU instruction set extension that enables fine-grained dynamic scheduling of individual tensor operations (calculations on multi-dimensional arrays) across multiple virtual NPUs in cloud systems.

micro-2024-070.method: Hestia creates an interpreter that lets you observe what's happening at multiple levels of detail—from your original software code down to RTL (the precise circuit instructions the hardware will execute). It maintains mappings between these levels, so when something breaks, you can pinpoint whether the bug is in the software, in the compiler's translation, or in the hardware itself. You can debug at any level using breakpoints and stepping, avoiding the need for slow full hardware simulations.
micro-2024-070.key_novelty: Hestia enables efficient debugging of compiler-generated hardware by maintaining mappings between software and hardware at different abstraction levels, avoiding the need for slow full simulations.

micro-2024-075.method: Surf-Deformer builds simple, modular deformation rules based on gauge transformations—mathematical ways of reorganizing the quantum code that preserve its corrective power. These rules can be freely combined to handle different types of defects, creating many more possible strategies than older methods that use the same approach for every situation. By customizing which combinations to apply based on the specific defects it encounters, the system fixes errors while maintaining efficient quantum operations and using fewer extra qubits than worst-case designs.
micro-2024-075.key_novelty: Combining simple deformation building blocks based on gauge transformations creates a larger space of possible solutions, enabling the system to customize its error correction strategy for each specific defect situation rather than using one generic approach.

micro-2024-080.method: Cambricon-LLM uses a chiplet-based architecture (multiple specialized chips working together) that combines an NPU (a processor designed for AI) with a dedicated NAND flash storage chip. They use a hardware-tiling strategy—a way of arranging data into blocks that minimize how much data has to move between the NPU and flash, saving time and power. The NAND flash has two advanced features: in-flash computing (it can do simple calculations right where the data is stored) and on-die ECC (error-checking built directly into the storage chips). The NPU handles the big matrix multiplications and special computations, while the flash handles lighter processing tasks directly on itself.
micro-2024-080.key_novelty: The single core idea is putting computing capability directly inside NAND flash storage—not just in the separate NPU—so the flash and NPU can work together without having to constantly move data between them.

micro-2024-081.method: The paper represents sparse tensor algebra applications as data dependency diagrams (showing which operations pass data to each other). This reveals where data from one operation can be reused by another—both as direct hand-offs between operations and across repeated iterations of the algorithm. Sparsepipe captures these opportunities using an execution strategy called OEI dataflow (Output-stationary-Element-wise-Input-stationary: keeping outputs in place while inputs flow in a specific order). The hardware implements this by arranging its memory and data paths to keep reused data nearby, minimizing expensive data movement.
micro-2024-081.key_novelty: The key insight is recognizing that sparse tensor algorithms can reuse the same data across multiple iterations instead of reloading it each time.

micro-2024-076.method: Different GNN models perform different operations, but they share common patterns in how data moves through computations. SCALE takes a structure-centric approach, designing hardware around these shared dataflow patterns rather than optimizing each model separately. It combines three techniques: a systolic array-like processor (a grid of coordinated units) supporting varied dataflows including all-reduce operations (combining results from multiple units), scheduling that considers vertex degree (how many connections each node has) to balance workload, and a unified data pipeline for both graph and neural operations without extra overhead.
micro-2024-076.key_novelty: Different GNN models share underlying dataflow patterns (how data flows through operations), so hardware optimized for those universal patterns can work across all models instead of separate model-specific designs.

micro-2024-085.method: The UFC accelerator analyzes different FHE encryption schemes to find common operations it can build hardware around. Instead of creating separate specialized pipelines for each scheme, it builds flexible hardware units that handle these core operations, which means the hardware stays productive whether you're running one scheme or switching between different ones. The design combines algorithm and hardware optimizations to reduce the cost of moving data around the chip, and uses a smarter compiler to keep all the hardware units working productively regardless of the specific encryption settings chosen.
micro-2024-085.key_novelty: A single accelerator that supports multiple FHE encryption schemes through general-purpose hardware units, rather than building separate specialized circuits for each scheme.

micro-2024-082.method: Atomic Cache solves the slowdown of atomic operations (updates that must complete without interruption) using two coordinated techniques. On the software side, it applies relaxed memory consistency based on non-ordering commutativity—detecting operations that produce the same result regardless of order and skipping the synchronization barriers that usually enforce strict ordering between them. On the hardware side, the In-Situ Store Atomic Cache Macro executes atomic operations directly in the processor's cache instead of sending them to main memory, eliminating the serialization bottleneck where threads queue up waiting to update shared variables.
micro-2024-082.key_novelty: Atomic operations execute directly in the cache using the In-Situ Store Atomic Cache Macro, paired with relaxed memory consistency that skips synchronization delays between operations that commute.

micro-2024-086.method: MeMCISA uses multiple separate banks of memristors (electronic elements that store data and perform computations) with computing circuits placed near each bank, enabling calculations to happen right at the storage level. It executes instructions in parallel whenever their input data is ready, not in fixed sequence (out-of-order scheduling), using four categories of operations: single-bit operations, element-by-element operations, vector operations on groups of data, and control instructions. The system automatically manages dependencies—when one operation needs the result of an earlier one—including complex vector patterns where one group-operation feeds into another, which traditional single-number instruction sets cannot handle efficiently. This allows the system to handle diverse database tasks like vector aggregation, convolution, and computing multi-hop paths through data.
micro-2024-086.key_novelty: The key innovation is using out-of-order scheduling (executing operations whenever their input data is ready) with vector instructions (operations on groups of values) on memristor-based multi-bank storage, enabling databases to efficiently compute the complex, interdependent calculations they perform without requiring strict instruction sequencing.

micro-2024-078.method: AdapTiV speeds up Vision Transformers by identifying and merging redundant tokens before processing. It combines three techniques: Local Matching restricts each token's search to nearby tokens rather than all pairs, Sign Similarity determines redundancy using just the sign (positive or negative) of values instead of full computation, and Dynamic Merge Rate automatically adjusts merge amounts based on the image. The merging work is performed invisibly by folding it into Layer Normalization—an existing computation step the model always performs.
micro-2024-078.key_novelty: The key insight is using just the sign (positive or negative) of values to detect similar tokens, combined with automatic image-adaptive merge rates, so all merging work runs invisibly within an existing Layer Normalization step.

micro-2024-079.method: RAHP avoids wasted computation by noticing which vertices (nodes) appear in multiple hyperedges (multi-node connections) and computing them once instead of repeatedly. It starts from high-degree vertices and preloads their related vertices into the accelerator's fast on-chip cache. Memory accesses follow the hypergraph's structure rather than being random, which minimizes slow external memory accesses. When multiple parts of the computation need to update the same vertex simultaneously, an adaptive synchronization scheme coordinates these updates efficiently, and intermediate results (computed features) are cached and reused across similar hyperedges.
micro-2024-079.key_novelty: By scheduling computation asynchronously (using flexible execution order), RAHP detects vertices that appear in multiple hyperedges (multi-node connections) and computes them once, reusing the results instead of recomputing them.

mlsys-2024-001.method: The paper tests compression techniques on intermediate training data (activations) that must be communicated between devices in model parallel training, where large models are split across multiple GPUs. It applies compression methods like quantization (representing data with fewer bits) and sparsity (removing unimportant values), then measures how much communication volume shrinks, whether training speed stays acceptable, and if models still converge correctly. Testing spans different model parallelism strategies to understand the tradeoff between communication savings and the overhead of compression itself.
mlsys-2024-001.key_novelty: The paper empirically tests whether compressing intermediate training data reduces communication overhead in multi-device model training while maintaining training convergence.

mlsys-2024-000.method: Instead of treating memory management and kernel optimization as separate problems, the system jointly schedules both together. It reduces memory usage through smart tensor allocation (placing data efficiently to minimize peak memory demand), in-place operations (modifying data without creating copies, reducing fragmentation), and operator fusion (combining operations to eliminate intermediate storage). The kernels themselves are optimized for MCU constraints using quantization-aware computation (processing lower-precision numbers that use less memory) and tiled execution (processing large tensors in smaller chunks that fit in available memory).
mlsys-2024-000.key_novelty: The core idea is to jointly optimize memory management and kernel execution as a single scheduling problem, rather than treating them as separate optimization targets.

mlsys-2024-002.method: AWQ compresses neural network weights (reducing bits per weight to save memory and speed up inference) by watching which parts of the network handle the largest values during actual use. Weights connected to channels with high-magnitude activations (the numerical data flowing through those channels) stay at higher precision, while weights in low-activation channels use lower precision, enabling sub-bit quantization while preserving accuracy. This per-channel adaptation is guided by observing real activation patterns rather than applying uniform compression everywhere.
mlsys-2024-002.key_novelty: AWQ uses real activation patterns (the actual data flowing through the network) to decide how much each weight should be compressed, instead of using the weights' own statistics or applying uniform compression.

mlsys-2024-008.method: The approach trains a machine learning model on examples of past neural architectures and how fast they actually executed. This model learns patterns about which design choices (like the number of layers or connection patterns) affect execution speed. Instead of building and running each candidate architecture to measure its speed, the search process now just uses the trained model to instantly predict speed for new candidates. This replaces slow physical execution with fast predictions, dramatically reducing the time needed to search for good architectures.
mlsys-2024-008.key_novelty: Instead of running each architecture candidate to measure speed, use a trained model to predict speed from design features.

micro-2024-083.method: DRCTL adds a translation layer—a middle software/hardware interface—that enables dynamic rescheduling (moving computations around to prevent hardware wear) while keeping communication fast. It works through three mechanisms: address conversion automatically updates instruction sequences (the steps telling hardware what to do) after rescheduling without recompiling the program; hierarchical wear-leveling reduces communication overhead by moving larger work blocks instead of individual pieces; and layout-aware selective remapping keeps related data physically close during rescheduling by exploiting data dependencies.
micro-2024-083.key_novelty: The key innovation is a translation layer that decouples dynamic task rescheduling (moving work to prevent hardware wear) from static data layout optimization (fixing data positions for speed), enabling both through automatic address conversion and data remapping based on data dependencies.

mlsys-2024-004.method: SLoRA serves thousands of different LoRA adapters (small model customizations) from a single GPU by swapping adapters in and out of memory as requests arrive, rather than keeping them all loaded. The system batches together requests for different adapters so the GPU processes them in parallel, uses shared memory pools instead of giving each adapter its own space, and reuses computation across requests (prefix caching). These techniques let thousands of specialized models run on a single commodity GPU without exhausting memory or compute resources.
mlsys-2024-004.key_novelty: SLoRA is the first system to serve thousands of LoRA adapters on a single commodity GPU by scheduling which adapters to load when and dynamically sharing GPU memory between them.

micro-2024-084.method: The compiler splits the program into chunks called epochs (recoverable sections of code). At the end of each epoch, it saves key register values that the next chunk will need. The hardware then repurposes an existing battery-backed buffer called the write pending queue (which normally holds memory writes waiting to be sent to storage) as a log of changes. At each epoch boundary, it sends all the collected memory writes together to permanent storage, so the data survives a crash.
micro-2024-084.key_novelty: The core idea is repurposing an existing piece of hardware—the battery-backed write pending queue—as a change log, so the system can recover from crashes using minimal added hardware (0.5 bytes per core) and without needing to predict how multiple memory controllers will behave.

mlsys-2024-006.method: During text generation, an LLM keeps cached attention data (the stored key-value pairs for every token seen so far) to help predict the next words. Keyformer identifies which of these tokens will actually matter for future predictions—using attention pattern analysis or scoring each token's predicted usefulness—then discards the cached data for less-important tokens. By keeping only essential cached data, it reduces memory bandwidth (the amount of data the GPU fetches per generation step) and storage overhead, while maintaining generation accuracy.
mlsys-2024-006.key_novelty: Keyformer prunes the KV cache to only the most-important tokens based on predicted usefulness, rather than always retaining the complete cache.

mlsys-2024-010.method: Punica combines requests from different customers' LoRA adapters (lightweight customizations of a base model) into larger processing batches that run together. It stores the LoRA weights in high-bandwidth memory (the fastest available memory tier), eliminating the overhead of shuffling data between slower storage. When certain adapter combinations can't run in the same batch, dynamic scheduling (real-time reordering) intelligently groups compatible requests together while maintaining high throughput.
mlsys-2024-010.key_novelty: Combining requests from different customers into shared processing batches lets them run the same base model computation together, even though each customer has different weight customizations, cutting per-request overhead.

mlsys-2024-007.method: VIDUR is a simulation tool that predicts how large AI language models will perform when running on computer systems. You input hardware specifications (the processors, memory systems, and network connections between machines), actual user request patterns, and the tool simulates the full execution to estimate system performance. It can model multiple machines working together and handle setups that mix different types of hardware.
mlsys-2024-007.key_novelty: A simulation tool purpose-built to predict AI language model inference performance by accurately modeling both how the language models compute and how real-world systems serve them.

mlsys-2024-013.method: ACROBAT predicts how data shapes and sizes will vary at runtime, then uses those predictions at compile time to determine the best batching strategy (grouping data into batches of similar size for efficient processing). It generates specialized code that handles multiple different data sizes efficiently without needing to make slow decisions during actual execution.
mlsys-2024-013.key_novelty: ACROBAT optimizes batching strategies at compile time, even though the actual data sizes won't be known until the program runs.

mlsys-2024-011.method: To run neural networks on encrypted data using homomorphic encryption (a method to compute on encrypted data without decrypting it), the paper replaces activation functions like ReLU and sigmoid—which can't be directly computed—with low-degree polynomials (simplified mathematical expressions). The technique carefully balances the number of polynomial terms to achieve accurate approximations while keeping computation fast, avoiding the expensive high-degree polynomials typically needed for private neural network inference.
mlsys-2024-011.key_novelty: The core method is using low-degree polynomials (simplified mathematical expressions) to replace activation functions like ReLU and sigmoid in encrypted neural networks, making it possible to run them efficiently without expensive high-degree polynomial approximations.

mlsys-2024-003.method: The system uses dynamic containers—wrappers that adjust the floating-point precision (how many bits represent each number) during training. Based on each training phase's needs, containers use lower precision (fewer bits, faster, more memory-efficient) when rounding error is tolerable, and higher precision (more bits, more accurate) when accuracy is critical. By adjusting precision on-the-fly rather than fixing it for the entire training run, the system trades computational efficiency against accuracy in a way that's optimized for each phase.
mlsys-2024-003.key_novelty: Dynamic floating-point containers that automatically adjust precision during training based on what each training phase requires.

mlsys-2024-009.method: COMET applies explanation techniques from explainable AI to reveal why neural cost models make their predictions. It likely uses methods such as feature attribution (identifying which architectural parameters matter most), attention visualization (showing which parts the model focuses on), or gradient-based analysis (tracking how input changes propagate). The framework translates these internal mechanisms into human-readable explanations connected to actual hardware design choices.
mlsys-2024-009.key_novelty: First framework to systematically explain neural cost model predictions, showing which hardware design choices actually cause changes in predicted latency, power, and area.

mlsys-2024-005.method: Q-Hitter works by predicting which tokens (words) the model truly needs to remember—this prediction happens during attention computation, which is when the model decides which past words are relevant for what comes next. Based on this prediction, it stores important tokens at high precision while compressing less important ones to lower precision in the key-value cache (the storage that holds information about every past word). By keeping important tokens at full detail and shrinking the rest, it reduces GPU memory consumption while maintaining the model's ability to compute attention correctly.
mlsys-2024-005.key_novelty: Q-Hitter combines a token oracle (a mechanism that predicts which tokens matter) with quantization (precision reduction) to selectively compress the key-value cache, reducing GPU memory use for LLM inference.

mlsys-2024-018.method: JIT-Q addresses training's memory bandwidth problem by reducing numerical precision (quantizing) on-the-fly rather than storing full-precision numbers. It uses processing-in-memory (PIM)—specialized hardware that performs calculations directly inside the memory system where data lives. By co-locating quantization with PIM, the system computes using lower-precision numbers in-place within memory, avoiding the data movement that would otherwise bottleneck training performance.
mlsys-2024-018.key_novelty: Combining on-the-fly quantization with processing-in-memory enables training computations to happen in-place within memory using reduced precision, eliminating data-movement overhead.

mlsys-2024-015.method: Proteus protects a machine learning model during compiler optimization by keeping its computation graph (the blueprint of operations and data flows) encrypted or scrambled. Even while locked this way, the system can apply standard speedup techniques: kernel fusion (merging small operations together), memory scheduling (deciding when and where to move data), and layout transformations (reorganizing how data is stored). The model remains encrypted throughout, so its architecture and parameters never get exposed.
mlsys-2024-015.key_novelty: Enables full compiler optimizations—kernel fusion, memory scheduling, and data reorganization—on encrypted machine learning models without decrypting the model's architecture or parameters.

mlsys-2024-020.method: HeteroSwitch measures how physical system factors—different device capabilities, variable network speeds, and uneven resource availability—create uneven data distributions in a federated learning system (where models train across many distributed devices). When it detects these patterns, it automatically switches the strategies for combining the data and training to adapt to what it finds. This adaptive approach helps the system converge faster and more reliably despite heterogeneous devices and network conditions.
mlsys-2024-020.key_novelty: HeteroSwitch treats system-induced data unevenness—caused by device differences and network variability—as a distinct problem from natural data skew, and addresses only the system-induced part.

mlsys-2024-016.method: When an LLM processes a prompt, it calculates how each word should pay attention to other words—an expensive step called attention. The system saves these precomputed calculations by breaking them into modular (reusable) pieces indexed by the prompt content. Whenever a new request arrives with an identical or overlapping prompt prefix, it retrieves and reuses these saved pieces instead of recalculating them.
mlsys-2024-016.key_novelty: Reusing precomputed attention work across similar prompts by organizing it into modular, reusable pieces.

mlsys-2024-014.method: The approach compresses the model's trillion parameters to less than 1 bit each—a dramatic reduction in storage and memory needs. It exploits the Mixture of Experts architecture, where multiple specialized sub-networks exist but only some activate for each input (this sparsity is key). By applying different compression settings to each expert module based on its weight patterns, the technique achieves extreme compression while preserving accuracy.
mlsys-2024-014.key_novelty: The key insight is that Mixture of Experts' sparsity—where only some expert modules activate per input—allows different experts to use tailored compression levels, enabling sub-1-bit compression of trillion-parameter models.

mlsys-2024-012.method: SiDA analyzes the characteristics of input data to guide its routing and batching decisions. For each token (a piece of text being processed), it routes only to the experts (specialized model components) needed for that token, rather than activating all experts. It also groups requests together in memory-efficient ways that fit hardware constraints. This approach exploits the natural sparsity in Mixture-of-Experts models—where each token typically uses only a subset of experts—to reduce the total processing time.
mlsys-2024-012.key_novelty: SiDA uses the characteristics of input data to guide routing decisions that exploit the sparsity of Mixture-of-Experts models, activating only the experts each token needs.

mlsys-2024-019.method: Lancet overlaps computation and communication in Mixture-of-Experts training by using pipelining (breaking work into stages) and scheduling to identify which computations don't depend on each other. These independent tasks can run while data moves between distributed experts (different processors) and parameter servers (where shared model parameters are stored). By coordinating this overlap across the entire computation graph rather than piece-by-piece at individual layers, Lancet hides communication delays behind productive work.
mlsys-2024-019.key_novelty: Lancet's core idea is overlapping computation and communication at the whole-graph level for Mixture-of-Experts training, instead of doing it piece-by-piece at individual layers.

mlsys-2024-026.method: UniDM uses a single large language model (an AI trained on vast amounts of text) to understand what data represents and handle multiple data tasks—cleaning errors, converting formats, and merging different sources—through one unified interface. The model's reasoning capabilities let it figure out what steps are needed for each task, rather than requiring separate specialized tools for cleaning, transformation, and integration.
mlsys-2024-026.key_novelty: Using a single large language model to handle all data manipulation tasks instead of relying on separate specialized tools for each type of work.

mlsys-2024-021.method: The system breaks a recommendation model into many small pieces and assigns each piece to run on a specific processor, using an algorithm that considers the hardware topology (how computers are physically connected), network bandwidth, communication latency, and compute capabilities. It then schedules the work so that pieces that exchange data run close together, which reduces how much data needs to travel between different parts of the hardware.
mlsys-2024-021.key_novelty: The core innovation is using hardware topology information (how processors are connected and how fast they can communicate) to guide where each piece of the recommendation model gets placed, which reduces unnecessary data moving between machines.

mlsys-2024-023.method: L-GreCo examines how the gradients (numbers that update the network during training) behave layer by layer, measuring their size and variability. Layers with small gradients can be compressed heavily without hurting accuracy, while layers with large or variable gradients need lighter compression to protect important information. The system assigns a different compression strength to each layer based on these measurements, typically by dropping small gradient values or reducing their numerical precision (storing them with less detail). This works because different layers contribute unequally to the final result—some can tolerate information loss during compression while others cannot.
mlsys-2024-023.key_novelty: Using different compression levels for each layer based on how its gradients actually behave, instead of compressing all layers the same way.

mlsys-2024-022.method: ReLU activation functions—which output the input number if positive or zero if negative—are costly to compute securely when multiple parties jointly perform the computation without revealing their data (a technique called Multi-Party Computation or MPC), normally requiring many rounds of back-and-forth messages between parties. This work accelerates ReLU by using a more efficient approach to calculate the sign (whether a number is positive or negative), which is the key decision ReLU needs to make, thereby reducing the number of communication rounds.
mlsys-2024-022.key_novelty: A faster way to compute the sign function (positive or negative) in ReLU for systems where multiple parties jointly perform calculations without revealing their data, reducing the messages they must exchange.

mlsys-2024-024.method: Torch2Chip takes PyTorch neural network models and automatically makes them smaller through compression techniques: quantization (using fewer bits to represent numbers) and sparsity optimization (removing unnecessary connections). It then converts these compressed models into hardware-specific code that maps each operation in the network to the right resources on the target accelerator.
mlsys-2024-024.key_novelty: Torch2Chip integrates neural network compression, compilation, and hardware mapping into a single customizable toolkit for deploying PyTorch models to custom accelerators.

mlsys-2024-028.method: Converts the weights and activations (the numerical parameters that determine how a neural network makes predictions) from full precision down to an 8-bit floating-point format—a compact representation that uses much less memory and computes faster. The technique uses calibration (systematically testing different ways to map the original numbers into the 8-bit range) and smart rounding strategies to keep accuracy loss minimal during the conversion. Because no retraining occurs, the method must find the right mapping purely by analyzing the original numbers, without teaching the network anything new.
mlsys-2024-028.key_novelty: An 8-bit floating-point format (FP8) enables you to shrink fully-trained neural networks without retraining them.

mlsys-2024-030.method: When training neural networks on graphs, you sample subsets of nodes and edges because the full graph won't fit in memory. Coordinating this sampling across multiple computers normally requires constant communication between them, which becomes a bottleneck. This approach converts sampling decisions into matrix multiplication—an operation that GPUs and CPUs are specifically designed to perform efficiently. By representing sampling as matrices, each computer can calculate locally what to sample using hardware acceleration, then exchange results, eliminating the synchronization overhead.
mlsys-2024-030.key_novelty: Using matrix operations to transform sampling coordination into hardware-optimized local computation in distributed training.

mlsys-2024-025.method: LIFL breaks federated learning into serverless functions (cloud programs that run on-demand without managing servers) that activate only when something finishes—like when a participant completes training—instead of constantly checking for updates. These functions handle participant registration, collect and average model parameters across sites, and send out updated models through event-driven triggers. This approach eliminates the overhead of long-running coordination processes, letting the system automatically scale based on demand.
mlsys-2024-025.key_novelty: Instead of always-on central servers, LIFL uses serverless functions triggered by events, so coordination only runs when participants finish work—cutting the overhead of continuously maintaining state.

mlsys-2024-036.method: FedTrans optimizes distributed neural network training across devices with varying capabilities—weak devices like phones and powerful servers mixed together—by transforming models to suit each device. It uses techniques like compression to make models smaller, or selective layer transformations to update only the most important parts of the network. This reduces the amount of data that must be communicated when devices sync their training progress, addressing the main performance bottleneck in federated learning systems.
mlsys-2024-036.key_novelty: FedTrans uses model transformation—reshaping neural networks to match each device's capabilities—as the core strategy to make federated learning efficient.

mlsys-2024-029.method: DiffusionPipe applies pipeline parallelism—splitting the model across multiple GPUs like an assembly line—but tailors it to how diffusion models work. The key insight is that diffusion's sequential denoising steps create different computational patterns than other models, so DiffusionPipe arranges pipeline stages to match these dependencies and schedules GPU execution to minimize idle waiting time. It also overlaps data transfer between GPUs with computation, hiding the communication cost.
mlsys-2024-029.key_novelty: DiffusionPipe's core contribution is pipeline parallelism (splitting model work across GPUs) built specifically to handle diffusion models' sequential denoising steps, rather than using generic parallelism strategies from other model types.

mlsys-2024-033.method: VQPy lets you build video analytics pipelines by composing reusable components—like combining video filters—instead of writing everything from scratch. You describe what you want analyzed (such as 'detect objects in each frame') using a query language (a declarative way to specify what operations you need) rather than writing detailed code. A compiler then optimizes by combining related operations into fewer steps, ordering them efficiently, and running them on fast hardware accelerators like GPUs.
mlsys-2024-033.key_novelty: VQPy applies object-oriented design to video analytics, letting you combine reusable components that are automatically optimized by the system.

mlsys-2024-017.method: The system avoids synchronization overhead by running operations asynchronously—letting them proceed without waiting for each other to complete. It optimizes matrix multiplication (GEMM) by improving the memory layout: instead of accessing memory in a scattered way that skips around (strided pattern), data is arranged to be read sequentially (contiguous layout), which improves cache efficiency and throughput. Heuristics then adaptively adjust the scheduling strategy and batch sizes based on the hardware and workload, preventing underutilization.
mlsys-2024-017.key_novelty: Combining asynchronous kernel execution with flat GEMM optimization to simultaneously reduce synchronization stalls and improve memory efficiency in token generation.

sc-2024-003.method: The approach continuously monitors kernel performance during execution and uses this data to automatically adjust tile sizes (the chunks of computation grouped together) on-the-fly. Rather than using fixed, pre-configured tile sizes, it adapts the tiling parameters in real time based on what the CPU and GPU hardware can actually handle.
sc-2024-003.key_novelty: Instead of manually tuning tile sizes separately for each computer setup, this technique automatically adjusts them during execution based on how fast the code actually runs.

mlsys-2024-027.method: FLASH speeds up model adaptation by strategically choosing which layers (stages of computation) of a pre-trained model to update rather than retraining the entire model. It organizes how data moves through cloud resources—GPUs for fast computation, CPUs for general processing, and storage systems—to minimize wasted transfer time. The system also schedules multiple adaptation jobs to run without idle gaps, keeping compute resources constantly in use.
