mlsys-2024-027.key_novelty: FLASH's core innovation is making adaptation faster by customizing the fine-tuning strategy to match the specific hardware capabilities and how data flows through the cloud platform being used.

mlsys-2024-035.method: The approach compresses language models using low-bit quantization (storing numbers with fewer bits of precision). Instead of applying quantization uniformly across all model parts, it tailors the compression specifically for the characteristics of language-model serving. This targeting preserves accuracy while cutting computation and memory requirements. The system then efficiently executes these compressed models on hardware.
mlsys-2024-035.key_novelty: Tailoring low-bit quantization to the specific requirements of language-model serving makes it possible to have both efficiency and accuracy, rather than trading one for the other.

sc-2024-002.method: DistGNN reduces training overhead using hierarchical sampling—processing only the most important neighboring nodes at each layer instead of all neighbors—which cuts computation. It splits the graph across multiple machines (graph partitioning) so most data stays local rather than being repeatedly sent between computers. This combination reduces communication overhead, the expensive step of synchronizing data across the cluster. Critically, the system maintains convergence properties, meaning the model can still reliably reach its best solution despite the distributed setup.
sc-2024-002.key_novelty: The core contribution is combining hierarchical sampling with graph partitioning to reduce communication between machines during training while preserving convergence—the mathematical guarantee that the distributed model reaches the same solution quality as training on a single machine.

sc-2024-001.method: The framework enables GPUs to send data directly to each other (called GPU-direct memory access) instead of routing through the CPU. It also offloads collective operations—coordinated tasks where all GPUs need to exchange or combine data—to specialized hardware, freeing the CPU to do other work. Together, these prevent communication from becoming a bottleneck, allowing the system to scale nearly linearly across thousands of GPUs.
sc-2024-001.key_novelty: Combining direct GPU-to-GPU communication with hardware offload enables efficient collective operations even when coordinating thousands of GPUs.

mlsys-2024-031.method: CloudEval-YAML is a testing toolkit for systems that automatically generate cloud configuration files in YAML format (a structured text format used to describe cloud settings). The toolkit provides example configurations showing correct outputs, test cases covering different cloud setup scenarios, and metrics to evaluate whether generated files are actually valid. It also includes baseline implementations—simple reference systems—so researchers can measure how their new systems improve over known baseline performance.
mlsys-2024-031.key_novelty: A standardized test suite for evaluating systems that automatically generate YAML cloud configuration files.

sc-2024-005.method: The system continuously watches how data is actually accessed during exascale simulations and uses those patterns to decide where to store each piece of data across the memory hierarchy (fast registers through caches and DRAM to slower persistent storage). Instead of following a fixed storage rule, it adapts its decisions based on what it observes—keeping frequently-used data closer to the processor and pushing rarely-used data further away. This targeted placement reduces unnecessary movement between memory levels, which is what causes bottlenecks in massive simulations.
sc-2024-005.key_novelty: It adjusts data storage placement during execution based on real access patterns, rather than using a fixed strategy decided before the simulation starts.

mlsys-2024-032.method: The approach uses formal verification (checking whether outputs satisfy strict logical safety specifications through techniques like model checking or theorem proving) to evaluate the model's behavior. When violations are detected, the verification produces training signals. The model then learns from them by adjusting its parameters (through gradient-based optimization) to minimize error signals derived from specification violations—teaching it to consistently follow the formal safety requirements.
mlsys-2024-032.key_novelty: The key innovation is integrating formal verification feedback directly into the fine-tuning process, so the model learns to produce outputs that satisfy formal safety specifications.

sc-2024-006.method: An AI language model reads descriptions of scientific workflows and automatically generates contracts—formal rules specifying what software the workflow needs and what correct results look like. This replaces the manual process of developers handwriting these specifications. The system was tested on real Nextflow workflows, showing the AI can create practical, verifiable contracts that encode both environment requirements and correctness checks without human intervention.
sc-2024-006.key_novelty: An AI language model automatically generates executable contracts from workflow descriptions, eliminating the need for manual specification.

mlsys-2024-034.method: HeteGen runs large language models on resource-constrained devices like phones by splitting the computational work across available hardware accelerators—CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. Rather than sending all the work to one chip, it dynamically decides at runtime which operations go to which hardware based on what each chip handles fastest. A scheduling layer coordinates execution and communication between the chips, keeping them all working in parallel to avoid idle time and delays.
mlsys-2024-034.key_novelty: HeteGen speeds up large language model predictions on phones and other resource-limited devices by dynamically splitting work across different hardware accelerators (CPU, GPU, NPU) so they all run in parallel.

sc-2024-008.method: The current Flang compiler translates Fortran using custom, handwritten transformation passes (intermediate steps) that don't connect to standard compiler infrastructure. The authors create a direct mapping from Fortran language constructs to standard MLIR dialects (reusable modules within a shared compilation framework), which replaces the custom passes and enables use of MLIR's shared optimizations. They benchmark this new approach against Flang's existing system and other HPC compilers to measure performance gains from accessing the shared optimization infrastructure.
sc-2024-008.key_novelty: A direct mapping from Fortran to standard MLIR dialects replaces custom translation passes and lets the compiler use shared optimization infrastructure.

sc-2024-009.method: The researchers tested both Frontier (with a dragonfly network) and Summit (with a fat-tree network) using three types of tests: simple synthetic benchmarks that isolate specific communication patterns, practice applications, and full real scientific applications. For each test, they measured 'scaling efficiency'—how much faster the system got when they added more processors—which reveals when communication becomes a bottleneck. This showed whether Frontier's cheaper network design caused communication to slow down real workloads more than Summit's.
sc-2024-009.key_novelty: This is the first empirical measurement of how dragonfly network cost optimizations impact performance on exascale supercomputers running capability workloads.

sc-2024-010.method: EcoLife uses particle swarm optimization (a search algorithm where simulated agents explore possible solutions, similar to how a flock of birds searches for food) to decide which machine should run each function. The scheduler looks at all the available hardware—machines of different generations with different power consumption rates—and searches through possible function assignments to find ones that reduce carbon emissions while keeping execution time acceptable.
sc-2024-010.key_novelty: EcoLife is the first serverless scheduler that factors carbon emissions into placement decisions, balancing environmental impact from power usage against execution speed.

sc-2024-015.method: The approach uses the Roofline model—a framework that displays hardware's maximum speed limits—adapted to track how workflows perform from start to finish. It analyzes four example workflows that hit different limits: LCLS (memory speed limits), BerkeleyGW (processor speed limits), CosmoFlow (CPU preprocessing before the main computations), and GPTune (control decisions and data dependencies). The method identifies what's actually slowing each workflow by comparing real execution measurements against the theoretical speed limits of the hardware at both individual-node and full-system scales.
sc-2024-015.key_novelty: The key insight is applying the Roofline model—a tool for understanding what hardware limits performance—to complete workflows instead of just individual computations, revealing which hardware bottleneck is actually constraining real scientific applications.

sc-2024-016.method: The system breaks down climate data into frequency components using spherical harmonic transform (a mathematical technique that decomposes patterns on a sphere, like Earth's surface), then uses stochastic modeling—adding controlled randomness—to simulate how climate varies across space and time, achieving ultra-high spatial resolution of 0.034 degrees. To speed up the calculations, it runs them on GPUs (graphics processors) using mixed-precision arithmetic, where different parts of the computation use different numerical precision levels based on how strongly that data is correlated. The parallel matrix operations are managed by the PaRESEC runtime system, and the code is tuned for efficient execution across multiple GPU architectures using BLAS3 (a standard library of optimized mathematical operations).
sc-2024-016.key_novelty: The core contribution combines spherical harmonic decomposition, stochastic modeling, and GPU-accelerated mixed-precision solvers (variable numerical precision across calculations) to achieve a climate emulator with ultra-high 0.034° spatial resolution and dramatically reduced storage requirements.

sc-2024-004.method: MPI-X enhances MPI (the standard interface for coordinating multiple processors on supercomputers) to automatically work with accelerators like GPUs. Instead of requiring separate code for CPUs and GPUs, you write once and MPI-X automatically sends operations to the appropriate hardware. It includes built-in knowledge of GPU memory management and collective operations (tasks that require multiple processors to coordinate), and it keeps all existing MPI programs working without modification.
sc-2024-004.key_novelty: MPI-X extends MPI to automatically support mixed CPU and GPU systems with a single program, eliminating separate code paths while keeping all existing MPI programs working.

sc-2024-007.method: CoRD combines two storage update approaches—RAID (which uses parity for recovery) and Delta (which tracks just what changed). It identifies places where multiple updated blocks overlap in where they store data (offset address intersections), then sends only the changed parts to update the parity information. For updates spanning multiple blocks, it changes which blocks it uses for parity calculations to reduce network traffic.
sc-2024-007.key_novelty: The core idea is leveraging offset address intersections—where multiple blocks being updated overlap in memory—to optimally combine RAID and Delta approaches, reducing update traffic for both partial-block and partial-stripe updates.

sc-2024-017.method: The researchers measured power consumption of MILC (a quantum physics simulation program) on a Perlmutter GPU system, testing its Generation and Spectrum components with varying numbers of parallel tasks and different data sizes. They then ran these same tasks with the GPU power limited to different levels and measured the resulting performance changes, characterizing the trade-off between power savings and performance loss.
sc-2024-017.key_novelty: When MILC's GPU power is reduced to 50% of TDP (maximum design power), performance drops by less than 15%, making it well-suited for power-capping strategies.

sc-2024-014.method: Hydrogen separates memory capacity from bandwidth for CPUs and GPUs, letting each processor get a flexible split rather than a fixed one. To prevent GPU data transfers from overwhelming the system, it uses a token-based throttle where transfers only happen when a processor has a token to spend. The system automatically finds the best configuration by testing different settings in repeating time cycles called epochs, switching between them with minimal overhead.
sc-2024-014.key_novelty: The key insight is decoupling memory capacity from bandwidth, then continuously optimizing how much of each the CPU and GPU get by testing different settings in repeating cycles (epochs).

sc-2024-019.method: SZOps lets you perform math operations directly on compressed scientific data without unpacking it first. It handles negation, addition, multiplication, and statistical operations like computing means and variance, while keeping results within a user-specified error bound (a controlled limit on how much accuracy you sacrifice for file size). Normally you'd have to decompress everything before doing any math—which is slow and memory-intensive—but SZOps works in the compressed domain instead. The system optimizes three competing goals: minimizing file size, keeping operations fast, and respecting the error bounds.
sc-2024-019.key_novelty: SZOps is the first lossy compressor that lets you do math directly on compressed data while maintaining specified error bounds, without unpacking first.

sc-2024-011.method: MixQ predicts where outliers (unusually large or irregular values) will appear before computation by analyzing patterns in nearby data, achieving 95.8% accuracy. A verification technique called quantization ahead of detection (QAD) confirms these predictions are correct. A specialized data structure then efficiently processes these predicted outliers during actual computation, enabling the system to use lower precision (fewer bits) for regular values and higher precision for outliers, reducing memory and computation needs.
sc-2024-011.key_novelty: The innovation is predicting outliers (unusual values needing special handling) as data flows through the system by analyzing nearby data patterns, enabling hardware-efficient mixed-precision quantization—using lower precision for regular values and higher only where needed.

sc-2024-022.method: The approach changes deep learning models so they output not just a single prediction, but a full distribution showing how likely each possible answer is—revealing how confident the model really is. When confidence is too low, the model can choose to abstain (decline to predict) rather than guessing. The researchers tested this on three tasks: predicting air pressure and velocity around airplane wings using RANS simulations, classifying images in ImageNet1K, and recognizing MNIST handwritten digits.
sc-2024-022.key_novelty: Instead of making a confident guess, deep learning models output their full uncertainty about each possible answer and can choose to skip predictions when they're not confident enough.

sc-2024-021.method: The system uses federated identity management—where users log in once through their home institution and access multiple systems without separate passwords—combined with zero-trust security (verifying every user and access request, not trusting by default). It enforces multiple verification layers: multi-factor authentication (passwords plus a second factor like a phone code), cloud-native protocols (industry-standard secure login methods), and time-limited role-based access that automatically expires. The system monitors all access attempts, alerts administrators to suspicious activity, and ensures compliance with security regulations, deployed on Isambard-AI and HPC supercomputing facilities in the UK.
sc-2024-021.key_novelty: The key idea is co-designing federated single sign-on (one login across multiple systems) and zero-trust security (verify all access rather than assuming trust) together as an integrated system for scientific computing that combines HPC and AI infrastructure.

sc-2024-012.method: MR-MTP (Multi-Root Meshed Tree Protocol) exploits folded-Clos topology (a data center network with many symmetrically arranged backup paths) by routing traffic from multiple sources simultaneously, automatically distributing load to avoid bottlenecks—unlike standard BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) with ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path routing that spreads traffic equally across routes) or BGP with BFD (Bidirectional Forwarding Detection for faster failure detection). The researchers tested it on the FABRIC testbed, measuring convergence time (recovery speed after failures), packet loss, control message overhead, and blast radius (how far failure impact spreads), by deliberately injecting failures at multiple network locations.
sc-2024-012.key_novelty: Multi-Root Meshed Tree Protocol that uses folded-Clos topology's redundant paths to simplify routing and reduce convergence time (network recovery speed from failures) and control messaging overhead.

sc-2024-013.method: CUSZ-i predicts data values using multiple layers of interpolation on the GPU—estimating values between known data points at progressively finer scales—to reduce redundancy. It then applies Huffman encoding (replacing frequent patterns with shorter codes) and NVIDIA Bitcomp lossless compression to further shrink the data. The whole process guarantees decompressed data won't deviate more than your specified error threshold.
sc-2024-013.key_novelty: The core mechanism is using multiple layers of interpolation-based prediction on the GPU (estimating values between known data points at different scales) for data compression.

sc-2024-024.method: Globus Compute connects Python programs to HPC systems through three capabilities. First, it provides an asynchronous task submission interface (you submit work and get back a 'future' to check the result later without blocking). Second, it wraps shell commands and MPI applications (programs that run on multiple computers) so they behave like Python functions. Third, it uses a shared endpoint—one managed connection point serving multiple authorized users—instead of requiring each user or configuration to have its own.
sc-2024-024.key_novelty: Instead of deploying separate endpoints for different users and configurations, a single shared endpoint serves multiple authorized users with different needs.

sc-2024-023.method: Fire-Flyer 2 combines hardware and software design to reduce HPC costs: it uses 10,000 PCIe A100 GPUs connected via HFReduce (an optimized way for GPUs to combine their results) and a Computation-Storage Integrated Network that prevents data traffic bottlenecks. The software stack (HaiScale, 3FS, HAI-Platform) lets computation and data transfer happen simultaneously instead of waiting for each to finish. Together, these achieve performance comparable to expensive DGX-A100 systems while costing 50% less and using 40% less energy.
sc-2024-023.key_novelty: The key insight is co-designing hardware and software as one system: optimized GPU-to-GPU communication combined with a bottleneck-free network cuts costs 50% while matching expensive standard systems.

sc-2024-018.method: To speed up file reading, the paper explores different file formats and parallel I/O via MPI-IO (a standard library that distributes file-reading work across multiple processors). It introduces OO_MPI_IO, a C++ tool that simplifies parallel I/O programming by hiding MPI-IO's complexity. The tool also helps teach Amdahl's and Gustafson's Laws, which describe how speedup improves when computational work is distributed across processors.
sc-2024-018.key_novelty: OO_MPI_IO is a C++ abstraction layer that simplifies parallel file reading by hiding MPI-IO complexity behind easy-to-use interfaces.

sc-2024-025.method: The system applies three optimization techniques—fusing loops together, reordering loop execution, and accumulating results in fast local memory—to reduce GPU idle time waiting for data. These techniques are implemented using Kokkos, a framework that allows the same code to run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs without modification. To guide these optimizations, the system measures actual execution time and data transfer volume, then selects the combination that improves performance on each GPU type.
sc-2024-025.key_novelty: A metric that measures real execution time and data transfer volume to identify which optimizations work best across different GPU brands.

sc-2024-028.method: The researchers used micro-benchmarks—simple tests of basic GPU operations—to understand Ponte Vecchio's capabilities, then validated that these results predicted performance on four test programs whose behavior was already well-understood. They measured performance on single nodes from Aurora and Dawn, two production systems with Ponte Vecchio GPUs, using the same tests on NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI250 GPUs to directly compare results. They also ran actual applications on large Intel GPU systems to demonstrate that these benchmarking insights have practical value.
sc-2024-028.key_novelty: This is the first measurement of Intel Ponte Vecchio GPU performance on actual production systems (Aurora and Dawn), compared directly against NVIDIA H100 and AMD MI250 GPUs under the same testing conditions.

sc-2024-029.method: The approach uses four coordinated techniques to reduce communication costs and memory constraints in large-scale graph search. Forest pruning eliminates vertices that won't contribute to the search, shrinking the work. Group reordering and multilevel bitmap compression (packing data more densely in memory) both reduce memory required per search step, enabling fewer computer nodes to handle larger graphs. Adaptive parameter tuning automatically finds the best algorithm settings.
sc-2024-029.key_novelty: The core insight is combining forest pruning (removing unneeded vertices) with multilevel bitmap compression (densely packing data) to simultaneously shrink the search space and memory needs, enabling the algorithm to scale to hundreds of thousands of compute nodes.

sc-2024-031.method: The approach trains a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO—a neural network that works in frequency space rather than processing raw physical coordinates) to learn how 2D turbulent flows evolve over time, using simulation data as examples. Instead of running expensive numerical solvers for each prediction, the trained model can forecast flow behavior much faster. The researchers then determine exactly how much training data and what time-step resolution the model needs to maintain accuracy and physical realism over long forecasting periods.
sc-2024-031.key_novelty: Fourier Neural Operators can effectively replace traditional numerical solvers for turbulence simulation, with systematic determination of the data volume and time resolution required for stable, accurate long-term predictions.

sc-2024-026.method: Fine-grain data blocking in BrickLib arranges stencil computation data in small blocks matched to access patterns, which reduces the amount of data that must move between memory and processing cores during geometric multigrid V-cycles (multi-resolution solvers). By measuring real-world performance with empirical linear models—mathematical equations that capture memory latency, communication overhead, bandwidth, and throughput—the researchers understand how stencil computations and MPI communication affect overall performance. Testing on NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPU supercomputers shows that this approach maintains consistent performance across different hardware types and scales efficiently when using multiple GPUs.
sc-2024-026.key_novelty: Fine-grain data blocking—organizing stencil data in small, strategically-arranged chunks—reduces data movement in geometric multigrid V-cycles and improves performance portability across different GPU architectures (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel).

sc-2024-020.method: The framework combines two tools: Hecate, which uses deep reinforcement learning (learning through trial-and-error) and traffic classification to find the best paths for data based on live traffic patterns, and PolKA, a source routing tool that dynamically sends data flows along those chosen paths. Hecate continuously watches traffic, learns which paths work best, and updates its decisions to improve routing. The combination was tested on a real network using P4 (a programmable network switch standard) to verify the approach works in practice.
sc-2024-020.key_novelty: The core idea is that machine-learning traffic control (Hecate) and source routing (PolKA) work together on real networks, letting networks automatically optimize their own routing based on traffic patterns.

sc-2024-037.method: The paper solves this by introducing a dynamic heuristic—a decision rule that adapts based on threshold times (Tn), which mark decision points for when to schedule exactly n checkpoints. It then uses dynamic programming (a technique for optimization that breaks problems into smaller overlapping subproblems) applied to a discretized time grid to find the mathematically optimal checkpoint placements with no restrictions. The method is tested through simulations comparing it against Young/Daly periodic checkpointing, the traditional baseline.
sc-2024-037.key_novelty: The core innovation is a dynamic programming approach with threshold-based checkpoint scheduling that finds optimal strategies by adapting the checkpoint times flexibly, rather than forcing them into periodic intervals or requiring checkpoints at fixed points like the reservation end.

sc-2024-033.method: They measured actual GPU activity across thousands of processors in NERSC's Perlmutter supercomputer while it ran real scientific workloads. They used roofline analysis—a method that identifies whether a machine is bottlenecked by computing power or memory bandwidth—to map where each workload fell. They measured both how precisely numbers were stored and how much actual computation happened per chunk of data fetched from memory, then compared these against the machine's physical limits.
sc-2024-033.key_novelty: They applied roofline analysis across an entire supercomputer's GPU population running real production workloads, rather than testing individual applications in isolation.

sc-2024-030.method: Develops spline-based matrix-solving operations in the Kokkos-kernels library, optimizing them to handle many equations with different right-hand sides together (batched processing). It merges multiple calculation steps into single operations to reduce data movement between memory levels (kernel fusion) and uses sparse matrix storage to only store and compute with non-zero values. The code runs efficiently on NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI250X GPUs while maintaining reasonable CPU performance, making it portable across different hardware.
sc-2024-030.key_novelty: It applies kernel fusion (merging operations to reduce data transfer) and sparse matrix storage (storing only non-zero values) to efficiently solve many matrix equations at once in Kokkos-kernels.

sc-2024-035.method: The method creates a neural network layer that shares information between connected data points, and it works even when a mesh (connected grid of points representing physical space) is split across multiple computers. It uses 'halo nodes'—extra boundary points connecting the separate sections—to properly handle information at partition edges. The system integrates with NekRS, an exascale fluid dynamics solver (software for large-scale physics simulations), so distributed neural network training and inference naturally align with the mesh's partitioning. By carefully handling boundary information during message passing, the system ensures identical results whether the neural network runs on one computer or distributed across many.
sc-2024-035.key_novelty: The core innovation is using halo nodes—boundary points in neural message passing—to ensure that graph neural networks distributed across multiple computers produce mathematically identical results to centralized versions, while scaling to billions of connected data points.

sc-2024-027.method: MCBound learns from 2.2 million historical job runs on Supercomputer Fugaku, identifying which ones were limited by how fast they could move data versus how fast they could compute. It then builds machine learning models based on these patterns and uses them to predict, as you submit a new job, whether it will be bottlenecked by data movement (memory-bound) or processor speed (compute-bound). These predictions are accurate 89% of the time (F1-macro score of 0.89, a standard metric for classification accuracy), with negligible added system burden.
sc-2024-027.key_novelty: MCBound automatically predicts at submission time whether a job will be limited by data movement or computing power, learning from patterns in past runs without needing user intervention.

sc-2024-034.method: MDLoader automatically chooses the best communication strategy for moving data across computers during neural network training, using Tree of Parzen Estimators (a technique that efficiently predicts which strategies work best under different conditions) to decide at training startup. The system learned that collective communication—sending identical messages to all computers—works best with large mini-batches and few computers, while one-sided communication—sending targeted messages to specific computers—is faster at larger scales. It picks whichever strategy fits your configuration.
sc-2024-034.key_novelty: MDLoader dynamically selects between one-sided and collective communication using Tree of Parzen Estimators to predict which strategy will be fastest.

sc-2024-038.method: The researchers added zero-copy support to OpenMP (a framework for parallel programming), which allows GPUs to read directly from unified memory (memory that both the CPU and GPU can access) without needing explicit data transfers. They tested this on MI300A APUs (AMD processors that combine CPU and GPU on one chip) using real production applications and SPECaccel 2023 benchmarks, comparing its performance against the traditional approach of copying data explicitly before GPU computation.
sc-2024-038.key_novelty: The authors measured zero-copy memory access on MI300A APUs and found its performance benefits vary significantly depending on the application type.

sc-2024-032.method: CUDASTF is a C++ library where you describe your computation as a task graph—specifying which tasks depend on which other tasks' data—and it automatically distributes those tasks across multiple GPUs with fine-grained placement control. It uses events—signals that fire when data is ready—to coordinate task execution. The library can transparently switch between CUDA Streams (traditional sequential GPU work) and CUDA Graphs (pre-optimized sequences of operations), preferring Graphs for small tasks where they're more efficient.
sc-2024-032.key_novelty: It bridges your task-level code with GPU optimizations using events (signals that fire when data is ready), enabling automatic and efficient execution across multiple GPUs without manual work distribution.

sc-2024-039.method: To create a complete Linux system for RISC-V processors, the approach systematically establishes the filesystem hierarchy (the directory structure Linux needs to run), develops a cross-compiler (a compiler that runs on standard computers but generates code for RISC-V), and uses it to bootstrap an initial system on the target platform. A native GCC compiler (one that compiles directly on RISC-V) is then installed on the bootstrapped system. Finally, a custom Python script automates the Koji build system (a tool for compiling and packaging software) to rebuild all necessary packages for the complete Linux environment.
sc-2024-039.key_novelty: A custom Python automation tool manages Koji builds to rebuild the entire Linux software ecosystem for RV64G.

sc-2024-040.method: The approach trains neural networks on sparsely sampled simulation data (recording only certain locations and times) to learn how to reconstruct the complete dataset. It uses a two-stage training process—pretraining for general patterns, then fine-tuning for specific data—balancing storage requirements, training time, and reconstruction speed. The networks generalize to timesteps and grid resolutions never seen during training, outperforming traditional Delaunay triangulation-based interpolation in quality, speed, and reliability.
sc-2024-040.key_novelty: Neural networks can reconstruct full spatiotemporal datasets from sparsely sampled data and generalize to timesteps and grid resolutions they never saw during training.

sc-2024-041.method: PRIF creates a standardized set of procedures that any Fortran compiler can call and any runtime library can implement, decoupling the compiler from being locked into one specific runtime library. The design supports both shared-memory systems (where processes on the same machine access the same memory) and distributed-memory systems (where processes on different machines communicate over a network), while remaining portable across different operating systems, toolchains, and hardware architectures. Caffeine is provided as a prototype implementation.
sc-2024-041.key_novelty: A standardized interface that lets any Fortran compiler work with any parallel runtime library, making parallel Fortran code portable across different high-performance computing systems.

sc-2024-044.method: The INTERSECT Open Architecture integrates resources across organizations using microservices—small, independent software components that each handle one specific task. The framework includes a toolkit that provides templates and abstracts technical complexity, allowing developers to focus on what each component should accomplish rather than wrestling with integration details. This approach connects experimental instruments, computing resources, and data management systems through reusable components to create integrated ecosystems across multiple scientific facilities.
sc-2024-044.key_novelty: A toolkit that uses microservices (small independent software components) to let diverse scientific facilities across different institutions connect their experimental instruments, computing resources, and data systems.

sc-2024-049.method: The authors created a plugin for Flang (Fortran's compiler component in LLVM) that automatically detects Fortran language features by analyzing the parse tree—the structured breakdown of code that compilers create when reading source files. The plugin works by searching through this parse tree for specific patterns that mark each language feature. They tested the plugin on four applications, comparing its results to manual expert analysis of three applications to verify accuracy and discover features the experts had missed.
sc-2024-049.key_novelty: Automatically finding which Fortran language features code uses by analyzing its parse tree, eliminating the need for experts to manually identify them.

sc-2024-045.method: The authors run MLPerf HPC's DeepCAM benchmark—a standardized test of machine learning workloads—across different hardware platforms to measure how efficiently AI systems use energy. They identify specific problems with how AI software frameworks integrate with traditional supercomputers (HPC systems), and they document why measuring actual power consumption is difficult and unreliable across supercomputers and virtualized systems.
sc-2024-045.key_novelty: They systematically measure AI energy efficiency on supercomputers using standard benchmarks and provide practical configuration recommendations for sustainable AI.

sc-2024-046.method: Intel SHMEM puts OpenSHMEM-style communication functions (a standard way for different parts of a system to send messages to each other) directly into GPU kernels using SYCL (a programming framework for writing code that runs on graphics processors). This means GPUs can initiate their own communication without needing the main CPU to coordinate. The system automatically picks the best method for moving data based on what's available: either reading and writing memory directly from the GPU, or using a GPU copy engine (specialized hardware that transfers data). They also added extensions that let multiple threads running on the same GPU collaborate on communication operations.
sc-2024-046.key_novelty: GPU kernels can now directly call OpenSHMEM communication functions using SYCL, with extensions that enable multiple GPU threads to collaborate.

sc-2024-047.method: The researchers tested the Jacobi iterative method (a technique that repeatedly updates values based on neighbors to solve equations) on a Tenstorrent Grayskull e150 accelerator. They optimized the code for the Grayskull's Tensix cores, which separate data movement from computation. They then benchmarked single and multiple accelerators against Xeon Platinum CPUs, measuring both performance and energy consumption.
sc-2024-047.key_novelty: RISC-V-based PCIe accelerators can match CPU performance on stencil computations (updating grid cells based on neighboring values) while using 5x less energy.

sc-2024-036.method: The system's code generator combines multiple GPU operations into persistent kernels—GPU programs designed to stay running and coordinate their execution without waiting for the CPU. These kernels use NVSHMEM (a library enabling GPU-to-GPU communication) to transfer data between devices directly. Accessible through Python, this lets multi-GPU systems execute autonomously, with GPUs independently organizing their computation and data flow.
sc-2024-036.key_novelty: The innovation is compiler support enabling autonomous multi-GPU execution, where GPUs independently manage their own computation and data transfers.

sc-2024-042.method: ExaDigiT combines three modules: a power simulator modeling electricity consumption under different workloads, a heat-and-coolant-flow model predicting how temperature and cooling liquid change over time, and an augmented reality visualizer. Using six months of Frontier supercomputer data for validation, it forecasts energy consumption (including losses from power conversion like rectification and voltage regulation) for real or synthetic workloads.
sc-2024-042.key_novelty: ExaDigiT is a digital twin—a computer model of hardware behavior—combining power simulation, temperature and coolant-flow modeling, and energy loss prediction for liquid-cooled exascale supercomputers.

sc-2024-052.method: The system uses two specialized processors working together: an FPGA (customizable hardware designed for specific tasks) accelerates the sampling stage—selecting relevant data points from the graph—while the GPU handles neural network training. Graph sampling normally becomes a bottleneck on GPU systems because graph data doesn't parallelize efficiently on standard GPUs, so moving this computation to an FPGA that can handle it better eliminates the slowdown. Sampled data flows directly from FPGA memory to GPU memory through PCIe peer-to-peer communication (a fast direct link between the two chips), bypassing the CPU and avoiding communication overhead. This allows the GPU to focus purely on training while the FPGA continuously feeds it prepared data.
sc-2024-052.key_novelty: The core innovation is using an FPGA to accelerate graph sampling and connecting it directly to the GPU through PCIe peer-to-peer communication, eliminating the CPU bottleneck that limits GPU-only graph neural network training.

sc-2024-048.method: PipeInfer speeds up language model inference by running multiple predictions in parallel. While computing the next word, it simultaneously makes several guesses about the following words. When a guess turns out to be wrong (because the actual next word doesn't match what was guessed), the system cancels that speculation mid-computation rather than finishing it wastefully—this is called early inference cancellation. The pipeline structure organizes all these parallel predictions sequentially through processing stages, reducing the time between generating each word and keeping the hardware busy even when most guesses fail.
sc-2024-048.key_novelty: By canceling wrong predictions mid-computation and organizing speculative inference as a pipeline, the system can generate text faster even when most guesses are incorrect.

sc-2024-043.method: Different GPU and CPU vendors (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) each have their own way to measure and report power consumption and performance metrics. hws creates a unified layer on top of all these vendor-specific interfaces, so one piece of code can collect the same measurements—power draw, total energy use, clock speeds, memory consumption, and hardware utilization—on any vendor's hardware. It's written in Python and C++ to work with different software environments. The authors tested it on real AI scenarios: finding optimal training settings for neural networks and running machine learning algorithms on GPUs.
sc-2024-043.key_novelty: hws is a vendor-independent library that lets you measure power consumption and performance metrics the same way across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs and CPUs.

sc-2024-050.method: SurePath adds a separate backup network pathway called an Up/Down escape subnetwork that runs alongside standard routing. When a physical link or node fails, packets automatically reroute through this backup pathway, which uses hierarchical routing (moving up then down through the network layers) that prevents deadlock—situations where packets get stuck in circular waits. This ensures reliable packet delivery even when the network experiences failures.
sc-2024-050.key_novelty: The core idea is pairing standard routing with an Up/Down escape subnetwork to simultaneously prevent deadlock (packets getting stuck in circular waits) and tolerate network failures in HyperX networks.

sc-2024-053.method: A security testbed embedded directly in live traffic at NCSA's supercomputer learns attack patterns from 200+ documented security incidents collected over two decades. Operators use a visualization tool to identify genuine threats amid the constant stream of false alarms. The system deploys statistical models (Factor Graphs, which map relationships between suspicious behaviors to calculate attack likelihood) to detect and preempt real-world ransomware families before they compromise the system in real-time.
sc-2024-053.key_novelty: Using statistical models (Factor Graphs) to automatically distinguish real attacks from false alarms in live supercomputer traffic and preempt ransomware before system compromise.

sc-2024-051.method: The paper maps out how attackers can compromise Jupyter Notebooks—interactive computing systems used for AI research—by identifying specific entry points (terminal access, file browser, malicious code in notebooks) and the types of attacks they enable (data theft, ransomware, unauthorized mining, security mistakes). It identifies a critical detection gap: Jupyter's encrypted network connections hide traffic from monitoring tools like Zeek, making attacks invisible to standard security systems. The paper proposes better auditing mechanisms to see inside Jupyter's traffic and discusses cryptographic designs that will remain secure against future quantum computers.
sc-2024-051.key_novelty: The paper provides the first comprehensive catalog of attacks on Jupyter Notebooks and proposes improved ways to see and audit what's happening inside them.

sc-2024-056.method: The technique bundles multiple messages together, which cuts the overhead of sending each one separately. It also considers where data lives in shared memory and places messages close to their destination (a strategy called locality awareness) to speed up delivery. By combining message batching with memory-aware placement, the approach reduces both the per-message overhead and end-to-end message latency. Validation used proxy applications that simulate realistic HPC workloads.
sc-2024-056.key_novelty: Message aggregation jointly optimizes for message latency and per-message overhead by accounting for shared memory characteristics.

sc-2024-058.method: The team redesigned the cluster infrastructure to better manage different hardware types. They replaced the job scheduling system to more effectively match computing tasks with available resources. They created new billing and resource allocation rules to ensure fair distribution of computing time across different research groups.
sc-2024-058.key_novelty: The paper documents how a real research institution successfully transitioned its computing cluster to handle diverse hardware types fairly and schedule jobs more efficiently.

sc-2024-062.method: LLM-Inference-Bench tests how fast large language models (specifically LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen models at 7 billion and 70 billion parameters) run on different specialized hardware accelerators—Nvidia GPUs, AMD GPUs, Intel Habana, and SambaNova chips—using various inference frameworks (the software that controls how the model executes). It measures the speed and resource efficiency of each hardware-software combination. An interactive dashboard lets you quickly see and compare results to find which configuration works best for your needs.
sc-2024-062.key_novelty: A benchmarking system that measures and compares LLM inference performance across different hardware accelerators and software frameworks, presenting results in an interactive dashboard.

sc-2024-059.method: The authors replace FIRAL's exact calculations with simpler approximations that reduce storage from O(c²d² + nc²d) to O(n(d+c) + cd²) and computation from O(c³(nd² + bd³ + bn)) to O(bncd²), while keeping the same prediction accuracy. To speed things up further, they implement this on GPUs working together in parallel. They then validate their approach using strong and weak scaling tests on large-scale vision datasets to show it scales well.
sc-2024-059.key_novelty: The core idea is to approximate FIRAL's calculations so it uses dramatically less memory and computation while maintaining prediction accuracy, enabling practical deployment across multi-GPU systems with million-point datasets.

sc-2024-060.method: They extended the Structural Simulation Toolkit (SST)—a simulator for supercomputer systems—to model different ways of synchronizing gradient data across many computers. They tested three synchronization approaches (Rabenseifner, ring, dissemination) and two barrier types (centralized and decentralized) across six network layouts and varying message sizes. This allowed them to measure which combinations performed best without having to run experiments on actual supercomputers.
sc-2024-060.key_novelty: SST was extended to systematically compare different synchronization algorithms across multiple network designs, measuring the performance advantage of algorithms that keep data movement local within the network.

sc-2024-057.method: Instead of NCCL collective communication (the standard synchronized approach where all GPUs coordinate and reshape data), they use PGAS-style one-sided asynchronous messages where each GPU directly sends data to others without waiting. They build this into a custom CUDA embedding retrieval backend for PyTorch. This asynchronous approach eliminates synchronization overhead (the cost of GPUs waiting) and data restructuring costs (rearranging data).
sc-2024-057.key_novelty: Replace collective communication with PGAS-style one-sided asynchronous messaging (where each GPU directly sends data without waiting for coordination) for multi-GPU embedding retrieval.

sc-2024-054.method: The authors compiled a production solar-simulation program using Fortran 'do concurrent' loops—a standard way to mark code for parallel execution. They ran it on GPUs from three vendors (NVIDIA, Intel, AMD) across both expensive data-center and cheaper consumer models, measuring how fast it ran. They tracked how each platform managed memory: whether it used unified memory (GPU automatically accessing CPU data) or needed explicit directives (manual instructions to move data between GPU and CPU). This revealed which memory strategy each vendor required for correct and fast execution.
sc-2024-054.key_novelty: First test of whether Fortran 'do concurrent' works the same way on NVIDIA, Intel, and AMD GPUs with a production solar-simulation application.

sc-2024-055.method: The implementation uses two parallel strategies for Barnes-Hut: an unbalanced octree (a 3D spatial hierarchy) that handles concurrent updates directly, and a balanced bounding-volume hierarchy (a tree of spatial boxes) pre-sorted by Hilbert spacefilling curve (which orders points while preserving spatial locality). Both use ISO C++ standard parallel algorithms with atomic synchronization primitives (specialized operations that prevent concurrent threads from interfering with each other), with each approach trading off GPU acceleration versus CPU efficiency to achieve competitive performance.
sc-2024-055.key_novelty: C++ Standard Parallelism's execution policies (particularly par) effectively optimize irregular tree-based algorithms (with unpredictable memory-access patterns) across heterogeneous CPUs and GPUs.

sc-2024-066.method: The curriculum teaches parallelization concepts through n-body simulations (calculating how many objects move under each other's gravitational forces). Bachelor students code galaxy collisions in C++ using Git and remote development, which teaches them how code complexity grows as problems get bigger. Master students parallelize solar system simulations using OpenMP (to speed up code by splitting the work within one computer) and MPI (to speed up code by splitting work across many computers), with the option to add GPU acceleration, molecular dynamics simulations, and interactive visualization.
sc-2024-066.key_novelty: N-body simulations form a single educational framework that teaches sequential programming, parallelization, and distributed computing through a visually compelling problem.

sc-2024-063.method: CoaXial replaces the standard memory connections (DDR) between processors and memory with CXL, which sends 4 times as much data through each connection pin. While CXL takes longer to respond (higher latency), servers with many cores making concurrent memory requests experience overall speedup because the extra bandwidth clears the queue of waiting requests much faster than the latency delay hurts performance.
sc-2024-063.key_novelty: Use CXL, which sends 4 times more data through each connection pin, as the main memory interface for servers instead of DDR, accepting slower responses to gain much more bandwidth.

sc-2024-068.method: The approach builds a performance model to predict how efficiently a scientific workflow will run. THman, an open-source scheduler, uses the Highest Contribution First (HCF) heuristic—a decision rule that prioritizes whichever computing or storage task will make the biggest difference to overall speed. THman makes these scheduling decisions in real-time while coordinating both computing resources and multi-tier storage systems (different storage layers optimized for different speeds and costs), and it integrates with existing HPC batch schedulers so it doesn't require replacing systems already in place.
sc-2024-068.key_novelty: THman jointly schedules when computing and storage tasks run (co-scheduling) while still working within existing HPC batch schedulers instead of replacing them.

sc-2024-064.method: The researchers modified Score-P (a tool that measures how fast parallel programs run) by adding a timing system that counts computational work instead of measuring elapsed time, which avoids noise from system interference. They tested three different methods to count work: tracking how many times OpenMP (a parallel programming standard) loops execute, counting individual instructions and instruction groups called basic blocks in LLVM compiler code, and reading hardware performance counters built into the CPU. They validated this approach by measuring MPI+OpenMP programs (which combine two parallel programming standards) and analyzing the results with Scalasca, a tool that visualizes performance traces.
sc-2024-064.key_novelty: A logical clock (work counter) in Score-P that eliminates performance measurement noise by tracking computational work instead of elapsed time.

sc-2024-065.method: The approach uses RFC8925—a standard allowing devices to disable IPv4 support—paired with RFC6145 (a translation algorithm) to maintain connectivity over IPv6 alone. For devices that cannot make this transition, it serves deliberately configured DNS records (called poisoned records) that explain why they cannot access the IPv6-only network. The system was deployed on the SC24v6 wireless network with safeguards to minimize disruption to devices supporting both IPv4 and IPv6, or those with RFC8925 support.
sc-2024-065.key_novelty: The core innovation is using poisoned DNS records—deliberately configured responses—to tell IPv4-only clients why they cannot access an IPv6-only network.

sc-2024-070.method: Students in small groups used a deck of playing cards to physically simulate parallel computation, dividing the sorting task among group members and measuring how much faster they completed it together versus one person working alone. This hands-on experience showed them directly how adding more 'workers' initially speeds things up, but the speedup diminishes as the group grows—a core principle of parallelization. The activity was tested across seven courses at five institutions during 2023-2024, with surveys administered before and after to measure students' understanding.
sc-2024-070.key_novelty: Teaching how parallel computing and performance scaling work through hands-on card-sorting group activities instead of traditional lectures.

sc-2024-061.method: The researchers tested different configuration settings for LLVM/OpenMP (the runtime system that executes parallel programs on multi-core CPUs) to see how they affected performance. They ran six benchmark programs (NAS Parallel Benchmarks, Barcelona OpenMP Task Suite, XSBench, RSBench, SU3Bench, LULESH) on three CPU architectures and collected 240,000 performance measurements showing how CPU type, program type, input size, thread count, and environment variables affected speed. Machine learning (using Linear Models) found patterns in these measurements and generated recommendations for which settings work best on different CPUs.
sc-2024-061.key_novelty: By analyzing 240,000 measurements across three CPU architectures and six benchmarks, the study determines which LLVM/OpenMP runtime settings perform best and derives optimal default configurations for each CPU type.

sc-2024-067.method: The paper evaluates Linux's current support for heterogeneous processors (systems with different types of cores) and documents the problems that arise when trying to add this support to PAPI, a performance measurement library. It identifies the specific challenges in tracking performance counters—low-level measurements of operations like cache misses—across cores with different capabilities. The paper then proposes solutions to extend PAPI's infrastructure so it can accurately measure performance on all these different core types.
sc-2024-067.key_novelty: PAPI supports heterogeneous processors by adapting how it tracks performance across different core types.

sc-2024-069.method: Each airline trains a predictive maintenance model on their own turbofan engine data from the NASA Turbofan Jet Engine Dataset (N-CMAPSS), then shares only the model updates (the patterns the model learned, not raw data) with a central aggregator. These updates are combined into a global model that improves using everyone's data while keeping each airline's operational information private. The system repeats this cycle—sending the improved global model back, receiving new local updates—until the model stops improving.
sc-2024-069.key_novelty: Airlines can collaboratively train a predictive maintenance model on the NASA Turbofan Jet Engine Dataset (N-CMAPSS) by having each airline train locally and only share learned model updates, preserving the privacy of their operational data.

sc-2024-072.method: The team adds an improved electron-interaction model (the self-consistent GW approximation, which accounts for how electrons affect each other) to QuaTrEx, a computational tool that simulates charge flow through transistors from first-principles physics using density functional theory (which predicts electron behavior) and Non-equilibrium Green's Function methods (which handle electron motion through devices). The simulations handle transistors with 10,560 atoms on GPU-accelerated supercomputers using parallel algorithms tuned for both weak scaling (more processors on the same problem) and strong scaling (more processors on larger problems).
sc-2024-072.key_novelty: The approach combines an improved many-body electron model (the self-consistent GW approximation) with first-principles quantum transport simulations, enabling nanoelectronic device modeling at exascale (supercomputer scale).

sc-2024-079.method: The framework watches each application's input/output operations in detail and simultaneously measures what the storage system is doing. It trains a machine learning model—a system that learns patterns from data—to understand how applications competing for the same storage resources interfere with each other. The trained model can then predict whether interference will occur and estimate how much each application's performance will suffer.
sc-2024-079.key_novelty: This method predicts how applications interfere with each other in shared HPC storage by tracking detailed I/O operations and using machine learning to find the patterns that cause slowdowns.

sc-2024-075.method: The researchers adapt Octo-Tiger—an astrophysics simulation built with HPX and Kokkos (C++ frameworks for parallel programming)—that models multiple physical systems in 3D with adaptive mesh refinement (uneven spatial partitioning that concentrates computation where it matters most), to run on RISC-V processors. They use std::experimental::simd, a C++ interface that exploits RISC-V's vector extension (hardware that processes multiple data values simultaneously) with variable-length vector support (adjusting to the processor's native width) and vector-chaining (efficiently linking multiple vector operations). They measure performance, scalability, and power consumption on RISC-V single board computers and directly compare the results against A64FX systems, an established Arm-based HPC processor.
sc-2024-075.key_novelty: This work provides the first thorough test of RISC-V vector processors on a real, production-grade HPC astrophysics application using HPX and Kokkos (modern C++ frameworks).

sc-2024-071.method: CANARI continuously monitors whether cluster nodes are working and runs test programs (synthetic benchmarks) to measure how fast each node performs. It stores the test results in a database and compares each node's current speed against its normal baseline to identify slowdowns. When nodes show degraded performance, the system automatically stops using them and sends alerts and summary reports to administrators through Slack.
sc-2024-071.key_novelty: CANARI combines continuous performance monitoring, automated detection of node slowdowns, and immediate Slack alerts into a single system that helps cluster administrators fix problems proactively.

sc-2024-081.method: The UCIS4EQ platform uses PyCOMPSs (a framework for coordinating parallel computations) to build workflows that can adapt as new seismic data arrives during execution. While 3D earthquake simulations run simultaneously across multiple computers (HPC jobs), the system continuously monitors for updates to earthquake measurements and incorporates them into the ongoing calculations without stopping. This maintains both computational efficiency and the consistency of results.
sc-2024-081.key_novelty: The key innovation is a workflow capable of adjusting itself in real-time as new earthquake data arrives, reducing the computational resources required by 40% while keeping the time to deliver results the same.

sc-2024-080.method: The researchers implemented the power method algorithm (a stencil code that updates grid values based on neighboring cells) using several different modern C++ shared memory programming models, which are different ways to write parallel code where multiple threads work with shared memory. For each implementation, they benchmarked both the ease of expressing the algorithm in code and the computational performance, revealing the practical tradeoffs between different approaches.
sc-2024-080.key_novelty: This work compares different modern C++ shared memory programming models (ways of writing parallel code where threads access shared data) to reveal which approach best balances ease of coding with runtime speed for stencil algorithms.

sc-2024-083.method: They ran experiments applying data compression techniques to volume rendering (visualizing 3D scientific data as semi-transparent, colored volumes). They tested how characteristics of the original data, along with the transparency and color settings in your visualization, affect image quality across different compression levels.
sc-2024-083.key_novelty: They systematically tested what people actually see when viewing compressed volume renderings, rather than just relying on mathematical compression error measurements.

sc-2024-076.method: The researchers benchmarked four Intel Xeon processor generations (Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids, and Sierra Forest) using bandwidth-bound applications—workloads that slow down waiting for data from memory rather than due to processor speed. They measured the runtime and energy consumption of each processor, then compared results across generations to evaluate the impact of new features like on-package HBM (high-speed memory built into the processor) and efficiency-focused processor variants.
sc-2024-076.key_novelty: This work provides a comprehensive empirical benchmark of recent Intel Xeon processor generations, including models with on-package HBM and efficiency-focused variants, on bandwidth-bound applications.

sc-2024-078.method: The approach generates training data on-the-fly during learning instead of pre-computing everything, with Melissa handling the streaming pipeline and Breed selecting which simulations to generate. Breed analyzes training loss statistics to find where the model performs poorly, then focuses new simulations on those difficult regions of the parameter space. It uses Adaptive Multiple Importance Sampling (AMIS: a technique that reweights simulation candidates as the model learns). The neural network learns to predict specified timesteps into the future for any combination of initial and boundary conditions.
sc-2024-078.key_novelty: Combining training loss statistics with Adaptive Multiple Importance Sampling (a technique that reweights simulation candidates based on learning progress) to intelligently select which simulations to generate, focusing computational effort on parameter space regions where the model performs poorly.

sc-2024-082.method: The work examines how data accesses repeat in specific mathematical patterns when programs access memory, using symmetric group theory (mathematical rules describing patterns that remain consistent under transformations). Instead of just studying known patterns like cyclic loops and sawtooth patterns, it generalizes them to work with any repeating access sequence. The researchers built a framework that compilers and machine learning tools can use to predict memory behavior and optimize how data moves between cache and main memory.
sc-2024-082.key_novelty: The work generalizes re-traversal patterns (repeated ways of accessing data) using symmetric group theory to create a single framework that characterizes and optimizes memory performance, rather than treating each known pattern separately.

sc-2024-074.method: The system pairs protein sequences with text descriptions of their chemical properties, then trains a generative model using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)—a machine learning method that learns by comparing pairs where one sequence is better than another. It incorporates data from actual lab experiments and computer simulations to teach the model which sequences work best. Mixed-precision computing (using different numeric precision levels for speed) across distributed supercomputers enables ExaFLOPS-scale sustained performance (a million trillion calculations per second).
sc-2024-074.key_novelty: This is the first application of Direct Preference Optimization to protein design using both text descriptions and sequences, achieving sustained ExaFLOPS-scale performance (a million trillion calculations per second) across multiple diverse supercomputers.

sc-2024-073.method: DFTracer watches data flowing in and out at every layer of the system—from the AI framework down to the operating system. To handle the millions of events it captures, it uses an optimized storage format that can load them all back in just seconds. It then tags each I/O operation (data read or write) with high-level workflow context—showing what task it belongs to and what work was happening—so you can connect performance problems back to the actual work, not just raw data patterns.
sc-2024-073.key_novelty: DFTracer traces data across all layers of AI systems while tagging I/O operations with their high-level workflow context, enabling performance analysis that existing tools cannot provide.

sc-2024-077.method: The authors optimize a computational kernel called MILC-Dslash for NVIDIA A100 GPUs using SYCL. They test different parallel strategies: varying how work is indexed and grouped (work-item ordering and work-group sizes), how memory is accessed, and which coordination methods to use (atomic operations—where multiple cores safely modify shared data—and synchronization barriers—points where the code waits for all cores). They measure how different choices affect performance, testing factors like atomic operations, shared variables, divergent instructions (when different cores run different code paths), and using SyclCPLX for complex numbers and SYCLomatic to guide decisions.
sc-2024-077.key_novelty: The key finding is that on NVIDIA A100 GPUs, different ways to organize parallel work (work-item indexing, work-group sizing, and memory patterns) have large performance effects, and keeping the GPU cores fully busy is more important than maximizing concurrent tasks.

sc-2024-084.method: Instead of using expensive switches with many connections (called high-radix switches), this approach builds high-speed communication networks directly into a wafer-scale chip structured according to the Dragonfly topology—a proven network design. The routing uses both shortest-path and longer-path algorithms that are guaranteed to avoid deadlock (where data gets stuck waiting in circles) and only requires one extra virtual channel (a logical communication pathway). By embedding the network directly in the chip itself, it eliminates expensive external switching hardware while maintaining all the performance advantages of the Dragonfly structure.
sc-2024-084.key_novelty: It replaces expensive high-radix switches (switches with many ports) with communication networks embedded directly in a wafer-scale chip, while maintaining the proven Dragonfly topology structure.

sc-2024-086.method: The approach reduces communication between GPUs by compressing embedding data—learned representations of users and products—using lossy compression (allowing small, controlled errors). Rather than using a fixed compression level throughout training, it adapts the compression strength separately for each embedding table and each training iteration, enabling more aggressive compression where the model can tolerate errors and less where accuracy matters. The compression and decompression are optimized to run directly on GPUs using PyTorch's tensor operations, minimizing any overhead.
sc-2024-086.key_novelty: It adjusts compression error limits separately for each embedding table and each training step instead of using one fixed compression level.

sc-2024-089.method: Lamellar is a high-performance computing runtime written in Rust that lets developers write distributed programs in a memory-safe way. It provides high-level abstractions—distributed arrays and active messages (a mechanism for sending computational tasks to remote machines)—that programmers use to express parallel work. All user code is written in safe Rust, while the runtime's rigorously tested code blocks handle the low-level unsafe operations that communication requires. Performance is validated by comparing execution speed against C, C++, and Chapel implementations running on the BALE kernel suite.
sc-2024-089.key_novelty: Lamellar is a Rust-based PGAS runtime that provides memory-safety guarantees while maintaining performance equal to unsafe C and C++ implementations.

sc-2024-087.method: Developers add directives (simple annotations) to their scientific code to mark where ML models can replace slow computational steps. The runtime system first executes the original algorithm to gather and prepare data through data assimilation. It can then dynamically replace those marked sections with fast ML predictions instead. This was tested across 5 benchmarks, evaluating over 5000 ML models to find the best options for each task.
sc-2024-087.key_novelty: A directive-based programming model that lets developers automatically switch between running the original algorithm or a fast ML prediction while the program executes.

sc-2024-090.method: The system simulates quantum circuits by representing them as networks of numerical arrays (tensors) and optimizing the computation at three levels—globally, at individual processing nodes, and at the device level. It distributes this work across 2304 graphics processors (GPUs) that collectively deliver 561 petaFLOPS of performance (561 quadrillion floating-point math operations per second). After the main computation, it uses post-processing to calculate XEB metrics, which measure how well a quantum processor performs.
sc-2024-090.key_novelty: Optimized classical tensor network simulation using thousands of GPUs achieves superior energy efficiency and speed compared to quantum processors.

sc-2024-093.method: The researchers collected real-world disk failure data from large-scale HPC storage systems (computer systems used for scientific computing) over five years, recording 5,000+ individual failures from 40,000+ disks. They examined these failures in three ways: when they happened over time, where they occurred in the storage system, and how one failure connected to or predicted others. This revealed patterns in how storage systems actually break down under real conditions—information that helps engineers design more reliable systems.
sc-2024-093.key_novelty: Five years of actual disk failure data from 40,000+ disks in production HPC systems reveals patterns that guide more reliable storage design.

sc-2024-085.method: UNR is a library that provides one unified interface for detecting when remote memory operations (data transfers between computers over a network) complete, regardless of what network hardware is being used. It works by gathering completion signals from multiple network adapters at once and coordinating between the software and the hardware. The library was tested by integrating it with PowerLLEL, a scientific application, and deploying it on four HPC systems that use different network technologies.
sc-2024-085.key_novelty: A unified library that tells programmers when remote memory transfers complete across different network types and multiple network adapters.

sc-2024-094.method: The research adapts Radical-Cybertools—a tool that manages ensembles (collections of related computational jobs that run together)—to work on Summit and Frontier supercomputers. It uses a pilot scheduler that divides the supercomputer's resources among multiple jobs simultaneously, rather than running one massive job at a time. The team tests this on three scientific applications: Chroma, NAMD, and LAMMPS, optimizing their performance. They develop data management strategies that follow the facility's operational constraints.
sc-2024-094.key_novelty: It enables production ensemble workflow management on leadership-class supercomputers by solving the integration challenges that arise when coordinating multiple related computational jobs alongside large-scale scientific applications.

sc-2024-088.method: Incoming RPC requests are intercepted by a Data Processing Unit (DPU), a specialized processor separate from the main CPU, which deserializes (converts from a compact binary format to usable objects) Protocol Buffers. This deserialization work no longer consumes host CPU cycles because it happens on the DPU instead. The processed data reaches the host where the application's business logic executes, freeing the CPU to do more valuable work.
sc-2024-088.key_novelty: Offloading Protocol Buffer deserialization to Data Processing Units (DPUs) eliminates this CPU overhead from the RPC datapath.

sc-2024-095.method: SurgeGuard is a decentralized system (one without a central coordinator) that manages computing resources for independent services called microservices. It works by understanding two things: how much slower each service can run before falling below its performance standards (called latency slack), and how the services communicate with each other. Using this knowledge, it rapidly detects when service quality will drop and intelligently allocates additional computing power during traffic spikes and network slowdowns.
sc-2024-095.key_novelty: By understanding how microservices communicate and their available timing margins, a system can rapidly detect quality failures and adjust resources without centralized control.

sc-2024-097.method: TCXL is a software library that adds ACID transaction support—data integrity guarantees—to CXL disaggregated memory (data on remote hardware connected via the CXL protocol rather than built into the processor). It deploys a backend controller that manages these transactions; this controller can run in three places: embedded in the CXL controller, as a standalone device, or on the host processor. The system supports both persistent memory transactions (data that survives power loss) and volatile in-memory transactions (regular RAM), with flexible resource management that adapts between these transaction types. It also integrates with the processor's Hardware Transactional Memory (the processor's built-in atomic operation mechanism), using hybrid execution that combines both hardware and software approaches.
sc-2024-097.key_novelty: TCXL is the first to provide ACID transaction support for CXL disaggregated memory without requiring changes to existing processor hardware.

sc-2024-091.method: AutoCheck automatically identifies which variables a program must save during checkpointing—the process of recording state to recover from crashes. It maps out how data flows through a program (building a data dependency graph, or DDG) by analyzing dependencies between variables and execution state. Using general-purpose heuristic rules on this map, it identifies which variables are critical to save. Programmers can identify necessary variables in minutes without specialized knowledge, and the approach was evaluated on 14 representative HPC benchmarks.
sc-2024-091.key_novelty: AutoCheck automatically identifies critical variables to checkpoint by systematically analyzing data dependencies using general heuristics, instead of requiring manual expert judgment.

sc-2024-098.method: The researchers asked over 100 people the same questions from a survey done ten years earlier, and compared the statistics from then and now to see what changed. They used large language models (AI systems trained to understand text and extract meaning from it) to automatically find patterns and insights in the interview transcripts. They also developed a toolkit that other researchers can use to assess research computing practices in the future.
sc-2024-098.key_novelty: This study revisited research computing practices by redoing a decade-old survey with new interviews and using AI to automatically find patterns in the results, revealing how researchers' use of computing resources has changed.

sc-2024-096.method: The researchers analyzed three years of actual network traffic from NERSC (a major supercomputing center) to understand how data moves and find bottlenecks. They tracked how data movement patterns changed over time and measured how much slower individual transfers become when multiple transfers compete for the same network resources.
sc-2024-096.key_novelty: Three years of NERSC network traffic analysis showing that data movement patterns have shifted, revealing infrastructure limitations when multiple transfers compete.

sc-2024-102.method: To understand why workflow performance varies unpredictably, the authors monitor what's happening at three system levels simultaneously: the job scheduler, the Dask.distributed workflow manager, and the operating system. They extend Dask.distributed with Mochi data services to track what each task does (task provenance), and they use Darshan to measure disk and network I/O precisely. By combining these three data streams, they can pinpoint where bottlenecks occur and whether results are reproducible.
sc-2024-102.key_novelty: They combine task provenance tracking (recording what each task does) with simultaneous performance measurements from three system levels—jobs, the workflow manager, and the operating system—to give a complete view of how Dask workflows run.

sc-2024-092.method: The authors develop Optimistic Tag Matching, a bin-based method (organizing messages into groups) for SmartNICs—network cards with built-in processors designed for parallel work, using simpler hardware than your main CPU. They analyze real MPI applications (programs that send messages between computers) and find most have short backlogs of waiting messages, making SmartNIC offloading practical. The method makes an optimistic guess about which message belongs where, fixes mistakes later in software if needed, and frees the CPU while matching messages at the same rate as traditional CPU-based approaches.
sc-2024-092.key_novelty: The key innovation is using optimistic guesses (make a fast match assumption, fix rare errors later) on SmartNICs to offload MPI message matching from the CPU while keeping speed and the ability to reprogram the logic.

sc-2024-100.method: The authors tested GPU power consumption in matrix multiplication operations by deliberately varying input data in four dimensions—value distribution, binary representation similarity, memory placement, and sparsity (how many empty values the matrices contain)—while keeping the matrix sizes constant.
