They measured the power consumption and found it varied by up to 40% based on the input data, which they attributed to differences in bit flip rates (how often bits switch between 0 and 1) in the GPU's hardware.
sc-2024-100.key_novelty: The content of input data—specifically its value distribution, binary patterns, memory placement, and sparsity—affects GPU power consumption in matrix multiplication with variations reaching up to 40%, creating new power-optimization opportunities.

sc-2024-107.method: SciTrust tests whether language models give reliable answers in science by creating question sets in four fields—Computer Science, Chemistry, Biology, and Physics—and running five different models on them. It checks each model's answers two ways: using traditional automatic scoring and having other language models evaluate truthfulness, accuracy, and whether models hallucinate (make up false details) or practice sycophancy (agree with incorrect claims). Finally, it measures how fast the models run and how they scale on high-performance computing systems.
sc-2024-107.key_novelty: SciTrust provides a way to test whether language models give trustworthy answers in science by checking them with both automatic metrics and AI-based evaluation across four scientific fields.

sc-2024-099.method: The system watches how much data is moving through Lustre (a shared file system used in computing clusters) right now and estimates how much storage each job needs. It then tells Slurm (the job scheduler) to reschedule jobs to prevent the storage from being over- or under-used. A two-group technique handles edge cases where some jobs don't use any storage.
sc-2024-099.key_novelty: The system automatically adjusts job scheduling based on actual real-time storage usage, eliminating the need for users to predict how much storage their jobs will need.

sc-2024-103.method: M3XU breaks high-precision calculations into multiple steps so that simpler matrix multiplication hardware (MXUs) designed for AI can handle both standard and complex 32-bit floating-point numbers (IEEE 754 single-precision) without needing expensive new multiplier circuits. The approach reuses all existing hardware infrastructure and memory systems without requiring changes to programmer code.
sc-2024-103.key_novelty: The core idea is that simple matrix multiplication hardware (MXUs) designed for low-precision AI work can handle high-precision and complex 32-bit floating-point matrix operations by performing the calculations in multiple steps instead of one, without adding new multiplier hardware.

sc-2024-105.method: The algorithm stores graphs as distributed sparse matrices—number grids stored across multiple computers where most positions contain zero. When you add or remove a batch of vertices or edges, the algorithm converts these updates into mathematical matrix operations instead of requiring computers to pass messages to each other. It reduces communication overhead through carefully designed algorithms and shared-memory parallelism (where multiple processors within a single computer access shared data without messaging), and it maintains balanced workload across computers by rearranging the matrix's rows and columns during updates.
sc-2024-105.key_novelty: The core insight is that graph batch updates can be framed as mathematical operations on sparse matrices, which inherently reduces communication between computers and keeps work balanced through matrix rearrangement.

sc-2024-108.method: The benchmark suite collects 16 real scientific applications—programs that researchers use in climate modeling, physics simulations, and other fields—to understand what computing power and features an exascale supercomputer actually needs. It identifies specific hardware and software requirements, documents each application's behavior and how it performs as you add more processors (called scaling), and releases the complete suite as open-source software so any institution can use and verify the results.
sc-2024-108.key_novelty: Unlike artificial test programs, this suite uses 16 real scientific applications to define what an exascale supercomputer must do, and this approach was proven by guiding the actual procurement of Europe's first exascale computer.

sc-2024-101.method: FRSZ2 uses block-based compression to shrink the Krylov basis (the working vectors generated by GMRES, an iterative equation solver) and stores them in GPU registers (the GPU's fastest memory) on NVIDIA H100. The key advantage is that decompression happens at GPU bandwidth speeds, so the memory savings don't get lost to slow decompression. This beats simpler approaches like using lower-precision numbers.
sc-2024-101.key_novelty: FRSZ2 demonstrates that block-based compression outperforms using lower-precision numbers (fewer bits per value) for the Krylov basis while decompressing at full GPU speeds.

sc-2024-110.method: Echo State Networks use a recurrent neural network (a machine learning model that remembers past information) with a fixed random 'memory bank'—only the final output layer is trained, using a pseudo-inverse matrix method (a mathematical technique for finding the best-fit solution). The system reads raw electrical power data from welding equipment and learns patterns automatically without requiring experts to manually prepare the data. Its efficient training means it can work from very few examples—sometimes even just a single weld.
sc-2024-110.key_novelty: Echo State Networks can spot equipment failures from just a single training example using pseudo-inverse matrix training, making them practical for factories with very limited historical data.

sc-2024-106.method: XCVerifier is a tool that automatically verifies whether implementations of density functional approximations—mathematical methods for simulating materials—satisfy known exact mathematical conditions. It does this by taking five implementations from the Libxc library and testing them against seven exact conditions derived by Pederson and Burke, using constraint solving (a computational technique that systematically determines which implementations pass or fail each condition).
sc-2024-106.key_novelty: This is the first tool to automatically verify whether implementations of density functional approximations—mathematical methods used to simulate material properties—satisfy known exact conditions.

sc-2024-109.method: The algorithm identifies which numbers in the sparse matrices actually participate in the multiplication, then fetches only those from other computers instead of everything. It uses 1D partitioning (splitting data along one dimension) rather than the typical two-dimensional or three-dimensional approaches to determine participation. When transferring data between computers, it employs MPI RDMA (direct memory-to-memory transfer that bypasses packing overhead) and groups small requests into larger blocks to reduce the number of individual messages. The approach is tested against CombBLAS 2D and 3D implementations across various configurations.
sc-2024-109.key_novelty: The algorithm uses 1D partitioning with sparsity-awareness to fetch only numbers contributing to the multiplication, employing direct memory transfers (MPI RDMA) and batched requests instead of standard multi-dimensional partitioning.

sc-2024-111.method: The system uses two neural networks (AI pattern-recognition systems) running on the telescope. The first one learns to distinguish genuine gamma-ray bursts from background radiation noise. The second analyzes individual gamma-ray particles (photons) to estimate where each burst originated and how certain that estimate is. Both networks were trained and validated using simulated gamma-ray data from ADAPT, a high-altitude balloon-borne prototype telescope.
sc-2024-111.key_novelty: The core innovation is running neural networks directly on an orbiting telescope to locate gamma-ray bursts in real time, instead of processing data on the ground.

sc-2024-112.method: hZCCL performs calculations directly on homomorphically compressed data (compression that allows math without decompressing), eliminating the wasteful decompress-operate-compress cycle in collective communication. The system uses two compressors working together: a lightweight one optimized for multi-core CPUs, and a homomorphic compressor with runtime heuristics that dynamically select the most efficient compression pipeline.
sc-2024-112.key_novelty: The core innovation is doing calculations directly on homomorphically compressed data (compression that lets math happen without unpacking), rather than decompressing before computation.

sc-2024-119.method: Shepherd is a workflow manager that treats long-running services (like databases or web servers) as regular tasks in a workflow. It figures out what each service is doing by watching what the service prints to its logs and what files it creates, without needing to change the service's code. This lets Shepherd coordinate when services start and stop so they work together properly.
sc-2024-119.key_novelty: Shepherd handles long-running services as workflow tasks by watching their logs and files to understand what they're doing, instead of requiring code changes.

sc-2024-114.method: CONDA analyzes the source code before compilation to understand what arithmetic operations it performs, then adds checking code during compilation that catches errors in those operations when the program runs. These runtime checks are made efficient because the analysis was done beforehand. The added checks don't change when decisions happen in the program or what data gets read and written.
sc-2024-114.key_novelty: By analyzing programs before they run and using those insights to make runtime error checks efficient, this approach detects errors in processor arithmetic circuits while using significantly less computing overhead than other methods.

sc-2024-115.method: Programs save memory snapshots called checkpoints to enable fast recomputation, but currently save every element in a variable even if some don't affect the result. This method uses automatic differentiation—which traces how changes in input values propagate through calculations—to identify which elements of each variable actually influence the final output. It then stores only these critical elements, omitting the rest.
sc-2024-115.key_novelty: By using automatic differentiation to distinguish which individual data elements impact the program's output, checkpoints can be optimized to save only the critical elements.

sc-2024-104.method: The team reimplemented the core algorithms from the production software (Mantid C++) in Julia, a scientific computing language, using JACC.jl—a library that automatically optimizes code to run on both CPUs and graphics processors without rewriting it for each hardware type. Two test applications were created—MDNorm in C++ and MiniVATES.jl in Julia—to compare the new approach against the original Mantid C++ production code. Performance was measured on real hardware: NVIDIA A100 and AMD MI100 graphics processors paired with AMD EPYC 7513/7662 CPUs.
sc-2024-104.key_novelty: One data reduction program in Julia and JACC.jl replaces separate CPU and GPU implementations, running efficiently on both hardware types.

sc-2024-116.method: CuSan is an LLVM compiler extension that instruments CUDA code, adding monitoring to track how parallel threads interact, synchronize, and access memory at compile-time and runtime. It connects this instrumentation to MUST (which checks MPI—a message-passing system for distributed computing) and ThreadSanitizer (which detects data races when threads access memory). By exposing CUDA's concurrency semantics to these existing race detectors, it enables comprehensive detection of data races in hybrid MPI+CUDA applications.
sc-2024-116.key_novelty: It catches data races in hybrid MPI+CUDA applications by using compiler instrumentation to expose CUDA's concurrency behavior to existing MPI and thread-level race detectors.

sc-2024-121.method: HiRace detects data races—when multiple threads access shared memory simultaneously without coordination—using a state machine tailored to GPU execution's structure. GPUs organize computation into synchronized blocks and warps that reach common sync points, creating a hierarchy. Rather than logging every access, HiRace tracks only a fixed-size summary at each synchronization boundary, exploiting this hierarchy to be both fast and memory-efficient.
sc-2024-121.key_novelty: Using GPU's hierarchical synchronization structure to compress memory-access tracking to constant size.

sc-2024-117.method: PIMnast determines how to arrange matrix data across multiple memory banks in Processing-In-Memory hardware (memory with compute cores embedded in each bank) to maximize speedup for matrix-vector multiplication. It works by identifying the competing performance factors that affect data placement, then using adjustable tuning parameters (called orchestration knobs) to test and optimize how rows and columns of the matrix are distributed across banks. The method coordinates this data placement strategy with PIM's execution model, where a single command is broadcast to all banks at once, ensuring the compute cores can efficiently access the matrix data they need.
sc-2024-117.key_novelty: PIMnast determines how to distribute matrix data across Processing-In-Memory banks by balancing competing factors, achieving near-roofline performance (close to theoretical hardware maximum) for matrix-vector multiplication.

sc-2024-120.method: NEO-DNND spreads the work of building a nearest neighbor graph across multiple computers using MPI (a system where computers coordinate by sending messages). To reduce communication overhead, it uses three techniques: avoiding duplicate checks of the same neighbor pairs, sharing data within each computer to use its fast local memory instead of sending over the network, and copying frequently-used data locally so computers don't repeatedly request it from others. This approach efficiently builds graphs from datasets with billions of data points.
sc-2024-120.key_novelty: NEO-DNND speeds up distributed nearest-neighbor graph construction by reducing duplicate work, sharing data within each computer, and copying frequently-used data locally to minimize network communication.

sc-2024-122.method: CARP partitions incoming data as it streams to storage, automatically discovering how the data is distributed (especially uneven distributions where some values appear far more often than others) and adjusting the partitions to handle this. By reorganizing the data during the streaming process itself, rather than sorting everything after collection, it avoids expensive post-processing overhead. This allows range queries to run nearly as fast as they would on pre-sorted data.
sc-2024-122.key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically adapting how data gets partitioned during streaming ingestion, enabling query performance matching fully sorted data even with uneven value distributions.

sc-2024-123.method: PAL measures how much GPU performance varies across different accelerators in a cluster and determines which machine-learning applications are most sensitive to these differences. When assigning jobs to GPUs, PAL uses this variability information to make placement decisions that minimize wasted resources while accounting for each application's performance sensitivity.
sc-2024-123.key_novelty: PAL identifies how sensitive each machine-learning application is to GPU performance variations and uses this knowledge when deciding where to place jobs in a cluster.

sc-2024-125.method: The approach creates a fingerprint of each application's executable code using fuzzy hashing (a technique that detects similarity even when code is slightly different), then uses a machine-learning classifier called Random Forest that learns to recognize applications by finding patterns similar to ones it has already seen. This allows it to identify both known and previously unseen applications. The method is evaluated on 92 application classes and 5,333 distinct samples.
sc-2024-125.key_novelty: Using fuzzy hashing, a technique from malware detection that finds similarities between code samples, to classify and identify HPC applications including previously unseen ones.

sc-2024-124.method: The researchers added two compression tools (SZ3 and ZFP) to Flash-X to shrink simulation output files. They tested both lossless compression (preserving all data) and lossy compression (trading some precision for smaller file sizes). They systematically measured how different settings—compression precision levels and chunk sizes (how many data points to compress together)—affected file size and simulation accuracy across different physics problems, running these tests on the Frontier exascale supercomputer.
sc-2024-124.key_novelty: The core contribution is integrating two compression tools (SZ3 and ZFP) into Flash-X so simulations produce smaller data files while keeping the results accurate, tested with different compression settings on the Frontier exascale supercomputer.

sc-2024-127.method: The simulator lets you build a custom superscalar RISC-V processor (a processor design where multiple instructions execute in parallel) by adjusting architecture parameters like pipeline depth, instruction-per-cycle throughput, and cache sizes. You write C code and compile it within the tool, then the simulator runs your code on your custom processor design and records detailed timing measurements. By comparing results across different architecture choices, you can directly see how design decisions trade off against each other—for example, more parallelism increases speed but also power consumption and chip complexity.
sc-2024-127.key_novelty: A web-based simulator combining customizable superscalar RISC-V processor design with C programming support, so you can immediately see how architecture choices affect program performance.

sc-2024-118.method: The approach splits equation-solving work between a CPU and GPU on the same high-performance nodes (GH200, which have fast connections between processors), using directives (special annotations like OpenMP and OpenACC that tell compilers which code to parallelize) that work the same way on different systems. Machine-learning techniques optimize the solving by learning patterns in the equation structure, while the system automatically sends heavier work to the GPU and lighter coordination tasks to the CPU.
sc-2024-118.key_novelty: The core idea is combining machine-learning, CPU-GPU computing, and portable directive-based code to accelerate time-evolution equation solving.

sc-2024-126.method: The paper discovers that imbalanced benchmark data—where there are many more correct code examples than buggy ones, or vice versa—makes it hard to interpret whether a tool is actually useful. To address this, it tightens the definition of a 'true positive' (correctly identifying a real bug) by requiring tools to also report the source line where the bug occurs and classify what type of error it is. The paper also adds a 'noise metric' to measure how many false alarms a tool generates. It tests these metrics on MPI-BugBench using three debugging tools: ITAC, MUST, and PARCOACH.
sc-2024-126.key_novelty: The contribution is tightening what counts as successful bug detection (tools must report source lines and error types), combined with a noise metric (counting false alarms that distract developers).

sc-2024-132.method: IRIS-GNN uses a machine learning system called a Graph Neural Network (which learns patterns in how tasks connect to each other) to automatically analyze incoming work. The system classifies each task graph into one of three types: ones where keeping data near the processor matters most, ones where running tasks in parallel matters most, or a mix of both. Based on this classification, it automatically selects the best scheduling strategy—the runtime method for assigning work to different accelerators—from IRIS's options.
sc-2024-132.key_novelty: It applies Graph Neural Networks for the first time to automatically classify task structures and select the right scheduling strategy for systems with different types of accelerators.

sc-2024-128.method: The approach tests two methods to make language models detect unusual activity in computational workflows (the sequences of tasks systems execute). First is supervised fine-tuning: taking a pretrained language model and training it on labeled examples of normal versus abnormal events until it learns to spot problems. Second is in-context learning: instead of retraining, you include task descriptions and examples directly in the prompt, letting the model figure out anomalies from just a few examples. The work compares different versions—zero-shot (no examples, just instructions), few-shot (a few examples), and chain-of-thought prompting (showing reasoning step-by-step)—across multiple real workflow datasets.
sc-2024-128.key_novelty: This work shows that language models can detect anomalies in computational workflows through either fine-tuning or prompting, enabling few-shot detection (learning from just a few examples) without expensive model retraining.

sc-2024-129.method: The authors add special annotations (OpenMP directives) to sum reduction code that tell the compiler to send the computation to an NVIDIA Grace-Hopper GPU. They systematically test different configurations by varying how many parallel teams do the work, how many numbers each team processes per iteration, and whether the CPU and GPU should work together on the problem using shared memory. For each configuration, they measure how fast the sum reduction runs.
sc-2024-129.key_novelty: This research systematically explores how sum reduction performance varies when both the CPU and GPU execute work together using shared memory on an NVIDIA Grace-Hopper system.

sc-2024-130.method: The approach uses program synthesis tools to automatically optimize how quantum gates are arranged for QFT algorithms on real quantum hardware. It combines relaxed ordering (allowing quantum gates to execute in flexible, non-strict sequences) and unit exploration (systematically trying different possible gate arrangements) to minimize SWAP gates (operations that move quantum information between qubits) and circuit depth (how many sequential operation layers are needed). The result is circuits that fit better on actual quantum processors with fewer total operations.
sc-2024-130.key_novelty: This is the first approach to guarantee linear-depth QFT circuits—meaning circuit depth that scales proportionally with qubit count—across multiple quantum architectures: Google Sycamore, IBM heavy-hex, and lattice surgery.

sc-2024-134.method: The system continuously processes millions of data points per second (10 million in exascale systems) using machine learning and deep learning algorithms to detect patterns that indicate approaching failures—such as abnormal temperature or power consumption. By identifying these early warning signs, it prevents outages before they occur and stops equipment from consuming power unnecessarily during failures. This approach operates fast enough to work in real-time across modern data centers.
sc-2024-134.key_novelty: An AIOps framework that uses machine learning and deep learning to predict failures and detect anomalies, tackling two critical data center challenges simultaneously—preventing outages and reducing energy waste.

sc-2024-113.method: cuSZp2 is a lossy compressor (it discards less-important data to reduce file size) that runs on the GPU as a single operation, avoiding slow CPU-GPU data transfers. It combines a new encoding method with memory access patterns optimized for GPU speed. The design hides delays from GPU synchronization (when cores coordinate their work) by performing useful work while waiting, achieving high compression and decompression throughput.
sc-2024-113.key_novelty: A GPU lossy compressor that runs as a single operation, combining a new encoding method with GPU-optimized memory access and synchronization-delay hiding to achieve high throughput.

sc-2024-136.method: The authors modified the Zig compiler to recognize OpenMP pragmas—special directives that tell the compiler to split a loop across multiple CPU cores. These pragmas are converted into parallel instructions using LLVM, the low-level system that Zig builds on, which handles the mechanics of running code simultaneously on multiple cores sharing the same memory. The results were tested against equivalent Fortran and C programs using NASA's NAS Parallel Benchmark suite, which measures how well different languages handle multi-core workloads.
sc-2024-136.key_novelty: Zig now supports OpenMP loop directives for the first time, letting programmers write simple annotations to run loops in parallel across multiple CPU cores.

sc-2024-137.method: The approach categorizes the types of portability bugs that appear in Kokkos programs—bugs that only manifest when code runs on specific hardware backends like CUDA GPUs, HIP (AMD's parallel computing platform), or OpenMP CPUs. Klokkos, a tool developed for this work, uses symbolic execution (a technique that tests code against many possible inputs simultaneously without actually running it) to detect these bugs on regular commodity hardware. This enables early bug detection before code deployment to supercomputers, avoiding failures that would only appear on those specific hardware systems.
sc-2024-137.key_novelty: The core idea is using symbolic execution—a technique that explores code without actually running it—to find portability bugs in Kokkos programs on commodity hardware, without needing to test on the specific hardware backends (CUDA, HIP, OpenMP) where they would occur.

sc-2024-131.method: CARAML is an automated benchmark suite that measures speed and power consumption of transformer-based large language models and computer vision models running on specialized hardware accelerators (chips optimized for AI) from different vendors. It uses a custom tool called jpwr to accurately measure power consumption. The design prioritizes compactness (minimal dependencies), extensibility (easy to add new tests or hardware), and reproducibility (consistent results across different systems).
sc-2024-131.key_novelty: CARAML automatically measures both speed and power consumption of AI workloads in a single unified framework designed to work across specialized hardware accelerators (chips optimized for AI) from different vendors.

sc-2024-143.method: Cholesky factorization breaks into dense matrix blocks and sparse structure management. The method uses a right-looking approach (processing the matrix from right to left), which naturally exposes dense sub-matrices that need intensive calculations. The GPU accelerates these dense blocks since it excels at large repetitive matrix math, while the CPU coordinates which blocks to compute and when, based on the sparse structure.
sc-2024-143.key_novelty: Sparse Cholesky factorization naturally contains dense sub-blocks that the GPU can handle much faster than the CPU, so the method offloads those blocks while keeping sparse coordination on the CPU.

sc-2024-141.method: The system bridges CWL and Parsl by automatically converting CWL CommandLineTool definitions (standardized descriptions of command-line tools) into Parsl apps (Python-based workflow components), so existing CWL workflows can run as part of Python code. It also provides a Parsl runner that executes CWL CommandLineTool definitions directly, without conversion, giving users flexibility in workflow style. As a proof-of-concept, it allows Python code to be embedded directly in CWL workflows. Performance is evaluated using image-processing workflows.
sc-2024-141.key_novelty: CWL CommandLineTool definitions can be converted into Parsl apps, enabling standard CWL workflows to run directly within Python code.

sc-2024-139.method: The code simulates how individual atoms move and rearrange in a material under electric and heat fields, using Kinetic Monte Carlo (a method that models random atomic movements based on probability). It runs these simulations on GPUs (graphics processors optimized for parallel computing) within the LUMI supercomputer, using high-speed direct connections between GPUs on the same node to efficiently coordinate the computation. The approach was tested on hafnium oxide (HfOx), the material stack used in resistive switching memory cells.
sc-2024-139.key_novelty: This is the first scalable GPU-accelerated Kinetic Monte Carlo code that efficiently simulates how atoms move under electric fields in resistive memory arrays through inter-GPU communication.

sc-2024-133.method: Mosaic categorizes how applications read and write data to storage by tracking three things: how often access patterns repeat (periodicity), when data is accessed (temporality), and how often the app checks file metadata (information about files, like size or timestamps). It automatically breaks down I/O traces (detailed logs of data access) into segments, identifies recurring patterns, and categorizes applications without manual analysis.
sc-2024-133.key_novelty: Automatically categorizing how HPC applications access storage by examining three dimensions: how often patterns repeat (periodicity), when they occur (temporality), and how the app accesses file metadata (properties like size or modification time).

sc-2024-140.method: They ran GPU tests to measure the power consumption of different applications under various conditions. Then they analyzed three months of data collected from Frontier, an operational exascale supercomputer, to identify which jobs were good candidates for energy-saving techniques like DVFS (reducing processor speed and voltage) and power capping (limiting power consumption). The analysis revealed which techniques would work best for different types of applications.
sc-2024-140.key_novelty: A method for determining the maximum possible energy savings from power management, demonstrated on real applications running on an operational exascale supercomputer.

sc-2024-144.method: MQSS uses a compile-at-runtime (JIT) optimization stack that works across any quantum hardware type (hardware-agnostic). When quantum circuits are too large for a single device, it splits them into smaller parts using quantum circuit cutting. It then dynamically selects which available quantum accelerator should handle each workload through a unified Quantum Device Management Interface (QDMI).
sc-2024-144.key_novelty: MQSS introduces a unified Quantum Device Management Interface that dynamically routes hybrid computing workloads (mixing classical and quantum tasks) to the best available quantum accelerator, enabling multiple different quantum computers to function as a shared resource.

sc-2024-138.method: The authors implement LULESH (a proxy application for evaluating supercomputer performance) using HPX, a framework that breaks work into small tasks and automatically assigns each to a processor based on readiness—instead of requiring programmers to manually specify parallel regions as in OpenMP. This dynamic assignment keeps processors busy by always having work ready and hides latency (delays from slow operations). They further optimize for single-node performance on multi-core systems to achieve faster execution than OpenMP.
sc-2024-138.key_novelty: HPX's dynamic task scheduling—automatically assigning work to processors as it becomes ready—achieves 1.33x to 2.25x faster LULESH execution than OpenMP.

sc-2024-135.method: ProTEA is an FPGA accelerator that speeds up transformer encoder blocks by breaking their matrix computations into smaller tiles (64-element chunks for attention, 6-element chunks for feedforward operations). These tile sizes can be reconfigured while the accelerator runs, making it adaptable to different transformer architectures. The system runs on a Xilinx Alveo U55C FPGA and processes 8 parallel attention heads across 12 layers with 768-dimensional embeddings, distributing tiles across the FPGA's memory and computing resources to maximize parallelism.
sc-2024-135.key_novelty: ProTEA's innovation is matrix tiling (splitting matrices into chunks) that can be adjusted while the accelerator runs, enabling efficient execution of dense transformer encoder computations on FPGA hardware.

sc-2024-142.method: NetCL lets you write in-network computing (code that processes data inside network switches) using C/C++ and special APIs for this task. You write simple programs called kernels that process data packets as they travel through the network. A compiler automatically translates your kernels into P4 code (the language network switches use), and a lightweight runtime handles low-level networking details.
sc-2024-142.key_novelty: NetCL enables ordinary programmers to write in-network computing (code that processes data inside network switches) using C/C++ with automatic compilation to P4, eliminating the need for specialized networking expertise.

sc-2024-147.method: The approach uses hardware multicast—a network feature that broadcasts data to multiple machines simultaneously—to create an efficient broadcast protocol that works in constant time regardless of how many computers participate. This broadcast becomes the foundation for scheduling Allgather operations (gathering data from all computers) in a way that fully saturates available network bandwidth. Instead of burdening the main CPU with coordination, the algorithm runs on a SmartNIC (a specialized network card), eliminating CPU overhead and enabling multiple data movements to happen in parallel.
sc-2024-147.key_novelty: Using hardware multicast to build bandwidth-optimal Allgather operations with execution offloaded to a SmartNIC (specialized network card) so the main CPU stays free.

sc-2024-146.method: The paper reformulates directed triad counting—identifying and counting specific patterns of directed connections between three nodes—as a linear algebra problem expressed through matrix operations. Using the FLAME methodology (a systematic framework for deriving algorithms from mathematical descriptions), they generate algorithms with mathematical proofs of correctness. By combining individual specialized algorithms (each designed to count one type of directed triad), they efficiently count all triads together, achieving faster results than previous graph-based approaches.
sc-2024-146.key_novelty: Using linear algebra and the FLAME methodology to systematically derive provably correct algorithms for directed triad counting.

sc-2024-145.method: Chapel is a programming language that treats parallelism (splitting work across processors) and locality (where data sits in memory) as concepts you directly express in your code. Instead of writing separate code for different GPU frameworks, you write once in Chapel, and the compiler translates it to CUDA, HIP, or whatever framework you're using. This avoids the tedious and error-prone work of managing multiple GPU programming models.
sc-2024-145.key_novelty: A programming language that lets you write GPU code once and automatically translates it to work with any vendor's GPU framework (CUDA, HIP, etc.).

sc-2024-149.method: The approach uses the actor model (a way to write parallel programs where independent computing units called actors send messages to each other) to handle hundreds of thousands of short-lived tasks efficiently. Instead of processing each message individually—which forces the system to pause and synchronize frequently—messages are batched together (grouped and processed in bulk). This batching reduces synchronization overhead (the expensive cost of coordinating between tasks), allowing the system to flexibly handle both uniform and varied computing tasks.
sc-2024-149.key_novelty: Batching actor messages together (processing them in groups rather than one at a time) reduces the overhead of coordinating between tasks, making the actor model competitive or superior to MPI and OpenMP on large-scale parallel computing problems.

sc-2024-152.method: The system uses Flux—a job scheduler designed to work across different vendors' hardware—as its foundation. It includes flux-power-monitor, which measures power usage across heterogeneous systems with only 0.4% overhead, and flux-power-manager, which controls power allocation through proportional sharing (dividing power fairly among running jobs) and a hierarchical FFT-based algorithm called FPP that automatically adjusts each job's power budget based on the job's characteristics.
sc-2024-152.key_novelty: A hierarchical FFT-based dynamic power management algorithm (FPP) that automatically adjusts power budgets for jobs running on any vendor's hardware, works reliably in production systems, and lets users customize power constraints for both traditional MPI applications and non-MPI workloads.

sc-2024-151.method: The system creates network diagrams for each time period showing how sensor readings from a compute node relate to each other, including both current and historical measurements. Machine learning models are trained on these diagrams to recognize which patterns of sensor relationships appear right before a node fails and needs maintenance. Once trained, the models can predict upcoming failures by spotting these warning patterns in new sensor data.
sc-2024-151.key_novelty: Predicting compute node failures in production HPC systems by representing sensor data as network diagrams that capture how the sensors relate to each other over time.

sc-2024-158.method: LLM-Pilot tests how well LLM (large language model) inference services perform on different GPUs under realistic workloads—with many users making requests at the same time—and tunes the service settings for each GPU to get the best performance. Instead of running expensive tests every time for a new LLM or GPU, it builds a predictive model (a machine-learning system trained on patterns from past tests) from the data it collects during testing. This model can then predict which GPU and configuration will work best for a new LLM without needing to benchmark it from scratch.
sc-2024-158.key_novelty: Instead of testing every new LLM on every GPU (which is expensive and slow), LLM-Pilot learns from past tests to predict which hardware and settings will work best for a new LLM without running all those expensive tests again.

sc-2024-155.method: The framework uses a scheduling method called Cyclic Queueing and Forwarding (CQF), which divides time into repeating cycles on network nodes that are synchronized to each other. It configures the length of these cycles so that any data packet starting at the beginning of a cycle will finish transferring to the next node before the cycle ends. The amount of data that can fit in each cycle depends on three things: how long the cycle is, how long it takes data to physically travel across the link, and how fast the link can send data. The system is tested by simulating it against two simpler approaches: one that always reserves a fixed amount of bandwidth, and another that reserves bandwidth dynamically as needed.
sc-2024-155.key_novelty: The key innovation is applying Cyclic Queueing and Forwarding to scientific data networks to guarantee data arrives by a specific deadline, potentially using multiple network paths to improve those guarantees.

sc-2024-156.method: The researchers tested a small-scale DAOS storage system (which combines NVMe drives, persistent memory, storage servers, and RDMA—a fast network technology) by systematically changing different settings. They varied the physical arrangement of hardware (topology), how many network requests could happen at the same time (concurrency), and which input/output API programs used to access data. They measured how fast data actually moved under each configuration to see which choices had the biggest impact on real-world performance.
sc-2024-156.key_novelty: DAOS storage performance on Aurora depends on how hardware topology, network concurrency (parallel operations), and I/O API design interact with each other.

sc-2024-154.method: The framework automatically generates random but structurally valid OpenMP programs using a grammar (a set of rules defining legal program structures), building on the Varity program generator. These generated tests run against three OpenMP compiler implementations (GCC, Clang, Intel) in parallel, comparing their outputs—a technique called differential testing—to identify cases where they disagree or produce incorrect results. Across 1,800 generated tests, the researchers found patterns indicating which types of programs most reliably expose compiler bugs.
sc-2024-154.key_novelty: Use grammar-based random program generation to automatically create diverse OpenMP tests for differential compiler validation, instead of writing tests manually.

sc-2024-150.method: The approach selects which functions to measure by framing it as an optimization problem (binary knapsack: choosing items for a limited-capacity backpack). It uses two sources of information: runtime measurements from actually running the program, and static information about how functions call each other in the code structure. Based on these, it estimates the measurement overhead for each function and automatically selects the set that maximizes visibility into hot spots (where execution time is spent) without exceeding the overhead budget. The method was implemented in the PIRA profiling infrastructure and evaluated on HPC proxy applications including LULESH, AMG2013, MILC, and ASTAR.
sc-2024-150.key_novelty: An optimization approach automatically selects which functions to instrument, maximizing visibility of program hot spots while staying within a measurement overhead budget.

sc-2024-148.method: DeLiBA-K operates at the Linux kernel level instead of as a user-space program, eliminating the overhead of context switching—the repeated transitions between user space (where programs run) and kernel space (where the OS manages hardware). It uses io_uring (an asynchronous I/O API that issues multiple requests in parallel rather than sequentially) to communicate directly with the block and network I/O stacks. This runs on a 16nm AMD Alveo U280 FPGA, a programmable hardware accelerator. The result is reduced latency and improved I/O parallelism by avoiding context-switching overhead.
sc-2024-148.key_novelty: The core innovation is implementing io_uring inside the Linux kernel instead of user space, eliminating context-switching overhead when applications access FPGA-accelerated storage.

sc-2024-160.method: The paper proposes disaggregated architectures (spreading computation across multiple separate computers) with near-data processing (placing compute next to data storage instead of moving all data to one processor). The researchers test this approach on different graph types and analytics tasks to identify what system-level mechanisms would let software frameworks effectively leverage this split architecture.
sc-2024-160.key_novelty: The key insight is using disaggregated, near-data processing—spreading computation across multiple machines with processors placed next to data storage instead of centralizing everything—to overcome memory bottlenecks that limit large-scale graph analytics.

sc-2024-157.method: The researchers extend OSACA (Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer), a tool that models CPU performance, to handle three modern CPU designs: Zen 4, Golden Cove, and Neoverse V2. They use microbenchmarks—small test programs that measure specific performance characteristics—starting with single-core analysis and scaling to full-node capabilities. They compare their results with another analysis tool, LLVM-MCA, with special focus on write-allocate evasion (a cache optimization that avoids unnecessary memory transfers when data changes).
sc-2024-157.key_novelty: The paper compares how three CPU architectures implement write-allocate evasion (a cache optimization that avoids unnecessary memory transfers), uncovering different architectural choices and optimization opportunities specific to each design.

sc-2024-161.method: ParvaGPU splits NVIDIA A100 GPUs into separate sections using Multi-Instance GPU (MIG), then runs multiple processes in each section at different times using Multi-Process Service (MPS), combining spatial division with time-sharing in a single system. By carefully managing resource allocation across both spatial sections and time slots, it reduces both the unused computing capacity sitting idle within sections and the wasted space from scattered available slots. Testing with 11 different deep-learning workloads showed the system meets latency requirements while using fewer total GPU resources.
sc-2024-161.key_novelty: The core idea is combining spatial GPU partitioning (dividing the GPU into sections) with temporal multiplexing (time-sharing) in one unified system to eliminate resource waste from either approach alone.

sc-2024-164.method: Copper places a shared cache between the processes and the storage system. The first time a process needs a file, it loads from storage into this cache; the next time any process needs that file, it comes from the cache instead of storage. By serving many processes from one cached copy, the storage system isn't overwhelmed with duplicate requests, and nodes spend less time waiting for data.
sc-2024-164.key_novelty: A shared cache layer that keeps initialization time nearly constant as jobs scale from 32 to 8,300 nodes by coordinating data access across all processes.

sc-2024-159.method: When a node fails in a large-scale cluster, its locally-cached data is lost, normally forcing remaining nodes to refetch from the slow shared parallel file system (PFS). Instead, the system uses a hash ring—a method that systematically distributes data evenly across remaining nodes—to recache the lost data locally. This balanced redistribution ensures no single node becomes overloaded with recached data. By maintaining data in fast local caches rather than relying on the PFS, the system avoids severe I/O bottlenecks and preserves performance during node failures.
sc-2024-159.key_novelty: The system uses a hash ring to redistribute data lost from failed nodes evenly across remaining nodes, keeping it in fast local caches instead of the slow parallel file system (PFS).

sc-2024-162.method: The framework provides an API to write unit tests that specify both regular assertions and expected OMPT events (notifications from the OpenMP runtime). When the test runs, the framework captures these runtime notifications and checks that they match your expectations, verifying both the code logic and runtime behavior at once. This eliminates the verbose manual event tracking that existing approaches require.
sc-2024-162.key_novelty: A testing framework that embeds OMPT event verification (checking expected OpenMP runtime notifications) into standard unit tests.

sc-2024-166.method: The code distributes simulation work across many computers (node-based parallelization), cutting the communication between computers by 81% through smart data organization—keeping related data on the same node so computers don't need constant back-and-forth. It accelerates the heavy calculations using SVE-GEMM (optimized matrix multiplication for Fugaku's A64FX processors) and mixed-precision arithmetic (performing some calculations in lower precision to reduce bandwidth usage). Finally, it balances the workload evenly across processing units within each computer (intra-node load balancing).
sc-2024-166.key_novelty: By organizing the simulation across nodes and cutting communication between them by 81%, the approach scales neural network molecular dynamics efficiently to tens of thousands of computers.

sc-2024-153.method: An automated system coordinates collection, preprocessing, AI analysis, and movement of satellite climate data across multiple research facilities run by different federal agencies. The system dynamically breaks satellite data into smaller pieces (tokenization and sharding) that are distributed and processed in parallel across 80 workers on multiple nodes at OLCF's Advanced Computing Ecosystem Testbed. This parallelized processing allows the system to handle massive amounts of climate data across multiple facilities.
sc-2024-153.key_novelty: The system enables petascale climate data processing—handling vast satellite datasets measured in petabytes—by coordinating across multiple research facilities managed by different federal agencies.

sc-2024-167.method: The authors improved a GPU implementation of pangenome layout by reorganizing data for cache efficiency (reducing wasted memory transfers), coordinating random memory accesses into coalesced requests (so multiple GPU threads fetch together), and merging warps (groups of GPU threads) to reduce idle threads. They tested this on 24 human whole-chromosome pangenomes.
sc-2024-167.key_novelty: The core innovation is coordinating three GPU optimizations—cache-friendly data layout, coalesced random accesses, and warp merging (combining GPU thread groups)—to overcome the memory bottleneck from irregular access patterns in pangenome layout.

sc-2024-165.method: PerfVec uses deep learning to learn two independent, non-overlapping representations: one capturing what programs need from a processor, the other capturing what a processor architecture can provide. A program's representation generalizes across different processor architectures for performance prediction, and a processor architecture's representation generalizes across different programs. The result is a foundation model that understands instruction-level performance and can predict outcomes without retraining on new programs or architectures.
sc-2024-165.key_novelty: Learning independent program and microarchitecture representations that enable a single trained model to predict performance whether the program is new, the hardware is new, or both.

sc-2024-168.method: The researchers created a measurement system that evaluates how productive different programming models are by analyzing three key factors: syntax (how the code is written), semantics (what the code actually does), and optimization overhead (the extra computational work needed for speed). They built analysis tools that work with GCC and Clang compilers to examine C/C++ and Fortran code. The measurement was tested on SPEChpc benchmark programs and other standard tests. Results are presented as visualizations that show how easily developers can write code (productivity) versus how fast the code runs (performance).
sc-2024-168.key_novelty: The paper proposes a way to measure how productive different programming models are by analyzing syntax, semantics, and optimization overhead, giving a more objective comparison than simply counting lines of code.

sc-2024-175.method: TROUT predicts job wait times in supercomputers by splitting the problem into two stages. First, a neural network (a computational model trained to learn patterns from data) classifies each job into a time bucket—like predicting 'this job will wait 1-10 minutes' instead of guessing an exact number. Second, it refines that bucket estimate to predict the precise wait time. The model trains on real data from the Slurm Workload Manager (the software that schedules jobs on HPC systems) and uses features like job priority, assigned partition (queue), and current job state to make its predictions.
sc-2024-175.key_novelty: The key insight is to predict job wait times in two stages—first guessing a rough time range, then narrowing down to an exact prediction—rather than trying to predict exact times all at once.

sc-2024-163.method: The authors built a conformance test suite—a set of 30 targeted tests that check whether different compilers correctly implement the OpenMP Tool Interface (OMPT), which is the standard way for profiling and debugging tools to observe what parallel programs are doing. The tests examine both the main CPU and GPU events, focusing on specific OMPT features. By running these tests on various compiler versions, particularly AMD's ROCm compiler, they identified which compilers have missing features and tracked their progress toward full compliance.
sc-2024-163.key_novelty: The key contribution is the first conformance test suite designed to systematically evaluate which compilers properly implement the OpenMP Tool Interface.

sc-2024-174.method: MegaMmap creates a single unified memory view across your computer's fast RAM and slower storage (like SSDs), letting you write programs as if all your data fits in RAM even when it doesn't. It watches how your program uses data and automatically moves frequently-accessed information into fast RAM while pushing rarely-used data to storage. To avoid slowdowns, it predicts which data you'll need next and brings it into fast memory ahead of time, using hints about critical data to keep the fast and slow memory layers in sync.
sc-2024-174.key_novelty: The core innovation is software that automatically moves data between fast RAM and slow storage based on actual program usage, making them work as a single unified memory system.

sc-2024-172.method: The method uses Convolutional Neural Networks—machine learning models that excel at finding patterns in data—to extract correlations (mathematical relationships) between different fields in scientific datasets. These cross-field patterns are then combined with traditional local field information to produce better predictions of what data values should be. With more accurate predictions, the lossy compression algorithm can represent data more faithfully while using fewer bits, achieving better compression ratios.
sc-2024-172.key_novelty: The innovation is using Convolutional Neural Networks to identify cross-field correlations (relationships between different measured fields in scientific data), which improves compression prediction accuracy more than using only single-field local information.

sc-2024-171.method: The authors write GPU code that assembles genome sequences by constructing de Bruijn graphs—networks where overlapping DNA fragments connect together—and use hash tables (fast lookup structures) to efficiently store sequence data. They evaluate this code across NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, identifying performance bottlenecks and hardware-specific differences. By analyzing these results, they uncover that existing GPU performance prediction tools don't accurately model integer-heavy bioinformatics workloads and propose specific improvements.
sc-2024-171.key_novelty: Existing GPU performance prediction tools fail to accurately model integer-heavy bioinformatics workloads, as revealed by cross-vendor testing.

sc-2024-173.method: Moirae treats multiple chained stencil operations as a single optimization problem. It uses a lightweight cost model (a tool that predicts performance by analyzing memory access patterns) to estimate how fast different optimization strategies would run. The framework explores different optimizations using evolutionary search (a method that generates and tests variations, keeping the best performers) while using domain knowledge to eliminate clearly bad options upfront, reducing the total exploration time needed.
sc-2024-173.key_novelty: Rather than optimizing individual stencil operations separately, Moirae optimizes chains of stencils together using evolutionary search (testing and refining variations) guided by memory-aware performance prediction.

sc-2024-170.method: The system pairs Cendio's ThinLinc (remote desktop software that streams graphics and user input over the network) with a custom scheduling framework called GfxLauncher. When users connect to a remote desktop, they can run graphics-accelerated applications in real time or submit Jupyter notebooks to the cluster. ThinLinc relays the graphics to the user's screen and captures their keyboard and mouse commands, while GfxLauncher manages the execution of graphics-accelerated applications and schedules notebook jobs on the cluster.
sc-2024-170.key_novelty: Combining Cendio's ThinLinc remote desktop with a custom GfxLauncher backend framework enables interactive graphics applications and Jupyter notebook access to HPC clusters.

sc-2024-180.method: GNU Parallel allows many computing tasks to run at the same time across multiple computers in a supercomputer by quickly dispatching each task to available machines. The tool was tested on two leading-edge supercomputers—OLCF's Frontier and NERSC's Perlmutter—with diverse workloads including GPU computing, containerized software, and fast storage operations (NVMe). GNU Parallel can work independently to manage entire computational workflows or integrate with other workflow systems to handle the final parallelization stage, all while using minimal computing resources for coordination.
sc-2024-180.key_novelty: GNU Parallel effectively manages high-throughput computing workloads (many independent computing tasks) at extreme scales on leadership supercomputers without significant overhead.

sc-2024-178.method: AmgT creates a unified way to store sparse matrices (matrices with mostly zeros) that enables specialized GPU units called tensor cores to speed up both the setup phase (matrix multiplication, or SpGEMM) and the solve phase (matrix-vector multiplication, or SpMV) of algebraic multigrid solving. The design uses mixed precision—storing some numbers at lower precision—to reduce memory bandwidth and overhead from converting between storage formats. The implementation is integrated into the HYPRE library, so existing software can use it without changes.
sc-2024-178.key_novelty: The first unified sparse matrix storage format enabling tensor cores to accelerate both SpGEMM (sparse matrix multiplication for setup) and SpMV (matrix-vector multiplication for solving) in algebraic multigrid, with mixed precision support.

sc-2024-179.method: PARALLAX avoids expensive SWAP operations (which physically move qubits during computation) by pre-planning how atoms should move through the quantum processor. The compiler jointly decides qubit placement and the timing of atom movements while respecting the hardware constraints of neutral atom systems. It can optimize multiple parts of the plan in parallel, keeping compilation fast and scalable. Since atoms are repositioned proactively rather than on-demand, the total number of error-prone operations is reduced.
sc-2024-179.key_novelty: Pre-scheduling atom movements eliminates costly SWAP operations in neutral atom quantum circuit compilation.

sc-2024-176.method: The approach harnesses specialized math units called tensor cores built into NVIDIA Ampere and Hopper GPUs. It redesigns how the algorithm calculates distances between data points to use the fastest, lowest-precision math (INT8) while exploiting symmetry in the data structure. Then it solves the resulting matrix equations using a Cholesky solver (a technique for solving systems of equations) that strategically picks the optimal precision level (FP64, FP32, FP16, FP8, or INT8) for each step. By organizing computation in small blocks and adapting precision on-the-fly, it reduces data movement while keeping the final results accurate.
sc-2024-176.key_novelty: A Cholesky-based matrix solver that strategically assigns different precision levels (FP64/FP32/FP16/FP8/INT8) to different operations to maximize GPU tensor core speed while preserving result accuracy.

sc-2024-183.method: The algorithm works by having each point in the graph greedily select its best-weighted neighbor as a match, using pointers to track these pairs. The computation is then distributed across multiple NVIDIA A100 and V100 GPUs on DGX systems, with the graph broken into batches. Graph matching normally causes two problems: unpredictable memory access patterns and frequent synchronization (waiting) between GPUs. The paper solves this by strategically assigning graph batches to different GPUs to reduce these bottlenecks.
sc-2024-183.key_novelty: The core innovation is pairing a locally greedy matching algorithm with multi-GPU batching and distribution strategies to efficiently handle graphs larger than a single GPU's memory.

sc-2024-181.method: The authors rewrote the LSQR algorithm (which computes astrometric parameters—measurements of star positions—for ~10^8 stars) in five GPU programming frameworks: CUDA, C++ PSTL, SYCL, OpenMP, and HIP. They tested each version on five GPU platforms from NVIDIA and AMD, verifying that all versions produced correct results. Performance consistency across different hardware and problem sizes was measured using ȹ, the harmonic mean (an average that emphasizes consistent rather than peak performance) of performance efficiency.
sc-2024-181.key_novelty: This work systematically compares performance portability—how efficiently GPU code runs when switching between different hardware makers—across five programming frameworks (CUDA, C++ PSTL, SYCL, OpenMP, and HIP) tested on NVIDIA and AMD platforms.

sc-2024-184.method: ProtoX uses two tools to automatically generate optimized GPU programs: Proto provides the high-level structure for equations on regular grids, and SPIRAL generates efficient low-level code. These create kernels (specialized GPU programs) that solve Euler equations (equations describing fluid flow) using a high-accuracy method (fourth-order finite volume). IRIS, a runtime scheduling system, then distributes these kernels across multiple GPUs and optimizes them through two techniques—fusing operations into computation graphs (DAG fusion) and merging separate GPU tasks—enabling efficient execution on any GPU type.
sc-2024-184.key_novelty: Combining automatic GPU code generation for structured-grid equations with intelligent runtime fusion of computation operations (DAG and task fusion) enables the same code to run efficiently on different GPU architectures.

sc-2024-187.method: The authors move the task of sending data between system components from CPUs to GPUs, since GPUs can do this work much faster. They reorganize how data is stored so GPUs can access it without wasting time. They also develop new algorithms that speed up the overall computation. They validate the approach on Polaris and Frontier supercomputers using real simulations involving millions of deformable cells.
sc-2024-187.key_novelty: The key idea is moving communication work from CPUs to GPUs and redesigning data structures so GPUs can access them efficiently.

sc-2024-186.method: The authors build a driver that uses PCIe shared memory (a way for multiple computers to read and write the same memory) to let multiple hosts directly access the same NVMe storage device, bypassing RDMA (which requires extra software steps on the critical path). They split the storage controller's request queue (I/O queue) so each computer can submit requests independently and in parallel. This direct approach achieves speeds nearly as fast as having local storage.
sc-2024-186.key_novelty: Splitting the NVMe controller's request queue across PCIe shared memory enables multiple computers to directly access the same storage device without RDMA overhead.

sc-2024-182.method: ChatVis uses a large language model to turn your natural language description of a visualization into actual Python code. It then runs that code, catches any errors that occur during execution, and sends those error messages back to the model with instructions to fix them. The model rewrites the faulty code, it runs again, and this cycle repeats until the code runs without errors.
sc-2024-182.key_novelty: Running visualization code, catching the error messages when it crashes, and using those messages to automatically guide a language model to fix the broken code.

sc-2024-188.method: OMPDart examines OpenMP code statically (without running it) to determine which data is used in host and device sections of the program. It then automatically generates instructions that tell the system exactly what data needs to transfer between the main computer and accelerators (like GPUs), and when. The approach was tested on nine HPC benchmarks, demonstrating that it reduces the amount of data moved between host and device.
sc-2024-188.key_novelty: The core idea is using static code analysis to automatically generate data-movement instructions instead of requiring programmers to write them manually.

sc-2024-177.method: SMIless jointly optimizes two decisions usually made separately: resource allocation and cold-start management (minimizing startup delay). For ML workloads with dependent functions organized as chains (DAGs), it pre-warms functions to minimize startup time, adjusting the intensity based on the workload and available hardware. Implemented on OpenFaaS, this approach balances speed against cost.
sc-2024-177.key_novelty: SMIless jointly optimizes resource allocation and cold-start delay for DAG-based ML inference on serverless platforms through adaptive pre-warming.

sc-2024-193.method: The researchers tested two different organizational structures for storage control on the Frontera supercomputer. One is flat (all nodes communicate directly with central control), the other is hierarchical (organized in layers, like a tree). As they added more computers to the system, they measured how well each design kept up with requests and at what point each one became too slow to be useful.
sc-2024-193.key_novelty: This is the first time anyone measured how flat versus hierarchical storage control designs actually perform when scaled to a real, working supercomputer.

sc-2024-185.method: DAOS is a distributed storage system that provides two different ways to access data: a direct object storage API, or a traditional file system interface built with FUSE (a technique for implementing file systems without kernel modifications). The researchers benchmarked both approaches using various I/O workload patterns on NVM-backed devices (fast solid-state storage) and measured their performance against competing distributed file systems and object storage systems on the same hardware.
sc-2024-185.key_novelty: The paper measures performance differences between accessing NVM-backed distributed storage (fast reliable storage devices) through a direct object API versus through a POSIX file system interface (traditional file management standard) built with FUSE (file system implementation technique avoiding kernel modifications).

sc-2024-197.method: The approach adds data compression to a roofline model—a tool for understanding what limits a computer's performance. It uses three compression techniques: low-precision floating-point numbers (using fewer decimal places), sparse matrix formulation (storing only non-zero values), and ZFP compressed arrays (a data compression format). By shrinking data size, these techniques reduce how much memory must move to and from processors, cut unnecessary repeated memory reads, and make data access more efficient. The framework automatically adjusts how much compression to use based on whether a given hardware is better at computing or moving data, tested on matrix multiplication at different scales.
sc-2024-197.key_novelty: Data compression serves as a tuning mechanism that lets applications automatically shift to either be limited by computing power or data transfer speed, whichever matches the hardware's strengths.

sc-2024-190.method: The authors tested single-precision matrix multiplication on the Cerebras CS-2, which packs 745,500 processors into a single wafer connected in a low-latency 2D mesh topology (ultra-fast grid-like wiring). They measured peak performance and tested two types of scaling: weak scaling (adding processors while keeping per-processor work constant) and strong scaling (using more processors on the same fixed problem). They built a performance prediction model by analyzing actual measurements across different matrix sizes.
sc-2024-190.key_novelty: They developed a performance prediction model for matrix multiplication on the wafer-scale Cerebras CS-2 that predicts results with 4.7% accuracy and achieves perfect weak-scaling efficiency (1.00), meaning adding processors doubles performance without communication slowdown.

sc-2024-200.method: The approach collects data from past Spack builds, recording which package version combinations succeeded and which failed. It trains a machine learning model on this data to discover patterns in what versions work together. When selecting versions for a new build, the model predicts the probability of success for each option, allowing Spack to automatically choose the combinations most likely to build without errors.
sc-2024-200.key_novelty: Instead of requiring humans to manually write dependency constraints, the system learns patterns from historical build data using machine learning to predict and automatically select version combinations most likely to succeed.

sc-2024-194.method: The problem is translated into a QUBO model (Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization—a mathematical formula where each choice is either 0 or 1). This formulation is sent to an Ising machine (specifically, Fixstars Amplify Annealing Engine), specialized hardware that uses quantum annealing principles to test many candidate solutions in parallel rather than sequentially. This parallel approach sidesteps the exponential time complexity that would make conventional computers timeout.
sc-2024-194.key_novelty: Reformulating video coding's intra prediction mode selection as a QUBO model (a type of optimization problem) and solving it with an Ising machine (Fixstars Amplify Annealing Engine) to achieve speedups over conventional computers.

sc-2024-191.method: The authors build a quantum machine learning framework using a Matrix Product State (MPS) simulator—a technique that efficiently encodes quantum states as a chain of connected mathematical structures, making large-scale quantum simulations practical. They arrange quantum bits (qubits) in a linear line and systematically increase the maximum distance over which qubits can interact with each other. They then evaluate performance on both standard processors (CPUs) and graphics processors (GPUs) to determine when GPU acceleration becomes beneficial.
sc-2024-191.key_novelty: They demonstrated quantum kernel models at practical scale (165 features, 6400 training points) using MPS simulation, far exceeding what earlier approaches could accomplish.

sc-2024-199.method: The work redesigns the OMPC runtime (the scheduling system in OpenMP) to handle clusters with different types of hardware. It uses the Heterogeneous Earliest Finish Time algorithm (HEFT): for each task, predict how long it would take on each available resource, then assign it to whichever resource would finish fastest. The approach is evaluated against Work Stealing, a method where idle processors grab pending tasks from busy ones, on real clusters.
sc-2024-199.key_novelty: The innovation is using a unified task scheduler based on the HEFT algorithm for OpenMP clusters with different hardware types, which assigns each task to the resource predicted to finish it fastest.

sc-2024-195.method: The approach trains a decision tree regression model—a machine learning system that learns to predict outcomes by finding patterns—on over 180,000 simulated data points showing how different CPU design choices affect execution cycles (the number of clock cycles it takes to run programs). It uses specialized search spaces and simulation frameworks designed to test realistic high-performance computing workloads, allowing designers to see how each architectural parameter impacts performance without testing every possible combination.
sc-2024-195.key_novelty: Using machine learning regression models to efficiently navigate CPU design space and measure how much each microarchitectural feature affects performance.

sc-2024-196.method: The approach diagnoses performance problems in RISC-V processors by using predefined formulas to combine measurements from hardware performance counters (sensors that track CPU activity) and classify issues into four categories. It validates this method by running standard benchmark programs (SPEC CPU2006) on SiFive RISC-V processors and checking whether the diagnosed problems match actual hardware behavior.
sc-2024-196.key_novelty: This is the first adaptation of Intel's Top-Down Microarchitecture Analysis methodology (a way to diagnose why processors run slowly) to RISC-V processors, with clearly-defined performance metrics validated through hardware performance counter measurements.

sc-2024-202.method: The researchers tested FABRIC—a distributed computing system with graphics processors (GPUs)—running brain-cell simulations using CoreNEURON across multiple geographically distributed sites. They compared different strategies for assigning cells to sites, then applied graph partitioning (a technique that divides interconnected networks into balanced sections while minimizing data transferred between sections) to optimize how the simulation workload was distributed. They measured how many cells could be simulated, how delays in sending data between sites affected performance, and how much GPU memory was required.
sc-2024-202.key_novelty: FABRIC, a distributed computing system, can scale neuronal network simulations to 25,000 cells by using graph partitioning to distribute the simulation workload efficiently across geographically distributed sites.

sc-2024-198.method: HPCAdvisor helps users select which cloud computers (VMs) and cluster size to use for HPC workloads (high-performance computing tasks) by analyzing their program's specific input needs against real performance measurements from cloud providers. The tool takes information about what your program will process and recommends which computer types and cluster size will perform best. This approach is better than generic recommendations because it's customized for your program instead of following one-size-fits-all rules.
sc-2024-198.key_novelty: The innovation is personalizing cloud computer and cluster recommendations based on what your specific program will process, rather than using one-size-fits-all benchmark data.

sc-2024-192.method: The authors develop a memory profiling tool using ARM's Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE, a hardware feature that periodically records memory accesses without stopping the processor by sampling events). They test the tool on ARM Ampere processors running HPC and cloud workloads. The evaluation measures two key metrics: execution overhead (how much profiling slows the system down) and sampling accuracy (whether sampled memory accesses represent actual behavior), across different sampling intervals and buffer configurations.
sc-2024-192.key_novelty: This paper provides the first measurements of ARM SPE's execution overhead and sampling accuracy for memory profiling at multiple system levels, establishing its feasibility for production HPC systems.

sc-2024-201.method: SMaT is a block-sparse SpMM (sparse matrix multiplication) library that directly uses Tensor Cores—specialized hardware circuits in GPUs designed for fast matrix math. It accesses these circuits through the low-level CUDA MMA (matrix-multiply-accumulate) API to maximize speed when working with unstructured sparse matrices, which have non-zero values scattered randomly rather than in patterns. The library reorganizes the sparse matrix data into blocks of non-zeros, which reduces wasted computation on empty space and improves efficiency. This block structure allows Tensor Cores, which normally require perfectly structured dense data, to work with irregular sparsity patterns instead.
sc-2024-201.key_novelty: Block-sparse data structures and the CUDA MMA API enable Tensor Cores to accelerate unstructured sparse matrix-matrix multiplication.

sc-2024-204.method: CEEMS plugs into existing system-monitoring tools (Prometheus and Grafana, which track server activity) to collect energy-usage data from CPUs and graphics accelerators made by NVIDIA and AMD. It calculates the carbon emissions from that energy consumption. The system also lets data center operators write custom rules for how their hardware actually uses energy, and it works with any resource scheduler—whether on HPC systems or cloud platforms.
sc-2024-204.key_novelty: The core innovation is a system that measures energy and carbon emissions while working with any resource scheduler and any combination of CPU and GPU hardware.

sc-2024-189.method: The framework converts directive-based GPU code (where programmers annotate code for compiler optimization) into single-assignment form (a representation where each variable is assigned exactly once), then uses equality saturation—a technique that generates all mathematically equivalent ways to rewrite the code while keeping the program intact. It explores this search space by strategically reordering calculations and memory accesses to reduce computational work and improve data-transfer efficiency. Finally, it selects the rewritten version that simultaneously improves computation speed, reduces memory-access overhead, and increases throughput.
sc-2024-189.key_novelty: Applying equality saturation (generating all mathematically equivalent rewrites of code) to directive-based GPU code in single-assignment form to select versions that simultaneously reduce computation, lower memory-access overhead, and improve throughput.

sc-2024-203.method: A coordinated set of software tools that tracks the complete lineage of data transformations throughout an AI research workflow. Starting from original data sources, the system records every processing step, creating a detailed history of how data evolves through all stages of computation. Researchers can then examine this record to document experiments, verify reproducibility, understand what happened in their pipeline, and pinpoint performance bottlenecks.
sc-2024-203.key_novelty: A coordinated ecosystem of tools designed specifically for AI research workflows that tracks data transformations at every computational level, enabling researchers to simultaneously solve documentation, reproducibility, interpretability, and performance diagnosis challenges.

sc-2024-212.method: The paper adds vector clocks—a technique that records the order of operations across parallel threads—to the MUST MPI correctness tool to track how OpenMP threads (code segments running simultaneously within the same program) synchronize with each other. It pulls synchronization information from the Archer race detector to understand thread interactions, then uses this data to identify four specific types of errors that occur when multiple threads attempt to make concurrent MPI calls (network communication requests) at the same time.
sc-2024-212.key_novelty: The innovation is using vector clocks to track OpenMP thread synchronization for detecting errors that occur when multiple threads invoke MPI calls concurrently in the same program.

sc-2024-206.method: AdaMBE redesigns how bicliques are found by using information from the active part of the graph (the computational subgraph) to avoid reading the same data from memory repeatedly. It represents this active region as bitmaps—fast, compact sets of 0s and 1s—and uses quick bitwise operations (like AND and OR) to find overlapping nodes between groups. A parallel version, ParAdaMBE, splits the work across multiple CPU cores.
