sc-2024-206.key_novelty: AdaMBE uses bitmaps of the active graph region with fast bitwise operations to eliminate repeated memory accesses and speed up finding node overlaps in biclique enumeration.

sc-2024-215.method: The researchers set up two HPC systems with different Ethernet interconnects—the networking technology that connects computers together—one operating at 100G speed and one at 200G speed (where G means billions of bits per second). They measure how much data can flow between computers per second (bandwidth) and how long it takes before data starts moving (latency), testing both small and large message sizes. They compare these results directly against InfiniBand, which is the networking standard currently used for high-performance computing.
sc-2024-215.key_novelty: Testing shows that modern Ethernet (at 100G and 200G speeds) performs just as well as InfiniBand when sending large amounts of data between computers.

sc-2024-205.method: Octopus links event sources and processors across edge devices, cloud data centers, and supercomputers by routing all events through cloud-hosted brokers—central hubs that organize and forward them. The system automatically activates responses to specific events, enforces detailed permission rules about what each component can access, and adjusts computing resources based on how many events arrive. When parts of the network fail, the system finds alternate routes so events still reach their destinations.
sc-2024-205.key_novelty: A unified system for routing events (messages about things happening) across the full range of scientific computing infrastructure—from edge devices to cloud systems to supercomputers.

sc-2024-207.method: Researchers continued training LLaMA-2 models (7 billion and 70 billion parameters) on astronomy papers from arXiv, then tested the results with astronomy multiple-choice questions. They compared the specialized models against the original base models to see whether high-quality astronomy data prevented catastrophic forgetting—the tendency for models to lose general knowledge when trained on a specific domain.
sc-2024-207.key_novelty: Large models (70 billion parameters) retain general knowledge when specialized on astronomy with high-quality data, unlike smaller models, as shown by AstroLLaMA-2-70B outperforming previous astronomy-specialized variants.

sc-2024-208.method: RecFlex combines computations for different feature fields into one optimized program (a fused kernel), giving each field its own schedule—the order and timing of operations—rather than forcing all fields to use the same strategy. To determine the best schedule for each field, it uses a two-stage tuner that simulates interference: how the fields slow each other down when competing for shared processor resources. A compiler then combines these different schedules into the single fused kernel. Since recommendation workloads vary during execution, RecFlex also adjusts how tasks are mapped to processor cores at runtime, not just at compile time.
sc-2024-208.key_novelty: RecFlex creates fused kernels where each feature field gets its own customized execution schedule, instead of applying one uniform schedule across all fields.

sc-2024-211.method: The authors trained four generative AI models (TVAE, CTAGGAN+, SMOTE, and TabDDPM) on over 2 million real job submissions collected during 150 days of operations. To verify the synthetic records were realistic, they measured whether the generated data matched the original data's patterns—checking individual feature distributions, relationships between pairs of features, how close synthetic records were to real ones, and whether pre-trained models responded similarly to real and synthetic data. They selected TabDDPM, a probabilistic diffusion-based model (which builds data step-by-step through a process similar to gradually adding noise to an image, then reversing it), because it best balanced data quality with privacy protection.
sc-2024-211.key_novelty: The core contribution is generating synthetic but realistic job records using AI, enabling machine learning to optimize workload placement without requiring direct access to real submission data while protecting privacy.

sc-2024-219.method: The researchers ran popular global climate models multiple times, comparing results with Fused Multiply-Add (FMA)—a CPU instruction that multiplies and adds numbers in a single operation—enabled versus disabled. Instead of requiring outputs to match exactly bit-for-bit, they analyzed whether the overall statistical properties and patterns of the simulations remained consistent across different hardware and software configurations.
sc-2024-219.key_novelty: Rather than treating Fused Multiply-Add's numerical differences as correctness failures, this work shows climate model consistency can be preserved when measured statistically rather than requiring exact bit-for-bit matching.

sc-2024-210.method: To predict missing connections in knowledge graphs, the model identifies the local area around each potential link, called an enclosing subgraph. It uses attention mechanisms—methods that learn to assign different importance to edges based on their properties. By using graph attention networks (which learn variable weights for each edge) instead of graph convolution networks (which weight all edges equally), the model can better use the information stored in edge attributes to make predictions.
sc-2024-210.key_novelty: Replacing graph convolution networks with graph attention networks to enable the use of edge attributes for knowledge graph link prediction.

sc-2024-216.method: SANReN deployed Data Transfer Nodes (computers that move large research datasets) capable of 100 Gbps speeds using Globus software at two locations—Cape Town and Johannesburg—connected by an upgraded high-speed network backbone. Instead of requiring separate machines for data transfer and network-performance monitoring (perfSONAR, a tool that watches how the network is performing), they built one combined system that does both jobs. This cuts equipment costs, reduces maintenance burden, and lets institutions with limited rack space actually participate in the national research network.
sc-2024-216.key_novelty: They built the first working shared national research infrastructure where a single Data Transfer Node and network-performance monitoring system (DTN/perfSONAR) serves multiple institutions, eliminating the need for separate specialized hardware.

sc-2024-209.method: The paper evaluates different methods for efficiently scaling small pre-trained models into larger ones by reusing their learned parameters (weights and biases—the internal numbers that encode what the model has learned) through either fixed mathematical transformations or learned mappings. It tests each method individually and in combinations, identifying which techniques work especially well together. This systematic comparison shows how to maximize training-efficiency gains from parameter reuse.
sc-2024-209.key_novelty: A systematic comparison shows that combining different model-growth techniques can achieve up to 80% reduction in training computation (measured in TFLOPs—trillions of floating-point operations).

sc-2024-217.method: The framework (DCMESH, combining divide-and-conquer optimization with Maxwell-Ehrenfest-surface hopping—a technique for simulating quantum molecular dynamics) runs simulations on Intel Data Center GPU Max Series 1550 GPUs. To speed up the calculations, it can use different numerical precisions (BF16, TF32, or Complex 3M) depending on the simulation's needs. The precision level is controlled entirely through environment variables—just a setting you change before running—rather than requiring code edits or recompilation. This makes it simple to deploy and tune across many different simulation jobs without extra engineering work.
sc-2024-217.key_novelty: Using environment variables to switch BLAS precision enables up to 3.91x faster quantum simulations while keeping the important output values accurate, all without modifying the code.

sc-2024-213.method: The RAJA Performance Suite includes computational kernels written in different GPU programming approaches. Using integrated Caliper and Thicket tools, it automatically identifies whether each kernel is limited by memory bandwidth or by processor computing speed (FLOPS—floating-point operations per second), then predicts performance on new hardware with different resource balances.
sc-2024-213.key_novelty: The key innovation is automatically detecting performance bottlenecks in code to predict how well it will perform on different hardware.

sc-2024-227.method: Multiple scientists can now work together on the same Jupyter notebook—an interactive tool for writing code and analyzing data—while running on supercomputers (HPC systems, or high-performance computing facilities). JupyterHub manages these shared notebook sessions, giving each team an isolated workspace so they don't interfere with each other. It connects to the supercomputer's resource manager—the software that allocates computing power—so teams can run real analysis on experimental data without leaving the notebook. The system keeps a complete record of who made each change, which is required for security compliance at large research facilities like NERSC.
sc-2024-227.key_novelty: Making Jupyter notebooks work collaboratively—multiple people editing the same notebook at once—directly on supercomputers, with automatic tracking of all user actions for compliance and security.

sc-2024-220.method: During container image builds, package managers request privileged system calls—operations that normally require root access. A Linux security tool called seccomp intercepts these calls and returns success without actually executing them, making the program think the operations completed. This allows unprivileged container builds to proceed, enabling Dockerfiles to be constructed without root access.
sc-2024-220.key_novelty: By faking successful privileged system calls (without tracking their effects), seccomp enables building container images without requiring root access.

sc-2024-214.method: The tool builds on Valgrind (a program inspection framework) by adding heavyweight monitoring that watches every instruction as the program actually runs—it's thorough but slows things down considerably. It records every memory access made by concurrent tasks (pieces of work running in parallel) and flags races: situations where two accesses to the same memory location aren't properly ordered and at least one is writing. Because it understands how Cilk and OpenMP organize parallel work, it avoids many false alarms that simpler tools raise, catching actual problems without noise.
sc-2024-214.key_novelty: By combining detailed runtime monitoring (watching every memory access) with awareness of parallel programming models, it detects races in Cilk and OpenMP programs that simpler tools miss.

sc-2024-225.method: The algorithm builds a conflict graph—a map showing which matrix operations will interfere when trying to write to the output vector at the same time. It then recursively breaks this graph into isolated subgraphs where operations don't conflict with each other. For subgraphs with few conflicts, it processes them in parallel using divide-and-conquer; for those with many conflicts, it falls back to traditional sequential processing. A machine learning model predicts which strategy is optimal for a given matrix and hardware.
sc-2024-225.key_novelty: The innovation is using recursive divide-and-conquer partitioning of the conflict graph—the map of which operations interfere—to eliminate data races (simultaneous writes to the same memory location) in parallel symmetric matrix multiplication.

sc-2024-226.method: The approach uses a score-based diffusion model (a generative model that learns gradients pointing toward likely data) without requiring expensive upfront training. Instead, it solves the backward stochastic differential equation (BSDE, a mathematical equation describing how to generate samples) using a parallel-in-time method that distributes computation across multiple time steps simultaneously on multiple GPUs and nodes. Because training is eliminated, the method immediately adapts to changes in the target probability distribution without retraining.
sc-2024-226.key_novelty: The core idea is using parallel-in-time distributed computation across multiple GPUs to enable a training-free score-based diffusion model that adapts immediately to changing probability distributions.

sc-2024-221.method: The system prevents users from interfering with each other by enforcing separation at four levels: isolating their running programs (processes), controlling which files they can access, blocking their network traffic from crossing, and restricting their access to hardware accelerators (like GPUs). Because all four barriers work together, each user sees only their own work and cannot access or affect what others are doing, even though they're all using the same physical hardware.
sc-2024-221.key_novelty: The key contribution is coordinating user separation across all four areas—processes, filesystem, network, and accelerators—to create strong isolation between users on shared HPC hardware.

sc-2024-222.method: Instead of finishing all computations first and then sending results between GPUs, this approach combines these operations into a single program (kernel) that runs on the GPU. Groups of GPU threads can immediately send their results directly to other GPUs while other thread groups continue computing—with the GPU itself managing the sending rather than the CPU (GPU-initiated communication). The team developed three specific combined operations: embedding plus All-to-All communication, GEMV (matrix-vector multiplication) plus AllReduce, and GEMM (matrix-matrix multiplication) plus All-to-All, each optimized for specific AI architectures—DLRM, Transformer, and Mixture-of-Experts. These are exposed as PyTorch operators and integrated into the Triton framework.
sc-2024-222.key_novelty: Fusing computation with direct GPU-to-GPU communication at the threadblock level (groups of GPU threads), enabling simultaneous data transfer and computation in a single kernel.

sc-2024-218.method: The combination technique partitions an extremely large high-dimensional grid across multiple supercomputers, with each computing a complete subgrid at full resolution. To coordinate work across these diverse machines, it uses load balancing to keep all systems equally busy, compresses data flowing between supercomputers to maximize network throughput, intelligently routes I/O operations to match each machine's strengths, and optimizes the algorithm itself for memory efficiency. The technique extends to work with three or more supercomputers simultaneously.
sc-2024-218.key_novelty: The key innovation is extending the combination technique to coordinate three or more supercomputers for extreme-scale high-dimensional simulations in a superfacility (a coordinated network of supercomputers).

sc-2024-224.method: When a virtual machine needs to access storage, requests normally have to switch from the Linux kernel to QEMU (the virtual machine software) running in user-space, creating overhead. EXO uses eBPF, a method for running programs directly inside the Linux kernel, to create a direct path that performs guest-to-host memory address translations (converting virtual machine addresses to real computer addresses) without needing to switch to QEMU. For complex operations that need full backend processing, the system falls back to the original slower path through QEMU.
sc-2024-224.key_novelty: EXO uses eBPF (a method for running code directly in the Linux kernel) to create a fast path for virtio-blk storage requests that bypasses the user-space QEMU backend by performing guest-to-host memory address translations (converting virtual machine addresses to real computer addresses).

sc-2024-233.method: Researchers tested NVIDIA's new Grace processors on Vista by running real scientific applications on them. They compared the performance directly against Intel and AMD processors running the same applications at TACC (the Texas Advanced Computing Center). By measuring actual workloads instead of synthetic benchmarks, they got the first reliable picture of how Grace performs for the kinds of scientific computing that researchers actually do.
sc-2024-233.key_novelty: This work provides the first performance measurements of NVIDIA's Grace CPU architecture when running real scientific HPC (high-performance computing) applications on an academic supercomputer.

sc-2024-236.method: The system collects detailed packet information directly from network switches and cards using in-band network telemetry (INT), which adds minimal overhead to the network. This data streams to a central control system that uses machine learning models to analyze it in real-time and detect DDoS attacks. The researchers then compared how well this INT-based detection performs against sFlow (a traditional traffic-sampling approach) in a real production network.
sc-2024-236.key_novelty: Real-time DDoS detection using in-band network telemetry in production networks, directly compared to sFlow.

sc-2024-235.method: OptME figures out which transactions can run in parallel while still producing the same final result as if they had run one after another in a predetermined order. It does this by analyzing which transactions depend on each other (by tracking which ones read or write the same data), creating a schedule that runs non-conflicting transactions simultaneously, and executing them according to that plan. To speed this up, it analyzes dependencies in parallel, stops transactions early if they conflict, and uses optimistic reordering—assuming transactions will succeed and rearranging them for speed, then rolling back if a conflict is discovered.
sc-2024-235.key_novelty: By analyzing which transactions depend on each other, you can find which ones can run in parallel while maintaining the correct predetermined order—doing both simultaneously instead of as separate phases.

sc-2024-231.method: The authors measure Apple M4's Scalable Matrix Extension (SME, a hardware feature for accelerating matrix math) by testing how fast it performs floating-point and fixed-point operations and measuring memory bandwidth when using matrix registers (fast on-chip storage). They discover that two-step loading and storing—rather than single transfers—achieves optimal bandwidth. They then build a just-in-time code generator that automatically creates optimized matrix multiplication code for Apple M4.
sc-2024-231.key_novelty: A code generator that automatically produces optimized matrix multiplication kernels for Apple M4 by measuring how its matrix extension hardware actually performs.

sc-2024-232.method: Laminar 2.0 improves the dispel4py framework—which builds data processing pipelines from modular elements that perform individual tasks—with better dependency tracking and a split client-server design. It finds similar processing elements two ways: structurally, by comparing simplified parse syntax trees (simplified maps of code structure that reveal matching patterns), and semantically, using deep learning models trained to understand what code does, with preprocessing that translates text descriptions into code.
sc-2024-232.key_novelty: Simplified parse syntax trees enable code-to-code searching that finds similar processing elements and workflows based on what they actually do, not just structure, even when code is incomplete.

sc-2024-230.method: It coordinates work across multiple processors using messages and independently schedulable tasks to enable highly asynchronous execution without waiting for synchronization. It reduces wasted speculative work by adapting how much data it groups together at once and using evolving time windows to prioritize which graph connections (edges) to process first.
sc-2024-230.key_novelty: It continuously monitors parallel execution and adjusts how asynchronously the algorithm runs to balance the benefit of doing many things at once against the cost of wasted speculative work.

sc-2024-234.method: The researchers adapted OpenFold—an efficient, open-source implementation of AlphaFold designed to train across multiple GPUs—to run on Intel's Ponte Vecchio data center GPUs. They trained it on a dataset of five million multiple sequence alignments (protein sequences aligned to find similarities) and systematically tested different configurations to measure performance and identify where it could be optimized.
sc-2024-234.key_novelty: The study is the first to measure how efficiently OpenFold's distributed training runs on Intel's Ponte Vecchio GPUs.

sc-2024-239.method: The method converts raw records of I/O system calls (requests to the operating system for file operations) into a Directly-Follows-Graph—a network diagram where each I/O operation is a node and arrows show their execution order. By comparing these graphs from different programs or configurations, the approach identifies behavioral differences. It tests this on the IOR benchmark, varying file output methods and software interfaces to analyze patterns of file access contention.
sc-2024-239.key_novelty: The key insight is representing I/O system call sequences as Directly-Follows-Graphs—networks showing which operations happen before others—to systematically identify behavioral differences between programs.

sc-2024-229.method: The team built a 0-75 km fiber network and used single photon coincidence detectors (sensors that detect when two photons arrive at the same time) to measure transmissivity—the fraction of the quantum signal that successfully reaches the destination. Using these measurements, they calculated theoretical capacity estimates using mathematical models, then converted those estimates to practical throughput predictions (in entanglement bits per second) using a scaling factor calibrated from the testbed detectors. They validated their predictions against the actual measured throughput across all test links.
sc-2024-229.key_novelty: They showed how to reliably convert theoretical capacity estimates into actual quantum network throughput by using matched physical measurements and mathematical models.

sc-2024-228.method: TSSpGEMM handles the specific case of multiplying two sparse matrices where one is tall and thin using 1D partitioning (dividing the work in one direction) instead of traditional 2D or 3D grid-based divisions, which is simpler for this matrix shape. It then uses sparsity-aware tiling—grouping calculations into chunks while being smart about where the actual non-zeros are—which minimizes how much data needs to be moved between processors. The algorithm strategically decides which computations each processor does locally and which ones need to communicate with remote processors, which further cuts down on expensive data transfers. This entire design is tuned specifically to how tall-and-skinny matrices are structured, rather than being a general approach for all sparse matrices.
sc-2024-228.key_novelty: Using 1D partitioning with sparsity-aware tiling, specifically tailored for tall-and-skinny sparse matrices instead of traditional 2D or 3D approaches designed for general sparse matrices.

sc-2024-223.method: Tango coordinates two system layers to handle I/O interference. The application layer reorganizes analytics data across different storage tiers (fast to slow), moving data away from busy lower-tier storage during interference while keeping results accurate. The storage layer adjusts how much bandwidth (data flow capacity) each application receives, based on how much data it processes, how accurate its results need to be, and how the application behaves.
sc-2024-223.key_novelty: Tango's innovation is coordinating application decisions about data placement with storage decisions about bandwidth allocation, enabling the system to automatically adapt to I/O interference while keeping analytics accurate.

sc-2024-243.method: BCSR (bit-CSR) modifies the standard CSR (Compressed Sparse Row) format, which is how graphs are typically stored efficiently in memory. When you partition a large graph across many processors for distributed processing, you create local subgraphs where most vertices have no edges—CSR format wastes memory storing empty slots for them. BCSR solves this by using bitwise operations to encode those empty vertices as individual bits instead of full data structures, shrinking memory use on GPUs without slowing down computation. The method is tested on Graph500 benchmarks using sparse random graph datasets containing hundreds of millions of vertices and edges.
sc-2024-243.key_novelty: BCSR applies bit-level compression to CSR format to eliminate memory waste from empty vertices in sparse graphs processed on GPUs.

sc-2024-237.method: The approach solves large systems of equations that come from Finite Volume discretization (a technique that approximates physics equations by dividing space into small volumes). Instead of computing and storing a complete matrix (a large grid of numbers), the algorithm computes only what it needs on-the-fly, which saves memory. It runs on a dataflow architecture—specialized hardware designed to pass data directly between calculations without going through slow main memory—which keeps data access fast and eliminates the memory delays that normally dominate simulation time.
sc-2024-237.key_novelty: Matrix-free Finite Volume kernels (computing results on-the-fly rather than storing a matrix) on dataflow architecture (specialized hardware for efficient data routing) overcome memory bottlenecks in large geological simulations.

sc-2024-238.method: The system automatically generates code to run high-order stencils (calculations that examine neighboring data values) on dataflow processors like the Cerebras wafer-scale engine. It automates the complex task of determining how to route data between processing units and coordinate their communication, optimizing for the processor's limited memory and routing capacity—constraints that would otherwise require manual code development.
sc-2024-238.key_novelty: The key idea is automating code generation for dataflow processors like the Cerebras wafer-scale engine to run high-order stencils, automatically solving the routing and memory constraint problems that normally require manual coding, while achieving performance comparable to hand-written code.

sc-2024-246.method: The authors built tests to measure data movement speed in AMD MI250X systems—clusters of four specialized processors called GPUs. They compared different communication paths (direct GPU-to-GPU links versus paths to multiple GPUs), storage locations (GPU memory or host CPU memory), and software libraries (AMD's specialized RCCL library versus the older general-purpose MPI system). Each test measured latency—how long before data starts moving—and bandwidth—how much data flows per second.
sc-2024-246.key_novelty: Direct GPU-to-GPU communication and AMD's RCCL library deliver higher bandwidth and lower latency than the traditional general-purpose MPI approach on Infinity Fabric interconnects.

sc-2024-248.method: The researchers created benchmarks that measure how fast GPUs exchange data within a single computer and between different computers. They ran these tests on three different supercomputers—Alps, Leonardo, and LUMI—that use different connection technologies. By testing with up to 4,096 GPUs, they could identify where communication slows down and what hardware and software changes could improve performance.
sc-2024-248.key_novelty: The paper directly compares GPU-to-GPU communication performance across exascale supercomputers with different interconnect architectures.

sc-2024-241.method: The system uses a Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine—a processor with thousands of cores densely packed together—and assigns one processor core to each atom being simulated. Because each atom can be processed independently, thousands of atoms get calculated in parallel rather than one after another. The system implements a dataflow algorithm (which moves data between cores only when needed) and uses the Embedded Atom Method physics model to calculate how atoms interact, allowing it to compute the time increments that molecular dynamics simulations require much faster than traditional supercomputers.
sc-2024-241.key_novelty: Mapping one processor core to each atom on a wafer-scale chip enables parallel molecular dynamics calculations.

sc-2024-242.method: The approach trains machine learning models (deep kernel methods, a technique for learning patterns from data) on microscopic images to predict differences in defect formation energy for various structures. It starts by fully training on simulated images to establish a baseline, then uses active learning (strategically picking examples that are either hard to predict or energetically interesting) to predict what structures appear at key points along simulated trajectories, reducing data and computational needs. The system uses an autoencoder-decoder neural network—which compresses images to extract essential features—to precisely align simulations with real experimental observations.
sc-2024-242.key_novelty: Deep kernel-based surrogate models combined with active learning map microscopic images to defect formation energy differences while strategically selecting which simulation paths to analyze, reducing data and computational requirements.

sc-2024-244.method: We adapted quantum chemistry code from CPUs to run on GPUs from three vendors (AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA) using OpenMP—a framework where the same code runs across different hardware. Each vendor's OpenMP compiler, however, optimizes code very differently, creating large performance gaps. We addressed this by developing strategies to restructure code for each GPU's memory constraints, fix branching logic that varies by vendor, and account for each compiler's unique optimization patterns.
sc-2024-244.key_novelty: We identified practical coding strategies that let you write a single OpenMP program that runs efficiently on multiple vendors' GPUs despite their different compiler optimization behaviors.

sc-2024-245.method: The system uses a reconfigurable hardware processor (a CGRA—custom silicon that can be reprogrammed to run different calculations) to simulate how particle bunches oscillate in the direction they're traveling. By running this simulation in real-time—fast enough to match actual physics—engineers can connect real beam control hardware and test whether it correctly handles the simulated behavior (hardware-in-the-loop validation) before deploying it to the actual accelerator.
sc-2024-245.key_novelty: The core contribution is using a reconfigurable hardware processor (a CGRA) to achieve real-time simulation of how particle bunches oscillate in the direction they travel, enabling engineers to test actual beam control hardware before deployment.

sc-2024-249.method: The paper introduces a bridge that enables interactive steering of running simulations by letting scientists pause between timesteps, adjust simulation parameters (like model inputs) or analysis settings, and resume without cold restarts. This bridge works with any in situ analysis system (the tools that examine simulations as they run), with Ascent as a reference implementation. Rather than relying on automated, hands-off analysis, the interface puts scientists in real-time control, letting them respond to emerging results immediately.
sc-2024-249.key_novelty: An interactive steering interface that's library-agnostic (compatible with any in situ analysis tool) and lets scientists pause running simulations to adjust parameters in real time, without restart overhead.

sc-2024-247.method: The researchers tested two Linux kernel features designed to speed up data transfer: MSG_ZEROCOPY (which sends data directly from user memory to the network instead of copying it multiple times) and BIG TCP (which reduces overhead by allowing larger packets to be sent at once). They ran controlled experiments at AmLight and ESnet testbeds, comparing Linux versions 5.15 and 6.8 on Intel and AMD processors across various network conditions. They measured how much faster data could be transferred when combining MSG_ZEROCOPY with packet pacing (spacing packets over time) and BIG TCP optimizations.
sc-2024-247.key_novelty: Systematic real-world testing reveals how two Linux kernel optimizations—MSG_ZEROCOPY and BIG TCP—improve data transfer speeds, with effectiveness varying across different processors and network conditions.

sc-2024-240.method: PULSE makes it cheaper to keep AI models ready to use instantly by using multiple versions of each model with different quality levels. Instead of keeping one full-size model running for a fixed duration (a simple but wasteful approach), PULSE dynamically chooses which version to keep alive based on current demand—using smaller, faster models when accuracy is less critical and upgrading when needed. This approach prevents sudden memory spikes and works with existing serverless platforms' warming strategies.
sc-2024-240.key_novelty: The core idea is dynamically switching between model variants of different sizes and accuracy levels based on demand, rather than keeping one fixed-size model running for a predetermined time.

sc-2024-250.method: The paper compares two approaches to connect quantum computers across Tennessee cities: deploying 108 orbiting satellites or using high-altitude platforms (stationary systems suspended high in the atmosphere). Researchers measure how well each covers the region, how many requests for quantum entanglement (the special connections that distribute quantum information) it can fulfill, and how accurately quantum information survives transmission (called fidelity).
sc-2024-250.key_novelty: The paper shows how satellites versus high-altitude platforms compare for connecting quantum computers across a region, revealing specific trade-offs in coverage, request fulfillment rates, and transmission accuracy.

sc-2024-253.method: Investigated how floating-point non-associativity—where adding numbers in different orders produces slightly different results because computers round intermediate calculations differently—affects parallel programs through direct measurement. Tested the performance and productivity impact of replacing atomic operations (synchronized actions between processors) with deterministic alternatives on GPUs. Examined PyTorch's built-in reproducibility features to assess how reliably they work. Evaluated whether specialized hardware like the Groq LPU accelerator can automatically enforce reproducible deep learning inference without requiring algorithmic or software changes.
sc-2024-253.key_novelty: A specialized hardware accelerator (Groq LPU) can automatically enforce reproducible results in deep learning inference without requiring algorithmic or software modifications.

sc-2024-258.method: The system combines two pieces: an HPC workflow generator (a tool for creating realistic scientific computing tasks) and a serverless workflow management system (which runs tasks on cloud platforms without needing to maintain servers). Researchers used these together to build benchmark workflows—realistic test workloads—then ran them on different serverless platforms and compared the results against traditional container-based execution.
sc-2024-258.key_novelty: The first system to combine HPC workflow management with serverless computing, proving that serverless platforms can handle complex scientific computing tasks.

sc-2024-256.method: The framework ingests and processes multi-terabyte data streams generated daily by supercomputers at Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, handling the entire pipeline from raw data collection through analysis. The researchers built and refined this system across two generations of hardware, documenting the design decisions, challenges encountered, and pipeline strategies that actually worked. By learning from the first generation and improving the second, they created a systematic approach to turning massive data volumes into useful operational insights.
sc-2024-256.key_novelty: A two-generation evolution of an operational data analytics system at Oak Ridge that shows how to transform daily multi-terabyte data streams from supercomputers into actionable operational insights.

sc-2024-260.method: They set up XDMoD (a tool that continuously monitors how fast programs run) to track performance on Ookami, a cluster of ARM computers using Fujitsu A64FX processors and SVE-512 vector acceleration. Over 3+ years of monitoring, they measured how quickly applications and numerical libraries (reusable math code) performed after each software update. By watching performance over such a long period, they could distinguish genuine improvements from natural fluctuations and see when software changes actually helped.
sc-2024-260.key_novelty: The largest performance gains happen when new technology support first becomes available, not through slow incremental software improvements.

sc-2024-257.method: This approach tackles the energy problem at every level of the system. It picks specialized hardware accelerators (circuits designed for specific types of computation) for each application, develops algorithms that do the same work with less power, and uses data-driven analysis to find the best operational settings. Rather than just optimizing for speed, it treats energy as the limiting resource and keeps performance within that budget.
sc-2024-257.key_novelty: The core idea is building energy efficiency into every layer of the system, from hardware choices to day-to-day operations, rather than optimizing each part separately.

sc-2024-259.method: LexiQL converts text into quantum circuits by gradually feeding in the text data step-by-step—a technique called incremental data injection—rather than loading it all at once. It uses quantum circuits of varying depths: some shallow (with fewer quantum operations, making them more stable on noisy hardware) and some deeper (capable of more complex transformations). The training process accounts for errors that naturally occur in NISQ devices—today's quantum computers with limited capacity and high error rates. This mix of circuit designs is tuned to classify text effectively despite these hardware limitations.
sc-2024-259.key_novelty: LexiQL performs text classification by using incremental data injection and shallow quantum circuits specifically tuned to handle the noise limitations of current-generation quantum machines.

sc-2024-251.method: The approach breaks down the correlation energy calculation into linear systems solved together using a block Krylov subspace solver, a technique that iteratively refines the solution approximation. It automatically adjusts the batch size (how many equations to solve simultaneously) based on system difficulty—using larger batches when efficient and smaller batches when needed. This adaptive balancing reduces computational scaling from quartic to cubic and improves memory efficiency.
sc-2024-251.key_novelty: The core innovation is automatically choosing the right batch size for solving equations together, dynamically adjusting it to trade off per-iteration cost against convergence rate depending on problem difficulty.

sc-2024-255.method: The paper develops I-mrDMD (incremental multiresolution dynamic mode decomposition), which extracts recurring patterns from massive monitoring logs by processing them in chunks at multiple time scales rather than all at once. This approach works by identifying dynamic modes—recurring patterns that emerge at different frequencies—like simultaneously detecting both daily trends and minute-by-minute fluctuations in system behavior. The extracted patterns are visualized using D3-based interactive charts in Jupyter Notebooks that align and display hardware, job, and environment logs together through a rack visualization that represents data in the physical layout of server racks.
sc-2024-255.key_novelty: I-mrDMD combines incremental processing (analyzing data in chunks) with multiresolution analysis (finding patterns at different time scales) to quickly extract patterns from terabyte-scale HPC system monitoring data.

sc-2024-252.method: The authors developed more efficient quantum mechanical algorithms for calculating Raman spectra—how molecules respond to light at different frequencies. They implemented these on the Sunway and ORISE supercomputers, which use different processor types, distributing computation across thousands of compute nodes. Critical to their approach was optimizing data communication and memory management between computers to prevent idle waiting time. This achieved near-linear scaling: adding more computers provided nearly proportional speedups, making simulations of 100 million atom biological systems feasible.
sc-2024-252.key_novelty: The researchers demonstrated the first quantum mechanical simulation of Raman spectra (how molecules respond to light at different frequencies) achieving near-linear scaling to biological systems with 100 million atoms across tens of thousands of compute nodes.

sc-2024-262.method: AxoNN splits the training work across four different dimensions of parallelism, speeds up GPU matrix-multiplication operations, and overlaps communication between GPUs with calculation time rather than pausing for messages. A performance model analyzes different configurations to find the optimal setup for each supercomputer. To prevent models from simply memorizing training data, the system limits model capacity in ways that force it to learn generalizable patterns instead of memorizing word-for-word.
sc-2024-262.key_novelty: Four-dimensional parallelism achieving Exascale training throughput on GPU supercomputers while integrating defenses against data memorization.

sc-2024-261.method: The researchers added measurement tools to SPH-EXA, an open-source astrophysics simulation program built for GPUs, to precisely track energy use across different computer configurations. They implemented dynamic frequency scaling—making the GPU automatically run faster or slower during different parts of the simulation to save energy. They benchmarked both fixed-speed and variable-speed approaches to understand the trade-offs between energy savings and how quickly the simulation runs.
sc-2024-261.key_novelty: The core innovation is dynamically adjusting GPU speeds during individual computational tasks to achieve measurable energy savings while maintaining acceptable performance in astrophysics simulations on production supercomputers.

sc-2024-268.method: Beatnik creates a simplified model that simulates 3D Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities—a type of fluid flow mixing pattern—using the Z-Model mathematical formulation developed by Pandya and Shkoller. It runs within the Cabana framework, which allows the same code to run efficiently across different hardware types. The application provides four benchmark configurations to evaluate how well HPC communication systems (the networks and memory that move data between processors) perform under weak and strong scaling tests—where weak scaling adds more hardware while keeping the problem size per processor constant, and strong scaling adds more hardware to solve a fixed problem faster—on GPU-accelerated systems.
sc-2024-268.key_novelty: A mini-application that reproduces data-movement patterns from production HPC codes to expose communication bottlenecks—places where slow data transfer between processors limits overall performance—in modern accelerator-based systems.

sc-2024-267.method: Fugaku Points gives users direct controls to reduce power consumption in their jobs (power control functions). When users achieve power savings, they earn reward points, creating a financial incentive to operate efficiently. This motivates users to both run individual jobs efficiently and optimize how they schedule their work across the supercomputer.
sc-2024-267.key_novelty: A reward-based power-control program deployed on a real supercomputer that motivates users to reduce power consumption in their jobs.

sc-2024-254.method: LLAMP uses mathematical analysis instead of specialized hardware or simulators to predict the maximum network latency—how long data takes to travel through the network—that HPC applications can tolerate before slowing down. It combines two techniques: the LogGPS model (which predicts how network latency affects message timing) and linear programming (an optimization method). The tool analyzes MPI applications—programs for parallel computing—to capture their communication patterns and extract key parameters, then uses linear programming to find the exact latency threshold. On real applications like LULESH, MILC, and ICON, it achieves prediction errors below 2%.
sc-2024-254.key_novelty: The key insight is applying linear programming (an optimization technique) to the LogGPS model to predict the maximum network latency that HPC applications can tolerate without requiring specialized hardware or simulators.

sc-2024-266.method: They test the deepseek-coder-33B-instruct model using agent-based prompting (a technique where the AI reasons through problems step-by-step), challenging it with intentionally buggy code to see if it can spot the errors. They define evaluation metrics and build an automated pipeline that validates whether LLM-generated compiler tests for OpenMP and OpenACC are correct.
sc-2024-266.key_novelty: An LLM acts as a judge for evaluating whether other LLMs' generated compiler tests for parallel programming (OpenMP, OpenACC) are correct, using step-by-step reasoning prompts and automated pipeline validation.

sc-2024-269.method: The approach fragments the biomolecule into smaller pieces and uses MP2 perturbation theory—a quantum method that improves basic calculations by adding computed corrections—to calculate each piece separately. To sidestep four-center integrals (the expensive quantum calculations needed for accuracy), it employs resolution-of-the-identity (RI), a mathematical trick that replaces these integrals with faster approximations in both the Hartree-Fock and MP2 calculations. It then accelerates execution using GPU processors on the Frontier supercomputer and overlaps computational phases asynchronously to keep processing units busy and avoid waiting for any single step to complete.
sc-2024-269.key_novelty: Combining molecular fragmentation with MP2 perturbation theory and resolution-of-the-identity approximation eliminates the four-center integral bottleneck, enabling quantum-accurate molecular dynamics on large biomolecules.

sc-2024-263.method: Instead of pausing all computation periodically to let every node catch up (bulk-synchronous parallelism), this approach lets compute nodes work asynchronously at their own pace and communicate only when needed. Each node holds its own slice of the graph data without redundant copies across nodes, cutting memory usage. On distributed-memory supercomputers like NERSC Perlmutter, this asynchronous communication improves network efficiency by sending data only when necessary rather than in synchronized batches.
sc-2024-263.key_novelty: Solving influence maximization with asynchronous algorithms where each compute node independently manages its slice of the graph, eliminating the need to replicate data or pause for synchronization.

sc-2024-271.method: The system creates digital copies of data centers (called Digital Twins) that work together in a federated way—coordinating with each other while operating somewhat independently. It continuously monitors key metrics like power consumption and network usage, using machine learning to detect unusual patterns that signal problems. The system automatically adjusts which metrics it watches most closely based on how conditions change. Results appear in real-time on an interactive dashboard showing current state, predictions, and alerts.
sc-2024-271.key_novelty: Digital copies of data centers that coordinate with each other (federated approach) and automatically adjust what they monitor based on conditions, using machine learning to detect problems.

sc-2024-264.method: High-energy physics analysis requires researchers to process enormous datasets repeatedly while testing different approaches—but long wait times for results slow scientific discovery. This paper restructures the analysis pipeline using TaskVine, software that distributes computing tasks across thousands of machines, along with two existing tools called Coffea and Dask. The changes span the full system: redesigning storage and how data moves through the pipeline, optimizing how machines coordinate their work, and modifying the analysis application itself. Together, these changes compress the iteration cycle from hours to minutes, enabling researchers to refine their analysis interactively.
sc-2024-264.key_novelty: TaskVine task coordination combined with redesigning storage, data flow, and application architecture compresses high-energy physics analysis iteration from multi-hour waits to near-interactive speeds.

sc-2024-274.method: The tutorial teaches NSDF—a unified platform combining data storage, streaming solutions, and visualization tools—through hands-on exercises using real Earth science datasets. Participants learn to build analysis pipelines (repeatable sequences of data processing steps) by integrating these services, progressing from basic pipeline construction to advanced techniques for data visualization and large-scale management.
sc-2024-274.key_novelty: NSDF provides a unified platform combining storage, streaming, and visualization for petabyte-scale scientific datasets, so researchers can build scalable analysis workflows without managing underlying infrastructure.

sc-2024-272.method: MN-Core is a processor where each core has its own memory built into the chip, rather than all cores sharing memory from a distant pool. This design, called distributed-memory SIMD (where the same instruction processes multiple pieces of data simultaneously), reduces the delay in fetching needed values. The researchers tested it by running three computational kernels from NICAM, a global climate model, to measure how efficiently it handles CFD (computational fluid dynamics) workloads that require moving massive amounts of data.
sc-2024-272.key_novelty: A processor with memory built into each core achieves efficiency comparable to the high-bandwidth Fujitsu A64FX supercomputer CPU on real climate simulations.

sc-2024-270.method: They developed a performance model—a tool for predicting training speed—to systematically study how transformer training scales with transformer type, parallelization strategy (3D parallelism distributes work across three dimensions; 4D across four), and hardware features like GPU memory bandwidth and network speed. The model measures how much each of these choices affects training efficiency at different scales.
sc-2024-270.key_novelty: Different transformer types require fundamentally different hardware: large language models (LLMs) achieve efficiency with 3D parallelism and low network dependence, while long-sequence transformers (scientific foundation models) require 4D parallelism and equally fast networks and large GPU memory.

sc-2024-265.method: The researchers automated the OMFIT CAKE workflow—which calculates plasma state, the physical properties of hot gas inside the DIII-D reactor—to run on both the local facility's computers and the Perlmutter supercomputer at NERSC, connected through the DOE Integrated Research Infrastructure. This system automatically splits the computational work between locations and manages data movement, running multiple reconstruction jobs in parallel to complete the analysis within the time window between experimental pulses.
sc-2024-265.key_novelty: Connecting the DIII-D plasma reconstruction workflow to the Perlmutter supercomputer (a leadership-class computer—one of the world's most powerful) via the DOE Integrated Research Infrastructure achieves a 5.6x speedup, enabling near-real-time decision support during experiments.

sc-2024-273.method: P-MoVE uses a structured knowledge base that organizes how to monitor different vendors' hardware components. An abstraction layer (a translator that converts different vendors' data formats into one common format) lets measurements from any manufacturer flow into the system. It then runs continuous cache-aware roofline modeling—a calculation that predicts the maximum speed the system can achieve based on how fast data moves between fast local memory and slow main memory—to show performance bottlenecks in real time without adding system overhead.
sc-2024-273.key_novelty: Combining a structured knowledge base designed for high-performance computing with a translation layer so a single monitoring system works across different manufacturers' hardware.

sc-2024-277.method: Serverless platforms sit between the workflow management system and the container orchestrator, acting as an abstraction layer. When a workflow task needs to run, it sends an event that triggers a serverless function, which automatically starts a container to execute the task. Containers are reused across multiple workflow tasks to reduce the overhead of repeatedly spinning them up and down. The event-driven architecture automatically scales resources up or down based on how many workflow tasks are waiting to run.
sc-2024-277.key_novelty: Serverless platforms automatically handle the complex job of connecting workflow systems to containers, spinning them up on demand and reusing them across tasks.

sc-2024-276.method: EE-HPC monitors power use across hybrid HPC clusters (systems with mixed processor types) using tools called ClusterCockpit and LIKWID. The framework detects when a program switches between different computational phases and automatically adjusts hardware power settings in response. This dynamic tuning applies to MPI (code distributed across multiple computers) and OpenMP (code running in parallel on one computer) regions. Testing involved molecular dynamics and earth system modeling simulations.
sc-2024-276.key_novelty: The framework automatically adjusts hardware power settings based on each program's computational phase, instead of using the same settings for all work.

sc-2024-278.method: LIDC uses a decentralized control plane (a management system spread across multiple locations rather than centralized) that assigns meaningful names to computational tasks and matches them to available computing resources labeled with those same names. When new clusters or computers join the system, they automatically become available to accept matching tasks without requiring manual configuration or advance setup. This allows the system to adapt to changing infrastructure—adding or removing resources—without disrupting work.
sc-2024-278.key_novelty: The system decouples computational placement from specific clusters by using semantic names as a universal matching mechanism, enabling multi-organizational collaborations without predefined cluster assignments.

sc-2024-275.method: The authors extend MPI 4.0's Partitioned Point-to-Point communication (a system for splitting messages into independent chunks) to let GPUs directly trigger message-sending while their code is running, without pausing. They also add support for Partitioned Collectives, which are group operations like broadcasting or reduction using the same split-message model. The implementation adapts proven techniques from existing GPU communication libraries, NCCL and NVSHMEM. Testing used NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper systems with NVLink and InfiniBand networks, benchmarked with a mathematical solver (Jacobi) and deep learning workloads.
sc-2024-275.key_novelty: The work extends MPI to let GPUs directly trigger messages and group operations while running code, using Partitioned communication—standardizing capabilities that previously required separate vendor libraries.

sc-2024-283.method: JACC is a system built on Julia (a programming language) that lets you write high-performance code once and have it automatically run fast on both CPUs and GPUs. It works by compiling your code at runtime—called just-in-time compilation—and using Julia's meta-programming features (code that writes other code) to automatically generate optimized versions for each specific hardware platform. The system relies on LLVM, a compiler technology that converts the generated code into efficient machine instructions for different CPU and GPU architectures.
sc-2024-283.key_novelty: The core idea is a high-level programming model where you write a single piece of code that runs nearly as efficiently on CPUs and GPUs as code hand-optimized separately for each specific hardware platform.

sc-2024-282.method: KaMPIng wraps MPI—the standard library for parallel computing across multiple computers—with C++ interfaces at different abstraction levels, ranging from direct low-level calls to high-level interfaces styled after C++'s standard library. It uses named parameters (you pass arguments by name, like keyword arguments in Python) and template metaprogramming (where the compiler generates specialized code during compilation). The compiler only produces code for the specific operations you actually use, achieving near-zero runtime overhead. The type system and safety features built into C++ catch programming errors at compile time instead of causing silent failures like the C version would.
sc-2024-282.key_novelty: Using C++ named parameters and compile-time code generation (template metaprogramming) to create a high-level, standard-library-style MPI interface where the compiler automatically infers most parameters with zero runtime overhead.

sc-2024-286.method: When computers work together to solve this problem, the results scatter across different machines and must be reshuffled between them. The paper proposes two strategies to make this reshuffling more efficient: one saves memory on each computer, the other saves communication time between computers. Both analyze how the computers are physically connected (the network topology) to identify the slowest communication routes and avoid them. The solutions were tested on Fugaku supercomputer.
sc-2024-286.key_novelty: The innovation is using the physical network layout of how computers connect to optimize how scattered results are reshuffled, with two strategies that trade off between memory and communication efficiency.

sc-2024-281.method: The approach uses EigenExa, a fast parallel eigensolver, to compute initial eigenvectors across distributed computers. It then refines these eigenvectors by repeatedly computing corrections using ordinary precision arithmetic, then applying those corrections using high-precision arithmetic. Alternating between fast (ordinary) and accurate (high) precision calculations improves the eigenvectors without requiring expensive arbitrary precision arithmetic.
sc-2024-281.key_novelty: Using alternating low and high precision iterations accurately computes eigenvectors when eigenvalues are closely spaced, eliminating the need for arbitrary precision arithmetic.

sc-2024-279.method: Instead of creating separate functions for each combination of communication mode and persistence style, the paper treats these as independent options that can be mixed and matched. The same core operations can then cover all the cases the old 81 interfaces did, using new persistence styles called pairwise and relaxed persistence to enable additional flexibility without new function names.
sc-2024-279.key_novelty: The innovation is treating communication modes and persistence as independent options rather than requiring separate functions for every combination, enabled by pairwise and relaxed persistence variants.

sc-2024-288.method: The system uses a task-based programming model—breaking the training workflow into discrete, independently schedulable tasks—to coordinate machine learning training across distributed resources spanning wearable edge devices and central servers. One unified programming interface manages these tasks, specifying where and when each computation runs and orchestrating neural network training on heart rhythm data from PhysioNet. Trained models are then deployable directly onto wearables for real-time atrial fibrillation classification.
sc-2024-288.key_novelty: A single task-based programming model coordinates machine learning training across the entire path from wearable edge devices collecting data, through central servers, and back to wearable deployment.

sc-2024-289.method: The system automatically moves ptychography measurement data (X-ray scanning data used for structural imaging) from X-ray beamlines to a computing center using files as the standard exchange format. Tests processed 98 scans from the Advanced Photon Source and 15 scans from the Linac Coherent Light Source, both sent to Argonne Leadership Computing Facility for reconstruction—the mathematical process of rebuilding images from raw measurements. This file-based design is portable: it works unchanged at any ptychography beamline.
sc-2024-289.key_novelty: The core innovation is using files as the standard exchange format, which lets ptychography measurement data from different X-ray sources (APS, LCLS) be moved to a centralized computing facility (ALCF) for reconstruction without needing facility-specific customization.

sc-2024-280.method: The new interface lets applications write custom code that controls exactly how MPI should pack complex data types (organize them into network-ready format). Instead of MPI's standard approach, this gives each application control over the buffer packing (arrangement in memory) and wire representation (how it appears when traveling between computers). The authors built a working version and tested it with three languages—Rust, Python, and C++—measuring how well it works across different language type systems and whether performance improves.
sc-2024-280.key_novelty: MPI now lets applications control exactly how complex data types get serialized (converted to network-ready format) and packed into messages, instead of using MPI's standard approach.

sc-2024-291.method: Long Exposure accelerates fine-tuning by detecting and exploiting shadowy sparsity—a distinctive pattern of sparse (unused) values that emerges during training. The system continuously identifies where sparse values occur, predicts which values will become sparse as parameters evolve during fine-tuning, and reorganizes computation to skip sparse values while efficiently grouping memory accesses together. By avoiding redundant computation and reducing memory bandwidth demands, it speeds up training time and lowers operational costs.
sc-2024-291.key_novelty: The key idea is recognizing shadowy sparsity—a distinctive pattern of sparse values that emerges during LLM fine-tuning—and building a specialized system to exploit it for faster parameter-efficient training.

sc-2024-285.method: The authors ran over 400 million simulations of radiation-induced faults in a surface code—a technique for detecting and correcting errors in quantum computers. They varied four factors: how strong the error correction is, what role each physical qubit plays in the code, how qubits are physically connected to each other, and the energies of the radiation particles. By measuring how these factors affect fault correction, they mapped out how real qubit errors translate into errors in the protected data.
sc-2024-285.key_novelty: Selecting and tuning the surface code without extra resources can increase radiation fault correction success by up to 10%, providing design guidelines for future quantum error correction systems.

sc-2024-284.method: The authors use ChatGPT to generate C/C++ code for basic vector-math operations, specifically BLAS level-1 routines. The generated code is then optimized for different hardware—CPUs and GPUs—by applying hardware-specific optimizations. They verify that the code runs correctly and performs as well as or better than vendor-optimized BLAS libraries.
sc-2024-284.key_novelty: An AI language model can generate BLAS code that's functionally correct and performs as well as or better than vendor-optimized libraries across different CPU and GPU platforms.

sc-2024-290.method: The workflow identifies important regions of uniform simulation data and restructures it into a multi-level format. It then tests three different compression methods to find which performs best on this multi-level structure. Finally, it uses visualization to show which areas are affected by the lossy compression process.
sc-2024-290.key_novelty: This compression-focused approach identifies important areas and restructures uniform simulations into multiple detail levels, which enables multi-resolution compression (a technique normally limited to data natively built in levels, like Adaptive Mesh Refinement) to work with any uniform simulation.

sc-2024-293.method: UpDown uses a two-level address translation system—a mapping between where programs think memory is and where it actually exists. The lower level controls access permissions efficiently for memory segments of any size, while the upper level controls how data is physically arranged. This separation lets applications directly optimize data placement for performance (keeping frequently-accessed data near each other) without needing special system privileges.
sc-2024-293.key_novelty: A two-level address translation where access control is separate from data placement, making the system scalable while letting applications precisely control where data is stored.

sc-2024-287.method: A custom tool automatically rewrites Fortran code in weather and climate models to identify calculations that can safely use lower numerical precision (fewer decimal places) without affecting accuracy. The tool systematically tries countless combinations of precision settings across the program, measures how fast each version runs and whether it stays accurate, then picks the best one. It was tested on three major models—MPAS-A (atmospheric), ADCIRC (coastal storm surge), and MOM6 (ocean)—replacing the manual work that domain experts previously did.
sc-2024-287.key_novelty: Researchers automated the process of finding which calculations in weather and climate models could safely use lower numerical precision by directly measuring speedup, the first time this was done at scale on real-world models using a custom Fortran tool.

sc-2024-295.method: xDM spreads memory across multiple storage backends (different storage device types) and automatically picks the best one and access path for each memory request based on your application's actual data-access patterns. It continuously adjusts settings to make full use of each device's available bandwidth. This beats older systems that were stuck using a single PCIe device with limited throughput.
sc-2024-295.key_novelty: xDM is the first disaggregated memory system to automatically switch between multiple storage backends based on application data patterns, rather than being locked into a single device.

sc-2024-301.method: The researchers created electron microscopy image datasets by applying data augmentation (techniques that artificially create image variations) in different combinations: using just one method, two methods together, or four methods together—drawn from six standard augmentation techniques. They tested these datasets on three image-recognition systems (DenseNet169, MobileNetV2, and ResNet101V2) to classify images into two categories. They then tracked how much the order of applying these methods mattered and whether using more methods at once improved accuracy.
sc-2024-301.key_novelty: Using more augmentation methods at once doesn't always improve accuracy—sometimes fewer methods work better—and the order in which methods are applied can shift accuracy by up to 2.6%.

sc-2024-303.method: The authors move computationally expensive parts of the FSBM (Fast Spectral Bin Microphysics) scheme—which simulates cloud droplets in weather models—from CPUs to NVIDIA GPUs on the Perlmutter supercomputer, using OpenMP device offloading directives (commands that tell code to run on the GPU instead of the CPU). They combine two complementary tools to guide the work: runtime profilers (which measure performance while code executes) and Codee (a static code inspection tool that analyzes code before it runs) to find bottlenecks and spots where the code can be reorganized for faster GPU execution.
sc-2024-303.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining static code inspection (analyzing code before it runs) with runtime profiling to systematically identify and optimize the computationally expensive parts of weather simulations for GPU execution.

sc-2024-297.method: The system profiles HPC and DNN workloads to measure their resource needs and how they slow each other down when combined (interference patterns). Using these measurements, it calculates the optimal way to allocate GPU resources for each pair of workloads. It then uses CUDA MPS—a mechanism that lets multiple programs share one GPU—to run them together with these tailored allocations, maximizing throughput and energy efficiency.
sc-2024-297.key_novelty: Measuring how workloads interfere with each other to better decide how to run multiple programs on shared GPUs.

sc-2024-294.method: EcoRec compresses the large lookup tables (embedding layers) used in recommendation systems using Tensor-Train decomposition—a technique that splits a massive data structure into smaller, interconnected pieces. It optimizes this compression by removing redundant calculations that normally occur when these pieces interact, and uses micro-batching where data is sorted by index so related items train together, reducing memory without slowing things down. To handle training across multiple machines, it uses a pipeline system for the embedding layers that keeps the data balanced and flowing smoothly between GPUs, all built on PyTorch and CUDA.
sc-2024-294.key_novelty: Eliminating redundancy from Tensor-Train compression through optimized operations, while combining it with sorted micro-batching and distributed pipeline training.

sc-2024-292.method: ORBIT is a vision transformer—an AI model trained on satellite imagery that learns patterns by analyzing images in small sections—scaled to 113 billion parameters, the individual numerical settings the model learns. To train this enormous model, the team distributed it across 49,152 AMD GPUs using a hybrid parallelism technique that divides both the model and the data simultaneously in orthogonal ways, keeping the computational work balanced across all hardware. Running on Oak Ridge's Frontier supercomputer, ORBIT sustained 684 petaFLOPS to 1.6 exaFLOPS with 41–85% scaling efficiency, achieving 41–85% of theoretical peak performance as tens of thousands of GPUs work together.
sc-2024-292.key_novelty: A parallelism technique called tensor-data orthogonal parallelism that splits both an AI model and its training data simultaneously across GPUs, enabling Earth system vision transformers to scale 1000 times larger than existing models.

sc-2024-298.method: APTMoE runs MoE fine-tuning by splitting experts (the sub-networks in a Mixture-Of-Experts model) between GPU and CPU: popular experts stay on GPU, less-used ones move to CPU. It loads these experts in three phases, deciding which phase based on how often each expert is used and how efficiently it runs on each processor. It then schedules these phases so they don't compete for bandwidth—the GPU and CPU pull data when it's least likely to interfere—maximizing overall bandwidth utilization.
sc-2024-298.key_novelty: The core idea is affinity-aware offloading (placing each expert on the processor best suited to it based on popularity and efficiency), which enables pipeline parallelism for MoE fine-tuning despite bandwidth constraints on GPUs.

sc-2024-306.method: GPU-BLOB is a portable benchmark—a standardized testing tool—that runs matrix multiplication (GEMM) and matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) on both CPUs and GPUs to find the break-even point: the minimum problem size where the GPU finishes faster even after paying the cost of copying data to it. The benchmark tests this on three production HPC (high-performance computing) systems with different hardware to see how thresholds vary. It also measures how the problem's shape (tall vs. square matrices) and running multiple operations back-to-back affect when GPU acceleration actually helps.
sc-2024-306.key_novelty: GPU-BLOB measures the exact point where GPU acceleration becomes faster than CPU execution, accounting for different hardware platforms and problem characteristics.

sc-2024-296.method: Speed Galerkin Transformer optimizes four GPU operations specific to solving PDEs with Fourier neural operators—algorithms that work in frequency space instead of direct space. It parallelizes matrix multiplication on thin matrices across independent chunks that are combined afterward (SliceK-SplitK-ReduceK strategy), reorganizes where transformer components like query, key, and value matrices sit in GPU memory to reduce latency, merges normalization across multiple attention heads (the transformer's parallel information-processing pathways) into a single operation, and optimizes how multiple matrix transpositions (flipping data rows and columns) happen together using strategic memory access patterns. These kernel-level optimizations eliminate the bottlenecks that make Fourier neural operators theoretically efficient but practically slow on hardware. The combination lets the algorithm approach the GPU's peak performance.
sc-2024-296.key_novelty: Four GPU optimizations integrated and co-designed for Fourier neural operators: parallelizing thin matrix multiplications (SliceK-SplitK-ReduceK), reorganizing memory layout, merging normalization across attention heads, and optimizing batched matrix transpositions.

sc-2024-300.method: Programmers add compiler directives (special annotations in their code) to mark code blocks that depend on remote-memory messages. The compiler translates these directives into information for the runtime system. The runtime system then automatically waits for aggregated messages (bundled memory operations) to complete before executing the marked code blocks, handling all the synchronization and coordination internally. This eliminates the need for programmers to manually verify when messages have arrived before using the data.
sc-2024-300.key_novelty: Compiler directives that automatically defer code execution until remote-memory operations (data transfers to other computers) complete, removing manual dependency management.

sc-2024-304.method: The platform combines two systems: Bluesky orchestrates the experiments (controlling and coordinating them), and Raydata analyzes the resulting data. Instead of keeping these separate, the integration automatically routes data from the experiment into analysis workflows that can be customized for each research domain. Because the workflow is tailored to the specific research type and equipment setup, different research groups get analysis that fits their needs without rebuilding the system each time.
sc-2024-304.key_novelty: The core idea is coupling experiment orchestration with adaptive data analysis to automatically enable domain-specific workflows at synchrotron facilities.

sc-2024-302.method: JUmPER creates a custom Jupyter kernel—the engine that runs code in notebooks—that collects CPU and GPU usage measurements while executing your code and displays them through special notebook commands. It integrates Score-P (a tool that identifies exactly where code spends its execution time) to provide detailed performance insights. To keep the notebook responsive, JUmPER passes data through RAM instead of disk (in-memory pipe communication) and efficiently converts Python's internal state in parallel, so measurement overhead stays minimal and doesn't interrupt your exploratory work.
sc-2024-302.key_novelty: A Jupyter-based kernel that combines low-overhead system monitoring, Score-P profiling, and interactive visualization for real-time performance analysis during coding.

sc-2024-307.method: PIKA collects performance measurements across the entire cluster, while Vampir is designed to analyze individual applications—they speak different technical languages but describe the same hardware. The approach automatically converts cluster-wide data from PIKA into formats that Vampir can read and analyze. This lets application-level tools now understand and study patterns happening at the cluster scale, by bridging the translation gap between site-wide and application-specific monitoring.
sc-2024-307.key_novelty: The solution is an automatic translation layer that converts cluster-level monitoring data into formats that application-level performance analysis tools can understand and use.

sc-2024-310.method: autoGEMM automatically creates fast multiplication code by combining pre-written code fragments with tuning customized to each Arm processor. It accelerates execution by reusing processor registers (fast on-chip memory) and overlapping load/store operations (reading and writing data while processing). A dynamic tiling scheme reduces this search by breaking the matrix into balanced chunks, shrinking TVM's configuration space so it can efficiently find the best parameters.
sc-2024-310.key_novelty: The innovation is a dynamic tiling scheme—breaking matrices into balanced chunks—that prunes TVM's search space when automatically generating efficient irregular matrix multiplication code for diverse Arm processors.

sc-2024-309.method: The system mathematically tracks how errors from raw data flow through calculations to produce derived quantities (values computed from raw data). Rather than controlling accuracy only in the raw data, it identifies each source of error and how they combine during the derived calculations. It then designs a progressive data delivery system (sending data in incremental chunks) that keeps these combined errors within user-specified limits.
sc-2024-309.key_novelty: This framework guarantees that derived quantities calculated from progressively retrieved data stay within acceptable error bounds—the first to extend precision control from raw data to computed quantities.

sc-2024-308.method: The system processes X-ray detector data in three stages. First, it compresses each incoming batch using ARAMS, a sketching algorithm that combines Priority Sampling (selecting the most informative measurements) with a modified Frequent Directions algorithm (extracting the main patterns in the data). The compressed data is then reduced to fewer dimensions using PCA, visualized using UMAP, and grouped into clusters using OPTICS. All three stages run in parallel across multiple processors, enabling real-time analysis as data arrives.
sc-2024-308.key_novelty: ARAMS enables rank-adaptive matrix sketching by combining Priority Sampling with a modified Frequent Directions algorithm, letting practitioners specify target error tolerance instead of choosing how many key patterns to keep upfront.

sc-2024-314.method: Atlas breaks quantum circuits into smaller pieces (subcircuits) and distributes them across multiple GPUs running in parallel.
