To minimize the expensive communication between GPUs, it applies Integer Linear Programming—a mathematical optimization method that finds the best arrangement where gates working together land on GPUs that are close together. Dynamic programming then optimally assigns each subcircuit to run on a specific GPU processor (kernel). For very large circuits exceeding single-GPU memory, overflow data is stored in the computer's main memory (DRAM).
sc-2024-314.key_novelty: Breaking quantum circuits hierarchically and using mathematical optimization (Integer Linear Programming) to arrange them on multiple GPUs while minimizing inter-GPU communication.

sc-2024-317.method: The approach uses two strategies. First, it fuses multiple rounds of matrix multiplication (general matrix multiplication or GEMM) together and keeps intermediate results in the fastest on-chip memory (L1 buffer) to reduce the constant shuffling of data back and forth—this overcomes the memory wall, the bottleneck where data movement becomes slower than computation itself. Second, it builds a pipeline that splits work between two different processor types: specialized processors called NPUs (neural processing units) handle the heavy matrix multiplication work while regular CPUs handle the remaining parts of LU factorization (a matrix decomposition technique), allowing them to work together efficiently.
sc-2024-317.key_novelty: The core idea is combining multiple rounds of matrix multiplication into a fused operation while keeping intermediate results in fast on-chip memory (L1 buffer), designed specifically to eliminate data movement bottlenecks in systems mixing specialized processors (NPUs) with regular CPUs.

sc-2024-305.method: It uses OpenACC compiler directives (instructions that tell the compiler to offload code to GPUs, with special parallelization clauses like gang, vector, and collapse) to move computation to GPUs, and reorganizes the data layout by packing user-defined types into coalesced arrays (memory structures organized for efficient GPU access). It also uses code generation (metaprogramming) to eliminate function-call overhead by replacing function calls with their actual code (inlining). These three optimization strategies combine to achieve cumulative speedups.
sc-2024-305.key_novelty: It combines three optimization techniques: OpenACC directives with gang/vector/collapse clauses, data packing into coalesced arrays (memory organized for efficient GPU access), and metaprogramming-based function inlining (code generation to eliminate call overhead), achieving 6-30x speedups on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs.

sc-2024-318.method: The overhead of launching kernels (sending work to a GPU) limits performance when each kernel must finish before the next one starts. The approach uses two techniques: OpenACC allows asynchronous execution, where multiple kernels are sent to the GPU without waiting for each to finish, reducing idle time. CUDA kernel fusion physically combines multiple loops into a single kernel, using block-index branching so the GPU executes the combined work as one operation instead of many launches.
sc-2024-318.key_novelty: The single core idea is systematically combining asynchronous kernel execution and kernel fusion to eliminate launch overhead in atmospheric models.

sc-2024-320.method: GPUFASTQLZ uses a GPU (graphics processor) to compress genomic sequence files by running multiple processing steps in parallel across thousands of cores. It quickly parses FASTQ records (the standard genomic data format) into separate fields, encodes DNA bases as 2-bit numbers to shrink file size, groups quality scores from Illumina sequencers into bins, and applies GPU-accelerated GPULZ compression.
sc-2024-320.key_novelty: The core idea is pairing 2-bit encoding for DNA bases with GPU-accelerated GPULZ compression, both specifically optimized for FASTQ data.

sc-2024-312.method: The method uses low-rank approximations—mathematical techniques that preserve essential information while discarding less important details—to reduce the scaling of computational cost and memory usage in GW excited-state calculations (shrinking from O(N^4) to O(N^3) computational complexity and from O(N^3) to O(N^2) memory complexity). It distributes these calculations across hundreds of thousands of processor cores on the Sunway supercomputer using plane-wave methods, with optimizations to minimize communication overhead between cores. This parallel efficiency enables the simulation of substantially larger systems.
sc-2024-312.key_novelty: Low-rank approximations (techniques that keep essential information while discarding redundancy) enable GW excited-state calculations to reach cubic scaling, making simulations of 13,000+ atom systems feasible where previously only roughly 2,700 atoms were achievable.

sc-2024-311.method: EFFICIENTIMM targets the bottleneck in parallelizing influence maximization on computers with multiple processor cores and separate memory regions (NUMA nodes): cores have to access memory that might be located far away, causing them to stall. The solution combines four techniques: redesigning how work is divided among cores, placing data close to the cores that use it (optimizing memory affinity across nodes), spreading work evenly across cores and memory regions so all cores stay busy (load balancing), and having data structures adapt to runtime conditions. By eliminating slow memory access and keeping cores equally loaded, the algorithm runs much faster on these systems.
sc-2024-311.key_novelty: The key insight is combining memory-aware data placement, dynamic work distribution, and adaptive data structures as an integrated system to parallelize influence maximization.

sc-2024-313.method: HyDRA combines sampling (selecting which neighbors to train on) and GPU data transfer into a single kernel operation (one unified GPU computation step) rather than doing them separately. It uses memory addresses to point directly to data across GPUs instead of copying, stores copies of high-degree vertices (nodes with many connections) locally on multiple GPUs to avoid redundant data fetches, and overlaps data transfers with computation (pipelining) so new data arrives while processing happens.
sc-2024-313.key_novelty: The innovation is combining sampling (selecting training neighbors) and GPU data transfer into one unified computation step instead of separate ones, eliminating the CPU-GPU bottleneck in multi-GPU graph neural network training.

sc-2024-315.method: The paper uses Compute Express Link (CXL, a high-speed connection standard between CPU and accelerator hardware) to create a memory space where both can coordinate data access. It adds a system that tracks which tensor data has changed since the last transfer. When the accelerator needs data, only the modified tensors are moved from CPU to accelerator memory, eliminating wasteful copies of unchanged data and allowing the system to hide the transfer time more effectively.
sc-2024-315.key_novelty: Using Compute Express Link to implement an extended update protocol that tracks changed tensor data, allowing only modifications to be transferred between CPU and accelerator instead of entire tensors.

sc-2024-299.method: LICOMK++ is an ocean simulation program built on Kokkos, a framework that lets the same code run on different types of hardware (Sunway processors, NVIDIA/AMD GPUs, and ARM CPUs). The authors extended Kokkos to support Sunway processors, CPUs used in supercomputers. It works by having Kokkos translate generic parallel computing instructions (kernels) into commands each specific hardware understands, and by handling memory allocation differently depending on the hardware.
sc-2024-299.key_novelty: This is the first kilometer-scale global ocean general circulation model that works on multiple hardware types (Sunway processors, GPUs, and ARM CPUs) using a single codebase.

sc-2024-316.method: The system tackles checkpoint overhead through two coordinated strategies. It regularly deletes old checkpoint files to reduce storage requirements, and it optimizes how checkpoint data moves between fast local storage and slower shared storage—routing data through faster paths to speed up the writing process. This approach was tested on GPT-2 models of different sizes.
sc-2024-316.key_novelty: The core innovation is combining automatic deletion of old checkpoints with coordinated movement of data between storage systems to simultaneously address storage and write-speed bottlenecks.

sc-2024-319.method: The researchers tested power measurements from over 70 different NVIDIA GPUs across 12 generations. They analyzed how the built-in power sensor measures by examining its sampling rate—how frequently it takes measurements—and found that it only measures during a small fraction of the GPU's runtime, leading to large errors. They then developed corrections that reduced energy measurement errors by 35% on average.
sc-2024-319.key_novelty: This work reveals that NVIDIA's built-in power sensor only samples 25% of the GPU's runtime on A100 and H100, and proposes corrections that reduce measurement error by 35%.

sc-2024-321.method: The work takes XBFS's adaptive strategy—which automatically picks the best frontier queue design (the way to organize which nodes to process) based on the search's characteristics at each level—and retunes it for AMD MI250X GPUs. New optimizations are developed specifically for AMD's hardware architecture, replacing the original NVIDIA-focused tuning. The implementation is evaluated on the Frontier supercomputer.
sc-2024-321.key_novelty: XBFS's adaptive frontier queue generation strategy is adapted for AMD MI250X GPUs with hardware-specific optimizations for the Frontier supercomputer.

sc-2024-325.method: The framework combines an ensemble score filter—which maintains multiple weather prediction guesses and updates them with new observations—with a vision transformer (a neural network that learns patterns in atmospheric data) that both adapt in real-time as observational data arrives. This system was validated on a surface quasi-geostrophic turbulence benchmark and demonstrated to scale efficiently up to 1024 GPUs on the Frontier exascale supercomputer.
sc-2024-325.key_novelty: The system combines ensemble score filtering (a technique for updating multiple weather predictions with observations) and a vision transformer (an AI model learning weather patterns) to enable real-time operational weather prediction that scales to 1024 GPUs on exascale supercomputers.

sc-2024-323.method: ActorProf uses hardware performance counters—built-in processor sensors that measure program behavior—to track direct messages between processes and automatically combined ones. It analyzes where time is spent in the program while accounting for FA-BSP structure: the synchronization barriers (checkpoints where the program pauses to let all parts catch up) and execution phases (stages of computation). Results are displayed in a format tailored to FA-BSP programs, making performance bottlenecks easy to spot.
sc-2024-323.key_novelty: ActorProf is the first profiler designed specifically for FA-BSP programs, tracking messages between processes with hardware counters while understanding the program's synchronization barriers (waiting points) and execution phases (stages).

sc-2024-328.method: Stellaris trains reinforcement learning models distributed across cloud servers that automatically scale. Instead of making all workers wait for each other (synchronous training), workers update the shared model independently (asynchronous training). To keep this stable when updates arrive out of order and at different speeds, Stellaris uses importance sampling truncation (a weighting technique that limits extreme updates) and staleness-aware gradient aggregation (which adjusts how updates are combined based on how delayed they are).
sc-2024-328.key_novelty: Stellaris shows how to train distributed reinforcement learning asynchronously on serverless cloud infrastructure.

sc-2024-322.method: DBSR reorganizes how sparse matrices are stored in memory to work efficiently with vector processing—where CPUs process multiple values simultaneously using SIMD instructions. It arranges data contiguously (next to each other) in patterns that vector operations can directly access, enabling the CPU to process many elements in parallel while keeping the memory footprint compact. It's evaluated with multigrid solvers and zero fill-in incomplete LU preconditioners on ARMv8 and x86 processors.
sc-2024-322.key_novelty: DBSR is a sparse matrix storage format that enables CPU vector instructions to efficiently solve sparse triangular systems by organizing data in memory for fast parallel access.

sc-2024-324.method: The solver organizes sparse matrix data into small tiles and runs the entire solving procedure in a single GPU kernel rather than calling the GPU multiple times. Within that kernel, GPU threads coordinate using atomic operations (built-in hardware that lets different threads synchronize safely), which eliminates the expensive overhead of stopping and restarting the kernel between computational steps. As the solver runs, it monitors each tile's progress toward convergence and automatically adjusts the numerical precision for that tile, switching to lower precision where the computation can safely use it.
sc-2024-324.key_novelty: A single-kernel GPU solver that dynamically adjusts numerical precision for each tile based on convergence progress, eliminating synchronization overhead while maintaining numerical stability.

sc-2024-329.method: A tool called Varity automatically generates thousands of test programs written in CUDA (NVIDIA's GPU programming language) and HIP (AMD's equivalent). These programs run on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs using the same compiler settings, and the numerical results are compared—this side-by-side testing reveals when identical code produces different numbers. When differences appear, AMD's HIPIFY tool (which automatically translates CUDA to HIP) helps determine whether the problem is in the translation process itself or in how each compiler fundamentally handles calculations.
sc-2024-329.key_novelty: This work runs randomly-generated test programs on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and systematically compares the results to measure compiler-induced numerical differences—cases where the two compilers calculate different values for the same input—including differences from automatic code translation.

sc-2024-332.method: The approach analyzes the image during preprocessing to identify regions with important details, then generates patches adaptively—using larger patches in simple areas and smaller ones where details matter, similar to Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), a technique from supercomputing. This reduces the number of patches fed to the transformer by orders of magnitude, with minimal overhead, and works with any transformer model without requiring architectural changes.
sc-2024-332.key_novelty: Using adaptive mesh refinement from supercomputing to generate image patches based on content importance for transformers, overcoming quadratic attention costs on high-resolution images.

sc-2024-330.method: When parallel processes finish at different times, faster ones wait at synchronization points, causing delays. The paper solves this by formulating load balancing as a quadratic optimization problem (a math problem certain computers can solve using quantum techniques), creating two versions that trade off between needing fewer quantum bits versus having simpler constraints. The hybrid approach—combining classical and quantum computation—is tested against three traditional heuristic methods (Greedy, Karmarkar-Karp, and ProactLB), measuring success by imbalance ratio, speedup achieved, and task migration count.
sc-2024-330.key_novelty: It uses hybrid classical-quantum computation to solve load rebalancing through constrained quadratic formulations.

sc-2024-327.method: The tool adds a monitoring point called device_mem (in OpenMP's tool interface) that watches each data transfer between CPU and GPU. It maintains a shadow memory—a tracking system that mirrors data state to detect when CPU and GPU copies become inconsistent. The tool uses vectorized dynamic analysis: it processes multiple data movements in parallel using SIMD instructions (special CPU operations that handle multiple pieces of data simultaneously), which reduces overhead compared to checking each transfer individually. By combining this parallel checking with better debug information from the LLVM compiler, it can accurately catch data inconsistencies with minimal performance cost.
sc-2024-327.key_novelty: The core innovation is introducing device_mem, an OMPT monitoring point that efficiently catches mismatches between CPU and GPU data by checking multiple transfers in parallel rather than sequentially.

sc-2024-326.method: GVARP examines code (without running it) to find which inputs and settings most affect speed in kernel functions. It breaks program execution into segments at points where external libraries are called or asynchronous operations occur (operations that don't wait for completion). For each segment, it builds a graph tracking how data flows and measures how much computation happens. By grouping segments with similar workloads, it detects when identical code unexpectedly runs at different speeds.
sc-2024-326.key_novelty: It tracks data flow through a program and groups segments by workload to detect when identical code runs at different speeds in large-scale heterogeneous systems.

sc-2024-335.method: The researchers tested VASP, a computational chemistry software, on Perlmutter, a supercomputer at NERSC with NVIDIA A100 GPUs. They changed different types of inputs to the software and adjusted how the computation was split across multiple processors to see how this affected power consumption. They also applied power caps to the GPUs, limiting them to 50% of their maximum power draw (called TDP), and measured both the resulting changes in power usage and the slowdown in performance.
sc-2024-335.key_novelty: VASP power usage depends much more on what computation is being run than on how many processors are used in parallel, and reducing GPU power to 50% of maximum causes less than 10% performance loss for most workloads.

sc-2024-337.method: The authors reverse-engineered how MPI (Message Passing Interface—a standard for programs to send messages to each other) actually decides when to check for incoming messages and process them. They mapped out common patterns in how programs handle asynchronous communication (messages arriving at unpredictable times), and pinpointed which parts of the system create performance bottlenecks. They then designed new MPI features that let programmers write custom code to manage message checking themselves, instead of being locked into MPI's hidden, one-size-fits-all approach.
sc-2024-337.key_novelty: MPI extensions enable users to explicitly construct and manage progress engines (systems that decide when the program checks for incoming messages), replacing reliance on MPI's built-in opaque mechanisms.

sc-2024-333.method: LoRAStencil speeds up stencil computations (repeatedly applying a pattern across a grid, common in physics simulations) on Tensor Cores—specialized matrix-processing hardware in GPUs—by decomposing weight patterns into low-rank components (simpler sub-matrices that combine to form the original). This simpler structure is easier to reorganize efficiently, so LoRAStencil uses three techniques: efficiently gathering misaligned data (Residual Dimension Gathering), organizing patterns hierarchically to match their structure (Pyramidal Matrix Adaptation), and using a butterfly algorithm for data rearrangement to avoid expensive shuffles (Butterfly Vector Swapping).
sc-2024-333.key_novelty: Decomposing stencil weight matrices into low-rank components to fix dimension residue (the performance loss when data dimensions don't align with Tensor Core hardware expectations) and enable efficient data gathering.

sc-2024-334.method: MCFuser fuses multiple compute-intensive operators (like matrix multiplies and convolutions) into a single GPU kernel by breaking the computation into tiles that fit in faster on-chip memory and analyzing the data flow to eliminate redundant memory reads. Rather than trying all possible kernel designs, it prunes bad options upfront and uses a mathematical model to predict performance, guided by heuristic search (smart, targeted search) to find an optimized kernel quickly.
sc-2024-334.key_novelty: The core idea is using tiling strategies combined with data-flow analysis to automatically combine multiple compute-intensive operations into a single GPU kernel, with mathematical performance prediction replacing exhaustive trial-and-error tuning.

sc-2024-331.method: TorchGT optimizes training at three levels. At the algorithm level, Dual-interleaved Attention (a technique for processing graphs) exploits sparsity—most node pairs don't connect—while keeping the model accurate. At the runtime level, Cluster-aware Graph Parallelism splits work across multiple machines while minimizing data transfer between them. At the kernel level, Elastic Computation Reformation dynamically reorganizes computations to reduce memory access delays.
sc-2024-331.key_novelty: TorchGT combines three levels of optimization—algorithm-level sparse attention, runtime-level communication-efficient distributed parallelism, and kernel-level dynamic memory reformation—enabling large-scale graph transformer training.

sc-2024-336.method: The visualization pipeline is split into pre-filters at storage nodes and post-filters at clients. Pre-filters use computational storage (processors built into the storage system) and smart network interface cards to filter and reduce data before it travels over the network, based on what downstream processing stages need. Post-filters complete the visualization work on the client side. Testing used two real-world simulation datasets.
sc-2024-336.key_novelty: The core idea is applying near-data processing to visualization pipelines—filtering data at storage nodes before network transfer—so clients receive only what they need, significantly reducing data traffic.

sc-2024-338.method: The paper describes a unified data-handling system within the SPH-EXA framework that enables two analysis approaches: in-situ (analyzing results while the simulation is running) and post-hoc (analyzing results after the simulation finishes). By combining both approaches in a single system, researchers can select whichever method works best for each analysis task without rebuilding the data pipeline. The researchers tested this system on the Piz Daint supercomputer across multiple dataset sizes to measure its performance and verify it works at scale.
sc-2024-338.key_novelty: The key innovation is combining both forms of analysis—examining results during simulation (in-situ) and examining results afterward (post-hoc)—into a single unified architecture for extreme-scale particle simulations, so scientists don't need separate systems for each approach.

hotchips-2025-015.method: Azure's architecture verifies software integrity through cryptographic attestation (proving code is genuine with mathematics), runs sensitive workloads in hardware-protected isolated zones called secure execution contexts, and stores encryption keys directly in the CPU so software cannot access them. This extends Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs—isolated processor regions that prove they're untampered) with protections for cloud's unique threats: attacks that exploit shared hardware where multiple customers' workloads coexist.
hotchips-2025-015.key_novelty: By unifying security across the CPU, firmware, and hypervisor, Azure gives cloud customers cryptographic proof that both the hardware they run on and the software inside it are genuine and unchanged.

hpca-2025-106.method: Buffalo solves a memory overload problem by organizing nodes based on their degree (how many connections each has) and spreading high-degree nodes across different chunks (partitions) of the graph so no single chunk gets overloaded. Instead of dividing the graph using expensive algorithms, it uses simple bucketing rules based on degree. Before loading data, it uses a lightweight mathematical model to predict how much memory each chunk will need, preventing overload before it happens. It also uses sampling to select a subset of data during block generation, speeding up the data preparation step.
hpca-2025-106.key_novelty: Buffalo uses degree-based node bucketization—a strategy that spreads high-degree nodes across different partitions—to eliminate the memory explosion caused by the long-tail distribution of connections in real-world graphs.

vlsid-2025-010.method: Convolutional neural networks for image processing often have many zero values; this approach exploits that sparsity by skipping zeros during computation instead of processing them. It organizes non-zero values in row-wise patterns that match how the processor's cache (fast memory attached to the processor) works, keeping related data together so the processor doesn't have to fetch from slower main memory as often. On resource-constrained hardware with limited cache, this reduces the bandwidth and power needed, making the network run faster.
vlsid-2025-010.key_novelty: Restructuring sparse CNN data to match row-wise cache patterns, so zero values don't waste precious cache space on resource-constrained hardware.

sc-2025-393.method: Following SC25 Supercomputing conference reproducibility standards, this work independently repeats the original paper's experiments on large language model inference resilience—testing how well language models continue functioning when failures occur during prediction. The researchers reproduced the complete end-to-end process, from input through to output, across multiple independent runs to verify the methodology produces consistent results that others can obtain.
sc-2025-393.key_novelty: This work verifies that the original paper's end-to-end methodology for evaluating large language model inference resilience produces consistent, reproducible results when tested independently.

mlsys-2025-003.method: QServe makes INT4-quantized weights efficient by keeping dequantization on Tensor Cores (specialized multipliers) rather than general-purpose CUDA cores. Progressive group quantization uses a protective range of [-119, 119] to ensure INT4 values remain safe when scaled back to INT8 for Tensor Core multiply-accumulate without overflow; SmoothAttention suppresses outliers in Key tensors by applying per-channel scales that absorb into preceding layer weights (exploiting RoPE's mathematical commutativity), enabling 4-bit Key/Value quantization without accuracy loss. Compute-aware weight reordering stores weights in their actual GEMM access order for efficient 128-bit/thread memory fetches, while fast dequantization via vadd4 instructions (processing 4 weights per instruction) reduces per-element operations from 5 to 2 in attention decoding.
mlsys-2025-003.key_novelty: Three techniques—protective-range quantization for Tensor Core safety, RoPE-based Key scale pre-absorption for quantization without loss, and compute-aware weight reordering for bulk memory access—enable INT4 serving without CUDA core dequantization overhead.

sc-2024-169.method: The system uses three techniques to fit billion-scale graph training into FPGA memory. It arranges data to match the neural network's access pattern for faster retrieval, uses compact lookup tables so vertices need only small index numbers instead of full identifiers, and reduces number precision to shrink data size. Combined, these reduce memory use enough to train billion-node graphs in FPGA memory at full speed.
sc-2024-169.key_novelty: The core idea is combining data arrangement, vertex renaming (giving nodes shorter names for smaller storage), and precision reduction so billion-scale graphs fit in FPGA memory during training.

sc-2025-373.method: The researchers tested the STZ compression framework by running it on scientific datasets and comparing compressed results to originals. They verified that STZ could process data in real time as it arrived, while retaining enough accuracy for analysis, confirming its usefulness for transferring large volumes of data to remote research facilities.
sc-2025-373.key_novelty: STZ processes scientific data as it flows, discarding less-important details to speed up transfer while keeping the measurements needed for research.
